## Volume front matter

### Series title page

The Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, and Economical Library of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reissue of all the surviving monuments of Catholic tradition from the first twelve centuries of the Church, according to the most accurate editions, compared with one another and with several manuscript codices, corrected with the greatest diligence; continuously illuminated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged with all works discovered after the extensive editions published during the last three centuries; supplied with particular analytical indexes following each volume or each author of any importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with headings distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating the subject matter below; augmented by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and by works possessing some authority or influence in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it is immediately clear to the reader which Fathers, and in which passages of their works, have commented on the individual texts of the individual books of Scripture.

An edition of the greatest accuracy, and easily preferable to all others, if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the extremely convenient format of the volumes, uniform and consistently similar throughout the entire work, and the low price; and especially this collection, a single, methodical, and chronological gathering of six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, but now for the first time assembled in our library from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.

**Second Series**, in which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III. Edited by J.-P. Migne, publisher of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of the complete courses in the individual branches of ecclesiastical learning.

# Life of Emperor Charlemagne, by Einhard

## Prologue

*(Pertz, Monumenta Germaniae historica.)*

[Col. 0009A] Among all the heroes who stood out in the Middle Ages, none equaled the fame of the emperor Charles; among historians, none equaled that of Einhard.

[Note: [Col. 0009B] That the name ought to be written in this way is shown by the charter granted by the emperor Louis to Einhard—one copy for the monastery of Blandinium writes Ainhardum—and by the catalogue of the nobles of Saxony for the year 803, which has Einhartus; then by Einhard himself in the Annals for the year 806, in two charters for the monastery of Lorsch, and in others that I recently inspected in Paris, written in Tironian notes; also in his letter to Lupus and in the History of the Translation of Saints Marcellinus and Peter, chapter 1; and likewise by his chief friends: Gerward, in the verses appended to the Life of Charlemagne; Lupus of Ferrières, letters 1, 2, 4, and 5; and Rabanus, in the epitaph. His contemporaries Ermoldus Nigellus, book II, verse 31, have Heinardus; Walafrid Strabo, in his work on Einhard; Frotharius of Toul, letter 16; the anonymous author of the Life of Louis, chapter 41, Heinhardus; the Chronographer of Fontenelle, Heinhardus and Einhardus; then the Annalist of Fulda for the year 874; and the Saxon Poet—to mention only the principal writers of the ninth century—show this most clearly. Nevertheless, one or two later works give his name as both Eginhardus and Agenardus; the recension of the manuscripts undertaken below will show that it was also distorted in various other ways. In the sole manuscript of his letters, which I found again at Lugdunum Batavorum in 1827, only the initial letter E is expressed.]

Both were German by race and character. The latter, at least, was born—as more recent writers, though led by a deceptive conjecture, relate—in the district of Moingau in eastern Francia, opposite the Ottonian Forest, toward the end of Pepin’s reign or during the first years of Charles’s reign.

[Note: [Col. 0009C] The manuscript of the royal library at Hanover, whose opinion on this matter will be printed below under B 8 in the discussion of the manuscripts; and writers of no little distinction nearer to our own age.]

[Note: [Col. 0009C–0010B] For he was brought up with Charles’s children, and in a letter to Lupus written in 836 calls himself an old man.]

When he soon entered Charles’s court, he was brought up by him,

[Note: [Col. 0010B] Life of Charlemagne, preface.]

and afterward became a participant both in the administration of the kingdom

[Note: [Col. 0010B] In the Preface, and in Ermoldus Nigellus II, 31, 34.]

and in the literary leisure in which the king took particular delight. He conducted himself in such a way that he became bound to the king and his children by a lasting friendship, one that would endure even after the king’s death.

[Note: [Col. 0010B] In the Preface.]

Together with the king he was a pupil of Alcuin, who declares him skilled in arithmetic.

[Note: [Col. 0010B] Alcuin’s letter 85, Works I, 126.]

He married the most noble young woman Imma,

[Note: [Col. 0010B] Lupus’s letter 4 to Einhard.]

whom later writers wished to make the king’s daughter,

[Note: [Col. 0010B] The first monk, author in the twelfth century of the Lorsch chronicle.]

and had by her a son, Vussin.

[Note: [Col. 0010B] Einhard’s letter 30.]

Thus held in the highest position and enriched with benefices,

[Note: [Col. 0010B] For example, Fredeslar, Einhard’s letter 37.]

he received, among other things, the abbeys of Saint Bavo

[Note: [Col. 0010B] Miraeus, Diplomatic Works I; from this source the Ghent annals above, p. 187, are shown to be mistaken in the number of the year 826. Einhard’s letters 12, 22, and 41; History of the Translation of Saints Marcellinus and Peter.]

and Blandinium at Ghent,

[Note: [Col. 0010B] The same source, and Einhard’s letter 12; History of the Translation of Saint Wandregisel.]

which had been granted judicial immunity.

[Col. 0010A] Under either Charles or Louis, the abbeys of Saint Servatius at Maastricht,

[Note: [Col. 0010B] Einhard’s letter 32, and a charter written in Tironian notes in the royal manuscript of Paris, no. 2, 16.]

Saint Chlodoald,

[Note: [Col. 0010B] Einhard’s letter 2.]

the church of Saint John at Pavia,

[Note: [Col. 0010C] Einhard, History of the Translation of Saints Marcellinus and Peter, chapter II, no. 12.]

and, in the years 816–823, the abbey of Fontenelle were added to these.

[Note: [Col. 0010C] Chronicon Fontanellense.]

In 803 he is listed among the nobles

[Note: [Col. 0010C] In the Prodromus of Sacred Germany, vol. I, from a manuscript that I copied again at Saint Paul in Carinthia.]

to whom the Saxon hostages had been entrusted for custody.

Appointed superintendent of the royal works,

[Note: [Col. 0010C] Chronicon Fontanellense; Walafrid Strabo’s poem about him; and Rabanus’s epitaph.]

he is to be regarded as having completed—although he may not have begun—the great buildings: the bridge at Mainz, the palaces at Ingelheim and Aachen, and especially the basilica at Aachen, which we still admire, an eternal witness to his genius through its simplicity, solidity, and harmony.

He always remained attached to the emperor at home and in the field,

[Note: [Col. 0010C] In the Preface.]

and seems to have left him only once, when in 806, as an envoy, he brought the emperor’s testament to Pope Leo for signature.

[Note: [Col. 0010C] Einhard, Annals, under the year 806.]

In 813, after the elder sons of Charles had died, he is said to have been Louis’s chief advocate for admitting him to a share in the empire.

[Note: [Col. 0010C] Ermoldus Nigellus, book II, verse 31 ff.]

In the years immediately following Charles’s death, as a sign of his grateful and reverent affection,

[Col. 0011A]

[Note: [Col. 0011C] Preface to the Life.]

he resolved to write his Life, and completed it before the year 820. For in the following year, 821, it is already found among the books of the monastery of Sindleozes-Auva,

[Note: [Col. 0011D] In Neugart, Episcopate of Constance, p. 540.]

and from a letter of Lupus to Einhard we understand that his reputation had already spread widely in 830 or 831.

In the preface he complains that the honor paid to learning at court had already begun to decline. Although he retained his former position of honor under the emperor Louis, he nevertheless already perceived that he was unequal to affairs from which his great friend had departed, and “he began, after much reflection, to meditate upon a leisure in which he might at some time take delight.”

[Note: [Col. 0011D] History of the Translation of Saints Marcellinus and Peter, chapter 2.]

For this reason, having obtained the estates of Michilinstat and Mulinheim, very remote from the crowds of ordinary people in the Odenwald, he asked that they be granted by the emperor to himself and his wife Imma.

[Note: [Col. 0011D] The same work, chapter 2, and Louis’s diploma in the Lorsch Diplomatic Codex I, p. 44.]

The emperor not only granted the request, but, after appointing Lothar king in 817, chose Einhard above all others to “look after him and diligently admonish him concerning the correction of his morals and the pursuit of honorable and useful things.”

[Col. 0011B]

[Note: [Col. 0011D] Einhard’s letter 34.]

Hence a close relationship afterward remained between the two.

[Note: [Col. 0011D] The same letter and letters 43, 48–50.]

In 818, with Imma’s consent, he transferred the estate of Michilinstat to the monastery of Lorsch.

[Note: [Col. 0011D] Lorsch Diplomatic Codex I, pp. 46, 48.]

A few years later he and his wife agreed that in future they would live as brother and sister. Yet this is shown not to have been a sign of diminished affection by the fact that Imma remained in her husband’s house until her death and continued to manage all his affairs as she had been accustomed to do.

[Note: [Col. 0011D] Einhard’s letter to Lupus, and Lupus’s letter 4.]

Einhard, meanwhile, after being ordained a priest,

[Note: [Col. 0011D] He celebrated Mass in 826, History of the Translation, chapter 42; he was abbot in 827, History of the Translation, chapter 69.]

built a basilica of respectable workmanship on his estate at Mulinheim, and in 825 sent his notary Radleic to Rome to obtain relics of the saints.

[Note: [Col. 0011D] History of the Translation.]

These relics, obtained only with difficulty, were deposited in that monastery of Mulinheim—now called Seligenstadt—in the years 826 and 827.

Since, then, he was famous among learned men

[Note: [Col. 0011D] Compare the Chronicle of Fontenelle.]

and easily first among the emperor’s advisers, together with Hilduin, abbot of Saint-Denis, exercising authority over a large part of the affairs of the kingdom, a grave and gradual change in court affairs took place.

For when Charles the child was born from the emperor’s second marriage, all Judith’s and Louis’s efforts were directed toward securing for him a portion of the kingdom distributed among the other sons. While they spent considerable time on this, the state was increasingly neglected, and everything began to deteriorate so badly that Einhard became entirely filled with a desire to withdraw to his estates.

[Note: [Col. 0011D] History of the Translation, chapters 2, 46, 50, and elsewhere.]

Nevertheless, he thought he ought not to refrain from first testing the emperor’s mind.

[Note: [Col. 0011D] He seems shortly beforehand to have incurred the emperor’s displeasure. For he writes to Gerward, librarian of the palace, chapter 14, that he had been ordered to remain at Seligenstadt and that an absence of seven days would be painful for him. In this letter he consults his friend about conveying Gabriel’s admonitions to the emperor.]

In 828 he presented him with the admonitions of the archangel Gabriel, arranged in twelve chapters, and indicated what needed to be done, predicting that rebellion would arise if he failed to fulfill it.

[Note: [Col. 0012D] History of the Translation, chapters 47–48; Annals of Fulda, under the year 874.]

After reading the little book, the emperor carried out some things and neglected others.

[Note: [Col. 0012D] History of the Translation, chapter 47.]

Two years later, when the emperor’s court was being increasingly divided into factions, and Judith had secured the appointment of Bernard, duke of Septimania, as chamberlain, the friends of the sons, on the other hand, summoned Lothar to their aid. Einhard earnestly pressed his former pupil not to oppose his father.

[Col. 0012A]

[Note: [Col. 0012D] Einhard’s letter 34.]

Meanwhile Bernard so abused his authority that the leaders of the opposing party thought it preferable to attempt the most desperate measures rather than tolerate him any longer. At the beginning of 830, when the emperor had come to Compiègne for the expedition to Brittany, they led the army away and stirred up a rebellion.

When he received this news, Einhard—who, ordered to follow Judith to Compiègne, had reached Valenciennes while seriously ill—returned by ship to Ghent and, with a new ordering of affairs already impending, asked the emperor for his dismissal.

[Note: [Col. 0012D] Letters 40, 41, and 42, and others not yet published.]

After obtaining it,

[Note: [Col. 0012D] Letter 42.]

he withdrew to Mulinheim in March. But when he saw the state, shaken by factions, being driven in different directions, in April or May

[Note: [Col. 0012D] Annals of Bertin, under the year 830.]

he sought an interview with the emperor Lothar, who had returned from Italy,

[Note: [Col. 0012D] Letter 43 and other unpublished letters.]

and afterward resolved to attend the great assembly at which the condition of the entire kingdom was to be investigated.

[Note: [Col. 0012D] Letter 44.]

When this assembly was held at Nijmegen on the Kalends of October,

[Col. 0012B]

Lothar was reconciled with his father through the intervention of friends. We are all the more led to believe that our Einhard also faithfully served in this matter because we read that, in the summer of 836, when the emperor was already considering only how sincerely to unite Lothar to himself, he voluntarily visited his old friend at Seligenstadt.

[Note: [Col. 0012D] Annals of Fulda, under the year 836.]

He spent the rest of his life devoted to religion, learning, and friends, living quietly amid the kingdom’s greatest turmoil.

[Note: [Col. 0012D] Beginning of letter 47.]

He did not cease either to use his influence kindly on behalf of the affairs of the peasants and neighbors

[Note: [Col. 0012D] Letters 6, 7, 15—where Boma should probably be read Imma—16, 17, 18, 25, 53, and 54.]

or to intercede with friends remaining at the palace on behalf of the oppressed.

[Note: [Col. 0012D] Letters 27 and 28, perhaps also 26 and 27; 48, 49, and 51.]

He adorned the church at Mulinheim, already famous far and wide for the merits of its martyrs, and roofed it with lead.

[Note: [Col. 0012D] Letter 46.]

He devoted less time to writing books than he once had amid the affairs of the kingdom.

[Note: [Col. 0012D] Letter to Lupus and letter 30.]

He decided not to continue beyond the year 829 the annals that he had published while established at the palace, concerning the affairs of Pepin, Charles, and Louis.

He also wrote books on the history of the translation of Saints Marcellinus and Peter,

[Col. 0012C]

and a little work for Lupus on the veneration of the cross.

His surviving letters contribute greatly to illuminating the history of the author and of his period.

The History of Saxony, or the little book on the arrival, customs, and superstition of the Saxons, and the History of the Translation of Saint Alexander, attributed to him by Adam of Bremen, are demonstrably owed to Rudolf and Meginhard of Fulda.

Lambecius,

[Note: [Col. 0012D] Commentary on the Imperial Library of Vienna II, pp. 395, 398.]

however, attempted to claim for him an abridgment of the chronicle from the foundation of Rome to the year 809, but rests on no foundation whatsoever. Nor with better right have others assigned to our Einhard a psalter of a certain Einhard recorded in the Bobbio library.

[Note: [Col. 0012D] Mansi, in Fabricius’s Library of Medieval and Later Latin, book V, p. 88.]

The works he did publish, however, are so constituted that they assign him a foremost place among historians. For he wrote with complete integrity of mind, not about foreign and alien matters, but about his own time and his own friend; and not merely as a learned man, but as one who had spent his life administering the state.

[Col. 0013A]

He cultivated Greek letters

[Note: [Col. 0013D] That he understood Greek is attested by both the proverb quoted in the Life of Charlemagne and Lupus’s letter 5, as well as by what he reports about Charles as a proficient speaker of that language.]

as much as Roman ones. From ancient authors he read not only historians and poets,

[Note: [Col. 0013D] Virgil’s Georgics, letter 30.]

mathematicians, grammarians,

[Note: [Col. 0013D] The same source; Lupus’s letter 1.]

and rhetoricians,

[Note: [Col. 0013D] Vitruvius, in the same place. Compare Lupus’s letter 5.]

but also the Fathers

[Note: [Col. 0013D] Einhard’s letter to Lupus.]

and writers of his own age.

[Note: [Col. 0013D] For example, Paul the Deacon.]

[Note: [Col. 0013D] Letters 30?]

Since he was regarded as the wisest and most learned man of his time,

[Note: [Col. 0013D] Anonymous Life of Louis, chapter 41; Ermoldus, cited above; Chronicle of Fontenelle.]

we shall readily believe that young men of excellent character sought his association.

He held as his foremost admirer Lupus, later abbot of Ferrières, who had been sent to Germany to be educated.

[Note: [Col. 0013D] Lupus’s letters to Einhard.]

He was joined in constant friendship with Rabanus, then abbot of Fulda, whom he esteemed highly for the abundance of his learning and the integrity of his character. He had shared with him the catalogue of his library,

[Note: [Col. 0013D] Lupus’s letter 1 to Einhard.]

lent him books,

[Note: [Col. 0013D] Lupus’s letter 5.]

and entrusted to him his only son, Vussin, to be formed in character and learning and trained as a monk.

[Note: [Col. 0013D] Letter 30, and Einhard’s letters to Lupus. Einhard seems to have inspected the library at Fulda, for he knows of a little box there in which obscure words and names could be displayed, letter 30.]

He also enjoyed for several years the companionship of Imma, his sweetest sister. When she died at the beginning of 836,

[Note: [Col. 0013D] She died in winter. Lupus, after the death of Aldric—on the sixth day before the Ides of October—returned to Gaul and visited Einhard in June; Lupus’s letter 41.]

he mourned her so deeply that he resolved to spend all the days remaining to him in grief.

[Col. 0013B]

[Note: [Col. 0014D] Einhard’s letter to Lupus.]

To remember her, to embrace her in his inmost heart, to commend himself to her intercession before God—this was the sole joy of his life and the sole consolation of his death. He had resolved to surrender his soul to the Creator with these prayers.

[Note: [Col. 0014D] Letters to Lupus, letter 32.]

He died on the eighth day before the Kalends of August, in the year 844.

[Note: [Col. 0014D] Those who maintain that Einhard survived until 848 should consider how they interpret Rabanus’s epitaph of Ratleic, Einhard’s successor. Ratleic is there said to have died young; but how could one call young a man who, twenty-five years earlier, had already been Einhard’s notary and had been sent by him as an envoy to Rome? Ratleic certainly died not long after Einhard—if we do not stretch the meaning of youth too far. The history of the abbey of Seligenstadt in the ninth century is shrouded in deep darkness; Weinckensius’s *Navarchia Seligenstadensis*, *Eginhartus*, and the *History of the Translation of Saints Peter and Marcellinus* are nauseating to read.]

His body was buried in the church at Seligenstadt, and Rabanus composed this epitaph for him:

> You who enter this temple, I ask you not to disdain to learn  
> What this place contains, and what its occupant teaches.  
>   
> Behold, a noble man lies buried in this tomb;  
> Einhard was the name his father gave him.  
>   
> Here he was wise in intellect, upright in conduct, and eloquent in speech,  
> And through his skill he was useful to many.  
>   
> Prince Charles raised him in his own court,  
> Through whom he also completed many great works.  
>   
> For, having performed fitting honor for these saints,  
> He sought out their bodies in Rome and brought them here,  
>   
> So that they might benefit many by their prayers and healing care,  
> And grant his own soul the kingdom of heaven.  
>   
> Christ God, savior, ruler, and creator of human beings,  
> In your mercy grant him eternal rest above the stars.

Einhard was short in stature, but he expressed the ardor of his spirit through the agility of his body. Testimony to this survives in a work by Theodulf, bishop of Orléans. I believe that his *Nardulus* is an abbreviated form of *Einardulus*; Alcuin calls him Bezalel, after the craftsman whom we read built the Ark of the Covenant.

Anyone can easily understand that, if such a man had undertaken to write the history of his own time, he would have produced a work remarkable for its wealth of material and its elegance of expression. That he possessed an abundance of material for writing is clear from what has been cited above, as well as from what he himself says about himself, his letters—which he says still exist—and his embassies to the emperor. We recognize him as no less devoted to truth than capable in reporting

[Note: [Col. 0014D] Under Louis’s rule, while he was the emperor’s chief adviser.]

the calamities of the Franks and the evil reputation of Charles’s

[Col. 0014A]

daughters, as well as the conspiracies that arose because of the monstrous cruelty of Fastrada.

Of his works that now survive, we have published the *Annals* in volume I, reserving the letters and the history of the translation of Saints Marcellinus and Peter for a future volume.

The *Life of Charlemagne*, however, surpassed them all among his contemporaries and among later generations. For we do not remember that any historian throughout the Middle Ages, with the single exception of Martin of Poland, had so many manuscripts survive, nor that the writings of any other historian were extracted so eagerly by all who treated of Charles’s deeds.

Einhard owes part of his glory to Charles and part to himself. Certainly neither in the centuries immediately preceding nor in those following will one find a historian who surpasses him in such force of thought, clarity of judgment, and skill of expression.

He owed this to his study of the Romans, especially Cicero and Suetonius, whom he valued so highly that he seems often to have borrowed from him not only the arrangement of his work but even complete sentences. Before his eyes stood especially the first of those emperors, Augustus Octavian, whom Charles had in a sense equaled by his deeds,

[Col. 0014B]

and Titus; but he did not disdain Tiberius or Claudius. This sheds light on several disputed passages of the work—for example, what he says in chapter 4, that he had been unable to learn anything, either from written sources or by hearsay, about Charles’s birth, childhood, or even boyhood.

Certainly, just as Suetonius transmitted accounts of certain Caesars, Einhard had no opportunity to draw similar accounts of Charles from books—at least not from written sources. For this reason some modern writers attacked him fiercely, boasting that they themselves possessed certain knowledge that Charles had been crowned in 754. If only they had wished to learn from his annals that Einhard was not ignorant of this!

He incorporated a few sentences into his book from Paul the Deacon’s little work on the bishops of Metz. Yet, just as no one imitates others with impunity, I readily admit that Einhard too paid the penalty for this in one or two places. Nor did he succeed, despite all his effort, in mastering the language of antiquity perfectly, since he occasionally sinned against grammar.

[Col. 0014C]

No further doubt about this can remain now that we have prepared a new edition with the aid of sixty manuscripts. No one would previously have been persuaded that so many copies of Einhard’s work survived; I myself examined most of them in the libraries of Germany, Italy, Switzerland, Belgium, France, and Britain.

In such an abundance of books, the first matter to be examined was the relationship by which one depended on another and all depended on Einhard’s authentic copy. I soon observed that all the manuscripts now surviving derive from two exemplars.

The manuscripts of the first class are therefore those which I believe descended from Einhard’s own authentic copy, although by different routes:

## 1

A manuscript of the Imperial Library of Vienna, listed in the catalogue of profane history under no. 667, written on parchment in quarto and dating from the end of the ninth century. We have given a specimen of its script on the plate appended to the work.

According to its subscription, it belonged in the tenth or eleventh century to the monastery of Saint Maximinus at Trier.

[Col. 0015A]

The prologue is missing. A second hand, contemporary with the scribe, corrected Einhard’s book in several places and seems to have appended no other work except the anonymous *Life of the Emperor Louis*.

Several passages, worn away through use, were restored or corrupted in the thirteenth century by the application of fresh ink. Words and sentences are so often joined together that one scarcely feels any force in the punctuation marks.

There are few abbreviations, all customary ones; *ae* and *oe* are expressed either by two letters or by a simple or tailed *e*; *t* and *c* are scarcely distinguished.

In place of the ancient title *Life of the Emperor Charles*, now almost erased, another title, *Life of the Great Emperor Charles*, was written over it in the thirteenth century.

I copied the entire work in 1820.

## 2

A manuscript of Queen Christina’s library in the Vatican, no. 637, written on paper in quarto and dating from the seventeenth century. Its heading reads:

> The Life of the Emperor Charles, published by Eginhard, a man exceedingly learned and educated in his own time by that same prince, begins successfully.

Besides Einhard, it contains the *Life of Louis*, a genealogy of the Frankish kings, and the ancestry from which Charles, who is called the Great, sprang.

It agrees astonishingly with the Viennese manuscript, so that it must be considered to have flowed from nearly the same source.

I collated it in 1821 and reported in the notes all the readings not adopted in the text.

The following manuscript comes closest to it:

## 2 b

A manuscript of the Royal Library of Paris, no. 5925, written on parchment in the fourteenth century. After Aimoin’s history of the Franks it contains the following:

> The Life and conduct of the most glorious emperor Charles, the most invincible Augustus, begins. Published by Eginhard, a man exceedingly learned in his own time and also highly experienced in the liberal arts, educated by the aforesaid prince, propagator and defender of the Christian religion. Read through it happily to the end, rejoicing in Christ.

The prologue of the work is missing. Einhard is followed by the deeds of Charles in Spain.

The principal passages were collated with the printed editions by the distinguished Faerber, with the generous consent of the directors of the learned society.

## 2 c

A manuscript of the Royal Library of Paris, no. 5943 B, written on parchment in the thirteenth century. It follows an anonymous *Life of Charles* published by Chesne, volume II, p. 50, from the same source, and precedes the *Deeds of the Emperor Charles the Great*.

The work is entitled:

> Here begins Einhard’s prologue to the Life of the Emperor Charles.

Selected passages were collated by Dr. Faerber.

## 3

A manuscript of the Royal Library of Paris, no. 5927, written on parchment in the eleventh century. It contains first the *Chronicle of Ademar* and a certain charter, followed by:

> The Life and conduct of the most glorious emperor Charles, the most invincible Augustus, published by Eginhard, a man exceedingly learned in his own time and also highly experienced in the liberal arts, educated by the aforesaid prince, propagator and defender of the Christian religion.

The manuscript breaks off at the word *basilica* in chapter 17.

The surviving portions were collated with the printed editions by Mr. Keller. When it was still complete, it was copied in the thirteenth century; that copy now survives as:

## 3*

A manuscript in the Paris Library, no. 5926. Selected passages were collated by Dr. Faerber.

[Col. 0015D]

## 3 b

A manuscript of Queen Christina’s library in the Vatican, which I examined completely in 1821, listed under no. 692. It is written on parchment in folio, dates from the twelfth century, and is written in Lombard script.

Its title is as in Codex 2 b, except for the words *Karoli* and *doctissime*.

It also contains the anonymous *Life of Louis* and a brief history of the Franks from Pharamond to the times of the emperor Henry II and King Robert.

## 3 c

A manuscript of the Royal Library of Paris, no. 5354, written on parchment in the eleventh century, collated with the printed editions by Mr. Schneegans.

Its title is the same as that of Codex 2 b above. The anonymous *Life of the Emperor Louis* follows. It is a copy of that manuscript.

## 3 c*

A manuscript of the Royal Library of Paris, no. 4631, dating from the fifteenth century, collated by Mr. Oberlin.

## 4

A manuscript of the Viennese Palatine Library, among the profane historians, no. 654, written on parchment in quarto and dating from the tenth century.

The inscription *Deeds and Life of the Emperor Charles* has now been erased. The preface is missing.

Since several leaves had fallen out before the thirteenth century, they were supplied by a man of that period with the aid of a manuscript of the second class that closely approached B 5. Some readings were also corrected as he thought appropriate; these I decided should be marked with the notation 4 B.

[Col. 0016A]

The scribe completed the work with great care, so that one encounters few errors in it. He used *ae*, *ce*, *ae*, and *e* more often than the usage of our own time requires.

## 4 b

The manuscript used by Marquard Freher for his edition in the *Corpus of Frankish Writers*, p. 433, seems for the most part to agree with the manuscripts so far reviewed. Freher, however, did not turn it to proper advantage for his own purposes, since he usually follows the Nuenarian edition so closely that he reproduces again even typographical errors corrected at its end.

For this reason I invoked Freher’s authority more rarely, and generally only when he departs from Nuenarius.

## 5

A manuscript of the Vatican Library, no. 3339, written on parchment in folio and dating from the thirteenth or fourteenth century, which I read in 1822.

Its inscription reads:

> Here begins the preface of the little book on the Life, Character, and Deeds of the most excellent king Charles.

[Col. 0016B]

## 6

A manuscript of the Royal Library of Paris, no. 4628 A, written on parchment in the tenth century, bearing the title:

> The Life of Charles the Great, dictated by Einhard.

It generally agrees with the manuscripts already reviewed in readings of greater importance. In writing such forms as *com*, *dicontur*, *cuncordia*, *cummuniter*, *cumpelleret*, *cumpositis*, *cumpletum*, *cumsimilis*, *cumvenientem*, and *nundum*, it departs from common usage.

It extends to the words of chapter 16, *There exists a proverb*, and ends with the superscription concerning Charles’s final will.

It was collated by Mr. Weber.

## 6 b

A manuscript of the Royal Library of Paris, no. 4955, written on parchment in the eleventh century, collated by Mr. Schneegans.

It is entitled:

> The Life of Charles the Great, king and emperor of France, by Einhard, once his pupil and sworn secretary, a German.

After the book ends, there follows a genealogy of the Carolingian line from Arnulf to the emperor Lothar, and only after it the formula:

> Here ends the Life of Charles, king and emperor.

[Col. 0016C]

## 7

A parchment manuscript of the Cotton Library, marked Tib. C XI, collated with the printed editions by Dr. Faerber.

## 7 a

A manuscript formerly at Gembloux, written on parchment in the eleventh century, in octavo or quarto. I examined it among the royal manuscripts at Brussels in 1826.

After Gerald’s poem, or the book of the two companions Waltharius and Haganus, it presents our book under the following title:

> Here begins Einhard’s preface to the Life of Lord Charles the Emperor.

Its readings most closely approach those of Codices 7, 7 b, c, 10 f, g, h, and 15.

## 7 b

A manuscript of the Bodleian Library, marked Laud H 39, which I examined at Oxford in 1827.

It is written on parchment in small folio and dates from the twelfth century. It contains Victor of Vita’s *History of the Vandal Persecution*, Paul’s *History of the Lombards*, and, after Einhard’s work, a book of beasts, a work on Alexander the Great, and finally a history of Apollonius.

## 7 c

A manuscript formerly belonging to the Jesuit Society at Paderborn, used by John Bolland for his edition in the *Acts of the Saints*, January, volume II, pp. 874–888, Antwerp, 1643. Its subsequent history is unknown; therefore I was able to consult not the manuscript itself, but only Bolland concerning it.

That it was not unlike the Cotton manuscript is shown by its reading in chapter 1, *the monastery of Sithiu*. Thus, in general, when I knew only a few things about the manuscript, it was necessary to follow a notable reading in placing it among the others.

Bolland’s edition, moreover, has an advantage over the earlier editions in that, with the aid of his manuscripts, he restored several passages after rejecting Nuenarius’s corruption.

## 7 d

A manuscript preserved in Sion College, London, several of whose readings Schminkius reports as having been sent to him by J. J. Schroeder.

You may recognize that it approaches the Paderborn manuscript from the same reading in chapter 1, *the monastery of Sithiu*.

Its inscription reads:

> The Life of Charles, the orthodox emperor, published by Meinard, his chaplain, a man exceedingly learned in his own time.

[Col. 0017]

[Col. 0019A]

## 8 and 8*

A manuscript of the Royal Library of Paris, from the library of Notre-Dame, no. 133, formerly H 4, written on parchment in folio and dating from the twelfth century, which I examined in 1827; and a copy of it, manuscript no. 6187 of the same library, written on parchment in the thirteenth century.

After the preface they contain:

> The Life of the Emperor Charles the Great, written by Einhard, his abbot and chaplain.

The readings are somewhat corrupt. They break off at the words of chapter 31, *In the seventh year of the indiction, on the fifth day before the Kalends of February*.

In the same volume are found Turpin’s work, excerpts from a certain letter of Alcuin (Bouquet V, p. 607), Charles’s letter to Offa (the same, p. 627), a vision concerning Charles Martel, and Bede’s *History of the English*.

### 8 b)

The manuscript which Count Hermann Nuenarius used in his edition, published at Cologne in 1521 in quarto together with Einhard’s *Annals*, either had already departed too far from the ancient exemplars, or—which I rather believe—was altered in many places by the editor in order to make the diction more polished and more Latin. The chief indication of this will be that, in such passages, all the other surviving manuscripts, without exception, generally depart from Nuenarius. Accordingly, very many readings peculiar to him ought to have been rejected as mere conjectures and not even reported in the notes. [Col. 0019B]

Its title is: “The Life and Deeds of Charles, surnamed the Great, the most valiant king of the Franks, illuminator of his Germany and its most worthy benefactor, by Einhard—a German, formerly his pupil and sworn secretary—happily begin.” The words of this title, which are lacking in Manuscript 6, were presumably added by the editor. It is closely related to Manuscript 8 c.

### 8 c)

The manuscript of the University Library of Bonn is related to it, at least in those passages which I compared with my edition in 1826. It is a parchment manuscript in large folio, of the twelfth century, and also contains several capitularies; on this matter, see the *Rheinisches Archiv*, vol. I.

### 9)

A manuscript formerly belonging to the monastery of Prüm and now in the public library of Trier, on parchment, in small quarto, written in the year 1084. The collation of the entire book, as well as of the more important passages, was undertaken for the public benefit and sent to us by the distinguished Wyttenbach. [Col. 0019C] Einhard’s work lacks both title and preface.

### 9 b)

A parchment manuscript of the Bodleian Library at Oxford, collated with the printed editions by J. J. Schroeder for Schminck’s use. Both men withhold its date; the preface is lacking.

### 9 c)

Manuscript 208 of the public library of the city of Bern, parchment, in folio, of the thirteenth century. A few lines after “Walah, Meginherius” are missing. I inspected some passages in 1823 and would have done more had the short period available allowed it.

### 10)

A parchment manuscript of the Royal Library of Hanover, in quarto, of the twelfth century, which I consulted for our purposes. As I shall explain more fully below, when introducing the monk of Saint Gall, this manuscript, together with the five following ones, recognizes the same source. For after our work they contain Einhard’s *Annals* and the monk of Saint Gall, and they are so closely connected by the affinity of their readings that it is permissible to suppose that the oldest manuscript of the monk of Saint Gall was attached to both of Einhard’s works. [Col. 0019D] The first four leaves of the Hanover manuscript, together with the preface, as I suppose, and the beginning of the work down to the words of chapter 9, “So that the location and configuration of the narrow places,” have fallen out. The final words of the *Life*, “He took care to complete,” are followed on the same line by the beginning of the *Annals*, “In this year.”

### 10 b)

A parchment manuscript of the Ducal Library of Gotha, in quarto, of the twelfth century, which, through the patriotic goodwill of the distinguished Jacobs, privy councillor and librarian, I was permitted to handle. The book is distinguished by an image of Charles seated upon a throne, with an armor-bearer standing on his right. After the monk of Saint Gall, it counts as the third and fourth book of Charles’s deeds; it also contains a few remarks on the death of Bede the priest and twelve verses on computation. The preface is lacking. Its title is: “Here begins the first book of the deeds of Charles.” The text not infrequently betrays a reckless scribe.

### 10 c)

A parchment manuscript of the Royal Library of Munich, formerly belonging to the monastery of Saint Mang at Stadt-am-Hof, in quarto, of the twelfth century, discovered by the distinguished Docen and collated for our purposes by D. Bachlechner. [Col. 0020A] Here too the preface is lacking. The following manuscript is a copy of it:

### 10 c*)

A parchment manuscript of the Imperial Library of Vienna, among the secular historians, no. 990, in quarto, of the fourteenth century. I collated it in 1820; I have rarely cited its readings here. Its title is: “Here begins the prologue of the books concerning the deeds of the Emperor Charles.”

### 10 c+)

Two manuscript books formerly reported by Justus Reuber as having been in his library exhibit almost the same readings as Manuscripts 9 b and, especially, 10, 10 b, and 10 c.

### 10 d)

A paper manuscript of the Ducal Library of Modena, of the fifteenth century, which I examined there in 1823; it needed to be consulted in only two or three passages.

### 10* e)

A parchment manuscript of the Electoral Library of Kassel, written in 1498. A copy of it was sent to Schminck; I inspected it in 1824 and, amid such a large collection of much older books, did not think it necessary to read it through again.

[Col. 0020B]

### 10 f)

A parchment manuscript of the Public Library at Leiden, collated by Schminck with the printed editions. Since, however, in chapter 6 it omits the same sentence as the Kassel manuscript, it is clear that the two must be connected. Its title is: “The life and conduct of the most excellent prince, our lord Charles, once great emperor of the Romans and king of the Franks.”

### 10 g)

A manuscript at Cambridge, in Caius College (formerly the church of Reading), examined by J. Gordon for Schminck’s use; it agrees with the Leiden manuscript in nearly the same readings. I examined it at Cambridge in 1827 and found it entitled: “Here begins Alcuin’s prologue to the life of Charles the Great, king of the Franks and emperor of the Romans.” It was written in the twelfth century, on parchment, and after Einhard contains the *Life of Alexander the Great*, his letter to Aristotle concerning the location of India, and an abridgment of the deeds of the Frankish kings.

### 11)

Manuscript 16 in the Hohendorf catalogue of the Imperial Library of Vienna, in folio, on parchment, of the twelfth century, which I read through in 1820. Paul’s *History of the Lombards* precedes it. Its title is: “Here begins the life of the Emperor Charles the Great.” It was copied from the same manuscript as the following four. [Col. 0020C]

### 11 b)

Manuscript 4877 of the Royal Library of Paris, on parchment, in folio, of the thirteenth century. Here Einhard is placed after Orosius and the history of the Lombards, and before the history of Alexander the Great and his letter concerning the location of India. The title is as in Manuscript 11. D. Faerber collated selected passages.

### 11 c)

Manuscript 5997 of the Royal Library of Paris, on parchment, of the thirteenth century, in which the *Life* is placed between the history of the Northmen and an abridgment of the deeds of the Frankish kings. Its title is: “Here begins the prologue to the life of Charles the Great, king of the Franks and emperor of the Romans.” D. Faerber collated selected passages.

### 11 c*)

Manuscript 4937 of the Royal Library of Paris, on parchment, of the fourteenth century, is a copy of Manuscript 11 c. We owe the selected passages to Faerber.

### 11 d)

Manuscript 5999 of the Royal Library of Paris, of the sixteenth century. [Col. 0020D] In it, Charles’s life precedes the history of the Normans, and an abridgment of the deeds of the Frankish kings follows. Its title is as in Manuscript 11 c. D. Faerber excerpted selected passages.

### 12)

A paper manuscript of the Public Library of Bremen, in quarto, of the seventeenth century. It was copied by Goldast’s hand from a sufficiently good exemplar, but differs from the one which I shall discuss below under no. 17. I thought it necessary to consult the book only in a few passages.

### 13)

Manuscript 547 of the Library of Saint Gall, on parchment, in large folio, of the eleventh or perhaps twelfth century. It contains Bede’s *History of the English*, the deeds of the Frankish kings, and our work. The preface is present; at the end of the work some material has fallen out.

### 14)

The Gladbach manuscript, used by Bolland in his edition; the readings he reports are so few that nothing certain can be established about it.

### 15)

A manuscript of the Wolfenbüttel Library, among the *Extravagantes*, marked no. 152; it is a parchment manuscript in octavo, of the fifteenth century.

### 16)

A parchment manuscript in duodecimo, of the fifteenth century, described by Jacopo Morelli in his *Bibliotheca manuscripta Graeca et Latina* (Bassano, 1802), pp. 395–397. As I learned at Venice from the distinguished Pietro Bettio, the most courteous librarian of Saint Mark’s and Morelli’s nephew, it has now been taken to Britain. Most of its readings agree with our edition; I reported in the notes two additions that certainly have no authority.

### 17)

Goldast’s manuscript, which he testifies that he received from Schobinger, generally agrees with our edition in the commentary on our work published by Schminck. In his commentary Goldast supplied much that was learned, very much that was less necessary, and some things useful to know.

### 18)

Manuscript 339 of the Palatine Library, on parchment, in quarto, consisting of sixteen leaves. The Most Illustrious L. B. de Stein inspected it at Rome in 1822, but it could no longer be found the following winter. I have therefore listed it here last among the manuscripts of the first class. [Col. 0021B]

All the manuscripts of the second class had descended from a certain exemplar to which Gerward, librarian of Charles and Louis and Einhard’s chief friend, had added three distichs in praise of Charles and Einhard. Since it is therefore clear that these manuscripts trace their origin to a very ancient exemplar contemporary with Einhard, they seem worthy of more careful examination by an editor. Nor is the quality of their readings unequal to their origin. For the most part they agree with the best and most ancient manuscripts of the first class, though in several places they depart from them entirely, especially in that they do not list Roland among those killed by the Basques. The preface is lacking in all of them except Manuscript B 2 b. Most of the manuscripts of this class are found in Germany, and a few in Italy and France. It will be useful to reproduce those distichs here:

> Gerward, your suppliant servant, has produced  
> these little verses for your praise, greatest prince,  
> and for your eternal memory.  
> With kindly mind he exalts  
> your illustrious name to the stars.  
>   
> Know, prudent reader, that Einhard wrote  
> this account of the great and magnificent Charles.

[Col. 0021C]

The manuscript reads *suplex* (“suppliant”) in B 1. [Col. 0021D]

*Einhardum* appears as *Einchardum* in B 3, 3 c, and 3 d; *Einardum* in B 5 b; and *Enchardum* in B 4 b.

*Magni* appears as *magnum* in B 2.

The manuscripts are therefore as follows:

### B 1)

Manuscript 90 of the Imperial Library of Vienna, among the ecclesiastical histories, on parchment, in large quarto, from the end of the ninth century. According to the scribe’s practice, it begins only with the words of chapter 18, “The remaining matters that concern the interior …” It writes the diphthong *ae* as *ae*, *æ*, or *e* more often than we do; individual words are often joined together or incorrectly separated. I read through it in 1820.

### B 2)

The Florentine manuscript in the Laurentian Library, on parchment, in large folio, of the eleventh century. In the same volume are Prosper’s *Chronicle*, Jordanes’ *Getica*, the deeds of the Franks, and Paul’s *History of the Lombards*. Its title is: “Here begin the deeds of Charles.” The text is so close to B 1 that it cannot have failed to derive from the same source as that manuscript. Extracts from the manuscript, sent to Besselius by Heinrich Meibom, were already used by Besselius when he was preparing to publish Einhard, but they had been made with insufficient care. Accordingly, when I was staying in Florence in 1822, I decided to read through it again more carefully. Besides the copy of this manuscript preserved at Florence, another exists.

### B 2*)

Manuscript 477 in the catalogue of secular history of the Imperial Library of Vienna, paper, in folio, of the fifteenth century, which I consulted for our purposes in 1820. Its title is: “Here happily begin the deeds of Charles.”

### B 2 b)

Manuscript 6264 of the Royal Library of Paris, of the fifteenth century, whose selected readings D. Faerber transcribed. It appears to have been augmented from a manuscript of the first class—perhaps 3 c—with a preface and title. The title reads:

“The life and conduct of the most glorious Emperor Charles and unconquered Augustus. Here begins the work published by Einhard, a man exceedingly learned for his time and highly experienced in the liberal arts, educated by the aforesaid prince, promoter and defender of the Christian religion. May you, hastening through it in joyful reading, rejoice in Christ.” [Col. 0022A]

### B 3)

Manuscript 338 of the Imperial Library of Vienna, among the secular historians, on parchment, in folio, written in the twelfth century under Emperor Conrad III and examined by me six years ago. Its title is: “The deeds of Charles.” It is preceded by Rutbert’s history of the Jerusalem expedition and Isidore of Seville’s *Chronicle*, and followed by Liutprand’s history. Anyone examining the readings excerpted from it, together with those of the three or five manuscripts about to be listed, will easily see that it flowed from the same source as they did.

### B 3 b)

A parchment manuscript in folio, of the twelfth century, belonging to the monastery of Klosterneuburg above Vienna on the Danube. In the same volume are Paul the Deacon’s *Miscellaneous History*, Liutprand’s history, and Regino’s *Chronicle*. Its title is: “The deeds of Charles.” I read through the manuscript in 1821.

### B 3 c)

Manuscript 1068 in the catalogue of secular history of the Imperial Library of Vienna, on parchment, in octavo, entitled: “The deeds of Charles the Great.” The book contains both Liutprand and Regino’s *Chronicle*. I examined it and the following four manuscripts in 1820.

### B 3 d)

Manuscript 1080 in Schwandner’s catalogue of the Imperial Library of Vienna, on paper, in quarto, of the fifteenth century, also entitled “The deeds of Charles.” In the same book one finds Liutprand and Regino.

### B 4)

A parchment manuscript of the monastery of Zwettl in Austria, in quarto, of the twelfth century. Besides Einhard, it contains Liutprand, Victor of Vita’s *History of the Vandal Persecution*, and Otto of Freising’s *Chronicle*. Its title is: “Here begin the deeds of Charles.”

### B 4 b)

A parchment manuscript in folio, of the thirteenth century, in the catalogue of secular history of the Imperial Library of Vienna, no. 178, without a title. It contains the same writers as the Zwettl manuscript and, in addition, Paul’s *Miscellaneous History*. The inscription is lacking. [Col. 0022C]

### B 5)

Manuscript 110 in the catalogue of ecclesiastical history of the Palatine Library of Vienna, on parchment, in folio, of the twelfth century. Einhard’s *Life* was copied from a manuscript of the second class, while the monk of Saint Gall was copied from the Hanover manuscript. The verses in praise of Einhard are lacking. Its title is: “Here begins the *Life of Charles the Great, Emperor and Apostle of the Saxons*, composed by Enhard, his chaplain.” I encountered in it a peculiar scribal abbreviation, *et[a]*, that is, *etiam* (“also”); in Migne, the letter in square brackets is printed above the preceding word.

### B 5 b)

The Moissac manuscript, written in 1127, which was in Chesne’s possession.

### B 6)

A parchment manuscript of the monastery of Einsiedeln in Switzerland, of the eleventh or twelfth century. Since, according to the report of the distinguished Dumge, it contains those three distichs, I have counted it among the manuscripts of the second class. Nothing further is known to us about its text.

### B 7)

A parchment manuscript marked F. IV 75 in the Chigi Library, in octavo, of the tenth century. It contains the *Chronicle* of Benedict, a tenth-century monk of Saint Andrew on Soracte, into which I observed that certain passages from Einhard’s *Life* of the second class had been inserted—namely, from chapters 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 20, 22, 24, 25, 26, and 30–33. The verses of Gerward are also present, though miserably corrupted.

### B 8)

A paper manuscript of the Royal Library of Hanover, formerly belonging to the congregation of nuns at Wittingen in the principality of Lüneburg, in quarto, written around the year 1400. It is entitled, if I am not mistaken, *Various Matters Concerning Charles the Great* by Scheid, and among other things contains excerpts from Einhard and Thegan. The third distich, which reveals the author of the little book, is appended to those excerpts. In place of the true preface—which, as I said, is lacking in the books of this class—the manuscript’s scribe prefixed another preface, which he attributed to Strabo, undoubtedly because he had seen him named before Thegan. He therefore attempted to divide the *Life of Charles* according to Strabo’s example into chapters; their arrangement differs somewhat from the more recent one, but does not deserve to be reproduced here.

The prefatory text reads:

> “The deeds of Charles the Great, according to Strabo. From the chronicle of Saint Alban of Mainz. The life and deeds of the most glorious Emperor Charles the Great. Einhart, a man among all the palace officials of his time, is known to have described him with outstanding praise, not only because of his knowledge of affairs and universal moral integrity, but also because he strengthened his account by the testimony of the purest truth, since he was present at nearly all these events. Born in eastern Francia, in the district called Maingau, he received his first instruction in the monastery of Fulda under the guidance of Saint Boniface the martyr. From there he was transferred by Baugolf, the abbot of the aforesaid monastery, to Charles’s palace, etc.
>
> “But now, as studies slip back into opposite directions, the light of wisdom, which is less loved, grows rare among many. Accordingly, that little man—for he appeared contemptible in stature—in the court of Charles, the lover of wisdom, attained such an increase of glory through his prudence and integrity that he was regarded as almost the sole man among all the servants of the royal majesty to whom the king, then most powerful and wise, entrusted many of the secrets of his intimacy, etc. We say this so that no one may have less doubt about his statements.
>
> “After this little work follows: ‘I, Strabo, have inserted titles and divisions wherever seemed appropriate, so that the reader seeking particular points may more easily find whatever he wishes. The prologue ends.’”

The supplied prefatory text preserves the following variant forms: *a baugolfo* (“by Baugolf”); *monasterio* / *monasterii* (“monastery” / “of the monastery”); and an asterisked uncertain reading after *abbate*. Baugolf, the successor of Sturm, governed the monastery of Fulda from 779 to 802.

### B 9 and 10)

Manuscript 837 of the University Library of Oxford and its copy in the library of the chapter of Salisbury in England, both examined by me in 1827. They are parchment manuscripts of the fourteenth century and also contain Jordanes’ *History of the Goths*, the *Miscellaneous History*, Paul’s *History of the Lombards*, and, after chapter 31 of Einhard, some excerpts from the monk of Saint Gall.

Besides these sixty manuscripts, the following must also be mentioned:

### C 1)

Manuscript 5943 A of the Royal Library of Paris, on parchment, of the twelfth century; and

### C 1 a)

The manuscript formerly belonging to Vossius, concerning which it is not yet established to which class it should be assigned.

### C 2)

The Vienna fragment in a manuscript of the Imperial Library of Vienna, on parchment, of the ninth or tenth century, containing the names of the winds. [Col. 0023B]

### C 3)

The Pest fragment, in a parchment manuscript of Virgil of the tenth or eleventh century, which I inspected in the museum of the Hungarian nation in 1821. It contains the names of the months and winds.

### C d)

The Oxford fragment, that is, the names of the months and winds transcribed by D. Faerber from one Junius fascicle, 116 f., in the Bodleian Library.

### C e)

The Hamelin fragment, that is, the same names found in a parchment manuscript of the convent of Saint Boniface at Hamelin, a copy of which is preserved in the Royal Library of Hanover.

It remains now to explain how I used these resources.

After arranging the manuscripts, as careful investigation permitted, according to their classes and families, scarcely anything remained except to emend the best and oldest of all, namely the Vienna manuscript, listed first, with the assistance of the others. For that it too contained defects, and obvious ones, was demonstrated not only by comparison with the others but also by a more careful reading of it. Therefore, even when its reading could in itself be tolerated but all the others departed from it, I judged that its reading should be corrected, reasoning that it was easier for one manuscript to be wrong than for sixty. This, however, was done so rarely and with the unanimous agreement of such widely differing manuscripts, as I have said, that the procedure itself seems able to stand on its own grounds.

I recorded in the notes all the readings of the Vienna manuscript that I did not adopt. If one or another of the remaining manuscripts departed from the others in some very minor matter, I indicated this only for the older or better manuscripts—for example, 2, 2 b, c, 3, 4, B 1, and 2. For it is of no interest to anyone to know every wretched error of scribes—not to mention editors—or their conjectures, and neither my leisure nor my inclination would have sufficed to collect them. So far from fearing that this will be counted against me as a fault, I rather foresee that learned men will complain that useless material has even thus been heaped together. [Col. 0023C]

Believing that Besselius’s division of the work should be retained for the convenience of readers, I changed it in only two places, which I trust can lead no one into error.

The earlier editions were as follows:

1. Nuenarius’s edition of 1521, preceded by a dissertation on the origin and settlements of the ancient Franks and followed by Einhard’s *Annals*, which I mentioned above under Manuscript 8 b. It was reprinted in 1532 at Basel in Frecht’s collection of German writers; in 1561 at Cologne in duodecimo (in the copies I examined, the final number was changed to 2, so that 1562 is now read); in 1616 at Leipzig, printed by Justus Jansonius, in quarto; and in 1707 in Heineccius and Leukfeld’s *Writers on German Affairs*. Schminck also says that it was included by the blessed Rhenanus in his *Books on German Affairs* in 1551, but neither I nor any of my friends has seen such a copy, and the structure of the book strongly argues against such an addition. All the remaining editions, although they often depart from it, nevertheless rest upon Nuenarius’s edition as their beginning and foundation.

2. Justus Reuber’s edition in his *Writers on German Affairs* of 1584, using two manuscripts closely related to Manuscripts 9, 10, 10 b, and 10 c, was the first to cast suspicion on the readings of Nuenarius’s book, though he did not undertake to correct them. You will find the same recension in the second edition of Reuber’s *Writers*, published in 1619, and in Franzius’s *History of Charles the Great*, Strasbourg, 1644, in quarto. The third editor of Reuber’s *Writers*, Johannes, appended a record of variant readings from Schminck’s edition in 1726.

3. Freher’s edition of 1613, which I discussed above under Manuscript 4 b.

4. André Duchesne’s edition in volume II of the *Writers of Frankish History*, 1636. He corrected the text with the aid of five manuscripts apparently belonging among those of the Royal Library of Paris listed above.

5. Bolland’s edition of 1643, concerning which I gave my judgment above under Manuscripts 7 b and 15. The editor prefixed a dissertation on the other lives of Charles and on Einhard, and appended notes to the text.

6. Friedrich Bessel’s edition, Helmstedt, 1667, in quarto. It is distinguished by the readings of the Florentine manuscript (B 2). His notes, though they testify to much learning, may almost always be compared to carrying owls to Athens. [Col. 0024C]

7. Johann Hermann Schmincke’s edition, Utrecht, 1711, in quarto. He was the first to provide the readings of the Bodleian, Leiden, Caius College, Sion College, and Kassel manuscripts, as well as of Albert of Stade and other writers who followed Einhard. He attempted with the greatest zeal to correct and elucidate the text, and appended to the work Bessel’s commentary, Bolland’s notes, Goldast’s observations, until then unpublished, Nuenarius’s dissertation on the origin of the Franks, Freher’s discussion of the stature of Charles the Great, and his own commentary on the life and writings of Einhard.

8. Bouquet’s edition of 1744, in volume V of the *Gallic Writers*, using nine Royal manuscripts of Paris, among which, one may suppose, were also the manuscripts of Chesne.

9. Nicolaas Heerkens’s edition, Groningen, 1755, in octavo; it generally follows Schmincke.

10. Gabriel Gottfried Bredow’s edition, Helmstedt, 1806, in octavo. In addition to the older resources of Albert of Stade and Henry of Herford, who copied Einhard, he supplied readings and, having gathered from everywhere whatever might serve to illuminate Einhard, seems to have wished above all to encourage the Germans, in their most sorrowful times, to renew their ancient virtue by this example. May national history always be capable of accomplishing that!

Einhard’s little book, as soon as it appeared, was received with immense applause by everyone, and soon was repeatedly stripped for use by historians who touched upon the period of Charles. Since their number continually increased throughout the Middle Ages, it will suffice here to name only the oldest of them and those contemporary with Einhard: Einhard of Fulda, who began his work around the year 830; the chronicler of Fontenelle; Thegan; and the anonymous author of the *Life of Louis*. We know with certainty that three of these copied Charles’s *Life*, while Thegan at least imitated it. In the middle of the ninth century, Ruodolf, a monk of Fulda, borrowed very much from it in his *History of the Translation of Saint Alexander*. Learned men had already observed that, under King Arnulf, a Saxon poet rendered the *Life* in verse, and that in the twelfth century Radevicus had it before his eyes when portraying Emperor Frederick. [Col. 0025A]

## EINHARD’S PREFACE TO THE LIFE OF THE BLESSED CHARLES THE GREAT

*(Pertz, Monumenta Germaniae historica.)*

[Col. 0025]

I have gathered, with as much brevity as I could, the life and conduct, and a considerable part of the deeds, of my lord and foster-father Charles, the most excellent and deservedly most famous king, after the impulse to write came upon me. I have taken care to omit nothing concerning matters that could come to my knowledge, and not to offend the minds of those who dislike anything new by the length of my narration—if indeed this can in any way be avoided, so that those who disdain ancient memorials composed by highly learned and eloquent men may not be offended by a new piece of writing.

Although I do not doubt that there are many people devoted to leisure and letters who do not consider the present age so unworthy of attention that everything now taking place should be handed over to silence and oblivion as though worthy of no remembrance, and who, attracted by love of lasting fame, would rather insert the splendid deeds of others into writings of whatever kind than deprive the memory of posterity of the renown of their own name by writing nothing, nevertheless I did not think that I should refrain from this kind of writing. I was conscious that no one could write more truthfully than I about matters in which I myself had taken part and which I had learned with my own eyes, as they say, through direct observation; nor could I clearly know whether anyone else was writing about them.

I judged it better to entrust these matters, shared as it were with others, to the memory of posterity in writing than to allow the glorious life and outstanding deeds—scarcely imitable by the people of our own time—of the most excellent king, the greatest of all men of his age, to be destroyed in the darkness of oblivion.

There was also another, as I think, not unreasonable cause, which by itself might have been sufficient to compel me to write these things: namely, the nourishment bestowed upon me, and the enduring friendship I enjoyed with him and his children after I began to live at his court. Through this he so bound me to himself and made me his debtor, both while he lived and after his death, that I could rightly appear and be judged ungrateful if, forgetful of so many benefits conferred upon me, I passed over in silence the deeds of a man who had earned such distinguished and illustrious merit from me, and allowed his life to remain without written record or due praise, as though he had never lived. [Col. 0025D]

For writing and explaining this life, not my own little talent—for it is meager and small, indeed almost nonexistent—but Tully’s eloquence ought properly to have labored. Here, then, is a book containing the memory of that most illustrious and great man. In it there is nothing to admire apart from his deeds—unless perhaps it is that I, a barbarian and very little practiced in Roman speech, should have thought myself capable of writing something decently or appropriately in Latin, and should have advanced to such impudence as to think that Cicero’s statement could be disregarded. [Col. 0026C] The note identifies this *homo barbarus* as Einhard, a German; compare Suetonius, *Caligula*, chapter 47.

In the first book of the *Tusculan Disputations*, speaking about Latin writers, he is reported to have said:

> “To commit one’s thoughts to writing when one can neither arrange nor illuminate them, nor attract the reader by any pleasure, is the act of a man who immoderately abuses both leisure and letters.”

This judgment of the outstanding orator could indeed have deterred me from writing, had I not resolved in my mind that I would rather test the judgment of men and put my little talent to the trial by writing than, out of consideration for myself, pass over the memory of so great a man. [Col. 0026D]

## THE LIFE OF THE EMPEROR CHARLES

[Col. 0027]

### 1

The dynasty of the Merovingians—from which the Franks had been accustomed to create kings for themselves—is thought to have lasted down to King Childeric, who, at the command of Stephen, the Roman pontiff, was deposed, tonsured, and thrust into a monastery. The manuscripts exhibit the forms *Merovingorum*, *merowingorum*, *meroingorum*, *meringorum*, *mervingorum*, *merwingorum*, and *mercvingorum*. For the monastery, one manuscript reads *Sithiu*.

[Col. 0027D] The historical note observes that, after Zacharias had died, Stephen may be thought to have confirmed the command of his predecessor before Pippin was crowned. The author of the Urstisian fragment understood the passage in the same way (*Scriptores*, vol. II, p. 76). The passage is not concerned with Pippin’s second coronation.

Although the dynasty may seem to have ended with him, it had long since possessed no real power and displayed nothing distinguished in itself apart from the empty title of king. For both the wealth and power of the kingdom were held by the prefects of the palace, who were called *maiores domus*—mayors of the palace—and to whom supreme authority belonged. Nor was anything else left to the king except, content with the royal name alone, to sit on his throne with his hair flowing loose and his beard hanging down, and to act out the appearance of a ruler; to hear envoys arriving from every direction; and, when they departed, to give from his supposed authority the replies he had been taught or even ordered to give. [Col. 0027B]

Apart from the useless title of king and the precarious allowance for his livelihood, which the prefect of the palace supplied to him as he thought fit, he possessed nothing of his own except a single estate, and that one of very small income. There he had a house and a few servants, who provided him with what he needed and rendered him service.

Wherever he had to go, he traveled in a cart drawn by oxen, with a peasant acting as driver in the rustic fashion. In this way he used to go to the palace, in this way to the public assembly of his people, which was held annually for the benefit of the kingdom, and in this way he used to return home. [Col. 0028D] The note glosses *ad* as “at/for.” The administration of the kingdom and everything that had to be done or arranged, either at home or abroad, was managed by the prefect of the palace. The manuscripts generally have this reading from the ninth and tenth centuries, and many from the eleventh.

### 2

When Childeric was deposed, Pippin, the father of King Charles, already held this office as though by hereditary right. [Col. 0027C] For his father, Charles, who crushed the tyrants throughout all Francia who were claiming dominion for themselves, and who defeated the Saracens attempting to occupy Gaul in two great battles—one in Aquitaine near the city of Poitiers, the other near Narbonne at the river Berre—so thoroughly that he compelled them to return to Spain, administered with distinction the same office that his father Pippin had left to him. [Col. 0028A]

The manuscripts vary in the names of the places: *Pictavium*, *Pictavim*, and *Pictavum*; *Narbonam* and *Arbonam*; and *Birram*, *Byrram*, *Pyrram*, and *Buram*. He administered the office which his father Pippin had left to him; the manuscripts also show the forms *administravit* and *amministravit*.

That honor was customarily bestowed by the people on no one except those who surpassed the others both in nobility of lineage and in abundance of wealth.

Witness 3 omits *paene* (“almost”); 5, 6, 6 b, 7, 8, 11, 11 b, 11 c, 11 d and 13 have *et haec sc.* (“and these, namely”) at the Cicero passage. The Cicero citation remains: one who commits thoughts to writing while unable to arrange, illuminate, or attract the reader is abusing leisure and learning without restraint.

**Second-class manuscripts and B 8.** Gerward’s verses have *Suplex* (“pliant/suppliant”) in B 1; the name is *Einchardum* in B 3, 3 c and 3 d, *Einardum* in B 5 b, and *Enchardum* in B 4 b; B 2 has *magnum* (“great”) for *magni*. B 1 **begins** only with chapter 18’s “The remaining matters that concern the interior …”; it does not end there. B 5’s abbreviation is *et[a]* = *etiam* (“also”), with the square-bracketed letter printed above the preceding word in Migne.

The B 8 marginal preface is separately translated: “**Deeds of Charles the Great, according to Strabo. From the chronicle of Saint Alban of Mainz.** Einhard, a man among all the courtiers of his time, is recognized not only to have described the life and deeds of the most glorious emperor Charles the Great outstandingly for knowledge of affairs (*sciencia rerum*) and for the whole honesty of his character, but also to have confirmed them with the testimony of the purest truth, as one who was present at almost all of them (*utpote quibus pene omnibus interfuit*). Born in eastern Francia, in the district called Moingenui, he received his first instruction in the monastery of Fulda under the teaching of the holy martyr Boniface. From there he was transferred by Abbot Augolf (*ab augolfo*; alternative *a baugolfo*) of the aforesaid monastery (*monasterio*; alternative *monasterii*) to Charles’s palace. … Now, when study has declined into contrary pursuits, the light of wisdom, less loved, grows rare among most people. This said little man (*homuncio*), for he seemed contemptible in stature, in the court of Charles the lover of wisdom, attained such an increase of glory through prudence and probity that he was considered almost unique among the ministers of royal majesty. … We say this so that no one may have doubt about his statements. **Strabo’s addition:** ‘I, Strabo, inserted titles and divisions (*tytulos et incisiones*) into this little work as seemed fitting, so that one seeking any point may more easily find access to what pleases him. The prologue ends.’”

**Chapter 1.** At [Col. 0027], spellings for *Merovingorum* are *merowingorum, meroingorum, meringorum, mervingorum* (9 b), *merwingorum* (7 c), and *mercvingorum* (8 c). *Creare* (“create”) becomes *recreare* (“re-create”) in B 2, 2 b, 3, 3 b and 3 d, and *procreare* (“beget”) in B 3, 3 b, 3 c, 4 and 4 b. *Hildericum* becomes *hildricum* (1, 4 b, 8 b, 11, 11 b, 11 c, 11 d, B 3, B 4), *hildiricum* (10 b, 10 c), and *childericum*.

B 2 reads *carpente* for *carpento*; 1 has the thirteenth-century corruption *regiam* and 10 b *regi* for *regni*; B 2 has *celebratur* for *celebrabatur*. The note on *ad* means “at/for,” not “in this manner.” 6 has *domui* for *domi*; B 2 *curabat* for *procurabat*.

**Chapter 2.** 1 has an insertion by a correcting hand at *tum*; 6’s sequence is corrupt. 3 b and 11 read *disponebatur* (“was arranged”) for *deponebatur* (“was deposed”). 8 b has *hereditario iure*. The common form is *tirannos* (1); 2 reads *dominantes vel tum sibi vindicantes* and 3 b *dominantes*, where the text has *dominat[u]m sibi vindicantes*. *Sarracenos* is spelled *saracenos* in 1, 2, 8 b and some later manuscripts. Geographic variants are *pictavim/pictavum*, *arbonam*, and *byrram/pyrram/buram*. Finally, *amministravit* is *administravit* in 3 b, 4 b, 5, 11, B 2, B 3 and B 5.

**Other manuscript data.** C d is a fragment copied by Faerber from one Junius fascicle, identified as 116 f., in the Bodleian Library; it is not a “June gathering.”

When Pippin, father of King Charles, had held it for several years, as though under the aforementioned king, after it had been left to himself and his brother Karlomannus by their grandfather and father and divided between them in the fullest harmony, his brother Karlomannus—for reasons that are uncertain, although it seems that he was inflamed by love of the contemplative life—abandoned the laborious administration of a temporal kingdom and withdrew to Rome for a life of leisure. There, changing his habit and becoming a monk, he enjoyed the long-desired peace for several years with the brothers who had come there with him, at a monastery built on Mount Soracte beside the church of blessed Silvester. But since many nobles from Francia were solemnly traveling to Rome to fulfill their vows, and did not wish to pass him by as though he were once their lord, interrupting the leisure in which he took the greatest delight with frequent greetings, they compelled him to change his residence. For when he saw that such a crowd interfered with his purpose, he abandoned the mountain and withdrew to the province of Samnium, to the monastery of Saint Benedict situated in the fortress of Casinum; there he spent what remained of his temporal life in religious conduct.

### 3

Pippin, having been made king from prefect of the palace by the authority of the Roman pontiff, ruled the Franks alone for fifteen years or somewhat more. After the Aquitanian war—which he had undertaken against Waifarius, duke of Aquitaine, and waged for nine continuous years—had ended, he died at Paris from intercutaneous dropsy, leaving his sons Charles and Karlomannus alive; by divine ordinance the succession to the kingdom had come to them.

The Franks, having solemnly assembled a general council, made both of them their kings, on the prior condition that they should divide the entire body of the kingdom equally, and that Charles should undertake to govern the part which their father Pippin had held, while Karlomannus should undertake the part over which their uncle Karlomannus had presided. The conditions were accepted on both sides, and each received the portion of the divided kingdom according to the arrangement proposed to him.

This harmony endured, though with the greatest difficulty, since many on Karlomannus’s side were trying to separate their alliance, to such an extent that some even contemplated setting them against one another in war. But the outcome itself showed that there had been more suspicion than danger in this matter: when Karlomannus died, his wife and sons, together with certain men who were foremost among his leading nobles, fled to Italy; for no apparent reason, rejecting her husband’s brother, she placed herself and her children under the protection of Desiderius, king of the Lombards.

Karlomannus, after administering the kingdom jointly for two years, died of illness. Charles, however, after his brother’s death, was made king with the consent of all the Franks.

### 4

Since nothing has ever been set out in writing about his birth, infancy, or even childhood, and since no one is now found to survive who claims to possess knowledge of these matters, I have judged it foolish to write about them. I have therefore decided to pass over what is unknown and proceed to explain and demonstrate his actions, character, and the other aspects of his life. I shall do so, however, in such a way that I first recount his deeds at home and abroad, then his character and pursuits, and finally the administration and end of his kingdom, omitting nothing concerning matters that are either worthy or necessary to know.

### 5

Of all the wars that he waged, he first undertook the Aquitanian war, begun by his father but not yet completed because it appeared that it could be finished quickly. His brother was still alive, and Charles had also asked him to provide assistance. Although his brother disappointed him in this promised aid, Charles carried out the expedition he had undertaken with the utmost vigor. He refused to abandon what he had begun or yield to the labor once undertaken before he had brought what he was striving to accomplish to a successful conclusion through a certain perseverance and continual effort.

For he also compelled Hunold, who after Waifarius’s death had attempted to seize Aquitaine and renew a war that was already almost finished, to abandon Aquitaine and seek Wasconia. Yet, unwilling to allow him to remain there, Charles crossed the Garonne and sent word through envoys to Lupo, duke of the Wascones, that he should return the fugitive; if he did not do so promptly, Charles would demand satisfaction from him by war. But Lupo, acting on wiser counsel, not only returned Hunold but also placed himself and the province over which he presided under Charles’s authority.
