### 6

When affairs in Aquitaine had been settled and that war had ended, and when his companion in the kingdom had already been removed from human affairs, he was prevailed upon by the requests and entreaties of Adrian, bishop of the city of Rome, and undertook war against the Lombards.

This had previously been undertaken by his father as well, at the entreaty of Pope Stephen, but only with great difficulty, because certain leading Franks with whom he was accustomed to consult resisted his will so strongly that they openly declared that they would abandon their king and return home. Nevertheless, the war against King Haistulfus was then undertaken and very quickly completed.

Although the same, or rather the identical, cause seemed to underlie the undertaking of the war by Charles and by his father, it is clear that the struggle was conducted with neither similar labor nor a similar conclusion. Pippin forced King Haistulfus, after a siege of only a few days at Ticenum, both to give hostages and to restore the towns and fortresses that had been seized from the Romans, and to guarantee by oath that they would not be reclaimed.

Charles, however, after beginning the war himself, did not desist until he had received King Desiderius, whom he had exhausted by a long siege, into surrender; forced his son Adalgisus, toward whom everyone’s hopes seemed to incline, to leave not only the kingdom but also Italy; restored to the Romans everything that had been taken from them; overthrew Hruodgausus, prefect of the duchy of Foroiulium, when he was plotting revolution; subjected all Italy to his rule; and installed his own son Pippin as king over the conquered territory.

I would describe here how difficult the passage through the Alps was for those entering Italy, and with how much labor the Franks overcame impassable mountain ridges, peaks rising to the heavens, and rugged cliffs, were it not that my purpose in the present work is rather to commit to memory the manner of his life than the outcomes of the wars he waged.

The end of this war, nevertheless, was the subjugation of Italy; the deportation of King Desiderius into perpetual exile; the expulsion of his son Adalgisus from Italy; and the restoration to Adrian, ruler of the Roman Church, of the possessions seized by the Lombard kings.

### 7

After this had ended, the Saxon war—which had seemed almost to have been interrupted—was renewed. No war was undertaken that was either longer or more savage, or more laborious for the Frankish people, because the Saxons, like nearly all the peoples inhabiting Germany, were naturally fierce, devoted to the worship of demons, and hostile to our religion; they considered it no disgrace either to violate or transgress divine and human laws.

There were also causes that could disturb the peace every day: namely, our borders and theirs touched one another almost everywhere on level ground, except in a few places where larger forests or mountain ridges intervened and separated the fields of both peoples by a fixed boundary. In these places killings, plunder, and fires continually took place in turn. The Franks were so provoked by them that they now judged it right not merely to repay each attack in kind, but to undertake open war against them.

War was therefore undertaken against them. It continued for thirty-three consecutive years, with great hostility on both sides, though with greater loss to the Saxons than to the Franks. It could have ended sooner had the treachery of the Saxons permitted this.

It is difficult to say how often, after being defeated, they surrendered themselves as suppliants to the king, promising to do what was commanded, giving without delay the hostages demanded, receiving the envoys who were sent, and sometimes being so thoroughly subdued and softened that they even promised that they wished to abandon the worship of demons and submit themselves to the Christian religion. Yet, just as they were sometimes ready to do these things, so they were always quick to reverse them. It is impossible to estimate adequately whether they should more truly be called readier for one course or the other, since after the war against them began scarcely a full year passed in which they did not exchange one such behavior for the other.

But the king’s greatness of spirit and his constant steadfastness of mind, in adversity as in prosperity, could neither be conquered by their fickleness nor wearied of the actions he had begun. He never allowed them to commit such acts with impunity: either he himself led an army, or he sent one under his counts, to avenge their treachery and exact a punishment worthy of them. This continued until, after all who were accustomed to resist had been defeated and brought under his power, he removed ten thousand people who inhabited both banks of the river Elbe, together with their wives and children, and distributed them in various settlements here and there throughout Gaul and Germany.

The war that had lasted so many years is said to have ended on the following condition, proposed by the king and accepted by them: that they should abandon the worship of demons and their ancestral ceremonies, accept the sacraments of Christian faith and religion, and, united with the Franks, become one people with them.

### 8

Although this war was prolonged over a very great span of time, he himself engaged the enemy in battle no more than twice: once beside the mountain called Osnengi, at the place known as Theotmelli, and again beside the river Hasa—and these two battles occurred within one month, with only a few days between them.

In these two battles the enemy were so thoroughly defeated and conquered that thereafter they did not dare either to challenge the king or to resist his approach unless protected by some fortification of the place. Nevertheless, many men of both Frankish and Saxon nobility, who had held the highest offices, were killed in that war. At last it ended in the thirty-third year.

Meanwhile so many great wars both arose against the Franks in different regions of the world and were conducted with the king’s skill that, to those who observe them, it may reasonably be doubted whether one ought rather to admire his endurance of toil or his good fortune.

For the Italian war began two years earlier. Although it was waged without interruption, nothing that had to be done elsewhere was neglected, nor did he cease anywhere from an equally arduous struggle. The king, the greatest in prudence and outstanding in greatness of spirit among all who in his age ruled nations, neither shrank from anything that had to be undertaken or carried out because of the labor, nor recoiled from it because of the danger. Rather, having learned to undertake and endure each thing according to its nature, he was accustomed neither to yield in adversity nor, in prosperity, to assent to fortune when it falsely flattered him.

### 9

While he was waging a constant and almost uninterrupted war against the Saxons, he stationed garrisons at suitable points along the frontier and attacked Spain with the greatest military force he could muster. After crossing the Pyrenean pass and receiving into surrender all the towns and fortresses he had approached, he returned with his army safe and unharmed.

Except that, on the very ridge of the Pyrenees, he had the misfortune to experience for a short time the treachery of the Wascones on his return. For when the army was proceeding in an extended column, as the nature of the place and the narrowness of the route permitted, the Wascones, having placed an ambush on the summit of the mountain—for the place, because of the dense forests, of which there is a very great abundance there, was suitable for setting ambushes—rushed down upon the rear of the baggage train and upon those who, marching at the back of the column, were protecting the troops ahead. They threw them into the valley below and, joining battle with them, killed them all to the last man. After plundering the baggage, they scattered in every direction with the greatest speed, protected by the advantage of the approaching night.

The Wascones were aided in this action both by the lightness of their arms and by the nature of the place where the battle occurred. The Franks, on the other hand, were made wholly unequal to the Wascones by the weight of their arms and the unfavorable character of the terrain.

In this battle Eggihardus, overseer of the royal table, Anselmus, count of the palace, and Hruodlandus, prefect of the Breton frontier, were killed together with many others. Nor could this deed be avenged at that time, because after carrying out the action the enemy scattered so completely that not even a report remained as to where in the world they could be sought.

### 10

He also subdued the Britons who, living in a remote part of Gaul in the west along the coast of the Ocean, did not obey orders. He sent an expedition against them, by which they were compelled both to give hostages and to promise that they would do what was commanded.

Later, entering Italy with his army and passing through Rome, he approached Capua, a city of Campania. Having set up camp there, he threatened war against the Beneventans unless they surrendered. The duke of that people, Aragisus, forestalled this by sending his sons Rumoldus and Grimoldus, together with a large sum of money, to meet the king. He asked that the king accept his sons as hostages and promised that he and his people would do what was commanded, except only that he should not be compelled to come into the king’s presence himself.

The king, taking account more of the strength of the people than of the obstinacy of his spirit, accepted the hostages offered to him and granted Aragisus, as a great favor, that he should not be compelled to come into his presence. He retained the younger of the sons as a hostage and returned the elder to his father. He dispatched envoys to Aragisus to demand and receive oaths of loyalty from the Beneventans, and then returned to Rome. After spending several days there in veneration of the holy places, he returned to Gaul.

### 11

The Bavarian war then both arose suddenly and was brought to a swift conclusion. It was provoked by the arrogance and carelessness of Duke Tassilo. At the urging of his wife, who was the daughter of King Desiderius and thought that through her husband she could avenge her father’s exile, he formed an alliance with the Huns, who border the Bavarians to the east, and attempted not only to refuse to do what was commanded but also to challenge the king in war.

The king’s spirit could not endure his defiance, because it seemed excessive. Accordingly, having gathered forces from every direction, he came with a large army to the river Lech, intending to march into Bavaria. This river divides the Bavarians from the Alamanni. Having established a camp on its bank, before entering the province he decided to test the duke’s disposition through envoys.

But Tassilo, judging that stubborn action would be useful neither to himself nor to his people, submissively placed himself in the king’s power. He gave the hostages that were demanded, among them his own son Theodo, and additionally gave a sworn pledge that he would not listen to anyone urging him to defect from the king’s authority.

Thus the war, which had seemed likely to be an extremely great one, was brought to a very swift end. Later Tassilo was summoned to the king, and was neither permitted to return nor allowed to govern the province he had held; it was instead entrusted to counts to administer.

[Note: [Col. 0035] “Bavarian”: *baioricum* (3 b); *bawoaricum* (10 b); *boioaricum* (B 3 d); the same forms occur below.]

[Note: [Col. 0035] “Urging”: *ortatu* in manuscript 1, 2, and several others.]

[Note: [Col. 0035] “And”: *hac* (“this”) in manuscripts 1 and 2.]

[Note: [Col. 0035] “Huns”: *Hunis*, with the gloss “Hungarians” in 10 c.]

[Note: [Col. 0035] “Bavarians”: *baioariis*, glossed as “Abarians” in 10 c; *bubatiis*, “Bubatians,” also in 10 c.]

[Note: [Col. 0035] “Bordering”: *conuertimini* in manuscript 4.]

[Note: [Col. 0035] “Excessive”: *nimio* (“excessive,” masculine or ablative) in B 2.]

[Note: [Col. 0035] “Large”: *maximum* (“very large”) in manuscripts 3 b, 4, 8 b, 4 b, 11, and B 3–5.]

[Note: [Col. 0035] “This river”: *His* (“these”) in manuscript 3 b.]

[Note: [Col. 0035] “Placed himself in the king’s power”: *subiecit* (“submitted”) in manuscript 8 b.]

[Note: [Col. 0035] “Theodo”: *teodonem* in manuscript 3.]

[Note: [Col. 0035] “Additionally gave a sworn pledge”: manuscript 1 reads *dedit insuper fidem* (“he additionally gave a pledge”); the remaining witnesses read *data insuper fide* (“with a pledge additionally given”).]

[Note: [Col. 0035] “That”: *quod illius ad* in manuscript 11 c; *quod ad illius* in manuscript 11 d.]

[Note: [Col. 0035] “From the authority”: *fide* (“by faith”) in 11 c*; omitted in 10 g.]

[Note: [Col. 0035] “To defection”: *ad defensionem* is omitted in 2 c; *ac defensione* (“and from protection”) occurs in manuscript 3.]

[Note: [Col. 0035] “To anyone urging”: *nullo* (“to no one”) in B 2, 3, 3 b, 3 d, 4, 4 b, and 5; *nulli* (“to no one”) in B 3 c. Manuscripts 8 b and 4 b read *nemini defectionem suadenti* (“to no one urging defection”); B 2 b has *nulli defectionem suadenti*. The reading *ac defensione nemini defectionem suadenti* in Chesne and Bouquet is certainly compounded at their discretion from differing manuscript readings.]

[Note: [Col. 0035] “Listen”: *adsentiri* (“to assent”) in manuscripts 5, 6, and 7; *assentiri* in 2, 3 b, 3 c, 11, and 11 b.]

[Note: [Col. 0035] “Thus”: *sique*, corrected to *sicque*, in manuscript 1.]

[Note: [Col. 0035] “Tassilo”: *tassalo* (3 b).]

[Note: [Col. 0035] “Summoned”: *vocatus*, corrected to *evocatus* (“summoned”) in manuscript 1.]

[Note: [Col. 0035] “Province”: *provinciam* (“province,” accusative) in B 2; manuscript 8 b reads *provinciae ... praeesse* (“to preside over the province”).]

[Note: [Col. 0035] “To the duke”: *uti* in B 3–4.]

### 12

When these disturbances had thus been settled, war was brought against the Slavs whom we, according to our customary usage, call Wilzi [Note: [Col. 0035] *wilci* 3; *uiulci* 3 b; *wilti* 6, 7; *willzi* 4 b; *vuilsi* 8 b; *uulci* 11; *uulzi* B 2; *vvlzi* or *vvlti* B 5], but who, properly speaking, are called Welatabi [Note: [Col. 0035] *uueletabi* 2, 3 b, 11; *welezabi* 3; *weletabili* 3 c; *velatabi* 7; *weltabi* B 5] in their own language [Note: [Col. 0035] *propria* 2, 3, B 4, 4 b; “their own”]. The Saxons also took part in it as auxiliaries [Note: [Col. 0035] *auxiliatores* 6, 6 b, 7, 10 b, B 2, 3–5; “helpers”], among the other nations that, ordered by the king, followed his standards, although with feigned and less-than-devoted obedience [Note: [Col. 0035] *iuste* 3 b; *iussa* 6 b; *et iussa* 7; *iussa*, corrected to *iussae*, B 3]. The cause of the war was that the Abodrites [Note: [Col. 0035] *abotritos* 3 b, 4, 8 b, 11; *abodritos* 6 b], who had formerly been allied with the Franks [Note: [Col. 0035] *fuerant* 7; “had been”], were harassing them with continual raids and could not be restrained by commands [Note: [Col. 0035] *lacessebant* 3, 4, 5, 8 b, 4 b, B 3–5 and perhaps others; *lacessabant* 3 b, B 2; *lacessaebant* 6 b].

There is a certain gulf [Note: [Col. 0036D] Compare Adam of Bremen, *Church History*, book II, chapter 9 and following, and *On the Situation of Denmark*, chapter 217 and following] which extends from the western ocean toward the east. Its length is unknown, but its width [Note: [Col. 0035] “exceeds one hundred thousand paces,” 10, 10 b, 10 c, 10 c*, Bredow, p. 170; he observed that the Bodleian manuscript also reads this way, though I do not know where he obtained the information, since Schminkius says nothing about the matter, p. 63] nowhere exceeds one hundred thousand paces [Note: [Col. 0035] *huius* q. 3; “of this”], and in many places it is found to be narrower [Col. 0037A] [Note: [Col. 0037] *contretior* B 2; “more contracted”].

Many nations dwell around it. The Danes [Note: [Col. 0037] *tam* 2, 3 b] and Swedes [Note: [Col. 0037] *suesones* 1; *suessones* 2, 3; *suaues* 3 b], whom we call Northmen [Note: [Col. 0037] *nordmannos* 4, 8 b, 4 b, and likewise below; *nordemannos* 5; *normannos* 2, 3, 3 b, B 2; *nortmanos* B 3; *normanos* B 4; *normiannos* B 4 b], hold both the northern shore and all the islands in it. The southern shore is inhabited by Slavs and Aisti [Note: [Col. 0037] *haisti* 11; *aistri* B 3 c and elsewhere; *agisti*, Bouq.] [Note: [Col. 0037D] From these Estonia received its name. Tacitus, in *Germania*, chapter 45, calls them *Aestyi*; compare Jordanes, *On the Gothic Affairs*, chapter 23], and by various other nations. Among them the most prominent were those against whom the king was then waging war: the Welatabi [Note: [Col. 0037] *uuelathabi* 1; *uuelatabi* 3 c; *uueletabi* 2, 3 b, 11, B; *weltabi* B 5].

With a single expedition, which he conducted in person, he so crushed [Note: [Col. 0037] *contulit* 1, 3, 6, 6 b, 8, 10 c, B 2 c; *conculit* 3 c; *perculit* 3 b; *contulit*, corrected to *contudit*, 10; *contrivit* 10 b] and subdued them that thereafter they judged that his commands were by no means to be refused [Note: [Col. 0037] *renuendum* 3 b, 8 b, 4 b, B 3 c and perhaps others; “to be refused”].

### 13

The greatest of all the wars he waged, apart from the Saxon war, followed this one: namely, the war undertaken against the Avars [Note: [Col. 0037] *auaros* B 2–4; *abaros* B 5] or Huns [Note: [Col. 0037] *hunnos* B 2*]. He conducted it with greater courage than the others and with far greater preparation.

He made only one expedition in person into Pannonia—for that province was then inhabited by this people [Note: [Col. 0037] *ea gestum* B 2; “that was accomplished there”]—and entrusted the completion of the rest to his son Pippin [Note: [Col. 0037] *pipino* 3 b, 8 b, B 2, 3 c] and to the governors of the provinces, together also with counts [Note: [Col. 0037] absent in B 2] and legates. When the campaign had been conducted by them with the utmost vigor, it was finally completed in the eighth year [Note: [Col. 0037] “the ninth year,” B 3, 3 b, 4, 4 b; *nonо* B 3 c].

How many battles were fought in it and how much blood was shed is shown by the fact that Pannonia was empty of every inhabitant [Note: [Col. 0037] “of habitation,” B 3–4], and that the place where the khagan’s palace stood [Note: [Col. 0037] *cagani* 3 b, 8 b; *kagan* 4 b; *pagani* B 2] was so deserted [Note: [Col. 0037] *disertus* 2; “open” or “cleared”] that not even a trace of human habitation appeared there [Note: [Col. 0037] *ne* 2, 4, 8 b, 4 b, 5, 10, 10 b, 10 c, 11, B 2–5; “not,” instead of *nec*, “nor”; perhaps also the Parisienses].

All the nobility of the Huns perished in this war; all their glory fell. All their money [Note: [Col. 0037] *peccunia* 1, 2, 5?, 6; the others *pecunia*] and the treasures accumulated [Note: [Col. 0037] *coniecti* 3; “cast together,” instead of *congesti*, “heaped up”] over a long period were seized [Note: [Col. 0037] *disrepti* B 2]. No war against the Franks can be recalled in human memory in which they were more enriched and increased in wealth [Note: [Col. 0037] *sunt*, corrected to *sint*, 1; *sunt* B 2]. For although until that time they seemed to be almost poor [Note: [Col. 0037] *poene* B 2], so much gold and silver was found in the palace and so many precious spoils were taken in the battles that it may rightly be believed [Note: [Col. 0037] *posset* 8 b, 4 b, 9, B 2, 2 b] that the Franks justly took from the Huns [Note: [Col. 0037] *hunis … huni*, corrected to *hunnis … hunni*, B 2] what the Huns had previously unjustly taken from other peoples [Note: [Col. 0037] *alius* 1; “others,” instead of *aliis*].

Only two of the Frankish nobles perished in that war: Aericus [Note: [Col. 0037] *oelricus* 1; *aricus* B 2 b; *ericus* 4, 8 b, 4 b, 6, 8, 10 c, B 2–5; *ericius* 10, 10 b; *erich* 5; *hericus* 2, 2 c, 3 b, 3 c, 6 b, 7, 11, 11 b; *herico* 3, 3*, *henricus* 2 b, 10 g, 11 c, 11 d], duke of Friuli [Note: [Col. 0037] *in foro. iulanus in l.*, B 2; *foroiulani* 3 c, B 2 b; *foroiulianus* 2, 8 b, 4 b, 5, 7, 10, 10 b, 10 c, 11 d, B 3–4; *foroiuliani* 9; *foroiulii* 2 c, 2 c, 11 c; *foroiulianorum* 8], who was intercepted by an ambush of the townsmen [Note: [Col. 0037] *opidariorum* B 2–4; “town-dwellers”] in Liburnia, near the coastal city of Tarsatica [Note: [Col. 0037] *thrarsaticam* 1; *tarsaticam* 8 b, 4 b, B 3–4; *tarsicam* 2, B 2; *asaticam* 3]; and Gerold [Note: [Col. 0037] *geroltus* 8 b, 4 b; *gerulus* 3 b, 3 c, 3 c*; *geruldus* 13; *giraldus* 3], prefect of Bavaria, who was killed in Pannonia while he was drawing up his battle line to fight the Huns [Note: [Col. 0037] *instrueret* 1, 2 b, 2, 8, 9, 8 b, 4 b; *instrueret*, corrected to *strueret*, 10; *construeret* 3 c; *strueret* 2, 3, 3 b, 4, 5, 6, 6 b, 7, 10 b–c, 10 f, 11, 11 b, 11 c, 11 d, B 2–5]. It is uncertain by whom; he was killed with only two men who rode beside him and accompanied him as he encouraged each individual soldier [Note: [Col. 0037] *commitabantur* B 2; “were accompanying”].

Otherwise this war was almost bloodless for the Franks [Note: [Col. 0037] *poene* B 2], and it had a most successful outcome, although it was prolonged for a long time because of its great magnitude [Note: [Col. 0037] *ita* 1; *sua magnitudine* 8 b, 4 b; the others *sui magnitudine*].

### 14

After this, the Saxon war also reached an end proportionate to its long duration [Note: [Col. 0037] *sua prolixitate* 3 b, B 2; “its length”; in the printed editions chapter 14 begins here]. The Bohemian war [Note: [Col. 0037] *boematicum* 3 b] and the Linonian war [Note: [Col. 0037] *linonicum* 3, 3 b; *limonicum* 6; *liuonicum* elsewhere; *liconicum* elsewhere; *lilonicum* 4; *hilinonicum* 8 b; *linomicum* B 5], which arose later, likewise could not last long; both were brought to a swift conclusion under the leadership of the younger Charles [Note: [Col. 0037] some witnesses read “the rest … to be completed”].

Finally, war was undertaken against the Northmen, who are called Danes. At first they practiced piracy [Note: [Col. 0037] *piraticam* 3 b, 8 b, 4 b, 11, B 3, 3 b]; later, with a larger fleet [Note: [Col. 0037] *maiori* in all witnesses examined except one], they ravaged the shores of Gaul and Germany. Their king, Godfrey [Note: [Col. 0037] *godofridus* 4, 5, 6 b, 10, B 2–4; *godifridus* 6; *gotefridus* 10 b; *gotofridus* 3 b, 11; *gotofredus* 3], was so puffed up with empty hope that he promised himself dominion over all Germany [Note: [Col. 0037] in one witness, *germarnie*]. He regarded Frisia [Note: [Col. 0037] *fresiam* 2, B 5] and Saxony no differently than his own provinces; he had already brought the Abodrites [Note: [Col. 0037] *abodricos* 1; *abotritos* 8 b; *abodyros* 3 c; *obodritos* 11]—his neighbors—under his power and had made them pay tribute to him.

He also boasted [Note: [Col. 0037] *enim* B] that he would shortly come with very large forces to Aachen [Note: [Col. 0037] *aquisgrani* 2, 3, 3 b, 11, B 2–4], where the king’s court was located. His statements, however empty [Note: [Col. 0037] absent in B 3–4], were not entirely disbelieved; rather [Note: [Col. 0037] absent in 8 b] it was thought that he was about to begin something of the kind, unless a hastened death had forestalled him. For, killed by one of his own guards, he hastened the end both of his life and of the war he had begun [Note: [Col. 0039] *accelerant*, corrected to *accelerauit*, 1].

### 15

These are the wars which the most powerful king waged with the greatest prudence and success in different parts of the world during forty-seven years [Note: [Col. 0039] *XLVIII*, 3 b; “forty-eight”; *quadraginta quatuor*, B 5]—for he had reigned that many years [Note: [Col. 0039] *quod* B 2]. Through them he so nobly enlarged the Frankish kingdom—which he had received from his father Pippin [Note: [Col. 0039] *pipini* 6; *pipinum* 3 b, 8 b, 11, B 2, 3 c], already great and strong—that he added to it almost twice as much [Note: [Col. 0039] *dupplum* B 2].

Previously, the kingdom included no more than that part of Gaul [Note: [Col. 0039] *galileae* 6] which lies between the Rhine [Note: [Col. 0039] *hrenum* 3, 3 c, B 2; *renum* 3 b, B 3–5] and the Loire [Note: [Col. 0039] *eligerem* 3; *ligerem* 4, 6, 6 b, B 5; *ligurem* 10], and between the ocean [Note: [Col. 0039] *occeanumque* 3 b, B 4 b] and the Balearic Sea; and that part of Germany which lies between Saxony and the Danube, and between the Rhine [Note: [Col. 0039] *rhenumque* 4, 11; *renumque* 3 b, B 2–5] and the River Saale, which divides the Thuringians [Note: [Col. 0039] *thuringos* 2, 3 b, 3 c; *thuringo* 6; *turios* B 2; *toringos* B 3, 3 c, d] from the Sorbs [Note: [Col. 0039] *sarabos* 11, B 3 b, 4 b]. This territory was inhabited by those Franks who are called eastern Franks [Note: [Col. 0039] *posita* 1, 2, 3, 7 c, 8 b, 4 b, 9 b, 10 f–h; “situated”]. In addition, the Alamanni and Bavarians belonged to the authority of the Frankish kingdom [Note: [Col. 0039] *pertinent* B 3–4].

In the wars already mentioned, he first brought under his rule Aquitaine and Gascony [Note: [Col. 0039] *guasconiam* 3], and the entire ridge of the Pyrenees [Note: [Col. 0039] *pirenei* 3 b, 11, B 3 b, 4 b; *pyrinei* 4, B 2, 5; *pyrenei* 8 b], as far as the River Ebro [Note: [Col. 0039] *hyberum* 4 b, 10 b, 10 c, B 4, 5]. The river rises among the Navarrese [Note: [Col. 0039] *naruaros*, corrected to *naruarros*, 1; *nauaros* 2, 5; *nouarnos* 3 b; *naoarros* 3 c], cuts through the most fertile fields of Spain, and flows into the Balearic Sea beneath the walls of the city of Tortosa [Note: [Col. 0039] *tortose* 3, 3 b; *dertusae* 8 b; *dertote* 10 b; *moenibus* 6, 6 b, 7; “beneath the walls,” rather than “beneath the city”; *ballearico* 3 b].

Next he brought under his power all Italy, which extends from Augusta Praetoria [Note: [Col. 0039] *angusta* 1; *augusto* 3 b] to lower Calabria [Note: [Col. 0039] *qualabriam* 3], where the boundaries of the Greeks and Beneventans are said to meet [Note: [Col. 0039] *beneventorum*, corrected by a second hand to *beneventanorum*, 1]. Its length is more than one million paces.

Then he subdued Saxony [Note: [Col. 0039] *saxonia* B 2], which is no small part of Germany and is thought to be twice as broad as that part inhabited by the Franks [Note: [Col. 0039] *dupplum* B 2; one witness reads “twice as broad in relation to that inhabited by the Franks”], although it may be of equal length.

Afterward he subdued both Pannonias, and Dacia, situated on the opposite bank of the Danube [Note: [Col. 0039] *dariam* B 2], as well as Istria [Note: [Col. 0039] *hystriam* B 2, 4, 4 b] and Liburnia [Note: [Col. 0039] *liburneam* B 2] and Dalmatia, except for the coastal cities, which the emperor of Constantinople was allowed to retain because of their friendship and the treaty joined with him [Note: [Col. 0039] *ab*, corrected to *ob*, 1; “because of”].

Then he completely subdued all the barbarous and savage nations that inhabit Germany between the rivers Rhine [Note: [Col. 0039] *renum* 1; others *rhenum*] and Vistula [Note: [Col. 0039C] The Vistula, which in the municipal law of Culm of the year 1251 is called *Wizele* and *Wizele], and between the ocean and the Danube. Though nearly alike in language, they were very different in customs and appearance [Note: [Col. 0039] *similes* B 2; “alike”]. He reduced them to tribute [Note: [Col. 0039] *eos tributarios* B 2, 5; masculine plural “them, tributary”] so that they became tributary.

Among these peoples the chief were the Welatabi [Note: [Col. 0039] *uueletabi* 3 b, 11; *muelatabi* B 3; *wéltabi* B 5], Sorbi [Note: [Col. 0039] *sorobi* B 3–4; *sorabe* B 4], Abodrites [Note: [Col. 0039] *obodriti* B 2–4; *abotriti* 8 b], and Bohemians [Note: [Col. 0039] *boemani* 3 b, 4, 6, 11, B 3–5; *boemanni*]—for he fought a war with these. He received the rest, whose number was much greater, into submission.

### 16

He also increased the glory of his kingdom by winning certain kings and peoples to himself through friendship [Note: [Col. 0039] *sibi per amicitiam* 1, 2?; “to himself through friendship”] [Note: [Col. 0039] *conciliatus* B 2; “having been won over”].

He so bound Alfonso [Note: [Col. 0039] *adefonsum* 2, 2 b, 2 c, 3, 3 b, 10 g–h, B 2; *adaefonsum* 3 c; *aedefonsum* 6; *adesconsum*, corrected to *adefonsum*, 6 b; *adefensum* 5; *adeffensum* B 3, 3 b, 3 c, 3 d; *ad effesum* B 4, 4 b; *haldefonsum* 8, 11 c; *hasdestinum* 7; *adelfonsum* 8 b, 9, 9 b], king of Galicia [Note: [Col. 0039] *galleciae* 4, 5, 6, 6 b; *galetiae* 8 b; *galatiae* B 2, 3 b; *galiciae* 3 b, B 5] and Asturias [Note: [Col. 0039] *arturicae* B 2; *asturiae* 3; *asurice* 5], to himself by such an alliance that Alfonso, whenever he sent him either letters or envoys, ordered that he be called by Charlemagne in no other way than “his own man” [Note: [Col. 0040C] That is, “him”] [Note: [Col. 0039] *his*, corrected to *is*, 1; *his* 3 b, 6, 6 b, B 2; the others *is*] [Note: [Col. 0039] *deest* 1, 2, 3 b, 5; absent] [Note: [Col. 0039] *apud illum* absent in B 2].

Through his generosity he also inclined the kings of the Scots [Note: [Col. 0039] *scottorum* 4, 6, B 2, 3, 3 d, 4, 4 b] so completely to his will that they never proclaimed him by any other title than “lord,” and themselves his subjects [Note: [Col. 0039] *subditus* 1] and servants. Letters sent by them to him still exist, revealing such sentiments [Note: [Col. 0039] *effectus* 4, B 2; “effects,” rather than *affectus*, “feelings”] on their part toward him.

Aaron, king of the Persians, who, except for India, held nearly the whole of the East, maintained so harmonious a friendship with him that he preferred Charlemagne’s favor to the friendship of all the kings and princes throughout the world, and judged that Charlemagne alone should be honored and treated with generosity by himself [Note: [Col. 0039] *regnum* B 2; “the kingdom,” rather than “the friendship of kings”] [Note: [Col. 0040C] That is, “him”].

Accordingly, when Aaron’s envoys, whom he had sent with gifts to the most holy tomb of our Lord and Savior [Note: [Col. 0039] *s. mundi* 3*; “of the world”] and to the place of the Resurrection, came to Charlemagne and announced their lord’s wishes, Charlemagne not only permitted everything that was requested to be done, but also granted that sacred and saving place be assigned to Aaron’s authority. When the envoys returned, Charlemagne attached his own envoys to them and sent Aaron immense gifts among clothing, spices, and the other riches of the eastern lands; a few years earlier, when Charlemagne had requested it, Aaron had sent him the elephant, which Charlemagne then possessed as his only one [Note: [Col. 0041] *miserit* 11; *elephantum* 6 b, B 4–5; *elefantem* 2, 11; *helefantem* 3 b].

The emperors of Constantinople also—Nicephorus [Note: [Col. 0041] *nuciforus* 1, 4, 10; *niniciforius* 6; *niciforus* 6 b; *niciphorus* 11 d; *nicoforus* 2; *nichoforus* 8; *nicheforus* 3; *nicephorus* 8 b, 7, 9; *naiforus* B 2; *naiphorus* B 2 b], Michael [Note: [Col. 0041] *michahel* 3, 4, B 2, 3, 3 b], and Leo—sent several embassies to him, voluntarily seeking his friendship and alliance [Note: [Col. 0041] *et* 3, 4, 8 b, 5, 9, 11, B 2–5; “and,” rather than “or”].

Nevertheless, because they were highly suspicious of the title of emperor which he had assumed [Note: [Col. 0041] the words *susceptum a* are absent, but were added by the author himself in 1], and therefore suspected that he wished to seize their empire from them [Note: [Col. 0041] *hoc eis*, corrected to *eis*, 1; *hoc ei* 9 b; *hoc eis* B 3–5], he established an exceedingly firm treaty with them, so that no opportunity for any quarrel might remain between the parties [Note: [Col. 0041] *quasi qui* absent in 10, 10 b, 10 c, B 2] [Note: [Col. 0041] *unde usque εχις* absent in 2 c, 5].

For the power of the Franks had always been suspect to Romans and Greeks. Hence there is also preserved that Greek proverb [Note: [Col. 0041] at this point, with a superscription of Charlemagne’s final will, manuscript 6 ends: “The race of the Franks has friends; it does not wish to have neighbors”; B 5]: 

**ΤΟΝ ΦΡΑΝΚΟΝ ΦΙΛΟΝ ΕΧΙϹ, ΓΙΤΟΝΑ ΟΥΚ ΕΧΙϹ**

[Note: [Col. 0041C] That is, “Have a Frank as a friend, but do not have him as a neighbor.” Since Greek *ει* and *η* were customarily pronounced as *i* at that time, this is apparent here.]

The other manuscripts transmit this in variously corrupted forms; none, however, reads exactly as the printed editions do: *τὸν φραγκὸν φίλον ἔχῃς, γείτονα οὐκ ἔχῃς*, “Have the Frank as a friend; do not have him as a neighbor” [Note: [Col. 0041] the source’s Greek has *ΓΙΤΟΝΑ*; the printed form is *γείτονα*].

### 17

Although he was so greatly occupied in enlarging his kingdom and subduing foreign nations, and was constantly engaged in such activities, he nevertheless began in various places many works pertaining to the dignity and usefulness of the kingdom, and completed some of them. Among these, the chief may reasonably be considered to be the basilica of the holy Mother of God at Aachen, constructed with marvelous workmanship [Note: [Col. 0041] manuscript 3 ends at this word; manuscript 1 has “Aachen, with marvelous workmanship”], and the bridge at Mainz [Note: [Col. 0041] *magontiacum*, corrected to *mogontiacum*, 1; *mongontiacum* B 2; *magontiacum* 11; *maguntiacum*, Bouq.] over the Rhine [Note: [Col. 0041] *rheno* 4, 11, Bouq.; *hreno* B 2], five hundred paces long—for the river is that wide there [Note: [Col. 0041] absent in B 2–5].

The bridge burned down in a fire one year before his death [Note: [Col. 0041] *deceret* 1; *conflavit* 4], and could not be rebuilt because his death came so quickly [Note: [Col. 0041] *discessum* B 2, 3 b, 3 c], although he had been planning to replace the wooden bridge with one of stone.

He also began palaces of outstanding workmanship: one not far from the city of Mainz, beside a village whose name is Ingelheim [Note: [Col. 0041] *cui* 2 b, 2 c, 3 c, 8 b, 6 b, 7, 8, 10, 10 b, 10 c, 11 b, 11 d, 13, B 2–5; *nomen* 7 c?, 8 b, 11 d; *Engilenheim* 1; *Ingilenheim* 4, 5, 4 b, 6 b, 10, 10 b, 10 c, 11, B 5; *ingiletheim* B 2; *ennigilecheim* B 2*; *engiletheim* 3 b; *ingilemheim* 11 c; *ingilemhem* 8; *ingelenheim* B 4 b; *ingelentheim* B 3, 3 b, 3 d; *ingelenteim* B 3 c; *ingelehem* 2 b, 3*; *ingelenhim* 9; *ingelebem* 3 c; *ingelhem* 2 c; *ingelheim* 8 b, B 2 b], and the other at Nijmegen above the River Waal [Note: [Col. 0041] *wahalem* 8 b], which flows past the Batavian island on its southern side.

Above all, wherever he found sacred buildings throughout his kingdom collapsed through age [Note: [Col. 0041C] Compare Suetonius, *Augustus*, chapter 30], he ordered the bishops and abbots responsible for them to restore them, taking care through his legates that they carried out his commands [Note: [Col. 0042C] Compare the *Capitulary of Salzburg*, 804, chapter 2, section 1, and the Aachen Capitulary of 807, chapter 7].

He also prepared a fleet for war against the Northmen [Note: [Col. 0041] *nordomannicum* 1 and others; *nortmannicum* 10, 10 c, 11, B 5, etc.; *nordismannicum* 5; *normannicum* 3 b; here, and throughout the work, *nortmannicum*, *nortmanni*, and so forth appear preferable], building ships for this purpose beside the rivers that flow from both Gaul and Germany into the northern ocean. Since the Northmen [Note: [Col. 0041] *nordmanni* 4, 8 b, B 3, 3 b, 3 c; *nordomanni* 3 b, B 2; *nordismanni* 5] were continually ravaging the Gallic [Note: [Col. 0041] “and German” is absent in B 3–4] and German coasts, he stationed guards and lookouts at every harbor and river mouth [Note: [Col. 0041] *ostia* 4, 8 b, B 3 b–c; *hortus* B 2] [Note: [Col. 0042C] That is, “mouths”], wherever ships seemed able to enter, and by this defense prevented the enemy from making an exit [Note: [Col. 0041] *qui* 1; *que* 2, 11 c, B 3 d; *qua* in the others].

He did the same on the southern side, along the coast of the province of Narbonensis and Septimania, and along the entire coast of Italy as far as Rome, against the Moors, who had recently begun practicing piracy [Note: [Col. 0041] *piraticam* 8 b, 11, B 3–4; *adgressus* 1; *aggressus* B 3, 3 c, 3 d; “having attacked,” rather than *adgressos*, “those who had begun”]. Consequently, during his lifetime neither Italy suffered serious damage from the Moors [Note: [Col. 0041] some witnesses read “from the Moors, Italy”] nor Gaul and Germany from the Northmen [Note: [Col. 0041] *nordomannis* 1, 2; *nardomannis* B 2; *normannis* 3 b; *nordimannis* B 3 d; the others *nordmannis* and *nortmannis*], except that Centumcellae, a city of Etruria [Note: [Col. 0041] *hetruriae* 8 b], was captured and devastated by the Moors through treachery, and that certain islands in Frisia [Note: [Col. 0041] *fresia* B 5] adjoining the German coast were plundered by the Northmen.

### 18

It is clear that he was such a man in defending, enlarging, and at the same time adorning his kingdom [Note: [Col. 0042C] Compare Suetonius, *Augustus*, chapter 61]. One may admire the qualities of his character and his extraordinary steadfastness in every kind of circumstance, whether prosperous or adverse [Note: [Col. 0041] this reading is found in manuscript 1, written by the same hand above the line; it is also present in 2, 2 b, 2 c, 3*, 3 b, 3 c, 3 c*; absent in the others. Manuscript 1 has *maldegradam*, whose meaning is uncertain].

I shall now begin to speak of the other matters pertaining to his private and domestic life [Note: [Col. 0041] *a* was written above the line by the author in 1 and 3 c; *iam ab* is absent in 8 b] [Note: [Col. 0041] *exordior* B 2; “The first book ends. The second begins,” B 3 c].

After his father’s death he divided the kingdom with his brother. He endured his brother’s hostility and jealousy with such patience [Note: [Col. 0041] *sapientia* 1, 2, 3 b; “wisdom”; the others *patientia*] that everyone found it astonishing that he could not be provoked by him even to anger [Note: [Col. 0043] *nec* 3 b, B 1–4; “nor even”].

Later, at his mother’s urging, he married the daughter of Desiderius, king of the Lombards [Note: [Col. 0043] *longobardorum* 3 b, B 3–3]. For an uncertain reason [Note: [Col. 0043] *caussa* 4], he repudiated her after a year, and married Hildegard [Note: [Col. 0043] *hildigardem* 4, 10, 10 b, 10 c; *hildigardam* 3 b, 5; *hildigardim* 4 b, 8 b], a woman of the Suevian people [Note: [Col. 0043] *suaborum* 4, B 2; *sueurorum* 10, 10 b, 10 c, B 3–5] and of the highest nobility.

By her he had three sons—Charles, Pippin [Note: [Col. 0043] *pipinum* 11, B 2], and Louis [Note: [Col. 0043] *hludouuicum* 4, B 1, 2; *ludoicum* 5; *ludouicum* 3 b, 8 b, 11; *luodewicum* B 3 b, 4, 4 b, 5; *ludwicum* B 3, 3 c; *ludobicum* B 3 d]—and just as many daughters: Rotrude [Note: [Col. 0043] *hruodtrudem* 2 b, 3 c, 11 c; *hruodthrudem* 5; *hruotrudem* 3 b, 11 d; *hraodthrudem* 6 b; *hroadtrudem* 7; *hruadrudem* B 1, 2, 2 b; *hruddrudem* 9 b, 12; *hrotrudem* 2 c; *hrutrudam* 4 b; *rotrudem* 3*; *ruodrudem* 10; *ruotrudem* and *routrudem* 8, 11, 11 b, B 3–5; *rotdrudim* 8 b; *gerdrudem* 10 b, 10 c], Bertha [Note: [Col. 0043] *berhtam* 4, 10 b, B 3 c; *berctham* 3 c; *bertam* 2 c, 3*, 3 b, 8 b, 6 b, 7, 8, 11, 11 b, B 2 b], and Gisela [Note: [Col. 0043] *giselam* B 2, 3 b, 4, 4 b, 5; *gisalam* B 1, 3, 3 c, 3 d; *gisilam* 10 c*].

He had three other daughters: Theodrada [Note: [Col. 0043] *theoderanam* 3*; *theodeiadam* 5; *theodoradam* B 2, 2 b; *theodoratam* 10, 10 b, 10 c; *theodradam* 2 c, 11, 11 b; *theothradam* 11 c; *theotradam* 11 d; *theodoram* 3 b, B 3–5; *thedradam* 8 b], Hiltrude [Note: [Col. 0043] *hittrudem* 3 b; *eltrudem* 3*; *hildrudem* 10; *hildrudim* 8 b; *hiberudem* B 3 d], and Ruodhaide [Note: [Col. 0043] *hruodhaidem* 4, 5, 6 b, 7; *hruohaidem* 9; *hruodhadem* 3 c, 11 c; *hruodhadam* 12; *hruothadam* 11 d; *hruodgadem* 3 b; *hrothadem* 2 b; *ruodhaidem* 1, 2, 10 b, 10 c; *ruothaidem* 10, B 5; *ruodharpam* 8; *ruodadam* 11, 11 b; *roladam* 3*; *ruadhaidem* B 1, 2, 2 b, 3, 3 c, 3 d; *ruathaidem* B 3 b, 4, 4 b; *routhaidem* B 5; *rothaidem* 2 c, 8 b; *rudhaidem* 10 c*].

He had two daughters by his wife Fastrada [Note: [Col. 0043] *uastrada* B 5], who belonged to the people of the eastern Franks, namely the Germans; and a third daughter by a certain concubine, whose name does not now come to mind.

After Fastrada’s death [Note: [Col. 0043] *uastrada* B 3, 3 b, 3 d, 4, 4 b], he married Liutgard [Note: [Col. 0043] *leodgardam* 11 c; *leotgardam* 2, 2 b, 3 b; *leotghardam* 3 c; *leogardem* 2 c; *letgardam* 3*; *leodegardam* 11, 11 b; *luodgardam* 11 d; *liutgardam* 4, 5, 6 b, 7, B 1, 3, 3 b, 3 d, 4, 4 b; *liuthgardam* B 3 c; *liutgradam* 8; *liutgurdam* B 2, 2 b; *luidgardim* 8 b], an Alamannian woman, by whom he had no children [Note: [Col. 0043] *liberum nihil* 1, 2; *liberorum nichil* B 3–4; *nil liberum* 3 b].

After her death [Note: [Col. 0043] “After her death,” 1], he had three concubines [Note: [Col. 0043] Witnesses 8 and 8 b read: “he had four concubines, namely Mathalgard, who bore him a daughter named Rothild, Gersuinda, etc.”; 10 f and 10 h likewise read “four,” with *Rothild*]:  Gersuinda [Note: [Col. 0043] *gersuuindam* B 1, 3 b, 3 d, 5; *gesuiundam* 3 b], of Saxon descent, by whom he had a daughter named Adaltrude [Note: [Col. 0043] *adatrud* B 1; *adaltrudis* 11, 11 b; *adalthrud* 2, 4, B 2, 2 b, 3, 3 d; *adatorud* 6 b; *adaltrut* B 3 b; *adaltrat* B 4, 4 b; *adalthrut* B 5; *adaltrhud* 5; *adaldrud* 10 b; *adalruht* 10; *adatrhud* 7; *altrud* 11 c, 11 d; *adeldrudis* 8 b]; Regina [Note: [Col. 0043] *reginam*, corrected to *re hinam*, B 3; *reinam* 8, B 3 b; *re hinam* B 3 c; *remam* B 4, 4 b; *regiam* 2 b], who bore him Drogon [Note: [Col. 0043] *dronem*, corrected to *drogonem*, 1; *drugonem* 10, 10 b, 10 c; *drougonem* B 5] and Hugh [Note: [Col. 0043] *hugonem* 3 c, 7, 10 c, 11 c, 11 d, B 1–4; *ugonem* 9]; and Adalind [Note: [Col. 0043] *allindem*, corrected to *adallindem*, 1; *adalindem* 6 b, 10; *adillindem* 10 b; *adallindam* 2, 2 b, 3 b, 8, 10 c, B 1–2, 2 b, 3; *adillindam* B 3 b, 3 d, 4, 4 b; *adlindam* B 3 c; *atlindam* 3*; *adalintam* 11 c*; *aluidam* 10 g; *adalindam* 2 c, 11, 11 b, 11 d; *adelluidam* 8 b], by whom he fathered Theodoric [Note: [Col. 0043] *theodericum* 2, 4, 4 b, 10, B 5; *theodoricum* 3 b, 5, 10 b, 10 c, B 3–4; *theodricus* B 2; *thederichum* 8 b].

His mother Bertrada [Note: [Col. 0043] *berhtrada* 4, B 3, 3 c, d; *berethrada* 11; *bertrada* 3 b, 8 b, B 3 b; *perhtrat* B 4; *bethrada* B 5] grew old in great honor with him. He treated her with the utmost reverence [Note: [Col. 0043] *reuentia* 1], so that no disagreement ever arose between them [Note: [Col. 0043] *inter eos* 8 b; “between them”], except over the repudiation of the daughter of King Desiderius, whom he had married at her urging [Note: [Col. 0043] *susceperat* B 2–4; “had taken”; *uxorem acceperat* 9 b, 10 f].

At last she died after Hildegard’s death [Note: [Col. 0043] *hildegharde* 7; *hildigardae* 3 b, 4, 11, B 5; *hildegardis* 8 b], when she had already seen three grandsons and as many granddaughters in her son’s household. He had her buried with great honor in the same basilica where his father lies, at Saint-Denis [Note: [Col. 0043] *dyonisium* 4, B 2] [Note: [Col. 0043] *deest* 4; “with great” is absent].

He had one sister, named Gisela [Note: [Col. 0043] *gysla* B 1; *gisela* B 5; *gisila* 10 b, c], who from girlhood had been devoted to a religious way of life [Note: [Col. 0043] *religione* m., B 2; “to religion”]. He likewise honored her with great affection, as he did his mother [Note: [Col. 0043] *summa* B 5; “the greatest”]. She too died a few years before his death in the monastery where she had lived.

## Apparatus register for chapters 12–18

**Chapter 12.** B 2 omits *id est* (“that is”); 4 b reads *elocutione* (“expression”) and 8 b *lingua* (“language”) for *locutione* (“speech”). The critical record also gives the reading *quidam* (“certain [people]”) and notes that 8 b omits *ab occidentali* (“from the west”).

**Chapter 13.** *Sive* (“or”) stands for *vel*; the source records defective or alternate *cetera*, *praefectis*, *commisit*, and *tandem*. *Quod* here means “how many.” Other actual readings are *vascua* (“pastures”), *qua* (“by which/where”), the authorial insertion *in*, and *intercoeptus/interceptus* (“cut off/intercepted”).

**Chapter 14.** The note at *ultimum* preserves that exact reading; witness 3 omits *adeo usque potestatem* (“power so far/so completely”), and manuscript 1 omits *a se* (“by himself”).

**Chapter 15.** The author adds *usque in* (“as far as into”); the record gives variants for *tum*, and corrects *fluvios* (“rivers,” accusative) to *fluviis* (“rivers,” ablative). It records variants for *oceanumque* and *paene*, and an erased supralinear *aquis* (“waters”) with *eas*. The Vistula quotation is closed before the apparatus resumes.

**Chapter 16.** *Quibusdam regibus ac gentibus per amicitiam sibi consiliatis* means “with certain kings and peoples won/reconciled to him through friendship.” Alfonso required that Charlemagne call him *proprium suum*, “his own man.” The source records *ultro* (“of his own accord”), *complures* (“several”), and authorial additions *propter* (“because of”) and *a se* (“by himself”). When the envoys returned, Charlemagne—not Aaron—attached his own envoys and sent Aaron eastern gifts.

**Chapters 17–18.** The record distinguishes *inter quae/inter quaeque*, *praecipua*, *fere*, and *repperit*; manuscript 4 omits *toto etiam*, and “see above” refers to the Northmen. At chapter 18 it gives *ampliando*, omission of *regno*, the *Ceteraque* variants plus the manuscript-start notice, *cuius* in 2, omission of *et* before Pippin, and omission of *uxorem* in B 1–2. Witnesses 8 and 8 b read four concubines, naming Mathalgard, mother of Rothild; 10 f and 10 h also read four, with *Rothild*. At Adaltrude the distinct apparatus is *nomen/nomine* (“name/by name”) and its omissions before the personal-name variants.

### 19.

He judged that his children should be educated in such a way that both sons and daughters would first be instructed in the liberal studies to which he himself also devoted attention. Then, as soon as their age permitted, he had his sons ride in the Frankish manner and be trained in arms and hunting; but he ordered his daughters to become accustomed to wool-working and to devote themselves to the distaff and spindle, so that they would not grow sluggish through idleness, and to be educated in every honorable pursuit.

Of all these children, before he died he lost only two sons and one daughter: Charles, who was the elder by birth; Pippin, whom he had placed in charge as king of Italy; and Hruodrud, his firstborn daughter, who had been betrothed to Constantine, emperor of the Greeks.

Pippin left one son, his own Bernhard, and five daughters—Adalhaid, Atula, Guntrada, Bertha, and Theoderada—as survivors. In these children the king displayed an exceptional proof of his affection, for, after their father’s death, he had the grandson succeed to his father’s position and had the granddaughters brought up among his own daughters.

He bore the deaths of his sons and daughter all too patiently, considering the greatness of spirit in which he excelled, though affection—by which he was no less distinguished—moved him to tears. When he was informed of the death of Hadrian, Roman pontiff, whom he regarded as his foremost friend, he wept as though he had lost a beloved son or a dearest brother.

He was exceptionally well balanced in his friendships, readily admitting people to them and retaining them with the greatest constancy; and he held in the highest reverence all those whom he had joined to himself by this bond. He took such great care in raising his sons and daughters that, whenever he was at home, he never dined without them and never traveled without them. His sons rode beside him; his daughters almost followed him, while the last part of their procession was protected by guards selected for that purpose from among his attendants.

Although they were extremely beautiful and greatly loved by him, astonishingly, he did not wish to marry any of them to anyone, whether one of his own people or a foreigner. Instead, he kept them all in his household with him until his death, saying that he could not do without their companionship. For this reason, although otherwise fortunate, he experienced the malignity of adverse fortune. He concealed it, however, as though no suspicion or rumor of any disgrace concerning them had ever arisen.

### 20.

He had a son named Pippin, born of a concubine; I postponed mentioning him among the others. He was handsome in face but disfigured by a hump.

When his father, having undertaken a war against the Huns, was wintering in Bavaria, Pippin, pretending to be ill, conspired against his father with certain leading Franks who had enticed him with a false promise of the kingship. After the fraud had been detected and the conspirators condemned, he allowed Pippin, once tonsured and already willing, to devote himself to religious life in the monastery at Prüm.

Earlier, a powerful conspiracy had also been formed against him in Germany. Its leaders were partly deprived of their sight, while others retained their limbs unharmed; all, however, were carried into exile. None of them was killed except three, who, when they defended themselves with drawn swords to avoid being captured and had even killed some people, were put to death because they could not otherwise be restrained.

It is nevertheless believed that the cruelty of Queen Fastrada was the cause and origin of these conspiracies. For this reason conspiracies were formed against the king on both occasions: because, by consenting to his wife’s cruelty, he seemed to have departed outrageously from the kindness of his nature and his customary gentleness.

For the rest of his life he conducted himself, both at home and abroad, with such universal love and favor that no one ever charged him with even the slightest mark of unjust cruelty.

### 21.

He loved foreigners and took great care in receiving them, so much so that their multitude often seemed, not without reason, burdensome not only to the palace but even to the kingdom. Yet, because of his greatness of spirit, he was not at all weighed down by such a burden, since he even compensated for immense inconveniences with the reward of a reputation for generosity and good character.

[Note: Cols. 0045–0046. *Amabat* (“he loved”) appears as *amaibat* in manuscript 1. *In eis suscipiendis* (“in receiving them”) appears in manuscript 8b as *et eorum suscipiendorum* (“and of receiving them”). *Plerumque* (“often”) is absent from the other manuscripts. *Prae* (“because of”) appears as *pro* in manuscript 8b. The continuation belongs, in the printed editions, to chapter 21, although its placement varies.]

### 22.

His body was large and robust, and his stature was tall, though it did not exceed proper proportion—for it is established that he was seven of his own feet in height. His head was rounded at the crown, his eyes very large and lively, his nose slightly larger than average, his hair beautifully white, and his face cheerful and bright. Thus he acquired great authority and dignity of appearance both standing and sitting, although his neck seemed thick and somewhat short and his belly rather prominent. The symmetry of his other limbs, however, concealed these features.

His gait was firm, and his entire bodily bearing masculine. His voice was clear, though it suited his bodily appearance less well. His health was good, except that during the four years before his death he was frequently seized by fevers and at the end even limped on one foot.

At that time he followed his own judgment more often than the advice of physicians, whom he almost hated because they urged him to give up the roast meats he was accustomed to eating and to become used to boiled foods. He exercised constantly by riding and hunting, which was traditional among his people, since scarcely any nation on earth can be found equal to the Franks in this art.

He also delighted in naturally hot water and exercised his body by frequent swimming. He was so skilled at it that no one could rightly be preferred to him. For this reason he built a royal residence at Aachen and lived there continuously during the final years of his life, until his death. He invited not only his sons to the baths but also nobles and friends, and sometimes even a crowd of attendants and bodyguards, so that on occasion one hundred or more people bathed together.

[Note: Cols. 0045–0047. The heading “22” is absent from manuscript 5 for chapters 22–26 up to the words “from childhood.” *Amplo* (“large”) is absent from manuscript 3c; *robusto* (“robust”) appears as *robusta* in B 1–2. Compare Suetonius, *Tiberius*, chapter 68; *Augustus*, chapter 79; and *Caligula*, chapter 50. *Septem suorum pedum proceritatem* means “a height of seven of his own feet”; one witness reads *figuram* (“form”) instead of *mensuram* (“measure”). The phrase describing the crown of the head is absent from manuscript 3c. *Paululum* (“slightly”) appears as *paulolum* in B 1. *In mediocritatem* (“beyond the average”) is found in manuscripts 1–2. Compare Suetonius, *Claudius*, chapter 30. Compare also Suetonius, *Augustus*, chapter 79, for his appearance and dignity; *Nero*, chapter 51, for the thick, short neck; and *Titus*, chapter 3, for the prominent belly. The phrase *haec ceterorum membrorum celabat aequalitas* means “the symmetry of the other limbs concealed these features.” *Hoc* (“this”) appears in B 1, 3, and 3b for *haec* (“these”). Compare Suetonius, *Claudius*, chapter 31, for his health, and *Augustus*, chapter 80, for his lameness. *Quattuor* (“four”) is written *quatuor* in B 1–2. *Febribus* (“fevers”) is corrected from *febrius* in manuscript 1. The manuscripts read *claudicaret, claudicarat, claudicabat,* and *claudicavit* (“he limped” in varying tense forms). The phrase concerning his lameness is compared with Suetonius, *Augustus*, chapter 80. *Cuius* (“of which”) is followed in manuscript 1 by a marginal addition meaning “which skill could be preferred to none of his.” *Peritus* (“skilled”) appears as *p.* in one witness, and *potuerit* (“could have been”) appears for *valeat* (“can be”). *Aquisgrani* (“at Aachen”) is corrected from *aquis granum* to *aquis grani* in manuscript 1. *Perpetim* (“continuously”) appears as *continuo* in manuscript 8b. Compare Suetonius, *Titus*, chapter 8, for the hundred or more bathers.]

### 23.

He wore the native dress, that is, Frankish dress. Against his body he wore a linen shirt and linen drawers; over these, a tunic bordered with silk and leggings. Then he wrapped his legs with bandages and fastened his feet with shoes. In winter he protected his shoulders and chest with a breastplate made from otter and mouse-skins (*pellibus lutrinis et murinis*; the editorial gloss identifies the latter as ermine or sable). He wore a Venetian cloak and was always girded with a sword whose hilt and baldric were either gold or silver.

Sometimes he also used a jeweled sword, but only on the most important festivals or when envoys from foreign peoples had arrived. He rejected foreign clothing, however beautiful, and never allowed himself to wear it, except that at Rome, once at the request of Pope Hadrian and again at the supplication of his successor Leo, he wore a long tunic and cloak and shoes made in the Roman fashion.

On festivals he walked about wearing a garment woven with gold, jeweled shoes, and a golden brooch fastening his cloak, and adorned with a diadem of gold and gems. On other days his dress differed little from ordinary and plebeian clothing.

[Note: Cols. 0047–0048. *Patrio* (“native”) appears as *pario* in manuscript 3b. *Francisco* (“Frankish”) appears as *francico, frantia, francio,* and *frantio*. Compare the Monk of Saint Gall, *Deeds of Charlemagne*, chapter 34. *Camisa lineam* means “a linen shirt”; in French, *chemise*. Manuscripts also read *camisiam lineam* (“linen shirt”). *Feminalibus* (“drawers”) appears as *femuralibus*. The manuscripts vary in the placement of *tibialia* (“leggings”) and *fasciolis* (“bandages”); some read “leggings with bandages,” others “leggings, then bandages.” *Caltiamentis* (“shoes”) appears as *calciamentis*. The words “otter and ermine skins” are absent from several witnesses; some read *vel* (“or”) instead of *et* (“and”). The editorial gloss explains that these were the skins of ermine or sable. *Umeros* (“shoulders”) appears as *umeros* in B 1. The phrase *pectus hieme muniebat* means “he protected his chest in winter”; *hyeme* is corrected from *hyme* in manuscript 1. *Sagum venetum* means “a Venetian cloak.” Compare Suetonius, *Augustus*, chapter 82, and *Caligula*, chapter 52, for the cloak and clothing. *Baltheus* (“baldric”) is a variant of *balteus*. *Gemmatum ensem* means “a jeweled sword”; *geminato* is a manuscript variant. The clause concerning foreign envoys is absent from some witnesses. *Hadriano* appears as *hadriano*. The clause concerning Leo’s supplication is absent from several manuscripts. *More* (“fashion”) is corrected from *opere* (“work”) in manuscript 1. *Texta* (“woven”) is corrected from *testa* in manuscript 1. *Gemmat is calciamentis* means “jeweled shoes”; one manuscript reads *geminatis*. *Astringente* (“fastening”) appears as *astringebat* in B 3–4. The manuscripts offer several readings of the sentence about his ordinary dress, including: “his dress differed little from ordinary and plebeian clothing”; “his ordinary dress did not differ from that of the common people”; and “his dress, being common, did not differ from plebeian clothing.”]

### 24.

In food and drink he was temperate, though more temperate in drink, since he detested drunkenness exceedingly in anyone, and especially in himself and his household. He could not abstain from food to such an extent that he often complained that fasting was harmful to his body.

He gave banquets very rarely, and only on the most important festivals; even then, however, there was a large number of people present. His daily dinner consisted of only four courses, apart from the roast meat that hunters usually brought in on spits, which he enjoyed eating more than any other food.

During dinner he listened either to some entertainment or to a reader. Histories and the deeds of ancient kings were read to him. He also delighted in the books of Saint Augustine, especially those entitled *The City of God*.

He was so sparing in wine and every kind of drink that at dinner he rarely drank more than three times. In summer, after his midday meal, he would eat some fruit and drink once; then, having removed his clothes and shoes, he would rest for two or three hours, as he was accustomed to do at night.

At night he slept in such a way that his sleep was interrupted four or five times, not only by waking but also by getting up again. While he was putting on his shoes or being dressed, he admitted not only friends but also—if the palace official said that a lawsuit existed which could not be settled without his order—he immediately ordered the litigants to be brought in. Sitting as though on a tribunal, he heard the case and pronounced judgment. Nor did he attend only to this at that time: on that day he also dealt with whatever official business had to be conducted or whatever task had to be assigned to any of his servants.

[Note: Cols. 0047–0049. Compare Suetonius, *Augustus*, chapter 76, for food and drink; chapters 74 and 78 for banquets and sleep; and *Vespasian*, chapters 19 and 21. *Temperans* (“temperate”) appears as *temperatus* and *temperate*. *Abominabatur* (“he detested”) appears as *abhominabatur*. *Assa* (“roast meat”) is written in some manuscripts with variant forms. *Veribus* (“spits”) appears as *verubus*. *Acroama* means “an entertainment” or “a performance”; the manuscripts read *acroma, incroama,* and related forms. Compare Suetonius, *Augustus*, chapter 74, and *Vespasian*, chapter 19. The manuscripts vary between “histories and the deeds of ancient kings,” “the deeds of kings,” and “the deeds of events.” *De civitate Dei* (“The City of God”) is corrected from *de civitate domini* (“of the City of the Lord”) in B 1–4. *Expergiscendo* (“by waking”) appears as *expergescendo* and *expergescendum*. The wording concerning getting up again varies among *deresurgendo, desurgendo, resurgendo, exurgendo, assurgendo,* and *surgendo*. Compare Suetonius, *Vespasian*, chapter 21. *Calciaretur* (“he was putting on shoes”) appears as *calcearetur*. *Amiciretur* (“he was dressed”) appears as *amictaretur*. The manuscripts vary between *aut* (“or”) and *et* (“and”). *Aliquam* (“some,” feminine) is corrected from *aliquem* (“some,” masculine) in manuscript B 1. *Definiri* (“be settled”) appears as *definire*. Several manuscripts alter the verbs to “he ordered the litigants to be introduced” and “he said.”]

### 25.

He was rich and overflowing in eloquence and could express whatever he wished with the greatest clarity. Nor was he content with his native language: he also devoted attention to learning foreign languages. Among these he learned Latin so well that he was accustomed to speak it as readily as his native language; Greek, however, he was able to understand better than to pronounce.

He was indeed so eloquent that he even seemed a teacher (*didascalus*). He cultivated the liberal arts with the greatest zeal, and, showing the highest reverence for their teachers, he honored them greatly. In grammar he listened to the aged deacon Peter of Pisa; in the other disciplines he had as his teacher the deacon Albinus, also called Alcuin, a man from Britain of Saxon descent, learned in every field. With him he devoted a great deal of time and effort to learning rhetoric and dialectic, but especially astronomy.

He studied the art of calculation and, with keen attention, investigated the courses of the stars with the greatest curiosity. He also tried to write and was accustomed to keep writing tablets and notebooks under his pillow in bed, so that, whenever he had free time, he might train his hand in forming letters. But this labor, begun too late and undertaken at an unsuitable age, achieved little success.

[Note: Cols. 0049–0050. Compare Suetonius, *Augustus*, chapter 84, for his eloquence; *Titus*, chapter 3, for his knowledge of Latin and Greek; and *Tiberius*, chapter 70, for his studies. *Contentus* (“content”) appears as *contemptus* in manuscript 1. The phrase concerning foreign languages is inserted by a second hand in manuscript 1. *Grecam* (“Greek”) appears as *gregam*. *Intellegere* (“to understand”) appears as *intelligere*. *Didascalus* (“learned,” or possibly “teacher”) appears as *didasculus, didaculus, dicaculus,* and *dialecticus*. Peter of Pisa is called *diaconus* (“deacon”), with some manuscripts reading *diaconem*. Albinus is also called Alcuin: the manuscripts read *Alcoinum, Alcuinum,* and *Alcuuinum*. *De Brittania* (“from Britain”) appears as *de Brittannia, britania,* and related forms. The description identifies him as a man of Saxon descent and exceptionally learned in every discipline. *Rhetoricae* (“rhetoric”) and *dialecticae* (“dialectic”) have numerous orthographic variants. *Astronomiae* (“astronomy”) is especially emphasized. *Syderum* (“of the stars”) appears as *siderum*. *Cursus* (“courses”) appears as *cursum* and *cursu*. *Codicellos* (“notebooks”) appears as *codicillos*. The verb meaning “forming letters” appears as *effingendis, effigiendis, effigiandis, effigendis,* and *efficiendis*.]

### 26.

He practiced the Christian religion, with which he had been imbued from childhood, with the greatest holiness and devotion. For this reason he built at Aachen a basilica of extraordinary beauty and adorned it with gold, silver, lamps, and solid-bronze screens and doors. Since he could not obtain columns and marble for its construction from elsewhere, he arranged for them to be transported from Rome and Ravenna.

He attended the church diligently morning and evening, during the night hours, and at the time of the sacrifice, as long as his health permitted. He took the greatest care that everything done there should be carried out with the utmost dignity, frequently warning the custodians not to allow anything indecent or dirty either to be brought in or to remain there.

He procured such an abundance of sacred vessels of gold and silver and priestly vestments that, when the sacrifice was celebrated, even the doorkeepers—the lowest rank of the ecclesiastical order—did not have to serve in private clothing. He corrected the disciplines of reading and chanting with the greatest diligence. He was highly learned in both, although he himself neither read publicly nor sang except softly and with the congregation.

[Note: Cols. 0049–0050. Compare Suetonius, *Augustus*, chapters 90 and 93. *Religionem* (“religion”) appears as *relionem* in one witness. *Sanctissime* (“with the greatest holiness”) appears as *sanctissima et summa* (“with the greatest and highest [devotion]”). *Aquisgrani* (“at Aachen”) appears as *aquis granis*. *Luminaribus* (“lamps”) is altered in some manuscripts to *liminaribus* (“lintels”). The phrase *ne ianitoribus quidem* means “not even for the doorkeepers.” The manuscripts vary in the wording and placement of the clauses concerning the abundance of sacred vessels and vestments. *Legendi* (“of reading”) is corrected from *legengdi*. *Submissim* (“softly”) is corrected in manuscript 1 to *submisse*; other manuscripts read *submissim, summisse,* or *submissum*. One manuscript continues: “He dedicated eight hundred and eighty-six churches at his own expense, with their furnishings and other ornaments, to the praise of God and the Blessed Virgin, and restored three thousand seven hundred throughout the world.”]

### 27.

In supporting the poor and in the free generosity that the Greeks call *eleemosynē* (almsgiving), he was exceptionally devoted. He ensured that this was done not only in his homeland and in his own kingdom but also across the seas, in Syria, Egypt, and Africa. At Jerusalem, Alexandria, and Carthage, whenever he discovered that Christians were living in poverty, he sympathized with their need and used to send them money. For this reason above all he sought the friendship of foreign kings, so that some comfort and relief might come to the Christians living under their rule.

He honored, above all other holy and venerable places, the church of the blessed apostle Peter at Rome. In its treasury he deposited a great quantity of money, both gold and silver, as well as jewels. He sent many and innumerable gifts to the pontiffs, and throughout his entire reign he considered nothing more important than ensuring that the city of Rome, through his efforts and labor, should retain its ancient authority, and that the church of Saint Peter should, through him, be not only safe and defended but also adorned and enriched from his resources above all other churches.

Although he valued it so highly, during the forty-seven years in which he had reigned he traveled there only four times, to fulfill his vows and offer his prayers.

[Note: Col. 0051. *Eleemosynam* (“almsgiving”) appears as *eleymosynam, heleymosinam, elymosinam, elemosinam,* and other forms. The Greek term is *eleemosynē*. The phrase *quam Graeci elemosynam vocant* (“which the Greeks call almsgiving”) is absent from B 1–2 and perhaps B 3–5. The manuscripts vary between *in patria et in regno suo* (“in his homeland and in his own kingdom”) and *in suo regno* (“in his own kingdom”). *Verum etiam* (“but also”) appears in B 3–4. The geographical names Syria, Egypt, Africa, Jerusalem, Alexandria, and Carthage display numerous manuscript spellings and case forms, including *Siria, Aegyptum, Affricam, Iherosolimis, Ierosolymas, Alexandriam, Chartagini,* and *Carthaginem*. One continuation reads: “He redeemed all captives and prisoners held in the hands of barbarians and freed them with his own money.” The church is called in some manuscripts “the church of the apostles Peter and Paul” or “the church of Peter and Paul.” *Missa* (“sent”) is the reading of the text; manuscript 1 has *misit* (“he sent”). *Toto* (“entire”) appears as *toti* in B 1–2. *Duxit antiquius* means “he considered more important.” Compare Suetonius, *Vespasian*, chapter 8. *Urbs Roma* (“the city of Rome”) is reordered as *Roma urbs* in manuscript 1. *Suo opere* (“by his own work”) appears as *sua opera* in the text. *Beati* (“blessed”) and *sancti* (“holy”) vary in the designation of Saint Peter’s church. *Ornata* (“adorned”) appears as *ordinata* in some witnesses. The forty-seven years are reckoned as the completed years 768–814. Compare Suetonius, *Tiberius*, chapter 72, for the number of visits.]

### 28.

These were not the only reasons for his final visit. The Romans also compelled Pope Leo, who had suffered many injuries—his eyes having been torn out and his tongue cut off—to appeal for the king’s protection. Accordingly, he came to Rome and spent the entire winter there in order to restore the condition of the Church, which had been thrown into great disorder.

At that time he received the name of Emperor and Augustus. At first he was so displeased by it that he declared that, even though the day was a major festival, he would not enter the church if he had been able to foresee the pope’s intention. Nevertheless, he endured with great patience the resentment caused by the title he had accepted, since the Roman emperors were indignant about it. He overcame their arrogance by the greatness of spirit in which he was undoubtedly far superior to them, sending them frequent embassies and addressing them in his letters as brothers—

[Note: Cols. 0051–0052. *Ultimi adventus sui* (“of his final visit”) has various manuscript readings. *Erutis* (“having been torn out”) appears as *eruti*. *Imperatoris* (“of Emperor”) is added by a second hand in manuscript 1; the source records no separate variant concerning *hiemis* (“winter”). *Aversatus* (“displeased by” or “opposed to”) appears as *adversatus* in manuscripts 2, 3b, 5, and B 2–4. The manuscripts vary in whether the phrase meaning “he declared” is present. *Romanis* (“Roman”) is replaced by *Constantinopolitanis* (“Constantinopolitan”) in manuscript 8b. *Patientia* (“patience”) appears as *pacientia*. *Magnanimitate* (“greatness of spirit”) appears as *magnimitata* in manuscript 2 and is corrected in manuscript 1. The word *eos* (“them”) in the phrase “calling them brothers” is supplied above the line as a correction in manuscript 1. The source ends here, with the sentence incomplete.]

## Apparatus register for chapters 19–28

**Chapter 19.** The grief sentence is retained as printed: Charlemagne bore his children’s deaths all too patiently for so great a spirit, yet affection moved him to tears. The apparatus is not an assertion of unspecified “expanded readings”: it preserves the witnesses’ exact additions/omissions at the sentence. At [Col. 0045C], the one editorial note identifies Hludowic as Louis, abbot of Saint-Denis, and says that Hruodrud bore a son to Louis and Bertha a son to Angilbert; it is stated once, not duplicated.

**Chapters 20 and 22–25.** The witness record retains spellings, corrections, omissions, and sigla individually rather than as “numerous variants.” In chapter 23 the foreign-envoy clause is not said to be absent: the source’s actual apparatus is *adessent Bouq.* (“were present, Bouquet”).

**Chapter 27.** The winter garment is *pellibus lutrinis et murinis*: otter and mouse skins; the editorial gloss identifies *murinis* with ermine or sable. *Didascalus* means “teacher.” Manuscript 1 has a second-hand addition only of *Imperatoris* (“of Emperor”); the source has no separate *hiemis* addition.

**Chapter 28.** No variants are invented for *Ultimi adventus sui*. The source-bound spelling/cross-reference record is retained as printed, including corrections and witness designations.

29. [Col. 0051] After assuming the imperial title, when he noticed [Note: *averteret*; corrected to *aduerteret* by the second hand in manuscript 1.] that much [Note: *de: esse* in manuscript 1.] was lacking in the laws of his people—for the Franks have two laws [Note: *im* in manuscript 4.], the Salic Law and the Law of the Ribuarian Franks [Note: *Legem Salicam et Ribuariorum*, “the Salic Law and the law of the Ribuarian Franks.”]—which differ greatly [Note: *valde* is absent in B 1 and 2.] in many respects, he considered adding what was lacking, reconciling discrepancies, and correcting what was wrong and improperly stated [Col. 0052B]. But he did nothing further in this matter except add a few chapters, and those incomplete, to the laws [Note: That is, additions to the Salic Law and to the Ribuarian Law, from the years 803–806.]. Nevertheless, he had the laws [Note: Manuscript B 1 reads *iure*, “by law,” for *iura*, “laws.”] of all the nations that were under his rule [Note: Manuscript 8b reads *ditione*, “dominion,” for *dominatu*, “rule.”], which had not been written down [Note: The laws of the Saxons, Thuringians, and Frisians.], recorded and committed to writing. Likewise, he wrote down and committed to memory the barbarian [Note: That is, Germanic.] and most ancient songs in which the deeds and wars of ancient kings were sung. He also began a grammar of his native language.

He likewise assigned names to the months according to his own language, since before that time [Note: Manuscript 8b reads *tempus*, “time,” for *temporis*, “of the time.”] among the Franks they were pronounced [Note: Manuscript 8b reads *appellarentur*, “were called.”] partly by Latin and partly by barbarian names. He also distinguished the twelve winds by their proper names, although previously scarcely more than four names of winds could be found [Note: Manuscript 1 reads *possent vocabula*; the remaining manuscripts read *vocabula possent*; the edition also refers to the variant on p. 8b.] [Note: The remainder of this chapter is missing in manuscript 2c.].

As for the months, he called January Wintarmanoth [Note: In manuscript 7c, *monath* is consistently read; *uuintaremanoth* in 9; *uuintarmanodh* in B 2 and 2b; *uuintharmanoth* in B 3 and 3d; *Wintarmanodum* in C 3; *uuintermanoth* in 3b, B 3b, and 5; *wintermanoth* in B 4 and 10b; *wintermanoch* in B 4b; *windermanoth* in 10c and Reuber’s manuscript; *uuindermanoth* in 10 (which everywhere has *manoht*); *nuntirmanoth* in 5; *Vuinthermonet* in 8b (where *monet* or *mont* is consistently read); *windermonot* in 4b; *winterman* in B 8; *uuuintermonet* or *uindermonoth* in C 4.], February [Note: *febroarium* in 3b and 4. The months February, March, April, May, June, and July are absent in B 1, 2, and 2b.] Hornung [Note: *hornungmanoth* in 7; *hornug* in 1; *horinuing* in 11c; *ornung* in 3*; *ornunhg* in 3c; *hornunch* in 10b, B 4, and 4b; *hornunt* in B 5; *hormunc* or *orminhg* in C 4.], March Lentzinmanoth [Note: *lenzinmanoth* in 2b, 3b, 3c, B 5; *lenzenmanoth* in 9; *lenzimanoth* in 2, B 3c, C 4; *linzinmanoth* in 5; *lentzmont* in 8b; *lenthinmanoth* in 10b; *lentinmanoth* in 7, 11, 11b; *lentinmanod* in C 3; *lentimanoth* in 3*, 8, 11c–d; *lencimanoth* in B 3b, 4, and 4b; *lentzin*, that is, “May-month” or “the beginning of spring,” in B 8; *lenzemont* in C 4; *lengtenmonath* in 7b.], April [Note: April and May, July and August are absent in 2. He gave the winds names in the following manner [Note: Manuscript 1 reads *ergo*, “therefore”; the others read *vero*, “however.”].
