*atromwint* in 2b; *ostrumuuind* in 11 and 11b; *ostruniwind* in 11c; *ostrunniwind* in 11d; *ostronowind* in 7; *ostronowint* in 6b; *oslronowinth* in B 3d; *osteruuint* in 3b and B 8; *ostrenwyndt* in 8b; *ostrowyndt* in 4b.], the Eurus Ostsundroni [Note: *ostsumdooni* in 3b; *ostsumdroni* in 11c; *ostsundron* in B 3b and 4b; *ostsundruni* in B 3d; *ostsundren* in 8b; *ostsuthronowind* in 7.], the Euroauster [Note: *eroaustrum*, corrected to *euroaustrum*, in manuscript 1.] Sundostroni [Note: *suntaustroni* in 1; *suadrostoni* in 8; *sundostroni* in C 2 and B 3d; *sundrostron* in B 3b; *sundostron* in B 4 and 4b; *sundostren* in 8b and 4b; *sondostroni* in 10c–d; *sudostroni* in C 3; *suthostronowind* in 7.], the Auster Sundroni [Note: *sumdroni* in 1; *sundron* in B 3b, 4, and 4b; *sundren* in 8b and 4b; *sudwint* in B 8; *suthronowind* in 7.], the Austroafricus [Note: *austro affricum* in 3b, 10, 10b–c, and B 1–5; *austrum africum* in 2b, 11, 11b, and 11d; *austricum africum* in 11c.] Sundwestrom [Note: *suntuuestroni* in manuscript 1; *suduuestroni* in C 3; *sunduuuestroni* in B 1; *sundiuuestroni* in 11 and 11c; *sundri [lacuna] undiuest [lacuna] ii* in C 2; *sondwesroni* in 11d; *sudwestron* in B 3b; *sunwestron* in B 4 and 4b; *sunduestren* in 8b; *suthwestronowind* in 7. *Sundwestroni africum* is absent in B 2.], the Africus Westsundroni [Note: *affricum* in 2b, 3b, 10, 10b–c, B 3, 3c–d, 4, 4b, and 5; the sequence from *Africum* through *Chorum* is absent in 3c. *uuestsundron* in B 3b and 4b; *westsondroni* in 8; *westsundren* in 8b; *westsuthronowind* in 7.], the Zephyr Westroni [Note: *zephyrom* in 1; *zefyrum* in 4 and 10c; *zefirum* in 6b and B 2; *zephirum* in 2b, 3b, 10, 11, 11b, and 11d; *epyrum* in B 3b and 4b.] [Note: In 10, 10b–c, and 10c*, *Westroni* appears and *Chorum* is absent; *uestroni* in B 3; *westron* in B 3b, 4, and 4b; *uestoumi* in B 3d; *vuestren* in 8b; *westronowind* in 7.], the Caurus [Note: *choriam* in 6b.] Westnordroni [Note: *uuesthnordoni* in B 2; *vestnordroni* in B 5; *westnordorni* in B 3; *westnordron* in B 4 and 4b; *westnordon* in B 3b; *westnordren* in 8b; *westnorthronowind* in 7.], the Circius Nordwestroni [Note: *norduuuestroni* in 1; *norduuesthroni* in B 2; *norduestroni* in B 3d; *nordenuestroni* in C 2; *nordwesten* in B 3b, 4, and 4b; *nordiuestruni* in 11; *nordwestruni* in 11b–c; *nordwestren* in 8b; *northwestronowind* in 7; *westroni* in 8; *nordwesdroni* in Reuber’s manuscripts.], the Septentrion Nordroni [Note: Manuscript 1 has *Septemtrionem*; *septentrionem* in 4, B 1, C 3, and other manuscripts. *nordron* in B 3b, 4, and 4b; *nordoni* in 3c and 8; *nordren* in 8b; *northronowind* in 7.], the Aquilo Nordostroni [Note: *nordostronii* in 1; *nordosthroni* in B 2; *nordenastroni* in C 3; *nordrostroni* in B 3d; *nordostruni* in 11, 11b, and 11d; *nodstruni* in 11c; *nordostron* in B 3b and 4; *nordostren* in 8b; *northostronowind* in 7; *nordostdroni* in Reuber’s manuscripts; *nordwestroni* in 8.], and the Vulturnus Ostnordroni [Note: *osonordroni* in 3b–c; *oustnordroni* in 8; *ostnordron* in B 4 and 4b; *ostnordrun* in B 3b; *ostnordren* in 8b and 4b; *ostnorthronowind* in 7. Moreover, manuscripts B 3, 3b–d, 4, and 4b print the winds in this order: *Subsol., Eur., Affr., Sept., Euroaust., Zeph., Aquil., Aust., Chor., Vult., Austroaff., Circius* (Subsolanus, Eurus, Africus, Septentrion, Euroauster, Zephyr, Aquilo, Auster, Caurus, Vulturnus, Austroafricus, Circius). Manuscript B 8 reads: *Subsol. vocaret Osterwint, Eurum Ostsud, Vulturnum Ostnord, Sefirum Westwint, Circium Nordwest, Favonium [lacuna], Austrum Sudwint, Affricum Sudwest, [lacuna], Septentrionem id est Borean Nordwint, Chorum Westnord, Aquilonem Nordost*; that is, it supplies the corresponding Latin and German wind names, with two lacunae. In manuscript c*, Aquilo precedes Circius and Septentrion.]

30. At the end [Note: *E. vero* in 4b, 10, 10b, and 10c.] of his life [Note: *vitae suae* in B 3–4.], when he was already [Note: *et* is absent in manuscript 1.] weighed down by illness and old age, he summoned [Note: *et vocatum* in B 1 and 2.] to himself his son Hludowic [Note: *hluduuicum* in 1; *hlodowicum* in 7; *ludouicum* in 3b, 8b, and 11; *luodeuicum* in B 3b and 4b; *ludouuicum* in B 2; *ludewicum* in B 5; *ludevicum* in B 3; *ludbicum* in B 3d.], king of Aquitaine, who alone of the sons of [Col. 0053B] Hildegard [Note: *hildigardae* in 6b, 11, B 1, 2, 3, 3d, and 5; *hildegardis* in 8b.] remained, and, after solemnly assembling the leading men [Col. 0054A] [Note: *principibus*, “princes,” in B 3, 3b, and 3c.] from the whole Frankish kingdom, by the counsel of all constituted him his associate in the whole kingdom and heir to the imperial title. Having placed a diadem upon his head, he ordered him to be called Emperor and Augustus.

All who were present received this decision with great favor, for it seemed to them divinely inspired for the good of the kingdom [Note: *regni*, “of the kingdom,” is absent in B 1 and 2.]. This act increased his majesty and [Note: *et* is absent in manuscripts 1 and 2.] struck no small terror into foreign nations.

Then, having dismissed his son to Aquitaine, he himself, as was his custom, although exhausted by old age, set out to hunt not far from the royal residence at Aachen [Note: *regiae*, “of the royal residence,” in B 1 and 2.] [Note: *Aquisgrani* is read as *aquisgrani* in 1; *aquasgrani* in 4, 5, 8b, 10, 10b, and B 1, and by most of the remaining manuscripts.]. Having spent the remainder of the autumn in this activity [Note: *in*, “in,” is absent in B 1–4.], he returned to Aachen around the Kalends of November [Note: *novembres* in B 5; *nouemb.* in B 1, 2, and 10.]. While wintering there [Col. 0054B] [Note: *hiemaret* in 3b, 4, 11, B 1, 2, and 3–4; *hiemaverat* in 7.], in the month of January, he was stricken by a severe fever and took to his bed [Note: *v. c.* in 4, 8b, 10, 10b, 11, B 1, 2, and others; the abbreviated reading is uncertain.].

Immediately [Col. 0055A], as he was accustomed to do during fevers, he imposed abstinence from food upon himself [Note: The second hand in manuscript 1 corrected *inedia* to *inediam*, “abstinence.”], thinking that by this restraint [Note: B 1–4 read *in hac*, “in this,” before “restraint.”] the illness could be driven away or at least mitigated. But when pain in his side was added to the fever [Note: Manuscript 1 reads *dolorem*, “the pain,” for *dolore*, “pain.”], which the Greeks call pleurisy [Note: *pleuresim* in 8b; *vocant*, “call,” in 2c, 11d, and 8b.], and while he continued fasting and sustained his body in no other way than by very infrequent drinking, on the seventh day after taking to his bed, having received Holy Communion [Note: *communia* in B.], he died, in the seventy-second year of his life [Note: *septagesimo* was corrected to *septuagesimo* in manuscript 1.], and [Note: *et*, “and,” is absent in B 1–4.] in the forty-seventh year since he had begun to reign, on the fifth day before the Kalends of February [Note: *febroarias* in 3b.], at the third hour of the day [Note: Manuscripts B 9 and 10 continue *tertia in basilica sancti salvatoris et sancte Dei genetricis marie honorifice sepultus est* (“at the third hour; he was honorably buried in the basilica of Saint Saviour and of holy Mary, Mother of God”) and end here.].

31. His body was washed and prepared according to solemn custom and, amid the greatest mourning of the whole people, was brought into the church and buried. At first there was uncertainty where he ought to be laid [Note: *reponeri*, corrected to *reponi*, in manuscript 1.], because while alive he had given no instruction about this [Note: Manuscript 1 reads *praecipisset* for *praecepisset*, “had instructed.”]. At last everyone agreed [Note: *insedit* in B 3–4.] that he could nowhere be buried more honorably [Col. 0055B] than in the basilica that he himself had built in that same settlement at his own expense, out of love for God and our Lord Jesus Christ and in honor of his holy and eternal Virgin Mother.

He was buried in this basilica [Note: This phrase is absent in B 1 and 2.] on the same day on which he died, and a gilded arch was erected above the tomb [Note: Manuscript 8b reads *super* for *supra*, “above.”], bearing an image and an inscription [Note: Manuscript 1 reads *extrutus* for *exstructus*, “erected.”]. The inscription was written as follows [Note: *erat*, “was,” in B 3, 3b, 3c, perhaps 3d and 4, and B 4b. The earlier part of the epitaph survives in a manuscript of the late ninth century in the Vienna Palatine Library, no. 354, theolog., fol. 55; there it reads “forty-six years”]: 

> BENEATH THIS SEPULCHRAL CHAMBER LIES THE BODY OF CHARLES THE GREAT, THE ORTHODOX EMPEROR, WHO NOBLY ENLARGED THE KINGDOM OF THE FRANKS AND HAPPILY RULED IT FOR FORTY-SEVEN YEARS. HE DIED A SEPTUAGENARIAN [Note: B 1, 2*, and 3–4 read *LXXII aetatis anno, indictione VI, V Kal. Febr.*, “in the seventy-second year of his age, in the sixth indiction, on the fifth day before the Kalends of February.”] IN THE YEAR OF OUR LORD [Note: *Christi*, “of Christ,” in 11c; *ab incarnatione Domini*, “from the incarnation of the Lord,” in 2b–c and 3c; *anno incarnatione Domini*, “in the year of the incarnation of the Lord,” in B 5; *anno 814 a Domini incarnatione*, “in the year 814 from the Lord’s incarnation,” in 11 and 11b. The phrase “in the year of our Lord 814” is absent in 3b, 5, 6b, and 7; “of the Lord” is absent in 8 and B 2.] 814. IN THE SEVENTH INDICTION [Note: So manuscript 1, as very frequently occurs in writers and documents of the Middle Ages; most of the other manuscripts have *indictione*, “indiction.” It is absent in manuscripts 2 and 5; B 5 reads “sixth.”] [Note: “VII” is absent in manuscripts 2, 3b, 5, 10, and 10c, and in Reuber’s manuscripts.] ON THE FIFTH DAY BEFORE THE KALENDS OF FEBRUARY [Note: *V Kal. Febr.*, “the fifth day before the Kalends of February,” is absent in manuscript 11. With these words manuscripts 8 and 8* end.]

32. As the end drew near [Col. 0055C] [Note: *Adpropinquantis* in 4, 5, B 1, 2, and C; *A. vero f.* in 10; *Appropinquante vero finis termino* in 10b and 10c.], there were many portents [Note: *praesagia*, “portents,” in manuscripts 1, 4, 8b, 4b, 9, 10, and 10b–c; *prodigia*, “prodigies,” in 2, 2b–c, 3*, 3b–c, 5, 6b, 7, 7c, 10g, 11, 11b–d, 13?, and B 1–5, 8.] [Note: Compare Suetonius, *Augustus*, chapter 97.], so that not only others but he himself [Note: *et* in 8b.] sensed that it was threatening him.

For three successive years, immediately preceding the end [Note: *terminos* in manuscript 1.] of his life, there were very frequent eclipses of both sun and moon, and [Col. 0056A] a certain spot of dark color was seen on the sun for seven days [Note: Einhard himself reports in the *Annals*, under the year 807, that it was Mercury; here, however, imitating Suetonius, he presents the matter more as a portent.]. The portico that he had constructed between the basilica and the palace with laborious workmanship collapsed suddenly on the day of the Lord’s Ascension, falling to its foundations [Note: The reading *c. est* occurs in 5, B 3, 3b, 3d, 4, 4b, and 5.].

Likewise, the bridge over the Rhine [Note: *rheni* in 4, 11, B 3c, and others; *remi* in B 3 and 3d; *reni* in 3b and B 3b; *in Rheno* in B 1.] at Mainz [Note: *mogontiacum* in 4, B 1, and 3b, and others; *mogontiam* in 3b, B 4b, and 5; *moguntiacum* in 8b.], which he himself [Note: Absent in B 1 and 2.] built of wood over ten years [Note: *decim* in B 1; the remaining manuscripts have the numeral *X*.] with immense labor and remarkable workmanship, so that it seemed capable of lasting forever [Note: *perenniter* in 4, 6b, 8b, B 1, 2, 5, and others.] [Note: *durare posse*, “to be able to last,” is absent in 2b–c, 3*, 3b, 3c?, 9, 11, and 11b–d.], was accidentally [Note: *fortuito* in 10, 11, 11b, 11d, B 3b, and 4b; *forti* in 10b; *for.* in 10c.] consumed by fire in three hours, so completely that, except for the part covered by water, not even [Note: *nec* in B 1–4.] a single splinter [Note: *astula* in 3b, 4, 5, 10, 10b–c, and Reuber’s manuscripts.] remained of it.

He himself, too, while conducting his final expedition into Saxony [Note: *saxonia* in 7, 10, 10b–c, and 11.] against Godfrey [Note: *gotofridum* in 3b and 11; *godefridum* in 8b, 10, and B 5; *dogofridum* in 10b; *togofridum* in 10c; *logofridum* in 10c*; *godfridum* in B 3c.], king of the Danes, had one day left the camp before sunrise [Note: “Before sunrise” was added by a second hand in manuscript 1.] and begun his march when suddenly he saw a torch descend from heaven with a great light [Note: B 3–4 read *luce*, “brightness,” instead of *lumine*, “light.”] and pass from right to left through the clear air [Col. 0056B]. While everyone was wondering [Note: *ammirantibus* in 4, B 1, 2, 3b, and 4b.] what this sign might portend [Note: Manuscript 1 has the abbreviation *qd* for *quid*, “what.”], suddenly the horse on which he was sitting [Note: *sedit* in 10b.] [Note: *quem super* in 4b, 9b, 10, and 10b; *super quem* in 10c and 11b; *in quo* in 3* and B 3c; *cui insidebat* in 2c, 8b, and 11d.] [Note: *De equo quem sedebat, cum velocitate descendens* (“descending swiftly from the horse on which he was sitting”), in the *Life of Saint Wandregisel*, seventh century, chapter 7, in Mabillon, *Acta Ordinis Sancti Benedicti*, century II, p. 528. *Quia expeditum equum sidebat* (“because he was sitting on a ready horse”), in the Anonymous of Salerno, in Muratori, *Scriptores*, vol. II, p. 300. Compare also below, Ermoldus Nigellus, book III, verses 565 and 596.] fell headfirst [Note: *deosum*, corrected to *deorsum*, in the second hand of 1.] and threw him so violently to the ground that the clasp of his cloak broke and the belt of his sword was shattered [Note: *baltheoque* in 8b, B 3, 3c–d, and 5.]. His attendants, who were hurrying to him, disarmed him and lifted him up [Note: *laevaretur* in manuscripts 1 and 4.], not [Note: Omitted in 8b, 10b, 10g, 12, 16, and B 5; *nec* in 6b and in 2b, 3b–c, 4, 5, 7, 9, 10c, 11, 11b–d, B 1, 2, and 2b; *non ut* in B 3–3d.] without assistance [Note: *aminiculo* in 2, 10b, and B 3c; *amiculo*, corrected to *aminiculo*, in 5; *amiculo* in 10g, 11, 12, 16, and 17; *exarmatus aut sine amiculo*, “disarmed or without a cloak,” in 7b; *adminiculo* in 8b, 10, and others.].

The spear that he happened at that moment to be holding in his hand [Note: *quem* for *quod* in manuscript 1; *manum* for *manu* in manuscript 1.] also slipped away from him and was thrown a distance of twenty feet or more.

In addition to this, there was frequent [Note: *crebre* in 3b.] trembling of the palace at Aachen [Note: *aquiensis* in B 1; *aquis* in 2; *equensis* in B 2.], and in the houses where he stayed there was a continual creaking of the ceilings [Note: *adsiduus* in B 1.]. The roof of the basilica, beneath which he was later buried, and a golden apple with which the ridge of the roof was adorned were shattered by a lightning strike [Note: *fluminis*, “of a river,” instead of *fulminis*, “of lightning,” in 4 and B 1.] and thrown onto the house of the bishop, which stood next to the basilica [Note: *quod* for *quo* in B 1 and 2.].

In the same [Col. 0056C] [Note: *eodem* in manuscript 1.] basilica, on the rim of the crown that surrounded the inner part of the building between the upper [Col. 0057A] and lower arches [Note: Manuscript 1 reads *artus*, “joints,” instead of *arcus*, “arches.” Manuscripts 2b–c, 3*, 3b, 10b–c, c, and 11b–d read *inferiorem*, “lower,” instead of *interiorem*, “inner.”], there was an epigram [Note: *synopide* in 8b, B 4b, and 5; *synope descriptum*, “written in red ochre,” in 11.] written in red pigment [Col. 0057C] [Note: *Colore rubro*, “in red color.”], identifying the builder of the same temple. Its final line read:

> CHARLES, THE PRINCE.

Some people observed that, in the same year in which he died, a few months before his death, the letters that expressed [Note: *exprimebat*, corrected to *exprimebant*, in manuscript 1; *exprimebat* in 3b.] the word “PRINCE” [Note: *principem*, “the prince,” in 6b and B 4b; *quas principes*, “which [letters] ‘prince’,” in B 3c.] had been so erased [Note: The words *ita esse deletas*, “had been so erased,” are absent in 3c.] that they could not be seen at all [Note: Compare Suetonius, *Augustus*, chapter 97.]. But he either concealed or disregarded all these matters as though none of them in any way [Note: *quodlibet*, corrected to *quolibet*, in manuscript 1.] concerned his affairs.

Source/review notes: Every supplied Testament witness reading and siglum is retained in a complete apparatus; damaged or uncertain readings remain marked rather than normalized.

### 33. Wills

He began to draw up wills by which he might make his daughters and children by concubines heirs to some portion of his estate [Note: [Col. 0058C] Ibid., c. 101; [Col. 0057] MS 1 reads *quibus ex concubinis filias et liberos* (“by which [he might make] daughters and children by concubines”); MSS 1 and 3* read *filios ex c.* [probably *concubinis*, “sons by concubines”]; MSS 11, 11b–d read *filios* (“sons”).]. But, having been begun late, they could not be completed. Nevertheless, three years before his death, in the presence of his friends and officials, he made a division of his treasures, money, clothing, and other household goods [Note: *suppellectulis* in one witness; *suppellectilis* in others]. He charged them that, after his death, the distribution he had made should remain valid through their approval [Note: “in the third year” in witnesses B 3–4]. He set down in a brief document what he wished to be done with the things he had divided; its arrangement and wording are as follows [Note: The following words through “HOLY SPIRIT” are written in one manuscript in larger letters. It seems clear that they occupied the very first line of the brief document and were written in the elongated script customary for the period]:

> **IN THE NAME OF THE LORD, GOD ALMIGHTY, FATHER, SON, AND HOLY SPIRIT.** An inventory and division made by the most glorious and most devout lord Charles, emperor and august [Note: Some witnesses omit “in the name of the Lord” and “august”; one begins “Here begins the inventory”], in the year from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 811, in the forty-third year of his reign in Francia [Note: Some witnesses read forty-four], and in Italy in the thirty-seventh year [Note: One manuscript alone reads XXXVII, but the final *I* was drawn below the line by the scribe, and this part appears later to have been erased by the same hand, which also slightly touched the *I*. Another witness reads XXXIII; all the others read XXXVI], and in the eleventh year of his empire [Note: Some read XII], in the fourth indiction [Note: The forms *indicione* and *indictione* occur in many witnesses], which he resolved to make with devout and prudent deliberation and completed with the Lord’s assent, concerning his treasures and money [Note: *peccunia* in several witnesses; the others have *pecunia*] found on that day in his chamber [Note: One witness reads *camara*, “chamber,” rather than *camera*].

> In this he wished especially to take precautions that not only should the distribution of alms, which is customarily made among Christians from their possessions, also be carried out on his behalf in due order and arrangement from his money [Note: One manuscript adds “alone,” or “also”], but also that his heirs, with every ambiguity removed, might clearly know what ought to belong to them and might divide their shares among themselves in a proper partition, without dispute or contention.

> With this intention and purpose, he first divided all his property and household goods [Note: *suppellectilem* is the reading of several witnesses; others have *suppellectilem* or related forms], consisting of gold, silver, jewels, and royal ornaments that, as stated, could be found in his chamber on that day, into three divisions; then, subdividing two of those portions, he made twenty-one parts from them, while reserving the third intact [Note: Some witnesses have the singular *eadem* rather than *easdem*; one has *partes*].

> The division of the two portions into twenty-one parts is arranged as follows: since twenty-one metropolitan cities are known to exist in his kingdom, each one of those portions is to reach each metropolis through the hands of his heirs and friends in the name of alms [Note: One witness omits “in the name of alms”]. The archbishop who is then ruler of that church shall receive the portion given to his church and divide it with his suffragans, in such a way that one-third shall belong to his church and two-thirds shall be divided among the suffragans [Note: One witness reads “that particular portion”].

> Of these divisions, made from the first two portions and corresponding to the number—twenty-one—of the metropolitan cities, each, separated from the others, lies stored separately in its own repository, with the name of the city to which it is to be carried written upon it [Note: Some witnesses omit “with”; one omits “to which it is to be carried”; another omits the whole phrase concerning the inscription]. The names of the metropolitan cities to which this alms or largess is to be given are these [Note: Some witnesses begin “The names, then”]:

> Rome, Ravenna, Milan [Note: *Mediolanium* in one witness], Forum Iulii [Note: Also *foro Iulii*], Grado [Note: Variants include *gradis*, *vradus* in the margin, *warendus*; one marginal gloss calls it “a city of Italy”], Cologne, Mainz [Note: Variants include *Mogontia*, *Magontia*, *Maguntiacum*, *Moguntiacum*, and others], Iuvavum, which is also Salzburg [Note: The name appears as *Iuuarium*, *Iuuauium*, *Iuuanium*, *Iuvaiun*, *Iuvausum*, *Vivanum*, and other forms; Salzburg appears as *Salzbur*, *Saltzburg*, *Salzburch*, *Salzeburch*, *Salzeburk*, *Salzeburg*, *Salzbruc*, *Salzburuo*, *Saliszburch*, *Saltburg*, *Salburg*, and *Saltzburgum*], Trier [Note: Also *Treveri*], Sens [Note: Also *Renones*], Besançon [Note: Also *Vesontium*], Lyon, Rouen [Note: Also *Rotamagus*, *Rotomagum*, *Rodomagum*, *Ratumagus*], Reims [Note: Also *Remi*], Arles [Note: Also *Arales*, *Arelatum*, and *Areles*], Vienne, Darantasia [Note: Also *Daratansia*, *Darentasia*, and *Tarantasia*], Embrun [Note: Also *Ebrodonum* and *Ebredunum*], Bordeaux [Note: Also *Burdegala*], Tours [Note: Also *Turonis* and *Turonus*], and Bourges [Note: Also *Biturigies*, *Bituries*, and *Bituricas*].

> In one witness the names Rouen, Trier, Sens, Besançon, and Lyon are preceded by two additional names; in witnesses B 3–4, Mainz, Grado, and Cologne are preceded by two; Trier, Iuvavum, Lyon, Arles, Embrun, and Bourges likewise receive preceding duplicate names in various witnesses.

> The arrangement of the one portion that he wished to be reserved intact is this: after the other two had been distributed among the divisions described above and stored under seal, this third portion was to remain in daily use [Note: Also “ordinary daily use”; several witnesses have *cottidiano*], as property clearly not alienated from the ownership of its possessor by any obligation of a vow [Note: One witness reads “as three things”; another “as property”], and this for as long as he remained alive or judged its use necessary for himself [Note: Some witnesses omit “or”; one has a different wording, “or until he judged its use necessary for himself”; another omits part of the sentence].

> After his death, or his voluntary renunciation of secular possessions, this same portion was to be cut into four subdivisions. One of them was to be added to the twenty-one portions mentioned above [Note: One witness has the plural “portions”; another reads “to one”], another was to be taken by his sons and daughters and by the sons and daughters of his sons and divided among them in a just and reasonable partition [Note: One manuscript adds *vero*, “indeed”; another reads *ad supra*, apparently “in addition”]. The third was to be distributed, according to the customary Christian practice [Note: One witness reads *morte*, “in death,” instead of *more*, “in the manner”], for the use of the poor [Note: Some witnesses have “the poor” rather than “among the poor”]. The fourth, likewise in the name of alms [Note: Variant spellings include *eleimosine* and *eleemosynae*], was to be distributed for the support of the male and female servants serving in the palace.

> To this third portion of the whole sum, which like the others consists of gold and silver, he wished to add all vessels and utensils of bronze, iron, and other metals, together with arms and clothing and other household goods, whether precious or cheap, made for various uses [Note: The witnesses vary between masculine, feminine, and plural forms of “made”; one corrects *patis* to *partis*, “portion”]. These include curtains [Note: Cloths or draperies; German *Gardinen*], coverlets, carpets, felt cloths [Note: A kind of woollen cloth, German *Filz*], hides, and pack-saddles [Note: *Sagmata* are saddles, loads placed upon saddles, and then vessels], and whatever might be found that day in his chamber [Note: Also *camara*] and wardrobe, so that from this larger portion further divisions could be made and the distribution of alms could reach more people.

> He ordered that the chapel—that is, the ecclesiastical establishment—which he himself had made and accumulated, as well as what had come to him from his paternal inheritance [Note: One manuscript has “what came to him from his paternal inheritance”; the others have “what came to him from his paternal inheritance” in a slightly different order], should remain whole and not be divided in any way [Note: One manuscript supplies *esset*, “should be”]. If any vessels, books, or other ornaments were found that clearly had not been contributed by him to that chapel [Note: One manuscript adds “not” in a different position], whoever wished to have them was to buy and keep them upon paying a fair assessed price [Note: Some witnesses read *praemium*, “reward,” rather than *pretium*, “price”]. He likewise decreed concerning the books [Note: One witness omits “and concerning”], of which he had gathered a great abundance in his library [Note: One witness omits “in his”; another reads “which he had already gathered”], that those who wished to have them should redeem them at a fair price and that the price should be distributed among the poor [Note: Some witnesses read “the poor”].

> Among the rest of his treasures and money, there are known to be three silver tables and one golden table, all of exceptional size and weight [Note: The witnesses vary between *pecunias*, “moneys,” and *pecuniam*, “money”; one may have *Parisienses*]. Concerning these he decreed that one of them, square in shape and bearing a representation of the city of Constantinople, should be carried to Rome, to the basilica of blessed Peter the apostle, among the other gifts assigned for that purpose [Note: One manuscript originally had *ab*, “from,” corrected to *ad*, “to”; another originally had “to the blessed” and corrected it to “to the basilica of blessed Peter”]; and that another, round in shape and decorated with an image of the city of Rome [Note: One witness has “image” rather than “effigy”], should be given to the episcopate of the church of Ravenna [Note: Some witnesses read “to the bishop”].

> The third [Note: On its fate, see Thegan, ch. 8, and the Annals of St Bertin, s.a. 842], which greatly surpasses the others both in workmanship and in heaviness of weight, being joined from three circles [Note: One manuscript first had “depicted” or “described” and then supplied or corrected it to “joined”; the witnesses have *conexa*, *connexa*, or *convexa*], contains a representation of the whole world in fine and minute delineation; and the golden one, which was said to be the fourth [Note: One manuscript has “and [lacuna] (the golden one?)—that which was called the fourth, namely the golden one.”], he appointed to be divided among his heirs and to increase the portion destined for alms [Note: Variants read “as an addition,” “for the increase of that portion,” “between the sons,” or “in its case and as an addition”].

> This constitution and arrangement he made and established in the presence of the bishops, abbots, and counts who were then able to be present, whose names are written here [Note: One witness has “whose names were written”; the note observes that the rest of the sentence is absent in one manuscript].

**Bishops:** Hildebald [Note: Cologne. Also *Burgardus*, *Burcardus*, *Burghardus*, *Buruchardus*, and *Burchartus*], Meginhardus [Note: Also *Mehingardus*, *Meginardus*, *Meingardus*, *Meinhardus*, *Mainardus*, and *Meginhartus*], Hatto [Note: Also *Atto*, *Ato*, and *Hazza*], Rihwinus [Note: Also *Riuhuinus*, *Richuuinus*, *Riuchwinus*, *Ricwinus*, *Riwinus*, *Richuinus*, *Richwin*, and *Riguinus*], Edo [Note: Also *Eddo* and *Etto*], Ercangarius [Note: Also *Ercamgarius*, *Erchangarius*, *Erchengarius*, *Erchemgarius*, *Erkengarius*, *Ermingerius*, *Archangarius*, and *Archarius*], Geroldus [Note: Also *Geraldus* and *Gerholthus*], Bero [Note: Also *Pero*], Hildigerus [Note: Also *Hildigerius*, *Hildigarius*, *Hilgerus*, *Hildigernus*, *Hildigern*, *Hildigerh*, *Hiltigern*, *Hildegern*, *Hildegernus*, *Hildecent*, *Aldegerius*, *Hiltegernus*, and *Hiltiegernus*], and Rocculfus [Note: Also *Rocculfus*, *Rhoculfus*, *Roculfus*, *Hroccolfus*, *Hrocolfus*, *Brocolfus*, *Riculfus*, and *Ricolphus*].

[Note: In one manuscript John is written immediately after Hildebaldus; in witnesses B 2–4 Edo is written before Rihwinus. See also above, Treatise I, page 310, line 55.]

All these provisions his son Louis [Note: The witnesses read *Hludowicus*, *Iudowicus*, *Iuodewicus*, *Iudewicus*, and *Iudouicus*], who succeeded him by divine command [Note: Some witnesses omit “succeeded him”], took care to fulfill as quickly as he could after his death, with the greatest devotion [Note: Several witnesses omit this phrase], having inspected the same brief document.

[Note: Some manuscripts add concluding formulas such as: “Here ends the life of the unconquered august Charles the Great”; “The life of the most excellent, most distinguished, and piously remembered Charles, illustrious august, is completed”; “The life of the most excellent and most distinguished, piously remembered, unconquered august Charles is finished”; “The book ends, thanks be to God, amen”; “After the genealogy from Arnulf to Lothair I, here ends the life of King and Emperor Charles”; “Here ends the first book. The second begins”; “Here ends the life of the emperor Charlemagne”; “Here ends the life of Charles the Great, emperor of the Romans and king of the Franks”; and “The life of Charles the emperor ends. Thanks be to God, amen.” In some manuscripts B verses follow. In B 2 b, however, the words “Here ends the life of Charles the Great” occur first.

Another group of manuscripts states: “The remaining deeds and exploits of his life, or those commonly sung of him in poems, are not fully described here; seek them in the life which Alcuin wrote about him.” The editor remarks that the life said to have been written by Alcuin is not different from the present work. In a twelfth-century canon-law collection in a manuscript of the Imperial Library of Vienna, catalogued as no. 91, the following is found among other material:

> “From the deeds of Charlemagne according to Alcuin: At the request and entreaties of Hadrian, bishop of the city of Rome, King Charles undertook war against the Lombards, which had earlier been undertaken by his father, after the pope’s supplication, only with great difficulty,”

together with other passages found above in chapters 6 and 18. See also the description of manuscript 10 g above, page 436.]

# THE COMPLETE WORKS OF BLESSED EMPEROR CHARLEMAGNE, WHETHER RELATING TO HIS WRITINGS, HIS DECREES, OR HIS DEEDS

## PART ONE: DIPLOMATIC CODEX

### FIRST SECTION: CAPITULARIES

## PRELIMINARY REMARKS

[Note: Before applying ourselves to transcribing the Capitularies themselves, we have decided to place before the eyes of readers the three prefaces of the most learned men who edited them long ago—namely, those of Baluze, Bouquet, and Pertz—in order that the nature and origin of those laws, as well as the method of their collection, may become clear. Edition of the *Patrologia*.]

[Col. 0063]

# PREFACE OF ÉTIENNE BALUZE OF TULLE

[Col. 0063A]

I have decided to collect into one body the Capitularies of the Frankish kings, by which they confirmed the reverence owed to the institutions of sacred councils and the decrees of the holy Fathers, and by which the Roman pontiffs once declared in writing before our princes that they too wished to obey; through whose protection and authority sound discipline was long preserved in the Gallican, Germanic, and Italian churches. I shall thereby show my fellow Franks my love for my fatherland and give neighboring and surrounding peoples an example, so that they may recall their minds to the memory of that blessed age when these same Capitularies established public prosperity among them.

For in the age of Charlemagne, as the monk of Saint Gall relates in the first book of his Life, it was considered a mark of distinction to be a Frank and to use Frankish laws. Basil Johannes Herold declares that he knows, from the testimony of the most authoritative writers, that these laws were regarded by the ancients as so august and sacred that they would have found it more tolerable for all other laws, both divine and human, to be disregarded and abolished than for those laws themselves to be violated [Col. 0063B].

[Col. 0063B]

Rome, formerly mistress of nations, oppressed by civil evils and afflicted by prolonged and frequent conflicts and rebellions, when it prayed for an end to the many troubles it had endured, fled here as to a sacred anchor, asking the emperor Lambert, through John IX, the pope, at the synod of Ravenna [Note: Council of Ravenna, chapter 1 and following], that the authority of the Capitularies of Charles and of his sons and grandsons be confirmed, and that whatever had been wrongly done be corrected lawfully—that is, according to those same Capitularies [Note: The reference is to Herold’s preface to the *Code of Ancient Laws*].

The Germans themselves, although separated from the Franks, preserved the name of the Franks and their laws with the greatest reverence for a long period, until the time of the Ottos. Then, as though German affairs were already rushing headlong toward ruin, they rejected the name of the Franks, which in the memory of their fathers had been glorious and distinguished among them, and abandoned reverence for the Capitularies. So evident was the anger of the divine power that thereafter their affairs gradually fell into decay, not without great harm to our religion [Col. 0063C]. Thus the public calamity of that kingdom may rightly be thought to have arisen, among its other causes, from neglect of the discipline prescribed in the Capitularies [Col. 0064A].

I find that the most learned German scholar Hermann Conring held this view in his book *On the Origin of German Law*, chapter 19. There he traces the unhappy condition of the German Church in the time of Burchard, bishop of Worms, when the canonical laws were held for nothing, to the fact that the collections of Ansegisus and Benedict Levita—containing the constitutions of Charlemagne and Louis the Pious—were then not at all in use among the Germans. Johannes Justus Winckelmann calls these collections “a precious treasure of German antiquity and wisdom” [Note: *Notitia veteris Saxo-Westphaliae*, p. 454].

“From the complaint of Burchard, quoted shortly before,” says Conringius, “it is clear how wretched the condition of the canonical laws in Germany then was. Certainly the Capitularies of Ansegisus and Benedict no longer appear to have been in use at that time. For Burchard transferred nothing from them into his books; indeed, he does not mention them even in a single word.”

But before I bring my undertaking together, it seems necessary first to say something about the name itself, then about the manner and method by which the Capitularies were composed by our princes; next about their dignity, authority, and use; when that use was interrupted and when it was restored; and finally about the various collections and editions of the Capitularies [Col. 0064B].

### II

The name *Capitularies* is general, and in the broadest sense refers to every written work divided into various chapters, as the most learned men have already observed. Saint Gregory confirms this interpretation in a letter to the subdeacon Anthemius:

> “John, our brother and fellow bishop, having sent us a *Capitulare* through his cleric Justus, is known, among many other matters, to have informed us that certain monks of monasteries situated in the diocese of Surrentum were moving from one monastery to another as they pleased.”

(*Book I, Letter 40.*)

Adrian I likewise speaks in his letter to Charlemagne, in which he refutes the *Capitulare* concerning the non-veneration of images:

[Col. 0064C]

> “Accordingly, because of your honey-sweet royal devotion, we have given a reply to each chapter.”

[Col. 0065A]

A codex in which the beginnings and endings of the readings and Gospels once sung in churches had been written bears this title in ancient copies:

> *Capitulary of the Gospels for the yearly cycle.*

### III

The name *Capitularies*, therefore, is general and extends to every kind of constitution, whether ecclesiastical or civil and political. These were called *Capitularies* or *Chapters*, as Boethius Epo (*Book II on Sacred Law*, p. 202) and Sirmondus (*Note on Theodulf*, p. 274) correctly observed, because they were composed and distinguished chapter by chapter. The word *Capitulary*, as Sirmondus elsewhere explains (*Note on the Capitularies*, p. 752), signifies a decree arranged and distinguished into chapters.

Nevertheless, a law consisting of only a single chapter was sometimes called a *Capitulary*, as happened with the decretal concerning the prayers of certain bishops, established in the year of Christ 779. Hence it happened that certain laws of the emperors Constantine and Valentinian, which are preserved in the Theodosian Code, are said in the very ancient manuscript codex of Saint Arnulf of Metz to have been taken from the *Capitularies of the Emperor Constantine* and from the *Chapter of Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius*.

[Col. 0065B]

The constitutions of Liutprand, king of the Lombards, which he himself calls *edicts* by the customary and familiar Lombard term, are also frequently called Capitularies in the old cartulary of the monastery of Casauria. It is worthwhile to excerpt several examples.

A charter of Ada, son of Incha, issued in the year 1026:

> “And because the lord Liutprand judged in his Capitulary that any Lombard concerning his property, and so forth.”

Likewise, a charter of Ursus, priest and abbot, issued in August of the year 1030:

> “Because lord Liutprand, king, established in his Capitulary that whoever concerning his property, and so forth.”

Certainly it is better known than needs to be pointed out that the laws of Charlemagne were called Capitularies. Yet they are sometimes also called *edicts* and *decrees*, as in the title of the Capitulary of the year 779, in the note appended to the earlier Capitulary of the year 790, and in Book I of the Capitularies, chapter 112.

[Col. 0065C]

This observation is confirmed by the authority of Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, who, speaking of the constitution issued by Charlemagne concerning the non-division of ecclesiastical property, says:

> “Concerning this edict, part of it is written in your book called the *Book of Imperial Chapters*, chapter 77, where it says: ‘Because, according to the tradition of the holy Fathers,’ and so forth.”

(Citation in the supplied source: *T. II, title 27, chapter 7, p. 320*.)

And in the codex of the Capitularies of Charles the Bald, where the same law of Charlemagne is discussed:

> “Accordingly, the lord Charles the emperor, while he still bore the royal title, issued an edict that neither he himself, nor his sons, nor his successors, should attempt to undertake such an act.”

Indeed, the Capitularies of our kings are generally called *edicts* in the tenth chapter of the third Council of Valence, so that we may understand the words *Capitulary* and *edict* to be synonymous. For the council itself reads:

> “It was agreed that, just as it was commanded by the edicts of the princes, the ninths and tenths should faithfully be paid to those churches from which they had been withheld.”

[Col. 0065D]

The bishops of that council are referring to chapter 276 of Book V and to chapter 99 of the fourth addition. Chapter 1 of the Council of Ravenna, held in the year 904, also refers to those chapters; it commands that those who have not observed what was established and enacted in the Capitularies of the most glorious emperors—namely, the emperor Charlemagne, Louis, and Lothair, and his son Louis—concerning ecclesiastical tithes, should be subject to excommunication.

Thus, the Capitularies call laws what the Fathers of the Council of Valence call edicts.

### IV

That ecclesiastical sanctions, whether general or particular, were once called *chapters* is shown by canon 1 of the seventh Council of Toledo, which reads:

> “For in this way neither the Chapters recently appended to the commands or threats of princes ought ever to be annulled.”

Lupus Servatus, abbot of Ferrières, writing in Letter 42 about the canons of the Synod of Verneuil, says:

> “I have sent you those same canons, or, as you call them, Chapters, once they had been gathered together by my pen.”

The Council of Calchuth in England, held in the year 787, states in its preface:

> “For we wrote a Capitulary concerning each matter and, discussing everything in order, brought it to their ears.”

[Col. 0066A]

Rabanus, in his letter to Bonosus, speaking of Martin of Braga’s collection of canons, says:

> “Likewise, in the Capitulary of the Eastern Fathers, which was established by Bishop Martin and the other bishops, it is found written: ‘If any woman takes two brothers,’ and so forth.”

The Council of Troyes of the year 878, chapter 3, states:

> “So that those Chapters which we established the preceding year at Ravenna in the synodal assembly may be observed by all without disturbance.”

The constitutions of Theodulf, bishop of Orléans; Haito of Basel; Herard of Tours; Hincmar of Reims; Walter of Orléans; Ricolfus of Soissons; and Atto of Vercelli are called Chapters and Capitularies by their authors.

### V

[Col. 0066B]

From what has been said so far it is easily gathered that the name *Capitularies* is general, as we stated, and that laws are understood by the term *Chapters*. Yet there are certain passages of the ancients from which it may appear that there was a distinction between laws and Chapters, and indeed that laws could in no way be understood by the name *Chapters*.

For Louis the Pious, in the preface to the Capitulary of the year 816, speaking of the constitutions he had recently issued concerning the life of canons and monks, discusses worldly laws and Chapters in such a way that he seems plainly to say that laws differ from Chapters:

> “We have also noted what should be inserted into worldly laws and what into Chapters.”

And Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, in Letter 15 to the bishops of the kingdom, chapter 15, speaking of judges acting wrongly, says:

> “When they hope to gain something, they turn to the law. But when they do not think they can acquire anything through the law, they flee to the Chapters. Thus it sometimes happens that neither the Chapters are fully preserved, but are regarded as worthless, nor the law.”

Finally, among the Capitularies of Charlemagne excerpted from the Lombard law, chapter 49, we read:

> “In general we admonish all that the Chapters which last year, with everyone’s consent, we judged should be added to the Salic law should no longer be called Chapters, but only laws; indeed, they should be held as part of the Salic law.”

[Col. 0066C] **VI.** Yet it may be objected against these arguments that there was indeed a distinction between laws and Capitularies, since some matters were contained in the laws that did not appear in the Capitularies, while certain matters were read in the Capitularies that were not contained in the laws; but that this did not prevent the Capitularies from being included under the general designation of “law.” Hincmarus makes this clear in Letter 14, chapter 8, where he immediately lists among the laws what he had first called Capitularies. “For,” he says, “kings and the ministers of the commonwealth have laws by which they ought to govern those dwelling in whatever province. They have the Capitularies of Christian kings and of their forefathers, which they have legally promulgated, by the general consent of their faithful, to be observed.” Concerning these blessed Augustine says: “Although men judge concerning them when they establish them, nevertheless, once they have been established and confirmed, it will not be permissible for judges to judge concerning them, but only according to them.”

Likewise, in the Capitularies of Charlemagne excerpted from the code of Lombard law, the constitutions of that same Charlemagne, commonly called Capitularies, are called laws in several places. For in chapter 22 of those same Capitularies it is ordered that advocates be chosen such as the law commands to be chosen—that is, as it is written in Book Three of the Capitularies, chapter 11. Again, chapter 23 of the same excerpted Capitularies reads in full: “We order that the witnesses be separated from one another, as the law provides.” This passage refers to a constitution of that same Charlemagne, found in the same Book Three of the Capitularies, chapters 10 and 52. Finally, chapter 36 of those same Capitularies contains the following: “As for other cases, let them live according to the common law which the lord Charles, most excellent king of the Franks and Lombards, added in an edict”—that is, according to the Capitularies that Charlemagne added to Lombard law in the year 801.

Finally, Pope John VIII of Rome, when confirming at the Synod of Troyes the capitulary, or constitution, of King Charles concerning the composition for sacrilege, refrains from the designation “Capitulary” or “constitution,” and simply calls it a law. “But we,” he says, “order that the milder law which was established by Charles, the pious prince, concerning the composition for sacrilege, be observed.” For this reason, in the Capitularies issued at Aachen in 816, chapter 20 (Laws, 817), Louis the Pious calls his constitutions “Capitularies of worldly law,” according to which he orders judgment to be rendered in cases involving boys tonsured against their parents’ wishes.

**VII.** Having spoken about the name “Capitularies,” we must next address the matter itself, and first explain how they were enacted and what formal procedures had to be employed in those times for their authority to be valid. Charles the Bald settles the matter in a single phrase in the Edict of Pîtres, chapter 6, attributing the promulgation of a law to the decision and will of the prince, and its enactment to the consent of the people. “A law,” he says, “is made by the consent of the people and by the constitution of the king.”

By “the consent of the people,” I mean not people gathered from the streets—for no one should insolently abuse the word “people” here—but the king’s faithful: that is, the leading men, nobles, and magnates who are the heads of the people. For kings used their counsel when the enactment and establishment of new laws were under consideration and when the question was how peace and tranquility should be secured for the people. “They have,” says Hincmarus, “the Capitularies of Christian kings, which they have legally promulgated, by the general consent of their faithful, to be observed.”

He said “general consent” because these measures were decreed in a general assembly of the nobles, at a general royal *placitum*, as Charlemagne clearly teaches in these words:

> And when, with life as our companion, with God’s help, we come to the general assembly, we desire, with the counsel of all our faithful, to confirm in writing for ourselves, our people, and future generations matters that, with the Lord’s assistance, must remain most firmly and irrevocably. At present we are prepared to establish what is general and concerns all orders, and to communicate it, for love and remembrance of almighty God, to all the faithful of holy God’s Church and to our own faithful. At our next synodal assembly and general *placitum*, where many bishops and counts will have gathered, we shall confirm these matters as you have requested.  
> (*Book VI of the Capitularies*, chapter 371)

Accordingly, in the year 823 Louis the Pious decreed that anyone who neglected to restore churches should undergo the following penalty: “We absolutely desire that he undergo what we have ordained concerning this matter in our Capitulary with the common counsel of our faithful” (*Book II of the Capitularies*, chapter 22; and Book V, chapter 272).

Charles the Bald, in the Capitulary of the year 873 at Quierzy, says:

> The Capitularies of our grandfather and father, which the Franks judged should be held as law, and which our faithful decreed should be preserved in our general *placitum*.  
> (*Volume II of the Capitularies*, p. 231, chapter 8)

Especially notable on this subject is a passage from the Capitularies of Charles the Bald issued at Quierzy in 877, where the prince speaks as follows:

> The Capitularies which our grandfather and father established for the stability and protection of holy God’s Church and its ministers, and for the peace and justice of the people and the tranquility of the kingdom; and those which we established jointly with our brothers, the kings, and with our faithful and theirs; and also those which, with the counsel and consent of the bishops and of our other faithful and God’s faithful, we established at our various assemblies for the causes stated above to be preserved, and which we decree shall remain undisturbed—in the same way we desire and command that they be preserved undisturbed by our son also.  
> (*Ibid.*, p. 269, chapter 2)

It is therefore clear that bishops and the other faithful—namely, abbots, dukes, counts, and others—were present at these assemblies, as is evident from the preface of the Capitulary of 779, the preface of the second Capitulary of 813, the preface to title 34 of the Capitularies of Charles the Bald, and many other passages.

Thus the learned Francis Florens correctly observed (*Dissertation on Canon Law*, p. 170) that in those times bishops, together with the nobles of the kingdom, were summoned to advise the kings in public assemblies convened by them. In these assemblies the decrees of councils were examined, matters relating to ecclesiastical government were arranged, and Capitularies, or laws, were promulgated for the common benefit with the consent of all orders—a consent that, as Marcus Antonius Dominicy writes, was desired so that the Capitularies might acquire the force of law (*Assertor Gallicus*, p. 52).

[Col. 0068A] **VIII.** Accordingly, once the Capitularies had been established by the prince, they were read before the people; and after everyone had consented, all subscribed the new Capitularies. The Third Capitulary of 803, chapter 19, says:

> Let the people be questioned concerning the Capitularies newly added to the law. And after everyone has consented, let them place their subscriptions and hand-confirmations upon those Capitularies.

Hence an old note appended to the Second Capitulary of that same year records that all the *scabini*, bishops, abbots, and counts signed with their own hands the Capitularies added that year to Salic law.

The preface of the Second Capitulary of 813 shows that it had been established in the palace at Aachen with the consent and counsel of the bishops, abbots, counts, dukes, and the other faithful; and that the emperor Charles had confirmed it with his own hand, so that all the faithful might strive to strengthen it with their hands.

The Capitularies of Charles the Bald enacted in the year 844, at an assembly held in a villa called Coulaines, were confirmed by the signature of that prince, the bishops, and the other faithful of God, with the consent of Warinus and the other nobles. Thus their preface reads:

> For this reason, having taken counsel together, we proposed that this document be drawn up, and we also decreed that it should be strengthened by the subscription of all our hands.

This was done, as I believe, so that the law accepted by the people could not be violated; so that what had been approved by the consent of all and strengthened by the hands of individuals would thereafter suffer no opposition and would not be exposed to the complaints of those who resisted it. For, as Melchior Canus teaches, laws that are both requested and enacted with the common consent of the nobles are more willingly accepted by the people than those issued by the king alone (*On Theological Places*, Book I, final chapter, toward the end).

**IX.** Although it is certain that the Capitularies were established by our kings in public assemblies of the kingdom, in the presence of a numerous company of noblemen and magistrates, it must nevertheless be admitted that not everything was established in such assemblies. Many Capitularies were also taken from episcopal councils and synods. Consequently, the judgment of the celebrated and learned Antonio Agustín, archbishop of Tarragona, is entirely correct. In his *Dialogues on the Emendation of Gratian* (Book I, Dialogue 10), he says that he suspects the source of the Capitularies to have been the councils and assemblies themselves in which the emperor, together with the bishops and other counselors, dealt with both ecclesiastical and secular matters.

The great archbishop of Paris, Peter de Marca, explains this observation at length and with his customary learning in Book VI, chapter 25, of *On the Concord of the Priesthood and the Empire*.

Those excerpts from synodal Capitularies, however, were not always made in public assemblies or synods, but sometimes through a delegation from the prince, in private gatherings of bishops and ecclesiastical men who happened at that time to be in his retinue. This can be inferred from the title of the Third Capitulary of 814, where we read:

> Capitularies excerpted by the lord Charles and his son Louis, together with their wisest bishops.

Charles was evidently concerned that, since he wished the Christian religion to remain safe and unharmed and wished the conduct of Christians, moreover, to be ordered according to the best model, Capitularies of the most sacred institutions should be collected from the decisions of the ancient Fathers and the canons of the councils, and should be ordered to have the place of law throughout the kingdom of the Franks.

Benedict the Levite bears witness to this in the preface to his Capitularies. “In the third book,” he says, “after the enumeration of the Capitularies of the same book, certain Capitularies collected piecemeal from the canons by Bishop Paulinus, Master Albinus, and the other masters, at the command of Charles, the unconquered prince, have been inserted.”

And in the brief preface to Book VII:

> Some of these Capitularies were excerpted by the lord Charles and his wisest men, for the sake of the brevity and lightness of the book of canons: some from the beginning of a statement, some from the middle, and some from the end. They must be regarded as highly necessary and retained in memory. The rest were augmented partly by the same men and partly later by the lord Louis, his son, and his nobles.

After those Capitularies had been collected at the prince’s command, they were endowed with his authority so that they might possess the force and strength of public law, just like the other royal Capitularies. This is clearly taught by the brief preface placed at the beginning of the Fourth Addition, where we read:

> We have taken care to collect certain following Capitularies from the decrees of the holy Fathers and the edicts of emperors, and we ordered them, with the general counsel, to be inserted by our chancellor Erchembald among our Capitularies, to be held by the firmest force of law.

It cannot be denied, however, that many Capitularies were established by our princes by their own authority outside the presence of synods and public assemblies. Later, if circumstances seemed to require it, they arranged for these Capitularies to be reread in the same assemblies and accepted by the public consent of all.

[Col. 0069B] **X.** Although these points are certain and beyond all controversy, Jacob Gretser nevertheless declares (*Salmonian Mysteries*, chapter 35, pp. 279, 298; and *Apology for Baronius*, chapter 3, p. 323, and chapter 7, p. 336) that Pippin, Charlemagne, and the other kings of the Franks who established ecclesiastical laws, or Capitularies, for the restoration of ecclesiastical discipline, did not do so strictly by their own authority, but by the direction and permission of the bishops, with the approval of the bishops and councils; indeed, that most of those Capitularies were established by the authority of the Roman pontiffs.

And because Goldastus had sharply avenged this notable and grievous injury inflicted upon the sacred dignity of princes in his *Reply in Defense of the Empire* (chapter 15), and had confirmed with many clear and evident testimonies that Charlemagne had enacted such laws by royal right, Gretser bore this audacity gravely and with an embittered spirit (*Book II against Goldastus*, chapter 4, p. 193). In a speech full of abuse, and moreover misusing the words of Christ the Lord by which he promised the keys of the kingdom of heaven to Peter and his successors, Gretser deprived princes of all authority to decree concerning ecclesiastical matters. He asserted that neither emperor nor king, as such, possessed any ecclesiastical jurisdiction, and that Charlemagne had claimed no right over ecclesiastical matters or persons.

Neither the nature of my undertaking nor the narrow limits of this preface permits me to refute Gretser’s writing at greater length. Its complete falsity must be obvious to anyone engaged in our studies, especially since several highly distinguished men have defended the dignity and authority of princes in learned commentaries. It will suffice to state briefly that, contrary to Gretser’s view, the power of our kings to enact ecclesiastical laws did not formerly depend upon the direction and permission of the bishops. On the contrary, it is established that in Charlemagne’s time ecclesiastical constitutions were customarily examined in the presence of princes and required their confirmation in order to have force (de Marca, Book VI, *On the Concord*, chapter 28, § 1).

Our kings certainly believed at that time that they were lords of the land, not the bishops’ vice-lords, stewards, and ministers, as Gretser seems to have wished to make them. Charles the Bald is witness to this in a letter written to Pope Adrian II in the year 871, concerning Hincmar, bishop of Laon:

> We, kings of the Franks, born from the royal line, have hitherto been regarded not as vice-lords of bishops but as lords of the land; and, as Leo and the Roman synod wrote, kings and emperors, whom divine power has commanded to preside over the earth, have permitted the holy bishops the right of compelling compliance in matters according to the imperial constitutions, but they have not become the bishops’ stewards.

And Saint Augustine said:

> Possessions are held by the laws of kings; kings do not become stewards and agents of bishops through episcopal authority.  
> (Hincmarus, vol. II, p. 706)

[Col. 0070A] **XI.** The same conviction led the most illustrious Cardinal Baronius, when he read in Benedict the Levite that the Capitularies of the kings of the Franks had been confirmed by apostolic authority, initially to understand this universally of all the Capitularies, and to suppose that the Capitularies had been chiefly confirmed by the Roman pontiffs Gregory IV, Sergius II, and Leo IV, contrary to Benedict’s clear and explicit words (Baronius, under the years 819, 845, and 847). He later inferred from this that kings—whom he had previously said possessed no right in ecclesiastical matters—could not, by their own authority, enact ecclesiastical laws; that is, as I interpret him, laws concerning ecclesiastical matters. Rather, they required the concordant judgment of the bishops and the authority of the Roman pontiff (the same, under the years 752 and 819).

If anyone carefully considers Benedict the Levite’s words, however, he will discover that the Capitularies of our kings were indeed confirmed by apostolic authority, but not all of them—only those established in synods held in the presence of legates of the Apostolic See. “For,” says Benedict, “the apostolic legation was especially involved in drafting these” (*Book VII of the Capitularies*, chapter 478).

Baronius is so inconsistent with himself here that what he had stated generally about the Capitularies of our kings being confirmed by the authority of the Roman pontiffs, he later explains of those Capitularies that Benedict himself excerpted from spurious letters of ancient pontiffs. Benedict, fully aware that the authority of those letters was not sufficiently secure but highly doubtful, never cited the name of any author of them, as he did with the others whose authenticity was secure—namely, the letters of the Roman pontiffs Innocent, Leo, Gelasius, Symmachus, and Gregory. Yet, exercising great caution because he knew that what he had taken from them was not considered entirely firm, he took care—as he himself testifies at the end—to have it confirmed by apostolic authority (Baronius, under the year 865).

[Col. 0070B] **XII.** This most learned cardinal went astray in this matter in many ways. First, Benedict did not take those Capitularies from the letters of the Roman pontiffs themselves, whether genuine or spurious, but from the Capitularies of our kings, who had themselves made those decrees, as he teaches in his preface.

Second, he does not say that he took care to have those Capitularies confirmed by apostolic authority, as Baronius supposed. He merely stated that, above all, the Capitularies of the last three books of his collection were entirely strengthened by apostolic authority, because the apostolic legation was especially involved in drafting them.

Finally, it is not true that Benedict distinguished between the genuine and spurious letters of the ancient Roman pontiffs, naming the authors of those whose authenticity was beyond dispute—such as Innocent, Leo, Gelasius, Symmachus, and Gregory—and refraining from naming the others because the authority of the letters attributed to them was uncertain.

Although he cites Capitularies excerpted from the decrees of Innocent, Boniface, Celestine, Leo, Hilary, Simplicius, Felix II, Gelasius, Anastasius, Felix III, and Gregory III approximately fifty times in his collection, he consistently—speaking frankly—refrains from naming them, praising only once a letter of Saint Leo to Theodore, bishop of Friuli. By contrast, he reports Capitularies collected from the spurious decrees of Anacletus, Evaristus, Alexander, Callistus, Fabian, Stephen I, Eutychian, Marcellinus, Julius, Felix II, Felix IV, and Pelagius II approximately fifteen times, without mentioning any of the pontiffs to whom these decrees are attributed.

**XIII.** David Blondel went astray in another way when explaining this passage (*Prolegomena to the Pseudo-Isidorian Decretals*, chapter 5, p. 27). He interpreted what Benedict the Levite says about the royal Capitularies being strengthened by apostolic authority as follows. He had read in a fragment of an ancient writer—whose reliability, however, is not especially certain—that Pope Gregory IV had entrusted his authority in Germany to Autgar, archbishop of Mainz, at whose command Benedict appears to have compiled his collection. Blondel therefore believed that those Capitularies were said to have been strengthened by apostolic authority because Autgar, as a legate of the Roman See and relying upon the counsel and authority of Pope Gregory, ordered them to be written down and later approved them.

Benedict, however, explicitly teaches in his preface that he inserted into his work the Capitularies contained in the last three books of the collection, which he had found scattered in various places and documents, just as they had been issued in various synods and general assemblies; and that he left them exactly as he had found them—that is, without changing anything.

If we are willing to trust Benedict’s own account of himself, as certainly seems entirely appropriate, it will be clear that Autgar did not order those Capitularies to be written down, as Blondel supposed. Consequently, the conjecture that applies Benedict’s words about the royal Capitularies being strengthened by apostolic authority to Autgar is not plausible.

Moreover, Benedict refers that apostolic authority, in unmistakably clear words, to the legates of the Apostolic See who were present at the public assemblies in which those Capitularies were established—namely, Leo, Sergius, George, and others, whose names he had found inserted for each assembly. “The Capitularies of the last three books,” he says, “are all strengthened by apostolic authority, because the apostolic legation was especially involved in drafting them. For we have not inserted their names—apart from the three, namely Leo, Sergius, and George—even though we found them inserted in each assembly, in order to avoid wearying readers and scribes.”

Thus what Blondel says about Benedict’s collection having been approved by Autgar easily collapses. Antonio Agustín, however (*Book II on the Emendation of Gratian*, Dialogue 9), thought that Leo, Sergius, and Gregory were Roman pontiffs—for that is how he read the name mentioned here by Benedict. [Note: [Col. 0071D] Baronius likewise read it so under the years 819 and 847.]

[Col. 0071C] **XIV.** Nevertheless, the most distinguished Peter de Marca, archbishop of Paris, wisely points out that the presence of such legates was not necessary in order to confer authority upon constitutions issued in synods and general assemblies of the Frankish Empire (*Book VI on the Concord*, chapter 27). He further observes that, among the canons of the Gallican synods held in ancient times, none were confirmed through the deliberate presence of legates except those of Liptina and Frankfurt. If legates are occasionally found to have attended public assemblies, this was an honor accorded to men who, having been sent by the Roman pontiff for other reasons to our princes, happened to be staying in their retinue at the time when the assembly was held.

Accordingly, he adds that Benedict the Levite must be read with caution when, in the preface to the Fifth Book of the Capitularies, he says—so as to lend them authority—that most of these measures had been established in assemblies attended by legates of the Apostolic See, who confirmed them by apostolic authority. This passage, he says, must be understood of the last three books of the Capitularies, not of the others.

It should nevertheless be observed that not everything contained in those three books should be considered confirmed by apostolic authority, but only what was established in the presence of legates of the Apostolic See—namely, the Capitularies of Prince Carloman and King Pippin, and perhaps the Capitulary of 826 at Ingelheim, which was issued in an assembly attended by a legate of the Roman pontiff.

Isaac, bishop of Langres, states in the preface to his collection that the Capitularies of Prince Carloman, in whose drafting Boniface, archbishop of Mainz and legate of the holy Roman and Apostolic Church, took part, were confirmed by apostolic authority in the year 742 by Pope Zachary, who established them to be observed irrevocably by all the faithful of God’s Church.

**XV.** Just as the Roman emperors of old sent their rescripts or constitutions to the prefects of the praetorium, so that these might be presented to the people and carried into execution under the prefects’ care, so our princes entrusted the promulgation and execution of their Capitularies to bishops, counts, and royal envoys (*missi dominici*) (see de Marca, Book I, *On the Concord*, chapter 4, § 4).

To make this easier to accomplish and leave no opportunity for evasion, Louis the Pious ordered in the year 823 that the archbishops and counts—that is, the senior officials—receive the Capitularies from the palace chancellor, and that they thereafter provide copies to the lesser counts, bishops, and other magistrates, arranging for them to be reread and transcribed in their counties and provinces.

The edict reads:

> We also desire that the Capitularies which have now, or at another time, been established by us with the counsel of our faithful be received from our chancellor by the archbishops and counts of their respective cities, either personally or through their envoys. Let each of them, throughout his diocese, arrange for these Capitularies to be transcribed for the other bishops, abbots, counts, and our other faithful, and have them reread before everyone in their counties, so that our ordinance and will may be made known to all. Our chancellor, however, shall record the names of the bishops and counts who have taken care to receive them and report those names to us, so that no one may presume to neglect this duty.  
> (*Capitulary of 823*, chapter 24)

Charles the Bald confirmed and renewed this constitution in 853 at Servais, as follows:

> As for the Capitularies of our grandfather and father, which we mentioned above, those among our envoys who do not possess them and require them in order to correct matters entrusted to them according to their provisions shall receive them from our treasury or from our chancellor, so that they may correct and arrange everything reasonably and lawfully.  
> (*Capitularies of Charles the Bald*, title 14, chapter 11)

At the same time, he wrote to the royal envoys—so I believe—as follows:

> We further command that, if you do not possess written copies of the Capitularies of our lord grandfather and our father, you send to our palace, following the custom of your predecessors, your envoy and a scribe with parchment. There he shall receive the Capitularies from our armory and copy them. Then, according to those Capitularies, you shall diligently and vigilantly take care to correct lawfully the necessary proclamations concerning the justice of God and of the people entrusted to you by God.  
> (*Ibid.*, chapter 13)

Again, in the year 864, the same Charles renewed this constitution of his father, copying it word for word (*Ibid.*, title 36, chapter 36).

**XVI.** This responsibility concerned not only bishops and counts, but also the royal envoys, as we have seen—in fact, chiefly the envoys, since it belonged to their office to remedy the negligence of bishops and counts and to correct what they had improperly done in the provinces against the public laws.

An instruction given to the royal envoys in the year 823, chapter 27, says:

> We also desire that everyone know that they have been appointed for this purpose: so that, through the envoys, what we have generally established in our Capitularies concerning all kinds of matters may be made known to everyone, and so that these matters may fall under their administration and be fulfilled by all. If, however, through some such obstacle as they cannot remedy, anything among the matters we have established and commanded should remain incomplete, let this be reported to us in due time through them, so that what they could not correct may be corrected by us.  
> (*Book II of the Capitularies*, chapter 27)

A constitution of Louis the Pious states:

> Let the envoys and everyone in his own jurisdiction arrange for these Capitularies to be reread before the people, and let them be known to all, so that no one may have an excuse. Let them not demand a fine from anyone until these matters have been made known to all.  
> (*Ibid.*, Book IV, chapter 72)

Another constitution of our kings—either Charles’s or Louis’s—concerning the same matter is found in the collection of Benedict the Levite, where we read:

> We command our envoys to inquire diligently into what we have ordered throughout our entire kingdom for many years through our Capitularies to be done, learned, observed, or held as customary; and we command them now to strive earnestly to renew all these matters for the service of God, for our benefit, and for the advancement of all Christian people, and, insofar as they are able by the Lord’s gift, to bring them to completion. Let them report to us fully who among them has undertaken this good struggle and fulfilled it, so that he may have grace from God and from us.  
> (*Ibid.*, Book V, chapter 260, and Book VI, chapter 290)

For this reason, when Charles the Bald issued an edict at the palace of Quierzy in the year 861, he decreed that it should be kept at the palace with the chancellor and sent out from there through the envoys. “For this reason,” he says,

> we have considered it necessary to ask that our instruction concerning this matter be written and, according to custom, retained in our palace with the chancellor, and sent out from there through our envoys, so that no one may deviate from it through ignorance or deliberately.

At the end of the edict the following is added:

> We command that this constitution of ours concerning the present time—while preserving for the future, as we have said, the constitution of our predecessors on this matter—be reread, acknowledged, and observed in our palace and in our cities, in the courts and assemblies, and in the markets.  
> (*Capitularies of Charles the Bald*, title 33)

**XVII.** After establishing a new law, our kings customarily ordered that many copies of it be made, so that it could thereby be preserved and circulated publicly. When Charlemagne issued the Capitulary of 812, which was given to the royal envoys for advancing the army, he ordered the following in chapter 8:

> We desire four copies of this Capitulary to be written. Our envoys shall have one; the count in whose jurisdiction these things must be done shall have another, so that neither our envoy nor the count may act otherwise than as it has been ordered by us in the Capitularies. Our envoys who are to be appointed over our army shall have the third. Our chancellor shall have the fourth.  
> (*Capitulary I*, 812, chapter 8)

In a general letter concerning the form of the canonical institution sent throughout the provinces in the year 816, Louis the Pious orders that a copy of that form be kept in the palace treasury, so that it might clearly be established who had transcribed it carelessly or who had cut away any part of it.

In the privilege that he granted in the same year to the Hispanics who had fled into the Frankish kingdom to escape the brutality of the Saracens, he orders that several copies of that constitution be made:

> We have ordered one copy to be kept at Narbonne, another at Carcassonne, a third at Roussillon, a fourth at Empúries, a fifth at Barcelona, a sixth at Girona, and a seventh at Béziers; and we have ordered a copy of them to be kept in the archive of our palace, so that the aforementioned Hispanics may receive and possess copies from those seven exemplars, and so that, if a complaint should again be brought before us, it may more easily be resolved by reference to the copy that we retain in the palace.

### XVIII

Yet although everyone was under the obligation of observing the constitutions contained in the Capitularies, they nevertheless possessed a particular and exceptional authority in ecclesiastical cases, so much so that bishops and other ministers of divine office accorded them the greatest honor and treated them with the same reverence as the sacred canons of the councils. Thus the bishops assembled at the martyr shrine of Saint Macra in 881 spoke as follows in the preface to the statutes enacted by them at that synod:

> We decree, with the Lord’s help, that the following provisions be observed by all who wish to live justly and devoutly in communion with the Catholic Church, which is Christ’s body. We are not establishing novelties, but summon forth, like lights amid the darkness of wicked men—darkness that blinds the children of distrust—those provisions which our forefathers established according to the path of the sacred Scriptures, which Christian emperors and kings promulgated, and which were observed down to these perilous times of our unhappiness.

But the testimony of the bishops assembled at Trosly in the district of Soissons in 909 appears especially remarkable. They call the Capitularies of the kings “attendants upon the canons,” an expression that, though not especially Latin, signifies that the Capitularies occupy the second place in the Church after the canons and possess equal authority with them. “The enactments of the canons,” they say, “and likewise their attendants, the Capitularies of the kings, as contained in Book I of the imperial Capitularies, chapter 28, prescribe that if clerics and monks have any dispute among themselves, they are to be judged by their own bishop and not by secular authorities” (Council of Trosly, c. 3).

Indeed, the Church approved the imperial Capitularies as regulatory provisions, as Hincmar teaches (Formula for the Promotion of a Bishop, tit. 18, c. 6)—that is, as consistent with the ecclesiastical rules and canons by which the Church is governed—and wished public discipline to be established according to them. For this reason, the Capitula of Herard, archbishop of Tours, which are evidently taken and abridged from the books of the Capitularies, are said to have been excerpted from the body of the holy canons. Likewise, the Capitula of Isaac, bishop of Langres, which were similarly excerpted from the last three books of the Capitularies collected by Benedict the Levite, are called “The Canons of Isaac” in the chronicle of Saint Benignus of Dijon.

> “He composed,” says the author of that same chronicle, “a book called THE CANONS OF ISAAC, because by selecting the most useful material from the books of the canons, he compressed it into a single volume” (vol. I of D’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, p. 416).

For the same reason, the bishops of the Synod of Meaux requested Charles the Bald to order that the ecclesiastical Capitula promulgated by the lord Emperor Charles the Great and also by the lord Emperor Louis the Pious be diligently observed (Council of Meaux, c. 78).

At the Synod of Ravenna, held in 904, at which Pope John IX and Emperor Lambert were present, the following was established above all concerning the observance of the Capitularies of those princes:
