> If anyone has despised the rules of the holy Fathers and has not observed what the most glorious emperors—namely Emperor Charles the Great, Louis, Lothar, and also his son Louis—established and enacted in their Capitularies concerning ecclesiastical tithes, both the one who gives and the one who receives shall, by the authority of the holy apostolic see and by the sanction of the holy synod, be subject to excommunication.

Lambert himself confirmed and explained this constitution by his edict, as I found it in an old manuscript of the Thuane Library. It reads as follows:

> Likewise, from the Roman laws promulgated by the lord Emperor Lambert, chapter 11. If anyone has despised the rules of the holy Fathers and has not observed what the most glorious emperors Charles, Louis, Lothar, and his son Louis established and enacted concerning tithes in their Capitularies, and has attempted to give them elsewhere than in baptismal churches without the bishop’s consent, or has presumed to retain them, both the one who gives and the one who receives shall be punished by those same constitutions. If he does not correct his conduct even then, he shall in every respect be subject to the authority and judgment of the holy apostolic see.

The same Thuane manuscript contains another constitution of Lambert:

> That every tithe be provided to the bishop or to the person appointed by him.

Baronius published this constitution, together with several other Capitularies, from a manuscript of Antonius Augustinus and appended it to the decrees of the Council of Ravenna. Binius, however, attached it to the Roman council of that same year and considered it to be a canon of an anonymous or unknown council. Goldastus followed him (*Imperial Constitutions*, vol. III, p. 299), asserting that these Capitula had been enacted by Emperor Berengar in 903 at the assembly of Pavia.

Yet there can be no doubt that the Capitula published from the manuscript of Antonius Augustinus belong to Emperor Lambert, in view of the testimony of the Thuane manuscript, especially if one compares the constitution of the Synod of Ravenna with the imperial enactment.

But, to return to the point from which we have briefly digressed: just as bishops and the other members of the ecclesiastical order accorded the Capitularies the same reverence as the canons, so our kings wished them to possess equal authority. They did not permit them to be broken or violated as superfluous by those who proclaimed that the sacred canons alone were sufficient for them.

For although civil laws do not disdain to follow divine rules, as the Emperor Justinian says (*Novella* 83; see also *Extra Decretum*, c. 1, *De novi operis nuntiatione*), our princes nevertheless knew that laws not contrary to the canons ought to remain inviolable, and that no one may violate a law enacted by those to whom God wished the authority of making laws to belong.

Accordingly, in the Capitulary of Toulouse of 844, after setting forth Capitula concerning public peace, Charles the Bald finally decreed that bishops should not reject them on the pretext of the canons, as though the canons were sufficient and more than sufficient for them:

> “So that the bishops, under the pretext that they possess the authority of the canons, may in no way resist or neglect these enactments of Our Excellence” (*Capitularies of Charles the Bald*, tit. 5, c. 8).

### XIX

Yet if we consider somewhat more closely the wisdom of the bishops of that age, this concern of Charles may perhaps appear superfluous. For the bishops understood well enough that the royal Capitularies were exceedingly useful for preserving ecclesiastical discipline, as we saw above. Everywhere they held them in high honor, read and turned them over continually, and used them on every occasion. Finally—and this is especially glorious for the praise and renown of the Capitularies—the bishops transcribed the decrees written in them into general and provincial councils, and also into the diocesan synods of their priests.

There is no need here to undertake a long and painstaking enumeration of the royal Capitularies whose words or meaning are found in episcopal constitutions promulgated after the Capitularies themselves had been issued. It is enough to consult the enactments of the councils and synods of that age, whether those written in our Gaul or those held in Germany and Italy, especially the Council of Meaux, the Council of Reims at Saint Macra, the Council of Mainz held in 888, the Council of Cologne celebrated under Emperor Charles III, the Councils of Tribur and Trosly, and also the Capitula of Herard, archbishop of Tours, and Walter, bishop of Orléans.

The bishops naturally devoted much effort to learning the Capitularies because they were required to give an account of them in the general assemblies—that is, in the public assemblies of the kingdom—as may be gathered from letter 28 of Frothar, bishop of Toul, to Hetti, archbishop of Trier:

> “Now the assembly is close at hand, at which the lord whose command it is will undoubtedly inquire whether his command has been obeyed.”

Moreover, since those same Capitularies were highly favorable to churches and ecclesiastical persons, who were greatly assisted and elevated by them, it was necessary to know them so that they could be useful whenever the preservation of ecclesiastical discipline or the affairs of churches came under discussion.

For this reason, in the codex of the Capitularies of Charles the Bald (tit. 46, c. 1), we see Frodoin, bishop of Barcelona, defending the rights of his see against Tyrsus, a priest of Córdoba, by the authority of the Capitularies of Charles the Great and Louis the Pious.

Similarly, Ermengaud, bishop of Urgell, who was a saint, recovered in 1024, with the protection of those same Capitularies, a certain church which the abbot of Saint Cecilia of Elins had seized (*Appendix to the Capitularies*, tit. 145).

At the same time, when consulted by a certain bishop of the province of Reims, as I believe, Drogo, bishop of Beauvais, about what should be done with those who beat clerics, after praising the bishop for excommunicating them, added the constitution on that matter found in Book VI of the Capitularies (ibid., tit. 146).

The Capitularies, as must often be stated, were exceedingly favorable and useful to the Church. This is also shown in the will of a certain Adeledis, who in the twenty-fifth year of the reign of King Henry gave, among other things, to the Church of Barcelona a book of Charles “most useful to the holy Church,” divided into three volumes—that is, as I interpret it, the last three books, which constituted the body of the Capitularies, though divided physically into separate volumes.

### XX

So true is it that the Capitularies were favorable to the Church that, in addition to the fact that their decrees were repeated and copied in the synods of bishops—as Antonio Augustinus also observed (*On the Correction of Gratian*, Book II, Dialogue 10)—those who composed collections of canons in later centuries, such as Regino, Burchard, Ivo, and Gratian, transferred a great deal from the Capitularies into their own collections, sometimes suppressing or supplying an attribution, as Franciscus Florens rightly noted (*Dissertation on Canon Law*, p. 170), a man exceptionally learned in our literature.

Regino, Ivo, and Gratian frequently name the Capitularies. But Burchard, when compiling Regino, preferred to be bold and deceitful: he attributed the Capitula he took from the Capitularies to certain councils or ancient Fathers rather than to our kings. The designation “Frankish,” by which the German kings still gloried in the age of Regino and Witikind, had ceased to be used in Burchard’s time, and thus all reverence for these Capitularies had been stripped away among the Saxons.

Burchard (*Book I*, c. 218 and following) cites the Capitula of Charles the Great by name only once, adding that they had been highly praised by the bishops at Aachen; otherwise, perhaps, he would not have used them. But we have often exposed his deceptions elsewhere, both in our notes to Regino and Gratian and in our notes to the Capitularies.

### XXI

Although many magnificent things have thus far been said in praise and glory of the Capitularies, nothing commends their dignity, majesty, and authority so greatly as the obedience and compliance of the Roman pontiffs. Learned men have noted that these pontiffs once obeyed the laws of our kings and bound themselves to observe them.

Proof of this is drawn from a letter of Leo IV to Emperor Lothar, which Ivo and Gratian quote. These are its words:

> Concerning the Capitula and imperial commands of Your Majesty and of your predecessors, which must be observed and preserved without contradiction: insofar as we have been and are able, with Christ’s favor, we openly profess that, insofar as we have been and are able, with Christ’s favor, we shall preserve them in every respect, both now and forever. And if anyone should have said or should say anything else to you, know for certain that he is a liar (Ivo, Part IV, c. 176; and *II Panormia*, c. 149; Gratian, Distinction 10, c. 9, “On the Capitula”).

Charles Molinaeus treats this argument harshly and tendentiously in his book *On the Origin, Progress, and Excellence of the Kingdom and Monarchy of the Franks* (§ 123 and following). He attacks, in severe terms, the ambition and usurpation of later Roman pontiffs, as well as the sophistries and fabrications of the canonists, who did not hesitate to accuse the aforementioned Leo of indolence and timidity, as though fear had caused him to write and profess this.

To show that their interpretation was vain and foolish, Molinaeus adds that Leo IV, who was subject to the emperor, pleaded his case before Louis II, the son of the aforementioned Lothar, and submitted himself to his judgment, thereby being released from the charge. He appeals to the chapter beginning “If we have acted incompetently” (2, q. 7, c. 41).

Finally, to remove the mark of timidity and indolence from Leo’s reputation, he cites the example of the Saracens whom Leo defeated. Some were strangled in the harbor of Ostia, while others were taken into slavery; Leo used their labor to restore the churches and walls of Rome that had been demolished in earlier Saracen incursions.

[Note: [Col. 0075] See Gratian 23, q. 8, c. 7, “Therefore,” and the observations made there by the Roman Correctors.]

Certainly, anyone who reads somewhat more carefully what is recorded in the *Pontifical Deeds* concerning the election of that same Leo will easily perceive that its principal cause was the Romans’ fear of the Saracens. Because of this fear, they inclined more toward Leo than toward anyone else.

### XXII

It must indeed be admitted that the canonists’ observation which Molinaeus refutes is neither true nor honorable to Leo and to the pontiff of the apostolic see. But it must be considered that this opinion entered their minds in a more unfortunate age, when those who devoted themselves to literary studies could scarcely learn anything except ignorance of those subjects, since the knowledge of the liberal arts and especially of ancient history had been completely excluded and driven into exile.

Accordingly, Baronius, neglecting and rejecting this opinion of the canonists, took another route to extricate himself from the difficulties that confronted a writer of Ecclesiastical Annals in Rome in this passage of Leo’s letter (Baronius, under the year 847).

First, he maintained that Leo had made this promise on the basis of a pact and agreement concluded between himself and the emperors Lothar and his son Louis: they had promised a free and canonical election of the future Roman pontiff, while Leo, in turn, had promised to preserve the imperial rights unimpaired.

Leo’s words to the emperors are as follows:

> Between us and you it has been established and confirmed by the terms of an agreement that the election and consecration of the future Roman pontiff must take place only justly and canonically (Ivo, Part V, c. 14; Gratian, Distinction 63, c. 31).

Baronius further says that Leo’s promise to preserve the imperial rights must be explained by a letter of Nicholas I to Emperor Michael, in which it is stated that pontiffs use imperial laws only for the administration of temporal matters.

### XXIII

Many objections may be brought against this opinion, or rather account, of Baronius—objections that preserve the authority of the royal Capitularies intact and unimpaired.

First, it is clear from the text of Leo’s letter that a complaint had been brought before Emperor Lothar against Leo, on the ground that he despised the Capitularies of the kings of the Franks. In response to this accusation, Leo, determined to avenge the wrong done to him and confident of his own position, replied that he wished to preserve those Capitularies forever and without contradiction, declaring that whatever had been said to the contrary before the emperor was a great and shameless lie.

This interpretation, which is otherwise obvious and apparent to everyone, is owed to Bartholomew of Brescia, whose words are these:

> Lothar had heard that Pope Leo did not wish to observe the imperial laws. Therefore he asked the pope whether this was true. Leo accordingly wrote to him and said that he himself wished to observe the laws without contradiction, and that whoever said otherwise was a liar (Gloss on Distinction 10, chapter 9, “On the Capitula”).

Next, although Baronius admits shortly afterward that Leo’s words must be understood of the books of the Capitularies, here, where the true meaning of this letter is at issue, he transfers what is said about preserving the Capitula and imperial commands to the imperial rights, thereby diminishing, through general language, the authority of what is said about observing the Capitularies.

Finally, he explains those imperial rights from the letter of Nicholas I to Michael, emperor of Constantinople. That letter contains no mention of the Capitularies, nor could it contain one. It says only in general terms that Christian emperors need the pontiffs for eternal life, while pontiffs need imperial laws only for the course of temporal affairs—that is, that pontiffs are subject to civil laws with respect to temporal matters, but not with respect to their persons.

For bishops are gods, and gods cannot be judged by men, as Emperor Constantine used to say.

Baronius interpreted Nicholas’s words as referring specifically to Roman pontiffs so that they might correspond with the letter of Leo IV, although they ought to be understood generally of all bishops. This is so alien to the meaning of Nicholas’s words that nothing could be more alien to it (Nicholas I, letter 8; Gratian, Distinction 10, c. 8).

### XXIV

Again, in order to confirm his opinion concerning a pact made between Leo IV and the emperors Lothar and Louis, Baronius says that at that time Leo requested from those same emperors that Roman law should henceforth retain its own force and proper vigor. He further says that Lothar agreed to the pope’s request and describes his decree on the matter from Book II of the Lombard law.

Before examining this observation of Baronius, however, the reader must be warned that it is not Baronius’s own, but belongs to the Roman Correctors, who, in their note on the chapter “Your Clemency,” Distinction 10, conjectured about a matter which Baronius later presented as certain (Ivo, Part IV, c. 181).

The pope’s words are these:

> We implore Your Clemency that, just as Roman law has hitherto remained in force without being shaken by any storms and is not remembered as having been corrupted for the sake of any individual, so now it may retain its own force and proper vigor (Gratian, Distinction 10, c. 15).

Ivo and Gratian, who preserved this passage for us, make no mention here of Louis, but only of Lothar, as though Leo’s letter had been written to him alone.

Baronius was therefore mistaken, or wished to deceive, when he wrote that this request had been made to Lothar and Louis.

Moreover, the decree of Lothar which the Roman Correctors, and Baronius after them, thought had been issued in response to Leo IV’s request, and which they transcribed from a manuscript of the Lombard law, had been promulgated long before Leo occupied the seat of Saint Peter. It was enacted by Lothar in 824, during the time of Eugene II, as is recorded in an old manuscript of the Thuane Library and in the canonical collection of Cardinal Deusdedit. From the latter, Holstenius published a Capitulary containing this chapter (see vol. II of the *Capitularies*, pp. 318 and 1291).

Thus, on this ground also, Baronius’s opinion concerning pacts concluded between Pope Leo and the emperors Lothar and Louis collapses.

### XXV

Nor is what Baronius says any truer: namely, that Leo had succeeded in ensuring that the election of the Roman pontiff would take place only according to the prescription of the canons, and that the same emperors had abandoned the confirmation of the elected Roman pontiff, which they claimed for themselves, or any other right which they had attempted to arrogate to themselves in his election or consecration.

For if Leo’s words, quoted shortly above, are read without prejudice, it will be clear that the emperors did indeed agree that the election of the Roman pontiff should take place justly and canonically. Yet they did not abandon their imperial rights; rather, they expressly retained them when they decreed that the election should be conducted justly—that is, according to ancient custom, with the imperial right preserved.

Thus the elected pontiff was not to be consecrated before taking an oath of fidelity in the presence of the emperor’s envoys, who were sent by the emperor according to “canonical rite” and custom, as is recorded in the Council of Ravenna (see vol. I of the *Capitularies*, p. 648).

This is so certain that, after Leo’s death, when Benedict III had been elected, the clergy and all the nobles, as is recorded in the *Pontifical Deeds*, drew up a decree and confirmed it with their own hands; and, as ancient custom required, they sent it to the invincible emperors Lothar and Louis.

Finally, Benedict himself was not ordained until imperial legates came to Rome and gave their consent to his election. Even long after these events, the elections of Roman pontiffs continued to require the presence of those envoys, as was formerly stated at greater length in the discussion of Agobard.

### XXVI

But, to return to the Capitularies of our kings: although we do not find that the Roman pontiffs who lived before and after Leo IV promised that they would observe the laws written in those Capitularies, we can nevertheless easily infer that they were subject to them. They themselves sometimes commended observance of the Capitularies, and their cases and disputes were judged by imperial judges.

It is established that at the Synod of Ravenna, held in 904, John IX suggested to Emperor Lambert, who was present at the sacred assembly, that he order the Capitula of Charles the Great and his successors to remain inviolate. Lambert issued a decree on the matter in accordance with the pontiff’s suggestion.

It is also established that the dispute concerning the subjection of the monastery of Acutianus, or Farfa, in the duchy of Spoleto—a dispute between Pope Paschal I and the monks of that monastery—was judged by imperial judges in 824, with Paschal present and offering no opposition. He accepted the judgment by which the liberty of that monastery was confirmed through an imperial command.

A copy edited by André Duchesne exists.

### XXVII

Nothing more illustrious can be brought forward to assert the dignity and authority of imperial judgments than what the author of that same chronicle relates about Gregory IV.

Perhaps at that time Emperor Louis the Pious sent Joseph, bishop—as I believe—of Ivrea, Count Leo, Adelbrand, and perhaps others to Rome as his envoys to administer justice. While they were seated in judgment at Rome in the Lateran palace, a dispute was brought before them concerning certain properties which Ingoald, abbot of the monastery of Farfa, claimed had been seized by Popes Adrian and Leo and unjustly retained by their successors Stephen, Paschal, and Eugene.

Since the case could not be concluded on the first day, it was postponed. Then, after the arguments of both parties had been heard and carefully examined, judgment was given in favor of the monastery.

But Pope Gregory refused to abide by the judgment and appealed from the sentence of the imperial envoys to the emperor. Here the force and extent of imperial authority shine forth most clearly.

We owe the memory of this remarkable and highly singular history to the same chronicle of Farfa. Although the passage is very lengthy, I thought it worthwhile to transcribe it here in full:

> While Joseph the bishop and Leo the count, envoys of the lord Emperor Louis, were seated in judgment at Rome in the Lateran palace in the presence of the lord Pope Gregory, and while Leo the bishop and librarian of the holy Roman Church, Theodore the bishop, Cirinus the primicerius, Theophylactus the moneyer, Gregory son of Mercury, Peter duke of Ravenna, and many others were present, the lord Ingoald, abbot of this monastery, came with Audulf his advocate and reported that the lords Adrian and Leo, pontiffs, had violently seized the property of this monastery—namely, the estate of Corvianum, the estate of Saint Vitus which is at Palms, the estate of Saint Mary in the New Village, and the estate at Bariliano, together with their goods and households. He had therefore continually lodged complaints during the times of Stephen, Paschal, and Eugene, but had been unable to obtain justice.
>
> Then the envoys and judges, to whom the lord emperor had commanded in the city that they administer justice in this matter, questioned, in the presence of the lord apostolic, the advocate of the apostolic see, named Gregory, asking what he had to say about it. He replied that those estates belonged in no way to that monastery.
>
> Then the advocate of the lord abbot produced documents concerning them. They stated that Ansilberga, abbess of Saint Saviour’s at Brescia, had transferred those same estates to this monastery by means of those documents. There was also another document recording that Duke Teudicus had given them to his daughter Ansilberga, as well as a command of King Desiderius and of the lord Emperor Charles, by which they had confirmed those estates, with everything belonging to them, to this monastery.
>
> Then the aforementioned envoys and judges caused the parties to provide sureties, appointing guarantors for both sides according to their law, and ordered them to return to the same assembly on another day.
>
> And so the lord abbot and his advocate came with witnesses, whose names were Gradolf and Guaspert of Rieti. They testified as had been reported. The advocate of the pontiff said nothing contrary to this and could say nothing, because the men appeared to him to be honest.
>
> Joseph the castald of Rieti then came with good and truthful men. They were questioned under the oath which they had sworn to the lord emperor, praised the testimony of the aforementioned men, and affirmed that it could properly be accepted in every respect. They were then questioned separately. The first said:
>
> “I know and remember well that, in the time of the Lombards and of the lord Emperor Charles, I saw those estates belonging to the monastery. I remember that John, Peter, and Christian, monks of that monastery, were administrators there until the aforementioned pontiffs caused them to be taken away by force.”
>
> The others likewise spoke.
>
> Then twelve good and more truthful men came: John, Clarissimus, Meitio, Teuto, Castinus, Audacius, Alboin the physician, Gualispert, Constantine the notary, Peter, Fratellus, and Hyderic the scabinus. When all these men were questioned about what they knew concerning the case, they gave the same testimony.
>
> After this Audulf the advocate swore, saying:
>
> “By these holy four Gospels, what these witnesses have said is true.”
>
> When the aforementioned envoys and judges heard this, they judged that Gregory, the advocate of the pontiff, should restore the estates to Audulf the advocate on behalf of this monastery. He refused to do so.
>
> The apostolic himself also said that he did not in the least trust their judgment until they should all come together in the presence of the lord emperor” (*Chronicle of Farfa*, in Duchesne, vol. III, p. 656).

### XXVIII

Finally, in order to confirm the authority of the Frankish princes and of Frankish laws even in cases involving the bishops of the Eternal City, whether those bishops were plaintiffs or defendants, one must not omit the letter of Pope Leo to Emperor Louis, a fragment of which is found in Ivo and Gratian.

Before quoting it, however, it should be noted that Gratian attributes this letter to Leo IV, whereas Conring believes it to belong to Leo III. His principal reason is that, while Leo IV was seated on the papal throne, supreme imperial power rested with Lothar, not with Louis.

Moreover, no ancient writer records that any hostility existed between Leo IV and Lothar. On the other hand, it is clear from the annals of Einhard that Louis the Pious was angered against Leo III in 815. When Leo discovered a conspiracy formed against him, all the leaders of that faction had been killed by his order, evidently through his own private authority, although he should have referred the matter to the ruler who was lord of affairs.

Einhard adds that Leo attempted to clear himself before Louis by sending envoys to him. It is therefore probable that Leo wrote and sent at that same time the letter of which we are speaking.

Conring’s conjecture is also supported by Ivo of Chartres, who says merely that the letter was written by Leo, without specifying whether he was Leo III or Leo IV.

It must further be noted that during this period there were imperial judges in Rome who remained there continually to deliberate contentious disputes, and that royal authority was always present in Rome and its surrounding regions until the end of that emperor’s life, as an ancient writer commonly cited under the name of “Eutropius the Lombard” teaches.

Accordingly, whenever cases, whether minor or serious, arose at that time, they were judged by imperial judges. If anyone complained that he had been wronged, an envoy was sent by the emperor for that particular matter to investigate the truth carefully, as the same author says.

Thus, when certain Romans had been mistreated by Leo, as I believe, contrary to the order of the law, and had consequently brought their complaint against him before Emperor Louis, as their supreme lord, and when Louis had undoubtedly rebuked Leo and written that he would send envoys to investigate the truth of the matter, Leo replied that he would obey their judgment, while nevertheless asking the prince to send wise men who feared God:

> If we have acted incompetently in anything, and have not preserved the path of just law toward our subjects, we wish to correct everything according to the judgment of Your Majesty and of your envoys. For if we, who ought to correct the sins of others, commit worse ones ourselves, then certainly we shall not be disciples of truth but, as we say with sorrow, teachers of error above all others.
>
> Therefore we earnestly implore the clemency of Your Greatness to send into these regions envoys who fear God in all things, to investigate the matters we have mentioned, and to examine everything carefully, just as they would if Your imperial glory were personally present.
>
> Nor do we ask them to examine only the matters mentioned above with exacting care. If any matters, whether lesser or greater, are reported to them concerning us, let all of them be settled by a lawful investigation, so that in the future nothing arising from them may remain unexamined or unresolved (Ivo, Part V, c. 22; Gratian, II, q. 7, c. 41).

### XXIX

Most interpreters of canon law and scholastic theologians—especially those whose origin or outlook was Italian—think that this should not be regarded as though the pope had been subject to the emperor’s authority. Rather, they say, because of excessive humility he voluntarily wished to submit himself to the emperor’s judgment; thus, as they put it, this was an act of supererogation, not of obligation. For a pope can, out of humility and for the sake of peace, submit himself to another’s judgment.

It is clear that they drew this interpretation from the gloss on this chapter of ours, which later admirers greatly embellished in grandiloquent language, as later adulation is generally wont to do. “Some,” says the author of the Gloss, “were complaining to Louis the emperor about an injury inflicted upon them by Pope Leo. The pope entrusts himself to imperial jurisdiction and asks the emperor Louis to send men to investigate the matter who fear God and who will examine and determine it in place of the imperial majesty in such a way that no doubt can remain in the future, even if greater charges than those already stated should be brought against him.” He immediately adds: “Here the pope submits himself to the judgment of others, which he may do; as is accepted in *ff. de juris. om. ju.*”

They claim that it is an established principle that no one can be judged by an inferior, that the pope is superior to the emperor and to all kings and princes, that he is subject to no judgment except the divine, and that he himself ought to judge all things. Clearly, they confuse the spiritual authority of the Roman pontiff with his temporal authority, and they do not distinguish his civil cases from criminal ones, although there is a very great difference between these matters.

For although it must be admitted that he is the spiritual father of Christian kings and princes, and that his person cannot be judged by secular judges [Note: [Col. 0081C] This is entirely true from the time when a large part of Italy was brought under the pope’s power. But when the Roman pontiff obeyed the emperors, his person, like that of the other faithful, depended upon the judgment of the civil authority. And if any Roman pontiff had happened to be guilty of treason or of any other public crime punishable by death, he could, by the authority of the prince, have been condemned to punishment. This would be easy to prove. But, leaving aside all dispute on that point, one thing must be carefully considered so that the truth of the principle stated may remain unshaken: if, while the Roman pontiff obeyed the emperors, his person had been free from their jurisdiction and supreme power, how many absurd consequences would have followed from this! For it would then also have to be inferred that the persons of all the other bishops—among whom, as Saint Cyprian says, the episcopate is one, of which each holds a portion in its entirety together with the pope, the head of the Church—would not depend upon the jurisdiction of the princes to whom they are subject, regardless of whatever crimes might defile them. Who today would dare defend such a proposition, contrary to the teaching of the Gospel and to right order? Christ said, John 18:36: “My kingdom is not of this world”; therefore neither is the kingdom of his vicars. For the same divine lawgiver says, Matthew 10:24: “The disciple is not above his teacher, nor the servant above his lord.” Hence the Apostle says, Romans 13:1–4: “Let every soul be subject to the higher powers . . . For there is no power except from God . . . Therefore whoever resists the power resists the ordinance of God . . . For rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to evil . . . But if you do evil, be afraid; for he does not bear the sword without cause . . .” The same truth will shine forth to anyone who attends in good faith to the civil laws. Once it is recognized, the opinion collapses that the pope’s person could formerly not be judged by the emperors. (Petrus de Chiniac.)]

—although this is certain, as can abundantly be gathered from what has so far been said and from many other records of ancient times—nevertheless, in antiquity, the civil cases of the Roman pontiffs belonged to the secular court, so long as kings and emperors held Rome in their power, that is, until the death of the Emperor Louis II.

Indeed, it seems to me, unless I am mistaken, that the example of Paschal I shows that accusations brought against them were sometimes submitted to the judgment of princes. [Note: [Col. 0082D] Leo III was judged and exonerated before Charlemagne as judge. See the Annals of Einhard and Regino.] For when a certain uprising occurred at Rome in the year 823, and Theodore, primicerius of the Roman Church, and Leo, the nomenclator, were seized and beheaded, this happened, as Einhard says, because they were acting faithfully in every respect on behalf of the young Emperor Lothair. Some people said that the deed had been carried out either by order or on the advice of Pope Paschal. The Emperor Louis the Pious therefore sent to Rome, to investigate the matter, Adalungus, abbot of the monastery of Saint-Vaast, and Hunfrid, count of Chur.

“When the envoys came to Rome,” says Einhard, “they were unable to ascertain the truth of the matter, because Pope Paschal cleared himself by oath, together with a large number of bishops, from participation in this deed” (that is, with thirty-four bishops and five priests and deacons, as Thegan reports), [Col. 0082A] “and, vigorously defending the killers of the aforesaid men because they belonged to the household of Saint Peter, condemned the dead as guilty of treason and declared that they had been justly killed.”

When the emperor had thus been satisfied, and Paschal had again sent him an explanation of his conduct through envoys, the accusation proceeded no further.

From all this it can be understood that accusations brought during those times against the Roman pontiffs, when the matter concerned the crime of homicide, were referred to the emperors, and that they sent envoys to investigate the truth of the case. For if the emperor had no authority in matters of this kind, why did Leo III send envoys to Louis the Pious, who fully satisfied him concerning the charges brought against his lord? Why did Paschal send him two embassies to prove his innocence? Why did he clear himself by oath before the emperor’s judges? Such things were not ordinarily done without reason or voluntarily, especially by supreme authorities.

Certainly, the rule and dominion of the emperors was evidently less agreeable than burdensome to the Roman bishops of those times, because the temporal monarchy of the Roman Church was already rising and vigorously flexing its muscles. Thus, at last, after various attempts, when, following the death of the Emperor Louis II, Charles the Bald, king of the Franks, had been summoned by them and had come to Rome with the hope of obtaining the Roman Empire held out to him, “he renewed the pact with the Romans,” as Eutropius the Lombard says, “pardoning them their royal rights and the customs associated with them. He also removed from them the royal embassies and the regular attendance or presence at the apostolic election. What more? He granted them everything they wanted, just as things are given which are neither rightly acquired nor expected to be retained. From that day onward, no emperor and no king acquired the honorable customs of royal dignity.”

### XXX

What Einhard says—that Pope Paschal undertook the defense of the killers for the reason that they belonged to the household of Saint Peter, and declared that the dead had been justly killed as guilty of treason—presents some difficulty. For an action for treason can be brought only against one who conspires against the prince or against the commonwealth. But these men had committed nothing of the kind [Note: [Col. 0082D] This is so true that their loyalty toward the emperor seems to have been the actual cause of their death. Yet, to excuse the killers more easily, could Paschal not have accused them of plotting something against public order, or represented them as guilty of some crime equally serious with treason? This is what Einhard may have expressed by the words: “He condemned the dead as guilty of treason.” They very frequently abused this charge of treason. (Petrus de Chiniac.)]

On the contrary, they are said to have been killed because they were acting faithfully in every respect on behalf of the young Emperor Lothair. It cannot be supposed that they were called guilty of treason because they had injured the majesty of the pontiff. For even if we granted that the privilege which they claim was granted to the Roman Church by Louis the Pious, fragments of which are preserved by Ivo and Gratian, was genuine and authentic, it would nevertheless always remain certain that the supreme lord of the city of Rome was not the pope but the emperor; and therefore the crime of treason could not have been committed against Pope Paschal.

For when Louis granted Paschal and his successors the city of Rome, together with the many extensive territories that his successors possess today, he retained for himself supreme dominion over the cities and regions granted: “With our dominion over those same duchies always preserved in every respect,” he says, “and with their subjection to our side” (*Tom. I Capitular.*, p. 594).

Perhaps, therefore, it should be said that the uprising was begun by Theodore and Leo, by whom the household of Saint Peter had been provoked and injured, and that they consequently committed treason because they had used force and laid hands upon men who were under the special protection of the Roman pontiff. It seems possible to infer from the chapters which the Emperor Lothair added at the shrine of blessed Peter in the year 824 that these men were then endowed with privileges equal to those enjoyed by persons under the special protection of the emperor. [Note: [Col. 0083] See the History of the Exoneration of Leo III, where the crime of injured majesty is discussed.] There one reads first:

“We decree that all who have been received under the special protection of the apostolic lord or under ours shall enjoy the protection granted to them inviolably. If anyone should presume to violate it in any way, let him know that he will incur danger to his life” (*Tom. II Capitular.*, p. 317).

### XXXI

Thus far we have treated generally of the capitularies of our kings, and of their dignity and authority, as well as of the fact that Rome and the Roman pontiffs were likewise subject to them. The plan of the work undertaken now requires that we say something separately about Charlemagne, that founder and author of the most flourishing empire of the Franks, and about the capitularies promulgated by him.

The most illustrious Cardinal Baronius (*Ad an. 801*) thought that Charlemagne had been extremely sparing in creating new laws, so that although he lived for so long as king and emperor—he reigned for forty-six years—he is said nevertheless to have enacted very few legal provisions.

Baronius’s opinion seems to be confirmed by Einhard in his *Life of Charlemagne*. Einhard writes that when Charlemagne noticed that much was lacking from the laws of his people [Col. 0083C] and that many contradictions were found in them, he considered adding what was missing and removing what was contradictory, but that he did nothing else except add a few, and imperfect, capitularies to the laws.

These are Einhard’s words:

“After assuming the imperial title, when he noticed that much was lacking from the laws of his people—for the Franks have two laws that differ greatly in many places—he considered adding what was lacking, reconciling what differed, and correcting what was wrong and improperly stated. Yet he did nothing else in this matter except add a few capitularies, and those imperfect ones, to the laws. Nevertheless, he caused the laws of all the nations under his rule that had not been written down to be recorded and committed to writing.”

These statements, I say, seem to favor Baronius’s opinion. Yet I think they should be understood to mean that after Charlemagne became emperor he considered correcting and reconciling the laws of the peoples subject to him, but did not carry out his plans and added only a few provisions to those laws. For he added certain capitularies to the Salic Law and the Ripuarian Law, and perhaps to others as well.

This does not, however, prevent him from having enacted very many general constitutions by which he wished all the nations subject to him to be bound.

### XXXII

John Aventinus, in his *Annals of Bavaria*, notes that Charlemagne continually administered justice with the greatest diligence, sometimes in the morning while he was dressing and putting on his shoes. He adds:

“At night, while lying in bed, he placed writing tablets beneath his head; if anything useful came to mind—as commonly happens in bed—he wrote it down so that it would not slip from his memory” (Aventinus, book IV, pp. 368–371, first edition).

Aventinus appears to have taken this observation from a council held at the martyr shrine of Saint Macra in the diocese of Rheims in the year 881, where the following is recorded:

“Emperor Charlemagne, who nobly enlarged the kingdom of the Franks and ruled it successfully for forty-six years, and who surpassed the kings of the Franks in wisdom both in the Holy Scriptures and in ecclesiastical and human laws, never at any time allowed himself to be without three of his wisest and most distinguished counselors. Rather, by turns and in succession, as it was possible for them, he kept them with him. He kept tablets and a stylus at the head of his bed, and whatever he meditated upon during the day or night concerning the welfare of holy Church and the advancement and stability of the kingdom, he wrote down on those same tablets. He discussed these matters with the counselors who were with him. When he came to his assembly, he carefully presented everything that had been discussed to his full council and endeavored to carry it into effect by common counsel” (*Council at Saint Macra*, chapter 8).

Aelius Lampridius tells a similar story about the Emperor Alexander Severus in his *Life of Alexander*. He says that Alexander enacted moderate and countless laws concerning the rights of the people and the treasury, and that he enacted no constitution without twenty jurists and highly learned and wise men.

But what is read in Aventinus and in the synod at Saint Macra—that Charlemagne, at night while lying in bed, placed writing tablets beneath his head and used to write down whatever then came into his mind—is indeed confirmed by the authority of Einhard, but in such a way that Charlemagne’s concern is restricted to the mere art of writing, which he had taken up late in life.

“He also tried to write,” says Einhard in his *Life of Charlemagne*, “and for this purpose he used to carry tablets and writing booklets around in bed beneath his pillow, so that whenever he had free time he might accustom his hand to forming letters. But the effort, begun too late and undertaken at an unsuitable time, had little success.”

### XXXIII

But to return to Baronius, whom we said shortly before held the opinion that Charlemagne had been extremely sparing in creating new laws and had enacted very few legal provisions during the many years in which he reigned and ruled: it should be observed that no king of the Franks in the ancient period issued as many laws as Charlemagne promulgated. More laws of Charlemagne alone now survive than of all the other kings who lived before and after him, down to Hugh, surnamed Capet.

For, besides the Salic Law and the others to which he added the weight of his authority, and besides the capitularies scattered through the books of the capitularies and through the Code of Lombard Law, whose origin we have been unable to discover, we possess more than sixty constitutions issued by him at various times, whether when he was merely king or after he had assumed the imperial title.

If the laws enacted by him are compared with those decreed by his successors, it is easy to discern in the former the lofty and upright intellect of Charlemagne, and in the latter the declining and downward-sloping magnitude and splendor of Carolingian glory.

It is certainly no wonder that so great a man, who devoted much effort to framing excellent laws and establishing good discipline, surpassed the other princes and left them far behind him. As Benedict the Levite says, “he surpassed the illustrious deeds of all the fathers.” He conquered barbarous nations, greatly expanded the kingdom of Christ, corrected the deteriorated morals of the clergy, and enriched, enlarged, and adorned the churches—especially the Roman Church—with extensive estates, possessions, and privileges (*Tom. II Capitular.*, p. 251; Lupus of Ferrières, Letter 1).

He also restored the study of good literature, established public schools, honored the other liberal arts, and adorned their teachers with rewards. Time would fail me if I wished to recount all the virtues of this greatest prince and review each of his illustrious deeds. I shall therefore pass over them and turn once more to the capitularies.

### XXXIV

There was recently a learned man—Thiers, *De festorum dierum diminutione*, chapter 13—who thought that the capitularies of Charlemagne had not been received in the bishopric of Tours during the time of Herard, archbishop of Tours; or, if it must be admitted that they had been received, that this should not be understood to mean that Herard, the bishop of Tours, had considered the custom of his Church concerning the observance of feast days in need of alteration because of them.

He took the foundation and basis of his opinion from chapter 61 of the capitularies which Herard himself issued in the year 838 at his diocesan synod. In that chapter, when the feast days to be observed by the Christian faithful are listed, certain days are omitted that Charlemagne had ordered to be celebrated in chapter 161, according to the Pithoean edition, or, according to ours, chapter 158 of the first book of the capitularies. These include the commemoration of the Paschal feast, Sunday, the Annunciation and Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary, the three days of Rogation, and the octave of Epiphany. Pentecost, moreover, is proposed as being celebrated on only one day.

I do not think either of these two conjectures of that most distinguished man is correct. It is established that Caesarodunum, the city of the Turones, was then situated in the middle of the Frankish kingdom; that it was counted among the metropolitan sees of Charlemagne’s kingdom (*Tom. I Capitular.*, p. 488; likewise, p. 641); that a council was held there in the year 813 by order of Charlemagne; and that Landrannus, archbishop of Tours, was appointed *missus dominicus* in the district of Tours in the year 823, together with Count Ruotbert, to command and enforce the execution of the royal capitularies.

As for the feast days, what the same learned man says about those omitted presents little or no difficulty. For the things Herard omitted in chapter 61 he mentioned elsewhere: the Paschal feast in chapter 97, and Sunday in chapter 2. In chapter 97 he joins the observance of Pentecost to Easter, saying that eight days of Easter ought to be kept as holidays, but saying nothing about Pentecost. This apparent contradiction must be removed by chapter 35 of the second book of the capitularies, from which Herard’s chapter was abridged. In that chapter of the second book, the Emperor Louis the Pious, son of Charlemagne, decrees that Easter Sunday should be observed with honor and sobriety, and that the entire week should likewise be observed. He then adds: “At Pentecost likewise as at Easter.”

Nor is it surprising that Herard omitted the Annunciation and Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary, since neither of these feasts is mentioned in the capitularies from which Herard excerpted his synodal constitutions.

As for the Nativity, it is indeed established that this day was not celebrated with public observance in the age of Charlemagne. The acts of the Council of Rheims under Sonnatius, whose authority the same learned man uses to show that its observance had been ordered before Herard’s time, are not beyond controversy. They appeared to Sirmond to be so poorly supported and of such doubtful authenticity that he considered them unworthy of inclusion in the collection of the ancient synods of Gaul.

The distinguished scholar further notes that Charlemagne commanded three days of Rogation in the passage cited shortly before from the first book of the capitularies, and that Herard nevertheless says nothing about them.

First, it is certain that no mention of a three-day Rogation appears in the first book of the capitularies, but only in the fifth book, chapter 150, where we read:

“It has pleased us that the greater litany be observed by all Christians for three days.”

This was taken from canon 33 of the Council of Mainz, held toward the end of Charlemagne’s reign.

Second, even if it were true that a mention of this kind of Rogation occurred in the first book of the capitularies, it would not equally be true that Herard omitted it. Although he does not discuss it in chapter 61, he explicitly treats the days of Rogation in chapter 95, even using the term “Rogation,” although that word does not appear in the cited chapter of the fifth book of the capitularies or in addition 3, from which Herard compiled this chapter.

As for the octaves of Epiphany, I admit that the observation is correct and that they are entirely omitted from Herard’s chapters. It cannot, however, be inferred from this that the capitularies of Charlemagne were then neglected in the bishopric of Tours. It may perhaps have been the error of a copyist, who, as we often see in ancient books, omitted the octaves of Epiphany because of the proximity of the word “Epiphany.”

### XXXV

The royal capitularies therefore possessed great authority everywhere and were revered as highly as the sacred canons. Their use continued for several centuries, namely until the time of Gratian and, it seems, even until the reign of Philip IV, surnamed the Fair, king of the Franks.

Nor were they effective only in the kingdom of the Franks; they were also effective in Germany and Italy. As for Germany, numerous records of the ancient period bear witness to this, especially the decree of Otto the Great, king of Germany, issued at Frankfurt in the year 952. In that decree, with the institutions of the preceding kings’ capitularies set before him, he established that no one should oppress virgins or widows or commit abduction (*Appendix prim. Reginon.*, chapter 53).

Many things prove that the capitularies continued to be observed longer among the Italians than among the Germans. Above all, this is shown by the collection of canons and decrees compiled by Gratian, in which constitutions transcribed from the capitularies of our kings are very frequently cited, as the most learned men have already observed.

It might nevertheless be objected that Gratian did not take his material from the books of the capitularies, but from the *Decree* of Ivo, bishop of Chartres, whom he seems to have used as a compiler, and therefore that the capitularies cited by Gratian cannot be used as evidence that the capitularies of the Frankish kings were known in Italy in Gratian’s age.

Indeed, it might seem that Gratian copied from Ivo the chapters of his collection that are cited from the capitularies, unless we could demonstrate by certain indications that he copied some things from the capitularies that do not occur in Ivo.

For Gratian copied a constitution of Charlemagne by which he renewed the law of the Emperor Constantine concerning episcopal judgment. Gratian could not have received this constitution of Charlemagne from Ivo, since it is not found in Ivo. He therefore took it from the capitularies, as he himself shows in these words:

“If anyone claims that this is obsolete because these provisions are not found inserted in this form in Justinian’s Code, let him recognize that they were renewed by Charlemagne, who says among other things in his capitularies: ‘We wish and command that all,’ etc.” (Gratian, XI, question 1, chapter 37, *Volumus*.)

In turn, Innocent III plainly copied from Gratian (*Book VI of the Capitularies*, chapter 366) in a letter written in the year 1204 to the archbishops and bishops established throughout France (Raynaldus, under the year 1203, §58). This letter is found in the second book of the *Decretals*, where it says, among other things:

“Nor should we omit that most humble provision which the Emperor Theodosius established and which Charles renewed, from whose lineage the king himself—Philip Augustus—is known to descend: namely, ‘Whoever has a lawsuit,’ etc.” (*Cap. Novit.*, extant under *de judiciis*.)

Gregory IX and Innocent IV likewise took from Gratian everything they say about this law of Constantine confirmed and renewed by Charlemagne. For at that time they did not return to the sources, but copied everything from Gratian while suppressing his name (see the Notes to the *Capitularies*, p. 1232).

### XXXVI

It was fitting that the Franks should retain the use of the capitularies longer than the other nations, since they had been established chiefly for them and enacted by their kings. Accordingly, their authority was widely effective not only in the age of King Robert and later under Philip I, as is known from the letters and canonical collections of Ivo, bishop of Chartres, but also—as we have said—under Philip IV, surnamed the Fair.

We have seen ancient parchment manuscripts containing a provincial council held at Avaricum of the Bituriges in the year 1286, which the distinguished Antoine Vyon Herovallius most graciously shared with us in accordance with his custom.

In chapter 32 of that council it is decreed that Sundays and feast days should be carefully and diligently observed by everyone, with all servile work prohibited.

At the end of the constitutions, chapter 75 of the first book of the capitularies is found inserted, though with its wording altered, as follows:

“Sunday is to be observed in such a way that . . . and the solemnities of the Mass and those things which pertain to . . . . . are observed, namely, that they neither perform servile work on it . . . . . nor cultivate the fields, nor dry the harvest . . . . . nor make a hedge, nor cut down the forest . . . . . nor cut trees, nor make gardens, except because of the necessity of food or cold; but that they in no way . . . . . grind, nor bake bread, nor work with stones, nor build houses, nor move carts, nor gather at markets, nor engage in hunting.

“Likewise, women shall not perform outdoor work, shall not card clothing, nor sew, nor wash, nor bleach, nor beat flax, nor presume to comb wool, nor shear sheep, so that in every way the rest of good people may be observed on Sunday.”

### XXXVII

Although these facts are certain, the opinion of the most illustrious Peter de Marca, archbishop of Paris, is nevertheless correct (*History of Béarn*, book V, chapter 2, §7). He teaches that the use of the capitularies was interrupted at the beginning of the third dynasty of our kings, because the changes in public affairs and the diminution of royal authority that then occurred necessarily brought about the abolition of received laws, which can rest on no other foundations than the pillars supporting royal dignity.

For the wars with the Normans and the civil wars caused the offices of the dukes, counts, and marquises, which had previously depended upon the king’s discretion, to become the personal possessions of each holder and hereditary. Hence various municipal laws were introduced, so that nothing might remain from the old order capable of obstructing the new possessors.

Thus, little by little, people withdrew from knowledge of the capitularies, until ignorance of them prevailed—the ignorance that existed before the beginning of the last century.

At last, however, when that brilliant star of literature, Francis I, the most Christian king of the Franks, had appeared—a king to whom learning in these latest times owes no less than it once owed to Charlemagne—men’s minds were awakened to various arts and studies. The ancient libraries were searched, and the works of earlier scholars that had previously lain hidden were brought back from darkness.

Then the laws of the capitularies were restored to the light, first by the Germans and afterward by our own countrymen.

### XXXVIII

The first person, so far as I believe, to bring the authority of the capitularies, or constitutions, of Charlemagne into the light of day after a long period of oblivion was the blessed Beatus Rhenanus, in the year 1531. He transcribed much material from the Code of Frankish Laws, whose ancient copies, he says, existed in various German libraries, in the second book of his *German Affairs*.

Then, in the year 1536, Joachim Vadianus, in book six of his *Aphorisms on the Eucharist*, p. 215, explicitly mentioned the collection of Ansegisus, abbot of Lobbes:

“There exists among us at Saint Gall,” he says, “an ancient codex of Ansegisus, abbot of Lobbes, in the library of the principal church, in which the passages we have just cited are read word for word: namely, that a priest should always have the Eucharist prepared for the sick.”

Then, in the year 1545, Vitus Amerpachius published at Ingolstadt a book of the Constitutions of Charlemagne [Note: [Col. 0087D] See the supplement to this new edition.], as we shall explain in its proper place.

Three years later, John Tilius, later bishop of Saint-Brieuc and Meaux, undertook an edition of the capitularies of Charlemagne and Louis the Pious, but neither completed nor published it.

It was then that the name “capitularies” first began to be heard. Previously they had simply been called the constitutions of Charlemagne or the Frankish laws.

In the following year, 1549, Charles Dumoulin, preparing to publish a style-book of the Parliament of Paris revised and enlarged by himself, says in the preface that he had added certain notable chapters from the constitutions of Charlemagne and Louis the Pious, “of which,” he says, “I possess a copy.” He repeats the same statement in the marginal notes to that same *Style*, part III, title 50.

It should not, however, be thought that the copy used by Dumoulin was one of those which Tilius had prepared for publication. Apart from the fact that Dumoulin, both in his additions to the *Style of the Parliament* and in his treatise *On the Origin, Development, and Excellence of the Kingdom and Monarchy of the Franks*, as well as in his commentary on the edict of Henry II against petty gifts, always cites the capitularies or constitutions of Charlemagne and Louis the Pious according to the numbers marked in ancient copies—which Tilius changed in his edition—Dumoulin further states in the same treatise *On the Excellence of the Kingdom of France*, §115, and in the preface to his commentary on Henry II’s edict against petty gifts, §7, that he had obtained his copy from the royal registers.

I know that this note by Dumoulin was removed from the treatise *On the Excellence of the Kingdom of France* in the later editions of his works, beginning with the one published at Paris in the twelfth year of this century. Those responsible for that edition allowed themselves the liberty of removing, changing, and adding as much as they wished.

For example, they corrected the numbers of the capitularies recorded in Dumoulin’s older editions according to the Pithoean edition of the capitularies, which was published long after Dumoulin’s death.

And when Dumoulin had written the following in paragraph 119 of the same treatise *On the Monarchy of the Franks*:

“Likewise, in book IV of the capitularies, the following chapters, which Ansegisus places in the first booklet of his compilation—namely, chapter 95—prohibited in every way and under penalty specified in the capitularies that boys should be tonsured without their parents’ consent, or girls veiled; and chapter 109, that girls of tender age should not be veiled before they knew how to choose what they wanted.”

The editors, with such audacity, replaced this with the following:

“Furthermore, in book IV of the capitularies, they wrote the following articles, which Ansegisus, in book I of his compilation, added in these words, chapter 101 [of the latest Paris edition, which we have followed]:

“‘It has been absolutely forbidden that boys be tonsured without their parents’ consent, or girls veiled; and whoever attempts to do this shall be compelled to pay the fine contained in the capitularies of the secular law established by us.

“‘And chapter 107: “But that girls should not be veiled indiscriminately, it has also pleased us to set out here what is to be observed according to the sacred canons. Concerning the age at which girls are to be veiled, the African Council, chapter 16, provides that they are not to be consecrated before the age of twenty-five.”’”

They ought, if they intended to reproduce Dumoulin’s complete statement, to have added chapter 115 of the first book of the capitularies according to the Pithoean edition, which is chapter 109 in ours, where we read:

“That girls of tender age should not be veiled before they know how to choose what they want.”

There was therefore considerable audacity on the part of those who prepared this edition of Dumoulin’s works.

First, they did not retain Dumoulin’s words, but substituted others that are not Dumoulin’s, as is also evident from the same treatise written in French, in which precisely the same meaning and the same order of words—even in their edition—are found as in the passage of Dumoulin that we cited from the old edition.

Second, although Dumoulin deliberately refrained from quoting the capitulary passages in full, which he mentions here, they inserted them contrary to the author’s intention.

Third, they mentioned the latest Paris edition of the capitularies in Dumoulin’s text, although it is certain that no such mention should have been made, since that edition, as we have already observed, appeared long after Dumoulin’s death.

Finally, having abused the authority they had assumed to correct and supplement Dumoulin, they omitted the final part of this paragraph.

That omission may have resulted from negligence. But the alteration made in paragraph 115, where they omitted Dumoulin’s words stating that he had obtained the books of the capitularies from the royal registers, was made deliberately by those who thought that this notice was no longer necessary once the books of the capitularies were in everyone’s hands, and that it was therefore no longer necessary to indicate where they could be found.

For Dumoulin had written there:

“And it is found in the original *Capitulary*, of which I possess a copy from the royal registers.”

The Paris editors completely deleted this clause, although they retained it in the same treatise written in French.

From this one may infer how faithfully they conducted themselves in their edition of Dumoulin’s works.

### XXXIX

Before the year 827, the capitularies of our kings had not yet been collected into a single volume, but were kept separately, written on sheets and [Col. 0089A] parchment leaves. At that time Abbot Ansegisus collected several capitularies of Charlemagne and Louis the Pious, so that they might not be consigned to oblivion, as he himself says, and arranged them into four books.

Most people believe that this abbot Ansegisus was from Lobbes, persuaded by the authority of Sigebert, who writes of him under the year 827 as follows:

> Ansegisus, abbot of Lobbes, arranged in two little books the edicts of the emperor Charlemagne and of his son Louis that pertain to ecclesiastical law. He likewise arranged in two similar little books their edicts pertaining to secular law.

John Trithemius later confirmed and disseminated this opinion. But I have found no one older than Sigebert who reports this. Indeed, Fulcuinus, an ancient author who described the origin and history of the monastery of Lobbes and provided a succession of its ancient abbots, makes no mention of Ansegisus. Nor does Giles Waulde, who in the twenty-eighth year of this century published the Life of Saint Ursmar and the history of the same monastery, [Col. 0089B] compiled from ancient records of Lobbes and of the neighboring churches and monasteries.

Those who think that he was the first abbot of Lobbes are seriously mistaken, and still more mistaken are those who maintain that he later became archbishop of Sens, in the final years of Charles the Bald. For although it is certain that the man who was archbishop of Sens had previously been an abbot, he must not be confused with the compiler of the Capitularies. Nor is it necessary to refute the arguments of those who hold this view; it would be easy to overwhelm them with the strongest evidence. The authority of the celebrated and most learned expert in these matters, Jacques Sirmond, will suffice. In a letter to Dom Constantine Cajetan, abbot of Saint-Barontus, he writes of Ansegisus as follows:

> There was a similar error concerning Ansegisus, who collected the Capitula of the kings Charles and Louis. Since it is clear from Sigebert that this Ansegisus was abbot of Lobbes, in the diocese of Cambrai, and was quite different from Ansegisus, archbishop of Sens—although the latter too had been an abbot before his episcopate, but of another monastery in the Beauvais region, named after Saint Michael—there were nevertheless some who confused the two Ansegisi and wrongly attributed to the archbishop the credit for arranging the Capitula into books  
> (in Labbe, vol. II, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, p. 692).

### XL

From what has been said thus far, it may reasonably be doubted whether the opinion of those who maintain that our Ansegisus was abbot of Lobbes is correct. In the *Chronicle of Fontenelle*, published in the third volume of D’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, I find that Ansegisus, appointed abbot of Fontenelle by Louis the Pious, was a learned man and a lover of books, of which he left a large number in the monastery of Fontenelle and in that of Flavigny; the author of the same Chronicle also indicates that he was abbot of the latter. [Note: [Col. 0089D] See *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, vol. IV, p. 457, at the beginning.]

It might therefore perhaps be thought that the abbot Ansegisus who collected the capitularies of the kings was the same man who was abbot of Fontenelle and died in the year 834, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August, after governing that abbey for ten years [Col. 0089D] and more.

### XLI

That collection of capitularies compiled by Abbot Ansegisus immediately acquired great authority because the emperor Louis the Pious adopted it as his own. For in constitutions issued after the year 827, when he cites words or the substance of laws previously issued by his father Charles or by himself, he writes that they are to be found “in the Capitularium.” By this designation he means the collection of Ansegisus.

Thus, in the Capitular of Worms of the year 829, title 1, chapter 5:

> For thus it is contained in the Capitular of our father of blessed memory, in book I, chapter 157: “That those who hold the benefices of churches,” etc.

And shortly afterward:

> Likewise, in our Capitular, book II, chapter 21, concerning the same matter.

Further, in chapter 9 of the same title of this Capitular of Worms:

> Whoever has neglected to carry out the restoration of the churches whose property he holds as a benefice, let it be carried out concerning them according to the earlier Capitular, in which regulations were made concerning labor, noval lands, and tithes;

that is, in book IV, chapter [Note: [Col. 0090D] See the Notes on the Capitularies.] 38, “Concerning the labor and restoration of churches,” etc.

And in title 2 of the same Capitular, chapter 1:

> Concerning destroyed benefices, let that be observed which is contained in the earlier Capitular;

that is, in book IV, chapter 36:

> Whoever [holds] a benefice, etc.

In the same place, chapter 8:

> Concerning good denarii which the people do not wish to accept, we wish that what was established in our earlier Capitular be observed and maintained;

that is, in book IV, chapter 30:

> That no free man, etc.

And in title 3, chapter 1:

> Concerning homicides committed in churches or in their atria, let that be observed and maintained which was established in the earlier Capitular;

that is, in book IV, chapter 13:

> If anyone for a trivial cause, etc.

Likewise, chapter 5:

> Concerning vicars and centenarii who very often hold placita more from greed than from a desire to administer justice, and thereby afflict the people excessively, let it be maintained as it is contained in the Capitular of the lord emperor Charles;

that is, in book III, chapter 40:

> That no one be summoned to a placitum, etc.

And shortly afterward:

> Likewise, concerning the same matter, in our Capitular, book IV, chapter 45: “Concerning placita, indeed,” etc.

And in chapter 8 of the same title:

> Concerning the suppression of feuds, let that be observed and maintained which is contained in our Capitular, book IV, chapter 25:

> If anyone, compelled by some necessity, etc.

### XLII

Charles the Bald likewise often praised the same collection as the public code of Frankish laws, accepted by royal authority and public usage. The passages from his Capitula that prove what we have said should be cited.

Title 36, chapter 1:

> Let counts be assistants in every respect to bishops and the ministers of the Church in their ministries, as is contained in the Capitular of our predecessors and forefathers, in book II, chapter 23, etc.

In the same place, chapter 4:

> We wish and expressly command our counts that, just as it is contained in chapter 24 of the second book of the Capitula of our predecessors, [Col. 0090C] etc.

Chapter 8:

> That denarii from all mints be pure and of good weight, as is contained in the Capitular of our predecessors and forefathers, book IV, chapter 32.

Chapter 9:

> According to secular law, let the perjurer be punished, as is contained in the Capitular of our predecessors and forefathers, at the end of chapter 10 of book III.

Chapter 18:

> But if he has fled for refuge to the immunity, power, or property of some powerful person, let it be according to what is contained in book III of the Capitular, chapter 26, etc.

Chapter 19:

> Let markets not be held anywhere on Sunday, as is found in book I of the Capitula, chapter 136.

Chapter 20:

> Let those men also who ought to have taken care that defective measures were not made, if they are convicted of the perjury which they swore because they ought not to have consented to this, be punished according to law, as is found at the end of chapter 10 of book III of the Capitula.

Chapter 22:

> We wish to consider the regulation which our predecessors, the kings, established in book IV of the Capitula, chapter 57.

Chapter 25:

> And since it is contained in the aforesaid Capitula, book III, chapter 75, that no one without royal permission—*brunia* [coat of mail], etc.

Chapter 27:

> And those who have dismissed an army expedition on such grounds shall pay the *heribannum* according to the regulation contained in book III of the Capitula of our forefathers, chapter 14.

Chapter 28:

> Let them make composition to our royal share, as is found in the aforesaid book III of the Capitula, chapters 15 and 86, and in book IV, chapter 36.

Further, in the same chapter:

> As is contained in the Capitula of book I, chapters 132 and 134, and in book II, chapter 31, and in book IV, chapter 19.

Chapter 34:

> Nevertheless, it is contained in book III of the Capitula, chapter 29, “Concerning a free man,” etc.

Title 40, chapter 9:

> As is contained in book I of the Capitula of our grandfather and father, and as is contained in the Capitula made by our father in the sixteenth year of his imperial rule.

Title 45, chapter 1:

> Whoever receives such a person under royal ban, let it be according to what was established in the Capitularies of our grandfather and father, in book III: if he is a Frank, etc.

In the same place, chapter 3:

> Let it be done with them as is contained in the Capitular of our grandfather and father, book III, chapter 47. And if they have already been convicted of theft, let it be done with them as with those who have been convicted. But if their lives have not yet been spared, and they have not been convicted, and they possess property, slaves, or movable goods, let it be done with them as is stated in book IV of the Capitula, chapter 29.

The same Charles also frequently cites the Capitularies of Charlemagne and Louis the Pious. But we have selected only those passages in which he praises them from the Collection of Ansegisus, in order to show that it was authentic and confirmed by royal authority.

### XLIII

The arrangement of this collection is as follows. In the first book, as Ansegisus himself indicates in his preface, are placed the Capitula of Charlemagne relating to ecclesiastical order; in the second, the ecclesiastical Capitula of Louis the Pious; in the third, the Capitula of Charles relating to secular law; and finally, in the fourth, those which Louis the Pious issued for the advancement of secular law.

Because this fact was not sufficiently noticed, several learned men fell into error and thought that the second and fourth books of the Capitularies belonged to Charlemagne. It should also be noted that in certain ancient copies of Ansegisus these two books are attributed to Louis and to his son Lothar. Yet it is certain, as Peter Pithoeus correctly observed, that nothing here belongs specifically to Lothar and that these two books are composed entirely of the Capitula of Louis alone (see the note on the Capitularies, p. 1121), except for the first two appendices of book IV, which were taken from Capitula of Charlemagne that Ansegisus had omitted from the earlier books.

Nevertheless, although Ansegisus’s intention was to place only the Capitula of Charlemagne in the first book, it is certain that several Capitula of Louis the Pious were accidentally mixed into it—namely, chapter 79 and the following chapters through 104. These were taken from Capitula enacted by Louis the Pious in the year 816. The cause of this error, as we explain elsewhere, can be no other than that, when Ansegisus discovered two Capitula of Charlemagne at the beginning of the Capitular issued by Louis the Pious in 816, he thought that the other chapters of that same edict also belonged to Charles (ibid., p. 1059).

Ansegisus later returns to his original plan. Chapter 105 and the following six chapters were taken from the first Capitular of the year 805; the next four from the second Capitular of that year; chapter 116 and the following ten from the fifth Capitular of the year 806; and the next seven from the sixth Capitular of the same year. The five chapters that are read afterward were copied from the second and third Capitularies of the year 803. Chapter 139 was taken from Capitula issued in the year 809. I have been unable to discover the origin and sources of what follows, through chapter 159. But the final four chapters of the same first book were taken from the first Capitular of the year 810.

### XLIV

Since Ansegisus had omitted many Capitula of Charlemagne and Louis the Pious, and had moreover refrained from reporting the constitutions of Pippin and Carloman, although they were frequently used, Benedict the Levite of Mainz undertook around the year 845 to collect the Capitularies into one body and distribute them in three books.

Baronius (*Ad ann.* 845 and 847), followed by others, believed that this Collection compiled by Benedict had been made at the command of the Council of Meaux, because, as we saw above, that council had requested Charles the Bald to order that the ecclesiastical Capitula promulgated by the lord emperor Charlemagne and by the lord Louis Augustus be strictly observed (Council of Meaux, chapter 78).

But Hermann Conringius correctly pointed out (*On the Origin of German Law*, chapters 15–17) that the opinion of those who think this collection was made by order of the Council of Meaux is false. Correctly, I say: for since it was made in the kingdom of Louis, king of Germany, outside which the city of Meaux was situated, it is entirely impossible to suppose that Benedict, a deacon of Mainz, undertook this work at the command of bishops from another kingdom.

Moreover, Benedict himself makes clear in wholly unambiguous words that he arranged this collection at the command of Otgar, archbishop of Mainz. After speaking of the four books collected by Ansegisus, he adds:

> Finally, at the command of pious Otgar,  
> who at that time held the highest pontificate at Mainz,  
> I, Benedict the Levite, added  
> three little books, in which the work of the law is recited.

### XLV

Nor is the complaint of learned men either recent or without foundation when they say that this collection of Benedict is confused and composed of various patches. Nevertheless, I do not consider correct the opinion of those who write that he acted here deceitfully, adulterating and interpolating in various places the Capitula he had collected for the benefit of the Roman See, and therefore making use of the archive of the Church of Mainz, where the Capitularies had been forged and their mines investigated. [The final phrase is materially obscure in the supplied text.]

I would more readily believe that he first collected the Capitula that had unquestionably been issued by the kings, and then those which, as we noted above, had been excerpted from the books of Holy Scripture by the kings themselves or at their command by bishops or learned men, as he found them scattered among their Capitula. To use Benedict’s own words, he also collected excerpts made by them from the canons of holy councils, from the decrees of the Roman pontiffs, from the sayings of the holy Fathers, from the synodal constitutions of the Gallican bishops, from the Theodosian Code or the interpretations of Anianus, from the *Sentences* of Paul, from the *Novels* of Julian the Antecessor, from the Code of the laws of the Visigoths, from the Salic Law, from the Ripuarian Law, and from the Bavarian Law.

From all these sources that collection of Benedict was patched together: certainly in a confused manner, with no chronological order maintained, and often with the wording of the chapters reported there altered. But I do not therefore think Benedict should be blamed, since he himself warned us that he had found those Capitula scattered about in such a confused and disordered state. Some of them, he says, had beginnings that agreed but endings that did not; others had matching endings but unlike beginnings; in some there was less, and in others more. For that reason he left them as he had found them—that is, he changed nothing, added nothing, and removed nothing.
