So far am I from thinking that Benedict deserves blame that I even believe we owe him a great deal. Without his diligence and labor, we would today lack many of the most sacred and excellent constitutions of our princes, which are found nowhere else.

### XLVI

That collection was published and accepted for public use not only in the kingdom of Germany but also in our France, before the year 858. For since in that year Herard, archbishop of Tours, published his Capitula and abridged a large part of them from those contained in Benedict’s collection, it is clear that he used it.

Later Isaac, bishop of Langres, also collected his Capitula from the same three books of Benedict the Levite. Finally, the Capitula of the same collection are frequently cited at the Council of Sainte-Macre, at Trosly, and by Hincmar, Regino, Fulbert, and Ivo.

As for Burchard, I think I must remain silent, because although he took much from that collection of Benedict, he preferred to be a liar—as we have often noted—rather than to cite the Capitularies of our kings. What is meant by Benedict the Levite’s statement concerning royal Capitula strengthened by apostolic authority has been discussed at length above, and there is no need to repeat it here.

### XLVII

Before we leave Benedict’s collection, it will not be superfluous to point out that, since it was made long after Ansegisus, it did not always form a single body with his work, and that the book of Capitularies which is our fifth book was sometimes counted as the first by the ancients.

Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, will serve as a witness in his treatise 48, entitled *Concerning Criminal Priests Whose Approval Is Lacking*. There, while citing chapter 35 of the fifth book of the Capitularies, which is the first book of Benedict the Levite, he says:

> What should be done concerning criminal priests whose approval is lacking is written in the first book of the Capitula of the lord emperor Charles Augustus, chapter 34: “This must be reconsidered by us with great care,” etc.

And the Council of Trosly, held in the year 909, while citing chapter 427 of the sixth book of the Capitularies, which is Benedict’s second book, says:

> Therefore, in the second book of the Capitularies, chapter 427, it is thus decreed: “Correcting ourselves and giving an example to those who come after us,” etc.

Moreover, Isaac, bishop of Langres, prepared his collection solely from the three books of the Capitularies published by Benedict the Levite.

We also possessed a very ancient codex of Saint Arnulf of Metz, in which many Capitula excerpted from those three books of Benedict are copied. At the beginning of the passages taken from book six, this is written: “From the Capitularies of the most glorious emperors, the lord Charles and the lord Louis, book II.” Shortly afterward: “Likewise, in the same book, from the law of the Old Testament.”

Again, below, where chapter 182 of the fifth book is copied, the heading reads: “Likewise, in the same [that is, in the Capitularies], from book I: ‘That bishops may have authority,’” etc.

Finally, as noted above, in the charter-book of the Church of Barcelona we found that a certain Adeledis, in the twenty-fifth year of the reign of King Henry, had given that Church a book of Charles, most useful to the holy Church, divided into three bodies—that is, Benedict’s collection divided into three books.

If these facts had been observed by the very learned Mariano Victorio, he would not have attributed the fifth book of the Capitularies to Ansegisus. He writes:

> In Abbot Ansegisus there is a certain synod held under Charlemagne, in which mention of such petitions is made in these words: “Let no priest presume to judge the sins of the people who confess them to him without the authority of the canons”  
> (Mariano Victorio, *On the Sacrament of Confession*, p. 139).

This is chapter 116 of the fifth book.

Nor are those who praise all the books of the Capitularies in which the constitutions of Carloman, Pippin, Charlemagne, and Louis the Pious are found as though they belonged solely to Charlemagne any less seriously mistaken. They commonly write in this fashion: “Charlemagne, book IV, etc., of the Capitularies.”

### XLVIII

After the seven books of the Capitularies come four additions, in which many things are found that appear neither in Ansegisus nor in Benedict. Sirmondus thought that these had been composed by Benedict the Levite (*Notes on the Capitularies*, pp. 752 and 754). But Benedict makes no mention of any of them in his preface.

Although in the codex of the Church of Beauvais the three later additions are read after the books of Ansegisus and Benedict, and in the Tilian manuscript most of the Capitula of the three final additions are also found after the seventh book, nevertheless, in the very ancient copies of Peter Pithoeus and Jacques Sirmond, in which there is nothing belonging to Benedict the Levite, four additions are found [Col. 0093D] appended after the four books of Ansegisus.

It should also be noted here that the first addition is not found in the Tilian codex, nor in the Beauvais or Palatine codices. Nevertheless, in the latter two it was copied in ancient times as though it formed part of the seventh book.

This is inferred from the fact that, in the headings prefixed to that seventh book in both codices, the headings of the chapters of the first addition follow in consecutive numbering. Thus, when the eighty chapters of the first addition are added to the 478 chapters of the seventh book, the total becomes 558 Capitula.

Indeed, it may also be inferred from those same copies of Pithoeus and Sirmond that this arrangement was anciently followed in some places. Although no other books of the Capitularies are copied in those manuscripts besides the four earlier books with the four additions, the beginning of the first addition is nevertheless written as follows:

> Chapter 478. That abbots, etc.

The same conclusion may be drawn from Ivo (Part I, chapter 133), who, when citing chapter 16 of the first addition, says that he took it from book VII of the Capitularies, chapter 493, as it is read in the published editions of Ivo and in the very ancient manuscript codex of Saint Victor of Paris.

Perhaps the bishops assembled at the Council of Trosly in the year 909 were also referring to this when, citing chapter 1 of the Capitular of the year 817, they praise it as being “from the Capitularies” (chapter 3).

Nevertheless, although this is completely certain, it is equally true that Benedict the Levite’s collection ends at chapter 478, with these words:

> Especially the Capitula of the final three books, etc.

Therefore the Capitula of the first addition were inserted into the seventh book after Benedict’s time, since in his preface he had granted every student permission to insert whatever he wished.

For this reason we did not wish to include those eighty chapters within the limits of the seventh book, and also so as not to disturb the order accepted among learned men. For what is now the second addition would have been the first had we chosen to follow the authority of the ancient books of Pithoeus and Sirmond and of Ivo.

Nevertheless, we assigned the first addition to the year 818, among the Capitula of Louis the Pious.

### XLIX

The first edition of the constitutions of Charlemagne was published by printers in the year 1545 through the work and scholarship of Vitus Amerpachius, a man exceptionally devoted to antiquities and good letters, under the supervision of Alexander Weissehorn, printer at Ingolstadt. It bore the following title:

> *Principal Constitutions of Charlemagne Concerning Ecclesiastical and Civil Affairs, Collected by Lothar the Grandson from the Books of the Constitutions of His Grandfather, and Recently Brought Forth from the Monastery of Tegernsee, with Notes and a Preface by Vitus Amerpachius.*

There follows a dedicatory letter from Amerpachius himself to the emperor Charles V and the Caesar Ferdinand, consisting almost entirely of their praises. On pages nine and following, however, he discusses the work he had undertaken in these words:

> For this purpose there came most opportunely before me a compendium of these canons and laws. The latter were issued by Charlemagne himself; the former were either approved by him or enacted by him together with the bishops. For they are, for the most part, like flowers gathered from the various volumes of this emperor’s laws and from the acts of councils held by him with the bishops—while everywhere preserving the authority of the Apostolic See, indeed treated with the utmost reverence—as is clearly indicated at the end of the work.
>
> Until now this jewel of antiquity had lain hidden in the monastery of Tegernsee. Although entrusted to parchment, in most places it was not merely considerably worn and damaged by moths and bookworms, but also hideously disfigured by the scribe, as I have noted throughout in connection with the laws and canons themselves. Even so, I have not changed something everywhere; and it is readily apparent that the book was written by a man both ignorant and negligent.
>
> This sort of arrangement caused me very great difficulty. First, the entire book had to be read. Besides the fact that, because of the unfamiliarity of the script, I was sometimes almost forced to become a child again—that is, to learn the forms of letters and syllables either by comparison or conjecture—I had to consider the meaning, and many words had to be examined with no less effort than was once expended, or is ordinarily expended, in examining oracles or riddles.
>
> Although in these matters I perhaps lack neither intelligence nor experience altogether, I was nevertheless often unable, without great labor, to find at least something probable amid such great antiquity of German customs and language. This is not because I think I never went astray; but, given my persistence in investigating, I could not help applying myself to every passage and bringing matters to the point at which, somehow or other, I could finally be satisfied somewhere.
>
> This difficulty was increased by the fact that I possess no great expertise in either laws or sacred constitutions. Nevertheless, in this respect too I did as much as my abilities and other labors permitted.
>
> I admit that many others could have produced this edition more successfully than I did, especially in matters of this kind. But those who might have wished to undertake it would not have been so readily available; and this labor required more a certain literary industry and expertise than any highly refined knowledge of law.
>
> Whether some jurist of exceptional ability could have rendered better service here than I have done, let the judgment belong to the fair-minded reader. Therefore I think that not only the most learned will grant me pardon, but will also praise my diligence, because amid my modest academic occupations I undertook this additional burden—especially since in the meantime I could have composed some work of my own, both much longer and perhaps more profitable to me and mine, as times now are; and, to confess the truth frankly, we are sometimes compelled to turn even these activities toward earning money.

### L

That collection contains, first, the Capitular of the year 779, divided into 24 Capitula; then, second, the three complete Capitularies of the year 789; third, the Capitular of the year 793 concerning the affairs of the kingdom of Italy; fourth, the Capitula issued at Nijmegen in the year 806; fifth, the Capitula issued to the royal agents in the same year; sixth, excerpts from the canon, which in our edition are published after the Capitula issued at Nijmegen; seventh, chapter 89 of the Ripuarian Law, which also appears among the Capitula of Charlemagne excerpted from the Lombard Law; eighth, the second, third, and fourth Capitularies of the year 803, the first three Capitularies of the year 805, and the fourth Capitular of uncertain date, followed by an edict of the emperor Charles concerning the honor and assistance to be rendered to bishops by counts and other judges, issued around the year 800.

There follow eight Capitula of Charlemagne added to the Lombard Law, and then a letter of the same king to his son Pippin, king of Italy, which we assigned to the year 807. After it come three Capitula of Charlemagne added to the Lombard Law, two of which are included among the Capitula we excerpted from that law. Since the third had escaped us, we added it at the end of the first volume, after the end of the index and the notice of typographical errors.

After the Capitula of Charlemagne, the Capitula issued by Louis the Pious in the sixteenth year of his imperial rule are copied. Finally, there are a few Capitula collected from here and there, and a chapter of Lothar concerning the confirmation of the preceding Constitutions.

This codex [Col. 0095C] was later reprinted at Mainz in 1602 by John Busaeus, a priest of the Society of Jesus, at the end of Hincmar’s letters, and also by Goldastus in his collection of imperial Constitutions.

### LI

At the same time, the man of supreme judgment and a leader in letters and virtue, John Tilius, later bishop of Saint-Brieuc and of Meaux, to whom we all owe the publication of many excellent books, considered publishing the books of the Capitularies collected by Abbot Ansegisus and Benedict the Levite. Finally, in the year 1548, he committed them to the press in this city of Paris.

He stopped, however, at chapter 289 of the sixth book. We do not know why this occurred, although Peter Pithoeus, who was closer to him, attempted to conjecture the reason.

Nevertheless, although the edition was not completed and perfected, some copies of it were released, which we still use today. Thus those who in Rome at that time were supervising the correction and revision of Gratian’s collection—as Pithoeus himself says (*Preface to the Capitularies*)—used them together with the remains of the Beauvais copy, which, as Pithoeus adds, they obtained through the favor of that most learned bishop, on our indication—that is, through the favor of Jacques Amyot, bishop of Auxerre. The Roman correctors frankly acknowledge this in the catalogue of books obtained from various places, which follows the preface:

> The seventh book of the Capitularies, they say, and the appended Capitularies, sent by Jacques Amyot, bishop of Auxerre, from the library of the Church of Beauvais.

The celebrated and very learned Antonius Augustinus, archbishop of Tarragona, also possessed a copy of this same edition. [Note: [Col. 0095D] In *Judgment Concerning Certain Ancient Collectors of Canons*, and in book II of *On the Correction of Gratian*.]

Speaking of the books of the Capitularies, he says:

> This mutilated collection came into my hands. For the six books of the Paris edition of the year 1548 were incomplete: the sixth ended at the beginning of chapter 289, although the headings indicated that the chapters of the sixth book numbered 330.

He adds that he had obtained it through the kindness of the very learned men Peter Chacon and Latino Latini. Latino himself informs us of the same thing in a letter written in 1576 to Augustine (vol. II, p. 166):

> You will have, partly through my work and partly through that of your Chacon, a little book of the Capitularies—indeed defective and incomplete, but of the same kind as all those that have so far been sent from Paris here to us.

Antonius Augustinus also writes in the passage cited above that he had obtained from Rome a copy of the seventh book and of the appended Capitularies. He adds:

> The copy of the seventh book which I received from Rome was diminished by many chapters. We have written above that the final chapter of that book is 478, although the headings of the chapters numbered 558. A double collection of the appended Capitularies followed.

Therefore, in addition to the leaves of Tilius’s edition of the Capitularies, a copy of the seventh book and of the appended Capitularies was also sent to Augustine. It had been copied from the exemplar that had reached Rome from the library of the Church of Beauvais.

For not only are these materials found in the Beauvais codex just as Augustine describes them, but the Roman correctors also state that the volume of the Capitularies obtained from Gaul contained headings for 558 chapters of the seventh book.

In the index of the seventh book of the Capitularies, under number 494—for the chapters themselves from 478 through 558 are missing from the volume obtained from Gaul—the following is read:

> That monks should not make one another godfathers and godmothers.

[Note: [Col. 0096D] Note of the Roman correctors on “Monks,” in distinction 4, “On Consecration,” chapter 104.]

Forty years later, Peter Pithoeus, that great ornament of our France, completed and published Tilius’s edition.

Since Tilius and Pithoeus removed many things from the books of the Capitularies that seemed superfluous to them, and often disturbed the order of Ansegisus and Benedict, it is worthwhile to note here what they did in this edition and what appears deserving of blame.

But before I discuss these matters, the plan of the work and the chronological order require that we say something about the Basel edition of the Capitularies.

### LII

That edition appeared in the year 1557 together with other ancient laws of the nations that once obeyed the empire of the Franks, which Basil John Herold copied from the oldest exemplars of the library of Fulda.

Among these are found the Capitularies of Charlemagne and Louis the Pious collected by Abbot Ansegisus, as they are found in the ancient books, except that the fourth book is mutilated and incomplete through much of it. Twenty-three chapters are missing there—namely, chapter 13 and those following through chapter 36; chapter 61 and the remainder of the fourth book are also missing.

The edition then contains, in volume II of the Capitularies, p. 339, chapter 37, the Basel edition of Lothar’s law concerning tithes, which we published among the Capitula of Lothar excerpted from the Lombard Law.

Afterward come chapters 196, 197, 199, 202, and 204 of the fifth book of the Capitularies. Then follow the second and third Capitularies of the year 789, the Capitular of the year 793 concerning the affairs of the kingdom of Italy, and several Capitula of the years 803 and 806.

Next comes chapter 61 of the fourth book of the Capitularies and the remainder through chapter 74, except that chapter 72 is missing. Afterward chapters 67 and several others from the third book and other books are repeated, without any order.

Following these comes the preface that is usually placed before the eight Capitula of Charlemagne added to the Lombard Law, together with the first two chapters of the fourth book and the first Capitular of the year 812. Then comes chapter 3 of the fourth book with the remainder of that book.

Attached to these is an edict of Charlemagne concerning the honor to be rendered to bishops, issued around the year 800, and the three Capitula that we said above, when discussing Amerpachius’s edition of the Constitutions of Charlemagne, had been added to the Lombard Law.

After all these come three appendices to the fourth book and the Capitular of Louis the Pious from the sixteenth year of his imperial rule.

Finally, there are the Capitularies and Constitutions of Pippin, king of Italy; Guido; Otto I; Henry II; Conrad I; and Charles IV, emperors.

### LIII

Thirty years later, Petrus Pithoeus produced a new and expanded edition of the *Capitularies*, following the Tilian edition and enlarging it with the Capitula that were missing from that edition. Both men, however, interpolated the collection of Ansegisus; and from the collection of Benedict the Levite they omitted many Capitula because they saw that these occurred elsewhere in the same work. Benedict foresaw that some would disapprove of this. Accordingly, he used the following wise defense before them in his preface:

> We therefore warn readers that, if they should find the same Capitula repeated twice or three times, they should not attribute this to our incompetence, since, as we have said, we found them in different documents.

When Antonius Contius and certain others detected repetitions of this kind in some of Justinian’s *Novels* edited by Haloander, they thought that the words repeated in these passages [Col. 0097B] had been inserted there by mistake and ought therefore to be removed. Joannes Leunclavius refutes their opinion as rash (*Notatorum*, Book II, chapters 240 and 256). He says that it is not unlikely that the same matters were sometimes repeated in two or more *Novels*, and that the very passages condemned there are also found in the books of the *Basilica*.

Precisely the same thing happened in this collection of Benedict’s. For when he transcribed the royal Capitularies as he found them in his documents, he could not avoid writing many of them twice or even three times, because princes often renewed either their own laws or those of their predecessors, as we see in the Capitularies of our kings. Thus, for example, Charlemagne enacted many laws transcribed word for word from those which his father Pippin had enacted; and he renewed many of those which he himself had promulgated, using exactly the same words as before.

Nothing, therefore, ought to have been removed from Benedict’s collection, nor anything changed. For—to pass over the fact that the Capitula omitted from it contain variant readings differing from those [Col. 0097C] found in the Capitula retained by Tilius and Pithoeus—there are sometimes passages in the omitted material that do not exist elsewhere, and consequently we lack them contrary to the intention of the authors.

The matter should be demonstrated by examples. Tilius, and after him Pithoeus, reproduced chapter 276 of Book V of the *Capitularies*, which is mutilated in the ancient copies of Benedict the Levite, just as they found it mutilated. In those ancient copies, however, the chapter beginning *Whoever pays a tithe* is referred to chapter 57 of Book I of the *Capitularies*, where no such passage exists. They therefore changed the number and substituted 163 for 57, thinking that the sense of this chapter was contained in the chapter of Book I cited by them.

Yet it is certain that the chapter of Book I in question, which is chapter 157 in our edition, has an entirely different meaning from the statement of the chapter beginning *Whoever pays a tithe*. Therefore, to fill the gap occurring in this chapter, it ought to have been repeated, as we have done, in the fourth addition, where it exists complete. But because Pithoeus saw that its first part had already been printed [Col. 0097D] in Book V, he thought it unnecessary to repeat this chapter in the addition. He did not notice that many things occur there which are absent from Book V, and that there is also a difference in the first part of the chapter between the editions found in Book V and in the fourth addition.

### LIV

Pithoeus committed a similar error concerning chapter 198 of Book V, which deals with the nones and tithes, or the census of the churches. This chapter existed twice in the collection of the *Capitularies*: once in Book V and again in the fourth addition. Since most of it was found in Book V, Pithoeus thought that everything found in the fourth addition was already present there. This is not true. For chapter 132 of that addition contains a considerable amount of material that can neither be considered superfluous nor rejected by us. It was added with public authority and has the force of law.

### LV

Again, Tilius and Pithoeus omitted chapter 108 of Book VI [Col. 0098A] because it had already been transcribed in Book V. Yet there is a significant difference between the two editions. For, besides the fact that Book VI reads, “and he himself must serve in the office of the fisc,” whereas Book V reads, “and he himself must serve in the office of the governor,” Book VI adds a very important clause, which is absent from Tilius and Pithoeus, namely:

> And he is not to be received in another monastery without the permission of his abbot and his own bishop.

The editors of the *Capitularies* ought not to have omitted this clause, since it occurs in the manuscripts. It was formed from monastic practice: in ancient times monks could not be transferred elsewhere without the permission of their abbot and their own bishop, as learned men have already observed.

Yet the author of the clause departed from the true meaning of the words from which he composed it. For it is certain that the chapter with which we are now concerned was taken from the *Novels* of Julian the Antecessor, which have an entirely different meaning, as we explain elsewhere.

### LVI

In another kind of error, the same men added certain material to chapter 106 of Book VI [Col. 0098B] that is not found in the ancient copies. The reading of the ancient copies is as follows:

> Likewise concerning the sick and penitents: that those who are dying may not perish without reconciliation and viaticum.  
> *(Isaac, title 4, chapter 6.)*

This is also the way it is read in the canons of Isaac, bishop of Langres. Tilius and Pithoeus, however, printed the passage as follows:

> Likewise concerning the sick and penitents: that those who are dying may not perish without the anointing of consecrated oil and viaticum.

I know that the words added here are found in the Capitular of the year 769 and in chapter 132 of Book VII of the *Capitularies*, and therefore that Tilius and Pithoeus are free from blame with respect to the sense of the chapter. Nevertheless, I maintain that these words ought not to have been transferred into Book VI from Book VII, since it is quite possible that when this law was first enacted—which perhaps occurred before the time of Charlemagne—the clause concerning the anointing with consecrated oil did not exist in that chapter and was added later by Charlemagne in the year 769.

### LVII

The same illustrious men committed the same fault in chapter 159 of Book VI [Col. 0098C]. Whereas the ancient books have simply:

> Those, however, who shall have been born from the same persons are to be admitted as witnesses,

Tilius and Pithoeus printed:

> Those, however, who shall have been born from the same persons are to be admitted as witnesses from the third generation.

I know that this clause is found below in chapter 352 of this book, and that Tilius transferred it from there, for which reason he omitted the second edition of that chapter. But I would have preferred that both passages be given rather than that the earlier one be interpolated contrary to the intention of the author and collector.

For in the *Code of the Visigothic Law*, from which this chapter was taken, the following alone is read:

> Those, however, who shall have been born from the same persons are in every respect to be admitted as witnesses.

This is exactly how it is read there, not only in the printed editions but also in the ancient copies.  
*(Book III of the Capitularies, chapter 12; and Book V, chapter 254.)*

### LVIII

They suppressed chapter 279 of the same Book VI because it had already been printed in Book III; and for the same reason they also omitted it [Col. 0098D] from the edition of Book V. Yet they ought to have noticed that the edition of Book III does not contain the clause found in Books V and VI.

Nor do I think that those who are curious about such matters are satisfied merely because they placed that clause within brackets after the end of the chapter in Book III. The works of ancient authors are not so subject to our discretion that we may supply their errors or gaps, as we have often said in connection with the corrections that the otherwise most learned Roman correctors made in the text of passages cited by Gratian in his work.

### LIX

In the same Book VI, chapter 382, a chapter taken from the *Law of the Bavarians* was transcribed. The other editors did not print it because it already constituted chapter 341 of Book V. If the learned men had observed that the edition of Book VI contains certain things absent from Book V, they would undoubtedly either have transferred those things into Book V or have placed the chapter again in Book VI.

[Col. 0099A] Since the copy of the *Law of the Bavarians* from which this chapter was taken does not contain the clause found in the chapter of Book VI that we have just cited, it is probable that the prince who approved the Capitula excerpted from the *Law of the Bavarians* did not insert that clause into his edict. It was added later, at another time, because it appeared necessary.

### LX

The same men were even more audacious in joining together chapters 73 and 75 of the same Book VI. Since these chapters are divided in the ancient copies of the *Capitularies* exactly as we have printed them, and since Isaac of Langres (title I, chapters 23 and 24) presents the part of chapter 75 that Tilius and Pithoeus added to chapter 73 immediately after the first part of that same chapter 73, it is clear that the passages ought to be distinguished.

Indeed, in a certain respect the illustrious men erred more seriously here than in other places where they interpolated and altered the text of the *Capitularies*: they removed certain material in order to create a continuous passage. Let only these chapters be read in our edition and compared with the Tilian and Pithoean editions, which read as follows:

[Col. 0099B]

> It was resolved by the entire synodal assembly that no priest should presume to claim more than one church for himself; for just as every layman ought to have no more than one wife, so also every priest ought to have no more than one church.

Thus, in order to join chapter 73 with the later part of chapter 75, they removed these words:

> Therefore it was resolved by all that no priest should claim more than one church for himself, because their meaning was contained in the preceding chapter.

But this is not to edit the Capitularies, when each person assumes the liberty of changing and removing whatever he pleases.

### LXI

Besides those errors common to Tilius and Pithoeus, there are some that belong to Pithoeus alone. Since Tilius did not complete the edition of the *Capitularies* and did not publish the additions, any error found in them was the fault of Pithoeus alone.

He too, however, fell into error here. For he omitted chapters 46 and 82 of the fourth addition, which are found nowhere else in the entire collection of the *Capitularies* [Col. 0099C]. They are nevertheless of great authority, since they were taken from the Council of Mainz (chapter 14), held in the year 813, and from the Sixth Council of Paris (Book III, chapter 2). From the latter were taken most of the Capitula that Benedict included in his collection, as well as a large part of those found in the second addition.

### LXII

The justice of the complaint we have brought against Tilius and Pithoeus can also be confirmed by Pithoeus’s own authority. In Book VI, chapter 143—which in our edition is chapter 145 [Book VII, chapter 234]—he had reproduced an African canon concerning clerics who appeal to secular judges (fourth addition, chapter 165). He then printed it again in Book VII and in the fourth addition because in those two later places it is read somewhat differently from the edition found in Book VI.

He likewise transcribed chapter 115 of Book VI again as chapter 466 of the same book, in exactly the same words, except that the edition of the earlier chapter is somewhat more accurate than the later one. Therefore, if the method of removing similar chapters was to be followed, [Col. 0099D] that chapter ought certainly not to have been printed in two places in the same book.

He also printed chapter 133 of Book V again in the fourth addition (chapter 77). According to the same method, it ought to have been omitted there.

### LXIII

After the Tilian edition and Petrus Pithoeus’s first edition, another edition followed, prepared by Franciscus Pithoeus in 1603 from those two editions, but once again interpolated and corrupted under the guise of correction.

This can be demonstrated by several examples. In Book III, chapter 23, the ancient copies and the Basel edition read:

> Because he is a thief and is disloyal to us and to the Franks.

This reading is confirmed by the Capitula of Charles the Bald, where the passage reads:

> Because he is a thief, and he is disloyal to us and to the Franks.  
> *(Title XIV, chapter 6.)*

Tilius and Petrus Pithoeus had restored the passage as follows:

> Because he is a thief and is disloyal to us and to the Franks.

Ivo had read it in nearly the same way (Part XVI, chapter 223), except that he omitted the two words *a thief*. But Franciscus Pithoeus thought that the passage should be corrected from the *Code of Lombard Law* [Col. 0100A], where it reads:

> Because whoever is a thief is disloyal in our kingdom of the Franks.  
> *(Book I, title 25, chapter 75.)*

Accordingly, he restored the passage in Ansegisus as follows:

> Because he is a thief and is disloyal in our kingdom of the Franks.

### LXIV

He likewise altered the final words of chapter 168 of Book V, which was transcribed from the Council of Mainz (chapter 56), held by order of Charlemagne.

The ancient books of the *Capitularies*, as well as the Mainz council held under Rabanus, Regino (Book II, chapter 197), Burchard (Book XVII, chapter 9), and Ivo (Part IX, chapter 71), retained the words of the Council, which read:

> And never again to be joined in marriage, but to be kept under severe constraint.

Tilius and Petrus Pithoeus printed the passage in this form.

Yet by the time of Regino (Book II, chapter 225), another reading had entered the tradition, which Ivo (Part IX, chapter 77) and Gratian likewise followed, namely:

> We command that they be separated and never again joined in marriage.

Franciscus Pithoeus retained neither of these readings. Instead, he supplied another that I have been unable to find elsewhere, writing:

> And never again to be joined in marriage [Col. 0100B] under strict discipline.

### LXV

Let us add one further example of the changes made by Franciscus Pithoeus in the *Capitularies*. Benedict the Levite reports in Book V, chapter 378, a Novel constitution of Justinian, which is number 79 in Julian the Antecessor’s edition by Antonius Augustinus and number 73 in Franciscus Pithoeus’s edition.

Benedict did not reproduce Julian’s actual words but only their meaning. At the end, where the penalty for those who failed to observe the law is established, he wrote:

> If anyone in public office violates this Constitution, he shall be fined ten pounds of gold. If he is an executor, he shall be confined in the chains of the churches to undergo punishment, and he shall lose his office.

The author of the third addition reads the same way (chapter 59); and this is certainly how it is read in all the ancient copies of the *Capitularies* and in the editions of Tilius and Petrus Pithoeus.

But Franciscus, who knew the source of this Constitution because he had edited Julian, removed the word *chains* from the passage and substituted *decanicis* (“the decanal prisons”) [Col. 0100C], because it was clear that Julian the Antecessor had used that word in his epitome of Justinian’s *Novels*.

### LXVI

In my judgment, we have acted more correctly by presenting the collections of Ansegisus and Benedict the Levite, together with the four additions, as they were composed by their authors, and according to the numbering recorded by Louis the Pious, Charles the Bald, Hincmar, Isaac, Regino, the Council of Trosly, Fulbert, and Ivo.

It will therefore not be difficult hereafter to find the Capitula cited by those ancient authors from the books of the *Capitularies*. It is worthwhile, however, to record how I conceived the plan for this work, on what occasion, with what assistance it was completed, and finally what I myself contributed according to the limits of my abilities.

### LXVII

The illustrious Petrus de Marca, archbishop of Paris—who rightly and deservedly often appears in the commemoration of my studies and labors—was, as though born by the highest gift of God for these studies, which he advanced wonderfully, an example that led me to turn toward them. He also seemed, as it were, to have imposed upon me by the testament of his final wishes the task of correcting and presenting a new edition of the Capitularies of our kings.

When he once held the office of chief magistrate in Tarraconensian Spain on behalf of our Most Christian King Louis, he discovered an old copy of the *Capitularies* in the library of the monastery of Ripoll. He borrowed it and ordered that certain portions not yet published be transcribed from it.

When the plague invaded Barcelona in 1651, and he wished to relinquish the province after seven years of administration, he left the manuscript at Barcelona and ordered that it be returned to the monastery of Ripoll. This was done as he had commanded.

But because the memory of that ancient manuscript repeatedly returned to his mind, and because he greatly desired to use it to correct the books of the *Capitularies*, he took advantage of a royal commission to investigate the boundaries of France and Spain in that part of the Pyrenees which separates the Tarraconensian region [Col. 0101A] from the Narbonensian.

He then wrote a letter full of benevolence and courtesy in the year 1660, on 8 March, to the marquis of Mortara, who at that time governed Catalonia as viceroy of Spain. Through the distinguished Petrus a Ponte, abbot of Arles, he instructed him in his name to ask the marquis to arrange for the Ripoll copy of the *Capitularies* to be sent to him, since he wished to compare it with the printed books, as he would have done had the plague not forced him to leave Barcelona.

Mortara replied most courteously that he would arrange for the book to be sought in the monastery of Ripoll and would send it as soon as it was found. Nevertheless, it was not sent until the following August. De Marca received it at Toulouse on 3 September, the day before he was to embark upon the Garonne, intending to travel first to Bordeaux and then to Paris.

Accordingly, [Col. 0101B] we boarded the boat on 2 September and compared the book of the *Capitularies* with the Pithoean edition: De Marca read the ancient copy, while I held the Pithoean edition and recorded the variant readings. The four days during which we traveled were spent on this work.

The Ripoll book was then sent to Toulouse and from there carried to Barcelona, where it was restored to its owners. It contains the first five books of the *Capitularies*, together with several Capitula of Louis the Pious and Charles the Bald, the Capitula of Walter, bishop of Orléans, several letters of Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, and finally a history of the translation of the relics of Saint Stephen.

Its title is as follows:

> *Capitularies: Here begins the preface of the book of Lord Ansegisus, abbot, which he composed for the lords Louis and Lothair, emperors, his two books on ecclesiastical order and two others on secular law.*

### LXVIII

Afterward, when I undertook the care of the Colbert Library, I found there a very ancient and excellent copy of the *Capitularies*, containing the first five books, some Capitula of Book VI, and also several Capitula of Book VII. I compared this manuscript with the Pithoean edition of the *Capitularies*, carefully recording the variant readings.

The title of the *Capitularies*, which is absent from many ancient books, as Petrus Pithoeus also observed, appears in the Colbert manuscript as follows:

> In the name of Christ. Here begin the Capitula of the kings and bishops, and especially of all the nobles of the Franks.

The remaining material found in the Tilian edition does not exist in this ancient copy.

### LXIX

Not long afterward, the manuscript books that had belonged to the eminent Cardinal Julius Mazarin were transferred to the royal library. Among them was found the very ancient manuscript used by Tilius in his edition of the *Capitularies*, corrected and interpolated in his own hand. It is therefore easy to see the source of everything enclosed in brackets in his edition and in the Pithoean edition.

This manuscript contains seven books of the *Capitularies*, but they are very incomplete, as Pithoeus seems to have warned. This, however, [Col. 0101D] must be understood of the three later books. It also contains the last three additions, though these too are incomplete.

### LXX

From the work I undertook in correcting the books of the *Capitularies* against those ancient copies, I easily understood that we do not today possess the collections of Ansegisus and Benedict the Levite in the form in which they were composed by them. Many passages had been torn from their proper places and transferred elsewhere; many things had also been added to the *Capitularies* themselves, although Ansegisus and Benedict had deliberately refrained from transcribing them.

I therefore resolved to restore the ancient edition entirely to use: to restore what the learned men had removed and to remove what they had added. I would not have anyone interpret this as though I were condemning the judgments of great men who had served the republic of letters so well. On the contrary, I rise to the level of their virtues and venerate and honor their memory with the greatest reverence.

Since, however, more copies still seemed necessary for preparing [Col. 0102A] the best edition, I searched for others and found two very ancient ones in the Thuana Library. One of them was certainly used by Petrus Pithoeus, since it had formerly been transferred from his library to the Thuan Library.

In that copy are transcribed the first four books of the *Capitularies*, the first two appendices of Book IV, and the four additions. The Thuana copy contains nothing besides the four books of Ansegisus and the three appendices of Book IV.

### LXXI

Antonius Sanderus, in the book entitled *Belgian Manuscript Library*, noted on page 352 that an ancient book existed in the library of the monastery of Cambron in Hainaut, bearing the following title:

> Statutes of Charlemagne, emperor of the Christians, and of his son Louis and Caesar Lothair.

We too obtained this manuscript through the kindness of the Reverend Fathers of the Order of Preachers residing in the parish of Saint-Honoré in Paris, in whose library it is now preserved. It contains only the first five books of the *Capitularies*, like the Ripoll copy.

### LXXII

[Col. 0102B]

I had previously noted that Joachim Vadianus and Jacob Gretser mention manuscripts of the library of Saint Gall containing Capitularies. Vadianus mentions them in Book VI of his *Aphorisms on the Eucharist*, page 215:

> There exists among us at Saint Gall an ancient codex of Ansegisus of Lobbes.

And in Book I of his *On the Ancient Colleges and Monasteries of Germany*, page 12:

> At Saint Gall there exists a very ancient codex, written in an uncultivated and barbarous style, which contains the Salic, Ripuarian, and Alemannic laws. There too are the books of Ansegisus on the laws of Charles and Louis, from which we have transcribed many passages.

Gretser, however, says in chapter 3 of his *Apology for Cardinal Baronius*, page 325, that he possessed a copy of the *Capitularies* from the library of Saint Gall.

It therefore happened conveniently that, at almost the same time as the Cambron manuscript was communicated to me, a catalogue of the books of the celebrated monastery of Saint Gall in Switzerland fell into my hands. In it [Col. 0102C] I found several manuscripts noted as containing the Capitularies of our kings.

Just as it was easy to conceive the desire to see these books, so it seemed difficult to obtain them from places separated by so great a distance. Yet the authority of the most illustrious and excellent Joannes Baptista Colbert—today the father of letters and of men of letters—brought it about that the manuscripts were conveyed here to me. He was especially assisted in this matter by the illustrious Melchior Arod of Saint-Romain, who at that time was our Most Christian King’s ambassador among the Swiss.

From this source, therefore, I obtained many very ancient manuscripts, but especially two in which the books of the *Capitularies* had been transcribed. One of them contained only Books III and IV and the three appendices of Book IV. The other contained the first five books and the first hundred chapters of Book VI, together with the three appendices of Book IV.

From the same source I also obtained an ancient copy of the Aachen Capitulary of the year 789 and several Capitula of Louis the Pious that had not yet been published, *Amalarius’s Extracts on the Office of the Mass*, and several Capitula relating to monks, which have been published in the appendix to the second volume.

Finally, among the other materials, I also obtained from there a very ancient codex of the letters of Ruricius, bishop of Limoges, and Desiderius, bishop of Cahors, from which Henricus Canisius published the same letters in the fifth volume of his *Ancient Readings*.

### LXXIII

After these materials, I obtained an ancient and excellent book of the Church of Beauvais—the best of all those I had yet seen—because it contains more material, and material in complete form, than the others. It was sent to me by the learned Godofredus Hermant, canon of that church and doctor of the Sorbonne.

Besides being written with great elegance, it contains the complete collections of Ansegisus and Benedict the Levite, including Book VII, which I had not yet seen complete anywhere else. The only exception is that, in the documents sent to me from Rome, I read that the same book, in the form in which it appears in the Beauvais manuscript, also exists in an ancient manuscript of the Vatican Library, as I shall [Col. 0103A] state shortly.

The same Beauvais manuscript then contains the Capitula of Charles the Bald—not all of them, but many more than are found in the other copies. Although this book is the most complete of all those I have seen, it does not contain the first addition, as I noted above.

### LXXIV

Next we obtained an ancient manuscript of Ansegisus from the library of the illustrious Philibert de la Mare, senator of Dijon; it also contains several Capitula of Charles the Bald.

We also used an ancient book of Saint Arnulf of Metz, in which many Capitula are transcribed, excerpted from the three final books of the *Capitularies*, by someone who clearly did not know the first four books. Excerpts of this kind are frequently found in ancient books, where they are said to have been taken from councils of kings at which Boniface, legate of the Apostolic See, was present, as we explain elsewhere.

### LXXV

[Col. 0103B]

The ancient copy that belonged to Franciscus Pithoeus and is now preserved in the library of the Oratory at Troyes was most courteously communicated to me by the illustrious Abel Sammarthanus, superior general of the Congregation of the Oratory in France.

The book is arranged as follows. First comes the preface of Ansegisus, then the preface of Charlemagne, followed by the prefaces of Books II, III, and IV. Next comes a letter of Pope Zacharias addressed to the Franks and Gauls, followed by a synod held under Prince Carloman.

Then are transcribed the verses customarily placed before the last three books of the *Capitularies*. After these verses come the acts of the Synod of Liptine and certain other Capitula collected here and there from the books of the *Capitularies*, without order.

The books of the *Capitularies* follow at the end, but they are not complete, since most of the Capitula have not been included; only those that suited the writer’s inclination or interests are present.

Moreover, the customary order has not been preserved in this collection. Whereas all the other collections of the *Capitularies* are divided into seven books, this one is divided, under a single numerical sequence, into nine books. These also contain Capitula excerpted [Col. 0103C] from the three final additions.

Finally, after chapter 447 of this collection, another 139 Capitula excerpted from the books of the *Capitularies* are added. It may perhaps be inferred from this that other additions after the fourth were also in use at the time when this book was written.

In all, it contains 587 Capitula.

### LXXVI

The library of the Society of Jesus at the College of Clermont in Paris alone supplied us with several ancient manuscripts, principally through the work and diligence of the illustrious René Rapin. Without him, this collection of the *Capitularies* might perhaps have remained incomplete. He made the entire manuscript library of the college accessible to me, so that the illustrious Joannes Garnerius, who had charge of the library, also gave me permission to examine the papers of Sirmond and copy whatever I wished.

From this source I obtained especially three very ancient manuscripts of the *Capitularies*.

The first, which belonged to Jacob Sirmond, contains the first four books and the first two appendices of Book IV, together with the four additions.

The second, which belonged to the monastery of Saint-Remi at Reims and was transferred from the Tilian library to the Clermont Library, contains only the first four books and the first two appendices.

The third, which belonged to Saint Vincent of Metz and which I have discovered was also used by the Pithoeus brothers and Bignon, likewise contains only the first four books together with the same two appendices.

[Col. 0103D] This manuscript also contains material that does not belong to the seven books of the *Capitularies*: Capitula of Prince and King Pippin; Capitula of Charlemagne, among which are many that had not yet been published; several Capitula of Louis the Pious and Charles the Bald; the laws of the Ripuarians, Alemannians, and Bavarians; and the Salic Law.

This is the celebrated Codex of Charlemagne’s *Capitularies*, which alone among all the manuscripts, as Sirmond says (*Gallican Councils*, vol. II, p. 244), contains more Capitularies of Charles Augustus than the others and assigns them to their proper places according to each year of his reign—except that in some cases it lacks the name of the place and entirely omits the first Capitulary, which concerns Italy rather than the Franks.

The Palatine Library nevertheless possessed a similar manuscript, which is now in Rome in the Vatican Library, as we shall say below.

Sirmond had also seen another ancient manuscript, namely the one that, as I conjecture, he calls the Ghent and Flemish manuscript, whose use he had obtained through Heribert Rosweyde. In his papers I found several additions to the Capitularies of Charlemagne that are not read elsewhere.

They have, however, certain and unquestionable authority, because they were found among the papers of that great man and transcribed in his own hand.

### LXXVII

I was subsequently informed that an ancient copy of the *Capitularies* existed in the library of the monastery of Saint Michael at Periculo Maris. The Reverend Father Lord Laurentius Hunaltus, prior of that monastery, willingly supplied me with a copy. The illustrious Lords Lucas Dacherius and Joannes Mabillonius, Benedictine monks—names well known among [Col. 0104B] students of good letters—had written to him about the matter out of friendship and courtesy toward me.

At the beginning of the manuscript the following was written in ancient times:

> In this volume are contained four little books of the Capitula of the Emperor Charles and his son Louis, collected by Ansegisus, abbot, and three others collected by Benedict the deacon, the last of which is missing.

Correctly so, for this manuscript ends at chapter 363 of Book VI.

Afterward we read:

> This book belongs to Saint Michael of Periculo Maris; Lord Robert, abbot, had it made.

I understand this to refer to Robert, abbot of Mont-Saint-Michel, whose additions and appendix to Sigebert survive. Henry, archdeacon of Huntingdon, informs Varinus in a letter that Robert was a most diligent investigator and collector of both sacred and secular books (*Appendix to Guibert of Nogent*, p. 736).

This interpretation also seems to be supported by what the aforementioned Lucas Dacherius reports: that he had seen a huge volume of Pliny’s histories, written with the greatest elegance and sent from the monastery of Mont-Saint-Michel, where the following, among other things, was written:

[Col. 0104C]

> Preface of Robert, abbot, to Pliny; he also brought the book itself into Normandy and corrected it after it had become corrupt.  
> *(Ibid., p. 716.)*

In his notes on the letters of Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, when he was compiling a catalogue of the abbots of Saint Michael of Mont-Tombe, he says the following about Robert:

> The history of Saint Michael, written in manuscript, reports that he produced 140 volumes, and that they rotted beneath the ruins and drip-eaves of the tower.

Everyone can see that this passage must be understood of the books that Robert ordered to be transcribed and deposited in the library of his monastery.

### LXXVIII

Besides the ancient codices mentioned thus far, we have also used three Palatine codices of the Vatican Library, whose variant readings were sent to us from Rome. But before beginning the account of what is found in those books, it is worthwhile to note here how it came about that I obtained access to them.

When I had observed that the most distinguished Philippus Labbe, in volume seven of the latest edition of the councils, pp. 1174 and 1180, reported that Holstenius had informed him that certain Capitularies of Charlemagne existed in an old Palatine Codex of the Vatican Library, partly published and partly not yet published, I wrote on 21 September 1674 to the eminent Cardinal Giovanni Bona, asking him to have the unpublished Capitularies copied from that codex for me, to order that the variant readings of the published ones be recorded, and to have the whole sent to me as soon as possible.

My letter found that excellent man confined to bed by the illness that carried him away from us. Yet, although he was oppressed by pains throughout his body, he immediately sent word to the Vatican Library; and when he had learned that three ancient copies of the Capitularies existed there, he instructed them to report to me that, as soon as he had recovered his health, he would gladly lend me his assistance in this matter.

But alas! That excellent man died shortly afterward, on 28 October of the same year. When news of his death spread here in Paris, the grief of those who love learning was so great that, although they openly testified it by their faces and voices, they mourned even more deeply in their hearts, as if a common father had been taken from everyone. For who would not grieve at the death of so excellent and holy an old man, placed at the highest rank of dignity, endowed with extensive knowledge of all good things, and both able and willing to adorn, assist, and advance the world of letters?

Accordingly, scarcely anyone in this city—namely, among those who love our studies and knowledge of ecclesiastical antiquity—failed to lament that his death had cut short his literary counsels. He bestowed his favor on all, lent his assistance to each, and moved and inspired everyone by his splendid and honorable example.

I, above all, suffered the greatest loss at the death of so great a man, who loved me and approved my labors, whatever their worth, by his most kindly support. Having lost this patron, I had to seek another not unlike him, who would assist my studies and arrange for the variant readings of the ancient codices mentioned above to be sent to me.

At that time the eminent Cardinal César d’Estrées, bishop and duke of Laon and peer of France, was conveniently in Rome. When I wrote to him concerning the edition of the Capitularies and requested his assistance, he used his authority to have those codices collated with the printed books and, in addition, to have the Capitularies not yet published copied.

From this source, therefore, I received several Capitularies of Charlemagne and Louis the Pious that had not yet appeared in print, together with the variant readings of the books of Ansegisus and Benedict the Levite, and of the Capitularies of Charles the Bald.

The codex whose variant readings first reached me contains the four books of Ansegisus, together with the first two appendices to the fourth book. Another contains seven books of the Capitularies and three later additions, like the book of the Church of Beauvais. The third contains the Capitularies of Charles the Bald.

But the papers sent to me do not indicate in which of these three the unpublished Capitularies made available to me are found.

### LXXIX

Finally, I used two other ancient codices, one of which is mine, while I obtained the other from the Royal Library. I join them to this group because, since both are of the same antiquity and are completely similar, and since one must have been copied from the other, it would have been useless to treat them separately.

In these codices are first placed the canons of councils and the decrees of the Roman pontiffs from the edition of Dionysius Exiguus; then the seven books of the Capitularies; certain excerpts concerning the nature of marriage and legitimate unions from Jerome, Augustine, and the Irish synod. After these follows a treatise *On the Benefit of Penance* and *On the Remission of Sins through Penance*, divided into three books, which the distinguished Dom Lucas Dacherius recently published in volume eleven of his *Spicilegium*.

But just as the collection of Dionysius is complete in the royal codex and mutilated in mine, so the royal codex does not contain that treatise on Penance, but only part of its preface, because the leaves that followed were cut out and removed. Moreover, the seven books of the Capitularies are not complete in these two codices, but are excerpted only, as has been said, from the codex of Troyes.

### LXXX

Thus far we have dealt with the ancient exemplars containing the collections of Ansegisus and Benedict the Levite. We must now say something about other ancient codices that we used in correcting the published Capitularies, and also about those that supplied us with Capitularies not previously published.

These sources are indeed recorded everywhere in their proper places in our notes, or at the beginning of the Capitularies now published for the first time. Nevertheless, a brief enumeration of them must also be undertaken here.

Accordingly, in correcting the complete Capitularies that circulate outside the books of the Capitularies and their additions, we used the very oldest codices of the Royal, Vatican, Colbert, Thuani, Bigot, Mazarin, and Tilius libraries; those of the Church of Albi, the Church of Poitiers, the monasteries of Corbie, Moissac, Corbie—or Saint-Laumer—Saint Gall, Saint Vincent of Metz, Saint Vincent of Laon, Saint Remigius of Reims; and also those of the monasteries of Aniane and Ripoll.

We used the Dijon codex of the distinguished Philibert de la Mare, senator, a man of great authority and learning; the Navarre codex, formerly belonging to the Navarre College of Paris; and the Helmstedt codex of the Julia Academy, from which the distinguished men Hermann Conring and Joachim Johann Mader copied variant readings and sent them to me.

We also used several excellent codices of the Parisian College of the Society of Jesus. The codices of the distinguished men Claudius Puteanus and Petrus Pithoeus were of great assistance to us, as was the codex of the very eminent Hieronymus Bignon, which had previously belonged first to Jean-Antoine Lescurier and had then been purchased from his heirs by Claude Expilly.

That Jean Tilius used this codex is evident from various places where corrections in his own hand have been written above the lines, as was his custom.

Finally, I published or corrected the provisions of Charlemagne and Louis the Pious for the Spaniards with the help of an old codex preserved in the archive of the archbishop of Narbonne.

### LXXXI

Furthermore, in correcting the Capitularies of Charlemagne, Louis the Pious, and others that concern the law of the Lombards or are excerpted from it, I used two ancient codices of the Royal Library. One belonged to the old Royal Library; the other was transferred to it from the Mazarin Library and once belonged to the jurist Paulus Ramus.

The following annotation, written in his hand in the codex itself, establishes this:

> As a gift from the most distinguished jurist, Lord Alexander de Agagiis, a nobleman of Bergamo, who gave these laws of the Lombards to me, Paulus Ramus, doctor of law, when I was serving as vicar at Bergamo, under the magnificent and most excellent doctor, Lord Marino Giorgio, my most respected magistrate.

These two codices also contain ancient glosses, many fragments of which I published among my notes.

### LXXXII

It remains, therefore, to explain what we have accomplished in this collection and edition of the Capitularies.

First, we collated the Capitularies with the ancient codices mentioned above, with the greatest accuracy and diligence that could possibly be applied, and with their assistance we corrected the older editions.

Next, we attempted to indicate in the margin the sources of the Capitularies, such as councils, the decrees of the Fathers, the laws of peoples, and the Capitularies themselves.

I also recorded the passages quoted from the Capitularies by the ancient writers Theodulf, bishop of Orléans; Hincmar, archbishop of Reims; Herard, archbishop of Tours; Isaac, bishop of Langres; Regino, abbot of Prüm; Burchard, bishop of Worms; Fulbert and Ivo, bishops of Chartres; and finally Gratian, compiler of the canons and decrees.

Since, however, it was difficult to discover everything in so great a number of Capitularies, and many things escaped us whose origin we did not record, we nevertheless later found the sources of most of them. We reported these either in the notes or in additions to the notes, or at least drew attention to them among the errata.

How much the whole undertaking cost us, and how harsh and thankless a labor it was, will be for you, learned reader, to judge. For my part, I prefer that it has now been accomplished rather than left undone.

### LXXXIII

I have illustrated the entire work with my notes, as was proper.

> Although we have not reprinted the text of the Capitularies edited by Baluzius, since we possess a more accurate one in the *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, we shall nevertheless append Baluzius’s notes beneath the text. — Editor.

In these notes I report variant readings from ancient manuscript codices and editions—not all of them, but only those that seemed to possess some importance.

I have also explained the reasons for the readings adopted in the text and attempted to confirm them by authority and examples. Finally, I explained those passages that contained some difficulty, or to which the distorted interpretations of others had done violence, according to the meaning, as I believe, of the authors from whom they were taken, while indicating their sense.

I have sometimes interpreted barbarous and obscure words, but often passed them over, partly because I was hindered by my other occupations, but chiefly because I saw that the distinguished and learned Charles du Fresne was seriously considering the publication of a very rich *Glossary of the Writers of Middle and Low Latin*, long desired by scholars, which is now under the press and being printed in the most elegant type.

In that work the reader will easily find explanations of the more difficult words occurring in our collection.

### LXXXIV

Finally, following my usual practice and custom, I added a very important and rich appendix of ancient records: namely, several short works concerning matters relating to ecclesiastical ceremonies; various Capitularies concerning monastic institutions; provisions of kings; decrees and letters of bishops; judicial assemblies of counts and *scabini*, royal envoys, and royal vassals; and many other materials of this kind.

We nevertheless point out that a large part of the material taken from chartularies was supplied to us by the distinguished Antonius Vion Herovallius, whose name frequently occurs both in the books published by us and in the scholarly works of those who devote themselves to letters.

There are also several items in this appendix that had previously been published, but in a very corrupt and mutilated form; for that reason we thought they ought to be reprinted. They are:

- The judgment issued in 783 against Count Milo on behalf of Daniel, archbishop of Narbonne;
- the provision of Louis the Pious confirming the authority of the archbishop of Sens over the monasteries of the diocese of Sens;
- the dowry charter by which Folradus settled property upon Helegrina, his bride;
- the provision of Charles the Bald for certain Spaniards;
- the letter of John VIII to Adalgarius, bishop of Autun;
- and the dowry document of Micza, daughter of John.

(*Appendix of Ancient Records*, titles 16, 38, 43, 59, 102, 147.)

These documents, I say, which previously abounded in many errors, have been corrected and supplemented by us with the aid of ancient books. All the rest are now published for the first time.

### LXXXV

You have here, learned reader, an account of my purpose and method in publishing the Capitularies, and of the aids and labors by which this work was brought to completion.

You may judge that I acted in the best faith when reviewing these Capitularies and correcting them against ancient exemplars, and that I have named no ancient codex which I did not collate with the printed editions, word for word.

Those that now appear for the first time I myself copied in my own hand; and those found in several ancient books I collated with each individual exemplar.

As for my notes and preface, I ask you to believe that I have written nothing out of hatred or favor toward anyone. I always pursue the truth, as far as the smallness of my talent permits.

I have also maintained modesty whenever I was compelled to dissent from the opinions of learned men. When I refute their judgments and views, I often do so with some preliminary expression of respect, and always without attack.

This is what I wished to tell you, reader. Farewell.

---

## Preface of Georg Heinrich Pertz

*(From the* Monumenta Germaniae Historica, *volume III.)*

The book that at last may be delivered to its readers contains the Capitularies of our Frankish kings and emperors from the sixth century through the tenth.

These are not merely the laws themselves, arranged in chapters and therefore called Capitularies, but also the other legal monuments that appeared relevant both to the formulation of laws and to their execution, and that have survived down to our own time in manuscript books or in printed form.

Here, therefore, in order that we may survey the process by which laws were enacted, are royal constitutions concerning the holding of a court or the mounting of a military expedition; chapters proposed by kings and emperors, with the advice of their men, at public assemblies; the judgments of nobles selected to examine them; the proceedings of individual assemblies and courts; reports to the ruler from individual assemblies and courts, bishops, or counts; petitions presented to the king by nobles; the king’s replies and public speeches; laws, constitutions, pacts, and general or special chapters publicly promulgated; royal edicts concerning the observance or interpretation of laws; encyclical letters; chapters entrusted to royal envoys for execution; the encyclicals of the envoys to the prelates and counts subject to them; formulas for the promulgation and acceptance of laws at individual assemblies, together with the subscriptions of free men; formulas of oaths, commendations, coronations, and other documents of this kind that can contribute to an understanding of the enactment of laws and the administration of the state.

They are so useful that the form, method, and supports of ancestral liberty may already be placed most clearly before our eyes.

These records of greater importance, written on parchment sheets in the royal palace and either presented publicly at an assembly for the knowledge of all or sent through the individual archbishoprics to bishops, abbots, and counts for promulgation to the people, were preserved both in the palace archive and in cathedral churches, monasteries, and public assemblies. So that they would not easily perish, they were usually inserted into legal books or codices of ecclesiastical law.

Almost all the authentic copies, whether retained in the palace or sent into the provinces, have perished, except for a delicate parchment sheet now surviving in the monastery of Saint Paul in Carinthia, by which Charlemagne orders the Saxon hostages distributed through Alamannia to come to Mainz, and the encyclical letters of Archbishop Riculfus preserved in the monastery of Saint Gall.

But numerous books of ecclesiastical or secular law containing the Capitularies have survived to our time, having been written in Germany, Italy, Gaul, and the Spanish March. We examined such books in the Church of Saint Martin at Mainz, the cathedrals of Augsburg and Freising, the monasteries of Saint Emmeram at Regensburg, Tegernsee and Chiemsee, Saint Gall, Weissenau, Weissenburg, and Corbie; in the Italian monasteries of Monte Cassino, Cava, and Susa; and in the Church of Saint Euphemia at Verona.

We also examined books written in the churches and monasteries of Gaul: Paris; Mâcon; Saint Vincent at Laon; Saint Peter at Beauvais; Saint Remigius at Reims; Anizy; Saint Vincent at Metz; Saints Mary and Stephen at Sens; Corbie; Saint Mary at Luçon; Tours; and the region of Bourges, besides many others whose origin is not sufficiently certain.

As for their age, some were written in the eighth century, most in the ninth or tenth, some in the eleventh and twelfth, and indeed some even in the fifteenth century.

Legal records were therefore transcribed for as long as their authority, still vigorous throughout the empire and the kingdoms derived from it, encouraged the renewal and multiplication of ancient books.

Only in the thirteenth century, when legal statutes written in the vernacular gradually began to claim great authority for themselves in Germany and Italy, did the older materials begin slowly to be neglected and soon handed over to oblivion. Yet neither the laws of the empire—the foundations of the public order—which were expressed in the Capitularies, nor the Capitularies themselves, were abrogated. Indeed, they continued to have the force of law, confirmed by emperors Frederick I and Otto IV and repeatedly reinforced by the oath of each new king until the final period of the empire.

> Otto I, emperor, issued the Frankfurt constitution in 951 “with the authority of the holy canons and Fathers, and also with the institutions of the preceding kings’ Capitularies, placed before us.”
>
> Emperor Frederick I, in the judgment concerning the property of deceased clerics issued at Worms on 26 September 1165, says:
>
> “Therefore, following the footsteps of our predecessors, the deified emperors—namely Constantine the Great, Justinian, and Valentinian—as well as those of Charles and Louis, and venerating their sacred laws as divine oracles . . . instructed by these sacred laws and by the institutions of Charles and Louis, whose zeal for divine worship and the Catholic faith was comparable, we grant perpetual firmness to the judgment of the venerable clergy of the Church of Worms . . . for this liberty.”
>
> The same emperor had said the following to the princes of Germany:
>
> “There are two things by which our empire must be governed: the holy laws of the emperors and the good customs of our predecessors and fathers.”
>
> According to the history of the landgraves of Thuringia, Emperor Otto IV, after defeating his rival Philip and gaining possession of the whole empire, in 1209 “held his court at Frankfurt, where he was confirmed by the princes of Germany; there he delivered to all the princes the laws, peace, and edicts of Charlemagne, with the requirement that they should all swear an oath of law concerning them.”
>
> Emperor Louis IV, in 1342, at the urging of the archchancellor of the empire, decreed that the imperial court should judge in the Roman Empire according to the laws of the kings and emperors who had preceded him and according to their written rights.
>
> Emperor Francis II, in 1792, in the capitulary of his election, article 2, § 4, declared that he would renew the laws and constitutions of the empire and, with the consent of the electors, princes, and estates of the empire, amend them; but that he would in no way alter, without the express consent of the electors, princes, and estates at the imperial diet, anything defined and concluded in earlier assemblies and not abolished by subsequent imperial constitutions, laws, or the rightful custom of the empire, but would firmly preserve it. This passage seems chiefly to refer to the statutes and laws of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries, but it is clear that the earlier ones were likewise to be preserved.

This seems to be understood especially of the collection of Ansegisus. Nevertheless, it is equally clear that the other records explaining the ancient constitution of the state must not be neglected either in elucidating the public law of the Middle Ages or even that of more recent times.

In Gaul, according to Baluzius, the authority of the Capitularies remained in force until the time of King Philip IV, that is, through the fourteenth century, although they appear to have been copied more rarely in the eleventh, twelfth, and thirteenth centuries.

In Italy, I do not know whether the chapters added to the edict of the Lombard kings and inserted into collections of laws ever entirely lost their force. Muratorius himself, in the preface to his edition of the Lombard law, inclines rather to the view that these laws, and therefore the Lombard Capitularies as well, retained some force in his own age.

Certainly the Lombard law, formed together with its appended Capitularies, was in use in the thirteenth century, and I remember having examined a charter concerning *morgengabe*, dated 1425, in the chartulary of the monastery of Cava.

In the sixteenth century, after the name “Capitularies” first began to be heard through Beatus Rhenanus and Vadianus, Vitus Amerpachius, in 1545, when he published the Tegernsee codex, provided material for a somewhat fuller knowledge of them.

Following closely in his footsteps, Tilius published a collection of ancient laws, but in 1548, after undertaking Ansegisus and Benedict, he did not complete the work, so that Herold surpassed him in publishing Ansegisus.

I have discussed these men below, together with Pithoeus and Lindenbrog, who used a single Wolfenbüttel codex.

At the end of the sixteenth century and the beginning of the seventeenth, Cardinal Caesar Baronius inserted in his *Annals* several Capitularies taken from Antonius Augustinus’s copy of the codex of Muretus, while Canisius inserted the assemblies of Emperor Louis II and Otto I in his *Ancient Readings*.

Goldastus collected into one body all the materials that, whether in the books of those who preceded him, in historical works, or in the ancient charters of emperors and kings, appeared to bear the character of written law or right, preserving them as he found them or ordering them to assume new forms. This was indeed a sufficiently arduous undertaking, but less pleasing to a lover of unadorned truth.

When the number of legal monuments had already become considerable, in 1623 and 1629 the work of Sirmond added several Capitularies of Charles the Bald and his successors, together with three volumes of the Councils of Gaul. We still rejoice that these works infused new light into the history of Gaul and Germany.

From Sirmond’s papers, Labbe also produced material in volume eight of the *Councils*. After Holstenius and Charles Dati, who published a few Capitularies, the true restorer of the Capitularies, Stephanus Baluzius, adorned the field with his labors.

Baluzius’s principal plan had been to correct the collections of Ansegisus and Benedict by collating codices. But, following the example of Goldastus and Sirmond, he also undertook to publish the individual Capitularies, arranged almost everywhere in chronological order, using many codices obtained from the Spanish March, Switzerland, Belgium, Rome, Helmstedt, and above all Gaul.

He inserted the laws of the Ripuarians, Bavarians, Alamanni, and Salian Franks; numerous letters and diplomas; and chapters excerpted from the books of Benedict. He added collections of formulas and many documents, together with the notes of earlier scholars—Pithoeus, Bignonius, Sirmondius—and his own.

With such an abundance of learning, such indefatigable zeal, and such fortunate acumen, he brought his work to completion in a manner that will secure for him among posterity the everlasting memory of a great name.

A decade after Baluzius, Mabillonius published in the *Museum Italicum* a few chapters taken from the Chisian codex.

In the eighteenth century, Muratorius, the glory of his Italy, published the chapters added to the Lombard edicts; Eccardus and Martenius brought several documents to light from the Helmstedt and Andechs libraries; and the Baluzius edition was reprinted and enlarged in Venice through the work of Georgisch, de Chiniac, and Canciniani.

Toward the end of the century, Brunsius once again published the *Capitulary on the Estates*, together with the formulas for describing royal domains. In the nineteenth century, when our edition had already begun to be prepared, E. Spangenberg made some readings of his codex public. With their assistance, as well as with that of the other materials newly discovered after Baluzius by Herold, Eccardus, Mabillonius, and Canciani, the distinguished Walter used them in arranging his *Corpus of German Law* according to the example of Baluzius.

The matter has now reached the point at which I must give an account of the aids and plan of the new edition.

The first suggestion for undertaking a new edition of the Capitularies was given to me by the codex of the monastery of Saint Paul in Carinthia. Besides a collection of ancient laws, I found in it several Capitularies of Charles and Louis I, and some of Lothair, appended to the edicts of the Lombard kings, with their original order and form preserved.

When this occurred in September 1820, I thereafter never failed, in all the libraries and archives that I investigated, to seek new additions to the work.

After examining the treasures of the Imperial Library of Vienna, in the years 1821, 1822, and 1823 I obtained in Italy several codices of great value, especially the Chisian, the Cava codex, and the Vatican codices. I was then able to undertake, with greater success, the restoration of the Capitularies of Charles, Louis, and Lothair I.

Nor did I fail to anticipate that our Germany would yield still greater treasures.
