I examined the codices of Saint Gall, and in the autumn of 1823, while inspecting the books of the ducal library at Wolfenbüttel, I came across, among the other valuable codices, a codex formerly belonging to Blankenburg, outstanding for its unpublished Capitularies of Emperors Charles, Louis, Lothair I, and Louis II.

The generosity of the distinguished librarians, our late Ebert, Eigner, and Schoenemann, allowed me to use it at leisure for a long time. With the same favor, the distinguished Friedrich Jacobs continued our work and allowed me to use, for as long as I needed it, an excellent Gotha codex to which we owe other unpublished records of those same emperors.

In 1826 and 1827 I turned to the codices of the Royal Library of Paris. With the support of the distinguished men Abel Rémusat, Gail, Hase, and Guérard, I examined and copied the codices formerly used by Baluzius for his edition, together with many others unknown to him, of which that library possesses an abundance.

Nor did Britain, when I visited it in 1827, deny me its resources, nor Germany when I returned once more. One of the Corbie codices was sent by the distinguished Wigand; another, already in Hamburg, by our Lappenberg; the Schaffhausen codex by the distinguished Zellweger, the learned man of Appenzell; and a collation of the Weissenau codex was voluntarily offered by the distinguished Maier of Esslingen, who, alas, died a few days before.

As the work gradually grew through these materials, one thing nevertheless seemed lacking: I had not yet visited the Royal Library of Munich for the preparation of the work.

I visited it in 1833, accompanied by our Boehmer. On the journey, with the support of the distinguished Laeckio, we put the codices of the Babenberg Library to our use. Then at Munich, whatever books the generosity of the distinguished Liechenthaler and Schmeller placed before me when I requested them—including the codex formerly belonging to Tegernsee—I either copied myself or later received in transcription from the most learned young man and most devoted student of our work, the distinguished Foringer.

Thus it became possible for the work, furnished with the most extensive aids, finally to be committed to the press.

The codices I used, besides those listed below in the preface to Ansegisus, and excluding those from which the work derived no benefit, are the following:

- **C. Casinas no. 257**, folio, eleventh century; and **Vaticanus Christinae no. 556**, eleventh century. In Gregory of Tours’s *Ecclesiastical History* they contain the pact designated in our index as number 4. On these, see our *Annals*, vol. V, pp. 53–60.

- **C. ducalis Guelferbytanus**, among the Weissenburg codices, no. 97, eighth century. It places the Capitularies of the Salian law, designated by numbers 5 and 7 in our index, under titles 77–90, and contains a summary of the *Breviary of Alaric*.

- **C. regius Monacensis Cimel. IV, 3, 9**, large octavo, late eighth or ninth century. It exhibits the Salian law; Capitularies 5 and 7; and titles 78, 42, and 75 of the Burgundian law. It was made public by the distinguished Ed. Aug. Feuerbach in 1831. It also contains the laws of the Ripuarians and Alamanni.

- **C. bibliothecae Sangallensis no. 731**, from the year 793. It contains part of the Theodosian Code, the Salian law, Capitulary 6, and the law of the Alamanni. See volume V of our *Annals*, p. 213.

- **C. of the same library no. 729**, ninth century. It contains the Theodosian Code, the Salian law, Capitulary 6, and the law of the Alamanni. See our *Annals*, vol. V, p. 215.

- **C. regius Paris. no. 4627**, tenth century. It contains the Salian law published by Schilter, Capitulary 6, and the formulas of Marculf.

- **C. regius Paris. no. 4409**, perhaps written at Tours (Colbert 1197, Regius 5184), ninth century. It presents the Theodosian Code and the Salian law, with a catalogue of the Frankish kings, the prologue of the Salian law, and Capitulary 6 added, as well as the Sirmondian formulas and the Breviary of Alaric.

- **C. Vaticanus no. 3827**, folio, eleventh century, formerly of Saint Peter at Beauvais. It exhibits a collection of councils and Capitularies, for example 3, 12, and 14.

- **C. Palatino-Vaticanus no. 577**, from approximately the year 800, formerly belonging to the Church of Saint Martin at Mainz. It exhibits the Capitularies indicated in our index by numbers 9, 10, 16, 11, and 14. A fuller description may be found in our *Annals*, vol. V, p. 303.

- **C. palatinus Vindobonensis, Theologia no. 259**, ninth–tenth century. Among the letters of Boniface it contains Capitularies 9, 10, and 18.

- **C. regius Monacensis**, formerly Mainz, ninth century; also a codex of the Karlsruhe Library, tenth century; and **D. Marci at Venice**, paper, fifteenth century, contain Capitularies 9 and 10.

- **C. regius Monacensis**, formerly Freising, C. F. 25, tenth century, contains Capitulary 9.

- **C. bibliothecae Babenbergensis D. II, 2**, ninth century, long octavo. It supplied the Salian, Ripuarian, and Alamannic laws, and on its final folio our Capitulary 20.

- **C. bibliothecae ducalis Guelferbytanae**, among the Helmstedt codices, no. 496, of a rather tall octavo format, approximately the year 800. It contains the ecclesiastical Capitulary of 789, together with an explanation of the Apostles’ Creed and the Lord’s Prayer, and a paraphrase of that prayer.

- **C. regius Monacensis**, formerly of Saint Emmeram at Regensburg, E. 91, quarto. Written in 821 at the order of Bishop Baturic, it contains, after many matters relating to the Church, a letter of Hadrian I to the bishops of Spain; Paulinus’s pamphlet against Elipandus; the synodal letter of the Council of Frankfurt; Charlemagne’s letter to Elipandus; some short questions of Saint Augustine; and Capitularies 30, 31, and 32.

- **C. regius Parisiensis no. 5577** (Colbert 4167, Regius 4382, 5, 5), tall octavo, tenth century, formerly of Saint Mary of Luçon. After the Passion of Saint Eustace and that of Saint Felicity, it contains an epitaph of Alcuin, various letters and treatises, and Capitulary 39, “which is appropriate to recall at such a time.” A fuller description of the codex is found in the catalogue of the manuscripts of the Royal Library, vol. IV, p. 134.

- **C. regius Monacensis**, formerly of Saint Emmeram at Regensburg, F. 11, quarto, ninth century, folios 118–119. It contains Capitulary 41.

- **C. of Saint Paul in Carinthia**, a leaf inserted into a canonical manuscript, ninth century. It provides an autograph copy of Capitulary 42.

- **C. regius Monacensis**, formerly of Saint Emmeram at Regensburg, G. 111, quarto, ninth century, folio 139. It contains Capitulary 49.

- **CC. regii Monacenses**, formerly of Freising, C. K. 3, ninth century, and C. 1, 26, tenth century. After Isidore, they exhibit Capitulary 50.

- **C. regius Paris. no. 4758** (Reg. 4490), small quarto, ninth century. It contains Capitularies 53 and 54, and the Salian and Burgundian laws.

- **C. Palatino-Vaticanus no. 773**, octavo, tenth century. After the Ripuarian law, it presents Capitularies 55, 53, and 54.

- **C. palatinus Vindobonensis, Civil Law no. 64**, twelfth century. It appends Capitulary 64 to the law of the Bavarians.

- **C. regius Monacensis Cimel. IV, 3, d**, octavo, ninth–tenth century, formerly of Tegernsee. It adds Capitulary 64 to the laws of the Bavarians and Alamanni.

- **C. regius Monacensis**, formerly of the Church of Augsburg, no. 153, quarto, tenth century. It presents a collection of penitential canons, the Alamannic law, Capitulary 64, and Ansegisus.

- **C. regius Monacensis Cimel. IV, 3**, formerly of Chiemsee, octavo, twelfth century. It adds Capitulary 64 to the law of the Bavarians and the decree of Tassilo. The Munich codex formerly belonging to the city of Augsburg, twelfth century, octavo, appears to have been copied from it.

- **C. palatinus Vindobonensis**, in the catalogue of canon law, no. 128, ninth century, large octavo. It exhibits our Capitularies 30 and 65.

- **C. regius Paris**, among the Latin supplements, no. 303, formerly of Clermont College, no. 629, ninth–tenth century. It exhibits the Salian law, with chapter 2 appended to title 71, and the Capitularies that immediately follow: 53, 71 a, and 71 b.

- **C. regius Paris. no. 4404**, from Narbonnese Gaul (Colbert 2436, Regius 4890, 22), ninth century. It contains the Breviary of Alaric, the Salian law, the prologue of the Salian law, the Alamannic and Ripuarian laws, and Capitularies 5, 7, 6, 53, 54, 78, and 68.

- **C. regius Paris. no. 4629**, tall folio, ninth century (Colbert 4059, Regius 5189, 3, 3). It exhibits the Salian law, defective at the beginning; Capitulary 6; a question concerning the Trinity; Capitularies 78, 53, 54, 55, 71 a, and 71 b; the Ripuarian law; a recapitulation of the solidi; an orthography; epitaphs; several other items; and a charter from Bourges.

- **C. Sangallensis**, containing a very mutilated autograph letter 94 b.

- **C. of Saint Paul**, tall octavo, tenth century. It exhibits Isidore and Capitulary 98.

- **C. ducalis Guelferbytanus**, among the Helmstedt codices, no. 254, early ninth century, tall format. It preserves Capitularies 101 and 102, and letters of Pope Leo III to Charlemagne.

- **C. Palatino-Vaticanus no. 289**, ninth century. It contains Capitularies 61, 62, 103 b, 27, and 35. See our *Annals*, vol. V, p. 305.

- **C. ducalis Guelferbytanus**, among the Gudian codices, no. 299, quarto, ninth century. It contains the Salian law; Capitulary 53; excerpts from Capitularies 54 and 71 a–b; Capitulary 106; the donation of Lambert; and the Ripuarian law.

- Codex of Saint Paul in Carinthia, copied at the beginning of the ninth century, namely between the years 817 and 823, with an image of the lawgiving king placed at the beginning. It contains our capitulary 52; the laws of the Ripuarian Franks, the Salian Franks, the Bavarians, and the Alamanni; part of the Breviary of Alaric; the Burgundian Law; our capitularies 21, 33, 26, 80, 83 (chapters 6–9, 12, and 13), 55 (chapter 3), 85, 88, and 53 (chapters 1–5), marked with continuous chapter numbers (1–92). These are followed by our capitularies 40, 23, 112, 113, and 114; in a different hand, capitularies 124 and 135 were added, apparently in the years 823 and 825. See our *Annals*, vol. III, pp. 78 ff.

- Royal Codex Paris, no. 4995 (Colbert 3287, Royal 5192, 2, 2), ninth century, contains, after annals for the years 708–799 [Col. 0113C] and interpretations concerning divine or human laws, our capitularies 112, 113, 53, and 54; a recapitulation appended to the Salian Law; and capitularies 78, 71, 44a, 51, 76, 70, 99, and 87. It was written for the use of some Parisian church, as is shown by the notice concerning the promulgated chapters (53) at the Parisian assembly, and by capitulary 44a. This is the Tilian Codex, from which a few passages copied by Sirmond’s hand were taken for Baluze’s use; Baluze, however, did not use the codex itself.

- The late Ernest Spangenberg’s Codex, ninth century, contains a fragment of the Ripuarian Law, the Saxon Law, the beginning of capitulary 53, then 112 (from chapter 6 onward), 113, the beginning of the Alamannic Law, the end of the Burgundian Law, and the beginning of capitulary 75.

- The Corbie Codex, quarto, tenth century, contains the Saxon and Thuringian Laws, capitularies 35, 112, 113, and 114, a Penitential Book, and the privileges of Corbie from the ninth and tenth centuries. See our *Annals*, vol. IV, p. 346.

- Royal Codex Paris, no. 4788, formerly belonging to Saint Vincent of Laon [Col. 0113D], octavo, ninth century (Baluze 864, Royal 4655a), contains the Salian Law, capitularies 53, 54, 111, and 112, with 114 inserted, 113, a homily of Augustine, and, on very badly damaged pages, capitularies 89 and 90.

- Royal Codex Paris, no. 4628 (Colbert 5453, Royal 5289, 6), from the end of the ninth or the beginning of the tenth century, contains the Salian Law, capitularies 53, 54, 72b, 112, 113, and 114, and the Ripuarian and Alamannic Laws.

- Royal Codex Paris, among the Latin Supplements, no. 215, formerly of Corbie, large octavo, contains the Theodosian Code, the Burgundian Law, capitulary 2, chapters 3, 4, 10, 12, and 11 of capitulary 112, a formula concerning a hand sent into the bronze vessel on account of theft, the Salian Law, capitularies 53, 54, and 71b (chapters 3, 6, 8, 9, 11, 15, and 22), and the Ripuarian and Alamannic Laws.

- Ducal Codex Wolfenbüttel, among the Augustean manuscripts, no. 50, 2, octavo, ninth century, contains the Salian Law, capitularies 53 and 71, and, in another ink, capitulary 112 (chapters 3, 4, 7, 9, and 18), with certain theological writings appended.

[Col. 0114A] Royal Codex Paris, among the Latin Supplements, no. 65, folio, ninth century, contains the Burgundian and Salian Laws, a fragment of capitulary 112, the prologue of Moses, and the Breviary of Alaric.

- Royal Codex Paris, no. 4280A, formerly of Saint Remigius of Reims (Colbert 3029, Royal 4240B), tenth century, after several works relating to canon law, contains a letter of Nicholas I and other capitularies—111, 112, 113, and 114—the letter of Heriveus of Reims to Witton, and a letter of Pope John to Heriveus concerning the imposition of penance on baptized pagans.

- Royal Codex Paris 2826, ninth–tenth century, contains capitulary 109.

- British Museum Codex, Cotton Tiberius A. III, ninth–tenth century, contains capitulary 109.

- Ducal Wolfenbüttel Codex, among the Helmstedt manuscripts, no. 532, contains capitulary 109.

- Royal Codex Paris, no. 1535, tenth century, contains capitulary 109.

- Ducal Wolfenbüttel Codex, no. 532, large octavo, tenth century, intersperses capitulary 115a among various writings and also contains the Law of the Bavarians [Col. 0114B].

- Royal Codex Paris, no. 1537, tenth century, contains capitulary 115b and books concerning the canonical life.

- Royal Codex Paris, no. 4632, folio, tenth century, contains the Ripuarian and Salian Laws, capitularies 53, 54, 112, and 117, and the Alamannic Law.

- Royal Codex Paris, no. 2718, ninth century—the specimen of whose script Carpenter published in the Tironian alphabet—is a handbook. After a catalogue of the Frankish kings, an exposition by Augustine on the Epistle of Saint John, and other similar works, it contains, from folio 72 onward, sheets written in Tironian notes, interspersed with capitularies 120, 108, 110, 111, 112, 113, and 114; 120 a second time; 118; and a letter of Charlemagne to Albinus and to the congregation of Saint Martin of Tours, which we shall include among the letters.

- Codex of Saint Gall, no. 733, from the year 824 or 825, contains our capitularies 21, 126, 30, 31, 32, 38, and 33, together with a collection concerning tithes to be given. The distinguished Wegelin collated it with the printed editions [Col. 0114C]. See our *Annals*, vol. V, p. 306.

- Royal Codex Paris, no. 4417, formerly belonging to the canons of Le Puy (then Colbert 826, Royal 5159, 5), folio, ninth century, contains the Breviary of Alaric; the Ripuarian, Salian, Alamannic, and Bavarian Laws; capitulary 64; the Burgundian Law; Ansegisus (p. 267); and capitularies 140, 145a–b, 146, and 141a.

- Royal Codex Paris, Notre-Dame collection, no. 247 (F. 4), octavo, ninth–tenth century, contains capitularies 111, 112, 113, and 114, one page of theological material, a fragment of Ansegisus, and the Salian Law.

- Royal Codex Paris, Notre-Dame collection, no. 252 (F. 9), formerly belonging to Antoine Loisel, quarto, ninth century, consists of three codices. The first contains a fragment of Ansegisus; the second, the Salian Law, capitularies 5, 6, and 7, and Isidore’s work *On the Authors of the Laws*; the third, written in the same hand as the first, contains the Alamannic Law.

- Codex formerly of Tegernsee, now the Royal Munich Codex (M.G. 43), ninth century, small octavo, contains our capitularies 21, 30, [Col. 0114D] 31, 32, 26, 76, 78, and 79; capitularies 53, 54, 55, 71, 83, 38, 40, and 82 (chapters 1–6); 112, 145, 146, and the beginning of 147; and, after five erased pages, chapters 9–14 of capitulary 150. Amerbach printed this codex in 1545, but neither accurately nor under its correct title. Since he took no account of the five erased pages and was guided by the final words of capitulary 150, he supposed that the whole codex contained chapters excerpted by order of Lothair from the constitutions of Charles and Louis. This error was followed by Goldast, the re-publisher of the *editio princeps*, in his *Imperial Customs*, pp. 102–125, and also by writers of our own age.

- Royal Codex Paris, no. 2853, quarto, ninth century, contains document 152 among the works of Agobard.

- Ducal Wolfenbüttel Codex, among the Helmstedt manuscripts, no. 32, formerly of Reims, folio, tenth century, contains document 153 among several other works concerning the church of Reims—for example, a synod of the year 991.

- Vatican Codex, no. 5359, quarto, from the end of the ninth or the beginning of the tenth century, concerning which see our *Annals*, vol. V, [Col. 0115A] pp. 239 ff., contains, after the edicts of the Lombard kings, capitulary 150a and, with two pages cut out, chapter 10 and 11 of 135, chapter 10 of 133, and chapters 2 and 3 of 135.

- Codex of the Chisian Library, tenth century, after the *Chronicle of Benedict, monk of Saint Andrew on Soracte*, presents the second part of a legal codex. The edict of the Lombard kings has been cut away—perhaps surviving at Madrid—and the Lombard capitularies of Charlemagne 104, 21, 52, 33, 26, 53 (chapters 1 and 2), 87, 47, 40 (apart from the preface and chapters 3 and 4), 83 (chapters 6 and 13), 60, 40 (the preface and chapters 3 and 4), and 23; the chapters of Louis I given below, joined to our capitularies 106, 129, 107, 112, 113, and 78 (chapters 1–3); those of Pippin 24, 33, and 26; those of Lothair 123, 130, 133, 134, 135, 128 (with chapter 18 added), 150, 114, and 124; and the capitulary of Louis II, 165.

- Codex of Cava, from the beginning of the eleventh century, exhibits the edicts of the Lombard kings and the capitularies in nearly the same form and order as the Chisian Codex. It differs in omitting, because a page has been cut out, chapters 1 and 2 of capitulary 104 [Col. 0115B] among the laws of Charlemagne; in writing, after the preface of capitulary 40, admonition no. 46; in placing 26 after 23; in inserting it among the laws of Charlemagne; and in ending with 128, omitting the remaining items that follow it in the Chisian Codex. Concerning this book, see our *Annals*, vol. V, pp. 247–262.

- Palatine Vienna Codex of Canon Law, no. 45, folio, twelfth century, contains capitularies 98 and 158 among many charters and letters.

- Codex of Bamberg, quarto, formerly of Mont-Saint-Michel, tenth century, contains capitulary 173.

- Royal Codex Paris 4613, large folio, tenth century (Colbert 1385, Royal 5192, 3), contains the edicts of the Lombard kings and capitularies: those of Charles 21, 33, 26, 28, 40, 53, 54, 30, 31, 32, and 43; 46 from the beginning; then, after several leaves have been cut out, chapter 29 of capitulary 114; those of Louis 145, 146, and 135; that of Lothair 150a; and those of Louis II, 187 and 189. Sirmond used this codex before me; Labbe published several passages from it using Sirmond’s papers; Baluze calls it the Thuaneus and Colbertinus Codex.

[Col. 0115C] Codex formerly of the cathedral church of Augsburg, now Ducal Wolfenbüttel, among the Blankenburg manuscripts, tenth century, folio, contains the edicts of the Lombard kings, capitularies, and the Salian, Burgundian, Ripuarian, Alamannic, and Bavarian Laws. The capitularies, preceded by a general index of chapters on folios 64–73, are divided by titles. They are as follows:

- Those of Charles, under his name: 30; 71a–b; 82; 38; 26; 78; 54, chapters 22 and 21; chapters 17–23; 36; 37; 48; 32, chapters 1–6; 33, chapters 12–14; and 55, chapter 5, with continuous chapter numbering; then 21 and 40.

- Those of Louis: 53, 54, 112, 113, 139, 120, 131, 111, 127, and 122.

- Those of Lothair: 125, 135, 169, 134, and 133.

- The chapters of Lothair omitted in the index are 104, namely chapters 1–41; the chapter headings of the Roman council of the year 826; then, with a new order of numbering, 148; 123, chapters 12–14; 47, chapter 14; 150, chapter 13; 124; and finally 128, 145a–b, 146, and 150, chapters 3, 11, 12, and 14, followed by 123, chapter 11.

- The Roman council of Eugenius in the year 826.

- Those of the emperor Louis II: 183, 186, 188, and 190.

Several notices and charters concerning the bishopric of Augsburg are also written in the book, as is a formula for the oath of the Jews, in different hands from the tenth through the twelfth century.

- Codex Cassinensis, no. 353, folio, tenth century, concerning which see our *Annals*, vol. V, contains, among several other capitularies, 109 and 220.

- Ducal Gotha Codex, formerly of Saint Martin of Mainz, from the beginning of the eleventh century, in very large folio, written in two columns per page, consists of four parts.

  The first, folios 1–146, preceded by an image of the lawgiver, contains the capitulary collections of Ansegisus and Benedict, with the capitulary of Otto the Great at Frankfurt and the spurious capitulary of the year 822 at Thionville added.

  The second, folios 147–223, contains the successions of the emperors down to Louis I; the prologues *Moses, People of the Jews* and *The Illustrious Frankish People*; images of lawgivers; the Salian and Ripuarian Laws; the chapters of the Lombard Law, or the concordance concerning the individual cases enacted by Rothari, Grimoald, Liutprand, Ratchis, and Aistulf, all joined and harmonized together [Col. 0116A] and divided into sixty chapters, though three leaves have been cut out; the Alamannic and Bavarian Laws; and the capitularies of Charlemagne and Pippin: 53, 54, 21, 30, 31, 32, 38, 26, 33, 40, 71, 53 chapter 1, again 21 Lombard [chapters 1–8 and 14], 53 chapter 2, and again 40 chapter 5.

  The third part, folios 224–337, is occupied by the Theodosian Code and a brief history of the Lombards.

  The fourth part, folios 338–413, contains the edicts of the Lombard kings; the capitularies of Ansegisus a second time; and, in addition, capitulary 144 of Louis and chapters 71 and 72 of Book IV of Ansegisus; those of Lothair 125, 148, 133, 135, 145a–b, and 146; and those of the emperor Louis II, 182, 183, 168, 171, 170, 184, and 185.

  The book was formerly noticed by Eckhard, but has now for the first time been fully excerpted. The distinguished Jacobs, with his outstanding kindness, permitted me to use it.

- Codex of the cathedral church of Modena, which Muratori used in publishing the capitularies in vol. I, part II, of the *Italian Saints*, eleventh century, contains, after excerpts from Isidore and from the institutions of Roman law [Col. 0116B], and a history of the Franks and Lombards, the prologue of Moses; the Salian and Ripuarian Laws; the chapters of the Lombard Law, or the concordance concerning the individual cases enacted by Rothari, Grimoald, Liutprand, Ratchis, and Aistulf, all joined and harmonized together as in the Gotha Codex and divided into sixty titles; the Alamannic and Bavarian Laws; and the capitularies of Charlemagne, Pippin, Louis I, Lothair I, and Louis II. Muratori transcribed the unpublished portion on pp. 113 and 151–155—capitularies 125, 133, 135, 145a–b, and 146—and on p. 162—capitularies 184 and 185. Concerning the book itself, see Muratori, vol. I, part II, preface, pp. 8–11, and our *Annals*, vol. V, p. 262.

- Palatine Vienna Codex, no. 106, of Canon Law, tenth century, contains capitulary 234, besides other material.

- Royal Codex Paris, among the Latin Supplements, no. 164 bis, folio, ninth century, formerly of Saint Remigius of Reims and later no. 620 of the Clermont College, contains, after the booklet of the bishops of Italy against Elipandus, capitularies 34 and 30; Pippin’s [Col. 0116C] questions and Alcuin’s answers; an index of the laws and prologue of 53 and 54; Salian Law 6; a catalogue of the Frankish kings; the collection of Ansegisus—103, 140, 145a–b, 146, 147, 141a, 148 chapter 5, 141b, chapter 148, and 117; the recapitulation of the solidi of the Salian Law; a notice concerning the estate of Nobiliacum; excerpts from the chapters of Charles and Louis; Einhard’s *Life of Charlemagne*; the coronation of Louis in the year 879; and *On Money Not to Be Exacted from a Poor Person with Interest*. The Paris codices 4628 and 4760 closely resemble this book.

- Royal Codex Paris 4628A, quarto, tenth century, contains catalogues of kings and peoples; the Salian Law; capitularies 112, 113, and 114; the law of the district of Xanten; 71, 87, 145, and 146; Paulinus’s refutation of Elipandus and Felix; 34 and 30. Then begins: “The booklets or decrees of Chlodovech and Childebert, or of Chlothar and Charles, have been lucidly corrected.” It contains *On Divine and Human Laws*, 5 and 7 (chapters 1–12 and 16–18); the Law of the Suebi without its text, 6 and 21; a memorandum [Col. 0116D] concerning the eight bans (concerning the seven sevens); a recapitulation of the solidi of the Salian Law; 7 (chapters 1–5, 9–11, and 13–15); 6; a catalogue of kings; the capitularies of Ansegisus—103, 140, 145a–b, 146, 147, 141a, 148 chapter 5, 141b, chapter 148, and 117; the recapitulation of the solidi of the Salian Law; a notice concerning the estate of Novilliacum; excerpts from the chapters of Charles and Louis; Einhard’s *Life of Charlemagne*; and several other items. The book appears to have been copied from Supplement 164 bis or from some other codex of the same type. Its apograph is Royal Codex Paris, no. 4631, written on parchment and paper in the fifteenth century.

- Royal Codex Paris, no. 4760 (Baluze 365, Royal 4263, 7), large octavo, tenth–eleventh century, after readings on the Trinity and an index of the laws, begins: “The booklets or decree of Chlodovech and Childebert, or of Chlothar and Charles, was lucidly corrected.” It contains *On Divine and Human Laws*, and so forth, almost as in Supplement 164 bis and 4628A, though it omits mention of the Law of the Suebi; 53 and 54 (chapters 11–13, 15, 16, and 20); the Salian Law; Pippin’s questions; and so forth; [Col. 0117A] 112, chapter 2; the blessing of the cross; and a reading from Paul’s Epistle to the Romans.

- Royal Codex Paris, among the Latin Supplements, no. 75, folio, tenth century, formerly of the Clermont College and perhaps of Saint Vincent of Metz, preceded by an image of the lawgiver, contains capitularies 13, 15, 14a–b, 12, 17, 30, 31, 32, 41, 44b, 53, 54, 55, and 57; an inserted recapitulation of the solidi; 58, 59, 61, 63, 71, 76, 81, 84, 86, 87, 92, 93, 95, 96, 22, 21, 103b, 99, and 100; the capitularies of Ansegisus—140, 145a–b, 146, 141a, page 355, laws 12–35, 103a, 175, 177, 193, 197, 199, 208, 207, and 214a–b; the synod of Meaux of the year 845; 160 and 162; the synod of Lauriacum of the year 844; 164; an inserted continuation of the Synod of Meaux; 174, 213, 215, and 249; a catalogue of the Frankish kings; the Salian Law, with the words of chapter 7 of capitulary 53 inserted into the prologue; the law of the district of Xanten; and the Ripuarian, Alamannic, and Bavarian Laws. The capitularies of Charlemagne are arranged in approximately chronological order. Their collection from several books is shown, for example, by capitulary 178, taken from the book of the missus of Sens, and 197, taken from the book of the missus of Thérouanne [Col. 0117B]. The codex which Baluze calls that of Saint Vincent of Metz agrees very closely with this book—if indeed it was an entirely different book, which I scarcely believe—and so does the Palatine Vatican Codex of Ansegisus, whose readings were transmitted to Baluze in Royal Codex Paris no. 4639 (Baluze 271, Royal 4243, 3) by De Bru’s hand in 1675. The book of the College of Navarre, which Baluze used, also appears to have closely approached these.

- Royal Codex Paris, no. 4626, folio, tenth century, formerly of the Mâcon library and later belonging to Bigot, contains the Salian Law; capitularies 53, 54, 72a, 21, 111, 112, 113, 114, 197, 178, 218, and 198; after the recapitulation of the solidi and other legal material, the Breviary of Alaric and the Burgundian Law. Its reading in capitulary 197 shows that the codex was written in the missaticum of Mâcon and Dijon.

- Royal Codex Paris, no. 4638, folio, tenth century, formerly of Pithou and later [Col. 0117C] of Jacques-Auguste de Thou (Colbert 1597, Royal 4243, 1), contains the collection of Ansegisus; capitularies 103, 140, 145a–b, and 146; 141a; Benedict’s additions I–IV; capitularies 160, 162, 163, 164, 161, 166, 167, 172, 174, 175, 176, 177, 178, 180, 181, 179, 194, and 193, together with material from capitulary 181. It appears to have been written at Reims. I would suppose that the Tilian Codex used by Sirmond in the capitularies of Charles the Bald was of the same content.

- Royal Codex Paris, no. 4761, formerly belonging to Philibert de la Mare of Dijon, tenth century, after Ansegisus contains the *Chapters Extracted by Lord Emperor Charles and His Son Louis and Their Most Wise Bishops*, namely excerpts from Books I–III of Benedict. Baluze, pp. 519 ff., wrongly regarded them as genuine capitularies of Charlemagne, though he assigned them to no particular year. It then contains capitularies 175, 213, 218, 103, 140a, 145a–b, 146, and 141a; certain chapters excerpted from Benedict’s books; and 242, 244, and 109.

- Royal Codex Paris 5095, tenth century, besides the letters of Hincmar of Reims and Laon [Col. 0117D] and those of Nicholas I, contains the Synod of Tusey of the year 860, capitulary 215, and the letter of the Synod of Quierzy to Louis, king of Germany.

- Royal Codex Paris 3878, tenth century, contains a Penitential Book and excerpts from chapters from page 158 onward, including those of Charles II, 174 and 215, and of Carloman from the year 884. Royal Codex Paris no. 4376 contains, at the end of Benedict’s collection of canons, Book I, chapter 279. Royal Codex Paris 1455, folio, tenth century, formerly belonging to Jacques Tavelli of Sens (then Colbert 3368, Royal 3887, 1, 1, A), contains Benedict I, 35 and 36, placed at the beginning of the page of the codex.

- Royal Codices Paris 2859, tenth century; 1750, eleventh century; and 2319, written on paper, contain chapter 177. They are joined by the Royal Munich Codex, ninth century; the Vienna Codex of Canon Law no. 99, folio, tenth century; and the Wolfenbüttel Augustean Codex 83, 21, folio, tenth century, which preserve the capitulary of Charles II concerning the Jews, namely a fragment of the Synod of Meaux of the year 845.

- Royal Codex Paris no. 4375, octavo, twelfth century, formerly belonging to Antoine [Col. 0118A] Faure (Royal 4654, 3), contains at the end of its collections of canon law certain excerpts from the capitularies of the kings and from customary law, as well as the formula of the royal oath.

- Ambrosian Codex Milan O, 53, 55, formerly of the monastery of Oscela or Susa in Savoy, early eleventh century, octavo, like the codices immediately following, contains abridged edicts of the Lombard kings and chapters of Charlemagne, Pippin, Louis I, Lothair I, and Louis II, as well as the laws of Wido, Otto I, Otto III, and Henry II. The capitularies, their original order having been dissolved and those which appeared to have been issued for a particular occasion rather than with permanent legislative force having been deleted, are written with continuous chapter numbers in the manner seen in Muratori’s edition. That they were produced by jurists is clear from the fact that, especially in the Vienna, Verona, and Este codices, laws are presented as they had been more tightly defined or explained by the practice of later centuries, and differ to some extent from the genuine ninth- or tenth-century text. In [Col. 0118B] one Ambrosian codex our capitulary 231 is found. See our *Annals*, vol. V, pp. 264–277. The following codex closely approaches it:

- The Florentine Codex of the Laurentian Library, Plut. 89 sup. 86, very large octavo, late eleventh century, contains the edicts of the Lombard kings and the capitularies, and breaks off in the constitution of Conrad II. See the *Annals*, vol. V, pp. 277–282. It agrees with it very closely.

- The London Codex in the British Museum, no. 5411, small folio, late eleventh century, formerly Venetian, which I examined in 1827, contains the edicts of the Lombard kings and the capitularies, sometimes preserving ancient titles, down to the laws of the emperor Henry II. It also contains, in a different hand of the eleventh or twelfth century, the constitutions of Conrad II and Henry III, with marginal and interlinear glosses scattered throughout.

- The Palatine Vienna Codex in the catalogue of civil law, no. 210, folio, eleventh century, contains the edict and the capitularies and ends with the constitutions of Henry III. It supplies many glosses and judicial formulas. Very similar to it is

[Col. 0118C] the Codex of the most illustrious Count de Gianfilippi of Verona, formerly belonging to the church of Saint Euphemia at Verona, very large octavo, from the end of the eleventh or beginning of the twelfth century. Concerning it, see our *Annals*, vol. V, pp. 282 ff. It ends with Henry III; a fragment of the Salian Law has been added.

The last is

- The Este Codex, fifteenth century, used by Muratori in publishing the Lombard edicts and capitularies. It no longer appears to be preserved in the ducal library at Modena.

To these are added the codices of the Lombard Law, whose text, greatly altered by jurists for practical use, often departs from the ancient and genuine reading. It therefore needed to be compared with this edition only in a few places, especially in the constitutions of the emperors of the eleventh century; and we did in fact examine them.

- Codex Casinensis, no. 328, quarto, from the end of the eleventh or beginning of the twelfth century. Concerning it, see our *Annals*, vol. V, p. 297.

- Palatine Vienna Codex, in the catalogue of civil law, no. 39 [Col. 0118D], from the end of the eleventh century, written in Lombard script.

- Vatican Palatine Codex, no. 772, folio, twelfth century. After the work had been completed, the constitutions of Lothair III, from the year 1127, and the Roncaglia constitutions of Frederick I from the year 1158 were written in another twelfth-century hand. The following codex is closely related to it:

- Royal Codex Paris, no. 4617, folio, twelfth century, in which the same constitutions of Lothair and Frederick were added by a twelfth-century hand.

- Vatican Codex, no. 3833, twelfth century, contains excerpts from capitulary 128 in the collection of canons of Cardinal Deusdedit.

- Vatican Codex, no. 3922, folio, written on paper, sixteenth century, contains capitulary 75.

Having found, examined, and carefully collated these books in the libraries of our Germany and Switzerland, Italy, France, and Britain, and having used the earlier editions, I first attempted to present the text exactly as I had found it in the oldest and most trustworthy codices, adding the principal readings of the codices and editions. I then judged that the genuine division and connection of the chapters—often erased both in the books arranged for the use of jurists and in the printed editions—should be restored, according to the evidence of the best codices and as the matter appeared to require. Next I undertook to assign each monument to the time and place in which it was issued, making extensive use of the assistance provided by the writers, letters, and charters I had collected, and by the registers of the diplomas compiled by our Boehmer.

I moved the laws of the peoples, together with the law of the district of Xanten, which Baluze had treated as the third capitulary of the year 813, into a separate volume. I also moved all the charters, and the few letters inserted chiefly by Goldast and Baluze in their collections, since they belong in our great collection of imperial diplomas and letters. I removed the capitularies excerpted from Benedict by Goldast and Baluze, as spurious and as having no authority recognized by me. Conversely, I restored to their proper place the capitularies which I had found, or [Col. 0120A] thought I had found, in the collection of Ansegisus. I added many previously unpublished items now discovered for the first time.

I deferred the three books of Benedict with their additions—which were never received under public authority in our Germany and of which only one codex exists among us—together with the twelfth-century constitution concerning Charlemagne’s Roman expedition and the spurious capitulary of Tribur, to the end of the remaining imperial constitutions to be presented in the second volume of the *Laws*.

By this plan it has been brought about that, from the genuine legal monuments arranged in their proper order, a clear and truthful image of the commonwealth among our forefathers may now emerge. I pray and desire that their sons and grandsons, contemplating it with discerning eyes, may draw from it the courage and examples needed to defend their homeland bravely against the enemy and to administer the commonwealth of Germany justly and wisely. Written at Hanover, on 10 July 1835.

[Col. 0119]

# NOTICE OF D. BOUQUET ON THE DIPLOMAS OF PIPPIN AND CHARLEMAGNE

[Col. 0119B] As we are about to publish the diplomas of Pippin and Charlemagne, we consider it worthwhile first to set out certain rules, borrowed from Mabillon, for distinguishing the genuine and authentic from the false and interpolated.

## I. Titles

Pippin generally retained in his diplomas the old title of the preceding kings, in this form: “Pippin, king of the Franks, illustrious man.” Sometimes he added “by the grace of God,” because he had come to the kingship in an extraordinary manner.

Charlemagne likewise did not depart from the ancient custom. Following his father’s example, he used the addition “by the grace of God” almost invariably.

Three periods must be distinguished in his diplomas. The first extends from the beginning of his reign over the Franks to his accession to the Lombard kingdom, from the year 768 to 774. The second extends from that year to 800, when he was crowned emperor. The third extends from then to the end of his life.

In the first period he used this formula: “Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks, illustrious man.” His brother Carloman also used this formula [Col. 0119C].

In the second period he used: “Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans,” very often adding “illustrious man.”

In the third period he used: “In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, Charles, most serene Augustus, crowned by God, great and peaceful emperor, ruling the empire of the Romans, who also by the mercy of God is king of the Franks and Lombards.” In some diplomas, however, the invocation is omitted, perhaps through the carelessness of scribes.

## II. Subscriptions

The Carolingian kings ordinarily mention both the subscription and the ring in their documents, except in judicial decisions and diplomas of lesser importance. In those documents kings often did not subscribe; only the chancellor or notary did so, and no mention was then made of a royal subscription or, usually, of the royal ring or seal.

In other diplomas of greater importance it was customary to mention both, approximately as follows: “We have confirmed it below with our own hand,” or “we have decided to sign below,” or “we have ordered it to be signed.”

Mabillon observes that, among the many royal diplomas he found, only a few mention neither the subscription nor the ring, although the king does subscribe and his seal is not attached. In all these cases, mention of the seal in the clause expressing the sealing is extremely rare, although it occasionally occurs in the body of the diploma.

## III. The Manner of Subscribing

The Carolingian kings departed from the Merovingians in the manner of subscribing, as in other matters.

Pippin used this formula: “The sign of Pippin, most glorious king,” with a cross-sign placed between the word “sign” and Pippin’s name. Only the sign of the cross was made by the hand of the ruler; the rest was written by the chancellor or notary.

Charlemagne [Col. 0120B] preserved the ancestral custom: “The sign of Charles, most glorious king.” His brother Carloman did the same. After receiving the imperial dignity, however, Charles used: “The sign of Charles, most serene emperor,” or “Augustus,” with a monogram inserted between the words “sign” and “Charles.”

## IV. The Monogram

Few of the Merovingians used a monogram in their diplomas, and none except those who, through lack of education, were unable to write their own name. Charlemagne was the first to introduce the permanent use and practice of the monogram into royal diplomas; the other kings retained this practice down to Philip III of France.

Charles arranged the monogram so that it represented the sign of the cross used by the earlier Frankish kings in their letters.

## V. The Chancellor’s Subscription

In ancient times, after the Frankish kings, the referendary or chancellor, archchaplain, or notary ordinarily subscribed to the diplomas opposite the king, if the size of the parchment allowed it; otherwise, somewhat below the king’s subscription. This [Col. 0120C] was especially observed under the second dynasty, whose chancellors almost always subscribed a little below the king.

Under the Carolingians there were several chancellors or notaries. One presided over them and was called the chief notary, archnotary, protonotary, sometimes the chief chancellor or archchancellor, and sometimes simply notary and chancellor; at other times he was called archchaplain.

When notaries subscribed in place of chancellors, they used this formula: “Widolaicus in place of Rado.”

## VI. The Names of the Chancellors and Notaries

The man whom others call Egius or Eguim, who customarily reviewed Pippin’s royal diplomas by order, should be called not a chief chancellor but a notary, as should Chrodingus and Widmarus.

Hitherius, however, was Pippin’s archchancellor, since by his authority he reviewed and subscribed the royal letters. Mabillon makes no mention of Badilo, although he appears to have held the office of chancellor before Hitherius, who had been his notary. For in an original diploma for the monastery of Fulda [Col. 0120D], Hitherius is said to have subscribed in place of Badilo; in certain other documents Hitherius is said to have written, while Badilo reviewed and subscribed.

Hitherius exercised the office of chancellor from the beginning of Charlemagne’s reign. His notaries were Rado, Wigbald, Gilbert, and Optatus.

Hitherius was succeeded by Rado, abbot of Saint-Vaast, who had as notaries Wigbald, Gilbert, Optatus, Jacob, Erkembald, and Widolaicus.

The third chancellor of Charlemagne was Erkembald, from approximately the twenty-ninth year of his reign. Erkembald’s notary was Genesius, although Rado is still recorded as chancellor in the Osnabrück diploma granted in the third year of Charlemagne’s empire [Col. 0121A], in place of whom Jacob subscribes.

The fourth chancellor of Charlemagne should be considered to have been Jeremiah, later archbishop of Sens; his notary was Wither. The monk of Angoulême adds Bartholomew to their number in his *Life of Charlemagne* under the year 769.

Some also add Abbot Autpertus to the Carolingian chancellors, but without sufficiently strong evidence. Autpertus was a monk at Vulturnum in Italy before Charles was called king of the Franks, and he never thereafter moved to Gaul.

If the author of the Chronicle of Lorsch is to be trusted, Einhard was Charlemagne’s notary and archchaplain.

That Ruotfrid was Charlemagne’s notary is clear from Einhard’s *Annals* under the year 809.

Amalbert is suggested by the second Osnabrück diploma, which some consider suspect, although Erkembald, in whose place Amalbert is said to have reviewed the letters, was Charlemagne’s chancellor.

Erkembald had other notaries: Altifred, Ibbo, Suavius, and the deacon Guidbert [Col. 0121B]. Those who reviewed Charlemagne’s judicial decisions were extraordinary chancellors, such as Theudegarius, Chrotardus, and Eldebertus.

## VII. Subscriptions of the Magnates

Pippin’s privilege for the monastery of Fulda was countersigned by the magnates. A decree of the same Pippin concerning the construction and endowment of the monastery of Prüm, published by Mabillon in volume II of the *Annals of the Benedictines*, p. 705, is supported by the subscriptions of bishops and counts.

Charlemagne arranged for his testament to be subscribed by the bishops, abbots, and counts who could be present at the time, as is recorded by Einhard in his *Life*.

This was preceded by a donation he made to the Roman Church. He himself confirmed it with his own hand and caused all the bishops, abbots, dukes [Col. 0122A], and also counts to subscribe to it, as Anastasius testifies in his life of Hadrian.

In the other diplomas of Charlemagne there is no subscription of magnates, only those of chancellors and notaries.

## VIII. The Year of the Incarnation and the Indiction

Under the second dynasty, almost all diplomas concerning the affairs of churches, monasteries, and private persons lack the years of the Incarnation. Some, however, which concern the commonwealth especially, have the years of the Incarnation added to the regnal years.

Mabillon found only one diploma of Charlemagne, for the monastery of Saint Arnulf at Metz, bearing the years of the Incarnation. He would not have considered it genuine had he not inspected an autograph of excellent quality, though no seal had been attached to it.

The common use of the indiction in diplomas began with Charlemagne’s empire, that is, at the beginning of the year 801, if one excepts the aforementioned diploma for the monastery of Saint Arnulf.

We omit diplomas that depart from these rules [Col. 0122B], not because we consider all of them false, but because we intend to publish only those free from every suspicion.

We already remarked in the preceding volume—and cannot emphasize sufficiently—that diplomas which do not bear the customary features of other documents should not immediately be regarded as false, but only as interpolated and suspect. For it is entirely possible, as Mabillon observes, that diplomas may bear false and inauthentic titles and subscriptions while their actual text nevertheless does not depart from the truth.

We shall not reproduce diplomas issued in Germany, Italy, and other regions that are no longer under French rule; we shall nevertheless provide their titles and subscriptions, provided that we judge the diplomas themselves indisputable.

[Col. 0121]

# CAPITULARIES OF CHARLEMAGNE

## GENERAL CAPITULARY (A.D. 769–771)

Published by Baluzius from the Codex of Saint Vincent of Laon, made public property, and assigned to the year 769—as may be inferred from chapter 18—this was certainly promulgated in the early years of Charles and while his brother was still alive. Its individual provisions seem to have derived from Carloman’s Capitularies of 742 and from other ecclesiastical constitutions (compare, for example, chapter 7 with Boniface’s letter 73, in Würdtwein, p. 197). The whole constitution, except chapter 16, was repeated in Benedict’s third book, chapters 123–140, in a form all the more dangerous for uneducated clerics. With its help I revised Baluzius’s text, since I had not found our capitulary in the former Laon manuscript of Saint Vincent, now numbered among the royal Paris manuscripts as no. 4788.

[Col. 0121C] Charles, by the grace of God king and ruler of the kingdom of the Franks, devoted defender and helper of the holy Church, and in all things an assistant of the Apostolic See [Note: These words are divided in this way in the Laon manuscript and in Burchard and Ivo, whereas in the seventh book of the Capitularies the final words are joined to what follows. There is, however, a major difference between the two readings. For in the seventh book of the Capitularies Charles says that he established these chapters at the urging of the Apostolic See; here, however, he calls himself an assistant of the Apostolic See. He then issues constitutions after consultation with his councillors, without any mention of intervention by the Apostolic See. Thus the capitulary of 779 was made without the urging of the Apostolic See, as was likewise the constitution on the correction of ecclesiastical books and offices. The capitulary of 789, too, was made with the counsel of the bishops and nobles of the kingdom. There is no mention of the Apostolic See in these matters. The same must be said of the Capitularies of the Saxons of 797. The Chapters added to the Lombard law in 801 press the point even more strongly: although they were issued in Italy, and perhaps under the eyes of Leo III, Roman pontiff, they nevertheless make no mention of the Apostolic See. It would be endless to pursue every example. Let what we have said suffice. The reading that we have retained here therefore seems more genuine. For the defense of the Roman Church had passed to Charles together with his paternal inheritance, and he left it as an hereditary possession to his sons and descendants, as Marca demonstrates at length in book 1, chapter 12, of *On Concord*. Thus, in writing to Eugene II, Louis and Lothar say that they are bound to owe assistance to this most holy See in every matter, referring, in my opinion, to the beginning of this capitulary. John VIII, in letter 47 to the emperor, says that he had been granted by heavenly majesty as a powerful and vigorous assistant of the holy Church. It is certain that the assistance Charles gave to the Apostolic See and to the Roman pontiffs won him immortal glory. The Roman pontiffs themselves readily acknowledge this; nor did the insulting thought of Valdesius concerning so great a prince ever enter the mind of any of them. Valdesius, in chapter 20, section 15, of his work *On the Dignity of the Kings and Kingdoms of Spain*, says that when Charles labored for the liberty of the Apostolic See, he “fought not so much for the altars and hearths of the Church as because it was in his own interest.” He was evidently forgetful of Charles’s supreme services to the Church, and ungrateful even toward the memory of a man without whom Christianity might once have been entirely extinguished in Spain, as a most learned man has already observed. Baluzius.]

At the urging of all our faithful men, and especially after consultation with the bishops and the other priests [Col. 0123A], we altogether prohibit the servants of God from carrying weapons, fighting, or going on campaign or to war in any circumstances, except only those who have been chosen for this on account of the divine ministry—namely, to fulfill the solemn rites of the Mass and to carry the protection of the saints. That is, each prince shall have one or two bishops with chaplains and priests accompanying him, and each prefect shall have one priest who can judge those confessing their sins and assign them penance.

2. That priests shed neither Christian nor pagan blood.

3. We forbid all servants of God to hunt or roam the forests with dogs, and to keep hawks or falcons.

[Col. 0123B] 4. We decree that, in accordance with canonical precaution, we shall not admit into ecclesiastical ministry any unknown bishops or priests arriving from anywhere until they have undergone synodal examination.

5. If priests have had several wives, or have shed Christian or pagan blood, or have acted contrary to the canons, they shall be deprived of the priesthood, because they are worse than laymen.

6. We have decreed that, in accordance with the canons, each bishop shall diligently exercise care in his parish, with the assistance of the count, who is the Church’s defender, so that the people of God do not practice pagan rites, but cast away and reject every impurity of heathenism: whether profane sacrifices to the dead, or diviners and sorcerers, or amulets and omens, or incantations, or sacrificial offerings [Col. 0123C] which foolish people make beside churches according to pagan ritual under the name of holy martyrs or confessors of the Lord—people who thereby provoke their saints to anger rather than to mercy.

7. We decree that every year each bishop shall diligently travel through his parish and strive to confirm the people, teach and investigate among the congregations, and prohibit pagan observances, diviners and sorcerers, omens, amulets, incantations, and every impurity of the heathen.

8. We have likewise decreed, in accordance with the canons of the saints, that each priest residing in a parish shall be subject to the bishop in whose parish he resides, and that every Lent he shall render the bishop an account and description of the order of his ministry—whether concerning baptism, the Catholic faith, prayers, [Col. 0123D] or the order of the Masses [Note: “and display it” in some manuscripts. Benedict III, 130]. Whenever the bishop canonically travels through the parish [Col. 0124A] to confirm the people, the priest shall always be ready to receive the bishop, with the gathering and assistance of the people who are to be confirmed there. On Maundy Thursday he shall always request new chrism from his own bishop. No one shall presume to baptize with the old chrism; rather, he shall cause it to be burned in the church lamps [Note: “Let the old one not remain” in the same place].

9. That no one receive a church within a parish without the consent of his bishop, nor transfer from one parish to another.

10. That priests take great care concerning incestuous and criminal persons [Note: “lest they perish in their crimes” is lacking in manuscript III, 132], lest they perish in their crimes and their souls be required of them by Christ, the strict judge. Likewise they shall care for the sick and penitents, so that the dying do not depart without anointing with consecrated oil, reconciliation, and [Col. 0124B] viaticum.

11. That the priests themselves observe the fast of the four Ember seasons [Note: “Let the priest himself observe it and announce it to the people” in another version], and announce that it is to be observed by the people.

12. That no one delay coming to the assembly: first, around summer; second [Note: “and another” in another version], around autumn. For the other assemblies, if necessity arises or the king’s summons presses, no one who is called shall delay coming.

13. Whenever it has been announced that prayers are to be offered for the king or for his faithful on any matter, no one shall thereby appear negligent.

14. No priest shall presume to celebrate Mass except in places dedicated to God, or while traveling, in tents or on stone altars consecrated by the bishop. Whoever presumes to do so shall be liable to the penalty of his rank [Note: “whoever” in another version].

[Col. 0124C] 15. Priests who do not properly know how to fulfill their ministry, and do not strive as far as they are able to learn in accordance with the command of their bishops, or who are contemptuous of the canons, are to be removed from their office until they have fully corrected these matters.

16. Whoever, after frequent admonition by his bishop concerning his learning, has neglected to take care to learn shall undoubtedly be removed from office and lose the church that he holds, because those who do not know the law of God cannot announce and preach it to others.

17. That no judge shall presume, without the knowledge of the bishop, to restrain or condemn a priest, deacon, cleric, or junior member of the Church on his own authority. Whoever does this shall be separated from the church to which he is known to have inflicted an injury [Col. 0124D] for as long as it takes him to acknowledge and correct his offense.

[Col. 0125A] 18. [Note: Compare canon 14 of the Fifth Council of Orléans, held in 549, in Sirmond, *Councils of Gaul* I, p. 281; this chapter appears to have derived from it. Pertz.] Let no bishop or layman presume to claim, retain, or regard as belonging to himself any property of another bishop, church, or private person, whether by division of kingdoms or by separation of provinces [Note: “or demand,” Council of Orléans]. If anyone attempts to do this, he shall be suspended from the charity of all and separated from the grace of communion until he restores what was taken, together with compensation for its fruits.

### CAPITULARY ON THE LORD’S BAN (Around 772)

[Col. 0125]

We have once again made public a constitution concealed in the pamphlet of the distinguished Ortloff on the Salic Law, p. 30, from a manuscript of the royal library at Bamberg containing the Salic, Ripuarian, and Alamannic laws. It is a parchment manuscript of the ninth century, in a somewhat elongated octavo format; I copied it the previous year from pages 306 and 307. It appears to have been issued in the early years of Charles, certainly [Note: Compare the Saxon Capitularies of 797, chapters 1–2. It will also be useful to compare Benedict’s Fourth Addition, chapters 42–45.] before the capitularies by which, in 797 and 803, he imposed these same laws on the conquered Bavarians and Saxons.

[Col. 0125B] Concerning those [Note: Eight, manuscript VIII] eight bans from which our lord wishes sixty solidi to be collected [Note: “to go out,” manuscript c.].

1. Chapter: dishonoring the holy Church.

2. Whoever acts unjustly toward widows.

3. Concerning orphans.

4. Against the poor who cannot defend themselves, who are called *ur uer magon*.

5. Whoever commits abduction—that is, whoever carries off a free woman against the will of her parents.

6. Whoever commits arson within the country—that is, whoever burns another person’s house or barn.

7. Whoever commits *harizhut*—that is, whoever violently breaks another person’s hedge, gate, or house.

8. Whoever does not go to the army.

These are the eight bans of the lord king, from each of which sixty solidi are to be collected.

### CAPITULARY, 779 (At Heristal)

[Col. 0125]

The following manuscripts served our edition of the capitulary previously published by Amerbach, Sirmond, and Baluzius:

1. Manuscript of the monastery of Saint Gall, no. 733, written at the beginning of the ninth century; our edition generally follows it. Baluzius collated it, and the distinguished Wechelin collated it for use in our edition.

2. Manuscript of the monastery of Saint Paul in Carinthia, written at the beginning of the ninth century and copied by me; it agrees with the preceding in many places.

3. Manuscript of the royal library at Paris, no. 4613 m., tenth century, formerly belonging to the Thuani family, collated first by Baluzius and again by me.

4. Manuscript of the Wolfenbüttel-Blankenburg library, tenth century.

5. Manuscript of the ducal library at Gotha, eleventh century; it follows manuscripts 2, 3, and 4 most closely.

6. Manuscript of the royal library at Paris, no. 4628 A., tenth century, where the capitulary is entitled: “Here begins the decree of Charles, precious king of the Franks.” Nearly the same title is found in:

6*. Another manuscript of the same library, no. 4626 m., tenth century: “Here begins the decree of Charles, most precious king.” This book, formerly belonging to the Bigot library, was collated first by Baluzius and then by me.

7. Manuscript of the royal library at Munich, formerly from Tegernsee, published by Amerbach.

8. Sirmond’s edition in the *Councils of Gaul*, or rather the manuscript that he calls Aquitanian.

9. Manuscript of the royal library at Paris, numbered among the Latin supplements as no. 75, collated by me with the printed editions, tenth century. It appears to be the same manuscript that Baluzius called Parisian and Clermont. The following agree with it very closely.

10. Manuscript of Saint Vincent of Metz, and 11. the Palatine manuscript, both used by Baluzius.

We now publish for the first time an edition of this same capitulary adapted for the recently conquered kingdom of the Lombards, on the authority of the following manuscripts:

1. The Chisian manuscript, tenth century;

2. The Cavense manuscript, eleventh century;

with which

3. The Gotha manuscript and 4. the Mutina manuscript, in Muratori, agree very closely; the Ambrosian, London, Florentine, Viennese, Veronese, and Este manuscripts in Muratori were also collated.

### FRANKISH CAPITULARY

[Note: In Migne, the texts headed “Frankish Capitularies” and “Lombard Capitularies” are printed in parallel.]

[Col. 0125B]

In the name of Christ [Note: “In the name of Christ,” from manuscript 1]. In the fortunate [Note: “most fortunate,” manuscript 1] eleventh year of the reign of our lord Charles, most glorious king, in the month of March, a capitulary was enacted concerning how, when the bishops, abbots, illustrious men, and counts had been gathered together in one synodal [Note: “synodal,” manuscript 2; “synodical,” manuscript 3] council, together with our most pious lord, they agreed, according to God’s will and for necessary matters, upon a decree [Note: This expression is absent from the Palatine and Albien manuscripts and from book III of the Lombard law. The Paris manuscript reads: “together with the counts, illustrious men.” Baluzius].

1. [Note: See the letter of Hadrian I to Bertherius, bishop of Vienne, published by Peter of Saint-Julian in his *On the Antiquities of the City of Mâcon*, p. 272; it is also found in the *Chronicle of Hugh of Flavigny*, p. 109, and finally in volume VI of the Councils, p. 1888. Idem.] Concerning metropolitan bishops: their suffragan bishops are to be subject to them according to the canons, and whatever they recognize as requiring correction in their ministry, they are to correct and amend willingly [Note: “and correct them,” manuscript 5].

2. Concerning bishops: where bishops have not been ordained, let them be ordained without delay.

3. Concerning monasteries [Note: Baluzius: “which were under a rule.” Paris manuscript: “That monasteries which were under a rule…”] that were regular: let them live according to the rule. Likewise [Note: “that,” manuscript 2] let the monasteries of women observe the holy order, and let each abbess reside continuously in her own monastery.

4. Let bishops, concerning priests, deacons [Note: This word appears in one copy], and clerics within their parish, have authority according to the canons [Note: The Thuani manuscript has “to correct” in place of these words. The same occurs in the Palatine manuscript. Baluzius].

5. Let bishops have the authority to correct incestuous persons; likewise, within their parish, let them have authority to correct widows [Note: “to correct” is lacking in manuscript 1].

6. Let no one be permitted to receive or ordain another person’s cleric in any rank.

7. [Note: This chapter is absent from manuscript 1.] Concerning tithes: let each person give his tithe, and let it be distributed by order of the bishop [Note: In the Tegernsee manuscript another chapter on tithes is inserted here; we shall present it below in chapter 8 of Charles’s Lombard Capitularies].

8. [Note: The following gloss is added in the margin of the Lombard law in the royal manuscripts: “That is, either the man who has killed his lord, or the wife who has killed her husband, or one who has plotted against the king’s life, or one who has attempted to flee outside the province, or one who has caused a scandal in a royal council or assembly: all these must be dragged away by the hands of good men, as is prescribed in the law, ‘If anyone has fled for refuge to the church of God.’” Idem.] Concerning murderers and other guilty persons who ought to die according to the laws: if they flee to a church, they are not to be excused [Note: Some manuscripts of the Laws of the Lombards read “not to be driven away”], nor is food to be given to them there.

[Col. 0127C] 9. Let thieves [Note: That is, those who commit theft within an immunity, or, alternatively, “remove [things] from an immunity,” as an interlinear gloss in one royal manuscript states. Idem.] from within the immunity [Note: That is, the immunity of that judge. “Namely, under whose jurisdiction the immunity itself is,” as an interlinear gloss in another royal manuscript states. Idem.] be presented to that judge at the count’s assemblies; and whoever fails to do this shall lose his benefice and honor. Likewise, if our vassal fails to fulfill this, he shall lose his benefice and honor. Whoever has no benefice shall pay the ban [Note: “band,” manuscript 1].

10. Concerning one who commits perjury: there shall be no redemption, except that he lose his hand. If the accuser wishes to pursue the matter of that perjury, let them stand at the cross. [Col. 0129A] If the person who swore wins, let the accuser make compensation according to his law. This is to be observed in lesser cases. In greater matters, or concerning the status of free birth, let them observe the law.

[10 bis. Concerning [Note: This law is found in Sirmond’s edition; it is absent from all the manuscripts.] thieves sent into custody. Concerning thieves who have been sent into custody: no public judge shall pay a price for them. If he does so, he shall lose his honor. Whoever has broken into a church shall die.]

11. Concerning vengeance [Note: That is, mutilation of limbs] and judgment [Note: That is, death] in the case of thieves. They say that the testimony of bishops is to be regarded as being without fault on the part of the count, provided that it is given without envy or evil pretext and that nothing else is introduced there except true justice for bringing the matter to completion [Note: “and confirming peace,” London manuscript]. If anyone, through hatred or evil intent, and not for the execution of justice, destroys a man, he shall lose his honor and shall make legal compensation to the one against whom he acted unjustly, according to the penalty that he inflicted.

12. [Note: The chapter is absent from manuscript 3.] We wish to preserve the chapters that our father, of blessed memory [Note: “Namely, our lord King Pippin,” manuscript 7], established in his assemblies and in synods [Note: “and in synods” is absent from manuscripts 4, 5, 6*, and 7].

13. Concerning the property of churches from which revenues now issue [Note: “now, revenues,” manuscript 2], let a tenth and a ninth be paid together with the revenue itself [Note: “payments,” manuscript 7]; and from property from which they formerly did not issue, likewise let a ninth and a tenth be given [Note: The words “with that revenue” or “let it be” are variously present or absent in the manuscripts]. From fifty households, one solidus; from thirty households, half a solidus; and from twenty, one tremissis. Concerning precarial grants: where they now exist, let them be renewed; where they do not exist, let them be recorded. Let there be a distinction between precarial grants made at our command and those that are made voluntarily from the property of the churches themselves.

14. Concerning the performance of *truste*, no one shall presume [Note: I think this chapter is mutilated. In book III, title 4, chapter 2, of the Lombard law it reads: “Concerning the performance of *truste*: let no one presume to forbid lodging to one who comes to us, and let him sell him what is necessary, as to his neighbor.” *Truste* means royal service, as an interlinear gloss in the royal manuscripts states. Other glosses reported in Lindenbrog’s *Glossary* say: “The performance of *truste*, that is, mounted service.” Nicolaus Boherius annotated this passage: “Explain *concerning the performance of truste*, that is, concerning the performance of royal service.” Baluzius.]

15. Concerning wax-makers, tablet-makers, and charter-writers, let the practice be observed as it has existed for a long time.

16. Concerning oaths sworn together through a *gildonia* [Note: The Albien and Saint Gall manuscripts and Sirmond’s edition read *gildonia*. The Bavarian and Basel manuscripts and the Metz manuscript read *geldonia*; the Bigotian manuscript has *gilduniae*; the Rheims manuscript, *ghilduniae*. In book I, title 17, chapter 7, of the Lombard Law: “Concerning oaths through a *gildonia*.” An interlinear gloss adds: “that is, an illicit association.” Thomas Reinesius, in letter 86 to Daumius, says that the associations of men in the laws of Charles connected with the Bavarian synod were groups, brotherhoods, fellowships, or guilds against robbers. Idem], let no one presume to establish such oaths with one another. In another manner, concerning their alms [Note: The Lombard law reads “alimonies,” which has the same meaning here], or concerning fire, or shipwreck, even if they make agreements, no one shall presume to swear an oath in this matter [Note: The words “even if they make agreements … presume” are absent from manuscript 9].

17. [Note: Absent from manuscript 11.] Concerning travelers: those who are going to the palace or elsewhere shall not be attacked by anyone with a band [Col. 0131A]. No one shall presume to take another person’s grass during a time of defense [Note: Here another chapter begins in manuscripts 1, 4, 7, and Gold], unless he is going to war or is our messenger. Whoever presumes to act otherwise shall make compensation.

18. Concerning tolls [Note: “tolls,” manuscript 1 and the Lombard version]: no one shall collect those that were previously forbidden [Note: “fraudulently imposed,” manuscript 7], except where they existed in ancient times.

[18 bis. [Note: From the Blankenburg manuscript, folio 85, since it is absent from the others.] It was likewise decided concerning consecrated women who have joined themselves to men or polluted themselves by adultery: they are to be separated, and both the men and the women are to enter monasteries, with their property and with the compensation that they ought to have paid publicly [Col. 0131B] or to her *mundoald*. Concerning those poor men who have nothing: they too are to be separated as above; and if they have no property with which to live in a monastery, their nearest relatives shall support them and take care that they do not sin again. If they subsequently commit further wrongdoing, her *mundoald* shall be liable for thirty solidi, and she shall enter a monastery with the penalty to which her *mundoald* had obligated her, and with the compensation for her adultery. A female servant who, with her master’s permission, has assumed religious clothing and afterward commits adultery or takes a husband: her master shall be liable for one solidus [Note: “if,” manuscript c.].]

19. Concerning those who sell slaves: the sale shall take place in the presence of a bishop or count, or in the presence of an archdeacon, or centenarius [Note: Absent from the London manuscript], or in the presence of a deputy of the lord, [Col. 0131C] or of the count’s judge [Note: That is, the *sculdahis*, London gloss], or before well-known witnesses. No one shall sell a slave outside the mark. Whoever does so shall pay as many bans [Note: Here manuscript 1 begins another chapter] as the number of slaves he sold. If he does not have the price, he shall give himself to the count as a pledge in place of the slave until he pays the ban [Note: “himself present,” manuscript 6; “being present,” manuscript 6*; “in place of the price,” manuscript 9].

20. Concerning *brunias*: no one shall presume to sell them outside our kingdom [Note: The Albien manuscript reads *brunias*. Amerbach and Herold published *prunias*, which has the same meaning. In other ancient copies I have seen written: “Concerning *brunias*: no one shall presume to sell them outside our kingdom.” Baluzius].

21. If a count does not render justice in his district, he shall cause our envoys to be lodged in his own household until justice has been done there [Note: This is the reading of the Thuani book. Amerbach and Herold published “our envoy.” The Palatine and Metz manuscripts have “our envoy”; likewise the Albien manuscript. The word “our” is absent from the Rheims and Bigotian manuscripts. Idem] [Note: The Ambrosian, Veronese, and Viennese manuscripts read “case”] [Note: An old gloss in one royal manuscript of the Lombard Laws says “that is, to take care.” In another: “namely, to inquire or investigate.” Both interpretations are false, in my opinion. For the prince seems to explain the word in the final part of this chapter. Idem] [Note: Other readings are *sonare*, manuscript 1; *somniare*, manuscript 5; *sommare*, Ambrosian manuscript; *sompniare*, Viennese manuscript]. If our vassal does not render justice, then both the count and the messenger shall sit in his house and live at his expense until he renders justice.

[Col. 0133A] 22. If anyone does not wish to accept a price for a feud, let him be sent to us, and let us assign him a place where he can cause the least harm. Likewise, whoever does not wish to pay a price for a feud and to render justice concerning it, we wish to send him to such a place that greater harm does not grow from the same matter [Note: Another chapter begins here in manuscripts 2, 5, 6, and 6*].

23. Concerning thieves. We command that the following be observed: for the first offense, let him not die, but lose an eye; for the second offense, let the thief’s nose be cut off [Note: “let him be mutilated,” manuscript B; “let him be mutilated,” manuscripts V, Viennese, and Este; “let him lose his nose,” manuscripts 2 and 3]; for the third offense, if he has not reformed, let him die.

Here ends the decree of King Charles.

### LOMBARD CAPITULARY

[Col. 0126B]

In the fortunate [Note: “Charles the Great with the Roman pontiff and the synodal council,” title in the Este manuscript] eleventh year of the reign of our lord Charles, most glorious king, in the month of March. A capitulary was enacted concerning how, when the bishops, abbots, illustrious men, and counts had been gathered together in one synodal council [Note: “noble men” instead of “illustrious,” Ambrosian manuscript], together with our most pious lord, they agreed, according to God’s will and for necessary matters, upon a decree [Note: The Viennese manuscript and the printed editions add here: “The people ask much; Charles fulfilled his commands; good king, honor of the world.”].

First chapter. Concerning metropolitan bishops: their suffragan bishops are to be subject to them according to the canons, and whatever they recognize as requiring correction in their ministry, they are to amend and correct willingly.

2. Concerning bishoprics: where bishops have not been ordained, let them be ordained without delay.

3. Concerning monasteries that were regular: let them live according to the rule; likewise [Note: Absent from manuscripts 1 and 2] let the monasteries of women observe the holy order, and let each abbess reside continuously in her own monastery.

4. Let bishops have authority, according to the canons, to act concerning priests, deacons, and clerics [Note: “priests and deacons” occurs in manuscripts V, Viennese, and Este, with “clerics” omitted; the Chisian, Cavense, Ambrosian, Mutina, and other manuscripts omit “deacons”] within their parish or concerning their ministry.

5. Let bishops have the authority to correct incestuous persons [Note: The words “have the authority …” are absent from manuscripts 1 and 2]; likewise, within their parish, let them have the authority to correct widows [Note: “to govern,” manuscripts 1 and 2]. If, after an episcopal judgment, any of these incestuous persons again involves himself in the same incest, and if he has allodial property, let the royal treasury receive it [Note: “our treasury,” manuscript 2].

6. Let no one be permitted to receive another person’s cleric or ordain him in any rank without a letter of dismissal from his bishop, in whose parish he is [Note: Some manuscripts add: “If he has a cleric from among his own men, let him under no circumstances presume to lead him to be ordained except to the bishop in whose parish he belongs, since he must have authority over him”; other manuscripts read: “or in whose parish he is”].

7. Concerning tithes: let each person give his tithe [Col. 0128C], and let it be distributed by the order and counsel [Note: “and counsel” is present in manuscripts 1, 2, 3, and 4] of the bishop in whose parish he is [Note: “in whose parish he may be,” adopted from manuscripts 1, 2, 3, and 4].

8. Concerning murderers and other wrongdoers [Note: The following text through the middle of chapter 14 is absent from manuscript 3] who are required by the laws either to die or to die in order to make peace: let no one permit them to enter his church for the sake of obtaining an excuse. [Col. 0130A] If anyone enters there without the pastor’s permission, then the person in whose church he is shall give him no food and shall not permit anyone else to give him any [Note: Thus manuscripts 1 and 2. The others read as in the Frankish capitulary].

9. Concerning thieves: let thieves from within the immunity be presented to those judges and advocates at the count’s assembly whenever it has been announced to them [Note: “whenever they have announced it,” manuscript 1 A]. If he says that he could not present that thief [Note: The words “could not present … could not” have fallen out of manuscripts 1 and 2], he must swear that he could not present those thieves [Note: “the thieves,” manuscripts V, Viennese, and Este] after it had been announced to him; that he did not consent to the thief’s escape by delaying any justice [Note: “that he did not allow the thieves to flee,” manuscripts V, Viennese, and Este]; and that he did not throw the thief out of his authority or jurisdiction on the pretext of delay. He shall swear that, if he can, he ought to present that thief to render justice. Whoever fails to do this shall lose his benefice and honor. Likewise, the royal vassals shall suffer the same penalty for this matter [Note: “If our vassals fail to fulfill this, let them lose their benefice and honor; and whoever has no benefice shall pay our ban,” manuscripts M, A, V, Viennese, and the printed editions]. Whoever cannot swear the aforesaid oath without perjury, if he has a benefice, shall lose the benefice or the office held through it; if he has no benefice, he shall pay the lord’s ban.

10. [Note: Manuscript 4 has the text as in the Frankish capitulary.] Concerning perjury: if anyone commits perjury, let him have no possibility of redemption except by losing his hand [Note: The remainder of the chapter is absent from manuscripts A, V, Viennese, and Este. Manuscripts V and Viennese nevertheless add: “and let him strive to make compensation.” Since the same law occurs in these manuscripts among the laws of King Pippin, it will be useful to set its readings below]. If the man who first swore that oath is convicted of perjury, and one of his fellow swearers says that he committed perjury unknowingly, let him either prove this to be true at the judgment of God or likewise lose his hand [Note: “Let him lose it as the other did, on whose account he committed perjury. If he has cleared himself by proving that he committed perjury unknowingly, then as the law …,” manuscripts V, Viennese, and Este].
