Concerning the matter on account of which he committed perjury, let him make compensation according to the law of the place where the perjury was committed, as it has existed for a long time [Col. 0130C] [Note: “Let him strive to make compensation from his own price,” that is, let him pay the *wergild*, manuscripts V, Viennese, and Este].

11. Concerning theft [Note: “Or concerning a challenge,” manuscript F; “or a chessboard,” manuscript A], or concerning lesser cases, we establish the following: if the man whose case has been sworn wishes to discover whether the one who swore knowingly committed perjury [Note: “Let him pay compensation or contest at the cross,” manuscript A; “or contest in the field,” manuscript P; “or contest at the cross,” manuscripts L, V, Viennese, and E], let them stand at the cross. If the one who swore [Note: “committed perjury,” manuscripts V and Viennese] is defeated, having knowingly committed perjury [Note: Absent from manuscripts 1 and 2], let him be subject to the judgment stated above. If the one who made the accusation does not prove the other’s perjury, let him who said that he had committed perjury pay his own legal compensation. In greater cases, let them observe the law that they have possessed for a long time [Note: The remainder of this chapter is absent from manuscripts 1, 2, 3, and 4]. For some people mentioned at an assembly that we held in the previous year, and it was said there that where it is openly apparent that either the accuser or the one wishing to defend himself must commit perjury, they should fight together in the field with clubs rather than secretly perpetrate perjury.

[Col. 0132B] 12. [Note: The London manuscript presents this chapter below, but here gives chapter 11 of the Frankish Capitularies of 779; the same arrangement appears to be found in the Mutina manuscript.] Concerning the vengeance [Note: That is, mutilation of limbs] and judgment [Note: That is, death] carried out against thieves. Let counts be able, without sin, to carry out vengeance and judgment against thieves on the testimony of bishops, provided that no envy, other evil pretext, or injustice has been introduced there, but only true justice for bringing the matter to completion and confirming peace. If a thief is convicted of one theft, let him lose one eye; if convicted of two thefts, let him lose an eye and let his nose be mutilated [Note: “Cut off,” manuscripts V, Viennese, and Este]; if convicted of three thefts, let him die. Concerning the two thefts for which he ought to lose one eye and his nose, we establish that the master of that slave shall pay according to the law under which the thefts were committed. Concerning the three thefts for which death is due, let his death discharge those thefts. If a count, without fault, destroys a man through envy or an unjust pretext rather than for the sake of justice and peace [Col. 0132C], let him lose his honor and make legal compensation to the one against whom he acted unjustly, according to the penalty that he inflicted.

13. Concerning the matters that our father, of blessed memory, Pippin [Note: Absent from manuscript 4], established in his assemblies and synods [Note: “and synods” is absent from manuscript 4], we wish to preserve them [Note: “And thus we also …,” manuscript 4].

14. [Note: [Col. 0132D] In the Mutinensis, the heading of chapter 13 of the Frankish Capitulary appears in place of this chapter.] Concerning the property of the churches which, until now, secular men have held as a benefice by command of the lord king: let them continue to hold it in the future in the same way, unless by command of the lord king they are recalled to those churches. And if, until now, a tenth and a ninth have proceeded from it for the church’s portion, let this continue in the future; moreover, let him pay to those churches one solidus for fifty holdings, half a solidus for thirty, and one tremissis for twenty [Note: Absent from manuscript 1.]; and whoever until now has paid another census shall continue to do so in the future as he did previously. But where no census has until now been collected, and the property belongs to the churches [Note: “By the king’s own laws”; manuscripts 1 and 2], let it be assessed [Note: “Let them be assessed”; two manuscripts], and [Note: Here the text continues in a third manuscript] where they are not, let them be recorded. And let there be a distinction [Note: “Let there be a description”; manuscript 2] between the precariae made by command of the lord and those which bishops, abbots, and abbesses make at their own discretion or disposition, so that, whenever it pleases them, they may receive back for the church’s portion the property which they have granted as benefices, arranging that every man serve God faithfully and firmly at God’s house, in honor of God [Note: “Cause” (*causa*); manuscript 1; “case” (*causam*); manuscript 2.].

# CAPITULARY OF THE BISHOPS [Note: Sirmond rightly observed that this should be joined to the capitulary of the eleventh year. Besides the fact that in the Palatine and Metz manuscripts it is joined to that capitulary, in the fifth book of the *Capitularies* and in the fourth addition it follows immediately after chapter 23 of the same capitulary [Col. 0134C]. There is therefore no doubt that it should be assigned to the year 779. Chapter 23 of the capitulary of Frankfurt undoubtedly refers to this constitution.] (A.D. 779)

[Col. 0133]

In the year 779, as the Alamannic annals report, “a great famine and mortality occurred in Francia, and, after the defeat suffered from the Gascons in the preceding year, a Saxon war threatened the Frankish army.” Since matters stood thus, the bishops, summoned by the king, ordered prayers to be offered for him and the Franks and for the present tribulation. We present here again their capitulary, published by Sirmond in volume II of the *Councils of Gaul*, p. 159, compared by Baluzius with two Palatine and three Metz manuscripts, and emended on the authority of manuscript 1 Paris, among *Suppl. lat.* no. 75.

[Col. 0133B] How the faithful should beseech God for the king and his army in this present tribulation, by prayers and almsgiving.

The capitulary established [Note: “That was decreed”; manuscript 2] in this assembly [Note: “Agreement”; manuscripts 1 and 3; “consent”; manuscript 2] of bishops is as follows: namely, that each bishop sing three Masses and three psalters, one for the lord king, another for the army of the Franks, and a third for the present tribulation. Each priest likewise shall sing three Masses; monks, nuns, and canons, three psalters [Note: “Each one of them shall sing three psalters”; manuscript B]. And all shall observe a two-day fast [Note: “Bishops, monks, nuns, and canons also”; manuscript B], as shall the men of their holdings, or those who are able. Each bishop, abbot, or abbess who is able to do this [Note: “Or has the means”; manuscript B] shall give a pound of silver in alms; those of moderate means, half a pound; the lesser, five solidi [Note: “The lesser likewise”; manuscript B]. Bishops, abbots, and abbesses must support four poor and hungry persons because of this scarcity [Col. 0134B] [Note: “By an arrangement among themselves”; manuscript 1; “according to the arrangement”; manuscript 2] until the time of harvest. Those who cannot support so many shall support as many as their means allow [Note: “Or three”; manuscript B], or two, or one. The stronger counts shall give one pound of silver or its equivalent [Note: “Let them give the equivalent as alms”; manuscript B]; those of moderate means, half a pound. A royal vassal with two hundred holdings shall give half a pound; with one hundred holdings, five solidi; with fifty or thirty holdings, one ounce. They shall observe two-day fasts, as shall their men in their holdings. Whoever is able to do this, and whoever wishes to redeem these fasts [Note: “To redeem these two-day fasts”; manuscript B], shall give: stronger counts, three ounces; those of moderate means, one and a half ounces; the lesser, one solidus. As for the poor and hungry, they too shall act as written above.

If it pleases God, all this shall have been completed, for the lord king, for the army of the Franks, and for the present tribulation, by the Mass of Saint John.

# CAPITULARY OF MANTUA [Note: In the *Codex Carolinus*, letter 65; in Cennius, 63.] (A.D. 781, perhaps March)

[Col. 0135]

We publish this constitution from the following manuscripts: 1, Saint Paul’s, beginning of the ninth century; 2, Chisianus, tenth century; 3, Cavensis, eleventh century, after Mabillon had printed the reading of the Chisianus manuscript in 1687, *Museum Italicum*, vol. I, p. 47. Since no one can easily suppose that it was issued during the king’s first expedition, in 773 or 774, I have assigned it to 781 rather than to 776 or 786, because shortly beforehand the king had complained to Pope Adrian about Italians selling slaves to the Saracens, and therefore a law against the perpetrators of such acts might have seemed necessary.

[Col. 0135] Concerning each chapter, we have made known to everyone what we have decided at the general assembly at Mantua [Note: “The assembly at Mantua”; manuscript 1] [Note: “To the men”; manuscript 1].

1. Concerning the rights of the churches of God, of widows, and of orphans, whether the powerful are great or small [Note: “Whether powerful or less powerful”; manuscript 1; “of the less powerful”; manuscripts 2 and 3], we wish and in every way command [Note: Manuscript 1 reads “by all bishops”] that all bishops, abbots, and counts fully administer and receive justice according to the law [Note: “Let them administer”; manuscript 2; “Let him administer”; manuscript 3].

2. We decree that every complainant shall appeal for the third time to his count [Note: “Every one who has been complained against”; manuscript 1], and shall have suitable men from that place who will truthfully attest what he has complained of and for which he has been unable to obtain justice. If anyone acts otherwise and has previously appealed to the palace, let him pay his legal composition.

3. The counts, for their part, shall affirm by witnesses that they wished to render justice to them [Note: Manuscript 1 reads *facerent*, “that they would do”], and shall have their notary write down how many people have appealed to them and how much justice they have rendered, so that, when they appeal [Note: The editor inserts *vocem*; it is absent from the manuscripts], the counts can have no excuse unless it is plainly true that they wished to render justice; and the count himself or his advocate must be able to confirm by oath that he has shown no negligence regarding their cases. From this document he shall be able to determine whether they appealed to him or not [Note: “We shall be able”; manuscripts 2 and 3; “whether he appealed to him”; manuscript 1].

4. Let this be known to all: if anyone, after a case has been legally settled, brings another complaint, he shall either receive fifteen *camacti* [Note: “*gamati*”; manuscript 2; “*gamaitoi*”; manuscript 3] or be compelled to pay a composition of fifteen solidi.

5. Let no one receive another man’s priest before he has been examined or investigated by the bishop of that place [Note: “Places”; manuscript 1], nor shall he be permitted to celebrate Mass there.

6. Whenever a bishop makes his circuit through his diocese [Note: The first manuscript lacks these words], let the count or *sculdaz* [Note: “Count or *sculdais*”; manuscript 2; “Count or *sculdahis*”; manuscript 3] provide assistance, so that he may fully carry out his ministry according to canonical ordinance.

7. Let no one sell Christian or pagan slaves, nor any weapons or *amissarius* (riding horse), outside our kingdom. Whoever does this shall be compelled to pay the king’s ban [Note: “The lord’s ban”; manuscript 2; “Our ban”; manuscript 3]; and if he cannot recover those slaves, let him pay his *wergild* [Note: “*Guidrigild*”; manuscript 3].

8. Concerning toll collectors [Note: Absent from manuscript 2; “Concerning tolls”; manuscript 3]: let no one dare to exact a toll otherwise than according to the ancient custom, and let it not be collected elsewhere except at the ancient, lawful places. Whoever exacts a toll unjustly shall make compensation according to the law and, in addition, pay our penalty to our envoys.

[Col. 0136A] 9. Concerning coinage: after these Kalends of August, let no one dare to give or receive the denarii which we are now seen to possess [Note: “August”; manuscript 1; “of August”; manuscripts 2 and 3]. Whoever does this shall pay our penalty.

10. Concerning thieves who have not come before our envoys: let the counts seek them out and keep them either under surety or in custody until those same envoys return.

11. Let no one receive any Lombard man into his vassalage or household before he knows where he is from and how he was born. Whoever acts otherwise shall pay our penalty.

12. Concerning hospitals, we wish and command that they be restored.

13. Concerning the king’s vassals and their rights: let them first receive and render justice before their own count.

## The following are appended in the manuscript of Saint Paul’s

### This is canonical law

**Chapter of the Apostles** [Note: The Canons of the Apostles, in Harzheim, *German Councils*, vol. I, p. 132, chapter 7].—Bishops, priests, and deacons shall in no way undertake secular concerns. If anyone acts otherwise, let him be deposed.

**Chapter 35, distinction 15** [Note: That is, “distinction”; it is written in manuscript h&Rbar].—Let bishops use the property of the church as property entrusted to them, not as their own.

**African canon, distinction 50.**—A gift, sale, or exchange of church property made by bishops without the agreement or written consent of the clergy shall be invalid.

**Canon of Arles, distinction 14.**—Let bishops in no way involve priests or deacons in guardianship or administration.

**Canon 54, distinction 3.**—Let a bishop not take upon himself the administration of any household matter, but devote himself solely to readings and prayer [Col. 0136C], to the word of God, and to preaching.

### Also concerning hunting: chapter 45, canon of Mâcon, distinction 20

[Note: *Council of Mâcon* II, chapter 13, in Sirmond, p. 387; this must be compared.]—Therefore we wish [Note: The manuscript has an apparently corrupt reading, “*ignit*”] that episcopal houses, which were established for this purpose, should receive everyone hospitably, without discrimination among persons [Note: “Without acceptance”; manuscript reading], and should have no dogs, lest those who hope to find relief from their miseries there be torn by the bites of savage dogs. The episcopal residence must therefore be guarded by hymns, not by barking; by good works, not by poisonous bites. Where there ought to be continual singing, it is a monstrous disgrace [Note: Perhaps “a mark of disgrace”] for dogs or hawks to dwell there [Note: Perhaps “to be kept there.”].

[Col. 0136D] **Canon of Épaone**, distinction 4 [Note: In Sirmond, vol. I, p. 195].—Bishops, priests, and deacons shall not be permitted to keep dogs for hunting or hawks. If a bishop presumes to do this, he shall be suspended from communion for three months; a priest shall abstain for two months, a deacon for one; and each shall cease from communion and office.

# CAPITULARY OF KING PIPPIN FOR THE LOMBARDS (A.D. 782, before Easter)

After Pippin, the second son of Charles and Hildegard, had been made king of the Lombards in 781, laws issued by Charles in his absence [Note: That his laws were promulgated under his name while he was nevertheless present is demonstrated by the Lombard capitulary of the year 801] from assemblies held in Francia and transmitted to his son [Note: Pippin himself says, “According to the schedule of our lord Charles, our father”; see his second capitulary], or laws issued in Italy by the Frankish and Lombard nobles at the son’s command, were promulgated in the name and with the authority of King Pippin. Since only a few examples of this matter had until now been known, more are presented below from the most ancient manuscripts; from them it will become clear that Charles’s general capitularies also possessed the force of law in Italy.

I thought that the first capitulary issued under Pippin’s name should be assigned to the year 782, since the texts following it were not promulgated before 783, and it cannot be assigned to 781, because it was issued shortly before Easter, whereas Pippin was consecrated king of the Lombards at Rome on Easter Day of 781. It is published here on the authority of manuscripts 1 Chisianus, 2 Cavensis, and the manuscripts containing the laws of the Lombards [Note: It was possible to compare the Ambrosian, London, Verona, and Florentine manuscripts with the printed editions only in general; the readings of the Vindobonensis manuscript, compared with great care, may be regarded as representative of all the others]: Ambrosianus, Florentinus, Londinensis, Vindobonensis, Veronensis, and Estensis, in Muratori. From their comparison with one another it will be shown most clearly that only the Chisianus and Cavensis transmit the text of the law itself, while the remaining manuscripts present a text prepared in a later age for the use of jurists.

[Col. 0137B] In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. How [Note: “Namely, how”; Florentine manuscript; “Hear how”; “Hear how” in the editions] it pleased us [Note: “Me”; Florentine, Vindobonensis, Veronensis, and Estensis manuscripts], Pippin, most excellent king of the Lombard people, when there were with us individual bishops, abbots, and counts, as well as our other faithful Franks and Lombards [Note: Manuscript L adds, “We add these chapters”; the Chisianus and Cavensis manuscripts lack the following words], who are with us or dwelling in Italy [Note: These words are absent from Ambrosianus, Londinensis, Florentinus, Vindobonensis, Veronensis, Estensis, and Muratori].

**Chapter 1.** Let those who restored baptismal churches or oratories long ago restore them again immediately; and let both the royal estates and the Lombards have there the same authority that has long been their custom.

**2.** Let each bishop organize and arrange his churches according to canonical order, and compel his priests and clerics to live according to canonical order. If any bishop does not wish to discipline his clerics so that they live according to canonical order [Col. 0137C] [Note: Another manuscript adds, “Let him be accursed, and let those men be transferred to Milan”], and has drawn them into a secular habit—which the canons forbid clerics to assume [Note: “If they have crossed over”; manuscript V.]—let the count appointed in that place discipline them in every respect for his portion, just like the other men liable to military service.

**3.** Let each person in whose protection monasteries of men and women are found—whether they are known to be under the protection of the palace, under episcopal protection, or under that of other men—discipline them so that they live according to the rule [Note: “Let them be disciplined”; manuscript 1. Cavensis, manuscript C, Vindobonensis, and the editions read: “Let them live. Chapter 4. Likewise …”]. Likewise, let this apply to hospitals of every kind. Let the brothers be fed in all respects according to the resources of their places [Note: “According to the resources of the places”; Muratori].

**4.** Let them generally undertake the restoration of churches and the construction of bridges and the restoration of roads, exactly as was the ancient custom; and let no exemption be put first, nor let any excuse arise on this account.

**5.** Let widows and orphans have a guardian according to their law, who will defend and assist them, so that they do not lose their justice through the oppression of evil men. If any one of them is unwilling to be guardian [Note: “Agent”; manuscript 1], let the judge provide a God-fearing man, according to their law, who by our command shall conduct their case [Note: One manuscript adds: “Yet in such a way that the lawful relative of the children, who appears rightly to be their guardian and defender, may at some time be compelled to render an account for them.”].

**6.** Whoever complains against a bishop that he has justice to seek shall have the count direct him to that bishop, either through his own envoy or by his own letter. If that bishop, whether Frank or Lombard, delays rendering justice [Col. 0138C], then, according to the choice made by those bishops themselves, wherever the custom of taking pledges has existed for a long time, let it continue in the same manner for the rendering of those judgments. We further decree that wherever a bishop has property, he shall have an advocate in that county who shall render and receive justice without delay [Note: “He shall have two advocates. And such a man …”; manuscript V.]. Let that advocate be a free man of good reputation, lay or cleric [Note: “Or not a cleric”; manuscript V.; absent from manuscript Estensis], who can carry through the oath concerning the case he has conducted [according to the extent of the property] [Note: These words are absent from manuscripts 1 and 2], as their law requires [Note: “So long as he or his envoy renders justice at some time”; manuscript Vindobonensis].

**7.** Concerning the whole people: whoever seeks justice anywhere [Note: “Wherever”; manuscripts V. and M.] shall receive it from his counts, from the *castaldii*, from the *sculdais* [Note: “*Sculdahis*”; manuscript 2; “*sculdais*”; manuscript V.; “*sculdasiis*”; manuscript M.], or from the officials appointed in the place [Note: “From the prefects”; manuscript M.], according to their law and without delay. If a Frankish count delays rendering justice and this is proved, let him suffer the penalty according to the choice that was made concerning them [Note: Absent from manuscripts 1 and V.], and let his honor be treated as is customary among the Franks [Note: “That is, let him die”; gloss in manuscript V.]. As for the Lombard counts, if one of them neglects to render justice, let him pay according to their law [Note: “And if this is proved, let them suffer the penalty according to the choice that was made concerning them, and let their honor be treated as …”; Baluzius]. If perhaps he favors his *gasindii*, relatives, or friends, or does not judge according to the payment and the law, and this is proved [Note: “Let him pay his *wergild*”; manuscript M.], let him make compensation and lose his honor [Note: “Let him forfeit it”; manuscript 1], as their law requires. If a *castaldus*, *sculdais*, or official appointed in any district [Note: “Judicial district”; manuscripts V., M., and B.] fails to render justice to his own villagers or to others who seek justice, let him make compensation according to their law. If a Frank or Lombard who holds a benefice is unwilling to render justice, let the judge in whose jurisdiction he remains withhold that benefice from him until he or his envoy renders justice.

**8.** Let every judge in each city cause believing men to swear by God’s judgments, as many as he considers appropriate, and likewise those living outside in estates or villages [Note: “Villages”; manuscripts V., M., and B.], so that whoever among them knows of homicide, theft, adultery, or unlawful unions may conceal none of these things. We further command that if someone comes to seek justice against any man, accusing him of homicide, theft [Note: “Adultery or plunder”; manuscript 2], or plunder, and the man accused wishes to deny it, then the complainant shall prove it if he can. If he cannot prove it, and the accused denies that either he or his men committed the wrong, and offers an excuse and says, “Name to me the men who did that wrong to you. I shall render you justice concerning them,” and the unknown complainant does not know the names of those men and cannot prove the charge, while those who know the truth about it wish to deny it, and the complainant says that the man knows the truth about it, then the judge who is in that place shall make the men swear—whoever they may be, Franks or Lombards—whom he has named specifically [Note: “Which”; manuscript 1], so that they may tell the truth. If they are believing men, let them give their right hands [Col. 0140A] into the hand [Note: “Hands”; manuscript 1] of their count [Note: “To the count”; manuscripts 1 and 2] [Note: “Their own”; manuscript 1] [Note: “Let them give their right hands”; manuscript 1; “let them swear”; manuscript 2]. If that robbery [Note: “That is, concealed homicide”; gloss in manuscript V.] or theft or plunder is discovered, let compensation be made according to their law [Note: “According to the law of the person against whom the wrong was committed; nevertheless, let the judge of the place from which the thief or robber came take care to do so.” This passage appears in manuscript V., M., B., and certainly several others, but is absent from manuscripts 1 and 2], so that the people dwelling here or arriving here [Note: “Living”; manuscript 1; “those dwelling and those arriving”; manuscripts M. and B.] may be able to live in peace.

**9.** Concerning fugitive male and female slaves: let every judge take care to seek them out according to what the edict provides. We further command that throughout Austrasia, Neustria, Emilia, and Tuscany [Note: “*Tustia*”; manuscript 1; “*Tussia*”; manuscript 2], and along the seacoast [Note: “The shores”; manuscript 2; “the shore”; manuscript M.], the fugitives written above be sought everywhere. Let them swear together in each place—*scultasii*, deans, *saltarii*, or local officials—that they conceal no one; and wherever the fugitives are found, let the person with whom they are found be brought to us together with an envoy of the count or of that place, so that they may be able to swear that they conceal no one. [Note: The remainder of this chapter is absent from the printed editions and survives only in manuscripts 1 and 2.] And a deadline has been established [Note: That is, the appointed time by which these matters must have been completed, etc.]: the fifteenth day [Col. 0140B] after Holy Easter. If anyone has fugitive male or female slaves, whether belonging to a church, an estate, or the people, at the appointed time the person who recognizes his own shall receive him.

**10.** Concerning visitors and pilgrims who, in God’s service, hurry to Rome or to the bodies of other saints, so that they may go and return safely under our protection: whoever among these pilgrims dares to kill one of them [Note: “If anyone [kills] any of these pilgrims other than a free Lombard or Roman”; manuscripts V. and Estensis] shall pay sixty solidi in our palace. In addition, the composition for the homicide itself shall be paid to the person to whom that *leud* belongs according to law.

We further command all bishops, abbots, counts, and our officials that all the justice written above must be carried out immediately and without delay, so that whoever has been unable to obtain justice for so many years [Col. 0140C], now, by the mercy of almighty God, by the command of my lord and father Charles, king of the Frankish and Lombard peoples and patrician of the Romans [Note: “Immediately” is absent from manuscript 1], and likewise by our command, may each receive his justice [Note: “Of the present time” is absent from manuscript 1. The remainder is absent from the printed editions and from all manuscripts except 1 and 2]. Nevertheless, everything must have been completed within fifteen days after Holy Easter. Then each of our judges shall send his envoy to us to give us an account of whether they have fulfilled our command. Afterwards, with God’s help, we shall arrange matters as we judge best.

# GENERAL CAPITULARY (A.D. 783)

[Col. 0139]

Queen Hildegard, wife of Charles, died on the second day before the Kalends of May in the year 783. Since the edict mentions the recording of her property, the law must have been promulgated either in May at Theodonis villa, or finally in the autumn, after Charles’s return from Saxony, at the assembly of Worms. It occurs only twice among Charles’s laws: namely, in manuscript 1, formerly Tegernsee and now the royal Munich manuscript, from which Amerpachius first published columns 41–44, and in manuscript 2, the ducal Gotha manuscript, folio 220. After carefully comparing both, we have arranged our edition so as to follow, as closely as possible, the traces of both books, but especially of the Tegernsee manuscript, from which all earlier editions derive. The result is that we now possess a text very similar to the second capitulary of Pippin, king of Italy, and one which can consequently be emended in several places.

We present the edition of the Lombard capitulary promulgated by King Pippin with the aid of the following manuscripts: 1, Saint Paul’s, ninth century; 2, the royal Paris manuscript no. 4613; 3, the Blankenburg manuscript of the ducal library at Wolfenbüttel; 4, Chisianus; 5, Cavensis; and the manuscripts containing capitularies added to the Lombard laws: Mutinensis, in Muratori; Ambrosianus, Florentinus, Londinensis, Vindobonensis, Veronensis, and Estensis, in Muratori.

# FRANKISH CAPITULARY [Note: In Migne, the sections “Frankish Capitulary” and “Lombard Capitulary” are printed in parallel.]

[Col. 0141A]

Here begins the capitulary in which the lord king commanded [Note: Absent from manuscript 2] concerning certain matters [Note: “Decreed”; manuscript 2].

**First chapter.** Concerning hospitals: he ordered that whoever possesses hospitals, if they are willing to feed the poor and manage them as they did formerly, should retain those hospitals and govern them in an orderly manner. If they are unwilling to do this, let them surrender them; and from now on let them be administered by such men as may thereby please God and us [Note: “Governed by such a man, with the counsel of the bishop, as Baluzius has it.”].

**2.** Concerning baptismal churches: laymen must in no way hold them, but they are to be administered by priests, as the order requires. Nor should the local inhabitants neglect what they ought to do there. Let the priests govern them in the manner required by canonical order.

**3.** Concerning advocates of priests: for the honor of the church and out of reverence for them, we wish them to have advocates.

**4.** Concerning the various peoples who dwell in Italy: wherever an offense occurs from which a feud may grow, let the offender make compensation according to the law of the person against whom he committed the offense, in satisfaction for that man [Note: Read “for satisfaction,” not “for the toils of that man”; manuscript 2 has “of the toils”]. Concerning the status of free birth and other disputes, let each man defend himself according to his own law.

**5.** Concerning compositions that belong to the palace: if the counts have taken up those cases for investigation, let them receive one-third for their own use [Col. 0141C], and the other two-thirds for the palace. If the cases have remained unresolved through their negligence, and the royal envoy has begun to investigate them, then we wish that the count receive no part of the third, but that the whole amount come to the palace.

**6.** Concerning monasteries and hospitals which appear to belong to various counts: let them be royal; and whoever wishes to possess them shall possess them as a benefice granted by the king.

**7.** Concerning property held by various counts, we wish it to belong to the palace [Note: “To the assembly”; manuscript 1].

**8.** If property has been given to someone as alms, and he dies before distributing it, then the royal envoy, together with the bishop of his parish, shall determine how that alms is to be carried out for the lord king’s spiritual recompense [Col. 0141D], and it must be completed within thirty nights.

[Col. 0143A] **9.** Concerning the daughter whose father, through the hand of an agent, ordered all his slaves [Note: “All men”; manuscript 1; “of the man”; manuscript 2] to be made free: because this appears to be contrary to law, we decree [Note: “We shall decree”; manuscript 1] that the daughter herself [Note: Absent from manuscript 1] may again enter into a third share [Note: The following words are absent from manuscript 1] of the aforesaid slaves [Note: The remainder is absent from manuscripts 1 and 2].

**10.** It has pleased us to insert that wherever there is a law, it shall prevail over custom [Note: “Custom”; manuscript 1], and no custom shall be placed above the law.

**11.** It has also pleased us that any woman who has the power, by her husband’s permission [Note: “By permission”; manuscript 2], to sell should also have the power to give.

**12.** Concerning the slaves of our palace and of our churches: we do not wish to receive protection over them, but to have those female slaves as our own [Note: “Protection”; manuscript 2].

[Col. 0143B] **13.** It has pleased us that our counts not oppress free men for their own servile labor; and whoever does this shall make compensation according to the judgment we have established [Note: “According to what must be judged”; manuscript 1].

**14.** Concerning the property handed over to Queen Hildegard: we wish written lists to be made of it [Note: “A list”; manuscript 1], and that those lists be brought to us.

**15.** It is not our will that the men of Piacenza, by their order [Note: “Orders”; manuscript 2], receive those *aldiones* from our palace estate [Note: “Those”; manuscript 1; “of that man”; manuscript 2].

**16.** Concerning fugitives from the regions of Benevento and Spoleto [Note: “The Spoletans”; manuscript 2], or from Romanía or the Pentapolis, who seek refuge: let them be returned, and let them go back to their own place.

[Col. 0143C] **17.** Just as it has been customary to take the seal [Note: “The sealed document”; manuscript 1] and letter, and to guard the roads or gates, so let it now be done.

# LOMBARD CAPITULARY

[Col. 0142A]

The capitulary which the lord king commanded [Note: Thus corrected by the editor; the manuscript reads “*cepi*.”] concerning certain matters.

**Concerning hospitals.** He ordered that whoever possesses hospitals, if they are willing to feed the poor and manage them by counsel as was formerly done, should retain those hospitals and govern them orderly. If they are unwilling to do this, let them surrender them, and from now on let them be governed by such men as may thereby please God and us.

**2. Concerning baptismal churches.** Laymen must in no way hold them, but they are to be administered by priests, as the order requires [Note: “Let them be established and governed in an orderly manner”; manuscript 2]. Nor should the local inhabitants neglect what they ought to do there; and let the priests govern them in the manner required by canonical order.

[Col. 0142B] **3. Concerning advocates of churches.** We wish them to have advocates for the honor of the church and out of reverence for the priests.

**4. Concerning an offense from which a feud may grow.** Concerning people of various origins who dwell in Italy, we wish that wherever an offense occurs from which a feud may grow, the offender make compensation, in satisfaction for the man against whom he committed the offense, according to the law of the person whose rights he violated. Concerning the status of free birth and other disputes, let each person defend himself according to his own law.

**5. Concerning compositions that belong to the palace.** If the counts have taken up those cases for investigation, let them receive one-third for their own use [Note: “Let them claim”; manuscript 1], and the other two-thirds for the palace. If the cases have remained unresolved through his negligence, and the royal envoy has begun to investigate them, then we wish that the counts receive no part of the third, but that the whole amount come to the palace.

**6. Concerning royal monasteries and hospitals.** Concerning monasteries and hospitals which appear to belong to various counts: let them be royal; whoever wishes to possess them shall possess them as a benefice granted by our lord king.

**7. Concerning forfeited property.** Concerning property forfeited through various counts, we wish it to belong to the palace [Note: “After a year and a day have elapsed”; Muratori].

**8. Concerning one to whom property has been given as alms.** If property has been given to someone as alms and he dies before distributing it, then the royal envoy [Note: The remainder of this chapter is absent from manuscript 1] together with the bishop of that parish shall determine [Note: “Shall sit in judgment”; manuscript 2; “Shall grant”; manuscript 3] how that alms is to be carried out for the lord king’s spiritual recompense and completed within thirty nights.

[Col. 0144A] **9. Concerning the daughter’s right to the property of slaves whom her father made free.** Concerning the daughter whose father, through the hand of an agent, ordered all his slaves to be made free, and because this appears contrary to law, we decree that the daughter herself may again enter into such a portion [Note: “A third portion”; manuscript 2] of the aforesaid slaves as was her portion of her father’s other property [Note: The remainder of this chapter is absent from manuscripts 2, 3, 4, and 5].

**10. Concerning the authority of law and custom.** It has pleased us to insert that wherever there is a law, it shall prevail over custom, so that no custom may be placed above the law.

**11. Concerning the power of a woman to sell and give.** It has also pleased us that whatever woman [Note: “A Lombard woman”; Mutinensis, Vindobonensis, and Estensis] has the power, by her husband’s permission [Note: “To sell her property”; manuscript 2], to sell shall also have the power to give.

**12. Concerning the slaves of the palace and churches.** Concerning the slaves of the palace and of our churches [Col. 0144B], we do not wish to receive protection over them, but to have those female slaves as our own [Note: The remainder is absent from manuscript 3].

**13. Concerning the prohibition against compelling free men to servile labor.** It has pleased us that our counts not oppress free men for their own servile labor; and whoever presumes to do this shall make compensation according to the judgment we have established.

**14. Concerning the queen’s property** [Note: This chapter is absent from manuscripts 4 and 5]. Concerning the property handed over to Queen Hildegard, we wish written records to be made of it on lists, and that those lists be brought to us.

**15. Concerning the palace *aldiones*.** It is not our will that the men of Piacenza [Note: “The Piacenzans”; manuscripts 2, 4, and 5], by their order, receive those *aldiones* from our palace estate.

16. **Concerning fugitives.** Concerning fugitives who take refuge in the regions of Benevento or Spoleto, or in Romagna or the Pentapolis [Note: *pentauoli* in witness 1], [it is ordered] that they be returned and restored to their proper places.

17. **Concerning seals and letters, and the guarding of roads and crossing-points.** Just as it was customary to take a seal and a letter, and to guard the roads or gates, so let it now be done.

# CAPITULARY OF PADERBORN (A.D. 785)

[Col. 0143]

There exists a single manuscript of these capitularies in the Vatican Library, among the Palatine manuscripts, no. 289, on parchment, of the ninth century. After the work of Holstenius, Fürstenberg, Conring, and Baluzius, I transcribed it again at Rome in the year 1822. I have therefore established a new edition on the authority of that manuscript. The date and place of this edict are not certain. Yet no one will fail to see that these bloody laws could not have been imposed and accepted either in the year 777, when for the first time the senate and people of all Saxony met at Paderborn and “with their hands made liberty and hereditary property [*ingenuitas et alodes*] secure, provided only that they preserved the Christianity and fidelity of the lord Charles, king of the Franks,” nor in the year 780, when at the synod at Lippibrunn churches were built and all Saxony was divided among bishops, priests, abbots, and counts, nor finally in the year 782, when at the general assembly at the same place counts were appointed from the most distinguished Saxon nobility. Rather, they could have been imposed and accepted only after three years had elapsed since the slaughter of Adalgisus and Geilo, when all Saxony had been utterly destroyed by the punishment at Verden, the battles at the Theotmelli, at the Hase, and at the Lippe, and by the continuous slaughter, plundering, and devastation inflicted by the Franks. For at that time, in the year 785, Charles held a public assembly of his people at Paderborn, “with Franks and Saxons.” When the matters belonging to that assembly had been completed, the churches throughout Saxony had been restored [Note: See the *Life of Saint Willehad*], and shortly afterward Widukind and Abbi had been converted to Christianity, all Saxony remained steadfast for seven years both in religion and in loyalty to the king. I therefore judge that this edict belongs especially to that time and place.

[Col. 0145A] **Chapters established concerning the regions of Saxony** [Note: The manuscript reads: “Capitulation: concerning the regions of Saxony these things have been established.” I corrected it. Baluzius emended it as follows: “Capitulation concerning the regions of Saxony. These things have been established concerning the regions of Saxony.”].

**1.** First, concerning the major chapters, all agreed to this: that the churches of Christ, as they are being built in Saxony and consecrated to God, should have no less honor, but greater and more excellent honor, than the temples of idols had had [Note: This is the reading of the Roman and German editions. They have *fana* (“temples”). Baluzius].

**2.** If anyone takes refuge in a church, no one shall presume to drive him from the church by force; rather, he shall have peace until he is brought before the assembly. And, out of honor for God and reverence for that church’s saints, his life and all his limbs shall be spared. He shall make amends for his case as far as he can and as judgment has determined; and thus he shall be brought into the presence of the lord king, who shall send him wherever his mercy pleases [Note: *domini* corrected to *domni* in the manuscript].

[Col. 0145B] **3.** If anyone enters a church by force and removes anything from it by force or theft, or burns the church itself with fire, he shall die by death.

**4.** If anyone, out of contempt for Christianity, despises the holy Lenten fast and eats meat [Note: *dispectu* corrected to *despectu*], he shall die by death. Nevertheless, the priest shall consider whether perhaps necessity caused that person to eat meat.

[Note: It is certainly harsh that a capital sentence should be pronounced against someone who eats meat during Lent, if he did so out of contempt for the Christian faith. But among a defiant people this had to be done, lest they continually relapse into paganism. In the age of Thietmar, bishop of Merseburg, this was the custom among the Poles: whoever ate meat after Septuagesima was punished by having his teeth pulled out. Thus he himself writes at the beginning of Book VIII: “Whoever is found to have eaten meat after Septuagesima is severely punished by having his teeth cut out. For the divine law, newly arisen in these regions, is strengthened by the bishops through such power more effectively than by fasting instituted by them.” The same editor.]

**5.** If anyone kills a bishop, priest, or deacon, he shall likewise be punished capitally.

**6.** If anyone, deceived by the devil, believes according to pagan custom that some man or woman is a witch and eats people, and for this reason burns that person, gives the person’s flesh to be eaten, or eats it himself, he shall be punished by a capital sentence [Note: *omnes* corrected to *homines*; *capitali* corrected to *capitis*].

**7.** If anyone causes the body of a dead person to be consumed by flame according to pagan ritual, and reduces the person’s bones to ashes, he shall be punished capitally.

**8.** If thereafter anyone among the Saxon people, hiding among them, wishes to conceal himself without being baptized, despises coming to baptism, and wishes to remain a pagan [Note: Alcuin, Letter 104: “For this reason the wretched Saxon people so often lost the sacrament of baptism, because they never possessed the sacrament of faith in their hearts.” See the *Chronicle of Moissac* under the year 792. The same editor], he shall die by death.

[Note: Although it is not proper for religion to compel religion, here the practice recorded by Thietmar recurs. Thus Andrew, the first king of Hungary, having been made secure from the disturbances of his enemies and wishing, as it were, to imitate Charlemagne, in the year 1047 “ordered all his people, under penalty of capital punishment, after abandoning the paganism previously granted to them, to return to the true faith of Christ,” as John of Thurócz says in chapter 42 of the *Chronicle of the Hungarians*. This is also reported by Antonio Bonfini in decade 2, Book II of the *History of Hungary*. The same editor.]

**9.** If anyone sacrifices a human being to the devil and offers him as a victim to demons according to pagan custom, he shall die by death.

**10.** If anyone makes a plot with pagans against Christians, or wishes to persist with them in hostility toward Christians, he shall die by death. And whoever agrees to this same thing by treachery against the king or the Christian people shall die by death.

**11.** If anyone appears unfaithful to the lord king [Note: *rege* corrected to *regi*], he shall be punished by a capital sentence.

**12.** If anyone abducts his lord’s daughter, he shall die by death.

**13.** If anyone kills his lord or his lady, he shall be punished in the same manner.

**14.** But if, for these mortal crimes secretly committed, anyone voluntarily takes refuge with a priest and, after making confession, wishes to perform penance, he shall be excused from death on the testimony of the priest [Note: *testimonia sacerdote* corrected to *testimonio sacerdotis*].

**15.** Concerning the minor chapters, all agreed that for each church they would grant a manor and two *mansi* of land, together with the dependents who resort to the church; and that among every one hundred and twenty men—nobles and free men alike, and also *liti*—they should assign to the same church a male servant and a female servant [Note: The manuscript reads: “nobles and free men likewise, and *liti*, a servant.” Baluzius punctuated it: “likewise *liti*, a servant.”].

**16.** And this also pleased Christ, by his favor: wherever any tax reaches the royal treasury, whether as a peace-payment, or under any kind of royal ban, and in every revenue belonging to the king, one-tenth shall be rendered to the churches and priests.

**17.** Likewise, according to God’s command, we order that everyone—nobles and free men alike, and also *liti*—give a tenth part of their substance and labor to their churches and priests. In accordance with what God has given each Christian, let them render a portion to God.

**18.** On Sundays they shall not hold assemblies or public courts, unless perhaps great necessity or enemy attack compels it. Rather, all shall resort to the church to hear the word of God and devote themselves to prayers or righteous works. Likewise, on the chief festivals they shall serve God and the church’s assembly, and set aside secular courts.

[Col. 0147A] **19.** It likewise pleased them to insert into these decrees that all infants be baptized before they are one year old. And we establish this: if anyone, without the advice or permission of a priest, neglects to present an infant for baptism within the cycle of the year, he shall pay to the treasury—if he is of noble birth, 120 solidi; if free, 60; if a *litus*, 30 [Note: The reading originally was “free men … *liti*.”].

**20.** If anyone contracts a forbidden or unlawful marriage, he shall pay, if noble, 60 solidi; if free, 30; if a *litus*, 15 [Note: The manuscript reads “to free men … *liti*.”].

**21.** If anyone makes a vow at springs, trees, or sacred groves, or offers anything according to the custom of the pagans, and eats in honor of demons, he shall pay—if noble, 60 solidi; if free, 30; if a *litus*, 15 [Note: *lucas* corrected to *lucos*; *aliquis* corrected to *aliquit*; *nobiles* corrected to *nobilis*; *litos* corrected to *litus*]. If they do not have the means to pay immediately, they shall be given to the service of the church until the solidi themselves have been paid.

**22.** We order that the bodies of Saxon Christians be carried to the church cemeteries, and not to pagan burial mounds.

**23.** We decree that diviners and sorcerers be handed over to the churches and priests.

**24.** Concerning thieves and criminals who flee from one county to another: if anyone receives them under his authority and keeps them with him for seven nights [Note: The manuscript reads six], unless it is in order to present them, he shall pay our ban [Note: *praesentendum* corrected to *praesentandum*]. Likewise, if a count hides him and refuses to present him so that justice may be done, and cannot excuse himself for this, he shall lose his office and honor.

[Col. 0147C] **25.** Concerning pledges: no one shall presume in any way to take another person as a pledge. Whoever does this shall pay the ban.

**26.** No one shall presume to block anyone’s way when he comes to us to seek justice. If anyone attempts to do this, he shall pay our ban.

**27.** If anyone cannot find a surety, his property shall be placed under the royal ban until he presents a surety. But if he presumes to enter his house while under the ban, he shall pay either ten solidi or one ox as compensation for that ban; and in addition he shall pay whatever he was indebted for. If the surety does not observe the appointed day, he himself shall suffer as much loss as the surety’s commitment had amounted to. But the person who was indebted to the surety shall repay double, because he allowed the surety to fall into loss.

**28.** Concerning rewards and gifts: no one shall accept gifts from an innocent person. If anyone presumes to do this, he shall pay our ban. And if, which God forbid, a count should do this, he shall lose his office and honor.

**29.** All counts shall strive to maintain peace and concord with one another. If some disagreement or disturbance should arise among them, they shall not on that account abandon our support or assistance.

**30.** If anyone kills a count, or gives counsel for his death, his inheritance shall pass to the king’s portion and be restored to his legal authority.

**31.** We have given the counts authority to impose a ban within their own jurisdiction: for a feud or major cases, 60 solidi; for lesser cases, we establish the count’s ban at 15 solidi.

**32.** If anyone owes an oath to any person, let him summon him to the church to swear the oath on the appointed day. If he refuses to swear, let him establish his good faith and pay 15 solidi—the penalty for appearing inactive [text uncertain: *inactivus apparuit*]; thereafter he shall be compelled to make full amends in the case.

**33.** Concerning perjurers, let it be according to the law of the Saxons.

**34.** We have forbidden all Saxons generally to hold public assemblies, unless perhaps our messenger gathers them by our order. Each count, however, shall hold courts and administer justice within his own jurisdiction. The priests shall see to it that he does not act otherwise.

# LOMBARD CAPITULARY (A.D. 786)

[Col. 0147]

After the rebellion of Count Hardrad and the Thuringians—which had created a great “disturbance” in Charles’s kingdom—had been suppressed in the year 786, when the king judged that the peoples subject to him ought to be bound by an oath and was planning the Beneventan expedition, I infer from chapters 6, 7, and 9 that this edict was promulgated by King Pippin. I have tried to restore the text from the single manuscript in the Paris Library, no. 4613, and have attempted, as far as conjecture allowed, to fill out the gaps in the final chapter.

[Col. 0147D] **1.** Concerning those women who had vowed themselves to God and had put on monastic clothing, but afterward joined themselves to husbands: each person shall investigate within the judicial district entrusted to him wherever he finds such women, so that they may separate them without delay from those unlawful unions and lead them from the aforementioned unlawful union back to the remedy of penance.

**2.** Concerning those men who practice any incantation or divination, or similar things that appear abominable in the sight of God: each person shall likewise investigate wherever he finds them, shall not release them without corrective discipline, and shall make them perform penance for these unlawful presumptions.

**3.** Concerning those wicked men who worship *brunaticus* [uncertain term] and those who burn wax candles beneath their *maida* [uncertain term] and make vows: each person shall make them desist from such iniquity. If they wish to offer bread to the church, let them offer it simply, without any admixture of that unlawful practice.

**4.** Likewise, each person shall investigate the people entrusted to him, wherever perhaps unlawful unions are found, so that if someone has taken as wife his *consobrinus* or his *insobrinus* [the transmitted forms are grammatically uncertain], or has joined any female relative to himself as a wife, they may be separated from one another without any leniency and assigned to the remedy of penance.

**5.** We also write this: all diligent officials shall investigate whether there is a man who has a wife and, as stated above, commits adultery with another woman and keeps a concubine [Note: *concubam* corrected to *concubinam*]. They shall therefore cause such people to be separated from this unlawful practice with every care [Note: *aut* in witness 1]. Thus it pleased the lord king: whoever neglects to correct these unspeakable crimes within the districts entrusted to him, as we have said, shall pay his *wergeld* in the holy palace.

**6.** Concerning the individual chapters in which the lord king instructed his messengers that they should hear and administer no oaths [Note: Reading uncertain: *illa? nova?*], they are to explain in due order, from ancient custom, why these oaths are necessary; and because these unfaithful men now wished to bring great disturbance to the kingdom of the lord King Charles, had plotted against his life, and, when interrogated, said that they had not sworn fidelity to him.

**7.** How the oath is to be sworn by bishops and abbots, or counts and royal vassals, as well as stewards, archdeacons, and canons. Clerics who do not appear fully to observe the monastic name and who maintain the rule of Saint Benedict according to its order shall promise verbally and truthfully; the abbot shall bring the relevant persons specifically before our lord. Then advocates, vicars, centenarii, and priests who are registered as *fore censiti*, as well as the entire body of the people—both those twelve years old and those elderly—who come to the courts and are able to fulfill the commands of their elders and preserve them, whether country-dwellers [Note: *palenses* in the manuscript], or men of bishops and abbesses or counts, and other men, treasury-slaves and tenant farmers, and ecclesiastical persons and slaves who hold honorable benefices and offices or are honored in vassalage with their lords and are able to possess horses, weapons, shield, lance, sword, and *sentespasium* [uncertain weapon], shall all swear. They shall bring with them in writing to the messengers the names and number of those who have sworn.

The counts likewise shall know the men of each hundred, both those born within the county who are country-dwellers and those who have been commended elsewhere into vassalage. If there is anyone who, by cunningly fleeing, has moved from one county to another on account of this oath, or who has refused to swear through arrogance, they shall report such persons separately in writing and either send them under sureties. If they do not have sureties who will bring them into the presence of the lord king, they shall be kept in custody. If they wish to live in that neighborhood, they shall swear like the others. If anyone becomes a fugitive, the messengers shall report it to the lord king.

**8.** The messengers must explain what has been said to the lord king: many complain that the law has not been preserved for them, whereas the lord king’s entire will is that each person’s law be fully preserved. If anything has been done against the law of anyone, it is neither his will nor his command. Nevertheless, if a count, messenger, or any other person has done this, it must be reported to the lord king, because he wishes to correct these matters completely.

They shall inquire of each person what law he has, by name, and shall in no way complete this mission without the count of that county [Note: *si* corrected to *sine*]. An exception is made if that count is absent on another service of the lord king, or if illness prevents him from being present there; in that case he need not be present.

**9.** [Note: The words printed in italics in this chapter have been supplied by conjecture.] Let the messengers, together with the counts who are in their jurisdictions, have the necessary service forces ready, so that all may come this year in military fashion to support the lord king, according to his command, and preserve peace while traveling within the kingdom. Through his letters he wishes to inform them of his will as to when and where they are to join one another.

**The chapters end here.**

# ENCYCLICAL ON THE CULTIVATION OF LETTERS

[Col. 0149]

(See this among the letters of Charlemagne in volume 98 of the *Patrologia*.)

# ECCLESIASTICAL CAPITULARY. A.D. 789 (23 March, Aachen)

[Col. 0149] In publishing this capitulary, the following manuscripts were available to me:

1. The manuscript of the Wolfenbüttel Library, formerly Helmstedt, in a large octavo format, written in Anglo-Saxon script, from the end of the eighth or the beginning of the ninth century.
2. The manuscript of the St. Gall Library, no. 733, on parchment, from the beginning of the ninth century.
3. The manuscript of the Palatine Library at Vienna, listed in the catalogue of canon law under no. 128, on parchment, from the ninth century, in a large octavo format.
3b. The manuscript of the Royal Library at Munich, among the books from St. Emmeram at Regensburg, marked E. 91, written in the year 821; I have not, however, collated it with the printed editions.
3c. The manuscript of the Royal Library at Munich, among the Tegernsee books, on parchment, from the ninth century, from which Amerbach’s first edition derived.
4. The Blankenburg manuscript of the Wolfenbüttel Library, from the tenth century.
5. The manuscript of the Ducal Library at Gotha, from the eleventh century.

I have marked Baluzius’s principal readings with the siglum B.

[Col. 0151A] **In the perpetual reign of our lord Jesus Christ.** I, Charles, by the grace of God and by his mercy’s gift, king and ruler of the kingdom of the Franks, and devoted defender and humble helper of the holy [Note: “holy church of God” in witness 2] Church, send to all the orders of ecclesiastical piety and to the dignities of secular power, in Christ the lord, eternal God, greetings of perpetual peace and blessedness.

Considering, with the peaceful and pious reflection of the mind, together with our priests and counselors, the abundant mercy of Christ the King toward us and our people [Note: Omitted in witnesses 2 and 5], and how necessary it is not only continually to give thanks to his piety with all our heart and mouth [Note: Witness 2 reads “with heart and mouth and piety”], but also to persist in his praises through the continual practice of good works, so that he who has bestowed such great honors upon our kingdom may deign by his protection to preserve us and our kingdom forever—

[Col. 0151B] therefore it pleased us to ask your diligence, O shepherds of the churches of Christ, leaders of his flock, and illustrious lights of the world, to strive through watchful care and diligent admonition to lead the people of God through the pastures of eternal life [Note: *pascuae* in witness 1; *docere* (“to teach”) in witness 2], and to labor to carry back the wandering sheep, upon the shoulders of good examples or exhortations, within the walls of ecclesiastical stability [Note: “by the example of good works” according to Baluzius]; lest the lurking wolf, finding anyone transgressing the canonical decrees or exceeding the traditions of the fathers and the universal councils—which God forbid—devour him.

Therefore, with great devotion [Note: “with great” in witness 5; Baluzius], they must be admonished and exhorted, indeed compelled, to remain within the decrees of the fathers with firm faith and tireless perseverance. In this work and devotion [Note: Baluzius reads “in the devotion of this work”], let your holiness know with complete certainty that our diligence cooperates with you [Note: Baluzius reads “cooperates with you”].

[Col. 0151C] Therefore we have also sent our messengers to you, who, by the authority of our name, would correct together with you whatever needed correction [Note: Witness 1 reads “with us”]. We have also appended certain chapters from the canonical institutions that seemed especially necessary to us [Note: Baluzius reads “to you”].

Please let no one judge this admonition of piety presumptuous, by which we strive to correct errors, cut away what is superfluous, and enforce what is right [Note: *cohartare* corrected to *cohortare*; *studemus* corrected by Baluzius to *studuimus*]. Rather, let him receive it with a benevolent spirit of charity. For we read in the books of the kings how the holy Josiah, traveling throughout the kingdom given to him by God, correcting and admonishing, strove to recall it to the worship of the true God.

I do not say this to make myself equal to his holiness, but because we must always follow everywhere the examples of the saints, and it is necessary to gather together as many as we can for the pursuit of the good life, to the praise and glory of our lord Jesus Christ.

[Col. 0152A] Therefore, as we have said, we ordered certain chapters to be noted, so that you might likewise strive to admonish them concerning these matters, as well as concerning whatever other things you know to be necessary [Note: Witnesses 4 and Baluzius read “you know,” rather than “you may know”], so that you may preach both these and those with equal earnestness. Do not omit anything that appears useful to your holiness and [Note: Omitted in witnesses 2, 3, 3c, 5, and Baluzius] to the people of God [Note: Witness 3 reads “do not omit”; witness 4, “do not leave out”; witness 3c omits the phrase], so that you may not fail to admonish them with pious zeal. Thus both your diligence and the obedience of your subjects may be rewarded by almighty God with eternal happiness.

## TO ALL [Note: “To all bishops” in witness 2; all rubric headings are absent in witness 5] — 1

[Note: Burchard reports this from the Council of Rouen, chapter 3. But here it should be observed—as we have very frequently pointed out regarding Regino and Gratian—that Burchard took the most diligent care that the chapters he copied from our kings’ capitularies should not appear to have been taken from them, and for this reason attributed them to ancient synods and Roman pontiffs; this is the source of so many errors in Gratian. Thus, although Burchard reports this chapter as from the Council of Rouen, it is nevertheless certain that he drew it from Book I of the *Capitularies*. Baluzius.]

There are some who, because their offenses require it, are excommunicated by their own bishop, yet are presumptuously received into communion by other ecclesiastics or laypeople. The holy Council of Nicaea, as well as the Council of Chalcedon, and likewise those of Antioch and Sardica, altogether forbid this.

[Note: Council of Nicaea, canon 5: “Concerning those who are excommunicated, whether clerics or laypeople, by the bishops in their respective dioceses, this judgment shall be observed: those who are excommunicated by some shall not be received by others. Let inquiry be made, lest perhaps they were cast out because of some personal resentment, contention, or similar irritation on the part of an angry bishop. Therefore, so that these matters may be investigated by a proper examination, it has seemed right that twice each year councils of bishops be held in every province, so that all, assembling together from the whole province, may examine such questions. In this way, those who have rightly incurred the displeasure of their bishops on account of their offenses may also rightly be held excommunicated by the others, until either all collectively or the bishop himself sees fit to adopt a more humane judgment concerning them. Let councils be held once before the days of Lent, so that, after all quarrels, if any exist, have been removed, a pure solemn offering may be presented to God. The second shall be held around the autumn season.

“Council of Antioch, canon 2: It is not permitted to communicate with the excommunicated, nor to enter their houses and pray with those who do not participate in the church, nor to receive into another church those who have been excluded from one. If any bishop, priest, deacon, or anyone enrolled among the clergy is seen to communicate with excommunicated persons, he too must be deprived of communion, as one who confuses the rules of the Church.

“Council of Antioch, canon 6: If anyone has been excommunicated by his own bishop, he ought not first to be received by others unless he has been received by his own bishop, or appears before a council and answers there. If he satisfies the synod and it determines that he should be received under another judgment, this shall also be observed concerning laypeople, priests, deacons, and all who are in the clergy.

“Council of Sardica, canon 16: Bishop Hosius said: Let this also please everyone: if either a priest, a deacon, or any cleric has been deprived of communion by his bishop, and has gone to another bishop, and the bishop to whom he has fled knows that he was rejected by his own bishop, he ought not to grant him communion. If he does so, let him know that he must give an account of the matter when the bishops have been convened. All said: This statute will preserve peace and guard concord.”]

## TO BISHOPS [Note: “To priests” in Baluzius] — 2

It is also stated in the same council that the faith and life of those who come to be ordained must first be carefully examined by the bishop, and only then are they to be ordained.

[Note: Pope Adrian, in his letter to Tilpinus, archbishop of the Church of Reims, preserved by Flodoardus in Book II, chapter 17 of the *History of Reims*: “We also enjoin upon your fraternity that, since certain matters concerning the ordination of a bishop named Lul of the holy Church of Mainz have reached us, you should take with you the bishops Viomagus and Possessor, together with the messengers of our glorious and spiritual son Charles, king of the Franks, and carefully investigate everything concerning his ordination, and examine his faith, teaching, conduct, character, and life.” Baluzius.]

[Note: Council of Nicaea, canon 9: “If some have been advanced as priests without examination, and, upon examination, have confessed their sins, and, after they confessed, men coming against the rule rashly laid hands upon them, the ecclesiastical order does not receive them. For in all things the Catholic Church defends what is irreprehensible.”]

## TO ALL — 3

It is also stated in the same council, and likewise in the Council of Antioch and the Council of Chalcedon, that fugitive and foreign clerics are to be received by no one and are not to be ordained without letters of recommendation and the permission of their own bishop or abbot.

[Note: Council of Nicaea, canon 16: “If any persons act without due regard and do not have the fear of God before their eyes or observe the ecclesiastical statutes, and leave their own church—whether priests, deacons, or persons placed in any ecclesiastical order—they must nowhere be received in another church. Rather, they must be compelled by every necessity to return to their own churches. If they remain, they are to be excommunicated.

“Canon 17: If anyone dares to ordain into his own church someone who belongs to another, without possessing the consent of the bishop from whom that cleric departed, such ordination shall be invalid.

“Council of Antioch, canon 3: If any priest, deacon, or any cleric, abandoning his own church, believes that he ought to transfer to another and there gradually attempts to remain permanently in the place to which he has migrated, he must no longer minister, especially if his bishop has urged him to return. If, even after being summoned by his bishop, he does not obey but persists, he must be removed from office in every way and must never have hope of restoration. If another bishop receives anyone deposed after this offense, he too shall deserve punishment by reprimand from the common synod, as one who dissolves ecclesiastical rights.

“Council of Chalcedon, canon 13: Foreign clerics and readers in another city may nowhere minister at all without synodal letters from their own bishop.”]

## TO ALL [Note: Omitted in witness 1; “to priests alone” in Baluzius] — 4

It was also forbidden in the same synod to priests and deacons, and to all who are in the clergy, to have a woman in their house on account of suspicion, except their mother, sister, or only such persons as avoid suspicion.

[Note: Council of Nicaea, canon 3: “Concerning persons under suspicion, the holy synod absolutely forbids a bishop, priest, deacon, or any cleric whatsoever to keep a foreign woman with him, unless she is his mother, sister, grandmother, or some such person. For in these persons and those like them all suspicion is removed. Whoever acts otherwise will endanger his clerical office.”]

## TO ALL [Note: Omitted in witness 1] — 5

It is also entirely forbidden—in the same council, in the decrees of Pope Leo, and in the canons called apostolic, just as the Lord himself commands in the Law [Note: *praecepit* in witnesses 2–4 and Baluzius]—for anyone to lend anything at interest.

[Note: Council of Nicaea, canon 17: “Since many clerics, pursuing shameful profits out of greed and forgetting the divine command that says, ‘He who has not lent his money at interest,’ engage in usury and demand hundredfold returns, this holy council establishes that if anyone is found after this definition to receive interest, pursue shameful profits from any such transaction, or even lend grain at sixfold return, anyone who devises such a thing for profit shall be cut off from the clergy and regarded as alien to the ecclesiastical order.

“Canons of the Apostles, canon 44: A bishop, priest, or deacon who demands interest from debtors must either desist or certainly be condemned.”]

## TO BISHOPS

**[Note: [Col. 0153] “to priests” in B.]**

**6.** It has been heard that certain priests celebrate Mass and do not communicate; this is altogether forbidden, as is read in the canons of the apostles. For how can he rightly say, if he has not communicated, “We have received the sacraments, Lord”? You can read this throughout the individual chapters in the statutes of the Council of Nicaea, or in the synodal decrees of other holy Fathers.

**[Note: [Col. 0154B] Regino did not record in his *Collection* the source from which he copied this chapter. Burchard reports it from the Council of Orléans, chapter 10. Fulbert correctly derives it from the first book of the *Capitularies*, chapter 6. Baluze.]**

**[Note: [Col. 0154B] By “celebrating Mass” Joachim Vadianus, in book VI of *On the Eucharist*, p. 215, understands the distribution of the Eucharist. These are his words: “In the same author—namely, Ansegisus—there exists another imperial constitution which provided that priests should celebrate Masses and abstain from communion. For there were men who, during the sacred celebration of Mass, gave the Eucharist to the people while themselves taking nothing. The emperor therefore orders that, in celebrating Masses, they should not only offer the Eucharist to others but also receive it themselves. He could not have issued this order unless they had retained that ancient rite of the public Mass in which the people communicated.” But, as I judge, Vadianus did not grasp the meaning of Charles’s words. The emperor wants only this: whenever a priest sacrifices the body and blood of Christ upon the altar, he should likewise communicate, as is evident from the words of the Twelfth Council of Toledo quoted below, book VI, chapter 120. Id.]**

**[Note: [Col. 0154C] That is, not to present themselves as participants in receiving the body and blood of Christ, as is read below, book VI, chapter 120, or not to receive the grace of holy communion, as is read in canon 5 of the Twelfth Council of Toledo. Hence the old synodal admonition prescribes that no one should sing Mass who does not communicate. In the new synodal admonition this is expressed as follows: “Celebrate Mass only while fasting, and in it receive the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ with all reverence and trembling.” And in the inquiry which the bishop conducted during his visitation, chapter 42, it is stated that the bishop ought to ask the priest whether he sings Mass and does not communicate. Simon Goulart is therefore seriously mistaken when, in his additions to the *Catalogue of Witnesses to the Truth*, p. 1020, he thinks that this chapter concerns a priest who does not admit those present to communion. Fulbert, however, seems to have read something there that is unknown to us. For, writing to the steward of the Church of Orléans about a certain priest who was found to have celebrated Masses without communicating, he says that, if he did so through indiscreet fear, he should be punished for a light fault with compassion, as is read in book I, chapter 6, of the *Capitularies*. Baluze.]**

**[Note: [Col. 0153] “in the canons” is misprinted “in the dogs” in one witness.]**

**[Note: [Col. 0153] “communicated” is misprinted “communicate” in one witness.]**

**[Note: [Col. 0155B] (Apostolic Canon 9.) If any bishop, priest, or deacon, or anyone whatsoever in the priestly catalog, after the offering has been made, does not communicate, let him state his reason; if it is reasonable, let him receive pardon. But if he does not state a reason, let him be deprived of communion, as one who has become a cause of injury to the people, giving rise to suspicion that the one who offered the sacrifice did not offer it rightly.]**

## TO ALL

**7.** Likewise, in the Council of Antioch, it is ordered that, when persons condemned by a synod or by their own bishop subsequently presume to minister, no one should dare to communicate with them. Whoever communicates with such a person shall be subject to the same sentence as the condemned person.

**[Note: [Col. 0155] “with them” is absent in B.]**

**[Note: [Col. 0155] “with him” is found in place of “with them” in one witness.]**

**[Note: [Col. 0155] “has communicated” is found in place of “communicates” in B.]**

**[Note: [Col. 0155] “to the same sentence” is found in place of “to the same judgment” in B.]**

**[Note: [Col. 0155B] (Council of Antioch, canon 4.) If any bishop has been deposed by a synod, or any priest or deacon by his own bishop, and he presumes to undertake any part of the sacred ministry, he shall no longer be permitted either to hope for restoration in another synod or to have any place for making a defense. Those who communicate with him shall all be expelled from the Church, especially if, after learning of the sentence pronounced against him, they have stubbornly communicated with him.]**

## TO BISHOPS

**8.** Likewise, in the same council, it is ordered that suffragan bishops look to the metropolitan bishop and dare to do nothing new in their parishes without the knowledge and counsel of their metropolitan; and that the metropolitan likewise act without their counsel in nothing.

**[Note: [Col. 0155] “suffragan” is written “suffraganean” in B.]**

**[Note: [Col. 0155] “nothing new” is written “nothing of a new kind” in another witness.]**

**[Note: [Col. 0155C] That is, in the canons of other synods—namely, canon 8 of the Second Council of Carthage, canon 37 of Martin of Braga, whose chapters are cited in ancient books under the name of Pope Martin or of the Council of Braga, and in the decrees of the Roman pontiffs cited by Gratian, 11. q. 3. For those passages concern bishops and priests who, although condemned, nevertheless minister. Baluze.]**

**[Note: [Col. 0155C] (Council of Antioch, canon 9.) The metropolitan bishop who presides ought to know that he has undertaken the care and concern of the whole province. Therefore those who have cases should without doubt hasten to the metropolitan city. Accordingly, it has seemed good that he should precede the others in honor, and that the remaining bishops should do nothing beyond those matters belonging to each Church within its own diocese without him, according to the ancient rule of our fathers that has prevailed. Each bishop ought to have authority over his own diocese, to govern it with the reverence appropriate to him and to provide for the region subject to his city, so that he may also, with sound judgment, ordain priests and deacons for it and decide each matter with moderation and due weight. Beyond this, nothing may be done without the knowledge of the metropolitan bishop.]**

## TO PRIESTS

**9.** Likewise in the same council, and also in the Council of Ancyra, it is ordered that chorepiscopi understand the limits of their office and do nothing without the permission of the bishop in whose parish they reside.

**[Note: [Col. 0155] “and also” is found in B in place of the reading referring to Ancyra.]**

**[Note: [Col. 0155D] (Council of Antioch, canon 20.) With regard to chorepiscopi established in estates and villages: although they have received the laying-on of hands from bishops and have been consecrated as bishops, the holy synod has decreed that they must retain the limits proper to them, govern the neighboring Churches entrusted to them, and be content with the care and governance they have received. They may appoint readers, subdeacons, and exorcists, who should be satisfied to have received authority only in these orders. But they must not dare to ordain a priest or deacon without the knowledge of the bishop of the city or of the Church to which the place adjoins, whether that bishop himself or the region over which he is known to preside. If anyone dares to violate these decrees, he is to be deposed and deprived of the dignity with which he is endowed.
