A chorepiscopus, however, must be ordained by the bishop of the city or place to which he is attached.]**

**[Note: [Col. 0155D] (Council of Ancyra, canon 13.) The representatives of bishops, whom the Greeks call chorepiscopi, may not ordain priests or deacons. Nor may they command the priests of the city to do anything further without the bishop’s instruction, or undertake anything in each parish without his written authorization.]**

## TO THE WHOLE CLERGY

**[Note: [Col. 0155] “everything” in one witness; “to all” in another.]**

**10.** Likewise in the same council, it is ordered that no bishop or anyone from the clergy dare appeal to the royal authority concerning his own cases without the counsel or letters of the bishops or of the metropolitan; rather, his case is to be examined in the common council of the bishops.

**[Note: [Col. 0156B] This appears among the Lombard laws in codex V. Vn. E. and in Muratori, chapter 146.]**

**[Note: [Col. 0155] “his case” is absent in B.]**

**[Note: [Col. 0155] “urteili” appears in the margin of one witness.]**

**[Note: [Col. 0156C] (Council of Antioch, canon 11.) If any bishop, priest, or anyone at all subject to ecclesiastical discipline goes to the emperor without the counsel and letters of the bishops within the province, and especially of the metropolitan, he ought not only to be deprived of communion and expelled, but also deprived of his own dignity, as troublesome and importunate to imperial ears and acting against ecclesiastical decrees. If necessity compels him to go to the emperor, he must go with the deliberation and counsel of the metropolitan of that province, with the knowledge of the bishops and others who are in the same province, and with letters.]**

## TO BISHOPS

**11.** Likewise in the same council, and also in the Council of Sardica and in the decretal letters of Pope Innocent, it is ordered that no bishop dare perform any ordinations in another bishop’s parish or conduct business that does not belong to him.

**[Note: [Col. 0155] “decretal” is written “decretal letters” in B.]**

**[Note: [Col. 0155] “of Innocent” is misread as “of the innocent” in one witness.]**

**[Note: [Col. 0155] “perform” is written “do” in B.]**

**[Note: [Col. 0156C] (Council of Antioch, canon 13.) No bishop is to pass from one province to another and ordain anyone in the Churches or advance anyone to the sacred ministry. Nor may he bring other bishops there with him, unless he has gone after being invited by letters not only from the metropolitan but also from the bishops of the province who are with him. If, however, he arrives disorderly without anyone inviting him and presumes either to ordain anyone or to usurp for himself any acts belonging to that Church and not pertaining to him, everything he has done shall be void and ineffectual. He himself shall suffer the penalties deserved by such an undisciplined presumption and irrational undertaking, as one deposed by the holy synod and already condemned for such presumption.]**

**[Note: [Col. 0156C] (Council of Sardica, canon 18.) Bishop Januarius said: “Let your holiness also decree that no bishop may solicit an ecclesiastical minister of another bishop’s city and ordain him in his own parishes.” All replied: “It is approved, because discord commonly arises from such intentions.” Therefore the unanimous judgment forbids anyone to dare do this.]**

**[Note: [Col. 0157A] (Innocent, letter 7.) Innocent to Florentinus, bishop of Tibur. Divine Scripture repeatedly declares that the boundaries established by the Fathers must not be transferred, for it is wicked if one person invades what another has always possessed. Our brother and fellow bishop Ursus has asserted that you have done this. He has complained with sorrow that you invaded the parish of Nomentum, or of Felicia, which from ancient times belonged to his diocese, and celebrated the divine mysteries there without consulting him and without his knowledge. If this is true, know that you have incurred no slight fault. Therefore, if you wish to avoid the odium of so great an usurpation, you ought, having been admonished by our letter, to abstain. Certainly, if you believe that justice supports your position, you must appear after the holy days of Easter, with everything intact and remaining in its former state, so that you may answer the accusations mentioned; when both parties have been brought before us, we shall investigate what antiquity or truth establishes.]**

## TO BISHOPS

**[Note: [Col. 0157] “one” is absent.]**

**12.** Likewise in the same council, it is ordered that a bishop have care of the Church to which he was ordained.

**[Note: [Col. 0157B] (Council of Antioch, canon 21.) A bishop must not pass from one diocese to another, neither if he intrudes of his own accord, nor if he is forcibly drawn by the people, nor even if other bishops advise him to do so. He must remain in the Church of God which he received by lot from the beginning and must not depart from it to another, according to the rule long ago established concerning this matter by the Fathers.]**

## TO BISHOPS

**[Note: [Col. 0157] “one” is absent.]**

**13.** Likewise in the same council, and also in the Council of Chalcedon, it is ordered that the provincial bishops, together with their metropolitan, hold councils twice a year on ecclesiastical matters.

**[Note: [Col. 0157C] (Council of Antioch, canon 20.) For the sake of ecclesiastical concerns and the resolution of disputes that arise, it has seemed sufficient that a council of bishops be held twice each year in every province. The first is to be held after the third week of the Paschal celebration, so that the council may be completed in the following fourth week, that is, in the middle of Pentecost. Those who live in the larger cities, namely, the metropolitan cities, are to summon the provincial bishops. The second council is to be held on the Ides of October, which among the Greeks falls on the fifteenth day of the month Hyperberetaeus. Priests and deacons ought to be present at these councils, as well as all who think themselves wronged, and they should await the synodal judgment. No one may hold synods privately, without the knowledge of the metropolitan bishops, who are entrusted with judgment in all matters.]**

**[Note: [Col. 0157D] (Council of Chalcedon, canon 19.) It has come to our ears that synods of bishops are not being held in the provinces according to the provisions of the canons, and that consequently many ecclesiastical matters requiring correction are neglected. Therefore the holy synod has decreed, in accordance with the canons of the Fathers, that bishops meet twice a year in each province, at the place designated by the metropolitan, and correct everything that has arisen. Bishops who fail to meet, if they remain in their own cities and are not absent because of travel—especially if their health permits and they are free from necessary and excusable occupations—are to be admonished out of regard for brotherhood.]**

## TO BISHOPS

**[Note: [Col. 0157] “Laodicene” is written “Laodicensian” in one witness and “Laodicean” in another.]**

**14.** In the Council of Laodicea, and also in the African council, it is ordered that monks and clerics not enter taverns for the purpose of eating or drinking.

**[Note: [Col. 0157] One occurrence is absent.]**

**[Note: [Col. 0158A] See the letter of Hincmar to Hadrian II, among the acts of the Synod of Douzy, p. 310 in Cellot’s edition.]**

**[Note: [Col. 0158B] (Council of Laodicea, canon 24.) Those who serve at the altar, from priests through deacons, and thereafter all members of the ecclesiastical order down to ministers, readers, singers, exorcists, and doorkeepers, as well as those devoted to continence, ought not to enter taverns.]**

**[Note: [Col. 0158B] (African Council, canon 7.) Clerics are not to enter taverns for the purpose of eating or drinking, unless compelled by the necessity of travel.]**

## TO ALL

**[Note: [Col. 0157] “to all” is absent in one witness; “to clerics” in another; “to everyone” in another.]**

**15.** Likewise in the same council, it is ordered that Sunday be observed from evening until evening.

**[Note: [Col. 0158B] (Council of Laodicea, canon 29.) Christians must not Judaize and rest on the Sabbath, but must work on that day. They should prefer Sunday and rest on it, if they wish, as Christians. If they are found Judaizing, let them be anathema.]**

## TO ALL

**16.** Likewise in the same council, it is ordered that unknown names of angels neither be invented nor pronounced, except those whom we have authoritative warrant for naming: Michael, Gabriel, and Raphael.

**[Note: [Col. 0158B] This decree was, I think, intended to restrain the insane superstition of those who invented various names of angels, such as Adelbert, who in his prayer named Uriel, Raguel, Tubuel, Michael, Adinus, Tubua, Sabaoc, and Sinuel. When this matter was being discussed in a synod assembled at Rome in the Lateran patriarchium, and Pope Zachary had questioned the bishops, they replied: “We judge that the names of angels which Adelbert invoked in his prayer were not the names of angels, except Michael’s, but rather that he invoked demons in his prayer to provide him assistance. We, however, instructed by your holy apostolate and by divine authority, recognize no more than the names of three angels: Michael, Gabriel, and Raphael.” It is surprising that Uriel, Raguel, and Tobiel are named in the litanies recently published by Dom Jean Mabillon in the second volume of his *Analecta*, p. 682, which he called Carolingian. For after that Roman synod it was not permissible to name these angels, since they lacked authoritative warrant, as is stated in our chapter. Nevertheless, that the name of the angel Uriel was known long before the time of Adelbert and Charlemagne is proved by an inscription found at Rome in the Vatican in 1544, in the tomb of Maria, wife of the emperor Honorius. As Surius reports in his *Commentary on Events in the World*, a gold tablet was found there bearing these names in Greek letters: Michael, Gabriel, Raphael, Uriel. See also the writing of Saint Angilbert on the buildings, relics, vessels, and so forth of the monastery of Centula in the Bollandists, February, vol. III: “In the churches of the holy angels Gabriel, Michael, and Raphael, three altars.” See Burchard, book III, chapter 198, and François d’Alteserre in his notes on Ferrandus’s *Abridgment of the Canons*, p. 124. Baluze.]**

**[Note: [Col. 0157] “those names” in B.]**

**[Note: [Col. 0158D] (Council of Laodicea, canon 35.) Christians ought not, abandoning the Church of God, go away and name angels and form congregations; all such things are forbidden. Whoever is found secretly devoting himself to this idolatry shall be anathema, because, abandoning our Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, he has approached idols.]**

**[Note: [Col. 0157] “to women” in one witness.]**

**[Note: [Col. 0157] “nuns” is written “nonnans” in one witness and “monks” in another.]**

**17.** Likewise in the same council, it is ordered that women must not enter the altar area.

**[Note: [Col. 0158D] (Council of Laodicea, canon 44.) Women must not enter the altar area.]**

**[Note: [Col. 0157] “to all” in one witness; “to priests” in B.]**

**18.** Likewise in the same council, it is ordered that persons called *cauclearii* [meaning uncertain], sorcerers, enchanters, and enchantresses not be permitted to become such.

**[Note: [Col. 0159] “coclearii” in one witness; “coglearii” in B.]**

**[Note: [Col. 0159B] (Council of Laodicea, canon 36.) Ministers of the altar and clerics ought not to be magicians or enchanters, or to make what are called *phylacteria*, that is, great bindings of souls. We have ordered that those who use such things be expelled from the Church.]**

## TO ALL

**[Note: [Col. 0159] “to bishops” in one witness.]**

**19.** Likewise in the same council, and also in the Council of Sardica, it is ordered that bishops not be appointed in small villages or in the countryside.

**[Note: [Col. 0159] “villages” in several witnesses and in B.]**

**[Note: [Col. 0159B] (Council of Sardica, canon 6.) A bishop should not be ordained in villages or hamlets; instead, let those be appointed who go around. Those who have been ordained from such places must do nothing without the knowledge of the bishop of the city. Likewise, a priest must do nothing without the bishop’s instruction and counsel. For if some village or small city, for which one priest is sufficient, suddenly wishes to have a bishop ordained for itself, so that the name and authority of bishop may be cheapened, men invited from another province ought not to make a bishop there, unless it is in cities that have had bishops, or unless some place is so substantial or populous that it deserves to have a bishop. Does this please everyone? The synod replied: It pleases us.]**

**[Note: [Col. 0159] “to appoint” in B.]**

## TO PRIESTS

**[Note: [Col. 0159] “to the whole clergy” in one witness.]**

**20.** Likewise in the same council, it is ordered that only canonical books be read in the church.

**[Note: [Col. 0159B] (Council of Laodicea, canon 59.) Psalms composed by private persons and common songs must not be recited in churches, nor may books outside the canon be read, except the canonical books of the Old and New Testaments alone. The books which ought to be read and received as authoritative are these: Genesis, the creation of the world; Exodus, the departure from Egypt; Leviticus; Numbers; Deuteronomy; Joshua son of Nun; Judges; Ruth; the four books of Kings; the two books of Chronicles; the two books of Ezra; the book of 150 Psalms; the Proverbs of Solomon; the Song of Songs; Ecclesiastes; Job; Esther; the twelve prophets, namely Hosea, Amos, Joel, Obadiah, Jonah, Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zephaniah, Haggai, Zechariah, and Malachi; also Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Daniel. Of the New Testament: the four Gospels, according to Matthew, according to Mark, according to Luke, and according to John; the Acts of the Apostles; the Catholic Epistles—two of Peter, one of James, three of John, and one of Jude; and the fourteen Epistles of Paul: to the Romans; the first and second to the Corinthians; to the Galatians; to the Ephesians; to the Philippians; to the Colossians; the first and second to the Thessalonians; two to Timothy; to Titus; to Philemon; and to the Hebrews.]**

## TO CLERICS AND MONKS

**[Note: [Col. 0159] “to bishops and the whole clergy” in one witness.]**

**21.** In the Council of Chalcedon, it is ordered that bishops or anyone from the clergy must not be ordained for money, since both are to be deposed: the one who ordains and the one who is ordained, as well as the person who acts as mediator between them.

## TO ALL

**22.** Likewise, concerning the same matter, it is read in the canons of the apostles; the prince of the apostles himself had already condemned this heresy terribly in Simon Magus.

**[Note: [Col. 0159] Thus in 1, 2, 3c, and 5; conversely, 3, 4, and B continue.]**

**[Note: [Col. 0159D] (Council of Chalcedon, canon 2.) If any bishop performs an ordination for money and sells a thing that is acquired only by grace, and for money ordains a provincial bishop, priest, or deacon, or anyone included among the clergy, or if, after receiving money, he appoints an economist, defender, doorkeeper, or anyone of this kind, he shall incur the peril of his rank for the disgraceful profit which he is proved to have sought. The one who is ordained shall acquire no advantage from an ordination that proceeded as a commercial transaction; he shall instead be excluded from the dignity or office entrusted to him for money. If anyone appears to have acted as intermediary in such shameful and criminal profits, then, if he is a cleric, let him be degraded; but if he is a layman or monk, let him be anathematized.]**

**[Note: [Col. 0160A] (Apostolic Canon 30.) If any bishop, priest, or deacon has obtained this dignity through money, let both him and the person who ordained him be deposed and, in every way, cut off from communion, just as Simon Magus was by Peter.]**

## TO ALL

**[Note: [Col. 0159] One occurrence is absent.]**

**23.** Likewise in the same council, two chapters below, and also in the decrees of Pope Leo, it is ordered that neither a monk nor a cleric engage in secular business.

**[Note: [Col. 0159] Among the Lombard laws, chapter 136, in Muratori.]**

**[Note: [Col. 0159] “nor priests” in B.]**

**[Note: [Col. 0160B] That is, commerce, as in Jerome’s letter to Rusticus. The best Corbie manuscript reads this way, instead of the reading “profits” found in the printed edition. Baluze.]**

It is also ordered that no one solicit another person’s slave to enter the clerical or monastic order without the will and permission of his master.

**[Note: [Col. 0160B] In book III, title 1, chapter 16, of the Lombard law, it reads: “No one shall solicit another’s slave to ascend to the clerical or monastic order without the permission and consent of his master.” The word “ascend” is superfluous here and does not occur in the ancient manuscript codices of the royal library. Id.]**

**[Note: [Col. 0160B] (Council of Chalcedon, canon 4.) Those who truly and openly pursue the solitary life shall exercise the honor appropriate to them. But since some people, under the pretext of monastic dress, disturb Churches, assemblies, and common property, wandering indiscriminately through cities and striving to establish monasteries for themselves, it has seemed good that no one should build or establish a monastery or oratory anywhere without the consent of the bishop of the city. Monks in each city and province are to be subject to the bishops, love quiet, and devote themselves to fasting and prayer; they are to remain in the places where they appear to have renounced the world. They must not in any way participate in ecclesiastical or secular affairs or cause disturbance after abandoning their own monasteries, unless they have been summoned by the bishop of the city for some necessary reason. In monasteries, a slave is certainly not to be received to become a monk without the will of his own master. Whoever transgresses this decree of ours shall, we have decided, be suspended from communion, lest the name of God be blasphemed. The bishop of the city ought to provide the monasteries with appropriate oversight.]**

**[Note: [Col. 0160D] (Leo, chapter 1.) People are admitted indiscriminately to the sacred order who have no support either from the dignity of birth or from good character. Those who have been unable to obtain freedom from their masters are advanced to the summit of the priesthood, as though servile lowliness could receive this honor. It is believed that a person can be approved by God who has not yet been able to prove himself to his master. There is therefore a double guilt in this matter: the sacred ministry is polluted by the lowliness of such an association, and the rights of masters are violated insofar as this involves the rashness of an illicit usurpation. Therefore, dearest brothers, let all the priests of your province abstain from such persons. We wish them to abstain not only from these but also from others who are bound by birth-status or by any other condition, unless the request or consent of those who claim some authority over them has been given. Whoever is to be enrolled in the divine service ought to be free from the claims of others, so that he may not be drawn away by any bonds of necessity from the Lord’s army in which his name is enrolled.]**

## TO PRIESTS

**[Note: [Col. 0159] “with S.” in one witness.]**

**24.** Likewise in the same council, two chapters below, and also in the Council of Sardica, it is ordered that neither bishops nor clerics be transferred from city to city.

**[Note: [Col. 0161] “c. not t.” in 2, 3, and B.]**

**[Note: [Col. 0161B] (Council of Chalcedon, canon 5.) Concerning bishops and clerics who transfer themselves from city to city, it has been decreed that the canons established by the holy Fathers concerning these very matters shall retain their force.]**

**[Note: [Col. 0161B] (Council of Sardica, canon 1.) Bishop Hosius said: “If anyone, whether bishop or cleric, moves from one city to another, let him remain excommunicated.”]**

## TO ALL

**25.** Likewise in the same synod, it is ordered that no one be ordained absolutely, without a declaration and secure designation of the place to which he is ordained.

**[Note: [Col. 0161] “and without” is found in one witness and B.]**

**[Note: [Col. 0161] “to which” is written “which” in one witness.]**

**[Note: [Col. 0161] “is ordained” is written “be ordained” in another.]**

**[Note: [Col. 0161B] (Council of Chalcedon, canon 6.) No one is to be ordained absolutely—neither priest, deacon, nor anyone at all among those in ecclesiastical orders—unless it has been specifically declared that he is being ordained for a church of a city, village, or martyr-shrine. The holy synod has decreed that ordinations of this kind, in which persons are ordained absolutely, are ineffective and can never prevail, to the detriment of the one who ordained them.]**

## TO MONKS AND THE WHOLE CLERGY

**[Note: [Col. 0161] “and the whole clergy” is absent in one witness; “to priests” in B; “to all” in several witnesses.]**

**26.** Likewise in the same council, it is ordered that clerics and monks remain in the purpose and vow which they have promised to God.

**[Note: [Col. 0161] One occurrence is absent.]**

**[Note: [Col. 0161C] (Council of Chalcedon, canon 7.) We decree that those who have once been ordained, or who have become monks, must not enter military service or secular dignities. If they undertake such a course, unless they return in repentance to what they chose for God’s sake, let them be anathematized.]**

## TO PRIESTS

**[Note: [Col. 0161] “to all” in B.]**

**27.** Likewise in the decrees of Pope Innocent concerning the same matter, it is ordered that, if a monk is advanced to the clerical order, he must not abandon the purpose of his monastic profession.

**[Note: [Col. 0161] “is examined” in one witness; “is advanced” in B.]**

**[Note: [Col. 0161C] (Innocent, canon 17.) Monks who, after remaining for a long time in monasteries, subsequently enter the clerical order must not deviate from their former purpose. For either, just as he was in the monastery, and as he long preserved it, he must not abandon it when placed in a higher rank; or, if he was corrupted and subsequently baptized, and while residing in a monastery wishes to enter the clerical order, he may not have a wife at all, since, having been corrupted, he cannot be blessed with a bride. This rule is observed among clerics, especially since the ancient rule provides that anyone who, after being corrupted and baptized, wished to become a cleric should promise that he would never take a wife.]**

## TO ALL

**[Note: [Col. 0161] In K and M, the Lombard laws, chapter 135, as in Muratori.]**

**28.** Likewise in the same council, it is ordered that, if clerics have any dispute among themselves, they be judged by their own bishop, not by secular authorities.

**[Note: [Col. 0161] “business” is misspelled in one witness.]**

**[Note: [Col. 0161] “judged” is written “be judged” in another.]**

**[Note: [Col. 0161D] This chapter is read as follows in chapter 3 of the Council of Trosly: “If clerics and monks have any dispute among themselves, let them be judged by their own bishop and not by secular authorities. For it is not right that ministers of the divine office should be subjected to the judgment of temporal powers.” Baluze.]**

**[Note: [Col. 0161D] (Council of Chalcedon, canon 9.) If any cleric has a case against another cleric, he must not leave his bishop and run to secular courts; rather, he must first have the case examined by his own bishop, or, with the bishop’s consent, let the case be heard by whatever judges both parties choose. Whoever attempts to act contrary to this shall be subject to canonical penalties. If a cleric has a case against a stranger, whether a bishop or his own bishop, he shall state the case before the provincial synod. If a bishop or cleric has a dispute with the metropolitan bishop, he shall appeal either to the chief see of the diocese or to the see of Constantinople, where the case is to be heard.]**

## TO ALL

**[Note: [Col. 0161] One occurrence is absent.]**

**29.** Likewise in the same council, it is ordered that neither clerics nor monks make conspiracies or ambushes against their shepherd.

**[Note: [Col. 0162B] (Council of Chalcedon, canon 18.) The crime of conspiracy or confederacy is entirely abolished even by secular laws; much more must it be prohibited from occurring in the Church of God. Therefore, if clerics or monks are found to have conspired or to be devising accusations against bishops or clerics through a conspiracy, let them lose their proper rank.]**

## TO ALL

**30.** Likewise in the same council, it is ordered that laypeople not accuse bishops or clerics unless their reputation and standing have first been examined.

**[Note: [Col. 0162B] (Council of Chalcedon, canon 21.) Clerics or laypeople who accuse bishops or clerics are not to be admitted to bring an accusation in any manner and without judicial examination unless their reputation has first been investigated.]**

Id.]**

**[Note: [Col. 0161] One occurrence is absent.]**

**32.** In the Council of Carthage: first of all, the faith of the holy Trinity and of the incarnation of Christ, his passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven is to be diligently preached to all.

**[Note: [Col. 0162D] The Rivipullian Codex reads: “the ascension into heaven, the coming of the Holy Spirit upon the Apostles, and the faithful expectation of the future judgment are to be diligently preached to all.” But these words do not occur in the capitulary of Aachen or in the Council of Carthage from which this chapter was taken. Baluze.]**

**[Note: [Col. 0162D] (Council of Carthage, in the profession of faith.) In the year 1036 from Alexander, in the month of June, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of July, the great synod declared: “We believe in one God, the almighty Father, maker of all things visible and invisible. And in one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God, begotten as the only-begotten from the Father—that is, from the substance of the Father—God from God, light from light, true God from true God, begotten, not made, *homoousios* with the Father, that is, of the same substance as the Father. Through him all things were made, both those in heaven and those on earth. For us and for our salvation he came down, was incarnate and became human, suffered, rose again on the third day, and ascended into heaven. From there he will come to judge the living and the dead. And in the Holy Spirit. But those who say, ‘There was a time when he was not,’ or ‘Before he was begotten he did not exist,’ or who say that he was made from things that did not exist, or from another subsistence or substance, or that the Son of God is changeable, the catholic and apostolic Church anathematizes.”]

**ALL** [Note: [Col. 0161] omitted in 1.]—33. Likewise, in the same work, concerning the prohibition of avarice, that no one usurp another’s boundaries or cross the limits established by the fathers [Note: [Col. 0163] between K, M, and the Lombard manuscripts, chapter 139, Muratori.] [Note: [Col. 0163B] (Council of Carthage, canon 5.) Bishop Aurelius said: “The desire for avarice—which no one doubts to be the mother of all evils—is therefore to be restrained, lest anyone usurp another’s boundaries or cross, for a reward, the limits established by the Fathers; nor should any cleric at all be permitted to receive interest on any matter. Although novel proposals, whether obscure or concealed under a general category, will receive a ruling after we have examined them, nevertheless, concerning matters expressly decreed by divine Scripture, a sentence is not to be passed but rather carried out. Therefore, what is condemned in laypeople ought much more to be condemned in clerics.”]

**ALL** [Note: [Col. 0163] omitted in 1.]—34. **ALL** [Note: [Col. 0163] omitted in 1.]—35. Approved.”]

**ALL**—36. Likewise, in the same work, that whoever presumptuously communicates with an excommunicated person [Col. 0164A] should himself be excommunicated [Note: [Col. 0163] “communicates” in 1.] [Note: [Col. 0163D] (Council of Carthage, canon 9.) Bishop Augustine, legate of the province of Numidia, said: “Deign to establish that if persons who have rightly been expelled from the Church because of their crimes have been received into communion by any bishop or presbyter, that person too should be held liable with them for the same offense, because he has evaded the regular judgment of his own bishop.” All the bishops said: “It pleases us all.”]

**TO PRIESTS**—37. Likewise, in the same council, two chapters below, that no presbyter should dare to act arrogantly against his bishop [Note: [Col. 0163] “nor any presbyter” in 2.] [Note: [Col. 0164B] (Council of Carthage, canons 10 and 11.) Bishop Alypius, legate of the province of Numidia, said: “Nor must this be omitted: if a presbyter, corrected by his bishop, becomes swollen with resentment or pride and thinks that sacrifices should be offered to God separately, or believes that another altar should be erected against ecclesiastical faith or discipline, he must not go unpunished.” Valentinus, first bishop of the province of Numidia, said: “What our brother Alypius has set forth is necessarily in harmony with ecclesiastical discipline and faith. Therefore, state what seems good to your affection.” All the bishops said: “If a presbyter has been corrected by his superior, he must certainly complain to neighboring bishops, so that his case may be heard by them and through them he may be reconciled to his own bishop. But if he does not do this and, inflated by pride—which God forbid—decides to separate himself from communion with his bishop, forms a schism with certain others, and offers sacrifice to God separately, let him be regarded as anathema and lose his position; [Col. 0164C] and if he has no just complaint against his bishop, the matter must be investigated.”

“(Apostolic Canon 32.) If any presbyter, despising his bishop, gathers separately and erects another altar, having nothing with which to reproach his bishop in a matter of piety and justice, let him be deposed, as one who loves primacy; for he is a tyrant. Let the other clerics who consent to such a person also be deposed. Let laypeople be separated from them. This should be done after the bishop has admonished him once, twice, and three times.”]

**ALL**—38. Likewise, in the same work, that clerics and ecclesiastical orders, if they incur a fault [Note: [Col. 0163] “and ecclesiastical orders” is omitted in 4 B.; “orders” in 2, 3 c., and 4 B.], should be judged before ecclesiastical authorities, not before secular ones [Note: [Col. 0164C] (Council of Carthage, canon 15.) “It was likewise agreed that any bishop, presbyter, deacon, or cleric against whom a criminal charge has been brought in the Church, or against whom a civil action has been initiated, if, abandoning ecclesiastical judgment, he wishes to clear himself before public tribunals, should lose his position, even if a judgment has been issued in his favor. This applies to a criminal action. In a civil action, he should lose what he has recovered if he prefers to retain his position.

“It was also agreed that when an appeal has been made from any ecclesiastical judges to other ecclesiastical judges of greater authority, this should not prejudice those whose judgment has been overturned, unless they can be proved either to have judged with hostile intent or to have been corrupted by some desire or favor. But if the judges were chosen by agreement of the parties, it is not permitted to appeal even from a smaller number than the established number.

“And let the sons of priests neither provide secular spectacles nor attend them, although this has always been forbidden to all Christians, so that they do not go where blasphemies occur.”]

**ALL** [Note: [Col. 0163] omitted in 1.]—39. Likewise, in the same work, that whoever lends money should receive money. If he lends another kind of thing, he should receive the same kind in the quantity he gave [Note: [Col. 0163] “than” in B.] [Note: [Col. 0163] “should receive” in 2, 3, 4, and B.; “unless something is paid in place of something else with the consent of the creditor or depositor,” in K, M, and the Lombard manuscripts, chapter 142.] [Note: [Col. 0164D] (Council of Carthage, canon 16.) “It was likewise agreed that if a cleric lends money, he should receive money; if he lends a thing, he should receive the same kind and the amount he gave. And that before the age of twenty-five neither deacons should be ordained nor virgins consecrated; and that lectors should not greet the people.”]

[Col. 0165A] **ALL** [Note: [Col. 0165] omitted in 1.]—40. In the African Council, that virgins consecrated to God should be kept under careful guardianship by persons of mature character [Note: [Col. 0165] “more serious” in 1.] [Note: [Col. 0165A] (African Council, canon 11.) “That sacred virgins, when they have been deprived of the parents by whom they were being guarded, should be guarded by the bishop. When the bishop is absent, they should be entrusted to responsible older women, so that, living together, they may guard one another; lest by wandering about indiscriminately they damage the reputation of the Church.”]

**TO BISHOPS** [Note: [Col. 0165] omitted in 1.]—41. Likewise, in the same work, that a bishop may not neglect the principal chair [Note: [Col. 0165B] Among ecclesiastical authors, the episcopal “chair” sometimes means the bishop’s actual seat in the church, and sometimes the church that we call the cathedral, as here. Chairs of the first kind were formerly wooden, even in the age of Charlemagne, as this passage from an old manuscript homiliary of the Church of Lyon shows: “The scribes and Pharisees have sat on Moses’ chair.” We must not understand the Lord’s words carnally, as though we should believe that the scribes and Pharisees sat on wooden chairs, as bishops and presbyters now ordinarily sit in church. In the other sense, as we said, it is the city in which the bishop’s proper see has been established, where he must remain continually unless necessary business requires him to be absent. Since some, driven by a desire for a freer and quieter life, were abandoning their cities and moving to rural parishes, Charlemagne, in accordance with the constitution of the Council of Carthage, restrained this permission and freedom of life [Col. 0165C]. See the notes on Regino, p. 542, and Francis Florens’s notes on the title of the decretals concerning the transfer of a bishop, p. 280. BALUZE.] of his parish and attend more frequently another church in his diocese [Note: [Col. 0165] “cathedral” in 1.] [Note: [Col. 0165] omitted in B.] [Note: [Col. 0165] “in his diocese” in 4 B.] [Note: [Col. 0165C] (African Council, canon 38.) “It was again agreed that no one should have the power, after abandoning his principal see, to move to a church established in his diocese, or, while remaining on his own property longer than necessary, to neglect the care of or attendance at his own see.”]

**TO BISHOPS** [Note: [Col. 0165] omitted in 1.]—42. Likewise, in the same work, that false names of martyrs and uncertain memorials of saints [Note: [Col. 0165C] That is, relics. Augustine, *City of God* XXII.8: “At the waters of Tibilis, when Bishop Projectus brought the memorial of the most glorious martyr Stephen.” Thus it is read in the ancient books, as Ludovicus Vives notes here, and in the oldest manuscripts of the Colbert Library, where this whole narrative bears the title: “A sermon of Saint Augustine, bishop, on Saint Stephen.” A little later in the same place we read: “The memorial of the aforementioned martyr, which had been placed in the Castle of Siniti, near the colony of Hippo, was carried by its bishop Lucian, with the people going before and following.” Again, shortly afterward: “Through the memorial of the aforesaid martyr, which Bishop Possidius had brought there, he was restored to health.”

In canon 50 of the African Council, however, from which this chapter is taken, “memorial” means the altar on which the martyrs’ relics had been placed. Charlemagne issued this constitution because in that age certain monks were selling false relics of saints, as Hugo Menardus shows at length in his notes on the *Concordia regularum*, p. 124. On this subject, among others, see Amulo, archbishop of Lyon, in his letter to Theobald, bishop of Langres. Moreover, as that age was eager to gather relics from everywhere, it mingled right and wrong, as Browerus says in book eight of the *Annals of Trier*, p. 399 of the latest edition [Col. 0166A]. Hence those stories about the bodies of saints stolen away. Thus the people of Regensburg think that they possess the body of Dionysius, bishop of Paris, stolen from Paris, as Aventinus writes in book four of the *Annals of Bavaria* [Col. 0166B]. The people of Salzburg likewise boast that they possess the body of Saint Martin, bishop of Tours, stolen away, as is clear from the account preserved in Henry Canisius, volume six of the *Ancient Readings*, p. 1221. We French too stole the body of Saint Gregory the Great in the time of Louis the Pious and deposited it in the monastery of Saint-Médard at Soissons, if the account preserved in Bollandus, volume two of January, p. 284, is true. In Flodoard, book III, chapter 24, Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, writes to Louis, abbot of Saint-Denis, requesting the return of the body of Saint Deodatus, which a certain Giso, driven by desire for the saint’s possessions, had secretly transferred from the diocese of Reims to the Parisian parish, without the knowledge of the bishop in whose episcopal residence it lay. In the *History of the Twenty-Three Abbots of Saint Albans*, p. 88, we read that the body of the same saint was retained by the people of Ely under a deceitful pretext and through sacrilegious crime. It would be endless to pursue everything.

Archbishop Anastasius Germonius of Tarentaise forbade uncertain relics of saints to be displayed for popular veneration and ordered them to be placed beneath the greater altar of his church, as is clear from the acts of that church, book III, title 45, chapter 1. BALUZE.] should not be venerated [Note: [Col. 0165] “memorials” in 1.] [Note: [Col. 0166C] (African Council, canon 50.) “It was likewise agreed that the altars established here and there throughout fields and along roads as though they were memorials of martyrs, at which no body or relics of martyrs are proved to have been buried, should, if possible, be overturned by the bishops in charge of those places. If popular unrest prevents this, the people should nevertheless be warned not to frequent those places, so that those who think rightly may not be held there by any superstition.

“In general, no memorial of martyrs should be accepted as credible unless there is either a body or some relics, or a trustworthy tradition establishes the origin of some dwelling, possession, or martyrdom. For altars established anywhere on the basis of dreams and empty revelations, as they are called, of just anyone must be rejected altogether.”]

[Col. 0166A] **ALL**—43. Likewise, in the same work, that neither a wife dismissed by her husband may take another husband while her husband is alive, nor may a husband take another wife [Note: [Col. 0165] “wife” in the Ambrosian manuscripts and other Lombard manuscripts.] while his former wife is alive [Note: [Col. 0165] “gold” in 1.] [Note: [Col. 0166C] (African Council, canon 69.) “It was agreed that, in accordance with evangelical and apostolic discipline, neither a man dismissed by his wife nor a woman dismissed by her husband may be joined to another; but they must remain as they are or be reconciled to one another. If they disregard this, they must be compelled to do penance. In this matter, an imperial law should be promulgated.”]

**ALL**—45. Likewise, in the same work, two chapters below [Note: [Col. 0166D] In the chapters of Charlemagne excerpted from Lombard law, chapter 24, it reads: “A false person shall not have the power to accuse.” BALUZE.], that persons of low standing should not have the power to accuse [Note: [Col. 0165] “to accuse” misspelled in 1.]. Nevertheless, all those to whom accusation is denied must not be denied the right to accuse in their own cases.

“(African Council, canon 97.) It was likewise agreed that whenever many crimes are brought against clerics by accusers, if they are unable to prove one of them, the one previously pursued, they should no longer be admitted to pursue the others.”]

[Col. 0167A] **ALL** [Note: [Col. 0167] omitted in 1.]—46. BALUZE.], that virgins should not be veiled before the age of twenty-five unless reasonable necessity compels it [Note: [Col. 0167B] (African Council, canon 93.) “It was likewise agreed that whenever any bishop, because the chastity of a virgin is endangered—whether a powerful suitor or some ravisher is feared, or whether she has been struck by some troubling fear of mortal danger lest she die unveiled—or at the insistence of her parents or those responsible for her care, has veiled or veils a virgin before she is twenty-five years old, the council’s decree concerning that number of years should not prejudice him.”]

**ALL** [Note: [Col. 0167] omitted in 1.]—47. **TO ALL PRIESTS** [Note: [Col. 0167] omitted in 1; “all” in 4 B.]—48. **TO PRIESTS**—49. In the Council of Ancyra there was found a severe and strict penance for those who sin against nature with quadrupeds or males [Note: [Col. 0167] “introduced” in B.]. Therefore, bishops and presbyters entrusted with the judgment of penance should strive by every means to prohibit or cut out this evil from customary practice [Note: [Col. 0167C] Flodoard, book III, chapter 21, concerning Hincmar’s letters: “To John, bishop of Rouen, replying to his question about a certain cleric who, although once promoted to govern a church, could not properly be ordained because of his age.” [Col. 0167D] BALUZE.]

**TO BISHOPS** [Note: [Col. 0167] the word is omitted, and 3 c. continues.]—50. In the Council of Neocaesarea, that no presbyter should be ordained before [Note: [Col. 0167] “ordain” in 1.] his thirtieth year, because the Lord Jesus did not preach before the age of thirty [Note: [Col. 0167D] (Council of Ancyra, canon 15.) The Greek words in the heading are: Περὶ τῶν ἀλογευσαμένων, ἤδε ἀλογευομένων, which we may translate as: “Concerning those who have acted irrationally or are acting irrationally.” The meaning of this sentence may be threefold, as is inferred from what follows: it may concern those who have had intercourse with animals, those who, in the manner of animals, have committed incest with relatives, or those who have had intercourse with males. (Thus far also in Benedict, book III, chapter 356; these passages are absent in Isidore.)

“Accordingly, all who committed such a crime before their twentieth year should, after completing fifteen years of penance, begin to participate only in prayer; and, remaining for another five years in simple communion, should after the age of twenty be received into communion with the offering. Their life during the period of penance should also be examined, and accordingly they should receive this concession of humanity. If some have persisted more obstinately in abusing themselves in this crime, they should spend a longer time in submission.

“But those who, after reaching the age of twenty and while married, fell into this crime should, after doing penance for twenty-five years, be admitted only to communion in prayers; remaining in this communion of prayer for another five years, they should receive full communion with the offering. But if some, while married and after passing their fiftieth year, have fallen into this sin, they should merit communion only at the end of life.”]

“[Council of Neocaesarea, canon 11.] A presbyter should not be ordained before the age of thirty, even if he is worthy, but should wait until the appointed time; for the Lord was baptized in his thirtieth year and then preached.”]

**ALL**—51. In the decretals of Pope Siricius, that no one may take another man’s fiancée [Note: [Col. 0168B] (Siricius, chapter 4.) “You have inquired concerning the violation of marriage, whether one man may marry a girl betrothed to another. We forbid this in every way; for that blessing which the priest bestows upon the married among the faithful is like a kind of sacrilege if it is violated by any transgression.”]

**TO BISHOPS, MONKS, AND VIRGINS** [Note: [Col. 0167] M and V B.]—52. Likewise, in the same author, that monks and virgins should observe their vows in every respect [Note: [Col. 0168C] (Siricius, chapter 6.) “Moreover, certain monks and nuns who had abandoned their holy purpose had sunk into such great wantonness that at first they secretly, under the pretext of monasteries, became involved in unlawful and sacrilegious intercourse; afterward, driven into the abyss by despair of conscience, they openly fathered children from their unlawful embraces. Both public laws and ecclesiastical statutes condemn this. We therefore order that these shameless and detestable persons be expelled from the communities of monasteries and churches, so that, shut away in their prisons and mourning such a great crime with continual lamentation, they may purge it in the cleansing fire of repentance, and that, at least at death, indulgence may come to their aid through the grace of communion, solely out of regard for mercy.”]

**ALL** [Note: [Col. 0167] “to priests” in O.]—53. In the decretals of Pope Innocent, that peace should be given by all after the sacraments of Christ have been completed [Note: [Col. 0168D] (Innocent, chapter 1.) “You assert that certain persons command the people to exchange peace before the mysteries have been completed, or that priests exchange it among themselves, although peace must necessarily be announced after everything that I ought not to disclose. Through it, it is clear that the people have given their assent to all that is performed in the mysteries and celebrated in the church, and the conclusion of the peace demonstrates that the seals have been completed.”]

**TO PRIESTS**—54. Likewise, in the same author, that names should not be publicly recited before the priestly prayer [Note: [Col. 0167] “name” in 1.] [Col. 0169A] [Note: [Col. 0168D] Augustine, at the Third Conference of Carthage, 230: “We are in the church in which Caecilian held the episcopate and died. We recite his name at the altar.” See Saint Gregory, book III, indiction 12, letter 37. The Council of Tulle, held around the year 1045: “Nor should their names be recited at the sacred altar among the faithful dead.” They placed on the altar the names that were to be recited, as is clear from an old Cologne manuscript cited by Pamelius in volume two of the *Liturgicon of the Latin Church*, p. 180, where it read: “Remember, Lord, your male and female servants, and those whose names we have written for remembrance and whose names appear to be written and present upon your holy altar.” The eminent man John Bona, cardinal, of learned, pious, dignified, and immortal memory, reports that he read these words in several ancient manuscripts, book II of the *Liturgy*, chapter 11.

“This is also confirmed by the very ancient sacramentary of the monastery of Gellone in Septimania, where, in chapter 316, it reads: ‘Extend, Lord, your mercy to your male and female servants whose commemoration we make, or whose names appear to be written before your holy altar; their number and names you alone, Lord, know. Grant the assistance of your heavenly right hand, so that they may seek you with their whole heart, and those who rightly ask may obtain what they seek. Grant also to the souls of all your male and female servants, all faithful Catholic and orthodox Christians who pleased you, whose commemoration we make or whose names appear written before your holy altar, remission of all sins, and let them obtain the indulgence they have always desired through devout supplication. Through the Lord.’

“From these passages it seems possible to conclude that it was not customary to recite the names of individuals, but of all in general—namely, those whose names had been written on the altar, so that the celebrating priest might think especially of them in offering the sacrifice. Yet in Amalarius’s *Eclogues* we read that in the age of Charlemagne it was customary in our churches to recite the names of the living and the dead faithful in that part of the Mass which we call the canon—not generally, but with the names of individuals pronounced. Sometimes the recitation of the names was performed by a subdeacon behind the altar. This is proved by the *Book of Sacraments* in Menardus’s edition, p. 264: ‘The subdeacons come forward from behind the altar, where they have named or recited the remembrance or names of the living and the dead, after the deacon.’

“The author of the exposition on the Canon of the Mass writes: ‘When it is first said, “Remember, Lord, your male and female servants,” and then ‘and all those standing around’ is added, it is clear that there is, as it were, a certain place where, after certain persons have been specially named, a commemoration of the others who are present in the church is also added. In that place the priest is either free to name individually whomever he wishes and commend them by name to God, or certainly it was observed by the ancients that the names of those making offerings were recited there.’

“I found it noted by the illustrious Paul Petavius, senator of Paris, that the author of this exposition was Florus. Among the papers of Pierre-François Chifflet, I found the beginning of this work copied from an old manuscript, in which it is attributed to this Florus. This confirms what was noted in Petavius, so that henceforth there can be no doubt that it is Florus’s work. BALUZE.]

[Col. 0170A] [Note: (Innocent, chapter 2.) “Concerning the names to be recited before the priest offers the prayer, and commends in his prayer the offerings of those whose names are to be recited: you yourself, in your prudence, recognize how superfluous this is. You do not yet offer the victim of one to God, and you announce his name beforehand, although nothing is unknown to God. Therefore, the offerings should first be commended, and then the names of those whose offerings they are should be announced, so that they may be named amid the sacred mysteries, not among the other things that we mention beforehand in order to open the way for the prayers that will follow to the mysteries themselves.”]

**TO BISHOPS** [Note: [Col. 0169] E and S B.] **AND PRIESTS**—55. Likewise, in the same author [Note: [Col. 0169] in the decrees of Pope Celestine B.], that no priest may be ignorant of the ordinances of the holy canons [Note: [Col. 0170B] (Celestine, distinction 38, canon 4.) “No priest may be permitted to be ignorant of his canons, or to do anything that could oppose the rules of the Fathers. For what worthy safeguard will remain for us if the standard of decretal ordinances is broken at the pleasure of some, with permission granted to the people?”]

**TO BISHOPS**—56 [Note: [Col. 0169] Chapters 56–60 are absent in 3.]. In the decrees of Pope Leo, as also in the Council of Sardica, that bishops should not entice another bishop’s cleric to themselves or ordain him [Note: [Col. 0170B] (Leo, chapter 39.) “No one may receive another’s cleric against the will of his bishop, unless perhaps, by an agreement motivated by charity, the matter has been arranged between the giver and the receiver. For he is guilty of grave injury who dares either to entice away or retain from a brother’s church what is more useful or more valuable. Therefore, if the matter occurs within the province, the metropolitan should compel the fugitive cleric to return to his own church. But if he has gone farther away, he should be recalled by the authority of your command, so that neither greed nor ambition may find an opportunity.”]

**TO BISHOPS** [Note: [Col. 0169] omitted in 1.]—57. Likewise, in the same author, that no bishop should presume to promote another’s slave to clerical office without the consent of his master. The Council of Gangra also prohibits this [Note: [Col. 0170C] (Council of Gangra, canon 3.) “If anyone, on the pretext of religion, teaches a slave to despise his master and abandon his service, and does not rather teach him to serve his master faithfully and with all respect, let him be anathema.”]

[Col. 0170A] **TO BISHOPS** [Note: [Col. 0169] omitted in 1.]—58. Likewise, in the same author, that if any priest presumptuously acts against the decretal ordinances and refuses to be corrected [Note: [Col. 0169] “refusing” in 1.], he should be removed from his office [Note: [Col. 0170C] (Leo, chapter 5.) “Our admonition therefore declares that if any of our brothers attempts to act against these ordinances and dares to do what has been forbidden, he should know that he is to be removed from his office and will not share in our communion, since he did not wish to share in discipline. To ensure that nothing seems to have been omitted by us, we order that all decretal ordinances—both those of blessed memory, Innocent, and those of all our predecessors, promulgated concerning ecclesiastical orders and the discipline of the canons—be guarded by your affection in such a way that anyone who violates them may know that forgiveness will thereafter be denied him.”]

**TO BISHOPS** [Note: [Col. 0169] “also” in 1.]—59. In the decrees of Pope Gelasius, that no bishop should presume to veil widows [Note: [Col. 0169] Here 25 manuscripts 1 and 4 continue without a distinction.] [Note: [Col. 0170D] (Gelasius, chapter 13.) “Let no pontiff attempt to veil widows, since neither divine authority delegates this power nor the form of the canons establishes it. It must therefore not be usurped at all; rather, ecclesiastical assistance should be provided to them in such a way that nothing unlawful is committed.”]

**TO BISHOPS** [Note: [Col. 0169] “other chapters” in B.]—For these matters, beloved, we have endeavored, with devout zeal and great concern born of affection, to admonish your unanimity—those matters that seemed most necessary—so that, adhering to the canonical ordinances of the holy Fathers, you may deserve to receive with them the rewards of eternal blessedness. For your prudence knows with what terrible censure of anathema those are struck [Note: [Col. 0171] “will be struck?” in 2; “may be struck” in 4.] who presumptuously dare to act against the statutes of universal councils [Note: [Col. 0171] “dare” in B.]. Therefore we admonish you even more carefully to strive with all your purpose to avoid that dreadful judgment of condemnation [Note: [Col. 0171] omitted in 1.], but rather, following the canonical statutes [Note: [Col. 0171] “ordinances” in 2, 4, and B.] and striving for peaceful unity, to become worthy of reaching the eternal joys of peace [Note: [Col. 0171] “to reach” in B.; “may you deign to be worthy” in 2 and 4.]. There are also certain chapters that seemed useful to us to append to this preceding admonition [Note: [Col. 0171] “other” in 4 and B.; “to you” in B.].

**ALL**—60. First of all [Note: [Col. 0171] “we admonish that” in B.], that the Catholic faith be diligently read by bishops [Note: [Col. 0171] “and presbyters” in B.; 4 and 3 c.], presbyters, and be preached to all the people; because this is the first commandment of the Lord God Almighty in the law: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God.” And that he be loved with all our heart, with all our mind, with all our soul, and with all our strength.

**ALL** [Note: [Col. 0171] omitted in 1.]—61. That there be peace, concord, and unanimity with all the Christian people—among bishops, abbots, counts, judges, and all persons everywhere, whether greater or lesser—because nothing pleases God without peace, nor does the offering of the holy sacrifice at the altar, as we read in the Gospel at the Lord’s own command. For this too is the second commandment in the law: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” [Note: [Col. 0171] “you love” in 1.]. Likewise in the Gospel: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.” And again: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.” By this commandment the children of God and the children [Col. 0171C] of the devil are distinguished; for the children of the devil always strive to stir up dissensions and discord [Note: [Col. 0171D] Eginhard, letter 62: “For, as is most plainly evident, demons rejoice in the dissension and disturbance of good people and delight in discord.” Sergius II, in a letter concerning Drogo’s vicariate: “On the contrary, it is plainly understood that those who desire wars are sons of the devil.”], while the children of God always devote themselves to peace and love.

**ALL** [Note: [Col. 0171] omitted in 1.]—62. That those who have been given the power to judge should judge justly, as it is written: “Judge justly, sons of men.” Not on the basis of gifts, because gifts blind the hearts of the wise and overturn the words of the just. Not through flattery, nor through regard for a person, as it is said in Deuteronomy: “Judge what is just.” Whether he is a citizen or a foreigner [Note: [Col. 0171] “whether he is a citizen” in 4 and B.; “let there be no” in 1.], there should be no distinction of persons [Col. 0172A], because it is God’s judgment.

First, the judge must diligently learn the law composed by wise men for the people, lest through ignorance he stray from the way of truth. And once he understands the right judgment, he must beware of turning away from it—whether through the flattery of certain persons, love for any friend, fear of someone powerful, or desire for a reward. And it seems proper to us that judges should hear and decide cases while fasting [Note: [Col. 0171] The final words of the chapter are found among the Lombard laws, K and M, chapter 42, Muratori.]

FOR ALL.—63. Likewise, we have in the law, by the Lord’s command: “You shall not swear falsely by my name, nor profane the name of the Lord your God, and you shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain” [Note: [Col. 0171] *vacuum* (“empty”) in manuscript 1.]. Therefore everyone must be carefully admonished to beware of perjury—not only in the holy Gospel, or at the altar, or over the relics of the saints, but also in ordinary speech. For there are some who swear by charity and truth, yet take care concerning an oath by the name of God [Note: [Col. 0171] *iuromento* (“oath”) in manuscript 1.] and do not know that the same God is charity and truth, as the apostle John says: “God is charity.” Likewise the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “I am the way and the truth.” Therefore whoever swears by truth and charity swears by God.

Likewise, care must be taken lest anyone, through Pharisaic [Note: [Col. 0171] *farisiaca* in manuscripts 1 and 2.] superstition, honor gold more than the altar, lest the Lord say to him: “Fool and blind man, which is greater, the gold or the altar that sanctifies the gold?” But it also seems honorable to us that whoever is to swear upon holy things [Note: [Col. 0171D] This is the true reading, supplied by nearly all the old manuscripts. In one Vatican manuscript, the Metz manuscript, and the Camberon manuscript, however, we read *audet jurare* (“dares to swear”). Regino also has this reading, followed by Burchard, Ivo, and Gratian. Burchard, moreover, because of his audacity, attributes this constitution to Pope Cornelius, since he did not wish to commend it from the books of the Capitularies. See the notes on Gratian, p. 532, and on Regino, p. 590.], do so fasting, with all propriety and fear of God. Let him know that he will render an account to God for every oath, wherever he may be [Note: [Col. 0171] *quicumque* (“whoever”) in manuscript 2.]—whether inside the church or [Col. 0172C] outside the church.

And [Note: [Col. 0171] The words that follow are found among the Lombard edicts, chapter 39 of Muratori.] let children who are not of rational age not be compelled to swear, as the Guntbodingi [Note: [Col. 0172D] After these words, the commonly circulated editions of the Capitularies add: *sicut Gunebodigni faciunt* (“as the Gunebodingi do”). It is certain, however, that this clause was added by Johannes Tilius. For it does not occur in the old manuscripts of Ansegisus, nor in the Basel edition. With equal license, the Roman correctors added it in Gratian, as we noted there. See also the notes on Regino, p. 590.] do [Note: [Col. 0171] Manuscript variants: *buntgodingi* in two manuscripts; *gundbondingi* in four; *gonebii digni* in five; *gunebodigni* in three; *gundebanda lege viventes* in the Ambrosian manuscript; *gundebada lege viventes* in the Vercelli and Vatican manuscripts.]. And whoever has once committed perjury shall thereafter be neither a witness nor take an oath, nor shall he be a swearer in his own case or in another’s [Note: [Col. 0172D] These words and those that follow are absent from the Colbertine manuscript, which has only: “nor shall he be an accuser against the Church or against clerics.” Baluze.] [Note: [Col. 0171] One manuscript adds: “unless he receives penance.”].

FOR ALL.—64. Likewise, we have in the law of the Lord the command: “You shall not practice divination”; and in Deuteronomy: “Let no one be found who consults diviners” [Note: [Col. 0171] *suscitetur* (“who raises up”) in manuscripts 1 and 2.], or observes dreams, or attends to auguries. Likewise: “Let there be no sorcerer, no enchanter, and no consulter of pythonic spirits” [Note: [Col. 0171] *nemo* (“no one”) in manuscripts 3 and Baluze.] [Note: [Col. 0172D] The royal, Troyes, Tilius, Thuane, and one Saint Gall manuscript, as well as Baluze’s manuscript, read *consulator* (“one who consults”); the Basel edition has the same reading. Another Saint Gall manuscript reads *Phitones consulantur* (“let pythonic spirits be consulted”). Ancient scribes often confused *consolatio*, *consultatio*, and *conlatio*. Examples must be used, for from them scholars can sometimes correct corrupt books of ancient authors. Petrus Pithoeus, in his notes on the collation of the Mosaic laws, p. 131: *Consultationis vet. consolationis* (“the old reading is *consolationis* for *consultationis*”). Thus it is written in the best manuscript of Servius at the passage in Book III of the *Aeneid*: *Augurium est exquisita deorum voluntas per consolationem avium aut signorum* (“Augury is an inquiry into the will of the gods through the consolation of birds or signs”). Faustus of Riez, Letter 5: *Pro cujus timore et amore consolatio ipsa tractatur* (“On account of whose fear and love, consolation itself is treated”), where *consultatio* (“consultation”) should be read. Likewise, in Letter 21 of Hormisdas, *consolatio* is used for what is called *consultatio* in Letter 17. When scribes were uncertain which reading should be preferred, they sometimes set down both, as in Letter 36 of Hincmar: *pro diversorum Patrum consolatione vel consultatione* (“for the consolation or consultation of various Fathers”). In the work of forty-five chapters, chapters 25 and 43, the reading is simply *pro diversorum Patrum consolatione* (“for the consolation of various Fathers”). This passage was taken from the decree of Gelasius on canonical and apocryphal books. Where Hincmar here has *consolatione*, Nicholas I wrote *consultatione* in Letter 42 to the archbishops and bishops established in Gaul; Gratian quotes part of it in Distinction 19, chapter *Si Romanorum* (“If the Romans”). In the Burgundian law, title 60, §1, we read: *nova lege futuris temporibus consulatur* (“let provision be made for future times under the new law”). For this, the Bigot manuscript has *consolatur*. In Saint Ambrose, Sermon 6, we read: *sine aliqua praedicationis consolatione dimiserim* (“I would dismiss him without any consolation of preaching”). Here, however, the very old manuscript of the church of Lyons has *consulatione*. Likewise in Book V of the Capitularies, chapter 35, where some manuscripts read *consultandum*, others *consulendum*, the Norman and one Saint Gall manuscript have *consulandum*. If anyone seeks further examples, let him consult Salmasius’s notes on Julius Capitolinus, p. 92. I will add only that *consulare* was sometimes used for *consolari*. Fortunatus, Book IV, chapter 6, in the epitaph of Exotius, bishop of Limoges:

> But since it was not permitted, may that hope console the people  
> which faith has carried to the stars according to his merits.

Baluze.]

“consultor” [Note: [Col. 0171] *consolator* in manuscripts 1 and 3; *consultur* in manuscript 2; *consulatur* in manuscript 4.]. Therefore we command that [Note: [Col. 0173] Baluze: *ut nec* (“and that they not”).] no calculators (*cauculatores*) [Note: [Col. 0173D] Most manuscripts read *cauculatores*. Others have *calculatores* (“calculators”). The royal, Troyes, and Baluze’s manuscript have *auguriatores* (“auguriators”); one Vatican manuscript, the Colbertine, and one Saint Gall manuscript have *auguratores* (“augurators”). Baluze.] nor enchanters [Note: [Col. 0173] *nec incantatores* (“nor enchanters”) is absent from manuscript 1.] nor storm-raisers [Note: [Col. 0174B] Those who claimed that they could produce lightning, thunder, and other storms of the air. See the notes on Agobard’s book *On Hail and Thunder*, p. 68, and on Regino, Book II, chapters 353 and 355. Baluze.] or binders become such; and wherever they are found, let them be reformed or condemned.

Likewise [Note: [Col. 0174B] See Gregory the Great, Book VII, Indiction 1, Letter 5; Saint Eligius in the homily published in Volume V of D’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, pp. 215–17; Regino, Book II, chapters 358 and 359, where see the notes. See also the chapters issued to priests, which Sirmond transcribed from the Vatican and Casinensis manuscripts. Baluze.] concerning trees, rocks, or springs where certain foolish people place lights or perform other observances, we command absolutely that this very wicked practice, abominable to God, wherever it is found, be removed and destroyed.

FOR ALL.—65. It is also necessary to preach how great an evil hatred and envy are, because it is written in the law: “You shall not hate your brother in your heart, but publicly rebuke him.” Likewise John the Evangelist: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer.” Likewise in the Gospel: “If your brother sins against you, go and rebuke him between yourself and him alone,” and the other things that are read there.

Concerning greed, we read the apostle saying: “Greed, which is the service of idols, must be avoided.” Likewise it is written concerning desire that it is the root of all evils. And in the law: “You shall not desire the property of your neighbor” [Note: [Col. 0173] *concupiscis* (“you desire”) in manuscript 1.].

[Col. 0174A] FOR BISHOPS, FOR ALL.—66. Likewise, homicides within the realm must not occur, as is forbidden in the law of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0173] This is absent from manuscripts 1 and 3.], whether for the sake of vengeance, greed, or robbery. Wherever they are found, they shall be punished by our judges according to the law and by our command [Note: [Col. 0173] *ad* (“by”) in manuscript 2.]. And no one shall be killed except at the command of the law.

FOR ALL.—67. Likewise, diligently forbid thefts, unlawful marriages, and false testimonies, as we have often requested, just as the law of the Lord also forbids them.

FOR ALL.—68. Also admonish this with great zeal [Note: [Col. 0173] Baluze: “It must be admonished.”], that children honor their parents, because the Lord himself says: “Honor your father and your mother” [Note: [Col. 0173] *tuum* (“your father”) in manuscript 1.], “so that you may live long upon the land that the Lord your God will give you.”

[Col. 0174B] FOR PRIESTS.—69. [Note: [Col. 0174C] Charles wisely and prudently commands this. For those who aspired to the rank of priest devoted themselves to letters until they reached ordination and received a title from the bishop. Afterwards, most abandoned the study of letters, as is clear from Flodoard, Book III, chapter 28, concerning Hincmar’s letters: “Likewise, concerning a certain priest who, after his ordination, through negligence had forgotten what he had once learned about his ministry. Thus, when the bishop was making his visitation of the diocese, he had to ask the priest whether he could read the Epistle and the Gospel well and at least explain their meaning word by word, as is read in the inquiry found in the first book of Regino on ecclesiastical discipline.”

“Then this unhappy state of the times returned, as may be gathered from Oration 26 of Isidore Clarius, bishop of Foligno, on the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount, where that excellent bishop addresses his clergy as follows: ‘Furthermore, take care to advance them in the study of letters, so that you may be able to engage daily in divine readings and complete in them the portions appropriate to men of your order. Otherwise, let none of you expect to be promoted by me to holy orders if he is not capable of understanding what he reads, at least in the text of the holy Gospels. For during this period of visiting the parishes I found scarcely any priest who knew how to interpret what he read.’ For this reason he issued this most salutary constitution at his synod in 1547: ‘Let that be guarded against above all which is the cause of many—indeed, I should say of all—evils in the Church of Christ: that priests, especially for the care of souls, not be received rashly and without judgment. For in this visitation we discovered in them the greatest ignorance, so that some not only understood nothing of what they read, but did not even know how to read correctly. In some provinces of this most flourishing kingdom, when there are several sons in one household, the first is destined to continue the family line, while another is handed over to the study of letters so that he may become a priest: *Il étudie pour être prêtre* (“He is studying to become a priest”); for this is how the parents speak. But once they have been ordained to the rank for which they had undertaken the study of letters, they no longer handle books; instead, they pass their lives in idleness and silence through the utmost laziness and inactivity—some entering taverns for the purpose of drinking and eating, contrary to the institutions of the holy canons and the provisions of the capitularies; others devoting themselves to hunting, bird-catching, and games, contrary to the ancient discipline. See the Council of Clovesho, chapter 10.’ Baluze.]

Let bishops carefully examine the priests throughout their parishes—their faith, baptism, and celebration of Mass—so that they hold the right faith, observe Catholic baptism, and properly understand the prayers of the Mass; and so that [Col. 0175A] [Note: [Col. 0175B] The author of the *Life of Alcuin*: “As a young man he loved the secret modulation of the psalms no less than any other reading.” Baluze.] they sing the psalms worthily according to the divisions of the verses, and understand the Lord’s Prayer themselves and preach it to everyone so that it may be understood, so that each person may know what he asks of God.

[Note: [Col. 0175B] In the Rivipullensian manuscript this passage reads: “And let the *Gloria Patri et Filio et Spiritui sancto* (‘Glory be to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit’) be sung among all with every honor; and let the priest himself, with the holy angels and dominions and powers, with the virtues of the heavens and of the heavens of heavens, with the cherubim and seraphim and the people of God, and so forth …” Baluze.] And let the “Glory be to the Father” be sung among all with every honor; and let the priest himself, with the holy angels and the people of God, sing with one voice: “Holy, holy, holy.”

And priests and deacons must be told in every way that they not carry weapons, but place their confidence more in God’s protection than in arms. [Note: [Col. 0175C] The laws had provided that priests should not handle weapons or be agents of bloodshed. Later, however, the rulers judged that they ought to provide assistance to the state in warding off enemy attacks. The priests, for their part, offered their prayers. Hence Hincmar, Letter 9 to the bishops of the province of Reims, chapter 4: “For this reason we bishops must take sufficient care that, in the counsel which the ministers of the state request from us according to the command of the Lord King, we do not withdraw from our ministry, and that we do not shrink from assistance to the extent that God has granted each of us the ability to provide, following the saying of the Lord: ‘Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s, and to God the things that are God’s.’ Let us therefore provide divine weapons in assistance—fasts, prayers, tears, appeals, and supplications for the aid of the saints—and divine assistance through ourselves and our parishes.”

“When the bishops excused themselves from providing support in the great dangers of the kingdom, the royal ministers replied that the state required other kinds of aid, and that when King Pippin had gone to Italy to defend the Apostolic See, he had not defeated King Aistulf, subdued Italy, and obtained the rights of Saint Peter through apostolic excommunication but by military force. Hincmar himself bears witness to this in Letter 41 to Pope Hadrian: ‘Pippin, not by apostolic excommunication but by military force, defeated Aistulf, a Christian king of whatever sort, subdued Italy, and obtained the rights of Saint Peter.’ And shortly afterward: ‘You therefore defend the kingdom by your prayers alone against the Northmen and others attacking it, and do not seek our defense.’

“Saint Ambrose, by contrast, says in Sermon 86: ‘Where are those who say that weapons can accomplish more than the prayers of holy men? Behold, one prayer of Elisha wounded an entire army, and through the merits of one prophet the whole number of the enemy was taken captive.’

“In the laws of King Edward of England, published in Bede’s appendix, chapter 11, it is written that the English Church, and also all land belonging to the Church, wherever it lay, was free and exempt from the tribute called *Danegeld*, ‘because they trusted more in the prayers of the Church than in the defenses of arms.’ And Pope Paul, in Letter 20 of the *Codex Carolinus*, addressed to King Pippin, says that the summit of royal power is surrounded and protected more by the strength of faith than by the arms and force of warriors.

“Moreover, William the Breton gives an elegant and lively account of Philip Augustus and the clergy of Reims in Book II of the *Philippid*. He relates that Philip, embroiled in a serious war, requested assistance from the ecclesiastical persons of the province of Reims; they replied in this manner:

> They say that they are rightly bound to pour forth  
> prayers for their king to the supreme King,  
> but not to give money or tribute, lest afterward  
> they perhaps bring harm upon the Church through custom.

“An old charter of Llandaff, published by the distinguished William Dugdale in Volume III of the *Monasticon Anglicanum*, p. 208, offers a noteworthy account of a deacon carrying weapons.” Baluze.]

SOMETHING FOR THE PRIEST [Note: [Col. 0175] *sacerdotibus* (“for priests”) in manuscript 3 and Baluze.], SOMETHING FOR THE PEOPLE [Note: [Col. 0175] *omnibus* (“for all”) in manuscript 3 and Baluze; the entire heading is lacking in manuscripts 1 and 4.]—70. We have also thought it right to admonish your graciousness that each of you should see throughout his parish that the Church of God receives its honor, and that the altars likewise be venerated according to their dignity; that the house of God and the consecrated altars not be accessible to dogs; that vessels consecrated to God be treated with great reverence; and that the sanctified offerings be gathered with great care by those who are worthy, or preserved with honor. Secular business and idle talk must not take place in churches, because the house of God ought to be a house of prayer, not a den of thieves. Let them keep their minds attentive to God when they come to the solemn celebration of Mass, and let them not leave before the completion of the priestly blessing.

FOR PRIESTS.—71. We also earnestly request your graciousness [Note: [Col. 0176C] The Basel edition has *altitudinem* (“your exaltedness”), but Herold inserted *almitatem* (“your graciousness”) in the margin. Saint Boniface, Letter 92: “Therefore I earnestly beseech, in God’s name, the mercy of your graciousness.” Baluze.] that the ministers of God’s altar adorn their ministry by good morals, whether they belong to canonical communities observing their order or to congregations of monastic discipline [Note: [Col. 0175] Baluze reads *seu et* (“and also”) for *seu* (“or”); *observantia* (“observance”) for *observantiae*; manuscript 4 and Baluze, *ordinis* (“order”) for *ordines*; manuscripts 2, 3, corrected 3, 4, and Baluze, *monachi* (“monks”) for *monachici*; Baluze, *proposito* (“profession”) for *propositi*, and *consecrationis* (“consecration”) for *congregationes* (“communities”).] [Note: [Col. 0176C] This is the reading of the Basel edition and of all the old manuscripts except the Tilius manuscript, which reads: “We beseech that they have a good and commendable life and conduct.” That reading occurs in the Aachen capitulary. Baluze.] We beseech them to have a good and commendable way of life [Note: [Col. 0175] Baluze: “a good life and conduct.”], as the Lord himself commands in the Gospel: “Let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven,” so that many may be drawn to the service of God by their good conduct.

And they gather to themselves and associate with them not only children of servile condition [Note: [Col. 0176D] The *Life of Saint Meinwerk, bishop of Paderborn*, chapter 2: “To gather boys, both noble and of lower condition, into the school and nourish them in instruction in divine reading.” Baluze.], but also the sons of free people [Note: [Col. 0175] *adgregent sibique socient* (“let them gather and associate them”) in manuscript 4 and Baluze.].

And let schools of boys learning to read be established. [Note: [Col. 0177B] Charles took great care with literary studies.
