Thus Lupus of Ferrières, in Letter 1, attributes to him the glory that through him literary studies began to be restored: “To him,” he says, “letters must show such honor that they may prepare an eternal memory for him.” Concerning the school at Paderborn that he himself founded, it is written in the *Life of Saint Meinwerk*, chapter 52: “Under him many exercises of study flourished, and young men and boys of good character were diligently instructed according to the rule, making notable progress in monastic discipline and in learning of every kind.” See the Council of Valence III, chapter 18; Regino, Book I, chapter 207; and Mader’s preface to the *Chronicle of Mount Serenus, or Lauterberg*, p. 9. Baluze.] [Note: [Col. 0177C] Saint Boniface, Letter 92: “There are certain monks in our cells, and boys have been appointed to read letters.” Leidrad, archbishop of Lyons, in a letter to Charles the Great: “I have schools of readers, not only those who are trained in the readings of the offices, but also those who may obtain the fruit of spiritual understanding through meditation on the divine books.” See Filesac, Book II of the *Selecta*, p. 208. Baluze.] Let them learn psalms, [Note: [Col. 0177C] That is, musical matters. Ademar, in the *Life of Charles*, chapter 8, says that in 787 Pope Hadrian gave him “antiphonaries of Saint Gregory, which he himself had written in Roman notation.” Shortly afterward he says: “All the singers of France learned the Roman notation, which they now call the Frankish notation.”

“In the very old book of Sacramentaries preserved in the library of the monastery of Compiègne, the following is written in ancient characters: ‘Gregory, a prelate worthy in merit and name, ascending to the highest honor, renewed the memorials of the earlier Fathers and composed this little book of musical art for the school of singers throughout the year.’”

“The school of singers is mentioned in the *Book of Sacramentaries*, p. 63 of Menard’s edition, and in Letter 1 of Leidrad, archbishop of Lyons, to Charles the Great: ‘I have schools of singers, many of whom have been so well trained that they can train others as well.’ The ruler therefore commands that those assigned to the ministry of the altars learn the art of singing psalms and chants. And indeed Eginhard shows that he took great care over these matters in his *Life*: ‘He most diligently corrected the discipline of reading and psalmody, for he was very well trained in both.’ Baluze.] notation, chants, [Note: [Col. 0177D] Eginhard, in the *Life of Charles the Great*: “He learned also the art of calculation.” Ademar, in the passage praised shortly before, reports that when Charles left Rome in 787 he took with him Roman singers, highly skilled grammarians, and calculators. The *Capitula of Walter of Orléans*, chapter 22: “Let all priests possess skill in calculation and diligently train their own people in it.” See chapter 15 of the *Chronicle of Fontenelle* in Volume III of D’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, and the notes on Regino, p. 541. Baluze.] computation, and grammar in every monastery or bishopric [Note: [Col. 0177] *discant* (“let them learn”) is supplied by some manuscripts; Baluze also has *sed et* (“and let them also”)]. Let them have thoroughly corrected Catholic books [Note: [Col. 0177] Baluze: *habeantque* (“and let them have”).], because often, while some wish to pray properly to God [Note: [Col. 0177] *aliquid* (“something”) in manuscript 2 and Baluze.], they pray wrongly through uncorrected books [Note: [Col. 0177] *libris* (“books”) in manuscript 1.].

And do not allow your boys to be corrupted either by reading or by writing. [Note: [Col. 0178B] That is, clerics of tender age, who, when they were maintained at the expense of priests, were called “priests’ fosterlings,” as may be gathered from the fifth Capitulary of Charles the Great, of uncertain date, chapter 5, and from Hincmar’s *Capitula*, title 4, chapter 5. Elsewhere, servants are understood by the word “boys,” as in Saint Ambrose, Book I *On Abraham*, chapter 9: “Thus we also say ‘boys’ when we mean little servants, expressing not their age but their condition.” Many likewise understand the Gospel passage according to John in this way: “There is one boy here who has five barley loaves.” Baluze.] And if it is necessary to write a Gospel book, a psalter, or a missal, let men of mature age write them with every care [Note: [Col. 0177] Manuscript 3 breaks off here.].

FOR PRIESTS.—72. We have likewise taken care to request that all who, wherever they may be, have bound themselves by a vow to the monastic life [Note: [Col. 0178C] This is the reading of the Basel edition and of the Reims, Pithoean, Saint Gall, Paris, and Metz manuscripts. The Norman, Vatican, Camberon, Colbertine, Troyes, another Saint Gall, and Baluze’s manuscript have *monasticae*. Others have *monachiae*. Baluze.], live in every way monastically and according to the rule [Note: [Col. 0177] *regulanter* in manuscript 1.] [Note: [Col. 0178C] Herold noted in the margin of the Basel edition that this should be the reading, although in the text he printed simply *monachi* (“monks”). It must indeed be admitted that most of the old manuscripts have the reading that Herold retained in the text. Nevertheless, the reading restored here, which seems more genuine, is found in the Paris, Pithoean, Reims, and one of the two Saint Gall manuscripts. Baluze.] according to their vow, as it is written: “Pay your vows to the Lord your God.” And again: “It is better not to vow than not to fulfill one’s vows” [Note: [Col. 0177] Manuscript 4 and Baluze read *quam vovere et non reddere* (“than to vow and not fulfill them”).].

And when they come to monasteries, let them first be tested in the receiving-house according to the regular order [Note: [Col. 0178D] The place in which those newly arriving for conversion are received is so called because they were admitted there only after they had knocked for a long time. It is unnecessary to prove this with examples. I will give only the testimony of Gerard, abbot of Silva Major, from chapter 1 of the *Life of Saint Adalard, abbot of Corbie*: “In this place, therefore, having knocked and been admitted through knocking, he was to be instructed according to the rule of Saint Benedict, and so forth.” Baluze.], and then be admitted [Note: [Col. 0177] Manuscripts 2 and 4 read *capiant* (“let them take”); Baluze has *recipiantur* (“let them be received”).]. Those who come from secular clothing into the monastery must not immediately be sent outside to the monastery’s tasks before they have been properly instructed inside [Note: [Col. 0178D] One Saint Gall manuscript has *enutriantur* (“before they are nourished”). Baluze.]. And let monks not go to secular lawsuits.

Likewise, those who enter [Note: [Col. 0177] Manuscript 1 reads *quod* (“that”) for *qui ad* (“those who … into”).] the clerical order—which we call the canonical life—we wish them to live in every way canonically according to their rule, and let their bishop govern their life, just as an abbot governs the monks.

FOR ALL.—73. Let everyone have equal and accurate measures and just and equal weights, whether in cities or in monasteries, whether for giving to them or receiving from them, as we also have the command in the law of the Lord. Likewise, in Solomon, the Lord saying [Note: [Col. 0177] The words “Likewise … we have” are absent from manuscripts 2 and 5.]: “A weight and a weight, a measure and a measure, my soul hates.”

FOR ALL.—74. It also seems fitting and honorable to us that guests, strangers, and the poor have regular and canonical places of reception in different locations [Note: [Col. 0178D] This is the reading of nearly all the old manuscripts. In the Reims, Pithoean, and Paris manuscripts, however, we read: “that regular and canonical communities have receptions for foreign guests and the poor in different places.” In all the old manuscripts of Ansegisus, moreover, the reading is *Canonici* (“canonical communities”), as it is also written in the Basel edition. Baluze.], because the Lord himself will say on the day of great recompense: “I was a guest” [Note: [Col. 0179] *hospes* (“guest”) in manuscripts 2 and 4 and Baluze.], “and you received me.” And the apostle, praising hospitality, said: “Through this some pleased God, having received angels as guests.”

FOR BISHOPS AND ABBOTS.—75. It has been heard that certain abbesses, contrary to the custom of the holy Church of God, give blessings [Note: [Col. 0179] *benedictiones* (“blessings”) is absent from manuscript 1.] with the imposition of hands and the sign of the holy cross upon men’s heads, and also veil virgins with a priestly blessing. Know absolutely, most holy fathers, that this must be forbidden by you throughout your parishes.

[Note: [Col. 0179B] The illustrious Francis Bosquet, bishop of Montpellier, in his notes on the letters of Innocent III, p. 97, admirably elucidates this chapter, citing also the words of the Sixth Council of Paris, Book I, chapter 43, from which it is understood that this abuse continued in the kingdom of the Franks even after this constitution of Charles.

“The observations of that most learned prelate were later transcribed by Christianus Lupus in his scholia on Tertullian’s *On Prescription Against Heretics*, p. 57 and following. He notes that this female presumption originated in the violent seizure by Charles Martel of ecclesiastical resources, which reduced all the churches of the Frankish kingdom throughout Gaul and Germany to extreme poverty and eventually deprived many of bishops and clerics. He says that this misery lasted until the apostolate of Saint Boniface, and that during the intervening period certain abbesses, because they had no bishops, began to veil and consecrate their nuns. These are Lupus’s words.

“I wish the learned man had confirmed this with the testimony of some ancient writer. For what a more recent author asserts about matters so ancient without the authority of an older source is disregarded, as the illustrious Cardinal Baronius rightly observes. Nowhere, however, is the memory of the prince attacked more unfairly than here—the same prince whom even the Roman pontiffs praised, and to whom Saint Boniface, before those same pontiffs, gave a substantial testimonial for the restoration of religion and ecclesiastical discipline. But here, as often elsewhere, Lupus reveals a restless disposition toward the Franks, though, so far as I know, none of us has injured him, and certainly none has provoked him.

“But to return to the presumption of the abbesses condemned in this chapter: it was also condemned in 829 at the Council of Paris, as we have said, and afterward by Louis the Pious, whose decree is found in the second addition to the Capitularies, chapter 16. ‘A similar decree,’ says Christianus Lupus, ‘the collection of Isidore Mercator attributes to the holy pontiff Eutychianus.’ It is certain, however, that it belongs to some Gallican synod. Whether it preceded or followed the Sixth Council of Paris, I do not know.

“The learned man is mistaken in several ways here. First, it is certain that the chapter in question does not occur in the collection of Isidore, but only among the decrees of Eutychianus collected from Ivo and Gratian and published after that pontiff’s letters in the commonly circulated editions of the councils. It is likewise certain that the chapter does not belong to any Gallican synod, but to Louis the Pious, who enacted it after the admonition of the bishops of the Council of Paris. The error arose because Burchard, who did not wish to commend the authority of the Capitularies, decided to include this chapter in his Collection, altered its title—as he often does—and attributed to Pope Eutychianus a constitution that belonged to the Emperor Louis. Baluze.]

FOR CLERICS.—76. [Note: [Col. 0180C] Burchard cites this chapter from the Council of Toledo, as he usually does. Baluze.] Clerics who pretend by their habit or name to be monks [Note: [Col. 0179] *monachus* (“monk”) in manuscript 1.], although they are not, must in every way be corrected and reformed, so that they may be either true monks or true canons [Note: This is absent from manuscripts 2, 3 corrected, and 4, and from Baluze.].

FOR ALL.—77. Likewise, pseudographical writings and doubtful narratives, or those that are wholly contrary to the Catholic faith, and [Note: [Col. 0179] *ut* (“that”) in corrected manuscript 3, manuscript 4, and Baluze.] that most wicked and utterly false letter [Note: [Col. 0180C] The Bavarian and Basel editions have *fallacissima* (“most deceptive”). Baluze.] which certain erring persons, misleading others into error, said in the preceding year had fallen from heaven [Note: [Col. 0180C] That is, in 788. For this Capitulary was issued at Aachen in 789. Therefore this passage cannot refer to the letter that the heretic Adalbert claimed had fallen from heaven and come to him, as recorded in the acts of the Roman council under Zacharias and preserved among the letters of Saint Boniface, p. 191.

“Perhaps it is the letter whose fragments I found among the papers of the illustrious Peter de Marca, archbishop of Paris, transcribed from an old manuscript of Tarragona in Spain. I found another letter of the same subject and, I believe, of the same period in a very old manuscript in the Colbert Library. Baluze.]—must not be believed or read, but must be burned [Note: [Col. 0179] *comburatur* (“let it be burned”) in manuscript 4; *comburantur* (“let them be burned”) in corrected manuscript 3 and Baluze.], lest the people be led into error by such writings. Let only canonical books, Catholic treatises, and the sayings of the holy authors be read and handed down.

[Note: [Col. 0180D] In the appendix to Regino it reads: *dicunt in Hierusalem de coelo cecidisse* (“they say that it fell from heaven in Jerusalem”). Baluze.]

[Note: [Col. 0180D] Consider the fate of human laws. Charles the Great had ordered that no one should believe those false letters. Later, a letter written in the name of the archangel Gabriel was presented to his son Louis the Pious. He rejected it—rightly so. Yet the author of the *Annals of Fulda*, under the year 874, therefore attacks his memory: “For, to omit the rest, if he had firmly and bravely resisted the heresy of the Nicolaitans, and had taken care to observe the admonitions of the archangel Gabriel, which Abbot Einhard presented to him in twelve chapters to be read and carried out, perhaps he would not have suffered such things.” Baluze.]

SOMETHING FOR PRIESTS, SOMETHING FOR ALL [Note: [Col. 0179] The heading is absent from manuscript 1.]—78. Likewise, these traffickers (*mangones*) and hawkers (*cotiones*) [Note: [Col. 0179] *cottiones* in manuscript 2; *scottones* in manuscript 4.] who wander about this land without any law must not be allowed to roam around and deceive people. Nor should these naked men carrying iron, who say that they wander after penance has been assigned to them, be permitted to do so. It seems better that, if they have committed some unusual and capital crime, they should remain in one place, laboring and serving and doing penance according to what has been canonically imposed upon them.

FOR ALL THE CLERGY.—79. [Note: [Col. 0179] Ansegisus reads *monachi ut* (“let monks …”).] Let them learn the Roman chant completely [Col. 0180B] [Note: *tantum* (“only”) in manuscript 1.], and let the nocturnal or gradual office be performed in due order [Note: *peragant* (“let them perform”) in manuscript 4.], according to what our father of blessed memory, King Pippin, decreed [Note: [Col. 0180D] The Thuane manuscript reads *decretavit* (“decreed”); the Metz manuscript, *decrevit* (“decided”). Amerbach printed *decertavit* (“contended”); Buzée printed *decretavit*. Herold retained *decertavit* in the text but noted in the margin that *decretavit* should be read. Baluze.] [Col. 0181A] should be done when he abolished the Gallican [chant] for the sake of unanimity with the Apostolic See and the peaceful concord of the holy Church of God [Note: [Col. 0181B] See what Pithoeus cites in the *Glossary to the Capitularies*, p. 711, from Book I of Charles the Great’s work *Against the Second Council of Nicaea*. Baluze.] [the supplied source ends here].

BISHOPS [Note: [Col. 0181] Absent in 1 and 4, B.] ALL. — 80. [Note: [Col. 0181B] Regino took this chapter from the Capitularies of Charles; Burchard and Ivo took it from the council held at Saint-Médard in the presence of Emperor Charles, chapter 5, and from the council held at Compiègne, chapter 6. ID.] We decree also, in accordance with what the Lord commands in the Law, that servile work not be performed on Sundays, just as [Note: [Col. 0181] “so” in 1.] my father of blessed memory also ordered in his synodal edicts [Note: [Col. 0181] “My [father], that” in 2 and B.] [Note: [Col. 0181B] Namely, in the capitulary of the year 755, established at the Synod of Verneuil. ID.], that is, neither should men perform agricultural work [Note: [Col. 0181] “Rural work” in 1.] nor work at cultivating vineyards, nor plow in the fields [Note: [Col. 0181] “Plowing, nor in” in B.] [Note: [Col. 0181B] A certain man yoked oxen on Sunday and began to plow a field. He was severely punished. Gregory of Tours recounts the event in Book II of *On the Glory of the Martyrs and Confessors*, chapter 11. ID.], reap [Note: [Col. 0181] Absent in 2 and 4.], or cut hay, or set hedges, nor clear land in the forests, or cut down trees, or work in the stone-quarries, nor build houses; nor should they work in gardens [Note: [Col. 0181] “They work” in 1; “to work” in 2 and 4.], nor assemble for lawsuits, nor engage in hunting. And three carting operations are permitted [Col. 0182A] on Sunday; that is, [Note: [Col. 0181B] That is, carts for military service, as in the *Census Register*, or polyptych, of Abbot Irminon of Saint-Germain in Paris, in volume IV of the *Acts of the Order of Saint Benedict*, p. 96. In Burchard it reads *hostilicia carra*; in Ivo, *hostilicidia*. In the polyptych of the monastery of Fosses I read that each tenant of the estate of Rokeniacum owes fourteen denarii for military service. A little earlier: “Each person pays two solidi for military service, that is, for an ox.” The same is called *hostelitia* in the polyptych of Saint-Remi of Reims: “The free man Hilmegandus holds a freeholding. He pays sixteen denarii for military service.” ID.] military carts, or carts carrying provisions, or, if it should happen to be necessary, transporting anyone’s body to the grave. Likewise, women shall not perform textile work, nor [Note: [Col. 0181] “They join together” in 1.] *capulent* garments [Note: The precise meaning of *capulent* is uncertain.], nor sew, nor [Note: [Col. 0181D] Thus the printed edition. An old book of the monastery of Tegernsee, from which the Bavarian edition was produced, had *aquapictile*, as Amerbach notes in the margin. One Saint-Gall manuscript has *aliquapictile*. These readings confirm the form we have retained. The Royal, one Vatican, Beauvais, Dijon, Troyes, and other manuscripts have *acupiculae*; Colbert, Ripoll, and Thuanus have *acupicule*; Herold has *acubiculae*; the book of Saint Michael in Periculo Maris has *acupicale*; Paris, Metz, and Rheims have *acupicula*; mine has *aucupiculae*; Camberon has *cupiculae*; another Saint-Gall manuscript has *apicule*; Pithou’s has *apicula*. See Spelman’s Glossary under *Acubicula*, where he criticizes Meursius, who thought this word should be changed to *acubitulae*, that is, “reclining cushions.” ID.] make embroidery [Note: [Col. 0181] “*Aquapictile*” in 1.] [Note: [Col. 0182B] The Basel edition reads “let them make.”], nor card wool, nor beat flax [Note: [Col. 0181] “*Battere*” in 2, 3, 4, and B.], nor wash clothing in public, nor [Note: [Col. 0182B] Incorrectly *cervices* in the Tilian manuscript. The Royal, Troyes, Camberon, one Vatican, Metz, Pithou’s, mine, and the Bavarian edition read *verveces*. The same form appears in Regino and Burchard, and in the polyptych of the monastery of Fosses. The other Saint-Gall manuscript, Ripoll, Thuanus, and the Basel edition have *berbices*. This last reading is especially frequent in old books, as Peter Pithou teaches in his notes on the *Comparison of Mosaic and Roman Laws*, title 11. “Later writers,” he says, “generally pronounced and wrote *berbix*, as in Anianus, Paul the Monk, and the Lombard and Frankish laws. Hence the word has remained with us.” In ancient copies of the Aachen Capitulary, *berbices* is written here. The same occurs in chapter 98 of the Alamannic Law. The memorandum of Abbot Ansegisus of Fontenelle, in volume III of D’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, p. 247, has “wethers, sheep, and chickens.” Hence *berbicine skins* appears there, p. 246, “for berbicine skins, from which garments are made.” Hence *berbicine fur* in the Saint-Gall monk’s second book *On the Military Affairs of Charlemagne*, chapter 27. Hence “berbicine mufflers” in the capitulary of 817, chapter 79, in the Saint-Gall manuscript. Finally, hence *berbices* and *berbicarii* in the ancient statutes of the monastery of Corbie, chapter 5. Besides the manuscripts mentioned above, *vervices* occurs in the Bigot manuscript in title 4 of the Salic Law and in title 38, chapter 3, and title 70, chapter 3 of the Burgundian Law. It also occurs in the polyptych of Abbot Irminon of Saint-Germain in Paris, praised by Mabillon in his notes to volume IV of the *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, p. 96: “wethers with lambs.” In Buzelin, Book II of *Gaul-Flanders*, p. 359, in the record of the donation made by the priest Walgarius to the monastery of Cison: “one hundred and eighty wethers.” ID.] be permitted to shear sheep [Note: [Col. 0182D] In the old copies—the Royal, Troyes, one Saint-Gall, Pithou’s, Colbert, Thuanus, Tilian, Paris, Rheims, Dijon, Beauvais, mine, and the Basel edition—the reading is “the repose of good people.”]. In every way, therefore, let the honor and repose of Sunday be preserved. But [Note: [Col. 0181] Absent in 2; “but also” in B.] let them all come from every direction to the church for the solemn celebration of Mass [Note: [Col. 0181] “From” in 1.] [Note: [Col. 0181] *aeclesias*, with an added *s*, in 1.], and praise God for all the good things that he has done for us on that day.

ALL [Note: [Col. 0181] Absent in 1.] — 81. [Note: [Col. 0182D] This is the reading found in the Aachen Capitulary and in the ancient copies of Ansegisus—Tilian, Dijon, Pithou’s, Thuanus, and Paris—as well as in the editions of Amerbach and Herold. In the Camberon, Beauvais, Rheims, Metz, and Regino: “But it must also be seen to by each of you.” In one Saint-Gall manuscript: “But it is also your concern, beloved”; incorrectly, I think. In another Saint-Gall manuscript, Colbert, and Ripoll, and in the editions of Tilius: “You must take the greatest care.” The Norman manuscript: “You must take the greatest care.” Regino correctly took this chapter from the Capitularies, Book I, title 66. Burchard took it from the Council of Rouen, and Ivo followed him. Burchard, therefore—as has often been said and must often be said—is responsible for most of the false headings found in the ancient collectors of canon law. BALUZ.] But it must also be your concern, beloved and venerable shepherds and rulers of the churches of God, that the priests whom you send throughout your parishes to govern and to preach to the people serving God preach rightly and honorably; and do not allow any of them to invent and preach to the people novelties or noncanonical teachings [Note: [Col. 0183D] That is, teachings “from his own heart,” as it is read in the inquiry found at the beginning of Regino’s books *On Ecclesiastical Discipline*. The prince therefore commands that the homilies delivered by priests to the ecclesiastical people be grounded in the text of Sacred Scripture, and that they not indulge the fantasies of their own thoughts, as though seeking fame through some novel and unusual method of preaching. Saint Gregory rightly condemned this sort of preacher long ago, as noted in the annotation to Agobard’s letter *On the Manner of Ecclesiastical Government*, chapter 11. ID.], from their own judgment and not according to the sacred Scriptures. You yourselves also must preach useful, honorable, and upright things—things that lead to eternal life—and instruct others to preach these same things.

First of all, it must be preached universally to everyone that they believe the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit to be one almighty, eternal, invisible God, who created heaven and earth, the sea, and all that is in them; and that there is one divinity, substance, and majesty in the three persons of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.

[Col. 0183B] It must also be preached how the Son of God was incarnate from the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0183D] Here we have adopted the reading found in the Bavarian and Basel editions, confirmed by one Saint-Gall manuscript. Most manuscripts have only “from the Holy Spirit and Mary.” The same is read in the *Sacrosyllabic Book* of the Italian bishops, in the very old manuscript of Saint-Remi of Rheims, and in Sirmond’s edition: “He was born from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary.” In place of this, however, Tilius printed “from Mary.” ID.] and from Mary ever-virgin, for the salvation and restoration of the human race; how he suffered, was buried, rose again on the third day, and ascended into heaven; and how he will come again in divine majesty to judge all human beings according to their own merits; and how the impious, because of their crimes, will be sent with the devil into eternal fire [Note: [Col. 0183] “Eternal” in 1.], while the righteous will enter eternal life with Christ and his holy angels.

It must also be preached diligently concerning [Note: [Col. 0183] Absent in 1.] [Note: [Col. 0184D] This passage was mutilated in the earlier editions, except the Bavarian and Basel editions. Regino rendered the sense, not the words, as follows: “It must also be preached that all human beings will rise in their own flesh.” Burchard copied Regino. ID.] the resurrection of the dead, so that they may know and believe that they will receive the rewards of their merits in those same bodies.

It must also be preached to everyone with the greatest care for which crimes they will be assigned with the devil to eternal punishment. For we read, as the Apostle says: “The works of the flesh are manifest: fornication, uncleanness, licentiousness, the service of idols, [Col. 0184A] sorcery [Note: [Col. 0183] “Benefits” in 1.], enmities, quarrels, rivalries, hostilities, angers, fights, dissensions, heresies, sects, envies, murders, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these. I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God” [Note: [Col. 0183] “Will attain” in 4 and B.]. Therefore, forbid with all zeal these same things, which the great preacher of the Church named individually, understanding how dreadful is what he said: “Those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God.”

But admonish them with every urgency concerning love of God and neighbor, concerning [Note: [Col. 0183] Absent in 1.] faith and hope in God, humility and patience, chastity and self-restraint, kindness and mercy, almsgiving and confession of their sins, and that, according to the Lord’s Prayer, they forgive their debtors their debts; knowing with absolute certainty that those who do such things will possess the kingdom of God.

We enjoin this upon your charity with all the greater diligence because we know that in the last times false teachers will come, as the Lord himself foretold in the Gospel, and the Apostle [Note: [Col. 0183] “Apostles” in 1.] Paul testifies to Timothy. Therefore, beloved, let us prepare ourselves with all our hearts in the knowledge of truth, so that we may be able to resist those who oppose the truth; and, by the grace of God, may the word of God grow, run, and multiply for the advancement of the holy Church of God, the salvation of our souls [Note: [Col. 0183] “Your souls” in 2, 3, and B.], and the praise and glory of the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Peace to those who preach, grace to those who obey, glory to our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen [Note: [Col. 0183] The remainder is absent in 4.].

In the year of the Lord’s incarnation 789, in the twelfth indiction, [Col. 0184C] the twenty-first year [Note: [Col. 0183] “Year XXI” is absent in 5; “year XX” in 3.] of our reign, this edict of the present mission was enacted in the public palace at Aachen [Note: [Col. 0183] “Aachen” in B.]. This document was issued on the tenth day before the Kalends of April [Note: [Col. 0183] “Tenth” in 1.]. [Note: [Col. 0184D] In manuscript 3 this very ancient prayer formula is appended: “Truhtin god thu mir hilp. indi forgip mir gauuitzi. indi godan galaupun. thina minna indi rehtan uuilieon heili indi gasunti. indi thina guodunhuldi,” that is: “Lord God, help me and grant me wisdom and good faith, your love and right will, health and soundness, and your good favor.”]

CAPITULARY CONCERNING MONASTIC MATTERS (A.D. 789)

[Col. 0183]

The following two capitularies, first published by Amerbach, now appear again with the aid of six manuscripts, namely:—1. Saint-Gall Library manuscript no. 733, parchment, ninth century. —2. Royal Bavarian Library manuscript among the books of Saint Emmeram at Regensburg, marked E. 91, written in the year 821. —3. Royal Bavarian Library manuscript among the Tegernsee books [Col. 0185], manuscript, ninth century, from which Amerbach’s edition was derived. —4. Royal Library of Paris manuscript no. 4613, parchment, tenth century. —5. Gotha Ducal Library manuscript, eleventh century. 6. —Royal Library of Paris manuscript among the *Supplementa Latina*, no. 75, manuscript, tenth century, corresponding to the Saint Vincent of Metz manuscript. Baluzius had also examined manuscripts 1 and 4.

[Col. 0185A] 1. Concerning gyrovagous monks [Note: [Col. 0185B] Those who, as is read in the first chapter of the Rule of Saint Benedict, “stay for three or four days in the cells of different people throughout various provinces, always wandering and never stable, serving their own pleasures and the enticements of gluttony.” See also the Rule of the Master, chapters 1 and 7. BALUZ.] or [Note: [Col. 0185C] The first capitulary of the year 802, chapter 23: “Without a master or discipline; these are called Sarabaites.” Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 1: “The third and utterly detestable kind of monks is that of the Sarabaites, who, approved by no rule or tested by experience, as gold in a furnace, but softened like lead, still keep faith with the world in their works. By the tonsure they are known to lie to God. They live in pairs, threes, or singly, without a shepherd, shut up not in the Lord’s but in their own folds. The desire of their pleasures is law for them; whatever they think or choose, that they call holy, and whatever they do not want, they consider forbidden.” We have thought it useful to transcribe this entire passage from the Rule in order to shed light on this chapter. Anyone wishing to know more should read the learned notes of Hugh Menard on the *Concordia Regularum*, p. 104. ID.] Sarabaites [Note: [Col. 0185] “Sarabatos” in 1.].

2. Concerning anchorites: it is better that they be encouraged to remain in the community than that their minds should attempt to wander elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0185] “Attempts” in 1.].

3. [Note: [Col. 0185C] These provisions are taken from chapter 2 of the same Rule. ID.] That the shepherds of the souls entrusted to them not be negligent, nor take greater care of earthly profits than of the souls entrusted to them.

4. Concerning the obedience which abbots must render [Note: [Col. 0185C] This is abbreviated from chapter 5 of the same Rule. [Col. 0185D] ID.], and that they perform it without murmuring.

5. [Note: [Col. 0185D] From chapter 21 of the Rule. ID.] Concerning deans and superiors, that their replacement be carried out according to the Rule.

6. [Note: [Col. 0185D] The Thuanus manuscript and the editions of Amerbach and Herold: “Concerning the cellarer.” The same is read in chapter 12 of the Frankfurt capitulary, from which it appears that the law was copied. ID.] Concerning the cellarers of the monastery: they must not be appointed as greedy men, but as men of the sort prescribed by the Rule.

7. Wherever the bodies of saints rest, there shall be another chapel in which the brothers may pray privately.

[Col. 0185B] 8. [Note: [Col. 0185D] That is, gifts given out of charity, as Menard correctly interprets it in the same place, p. 875. This chapter must further be explained from chapter 54 of the Rule of Saint Benedict, from which it is taken: “A monk may by no means receive or give letters, blessings, or any small gifts, either from his parents, or from anyone, or to one another, without the command of the abbot.” See the Rule of the Master, chapter 76. ID.] Concerning *eulogies*.

[Col. 0186A] 9. [Note: [Col. 0186C] See the Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 53. ID.] Concerning the reception of guests, as the Rule prescribes.

10. [Note: [Col. 0186C] See the same Rule, chapter 55. ID.] Concerning the clothing of monks: where there is excess, let it be cut away; where there is deficiency, let it be increased.

11. [Note: [Col. 0186C] Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 58; Rule of the Master, chapter 88. ID.] Concerning those newly coming to the religious life [Note: [Col. 0185] “Thus” in 1, 2, and 5; “conversion” in 3 and B.], that they be tested according to the Rule and not received beforehand except as the Rule commands. No one is to be compelled to make a promise unwillingly. Concerning obedience and the stability of remaining, let it be as the Rule provides.

12. [Note: [Col. 0186C] Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 59: “If someone from the nobility should offer his son to God in a monastery, and the boy is still under age, his parents shall make the petition mentioned above, and, together with the offering, wrap that petition and the boy’s hand in the altar cloth, and thus offer him.” See the Rule of the Master, chapter 91. ID.] Concerning the sons of nobles who are offered.

13. [Note: [Col. 0186C] The Thuanus manuscript: “Concerning abbots who have been ordained.” We have preferred another reading because it is supported by a larger number of old books and because these words appear to have been copied from the heading of chapter 64 of the Rule of Saint Benedict. The words of the Rule, which explain this passage, are: “In the appointment of an abbot, this principle must always be observed: that he be appointed whom the whole harmonious community, according to the fear of God, or even the smaller, more sound-minded part of the community, shall choose by common counsel. Let the one to be ordained be chosen for the merit of his life and the wisdom of his teaching, even if he is last in the order of the community.” ID.] Concerning abbots to be ordained [Note: [Col. 0185] “In ordaining an abbot” in 2 and 3.].

14. [Note: [Col. 0186D] This is the heading of chapter 59 of the Rule of Saint Benedict. ID.] Concerning brothers sent on a journey.

15. [Note: [Col. 0186D] See below, chapter 14 of the Synod of Frankfurt. ID.] That no abbot seek a payment for receiving a monk.

16. [Note: [Col. 0186D] See the Frankfurt chapter 16. ID.] That regular monastic discipline be imposed on monks [Note: [Col. 0185] “On monks” in 2, 3, 5, and 6; Baluzius.], not secular discipline; that is, they must not be blinded [Note: The text appears corrupt; *orbentur* may refer to blinding or mutilation.], nor suffer other [Col. 0186B] mutilations except by authority of the Rule.

CAPITULARY OF GENERAL MATTERS (A.D. 789)

[Col. 0185]

I have used the same manuscripts as in the preceding capitulary.

[Col. 0185D] 1. That the counts first hear the cases of wards and orphans [Note: [Col. 0185D] Absent in 1.]. They are not to go hunting on the day when they must hold court, nor go to a meal.

2. Concerning oaths of fidelity, which they must swear to us and our sons, and which must be affirmed in these words: “Thus do I, N., promise to my lord King Charles and his sons: I am and shall remain faithful throughout the days of my life, without fraud or evil intent.”

3. Concerning small monasteries, where nuns sit without a Rule: we wish a regular community to be formed in one place, and the bishop is to take care where this can be done. No abbess shall presume to leave the monastery without our command, nor permit women to make themselves subject to her; their enclosure must be securely fortified, and no one there shall presume to write or send love songs (*winileudos*) [Note: [Col. 0187] *Uninileodos* in 2; *vuinileodus* in 3; *uenileudus* in 5; *uuinileodes* in 6 and B. “*Melius dis.*” in 4. The word is obscure.]; and concerning their pallor, because of the reduction of blood [Note: [Col. 0187] “Reduction of blood” in 6 and B.].

4. Concerning the books or manuscripts that are to be sought. No one shall presume to cast lots in a psalter, or in the Gospel, or in other matters [Note: [Col. 0187D] Formerly certain people, as the gloss on *Decretum* 26, question 2, chapter 3, “Those who,” says—the passage being taken from Augustine’s Letter 119 to Januarius—used certain verses of the Psalter or Gospel to divine the future. Januarius therefore asked Augustine whether this should be done. Augustine replied: “As for those who read lots from the pages of the Gospel, although it is preferable that they do this rather than resort to demons for consultation, nevertheless this practice also displeases me: to turn the divine oracles, which speak for another life, toward secular business and the vanity of this life.” It is worthwhile here to transcribe a notable passage from the *Life of Saint Hubert, Bishop of Liège*, written, I believe, by Jonah, Bishop of Orléans, from which it is easy to understand how this inquiry through sacred books was carried out. These are his words in chapter 15: “Accordingly, turning to the aids dear to them, they devoted themselves to prayer and a three-day fast, and, so that they might know the Lord’s will concerning this matter, they asked him with all their strength. Finally, as the third day of the fast was approaching, they placed two books upon the altar: one contained the most sacred text of the Gospel, while the other contained the blessings and consecrations by which the sacrament of the Mass is performed, namely, so that they might learn from the divine books what they ought to do in this matter. When the Gospel was opened, it first offered this sentence to the one reading: ‘Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found favor with the Lord.’ The Sacramentary, when opened, likewise presented these words first to the one who saw them: ‘Direct the way of your servant.’ Concerning the lots of the saints, see the Council of Venice, chapter 16; Agde, chapter 42; Orléans I, chapter 30; Auxerre, chapter 4; Regino, Book II, chapter 358; and Ivo, Part II, chapter 37.] nor observe any divinations [Note: [Col. 0187] Absent in 1.].

5. That no one boast of acquiring or retaining anything through an unjust procedure.

6. That those regulations established for preserving the king [Note: [Col. 0187] “For preservation” in 1; “for preserving” in 5.] not be abandoned for the sake of a reward.

7. That the bishops inspect the baptisteries of the priests, so that they baptize according to Roman custom [Note: [Col. 0187] “Name” in 4.].

8. Concerning footwear according to Roman usage.

9. That on feast days and Sundays everyone come to church, and that they not invite priests to their houses to celebrate Mass.

10. The evil of drunkenness must be prohibited altogether. We also prohibit those oaths that they make by Saint Stephen, or by us, or by our sons. And we command that bishops and abbots not go around the houses mixing [Note: The precise sense of *misciendo* is uncertain.].

11. Concerning what our envoys must investigate [Note: [Col. 0187] “Must investigate” in 6 and B.], lest some complaint arise against a bishop or abbot [Col. 0187C], or abbess, or count, or anyone holding any rank, and that they report it to us.

12. Concerning unjust tolls [Note: [Col. 0187] “*Cedoneis*” in 4.].

13. Concerning the hand of a leper.

14. That monks and those established in priestly orders not engage in secular business. As for the other tonsured men, time is to be granted until our synod.

15. That bishops, abbots, and abbesses not keep packs of dogs [Note: [Col. 0187] “*Coppla*” in 4; “*cuplas*” in 5; “*cupplas*” in 6 and B.], nor falcons, nor hawks [Note: [Col. 0187] “*Acceptores*” in 4 and 5.], nor jesters.

16. [Note: [Col. 0187] Chapters 16–18 are absent in 4.] Concerning the poor lying in the streets or at crossroads: they are to come to the church, and their confessions [Note: [Col. 0187] “Confession” in 1.] are to be heard.

17. That coverings or panelled ceilings be made over the altars.

18. That no one baptize bells [Note: [Col. 0188D] Elsewhere *signa*, that is, little bells or church bells. *Acts of Aldric, Bishop of Le Mans*: “lawful vesting through the *cloacae*.” Polyptych of Saint-Remi of Rheims: “three bronze *cloaccae*, two of iron.” See Lindenbrog’s Glossary and Vossius, *On the Vices of Speech*. BALUZ.], nor hang papers on poles [Note: [Col. 0187] “They hang” in 2; “he hangs” in 3.] on account of hail.

19. That our envoys inspect how our benefices have been put in order, and know how to report it to us.

20. Concerning lepers: they must not mix with the rest of the people.

[Col. 0188B] 21. We command our envoys above all that they demonstrate by their own deeds the good things which they teach others to do by our word.

After the foregoing chapters, the following two, addressed to the Lombards, appear in manuscript 4.

1. Likewise, concerning church property. We wish that if anyone wishes to take away any property from it on the testimony of witnesses, five or seven witnesses should give their testimony, and thus the property, whatever it may be, shall be taken away. For a testament of the kind the Romans make could not be made secure unless it were confirmed by five or seven witnesses.

2. Likewise, concerning treasure found beneath the earth: if it is found in church land, one third is to be assigned to the bishop. But if any Lombard or any other person should dig it up of his own free will, and the lord should give him something from it as his own, one quarter of it is to be taken from him, while the other three quarters are to come to us; and by our command no one shall presume to act otherwise.

CAPITULARY WHICH KING PIPPIN ESTABLISHED WITH HIS JUDGES AT PAVIA [Note: [Col. 0189D] Thus in 6 and 6b.] (A.D. 789 or 790)

[Col. 0189]

Each chapter of this edict had previously been published among the laws of the Lombards. We have revised it with the aid of the following manuscripts: 1. Saint-Gall manuscript of the ninth century, which nevertheless contains only chapters 5–9 and 12–14. 2. Saint Paul’s manuscript of the ninth century. 3. Paris manuscript no. 4613, tenth century, from which Baluzius had published it. 4. Chisian manuscript of the tenth century. 5. Cava manuscript of the eleventh century. 6. Gotha manuscript of the eleventh century. b. Modena manuscript in Muratori, together with the Ambrosian, Florentine, London, Vienna, Veronese, and Este manuscripts in Muratori [Note: [Col. 0189D] Chapters 2, 4, 5, 12, and 14, which mention Pavia, are also found in the manuscript formerly belonging to the Royal Bavarian Library at Munich.].

Although this capitulary precedes the constitution of the year 783 in the Lombard manuscripts and likewise in the Saint Paul’s, Paris, and Chisian manuscripts, I nevertheless have thought it should be assigned to a later period: first, because chapter 10, “Concerning women whose husbands appear to be in Francia,” seems to have been issued only after the year 787, when Charles brought the noble Lombards to Francia; and second, because chapters 1, 2, and 7 appear to refer to the capitularies of the years 783 and 789.

[Col. 0189A] In the name of the Lord. Here begin the chapters concerning various matters of justice, according to the memorandum of our lord Charles, our father [Note: [Col. 0189] Thus in 4.].

1. It has pleased and been agreed by us that all claims throughout our kingdom must be fully settled without any delay [Note: [Col. 0189D] Compare the capitulary of the year 781, chapter 12, and that of 783, chapter 1.] [Note: [Col. 0189] “Postponement” in V; “affection” in 2.] [Note: [Col. 0189D] Compare 781, chapter 1.] concerning churches as well as hospitals, the poor and widows, orphans, and all other people [Note: [Col. 0189] “People, as our lord Charles commanded” in V and Este], according to the order of our lord King Charles [Note: [Col. 0189D] Compare 789, II, 1.].

2. For we have established that, just as our lord King Charles [Note: [Col. 0189D] Compare 789, II, 1.] ordered concerning those monks who came from Francia or elsewhere and abandoned their monasteries, they must immediately return to those regions and to their monasteries, and none of you is to detain them.

3. Concerning priests who come from another parish [Note: [Col. 0189] “Province” in 2 and 5.], no one is to receive them without a letter of release from their bishop.

4. Concerning bishops, priests [Note: [Col. 0189] Absent in 6.], abbots, counts [Note: [Col. 0189] Absent in 2, 3, and 4.], royal vassals, and other men who come to the palace or depart from it, or travel anywhere through our kingdom: they themselves and their men must not presume to take away any man’s property or the fruit of his labor, unless they have purchased it or that man has given it to them of his own free will. When it is winter, no one is to deny lodging to those travelers, so long as they themselves take no case away unjustly. If anyone should presume to do this—whether a lord, a vassal, or the man himself—and that person should lodge a complaint against them, then we wish that the man who committed this wrong immediately make restitution, according to his law, for what he took from the complainant, and pay our fine to the palace [Note: [Col. 0189] Thus manuscripts 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, 6b, and the other Lombard manuscripts have the following, omitting the final seven words: “And if it happens that the matter was not immediately settled there according to law, and a complaint concerning it reached the palace, then we wish that the person who committed this wrong make restitution according to his law to the man who complained, and pay our fine to the palace, because he dared to do this in violation of our fine.”].

5. It has been agreed by us concerning those men who here in Italy leave their lords [Note: [Col. 0189D] Compare 781, chapter 11; absent in A, Fl, L, V, Vn, and Este.] [Col. 0190A], that no one should receive them into vassalage without the permission of their lord, before he has learned truthfully for what reason or fault the man left his lord. The man who wishes to receive him and keep him with him must present him in our presence—either personally or through his envoy—within forty nights after that man has come to him, if we are in Italy. If we are not in Italy, then, after we have returned in God’s name, he must present him in our presence within forty nights, as we have said above. If anyone presumes to act in this matter and does not fulfill it, he shall pay our fine to us.

6. It has been agreed by us concerning the *libellarii* [Note: [Col. 0190D] *Libellarii* are people who were made free by a charter. BALUZ.] that no count or their subordinates shall further constrain or harass them, except according to the custom that existed from the time of the Lombards [Note: [Col. 0189] “In” in 1 and 6.].

7. It has pleased us concerning the baptismal churches [Note: [Col. 0190D] Churches in which baptisteries have been established. ID.] that everywhere they must be ordered and maintained in the manner commanded by our lord King Charles [Note: [Col. 0190D] 782, chapter 1; 783, chapter 2.] and contained in his capitulary.

8. We have also established that the immunities confirmed by the aforesaid lord must be preserved in every respect as they are prescribed by the command of that lord, King Charles.

9. We have determined that the roads, ferries, and bridges throughout our kingdom must everywhere be fully repaired in the places where they have always existed. Under no circumstances are ferries to be established elsewhere across those rivers.

[Col. 0190C] 10. [Note: [Col. 0190D] This chapter is attributed to Charlemagne in the common edition of the Lombard Law. But the old copies have the name of Emperor Pippin written here. BALUZ. It is absent in A, Fl, L, V, Vn, and Este.] It has pleased us concerning those women whose husbands appear to be in Francia that our envoys investigate throughout our kingdom whether their rights are being fully upheld in the manner commanded by our lord [Col. 0191A], or not. If they are being upheld, good. If not, then we wish our envoys [Note: [Col. 0191] “Together with the count in whose jurisdiction she is” in 6; “together with the count whose jurisdiction it is” in 5.] to complete the matter as our lord commanded.

11. It has been agreed by us that we should send our envoys—one monk and one chaplain—throughout our kingdom to inspect and investigate the monasteries of men and women who ought to live under the holy Rule: how their dwelling is arranged, what their life and conduct are like, and what property each monastery appears to possess from which its members can live.

12. It has pleased us that no count or his subordinates should in any way presume to take away or withhold any man’s witnesses [Note: [Col. 0191] “To take away witnesses” is absent in 2, 3, and 5.], unless the person who is able to obtain and request those witnesses is permitted to have them. [Col. 0192A] If anyone presumes to act against this, it is our will that he come into our presence and there receive such a judgment concerning the matter as we shall wish to pronounce.

13. Concerning those free Lombards [Note: [Col. 0191] “men” in 1.], it was decided that they should have permission to commend themselves wherever they wished [Note: [Col. 0191] The remainder is missing in 3.], provided that they did not have a senior lord [Note: [Col. 0191] “if he has not been commended” in 1 and 6.], just as they had done from the time of the Lombards, to the extent that they should reasonably render to their own count [Note: [Col. 0191] “to his count” in 1 and 30.] what they owed.

14 [Note: [Col. 0191] This chapter is present in 1, 2, 4, 5, and 6, in the Lombard Laws, and in the Augsburg manuscript in Munich; it is absent from Baluze’s edition.]. No one shall presume to take away or invade another’s property, or anything else, without a judgment; and whoever presumes to do this shall pay our ban as a composition to us.

*(Here end the capitula.)*

# THE CAPITULARY OF FRANKFURT

[Note: [Col. 0191C] We have placed these chapters among the capitularies of Charlemagne because it is clear that they were issued by him at the synod of Frankfurt, which he himself calls his synodal council in the charter for Anianus, abbot of the monastery of Caunes; moreover, a large part of them was repeated from capitularies that preceded this year. We compared them with the same Rheims manuscript from which Sirmond published his edition, and likewise with another, more recent manuscript mentioned by Sirmond. François Pithou thought that these chapters had been enacted at the synod of Aachen held against Felix and Elipandus, at the word “Gunebodigni.” Peter Bonifantius held the same opinion, as I found recorded in his hand in the collection of councils published by Johannes Sagittarius in 1553: “Our friend D. Puteanus has in his possession manuscript canons of the council published at Aachen under Charlemagne against the impious heresy of Felix and Elipandus.” Certainly, in the Rheims manuscript from which, as we said, these chapters were published, there is no title and no mention of the place where the synod was held. Nevertheless, it may be gathered from the Annals of Einhard that they belong to the Synod of Frankfurt, which was assembled in the year 794 by order of Charlemagne. This synod was attended, together with legates of Hadrian, Roman pontiff, by Paulinus, patriarch of Aquileia, and Peter, archbishop of Milan, along with many other bishops, priests, and deacons. The Annals of Aniane add: “Among them also were the venerable and most holy abbot Benedict, who was called Vitiza, of the monastery of Aniane in the region of Gothia, and his religious monks Bede and Ardo, who is also Smaragdus, together with all his brothers and disciples. These are Ingila, Rabanus, and George.” Anianus, abbot of Caunes, also attended this synod with his monks, as is clear from the charter of Charlemagne cited shortly above. BALUZ.]

*(A.D. 794.)*

[Col. 0191]

I restored the text of this constitution with the aid of manuscripts in the Royal Library of Paris:

1. No. 164 bis among the Latin Supplements, from which Sirmond was the first to publish it in *Councils of Gaul*, vol. II, pp. 194 ff.; 2. No. 4628 A, together with copies made from it, namely 3, No. 4631, which I have attempted to present in an emended form. It remains to note that Baluze, in his edition, cut away chapters 1 and 2, contrary to the authority of the manuscripts.

[Col. 0191B] 1. With the apostolic authority and the command of our most pious lord, King Charles, having been joined together by God’s favor in the twenty-sixth year of his reign, all the bishops and priests of the kingdom of the Franks, as well as of Italy, Aquitaine, and Provence, assembled in a synodal council. Among them, he himself, the most gentle lord, was present at the holy assembly [Note: [Col. 0191] “assembly” in 2.]. At the beginning of the chapters, the matter arose concerning the impious and abominable heresy of Elipandus, bishop of the see of Toledo, and Felix, of Urgell, and their followers, who, thinking wrongly, asserted adoption in the Son of God. All the most holy fathers named above rejected this and unanimously opposed it; and they decreed that this heresy should be utterly eradicated from the holy Church [Note: [Col. 0191] 2 reads *heresim … eradicandam* (“the heresy … to be eradicated”) for *eresi … eradicandum*.]. [Textual variants: 2 reads *iussione* for *iussionem*, *primordio* for *primordia*, *e. est* for *exortum*, *eliphandi* for *Elipandi*, and *s. dicti sunt* (“the aforesaid”) for *supra*.]

[Col. 0192B] 2. A question was brought forward concerning the recent synod of the Greeks, which they held at Constantinople concerning the images that are to be worshiped [Note: [Col. 0191] 2 reads *nova* for *novo*, *q. de* for *quam*, and corrects *imagines* to *imaginibus*.]. It had been written there that they judged those who did not offer to the images of the saints the same service or adoration as to the divine Trinity to be anathema [Note: [Col. 0191] “to the images” corrected to “to the images” in 2]. Our most holy fathers named above, utterly rejecting both adoration and prayer and service [Note: [Col. 0191] “adoration” in 2.], despised and condemned this together with those who consented to it. After these matters had been completed [Note: [Col. 0191] 2 reads *quam* for *qui*, *o. adorationem* for *omnimodis*, and *peractis* (“completed”) for *peragratis* (“gone through”).].

3. A chapter was determined concerning Tassilo, who had formerly been duke of Bavaria [Note: [Col. 0192C] The *Chronicle of Moissac* says: “And at that same synod Tassilo came, who had formerly been duke of Bavaria, being the king’s cousin; and there he was reconciled with King Charles, renouncing all the authority he had held in Bavaria and handing it over to the king.” His mother was Hiltrude, sister of King Pippin, as is evident from the grants of the church of Salzburg in Canisius, vol. VI, p. 1157.], namely, the cousin of our lord King Charles. He stood in the midst of the most holy council, asking pardon for the offenses he had committed, both those which he had committed against King Pippin and the kingdom of the Franks and those which he had later committed under our most pious lord King Charles, in which he had proved false to his faith [Note: [Col. 0193] 1 corrects *fraudatur* to *fraudatus*.]. He appeared to request, by humble petition, that he might receive pardon from him. In a pure spirit he laid aside anger and every grievance on his own part, and whatever had been perpetrated against him and of which he was aware; moreover, he abandoned and renounced every legal claim and property belonging to him, insofar as these ought lawfully to have belonged to him or to his sons or daughters in the duchy of Bavaria. Thereafter he relinquished every dispute to be brought forward, without any claim for restitution, and commended his sons and daughters to the king’s mercy.

Therefore our lord, moved by mercy, freely forgave the aforesaid Tassilo the offenses he had committed [Col. 0193B], granted him complete favor, and appeared to receive him into his almsgiving in the affection of love, so that thereafter he might remain secure through God’s mercy. For this reason he ordered three briefs to be written concerning this chapter in identical form: one to be retained in the palace, another to be given to the aforesaid Tassilo so that he might keep it with him in the monastery, and the third to be deposited in the chapel of the sacred palace.

4. Our most pious lord the king, with the consent of the holy synod, decreed that no one, whether ecclesiastical or lay, should ever sell grain [Note: [Col. 0193] 1 corrects *uindat* to *uendat*.] at a higher price, whether in a time of abundance or in a time of scarcity, than the publicly established and newly fixed measure: one denarius for a measure of oats, two denarii for a measure of barley, three denarii for a measure of rye, and four denarii for a measure of wheat. If anyone wished to sell it as bread, he was to give twelve loaves of wheat, each weighing two pounds, for one denarius; fifteen rye loaves of equal weight for one denarius; twenty barley loaves, likewise weighed; and twenty-five oat loaves, likewise weighed.

As for the king’s public grain, if it is sold: two measures of oats for one denarius; one measure of barley for one denarius; two measures of rye for one denarius; and three measures of wheat for one denarius. Whoever holds a benefice from us must take the greatest care, insofar as God grants him ability, that none of the dependents belonging to that benefice dies of hunger; and whatever remains after the needs of his household may be sold freely according to the law prescribed above.

[Col. 0194A] 5. Concerning the denarius, know with absolute certainty our edict: in every place, in every city, and in every market [Note: [Col. 0193D] So the old manuscript reads throughout, with a word derived from *emere*, “to buy,” in the same manner as in Book 1 of the *Capitularies*, chapter 69, where *pulsaturio* is read in the Orléans manuscript instead of the reading *pulsatorio* found in others. Duchesne and Sirmond published *emporio*.], these new denarii shall circulate and be accepted by everyone. If they bear the image of our name and are pure silver, fully weighing their proper amount, and anyone rejects them anywhere in any transaction of purchase or sale, then, if he is a free man, he shall pay fifteen solidi for the king’s use; if he is of servile condition and the transaction is his own, he shall lose the transaction or be flogged naked publicly before the people. But if he acted on the order of his lord, then that lord shall pay fifteen solidi, if this is proved against him.

6. It has been decreed by our lord the king and the holy synod that bishops shall administer justice in their dioceses. If any person in a bishop’s diocese—abbots, priests, deacons, subdeacons, monks, other clerics, or anyone else—does not obey his bishop, they shall come before their metropolitan, and he shall judge the case together with his suffragan bishops. Our counts also shall come to the judgment of the bishops. If there is anything that the metropolitan bishop cannot correct or settle, then at last the accusers shall come, together with the accused, with letters to the metropolitan, so that we may know the truth of the matter [Note: [Col. 0193] “of it” in 1.].

7. It has been decreed by our lord the king and the holy synod that a bishop shall not move from city to city, but shall care for his own church. Likewise, a priest and a deacon shall remain in their own churches canonically.

[Col. 0194C] 8. Concerning the dispute between Ursio, bishop of Vienne [Note: [Col. 0193] 1 reads *usione uieniensis*.], and Eliphantus, advocate of the bishop of Arles [Note: [Col. 0193D] This word has been restored from an old copy; it had dropped out of Sirmond’s edition. From this it may be inferred that Eliphantus, bishop of Arles, was not present at the Synod of Frankfurt. BALUZ.], the letters of the blessed Gregory, Zosimus, Leo, and Symmachus were read. They determined that the church of Vienne ought to have four suffragan sees, over which it should preside as the fifth; and that the church of Arles ought to have nine suffragan sees, over which it itself should preside. Concerning Tarentaise, Embrun, and Aix, a delegation was sent to the apostolic see; whatever the pontiff of the Roman Church should determine was to be observed.

9. It was also decreed by the same lord king and by the holy synod that Peter [Note: [Col. 0193] 1 reads *Petus* for *Petrus*.] [Note: [Col. 0194D] Verdun is in Belgica Prima, as the most learned Charles Le Cointe correctly notes in his *Ecclesiastical Annals of the Franks*. In Book III of his *Antiquities of Belgic Gaul*, fols. 140–141, Richard Wasseburg relates that he was suspected, about the year 784, of having participated in the conspiracy against Charlemagne made by Count Ardico in Austrasia; although he could not be convicted, he nevertheless fell from Charles’s favor and was forbidden to be at court for twelve years. At last he cleared himself at the Synod of Frankfurt and afterwards received permission to come to the palace. That conspiracy of Ardico, or Hardrad—for this is the true name—occurred in 785, as Einhard says in the *Annals*: “In that same year an excessive conspiracy against the king took place beyond the Rhine among the eastern Franks, and Count Hartrad was known to have been its author. But information about it was quickly brought to the king, and through his prudence so strong a conspiracy subsided in a short time without any great danger, its authors being condemned, some to loss of sight and others to exile.” Einhard also mentions the same conspiracy under the year 817. Likewise Thegan, in Book 22 of the *Deeds of Louis the Pious*, explains Hardrad’s plans more openly: “He [Reginharius] was the son of the daughter of Hardiat, the most faithless duke of Austria, who had long before wished to rise against Lord Charles and diminish his kingdom.” The author of the *Ecclesiastical Annals* cited above nevertheless thinks that Peter, bishop of Verdun, cleared himself at the Synod of Frankfurt because he was said to have taken part in the conspiracy recently undertaken against King Charles and his kingdom by his son Pippin. See the *Chronicle of Verdun* by Hugh, abbot of Flavigny, p. 117. BALUZ.] bishop of Verdun, should swear before God and his angels, with two or three men, as he had received the oath [Col. 0195A], or certainly with his archbishop, that he had not plotted either the king’s death or anything against his kingdom, and that he had not been disloyal to him [Note: [Col. 0196D] Sirmond thought that this referred to the conspiracy exposed at Regensburg in 792, whose author was Pippin, king of Italy. But from the material reported from Wasseburg it appears that this story must be assigned to another period. ID.]. Since the bishop could not find men with whom he might swear, he chose for himself that his own man should go to the judgment of God, and that this man should testify, without relics and without the holy Gospels, solely before God, that he himself was innocent in this matter; and that, according to his innocence, God should help that man of his who was to go to that judgment—and who did go.

Nevertheless, the bishop’s man went to the judgment of God neither by the king’s arrangement nor by the judgment of the holy synod, but by his own spontaneous will; and he emerged competent, having also been delivered by the Lord. Yet the clemency of our king [Note: [Col. 0195] “the clemency of the kingdom” in 1.] granted its favor to the aforesaid bishop [Col. 0195B] and enriched him with his former honors, not allowing him to remain without honor, since it had found that he had deserved no harm from the fabricated accusation.

10. It was indeed decreed by our lord the king, and is recognized as having been decreed by the holy synod, that Gaerbodus, who claimed to be a bishop but had no witnesses to his own ordination, although he had received episcopal status through Magnardus, the metropolitan bishop [Note: [Col. 0196D] Archbishop of Rouen.], and who had also confessed that he himself had been ordained deacon and priest not according to canonical ordination, should be deposed from the episcopal rank which he claimed to possess, by the aforesaid metropolitan or by the bishops of the province [Note: [Col. 0195] Sirmond conjectured *consecutus* (“obtained”) for the manuscript reading.].

11. [789. Genesis 14.] Monks shall not go out to engage in secular business or secular lawsuits, unless they act as the Rule itself has prescribed.

12. Recluses shall not be made except those whom the bishop of the province and the abbot have previously approved; and they shall enter the place of enclosure according to their direction.

13. The abbot shall sleep with his monks, according to the Rule of Saint Benedict.

14. [789. Monastic chapter 6.] Cellarers in monasteries shall not be chosen for their greed; rather, such men shall be elected as the Rule of Saint Benedict teaches.

[Col. 0196A] 15. [Chapter 7.] Concerning monasteries where the bodies of saints are located: they shall have an oratory within the cloister, where a special and continuous office shall be performed.

16. [Chapter 15.] For we have heard that certain abbots, led by greed, demand payments from those entering the monastery. Therefore it has pleased us and the holy synod that no money whatsoever be demanded for receiving brothers into the holy order; rather, they shall be received according to the Rule of Saint Benedict.

17. [Chapter 13.] An abbot shall not be elected in a congregation where there is a royal command, except with the consent of the bishop of that place [Note: [Col. 0196D] This clause is of great importance. It shows that privileges once granted to monasteries must be understood in such a way that the rights of bishops nevertheless remain unharmed. More will be said about this in the notes on chapter 81 of Book 1 of the *Capitularies*.].

18. [Chapter 16.] Whatever offense monks may have committed, we by no means permit abbots to have them blinded or to inflict mutilation of their limbs, unless they are subjected to regular discipline.

19. [789. Ecclesiastical chapter 14.] Priests, deacons, monks, and clerics shall not enter taverns for drinking.

20. [Chapter 55.] A bishop may not be ignorant of the canons and the Rule.

21. [Chapter 15.] Sunday shall be observed from vespers until vespers.

22. [Chapter 19.] Bishops ought not to be ordained in little villages or in villages.

23. [Chapter 23.] Concerning other people’s slaves: no one shall receive them, nor shall bishops ordain them, without the permission of their masters.

24. [Chapter 27.] Clerics and monks shall remain in their chosen way of life.

[Col. 0196C] 25. [779. Chapter 13.] All those who owe them by reason of benefices and church property shall pay tithes, ninths, and all dues generally, according to the earlier capitularies of our lord the king. Every person shall also contribute a lawful tithe from his own property to the church. We learned by experience that in the year [Note: [Col. 0195] 1 reads *anna* for *anno*.] *(A.D. 779)* when that severe famine came upon us, empty granaries boiled over, devoured by demons, and voices of reproach were heard.

26. The houses of churches and their roofs shall be repaired or restored by those who hold benefices from them. Wherever truthful men are found to testify that timber, stones, or tiles which had belonged to church buildings are now in someone’s own house, all of it shall be restored to the church from which it was taken.

27. [789. Ecclesiastical chapter 24.] Clerics shall by no means transfer from one church to another, nor shall they be received without the knowledge of their bishop and letters of commendation from the diocese in which they had been. Otherwise discord might arise in the church. Wherever such men are now found, they shall all return to their own church, and no one shall dare to retain one of them after his bishop or abbot wishes to receive him back. If perhaps the senior does not know where he ought to seek his cleric, whoever has him shall keep him under [Col. 0197B] custody and shall not permit him to wander elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0197] That is, “to wander.”] until he is restored to his master.

28. [Chapter 25.] They shall not be ordained unconditionally.

29. Each bishop shall teach and instruct his subjects well, so that worthy men may always be found in the house of God who can canonically be chosen [Note: [Col. 0197] “can” is misspelled *possi* in 1.].

30. [Chapter 28.] Concerning clerics who quarrel with one another or act against their bishop: they shall proceed in every respect as the canons teach. If a quarrel should arise between a cleric and a layman, the bishop and the count shall meet together and, in agreement, determine the case between them according to justice.

31. [Chapter 29.] Concerning oaths and conspiracies: they shall not be made; and wherever they are found, they shall be destroyed.

32. [Chapter 31.] Monasteries shall be guarded according to canonical institution.

33. [Chapter 32.] The Catholic faith of the holy Trinity, the Lord’s Prayer, and the creed shall be preached and taught to everyone.

34. [Chapter 33.] Greed and covetousness are to be trampled underfoot.

35. [Chapter 74.] Hospitality is to be practiced [Note: [Col. 0197] 1 reads *sectenda* for *sectanda*.].

36. [Chapter 35.] Criminals shall not have the right to accuse elders or their bishops.

37. [Chapter 34.] Concerning reconciliation in time of necessity.

38. Priests who are obstinate against their bishops shall by no means communicate with the clerics who live in the king’s chapel [Note: [Col. 0197D] Flodoard, Book III, chapter 23, concerning Hincmar’s letters: “to have brought them from the old royal chapel.” *Capitulary of the year 756*, chapter 6: “let them come into the king’s chapel.” See Charlemagne’s *Capitulary concerning estates*, chapter 6. BALUZ.], unless they have been reconciled by their bishop, lest canonical excommunication thereby come upon them.

39. If a priest is caught in a criminal act, he shall be brought before his bishop and restrained according to canonical institution. If he wishes to deny it, and the accuser cannot provide proof, and the matter cannot be settled before the bishop, then the case shall be referred to their general council.

[Col. 0198A] 40. [Chapter 40.] Girls who have been deprived of their parents shall be entrusted, under the supervision of bishops and priests, to respectable women, as canonical authority teaches.

41. [Chapter 41.] No bishop shall lose his own see by frequenting another place, nor shall he dare to remain in his own properties for more than three weeks. The relatives or heirs of a bishop shall by no means inherit, after his death, property acquired by him after his ordination, whether by purchase or by gift; rather, it shall belong canonically to his own church. Those possessions which he had previously held shall pass to his heirs and relatives, unless he had made a gift of them to the church.

42. [Chapter 42.] No new saints shall be venerated or invoked, nor shall memorials of them be erected along the roads; only those shall be venerated in the church who have been approved by the authority of their passions or by the merit of their lives.

43. [Chapter 64.] With regard to the destruction of trees and sacred groves, canonical authority shall be observed.

44. [Chapter 44.] Chosen judges from both sides shall not be rejected.

45. [Chapter 63.] Canonical observance shall govern the witnesses of these matters. Little children shall not be brought to the oath, as the Guntbadingi do.

46. [Chapter 46.] Concerning virgins: at what time they should be veiled, and for what occupations [Note: [Col. 0197] Sirmond conjectured *occasionibus* (“circumstances”) for the manuscript reading *occupationibus*.] before the age of twenty-five; if necessity compels, let those matters be sought which are written in the canon.

[Col. 0198C] 47. Concerning abbesses who do not live canonically or according to the Rule: the bishops shall investigate and report them to the king, so that they may be deprived of their honor.

48. [Chapter 47.] In the case of offerings contributed to the church or for the use of the poor, canonical procedure shall be observed; they shall not be administered by anyone other than the person whom the bishop has appointed.

49. Priests are not to be ordained before their thirtieth year of age.

50. [Chapter 50.] When the sacred mysteries have been completed, during the solemn celebration of Mass, everyone in general shall offer peace to one another.

51. [Chapter 53.] Names shall not be recited before the offering is made.

[Col. 0198D] 52. [Chapter 54.] No one shall believe that God may be prayed to only in three languages; for God is adored in every language, and a person is heard if he asks for what is just.

53. [Chapter 55.] No bishop or priest may be ignorant of the sacred canons.

54. Concerning churches built by free men: they may lawfully be transferred or sold, provided only that the church is not destroyed, but that its services are maintained every day [Note: [Col. 0199B] Sirmond published “be preserved.” Sirmond’s emendation may perhaps be correct. For it may be inferred that the words *servire* and *servare* were sometimes interchanged, from chapter 67 of Book 1 of the *Capitularies*, where the better manuscripts read *honores serventur*, “the services shall be preserved,” while the Pithoean, Camberon, Orléans, Thuane, Parisian, Dijon, and Metz manuscripts have *serviant*, “let them serve,” and the Tilian has *servant*. The Basel edition likewise has *serviant*. Herold, however, noted in the margin that *serventur* should be read. Antonius Augustinus observes in his *Glossary to Julian the Antecessor* that the word *observent* in chapter 29 of Novel 123 is used for *observentur*. BALUZ.].

55. Our lord the king also said in the same synod that he had received permission from the apostolic see [Note: [Col. 0199B] In those times our kings were accustomed to request from the Roman pontiffs bishops and priests who would remain continually at the palace. I find the origin of this practice in letter 26 of the *Caroline Code*, which is a letter of Pope Paul to King Pippin. It contains these words: “Your exalted Christianity has asked us, through the same letters, to grant that Bishop George and Priest Peter should remain in your service. Indeed, let your most excellent benevolence recognize that we long ago complied with this wish of yours.” But the following admonition of Pope Paul is both excellent and full of holiness. He adds: “For this reason, write to us what we ought to do concerning the episcopate of the aforesaid George and the church entrusted to the aforementioned Peter, lest, after being warned, they fall into excessive negligence.” Paul therefore thought that George and Peter could not govern their churches at the same time as they were at the palace. He accordingly asks Pippin to write back what he wishes to be decided concerning George’s episcopate and the church entrusted to Peter, lest, after their removal, their absence as rulers cause loss and damage. I believe that *amotis*, “after their removal,” should be read there instead of *admonitis*, “after being warned,” which the printed editions have.

Moreover, in addition to the authority of the Roman pontiff, the consent of the bishops or Gallican councils was also necessary for bishops and priests to have permission to reside at the palace. In this chapter from Frankfurt we read that Charlemagne acted in this way when he wished first to have Angilramnus and then Hildeboldus at his palace for ecclesiastical purposes. Hincmar is also a witness to this in Letter 14, chapter 14, where he speaks of the ministry and office of the archchaplain: “From the time of Pippin and Charles, this office was sometimes carried out by priests, sometimes by bishops, by royal will and episcopal consent, and more often by deacons or priests than by bishops, because bishops ought continually to watch over their flocks by example and word, and according to the sacred canons must not remain away from their dioceses for a longer time.” In the following chapter he lists the priests who were archchaplains under Pippin, Charles, and Louis. ID.], namely, from Hadrian the pontiff, to keep Angilramnus [Note: [Col. 0199] “Angliramnus” in 1.] the archbishop [Note: [Col. 0200B] Of Metz. He was called an archbishop, although he was not a metropolitan, because he was the chief chaplain of the sacred palace; in the same way Fulradus, abbot of Saint-Denis, who held the same dignity in the palace of Pippin and Charles, was called archpriest of France in a letter of Pope Hadrian to Tilpin, archbishop of Rheims, preserved by Flodoard. Angilramnus is also said to have been Charlemagne’s chancellor in the *Chronicle of the monastery of Senones*. If this is true, it confirms the opinion of those who think that under the second dynasty of our kings the offices of archchaplain and archchancellor were combined. ID.], continually in his palace for ecclesiastical purposes.

He asked the same synod that, just as he had had Angilramnus, he should likewise have Bishop Hildeboldus [Note: [Col. 0200C] He presided over the see of Cologne.] because he had apostolic permission concerning him just as he did concerning Angilramnus. The entire synod consented, and it pleased them that Hildeboldus should be at the palace for ecclesiastical purposes.

56. He also requested that the holy synod itself should deign to receive Alcuin [Note: [Col. 0200C] This concerns Alcuin. The old manuscript has *Aliquinum* instead of *Alquinum*. In the will of Count Evrard, in Aubert Miraeus’s *Code of Pious Donations*, p. 99: “Alcuin’s book to Count Wido.” Thiofridus, abbot of Echternach, also calls him *Alicuinus* in the prologue to the *Life of Saint Willibrord*, as Johannes Roberti reports in his notes on Thiofridus’s epitaphs, p. 81.
