The *Annals of Aniane* in our old manuscript say: “This book”—that is, the Gospel text—“was copied in his own hand by Alcuin, the teacher and instructor of the same king, who is also called Albinus.” ID.] into its fellowship [Note: [Col. 0199] “fellowship,” conjectured by Sirmond for *confortio* in 1.] and prayers, because he was a man learned in ecclesiastical teachings. The entire synod, following our lord the king’s admonition, consented and received him into their fellowship and prayers.

# THE SAXON CAPITULARY

*(A.D. 797, October 28, Aachen.)*

[Col. 0199]

I restored the constitution, made public by Holstenius from a Roman manuscript, to its integrity with the aid of: 1. the same manuscript, among the Palatine manuscripts of the Vatican Library, no. 289, fols. 62–64, ninth century; and 2. the Corbie manuscript, ninth or tenth century, pp. 28–33.

[Col. 0199D] In the year 797 from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ [Note: [Col. 0199] “1294” in 2.], and in the thirtieth and twenty-second years [Note: [Col. 0199] “twenty-fifth” in 2.], while our lord Charles, most excellent king, was reigning, venerable bishops and abbots, illustrious counts, and others assembled at the palace at Aachen [Note: [Col. 0199] “palace” in 1; “of the palace” in 2.] in his service, on the fifth day before the Kalends of November. At the same time Saxons gathered from various districts, both Westphalians and Angarians and also Eastphalians [Note: [Col. 0201] “Westphalians and Angarians … Eastphalians” in 2.], and all unanimously agreed and arranged that, concerning those chapters for which Franks pay a composition of sixty solidi if they transgress the king’s ban, the Saxons should likewise pay if they violated those bans anywhere.

## THESE ARE THE CHAPTERS

1. [Note: [Col. 0201D] This chapter is composed from chapters 2, 3, and 4 of the capitulary of the year 788. Indeed, it may be inferred that the remaining chapters of that capitulary are also missing here from the next chapter of this capitulary, for there it is written: “If anyone transgresses the eight chapters mentioned above,” and so forth. ID.] Churches, widows, orphans, and the less powerful [Note: [Col. 0201] “the powerful” in 1.] shall have just and peaceful protection. No one shall presume to commit abduction, violence [Note: [Col. 0201] “theft” in 2.], or arson within the country. No one from the army shall presume to remain behind in violation of the lord king’s ban.

2. If anyone transgresses the eight chapters mentioned above [Note: [Col. 0201] “four” in 2.], all agreed and arranged that the Saxons should likewise pay a composition of sixty solidi, just as the Franks do.

3. It also pleased all the Saxons that wherever Franks are required by law to pay fifteen solidi, the more noble Saxons should pay twelve solidi, free men five, and *liti* four.

4. They also decreed that whenever any case within the country has been settled with its own neighbors, the local people should, according to customary practice, receive twelve solidi as a penalty, and should be granted what they customarily exacted as *wargida*. If cases are settled in the presence of royal envoys, the local people shall likewise be granted the aforesaid twelve solidi for the *wargida*. Because the royal envoy has been burdened by this matter, he shall receive another twelve solidi from it for the king’s share [Col. 0201C].

If the case has been brought to the palace to be settled in the king’s presence, then both sums of twelve solidi—that is, the amount for the *wargida* and the amount that he ought to have paid his neighbors because the case was not settled within the country—shall be paid to the king’s share [Note: [Col. 0201] “to the kings” in 1.], making twenty-four solidi.

If there is someone who, in the country, refuses to settle according to what his neighbors have judged, and comes to the palace for this reason, and it is there judged that the neighbors had pronounced a just judgment, then, on the first occasion, as stated above, he shall pay twenty-four solidi to the king’s share. If, after returning from there, he refuses to settle and do justice, and is summoned again to the palace and judged there concerning this matter, he shall pay twice twenty-four solidi. But if, still not corrected [Col. 0201D], he returns to the palace a third time for the same matter, he shall make a triple composition for it to the king’s share.

5. If one of the nobles, having been summoned, refuses to come to the court, he shall pay four solidi; a free man, two; a *litus*, one.

[Col. 0202A] 6. Concerning priests, they decreed that if anyone presumes to do or take anything contrary to justice against them or their men, he shall restore everything to them twofold and pay a composition.

7. Concerning the king’s envoys, they decreed that if one of them is killed, whoever presumes to do this shall pay a triple composition for him. Likewise, whatever is done to them or to their men, they shall cause everything to be restored threefold and shall pay a composition according to their law.

8. Concerning arson, it was agreed that no one should presume to commit it within the country out of anger, hostility, or any malicious desire. The exception is if someone is such a rebel that he refuses to do justice, cannot otherwise be constrained, and has refused to come to us to render justice in our presence. In that event the local people shall come together in a common assembly according to the agreed arrangement; and if they unanimously consent, the house [Note: [Col. 0201] Thus in 1 and 2; that is, “the dwelling.”] of that person may be burned as a means of coercion. Then, after a common decision has been made in that assembly, the matter shall be carried out according to their law, and not on account of any anger or malicious intention, but solely as a means of enforcing our authority.

If anyone dares to act otherwise, he shall pay a composition of sixty solidi, as stated above.

9. It was agreed that, whenever the lord king wished—for the sake of peace, because of a feud, or for more important causes—to establish a stronger ban, he might, with the consent of the Franks and the faithful Saxons, double the sixty-solid penalty, or impose a penalty of one hundred solids or even up to one thousand, according as he deemed appropriate and as the case and circumstances required, on anyone who transgressed his command.

10. Concerning wrongdoers who, according to the Saxon law, ought to incur the penalty of death: it was agreed by all that, if any one of them should flee for refuge to the royal authority, it should lie within the king’s power either to return him to them for execution, or, with their consent, to have the right to place that wrongdoer, together with his wife, household, and all his property, outside the homeland, within his kingdoms or in the borderlands, wherever he wished; and they were to regard him as though dead. [Note: MS 1 reads *regium*; MS 2 corrects *regium* to *regiam*. MS 1 reads *foras*, corrected to *foris*.]

11. It must be noted what the solids of the Saxons are: namely, an ox of either sex, in the autumn, when it is brought into the stall, is valued at one solid; likewise in spring, when it leaves the stall. Thereafter, as it increases in age, so let its value increase. As for grain, they give forty *scapili* of bortrine grain for one solid, and twenty of rye. The northern people, however, give thirty *scapili* of oats and fifteen of rye for one solid. [Note: MS 1 reads *aut* (“or”); MS 2, *et* (“and”).] For one solid of bortrine value they give one and a half *sigla* of honey; the northern people, however, give two *sicli* of honey for one solid. Likewise, they are to give cleaned barley, like rye, for one solid. In silver, twelve denarii make a solid. [Note: MS 2 reads: “in silver, fifteen, and thereafter in commodities.”] And in other commodities the entire valuation of the compensation is to be made according to this price. [Note: The words *compositionis sunt* (“of the compensation is”) are absent from MS 2.]

# RHISPACH AND FRISING STATUTES (20 August 799)

Bernard Pez, in his *Codex diplomaticus*, p. 1, col. 74, had published an encyclical of Arno, bishop of Salzburg, by which he invited the bishop of Bavaria to a synod to be held on 20 August at Rhispach, in the diocese of Regensburg. The names of those who attended are preserved in the *History of Freising* by Meichelbeck, vol. I, p. 94; the decrees, however, are now published for the first time from the Blankenburg manuscript of the ducal library at Wolfenbüttel, tenth century, where they are found on fols. 83–85. The year in which the synod was held is not entirely certain; but, contrary to Mansi’s arguments, that it preceded the year 801 is clear from chapter 5, which prescribes prayer for the king’s welfare. We append what immediately follows in the manuscript, fols. 85–86: the equally unpublished Synod of Salzburg.

## SYNODAL DECREE OF THE BISHOPS BY ORDER OF THE LORD CHARLES

1. Therefore it was agreed that the aforesaid holy assembly should, with the help of the Lord God almighty, establish among its members an indissoluble bond of charity, so that, united and with one voice, they might honor God the Father in heaven and perpetually secure among themselves the concord of peace by a lasting bond—which the whole Christian people ought unceasingly to preserve, but especially those who are devoted to the duties of the ecclesiastical order. For themselves and for the salvation of all Christendom they ought to offer spotless sacrifices to the Lord Christ.

2. For they warned in that council that none of them—whether bishop, abbot, presbyter, monk, or any other minister of the holy Church of God, or nun—should presume to deviate from the straight path. Whoever ought to live a canonical life was to preserve that canonical life rightly and according to due order, without any transgression; and those who had vowed to observe the monastic life under a rule were likewise to do so.

3. They decreed that no one among the ecclesiastical orders should, for any reason, dare to resort to secular courts without the judgment of his own bishop or even the consent of the metropolitan. But if some matter should arise within the holy churches, it must be sought and settled with complete charity and mutual concord. If a bishop, abbot, or presbyter should have a dispute among themselves concerning a secular matter, then, with charity moderated and the bond of peace unbroken, and with the counsel of their bishop, they should faithfully and devoutly agree with one another concerning the matters at issue, without injury or condemned oaths, after justice had been carried out between them, in the fear of the Lord. If justice could not be achieved between them with the counsel of the bishop, then the matter should be referred to the metropolitan bishop, and everything should be completed with his counsel, consent, and command.

4. They also decreed that, with the counsel and consent of all, alms should be given four times a year for the remedy of souls: namely, on the Saturday before Palm Sunday; on the Saturday of Pentecost; on the third day of the seventh month; and on the Saturday immediately before the Nativity of the Lord. This should be done publicly, not for human praise or the reward of empty glory, but for eternal recompense and as an example to the Christian people. Hence the Lord himself says in the Gospel: “Let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.” No one is to do this unwillingly or under compulsion; rather, each person should strive to give according to his means by his own free judgment, for God will not ask how much was given, but with what willingness it was offered. A good intention will be reckoned as the deed itself.

5. It was likewise agreed by the holy council that on Wednesday and Friday all clergy should abstain from meat and wine and recite the litany at the ninth hour, with the solemnities of Mass, for the safety, prosperity, and stability of the whole holy Church of God, for the eternal salvation and perpetual life of the Christian people and their souls, and for the life, safety, and stability of the empire of the lord king and his sons. The following days are excepted: from the Nativity of the Lord through the octave of Epiphany; from Easter through holy Pentecost; and the principal feasts, namely those of Saint Mary, Saint John the Baptist, the twelve apostles, Saint Michael the archangel, and Saint Martin, as well as the revered feast of the particular parish. We also grant exemption when the duty of charity must be fulfilled for the arrival of visiting brethren, for those stationed in the army or on a journey, for those coming to the palace of the lord king, and for those detained by illness.

As for Lenten foods and drinks, their use is left to each person’s discretion. Above all, however, care must be taken not to consume food and drink to satiety, but more sparingly. [Note: That is, *parcius*.] Whoever abstains more is to know that he will have the greater reward. If anyone in the ecclesiastical order or clerical office voluntarily strives to fulfill this, he is exhorted always to advance toward what is better. But if anyone among them is negligent and sluggish, he is to be corrected and, unwillingly and even under compulsion through our admonition and correction, made to do it. We also admonish that this be proclaimed among the people, so that through exhortation, persuasion, and every suitable opportunity we may persuade the people to observe it; let us carry this out faithfully and devoutly with every effort. Likewise, we have decreed that the remaining chapters of our agreement be briefly set down one by one.

6. That councils be held twice a year, as is contained in chapter 19 of the Council of Chalcedon.

7. Concerning the ordination of presbyters and deacons only at the proper times, as is contained in chapter 3 of the decrees of Pope Zosimus and likewise in chapter 11 of the decrees of Pope Gelasius.

8. That peace be commanded to be preserved by all in the Church, as is contained in chapter 1 of the rule of Pope Innocent.

9. That no one, rejecting ordinary clothing, assume new and unusual garments—namely what is commonly called *cotzos* or *trembilos*—as is prohibited in the preface to the Synod of Gangra and stated in the decrees of Gelasius. [Note: C reads *gangensis* for *Gangrensis*.]

10. That no presbyter or other member of the clergy exact usury, as in chapter 3 of the decrees of Pope Leo and likewise in chapter 15 of the decrees of Pope Gelasius.

11. That no bishop or abbot dare seize the property of nobles for the sake of ambition, as is contained in canon 5 of the Council of Carthage. [Note: C reads *attrahere* for *atrahere*.] [Note: MS 1 reads *mobilium* (“of movable property”) for *nobilium*.]

12. If any priest acts presumptuously against the decretal statutes and refuses to reform, he is to be removed from his office and marked out to all, so that no one may receive him into his fellowship. Whoever does so will likewise be subject to the same sentence. We establish the same rule for laypeople, as is contained in chapter 5 of the decrees of Pope Leo.

13. [Note: Chapters 13–15 are also found in the formerly Tegernsee manuscript, now in the Royal Library at Munich; in the Gotha manuscript they were incorrectly treated and numbered as a continuation of the capitulary, from which I have added various readings. Chapter 13 is also found among the Lombard laws of Charles, chapter 95, in Muratori.] That the tithes of the people be divided into four parts: one part for the bishop, another for the clergy, a third for the poor, and a fourth to be applied to the construction of churches. [Note: C reads *amplificetur* (“be enlarged”); the Tegernsee and Gotha manuscripts have *amplicetur* (“be applied”).] This is contained in chapter 27 of the decrees of Pope Gelasius. [Note: Chapter 27 is absent from the Gotha manuscript.]

14. That we provide widows, wards, orphans, the blind, and the lame with protection and assistance according to our ability and means, as is contained in the lord king’s ordinance.

15. Concerning incantations, auguries, divinations, and those who cause storms or perform other harmful magic: it pleased the holy council that, wherever such people are discovered, the archpresbyter of that diocese should see to it that they are subjected to the most diligent examination, in case they should confess the evils they have committed. [Note: Tegernsee reads *reprehensi* (“rebuked” or “detected”) for *depraehensi* (“discovered”).] But this punishment must be imposed with such moderation that they do not lose their lives, but are saved while afflicted in prison, until, by God’s inspiration, they promise to amend their sins. [Note: The word *afflicti* (“afflicted”) is absent from C but present in T and Goth.] They are in no way to be released by counts or centenarii through any gifts without a strict examination. [Note: C reads *aliquam* for *aliqua*.] If they do this, the archpresbyters, when they learn of it, must not dare to conceal it from the bishops; and the bishops are to correct them for this as is proper.

16. That all presbyters teach the people to avoid the wicked use of oaths, as is contained in chapter 19 of the Council of Chalcedon.

17. That no member of the clergy permit a woman to live with him in his house, because of the danger of suspicion, except his mother, sister, or aunt, or women who are beyond evil suspicion, as is contained in the Council of Nicaea. If, after this agreement, anyone keeps women in his house, he is to be deposed. If a cleric has committed this offense, he is to be beaten.

18. That laypeople not enter the cloisters of monks or disturb the brethren living in silence, except perhaps when they are persons of high rank, a circumstance we cannot entirely avoid.

19. That Novatians who come to a monastery not be admitted into the community’s order until they have been fully examined according to the rule, and that they not be placed above the others in the monastery until they have been fully instructed in the order of regular life, as is contained in the rule of Saint Benedict.

20. That no one use the cowl unless he has bound himself by a monastic vow; or, if necessity demands it because of cold, a religious priest may use it.

21. That neither clerics nor laypeople enter a monastery of women, except only the presbyter who sings Mass or visits the sick; he must leave immediately at the proper hours.

22. That a nun be permitted to ring the church bell and light the lamp.

23. We earnestly admonish the entire Christian people to abstain from unlawful and criminal marriages.

24. That monks not presume to attend lay banquets. Whoever is bound by a monastic vow must in no way hold a parish or presume to resort to secular courts.

25. That no member of the clergy dare trouble the lord king before the matter has first been brought to the attention of his own bishop. If the bishop cannot settle it, he is then to direct the person to the metropolitan bishop. If the metropolitan himself cannot deliberate the matter with his counsel, he should endeavor to send the person to the king with letters of recommendation.

26. That abbesses in no way leave their monasteries except with the consent and permission of their bishops; and that the bishops take care that permission not be denied them when they ought to leave their monasteries for their own benefit. The abbesses themselves are to take such persons with them that, upon returning, they may in no way presume to recount matters to the other nuns, for this causes great destruction, as is contained in the holy rule.

27. That nuns not wear men’s clothing—namely, *rocho* or *fanones*—but only women’s garments.

28. That abbots, monks, and nuns abstain from the flesh of four-footed animals, as is contained in the holy rule, except when they are ill and require it for the restoration of their bodies. We do not forbid this if it happens that they must fulfill the duty of charity, or if some necessity or lack of food should arise; but it must be done with great consideration and the counsel of the bishops. No one should claim that he cannot observe this because of various journeys, since the Lord, when sending his disciples to preach, commanded them to take neither purse, nor shoes, nor two tunics—how much more should this apply to us, who have sufficient provisions and clothing.

29. That no bishop or abbot dare seize for himself the property of the lord king’s tributaries—that is, bless their basilicas or anything else that appears to belong to such a condition—before the lord king has fully determined the matter.

30. That no one presume to appoint another person’s slave as a minister of the Church or to bless him before his master has handed him over into the hands of the bishop, to remain in complete freedom for all his days. His master is to know that after that day he may exercise no right of domination over him. Then, if he is worthy, he may enter the sacred order.

We decreed that the matters set out above should first be observed at the place called Rhispach, secondly at Freising, and that the matters which follow should be added at the monastery of Salzburg.

# SALZBURG STATUTES (799)

[Note: The manuscript has the heading “Title VI: Concerning those things added afterward.” But this rubric was eventually inserted erroneously after the first chapter.]

1. That in every diocese lawful baptisteries be established and that a sacred font be honorably built there.

2. That during Lent they hold three litanies every week, namely on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday.

3. That the entire people proceed with all supplications, devoutly, humbly, and reverently, honorably, without adornment of costly clothing, seductive songs, or secular games; and that they learn to cry out “Kyrie eleison” (“Lord, have mercy”), so that they may learn to do so better and not as rustically as they have until now.

4. That, with God’s help and under the guidance of his counsel, we carefully consider what ought to be done concerning those whom we wish to ordain to the sacred ministry, and that they be examined by judgment to determine whether they are worthy of advancement.

5. That those who have been ordained to the sacred ministry as presbyters in no way dare to omit celebrating the solemnities of Mass continually, except for definite reasons that we are to determine, on account of which it is more appropriate for them to abstain for a time.

6. That bishops, abbots, and presbyters divide among their relatives and close associates the property of the holy Church entrusted to them, no more than the canonical permission authorizes, so that murmuring or criticism may be removed from the rest of the people and from those who offer their property there.

7. That the archpresbyters who customarily investigate and examine the other presbyters be admonished carefully to consider themselves and not neglect those over whom they preside, but diligently remember that they have been appointed for this purpose: so that their bishop may share his burdens among them.

8. Let deacons live soberly, chastely, and modestly; let them in no way pursue drunkenness. Rather, as ministers of God, let them always display examples of humility in themselves.

9. That the monks who, by turns, are appointed superiors, deans, porters, cellarers, and other ministers in the monastery not dare to appropriate or collect anything as private property, which we know to be anathema.

10. That Mass of holy Mary, Mother of God, be solemnly celebrated four times a year: her Purification, on 2 February; her Conception, on 25 March; her Assumption, on 14 August; and her Nativity, on 8 September.

11. That on the Wednesday before the beginning of Lent, which the Romans call the beginning of the fast, a solemn observance be held with a litany and Mass after the ninth hour.

12. If it seems good to you to adopt Roman usage, then on the Wednesday before the Lord’s Supper, let the prayers written for Good Friday be recited by bishops or presbyters at the third hour of that Wednesday in the church, with genuflection, except only for the Jews; likewise on Good Friday at the ninth hour, as the Romans do. As the missal contains the prayer for the collect, let us perform it according to Roman custom.

13. That no one of the nobility, nor any abbot or presbyter, dare be tonsured before his case has been examined in the presence of the bishop to whose diocese he belongs. If he has given any property either to the monastery or to the church where he was tonsured, there he is to remain in canonical or regular life. But if he later wishes to reside on his own property, he is to perform military service like other laymen.

14. Abbots are to be warned that no brother in the monastery is to be loved more than another, except the one found to be better in good works, so that murmuring may be removed from the rest. No one is in any way to consent to another’s collecting or possessing anything private. Every dispute and contention is to be removed from the monastery with the greatest diligence; and whoever stirs up a quarrel there is to be corrected with such discipline that the others will fear committing such acts.

15. If a dispute should arise between a man and a woman concerning marital union, so that they deny between themselves carnal intercourse, the holy synod decreed that, if the man denies having made her his wife, he should stand with her for the trial by the cross. If he refuses, he must find another woman to stand with her. If the man alleges that same union against her and she denies it, then the woman is to clear herself according to the law.

16. Therefore the holy synod agreed that, whenever anyone departs from this world by God’s command—whether bishop, abbot, monk, presbyter, or nun—letters should be sent from that place or monastery to each episcopal household. The bishop of the diocese is to designate someone to receive those letters and, through his own letters, make known to the other abbots and abbesses, as well as to all presbyters, the name and time of the deceased, so that prayers may be offered for that soul.

# EDICT FOR THE BISHOPS (800)

First published by Amerpach from the Tegernsee manuscript; I collated it with the following manuscripts: 1. Saint Gall no. 733, ninth century, beginning; 2. the Blankenburg manuscript of the ducal library at Wolfenbüttel, tenth century; 3. the Gotha ducal-library manuscript, eleventh century; 4. the formerly Tegernsee manuscript, now in the Royal Library at Munich, tenth century. It is clear that it was promulgated before the year 801.

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, to our beloved counts or judges, vassals, vicars, centenarii, and all our envoys and agents.

Let your administration know that a considerable presumption on the part of certain people has sounded in our ears: that you do not obey your bishops and priests in the manner required by the authority of the canons and laws. Thus, with some unknown rashness, you refuse to present presbyters to bishops, and moreover are not afraid to seize the clerics of others and dare to place them in your churches without the bishop’s consent. Nor do you allow our bishops to possess such authority in your ministries as ecclesiastical rectitude teaches. [Note: MS 4 reads *donet* (“may give”) for *docet* (“teaches”).]

Furthermore, in wicked greed you strive to withdraw the ninths and tenths, or rents, from the churches from which those benefits derive; and you neglect to accept leases of those properties, as was established by us earlier in our capitulary. [Note: See *Capit.* 779, 13; 794, 25.] You also refuse, according to your ability, to assist in reforming the holy Church of God together with those bishops and abbots. [Note: MS 1 reads *vestros* (“your,” masculine plural) for *vestras* (“your,” feminine plural).]

Therefore, with the consent of our bishops, abbots, and other priests, we have sent these ordinances to your districts. [Note: MS 1 reads *nostris* (“our”) for *vestris* (“your”).] We command that no one whatsoever among our faithful, from the least to the greatest, dare show disobedience to his bishop in matters belonging to God, whether concerning the chapters mentioned above or other instructions pertaining to their ministry. [Note: MS 1 omits *ex* (“from,” “among”).] Rather, with goodwill and complete gentleness and submission, let each person strive, for God’s sake and for the sake of peace, to obey his priest. [Note: MSS 2–4 read *inoboediens* (“disobedient”) for *inoboedientia* (“disobedience”); MSS 2–4 read *parere* (“to obey”) for *parare* (“to prepare”).] [Note: MS 1 reads *pertinentes* (“pertaining,” plural) for *pertinentibus* (“pertaining,” dative plural).] [Note: MSS 2–4 read *mansuetudinis subiectione* (“with the submission of gentleness”) for *mansuetudine* (“gentleness”).]

But if—as may it not happen—any one of you is found negligent in rendering the ninths, tenths, and rents, [Note: MS 1 reads *redditis* (“rendered”) for *reddendis* (“to be rendered”).] or in renewing the leases, and presumes stubbornly to contradict our bishops concerning matters known to belong to their ministry, or concerning what is contained in the capitulary previously issued by us, let him know without doubt that, unless he corrects himself quickly, he will thereafter have to give an account of this in our presence. [Note: MS 1 omits *se* (“himself”); MS 1 reads *inportune* (“inopportunely”) for *importunus* (“stubborn”); MSS 2–4 read *deducere* (“to bring forward”) or *ducere* (“to lead”) for *dicere* (“to say”).]

And so that you may believe these letters more firmly, we have ordered them to be confirmed below with our seal ring.

# CAPITULARY FOR THE COUNTY OF LE MANS (800)

I copied this from the Paris manuscript of the Royal Library, no. 5577, formerly Colbert no. 4167, Royal no. 4382, a somewhat elongated octavo parchment manuscript of the tenth century, where it is found after several letters and treatises of Alcuin. It is also read in Benedict, *Book of Capitularies* I, chapter 303; and it is clear that it was promulgated after Charles’s return from his journey through the counties of Le Mans and Tours.

## CAPITULARY OF THE LORD CHARLES

Because of the excessive complaint that reached us concerning ecclesiastical or fiscal people who had not been assigned their duties when we were in the county of Le Mans, it seemed good to us, with the advice of our faithful, to establish that anyone among the aforesaid people who held a quarter of a hide should plow one full day with his animals and plow in his lord’s demesne field; thereafter, no annual service should be demanded of him by his lord during that week. Whoever did not have enough animals to complete this in one day was to perform the aforesaid work over two days. Whoever had only four weak animals, unable to plow by themselves, was to plow with them joined to other animals for one day in his lord’s field, and afterward perform one day of hand labor during that week. [Note: “Hand labor” was added in another ink.] Whoever could do none of these things and had no animals was to work for his lord with his hands for three days, from morning until evening; his lord was to demand nothing more from him.

These practices had been carried out in various ways: some worked the entire week, some half the week, and some two days. Therefore we established this rule, so that the household could neither withdraw from the aforesaid works nor be required by its lords to do more. [Note: *ne* means “nor” (*nec*).] [Note: That is, “required” or “demanded.”] Whoever possessed less than a full quarter of the best land was to perform labor in proportion to the value of his land. We ordered Count Adalard to command this in our place and to announce it publicly, together with our other faithful, for their satisfaction.

# TICINUM CAPITULARY (June 801)

The historical notes found in the preface demonstrate that this addition to the Lombard laws was promulgated in June, when the emperor, returning from Rome, was staying at Pavia. We present it with the aid of the following manuscripts: 1. the parchment manuscript of Saint Paul, early ninth century; 2. the Royal Library in Paris, no. 4613; 3. the Blankenburg manuscript; 4. the Gotha manuscript; 4b. the Tegernsee manuscript, from which the first edition of the capitulary, by Amerpach, derives; 5. the Chisian manuscript; 6. the Cavensis manuscript, together with readings from the remaining manuscripts that transmit Charles’s Lombard capitularies, namely the Ambrosian (A.), Florentine (Fl.), London (L.), Vienna (V.), Veronese (Vn.), and Estense (E.) manuscripts cited by Muratori.

We have appended a twofold addition. The first derives from the Saint Paul manuscript; all its chapters except the last are also transmitted by the Chisian and Cavensis manuscripts among the laws of Louis, and by Ansegisus, book IV, chapters 74 and 75. The authority of the oldest of all the manuscripts is further supported by the fact that the chapters which follow these laws in the Chisian and Cavensis manuscripts—those to be published below under the third year of Louis—are of nearly the same subject, so that they could scarcely, if at all, have been issued in the same enactment. We present the second addition from the Blankenburg manuscript.

## CHAPTERS ADDED TO THE LAW OF THE LOMBARDS

[Note: These chapters were first published by Vitus Amerbach. He himself writes in book IV of *On the Kingdom of Italy* by Sigonius that an old copy of them existed at Modena in Sigonius’s time. We found the oldest copy in the Thuana Library; in addition, we emended these eight chapters with the aid of two old manuscript codices of the Royal Library. There is no doubt about the time when they were enacted, but the place is unknown. Sirmond thought that they had been promulgated at Rome. Nevertheless, it seems possible to infer from the Chronicle of Moissac that they were composed at Ravenna, to which the emperor Charles is attested by Einhard to have gone in June of the year 801. Certainly, from the preface to these chapters it is clear that the correction of the laws did not take place in one location, but that various questions were debated in each city before the prince, and various chapters necessary for the laws were added. — Baluze.]

[Note: This heading appears only in the Tegernsee manuscript; in that manuscript the formula “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ” is absent.]

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Charles, crowned by divine will, ruling the Roman empire, most serene Augustus, to all dukes, counts, gastalds, and all those appointed by our clemency over public affairs throughout the provinces of Italy.

In the year from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 801, in the ninth indiction [Note: The numeral VIII is written above it in MS 1; MS 2 reads VIII.], in the thirty-third year of our reign in Francia and the twenty-eighth in Italy, and in the first year of our consulship, when we had come to Italy for the benefit of the holy Church of God and for the ordering of the provinces, and when many different questions concerning ecclesiastical, public, and private matters were being discussed in the various cities before our presence, most were immediately settled, once read out, by an appropriate judgment according to Roman or Lombard law. Some, however, were temporarily deferred for our examination, matters whose judicial ruling had either been entirely omitted by the legislators [Note: MS 4 reads *legis latronibus*, apparently an erroneous form, for “legislators.”] or had been handed down by later generations into oblivion.

Therefore, considering our own welfare and that of the people granted to us by God, we have taken care to add, in accordance with the nature of the matters and the circumstances of the time, those provisions omitted by our predecessors, the kings of Italy, in the edicts of the Lombard law—so that what was necessary and lacking in the law might be supplied, and so that in doubtful matters not just anyone’s judgment or discretion, but the sanction of our royal authority, might prevail. The chapters that we have decided to add are these.

### 1. Concerning the Making of Donation Charters

[Note: C reads *faciendum statuimus* (“we establish that it be done”) for *faciendum*.]

If a Lombard, considering in advance the condition of human frailty, wishes to make a charter of donation from his property for the salvation of his soul, [Note: MS 1 reads *si voluerit iudicare vel cartula donationis facere* (“if he wishes to dispose of it or make a charter of donation”); MSS 5, 6, V, Vn., and M have related variant readings.] he is not to reserve for himself, as had hitherto been customary, the right to sell, exchange, or alienate the same property by another charter. [Note: C, MSS 5–6, Vn., and M read *donandi* (“of donating”) for *vendendi* (“of selling”).] Rather, each person is to dispose absolutely of his property as he wishes. [Note: V and Vn. read: “as he wishes, unless he has reserved for himself an arrangement and usufruct from property given to a place dedicated to God, if he should prefer otherwise, and should know…”] He is to know that our authority has entirely forbidden him to make two donations of the same property. But after he has made one transfer of his property, he is to have no power to make another concerning it. [Note: V, Vn., and E add the corrupt qualification *exceptis rebus traditis euntis. In hostem sepe quidem. Ita etc.*: “excepting property transferred when going on campaign. Often indeed on campaign. Thus, etc.”; the wording is materially uncertain.]

The arrangement is nevertheless such that, if he wishes to retain the usufruct, he may be granted the right to possess the transferred property by a lease until the defined term. [Note: MSS 1 and 3 omit *si voluerit habere* (“if he wishes to have it”).]

### 2. Concerning the *Heribannus*

[Note: One manuscript has *aribannum*.]

If any free man, despising our command while the others are going to the army, presumes to remain at home, let him know that he must pay the full *heribannus* according to Frankish law, namely sixty solids. Likewise, for contempt of each of the chapters that we have promulgated by the ban of our royal authority—namely, whoever violates the peace of the churches of God, widows, orphans, and minors or persons of lesser power, or commits robbery within the homeland, burns another’s house, or uses force against anyone with an assembled crowd—he is to pay a fine of sixty solids. [Note: MSS 5–6 add after “violates”: “or commits robbery within the homeland, or burns another’s house, or uses force against anyone with an assembled crowd”; the Estense manuscript is excepted.]

### 3. Concerning Deserters

If anyone is so obstinate or proud that, having abandoned the army, he returns home without the king’s command or permission, and commits what we call *herisliz* in the German language, [Note: MS 3 reads *theodisca* for *Teudisca*. MSS 1, 4, 4b, V, Vn., and 6 read respectively *ereslig*, *erilex*, *eris lex*, *eriliz*, *eriz*, and *erislig*.] he is to incur the penalty of death as guilty of treason, and his property is to be joined to our treasury.

### 4. Concerning Robbers

[Note: “After the third theft,” says an interlinear gloss in one Royal manuscript.]

If anyone preserves a robber who has been handed over to him for execution as deserving death, and grants life to one unworthy of it, he is to pay half the compensation for the damage on account of which the robber was handed over. [Note: MS V and Vn. read: “He is to pay the compensation for the robber to the public treasury.”] If that same robber is subsequently caught again in robbery, he is to pay the penalty owed for the earlier offense and discharge the debt of the capital sentence. [Note: MS 1 reads *sententiam vitam* (“the sentence of life”) for *sententiae debitum* (“the debt of the sentence”).]

### 5. Concerning Any Mutilation

If anyone, presumptuously and of his own accord, castrates another and cuts off both his testicles, he is to pay his full *wergild* according to the status of the person. If he cuts off the penis, the same rule applies. If he cuts off one testicle, he is to pay half. [Note: “Of one who has two,” says the same gloss. “But if he cuts off the only one possessed by someone who has only one, he is to pay two-thirds of that person’s value, as in the case of an eye.”]

We enact the same concerning eyes, hands, feet, or the tongue: if one of them is cut off, half the *wergild* is to be paid; if both, the full amount is to be paid as compensation for the deed. [Note: MS 1 omits *et pedibus* (“and feet”).] [Note: “This indicates that the law pertains only to Lombards,” as stated in the same gloss.]

### 6. Concerning Public *Aldiones* Belonging to Public Law

The *aldiones* or *aldianae* belonging to public law are to live in Italy under the servitude of their masters according to the law by which the fiscal dependants or *lites* live in Francia. [Note: MS 6 has the corrupt reading *s. quaris hoc aritur vel I. v. in Italia*, materially uncertain. One Royal manuscript reads: “According to which the fiscal dependants live as free people, either there or in Francia.”]

7. Concerning thieves. If anyone apprehends a thief or robber and releases him unharmed, and does not bring him before the presence of the duke or count, or of the local official [Note: [Col. 0213] “of the duke, count, or local judge,” according to P, V, and Un. (C has “or local judge”).], who is the count’s envoy, and if thereafter he is convicted in the presence of the judges of this deed or misconduct, he shall be compelled to pay the assessed amount of the damage for which the thief or robber was apprehended [Note: [Col. 0214A] “to the public treasury,” according to C, V, and Un.].

8. Concerning fugitive slaves [Note: [Col. 0213] The entire chapter is missing in MSS 1, 2, 3, and 4; it appears elsewhere in another codex.]. Wherever within Italy a slave—whether royal, ecclesiastical, or belonging to any other person—is found as a fugitive, his master shall reclaim him without any limitation of years; provided, however, that the master is a Frank, Alamannian, or of any other nation. But if he is a Lombard or Roman, he shall acquire or lose his slaves according to the law that has been established among them from ancient times.

## Chapters added in the Codex of Saint Paul

9. Concerning any case [Note: [Col. 0213] Louis I repeated this law, with some alterations, in the year 817; see below.]. If anyone has a dispute with another concerning any matter, and witnesses have been produced against him in court, and he suspects them of being false, he may oppose other witnesses to them [Note: [Col. 0213] “he [may set] others against them,” in Ch and C.], as many better ones as he can obtain, so that the perversity of false witnesses may be overcome by the testimony of truthful ones [Note: [Col. 0213] “testimony,” in MS 1.]. But if the two groups of witnesses disagree with one another so completely [Note: [Col. 0213] “agree,” in MS 1.] that neither side will yield at all to the other, let two of them be chosen, one from each side [Note: [Col. 0213] “from” is absent in MS 1.], who, with shields [Note: [Col. 0213] “discusses,” in C; “fight,” in Ch.] and clubs, shall determine in the field which side follows falsehood and which truth in its testimony. The champion who is defeated shall, on account of the perjury he committed before the combat, have his right hand cut off. The other witnesses of the same side who are shown to have given false testimony shall redeem their hands; two parts [Note: [Col. 0213] “two,” in MS 1.] of their composition shall be given to the party against whom they testified [Note: [Col. 0213] The words “of whose composition ... shall be paid” are missing in C and Ch.], and the third shall be paid as the *fred* (peace-fine). In a secular case, therefore, such a disagreement between witnesses shall be settled by the field; but in ecclesiastical matters the truth of the matter shall be sought through the judgment of the cross [Note: [Col. 0213] “of the truth,” in MS 1.]. We have decreed that this shall also be done in the case of the timid, the weak [Note: [Col. 0213] “the feeble,” in MS 1.], and the infirm, who are unable to fight, so that they may not on this account lose their justice [Note: [Col. 0213] i.e., “so that they may in no way [lose it],” according to Ch and C.]. Witnesses for any case [Note: [Col. 0213] “any,” in MS 1.], however, should be sought nowhere else than from the county in which the property at issue is situated, because it is not credible [Note: [Col. 0213] “decrepit,” in MS 1; “credible,” in Ch and C.] that the truth concerning a person’s status [Note: [Col. 0213] “testimony,” in MS 1.] or anyone’s possession can be learned [Note: [Col. 0213] “is learned,” in MS 1.] better through others than through those who live nearer.

10. If anyone habitually resides in another homeland [Note: [Col. 0213] “homelands,” in MS 1.], whether because of a benefice or for any other reason [Note: [Col. 0213] “occasion,” in MS 1.], and is summoned concerning any matter [Note: [Col. 0213] “matter,” in C; “a matter,” in A.], for example, concerning his acquired property or slaves [Note: [Col. 0213] The words from “by virtue” to “Lombards” are absent in C, Ch, and the Lombard codex.], let him receive justice there according to his own law, and let him swear the lawful oath with such oath-helpers—who must nevertheless be freeborn [Note: [Col. 0215] “with oath-helpers nevertheless freeborn,” in I, V, Un, and E.]—as he can have with him in that region or province [Note: [Col. 0215] “Except in proving the truth of a document called false,” according to V, Un, and E.]; except if someone has summoned him concerning his status [Note: [Col. 0215] “in such a way that the plaintiff either does not wish or is unable to prove,” according to V, Un, and E.], that is, concerning his freedom or the inheritance that his father left him when he died [Note: [Col. 0215] “that his father left him,” in MS 1.]. [Note: [Col. 0215] “unless the action concerns an investiture,” according to V, Un, and E.] In these two matters he may offer to swear the oath in his homeland, that is, in the lawful place for his oath [Note: [Col. 0215] “namely, if the accuser cannot prove that he is his slave in the same homeland where the accusation is made,” according to V, Un, and E.]; and the person litigating against him may, if he wishes, follow him to his homeland to receive that oath. Nevertheless, he must first satisfy, in the same place where he was summoned, both the count and the judges and his adversary, by proving through witnesses that he has inherited from his father the property that is being demanded from him [Note: [Col. 0215] “that his father left him,” according to Ch, C, A, V, Un, and others.].

41. Let every payment and composition contained in the Salic Law among the Franks be made in twelve-denarius solidi [Note: [Col. 0215] “in Francia,” in Ch; “in Francia and wherever,” in V, Un, and E.], except where a dispute has arisen against Saxons and Frisians. There we decree that the solidus shall have the value of forty denarii [Note: [Col. 0215] Muratori reads “sixty”; all codices read either “forty” or “XL”], which the Saxon or Frisian and the Salic Frank who is litigating with him must pay [Note: [Col. 0215] “the Salic Frank,” in MS 1; “the litigants,” in MS 1.].

12. Concerning status, that is, freedom or inheritance: anyone summoned concerning these matters shall be summoned according to the provision of the law. But in other cases for which a person must render an account, if, after the count’s second admonition, anyone refuses to come to the assembly [Note: [Col. 0215] “you refused,” in MS 1.], he shall be compelled to come and render justice after his property has been placed under the ban.

13. If anyone’s property is placed under the ban on account of a crime committed by him, and, after learning of the matter, he delays coming to do justice and allows a year and a day to pass while remaining under that ban [Note: [Col. 0215] “if he were under the ban,” in MS 1.], he shall not acquire it thereafter, but it shall be joined to the king’s fisc. The debt that the person to whom the property belonged was required to pay shall, according to the assessment of the damage [Note: [Col. 0215] “damage,” in MS 1.], be paid by the count and his officials, from the movable property found in that estate [Note: [Col. 0215] “property,” in MS 1.], to those to whom the same debtor was liable. If the quantity of movable goods found there is insufficient for the composition [Note: [Col. 0215] “of the quantity,” in MS 1.], it shall be supplemented from the immovable property; whatever remains shall, as stated, belong to the king’s fisc. If nothing can remain after the composition, everything shall be expended on it. But if that man has not yet divided his property with his co-heirs, let the count summon them and make a lawful division with them; then, as already stated, let him assign that man’s share to the king’s fisc, and let him pay the composition from it, according to the amount specified above, to those to whom that man is legally liable [Note: [Col. 0215] That is, “pay it.”].

## Chapters added in the Blankenburg Codex, fols. 89–90

[Col. 0216A]

14. We must make this known to all: throughout our realms, by the favor of Christ, no one shall refuse lodging to anyone traveling; no one shall demand lodging and fire, or likewise provisions, except in a meadow or standing crop.

15. Free men shall render no service to counts or to vicars, whether in a meadow, in a standing crop, in plowing, or in a vineyard, and shall pay no levy or residue, except to those summoning the army or carrying a royal commission.

16. [Note: [Col. 0215D] Compare 755, Vern. 7.] A public baptistery shall exist in no parish except where the bishop who is in charge of that parish has established one, unless necessity arises because of illness or some other emergency [Col. 0216B]. The priests whom the bishop has appointed in his parish shall have permission, wherever the need arises, to ensure that no one dies without baptism.

17. Concerning the forms of excommunication, both of clergy and of laity [Note: [Col. 0215D] Compare 755, Vern. 9.]. If a priest has been degraded by his bishop, and thereafter, contemptuously, presumes to perform any part of his office without authorization, and is subsequently corrected or excommunicated by his bishop, anyone who knowingly communicates with him shall know that he is excommunicated.

18. Likewise, whoever—cleric, layman, or woman—commits incest, and, after being corrected by his or her bishop, refuses to amend, and is excommunicated by him or her knowingly [Col. 0216C], shall know that he or she is excommunicated. And so that you may know the nature of this excommunication: the person must not enter a church, take food or drink with any Christian, accept gifts from anyone, offer a kiss, join in prayer, or give a greeting, until reconciled by his or her bishop. If anyone declares that he or she has been unjustly excommunicated, that person shall have permission to come before the metropolitan bishop and be judged there according to canonical rule; meanwhile, however, the person shall observe the excommunication. If anyone disregards all these provisions, and the bishop is unable to correct him, he shall be condemned by the king’s judgment.

19. Moreover [Note: [Col. 0216D] In Muratori, among the capitularies of Charlemagne, ch. 145.], taking every precaution, we have decreed that no one presume to join a boy or girl in marriage before the years of puberty, that is, below the proper age, or at unequal ages; rather, the parties should be of the same age and mutually consenting [Note: [Col. 0215] “Consenting together,” in the codex.]. We have often heard that from marriages of this kind many destructions of souls have resulted [Col. 0217A], and that such fornications have been committed as have not even occurred among the nations: plainly, when it happens that a boy is grown and the girl still a child, or conversely that the girl is of mature age while the boy is still young, and that, through the man, a female relative and mother-in-law are discovered to be adulteresses, and that, because of the girl, the boy’s brother or father perishes entangled in so great a disgraceful sin. Therefore, whoever thereafter presumes to undertake what is prohibited shall be excluded from all ecclesiastical fellowship, but shall not thereby be exempt from public judgments [Note: [Col. 0217] That is, “from” public judgments.].

20. Concerning the joining of kin: no one shall presume to marry within the fourth or fifth degree of relationship; and if anyone presumes to do so, he shall be excluded from holy communion.

21. As for churches built in each locality, no bishop shall dare consecrate a church without an endowment; and those that have been consecrated shall be under the bishop’s authority. If any layman thereafter presumes to claim a share, the churches themselves shall be closed, and the people themselves shall be deprived of communion.

22. As for a slave or freedman, no one shall presume to promote him to the priesthood unless his master delivers him into the hand of the bishop.

[Col. 0218A] 23. Concerning a church that was previously consecrated, but whose altar has been destroyed for any reason or by fire: the bishop shall have permission to build an altar there again. If the bishop, whether because of old age or illness, is entirely unable to travel to that holy place, then that priest or whatever custodian is appointed shall, with the counsel of the people, bring the altar to his bishop for consecration; and that priest, by the authority of his bishop, shall set it up in the appointed place. If the church has been newly built, no bishop shall have permission, as stated above, to send a priest; rather, the bishop himself shall go to install the relics or consecrate the altars.

24. [Note: [Col. 0217] The number is absent in the codex.] [Note: [Col. 0217B] The same, chapters 90 and 127.] [Note: [Col. 0217] We print this from the Tegernsee and Blankenburg codices.] Judges or royal envoys shall not demand *freda* (peace-fines) before the offense has been composed [Note: [Col. 0217] “before they compose it,” in Bl.]. We further order that the judges named above, or royal officials, shall not demand *freda* (peace-fines) in any case before the offense has been composed. If anyone, out of greed [Note: [Col. 0217] “out of greed,” in Bl.], transgresses this provision, let him make legal compensation [Note: [Col. 0217] “let it be imposed on him,” in T; “let him make compensation,” in Bl.]. The *fred* (peace-fine), however, shall not be given to the judge to whom the offense was committed [Note: [Col. 0217] “that is, the defendant,” in V.], but to the person who receives the payment; let him give a third part to the fisc in the presence of witnesses, so that lasting and stable peace may endure.

## Capitular of Aachen (November 801)

[Col. 0217]

The oldest of the codices in which this capitular is found is: 1. Codex C of the Royal Library of Munich, among the books of Saint Emmeram of Regensburg, marked F. 11, a ninth-century parchment manuscript. I also examined: 2. Codex C of the Royal Library of Paris, among the manuscripts marked Supplement latin no. 75, a tenth-century manuscript, with which 3. the codex of Vincent of Metz agrees; Sirmond’s and Baluze’s editions are based on it, as noted above. 4. The codex of the monastery of Andain, tenth century, in Martène and Durand, *Veterum Scriptorum et Monumentorum Collectio*, vol. VII, p. 26, presents the same chapters under the same heading as ours, but in a somewhat different order, namely chapters 3, 8, 4, 6, 7, 5, 1, 2, 9, 10–16, and 17–21, followed by six chapters that are absent from the other codices. In both Paris codices the capitular is assigned to the first year of the emperor’s reign, in which, according to the Salzburg annals, Charles held a synod for the examination of bishops and clergy in November.

[Note: [Col. 0217C] In the Oxford Codex, from which Spelman published these chapters in volume I of the *Councils of England*, p. 258, the title here was: “These are the laws of the priests which they ought to observe.” It is certain that they are not by Egbert, archbishop of York, under whose name Spelman published them. Indeed, as he himself writes, in the Oxford Codex they are inserted before Egbert’s penitential. —Baluze.]

THESE ARE THE CHAPTERS FROM THE WRITINGS OF DIVINE SCRIPTURE [Note: [Col. 0217] “writings,” in MS 1.], WHICH THE ELECTED PRIESTS JUDGED SHOULD BE OBSERVED AND FULFILLED [Note: [Col. 0217] Absent in MS 1.].

[Col. 0217C]

1. Let all priests pray continually for the life and reign of our lord the emperor, and for the safety of his sons and daughters.

2. Let every priest attend daily prayers for the bishop under whose governance he is ruled.

3. Let every priest build his church with every diligence [Note: [Col. 0217] “builds,” in MS 1.], and preserve the relics of the saints with the greatest devotion through nightly vigils and divine services [Note: [Col. 0217] Thus in MSS 1–4; B corrects this to “daytime services.”] [Note: [Col. 0217] “preserves,” in MS 1.].

4. On all feast days and Sundays, let every priest preach the Gospel of Christ to the people [Note: [Col. 0217] “preaches,” in MS 1.].

5. Let every priest carefully teach the Lord’s Prayer and the Creed to the people entrusted to him, and display to their minds the zeal of the whole religion and the observance of Christianity.

6. Let every priest instruct all those belonging to him so that they know how to offer to the churches of God, as they ought, the tithes of all their possessions [Note: [Col. 0217] “duly,” in MS 1.].

7. Let the priests themselves also receive the tithes of the people, keep written records of their names [Note: [Col. 0217] “their names,” in MSS 2 and 3.], and of all who have given [Note: [Col. 0217] “whatever they have rightly given,” in MS 4.], and divide them before witnesses according to canonical authority. For the adornment of the church, let them choose the first part [Note: [Col. 0219] “choose,” in MSS 2 and 3.]; the second part they shall mercifully distribute through their hands, with all humility, for the use of the poor or pilgrims [Note: [Col. 0219] “the poor and,” in MS 1.]; but the priests alone shall reserve the third part for themselves [Note: [Col. 0219] “for themselves,” in MS 2.].

8. Let all priests ring the bells of their churches at the appropriate hours of day and night [Note: [Col. 0219] “ring,” in MS 1.], and then celebrate sacred services to God [Note: [Col. 0219] “and sacred,” in MSS 2 and 3.], and teach the people at what hours and in what manner God is to be worshiped [Note: [Col. 0219] “celebrate,” in MS 1.].

9. Let no priest dare celebrate Mass in houses or other places, but only in dedicated churches, unless necessity compels it [Note: [Col. 0219] The final words are absent in MSS 2 and 3.].

10. Let the law and proper time of baptism be most carefully observed by all priests, at the appropriate times, according to canonical regulation [Note: [Col. 0219] Absent in MSS 1 and 4.].

11. Let all priests most diligently administer baptism at whatever hour to all who need it because of illness.

12. Let no priest presume to sell for any price the sacred office, the sacrament of baptism [Note: [Col. 0219] “the sacrament of baptism,” in MS 1; “baptismal,” in MS 4.], or any spiritual gift [Note: [Col. 0219] “anything,” in MS 1.], lest sellers and buyers imitate those who sold and bought doves in the Temple; so that, for what they have obtained, they may not seek earthly gain as the price of divine grace [Note: [Col. 0219] “may not desire a price,” in MS 1.], but may deserve to receive only the glory of the heavenly kingdom.

13. Let no priest, out of ambition [Note: [Col. 0219] “admonition,” in MSS 1 and 4.], leave the seat of his own holy church under whose title he was ordained and go to another church; rather, let him remain devoted in that church until the end of his life.

14. Let no one from the number of priests nourish the vice of drunkenness [Note: [Col. 0219] “nurture,” in MS 1.], nor compel others to become drunk by his command.

15. Let no priest maintain familiarity with foreign women; nor let him ever allow any woman [Note: [Col. 0219] “any woman,” in MSS 2 and 3.] to live in the house in which he himself resides [Note: [Col. 0219] “his house,” in MS 1.].

6. No priest may be a guarantor [Note: [Col. 0219] “of a guarantor,” in MS 1.]; nor, abandoning his own law, may he presume to go before secular courts [Note: [Col. 0219] “secular matters,” in MSS 2 and 3.] [Note: [Col. 0219] “to,” in MS 1.].

16b. [Note: [Col. 0219] This chapter is absent in MSS 1 and 4.] Whoever has held a church possession or parish for thirty years without anyone’s bringing a claim shall possess it by perpetual right. But if it is repeatedly claimed, careful inquiry shall be made. And if it becomes clear that the claimant has a just claim, he shall recover what he claims by confirming it with truthful and noble witnesses.

17. No one from the number of priests shall ever carry the weapons of combatants [Note: [Col. 0219] “carries”; “provokes,” in MS 1.], nor shall he stir up any quarrel against his neighbor.

18. Let no priest enter taverns for the purpose of eating or drinking [Note: [Col. 0219] “taverns,” in MSS 2 and 3.].

[Col. 0220A] 19. Let no priest swear anything by an oath [Note: [Col. 0219] “anything,” in MS 1.], but let him say everything simply, with purity and truth.

20. Let all priests impose an appropriate penance, with the greatest vigilance, on all who confess their offenses to them [Note: [Col. 0219] “impose,” in MS 1.]; and let them mercifully give all the sick, before the end of life, the viaticum and communion of the body of Christ.

21. According to the definition of the holy fathers, if anyone falls ill, let the priests carefully anoint him with consecrated oil, accompanied by prayers.

## In Codex IV the following are added

22. Concerning ninths and tithes. We wish and command that from all produce, wine, and hay, the ninth and the tenth be faithfully and fully paid by everyone. As for the produce of livestock, let the customary arrangement concerning the tithe be observed by all, as it has been until now. If, however, any bishop wishes to accept money for this, it shall remain within his authority.

23. Concerning the ancient churches, so that they may retain their property [Note: [Col. 0219] “so that they may not lose their property,” in M.]. They shall not be deprived of tithes or other possessions, so that these may be assigned to the oratories.

24. Concerning spiritual godchildren. We further command that each godfather and each spiritual relative instruct his spiritual children in the Catholic faith.

25. Concerning priests. Let them be irreproachable and adorned with good morals, according to the apostle’s word, and let them in no way devote themselves to shameful profits, in accordance with what Scripture says: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular business, so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself.” Let them themselves abstain from shameful profits and usury, and also instruct the peoples subject to them to abstain.

26. Concerning those who commit incest. Let incestuous persons be punished with penance according to canonical judgment. Those, however, who, after repeated admonitions and preaching by the priests, neglect to give tithes shall be excommunicated; we do not wish to bind them by oath.

27. Concerning discernment in receiving the body and blood of the Lord. It must be guarded against lest, if reception is deferred for too long, this prove destructive to the soul, since the Lord says: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves.” But if it is received without discernment, one must also fear what the apostle says: “Whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself.” Therefore, according to the apostolic teaching, a person must examine himself and then eat of that bread and drink from the cup, abstaining for some days from the works of the flesh and purifying body and soul, so that he may prepare himself [Col. 0221A] to receive so great a sacrament, following the example of David; for unless he had confessed that he had abstained from conjugal relations since yesterday and the day before yesterday, he would by no means have received the bread of the Presence from the priest [Col. 0222A].

## Mandate concerning the Saxon hostages to be presented to the emperor at Mainz  
*(802, January or February, Aachen)*

[Col. 0221]

In 1820, while stationed at the monastery of Saint Paul in Carinthia, I again copied out in full the parchment through which the late Ussermann had made this mandate public in volume I of the *Prodromus Germaniae Sacrae*, no. 3. It consists of two leaves of thin parchment, sewn, as can be seen, in the fourteenth century into a parchment codex containing ecclesiastical canons and written in the ninth century. The script dates from approximately the year 800 after the birth of Christ. It is clear that the edict should be assigned to the first months of 802, when the emperor was staying at Aachen, because Charles stayed at Frankfurt, in the suburbs of Mainz, at Easter only in that year and in 794. It would be less suitable to assign it to 794, since it was only in later years that the greatest number of Saxon hostages fell into the king’s hands.

Moreover, the names of the bishops and abbot—namely, the bishops of Basel, Constance, Augsburg, and Reichenau—show that the document concerns only those Saxons who were being held in Alamannia and who were to be brought to the emperor by the bishop of Basel and Count Hitto. Ussermann observes that some of the counts’ names occur in Alamannian charters of this period: Hitto in 809 in Albwinipara near the Danube; Richoin in 817; Wanning in Nibelgau in 802; Unroc and Ripoin in Nibelgau in 802; and Birtilo in Bertoldsbaar.

### From the Westphalians, Bishop Haito and Count Hitto shall receive these:

[Note: [Col. 0221D] The word *habuit* (“held”) is written almost everywhere, except at the places marked with an asterisk.]

Leodac, son of Bodolo.

Adalrad, son of Marcrad, was held by Bishop Aino [Note: [Col. 0221D] Basel.]

Odo, son of Emmo, was held by Count Ansbert.

Eruin, son of Rano, was held by Richoin.

Crailinc, son of Thetmaer, was held by Richoin.

Gerimfrid, son of Egloin, was held by Bishop Egino [Note: [Col. 0222D] Constance.]

Aichardh, son of Fredred, was held by Ado of Alamannia.

Theodoar, son of Audrad, was held by Count Winang.

Baldric, son of Rotger, was held by Count Geremannus [Note: [Col. 0222D] The word was omitted, leaving a blank space.]

Adalgaud, son of Suigaut, was held by Count Unroc.

### From the Eastphalians:

Gerard, son of Macco, was held by Bishop Sinbert [Note: [Col. 0222D] Augsburg.]

Hisi, son of Brunard, was held by Bishop Agino.

The son of Maing was held by Lantfred.

Titbald [Note: [Col. 0221C] “Titbaldus” corrected to “Titbald” in C.], son of Sigibald, was held by Count Ripoin.

Vulfer, son of Sier, was held by Count Audrac.

Hernald, son of Suithard, was held by Abbot Waldo [Note: [Col. 0222D] Reichenau.]

Eriward, son of Herigild, was held by Eriwald the Alamannian.

These men shall come to Mainz in the middle of Lent.

Fredeger, son of Ermamenar, was held by Birtilo.

The son of Macco was held by Count Vulfald.

Wendulf, son of Bernulf, was held by Vulfald.

Dodo, son of Attost, was held by Torro.

Sidugath, son of Benninc, was held by Count Bertald.

Ricohard, son of Unvan, was held by Count Bertald [Note: [Col. 0221C] “Was held,” in the codex.]

Fredegarius, son of Wichar, was held by Walah.

Alabern, son of Tuto, was held by *Vulvaldus.

### From the Angrivarians:

Bunun, son of Theotaker, was held by Wichart.

Altbert, son of Wilbern, was held by Bishop Sindbert.

Hetti, son of Megi, was held by Sciltung.

Hadamar, son of Sigimar, and Hitto, son of Fridileih, and Brunher, son of Liuther, were held by Wolfolt.

Ditmann, son of Osmann, was held by Waldo.

Einhart held Fridamund, son of Warmund, and Macrin, son of Megitod.

Ruadhart, son of Danctag, was held by Ruadhari.

Hadabern, son of Witrad, was held by Reccho.

Wolfurich, son of Eorich, was held by Bishop Egino.

These amount in total to thirty-seven.

## Capitular of Aachen, 802  
*(March, Aachen)*

[Col. 0221]

The Lorsch, Saint-Amand, Wolfenbüttel, and Salzburg annals report that Charles, having assumed the imperial dignity and returned to Francia, held an assembly at Aachen in March of the year 802, at which he received new oaths and sent envoys throughout all his realms to exact them from the entire people and to administer justice everywhere. The chapters issued concerning this matter have been preserved in Codex no. 4613 of the Paris Library, a tenth-century manuscript, from which Baluze first published them; after careful comparison with it, they are reproduced here again.

[Col. 0223A] 1. Concerning the mission sent by our lord the emperor. Our most serene and most Christian lord Emperor Charles therefore chose from among his leading men the wisest and most prudent persons, both archbishops and other bishops, together with venerable abbots and religious laymen, and sent them throughout his entire realm. Through them he granted that all who followed them should live according to right law. Wherever anything had been established in the law otherwise than rightly and justly, he ordered them to investigate it with the greatest care and make it known to him, since, by God’s gift, he wishes to improve it. And let no one dare or be able, through his own ingenuity or cunning, to violate the written law, as many are accustomed to do, or to pervert his own justice [Note: [Col. 0223D] “To violate, to break through,” as above in the Capitular of the Bavarians, 788, chapter 1. Thus *marrire* here means “to break” or “to break through” the law, a metaphor taken from travelers who, deviating from the straight road, are still said by the Limousins to *marrire* the road. Hence, in title 19 of the Capitularies of Charles the Bald, chapter 13, *marritio* means “injury,” because one who inflicts an injury turns aside from the law. Again, in old charters of Saint Gall cited here by Sirmond, *marritio* means “diminution,” because one who diminishes or withdraws some part of a thing that ought to be whole deviates from equity. In a charter of Ariulf and his wife Adoara in the cartulary of the church of Vienne, the following is found: “After the death of us both, finally, let the aforesaid property be restored to the use of the canons of blessed Maurice without diminution.” Likewise in another charter of Constantius, chorepiscopus, and his brother Adrulf, deacon: “After our death, let the farmers of blessed Maurice be restored without diminution or prejudice to the power and lordship of the mother church.”].

Nor shall anyone violate the churches of God, the poor, widows, orphans, or any Christian person [Col. 0223B]. Rather, let everyone live entirely according to God’s command, in a just order and under just judgment; and let each person remain unanimously in his own purpose or profession. Let the canons fully observe canonical life without the business of shameful profit; let the nuns guard their lives under careful supervision; and let laymen and secular persons rightly use their own laws without fraud or malice. Let all live perfectly with one another in charity and peace. Let the envoys diligently investigate wherever anyone complains that another has done him an injustice, just as they desire to preserve for themselves the grace of almighty God [Note: [Col. 0223] Thus I have corrected the text; the codex has a different reading.] and to maintain the fidelity promised to him. Thus, everywhere and in all things—whether in the holy churches of God, or among the poor, orphans, widows, and the whole people—let them fully and justly administer the law according to the will and fear of God. If there should be anything that they themselves, together with the provincial counts, are unable to correct and restore to justice, let them without hesitation refer it, with their written reports [Note: [Col. 0224D] “Briefs,” “short records,” or “inventories.”—Id.], to his judgment. And let no one obstruct the straight path of justice through anyone’s flattery or reward, or through kinship, protection, or fear of the powerful [Note: [Col. 0223] “Or other,” in C.].

2. Concerning the fidelity to be promised to our lord the emperor [Note: [Col. 0223] The remaining rubrics are absent in C.]. He therefore commanded that every person throughout his entire realm, whether ecclesiastical or lay, each according to his vow and purpose, who had previously promised fidelity to him in the name of the king, should now make that same promise in the name of the emperor. And those who had not yet fulfilled that promise should likewise make it, down to the age of twelve. And so that it might be publicly explained how everyone could understand how great and how many matters are contained in this oath [Note: [Col. 0223] Absent in C.], let no one, as many have until now supposed, think that it concerns only fidelity to our lord the emperor throughout his lifetime, not admitting an enemy into his realm out of hostility, and not consenting to or concealing anyone’s infidelity toward him; rather, let everyone know that this oath contains the following obligation toward him [Note: [Col. 0223] Baluze thus emended the codex’s reading, “this compassion.”].

[Col. 0224B] 3. First, each person must strive, with his own person, to preserve himself fully in the holy service of God, according to God’s command and according to his promise, in accordance with his understanding and strength; for our lord the emperor cannot individually provide the necessary care and discipline for everyone.

4. Second, no one, whether through perjury or by any other device or fraud, through anyone’s flattery or reward, shall in any way oppose, remove, or conceal either a servant of our lord the emperor, a boundary, land, or anything that remains under his lawful authority. Nor shall anyone presume to conceal or remove his own royal fugitives, who unjustly and fraudulently claim to be free, through perjury or any other device [Note: [Col. 0223] “No one,” in C.].

[Col. 0224C] 5. No one shall presume to inflict fraud, robbery, or any injury upon the holy churches of God, widows, orphans, or pilgrims, because our lord the emperor, after the Lord and his saints, has been appointed their protector and defender [Note: [Col. 0223] “whose,” in C.].

6. No one shall dare abandon the benefice of our lord the emperor in order to establish his own property from it.

7. No one shall presume to disregard the military ban of our lord the emperor, nor shall any count be so presumptuous [Note: [Col. 0223] “Companion,” in the codex.] as to release from it anyone who is required to go to war, whether through any defense based on kinship or through the flattery of any gift [Col. 0225A].

8. That no one at all presume in any way to obstruct any ban or command of the lord emperor, nor to hinder, impede [Note: [Col. 0225] “bind/tighten” (*stricare*) in c.], diminish, or in any other way act contrary to his will or commands. And that no one dare obstruct his due or census.

9. That no one in court presume to plead on behalf of another, or unjustly undertake another’s defense, whether out of greed [Note: [Col. 0225] “cuditate” in c.] for someone unable to plead adequately, or by some contrivance of his own pleading to obstruct a just judgment, or with the aim of oppressing someone unable to make his case. Rather, each person shall answer for his own cause, census, or debt, unless someone is infirm or ignorant of legal proceedings; in such a case, the envoys or officers present at that court, or the judge who knows the substance of the case, shall plead for him. Or, if necessity requires, a suitable person shall be appointed [Note: [Col. 0225] “ad?” in c.] to plead, acceptable to everyone and well acquainted with the case; this, however, shall be done entirely according to the agreement of the officers or envoys who are present. In every respect it shall be done according to justice and law, so that through reward, payment, some device of evil flattery, or defense based on kinship, no one may obstruct justice. And no one shall unjustly support anyone else; rather, all shall be prepared with every effort and good will to bring justice to completion.

[Col. 0225C] For all the foregoing matters must be observed by imperial oath.

10. That bishops and priests live according to the canons, and thus teach the others.

11. That bishops, abbots, and abbesses, who are placed over others, diligently strive to govern their subjects with the greatest reverence and care [Note: [Col. 0225] “precesse” in c.]. They shall not oppress those subject to them through domineering authority or tyranny, but shall carefully guard the flock entrusted to them with simple love, gentleness, and charity, and by the example of good works.

12. That where there are monks, abbots live fully with the monks according to the Rule, and diligently learn and observe the canons [Note: [Col. 0225] “canonicis” in c.]. Abbesses likewise shall do so.

13. That bishops, abbots, and abbesses have as advocates and stewards, and as centenarii, men who know the law, love justice, and are peaceful and gentle, so that through them the prosperity [Note: [Col. 0225] “command” in c.] or reward of the holy churches of God may increase. For we by no means wish to have in monasteries superiors or advocates who are harmful and greedy, from whom blasphemy or damage may instead arise for us. Rather, let them be such as canonical or regular discipline [Note: [Col. 0225] “by consideration” (*intuitu*) in c.] commands them to be: subject to the will of God [Note: [Col. 0225] “of God; subject” in c.], always ready to accomplish justice for everyone, fully observing the law without malicious fraud, and always exercising just judgment in all matters. Make your superiors such as the holy Rule teaches them to be. Let them observe this above all: that they in no respect depart from canonical or regular discipline [Note: [Col. 0225] “from us in greater unanimity” in c.], but display humility in all things. If, however, they presume otherwise, let them experience regular discipline. And if they refuse to correct themselves, let them be removed from office, and let worthy men be substituted in their places.

14.
