That bishops, abbots, abbesses, and counts be unanimous with one another [Note: [Col. 0225] “with certain other evils” perhaps; the passage is corrupt.] and agree to bring just judgment to an end with complete charity and peaceful concord; and that they live faithfully according to the will of God, so that everywhere and always, both through them and among them, just judgment may be completed, and that the poor, widows, orphans, and pilgrims may receive consolation and protection [Note: [Col. 0225] “declaration” in c.] from them. Thus, through their good will, we too may deserve the reward of eternal life rather than punishment.

15. [Note: [Col. 0225] In c. this chapter is joined to the preceding one.] We wish and command in every way that abbots and monks be subject to their bishops with complete humility and obedience, as canonical constitution commands. Every church and basilica shall remain under ecclesiastical protection and authority. No one shall dare to place the property of a basilica into division or allotment. What has once been offered shall not be reclaimed, but shall remain sanctified and protected. If anyone presumes otherwise, let him make satisfaction [Note: [Col. 0225] “be released” in c.] and pay our ban. The monks shall be disciplined by the bishop of that province. If they do not correct themselves, then the archbishop shall summon them to a synod. And if they still do not reform [Note: [Col. 0225] “if they likewise do not rise up” in c.], then they shall come into our presence together with their bishop.

16. Concerning the choice of persons for ordination: the lord emperor long ago granted by a Frankish ban, and has now confirmed, a provision concerning bishops and abbots [the wording is corrupt], but on this condition: that neither bishop nor abbot prefer an inferior person in the monastery to a better one, or strive to advance someone on account of kinship or any kind of flattery, and present such a person to us for ordination while concealing and suppressing someone better than he. We absolutely do not wish this to happen, since it appears to be an insult [Note: [Col. 0225] “a greater insult” in c.] and mockery of us. Rather, let such men be raised in the monasteries for ordination [Note: [Col. 0225] Baluze reads “for prayer”], in whom both our reward and the prosperity of those who recommend them may increase.

17. Monks, however, must live firmly and steadfastly according to the Rule, since we know that whoever is lukewarm in his own way of life displeases God, as John testifies in the Apocalypse: “Would that you were hot or cold; but because you are lukewarm, I shall begin to vomit you out of my mouth.” They must by no means claim for themselves worldly negligence. They shall have no permission to go outside the monastery unless compelled by the greatest necessity. Nevertheless, the bishop in whose diocese [Note: [Col. 0227] “teaches” in c.] they are shall take every care that they do not acquire the habit of wandering outside the monastery. If necessity requires someone to go outside for some obedience, this shall be done with the counsel and consent of the bishop, and such persons shall be sent out with letters of testimony, so that there is no evil suspicion concerning them and no evil report arises from them.

As for property or goods outside the monastery, the abbot, with the permission and counsel of his bishop, shall appoint someone to supervise them—not a monk, unless [Note: [Col. 0227] “another” in c.] he is a faithful man. They shall entirely avoid secular profit and desire for worldly things, since avarice and desire for this world must be avoided by every Christian, and especially by those who appear to have renounced the world and its desires. No one shall presume to stir up lawsuits or quarrels either within or outside the monastery. Whoever presumes to do so shall be corrected by the gravest regular discipline, so that the others may fear to commit such acts.

They shall entirely shun drunkenness and gluttony, since it is well known that these especially lead to defilement by lust. For a most pernicious report has reached our ears: that many cases of fornication have already been discovered in monasteries, together with abomination and impurity. It greatly grieves and disturbs us—for it can be said without error—that from the very place from which all Christians were believed to derive the greatest hope of salvation, namely, from the life and chastity of monks, damage should instead arise, so that it has been heard that some monks are sodomites. Therefore we beg and admonish them most earnestly to guard and preserve themselves from these evils from this day forward, so that nothing of this kind may ever again reach our ears.

Let this be known to everyone: we will never again dare to tolerate these evils anywhere in our realm, and still less among those who ought to be more exemplary in chastity and holiness. Certainly, if any such matters continue to reach our ears, we shall inflict such vengeance not only upon those involved but also upon the others who permit such things, that no Christian who hears of it will thereafter presume to commit anything of the kind [Note: [Col. 0227] “such a thing” in c.; the preceding phrase is corrupt in the source].

18. The monasteries of women must be strictly observed, and they must never be allowed to wander about; rather, they must be guarded with every care. No one shall presume to stir up lawsuits or quarrels among them, nor shall they dare to be disobedient or opposed in any matter to their superiors and abbesses. Where they are under a Rule, they must observe it in every respect: they must not devote themselves to fornication, drunkenness, or greed, but must live entirely justly and soberly.

No man shall enter their enclosure or monastery, except a priest who enters to visit the sick with written testimony, or who enters only for Mass and immediately departs. No one shall receive another person’s daughter into the congregation of holy women without the knowledge and consideration of the bishop to whose diocese that place belongs. The bishop himself shall carefully inquire how she wishes to remain in that holy place [Note: [Col. 0227] absent in c.] in the service of God, and whether she intends to establish her stability there or make her profession. Maidservants belonging to other people, and women of the sort who wish to live in the holy congregation according to the customary manner of life, must be entirely expelled from the congregation.

19. Bishops, abbots, priests, deacons, and no one at all from the clergy shall presume to keep dogs for hunting, or hawks, falcons, or sparrowhawks. Each person must instead preserve himself fully in his own order, canonically or regularly. Whoever presumes to do so shall know that he will lose his honor. The others shall suffer such a penalty for this that the rest may fear to appropriate such things for themselves [Note: [Col. 0227] “may fear” in the manuscript].

20. Abbesses, together with their holy women, must keep themselves unanimously [Note: [Col. 0227] “unanimously” as written in c.] and diligently within the enclosure, and must never presume to go outside it. If an abbess wishes to send out some of the holy women, she must under no circumstances do so without the permission and counsel of her bishop. Likewise, whenever she must arrange anything in the monasteries or receive anyone into the monasteries, she must first discuss it fully with her bishops. Whatever they determine should be done for the greater health or usefulness, they shall announce to the archbishop, and the necessary actions shall be completed with his counsel.

21. Counts must present the priests and other canons whom they have with them in their ministries [Note: [Col. 0227] “or” in c.] as entirely subject to their bishops, as canonical institution commands. They must agree that their bishops fully instruct these men under holy discipline, just as they desire to retain our favor and their own honors.

22. Canons must fully observe the canonical life, and in the bishop’s household or in monasteries they must be educated with every care according to canonical discipline. They must not be allowed to wander outside, but must live under strict supervision: not devoted to shameful profit, not fornicators, not thieves, not murderers, not robbers, not quarrelsome, not angry, not arrogant, not drunkards, but chaste in heart and body, humble, modest, sober, gentle, and peaceful, so that they may be worthy sons of God to be advanced in the sacred order.

They must not wander through streets or villages to neighboring churches or boundaries [Note: [Col. 0227] “wine” in c.] without instruction or discipline, like those called sarabaites, indulging in luxury or fornication or committing other wicked acts which it is abhorrent to tolerate.

23. Priests must carefully oversee the clergy whom they have with them, so that they live canonically and do not engage in empty amusements, secular banquets, songs, or luxurious practices, but live chastely and in a wholesome manner.

24. If any priest or deacon thereafter presumes to keep women with him in his house outside canonical permission, he shall be deprived both of his honor and of his inheritance [Note: [Col. 0229] “deprived of both” in c.] until he comes into our presence.

25. Counts and centenarii must enforce all justice, and must have in their ministries [Note: [Col. 0229] “or” in c.] such younger officials as they can trust with confidence—men who faithfully observe law and justice, and who will by no means oppress the poor. No one shall dare to conceal, through flattery, reward, or any protection, thieves, robbers, murderers, adulterers, evil-doers, magicians, female diviners, or any sacrilegious persons; rather, they must expose them, so that they may be corrected and punished according to law, and so that, by God’s gift, all these evils may be removed from the Christian people.

26. Judges must judge justly according to the written law, not according to their own discretion.

[Col. 0229B] 27. We command that throughout our entire realm no one, rich or poor, dare refuse lodging to any traveler [Note: [Col. 0229] “services” in c.]. Whether it is a pilgrim traveling through the land for God’s sake, or anyone journeying for the love of God and the salvation of his soul, no one shall deny him roof, fire, or water. If anyone wishes to do more good for them, let him know that he will receive the best recompense from God, as he himself said: “Whoever receives one little child for my sake receives me.” And elsewhere: “I was a stranger [Note: [Col. 0229] “poor, and no one inspected me” in c.], and you received me.”

28. Concerning envoys coming from the lord emperor and messengers sent by him: counts and centenarii must oversee them with every diligence, as they desire the favor of the lord emperor, so that they may proceed without delay [Note: [Col. 0229] “it was delayed” in c.] through their jurisdictions [Note: [Col. 0229] “may arise anywhere” in c.]. He has commanded everyone in every respect, since this is their duty, to ensure that the envoys suffer no delay anywhere, but that they make their journey with all speed, and that they arrange their responsibilities in such a way as our envoys direct.

29. Concerning the poor whom the lord emperor commends to his alms, though they are liable to pay his ban: judges, counts, and our envoys must not, under colour of that concession, constrain them for their own advantage [Note: [Col. 0229] “service” in c.].

30. Concerning those whom the lord emperor wishes, with Christ’s favor, to have peace and protection throughout his realm: namely, those who hasten to his clemency wishing to announce something, whether they are Christians or pagans [Note: [Col. 0229] “from the side of?”], or whether they seek assistance because of want or hunger. No one shall dare to compel them into his service or seize them, nor alienate or sell them. Wherever they voluntarily wish to remain, there, under the protection of the lord emperor, they shall receive assistance as part of his alms. If anyone presumes to transgress this, let him know that he will suffer such a penalty as the lord emperor’s command has determined [Note: [Col. 0229] “and so forth” in c.; the passage is corrupt].

31. No one shall presume to contrive any harm or injury against those who announce the justice of the lord emperor, nor stir up any hostility against them. Whoever presumes to do so shall pay the imperial ban. Or, if he is guilty of a greater debt, he shall be brought into his presence by command.

[Col. 0230A] 32. We command that homicides, through which much Christian people perish before God [Note: [Col. 0229] “for whom” in c.], be entirely abandoned and forbidden. The immediately preceding words are corrupt, but may be rendered: “which the Lord himself heard … opposed to his faithful on account of his enmity”; homicides all the more [must be forbidden]. For how can someone trust that he will be pleasing to God [Note: [Col. 0229] “that he hated, hates”], who has killed his own son, one close to him? How can he suppose that Christ the Lord will be favorable to him [Note: [Col. 0229] “according to God”], when he has killed his brother?

It is also a great and unbearable danger, before God the Father and Christ, ruler of heaven and earth, to stir up the hostility of men. A person may escape men by hiding for a time [Note: [Col. 0229] “cherish” in c.], but eventually he may fall into the hands of his enemies [Note: [Col. 0229] Baluze reads “and flee”]; where, however, can he flee from God, to whom all secrets are manifest? With what presumption does anyone think he can evade his anger [Note: [Col. 0229] “on what grounds” in c.]?

So that this evil may not destroy the people entrusted to us for governance [Note: [Col. 0229] the editor corrects the corrupt text as: “who, in the recklessness of his anger, thinks he can escape this”], we have taken care to avoid it with every discipline. For we cannot in any way have God appeased or favorable toward us if someone does not fear that God is angry with him. Rather, we wish to avenge with the harshest severity [Note: [Col. 0229] “with any punishment” in c.] anyone who has dared to commit the evil of homicide.

Nevertheless, lest sin increase and the greatest hostility arise among Christians when homicides occur through the persuasion of the devil, the guilty person must immediately turn to make amends. With all speed he must make suitable compensation to the relatives of the slain for the evil committed [Note: [Col. 0229] the text is defective; c. lacks a phrase]. We firmly ban this as well: the parents of the murdered person must not dare to increase their hostility over the evil committed [Note: [Col. 0229] “increase it” in c.], nor refuse peace to one who asks for it [Note: [Col. 0229] “faith in asking” in c.]. They must accept the pledged faith and the compensation prepared, and restore perpetual peace; the guilty person, meanwhile, must cause no delay in making compensation [Note: [Col. 0229] “property” in c.].

When, by the deserved judgment of sins, it happens that someone kills his brother or kinsman, he must immediately undertake the penance assigned to him and, without hesitation [Note: [Col. 0229] “and” in c.], strive to complete his remedy as his bishop directs. He must compensate for the slain according to law and reconcile himself completely with his relatives; once faith has been given, no one may dare to stir up hostility thereafter. Whoever refuses to make suitable amends shall be deprived of his inheritance until our judgment.

[Col. 0230D] 33. We absolutely prohibit the crime of incest [Note: [Col. 0229] “uncertain” in c.]. If anyone has been polluted by abominable fornication [Note: [Col. 0229] “n. a. f.” in c.], he must under no circumstances be released without severe punishment. He must be corrected in such a way that the others may fear to commit such acts, so that impurity may be entirely removed from the Christian people. The guilty person must make full amends for this through penance, as his bishop determines, and the woman must be placed in the hands of her relatives [Col. 0231A] until our judgment. If he refuses to accept the bishop’s judgment for his correction, then they shall be brought into our presence, remembering the example of what was done in the case of the incest committed by Fricco [Note: [Col. 0231] “which I committed” in c.] with a holy woman of God.

34. Everyone must be fully prepared whenever our command or announcement arrives. If anyone then says that he is unprepared and disregards the order, he shall be brought to the palace—not only he, but also all who presume to transgress our ban or command.

35. Everyone must honor his bishops and priests in every respect, in the service and will of God. They must not dare to defile themselves or others through incestuous [Note: [Col. 0231] “unlawful” in c.] marriages, nor presume to form unions before the bishops and priests, together with the elders of the people, have carefully investigated the kinship of those being joined. Then they shall be united with a blessing. They must avoid drunkenness, shun robbery, and commit no theft. Lawsuits, quarrels, and blasphemy, whether at banquets or at court, must be entirely avoided [Note: [Col. 0231] “doubted” in c.]; rather, they must live with charity and concord.

36. Everyone must be willing to carry out all justice and to cooperate with our envoys. They must not permit the practice of perjury at all [Note: [Col. 0231] Baluze inserts “at all”], for it is necessary to remove this most wicked crime from the Christian people [Note: [Col. 0231] “to offer it” in c.]. If anyone thereafter is convicted of perjury, he must know that he will lose his right hand [Note: [Col. 0231] “be completely deprived” in c.]; nevertheless, he shall not be deprived of his own inheritance until our judgment [Note: [Col. 0231] a word is lacking in c.].

37. Those who have committed parricide or fratricide [Note: [Col. 0231] “fratricide” abbreviated in c.], killing an uncle, a paternal uncle, or any of their relatives, and who refuse to obey or accept the judgment of the bishops, priests, and others, shall be confined by our envoys and counts in such custody [Note: [Col. 0231] “in such a custody” in c.] as is necessary for their salvation and for the rendering of just judgment, so that they remain secure and do not contaminate the rest of the people, until they are brought into our presence. In the meantime, they shall have nothing of their own property.

38. The same shall be done to those who have been convicted and corrected for unlawful and incestuous unions, yet refuse to amend themselves, obey neither their bishops nor their priests, and presume to despise our ban.

39. No one shall dare to steal our game in our forests; we have already forbidden this on many occasions. Now again we firmly ban it [Note: [Col. 0231] “but” in c.], so that no one does so any longer. Let each person take care to preserve for himself the fidelity he has promised us.

If any count, centenarius, our vassal, or anyone among our officials steals our game, he must be brought entirely into our presence for a reckoning. As for other common people who commit such theft of game, each must make the compensation that is just, and no one shall receive any remission for it. If anyone knowingly learns that another has committed this act, no one shall dare to conceal it, under the fidelity which they have promised us and must now promise again.

40. Finally, concerning all our decrees, we wish to know throughout our entire realm, and through our envoys now sent out, how each person—whether among ecclesiastical men, bishops, abbots, priests, deacons, canons, all monks, or holy women—has preserved our ban or decree in his ministry or profession; where it is appropriate to give thanks to any of them for their good will or to provide assistance; and where something still needs correction.

Likewise, concerning the laity, and in every place whatsoever, we wish to know about the protection of the holy churches, widows, orphans, and the least powerful, as well as robbery, the established military court, and all these matters: how they obey our command or will, how each person has preserved our ban [Note: [Col. 0231] “how” in c.], and above all how each person strives in holy service to keep himself devoted to God. Thus may all these things be good and well ordered for the praise of almighty God, and may we give thanks as is fitting.

Where we believe that something else remains unpunished [Note: [Col. 0231] “much” in c.], let us strive with every effort and good will to correct it [Note: [Col. 0231] “let it be” in c.], so that with God’s help we may bring it to correction, to our eternal reward and that of all our faithful. Likewise, concerning our counts, centenarii, and officials, we wish to know happily among ourselves all the matters mentioned above.

## Chapters Given to the Imperial Envoys

*(802, March, Aachen)*

[Col. 0231]

It is clear from the annals that, after the assembly at Aachen, Charles sent his envoys throughout all his realms to administer justice and to exact the oath of fidelity from everyone. Codex 1, the royal Paris manuscript no. 4995, has preserved for us chapters given to the envoys for the Parisian and Rouenese circuits. We publish them here for the first time in their entirety, since Baluze mixed only five of their chapters—taken from an uncertain source—with the chapters of the envoys for the Sens circuit. He had published these from Codices 2, the Palatine manuscript, and 3, that of Saint-Vincent of Metz; we present them again, revised also with the aid of Codex 4, the royal Paris manuscript among the Latin Supplements, no. 75.

[Col. 0233A] Chapters of the envoys for the Parisian and Rouenese circuit.

### Likewise, Chapters of Charles the Great, Emperor

[Note: [Col. 0233] Flodoard, Book II of the *History of Rheims*, chapter 18, states that Wulfarius, archbishop of Rheims, was appointed an envoy over all Champagne and the districts named there. It is preferable to set down the complete passage here, since it will shed much light on these capitularies:

“Wulfarius followed Tilpinus. He had been appointed, before becoming bishop, by the emperor mentioned above, the great Charles, as an imperial envoy to determine just judgments throughout all Champagne and in the following districts: Dolomense, Vogense, Castricense, Stradonense, Catalaunense, Otmense, Laudunense, Vadense, Portianus, Tardunense, and Suessionense. In the same way, certain other wise and God-fearing abbots were appointed throughout Gaul and Germany by the aforementioned emperor, so that they might diligently investigate how bishops, abbots, counts, and abbesses conducted themselves in each district, what concord and friendship they maintained with one another, and whether they had good and suitable stewards and advocates. They were also to investigate and complete, wherever necessary, both royal justice and the justice of the churches of God, as well as that of widows, orphans, and other people; they were to strive to correct whatever required correction as far as they could do so well, and whatever they could not correct themselves they were to have brought into the emperor’s presence. They were to strive faithfully to report all these matters to that prince.

Thus the aforementioned illustrious man Wulfarius, while residing to determine the judgments entrusted to him with certain counts in public courts, is found to have recovered certain properties for the church of Rheims, as well as some slaves or colonists, and to have vindicated them by law through the church’s advocates.”

That same imperial envoy was also at that time in Rhaetia, as Rupert, a monk of Saint Gall, teaches in the passage cited shortly before. Perhaps he was there with Unfred, count of Rhaetia, whose mention appears in a charter of Saint Gall preserved by Goldast in the second volume of *Rerum Alamannicarum*, p. 81. Arno, archbishop of Salzburg, fulfilled this mission in Bavaria together with his fellow bishop Adalwin—that is, the bishop of Regensburg—and the judge Orendil, as the old charters published in volume three of the *Metropolis Salisburgensis*, pp. 321–322, show. Baluze.]

1. Concerning the oath of fidelity: let everyone renew it.

[Note: [Col. 0233] It is evident from an old charter of Saint Gall, preserved by Goldast in volume II of *Rerum Alamannicarum*, p. 81, that the Rhaetians renewed it: “By the very oath which we have given to our lord.” Likewise the Bavarians, as is read in volume III of the *Metropolis Salisburgensis*, p. 322: “By the oath of fidelity which they swore to the lord emperor Charles in the presence of Arno himself.” From this it follows that the other peoples of the Frankish Empire also rendered the same oath. Baluze.]

2. Concerning bishops and the other priests: whether they live according to canonical institution, and whether they understand and fulfill the canons properly.

3. Concerning men’s monasteries where there are monks: whether they live according to the Rule or canonically, and whether they properly understand the Rule and the canons where these have been promised.

4. Concerning women’s monasteries: whether they live according to the Rule or canonically, and concerning their enclosures.

5. Concerning secular laws.

6. Concerning perjuries.

7. Concerning homicides.

8. Concerning adulteries and unlawful acts committed, both in episcopal establishments and in monasteries of men and women, and also among secular people.

9. Concerning those men whose benefices we have had destroyed and whose allods have been restored. Likewise concerning the property of churches.

10. Concerning those Saxons who have our benefices in Francia: how or in what manner they hold them restored [the wording is corrupt].

[Col. 0233C] 11. Concerning the oppression of poor free men who are required to go on campaign and have been oppressed by judges.

12. That everyone be properly prepared whenever our command arrives.

[Col. 0235A] 13. Concerning the preparation of ships along the seacoasts.

14. Concerning free men who live near the maritime regions: if a summons arrives that they must come to give assistance and they neglect to do so, each shall pay twenty solidi—half to the treasury and half to the people. If there is a landing [Note: [Col. 0235] perhaps “shore”], he shall pay fifteen solidi to the people and the lord’s fredum.

15. Concerning envoys coming to us and messengers sent by us.

16. Concerning those whom we wish, with Christ’s favor, to have peace and protection throughout our realms.

17. Concerning those men who have been killed while announcing our justice.

18. Concerning tithes and ninths, and the justice [Note: [Col. 0235] “chastity” in c.] of the churches of God: let everyone strive to give and render them.

[Col. 0235B] 19. Concerning the ban of the lord emperor and king, which he is accustomed to proclaim personally: namely, the protection of churches, widows, orphans, and the least powerful, as well as robbery and the established military court. Those who violate these matters must pay the lord’s ban in every respect.

20. Let them diligently inquire among bishops, abbots, counts, abbesses, and our vassals what concord and friendship they have with one another in each jurisdiction, and, if any disagreement appears to exist among them, let them not neglect to report the entire truth about it to us under oath. Let everyone have good stewards and advocates.

21. [Note: [Col. 0235] This does not appear in the Palatine and Metz manuscripts and was taken from the same copy of Sirmond. Baluze.] For Paris, Meaux, Melun, Provins, [Col. 0235C] Étampes, Chartres, and Poissy: Fardulfus and Stephen.

[Note: [Col. 0235] I agree with the distinguished author of the *Annals of the Church of the Franks*, who explains this passage as referring to Fardulf, abbot of Saint-Denis. Id.]

[Note: [Col. 0235] Count of Paris. Id.]

Moreover, wherever necessary, let them investigate and complete matters both concerning our justice and concerning the justice of the churches, widows, orphans, minors, and other people. Whatever they find requiring correction, let them strive to correct as well as they can. Whatever they cannot correct themselves, let them have brought into our presence.

[Note: [Col. 0235] I find this observed by Wulfarius, archbishop of Rheims, who was an imperial envoy in Rhaetia at that time. Rupert the monk, in Book 5 of *On the Origin and Fate of the Monastery of Saint Gall*: “He urged them to send the same charter of confirmation to the lord emperor through some trustworthy man.” Baluze.]

In Le Mans, Hoxon, Lisieux, Bayeux, Coutances, Avranches, Évreux, and Madrie, and on that side of the Seine belonging to Rouen, [Note: [Col. 0235] Rouen, mentioned in chapter eight of the Frankfurt capitulary. Id.] Bishop Magenardus [Col. 0235D] and Madelgaudus.

[Note: [Col. 0235] Perhaps the brother of Angilbert, abbot of Centula. Nithard, Angilbert’s son, states in Book IV of *On the Dissensions of the Sons of Louis the Pious* that Madelgaudus and Richard were his brothers. These three brothers, he says, were held in high regard by Charles the Great. Id.]

## Chapters of the Envoys for the Sens Circuit

First, from the city of Orléans to the Saône, as is right; then to Troyes with the whole territory of Troyes; from there to Langres; from Langres to Besançon, in a place belonging to Burgundy; from there to Autun; afterward along the Loire as far as Orléans. The envoys are Archbishop Magnus [Note: [Col. 0233] of Sens. Id.] and Count Godefridus.

1. Concerning the oath of fidelity: let everyone renew it.

2. Concerning bishops and the other priests: whether they live according to canonical institution, and whether they properly understand and fulfill the canons.

3. Concerning abbots: whether they live according to the Rule or canonically, and whether they properly understand the Rule or the canons.

4. Concerning men’s monasteries where there are monks: whether they live according to the Rule, where the Rule has been promised.

5. Concerning women’s monasteries: whether they live according to the Rule or canonically, and concerning their enclosures.

6. Concerning secular laws.

7. Concerning perjuries.

8. Concerning homicides.

9. Concerning adulteries and unlawful acts committed, both in episcopal establishments and in monasteries of men and women, and also among secular people.

10. Concerning those men whose benefices we have had destroyed and whose allods have been restored. Likewise concerning the property of churches.

11. Concerning those Saxons who have our benefices in Francia: how or in what manner they hold them restored [the wording is corrupt].

[Col. 0234C] 12. Concerning the oppression of poor free men who are required to go on campaign and have been oppressed by judges.

13. That everyone be properly prepared whenever our command arrives.

[Col. 0236A] 14. Concerning embassies coming to us and envoys sent by us.

15. Concerning those whom we wish to have peace and protection throughout our realms, with Christ’s favor.

16. Concerning those men who have been killed while announcing our justice.

17. Concerning tithes and ninths, and the justice of the churches of God, so that [Note: [Col. 0235] “so that all may give,” Bal.] they may strive to give and make restitution.

[Col. 0236B] 18. Concerning the ban of the lord emperor Charles, which he is accustomed to proclaim personally—that is, concerning the mundoburdium [Note: [Col. 0235] Thus, but corrected to *mundiburgium* in 4 and 55.] of churches, widows, orphans, and the less powerful, as well as concerning robbery and the military court that has been established—so that those who violate these matters may in every way pay the lord’s ban.

19. Concerning every matter, moreover, whatever may be necessary wherever it may be [Col. 0236C], whether concerning our own rights or the rights of the churches of God, widows, orphans, minors, and other people: let them investigate and bring these matters to completion. Whatever they find requiring correction, let them strive to correct as well as they can. Whatever they cannot correct themselves, let them have brought before us.

[Note: [Col. 0235] This exists among the formulas of Lindenbrog, chapter 40. Andreas Duchesne thought that these matters belonged to the year 770, because he saw that they had been enacted in Charles’s second year. It is certain, however, that they must be referred back to the year 802. Ed.]

### Oath

This is the form in which I promise: from this day forward I am faithful to the lord Charles, most pious emperor, son of King Pippin and Queen Bertrada, with a pure mind, without fraud or evil intent, on my part toward his part and for the honor of his kingdom, as a man ought by right to be toward his lord. So may God help me, and these relics of the saints that are in this place: throughout the days of my life, by my own will, insofar as God grants me understanding, I will so attend and consent.

Another form. This is the form in which I promise to the lord Charles, most pious emperor, son of King Pippin and Bertrada: I am faithful to him as a man ought by right to be toward his lord, for his kingdom and his rightful authority. And the oath that I have sworn I will keep, and I wish to keep it, insofar as I know and understand, from this day forward. So may God help me, who created heaven and earth, and these relics of the saints.

## EXCERPTED CHAPTERS

*(Year 802, March, Aachen.)*

[Col. 0237]

These chapters were first published by Baluze from the notes of Jacques Sirmond. They should be referred immediately to the foregoing capitulary. For they contain a few items that are not found there, or in the capitulary of 789 concerning ecclesiastical matters, in the same words.

[Col. 0237A]

1. [Chapter 2] That the faith, life, and knowledge of those who come to be ordained should first be examined by the bishop.

2. [Chapter 3] That fugitive and foreign clerics should be received by no one without letters of recommendation.

3. [Chapter 4] That presbyters, deacons, or other clerics should not have an unrelated woman in their house.

4. [Chapter 14] That monks and clerics should not enter taverns for the purpose of eating or drinking.

5. [Chapter 16] That unknown names of angels should neither be invented nor pronounced.

6. [Chapter 17] That women should not enter the altar area.

7. [Chapter 20] That only canonical books should be read in church.

8. [Chapter 21] That no one should be ordained for money.

9. [Chapter 22] That a monk or cleric should not turn to secular business.

10. [Chapter 24] That clerics should not migrate from one city to another.

11. [Chapter 25] That no one should be ordained without qualification.

12. [Chapter 26] That clerics and monks should remain in their chosen way of life.

13. [Chapter 28] That clerics who have a dispute among themselves should be judged by their bishop, not by secular authorities.

14. [Chapter 29] That clerics and monks should not lay plots against their pastor.

15. [Chapter 31] That places once dedicated to God as monasteries should remain monasteries perpetually, and should not thereafter become secular dwellings.

[Note: [Col. 0237] Among the laws of the Lombards, K. M., Muratori, chapter 135.]

16. [Chapter 37] That no presbyter should dare to act arrogantly toward his bishop.

[Col. 0237C]

17. [Chapter 38] That clerics of ecclesiastical rank, if they incur guilt, should be judged among ecclesiastical persons, not among secular persons.

18. [Chapter 39] That whoever lends money should receive money. If he lends some other kind of thing, he should receive the same kind, in the quantity he gave.

19. [Note: [Col. 0237] From the Council of Carthage, chapter 16; cited in the ecclesiastical capitulary of 789, book I, chapter 38.] That before the age of twenty-five neither deacons should be ordained nor virgins consecrated.

20. [Note: [Col. 0237] Council of Africa, chapter 11, whence chapter 39 of the ecclesiastical capitulary of 789.] That consecrated virgins living together should watch over one another and should not, by wandering about indiscriminately, damage the reputation of the Church.

21. [Chapter 42] That false names of martyrs should not be venerated.

22. [Chapter 43] That neither a wife dismissed by her husband should take another husband while her own husband is alive, nor should a husband take another wife while his former wife is alive.

[Col. 0238A]

23. [Chapter 48] That ecclesiastical fasts should not be broken without reasonable necessity.

24. [Chapter 50] That a presbyter should in no way be ordained before his thirtieth year.

25. [Chapter 55] That none of the priests should be permitted to be ignorant of the regulations of the holy canons.

26. [Chapter 57] That no bishop should presume to promote another person’s slave to clerical office without the consent of his master.

27. [794, 51; 802, 1, 10] That bishops and the other priests should understand the canons well and live according to canonical institution.

28. [789 ecclesiastical, chapter 69] That bishops should carefully examine throughout their dioceses the presbyters—their faith, baptism, and celebration of Mass—and that they should hold the correct faith, observe Catholic baptism, understand the prayers of the Mass properly, and sing the psalms worthily according to the melodies of the verses.

[Col. 0238B]

29. [Chapter 60] That the Catholic faith should be read carefully by bishops and presbyters and preached to all the people. [Chapter 68] And that they themselves should understand the Lord’s Prayer and preach it to everyone so that it may be understood, so that each person may know what he asks from God.

30. That all Christian people should know the Catholic faith and the Lord’s Prayer by heart.

31. [Chapter 61] That among bishops, abbots, counts, judges, and all persons everywhere, both greater and lesser, there should be peace, harmony, and unanimity; for nothing pleases God without peace.

32. That canonical abbots should understand and observe the canons, and that canonical clerics should live according to the canons.

33. That regular abbots and monks should understand the Rule and live according to the Rule.

34. That canonical abbesses and nuns should live canonically according to the canons, and that their enclosures should be properly arranged.

35. That regular abbesses and [Note: [Col. 0237] Absent in Baluze.] nuns living according to the monastic vocation should understand the Rule and live regularly, and that their enclosures should be arranged reasonably.

36. [Chapter 70] That the Church of God should have its honor; likewise, that altars should be venerated according to their dignity. The house of God and the sacred altars should not be accessible to dogs. Secular business or empty chatter should not be conducted in churches.

[Col. 0239A]

37. [Chapter 69] That presbyters, deacons, and other clerics should not carry weapons, but should place their confidence more in God’s protection than in arms.

38. [Chapter 62] That those to whom the power of judging has been given should judge justly, not for gifts, because gifts blind the hearts of the prudent. And that judges should judge and discern cases while fasting. [Note: [Col. 0239] “Let them hear,” 789, book I, chapter 61.]

39. [Chapter 63] That everyone should beware of perjury, not only in the holy Gospel, at the altar, or over the relics of the saints, but also in ordinary speech. Whoever must swear by holy things should do so fasting, with all propriety and fear of God. Whoever has once committed perjury should thereafter be neither a witness nor a juror, either in his own case or in another’s.

40. [Chapter 64] That no one should consult diviners, observe dreams, or attend to omens; and that there should be no sorcerers, enchanters, pythonesses, calculators, storm-makers, or spell-binders. Wherever such people are found, they should be corrected or condemned.

[Col. 0239B]

41. [Chapter 64] That the observances practiced by fools at trees, stones, or springs should everywhere be removed and destroyed.

42. [Chapter 66] That homicides should not be committed within the country for the sake of vengeance, greed, or robbery. No one should be killed unless the law commands it.

43. [Chapter 67] That thefts, unlawful marriages, and illicit causes should be prohibited.

44. [Chapter 73] That everyone should have equal and correct measures and just and equal weights. [Note: [Col. 0239] What follows is not found at this place.] And whoever formerly gave three *modii* should now give two.

[Col. 0239C]

45. [Chapter 78] That slave-dealers, brokers, and unarmed men who go about with iron should not be allowed to wander about and deceive people.

46. [Chapter 80] That servile work should not be done on Sundays. Sunday should be celebrated from evening to evening.

47. [Note: [Col. 0239] Compare the capitulary for the envoys of Rouen, above, col. 233, chapter 1.] That everyone should promise fidelity to the lord emperor.

[Col. 0240A]

48. [Same place, perhaps chapter 5.] That counts and judges should declare by what law they ought to live, and should judge according to it.

49. [Chapter 9] That the benefices of the lord emperor and of the churches should be examined, lest someone, restoring his own allod, destroy the benefices.

50. [Chapter 10] That the benefices of the Saxons in Francia should be examined as to how they have been regulated.

51. [Chapter 11] That poor free men should not be unjustly oppressed by anyone.

52. [Chapter 12] That everyone should be prepared whenever the lord emperor’s command should come.

53. [Chapter 15] That envoys coming to the lord emperor and those sent by him should be received honorably.

54. [Chapter 16] That those who are under the lord emperor’s mundeburdium [protection] should have peace and protection from everyone.

[Col. 0240B]

55. [Chapter 17] That inquiry should be made whether any man has been killed, or suffered some other harm, because he announced the lord emperor’s justice.

56. [Chapter 18] That those who hold ecclesiastical property through a benefice of the lord emperor should strive to give a tenth and a ninth and to restore the churches.

57. [Chapter 19] That the ban which the lord emperor has proclaimed personally should be paid at sixty solidi. Other bans imposed by counts and judges should be compounded according to the law of each person.

58. [Chapter 20] That everyone should have good and suitable subordinate officials, advocates, and judges.

[Col. 0240C]

59. [Chapter 20] That our envoys, wherever necessary, should investigate and complete matters concerning the rights of the churches of God, widows, orphans, minors, and all other people; whatever they find requiring correction, they should strive to correct as well as they can. Whatever they cannot correct themselves, they should have brought before us.

## GENERAL ADMONITION

[Col. 0239]

The foregoing capitulary (cols. 223–232) is followed in Paris Codex 4613 by a few lines, regarded by Baluze as chapter 41, but incomplete because the remaining part of the codex has been lost, and apparently not belonging to the capitulary itself. I copied the lost portion from the Cavensis Codex, and it appears to be an address of the emperor in which he orders the nobles to return home after the assembly has been dissolved. It seems to have been delivered at the end of the preceding assembly, both from the place where it is read in the Paris Codex and from what is said near the end to the dukes, counts, and judges concerning the administration of justice. I did not wish to remove the countless defects of the speech, which are not difficult for anyone experienced in these matters to understand. Number 1 indicates the Cavensis Codex; 2, the Parisian.

### THE ADMONITION OF THE LORD EMPEROR CHARLES

[Col. 0239D]

Hear, beloved brothers. We have been sent here for your salvation [Note: [Col. 0239] “our salvation,” corrected to “your salvation,” 1.], so that we may admonish you how you should live justly and well according to God, and how, in accordance with this world [Note: [Col. 0239] Absent in 2.], you should conduct yourselves with justice and mercy [Note: [Col. 0239] “Conduct ourselves,” 1; “let us live,” 2.].

I admonish you first of all to believe in one God, the almighty Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. This is one and true God, perfect Trinity and true unity [Note: [Col. 0239] “And true unity” is absent in 1.], creator [Note: [Col. 0239] From “Creator” through “author” is absent in 2.] of all visible and invisible things, in whom is our salvation and the author of all our good.

Believe that the Son of God was made human for the salvation of the world, born of the Holy Spirit from the Virgin Mary. Believe that he suffered death for our salvation, rose from the dead on the third day, ascended into heaven, and sits at the right hand of God. Believe that he will come [Note: [Col. 0241] “He will come” is absent in 1.] to judge the living and the dead, and then will repay each person according to his works.

Believe in one Church—that is, the congregation of good people—throughout the whole world. Know that only those will be able to be saved, and only those belong to the kingdom of God, who persevere to the end in the faith [Note: [Col. 0241] “Who have the beginning,” 1.] and communion and charity of this Church [Note: [Col. 0241] “Of the seat,” 2.] . But those who are excommunicated from this Church for their sins [Note: [Col. 0241] I have supplied “for their sins”; it is absent in 1.] and do not return to it through repentance cannot do anything acceptable to God in the world [Col. 0241B].

Believe that in baptism you have received remission of all sins. Hope in God’s mercy that our daily sins may be redeemed through confession and repentance. Believe in the resurrection of all the dead and eternal life; and in the eternal punishment of the ungodly.

This, then, is our faith, through which you will be saved if you hold it firmly and fulfill it by good works, because faith without works is dead, and works without faith, even if they are good, cannot please God.

Therefore, first love God the Almighty with all your heart and all your strength. Whatever you are able to know that pleases God, always do that as far as you can with God’s help. Flee whatever is contrary to God; for whoever says that he loves God but does not keep his commandments is a liar.

Love your neighbors as yourselves, and give alms to the poor according to your means. Receive strangers into your homes; visit the sick; show mercy to those who are in prisons. Do no evil to anyone, as far as you truly can; do not consent to those who do such things. For not only those who do them are guilty, but also those who consent to the doing of them.

Forgive one another your debts, as you wish God to forgive you your sins. Redeem captives; help those unjustly oppressed; defend widows and orphans; judge justly; do not consent to wrongdoing; do not retain prolonged anger; flee drunkenness and excessive feasting.

Be humble and kind among yourselves. Serve our lord faithfully. Do not commit theft or perjury, nor consent to those who commit them. Hatred and envy [Note: [Col. 0241] Perhaps “violent [hatred]”; the reading *violinque* is uncertain.] separate people from the kingdom of God.

Reconcile yourselves quickly to peace among yourselves, because it is human to sin, angelic to correct one’s fault, and diabolical to persevere in sin.

Defend the Church of God and assist their causes, so that the priests of God may be able to pray for you. Remember what you promised God in baptism: you renounced the devil through his works. Do not return to those things which you renounced, but remain in God’s will as you promised, and love him who created you and from whom you have received every good.

Let each person serve God faithfully in the rank in which he is.

Let women be subject to their husbands in all goodness and chastity. Let them guard themselves from fornication, sorcery [Note: [Col. 0241] That is, *veneficia*, “poisonings” or “witchcraft.”], and greed, because whoever does these things resists God. Let them raise their children in the fear of God, and give alms as much as they have, with a cheerful mind and good will.

Let men love their wives, and not speak dishonorable [Note: [Col. 0241] “Honorable,” 1.] words to them. Let them govern their households. In goodness, let them come frequently to church. Let them render to people what they owe without murmuring, and to God what belongs to God with good will.

Let children love and honor their parents. Let them not be disobedient to them. Let them beware of theft, homicide, and fornication. When they reach lawful age, let them take a lawful wife—unless they should prefer to enter God’s service.

Let canonical clerics diligently obey the commands of their bishops. Let them not wander from place to place. Let them not involve themselves in secular business. Let them remain in chastity. Let them frequently attend to God, as the reading of the holy Scriptures admonishes them, and let them diligently carry out ecclesiastical duties.

Let monks keep what they have promised to God. Let them do nothing without the command of their abbot. Let them not pursue shameful profit. Let them keep the Rule in memory and observe it firmly, knowing the command that it is better not to make a vow than, after making a vow, not to fulfill it.

Let dukes, counts, and judges administer justice to the people and mercy to the poor. Let them not alter equity for money or condemn the innocent out of hatred.

Let that apostolic saying always be held in the heart: “We must all stand before the tribunal of Christ, so that each may receive according to what he has done, whether good or evil.” As the Lord himself says: “With the judgment with which you judge, you will be judged.” That is: act mercifully, so that you may receive mercy from God.

Nothing is hidden that will not be known, nor covered that will not be revealed. And for every idle word we shall give an account on the day of judgment. How much more, then, should we all act with God’s help so that we may please God in all our works and, after this present life, deserve to rejoice forever with God’s saints.

This life is brief, and the time of death is uncertain [Col. 0242D]. What else should we do except always be prepared? Let us consider how terrible it is to fall into the hand of God.

With confession, repentance, and almsgiving, the Lord is merciful and compassionate. If he sees us turn to him with all our heart, he will immediately have mercy on us, so that he may grant us his mercy [the Latin is defective], and grant us prosperity in this life and the future life with his saints forever.

May God preserve you, beloved brothers [Note: [Col. 0241] “May God conserve,” 1.].

## LOMBARD CAPITULARY

*(Year 802, March, Aachen.)*

[Col. 0243]

We publish this capitulary from the codices: 1, the Chisianus; and 2, the Cavensis, with the readings of the Ambrosian Codex and of the others that contain the Lombard laws placed beneath them. It is found in the codices among the laws of Charles, but chapters 3 and 5 demonstrate that it was promulgated by King Pippin. I have assigned it to the year 802 because its chapters 2 and 3 also occur in the Frankish chapters of the same period, and because others—for example, those concerning tithes—seem to be alluded to in the capitularies of Pippin that follow shortly afterward.

### HERE BEGIN THE CHAPTERS: HOW THE LORD KING ADMONISHED HIS FAITHFUL AT HIS COURT

[Col. 0243A]

1. We wish and admonish [Note: [Col. 0243] “We command,” A, V, Vn, and others.] that bishops strive to perform their ministry in every respect within their dioceses, according to their ability, and that they complete preaching and confirmation there. Let them also diligently care for the monasteries located within their dioceses, so that the canons live according to the canons and the regulars according to the Rule. Wherever they find matters otherwise than order requires, let them strive to correct them; and if they cannot correct them, let them report them to us.

2. We wish and command that the abbots who preside over regular monasteries [Note: [Col. 0243] Absent in 2.] live and teach according to the Rule. In this respect [Note: [Col. 0243] “In this respect” is absent in 2; *quot* is printed in 1, “that” in 2.], let them provide for their subjects both materially and spiritually, and maintain vigilance.

3. The abbots who are responsible for the canonical standard should likewise provide for their clerics, as the canonical order teaches. Let them strive according to their ability to ensure that this order is observed there and that they are able to fulfill the proper office. Wherever necessary, let them arrange for their monasteries to be corrected.

Let abbots take greater pleasure in frequently visiting the monasteries entrusted to them and instructing their clerics so that they may fulfill God’s service and keep their order, than in allowing them to be idle in other diversions of secular desires [Note: [Col. 0243] “Desire,” 1.]—unless it should happen that they are occupied in the service of the lord emperor and of us. Even then, this will be for a time, not forever [Note: [Col. 0243] The phrase “and … fulfill” is absent in 2; *sinat* in 1; *desinant* in 2.].

[Col. 0243C]

4. Let counts love justice fully and carry it out according to their ability. Let them diligently attend to the justice of the holy Church of God, and strive to settle, with the fullest and most just deliberation, the cases of orphans, widows, and the poor, and of all who reside within their jurisdiction, as well as every complaint brought to them for any reason. Let them act in whatever way is more right and just. Let them first consider at their courts the cases of orphans, widows, and also the poor; and let their justice not be delayed by judges on account of any postponement.

5. We wish bishops and counts to have harmony and affection among themselves, in order to carry out the affairs of God and of the holy Church [Col. 0243D] [Note: [Col. 0243] *protractum* in Est.; *pertractatum* in Mur.]. When necessity requires it, let the bishop be a helper and adviser to his count, so that the count may fulfill his ministry. Likewise, let the count act toward his bishop so that he may be his helper in all things, enabling him to fulfill his canonical ministry within his diocese.

6. We also command counts and all the faithful of the lord emperor and of us [Note: [Col. 0243] “Our faithful,” Mur.] that everyone who holds ecclesiastical property as a benefice should give the ninths and tithes fully [Note: [Col. 0243] “According to the custom of the region, the ninths and tithes,” Mur.] to those churches, without any diminution or delay, insofar as they can. According to their means [Note: [Col. 0243] “As they can, and according to their means,” V and Vn.], whenever necessity requires [Note: [Col. 0243] “Whenever necessity requires it, let assistance be given for the restoration of the churches,” M.], let them provide assistance in labor for restoring those churches [Note: [Col. 0243] “Restoration and assistance,” M.].

7. And you bishops, who receive the ninths and tithes of everyone [Note: [Col. 0243] “In all things,” M.], must see to it that the churches and chapels in your dioceses are repaired, that you provide them with lighting, and that the presbyters may be able to live in them.

8. No one should dare to receive another person’s cleric without letters of recommendation or letters of release.

9. Let bishops and abbots establish hospitality at their hospices and monasteries wherever it formerly existed [Note: [Col. 0243] “Hospitals/guesthouses,” 2.], and let them take the greatest care that it is in no way neglected.

10. Let our vassals and officials in your jurisdictions receive the honor and full justice that is proper. If they cannot be present, let them have advocates who can defend their property before the count. Whatever complaint is brought against them, let them receive justice.

11. We wish advocates to be chosen in the count’s presence. They must not have a bad reputation; rather, such men should be chosen as the law commands.

12. We also wish and command that counts and their judges not allow witnesses of bad reputation to give testimony. Rather, let those be chosen who have a good reputation for testimony among their fellow countrymen. Let the judges first investigate them, and let them act according to what the judges have been able to investigate more correctly from others [Note: [Col. 0243] “Through them,” 2; “through those,” M and Est.; absent in Est. after “judges”], without giving assent to the will of evil men.

Let the counts or their judges, when they know that the case under dispute between the parties has been ascertained [Col. 0245A] [Note: [Col. 0245] “Revealed,” 2; “covered,” M and Est.], have the witnesses come to the same case without favoring the person who has the case [Note: [Col. 0245] “Let the witnesses come,” Est. and M.], and let the case be decided through their inquiry. We command that the witnesses be separated from one another, as the law orders, because if this is done many false witnesses can be convicted [Note: [Col. 0245] “If they have not been questioned and have been joined together,” 2; “if they have been questioned separately,” A, V, Vn, E.].

13. We also wish counts to administer full justice concerning robbers through their jurisdictions. Let them not tolerate evildoers and thieves remaining at peace, but let them always harass them as far as they are able.

14. No criminal action should be decided before subordinate officials, except only lighter cases that can easily be judged. No one should bring a claim to another person as a slave before their judgment; rather, he should be released through sureties [Note: [Col. 0245] “Through faith,” 1; “through a pledge,” 2; “through sureties,” M.] until the count’s presence.

They should not have free men detained for any court sessions after they have attended the three established courts, unless it should happen that someone accuses someone else—except for the *scabini* who must sit with the judges.

15. We wish that, just as we observe the law for everyone, everyone should likewise cause the law to be observed for us [Note: [Col. 0245] “All counts,” V, Vn, E, M; perhaps “our counts.”], and should strive to administer full justice in their jurisdictions in everything that concerns us.

16. For we command that, on account of any distraint that we order to be carried out, or for any other reason [Col. 0246A], slaves should not be sent into distraint. Rather, our envoys, their masters, or the advocates of those masters [Note: [Col. 0245] “The advocate,” A; “the masters,” V; “the advocates,” V.] should distrain the slaves [Note: [Col. 0245] “The slaves … on behalf of,” absent in 2; “the slaves themselves,” V.] and, as the law orders, the masters themselves [Note: [Col. 0245] “Their masters themselves,” V.] should give an account concerning the slaves, whether they are guilty or not.

The masters themselves should distrain and investigate their slaves as they themselves wish [the final clause is uncertain].

17. No one should presume to set snares in the lord’s forest [Note: [Col. 0245] “Forest,” 2; “in the forest,” M.] or in any place [Note: [Col. 0245] “In any royal place,” A, V, Vn, E, M.] belonging to the king. If free men commit this offense, let them pay the lord’s ban; if slaves do so, let their masters make restitution according to the law [Note: [Col. 0245] “That is, so that the slave receives 120 blows,” V, Vn, E.].

18. No one should presume to sell or buy a person except in the presence of counts or their envoys [Note: [Col. 0245] This chapter is absent up to this point in M.]. No one should dare to buy slaves illicitly and secretly take them to another region. Wherever such a person is found, he should be subject to legal judgment.

[Col. 0246B]

19. No one should presume to receive a *forcapium* concerning slaves or any matter [Note: [Col. 0245] “They should seize the thief,” 2; “a fugitive thief,” V, Vn, Est., M.], as the lord emperor has often instructed [Note: [Col. 0245] “By his words, not by law,” V, Vn, E.].

20. No one should presume to receive newly arrived or fugitive slaves.

21. [Note: [Col. 0245] Another chapter, “Concerning summons,” 2.] Concerning summonses, nothing need be observed except in cases concerning free status or inheritance. In all other inquiries [Note: [Col. 0245] “Matters,” V and Vn; “cases,” Est. and M.], let them come to the assembly through the count’s distraint and be examined justly so that justice may be done. Counts, however, should not continually oppress the poor through court proceedings.

## GENERAL CAPITULARY OF AACHEN

*(Year 802, October, Aachen.)*

[Col. 0245]

In October Charles once again assembled a great council to deal with the ecclesiastical and secular affairs of the empire. The Annals of Lorsch and of Moissac provide extensive testimony concerning this and report that “a general command of the emperor went forth concerning all bishops, abbots, presbyters, deacons, and the whole clergy, that clerics should live according to the canons, and monks according to the Rule of Saint Benedict; that, after their former vices had been corrected according to that standard, they should also sing the office according to the custom of the Roman Church and establish schools for singers. At that time, when dukes, counts, and the rest of the Christian people had been assembled together with the legislators, the emperor caused all the laws in his kingdom to be read, explained, and corrected, and ordered that judges should judge in writing and, without accepting gifts, grant justice to each person.”

Since the acts of this assembly had not previously been published, we now present: 1, from the Blankenburg Codex of the ducal library at Wolfenbüttel, the general command that seems to belong here; 2, from Codex G. 111 of the royal library at Munich, among the Ratisbon codices of Saint Emmeram and written in the first years of the ninth century, the capitulary for examining presbyters, canons, abbots, and laymen; 3, from two codices of the royal library at Munich, among the Freising codices written in the ninth and tenth centuries, chapters concerning what all ecclesiastics were ordered to learn; and 4, from Royal Paris Codex no. 4995, excerpts from the canons sent by Pope Hadrian to Charles, together with chapters for examining abbots and monks.

The laws committed to writing at the same assembly—those of the Saxons, Thuringians, and Frisians—will be presented in the second volume of our collection.

### GENERAL CAPITULARY. ALSO, THE COMMANDS OF CHARLES THROUGHOUT THE WHOLE KINGDOM, CONCERNING BISHOPS, ABBOTS, AND PRESBYTERS

[Note: [Col. 0245] “Title VII,” codex.]

[Col. 0245C]

1. All ecclesiastics are to be carefully examined concerning their learning and instruction. In this examination, although we are unlearned, it has been ordered that throughout this province [Col. 0246C] not only the doctrine of ecclesiastics but also that of laymen be investigated, as support or goodwill for the exercise of holy justice.

2. First, they are to examine how each ecclesiastic—whether bishop, abbot, or presbyter, and all canons or monks—has his office prepared: what has been neglected and what is worthy of correction. Whoever knows his office well should receive thanks for it and be urged always to advance toward better things. Whoever is negligent or sluggish in this matter should be constrained by suitable satisfaction until he makes an appropriate correction.

3. Also, how presbyters know the psalms, and how they are able to fulfill their course, whether by day or by night, according to Roman usage.

4. How they customarily instruct catechumens in the Christian faith, and thereafter how they know reasonably to adapt special Masses, whether for the dead or for the living, according to both genders, whether in the singular or plural number.

5. Likewise, in the instruction of the peoples and in the office [Col. 0247B] of preaching, as well as in the confession of sins: how they teach people to act, and how they know or arrange to impose a remedy for their sins [Note: [Col. 0247] *procurrent* in the codex].

6. Above all, concerning their conduct and chastity: how they provide a model and example to Christians.

7. How obedient they are to their bishops, and with what modesty, peace, and charity they live among one another.

### CONCERNING THE REST OF THE PEOPLE

8. They are to know that their bishops ought to preside over them humbly with pious concern, not exercise tyrannical power over them [Note: [Col. 0247] “Over him,” codex.]. But just as they wish their subjects to obey them, so they themselves must carefully take care not to dare to afflict anyone unjustly or in anger and without reason. Rather, they should consider themselves their companions and should strive more to love than to be feared [Note: [Col. 0247] Read “to be loved rather than feared.”].

9. Thereafter, each person is to be fully examined concerning his faith: how he himself believes and how he teaches others to believe.

10. Likewise, how they understand the Lord’s Prayer; and they are to learn fully the prayer itself and the meaning of the Creed, know them for themselves, and be able to explain them to others.

11. They are to learn the canons, the pastoral book, and the homilies for the instruction of the people, appropriately for each feast day.

12. No tonsured person is to be without a canonical or regular life; and no presbyter, deacon, or abbot is to be unattached (*absolutus*) without episcopal direction, because we know that those without discipline or instruction displease God.

13. No layman should presume to keep a presbyter, deacon, or cleric with him, or to ordain one for his churches, without the permission or examination of his bishop, so that the bishop himself may know whether he can rightly be called a cleric or presbyter and whether he is without reproach.

14. All Christians without exception are commanded to learn the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer.

[Col. 0248A] 15. No one is to take up an infant or another person from among the pagans from the sacred font before that person has recited the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer to his priest.

16. They are to be taught to avoid incestuous marriages altogether and to abstain from fornication, homicide, theft, perjury, sorcery, divination and incantations, sacrilege, drunkenness and abuse, robbery, hatred, and envy; and they are to receive Holy Communion worthily.

17. No member of the clergy is ever to presume, on any pretext, to do anything outside the canonical or regular permission.

18. Furthermore, a command has been given to the monks of God by the word of God, and it has been ordered and decreed by our lord and all his leading men, that no monk shall be occupied with secular affairs beyond what was decreed at the Council of Chalcedon.

19. Those who truly and sincerely pursue the solitary life are to be honored appropriately.  
[Note: The manuscript reads *quam* (“although”) instead of *quoniam* (“since”).]  
Since, however, certain persons wearing the monastic habit disturb ecclesiastical and civil affairs, wandering indiscriminately through cities and also attempting to establish monasteries for themselves, it has been decided that no one may anywhere build or construct a monastery or an oratory without the knowledge of the bishop of the city. Monks, moreover, are to be subject in each city or region to the bishop, to love quiet, and to devote themselves solely to fasting and prayer, remaining in the places where they renounced the world. They are not to involve themselves in ecclesiastical or secular business, nor be troublesome in any way by abandoning their own monasteries.

## CHAPTERS OF THE GENERAL EXAMINATION

[Col. 0248C]

In the king’s palace they have established that priests are not to be ordained before they have been examined.

1. Chapter. I ask you priests how you believe, so that you may hold the Catholic faith, and how you know or understand the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer.  
[Note: The manuscript reads *interro* instead of *interrogo*.]

2. How do you know or understand your canons?  
[Note: The manuscript reads *Canonones* instead of *Canones*.]

3. How do you know or understand the Penitential?

4. How do you know or understand your Mass according to the Roman order?

5. How can you read the Gospel, or teach others who are unlearned?

6. How do you understand the homilies of the orthodox Fathers, or know how to instruct others?

7. How do you know the divine office according to the Roman rite, for chanting at the appointed solemn celebrations?  
[Note: *ad tecantandum* means *ad decantandum*, “for chanting.”]

8. How do you know or understand the Baptismal Office?

9. I ask the canons whether or not they live according to the canons.

10. But I ask you abbots whether you know or understand the Rule, and whether those under your governance live according to the Rule of the most blessed Benedict; also, how many of them know or understand the Rule.

11. I also ask the laymen how they know or understand their law.

[Col. 0249A] 12. Each person is to send his son to learn letters, and he is to remain there with every diligence until he becomes well instructed.

## CHAPTERS ON THE INSTRUCTION OF THE CLERGY

These are the things that all members of the clergy have been ordered to learn.

1. The Catholic faith of Saint Athanasius and everything else concerning the faith;

2. Also the Apostolic Creed;

3. The Lord’s Prayer, fully understood together with its exposition;

4. The Book of Sacraments in full, both the canon and the special Masses, for complete adaptation (*ad commutandum*);

5. The exorcism over catechumens or over the possessed;

6. The commendation of the soul;

[Col. 0249B] 7. The Penitential;

8. The computation;

9. The Roman chant at night;

10. And likewise the chant at Mass;

11. To understand the Gospel, or the readings of the Book of Comes;

12. The homilies for Sundays and feast days, for preaching according to the canon; likewise the monks’ Rule and the canon, firmly;

13. The Pastoral Book of the canons and the Book of Offices;

14. The pastoral letter of Gelasius;

15. To write charters and letters.

1. Priests and ministers of the altar are to abstain from secular concerns.  
[Note: From chapter 7 in Harzheim, *Councils of Germany*, vol. I, p. 132.]

Likewise in the same chapter 13:

2. No one among the faithful is to receive a foreign cleric without letters of recommendation, and those who have been received are to be returned; and no one is to expel from a church, without the bishop’s consent, a priest whom the bishop has ordained for that church.  
[Note: This is found only this far in Harzheim, chapter 13, cited above.]

Likewise in the same chapter 16:

Likewise in the same chapter 18:

Likewise in the same chapter 19:

9. Concerning women living under the same roof.

Likewise in the same council:

10. Concerning those who have been advanced to the dignity of the priesthood without examination.  
[Note: Chapter 9, p. 138. The manuscript has *preb. ij* for *presbiterii*.]

Likewise chapter:

11. Concerning clerics who receive interest.  
[Note: Chapter 17, cited above.]

[Note: Chapter 12, p. 147.]

13. Concerning priests who have taken wives and those who have continued in fornication: that they are to be expelled.  
[Note: Chapter 1, p. 150.]

Likewise chapter:

Likewise chapter:

[Note: The following words are absent from the canon. The reference is to chapter 15 of the Council of Gangra in Harzheim, vol. I, p. 154: “Concerning those who, under the pretext of Christianity, despise their children.”]

Likewise in the Nicene Council:

16. Concerning those who are called Cathari.

### From the Council of Sardica
