### From the Sixteenth Council of Carthage

[Note: p. 201.]

18. Concerning the ordination of virgins.

19. Concerning equal measure and denarii.

20. It must be considered with regard to poor people according to what measure they ought to pay their annual assessment.

21. Let each person learn about the Holy Trinity according to what the holy Fathers have prescribed and discussed, and understand it faithfully. Let this suffice; nothing more is to be required.

22. Concerning fugitives from the regions of Ravenna and the Pentapolis: if it pleases my lord, let chapters 7, 3, 6, 8, 59, 60 [chapter 70], and 61 be read.  
[Note: Compare 783, 16.]

23. That is, concerning the kinds of monks; what an abbot ought to be; and the obedience of disciples.

24. Concerning the discipline governing the reception of novices, and concerning the sons of nobles or poor people who are offered.

25. Concerning priests who wish to live in a monastery, and concerning clerics as well as foreign monks. These contain regulations sufficient for the number of twenty abbots.

26. In addition, certain questions about these matters may be put to them, so that they may be asked in which chapter something is written or how it is to be understood: “Let no one in the monastery follow the desire of his own heart.” Likewise, where or what the *synaxis* is; where or what the *senpectas* is; where also, and what, is “not a completely healthy tyranny”; where it is written in Scripture, “The will has punishment, and necessity brings a crown”; whether the Gospel is read according to the Rule on Sunday nights; where it is commanded that a monk be struck; whether the brothers sleep after the nocturnal office, and where this is commanded. All these matters are contained in the second degree of humility, and in chapters 3, 11, 17, and 28; and also what each person is to drink, or to receive mixed.

## DOUBLE LOMBARD CAPITULARY (803, spring)

[Col. 0251]

We make this edict public law on the basis of one manuscript, the ninth-century Codex of Saint Paul, folios 3–6; the Chisian Codex; and the Cavense Codex, where it is numbered among the laws of Charles as chapters 14–24 and 15–25. That it was promulgated by Pippin is indicated by chapter 16 and by the concluding formula. It appears to have been issued at the time when Charles began arranging ecclesiastical affairs in Germany, thus in the autumn of the year 802 or, more probably, as the concluding statement shows, in the spring of the following year. The first part of the edict concerns the Church alone, while the second concerns the entire people; another example of this distinction is provided by the capitulary of the year 805. Two chapters of the latter part, namely chapters 12 and 16, divided into five sections, are also read in the Tegernsee Codex immediately after Charles’s letter to Pippin in the year 807, followed by a chapter concerning the maintenance of roads; we shall report this below as an appendix. The readings of the Ambrosian and other codices containing the laws of the Lombards are supplied at the foot of the page.

[Col. 0251B] It pleased us above all  
[Note: “It pleased us, Charles, most glorious king,” in manuscripts 2 and 3.]  
that the vices which have arisen in our time in the holy Church of God be uprooted from the roots.  
[Note: “Be eradicated,” in manuscripts 2 and 3.]

1. Chapter. Therefore, with the Lord ordering it beforehand, we wish to arrange our churches according to the authority of the canons and to establish the order of the clergy.  
[Note: Manuscript 1 has *autoritatum*, “of authorities.”]

2. The monasteries that have long been regular monasteries, both of men and of women, which are situated under our rule, we wish to be arranged and to live according to the Rule. If abbots or abbesses are found to live without the Rule or disorderly, and, after being admonished, they do not wish to amend, they are to be expelled; and from that same congregation, if suitable persons are found, an abbot or abbess is to be chosen; otherwise, from elsewhere. The royal monasteries likewise, if it pleases him.  
[Notes: Manuscript 1 has *auitiantur* for *abitiantur*. Manuscripts 2 and 3 read “regular monasteries” rather than “royal monasteries.” The words “if it pleases him” are absent from manuscripts 2 and 3.]

3. Concerning the hospitals belonging to us: those that are well ordered are to remain as they are; but those that have been ruined we wish to restore, according to the conditions of the times, to their former cultivation, so that the poor of God may be refreshed there, and so that they may be administered by persons who govern them according to God and take nothing away from the provisions of the poor.  
[Note: The rest of the chapter is absent from manuscript 3.]

4. Concerning baptismal churches, we decree that they are to be properly administered by priests, and that they are to suffer no violence, imposition, or diminution from their bishops in their revenues; rather, they are to act according to canonical institution and ancient custom.  
[Note: The words “Concerning baptismal churches” are absent from manuscript 3.]

5. When a bishop visits his diocese, he is not to demand or receive more from it than is prescribed by the canons or ancient custom, and the people of that bishop are not to suffer oppression from his men.  
[Note: Manuscript 1 reads “from all men.”]

6. We decree that bishops, priests and deacons, abbots and monks alike are not to presume to hunt on their own, nor, when they themselves are present, to permit any kind of games to be held before them that violate the authority of the canons.  
[Note: Manuscripts 2 and 3 read *tam* (“equally” or “as well”); manuscript 1 has *ullo*, “any,” instead of *ulla*, “any kind.”]

7. Concerning the stipends of the clergy, we wish the clerics themselves to have a fuller share, according to the canon, both from revenues and from the offerings of the faithful.

8. Let the provosts of the cardinal churches be obedient to their bishops, and let bishops not presume to expel them from their churches without fault and just cause, nor impose anything on them by force.  
[Note: Manuscript 1 has *prepositis* (“to the provosts”) for *prepositi*, and *obediente* for *obedientes*. Manuscripts 2 and 3 read: “nor may bishops expel them from their own or others’ lawful and useful positions”; the editorial note explains that *ad* means “from.”]

9. We promise that henceforth we shall accept no rewards for the ordination or consecration of priests or other clerics, neither from them, nor from their parents or friends, neither openly nor secretly.  
[Note: Manuscript 1 has *consegationes* for *consecrationes* and *pala* for *palam*, “openly.”]

[Col. 0252C] 10. The gifts that have recently been imposed upon churches belonging to us are to be abolished, and we decree that no gifts larger than those customary are to be received.  
[Notes: The phrase “belonging to us” is absent from manuscripts 2 and 3. *nobiter* is understood as *noviter*, “recently.”]

11. Concerning the tithes that are offered by the people in parish or baptismal churches: no part of them is to be transferred to a larger church or to a bishop.  
[Note: Manuscripts 2 and 3 read “imposed” instead of “transferred.”]

12.  
[Note: Codex 1 numbers this as “Chapter XII,” and similarly numbers the following chapters XIII, XIV, and so forth. Chapters 12 and 15–19 are found in Muratori among the laws of Charles, chapters 99, 120, 100, 121; and among the laws of Lothar, chapter 41, and Louis, chapter 34.]

We wish first that neither abbots and priests, nor deacons and subdeacons, nor anyone of the clergy, be dragged or compelled in their own persons into public or secular courts; rather, having been judged by their bishops, they are to render justice. If a complaint concerning their possessions, whether ecclesiastical or personal, comes before a judge against them, the judge is to send the complainant with his envoys to the bishop, so that the bishop may cause him to obtain justice through an advocate. If any such dispute arises among them which they are unwilling or unable to settle peaceably themselves, then the case is to come before the count or judge through such an advocate of the bishop as he himself orders, and there be concluded according to the law, after the person of the cleric has first been set aside, as stated.  
[Notes: Manuscript 1 reads *publico* (“in public”) for *publica* and *ante ei posito*; manuscripts V, Vn., and E., chapter 99, read *clero praeter episcopos, abbates, abbatissas* (“of the clergy, except bishops, abbots, and abbesses”), *episcopi suum clericorum*, *lex ipsa* (“the law itself”), *clericorum* (“of the clerics”), and *anteposita*.]

[Col. 0253A] 13. Clerics or monks who are at large—that is, wandering—whether from that parish or arriving from elsewhere, are not to be received by anyone without the bishop’s consent.  
[Note: *vacantes* is explained as “wandering,” which is what manuscripts 2 and 3 read.]

14. Baptismal churches are to be restored by those who are responsible for them, and each is to be assigned a measure of restoration proportionate to its means. We say this because we have heard that in certain places some people, with the consent of their masters, are withdrawing themselves for money; but all ecclesiastical persons ought to be ordained through the minister of the church.  
[Notes: Manuscript 1 has *et* for *haec*. Manuscript 1 reads *seu* for *se*. The phrase “through the minister of the church” is corrupt or uncertain in the manuscripts.]

15. Public or secular courts are in no way to be held either by a count or by any of his ministers or judges, whether in a church or in the buildings surrounding or adjoining a church.  
[Note: A marginal provision adds: “Unless the count holds minor courts. He is to hold them wherever he is able to obtain them.”]

16. Serfs, *aldiones*, old *libellarii*, or those newly made *libellarii*, who do not withdraw themselves from the public domain through fraud or evil intent, but inhabit or undertake to cultivate church lands solely because of poverty and necessity, are not to be compelled or forced by a count or any of his officials into any public or private compulsory labor or service; rather, whatever must justly be done by them is to be arranged by their patron or lord. If they are accused of some crime, the bishop is first to be summoned, and he, through his advocate, is to administer justice according to the law and in accordance with the status of each person. But otherwise, let it be done as it is written in the capitulary of our lord the emperor. Other free men who have either a commendation or an ecclesiastical benefice are to render justice like the rest of the people.  
[Notes: Manuscript 1 has “with evil intent.” Manuscript 1 reads *colivet*, explained as *quolibet*, “any.” The words “if they are guilty” are added by V, Vn., and the edition. Manuscripts 2 and 3 read “in our capitulary.”]

[Col. 0253C] 17. We have also heard that the young men of counts, or certain officials of the public administration, and even some of the more powerful vassals of counts, customarily demand various payments or levies—some in return for food, some without food, as though by way of a request. Likewise, they have been accustomed to exact from the people by the same or other devices labor services, collections of crops, plowing, sowing, clearing, hauling, cutting, and other similar services, not only from ecclesiastical people but also from the rest of the population. All these practices, if it pleases you, seem to us and to the whole people rightly to be removed, because in certain places the people have been oppressed by them to such an extent that many, unable to bear it, have fled from their lords or patrons, and the lands themselves have been reduced to desolation. From the more powerful or wealthier people, however, we do not at all forbid mutual assistance when they wish, by voluntary consent and mutual affection, to provide one another with support.  
[Notes: Manuscript 1 has *aliquit* for *aliqui*, “some.” Manuscript 1 has *etia* for *etiam*. One edition reads “some indeed”; another adds “from the people.” Manuscript 1 has *volentes*, “willing,” instead of *valentes*, “able.” The words “if it pleases you, and by us” are absent from manuscripts 2 and 3.]

[Col. 0254A] 18. Concerning bridges and other similar works which ecclesiastical people ought, according to just and ancient custom, to undertake with the rest of the people, we command this: the rector of the church is to be approached, and a share is to be assigned to him according to his means; and ecclesiastical people are not to be compelled to work by another exactor. If he has not completed his work by the appointed day, the count may, as a penalty, seize the provost of the work as security, in proportion to the estimated value or extent of the unfinished work, until it is completed. If the count neglects this duty, he is to be judged by the king or the king’s envoy.  
[Notes: Manuscript 1 reads “we request” instead of “we command.” Manuscript 1 has “let the rectors be approached”; manuscript 2 has “let the rector approach them”; manuscript 3, “let the rectors approach them.” The variants include “for a penalty” and “the overseer of the work.” Manuscript 1 has “by the king” rather than “by the king’s envoy.”]

19. Concerning tithes: they are to be paid, and those unwilling to pay are to be compelled by the officials of the public administration according to what was announced in the previous year. That is, four or eight men, or as many as may be necessary, are to be selected from each parish, according to its circumstances, one from each locality, so that they themselves may serve as witnesses between the priests and the people wherever tithes have or have not been paid. This is so that there may be no necessity of taking an oath there. We do not, however, say that so many witnesses are to be sent so that it is always necessary for all of them to be present together whenever tithes are paid, but so that the burden may be lessened by entrusting it to several; if two are present, we believe that they are sufficient. The negligent are to be admonished by the priests of the churches, up to the third time, to pay the tithe itself. If they despise this warning, they are to be prohibited from entering the church; and if they do not amend in this matter, they are to be distrained by the officials of the public administration, and each of them is to pay six solidi to the church as a penalty, while also being compelled to pay the tithe. If they again prove contemptuous, then by public authority their houses or huts are to be *wiffed*—that is, subjected to a legal seizure—until they make satisfaction for the tithe as stated above. If they again wish to be rebellious or oppositional, and presume by their own authority to intrude upon that *wiffa*, then they are to be placed in custody by the officials of the public administration until they are brought before the public court, and there they are to make composition according to the law to the count or the public party. For the rest, as stated above, they are to make satisfaction to the church concerning the tithe and the six solidi.  
[Notes: Manuscript 1 has *octos* for *octo*, “eight.” One edition adds “the best men.” The Tegernsee manuscript and the edition add “of each parish,” while manuscripts 2 and 3 omit it. Manuscript 1 reads *plurimus* for *pluribus*. The variants include *guiffentur*, *giffentur*, and *wiffentur*; the remainder is absent from the edition.]

These provisions, as stated above, are to be observed among the other pious works of Christianity until, at the assembly to be held in mid-October in the city of Pavia—unless the king should otherwise command—something better is found, with God as guide, to be added, joined, or changed.  
[Note: The words “at the assembly to be held” are absent from manuscripts 2 and 3; the wording *mutandumve* varies in manuscript 1.]

### The Tegernsee Codex Contains Only the Following

[Col. 0255A]

1. We wish first that neither abbots and priests, nor deacons and subdeacons, nor anyone of the clergy, be dragged or forced from their persons into public or secular courts; rather, after judgment by their bishops, they are to render justice. If a complaint concerning their possessions, whether ecclesiastical or personal, comes against them before a judge, the judge is to send the complainant with his messenger to the bishop, so that the bishop may cause him to receive justice through an advocate.

2. If some dispute has arisen between them that they do not wish or are unable to settle by themselves, then through an advocate of the bishop whom the bishop himself appoints, the case is to come before the count or judge and be settled there according to the law, with the cleric’s person placed under protection, as stated.

3. Serfs, *aldiones*, old *libellarii*, or those newly made *libellarii*, who do not withdraw themselves from the public domain through fraud or evil intent, but solely because of dire poverty and necessity inhabit or undertake to cultivate church lands, are not to be compelled or forced by a count or any of his officials into any public or private compulsory labor or service; rather, whatever must justly be done by them is to be arranged by their patron or lord.  
[Note: The manuscript reads *pro malo ingenio* (“through evil intent”), while the textual note has *lege sola* in place of *per sola* (“solely”).]

4. If they are accused of some crime, the bishop is first to be summoned, and he, through his advocate, is to administer justice according to the law and in accordance with the status of each person.

5. But if they are found guilty, let it be done as it is written in our capitulary; other free men who have either a commendation or an ecclesiastical benefice are to render justice like the rest of the people.

6. We also wish and decree concerning the roads or sewers of each city belonging to the kingdom of Italy that they are to be maintained every year. We do not, however, wish anyone to pay any *pandum* from this to the palace treasury. Rather, we command that the officials of each city take care that the year not end before the roads and sewers have been cleaned; and each public administrator of a city is to give this command, by admonition from our imperial authority, so that it is not neglected.  
[Note: The codex reads *clocleis*, with an I written above the word; Amerbach corrected it here and below to *cloacis*, “sewers.” It is clear that the subject cannot be the cleaning of *cocleae*, that is, bell towers.]

## CHAPTERS TO BE INSERTED INTO THE SALIC LAW

[Note: Thus the manuscripts: Paris 4629, *Capitulum q. i. l. saligam mitenda sunt*; 4404, 4995, Vatican 773, and 4758, variants of this title; 4758, *Incipit c. q. ad l. s. m. sunt*; and 4632, *in legem salicam* (“into the Salic law”).]

[Col. 0255]

We publish these chapters on the basis of the following manuscripts: the Royal Library of Paris codices nos. 4629, 4404, 4995, 4758, 4626, and 4632; among the *Supplementa latina*, no. 75, of the ducal library at Wolfenbüttel; the Gudian, Augustan, and Blankenburg manuscripts; the Tegernsee manuscript in the Royal Library at Munich; the ducal library at Gotha; the Saint Gall manuscript no. 728; the Vatican manuscript among the Palatine codices, no. 773; and the codices that contain the laws added by Charles to the Lombard laws, namely the Codex of Saint Paul in Carinthia, Paris 4613, the Chisian, Cavense, Ambrosian, Florentine, London, Vienna, Veronese, and Este codices, as reported by Muratori. We have also taken Baluzian’s edition into account, but have included only those readings that seemed likely to be of some importance.  
[Note: They are also found in the Royal Paris codices 4628, 4628A, and 4788, in *Supplementum latinum* 164 bis and 4760.]

The Paris Codex no. 4995 has the following inscription:

“In the name of Christ, here begin the chapters of the law of the emperor Charles, recently discovered. In the third year of our most merciful lord Charles Augustus, in that same year these chapters were made and entrusted to Count Stephen, so that he might make them known in the city of Paris at a public assembly and have them read before the judges; and this he did. And all unanimously agreed that they wished to observe them for all time into the future. All the judges, bishops, abbots, and counts also confirmed them below with their own hands.”

[Note: The codex identifies Stephen as “of Paris.” A note quotes the following from a small chartulary of the Church of Paris, folio 71:

“To the holy lord in Christ, the apostolic lord of the most holy church of Mary, Mother of God, and of Saint Stephen the proto-martyr, and also of Saint Germanus, where Inchadus appears to preside as rector and bishop of the city of Paris, which church has been built within the walls of Paris. Therefore, in the name of God, I, Stephen, a humble count of Christ by the grace of God, and Amaltrudis, countess, together, for the sake of mutual love, give our possessions situated in the county of Paris, in the place called Sulciacus, and so forth. Done at the estate of Bonoilus, where this was made and confirmed in the eleventh year of the reign of our lord Charles, glorious Augustus, the thirteenth year of his reign in Francia, and the thirty-sixth in Italy, in the fifth indiction.”

A charter of Inchadus, bishop of Paris, issued at a general council, reads: “Sulciacum, which Stephen, an illustrious man and count of pious memory, and his wife Amantrudis, assigned for their own use.” He was likewise the royal envoy in Paris in the year 802, and so forth. He is also found subscribed to the document recording the division of the treasures of Charlemagne. —Baluz.]

The inscription then continues:

“Chapters to be inserted into the Salic law.”

In the Saint Gall Codex, however, it reads:

“Here begin the chapters which the lord Augustus Charles, in the year from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 803 and in the third year of his reign, ordered to be prefixed and added to the Salic law.”

In the Paris Codex no. 4613:

“These are the chapters which the lord Charles the Great, emperor, ordered to be written in his council and ordered to be placed among the other laws.”

Finally, the Gotha Codex reads:

“Here begin the chapters which the emperor Charles established for the Salic law.”

They are found in Muratori among the laws of Charles as chapters 101–108, 91, 92, and 24.

[Col. 0255C] 1. Concerning the homicides of clerics.  
[Note: V, Vn., and K read *Salicha* (“Salic”); in E. “law” is now understood. In the Gotha Codex, the fines at the beginning stood as in the printed editions, but were corrected by a contemporary hand so that 400, 600, and 900 solidi are now read (in the cases of the priest and monk); then: “Whoever kills a bishop shall become a monk.”]

If anyone kills a subdeacon, let him pay 300 solidi; whoever kills a deacon, 400 solidi; whoever kills a priest, 600; whoever kills a bishop, 900 solidi.  
[Note: The old royal codex reads, “let him pay 900 solidi”; in other manuscripts, “let him pay six hundred solidi.”]

Whoever kills a monk is to be judged liable to 400 solidi.  
[Notes: The Paris and Mazarin codices read: “Let him be judged liable to 600 solidi.” The Cavense Codex has 445 solidi. Other manuscripts add “the guilty person”; the remainder is absent from the Saint Paul, Palatine 773, and Gudian codices. One manuscript gives “400 solidi for the deacon or monk”; another gives “400 for the deacon, and likewise for the monk.”]

[Note: The edition of Pithou adds after these words, “and if it has been proved against him.” We have removed these words because they occur in none of the ancient exemplars that we have seen, nor in Canisius’s edition, nor in the third book of the *Capitularies*. —Baluz.]

[Col. 0258A] 2. Concerning those who take refuge within an immunity or cause some damage there.  
[Note: That is, in a church or in church property that is regarded as protected under the name of immunity.]

If anyone causes any damage within an immunity, let him pay 600 solidi. If a person commits theft, homicide, or any other crime outside and then flees within an immunity, let the count order the bishop, abbot, vicedominus, or whoever holds the place of the bishop or abbot to hand over the accused.  
[Note: The Saint Paul manuscript reads “priest”; Paris 4404 reads “judge or vicedominus” and “bishop, abbot, or abbess.”] If that person refuses and will not hand him over, at the first refusal he is to be judged liable to 15 solidi. If, when sought a second time, he refuses to hand him over, he is to be judged liable to 30 solidi. If he refuses even at the third request, whatever damage the accused has caused, the entire amount is to be paid by the person who keeps him within the immunity and refuses to hand him over; and the count himself, on coming, is to have permission to search for that man within the immunity wherever he may be able to find him.

If, however, at the count’s first inquiry he is told that the accused had indeed been within the immunity but had escaped, the person holding the place of the bishop or abbot is immediately to swear that he had not caused him to flee in order to evade justice in any matter, and satisfaction is to be accepted from him on this point.  
[Note: Three codices—*Supplementum* 75, Saint Vincent of Metz, and Vatican—add “let the person holding the place of the bishop or abbot swear.” The Saint Paul Codex omits the words from “within the immunity” through “immunity.”]

If, when the count enters the immunity, anyone attempts to resist him with an assembled force, the count is to report this to the king or prince, and the matter is to be judged there. Just as the person who caused damage within an immunity must pay 600 solidi, so whoever presumes to resist the count with an assembled force is to be judged liable to 600 solidi.  
[Notes: A second hand in the Gotha Codex has 900 solidi instead of 600. Some manuscripts read “ought to pay” instead of “must pay.”]

3. Concerning those who flee for refuge to a church. If anyone flees for refuge to a church, let him have peace in the church’s atrium. It is not necessary for him to enter the church, and no one is to presume to drag him away from there by force. Rather, he is to be permitted to confess what he has done and then, by the hands of good men, be brought into the public court for examination.

4. Concerning those who maliciously assist another. If anyone presumes, through evil contrivance, unjustly to assist a man disputing against another in court, and is consequently rebuked before the judges or the count and cannot deny it, he is to be judged liable to 15 solidi.

[Col. 0258A] 5. Concerning those who wish to establish free status. If anyone’s freedom is challenged, and, fearing that he may fall into servitude, he kills one of his relatives through whom he fears he will fall into servitude—that is, his father, mother, a paternal relative (*patruelis*), a maternal uncle, or any person of comparable kinship—the perpetrator himself is to die, while his kindred and blood relatives are to fall into servitude. If he denies that he killed him, he is to undergo the judgment of God by approaching nine heated plowshares.  
[Notes: Baluz adds “maternal aunt,” contrary to the evidence of nine of the oldest codices. Manuscripts of the Vatican and Metz add “or concealed him.” One note explains “kindred” as “sons” and “blood relatives” as “brothers.”]

6. Concerning those who wish to give their property to the house of God. If anyone wishes to give his property for the sake of his soul to the house of God, let him make the transfer at home before lawful witnesses. The transfers made up to now in the army, concerning which there is no dispute, are to remain valid. If, however, someone has transferred his property to another and has gone on campaign, and the person to whom the property was transferred dies in the meantime, the person who transferred the property, when he returns, is to recover his property after producing the witnesses before whom the transfer was made. If he too has died, his lawful heirs are to recover the transferred property.  
[Notes: The Paris Codex 4404 reads “at the house of the lord”; other manuscripts have forms of *domini*. The V, Vn., and E. editions understand this as “at the principal church.” Other manuscripts read “who transferred the property itself.”]

Source/review notes: Inherited source breaks remain explicitly fragmentary. All supplied manuscript and edition readings are retained in the complete apparatus.

### 7. Concerning a man who has obtained freedom by a charter

If anyone has lawfully obtained freedom from his lord through a charter of emancipation, he shall remain free. But if anyone unjustly attempts to reduce him to servitude, and he produces his charter of emancipation and proves that his adversary wishes to enslave him unjustly [*“unjustly” is absent from the Regius and Lingon manuscripts 4629, 4995, 4758, the Augustinian and Palatine manuscripts, and in Ansegisus], the man who made the attempt shall be compelled to pay the fine written in the charter [*“written” appears as “inscribed” in 4995; “inscribed” or “described” in the manuscripts of St Gall and others]. But if the charter cannot be produced, because it has already been destroyed by the one who wished to enslave him, let him pay his *widrigild* [*also *wedregildum* in 4629; *wadregillum* in 4404; *widregildum* in 4758; *widrigyldum* in the Augustinian manuscript; *uueregeldum* in 4995; *uuildrilgeldum* in the manuscript of St Gall]. Let two parts go to the man whom he wished to enslave, and the third to the king; and let that man then recover his freedom again by royal order [*absent from 4995].

[*Whoever destroys another’s charter shall likewise make compensation for all the property contained in the charter. V. Vn. E. In the margin of the Veronese manuscript is added, in a later hand and by interpretation: “through custom.”]

### 8. Concerning a free man who has given himself in pledge

A free man who has placed himself in another’s power as a pledge, and who, while held there, has inflicted some injury upon anyone, must either have the person who received him as a pledge pay the compensation, or have that person produce him in court and release him, thereby also forfeiting the debt for which he received him as a pledge. The one who caused the injury, once released, shall be compelled to make compensation according to the nature of the matter [*that is, of the property; thus the oldest manuscripts read it]. But if he has taken a free woman as his wife while he remains in pledge, and they have children, their children shall remain free [*“and they have children” is absent from V. Vn.].

[Col. 0259A] **9** [*The chapter is absent from Blank.]. Concerning royal debts and how they must be paid. All debts that must be paid to the king’s treasury shall be paid in solidi of twelve denarii [*“twelve denarii per solidus” in V. Vn.], except the fines written in the Salic Law. Those shall be paid in the same solidus in which the other compensations must be paid.

### 10. Concerning one who presumes to reopen a case already adjudicated

If anyone presumes to reopen a case that has been adjudicated in court [Col. 0260A], and is there convicted by witnesses, he shall either pay fifteen solidi or receive fifteen blows from the *scabini* [*“from the judges” in 4404 and 4629; “from the *scabinei*” in 4995; “from the *scavini*” in Blank.] who previously adjudicated the case [*“who previously adjudicated that very case” in C. and Lugdunensis].

### 11. Concerning one who is called as a witness and what sort of person he must be

The best men in the district [*“in a small number” in 4758] or city shall be summoned as witnesses, and the person against whom they must testify must be unable to bring any accusation against them [*the Gothic reads “bring forward”; V. Vn. has “impose”; M. “induce”; Baluz. “say”; no manuscript reads “object,” though that is the meaning supplied by the context].

In the manuscript of St Gall the following is added after the final chapter: “These eleven chapters are to be sent to all the laws.”

## MINOR CHAPTERS

[*They have been compared with the same exemplars by whose aid we corrected the preceding eleven chapters. Sigebert mentions them in his *Chronicle* under the year 803: “Charles establishes justice throughout the whole empire and institutes twenty-nine chapters of law.” They are likewise found in an old manuscript chronicle, whose following fragment I discovered among Sirmond’s papers: “In the third year, Charles the emperor establishes justice throughout his whole empire and institutes twenty-nine chapters of law.” — Baluzius.]

[Col. 0259]

In all the manuscripts except that of St Gall, the following minor chapters are appended to the chapters to be added to the Salic Law; we now publish them again with their assistance. They are headed as follows: “Here begin the minor chapters” in manuscript 4995; “Likewise, the first chapter” in manuscript 4629; “Likewise, concerning the chapters” in the Gotha manuscript; “The emperor’s command” in the Vatican manuscript. Among Charles’s Lombard laws they are found as chapters 1, 4–6, 8, 10–13, 15, 17, 20, and 22; in Muratori, chapters 154, 93, 98, 110–113, 126, and 14–117.

[Col. 0259B] **1.** Concerning cases requiring admonition, churches requiring correction, and places where there are more churches in one locality than are necessary [*“are” in 4629], so that those which are unnecessary may be demolished and others built.

**2.** That priests not be ordained before they have been examined; and that excommunication not be imposed indiscriminately and without cause [*“not impose it” in 4629].

**3.** That our envoys select *scabini*, advocates, and notaries [*“vicars and notaries” in the Vatican manuscript] in each locality; and that, when they return, they bring with them a written record of their names.

**4.** Concerning those who refuse to observe the law [*The Codex Thuaneus reads “who consented”; in the Mazarin manuscript it is written “who did not consent.” — Baluzius], that they be brought before the king through sureties [*“brought” in 4629].

**5.** That those who are obliged to pay the *haribannum* make a levy [*that is, a *gaforium*, Vn., chapter 98] for the *haribannator* [*Benedict, book I, chapter II, p. 221, adds: “and render no other service to counts or vicars.”].

[Col. 0259C] **6.** Concerning fugitives [*“and fugitive female slaves, newcomers, and pilgrims” in M.] and pilgrims: they are to be subjected to restraint, so that we may know who they are and from where they have come.

**7** [*The chapter is absent from manuscript 4404.] That rings (*bauga*) [*4758 reads *baoca*, “rings,” and *bronias*, “coats of mail”] and coats of mail (*brunias*) [*the Vatican manuscript reads *brunias vel spata*, “coats of mail or a sword”] not be given to merchants [*the Vatican manuscript adds *foras marca*, “outside the district/frontier”].

**8.** Concerning measures: that they be made equal according to our command [*“the emperor’s command” in the Vatican and Metz manuscripts].

**9.** That no testimonies be sent concerning the investiture of the lord King Pippin [but that such honor be preserved for us in this matter as is known to have been preserved for our predecessors and for the emperors [*“was” in the manuscript]; this final clause is supplied only by Blank.].

**10** [*Absent from the Vatican manuscript.] [*The Corbie manuscript reads: “That neither a colonus nor a royal fiscal dependent be able to make a transfer elsewhere outside.” The Bigotian manuscript reads: “That neither a colonus nor a royal fiscal dependent be able to be sent outside elsewhere or make transfers.” Lindenbrog reads: “that he may be able to make transfers elsewhere of those sent outside.” He took this reading from book II of the Lombard Law. — Baluzius.] That neither a colonus nor a royal fiscal dependent be able to make transfers anywhere outside [*“outside transfer” is absent from B.; the oldest manuscripts read *foras mistio*, that is, “unless in a transfer”; Amb. has *foras mistos*; Vn. *foras mixtos*] [*“to anyone” in 4629].

**11.** That no one presume to bring a man to court without cause [*some manuscripts add “without cause.” All editions have this wording except the edition of Lindenbrog. We have followed it because it is supported by the greater number of ancient exemplars. — Baluzius], unless judgment has been rendered [*“without cause” is absent from the editions].

**12.** That a free man who has tonsured himself in a regular monastery and has transferred his property there shall firmly keep the promise he has made according to the rule [*In Blank.’s manuscript, chapter 9 is inserted here: “That all debts be paid until they are settled,” added to the Salic Law].

**13.** That everything which must be pledged [*“all who must pledge” in 4629] be fully re-pledged according to what the law provides, entirely in accordance with that law [*the edition reads *inuuadiata*, “pledged anew”]; and afterward let either the lord king or the person whose case it is show mercy according to his pleasure.

**14.** Concerning bishops, abbots, and counts who have not come to our assembly.

**15.** That no drunk man be able to prosecute his case in court or give testimony. Nor shall a count hold an assembly unless he is fasting.

**16** [*The chapter is absent from 4629.] That no one be permitted to compel another to drink [*The manuscript of St Rémi of Reims adds: “unless as much as suffices for him”; the Regius manuscript reads: “unless what was necessary for him.” The Bavarian edition likewise has this reading. — Baluzius] [unless what will be necessary for him].

[*“It must be investigated” according to the edition.]

[Col. 0261A] **17.** Concerning our envoys traveling about, and other men journeying on our business: no one shall presume to deny them lodging [*“in wintertime” in V. Vn. E.].

**18.** Concerning dogs that have been shorn on the right shoulder: the man who has such a dog must come with it into the presence of the lord king [*“with the dog” in 4629, 4404, 4995, and 4758].

**19.** That the people be questioned concerning the chapters recently added to the law [*that is, the immediately preceding Capitulary]. And after everyone has consented [*the Vatican manuscript ends here], let them make their subscriptions and attestations by hand to those chapters [*This was done in the Paris assembly. See above, Col. 255 B–C, paragraph “They are headed.”].

**20.** That no one be summoned to an assembly [*“to the daily assembly” in V. Vn. E.] unless he has a case to pursue, or unless another must pursue a case against him; except the seven *scabini*, who must preside at all assemblies [*“who must be present” in 4995, V. Vn. E., and Muratori] [*the remainder is absent from 4404 and Blank.].

**21.** Concerning false witnesses: that they not be admitted.

**22.** That no one presume to swear by the life of the king and his sons.

**23.** Concerning those Saxons who have no wives.

**24.** Concerning the marked men [*“the *sinnadis*” in 4995] who travel about by lying.

**25.** That our envoys who have already brought a written report concerning the announcement shall, as we wish, bring further information concerning the work [*“further” is absent from 4629; “concerning the work” is absent from 4995].

**26.** How long they remain in each locality, and how many men they have with them.

**27.** Concerning the prudence and steadfastness of our envoys.

**28.** Concerning false moneyers: the matter must be investigated.

**29** [*The chapter is absent from 4995 and the Mazarin manuscript; “if” is absent from 4629.] If other matters do not happen to intervene [*4929 has singular *praeoccupauerit*, followed by “Here end the chapters concerning the Salic Law”; the remainder is absent from 4758], we wish to hold a general assembly on 24 June, the feast of Saint John the Baptist, at Mainz or at Chalon [*the edition reads *Cabillonem*, Chalon].

In manuscript 4632 of the Royal Library the following follows:

### Chapter concerning the freedom of charters

If anyone has been released as a free man by a charter and is challenged by any person for service [Col. 0262A], let him first produce the lawful author of his freedom and remain in his freedom. But if the author is unavailable, let him be allowed to defend himself with the testimony of good men who were present when the free man was released. But if the witnesses too are unavailable, let him confirm that his charter, which is the third, is true and lawful by means of two charters signed or subscribed by the hand of the same chancellor, whatever sort those comparison charters may be. But if he is challenged for service and has neither an author nor witnesses, and cannot find two other charters to confirm his own [*“charter” is printed *carcam* in C.], then let the person who challenged him, according to the law itself, prove that charter false and claim him as his slave. But if the challenger [*that is, the *interpellator*] is defeated by an author, by witnesses, or by the comparison of charters, and cannot accomplish what he wished, he shall be compelled to pay the fine contained in the charter of emancipation itself [*Baluzius conjectures *absolvere*, “to release,” from Ansegisus].

In manuscripts 1 Gudianus and 2 Paris. 4626 the following chapters are added:

**1.** Let no toll or tax be demanded from anyone where there is neither navigable water nor a bridge to cross.

**2.** We must also command that whoever brings a horse as a royal gift have his name written on each one. Likewise on the clothing of abbesses.

**3.** We must also command that wherever vicars are found consenting to or committing some wrongdoing [*“some people” in manuscript 1], they themselves be expelled and better men appointed in their place [*“those men” in manuscript 1].

**4.** That counts and their vicars know the law, so that no one may judge anyone unjustly before them [*absent from manuscript 1], nor alter the law itself.

# LOMBARD CAPITULARY

[Col. 0261]

It is found in the Chisian and Cava manuscripts as chapters 42–64 and 69–90, and among the Lombard laws in Muratori as chapters 97, 91–93, 98, 102–108, 93, 110, 111 (chapter 15 is absent), and 112–119. It contains chapters 1–21; chapters added to the Salic Law, 9 and 10; minor chapters 4 and 5; chapters of the Salic Law 2–8; and minor chapters 4, 6, 8, 9, 11, 12, 15, 17, 20, and 22.

[Col. 0261D] **22.** Concerning free men who take royal fiscal women as wives, and free women who likewise take royal fiscal men, and so forth: see below, 805 B, chapter 22.

**23.** That a case which has not yet been before the count, and in which those who are making complaint, because of their violence [*“folly” in V. Vn. E. M., chapter 118] or stubbornness, have been unwilling to appeal to the count concerning it, be referred again to the count [*“from ‘that was’ onward” is absent from Ch. C.].

**24** [*A later hand in Vn. adds: “Concerning benefices and tributary lands.”] Whoever has abandoned a benefice on account of his own property, and, within a year after this has been made known to him by the count or by our envoy, has not restored it, shall lose that benefice.

# CHAPTERS TO BE SENT TO THE RIBUARIAN LAW

[Col. 0263]

We publish these with the aid of: (1) the Royal Paris manuscript 4629; (2) Vatican manuscript 773 among the Palatine manuscripts; (3) the Tegernsee manuscript, now in Munich, from which Amerbach first made them public; (4) Paris manuscript, Supplement latin 75; and also the manuscript of St Paul in Carinthia, which contains the third chapter, together with the other manuscripts [*The London manuscript places chapter 3 among Pippin’s chapters] in which chapters added to the Lombard laws are found. In the Vatican manuscript it is headed as follows: “Here begins the new constitution of the law of the Emperor Charles, which is to be sent to the Ribuarians.” Manuscript 4629 has only this: “Likewise, other chapters.”

In manuscript Suppl. lat. 75 we read: “This was issued at Aachen in the third year of the reign of the lord Charles Augustus, when a great synod was held there.” According to Baluzius, this statement was also found in the manuscripts of Metz and the Vatican, and must refer either to these chapters or to those immediately preceding them—or rather to both.

Among Charles’s Lombard laws there are chapters 2–5, 7, and 8–13; in Muratori, chapters 109, 119, 26, 27, 94, Pippin 13, and Charles 38 and 132.

[Col. 0263A] **Chapter 1.** *(To title 1 of the Ribuarian Law.)* If a free man strikes a free man with a blow, he shall pay fifteen solidi.

**2.** *(10.)* If a royal man, that is, a fiscal dependent, an ecclesiastical man, or a *litus* is killed, one hundred solidi shall be paid in compensation.

**3.** *(12; this chapter alone is present in the manuscript of St Paul and in the Chisian manuscript.)* A free man who is unable to pay any fine and has no sureties [*absent in manuscript 3] may place himself in pledge [*“in judgment” in manuscript 1] with the person to whom he is indebted, until he has paid the fine that he owed [*“to pay” in this same chapter in manuscripts 1, 3, and 4 of St Paul].

**4.** *(18.)* Concerning a *sonesti* [*“soniste” in manuscripts 3 and 4 of St Paul]: let him either pay six hundred solidi or swear with twelve men. Or, if the person pursuing the case refuses to accept the oath of twelve men, let him fight against him by the cross, or with shield and club.

**5.** *(20; XVIII in manuscripts 2, 3, and 4.)* No one may abandon his slave because of damage inflicted by him on anyone [*“by someone” in manuscript 1]; instead, according to the nature of the damage, the lord shall answer for him, or offer him in compensation or for the plaintiff’s punishment [*“take him away” in manuscript 1]. But if the slave flees after committing the crime, so that his lord is utterly unable to find him, his lord shall endeavor to clear himself by oath, declaring that it was neither by his will nor with his knowledge that his slave committed such a deed [*“and let him be absolved?” in Vn.? M.].

**6.** *(30.)* As they requested, so the lord emperor consented [*this is found only in manuscript 1; Benedict II, p. 310].

**7.** *(34; XXXIII in manuscripts 2, 3, and 4.)* If anyone is summoned to court according to the law [*“a Salic man” is added in V. Vn. E.] and does not come, unless an unavoidable necessity has detained him, he shall be judged liable to a fine of fifteen solidi [*“summoned” in manuscript 4; “only concerning freedom or inheritance” in V. Vn. E.]. The same applies to the second and third summons. But if he refuses to come at the fourth, his property shall be placed under the ban [Col. 0263C] until he comes and does justice concerning the matter in which he has been challenged. If he does not come within a year, the king shall be consulted concerning the property placed under the ban [*“which they placed under the ban” in manuscript 1], and whatever he decides concerning it shall be done.

The first summons shall be after seven nights, the second after fourteen nights, the third after twenty-one, and the fourth after forty-two [Col. 0264A]. Likewise, if a man has no property of his own, his benefice shall be placed under the ban until the king is consulted [*“His benefice shall indeed be denied to him until he himself or his envoy comes and does justice.” V. Vn. E.].

**8.** *(35.)* If the claimant comes and refuses to accept the disputed property, the matter shall be contested in the field or by the cross.

**9.** *(48.)* Whoever has no children and wishes to make anyone else his heir shall make the transfer before the king, or before the count and the *scabini*, or before the royal envoy who has then been appointed to administer justice in the province [*“parish” in manuscript 1].

**10.** *(57; LVIII in manuscript 2; XVII in manuscript 3.)* A *denarius-man* shall not be able to inherit into his kinship [*the reading of manuscripts 1 and 2; manuscript 1 corrects *agnitionem* to *agnationem*, while manuscripts 3 and 4 read *agnationem*] until he reaches the third generation.

**11.** *(64.)* The *cartellaris* man likewise [*“cartularis” in manuscript 2; “cartularius” in manuscripts 3 and 4].

[Col. 0264B] **12.** *(67.)* Every oath shall be sworn in a church or over relics. And what must be sworn in church shall be sworn either with six [*seven in manuscript 4] chosen men, or, if twelve are required [*absent in manuscript 1], with as many as he is able to find [*that is, “let him swear thus”; so Amb. and the other Lombard-law manuscripts]. May God and the saints whose relics these are so help him that he speak the truth [*“Let these oaths belong to minor cases” in V. Vn. E.].

**13.** *(72.)* If disputed property has been taken away by theft, the person against whom the disputed property has been claimed may clear himself by oath concerning the theft, declaring that what was taken was neither by his will nor with his knowledge; and he shall restore an equal amount without the damages [*the remainder is absent from manuscripts 2, 3, and 4: “If the claimant comes and refuses to accept the disputed property, let him contest it in the field or by the cross.” V. Vn. E.; see above, chapter 8. The Tironian notes of manuscript 1 are expressed in an added table].

Manuscript 1 adds:

Let no one presume to collect a toll on roads or through villages, nor a *rotaticum*, *cepstaticum* [*that is, *cespitaticum*], or *pulveraticum*.

The following is added in manuscript 3:

### Concerning a man who captured a slave and ordered him to kill his two masters’ children

A man captured a slave and ordered him to kill his master’s two children, one aged nine and the other eleven [*the printed plural *dominos suos* is glossed “his master” in the note]. Finally, after the slave had killed those children, he threw the slave into a certain pit [*in *occisit*, a later hand has written *d* over the final letter]. It was adjudged that he should pay triple *weregild* for the nine-year-old, double for the eleven-year-old, triple for the slave whom he had murdered, and our ban in full.

# CAPITULARY CONCERNING THE ADVANCEMENT OF THE ARMY

[Col. 0265]

This constitution was first published by Herold in his addition to the Lombard laws, chapter 3, p. 320. Baluzius assigned it to the year 811 because it seemed to be mentioned in the Capitulary of Bologna, whose chronological notices he referred to the year 812. But since the Capitulary of 805, chapter 6, already mentions an edict concerning the advancement of the army in which nothing had yet been established concerning *brunias*, and since that fits our constitution, it is clear that this constitution is earlier than 805. I have therefore assigned it to the year 803, since neither in that year nor in the immediately preceding one did Charles himself undertake an expedition, but, remaining at home, sent his envoys to the army; this agrees especially well with chapters 8 and 9 of this Capitulary. Our edition rests on the authority of the manuscript from which Herold also appears to have copied the law: the Weissenau manuscript of the tenth century, collated for our use with the printed editions by the distinguished and indefatigable promoter of our studies, D. Maier, jurist of Esslingen.

## SUMMARY OF THE CHAPTERS THAT THE ROYAL ENVOYS MUST HAVE FOR THE ADVANCEMENT OF THE ARMY

[Col. 0265B]

**1.** That every free man who possesses four stocked hides of his own property or from someone’s benefice shall prepare himself and go to the army in person, either with his lord if his lord goes, or with his count. Whoever has three hides of his own shall be joined by one who has one hide, and the latter shall give him assistance so that he can serve for both. Whoever has only two hides of his own shall be joined by another who likewise has two hides, and one of them, assisted by the other, shall go to the army. Whoever has only one hide of his own shall have three men joined to him who likewise have one hide, and they shall give him assistance; he alone shall go, while the three who gave him assistance shall remain at home.

**2.** We wish and command that these same envoys of ours carefully investigate who remained behind from the army to which he had been summoned in the previous year, contrary to the arrangement we have just ordered above concerning free and poorer men; and whoever is found neither to have assisted his equal in serving in the army according to our command nor to have gone himself shall fully repay our *haribannum*, and shall give security and pay it according to the law [*Compare 811, October, chapter 4].

**3.** [*The editor corrects the text to *hoc de quo*; the manuscript and Herold read *hoc quoque*. Compare 811, October, chapter 9.] If a man is found who says that, at the command of his count, vicar, or centenarius, he gave to that count, vicar, centenarius, or any of their men the thing with which he himself ought to have equipped himself, and for that reason abandoned the journey, and our envoys are able to establish that this is true, the person by whose command he remained behind shall repay and pay our ban, whether he is a count, a vicar [*“vicar” is written twice in the manuscript], or the advocate of a bishop or abbot.

**4.** Concerning the household men of counts [*Compare 811, October, chapter 9]. The following are to be excepted and are not to be ordered to repay the ban: two who were released to remain with his wife, and two others who were ordered to remain behind to guard his household and perform our service. In this matter we now command that, however many administrative duties each count has, he leave at home two men for each duty to guard it, in addition to those two whom [he had] with his wife. [The supplied source breaks off after *praeter illos duos quos cum uxore sua*; no governing verb is supplied.] He shall have all the rest fully with him; or, if he himself remains at home, they shall be sent with the man who goes to the army in his place [*“he shall be sent” in manuscript 1]. A bishop or abbot, however, shall leave at home only two of his household and laymen.

**5.** Concerning our men and those of bishops and abbots [Col. 0266C] who possess either benefices or sufficient property of their own to enable them to go properly to the army according to the command, except those whom we have permitted them to leave at home with them. If any are found who have bought themselves off, or who have remained at home with the permission of their lords [*“households” in manuscript 1], they shall repay our ban, as stated above [*the word is absent from the manuscript and from Herold, and was restored by Baluzius], and shall give security and pay it. Their lords, however, who permitted them to remain at home [*“permitted him” in manuscript 1], or their officials who accepted payment from them, shall likewise repay our ban [*“repay the ban” in manuscript 1] and give security, until word has been brought to us.

**6.** We wish our envoys carefully to investigate in which places the following occurred, which has come to us [*“which concerns us” in manuscript 1]: certain men, after giving assistance from their pay to their companions who had gone to the army according to our command, gave money, at the order of the count or his officials, to buy themselves off, so that they might be allowed to remain at home, even though they ought not to have gone to the army because they had already given their companions the assistance prescribed by us. Let this be investigated and reported to us.

**7.** We wish these envoys of ours who are to perform this mission to receive a levy from those men who ought to have gone to the army but did not go. Likewise, they shall receive it from the count, vicar, or centenarius who agreed that they should remain at home; and they shall also receive the aforesaid levy from all who, in the previous year, made void the order issued by us concerning the army’s march [*Compare 811, October, chapter 9].

**8.** We wish four copies of this Capitulary to be written. One shall be held by our envoys; another by the count in whose administration these things are to be carried out, so that neither the envoy nor the count may act otherwise than as ordered by us in these chapters. A third shall be held by our envoys who are to be placed in charge of our army. The fourth shall be held by our chancellor.

**9.** We wish the men of our faithful subjects whom we have ordered to remain at home with us for our service not to be compelled to go into the army; they shall remain at home or in the service of their lords. Nor shall those men who were with us in the previous year be ordered to repay the *haribannum* [*Einhard calls this “remaining behind” in letter 17, written to Rabanus, abbot of Fulda. — Baluzius].

# OTHER CHAPTERS TO BE ADDED

[Col. 0267]

These chapters were first published by Baluzius from the Palatine manuscripts of the Vatican Library and from the manuscript of St Vincent at Metz. I have revised them with the aid of the first Royal Paris manuscript among the Latin Supplements, number 75.

## OTHER CHAPTERS ARE TO BE ADDED, THOSE THAT WE HAVE RECENTLY HEARD AND ASCERTAINED

[Col. 0267B]

**1.** Concerning clerics and laymen who give or receive chrism in excessive quantities. If any priest or deacon presumes to give or receive it, let him lose his rank. The other clerics and nuns (*nonnanes*) [*This is not found in the Palatine manuscript and appears superfluous. — Baluzius] shall undergo corporal discipline and imprisonment. Laymen who receive it or give it to someone else shall lose a hand.

**2.** Above all, concerning commerce, it must be commanded that no one dare trade at night in gold or silver vessels, slaves, gems, horses, or animals, except food and fodder, which are necessary for travelers; but during the day, in the presence of everyone and before witnesses, let each person conduct his trade.

**3.** The remaining chapters written in the preceding Capitulary, concerning the sale of grain, other judicial matters, the restoration of churches, peace, fugitives, and each individual matter, shall all be observed in this way [*In manuscript 1 the following is added: “It must be understood that in certain booklets of the Salic Law, and so forth”—the entire recapitulation of solidi printed with the editions of the Salic Law. After removing this, Baluzius wrote: “Eight chapters are missing here.”].

**12.** [*Above, Col. 263, section C, chapter 5.] No one may abandon his slave because of damage inflicted by him; instead, according to the nature of the offense, his lord shall answer for the slave, or pay compensation for whatever he did up to the full *leud* (wergild) of a free man. Whatever exceeds this appears to belong to the king’s judgment [*I have corrected the reading to “in the king’s judgment”; the manuscript and editions have *inregauditio*].

**13.** If anyone is found to have made a false charter or given false testimony, let him lose a hand [*“his hand and foot” in manuscript 1] or buy himself off.

**14.** If a free man, under the pressure of sin—which God forbid—kills his father or mother, uncle, or nephew, let him lose his inheritance. And if anyone has sexual relations with his mother, sister, paternal aunt, or niece, let him likewise lose his inheritance.

**15.** If fiscal dependents, coloni, or slaves residing under another’s authority are demanded by their former lord, they shall not be handed over to him in any other way than this: they must return to the former place where they were previously seen to have lived, and there an inquiry must carefully be made concerning their condition and that of their kin. We command that this be made known to everyone.

**16.** [801, 14.] That, throughout our kingdoms, with Christ’s favor, no one deny lodging to any traveler: only a place to stay and a fire. Likewise, no one shall compel the provision of fodder, except in respect of meadow and harvest.

[Col. 0268C] **17.** [801, 15.] That free men render no service to counts or vicars, whether in meadow, harvest, plowing, or vineyard work, and pay them no levy or remainder; except the service owed to the king, to the *haribannitores*, or to those who carry an embassy.

**18** [*This is connected with the preceding chapter 1.] [*Above, Col. 262, chapter 3.] Wherever vicars are found consenting to or committing some wrongdoing, we order that they themselves be expelled and better men appointed.

**19.** [*Chapter 4.] That counts and their vicars know the law, so that no one may judge anyone unjustly before them or alter the law itself.

**20.** [*Chapter 2.] Whoever presents horses as royal gifts [*They are called royal gifts because at that time it was customary to offer horses to kings, as Charles du Fresne shows in his *Observations on Joinville*, p. 155. A precept of Louis the Pious for the church of Brioude reads: “No one should have rendered any service to anyone for the aforesaid matters, except that each year they presented to the king one horse with shield and lance.” — Baluzius] shall have his name written on each one [*Likewise, on the candles that the nuns offered to the tomb of Saint Radegund after her death, “each had written her name on her candles,” as it is in her life written by Baudonivia. — Baluzius].

**21.** Whoever has, or wishes to have, a consecrated oratory shall, with the counsel of the bishop, give some of his own property there, so that those canonical *vici* (settlements) are not neglected on that account.

**22** [*Connected with the preceding chapter 1.] [*Chapter 1.] No one shall presume to collect a toll anywhere except where bridges have been constructed from ancient times, where boats pass by [*perhaps “where boats cross”], and where the custom appears to be ancient. Likewise, no one shall presume to collect a *rodaticum* or *pulveraticum*, because whoever attempts to do this must in every way pay the lord’s ban [*Col. 264, line 39].

# CHAPTERS GIVEN TO A CERTAIN ROYAL ENVOY

[Col. 0269]

I have revised these chapters, which were given in response to the questions of a certain royal envoy and are drawn from chapters 5 and 6, with the aid of the Royal Paris manuscript among the Latin Supplements, number 75. They had first been published by Baluzius from the Palatine manuscripts of the Vatican Library and from the manuscript of St Vincent at Metz.

[Col. 0269B] **1.** The first chapter concerned whether, when a slave of someone has taken a female colonus as his wife, their children should belong to the female colonus or to the male slave. Consider, then, if your own slave has joined himself to another person’s own female slave, or another person’s own slave has taken your own female slave as his wife: to which of you should their offspring belong? Deal with these cases in the same way, because there is nothing further at issue than free and slave.

**2.** Concerning the second matter about which you questioned me: whether a count ought to receive one solidus for a notice, and likewise the *scabini* or the chancellor. Read the Roman law and act accordingly to what you find there. But if the matter belongs to the Salic Law and you find nothing there concerning what you should do, have the matter questioned at our general assembly.

**3.** The third chapter concerned those who obtain freedom through false witnesses, and you asked what should be done with them. We have everywhere commanded you that no one should be able to free himself from servitude by false testimony. If he has been able to free himself according to the procedure of the law, let him remain free. But if he did so with false witnesses, do not consent to him in any way.

**4.** The fourth chapter explained what should be done concerning those who, having been summoned once, twice, or three times [*“having been admonished,” in the Palatine manuscript. — Baluzius], refuse to come into your presence. We have likewise instructed you concerning what must be done with them.

## Complete supplied apparatus

The following reproduces all 129 canonical apparatus notices with their exact readings and witness or edition associations. In the English accounts, *deest/desunt* means “is/are omitted,” *addit/inseritur* means “adds/is inserted,” *corr.* means “corrected,” and *cf.* introduces the exact cross-reference. Latin forms remain visible because their spelling is the textual evidence; their English context is the translated clause identified on each line. Key distinctions include *scripta* (“written”) versus *disscripta/discripta/descripta* (“written/described” variants), *rewadiata* (“secured or paid by legal pledge”) versus *inuuadiata* (“pledged”), *mannitus* (“summoned”) versus *bannitus* (“placed under the ban”), and *ammonitio/mannitio* (“summons”) versus *bannitio* (“ban-notice”).

5. In the fifth chapter, however, there was mention of bishops, abbots, or other men of ours who had refused to come to your assembly. Have them summoned to your assembly by our ban. And those who then refuse to come, present their names, recorded in writing, to us at our general assembly.

6. In the sixth chapter it was written about established ancient bridges and about [Note: This word is absent from the Palatine Codex. ID.] unlawful tolls. Accordingly, we decree that wherever there has been an ancient custom of collecting a toll, they shall collect the lawful toll. For we previously commanded this to you personally, but you did not understand it at all.

7. In the seventh chapter, where it was stated how, after the complaints of their masters, slaves are to produce their documents, and how the slaves themselves, after receiving a judgment from the *scabini*, must prove that those documents are genuine: we by no means wish the slave to have to prove his own document; rather, the master who is claiming that slave must himself, if he can, detect that the document is false.

8. In the eighth chapter there was mention of slaves who take Frankish women, after which their masters make documents for them in these terms: if any offspring, male or female, should arise from them, they shall remain free. You wrote that you do not know whether they ought to possess them or not. We therefore decree that if a man makes a document for a male or female slave in his own presence, and the man or woman who is to possess the document of freedom is present, that document shall remain valid. But anyone born after the departure of his or her master shall remain in servitude. And those documents made by certain masters for persons who were not yet known to have been born, but who were born after their masters’ departure, shall have no effect [Col. 0270D], nor shall those persons be able to become free by means of those documents.

# CAPITULARY ISSUED BY THE ROYAL ENVOYS

[Col. 0269]

I have revised this capitulary, edited by Baluze, from an old manuscript Codex of Saint Vincent of Metz, with the assistance of Codex 1 of the Royal Library of Paris, among the *Supplementa latina*, no. 75.

[Col. 0271A] 1. First, concerning the ban of the lord emperor and king, which he is accustomed to proclaim personally: namely, the protection (*mundoburdium*) of churches, widows, orphans, and persons of lesser power, as well as [Note: I have inserted the words “and abduction,” since they are lacking in the Parisian Codex and in both of Baluze’s editions.] abduction, and the military assembly that has been established: those who violate these protections shall in every respect pay the lord’s ban.

2. Concerning tithes and ninths, and the justice of the churches of God: take care to give and do what the law requires.

3. Whoever possesses a benefice of the lord emperor or of the churches of God shall not divert anything from it into his own inheritance, so that the benefice itself may be destroyed.

4. No one shall receive another man’s cleric or dependent into his own power.

5. No one shall keep a robber in his power, nor conceal him [Col. 0271B].

6. No one shall presume to commit perjury or give false testimony.

[Col. 0272A] 7. No one shall dare to pronounce anything contrary to a rightful judgment.

8. No one shall presume to harm the man who has spoken the emperor’s rightful judgment [Note: Printed *impr.* in ed. 1.].

9. No one shall presume to oppress another without legal process or to do anything evil.

10. No one shall presume to sell, buy, or measure in any other way than the lord emperor has ordered.

11. Observe the Lord’s Day with all diligence, as the law requires or as the lord emperor has ordered.

12. Let no one violate the fidelity that he has promised to the lord emperor; nor let anyone consent to one who has violated it [Note: Thus ed. 1; corrected in the edition to “let him not be consented to.”].

[Col. 0272B] 13. Likewise, concerning those pagan practices [Note: “Pagan practices,” with an additional *c* in Codex 1] that some people observe: let no one perform them or consent to anyone performing them [Note: Thus ed. 1; corrected in the edition to “consent to one performing them.”].

# CAPITULARY AT SALZ

*(An. 803, summer)*

[Note: The royal palace in Germany on the River Saale. Germany has two rivers of this name: one flows into the Elbe, the other into the Main. The latter is meant here. For it is established from Einhard’s Annals that in 790, after leaving Worms, Charlemagne sailed along the Main to his palace at Salz in Germany, built beside the River Saale. Moreover, the Annals of Metz and of Fulda state that Louis the Pious, shortly before his death, returned to the royal estate at Salz—which the same Fulda Annals, under the year 897, call the estate known as Salz—and, after falling ill there, traveled by boat along the Main to Frankfurt; a few days later he was carried to an island in the Rhine near Ingelheim. The position of this palace is indicated by the Saxon poet, who still saw it standing in his own time, under the year 790, where, speaking of Charlemagne, he says:

“He undertook a naval journey along the River Main,

and ascended it until he came near the walls

of the great palace seat called Salz by name,

near the young Saale; for a small stream of this river

still surrounds these very palaces,

scarcely raising a hoarse murmur through the echoing stones.”

Baluze.]

[Col. 0271]

I have restored the text of this capitulary from Codex 1 of the Vatican Library, marked among the Palatine manuscripts as no. 289, of the ninth century, comparing it with Codex 2 of the Royal Library of Paris, among the *Supplementa latina*, no. 75. The Palatine Codex has no heading, whereas the Parisian one reads, “In the fourth year, at Salz.” The same material was contained in the Codex from which Sirmond first published this law in volume II of the *Councils of Gaul*, p. 252; for that reason both he and Baluze thought it should be assigned to the year 804. It nevertheless remains to be noted that Charles stayed at the palace of Salz in Franconia not in that year but in the preceding year, 803. Accordingly, this capitulary should be assigned to the summer of 803, or its year should be left entirely uncertain.

We append what follows immediately in these Codices: from the Palatine Codex, a capitulary of some metropolitan, perhaps promulgated at a synod; and, on the authority of the Parisian Codex, chapters addressed to priests, formerly published by Sirmond and Baluze with the assistance of the Rheims and Vatican Codices.

[Col. 0271C] 1. Let the churches of God be properly built and restored, and let each bishop exercise good oversight over them within his own parish, both concerning their service and lights and concerning all other restoration.

2. Concerning tithes where in ancient times there were [Note: Churches in which there was a public baptistery, as is read in chapter 7 of the synod held at Verneuil under King Pippin. Liutprand, king of the Lombards, says in a grant for Lupertian, bishop of Arezzo, published by Jacopo Burali in his *History of the Bishops of Arezzo*, p. 25: “The case that was disputed between you and Donatus, bishop of the city of Siena, concerning the churches of the holy God in which it is customary to perform baptism.” These were called baptisteries in a grant of Charlemagne and in letters of Ambrose, mayor of the palace under Liutprand, preserved by the same Burali. Flodoard calls them baptismal titles in book II, chapter 19 of his *History of Rheims*, p. 261 in Colvenerius’s edition. Those churches, therefore, were called baptismal churches in order to distinguish them from others that did not have baptisteries.

For I consider the observation of Joseph, viscount, entirely sound: he believes that in ancient times there was only one baptismal church in each city, to which all those being baptized were required to come. This is also clear from an old account preserved by Chifflet, part II of *Besançon*, chapter 26, p. 163. The same practice existed not only in cities but also in villages, as may be inferred from canon 48 of the synod of Meaux and from an old charter of Patriacum published by Perard in the *Monuments of Burgundian History*, p. 42: “Declaring that they ought not to hold an episcopal reception at Saint Marcellinus, which is a chapel, not a public village.”

Burchard confirms this in book III, chapter 22, from a certain Council of Aachen, if the attribution is reliable: “There cannot be several baptismal churches within one district, but only one, together with its dependent chapels.” Gratian, 16, question 1, chapter 53, cites this from the Council of Toledo. Chapels anciently subject to churches are mentioned in chapter 2 of Hincmar’s letter to the clergy and people of Laon, which appears below among the *Formulas of Episcopal Promotions*, title 18.

In those chapels, which ancient synods and Fathers also call oratories, it was not permitted to establish a baptistery. Gregory the Great is witness in book II, indiction 10, letter 9, to the bishop of Rimini. Speaking of the oratory that Themothea had built within the city of Rimini, he says: “You shall solemnly consecrate the aforesaid oratory without public Masses, so that neither a baptistery may be built in that place in future times nor a cardinal priest appointed.” The same provisions are made concerning another oratory in the city of Naples, book VIII, indiction 3, letter 3. Saint Gregory was later copied by Pope Zachary in his response 15 to the chapters sent by Pippin through Ardovain.

Indeed, those who came throughout the year to such oratories or chapels were required to come three times a year to the mother church, as was established by several councils. This holy institution remained in force for a long time, certainly until the eleventh century of the Christian era. We possess a letter of Pibo, bishop of Toul, dated 1079, in which we read: “The church of Munz was anciently the chapel of Blano, and the people living in the same village of Munz were accustomed to assemble three times a year—namely, at Easter, Pentecost, [Col. 0273C] and Christmas—at their mother church of Blano, and there to pay the prescribed offerings to the priest of Blano.” The people of Munz were then freed from this obligation, and Pibo also granted them a baptistery and free burial. Pibo was certainly able to do this, as Gratian observes in the passage cited shortly before. Nevertheless, the consent of the clergy was necessary.

Augustine Valerius, cardinal and bishop of Verona, knew this episcopal right. In his annotations on the synodal constitutions of Matthew Giberti, bishop of Verona, he writes on p. 296: “From these words it may be inferred that not every parish church has been granted the right to possess a baptismal font. This appears to be confirmed by the practice of many parish churches in which there are no baptismal fonts. Therefore, in order to remove all ambiguity, we decree that no parish priest may, by virtue of this constitution, erect a baptismal font at his pleasure unless he has first obtained our specific order and permission. If anything is done otherwise, the font itself shall be completely destroyed from its foundations, and that parish priest shall be punished at our discretion.”

According to the law of Charlemagne—which appears in the following chapter of this capitulary and in chapter 19 of the first capitulary of 823—the tithes of villages in which new churches had been established belonged to the older churches within whose boundaries the new churches lay. The same rule is found in book II of the *Capitularies*, chapters 36 and 47, and in book V, chapter 97, as well as in the decree of Leo IV cited by Gratian, 16, question 1, chapter 45, “On Tithes.” Gratian therefore concludes that tithes are to be given only to baptismal churches. The Gloss adds that tithes must always be paid to baptismal churches and not to chapels.

In Giraldus Cambrensis’s *Description of Wales*, chapter 18, we read [Col. 0274A] that the Britons customarily gave two parts of the great tithe to baptismal churches and the third to diocesan bishops. I shall also cite a notable passage of A. Amulo, archbishop of Lyon, in which he explains the dignity and authority of baptismal churches in words that are by no means obscure. These are his words from a letter to Theobald, bishop of Langres:

“Let every people remain peacefully in the parishes and churches to which it has been assigned, and let it go to those sanctuaries where it receives holy baptism, where it receives the body and blood of the Lord, where it is accustomed to hear the solemnities of Mass, where from its priest it receives penance for guilt, visitation in illness, and burial in death, where it is also commanded to offer its tithes and first fruits, where it rejoices to have its children initiated by the grace of baptism, where it continually hears the word of God and learns what must and must not be done. Let it, I say, gladly carry its vows and offerings there.”

In the Chartulary of the Church of Vienne I found that at a synod held by Archbishop Alexander in 907 it was judged, according to Bernard, abbot of Saint Maurice, who maintained that the tithes of the chapel of Saint Severus—which had been built within the boundaries of the church of Saint Primus at Taizé—ought to belong to the church of Taizé.

Louis the Pious nevertheless established in the capitulary of 816, chapter 12, that tithes from new villages should be assigned to the churches newly established in them. Apart from tithes, however, a foundation endowment was also required from the founders, as was stated in the notes to Regino, p. 543.

In an old Chartulary of the Church of Brioude there are letters of Adalard, bishop of Clermont, dated 906. After recounting the endowment of a newly built church in the village of Blanède, he adds that it should pay the Church of Clermont the service owed to it, like the other chapels subject to it. There are likewise letters of Arnald, bishop of Clermont, dated 923, concerning the consecration and endowment of the church of Canet, in which we read that he dedicated the same chapel on the seventh day of the last month and established that, for as long as John the founder lived, he should retain the chapel.

To return to baptismal churches: they were also called *plebes*, as will be said in the chapters of Charles the Bald.
