They were also called *oracula*, as in the chapters of Pippin, king of Italy, excerpted from the Code of Lombard law, chapter 16, and in a grant of Emperor Charles III for the church of Bergamo, published by R. P. Celestine the Capuchin in book XXII of the *History of Bergamo*, p. 399.

Since the dignity and reverence of such churches were so great, Charlemagne rightly decreed in the capitulary of 793, chapter 2, that laymen should not hold them—that is, that they should not be granted to laymen as benefices. The same was enacted in a capitulary of Pippin, chapter 15.

Nevertheless, in the Chartulary of the priory of Paray I find that the church of Saint Benignus, which possessed a cemetery, burial rights, and a baptistery, was long held by laymen by beneficiary right, until those who possessed it returned it to the monastery of Paray in the time of Prior Hugh.

The dignity of baptismal churches may also be inferred from the fact that, whereas one priest was sufficient in other churches, in these one deacon together with the priest was necessary. I found this in ancient chapters transcribed by Sirmond from the Vatican and Casinensis Codices. The eighth reads as follows: “Let no church of any diocese where baptism is performed be found with a priest without a deacon.” Baluze.]

baptismal churches, and a devotion has been made, let them be endowed in every respect, according to what the bishop of that parish has ordered. And if, through donations of kings or of other good men who fear God, certain properties have been assigned to bishoprics or monasteries, and anciently tithes from those properties were given to the older churches, let that ancient donation or endowment remain entirely firm and stable, and let the properties remain where they appear to have been assigned. Nevertheless, as we have said above, let the person who appears to possess those properties pay the tithes from them.

[Col. 0275A] 3. [Note: Regino reported this chapter from the capitularies; Burchard, following his usual practice, reported it from the Council of Worms, altering the words of the capitulary so that no one would suspect fraud. Baluze.] Whoever wishes to build a church on his own property shall have permission to do so with the consent and will of the bishop in whose parish it will be. Nevertheless, it must be carefully ensured that older churches do not on this account lose any of their rights or tithes, but that these always continue to be paid to the older churches.

4. Let each bishop arrange for priests to be ordained in his parish according to canonical institution.

5. Let no one presume to enter a monastery of women or of female servants of God: neither a priest, deacon, subdeacon, cleric, nor layman, unless only a priest enters at the proper time to celebrate Mass, subject to the needs of the monastery according to canonical institution and according to what the bishop of that parish has ordered there. [Col. 0276A] After celebrating Mass, the priest shall immediately leave.

6. Whoever wishes to offer his daughter, granddaughter, or female relative to Almighty God shall have permission to do so. Otherwise, let him raise his children at home, and let no one presume to send another child into the monastery for the purpose of being raised there, unless the child wishes firmly to persevere in God’s service in that place, or unless this is done according to the institutions of the holy Fathers or canonical authority.

7. We strictly prohibit anyone from presuming to place a male child, grandson, or male relative in a monastery of women for upbringing, and no one shall dare to receive him [Note: Thus Codex 1; compare chapter 6.].

8. Let no one from the clerical order—namely, priests or other clerics—or any layman presume to deposit coats of mail or other weapons within a monastery of women, nor let anyone dare to receive them, except when they have been given as alms.

# CAPITULARY OF A CERTAIN METROPOLITAN PROPOSED AT A SYNOD

[Col. 0275]

## Further Chapters

[Col. 0275B]

Chapter 1. Let us give thanks to God, because God has gathered us together in health [Note: “Together” is written twice in the Codex.].

2. Let prayer be made for the lord emperor, his sons, and the entire Christian people.

[Col. 0275C] 3. If any one of you has some matter to bring before us which he has not been able to remedy by himself.

4. Let each bishop admonish the priests [Col. 0276B] and clerics in his parish to act and live according to the canons.

5. Let bishops and abbots who have monks govern and teach them according to the Rule of Saint Benedict.

[Col. 0276C] 6. [The text reads “fl.”]

Let them pray for me, a sinner, as they desire.

[Note: These chapters are not complete but are merely brief summaries of chapters. It is unnecessary to proceed through every individual chapter, since they are described in various places in the capitularies. It will suffice here to note that the third chapter, which is not found in the books of the *Capitularies*, is found in full in volume IX of D’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, p. 64, among the chapters attributed to Archbishop Boniface, although they are not his. It reads there as follows:

“Let each bishop carefully examine his priests in his parish and ensure that they know [read *sciant* for *faciant*] their *signacula* and baptismal rites, and teach the priests what each individual word or clause in that baptism signifies.”

Baluze.]

# CHAPTERS GIVEN TO PRIESTS

[Col. 0275]

[Col. 0275C] I wish to admonish you, my brothers and little sons, to listen attentively to these few chapters written here.

1. First, let the priest of God be learned in sacred Scripture, rightly believe the faith of the Trinity, teach it to others, and be able to fulfill his office properly.

2. Let him know the entire Psalter by heart.

3. Let him know the *signaculum* and the baptismal rite by heart.

[Col. 0275D] 4. Let him be learned in the canons and know his penitential book well.

5. Let him know chant and computation.

[Col. 0276C] 6. Let no priest permit women to live with him, except his mother, sister, or aunt.

7. Let priests not presume to drink in taverns.

8. Let no one pursue greed; let him not be proud, drunk, addicted to wine, or drowsy.

9. Let no one presume to break his fast at the Lord’s Supper.

[Col. 0276D] 10. Let no one presume to baptize except at Easter and Pentecost, except in the case of a sick person.

11. Let no priest, deacon, or cleric presume to give chrism to anyone [Col. 0277A] under the pretext of any necessity [Note: That is, under the pretext of medicine or of anything else, as is stated in Addition III, chapter 99, from canon 18 of the Fourth Council of Arles; or under the pretext of medicine or sorcery, as in book V of the *Capitularies*, chapter 145, from canon 27 of the Council of Mainz. Sometimes they also used chrism to conceal crimes, believing that criminals anointed with or made to drink chrism could in no way be detected by any examination, as canon 20 of the Council of Tours, held in 813, teaches. See the chapters attributed to Archbishop Boniface, chapter 5. Baluze.]. If he does this, let him be deposed.

12. Let no priest refuse to come to the synod. If he presumes to act otherwise, let him be compelled to come and be judged according to the canons.

# ADDITIONS TO THE LAW OF THE BAVARIANS

*(An. 803, September or November)*

[Col. 0277]

In organizing Bavaria, which had been completely subdued in 788, Charles spent a considerably longer period of time—namely, in the years 788, 792, 793, and 803. It is not easy to say to which of these years the chapters added to the law of the Bavarians should be assigned. M. Welser assigned them to 788, Cointius to 792, and Baluze to 788 and 806, believing that they had been repeated after the division of the empire in 806.

Since we were uncertain, the word “emperor” seemed to us capable of settling the dispute. In more recent Codices it is omitted, as it is in all the oldest manuscripts from which the later copies were made, where it is present. The manuscripts available to us were:

1. Codex 4417 of the Royal Library of Paris, in folio, ninth or tenth century.
2. Codex 64 of the Palatine Library at Vienna, in the catalogue of civil law, a manuscript of the twelfth century, in which, as in the preceding and following manuscript, it appears after the laws of the Bavarians.
The edition of Joannes Tilius, without place or year, in sextodecimo.

In addition, the distinguished Foringer reported to us concerning the manuscripts preserved in the Royal Library at Munich and most generously noted their readings. They are these:

3. A former Tegernsee Codex, *Cimelium* IV.3.d., ninth or tenth century, in octavo, containing the laws of the Bavarians and Alamanni.
4. A former Codex of the cathedral church of Augsburg, no. 153, tenth century, in quarto, containing a collection of penitential canons, the laws of the Alamanni, and Ansegisus; as in the Tegernsee manuscript, it places the law of the Alamanni afterward.
5. A former Chiemsee Codex, later belonging to D. Lippert, now *Cimelium* IV.3.c., twelfth century, in large octavo, in which the law of the Bavarians is followed by the decree of Tassilo. As the distinguished Foringer observes, this book derives from the Tegernsee Codex, perhaps with another manuscript also used, and is the source of the sixth Codex.
6. A former manuscript of the city of Augsburg, twelfth century, in octavo, containing the laws of the Bavarians. From it H. Canisius, having obtained Welser’s copy, prepared his edition after Victor of Tunnuna’s *Chronicle*, Ingolstadt, 1600, in quarto; and Welser prepared his edition in book V of his *Bavarian Affairs*, Augsburg, 1602.

[Col. 0277B] The chapters which the most serene lord Charles [Note: *cartula* (“charter”) in Codex 1.] [Note: “Of the Bavarians” in Codex 2; the words “to the law of the Bavarians” are absent from manuscripts 3, 4, 5, and 6.] [Note: “Lord Charles most serene” is absent from manuscript 2.] emperor [Note: Absent from manuscripts 5 and 6.] ordered to be added, so that whoever [Note: “and” in Codex 1; “so that if” in Codex 2.] violates his ban [Note: *pannum* in manuscripts 3, 5, and 6; manuscript 4 corrects *pannum* to *bannum*, and likewise below in chapters 2 and 3.] [Note: *in hislibet* in Codex 1; *quilibet* in Tilius.] [Note: *irrumperet* in manuscript 4, *irrupere* in manuscript 3, *inrumperet* in manuscripts 5 and 6, and *inruperit* in Tilius.] must pay the composition.

1. Let the church [Note: *ecclesiae* in manuscript 4.], widows, orphans, and persons of lesser power have rightful peace. Wherever it is violated, let compensation of sixty solidi be paid [Note: The variant readings are printed as “XLX 49. 2” and XL in manuscript 4.].

2. Let no one presume to commit abduction [Note: *raptam* in Codex 1.] or violence [Note: *vim* in manuscripts 2, 4, 5, and 6.] through a gathering of men and burnings within the country [Note: Manuscripts 2, 4, 5, 6, and Tilius read “the country,” rather than “within the country.”]. Whoever commits this shall pay sixty solidi into our ban [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “whoever commits these things shall pay sixty solidi.”].

3. Likewise [Note: Absent from manuscript 2.], whoever violates the royal order, having been summoned under the ban, in the army [Note: Manuscripts 4, 5, and 6 read *hostem*, “the army,” rather than *hoste*, “in the army.”].

These eight chapters [Note: The words through “are to be observed” are absent in Welser, Tilius, and Baluze at this point; Tilius and Baluze nevertheless print the sentence at the end of the entire capitulary, contrary to all the manuscripts. The number has already been erased in Codex 3 and is absent from manuscripts 5 and 6.] are to be observed constantly [Note: That is, they are to be observed continually and in every case. In the remaining matters, however, the judgment of the kings—that is, of the king who is in power at the time—is to be sought in each individual case. Baluze refers the words “to the kings” to the sons of Charles, established as heirs to the kingdom in 806; but since Bavaria fell to only one of them, Pippin, king of Italy, it is clear, even according to Baluze’s view, that the plural has been used for the singular.]; the remaining matters, however, have been reserved to the kings, so that they may have the power to assign [Col. 0277C] where they must go forth [Note: Manuscripts 3, 5, and 6 read “from there.”].

[Col. 0278B] 4. Concerning the *denariales* [Note: Manuscript 2 reads *derinales*; manuscripts 3, 5, and 6 *dineriales*; manuscript 4 corrects this to *denerales*.], if anyone kills them, let compensation be paid to the king [Note: The words “if anyone kills them” are absent from manuscripts 3, 5, and 6.].

5. Likewise concerning those who have been released as free by a document in a church beside the altar [Note: The words “beside the altar” are absent from manuscript 1]: let compensation of forty solidi be paid to the king [Note: Absent from manuscript 4.].

6. Those who have been released as free by a document of emancipation, where they have chosen no patronage or protection, shall likewise be paid for to the king with forty solidi [Note: Manuscripts 5 and 6 read “with forty solidi.”].

7. Let no one dare to receive a cleric without the consent of his bishop. If anyone has accepted him, let him not act otherwise once the bishop’s permission has been granted; unless the man is brought into the bishop’s presence to be examined [Note: Manuscript 1 reads *praescrutandum*, “to be searched beforehand.”] as to whether he is worthy [Note: Tilius reads “let him bring him.”].

# BAVARIAN CAPITULARY

*(An. 803, September or November)*

[Col. 0277]

Having departed from the palace of Salz in August, Charles came into Bavaria and remained there for three months, awaiting the return of the army from Pannonia. During this time he appears to have stayed chiefly at Regensburg, the metropolis of the province, although in October he also inspected the remarkable site and surroundings of the city of Salzburg. It seems possible that the chapters concerning the Bavarian regions were composed at that time. Baluze, I do not know for what reason [Col. 0279], assigned them to the year 806.

Our edition is based on the single Codex 1, which I examined in the Imperial Library at Vienna, marked in the catalogue of canon law as no. 128: a ninth-century parchment manuscript in large octavo. A few words have nevertheless been supplied from Benedictus. Baluze’s edition derives either from the same source or from Benedictus’s second book [Note: Baluze entitled it: “And let our envoys make these matters known to everyone before the birth of the Lord.” This is absent from manuscript 1; compare below, under 806, “Chapters given to the envoys.”].

[Col. 0279A] First of all, it must be ordered [that they possess [Note: Absent from manuscript 1.]] that the churches have their rights, both concerning the lives of those who dwell in those churches and concerning their money and property.

2. Let all bishops, with authority according to canonical rule, teach and govern their ministries, both in monasteries of men and of women, among secular priests, and among the rest of God’s people.

3. Let widows, orphans, and persons of lesser power enjoy peace under God’s protection and our *mundeburdium*, and let them obtain their rights [Note: Absent from manuscript 1.].

4. Let bishops stand together with counts, and counts with bishops, so that each may be able to perform his ministry fully [Note: Manuscript 1 reads “gently” or “mildly.”].

5. Let robbers, murderers, adulterers, and incestuous persons be corrected under severe discipline [and correction [Note: Absent from manuscript 1.]] according to the custom [Note: The edition reads *euvam*; the intended word is uncertain.] or law of the Bavarians.

[Col. 0280A] 6. Concerning proprietary matters: let those involved come before our envoys, counts, or judges [Note: Benedictus adds: “let those who have done this come before them,” book II, p. 251], and there receive a final judgment. Henceforth let no one presume to lay claim to another’s property, unless he first seeks his own case before our judges, as we have said, and there receives what is just.

7. If anyone wishes to say that judgment has not been rendered justly in his case, then let him come into our presence. Otherwise, let him not presume to come into our presence in order to delay another person’s justice.

8. At present our envoys are to make no further determinations concerning those rights, except concerning matters from the time of Tassilo or Liutperga, with the exception of those who came to the faith of our grandfather and father or to us [Note: Manuscript 1 reads *illes*, an uncertain form].

9. Let them guard our frontier, according to what we have ordered or established [Note: The edition reads “sanctioned.”], together with our envoys [Col. 0280B].

# CAPITULARY CONCERNING ROBBERS

*(An. circa 804)*

[Col. 0279]

I have copied this constitution, hitherto unpublished, from Royal Parisian Codex 4404, parchment, in folio, ninth century, on whose last page it is found. It was issued before the year 805, as is shown by chapter 21 of the capitulary of that year, where it is evidently being discussed.

[Col. 0279C] A capitulary concerning how our envoys are to deal with robbers.

1. Wherever they find them [Note: *Reperint* is the reading of the Codex], let them investigate them carefully and examine them with discernment [Note: That is, with discretion], so that they neither do anything excessive where it is not appropriate nor omit what they ought to do.

2. If a robber is from among free persons, after he has been found guilty, let him be judged according to ancient custom. If someone is called a robber but has not been apprehended, let the person who wishes to establish this make the proof according to law. And if someone, in anger, calls another a robber, but cannot prove it, let no one believe him [Note: The Codex reads “let him not believe them.”]. If the man who has been publicly accused can swear to this or submit to judgment, whichever seems preferable, and a full investigation of him has been carried out, let him suffer nothing without due process [Col. 0279D] [Col. 0280C]—provided only that he is willing to do what we have stated.

3. If someone wishes to establish his innocence by oath [Note: That is, to clear himself], and there is someone who wishes to contend against him, let the other withdraw his hand from above the altar before his oath-helpers swear, and let them go out into the field with staffs. If the robber is defeated, let him pay compensation for everything of which he has been found guilty, unless it should happen that he is deserving of death. If the other man is defeated—the one who rose against an innocent man—let him know that he has spoken falsely, and let him endure whatever judgment they pronounce.

4. Concerning free men, ecclesiastics, or fiscal dependents: wherever a guilty person is found, let him be judged according to law, but not until [Note: That is, “beforehand”] he has been convicted through the testimony of good free men of good reputation [Col. 0280D].

# ECCLESIASTICAL CHAPTERS

*(An. circa 804)*

[Col. 0279]

I have judged that these two chapters, copied for me and communicated to me by the distinguished Foringer from a Codex of the Royal Library at Munich, formerly belonging to Augsburg, should be assigned to this year, because they renew in them the command of the preceding year concerning the learning of the Lord’s Prayer and the creed. In Ansegisus’s Codex they are inserted in an ancient hand between the index and the text of the third book.

[Col. 0279D] 1. If anyone residing in a bishop’s parish commits an injustice, the bishop shall summon him once, twice, and, if necessary, a third time, through his messenger and by his admonition, canonically to make correction or composition and to do penance, so that he may make satisfaction to God and to the church that he has injured. But if he despises and refuses his admonition and most salutary invitation, let the bishop strike him with the pastoral staff—that is, with the sentence of excommunication—and let him be separated from the communion of the holy church and of all Christians until he has made suitable satisfaction and worthy correction. The same bishop must make this excommunication known [Note: The Codex reads *excommutionem*, “excommunion.”] to that man’s superior [Note: The Codex reads *fecere*, “to make.”] and to all his fellow bishops, so that they do not receive him until he has made worthy satisfaction.

2. Let everyone be compelled to learn the creed, the Lord’s Prayer, and the *signaculum* [Col. 0282A]. If anyone does not now know them, let him either be beaten or fast from every drink except water until he fully masters them. Whoever refuses to consent to these measures shall be sent into our presence. Let women be compelled either by beatings or by fasts [Note: The Codex reads *ieiunis*, “by fasts.”]. Let our envoys [Note: The Codex reads *iussi*, “ordered.”], together with the bishops, take care that this is carried out; and let the counts likewise assist the bishops—if they wish to have our favor—in compelling the people to learn these things.

# CAPITULARY OF AIX (805, spring, Aachen)

[Col. 0281]

Up to the present I have copied this unpublished text from Codex 4995 of the Royal Library at Paris, ninth century, folios 33 and 34, and have assigned it to the year 805, in which Charles the king, the emperor’s namesake, was also sent by his father with an army into Bohemia; moreover, according to the capitulary immediately following, a severe famine occurred [Note: [Col. 0281C] In the year 808, when King Charles undertook his third expedition, no famine is mentioned; in 806 the same king was sent with an army not from the assembly, but only afterward.]. These capitula, therefore, were entrusted to the other envoys and to the nobles who had not been ordered to accompany King Charles, so that they might make them generally known.

[Col. 0281B] Other capitula of the lord emperor.

These are the capitula which we wish the bishops, abbots, and counts who are now returning home to make known at each of their localities and to see observed, both within their dioceses and districts and within the jurisdictions [Note: [Col. 0281] “misteria,” c.] of those living near them who went on campaign together with our namesake.

1. They shall strive to assist those in need with grain, so that they do not perish from the danger of famine.

2. By the middle of August they shall be present with us with the men summoned, unless our order has reached them earlier [Note: [Col. 0281] “has reached them,” c.] because of some necessity.

3. Everyone shall be prepared for God’s service and for our usefulness whenever one of our envoys or letters arrives, so that you may bring them immediately to us [Col. 0281C].

[Col. 0282B] 4. If someone does harm at home to any of those men who are able to go out on campaign and who appear to be with our beloved son Charles—whether to his wife, his house, or in any other matter—the envoys shall seize the wrongdoers and place them in the stocks and in prison, keeping them safe under guard until those against whom the wrong was committed have returned home [Note: [Col. 0281] “have returned,” c.]. [Note: [Col. 0281] “against whom” is absent in c.]

5. They shall take the best possible precautions concerning thieves and wrongdoers, together with the envoys of those who are on campaign.

6. In the cities and monasteries of men and women they shall have it proclaimed that everyone should strive to live piously and chastely in God’s service, and shall arrange that the poor and dependents of those institutions be fed according to their ability.

# DOUBLE CAPITULARY PROMULGATED AT THEODONIS VILLA (805, December)

[Col. 0281]

A very important edict promulgated at the assembly at Theodonis villa, where the emperor stayed during November and December of 805 and the following January and February, was first published by Amerbach from the Tegernsee Codex and afterward by Sirmond and Baluze. Neither of them, however, had the extensive aids available to us: besides the codices containing the Lombard capitularies—the Saint Paul, Chisian, Cava, Ambrosian, Florentine, London, Vienna, and Verona codices—and the editions of Muratori and Baluze:

1. Codex of the Royal Library at Paris, no. 4629, ninth century.  
1 b. Codex of the Ducal Library at Wolfenbüttel, the Gudianus, ninth century.  
2. Codex of the Royal Library at Paris, among the *Supplementa Latina*, no. 303, designated by a sign, ninth century.  
2 b. Codex of the same library, no. 4628 A, apparently copied from the preceding one, tenth century.  
3. Codex of the Ducal Library at Wolfenbüttel, the Augustaeus, ninth century.  
4. Codex of the Royal Library at Paris, no. 4995, ninth century.  
4 b. Codex of the Royal Library at Munich, formerly Tegernsee, tenth century.  
5. Codex of the Ducal Library at Wolfenbüttel, the Blankenburgensis, tenth century.  
6. Codex of the Ducal Library at Gotha, eleventh century.  
7. Codex of the Royal Library at Paris, among the *Supplementa Latina*, no. 75, a distinguished manuscript, tenth century; the codices of Saint Vincent at Metz, the Vatican, and Navarre, used by Sirmond and Baluze, agree with it. Baluze also used the Corbie Codex and the Paris Codex—our no. 2.

At the end we append an excerpt from this double capitulary: first, one given to Jesse, bishop of Amiens and royal envoy, first published by Baluze from Paris Codex 4626, tenth century, and now again corrected on the authority of that same codex; second, another given to a different envoy, not previously published, from Paris Codex 4628, parchment, ninth or tenth century. What Baluze presents as a second edition of the second part is nothing other than the reading of Codex 7 and the Metz manuscript.

[Col. 0283] GIVEN AT THEODONIS VILLA IN THE FIFTH YEAR OF THE EMPIRE, BEFORE THE NATIVITY OF THE LORD [Note: [Col. 0283] This heading occurs in Codices 7 and Saint Vincent of Metz. Codex 4 has: “Here begins the third capitulary”; Codex 5: “The lord’s capitulary given in the year of the Lord 806 at Theodonis villa, in the sixth year of Charles’s empire.” Heading II: “Also, Charles’s provisions concerning ecclesiastical matters.”]

## CAPITULA CONCERNING THE CHURCH [Note: [Col. 0283] Thus Codices 1, 2, 2 b, 3, 4, 4 b, 5, 6, and 7; in some, the first word is absent.]

[Col. 0283A]

1. Concerning readings.

2. Concerning singing [Note: [Col. 0283] c: “so that it may be learned, and so that the singers may return from Metz,” 7.].

3. Concerning scribes [Note: [Col. 0283] “so that they do not write incorrectly,” 2, 2 b, 3, 7; “so that they do not write wrongly,” 4 b.].

4. Concerning notaries.

5. Concerning various disciplines [Note: [Col. 0283] “concerning the other disciplines to be learned,” 7; “concerning the remaining disciplines,” 4 b.].

[Col. 0283B] 6. Concerning computation.

7. [Note: [Col. 0283D] In the Codex used by Amerbach it simply read “concerning medicine.” The same form is found in an old Parisian exemplar. Baluze.] Concerning the medical art.

8. Concerning churches that remain without honor, without services and lights; concerning those who collect tithes [Note: [Col. 0283] “consume them,” 4 b; “take them,” 2; “assume them,” 2 b.] but do not care for the churches; and concerning altars, so that they are not excessive in the churches.

[Col. 0283A] Baluze has the following text:

1. That the readings be read distinctly in church.

2. That singing be learned and be performed according to the order and custom of the Roman Church; and that [Note: [Col. 0283D] See the *Life of Charlemagne* by an uncertain author, chapter 8, and the monk of Saint Gall, book I, chapter 11. Alcuin’s Life, speaking of the priest Sigulf, says that he was sent to the city of Metz on account of singing. Baluze.] the singers return from Metz.

3. Concerning scribes, that they do not write incorrectly. Every bishop, abbot, and each of the counts shall have his own notary.

4. Concerning the other disciplines of the Church, that they be conducted according to the canons or the rule.

[Col. 0283B] 5. Concerning computation, so that everyone may learn it accurately. Concerning the medical art, so that children may be sent to learn it.

6. Concerning churches that remain without honor, without services and lights, and concerning those who indeed collect tithes but do not care for the churches, so that this may be completely corrected. And concerning altars, so that they are not excessive in the churches.

7. Concerning those newly coming to a monastery, so that they first learn the rule before they are sent outside [Col. 0283C] for duties, and so that they do not go to secular courts.

8. [Note: [Col. 0283] Baluze copied this chapter from the Corbie Codex and from Benedict II, 260.] Concerning those who leave the world in order to impede the lord’s service, and then do neither thing: they must choose one of the two, either to live fully according to the canonical or the regular constitution, or to perform the lord’s service.

[Col. 0284A] 9. Concerning laymen newly converted, that before they learn their law fully by living according to it, they not be sent to other [Note: [Col. 0283] “other,” 1.] affairs.

10. Concerning those who abandon the world: they shall choose one of the two, either to live fully according to the canonical or according to the regular institution.

11. Concerning personal male and female servants, that they not be beaten or veiled beyond measure, and that provision be made where sufficient [Note: [Col. 0283] “and there,” 4 b.], and that the estates not be left desolate.

12. Concerning excessive congregations, that they in no way be formed, but that as many be gathered as the available resources [Note: [Col. 0283] “assistance,” 5.] can support.

13. [Note: [Col. 0283] Between the Lombard capitularies of Charlemagne, chapter 141. Muratori.] Concerning those who are not struck according to the rule, that henceforth they be corrected [Note: [Col. 0283] “so that they not be…” 4.] and struck according to the rule [Note: [Col. 0283] The remainder of the chapter is omitted by Codices 2, 2 b, 3, and 5.].

[Col. 0284B] 14. That girls of tender age not be veiled before they know how to choose what they wish [Note: [Col. 0283] “what they wish, and that they be struck according to the same judgment and authority,” in Sirmond’s and other editions.], without prejudice to canonical authority [Note: [Col. 0283] “authority,” that is, before the age of twenty-five, except in fear of death or abduction; Codices V, Vn, and E. The later hand in V adds: “unless with the consent of the parents”; E also has this.].

15. That laymen [Note: [Col. 0283] “nor clerics” is added above the line, 1.] not be placed over monks within monasteries, nor be lay archdeacons.

16. Concerning incestuous persons, that they be examined according to the canons, and that because of anyone’s friendship some not be released while others are subjected to constraint.

## MATTERS COMMON TO THE CHURCH AND THE PEOPLE [Note: [Col. 0283] Thus 1 and 4; “generally for all,” 2, 2 b, 3, 7; “also Charles’s provisions generally for all,” 5; “also the capitulary,” 6.]

1. Concerning peace: all who are rebellious against it through any crimes shall be constrained.

2. Concerning the rights of the churches of God, widows, orphans, and wards [Note: [Col. 0283] Codex 7, after making a division here, numbers two chapters.], that those who cry out not be disregarded in public courts [Note: [Col. 0283] “those hearing,” 1, 1 b, 4.], but be carefully heard.

[Col. 0284C] 3. Concerning royal rights [Note: [Col. 0283] Thus 2, 3, 4 b, 5, and 6, and Ansegisus, book I of the lord emperor, chapter 4; compare below chapters 10 and 15.], that they be fully investigated.

4. If famine, devastation, pestilence, unseasonable weather, or any other tribulation should occur, our edict is not to be awaited; rather, God’s mercy is to be entreated immediately. [Note: [Col. 0283] Here Codex 7 begins another chapter.] And in the present year, concerning the scarcity caused by famine, each person shall help his own people as he can and shall not sell his grain too dearly. Nor shall any food be sold outside our empire [Note: [Col. 0283] absent in 1 and 4.].

5. Concerning the carrying of weapons within the homeland, namely [Col. 0285A] shields, lances, and coats of mail. If there is a feud, it shall then be investigated which of the two is at fault, so that they may be at peace; they shall be compelled to make peace, even if they do not wish it. If they are unwilling to make peace in any other way, they shall be brought before us. If anyone kills another after reconciliation, he shall pay compensation for him [Note: [Col. 0285] “if he did it in self-defense; but if otherwise, he shall lose all his property,” Vn and E.], and shall lose the hand by which he swore falsely [Note: [Col. 0285] “the hand by which he swore, without any redemption,” in some manuscripts and Benedict, I, 247; II, 271.], and shall moreover pay the lord’s fine. [And serfs shall not carry lances; if anyone is found doing so after the ban, his spear shall be broken over his back [Note: [Col. 0285] Thus 5 and Benedict, cited above.].]

6. (Above, column 265.) Concerning armor in the army: as we already prescribed in another capitulary, so it shall be observed. Moreover, every man holding twelve manses shall have a coat of mail. Whoever has a coat of mail but does not bring it with him shall lose the entire benefice together with the coat of mail.

[Col. 0285B] 7. Concerning merchants who travel into the lands of the Slavs and Avars, how far they are to proceed with their merchandise, namely through Saxony as far as Bardowick [Note: [Col. 0285] Manuscript forms: *bardaenouuio*, *bardenuui*, *bardanuuih*, *bardenuuih*, *bardouuich*, *bardenuuich*, *partemnuuih*.] [Note: [Col. 0285C] Bardowick.], where Hredi shall take charge [Note: [Col. 0285] Manuscript forms: *redi*, *beredi*, *arethi*, *heretus*.]; and to Schelza [Note: [Col. 0285] Manuscript forms: *sedzela*, *schzela*, *hereditaskaesla*, *hredi et ad sclesla*, *skaesla*, *kesla*, *skerba*, *schesla*, *skesba*.] [Note: [Col. 0285C] Schesel in the duchy of Lüneburg.], where Madalgaud shall take charge; and to Magdeburg, where Aito shall take charge [Note: [Col. 0285] Manuscript forms: *haito*, *hatto*, *atto*.]; and to Erfurt [Note: [Col. 0285] Manuscript forms: *herpesfur*, *erpisfurt*, *herbisfurt*, *erpesford*, *alpesfrud*, *hernesfurt*, *ferpfesfur*.] [Note: [Col. 0285C] Erfurt.], where Madalgaud shall take charge; and to Hallstadt [Note: [Col. 0285] Manuscript forms: *alaraestat*, *aletat*, *halazstad*, *alazstad*, *halastat*, *chalazstat*, *alugestat*, *aluesstat*.], [Note: [Col. 0286C] Near Bamberg.] where Madalgaud likewise shall take charge [Note: [Col. 0285] The words “and to Hallstadt … Madalgaud” are absent from the printed editions.]. At Forchheim [Note: [Col. 0285] Manuscript forms: *foraabeam*, *forachim*, *furcham*, *forachmirin*, *foramheim*.], at Breemberga [Note: [Col. 0285] Manuscript forms: *breberg*, *breembercg*, *berebemberg*.], and at Regensburg, Audulf shall take charge [Note: [Col. 0285] *aotolfus* in 5.]; and at Lauriacum [Note: [Col. 0285] Manuscript forms: *lauriago*, *lauoriacum*.] [Note: [Col. 0286C] Lorch near Enns.], Warnarius shall take charge [Note: [Col. 0285] *werinheri* in 4 b.].

They shall not transport weapons or coats of mail for sale. If they are found carrying them, all their property shall be taken from them: one half shall go to the palace, and the other half shall be divided between the envoy and the discoverer [Note: [Col. 0285] “between the count and the discoverer, and between the aforesaid envoy,” 7.].

[Col. 0285C] 8. Concerning claimants or litigants who wish neither to acquiesce in the judgment of the scabini nor to blaspheme, the ancient custom shall be observed: they shall be confined in custody until they do one of the two things. If afterward they appeal to the palace on this matter and bring letters, they are not to be believed, but they are nevertheless not to be put in prison; rather, they and the letters are to be sent together under guard to our palace, so that the matter may be examined there as is proper [Note: [Col. 0285] “If he carries a written decision from the court, he shall not be sent to prison, but shall be sent under guard with that decision to the court,” 7.].

9. Concerning the oath: no one shall promise fidelity by oath [Col. 0286A] to anyone else except to us and to each person’s own lord, for our benefit and that of his lord; except for those oaths which, according to law, are justly owed by one person to another [Note: [Col. 0285] The rest of the chapter is absent from 1, 1 b, 4, 4 b, and 6. Codex 4 nevertheless adds at the end of the capitulary: “Concerning those who were then children, so that those who did not swear may now swear fidelity to the lord emperor and their children.” See below, column 290, excerpt from Codex 4628, chapter 6.]. Children who previously could not swear because of their youth shall now faithfully renew their promise [Note: [Col. 0285] The word “fidelity” has been supplied from the Saint Paul Codex.].

10. Concerning conspiracies: whoever presumes to form one, and confirms any conspiracy by oath, shall be judged in three ways. First, wherever some evil has been perpetrated through it, the authors of the deed shall be killed; their helpers shall each be flogged by the others and shall cut off one another’s noses. Where no evil has been perpetrated, they shall likewise be flogged among themselves and shall cut one another’s hair. If a conspiracy has been confirmed by [Col. 0286B] handshakes, then, if they are free, they must either swear with suitable oath-takers that they did not do this with evil intent, or, if they cannot do so, pay the composition prescribed by their law; if they are serfs, they shall be flogged. Henceforth no such conspiracy shall occur in our kingdom [Note: [Col. 0285] “empire,” 1; “realm,” 2 and 3; “kingdom,” 2 b, 4, 4 b, 5, 6, and the Saint Paul Codex, and Benedict I, 251; II, 276. See above, chapter 3, and below, chapter 15.], either by oath or without oath.

11. Concerning perjury: it must be guarded against, and witnesses must not be admitted to an oath before they have been examined. If they cannot otherwise be examined, they shall be separated from one another and questioned individually. It shall not be permitted for the accuser alone to choose witnesses in the absence of his opposing litigant [Note: [Col. 0285] “prosecutor,” 1, 1 b, 2 b; V and M.]. Absolutely no one shall be admitted to an oath or testimony unless fasting. If someone brought forward as a witness is rejected, the person rejecting him must state and [Col. 0286C] prove why he does not wish to admit him. Witnesses shall be chosen from that same district, not another, unless perhaps the case must be investigated farther outside the county. If anyone is convicted of perjury, he shall lose his hand [Note: [Col. 0285] “Let him lose his hand if he did it knowingly, or redeem it—that is, pay the *wergild*—if he did it unknowingly,” V, V, Vn, and E.], or redeem it.

12. Concerning advocates: bad advocates, vice-lords, vicars, and centenarii are to be removed, and such men appointed as both know and wish to discern and settle cases justly [Note: [Col. 0285] “who know well,” Codex C and the Saint Paul Codex.]. If a bad count is discovered, it must be reported to us.

[Note: [Col. 0287] [This note appears at the foot of column 287, but the callout number (5) is not printed in the text.] p. If they are married, as husband and wife, this must not be done without the bishop’s consent, V, Vn, E.]

[Col. 0287A] 13. Concerning tolls: it pleases us that ancient and just tolls be collected from merchants, both at bridges and on boats or at markets. New or unjust tolls, however—where ropes are stretched, or where one passes under bridges by boat, or in similar situations in which no assistance is provided to travelers—must not be collected. Likewise, nothing shall be collected from those who, without trading, transport their property from one of their houses to another, or to the palace, or to the army. If there is anything about which doubt arises [Note: [Col. 0287] This is omitted in Ansegisus.], it shall be asked about at the next assembly that we shall hold with those envoys.

14. Concerning fugitive clerics, laymen, or women, what we already prescribed in another capitulary (above, column 237, chapter 2) shall be observed.

[Col. 0287B] 15. Concerning free men [Note: [Col. 0287] “of various kinds,” Codex and Saint Paul Codex.] [Note: [Col. 0287] “unmarried men,” V, Vn, E.] who wish to dedicate themselves to God’s service: they shall not do so before first requesting permission from us [Note: [Col. 0287] Absent in 1, 1 b, and 4.]. This is because we have heard that some of them do so not so much from devotion as by fleeing military service or another royal duty; and we have also heard that others are deceived through greed by those who covet their property. We therefore prohibit this from being done.

16. Concerning the oppression of poor free men: they must not be oppressed by the powerful through any evil scheme contrary to justice, so that they are forced to sell or surrender their property. For this reason we have spoken above and here about free men, lest perhaps parents be disinherited contrary to justice, royal service be diminished [Col. 0287C], and the heirs themselves, through poverty, become beggars, thieves, or wrongdoers. They are not to be summoned repeatedly to assemblies [Note: [Col. 0287] “to assemblies” is absent in 1, 1 b, and 4.]; what we prescribed in another capitulary (above, column 245, chapter 14; 246, chapter 21; 261, chapter 20) shall be observed.

17. Concerning churches or saints newly discovered without authority: they are not to be venerated unless approved by the bishop [Note: [Col. 0287] “approved,” 1.]; canonical authority concerning this and all churches is also to be preserved.

18. [Note: [Col. 0287] The chapter is absent in 1 b.] Concerning false coins: since they are being produced in many places contrary to justice and to the edict, we wish there to be no mint anywhere except in our palace, unless we should again order otherwise. Those denarii that have now been minted, however, are to be accepted if they are of full weight and pure.

[Col. 0287D] 19. Concerning the *heribannum* [Note: [Col. 0287] Manuscript forms: *agrebannum*, *haribannum*, *aribannum*, *herebannum*, *arinannum*.], we wish our envoys this year [Note: [Col. 0287] Absent in the Saint Paul Codex, Ansegisus III, 14, and Benedict I, 258; II, 285.] to collect it faithfully, without favor, flattery, or fear of any person, according to our order. That is, from a man possessing six pounds in gold, silver, coats of mail, bronze, whole garments [Col. 0288A] [Note: [Col. 0287] Absent from Codices A, V, Vn, and E; Muratori.], horses, oxen, cows, or other livestock, his wife and children must not be stripped of their clothing on this account; he shall pay the lawful *heribannum*, namely three pounds. Whoever possesses no more than property worth three pounds in the value stated above shall be charged thirty solidi, that is, one and a half pounds [Note: [Col. 0287] “that is, one and a half pounds” occurs in 1, 1 b, 4, 4 b, and the Saint Paul Codex; it is absent from the others.]. Whoever has only two pounds shall pay ten solidi. If he has one pound, five solidi, so that he may again be able to prepare himself for God’s service and our usefulness. Our envoys shall take care and investigate diligently lest, through any evil scheme, they withhold our due by transferring or entrusting it to another.

20. Whatever royal census lawfully arose from any source, we wish it to be paid from there, whether from the person of the man himself [Col. 0288B] or from his property.

21. Concerning thieves, what we already prescribed in another capitulary shall remain in force [Note: [Col. 0287D] See the capitulary concerning thieves, above, column 279.].

22. Concerning free men who take royal fiscal wives, and free women who likewise take royal fiscal men: they must not be excluded from inheritance, from seeking their property, or from testimony on this account; rather, in this matter the same honor shall be preserved for them that is known to have been preserved for our predecessors, kings and emperors [Note: [Col. 0287] “is known to have been preserved. Thanks be to God,” 4 b. There follow there chapters 13, 14, and 15 of the Synod of Rispach; the same chapters are appended in the Gotha manuscript—and perhaps also in the Modena manuscript, where chapter 25 is found (see Muratori, chapter 165)—as a continuation of the capitulary, with the numbers XXIII, XXIV, and XXV prefixed.].

Codex 5 continues as follows:

23. We wish, and have ordered our envoys to command, that true canonical books be kept in the churches [Col. 0288C], as we have often commanded in another capitulary (above, column 237, chapter 7).

24. Let laymen fully learn the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer. Counts, centenarii, and other noble men also shall fully learn their law, as has been decreed elsewhere (above, column 262, chapter 4; 249, chapter 11). We command our envoys that the things which for many years we have ordered throughout our entire kingdom through our capitularies to be done, learned, observed, or kept as custom—all these things they must now investigate carefully and strive to renew completely, for God’s service, for our benefit, and for the advancement of all Christian people; and, as far as they are able with the Lord’s gift, they must bring them to completion. They must report to us fully which persons have undertaken this good contest and fulfilled it, so that they may be pleasing to God and to us. Whoever has been negligent in this matter shall receive such discipline as one who despises it deserves to receive, so that the others may be afraid to do so again.

[Col. 0289A] Excerpt from the capitulary of the lord emperor Charles, which Jesse [Note: [Col. 0289D] Bishop of Amiens, frequently mentioned throughout the records of that period. Jean Cordesius, canon of Limoges, published his letter to the priests of the diocese of Amiens; some think that he wrote it when he was serving as an envoy to the empress Irene at Constantinople, that is, in 802. I, however, think it was given in 811, since it clearly contains a response to questions that the emperor Charlemagne then put to all the bishops of his kingdom. He was finally deposed from the bishopric in 831. I.D.] the bishop carried with him, by order of that august ruler, so that it might be made known to everyone.

[Note: [Col. 0289D] This is how they then said “excerpt.” An old glossary in Codex 1197 of the Royal Library gives *excerpta*, *excarpsa*. An old codex of the Church of Lyons, written in Saxon letters, has: “Excerpted from the book of Saint Jerome the priest, in his exposition of the prophet Isaiah.” Likewise there: “Excerpted from the book of Blessed Pope Gregory, on the prophet Ezekiel.” An old manuscript martyrology has: “Here ends the excerpt.” At the beginning of the Theodosian Code, the following is found in an old manuscript codex of the most distinguished man Hieronymus Bignon: “Under the reign of Alaric, king of the Goths, a judgment was given concerning the five books of laws that had been shut away in the king’s treasury; an excerpt was written from all the books into one volume.” Lambecius, book II of his *Commentary on the Vienna Library*, page 854, mentions an old manuscript chronicle of the imperial library bearing this title: “Excerpt from the chronicle of Gregory, bishop of Tours.” The same title, but corrected, occurs in the Codex of Alexander Petavius, senator of Paris, as Andreas Duchesne attests, volume I, page 722: “Excerpt from the chronicle of Gregory, bishop of Tours.” See Mabillon, volume IV of the *Analecta*, page 569. Baluze.]

Chapter 1. Concerning laymen newly converted: before they learn their law fully by living according to it, they are not to be sent to other affairs.

2. Laymen are not to be placed over monks in a monastery, nor are archdeacons to be laymen.

3. Concerning the rights of the churches of God, widows, orphans, and wards: in public courts they are not to be disregarded when heard, but must be carefully heard.

4. Concerning the rights of the lord emperor: they are to be fully investigated.

5. If famine, devastation, pestilence, unseasonable weather, or any other kind of tribulation occurs, our edict is not to be awaited; rather, God’s mercy is to be entreated immediately. And in the present year, concerning the scarcity caused by famine, each person shall help his own people as he can and shall not sell his grain too dearly. Nor shall any food be sold outside the empire.

6. Concerning weapons not to be carried within the homeland, namely shields, lances, and coats of mail. If there is a feud, it shall be investigated which of the two is at fault, so that they may be at peace; they shall be compelled to make peace, even if they do not wish it. If they are unwilling to make peace in any other way, they shall be brought before us. If anyone kills another after reconciliation, he shall pay compensation for him, lose the hand by which he swore falsely, and moreover pay the lord’s fine.

7. Concerning armor in the army: as we already prescribed in another capitulary, so it shall be observed. Moreover, every man holding twelve manses shall have a coat of mail. Whoever has a coat of mail but does not bring it with him shall lose the entire benefice together with the coat of mail.

8. Concerning claimants or litigants who wish to acquiesce in the judgment of the scabini and to blaspheme [reading as transmitted; the syntax is corrupt], the ancient custom shall be observed [Col. 0289C]: they shall be confined in custody until they do one of the two things. If afterward they appeal to the palace on this matter and bring letters, they are never to be believed, but they are nevertheless not to be put in prison; rather, they and the letters are to be sent together under guard to our palace, so that the matter may be examined there as is proper.

9. Concerning the oath: fidelity by oath shall be granted to no one else except to us and to each person’s own lord, for our benefit and that of his lord, except for those oaths which, according to law, are justly owed by one person to another.

10. Concerning conspiracies: whoever presumes to form one and confirms any conspiracy by oath shall be judged in three ways. First, wherever any evil has been perpetrated, the authors of the deed shall be killed. Their hearers shall each be flogged by the others and shall cut off one another’s noses [Col. 0291A]. Where no evil has been perpetrated, they shall likewise be flogged among themselves and shall cut one another’s hair. If a conspiracy has been confirmed by handshakes, then, if they are free, they must either swear with suitable oath-takers that they did not do this with evil intent or, if they cannot do so, pay the composition prescribed by their law. If they are serfs, they shall be flogged. Henceforth no such conspiracy shall occur in our empire, either by oath or without oath.

11. Concerning perjury: it must be guarded against, and witnesses must not be admitted to an oath before they have been examined. If they cannot otherwise be examined, they shall be separated from one another and questioned individually. It shall not be permitted for the accuser alone to choose witnesses in the absence of his opposing litigant. Absolutely no one shall be admitted to an oath or testimony unless fasting. If someone brought forward as a witness is rejected, the person rejecting him must state and prove why he does not wish to admit him. Witnesses shall be chosen from that same district, not another, unless perhaps the case must be investigated farther outside the county. If anyone is convicted [Col. 0291B] of perjury, he shall lose his hand or redeem it.

12. Concerning advocates: bad advocates, vice-lords, vicars, and centenarii are to be removed, and such men appointed as know and wish to discern and settle cases justly. If a bad count is discovered, it must be reported to us.

13. Concerning the oppression of all poor free men: they must not be oppressed by the powerful through any evil scheme contrary to justice, so that, being forced, they sell or surrender their property. For this reason we have spoken above and here about free men, lest perhaps parents act contrary to justice and be disinherited, royal service be diminished [Col. 0291C], and the heirs themselves, through poverty, become liars, thieves, or wrongdoers. They are not to be summoned repeatedly, except as we prescribed in another capitulary; that provision shall remain in force.

14. Whatever royal census lawfully arose from any source, we wish it to be paid from there, whether from the person of the man himself or from his property.

15. Concerning thieves, what we already prescribed in another capitulary shall remain in force.

16. Concerning free men who take royal fiscal wives, and free women who take royal fiscal men: they must not be excluded from inheritance, from seeking their property, or from testimony on this account; rather, in this matter the same honor shall be preserved for them that we know was preserved for our predecessors, kings and emperors.

[Col. 0290A] Excerpt from a capitulary given to a certain royal envoy.

Chapter 1. Concerning royal rights: they are to be fully investigated.

2. If famine, devastation, unseasonable weather, or any other kind of tribulation occurs, our edict is not to be awaited; rather, God’s mercy is to be entreated immediately. And in the present year, concerning the scarcity caused by famine, each person shall help as he can and shall not sell his grain too dearly [Col. 0290B]. Nor shall food be sold outside our empire.

3. Weapons must not be carried within the homeland, namely shields, lances, and coats of mail. If there is a feud, it shall be investigated which of the two is at fault, so that they may be at peace; they shall be compelled to make peace even if they do not wish it. If they are unwilling to make peace in any other way, they shall be brought before us. If anyone kills another after reconciliation, he shall pay compensation for him, lose the hand by which he swore falsely, and moreover pay the lord’s fine.

4. Concerning armor in the army: as we prescribed earlier in another capitulary, so it shall be observed. Moreover, every man holding twelve manses shall have a coat of mail. Whoever has a coat of mail but does not bring it with him shall lose all the benefice [L.; reading uncertain] together with the coat of mail.

5. Concerning claimants or litigants who wish neither to acquiesce in the judgment of the scabini nor to blaspheme, the ancient custom shall be observed [Col. 0290C]: they shall be confined in custody until they do one of the two things. If afterward they appeal to the palace on this matter and bring letters, they are not to be believed; nevertheless, they are not to be put in prison, but are to be sent together with the letters under guard to our palace, so that the matter may be examined there as is proper.

6. Concerning the oath: no one shall promise fidelity by oath to anyone else except to us and to each person’s own lord, for our benefit and that of his lord, except for those oaths which, according to law, are justly owed by one person to another; and children who previously could not swear because of their youth shall now faithfully renew their promise.

[Col. 0292A] 7. [Note: [Col. 0291] Chapters 7, 8, and 9 are printed according to the order of the Codex’s writing.] Concerning perjury: it must be guarded against, and witnesses must not be admitted to an oath before they have been examined. If they cannot otherwise be examined, they shall be separated from one another and questioned individually. It shall not be permitted for the accuser alone to choose witnesses in the absence of his opposing litigant. Absolutely no one shall be admitted to an oath or testimony unless fasting. If someone brought forward as a witness is rejected, the person rejecting him must state and prove why he does not wish to admit him. Witnesses shall be chosen from that same district, not another, unless perhaps the case must be investigated farther outside the county. If anyone is convicted [Col. 0292B] of perjury, he shall lose his hand or redeem it.

8. Concerning free men who wish to dedicate themselves to God’s service: they shall not do so before first requesting permission from us. This is because we have heard that some of them do so not so much from devotion as by fleeing military service or another royal duty; and we have also heard that others are deceived through greed by those who covet their property. We therefore prohibit this from being done.

[Col. 0292C] 9. Concerning free men who take royal fiscal wives, and free women who take royal fiscal men: they must not be excluded from inheritance, from seeking their property, or from testimony on this account; rather, in this matter the same honor shall be preserved for them that we know was preserved for our predecessors, kings and emperors.

# CAPITULA OF THE LORD’S ENVOYS (806)

[Col. 0291]

The most learned men, Martene and Durand, first published this capitulary promulgated by the envoys of Charlemagne in volume VII of the *Veterum Scriptorum et Monumentorum*, p. 12, from a tenth-century manuscript of the monastery of Andain. It ought to be assigned by the years of the emperor’s reign; and since, in the preceding capitulary of Thionville, at the previously unpublished chapter 24 given here, the envoys are instructed to investigate diligently and endeavor to renew whatever the emperor had ordered throughout his kingdom for many years through his capitularies—namely, what was to be done, learned, observed, or held as customary—the mission of Adalhard, abbot of Corbie, Fulrad, abbot of Saint-Quentin, Unroc, and Hrocculf—the latter two of whom occur in Charlemagne’s *Breviary*—appears to belong to the first months of the year 806.

Hadalhard, Fulrad, Unroc, and Hrocculf [Note: [Col. 0291] I have corrected it thus; Martene’s edition has *SENHROCCULFUS*], envoys of our lord the emperor, to that count beloved by us in the Lord: greetings in the Lord.

It is not unknown to your goodness how our lord the emperor had entrusted us—namely, Rado, Fulrad, and Unroc—with his mission in these regions, so that, insofar as we were able, we should strive in this mission to carry out the will both of God and of the emperor himself. But because Rado is now partly ill and cannot on this occasion undertake the mission as necessity requires, it pleased our lord the emperor to add Adalhard and Hrocculf to the aforesaid mission, so that all of us together, insofar as reason permits or necessity dictates, may strive and labor, as has been said, to accomplish the will of God and of the emperor.

We therefore, having been appointed to this mission [Note: [Col. 0293] thus I have corrected it; manuscript reading M.], have sent you this letter so that, on behalf of our lord the emperor, we might command you, and on our own behalf exhort you, to strive with all your strength in every matter pertaining to your office—both in matters relating to the worship of God and in those relating to the service of our lord [Note: [Col. 0293] *domni* … *domno* M.] or to the salvation and protection of the Christian people.

For we and all the other envoys have received a very definite command from our lord to report truthfully to him by the middle of April what, in his kingdom, has been done of those things which he himself ordered in these years to be done through his envoys, and what has been left undone, so that he may render fitting thanks to those who have acted and, according to his pleasure, impose deserved reprimands on those who have not acted. And what more can we say to you about this? He wants nothing else except that we report to him that everything has been fulfilled as he ordered, and what has thereby been left undone, and through whose negligence it has been left undone.

Now we admonish you to reread your capitularies, to recall whatever has been entrusted to you orally, and to strive thereafter in such a contest that you may receive a reward from God and a fitting recompense from that great lord of ours.

1. First, therefore, among other matters we command and admonish that you yourselves, as well as all your subordinates and district inhabitants, obey your bishop in every respect, insofar as this pertains to his office, whether he is present or gives orders through his envoy, and that you show no negligence in this matter. Next, concerning the justice of our lord the emperor, according to what has been told you either in writing or orally, strive in such a way as you recognize that you are thereby bound to do.

2. Next, carry out fully, irreproachably, justly, and rightly the justice owed to churches, widows, orphans, and all others, without any evil stratagem, unjust payment, delay, or unnecessary postponement [Note: [Col. 0293] *ora* M.], whether the matter concerns you yourselves, your subordinates, or any other person, so that you may receive from God a reward and from our lord a good recompense.

3. Next, if anyone is rebellious or disobedient to you and unwilling to heed you according to justice, make a written record of them, however many they may be; and, if necessary, send word beforehand, or tell us ourselves when we are together, so that we may deal with the matter according to what our lord has entrusted to us.

4. Next, take the greatest care that, if you have doubts about anything in the whole of that command—whether concerning God or worldly affairs—which has been entrusted to you by our lord either in writing or orally [Note: [Col. 0293] perhaps *esse*?], you promptly send an intelligent envoy to us, so that you may understand everything properly and, with the Lord’s help, carry it out properly.

5. Next, take great care that neither you yourselves nor anyone else, insofar as you can foresee it, is found guilty of this evil stratagem in your office: “Be quiet, be quiet until those envoys have passed, and afterward let us do justice to one another!”—with the result that, on this pretext, the justice itself either remains undone or is certainly delayed. Rather, strive to have it done before we come to you.

6. For if any such evil stratagem is practiced among you, or if the justice which you can carry out without us is postponed through negligence or malice until we arrive, know with absolute certainty that we shall demand a great accounting from you.

7. Next, read this letter frequently and preserve it carefully, so that it may itself serve as testimony between us and you as to whether you have acted as it is written here or have not done so.

## Capitularies of the Priests

These first appeared from the tenth-century manuscript of Andain in Martene and Durand’s *Amplissima Collectio*, volume VII, after the capitularies of Adalhard and the other envoys.

## Capitularies

1. As the holy Synod of Nicaea forbids, no priest shall ever permit a strange woman to live with him in his house, except his mother, sister, paternal aunt, or maternal aunt; nor shall any priest permit any woman to enter the private chamber or storeroom. If he does so thereafter, let him know that he will be deposed from the dignity of the episcopate [Note: [Col. 0293] perhaps “priesthood”]; for we have frequently forbidden this according to canonical institution, and it has not been fully observed by priests. Therefore we command that anyone who wishes to retain his rank of honor must abstain in every way from intimacy with strange women, so that no opportunity may be given to the enemy to suggest sin and none of them may incur an evil reputation among the people.

2. No priest, having abandoned his own church, shall presume to go to the house of any woman, whether dedicated to God or secular, to sow blood [Note: [Col. 0295] The passage is corrupt; perhaps: “having abandoned his church, he shall not presume to establish himself as a kinsman,” etc.]. Rather, let each priest carry out his duties in the house of his own church, so that he may always be found there, at his own church, by anyone seeking any of his ministries.

3. As we formerly forbade and the holy canons prohibit, no priest shall dare to carry weapons.

4. No priest shall dare to enter taverns for drinking, nor involve himself in such a gathering with secular men where he may hear or speak shameful words, or hear or participate in any disputes there, as often tends to happen.

5. No priest shall cause any payment to be exacted for the purpose of baptizing or administering communion, whether small or great, because we have received freely and must give freely; for they must not sell the gift and grace of God, which is given freely. If anyone does so and it comes to our attention, let him know that thereafter his position in his order will be endangered.

6. When priests are invited to a banquet by any of the faithful, they shall not engage in disputes among themselves about anything, but shall use only words of charity and sobriety, pleasing to God and expressing proper restraint, as is fitting for priests [Note: [Col. 0295] thus I have corrected it; *ut det* M.].

7. No priest shall seek his own basilica, and no priest shall dare to accept another church within the parish for celebrating Mass, except the one in which he was ordained, without the license and permission of the bishop.

8. Each priest shall be ready at every hour, by day or by night, to perform his office, so that, if by chance a sick person comes to be baptized, he may fully perform his duty [Note: [Col. 0295] absent in M.]. He shall guard against drunkenness, lest because of drunkenness he be unable to fulfill his office or stumble while performing it.

9. Let each priest, according to his means, strive to provide ornaments for his church—namely, a paten and chalice, a chasuble and alb, a missal, lectionary, martyrology, penitential, psalter, and as many other books as he can, as well as a cross and a chest—just as we have said, according to his means.

10. A priest shall order those who have confessed to homicide to abstain from the church and communion for forty days before they are reconciled by the bishop, or before the bishop orders them to be reconciled by priests.

11. Every priest shall exercise care and concern that he does not allow anyone who, lying in sickness and approaching his end, can be reached by him to depart from this world without viaticum. If he is negligent in this matter, he shall be subject to danger to his honor.

12. Each priest shall give some admonition and exhortation to the people at his church, so that each person may correct himself from wickedness and pass over to goodness, as he has directed in the writing sent to them [Note: [Col. 0295] The text appears corrupt; M. reads *scriptum est declinauerit*].

13. Water shall always be mixed in the chalice in the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood.

14. No priest shall lend his money at interest, lest he receive from anyone more than he has lent.

15. If a priest comes to a sick person who has already lost the ability to speak, and witnesses are present who heard him say that he wished to make his confession, let the priest perform everything required around him according to his ministry, just as he ought to do for a penitent.

16. A priest shall not be a merchant, nor gather money through any shameful profit [Note: [Col. 0295] M. reads “shameful speech”].

17. No priest shall act as a guarantor anywhere.

18. No priest shall presume to receive any cleric from another parish.

19. When priests go to a sick person, they shall come with consecrated oil, anoint him with holy oil in the name of the Lord, and pray for him. The prayer of faith, as it is written, shall save the sick person, and the Lord shall raise him up; and if he is in sins, they shall be forgiven him.

20. A priest shall not go anywhere to baptize without chrism [Note: [Col. 0295] M. reads *chrimate*] and consecrated oil, nor without the sacrifice, so that wherever the occasion arises he may fulfill his ministry toward the sick. He shall guard that oil together with the chrism and the sacrifice with every care, reverence, and religious devotion, and shall not allow that sacred substance mentioned above to be dishonored through drunkenness or any negligence of his.

[Note: [Col. 0295D] Peter Pithaeus writes in the preface to the twelve contemporary writers of the *History of the Franks* that this division of the kingdoms of Emperor Charles is of doubtful authenticity and may rightly be numbered among the many products of idle leisure and the imaginations produced for us by later ages. He was persuaded of this because it had been appended by a later hand to a paper copy of Thegan’s work. But I found its very ancient exemplar in the Thuana library, although it was not complete; the same document had previously been published by Johannes Nauclerus, and Aventinus mentions it in the *Annals of Bavaria*. Indeed, Einhard makes explicit mention of it and says that he carried it to Pope Leo at the emperor’s command so that it might be confirmed by his subscription. Its authenticity and authority are further strengthened by the charter of the division of the empire made by Louis the Pious in 837, almost all of whose clauses are copied word for word from Charles’s document; yet Pithaeus, who first published it in the same volume of contemporary writers, did not accuse that document of being false. Finally, the division made by Charles is clearly and explicitly mentioned in chapter 3 of the Capitularies published at Nijmegen immediately after the division of the empire. BALUZ.]

# Division of the Empire (A.D. 806, February 8)

Einhard mentions in his *Annals* [Note: [Col. 0298D] *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, *Scriptores*, vol. I, p. 193] that the division of the kingdom, confirmed by oath at Thionville in the year 806, and the testament drawn up concerning it, were personally brought to Rome to Pope Leo. We also owe the date to a contemporary author who recorded it in a very ancient book at Saint Gall [Note: [Col. 0298D] Ibid., p. 70].

Peter Pithoeus [Note: [Col. 0298D] *Scriptores coaetanei* XII, in the preface and p. 283] found the text of the document appended by a later hand to the paper manuscript containing Thegan’s work. But it was so corrupt—the formulas not merely uncorrected by some idle person but genuinely perverted—that Pithoeus believed it “to be of doubtful authenticity, so that it may rightly be numbered among the many products of idle leisure and the imaginations produced for us by later ages.”

All doubt on this matter, however, was removed by, first, a manuscript rescued from destruction by the most deserving jurist Ernst Spangenberg of Celle, which was written in the ninth century and contains the Saxon law and, on its final folio, the beginning of this testament. When Spangenberg made it available to me for examination, I restored from it almost the entire preface. Baluzius reports that he saw a parchment manuscript in the Thuana library, but, having made no use of it, was content to repeat the text of Pithoeus. I therefore had no alternative but, secondly, to admit into the text in several places the readings of manuscript no. 3922 of the Vatican Library, a paper folio manuscript of the sixteenth or seventeenth century, which in some passages follows the true reading of the very ancient fragment.

## Here Begins the Division of the Kingdoms

In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. Charles [Note: [Col. 0297] *Carolus* Sp.], most serene augustus, crowned by God, great and peaceful emperor, ruling the Roman Empire, and by the mercy of God king of the Franks and Lombards [Note: [Col. 0297] *longobardorum* Sp.], to all the faithful of the holy Church of God and to our own people, present and future.

As is known in all things [Note: [Col. 0297] *ominbus* Sp.], and we believe is hidden from none of you, divine clemency—by whose will the ages tending toward their setting are renewed through the succession of generations—has enriched us with the great gift of its mercy and blessing by giving us three sons [Note: [Col. 0297] *dandos* Sp.], a great [Note: [Col. 0297] *magna* Sp.] gift. Through them it has confirmed the kingdom according to our prayers and hope [Note: [Col. 0297] *sep* Sp.], and has relieved the care owed to posterity liable to oblivion [Note: [Col. 0297] *obliuianam* Sp.; Pithoeus: *oblivioni*; I have attempted to correct it; *reuelauit* Sp., corrected to *relevavit*].

We therefore wish this also to be known to you: by the grace of God [Note: [Col. 0297] *gratia* Sp.] we desire to have these same sons as partners in the kingdom granted to us by God for as long as we remain in the body, and, after our departure from this mortal life, to leave them as heirs—if the divine majesty so wills [Note: [Col. 0297] *maiestatis* Sp.]—of the empire or kingdom preserved and to be preserved by God.

We do not wish to leave it to them confusedly and disorderly [Note: [Col. 0297] Sp. has *confus ...... que*], or under the single designation of the whole kingdom, as a matter of quarrel [Note: [Col. 0297] *iurgiis* Sp.] or litigation [Note: [Col. 0297] *relinquimus* Sp.]. Rather, we have caused the whole body of the kingdom to be divided into three portions, and have had it described and designated which portion each of them is to protect or govern. The arrangement is to be such that each, content with his own portion [Note: [Col. 0297] *suo* Sp.; after *quisque* the Spangenberg manuscript has a lacuna], may strive, with God’s help, to defend it according to our ordinance and the boundaries of his kingdom, which extend to foreign peoples, and may preserve peace and charity with his brother.

1. We have decided to make the divisions of our empire or kingdom, preserved and to be preserved by God, as follows: we have assigned to our beloved son Louis all Aquitaine and Gascony, except the county of Tours, and everything extending from there westward toward Spain; also from the city of Nevers, which lies on the Loire River, together with the county of Nevers, the counties of Avallon, Alsace, Chalon, Mâcon, Lyon, Savoy, Maurienne, Tarentaise, Mount Cenis, and the valley of Susa as far as the passes; and from there, along the boundaries of the Italian mountains, as far as the sea. These counties with their cities, and everything contained from them southward and westward as far as the sea or as far as Spain—that is, that part of Burgundy, Provence, and Septimania or Gothia—we have assigned to Louis, our beloved son.

2. Italy, also called Lombardy, and Bavaria as Tassilo held it, except for the two villages named Ingolstadt and Lutrahahof [Note: [Col. 0297] *angolstat* and *intrahahaff* 2], which we formerly granted to Tassilo as a benefice and which belong to the county called Nordgau [Note: [Col. 0297] *norigorre* 2]; and that part of Alemannia which lies on the southern bank of the Danube, from the very source [Note: [Col. 0297] thus in 2; *flumine* Bal.] of the Danube, following the boundary as far as the Rhine River, at the boundary of the counties of Kletgau [Note: [Col. 0297] *Vergonree* 2] and Hegau, to the place called Engen; and from there upstream along the Rhine as far as the Alps, whatever lies within these boundaries [Note: [Col. 0297] *inter* B.] and faces south or east, together with the duchy of Chur and the county of Thurgau [Note: [Col. 0297] *turgonroe* 2], we have assigned to Pippin, our beloved son.

3. Whatever remains of our kingdom outside these boundaries—that is, Francia and Burgundy, except for the part we gave to Louis; Alemannia, except for the portion we assigned to Pippin; Austria, Neustria, Thuringia, Saxony, Frisia, and the part of Bavaria called Nordgau [Note: [Col. 0297] *noregomoe* 2]—we have granted to our beloved son Charles.

This is arranged so that Charles and Louis may have a route into Italy to bring aid to their brother if necessity should arise: Charles through the valley of Aosta, which belongs to his kingdom, and Louis through the valley of Susa; while Pippin shall have both an entrance and an exit through the Noric Alps and Chur [Note: [Col. 0299] *cureas* 2].

4. We arrange the following order: if Charles, who is the eldest, dies before his other brothers [Note: [Col. 0299] B. has *diem obierit*, “dies”], the portion of the kingdom which he has [Note: [Col. 0299] *habeat* B.] shall be divided between Pippin and Louis, just as it was formerly divided between us and our brother Carloman. Pippin shall have the portion which our brother Carloman had, while Louis shall receive the part which we acquired in that portion.

But if, while Charles and Louis are still living, Pippin fulfills the debt of human destiny, Charles and Louis shall divide between themselves the kingdom which he possessed. The division shall be made in this way: from the entrance into Italy through the city of Aosta, Charles shall receive Ivrea, Vercelli, and Pavia, and from there, with the boundary running along the Po River, as far as the territory of Reggio, together with Reggio itself [Note: [Col. 0299] *ipsum Regium* 2], Civitanova, and Modena, as far as the territories of Saint Peter.

These cities, with their suburbs and territories and the counties belonging to them, and whatever lies to the left of a person traveling from there toward Rome, from the kingdom Pippin held, together with the duchy of Spoleto, shall be Charles’s portion, as we have stated.

Whatever from the aforesaid cities or counties lies to the right of one traveling toward Rome from that kingdom—that is, the portion remaining of the Transpadane region, together with the duchy of Tuscany [Note: [Col. 0299] *Tusculanum* 2] as far as the southern sea and as far as Provence—Louis shall receive as an addition to his kingdom.

If Louis dies while the others survive, Pippin shall receive that part of Burgundy which we added to his kingdom, together with Provence and Septimania or Gothia as far as Spain, while Charles shall receive Aquitaine and Gascony.

5. If a son is born to any one of these three brothers whom the people wish to succeed his father as heir to the kingdom, we wish his paternal uncles to consent to this [Note: [Col. 0299] The variant is printed as *ut huic c. patrui sui*, and in manuscript 2.] and allow their brother’s son to reign in the portion of the kingdom which his father, their brother, possessed.

6. After this disposition of our authority, we have decided and commanded the following among our aforesaid sons, because we desire peace to remain perpetually among them: none of them shall presume to invade his brother’s territory or the boundaries of his kingdom, nor fraudulently enter it to disturb his kingdom or reduce his borders. Rather, each shall help his brother and provide him assistance against his enemies according to reason and ability, whether within the homeland or against foreign nations.

7.
