None of them shall receive a man of his brother who flees to him for any cause or fault [Note: [Col. 0299] Manuscript 2 has *sustineat ad intercessionem pro eo faciendam*, “support him in order to make intercession for him”], nor shall he even intercede on his behalf. For we wish every person who sins and needs intercession to flee within the kingdom of his own lord, or to holy places, or to honorable men, and there to deserve just intercession.

8. Likewise, we command that no king receive any free man who has left his lord against his lord’s will and gone from one kingdom to another, nor allow his men to receive such a person or presume to retain him unjustly. We establish that this is to be observed not only concerning free men but also concerning fugitive slaves, so that no occasion for discord may remain.

9. Therefore, it seems necessary for us to command that, after our departure from this mortal life [Note: [Col. 0299] *ab* B.], the men of each of them receive benefices only in the kingdom of their own lord, and not in another, lest otherwise some scandal arise from this. Each of these men shall possess his inheritance without contradiction, in whatever kingdom it happens that he lawfully has it.

10. After the death of his lord, every free man shall have permission to commend himself in these three kingdoms to whomever he wishes. The same shall apply to one who has not yet commended himself to anyone.

11. Concerning transfers and sales which commonly take place between the territories, we command that none of these three brothers receive from the kingdom of another, from any person, a transfer or sale of immovable property—that is, lands, vineyards, forests, and slaves who are already settled in households, or other things counted as inheritances. The exceptions are gold, silver, gems, weapons, clothing, unhouseholded slaves, and those commodities known properly to belong to merchants. We have judged that this prohibition should by no means be imposed on other free men.

12. If women, as commonly happens, are sought in marriage between the territories and kingdoms, they shall not be denied to those who ask justly. Rather, it shall be permitted to give and receive them in turn, and to join the peoples to one another through kinship. The women themselves shall retain authority over their property in the kingdom from which they departed [Note: [Col. 0299] 2 has: “to enjoy it in the other kingdom also, wherever they may dwell with their husbands”], even though, because of their marital union, they must live in another kingdom.

13. Concerning hostages who were given on account of pledges and sent by us to various places for safekeeping, we wish the king in whose kingdom they are not to allow them to return to their homeland without the consent of their brother, from whose kingdom they were taken. Rather, in the future, when hostages are received, let each brother provide mutual assistance to the other if one brother reasonably asks the other to do so. We command the same concerning those who have been or are to be sent into exile for their crimes.

14. If a cause, claim, or dispute should arise between the territories concerning the boundaries or frontiers of the kingdoms which cannot be clarified or settled by human testimony, we wish the will of God and the truth of the matter to be sought in the judgment of the cross for the clarification of what is doubtful; and never shall a fight or judicial combat of any kind be ordered as an examination for such a cause.

But if someone from one kingdom accuses a man from another kingdom before his own lord of disloyalty toward his lord’s brother, let his lord send him to his brother, so that there he may prove what he said about that man.

15. Above all, we command and order that these three brothers jointly undertake the care and defense of the church of Saint Peter, just as formerly our grandfather Charles, our father of blessed memory, King Pippin, and later we ourselves undertook it. With God’s help, they shall strive to defend it from its enemies and ensure that it receives its justice insofar as this pertains to them and reason demands.

Likewise, concerning the other churches which shall be under their authority, we command that they have their justice and honor, and that the pastors and governors of the venerable places have authority over the property belonging to those holy places [Note: [Col. 0301] *pia* or *propria* 2], in whichever of these three kingdoms the possessions of those churches may be located.

16. If anything in these statutes and agreements should be violated by chance or through ignorance—something we do not wish—we command that they strive to correct it as quickly as possible according to justice, lest greater harm arise through delay.

17. Concerning our daughters, that is, the sisters of our aforesaid sons, we command that, after our departure from this body, each one have permission to choose under the guardianship and protection of whichever brother she wishes to place herself. If any of them chooses the monastic life, she shall be permitted to live honorably under the protection of her brother in whose kingdom [Note: [Col. 0301] *domo* 2] she wishes to dwell.

If one of them is justly and reasonably sought in marriage by a worthy man, and she herself desires married life [Note: [Col. 0301] absent in B.], her brothers shall not deny her this, provided that the desire of the man asking and of the woman consenting is honorable and reasonable.

18. Concerning our grandsons—that is, the sons of our aforesaid sons, those already born to them or still to be born—we have decided to command that none of the three brothers, on any pretext, cause any one of those grandsons who has been accused before him to be killed, mutilated, blinded, or forcibly tonsured without a just inquiry and examination.

Rather, we wish them to be honored by their fathers and paternal uncles, and obedient to them [Note: [Col. 0301] absent in B.] with all the submission appropriate to such kinship.

19. Finally, it seems necessary for us to establish that whatever else we may wish to add to these decrees and commands of ours concerning matters and constitutions relating to their advancement and benefit shall be observed and guarded by our aforesaid beloved sons just as we command them to guard and observe what has already been established and set out here.

20. We have arranged and decided to confirm all these matters in due order, so that, for as long as it pleases the divine majesty that we continue this bodily life, our authority over this kingdom and empire, preserved by God, shall remain as it has been until now—in its government and ordering, and with every royal and imperial dominion—and so that we may have our aforesaid beloved sons obedient to us, as well as our people beloved by God, with all the submission which sons show to a father and subjects to an emperor and king. Amen.

# Double Capitular of Nijmegen (A.D. 806, March)

These chapters have been restored with the aid of the following manuscripts: 1. Paris, Royal Library, no. 4495, ninth century; 2. the Royal Bavarian Library manuscript formerly at Tegernsee, tenth century, with whose aid Amerbach first published them; 3. Paris, Royal Library, among the *Supplementa latina*, no. 75, tenth century. Some chapters are also found in the manuscript of Saint Paul. The edict was delivered to the lordly envoys during Lent—therefore in March—at Nijmegen, where the emperor celebrated that year’s Easter feast.

## Chapters Added at Nijmegen in the Sixth Year of the Emperor’s Reign, during Lent

[Note: [Col. 0301] The words “in the sixth year” through “Lent” are absent from manuscripts 1 and 2. “The chapters added at Nijmegen” is found in the manuscript of Saint Paul, which contains chapters 4, 7, and 9.]

[Note: [Col. 0301] Einhard reports that in this year Charles celebrated the Lenten fast and the most sacred solemnity of Easter at Nijmegen. BALUZ.]

1. Let everyone in his own circuit of visitation exercise the greatest care in foreseeing, ordering, and arranging matters according to the will of God and according to our command [Note: [Col. 0301] absent in 1].

2. Concerning the oath. Let those who have not previously promised fidelity to our interests be made to promise it; and, in addition, let every man [Note: [Col. 0303] Manuscripts 2 and 3 have *omnes*, “all”] promise it anew [Note: [Col. 0303] Manuscript 2 has *r. III. Ut etc.*] so that all must fully consent to what we have established among our sons for the sake of peace and concord.

3. Let the aforesaid envoys, in each city and in the monasteries of men and women, investigate how and in what manner the houses of the churches and the ornaments of the churches appear to have been repaired or restored. Let them diligently inquire into the conduct of each person and how well they have fulfilled what we ordered concerning their reading and singing and the other disciplines pertaining to ecclesiastical rule [Note: [Col. 0303] 2 and 3: “the disciplines and …”] [Note: [Col. 0303D] Compare the Capitular of A.D. 805, p. 131].

4. Let each bishop, abbot, and abbess carefully examine the ecclesiastical treasures, lest through the faithlessness [Note: [Col. 0303] *fiduciam* 1] or negligence of the custodians anything of the gems [Note: [Col. 0303] “of the gems” is absent in 2] or vessels, or any other part of the treasure, be lost. For we have been told that Jewish merchants [Note: [Col. 0303] absent in 1], as well as others, boast [Note: [Col. 0303] “that they can buy whatever pleases them from them” is absent in 1] that they can buy from them whatever pleases them.

5. We wish our envoys to act equally in each case, whether concerning the *haribannum* [Note: [Col. 0303] *agribannum* 1], newcomers, or any other matters. Concerning newcomers, we wish those who have been married for a long time in the various places to remain there and not be expelled without cause or fault. Fugitive slaves [Note: [Col. 0303] absent in 2] and robbers, however, shall return to their proper places.

6. We have heard how counts [Note: [Col. 0303] *comes* 1] and other men who appear to hold our benefices purchase private properties for themselves from the very benefice belonging to us, and make the servants of our benefices serve those private properties; meanwhile our estates remain deserted, and in some places the neighbors themselves suffer many wrongs.

7. We have heard that some transfer our benefice to other men as private property, and, once a price has been paid in that transaction, buy those same things back for themselves as allodial property. This must be avoided altogether, for those who do this do not faithfully preserve the loyalty they have promised us. They must beware lest they be found in any disloyalty, since the fact that such people do these things by their own will does not allow reports of their actions to reach our ears.

8. There are also others who ought to receive justice according to the laws, but who in certain places are harassed to such an extent that, until they surrender their justice through the hands of guarantors, they are able to retain only something, however small, while stronger men take the greater portion.

9. Concerning beggars who roam through the regions, we wish each of our faithful to support his own poor person from his benefice [Note: [Col. 0303] “to support him from our benefice” in the manuscript of Saint Paul] or from his own household, and not allow him to go elsewhere begging. Wherever such people are found, unless they work with their hands, no one shall presume to give them anything.

10. Concerning tolls and *cespitaticia*, let them observe what we established in another capitulary: that is, where an ancient custom existed, they shall be collected in that manner; where new ones have been discovered, they shall be abolished [Note: [Col. 0303] The following chapters are placed before the preceding ones by manuscript 1; manuscripts 2 and 3 number them continuously].

## Again, Chapters of Emperor Charles
1. Usury is when more is demanded than is given; for example, if you give ten solidi and demand more; or if you give a modius of wine [Note: [Col. 0303] manuscript 1: *modiam*] or grain [Note: [Col. 0303] manuscript 1: *uni*; manuscript 2: *unum*; manuscript 3: *unum*; I corrected the text from Ansegisus], and again demand something in addition [Note: [Col. 0303] manuscript 1: *nerum*].

2. Desire (*cupiditas*) may be understood in a good sense and in a bad sense. In the good sense, according to the Apostle [Note: [Col. 0303D] Philippians 1]: “I desire to depart and to be with Christ” [Note: [Col. 0303] manuscript 1: “to be desolated”]. And in the Psalm [Note: [Col. 0303D] Psalm 83]: “My soul has greatly desired the courts of the Lord.”

3. Desire, however, is understood in the bad sense when someone wishes unjustly to covet anything beyond measure [Note: [Col. 0303] manuscript 2: “which, in the bad sense, beyond measure”], according to Solomon [Note: [Col. 0304D] Ecclesiasticus 18]: “Do not follow your desires.”

4. Avarice is desiring what belongs to others and giving none of what one has acquired to anyone. And according to the Apostle [Note: [Col. 0304D] 1 Timothy 6], “this is the root of all evils.”

5. Those practice shameful gain who, through various deceptions and for the sake of profit, strive dishonestly [Note: [Col. 0303] manuscript 1: “honestly”] to gather whatever possessions they can.

6. A loan (*foenus*) is made when someone lends something. A loan is just when he demands no more than he has lent [Note: [Col. 0303] manuscripts 2 and 3: “as much as he lent”].

[Col. 0304C] 7. Whoever, at the time of harvest or the time of the vintage, purchases grain or wine—not from necessity but out of greed—for example, buys one modius for two denarii and stores it until he can sell it again for four or six denarii, or more, this we call shameful gain. But if he purchases it out of necessity, so that he may have it for himself and distribute it to others, we call it commerce [Note: [Col. 0303] manuscript 2: “This we do not call commerce”].

8. We have therefore determined that, in the present year, since severe famine appears to prevail in very many places, all bishops, abbots, abbesses, nobles, counts, household officers, and all our faithful who appear to possess royal benefices, whether from ecclesiastical property [Note: [Col. 0303] manuscripts 2 and 3: “ecclesiastical possessions”] or from other sources, shall each cause his household to be fed from his benefice, and shall feed his household from his own property. And if, by God’s gift, he has grain beyond what is needed for himself and his household [Note: [Col. 0303] absent from manuscript 1], whether in his benefice or in his allod [Note: [Col. 0303] manuscript 2: “dole”], and wishes to sell it, he shall not sell it at more than these prices: one modius of oats for two denarii; one modius of barley for three denarii [Note: [Col. 0305] manuscript 2 omits “not”]; one modius of spelt for three denarii if it is sifted [Note: [Col. 0305] manuscript 3: “separated”]; one modius of rye for four denarii; [Col. 0306A] and one modius of prepared wheat [Note: [Col. 0305] absent from manuscript 1] for six denarii. The modius itself shall be the measure established for everyone to possess, so that each person may have an equal measure and equal modii [Note: [Col. 0305] manuscript 2: “measure”].

# ENCYCLICAL ON HOLDING THE GENERAL ASSEMBLY

[Col. 0305]

(See among the letters of Charlemagne, *Patrologia*, volume 98.)

# CAPITULARY OF AACHEN (806, Aachen)

[Col. 0305]

These chapters, issued at the autumn assembly—chapter 6, therefore, at Aachen, where Charles was then residing—were first published by Amerbach from the Tegernsee Codex; we now publish them with the assistance of that codex and seven others. They are as follows:

1. Royal Library of Paris, manuscript no. 4629, ninth century;

2. The same library, manuscript no. 4404, ninth century;

3. The same library, manuscript no. 4995, ninth century;

4. Codex of the monastery of Saint Paul in Carinthia, ninth century;

4a. Codex of the Chisian Library, tenth century;

4b. Codex of the Cavense Library, eleventh century;

5. Royal Library of Munich, formerly the Tegernsee Codex, tenth century;

6. Ducal Library of Wolfenbüttel, Blankenburg collection, tenth century.

That these were sent to the royal envoys so that they might make them known everywhere is clear from the following inscription.

[Col. 0305B] “Let our envoys make these chapters known to everyone in every part” [Note: [Col. 0305] “in all places” is absent from manuscript 1; “to all men in all parts,” manuscript 4; “to everyone in every part,” manuscript 2; “to everyone in all parts,” manuscript 3; the inscription is absent from manuscript 5; “to all,” manuscript 6].

First chapter. No one shall come to the mallus or assembly within his district without bearing weapons—that is, a shield and a lance [Note: [Col. 0305] absent from manuscripts 3, 4, 5, and 6].

2. Concerning thieves. Whoever, after the feast of Saint John the Baptist, gives lodging to a thief shall, if he is a Frank, swear with twelve of his peers [Note: [Col. 0305] the remainder of the phrase is absent from manuscript 6] that he did not know him to be a thief, even if he is his father, brother, or kinsman [Note: [Col. 0305] absent from manuscript 1]. If he cannot swear this, and is convicted by someone that he received a thief into his lodging, he shall be judged a thief and a traitor [Note: [Col. 0305] manuscripts 2, 3, and 5: “as a thief”]; for whoever is a thief is a traitor to us and to the Franks, and whoever receives him is like him. But if he heard that the man was a thief, yet did not know it with certainty [Note: [Col. 0305] “If he did not know that he was a thief,” manuscript 1], he shall either swear alone that he had never heard him called a thief, whether truthfully or falsely; or he shall be prepared, if that man is later convicted of theft, to be condemned in the same manner [Note: [Col. 0305] manuscripts 2, 3, and 6: “likewise”; manuscript 1 ends here].

3. No one shall purchase a horse, ox, or beast of burden, or anything else, unless he knows the man who sold it to him, or knows from what district he comes, where he lives, or who his lord is [Note: [Col. 0305] manuscript 4 ends here, together with the Chisian and Cavense codices].

4. Concerning newcomers. Whenever any of our envoys come to our assembly, they shall have written down how many newcomers there are in their mission, from which district they come [Note: [Col. 0305] manuscript 3: “from which district”; manuscript 5: “from what district”], their names, and who their lords are [Note: [Col. 0305] manuscripts 2 and 5 continue the remainder without division into separate chapters].

5. We have likewise sent envoys into Aquitaine and Lombardy, so that all fugitives and newcomers may be brought to our assembly [Note: [Col. 0305] manuscript 1: “similar”; manuscript 5: “envoys”].

6. Whoever possesses these chapters shall transmit them to other envoys who do not possess them, so that no excuse of ignorance may be offered. And all parts shall be informed of these chapters before the Nativity of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0305] the remainder is absent from manuscript 3; manuscript 6 adds: “and our envoys shall make this known to all without fail before the Nativity of the Lord”; manuscript 5 has the same wording, omitting “without fail” and “to all”].

# EXCERPTED CHAPTERS FROM THE CANON

[Col. 0305]

These chapters have been restored in full from the sole codex from which Amerbach formerly published them—namely, the Tegernsee Codex of the tenth century—by comparison with the reading of Ansegisus.

# HERE BEGIN THE EXCERPTED CHAPTERS FROM THE CANON [Note: [Col. 0305] manuscript C: *excarps*]

[Col. 0305D]

1. That a synod be held twice each year.

2. What kind of person cannot enter the priesthood or the sacred orders, according to what we read in the canon.

3. That a province must never be divided between two metropolitans.

[Col. 0306D] 4. That there must not be two bishops in one city, and concerning the vicars of bishops.

5. That the ordinations of bishops ought not to be long delayed.

6. Concerning bishops who have been ordained but not received.

7. That no one should ordain anyone without qualification [Note: [Col. 0305] manuscript 1 reads *absolute* (“absolutely”) for *solute*].

[Col. 0307A] 8. Concerning a slave who has been ordained without his master’s knowledge.

9. That a cleric may not minister in two cities, nor abbots possess several monasteries or cells.

10. That a bishop may not move from one place to another without a decree of the bishops, nor a cleric without the command of his bishop.

11. Concerning foreign bishops and clerics.

12. Concerning letters of foreigners and clerics traveling without letters.

13. What persons, and for what offenses, someone is degraded from priestly office according to canonical discipline.

14. Concerning one expelled from the church and excommunication [Note: [Col. 0307] manuscript C: *excommunicato* (“the excommunicated person”)], or one condemned to removal from office.

[Col. 0307B] 15. Concerning ecclesiastical order and the office of the Mass; concerning the relics of the saints and rural oratories.

16. That altars may not be consecrated unless they are made of stone.

17. Concerning confirmation with chrism.

18. Concerning baptism.

19. Concerning Easter, the Lord’s Day, and the other festivals.

20. Concerning fasting and Lent [Note: [Col. 0307] manuscript C: *quagragesimo*], and the litanies.

[Col. 0308A] 21. That the principal festivals [Note: [Col. 0307] manuscript C: *praeplaras*] be held only in cities or public villages.

22. Concerning this office.

23. That all the faithful receive Communion and remain at Mass during the synodal prayer [Note: [Col. 0307] “final prayer,” manuscript 1].

Here begins the canon of Saint Sylvester and 284 bishops.

He established these grades [Note: [Col. 0307] manuscript C: *grandus*] within the synod, so that no priest might bring any accusation against a bishop, no deacon against a priest, no subdeacon against a deacon, no acolyte against a subdeacon, no exorcist against an acolyte, no lector against an exorcist, and no doorkeeper against a lector. And a prelate shall not be condemned without seventy-two witnesses; nor shall the supreme prelate be judged by anyone, since it is written [Note: [Col. 0307B] Matthew 10]: “The disciple is not above his teacher.”

A priest, however, shall not be condemned without forty-four testimonies. A deacon appointed to the principal church of the city of Rome shall not be condemned without thirty-seven [Note: [Col. 0307] manuscript C: “constructed”; manuscript C has a corrupt form of “condemned”]. A subdeacon [Note: [Col. 0307] manuscript C: “deacon”], acolyte, exorcist, or lector shall not be condemned except with seven testimonies, having sons and a wife, and while altogether preaching Christ. Thus the mystical truth is given.

# LOMBARD CAPITULARY (806)

[Col. 0307]

It survives in the Codex of Saint Paul, chapters 55–66. Since a twofold capitulary of 805 and the capitularies of 806 were issued in France in the presence of Pippin, this capitulary appears to have been promulgated in Italy only after his return, in the autumn of 806 or the spring of the following year.

[Col. 0307C] Chapter 1. It has pleased us concerning those documents made about individual persons who delivered themselves, their wives, and their sons or daughters into servitude, that wherever they are found [Note: [Col. 0307] manuscript 1: “wherever they were found”] they shall be returned, and shall be free as they were at first.

Chapters 2–12. See above, columns 285–288, year 805, chapters 6, 8, 9–13, 15, 16, 19, and 20.

[Col. 0308C] Chapters 13–15. See above, columns 303–304, capitulary of Nijmegen, chapters 5, 8, and 10.

Chapters 16–19. See above, columns 305–306, general capitulary, chapters 1, 2, and 3.

Chapter 19. See above, column 214, capitulary of 801, chapter 8.

# CAPITULARY OF AACHEN (807, AROUND MARCH)

[Col. 0307]

Edited by Baluze from the Codex of Saint Vincent of Metz; I have revised it with the aid of the Codex of the Royal Library of Paris among the *Supplementa Latina*, no. 75.

# “THIS CHAPTER WAS GIVEN IN THE SEVENTH YEAR AT THE PALACE OF AACHEN.”

[Col. 0307C]

Memorandum of how we made arrangements, because of the scarcity caused by famine [Col. 0307D], concerning the requirement that all those beyond the Seine undertake military service.

1. First, all who appear to possess benefices shall come to the army.

2. Every free man who appears to possess five manses of property shall likewise come to the army. He who has four manses shall do the same. He who appears to possess three shall likewise act. Wherever two men are found, each of whom appears to possess two manses, one shall have the other equipped [Col. 0308D], and whichever of them is better able shall come to the army. Wherever two are found, one of whom has two manses and the other one manse, they shall likewise join together, and one shall equip the other; and whichever is better able shall come to the army. Wherever three are found, each possessing one manse, two shall equip the third [Col. 0309A], and whichever of them is better able shall come to the army.

Those who possess half a manse shall have five equip a sixth [Note: [Col. 0309] manuscript 1 thus reads; it has been corrected to “half manses,” with the same meaning]. And if someone is found so poor that he possesses neither slaves nor land of his own, but nevertheless has property worth five solidi, five shall equip a sixth; and wherever there are two such men, they shall equip a third, among those who appear to possess small landholdings.

For each of those who go to the army, five solidi shall be contributed by the poorer men mentioned above who appear to possess no landholding. And because of this arrangement, no one shall abandon his lord.

3. Accordingly, all our faithful captains, with their men, wagons, and gifts, shall come to the appointed assembly with the best equipment they can prepare. [Col. 0309B] Each of our envoys shall arrange, in every administrative district, for one of our vassals to be selected, and shall command in our name that he come with the smaller contingent and wagons from each county and escort them peacefully behind us, so that nothing remains behind; and they shall be at the Rhine by the middle of August.

We wish all those who appear to reside beyond the Seine to observe these arrangements generally in the present year.

4. We wish and command that our counts not abandon their assemblies on account of hunting or other amusements, nor make them insignificant; but just as we customarily hold assemblies with them, so they shall hold assemblies with their subjects and administer justice. They shall personally see to each of the chapters that we have commanded them, so that nothing is omitted of what we enjoin them to do, whether within the country or outside the country, in the army.

5. If it should be necessary to provide assistance in the regions of Spain or Avaria [Note: [Col. 0309D] the old codex reads “Avarice.” I do not doubt that “Avaria” must be restored. Blessed Rhenanus appears to have read it this way in book 2 of his *Germanic History*, p. 94, where, discussing the condition of Gaul and Germany under Frankish kings and emperors, he writes: “Much was accomplished with the aid of the conquered Saxons. If it was necessary to proceed into distant regions, for example Spain or Avaria, which bordered Noricum from the Alps, five Saxons equipped a sixth. If, on the other hand, it was against the Bohemian Slavs, two equipped a third. If against the Sorbs, all were compelled to come. Thus six poorer Frisians armed a seventh.” This therefore confirms the authority of this capitulary. Baluze], then five Saxons shall equip a sixth. If it is necessary to provide assistance in the region of Bohemia, two shall equip a third. But if there is a need to defend the country around the Sorbs [Note: [Col. 0309] manuscript 1 originally reads “Surabs,” corrected to “Sorabs”], then everyone without exception shall come.

6. Concerning the Frisians [Note: [Col. 0309] manuscript 1 originally reads “Fresons,” corrected thus], we wish counts and our vassals who appear to possess benefices, as well as the horsemen [Note: [Col. 0310D] that is, those so called from their horses. An old charter of Brioude reads: “I shall not kill any cleric or horseman, nor any man or woman, within these boundaries.” Elsewhere *caballarii* signifies noblemen, knights, or chevaliers, as in an old charter of Rodez. Editor], all without exception, to come well equipped to our assembly. The remaining poorer men shall have six equip a seventh, and shall likewise come well equipped and in military order to the appointed assembly.

7. We wish and command that our envoys carefully inspect, in every district, all the benefices that our men and the men of others appear to possess, and determine how they have been restored in accordance with our proclamation, or whether they have been destroyed.

First, they shall inspect the churches: how they are built or destroyed in their roofs, walls of rubble or masonry, and pavements, as well as in their paintings, lamps, and furnishings. They shall inspect the other benefices in the same way—houses with all their appurtenances and cultivated or acquired lands—and also what each person, after we prohibited it, has transferred from that benefice into his own allod, or what he has worked there from it.

Each vicar shall inspect the condition of these matters in each county within his administrative district, together with our envoys, and shall be able to swear to the truth of his findings. He shall put everything he discovers into a written report [Note: [Col. 0309] absent from the codices], and they shall bring the reports to us.

All those who hold these benefices shall come together with our envoys, so that we may know who they are and who possesses his benefice in good order or in ruin. They shall likewise inspect their allods, to determine whether the allods themselves or the benefice have been better restored [Note: [Col. 0309] manuscript 1 corrected from the masculine “restored” to the neuter “restored”]; for we have heard that some men have left their benefices deserted while restoring their allods.

# LETTER TO PIPPIN, KING OF ITALY

[Col. 0309]

(See among the letters of Charlemagne, *Patrologia*, volume 98.)

# CAPITULARY OF INGELHEIM (807, AUGUST)

[Col. 0309]

We have assigned this edict, from chapter 13 and promulgated between the years 806 and 810, on the authority of the Annals of Moissac, to the assembly held near the palace of Ingelheim around the month of August. We publish it again from the codex from which it was first brought to light by Amerbach: the royal Munich codex, formerly belonging to the monastery of Tegernsee, tenth century. We have corrected several passages with the aid of the codex of the monastery of Saint Paul in Carinthia, from the beginning of the ninth century, in which chapters 6–9, 12, and 13 survive, as they also do in the Chisian and Cavense codices.

These codices differ especially from the Tegernsee codex in that chapters 9 and 13 mention several of Charles’s sons, whereas the Tegernsee codex speaks of only one. Thus, as the Codex of Saint Paul surpasses the Tegernsee codex in age, it also evidently surpasses it in the antiquity of its reading.

# ANOTHER CAPITULARY

[Col. 0311A]

1. Concerning ecclesiastical organization [Note: [Col. 0311] manuscript 1: “ecclesiastical”] and the restoration of the churches of God: let everyone without exception exercise proper care.

2. That our faithful maintain peace and concord with one another.

3. How our march is organized, and what our border-dwellers have themselves done in particular during these past years [Note: [Col. 0311] manuscript 1 reads: “what those who have made our frontier arrangements have done”].

4. Concerning the appointed assembly for the march: it is necessary that everyone come from every side in every way, as it has been organized.

5. Concerning those men whom our margraves must not receive—those who flee from their lords because of injuries which they have inflicted upon them.

[Col. 0311B] 6 [Note: [Col. 0311B] found in the codices of Saint Paul, Chisian, and Cavense]. Concerning wicked judges, advocates [Note: [Col. 0311] the Saint Paul codices read “judges and advocates”], governors, vicars, centenarii, and other malicious officials: such men must not be retained.

7 [Note: [Col. 0312B] present in the Codex of Saint Paul, as are chapters 8, 9, 12, and 13]. Concerning the ability of free men, so that they may undertake military service according to the quality of their property.

[Col. 0312A] 8. No one shall consent to his men doing evil within the country; and concerning those who say that they cannot obtain men to defend the march, if they discipline them properly [Note: [Col. 0311] manuscript 1 reads “if they discipline them”].

9. Concerning royal vassals: that they receive honor and hold their position directly, either under us or under our sons [Note: [Col. 0311] manuscript 1 reads “our son”; the Saint Paul codex omits this phrase].

10. Concerning hostages, who are not properly guarded and flee from those responsible for them.

11. Concerning those who suffer hardship: that they receive better consolation in pursuing their justice [Note: [Col. 0311] manuscript 1 reads “better” in the comparative form].

12. That free men not be placed under a ban at assemblies, except if a complaint has been brought against someone, or if there is no scabinus or judge; and that the poorer men not be condemned on this account [Note: [Col. 0311] wording taken from the Codex of Saint Paul; absent from manuscript 1].

[Col. 0312B] 13. Counts shall not presume to receive or demand a military levy or any other contribution from free men for military purposes [Note: [Col. 0311] absent from manuscript 1], except if an envoy comes from our palace or from our sons [Note: [Col. 0311] manuscript 1 and the Lombard capitulary, chapter 97, read “or from our son”], to demand that levy.

# DOUBLE CAPITULARY OF NIJMEGEN (808, APRIL)

[Col. 0311]

Edited by Baluze from the Codex of Saint Vincent of Metz; I have revised it with the aid of the royal Paris codex among the *Supplementa Latina*, no. 75.

# “IN THE EIGHTH YEAR, CHAPTERS TO BE COMPARED WITH THE FIRST” [Note: [Col. 0311] it apparently should be read “to be compared with one another.” Baluze].

[Col. 0311C]

1. Concerning thieves and robbers.

2. Concerning false witnesses.

3. Concerning perjuries.

4. Concerning fugitives.

5. Concerning men hanged for minor offenses.

6. Concerning coinage.

7. Concerning furs and cloaks.

8. Concerning the market of our palace.

9. Concerning the guarding of our march by land and sea.

10. Concerning the ships that we ordered to be built.

11. That the provisions established be observed by our faithful, and that our commands be carried out.

12. Concerning the time of our next assembly, and who must come to that assembly again.

[Col. 0311D] 13. Concerning the men of our sons and daughters, whom the envoys and counts do not dare to compel [Note: [Col. 0311] manuscript 1 originally reads “dare”; Baluze reads “may dare”].

# ALSO, IN THE SAME PLACE

1. Concerning the march [Note: [Col. 0311D] see above, chapter 9]: each person must be ready to hasten there whenever necessity arises, in order to inspect it.

2. Concerning thieves [Note: [Col. 0311D] see above, chapters 1 and 5]: that they be more strictly disciplined. No one shall presume to hang a man except by judicial sentence. If someone is hanged without guilt and dies there, the person who hanged him without a trial shall pay compensation to his nearest relatives. If he does not die there but escapes alive, compensation shall be paid to him personally, and his property and slaves shall not fall to the fisc.

As for slaves, if someone hangs another man’s slave without a trial and without guilt, and the slave dies there, his weregild shall be paid to his master. If he survives that death, he shall receive the compensation due for the injury and shall thereafter remain free.

3. No one shall presume to bring witnesses into court [Note: [Col. 0312D] see above, chapter 2]; rather, the count shall investigate the matter by oath through truthful men living nearby, so that they may declare in every respect what they know about it.

4. No one shall presume to commit perjury [Note: [Col. 0312D] see above, chapter 3]. If he does so, as was commanded in the earlier chapters, he shall lose his hand or redeem it by payment. Let it be announced to everyone what harm perjury or false testimony causes.

5. Concerning purchases and sales [Note: [Col. 0313B] see above, chapter 7]: no one shall presume to sell or buy a better *sagellum* for more than twenty solidi, or an ordinary one for ten solidi. The others shall cost less. A better marten or otter pelt shall cost thirty solidi; the best *sismusinum* ten solidi [Note: [Col. 0313B] that is, made from the skins of *cissimi*, namely sables]. If anyone sells or buys for more, he shall be compelled to pay forty solidi into the ban, and twenty solidi to the person who discovers and proves the offense.

6. Concerning fugitive men [Note: [Col. 0314B] see above, chapter 4]: wherever they are found, the person who retains one shall be compelled to pay the lord’s ban, and the fugitive shall without question return to his country and his lord.

7. Concerning mints [Note: [Col. 0314B] see above, chapter 6]: coin shall be struck nowhere except at the court. Let the palace denarii be used in trade [Note: [Col. 0313] manuscript 1 originally reads “be traded,” corrected to “be used in trade”] and circulate everywhere [Note: [Col. 0314B] see above, chapter 8].

# LOMBARD CAPITULARY (808)

[Col. 0313]

It survives in the Codex of Saint Paul, chapters 81–85, after the Ingelheim capitulary of 807; I have therefore assigned it to the year 808.

[Col. 0313B] 1. Concerning those who abandon the world: they must choose one of two alternatives—either live fully according to the canon, or live according to a monastic rule.

2. Concerning justice for the churches of God, widows, orphans, and minors: in public courts [Note: [Col. 0313D] that is, judgments] they must not be despised when they bring complaints, but must be heard attentively [Col. 0313C].

3. If one of our slaves is killed, our court shall take two parts of the compensation, and the third part shall go to the parents of our deceased slave, as we stated above. We establish this for our days and during the time of our reign, although it is not our law [Note: [Col. 0313] I have corrected this with the aid of Lothair’s capitulary of 832, II, chapter 33, which derived from this text].

After our death, whoever is ruler at that time shall do what God inspires him to do, or what he judges right according to his conscience. For we have learned and recognized repeatedly that, whenever such cases have arisen, nothing has benefited either the public treasury or the palace from what our officials took on that account. Moreover, we have found and learned that many of our officials took from one person ten solidi, from another six, and from another more, and gave the killer such a period and respite that the one who had committed the homicide was able to secure that nothing should be paid from it.

Therefore we have decided that our court shall receive half of the compensation for aldiones and two parts for slaves, as we said above, so that their parents and kinsmen may, amid their grief, receive some consolation by way of compensation [Note: [Col. 0313D] “let the parents and kinsmen themselves have it,” manuscript C].

4. For God’s sake and because of his mercy, we command and establish, solely as an act of piety, that if one of our aldiones is killed, our court shall take half of the compensation and half shall go to the parents of the deceased, if our aldio has a living father, or mother, or brothers, or sons.

[Col. 0314B] 5. We command that no one presume to buy anything from either our slave or our aldio. For the sake of caution and for the future, we are having registers made throughout all our courts of every tract of land belonging to those courts. Therefore, if anyone is henceforth found to have purchased anything from a slave, an aldio, or an *abthin* of our court [Note: [Col. 0313] this word occurs again below and is absent from the glossaries], he shall lose the purchase itself, like one who wrongfully seizes another’s property. If an official has consented to the act or been aware of it, he shall have his property taken and confiscated.

Every man must consider, for God’s sake and for the sake of his soul, that we have remitted to the free *eremanni* (*liveri eremanni*) that which belonged to us in our courts according to the ancient edict and the laws [Note: [Col. 0313] *illum*, that is, *illud* (“that thing”)]. For when someone left one daughter, only a third part of his estate passed to the daughter as successor to her father, while two parts reverted to the public treasury if he had no close relatives [Note: [Col. 0313] “if he had no close relative,” manuscript C]. If someone had two daughters or more, they succeeded to half of their father’s estate, and half went to the public treasury.

And behold, we have now, for God’s sake and for the salvation of my soul, released all such property. Therefore each person ought to be satisfied with his own substance and ought not, contrary to reason, desire to purchase anything from our slave, aldio, or *abthin*. Whoever presumes to do so shall pay compensation as it is written. Moreover, it appears to us that he incurs the guilt of perjury, since he has sworn to us that he is faithful to us.

What kind of fidelity is it when he conspires with a judge, official, aldio, or slave and seizes our property against our will? For it has been established in the edict that whoever purchases from a slave or aldio shall lose the price he paid. Whatever law each Lombard wishes to have for himself, he ought to preserve in our court.

Whoever has now purchased or pledged such property [Note: [Col. 0315] that is, “has pledged it”] shall lose his price according to the tenor of the edict. Whoever presumes to act in this way shall both lose the price and, like one who wrongfully seizes another’s property without the owner’s knowledge, pay compensation. The official, however, shall forfeit his substance if he has consented to this, as is read above. For if we have released such property, each person ought to have whatever we have commanded or shall command him to have.

# CAPITULARY OF AACHEN (808)

[Col. 0315]

Edited by Baluze from the Codex of Saint Vincent of Metz; I have revised it with the aid of the royal Paris codex among the *Supplementa Latina*, no. 75, and assigned it to the assembly customarily held in August or autumn, which appears to have been held at Aachen in this year. The comparison of the chapters of the two texts, together with the heading of these chapters, proves that it should not be referred to the assembly at Nijmegen.

# ALSO, FROM THE EIGHTH YEAR

[Col. 0315B]

1. Concerning peace within the country.

2. Concerning canons and monks.

3. Concerning false testimony and perjury.

4. Concerning those who fraudulently wish to make themselves free, and those who become arrogant.

5. Concerning counterfeit coins.

6. Concerning the search for those men who were recently led outside [Col. 0316B] and later acquired property after their fathers and relatives had been led away [Note: [Col. 0315B] that the property of those who were led outside the country was confiscated into the fisc is proved by a diploma of Charles, by which, on 17 July of this year at Aachen, he restored such property to Manfred, bishop of Reggio. Muratori, *Antiquities*, III, 78 (VIII, 430).].

7. Concerning tithes and ninths.

8. Concerning thieves and their discipline.

9. Concerning the palace works at Vermeria [Note: [Col. 0316B] manuscript 1 reads this; corrected to “Vermerium”].

10. Concerning the *broilum* at our palace of Attigny [Note: [Col. 0316B] a wooded place enclosed by a wall, ditch, or hedge and used for hunting].

# CAPITULARY OF AACHEN (809)

[Col. 0315]

Baluze published two capitularies for the year 809: the first from the Codex of Saint Vincent of Metz, the second from the Navarre Codex. Comparison of the individual chapters shows, however, that they are one and the same. Nor have I thought that they should be distinguished as two capitularies merely because of their different order, which also occurs in other capitularies—for example, in the codices of the twofold Nijmegen capitulary of 806.

I have therefore published one capitulary, whose readings also agree with those of Ansegisus, with the aid of three codices that I examined in the Royal Library of Paris: 1. the one numbered 4995, which I used as the basis of the edition; 2. no. 4628 A, which may be regarded as Baluze’s “Navarre Codex”; 3. the codex among the *Supplementa Latina*, no. 75, which follows the same order of chapters as Baluze’s Metz codex [Note: [Col. 0315C] namely chapters 16, 16 note, 17, 18, 20, 21, 21 note, 4, 3, 3 note, 5, 6, 9, 8, 25, 10, 11, 15, 12, 13, 19, the heading of chapter 1, 14, 1, 2, 4, 7, 12, 22, 23, and 24].

In addition, for chapters 1–12 I used the Lombard, Chisian, Cavense, Ambrosian, Florentine, London, Viennese, Veronese, and Este codices cited by Muratori. I placed the readings of codex 3 and of the Saint Vincent of Metz codex, as reported by Baluze, alongside the primary text.

# CHAPTERS WHICH THE LORD EMPEROR ESTABLISHED AT THE PALACE OF AACHEN [Note: [Col. 0315] manuscript 2: “Lord Charles”]

[Col. 0315C]

Chapters established for the administration of justice within the country [Note: [Col. 0315] absent from manuscripts 2, Chisian, and Cavense].

1. Concerning those men who, on account of their offenses, have been sentenced to death, but afterward have been granted their lives: if they themselves seek justice from others, or if someone wishes to seek justice from them, how judgment shall be concluded between them. [Note: [Col. 0315] Codex 3, chapter 28, reads: “After anyone has been sentenced to death, he shall neither become a judge, nor a scabinus, nor a witness, nor be admitted to an oath; but in matters in which others ought to swear, he shall always come to be examined by the judgment of God.”]

First of all, concerning the cases for which he was sentenced to death, he may make no claim, because all his property was publicly confiscated according to the judgment of the Franks. If afterward, once his life has been granted, he is able to acquire anything lawfully, he shall retain and defend it in his freedom according to the law.

He shall not be admitted as a witness, nor shall he hold a place among the scabini for judging according to law [Note: [Col. 0315] the Ambrosian, Viennese, and Muratori manuscripts read: “nor shall he hold a place for judging and defending according to law”]. If he is adjudged to swear an oath concerning something, and someone makes a claim against him concerning that oath [Note: [Col. 0315] manuscripts 2, 3, Chisian, Cavense, Ansegisus, Viennese, and Este instead read: “if someone wishes to accuse him of making a false statement under oath, let him contest it by arms”], he must always submit to the judgment of God.

[Col. 0317A] 2. If someone is granted his life after the judgment of the scabini, and afterward commits some evil and refuses to render justice, saying that he is dead and therefore ought not to render justice, it is established that he shall undergo the higher judgment which he previously ought to have undergone.

If someone wrongs him, however, he shall have permission, according to the order of equity, to seek his justice in cases committed after he was sentenced to death. As for what occurred before, it shall remain as it was judged above.

3. [Note: Concerning *meziban*, that is, [reading uncertain: “l. f. 3.”]] Concerning the outlawed robber: let a free man who has sheltered him pay 15 solidi, and let a slave be beaten with 120 blows.  
[Note: “Let … be beaten” is absent in two witnesses. “Unless he gave him lodging,” V. and Vn. In Codex 3 this is appended: “Let no one presume to despoil a poor and needy person without legal process.”]

4. Let the count who has placed a robber under the ban notify his neighboring counts that the same robber has been outlawed by him, so that they do not receive him.  
[Note: “His other” in two witnesses; “and his other counts” in V., Vn., and M.]

[Col. 0317B] 5. Let no other free man be compelled to come to a placitum or mallus, except the scabini [and the counts’ vassals (these words are absent from witness 1 but present in the others and in Ansegisus)] and those who are required to prosecute or answer their cases.  
[Note: “Their cases” in witness 1. “Except one who must prosecute and answer his own case,” in two witnesses and A., V., Vn., E.]

6. Let witnesses not be hired for giving testimony by means of a reward.  
[Note: “By a price imposed” or “by a reward,” in two witnesses.]  
And let no one give testimony or swear an oath unless fasting. Let the witnesses, before they swear, be examined separately as to what they intend to say concerning the matter about which they must give testimony.  
[Note: The words from “before they swear” through “they swear” are absent from witness 1.]

[Note: In Migne, paragraphs 13–17 are printed in parallel with paragraphs 5–6.]

[Col. 0317B] Codices Supplementum latinum 75 and Mettensis.

13. Let no one be compelled to come to a placitum unless he has a case to prosecute; except the scabini and the counts’ vassals.

14. Let no one dare to give assistance to one who does wrong, or to answer on his behalf.

15. Let our envoys act vigorously in all things through mercy.

16. Concerning witnesses, as is contained in the preceding chapters: let them come fasting to the placitum, and after they have eaten let them be unable either to give testimony or to swear an oath. And let them be examined separately before they swear.

17. Let no one receive a reward for suppressing justice.

7. Let no one of our officials—neither count, judge, nor scabinus—presume to delay anyone’s justice, if it can immediately be completed according to right; nor let them presume to accept rewards from anyone by any device on this account.  
[Note: “Our envoy” in two witnesses, Ch. and the others, Langobardic law, and Ansegisus. “Scabini” in witness 1. “Immediately” is read “the present evil” in witness 2. Witness 2 places this chapter before the following one; so also Ch. and the other Langobardic witnesses.]

8. [Note: “Pontum” in witness 1.] Let no one be compelled to go to a bridge over a river in order to cross it for the sake of tolls, when he can cross that river more conveniently elsewhere. Likewise, in an open plain where there is neither a bridge nor a ferry, we absolutely command that no toll be exacted.  
[Note: “Tolls” is read in witness 1.]

9. Let no market be held anywhere on Sunday, except where it existed from ancient times and ought lawfully to exist.  
[Note: “Expolitus,” “expullus,” and “expulsus” are variant readings.]

10. Let the priest who has given holy chrism in order to overturn a judgment, after he has been stripped of his rank, lose his hand.  
[Note: “His hands” in Ch. The remainder of this note is absent from Migne’s printed edition.]

11. Let judges, advocates, provosts, centenarii, and scabini be appointed to exercise their offices—men of the best quality who can be found and who fear God—together with the count and the people; let gentle and good men be chosen.  
[Note: “Judges” is read “vice-domini” in witness 3. Variants occur for “centenarii,” including “vicarii.” The words “together with … good men” are absent from Ch. and the other Langobardic witnesses.]

12. Let no one, out of desire for money and his own avarice, first be given a price and prepare a future claim for himself, so that he may then receive double or triple; but let him purchase them only when the present harvest is available.  
[Note: “Purchase” is read “buying” in witness 3, A., V., and Vn.; “contention” in Ch. The remainder is absent from Ch. and the other Langobardic witnesses.]

13. In places where public malluses are customarily held, let such a roofed structure be established that it can be used for holding placita both in winter and in summer.  
[Note: “In winter” and “in summer” are corruptly written in witness 1.]

[Note: In Migne, paragraphs 21–25 are printed in parallel with paragraphs 10–13.]

[Col. 0318A] 21. If a priest gives chrism, let him be degraded by the bishop, and afterward let him lose his hand at the hands of the judge, if he did this in order to overturn a judgment.

22. Let judges, vice-domini, provosts, advocates, centenarii, and scabini—good, truthful, and gentle men—be chosen and appointed with the count and the people to exercise their offices.

24. Concerning the earlier debts of the poor, and concerning business to be conducted before the harvest is gathered: we have expressly forbidden these things beforehand, speaking with our own mouth. Let each person, in the present year, whether for his free man or his slave, provide assistance against the scarcity of food.

25. Let the places where placita are to be held be properly restored, as we stated with our own mouth, so that they may be used for holding placita both in winter and in summer.

14. Let oaths that have been referred to the palace be completed at the palace. If the coniuratores refuse to come with him, let them, by the lord’s command, be compelled to come to the palace with a written notice or seal.  
[Note: “Placitum” for “palace” in witness 1 and Weissenzug. “Co-oath-takers” is written differently in witness 1. “Or” for “with” in witness 2. “Placitum” for “palace” in witness 1.]

15. But if an advocate has an oath against another and is unable to swear, or has rendered something by legal process, let him not lose his benefice on that account.  
[Note: Everything else, except chapters 22 and 24, is absent from witness 2.]

16. Concerning churches not yet properly restored; concerning cases that do not cease day by day.  
[Note: In Codex 3 the following is inserted here: “Concerning the peace of robbers.”]

[Col. 0319A] 17. Concerning the harmony of our faithful; concerning fugitives whom people do not cease to receive and conceal.  
[Note: “Fugitive” is misspelled in witness 1.]

18. Concerning foreign ships.  
[Note: “Concerning wandering pilgrims who do not go for God’s sake” in witness 3.]  
Concerning homicides.

19. Concerning transfers or purchases: let no one make them secretly.

20. Concerning coinage, or measures of modii and sestarii.

[Col. 0320A] 21. Concerning our benefices that have not been properly constructed.  
[Note: “Properly repaired.” “And let the nonae or tithes be given in full. Concerning clerics and vassals: let no one be received without his lord’s permission,” in witness 3.]

22. Concerning hospitality and the reception of travelers, both our envoys and all other good men.  
[Note: “All” in witness 1.]

23. That we send our envoys in our place.

24. Concerning those who sell wine and grain before they harvest them, and who thereby become poor.  
[Note: “Who make the poor” in witness 1.]

25. Let every person believe in God’s judgment without any doubt.

26. Concerning transfers: let them not be made secretly on account of various disputes.

27. Let no one make deceitful purchases from a poor man, except by legal process.

# LANGOBARDIC CAPITULARY (A.D. 809)

[Col. 0319]

These chapters, marked with the numbers 86 and 87 in the Codex of Saint Paul, follow the capitulary of the year 808 and were later repeated by the emperor Lothar. It is evident that they were promulgated by Pippin, who died the following year.

[Col. 0319B] 1. How the lord king commands all his officials who have charge of his estates: first, concerning what has now been published in our time, namely, that each official shall swear and say by the Gospels: “Whatever I discover to have been taken from anyone contrary to right, I shall make known to my lord the king, so that it may be released”; yet he must state in that oath that he has not consented out of friendship, nor for a relative, nor having been corrupted by a reward, but only because he certainly knows that something was taken contrary to right. When it has been reported to us, let it be released by our command.

2. Therefore we decree that possessions derived from public property shall be investigated for forty years, because [the reading *peccatis eminentis* is materially uncertain], no one remembers anything from forty years ago, and few are found who have so many years. We decree that, except where the matter has already been publicly adjudicated by law, if any invasion or fraud concerning public property occurred within thirty years, let the matter itself be sought out and brought to our attention. Yet he must not presume beforehand to mark it with his sign, seize the possession, or pledge it, because we wish to hear this matter ourselves and order it according to God’s will. For it has appeared to us that, if we ourselves hear the matter, with God favoring us we can investigate it without sin and order it in such a way that we may receive a reward, since our judges, nor the arimanni, nor our officials can discipline them as strictly as we can.

But whoever has been proved to have held anyone’s possession for thirty years or more, let him have it henceforth; let no official presume to disturb him, whether concerning a slave or by marking it with his sign, or otherwise molesting him. Whoever presumes to do so, let that official himself pay his wergeld, except where a false royal order is found, in which case the matter is plainly open to investigation.  
[Notes: “That is, to place his sign there and seize the possession.” The text is corrupt in several places; “wergeld” is the reading of the source term *widriguildum*.]

# CAPITULARY CONCERNING THE DISCIPLINE OF THE PALACE AT AACHEN (A.D. 809)

[Col. 0319]

Baluzius had published, under the title “Capitulary concerning the palace officials,” from the Codex formerly belonging to Saint Vincent of Laon, now Paris, Royal Library no. 4788, ninth century, fragments of an edict which, now that I have examined the same codex again, has emerged complete. It seemed assignable to the later years of the emperor, when, as the anonymous author of the *Life of Louis the Pious* testifies, the court and palace were overflowing with worthless men.

[Col. 0319C] 1. Let each palace official, with the most diligent investigation, first examine his own men and afterward his peers, to see whether he can find among them or among their dependents any sick person or prostitute lying concealed.  
[Note: *Igrotum*, that is, “sick.”]  
If any man or woman of this sort is found, let that person be guarded so that he or she cannot flee, until the matter is reported to us. Let the man who kept such a man or woman with him, if he refuses to correct himself, be held under guard in our palace. We likewise wish the officials of our beloved wife and of our sons to do the same.

2. Let Ratbert, the official, conduct a similar investigation through his office—that is, through the houses of our slaves—both at Aachen and in the small neighboring estates belonging to Aachen. But let Peter and Gunzo do likewise through the *scruas* and other residences of our officials.  
[Note: These appear to differ from the *screonae*.]  
And let Ernald conduct the investigation through the lodgings of all merchants, whether they trade in the market or elsewhere, both Christians and Jews. Let the lodging-master likewise do this with his juniors through the residences of bishops, abbots, and counts who are not officials, and of our vassals, whenever their lords are not in those residences.

3. We wish and command that no one among those who serve us in our palace presume to receive anyone who has committed theft, homicide, adultery, or any other crime, and who on that account has come to our palace and wishes to lie concealed there. If a free man transgresses this constitution and receives such a person, let him know that he must carry the same man found with him on his neck, first around the palace and then to the stocks into which the criminal is to be put. If it is a slave who has contemptuously failed to observe this command of ours, let him likewise carry the malefactor on his neck to the stocks; afterward let the slave be brought to the market and flogged there according to his deserts.

We likewise wish that lustful men and prostitutes, wherever they are found, be carried by those with whom they are found to the market, where they are to be flogged. Or, if the person refuses, we wish him to be flogged together with her in the same place.  
[Note: “The lustful,” literally “those given to sexual desire.”]

4. Whoever finds men fighting in the palace and is able but unwilling to reconcile them shall know that he must share responsibility for the damage done between them. If he sees men fighting but cannot reconcile them, and refuses to learn who those are who are fighting among themselves so that he can report it, we likewise wish him to share in the compensation for the damage committed between them.

5. Whoever receives or brings to our palace a man coming from anywhere, and does not take care to expel him, shall either produce him, if damage has been done by him in our palace, or, if he cannot produce him, pay compensation for the damage that the man himself caused.

[Col. 0322B] 6. Let the counts of the palace take every care that, after the accusers have received a written notice from them, they do not remain in our palace.

7. Let masters be appointed over beggars and poor people who will take great care and make careful provision for them, so that … and impostors cannot conceal themselves among them.  
[Note: Three or four letters could not be read.]

8. Every week, on Saturday, let our agents or officials report what they have accomplished in this investigation. Let them investigate and examine what they report to us so diligently and truthfully that, if it pleases us, they will be able to affirm in our presence that they reported nothing to us except the truth.

# CAPITULARY CONCERNING COINAGE

[Col. 0321]

I have with difficulty saved only the remnants of this edict from scraps of the Codex formerly belonging to Saint Vincent of Laon, now Paris, Royal Library no. 4788, ninth century. I greatly hope that, with the aid of another codex, the complete capitulary may eventually come to light. I have indicated the lacunae wherever possible. Letters printed in italics I have either supplied by conjecture or regarded as readings of doubtful certainty.

[Col. 0321C] 1. These chapters must be observed in each locality: that the coinage of that city be produced publicly under the count’s supervision.

2. Let the moneyers themselves presume to produce coinage publicly neither elsewhere nor below nor outside that city, except at the place appointed for them.

3. If anyone is found, whether one of the moneyers themselves or any other person, producing coinage in that district, [the text continues: “with all his property and the whole m…; further …”].  
[The surviving text is materially corrupt and incomplete.]

4. Let the moneyers not be able to strike coin. Therefore we wish the count … to have this investigated … through this [the matter] is falsified … and proclaimed …

5. [Lacuna.] Nothing … and with fish … a hide on the back and head, and let “counterfeiter of coin” be written on his face. In the other cities where no coinage has been authorized, let the count act in the same manner. The count himself shall not only take responsibility for what the moneyers do, but shall also ensure that the count … and shall investigate through his peers or merchants traveling here and there, so that he may bring forward … and subject the property to the established penalty …  
[The remainder is fragmentary and materially uncertain.]

[Note: This capitulary was formerly published by Johannes Cornesius as though it were the work of Jesse, bishop of Amiens. It is not Jesse’s, however, but, in my opinion, was issued by Charlemagne to the royal envoys. The error arose because, in the codex used by Cordesius, it was attached to Jesse’s letter of Amiens, mentioned above. But it does not appear in the old codex of the monastery of Saint Gall, and Jesse’s letter ends with the chapter that bears this title in Cordesius’s edition: “Concerning the confirmation of the body and blood of Christ.” Quite correctly, for this is the last of the questions about which Charlemagne had asked the bishops, as is clear from his letter to Odilbert, archbishop of Milan, and from Bishop Theodulf of Orléans’ book *Concerning the Order of Baptism*. Thus this ought to have been the end of Jesse’s letter. Later, some learned man added another treatise concerning the tradition of baptism because of the similarity of its subject, and then added that capitulary. Since it was joined in the old codex to Jesse’s letter, it was easy to suppose that all these writings had the same author. — Baluzius.]

# ECCLESIASTICAL CAPITULARY (A.D. 809, November, Aachen)

[Col. 0323]

In November of the year 809, a council was convened at Aachen concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit. The condition of the churches and the conduct of those who serve God in them were also discussed there, although Einhard reports that nothing was settled because of the magnitude of the matters involved. The following may belong to that discussion: (1) a fragment of chapters published in Cordesius’s edition of the works of Hincmar, p. 683, and again brought to light by Baluzius from Sirmond’s papers, together with a fifth capitulary of uncertain date; (2) the *Capitulary concerning Priests*, preserved by Ansegisus, book I, chapters 140–158, which we have judged should be reproduced in full.

For Einhard’s words should not be understood so absolutely that we conclude that nothing at all was settled; this will be clear from comparison with another passage of his, in the *Life of Charlemagne*, chapter 29, in the *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, Scriptores, vol. II, p. 458. Only those matters that were settled should be thought to have constituted the smallest part of the undertaking. It appears from the order in which these chapters are reported by Ansegisus within the Aachen capitulary of 809, published above in columns 315–316, and within the Aachen capitulary of 810, that they were promulgated at the autumn assembly.

[Col. 0323A] 1. First, all must be admonished concerning the soundness of their faith, so that they themselves may hold and understand it and announce it in living speech to the peoples subject to them. Let each person know those whom he has in his ministry, whether men or women, so that he may know the confession and conduct of each, since he will have to render an account to God for them all.

2. Second, let the priests themselves display to the peoples subject to them such conduct as can be imitated—namely, as the Apostle said, in chastity and sobriety. Let them not serve gluttony and the desires of this world. Let them show in themselves what they admonish others to observe, and let them guard themselves from every avarice and covetousness. For many labor day and night to acquire temporal things—namely, property, slaves, wine, and grain—with interest, from which both God, all divine Scripture, and the holy canons prohibit them.

Let them also avoid the company of women and not permit them to live with them, as canonical authority requires.

3. Third, let them impress upon all subject to them the Lord’s Prayer, that is, the *Our Father*, and the *Credo in Deum*, the “I believe in God,” and have both men and women, as well as children, recite them back to them.

4. Fourth, let the priests themselves withdraw from feasting and drinking, as the Apostle admonishes. For some of them remain drinking with certain neighbors until midnight and beyond. Others, who appear religious and holy, do not indeed remain there at that time, but nevertheless return to their churches full or drunk; and neither by day nor by night do they perform the divine office in the church entrusted to them. Some even sleep in the very place to which they have gone for the banquet.

5. Fifth, let the priests themselves have such schoolboys—properly nourished and instructed [Baluzius: “impressed upon”]—that, if it should happen that they cannot reach their own church at the proper time to perform the office, namely, terce, sext, none, and vespers, the schoolboys themselves may ring the bell at the proper time and perform the office honorably for God.

6. Sixth, ascertain diligently what each priest has done in his ministry after his ordination. For those who were poor before ordination afterward purchase for themselves an inheritance, slaves, and other possessions from the goods with which they ought to have served the churches. They have made no progress in their learning, collected no books, and increased none of the things that pertain to religious worship; instead, they live continually by insults, oppression, and plunder.

7. Seventh, let them diligently take care of their household members—that is, those who are with them in their residence, whether schoolboys or other servants—guarding them against every vice, especially drunkenness, lust, and various impurities. For, as the Apostle says, whoever neglects the care of his household will be unable to benefit the conduct of others.

8. Eighth, let them be hospitable, because many who know that a guest is approaching their church flee. But, contrary to what the Apostle and the rest of divine Scripture command them to practice, they are afraid to assist the poor.

9. Ninth, the Apostle commands all the faithful that their speech should always be gracious, seasoned with salt—that is, that a Christian should say things appropriate to religion  
[Note: Another manuscript reads “that serve religion.”]  
so that someone may thereby have his mind seasoned and be cleansed from the corruption of sins. If all the faithful …  
[The remainder is absent.]

# CHAPTERS CONCERNING PRIESTS

[Col. 0325]

I have taken these from Ansegisus, book I, chapters 140–158, and from Appendix I, chapter 20; two of them are also found among Charlemagne’s chapters added to the Langobardic laws, chapters 96 and 137.

[Col. 0325A] 1. Let no priest give an offering at the entrance of a church.

2. Let no layman presume to install or remove a priest in a church except with the consent of the bishop.

3. Let the bishops make provision for what honor priests are to grant for the churches of their lords.

4. Let tithes be in the bishop’s power, so that he may determine how they are distributed by the priests.

5. Let churches and altars be built better. Let no priest presume to place grain or hay in a church.

6. Let churches or altars whose consecration is uncertain be consecrated.

7. Let priests preach throughout their parishes to women, so that they may prepare linens for the altars.

8. Let no priest receive anyone belonging to another parish for Mass, unless he is traveling or has a placitum there.

9. Let no priest presume to sing Mass in another’s parish, unless he is traveling; nor let him dare to receive a tithe belonging to another.

10. Let each church have a defined territory, specifying from which villages it is to receive tithes.

11. Let each priest leave to the church as its property the goods he acquired after the day of his consecration.

12. Let no priest or layman invite a penitent to drink wine or eat meat unless, at that time, he has given one or two denarii on his behalf, according to the nature of the penance.

13. Let no priest write charters, nor act as his lord’s tenant or administrator.

[Col. 0326A] 14. From now on, let no one bury a dead person in a church.

15. Let each priest have chapters concerning major and minor vices, by which he may be able to recognize or preach to his subjects the dangers of the devil, so that they may avoid them.

16. Let the priest always have the Eucharist prepared, so that whenever someone falls ill, or a small child is ill, he may immediately give that person Communion, lest he die without Communion.

17. On the Lord’s Supper, let the priest carry two flasks with him: one for chrism, the other for oil for anointing catechumens or the sick, according to the Apostle’s teaching. When someone falls ill, let him bring in the priests of the church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the Lord’s name.

18. Let those who hold church benefices give the ninth and the tenth from them to the church whose goods they are. Those who hold such a benefice shall labor for half of it, and from their share give tithes to their own priest.

19. These are the festivals of the year that must be honored everywhere: the Nativity of the Lord; Saint Stephen’s; Saint John the Evangelist’s; the feast of the Innocents; the octave of the Lord; Epiphany; the octave of Epiphany; the Purification of Saint Mary; the eight days of Easter; the greater litany; the Ascension of the Lord; Pentecost; Saint John the Baptist’s; Saints Peter and Paul’s; Saint Martin’s; and Saint Andrew’s. We have left the question of the Assumption of Saint Mary for further inquiry.

[Col. 0326C] 20. We have left for inquiry the judgment concerning penance: by what penitential book or in what manner penitents are to be judged; and concerning incestuous unions, which persons may be joined and which may not.

# AACHEN CAPITULARY (A.D. 810)

[Col. 0325]

Published by Baluzius from the Codex of Saint Vincent of Metz, this has now been revised by us with the aid of Codex 1, Paris, among the *Supplementa Latina*, no. 75. We have judged that we must depart from Baluzius in this respect: the rubrics of the capitulary, which are arranged in another order and attached to it in the codices, should not be treated as part of the capitulary itself, but as references to it.

# CHAPTERS ANNOUNCED IN THE TENTH YEAR OF THE REIGN OF OUR LORD CHARLES, MOST SERENE AUGUSTUS, AT THE PALACE OF AACHEN

[Col. 0325C]

1. [Note: Compare below, col. 328, chapters 8 and 10.] Concerning the accusers who cause great obstruction in the palace before the ears of the lord emperor: let the envoys or counts send their own envoys against those who go about lying, so that they may convict them.

2. Before the vicar and centenarius, let no judgment concerning ownership or liberty be concluded or acquired except always in the presence of the imperial envoys or in the presence of the counts.  
[Note: Compare below, chapter 15.]

[Col. 0326D] 3. [Note: Compare below, chapter 7.] Concerning homicides committed in the present year among ordinary people, which have been caused by the mortal plague.  
[Note: “Mortal” is misspelled in witness 1.]

4. [Note: Compare below, chapters 1 and 6.] Let the priests admonish the people to give alms and to offer prayers, because of the various plagues that we continually suffer on account of our sins.

5. [Note: Compare below, chapter 2.] Let each priest, according to his rank, strive to preach and teach the people entrusted to him.

6. [Note: Compare below, chapter 4.] Concerning drunkenness: first of all, let the lords forbid themselves this, and let them show their juniors an example of good sobriety.

7. [Note: Compare below, chapter 3.] All must generally be admonished, according to evangelical authority: “Let your works so shine before men that they may glorify your Father who is in heaven.”

8. Concerning fugitives who are detained and concealed throughout various provinces contrary to the command of the lord emperor: whoever received or retains them after the appointed time has passed shall pay the lord’s ban.

9. Let peace and justice within the realm be fully carried out, as we have often commanded in other chapters.

[Col. 0327B] 10. [Note: Compare below, chapter 16.] Concerning robbers who have committed great blasphemy: whoever apprehends one of them shall suffer no loss on that account.

11. [Note: Compare below, chapters 11 and 12.] Concerning the military levy: let the envoys diligently investigate who could perform military service but did not, and let him pay the ban if he has the means to pay it. If he has no means by which he can pay it, let the debt be secured and entered in the record, and let nothing be exacted on this account until it comes to the lord emperor’s attention.

12. Let those who have committed *herisliz* be sent to the king through sureties.  
[Note: Compare below, chapter 14.]

13. [Note: Compare below, chapter 9.] Concerning destroyed benefices and restored allods.

14. [Note: Compare below, chapter 13.] Concerning the exaction of compensation payments.

15. Concerning timber for building ships.  
[Note: The word is formed from *materia* with the addition of *-mine*.]

[Col. 0327C] 16. [Note: Compare below, chapter 5.] Concerning the common people: let each person discipline his juniors, so that they may obey and consent more and more fully to the imperial commands and orders.

17. Concerning alms to be sent to Jerusalem for restoring the churches of God.

18. Let no one consent to evil men, but rather resist them as far as he can. Let the poor, orphans, widows, and churches of God have peace.

# ALSO, CONCERNING THE TENTH YEAR

*(Proposed chapters.)*

1. Concerning the general tribulation that we all suffer, namely, the mortality of animals and the other plagues.  
[Note: That is, of oxen. Einhard, under the year 810, says: “So great was the plague among the oxen on that expedition that scarcely any remained for so large an army; nearly all perished, down to the last. And not only there, but throughout all the provinces subject to the emperor, a devastating mortality raged most violently among animals of that kind.” Agobard, in *Concerning Hail and Thunder*, chapter 16, says: “A certain foolishness was spread a few years ago, when there was a mortality among oxen, so that people said that Grimoald, duke of Benevento, had sent men with powders which they scattered through fields and mountains, meadows and springs.” — Baluzius.]

2. Concerning preaching throughout each parish.

3. Concerning the Gospel: let your light shine before men.

4. Concerning the avoidance of all vices and drunkenness.

[Col. 0328B] 5. Concerning each person’s correction of himself and his household.

6. Concerning prayers offered for one another.

7. Concerning the investigation of the innocent who have been killed.

8. Concerning the manner in which accusers are to be punished.

9. Concerning benefices that have not been properly repaired, which must be investigated.

10. Concerning the avoidance of lies and perjury.

11. Concerning the exaction of the military levy.

12. Concerning the poor who are entirely unable to pay.

13. Concerning the exaction of compensation payments.

14. Concerning those who have committed *herisliz*: let them provide sureties.  
[Note: “Brisliz” in witness 1.]

15. Concerning property and slaves: let them not be claimed before the vicars and centenarii.

[Col. 0328C] 16. Concerning robbers: how they are to be disciplined.
