# CAPITULARY CONCERNING THE INSTRUCTION OF ENVOYS (AACHEN)

[Col. 0327]

Published by Baluzius from the Codex of Saint Vincent of Metz, this has now been revised by us with the aid of Codex Paris, among the *Supplementa Latina*, no. 75.

[Col. 0327D] 1. Let the envoys in their mission be such as it is fitting for vigorous envoys of the emperor to be, and let them accomplish what has been entrusted to them. If they cannot do so, let them make known to the lord emperor what difficulty prevents them from accomplishing it.

2. Whatever they must command or entrust to anyone by his order, let them announce and command with authority. Let them not make men of inferior rank their companions—men who always wish to discuss and reconsider whatever matters arise—but let them associate with themselves those who wish to bring each matter to completion.

3. When they have ordered justice to be done to the poor, let them command once or twice that justice be carried out. On the third occasion, if it has still not been done, let them themselves go to the place and to the man who refused to do justice, and forcibly take from him what he unjustly took from another, returning it to the person to whom it ought to have belonged by justice.

4. Whoever owes the lord emperor’s ban or compensation payment: let that payment be received and brought to him, so that he himself may give it to whomever he wishes.

5. Whoever attempts to resist those who wish to do justice, let them report him to the lord emperor. Likewise, whoever wishes to defend another against justice at a placitum shall incur the lawful penalty, whoever he may be—whether a man of the lord emperor, of any of his sons or daughters, or of any other powerful person.

# ENCYCLICAL CONCERNING GENERAL FASTS

[Col. 0329]

(See among the letters of Charlemagne, volume 98 of *Patrologia*.)

# DOUBLE AACHEN CAPITULARY (A.D. 811)

[Col. 0329]

The first of the two capitularies, under the title “Capitulary of Questions concerning those matters which Charlemagne established should be asked for the common benefit of all,” was published by Sirmondus and Baluzius from the Codex of Saint Vincent of Metz; we have revised it with the aid of Codex Paris, among the *Supplementa Latina*, no. 75.

# CONCERNING THE QUESTIONS OF THE LORD EMPEROR IN THE ELEVENTH YEAR

[Col. 0329A]

1. First of all, we wish to separate our bishops, abbots, and counts and address them individually. What causes make one unwilling to provide assistance to another, whether on the frontier or in the army, where each ought to do something useful in defense of the fatherland?

2. What is the cause of those very frequent disputes in which one person claims whatever he sees his equal possessing?

3. Concerning the person who receives into his household another’s man fleeing to him.

4. They must be asked in what matters or places ecclesiastics impede the ministry of laymen, or laymen that of ecclesiastics. Here it must be examined and discovered to what extent a bishop or abbot ought to involve himself in secular affairs, or to what extent a count or another layman may involve himself in ecclesiastical business. Here the sharpest inquiry must be made into the meaning and the persons to whom the Apostle’s statement applies: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs.”  
[Note: 2 Timothy 2:4. The manuscript reading *inveniendum* is corrected by editors and witness 1 to *interveniendum*.]

5. What is it that every Christian promises at baptism, and what things he renounces.  
[Note: The phrase “what each Christian promises” is absent from witness 1.]

6. By pursuing or neglecting what things he makes that very renunciation or abrenunciation invalid.

7. The person who believes rightly in God is not one who thinks he may disregard his commands with impunity, or who despises as though they would not come to pass the things that God has threatened.

8. That we must examine whether we are truly Christians. This can very easily be recognized by considering our life and conduct, if we are willing carefully to examine our way of life before God.

9. Concerning the life and conduct of our shepherds, that is, the bishops, who ought to give the people of God a good example not only by teaching but also by living. For we believe that the Apostle said to them what he says [Note: Philippians 3:17]: “Be imitators of me, and observe those who walk in this way, as you have our example.”

10. Concerning the life of those who are called canons, what it ought to be like.

[Col. 0329D] 11. Concerning the way of life of monks, and whether any can be monks apart from those who observe the Rule of Saint Benedict. It must also be investigated whether there were monks in Gaul before the transmission of the Rule of Saint Benedict reached these parishes.

12. Preserve these matters as is fitting for you; and I trust in you, most devout bishops, and insofar as I am able to investigate, I do not hesitate to send or write to you. Farewell in the Lord.

## BRIEF LIST OF CHAPTERS IN WHICH WE WISH TO ADDRESS AND ADMONISH OUR FAITHFUL BISHOPS AND ABBOTS CONCERNING THE COMMON BENEFIT OF US ALL

1. First, it must be recalled that last year [Note: Cf. above, chapter 4] we observed three three-day fasts, praying God that he might deign to show us in what respects our conduct before him ought to be corrected; and this is what we now desire to do.

2. First of all, it must be asked of the ecclesiastics, that is, the bishops and abbots, that they disclose to us how they ought to live in their conduct, so that we may be able to know whether we ought to believe something good or something else concerning them, with due restraint; and so that we may know to what extent any ecclesiastic—that is, a bishop, abbot, or monk—may involve himself in secular affairs; and what properly belongs to those who are called, and ought to be, shepherds of the Church and fathers of monasteries. Thus we may ask nothing else of them than what they are permitted to do, and so that none of them may ask from us those things in which we ought not to agree with them.

[Col. 0330C] 3. We wish to question those ecclesiastics who ought not only to learn the holy Scriptures themselves but also to teach them to others: who are those to whom the Apostle says, “Be imitators of me”; or who is the one of whom he likewise says, “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs”; and how the Apostle is to be imitated, or how one serves as a soldier for God.

4. Again [Note: This note is missing in Migne’s printed edition.], they must be asked to disclose truthfully to us what is meant among them by “leaving the world,” and by what signs those who leave the world can be distinguished from those who still pursue the world—whether solely by the fact that they do not bear arms and are not publicly married.

5. It must also be asked whether the person who is said to have left the world [Note: The *Book of Prayers of Marcellinus and Faustinus*, p. 83: “through contempt for secular things and human glory, which many strive after—even those who boast that they have renounced the world and the desire of the flesh.” Jerome, in his letter to Rusticus: “I have seen some who, after renouncing the world, changed nothing of their former way of life, except in clothing and verbal profession, not in reality.” Baluze.] has truly left it if he does not cease by any means or craft to increase his possessions each day, persuading the rich and poor—who are naturally more simple and are found to be less learned and cautious—by speaking of the blessedness of the heavenly kingdom, threatening eternal punishment in hell, and, in the name of God or of some saint, stripping them of their property, disinheriting their lawful heirs, and thereby compelling many, because of the poverty into which they have been driven, to commit shameful and criminal acts, so that they practice theft and robbery as though compelled by necessity because another has seized their paternal inheritance [Note: MSS 1 and 2 read *paternarum* (“of ancestral possessions”).] before it could come to them [Note: MS 1 reads *qui* (“who”) for *plerosque* (“many”). Jerome, in the epitaph for Nepotianus: “Let others add coin to coin and, while choking their purses, hunt down the wealth of matrons through their attentions; let monks be richer than they were as secular men.” Idem.]

6. Again, it must be asked how someone can be said to have left the world if, driven by greed to acquire property that he has seen another possess, he hires men for money to commit perjury and give false testimony, and seeks not a just advocate or administrator who fears God, but a cruel and greedy one who thinks little of perjury, and in investigating property asks not how much he acquires lawfully, but how much he acquires.

7. What should be said about those who, ostensibly out of love for God and the saints—whether martyrs or confessors—transfer bones and relics of holy bodies from one place to another, build new basilicas there, and urge as vigorously as they can all whom they are able to persuade to transfer their property there? The man in question wants to appear to be doing good and, because of this deed, to become deserving before God in the eyes of whatever bishops he can persuade. It becomes clear that this was done so that the property might pass under another authority.

8. We are astonished how it could happen that someone who confesses that he has left the world, and absolutely refuses to consent to being called secular by anyone, nevertheless wishes to retain armed men and his own property, although this belongs to those who have not yet entirely renounced the world. As for ecclesiastics, how it can rightly belong to them we utterly do not know, unless those who do not hesitate to usurp such things as though they were lawful explain it to us [Note: I have thought it right to restore the text thus. MS 1 reads, after correction, *armatus homo cum sit, et propria vellit retinere* (“though he is an armed man and wishes to retain his own property”); the earlier reading was damaged: *armatos hom… et p. retinere*.].

9. What does each person promise Christ in baptism, and for what reasons does he renounce? Although every Christian ought to consider this, it must nevertheless be asked especially of the ecclesiastics, who ought in their own lives to provide the laity with an example of this promise and renunciation. Here it must be considered with the greatest care and distinguished with the utmost precision what each of us, by pursuing or neglecting certain things, either preserves or makes void that very promise and renunciation; and who Satan is, or the adversary, whose works or pomp we renounced in baptism [Note: The source has *cuius* (“whose”); one manuscript reads *quae* (“which”).]. Care must also be taken lest, by acting perversely, any one of us follow the one whom we renounced long ago in baptism.

10. In which canon, or in whose rule as a holy father, is it established that anyone may unwillingly be made either a cleric or a monk? Or where did Christ command, or which Apostle preach, that a congregation should be formed in the Church—whether of canons or of monks—from unwilling, reluctant, and worthless persons?

[Col. 0332B] 11. What benefit does it bring to the Church of Christ that a person who ought to be the shepherd or teacher of some venerable place is more concerned to have many rather than good men in his community, and does not so much cultivate, train, correct, and make them better [Note: That is, exercise, cultivate, correct, and make them better.] as delight in the multitude of men; that he is more concerned that his cleric or monk sing and read well than that he live justly and blessedly? Certainly, the discipline of singing and reading should not merely be despised in the Church; it ought rather to be practiced in every way. But if both qualities can belong to any venerable place, it nevertheless seems more tolerable to us to endure imperfection in singing than in living.

And although it is good for the buildings of churches to be beautiful, the adornment and summit of good conduct must nevertheless be preferred to buildings, because, as it seems to us, the construction of basilicas derives a certain custom from the Old Law, whereas correction of conduct belongs properly to the New Testament and to Christian discipline. If Christ and the Apostles, and those who rightly followed the Apostles, are to be followed in ecclesiastical discipline, then in many matters we must act differently from the way we have acted until now: much must be removed from our usage and custom, and no less must be done that we have not done until now.

12. By what rule did monks live in Gaul before the Rule of Saint Benedict had been transmitted there, since we read that Saint Martin was both a monk and had monks under him, and that he lived long before Saint Benedict?

[Col. 0332D] 13. Concerning the conduct of nuns and of the servants of God.

## CAPITULARY CONCERNING THE MILITARY EXPEDITION (A.D. 811, AACHEN)

[Col. 0333]

Published by Baluze from the manuscripts of the Palatine Library of the Vatican and of Saint Vincent of Metz; we have revised it again with the help of the Paris manuscript among the *Supplementa Latina*, no. 75.

## ALSO, CONCERNING THE ABOVE, FROM THE ELEVENTH YEAR

[Col. 0333A]

Concerning the reasons why men are accustomed to abandon their obedience in the military expedition [Note: So the manuscripts; *expeditionem* (“expedition”) seems to be the correct reading.].

1. First, there are disputes, and they say that bishops, abbots, and their advocates have no authority over their tonsured clerics and other men. Likewise, counts have no authority over their own men of the county.

2. They complain that the poor have been stripped of their property. They raise this complaint equally against bishops and abbots and their advocates, and against counts and their centenarii.

3. They also say that, if anyone is unwilling to give his property to a bishop, abbot, count, judge, or centenarius, they seek pretexts against that poor man, by which they can condemn him, and continually make him go to the army until, having become poor, he willingly or unwillingly hands over or sells his property; while others who have handed over their property remain at home without anyone troubling them.

4. They say that bishops and abbots, or counts, leave their free men at home under the designation of *ministeriales* (household officials). The abbesses do likewise. These officials are falconers, huntsmen, toll collectors, administrators, deans, and others who receive the royal envoys and their followers.

5. Others also say that they compel the poorer men and make them go to the army, while they release those who have something that they can give for their own use.

6. The counts themselves say that some of their men of the county do not obey them and do not wish to fulfill the ban of the lord emperor, saying that they ought to answer to the lord emperor’s envoys concerning the military levy, but not to the count. Even if the count places his own household under their ban, they show him no respect unless he enters their house and does whatever he pleases.

7. There are also others who say that they are men of Pippin [Note: Pippin died in 810.] and Louis, and then claim that they go to the service of their lords when the other men of the county ought to go to the army.

8. Again, there are others who remain behind and say that their lords stay at home, and that they ought to go with their lords wherever the command of the lord emperor may be. There are others who for this reason commend themselves to certain lords whom they know will not go to the army. Above all, those men of the county thereby become more disobedient to the count and evade the envoys more than they had previously done.

9. Concerning those men who kill their relatives—their mother, maternal aunt, paternal aunt, or anyone of their family—in order that they may not be pursued on account of them. There are also others who ought not to be implicated through that kinship, yet are implicated because of that pretext.

## CAPITULARY CONCERNING THE MILITARY LEVIES (811)

[Col. 0333]

This capitulary appears in Book III of Ansegisus, chapters 64–66, and in Appendix II, chapters 34 and 35, after the capitularies of the years 809 and 810 and before those of the years 811 and 812. I have taken its Lombard edition from the capitularies of Charlemagne with the Lombard laws added.

[Col. 0333C] 1. If anyone comes against a royal envoy with a levy and arms, and refuses, or wishes to refuse, the assignment entrusted to him, and it is proved against him that he knowingly came to resist the royal envoy, he shall pay with his life [Note: “And his property shall pass to the public,” according to V. and E.]. If he denies it, he shall strive to clear himself with twelve oath-helpers [Note: “Let him do so,” according to V. and Ansegisus]. But because he came armed with a levy to resist the royal envoy, he shall pay the royal ban [Note: “He came to resist,” according to V. and Vn.]. The lord emperor judged the same way concerning his vassals. If a slave does this, he shall be subjected to corporal punishment.

[Col. 0334C] 2. [Note: In editions of the Lombard law, chapters 2–6 are numbered 30–34; there, and in manuscript Vn., a title is added: “Chapters concerning the military levies.”] If anyone breaks into another person’s house [Note: V., Vn., and E. read “in the emperor’s expedition”], and whatever he takes from it by force, carries off, or steals [Note: “Or has stolen,” according to V., Vn., and E.], he shall make full restitution in triplicate, according to the law and the *eua* [Note: “And the *eua*” is absent from the Lombard-law manuscripts.], to the person whose house was broken into and plundered, and shall additionally pay our ban [Note: The printed edition has “our royal ban”; it is absent from V.]. If a slave does this, he shall receive the preceding sentence and shall additionally make compensation according to his own law.

3. If a free man causes anyone such damage that he is unable to make full compensation, he shall strive to give himself as a slave by way of pledge [Note: V., Vn., and E. read “he shall strive to pledge himself to him”] until he fulfills the full compensation [Note: So Ansegisus, V., Vn., E., and M.; the other manuscripts read “let him do so.”].

4. If anyone, during the expedition [Note: In the Fl. manuscript this chapter precedes the preceding one.], seizes or steals crops or grain in the army in violation of the royal ban, or feeds upon them [Note: The printed edition reads “uses them”], or devastates them with horses, he shall make compensation in triplicate for the assessed damage according to the law. If a free man does this, he shall be compelled to pay the royal ban for it [Note: These words are absent in the damaged passage of A.]. A slave, however, shall restore the damage on the spot in triplicate according to his own law and, in place of the ban, shall be subjected to corporal punishment [Note: A. and Ansegisus read “for the damage”; the others read “in place of the ban.”].

## FRANKISH CHAPTERS

[Col. 0335A]

5. If a Saxon apprehends a man without theft or without any property of his own, saying that the man has caused him damage [Note: Corb. reads “that he may do so.”], and wishes to pursue the matter, he shall have the right to do so in court, in the field, or by the ordeal of the cross. If he does not wish to do this, the free man himself shall clear himself with his oath-helpers. If he apprehends anyone’s slave without any proof, the slave himself shall clear himself by boiling water or by another judgment.

6. If a Saxon finds horses in his crop and wishes to lead those horses away from it in order to prove his damage, and if any free man contradicts him or does him any harm on this account [Note: Absent in Corb.], he shall strive to make compensation to him in triplicate according to the law and the *eua* [Note: *Eouam* corrected to *euuam*; above, “that is, the law,” in Corb.], and shall additionally pay the royal ban. He shall also lose his hand because he was disobedient to the command of the lord emperor, which he ordered to be established for the sake of peace. If a slave does this, he shall restore everything in triplicate according to his own law and shall be subjected to corporal punishment.

## LOMBARD CHAPTERS

[Col. 0336A]

5. Likewise, whatever person is challenged concerning this matter [Note: V., Vn., and E. read “a person in the same expedition”; the printed edition has “the person challenged.”] shall either make immediate compensation or, alone, give an oath that neither he himself did it nor does he know who did it. The accuser, however, shall first swear that, to his knowledge, he did not unjustly accuse him [Note: A. adds: “And if he does not dare to swear, let him give the oath itself”; Fl. reads: “And if he does not dare to swear, let him pay fifteen solidi.”].

[Col. 0336B] 6. [Note: This chapter is absent from A., Fl., and Lond.; it was published from Est. and M.] Concerning those persons who remain far from the palace, as though on the road, waiting for their lord, and commit acts of plunder: the count or his official shall compel them to make compensation, without any excuse, for whatever they have done against the law. If they wish to dispute the injustice, he shall constrain them, whether they wish it or not, to render justice. If anyone, in his pride, contends so obstinately that he is killed there, let him lie without compensation; neither his lord nor his relative shall incur any feud or cause any disturbance on this account. If he does so, let him be marked as an enemy of us and of our people.

## ENCYCLICAL TO THE ARCHBISHOPS CONCERNING DOCTRINE

[Col. 0335]

(See this encyclical among the letters of Charlemagne in volume 98 of the *Patrologia*; Odilbert’s reply is in the appendix to the same letters, in the same volume.)

## CAPITULARY OF BOLOGNA (October)

[Col. 0335]

It was issued in the year 811 after the seventh day before the Ides of October, when Charles had entered the forty-fourth year of his reign, at Bologna, where, as Einhard testifies in the *Annals*, he was inspecting a recently constructed fleet. Published by Baluze from the manuscripts of the Vatican Palatine Library and of Saint Vincent of Metz, we now issue it again, revised on the authority of two Paris manuscripts: (1) Royal Library no. 4995, and (2) another manuscript of the same library among the *Supplementa Latina* no. 75, and restored to its proper year.

## CHAPTERS WHICH THE LORD EMPEROR ESTABLISHED AT BOLOGNA, WHICH IS ON THE SEASHORE, IN THE FORTY-FOURTH YEAR OF HIS REIGN, IN THE MONTH OF OCTOBER, IN THE FIFTH INDICTION [Note: “Sixth,” in the second manuscript and Baluze; incorrectly.]

[Col. 0335D]

1. Whoever among the free men has been summoned to the army by the ban and has refused to come shall pay the full military levy, that is, sixty solidi [Note: “The military levy, according to Frankish law, that is, sixty solidi,” as V., Vn., E., and M. consistently read.], or, if he does not have the means to pay that sum, shall hand himself over as a pledge into the service of the prince until, over time, that levy has been paid by him [Note: The words from “service” to “service” are absent in manuscript 1.]. Then he shall return again to the status of his freedom.

If the man who handed himself over into service because of the military levy dies in that service, his heirs shall not lose the inheritance belonging to him [Note: That is, “which belongs to his heirs.”], nor their freedom, nor shall they become liable for that military levy.

2. [Note: K. and M.; Lombard law, chapter 128; V., Vn., and E.; absent from the other manuscripts.] No count shall presume to exact the military levy on any pretext—whether for watch duty, the army division, guard duty [Note: That is, custody.], the provision of lodging [Note: “Military levy,” in manuscript 1.], or any other ban—unless our envoy first receives the military levy on our behalf and, by our command, gives him his third part of it [Note: Manuscript 1 reads “until.”].

The military levy itself shall not be exacted in land or slaves, but in gold and silver, clothing and arms, animals and livestock, or such kinds of property [Note: Manuscript 1 reads “useful goods in particular.”] as contribute to practical utility.

3. Whoever among those holding our honors has been summoned to the army and does not come to the appointed assembly shall abstain from meat and wine for as many days as he is proved to have arrived after the appointed assembly [Note: That is, “as many days as.”].

4. Whoever returns from the army without the permission or authorization of the prince—a deed which the Franks call *herisliz* [Note: The Weissenau manuscript in Alamannia reads *franci et alamanni heresliz* (“the Franks and Alamanni call it *heresliz*”)], shall be punished according to the ancient constitution, that is, the capital sentence.

5. Whoever among those who hold a benefice of the prince abandons his peer while the latter is proceeding in the army against common enemies, and refuses to go or remain with him, shall lose his honor and his benefice.

6. No one in the army is to ask his peer or any other man to drink. Whoever is found drunk in the army shall be excommunicated in such a way that he may use only water in drinking until he recognizes that he has done wrong [Note: That is, “drunk.”].

7. Concerning the royal vassals who still serve within the household but are nevertheless known to hold benefices [Note: C. and the Weissenau manuscript of Ansegisus read “who do not hold benefices”]: it has been established that, if any of them remain at home with the lord emperor, they are not to keep their household vassals with them, but must allow them to go with the count whose men of the county they are.

[Col. 0338A] 8. It has been established that, according to the ancient custom, preparations for an expedition are to be announced and observed: provisions for three months from the boundary-point, and arms and clothing for half a year. This is nevertheless to be observed in such a way that, for those who travel from the Rhine to the Loire, the beginning of their provisions is reckoned from the Loire. For those who travel from the Loire to the Rhine, it shall be stated that they must have three months’ provisions from the Rhine [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “let it be recognized.”].

Those who are beyond the Rhine and travel through Saxony are to know that the March is at the Elbe [Note: Manuscript 2 has “Libia,” falsely, as is evident]. Those who remain beyond the Loire and must proceed to Spain are to recognize the Pyrenees as their March.

9. Every free man found not to have been with his lord in the army in the present year shall be compelled to pay the full military levy. If his lord or count has left him at home, he himself shall pay the same levy for him [Note: Absent in manuscript 1.], and as many military levies shall be exacted from him as the number of men he left at home [Note: That is, “as many as.”]. Since this year we granted each lord permission to leave two men at home, we wish them to show these men to our envoys, because we grant the military levy only for those men.

10. It has been established that no bishop, abbot, abbess, or any rector or custodian of a church shall presume, without our permission, either to give or sell a coat of mail or sword to any outsider, except to his own vassals. If it happens that any church or holy place has more coats of mail than suffice for the men who administer that church, then the rector of that church is to ask the prince what should be done with them [Note: That is, “the same rector,” according to manuscripts 1 and 2.].

11. Whenever we wish to send a ship, the lords themselves are to go in those ships and be prepared for this [Note: Manuscript 1 reads “and for this purpose.”].

## CAPITULARY OF AACHEN (A.D. 812)

[Col. 0337]

Published by Baluze from the manuscripts of Saint Vincent of Metz and the Vatican Palatine Library; we have revised it again with the help of one manuscript of the Paris Royal Library among the *Supplementa Latina*, no. 75, and of the manuscripts containing the Lombard capitularies, namely the Ambrosian and the others, as well as Ansegisus.

## ALSO, CHAPTERS ESTABLISHED FOR THE ADMINISTRATION OF JUSTICE WITHIN THE REALM

[Col. 0337D]

1. Concerning the limitation of cases and disputes, we decree that, from the death of the lord King Pippin of blessed memory and the beginning of our reign, cases or disputes made and arising between the parties are to be examined and concluded by a suitable judgment [Note: So Ansegisus; manuscript 1 and Baluze read “their peers.”]. Cases entrusted before that time—that is, before the death of the aforesaid lord King Pippin—are either not to be reopened at all or are to be preserved pending our inquiry.

2. If bishops, abbots, counts, or any other powerful persons have a case among themselves and do not wish to make peace, they are to be ordered to come into our presence. Their dispute is not to be judged elsewhere [Note: I have corrected the text in this way; the manuscript has “divided,” corrected to “brought to an end.”], nor on account of it is justice for the poor and less powerful to be neglected. Nor shall the count of our palace presume to settle the more powerful cases without our command; he is to know that he must devote himself only to administering justice in the cases of the poor and less powerful [Note: Manuscript 1 has: “so that in all cases they may render an account on their behalf,” in Muratori, chapter 43, and K. and M., without manuscript authority.].

3. Whenever witnesses must be sought and chosen for investigating any matter, our envoy and the count in whose jurisdiction matters of whatever kind are being handled are to select men of such character as can be found to be the best in that county. Litigants are not to be permitted to bring false witnesses by means of rewards [Note: So the Lombard-law manuscripts and Ansegisus; manuscript 1 and B. read “very many.”], as they have been accustomed to do until now.

4. No man in the court of a centenarius is to be judged either concerning death or the loss of his freedom, or concerning the return of property or slaves. Such matters are to be judged either in the presence of the count or of our envoys [Note: The Lombard-law manuscripts present a second chapter concerning centenarii, which we shall give below.].

5. Our envoys are diligently to investigate and have recorded, each in his own district, what each person holds as a benefice, and how many settled men he has in that benefice.

[Col. 0339C] 6. How those same benefices were encumbered or contracted, and who bought or built an allod from his benefice.

7. Not only the benefices of bishops, abbots, abbesses, and counts, or of our vassals [Note: Manuscript 1 reads “your vassals.”], but also our royal fisc is to be recorded [Note: “In a summary,” as Ansegisus reads], so that we may know how much of our own property [Note: That is, “our substance”; Ansegisus reads “of our property.”] we possess in each person’s district.

8. Since justice has until now been neglected on the counts’ side, we wish our envoys to exercise our commissions in only four months of the year: in winter, January; in spring, April; in summer, July; and in autumn, October. In the other months, each count is to hold his own court and administer justice. Our envoys, however, are to hold their courts four times a year, for one month [Note: This word is added above the line in manuscript 1.], and in four places, with those counts for whom it is suitable to assemble at that place.

9. Whatever that envoy finds to have been done in his district otherwise than is our command, he is not only to order it corrected but also to report the matter itself to us, exactly as he found it.

10. Our envoys are diligently to investigate our customary dues, wherever they were formerly accustomed to come to the king’s share. The same applies to fines. They are to report to us, so that we may determine what should be done with these in the future.

11. Concerning properties from which a customary due used to go to the king’s share: if they have been given to a church, they are either to be handed over to their lawful heirs, or whoever retains them is to pay that customary due.

12. Each of our envoys is to make known at his court to the counts belonging to his district that, in those months when he does not exercise his commission, they are to meet among themselves and hold common courts, both for restraining robbers and for administering other forms of justice.

[Col. 0340C] 13. Our envoys are to make our people promise us fidelity again, according to the custom established long ago. They themselves are to explain and interpret to those men how they ought to preserve that oath and fidelity toward us.

## FORMULAE FOR RECORDING BENEFICES AND ROYAL FISCAL PROPERTY

[Col. 0339]

When, in the seventh chapter of the Aachen capitulary of the year 807, the emperor had ordered the royal envoys to summarize both ecclesiastical and other benefices throughout his empire, in the seventh chapter of the immediately preceding capitulary, from the year 812, he established that “not only the benefices of bishops, abbots, abbesses, and counts, or of his vassals, but also the royal fiscal estates, should be recorded” [Note: The properties of certain monasteries or churches had already been recorded earlier when necessity required it—for example, in the year 787, by Charlemagne’s envoys, the property of the monastery of Fontenelle (*Monumenta Germaniae* II, 290); and, at Alcuin’s command, the property of the monastery of Saint Martin of Tours.].

To ensure that this would be done throughout the empire according to one plan and in the same manner, formularies were needed, prepared as instructions for the envoys [Note: That these were formularies is clear especially from expressions such as “and thus you must summarize the rest,” and “and thus you must summarize the rest of such matters”; also from the words *ille*, *illa*, *illud*, *illius*, and so forth, sometimes used in place of an omitted noun; and from the direction, “You will likewise enumerate all the other past, present, or remaining items.” A fragment of the description itself, now lost, seems to survive in the polyptych of the monastery of Fossé, in Baluze, volume II, columns 1387–1391. The polyptych of the Abbey of Saint-Germain in Paris, famous under the name of Irminon, who assumed administration of the abbey in this year, is a most valuable document of the Carolingian age and will soon be brought to light through the work of the learned Guérard; it is much more extensive than would correspond to the instructions of our formularies.].

A portion of these formularies has been preserved for us by a manuscript of the Ducal Library of Wolfenbüttel, among the Helmstedt manuscripts no. 254. It was written at the beginning of the ninth century on unusually elongated parchment. It was first published by Eckhart in *Commentaries on Eastern Francia*, volume II, pp. 902–910, and then by Bruns in *Contributions to the German Laws of the Middle Ages*, pp. 57–79; we now publish it for the third time, having transcribed it with the greatest care.

In any event, it is impossible to determine how large a portion of the formulary survives in our fragment, since the number 12 written on the surviving quire indicates that the preceding eleven quires of the book have perished. What remain are examples for summarizing bishoprics, monasteries, and royal fiscal estates: namely, part of the description of the bishopric of Augsburg; a register of the prayer-men and beneficiaries of the monastery of Weissenburg; and a description of Asnapium, Treola, and three other royal fiscal estates. Concerning the commentators, the same observation applies as in the following capitulary.

[Col. 0341A] [lacuna] it does not continue: for two years, one excellent wether [*vervicem*] [Note: The supplied correction *vervicem* means “wether”]; in the third year, four modii of grain.

Also concerning the same matter.

On the island called Staphinseie [Note: The reading is not entirely clear because of an erasure of the penultimate letter; *staphinseie* appears, but *staphinseo* seems to require restoration. Eccard had printed *staphinsere*, which Bruns retained.]—the island of Staffelsee, in the bishopric of Augsburg, where Landfrid, founder of the monastery of Benediktbeuern, built an ascetic house in honor of Saint Michael the Archangel [Note: *Monumenta Boica* VII, 83.]—we found a church constructed in honor of Saint Michael. In it we found one altar furnished with gold and silver [Note: That is, adorned with them.].

Five gilded reliquary boxes decorated with glass and crystal gems; one copper box gilded in places. One small reliquary cross with a key, gilded with silver plates; another small reliquary cross fashioned from gold and glass; and another larger cross, furnished with gold and silver and with glass gems.

Above the same altar hangs one silver crown gilded in places [Note: The manuscript abbreviation means “gilded”], weighing two pounds. In its middle hangs one small gilded copper cross [Col. 0341B] and one crystal sphere. Around the same crown hang rows of pearls, thirty-five in various colors.

There are three solidi of refined silver [Note: That is, coined silver]. There are four golden earrings, weighing seventeen denarii.

There are two silver chalices. One of them, carved and gilded on the outside, weighs, together with its paten, thirty solidi; the other, likewise carved and gilded on the outside, weighs, together with its paten, fifteen solidi.

One silver offertory vessel, weighing six solidi. One silver box with a lid for carrying incense [Note: A small chest or pyx.], weighing six solidi. Another silver box weighing five solidi.

[Note on omitted apparatus: Above, chapter 2 has the reference “Cf. above, chapters 4 and 9”; chapter 3, “Cf. above, chapters 5 and 6”; chapter 9, “Cf. above, chapters 5 and 6”; and chapter 12, “Cf. above, chapter 11.” In chapter 7, MS 1 reads *episcopis palam sit* for *episcopis. Palam fit*. In chapter 11, MS 1 corrects *paucitatem* to *utilitatem*, *probis* to *probet*, and *reuerendus* to *praeferendus*.

In the capitulary concerning military levies: chapter 1 has *qui liber* in M.; *dominicum missum* in V. and Vn.; and *et si hoc ei* in V. and Vn.; Vn. and E. add, “and his property shall pass to the public.” Chapter 2 has *cujuslibet* in V., Vn., and Est.; *vim* for *virtutem* in A., V., and Vn. Chapter 3 is absent from A.; V., Vn., and Est. read “a free man in the same expedition”; chapter 4 has “in the same expedition” in V. and Vn. and “crop or grain” in V., Vn., and the others. In the Frankish chapters, Corb. omits both *pro hoc* and *ei* in chapter 6. In the Lombard chapters, the editor corrects *Si q.* in the manuscripts to *Sic quoque*; V., Vn., E., and the printed edition have feminine *interpellata*; V. has *quiquam* and Vn. *quinq* for *quisquam*.

In the Bologna capitulary: manuscript 1 reads *heir bare* for *heribergare* (“providing lodging”); it omits “does not come” in chapter 3; manuscript 1 reads *ad in hostem* in chapter 8, and manuscript 2 reads *victus* for *viatus*. In the Aachen capitulary, Ansegisus adds at chapter 2, “Nor shall any count of our palace presume [to settle] the cases of the powerful.”

In the Staffelsee inventory, the manuscript has *sca* for *sancti*, *capsa* for *capsas*, and *deaura* for *deaurata*.]

We found there a silver thurible, gilded in places, 1, weighing 30 solidi. Also another old bronze thurible, 1. One bronze flask, [Col. 0341C] and another tin flask, 1. One bronze pitcher with a ewer, 1. One large glass vessel, 1. Two small glass flasks with balsam. Above the same church hang two good bells, having two gilded bronze rings on their ropes. We found there two chestnut-colored chasubles, one made and dyed of wool. One dalmatic, one silk garment, seven albs. Four amices. Thirteen linen fanones prepared with silk for offering at the altar. Eight cloths for covering the altars. Two woolen cloths [Note: [Col. 0341] the manuscript reads *para c*.] made and dyed for covering the altar. Two dyed linen cloths. Twenty linen cloths prepared with silk for dressing the altars. [Col. 0342A] Four silk sleeves prepared with gold and pearls, and four other silk ones. Four corporals. Two oraria. One cushion covered with silk [Note: [Col. 0341C] *Pulvinar*, “cushion.”]

As for books: one Mosaic Heptateuch [Note: [Col. 0341C] “Heptateuch, or the five books of Moses, the book of Joshua, and the book of Ruth.” Eccard; Col. 0342C], the book of Joshua, the book of Judges, Ruth, and the four books of Kings; and the two books of Paralipomenon in one volume; the book of David’s Psalms, the book of Solomon’s Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, the Song of Songs, the book of Wisdom, the book of Jesus son of Sirach, the book of Job, the book of Tobit, the book of Judith, the book of Esther, and the two books of Maccabees in one volume; the twelve books of the Prophets and the two books of Ezra in one volume; the book of the Acts of the Apostles, the book of Paul’s Epistles, the seven books of the canonical Epistles, and the book of the Apocalypse in one volume; one lectionary, having prepared boards with gilded bronze plates; one book of homilies by various authors; one book of forty homilies by blessed Gregory; three books of sacramentaries; two books of lectionaries; one excerpted book of canons; one book of expositions of the Psalms without an author; one old book of the four Gospels; two books of antiphons; one book of Jerome’s commentary on Matthew; one book of the Rule of Saint Benedict. There are there two large glass vessels [Note: [Col. 0342C] “Large vessels.”] filled; three lead tablets, one lump, and 170 quills; one faldstool for sitting.

Again, concerning the foregoing. We found in the same place a demesne court and house, with the other buildings belonging to the aforesaid church. To the same court belong 740 day-lands of arable land; from the meadows, 610 wagonloads of hay can be gathered. We found no grain, except that we gave [Note: [Col. 0341] the manuscript reads *dedmus*.] [Col. 0342C] 30 wagonloads to the prebendaries [Note: [Col. 0342C] “those receiving prebends”]; they are provisioned until the feast of Saint John, and there are 72 of them. Twelve modii of malt [Note: [Col. 0342C] German *malz*, from which beer is made]. One broken-in horse [Note: [Col. 0341] the manuscript reads *cababallum*.], 26 oxen, 20 cows, one bull, 61 smaller animals, five calves, 87 wethers, 14 lambs, 17 he-goats, 58 she-goats, 12 kids, 40 pigs, 50 piglets, 63 geese, 50 chickens, and 17 beehives. Of bacon, 20 sides [Note: [Col. 0342C] a pork ham, English “bacon.”], together with the small portions [Note: [Col. 0342C] intestines, *pflaumen*, *Kinderling*, according to Bruns]; 27 measures of lard [Note: [Col. 0342C] fat, *schmalz*; perhaps “vessels of lard measured by the modius”?]. One boar slaughtered and hung up; 40 cheeses [Note: [Col. 0342C] “cheeses.”] Half a modius of honey; two sicli of butter, five modii of salt, and three sicli of soap. Five feather mattresses, three bronze cauldrons, and [Col. 0343A] six iron ones, five crane-hooks [Note: [Col. 0343D] *Gramaculum* and *cramaculus*, French *crémaillère*: an iron instrument suspended above the fire, from which cauldrons are hung], one iron lamp, 17 tubs bound with iron, ten sickles, 17 small sickles, seven adzes, seven axes, ten goat hides, 26 sheepskins [Note: [Col. 0343] the manuscript reads *uernicinas*.], and one fishing net. There is a women’s quarter [Note: [Col. 0343D] *Gynaeceum*, a women’s chamber], in which are 24 women; there we found five pieces of lighter woolen cloth [Note: [Col. 0343D] a type of lighter woolen cloth, commonly called *serge*. Eccard], with four bands, and five camisiles. There is one mill; it yields 12 modii each year.

To the same court belong 23 occupied free holdings [Note: [Col. 0343D] holdings assigned to free men, occupied by cultivators; German *besetzte Freihufen*.][Note: [Col. 0343] the manuscript reads 24]. Of these, there are six whose occupant each year renders 14 modii of grain, four *friskingae*, one *seiga* of flax for the women’s quarter [Note: [Col. 0343D] “women’s quarter”], two chickens, ten eggs, one sextarius of flax seed, one sextarius of lentils; he works five weeks each year, plows three day-lands, cuts one wagonload of hay in the demesne meadow, and brings it in; he performs *scara* [Note: [Col. 0343D] German *Schaarwerk*, corvée labor]. The remaining six are such that each one plows two day-lands annually, sows and brings in the crop; cuts five wagonloads in the demesne meadow and brings them in; works two weeks; and between two of them they provide one ox for the army. When they do not go on campaign, he rides wherever he is ordered.

There are five holdings which together render two oxen annually. He rides wherever he is ordered. There are four holdings whose occupant each year plows nine day-lands, sows and brings in the crop; cuts three wagonloads in the demesne meadow and brings it in. He works six weeks per year, performs *scara* for hauling wine, manures one day-land of demesne land, and supplies ten wagonloads of wood. There is one holding whose occupant each year plows nine day-lands, sows and brings in the crop; cuts three wagonloads of hay in the demesne meadow and brings them in; performs *scara* and provides a packhorse. He works five weeks per year.

There are 19 occupied servile holdings. The occupant of each renders one *friskinga* annually, five chickens, ten eggs, raises four demesne piglets, and plows half a plowing. He works three days per week, performs *scara*, and provides a packhorse. His wife makes one camisile and one piece of woolen cloth. She prepares malt and bakes bread.

There remain seven courts belonging to that bishopric, for which no abridged account is given here; everything is contained in the total. The total of the bishopric of Augsburg is 1,006 occupied free holdings, 35 vacant; 421 occupied servile holdings, 45 vacant. The combined number of occupied free and servile holdings is 1,427; the number vacant is 80. End.

[Col. 0343D] Concerning those clerics and laymen who gave their properties to the monastery called Wizunburch and, in return, received them for usufruct.

The priest Hartwic transferred to the aforesaid monastery, in the Worms district [Note: [Col. 0344D] Among the places of this district mentioned below, Lamey’s description of it (*Acta Palatina*, vol. I) includes Unkenstein, p. 247; Hessihaim, p. 246; Franconadal and Marisga, p. 245; Wanesheim, now Wonsheim, p. 279; Alasenza, now Alsenz, p. 280; and Lorenzenvillare, now Lorzweiler, p. 267], half of the church built in the village of Hessiheim [Col. 0344A] [Note: [Col. 0343] the manuscript reads *hessicheim*.], together with a demesne house, four occupied servile holdings, and five *picturae* of vineyards [Note: [Col. 0344D] a measure of land]; and in return he received that church in the village of Unkenstein, together with a demesne house, six occupied servile holdings, five *picturae* of vineyards, and 20 wagonloads of meadowland, on the condition that he should hold for the days of his life, by precarious tenure, the very property that he had transferred.

Motwinus and his wife likewise transferred to the same monastery, in the village of Hessiheim in the same district [Note: [Col. 0343] the manuscript reads *hessichaim*], together with a demesne house, six occupied servile holdings, five *picturae* of vineyards, and 12 wagonloads of meadowland; and in return they received, in the same village, together with a demesne house, six occupied servile holdings, seven *picturae* of vineyards, and 15 wagonloads of meadowland.

[Col. 0344B] Unroh likewise holds in that district, in that village, by precarious tenure, for the days of his life, one occupied holding, two vacant servile holdings, one *pictura* of vineyard, and 20 wagonloads of meadowland.

The priest Birniho transferred to the same monastery, in the same district, in the village of Franconadal, one church, together with a demesne house, seven occupied servile holdings, three *picturae* of vineyards, and 20 wagonloads of meadowland; and in return he received, in the same district, in the village of Marisga, three vacant servile holdings, one *pictura* of vineyard, and 20 wagonloads of meadowland.

Similarly, Gomoldus transferred to the same monastery, in the same district, in the village called Wisa, together with a demesne house, five occupied servile holdings, three *picturae* of vineyards, and 20 wagonloads of meadowland; and in return [Col. 0344C] he received, in the same village, together with a demesne house, four occupied servile holdings and two *picturae* of vineyards.

The cleric Graolfus transferred to the same monastery, in the same district, in that village, together with a demesne house, five occupied servile holdings and four *picturae* of vineyards; and in return he received, in the same district, in that village, together with a demesne house, five occupied servile holdings and five *picturae* of vineyards. And so you must abbreviate the rest.

Concerning the beneficiaries who appear to hold benefices from the same monastery.

Hunbertus holds as a benefice, in the Worms district, in the village called Wanesheim, together with a demesne house, six occupied servile holdings, two occupied free holdings, four vacant free holdings, 20 wagonloads of meadowland, six *picturae* of vineyards, and a common woodland; in the same village Friduricus holds a benefice.

Baldrih holds a benefice in the same district, in the village called that village, together with a demesne house, five occupied servile holdings, four vacant servile holdings, 30 wagonloads of meadowland, five *picturae* of vineyards, one mill, and a common woodland.

Gerbertus holds a benefice in the same district, in that village, with a demesne house, five vacant servile holdings, and five *picturae* of vineyards.

Meginhartus holds as a benefice, in the same district, in the village of Alasenza, together with a demesne house, two occupied servile holdings, three vacant servile holdings, 15 wagonloads of meadowland, one *pictura* of vineyard, one mill, and a common woodland.

Herigis holds a benefice in the same district, in that village, four occupied servile holdings, one vacant servile holding, and two *picturae* of vineyards.

Waltheri holds a benefice in the same district, in that village, together with a demesne house, six occupied servile holdings, six *picturae* of vineyards, and six wagonloads of meadowland; and between Lorenzenvillare, Hepfanheim, and Winolfesheim, two occupied servile holdings and two vacant servile holdings. The same Waltheri holds in the Speyer district, in the village of Tatastat [Note: [Col. 0345D] now Danstat; see Lamey’s description of the Speyer district in *Acta Palatina historica*, vol. III, p. 231], one church with a demesne house, four occupied free holdings, ten occupied servile holdings, one vacant servile holding, five *picturae* of vineyards, and 20 wagonloads of meadowland. And so you must abbreviate the rest concerning such matters.

An item to be abbreviated concerning livestock.

Concerning the office of that major-domo and the others.

We found at Asnapio [Note: [Col. 0345D] Its location is unknown; Eccardus identifies it with Gennapio on the Meuse], in the royal demesne, a very fine royal hall made of stone, with three chambers; the entire house surrounded by upper rooms, with eleven women’s quarters [Note: [Col. 0345D] women’s quarters]; one cellar below; two porticoes; and 17 other wooden houses within the court, with an equal number of chambers and the other appurtenances properly arranged; one stable, one kitchen, one bakehouse, two granaries, and three barns. The court is strongly fortified with a hedge [Note: [Col. 0345D] *tunimus*, “hedge”], with a stone gate and an upper room above it for administration. Likewise, a small court enclosed by a hedge, properly arranged and planted with trees of various kinds.

Clothing: one bed-covering, one tablecloth prepared for the table, and one towel [Note: [Col. 0345D] English “towel,” *toacla*].

Utensils: two bronze basins, two drinking vessels, two bronze cauldrons, one iron one, one frying pan, one crane-hook, one iron support, one fire-dog, two axes, one adze, two augers, one hatchet, one chisel, one large plane [Note: [Col. 0346D] *Plana major*, “large plane”], one plane [Note: [Col. 0346D] German *Hobel*], two sickles, two small sickles, and two iron-shod spades. Wooden utensils sufficient for service.

Of the produce: old spelt from the previous year, 90 baskets, from which 450 pounds of flour could be made; 100 modii of barley. In the present year there were 110 baskets of spelt; 60 baskets were sown from these, and we found the remainder. One hundred modii of wheat; 60 were sown, and we found the remainder. Ninety-eight modii of rye [Note: [Col. 0345] the manuscript reads *sigil*.]; the same amount was sown. Eighteen hundred modii of barley; 1,100 were sown [Note: [Col. 0345] the manuscript reads *O. c*.], and we found the remainder. Four hundred and thirty modii of oats, one modius of beans, and 12 modii of peas. From five mills, 800 modii according to the smaller measure; 240 modii were given to the prebendaries, and we found the remainder [Note: [Col. 0345] the manuscript’s *Ded c.* clearly should be read *dedit*; compare *Capitulare de villis*, chapter 31]. From four breweries [Note: [Col. 0346D] “houses for making and selling beer.” The manuscript has *camb*; if one reads *cambonibus*, with Bruns and Anton, it must be explained from *campis*], 650 modii according to the smaller measure. From two bridges, 60 modii of salt and two solidi. From four gardens, 11 solidi. Three modii of honey; by way of rent, one modius of butter. Bacon from the previous year, ten sides; 200 new sides, together with small portions and lard; 43 pounds of cheese from the present year.

Of the livestock: larger draft animals, 51 head; five from three years ago, seven from the previous year, and seven from the present year; ten two-year-old colts, eight yearlings; three breeding stallions; 16 oxen; two donkeys; 50 cows with calves; 20 young cattle; 38 yearling calves; three bulls; 260 larger pigs; 100 piglets; five boars; 150 wethers with lambs; 200 yearling lambs; 120 rams; 30 she-goats with kids; 30 yearling kids; three he-goats; 30 geese; 80 chickens; 22 peacocks.

Concerning the foregoing. Also concerning the mansion buildings belonging to the aforesaid holding. In the village of Grisione we found demesne mansion buildings, where there are three barns and a court surrounded by a hedge. There is one garden there, with trees; ten geese, eight ducks, and 30 chickens.

In another village we found demesne mansion buildings, a court strongly protected by a hedge, and within it three barns, one *arripennis* of vineyard, and one garden with trees; 15 geese and 20 chickens.

In that village there are demesne mansion buildings [Note: [Col. 0345] the manuscript reads *masionil domo*]. It has two barns, one granary, one garden, and a court well fortified by a hedge.

[Col. 0346C] Again, concerning the foregoing. We found the measure of modii and sextarii to be the same as at the palace. We found no officials, goldsmiths, silversmiths, smiths, men assigned to hunting, or men assigned to the other services. Of the garden herbs that we found: lily, costmary, mint, parsley, rue, celery, lovage, sage, savory, savin, leek, garlic, tansy, water mint, coriander, shallots, onions, cabbages, turnip-cabbages, and betony [*vittonica*; corrected to *vettonica*; see below, chapter 70]. Of the trees: pear trees, apple trees, medlar trees, peach trees, hazel trees, walnut trees, mulberry trees, and quince trees.

In that royal demesne we found a royal house, externally of stone and internally of wood, well built; two chambers and two upper rooms. Eight other wooden houses within the court; one women’s quarter with a chamber, properly constructed; one stable. The kitchen and bakehouse are joined together. Five granaries, three grain stores. The court is surrounded by a hedge and fortified above with thorn bushes, with a wooden gate. It has an upper room above. A small court likewise enclosed by a hedge. An adjoining orchard, thickly planted with trees of various kinds. Within it, one fishpond with fish; one well-arranged garden.

Clothing: one bed-covering, one tablecloth prepared for the table, and one towel.

Utensils: two bronze basins, one drinking vessel, one basin, two bronze cauldrons, one iron one, one frying pan, one crane-hook, one iron support, one fire-dog, one large plane [the gloss reads “*iuta*”], one axe, one adze, two augers, one chisel [the gloss reads “*bursa*”], one hatchet, one large plane [the note reads “*noil*”], one plane, two sickles, three small sickles, two digging tools, and two iron-shod spades; wooden utensils sufficient.

Produce: old spelt from the previous year, 80 baskets, from which 400 pounds of flour could be made; spelt from the present year, 90 baskets, from which 450 pounds could be made. New barley: 700 modii for service, 600 modii for seed. Old bacon from the previous year, 80 sides; new bacon from the breeding stock, 100 sides, with small portions and lard; bacon paid as rent, 150 sides, with small portions and lard: 330 sides in all. Twenty-four pounds of cheese.

Of the livestock: larger draft animals, 79 head; 24 three-year-old fillies, 12 two-year-olds, 13 yearlings; six two-year-old colts, 12 yearlings; four breeding stallions or mules; 20 oxen; two donkeys; 30 cows with calves; three bulls; ten other animals; 150 larger pigs; 100 smaller pigs; 80 wethers with lambs; 58 yearling lambs; 82 wethers; 15 she-goats with kids; six yearlings; six he-goats; 50 beehives; 40 geese; six ducks; 100 chickens; eight peacocks.

We found in that royal demesne a royal house [Col. 0347C] with two chambers and the same number of heated rooms, one cellar, two porticoes, and an enclosed small court strongly fortified with a hedge; within it, two chambers with the same number of women’s quarters; three women’s lodgings; a well-built stone chapel; two other wooden houses inside the court; four granaries; two barns; one stable; one kitchen; one bakehouse; a court strongly fortified by a hedge, with two wooden gates and upper rooms above them.

One prepared bed, one tablecloth prepared for the table, and one towel.

Utensils: two bronze basins, two drinking vessels, two bronze cauldrons, one iron one, one dish, one axe, one adze, one auger, one chisel, and one plane; wooden utensils sufficient for service.

Produce: old spelt from the previous year, 20 baskets, from which 100 pounds of flour could be made. In the present year there were 20 baskets of spelt; ten baskets were sown from these, and we found the remainder. One hundred and sixty modii of rye; 100 were sown, and we found the remainder. Four hundred and fifty modii of barley; 300 were sown, and we found the remainder. Two hundred modii of oats; the same amount was sown. Old bacon from the previous year, 60 sides; new bacon from the breeding stock, 50 sides, with small portions and lard; bacon paid as rent, 15 sides, with small portions and lard. There are so many sides of bacon in all.

Of the livestock: larger draft animals, 44 head; ten three-year-old fillies, 12 two-year-olds, and 15 yearlings; seven two-year-old colts; two breeding stallions or mules; 24 oxen; six cows with calves; five other animals; 90 larger pigs; 70 smaller pigs; 150 wethers with lambs; 200 yearlings; eight wethers; 20 she-goats with kids; 16 yearlings; five he-goats; and ten geese.

We found in that royal demesne a royal house properly built of wood, one chamber, one cellar, one stable, three lodgings, two granaries, one kitchen, one bakehouse, and three barns. The court is surrounded by a hedge and fortified above by another fence. A garden planted with trees of various kinds. Two wooden gates. Three fishponds with fish.

Utensils: two bronze basins, two bronze drinking vessels, one crane-hook, one iron support, one dish, one axe, one adze, one auger, one chisel, and one iron-shod spade; wooden utensils sufficient.

Clothing: one prepared bed, one quilt, one feather cushion, two linen cloths, one tablecloth, one napkin, and one towel.

Of the produce: old spelt from the previous year, 20 baskets, from which 100 pounds of flour could be made; in the present year there were 30 baskets of spelt, one basket was sown, and we found the remainder. Eight hundred modii of barley; 400 were sown, and we found the remainder. Old bacon from the previous year, 200 sides; new bacon from the breeding stock, 50 sides, with small portions and lard; bacon paid as rent, 80 sides, with small portions and lard.

Of the livestock: only so many larger draft animals; so many three-year-old fillies; two-year-olds, ten; yearlings, 11; so many three-year-old colts; two-year-olds, ten; yearlings, five; two breeding stallions; so many oxen; so many cows with calves; eight young cattle; three yearling calves; one bull; 150 larger pigs; 100 smaller pigs; 150 wethers with lambs; 200 yearling lambs; 100 wethers; 30 she-goats with kids; 90 yearlings; ten he-goats; 20 geese; four ducks.

At Treola we found, in the royal demesne, a demesne house very well made of stone, two chambers with the same number of heated rooms, one portico, one cellar, one winepress room, three wooden men’s lodgings, one upper room with a women’s quarter; three other buildings made of rubble, one granary, two barns, and a court surrounded by a wall, with a stone gate.

Clothing: one quilt, one feather cushion, one bed, one linen cloth, one coverlet, and one bench-cover [Note: [Col. 0347D] a cloth spread over a bench].

Utensils: one iron-bound wine vessel [Note: [Col. 0348D] a wine vessel bound with iron] and one leaden dish. From the demesne vineyards, 730 modii of wine; [Col. 0348D] as rent, 500 modii. Two pounds of hemp.

Of the garden herbs: costmary, mint, lovage, celery, beets, lily, southernwood, tansy, sage, savory, catmint, savin, clary sage, heliotrope, water mint, betony, agrimony, mallows, marsh mallows [Note: [Col. 0347] gloss: that is, hollyhock, called *ibischa*], cabbages, chervil, coriander, leek, onions, shallots, brittles, and others.

Of the trees: pear trees of various kinds, apple trees of various kinds, medlar trees, peach trees, walnut trees, plum trees, hazel trees, mulberry trees, quince trees, and cherry trees.

[Note: [Col. 0349; Col. 0350D] This note appears at the foot of columns 349 and 350, but the callout letter (c) has not been printed in the text: “Those who enjoy the rights of the community and bear its burdens in rotation.”]

[Col. 0349A] This is the total for the villages mentioned above.

In total there are: so many baskets of old spelt from the previous year, from which so many pounds of flour can be made; old wheat, and so you shall reckon all the other things, past, present, and remaining.

# CAPITULARY CONCERNING THE IMPERIAL VILLAS (A.D. 812)

[Col. 0349]

Since this capitulary, like the Helmstedt manuscript, now called Wolfenbüttel, follows the formulas for the description of royal benefices and demesnes, it has seemed most appropriate to place it here. Moreover, in the capitulary of the following year, chapters 10, 18, and 19, we read certain provisions promulgated generally in our capitulary. We have prepared our edition according to the authority of the sole manuscript. Earlier editions were those of Hermann Conring (A.D. 1647, after the letters of Leo III, in quarto), followed by both editions of Baluze and that of Georgisch (in the *Corpus Juris Germanici*), Eckhart’s much more emended edition, and Bruns’s, who added a substantial commentary by Kinderling in the book mentioned above (*Beiträge*, etc.). Among the commentators, Heumann, Tresenreuter (*Dissertatio*, Altdorf, 1758, quarto), Ress, and Anton (in the German work *Geschichte der deutschen Landwirtschaft*, pp. 177–243) are outstanding. The text, in the scribe’s hand, was corrected in several places either immediately or shortly afterward; the earlier reading is indicated by the number 1.

## HERE BEGINS THE CAPITULARY CONCERNING THE IMPERIAL VILLAS OR COURTS

[Col. 0349B]

1. We wish our villas, which we have established for the purpose of serving our needs, to serve our interests in full and not those of other men.

2. Our household is to be well maintained and not reduced to poverty by anyone.

3. The judges must not presume to place our household in their service, nor compel its members to perform corvées, cut timber, or do any other work for them; nor may they accept any gifts from them—not a horse, not an ox, not a cow, not a pig, not a wether, not a piglet, not a lamb, nor anything else, except little vessels and produce from the garden, apples, chickens, and eggs.

4. If any member of our household commits fraud against our interests, whether by theft or through some other negligence, he shall make full compensation; for the rest, however, he shall receive the discipline prescribed by law, by flogging—except in cases of homicide and arson, from which a *fredum* [Note: [Col. 0349D] that is, *freda* or *fredum*, a penalty payment] may arise. To other men they shall strive to render the justice that is theirs, whatever it may be, as the law requires. But for our *fredum*, as we have said, the member of our household shall be flogged. As for the Franks who live in our demesnes or villages [Note: [Col. 0349] added above the line], they shall strive to make amends according to their law for whatever they commit; and whatever they give as the *fredum* [Note: [Col. 0349] the manuscript reads *fauda*] shall come to our use, whether in livestock or in another payment.

5. When our judges must perform our labors—sowing or plowing, gathering the harvest, cutting hay, or harvesting grapes—each of them shall, at the time of the work, inspect every place and arrange how the work is to be done, so that everything may be safely preserved [Note: [Col. 0349] the earlier reading is *salue*]. If he is not within the country and cannot come to a particular place, let him send a good man from our household, or another man who is fully trusted, to oversee our affairs [Note: [Col. 0349] the earlier reading is *providendo*] and ensure that they are brought to a successful conclusion; and let the judge carefully see to it that he sends a trustworthy man to supervise this matter.

6. We wish our judges to give the full tithe from all produce to the churches that are in our demesnes; our tithe is not to be given to another church except where this was established in ancient custom. And no other clerics are to have those churches except our own men, whether from our household or from our chapel [Note: [Col. 0349] added above the line].

7. Each judge shall fully perform his service, as it has been announced to him. And if a necessity arises by which he must serve more, he shall have it calculated whether he must multiply the service or the number of nights.

8. We wish our judges to take charge of our vineyards that belong to their office, care for them properly, and put the wine itself into good vessels; they shall carefully ensure that it is in no way damaged. They shall also arrange to buy other wine for household use [Note: [Col. 0349] the earlier reading is “other wine”], so that they can provision the demesne villages. And whenever more of that wine has been purchased than is needed to be sent for provisioning our villages, they shall inform us, so that we may determine what our will is concerning it. They shall have vine cuttings from our vineyards [Note: [Col. 0349D] French *cep de vigne*, German *Weinfechser*] sent for our use. The rents from our villages that owe wine shall be sent to our cellars [Note: [Col. 0349] the earlier reading is “to our cellar”].

9. We wish each judge to have in his office the same measures of modii, sextarii, and jars measured by eight sextarii, and the same measure of baskets, as we have at the palace.

[Col. 0350D] 10. Our majors and foresters, keepers of colts, cellarers, deans, toll-collectors, and the other officials shall perform [lacuna] and provide pigs [Note: [Col. 0350D] “pigs”] from their holdings; but they shall carefully provide for the manual labor required of them. And whatever major has a benefice shall arrange to send his deputy, so that the manual labor and the rest of the service owed in his place may be fulfilled.

[Col. 0351A] 11. No judge shall exact lodging-service [Note: [Col. 0351D] a place where lodging is provided for public officials] for his own use or for his dogs from our men or in the forests [Note: [Col. 0351D] no judge is to impose on our men the burden of providing lodging for himself, his people, or his animals].

12. No judge shall have our hostage assigned to stay in our village.

13. They shall carefully attend to the breeding stallions, that is, the *waraniones*, and shall never allow them to remain long in one place, lest they perish because of this. If any one of them is such that it is not good, or is old, or if it has died, they shall have this reported to us at the proper time, before the time comes when they must be put among the draft animals.

14. They shall carefully guard our draft animals and separate the colts at the proper time. If the fillies multiply [Note: [Col. 0351] the manuscript reads *putrelle*], they shall be separated, and they shall arrange for the herd to be gathered separately.

15. They shall in every way have our colts [Note: [Col. 0351] the earlier reading is *puledros*] at the palace by the winter feast of Saint Martin.

16. We wish that whatever we or the queen have ordered for each judge, or whatever our officials—the seneschal and the butler—have ordered those judges in our or the queen’s name, they shall have completed at the appointed time, exactly as it was prescribed to them. Whoever fails through negligence shall abstain from drink after it has been announced to him, until he comes into our or the queen’s presence and asks us for permission to be released. If a judge is with the army, on watch, on an embassy, or elsewhere, and something is ordered to his juniors, and they do not complete it [Note: [Col. 0351] the manuscript reads *conplacuerint*, corrected here], then they shall come on foot to the palace [Col. 0351C] and abstain from drink or meat while they explain the reasons for which they neglected it; and then they shall receive their sentence, whether on their back or in whatever manner pleases us or the queen [Note: [Col. 0351] the manuscript reads *quomo*].

17. However many villas each person has in his office, so many appointed men shall he have who will care for bees for our use.

18. At our mills they shall keep chickens and geese according to the capacity of the mill, or as many as they can best provide.

19. At our barns in the principal villas they shall keep no fewer than 100 chickens and no fewer than 30 geese. At the mansion buildings they shall keep no fewer than 50 chickens and no fewer than 12 geese.

[Col. 0351D] 20. Each judge shall always arrange for abundant fruit to come to the court every year; apart from this, they shall send their visits by turns three or four times, or more.

21. Each judge shall have fishponds in our courts wherever they previously existed; and if they can be enlarged, he shall enlarge them. [Note: [Col. 0352D] This note appears at the foot of column 352, but the callout letter (g) has not been printed in the text: *Curare*, French *soigner*, “to care for.”] Where they did not previously exist but can now be made, they shall be newly constructed.

22. Those who have vineyards shall have no fewer than three or four taverns marked by vine-branch crowns [Note: [Col. 0351D] that is, taverns, conspicuous because a crown is displayed].

23. In each of our villas the judges shall have cowherds, swineherds, shepherds, goatherds, and keepers of he-goats, as many as they can provide, and they must never be without them. In addition, they shall have cows entrusted to them by our servants for the completion of their service, so that for the demesne service the cowherds or plow-teams are in no way diminished. When they perform service for the provision of dogs, they shall have sound, non-lame oxen [Note: [Col. 0352D] “crippled,” that is, neither lame nor sick], and cows or horses without mange, or other livestock that is not diseased. And, as we have said, they shall not reduce the number of cowherds or plow-teams [Note: [Col. 0351] the earlier reading is *carrugas*] on this account.

[Col. 0352B] 24. Whatever each judge must provide for our table, he shall have in his *plebium* [Note: [Col. 0351] the manuscript has *habet*; *habeat* is required], so that everything he supplies is good, excellent, carefully prepared, and clean. Each shall also have two *pastos* of grain daily for his service when he serves at our table [Note: [Col. 0352D] *Vicus*. See also chapter 42 and Muratori, *SS* VI, 327; Anton interprets it as “authority”]; and the rest of the provision shall likewise be good in every respect, both the flour and the livestock.

25. Concerning pasturage, they shall have it reported on the Kalends of September, whether it has been available or not.

26. The majors shall not have more in their office than they can travel around or inspect in a single day.

27. Our houses shall have fires and guards without interruption, so that they remain safe. When messengers or embassies come to or return from the palace, they shall in no way take lodging in the demesne courts unless there has been a specific order from us or the queen. The count, from his office, or those men who have traditionally been accustomed to entertain messengers or embassies, shall continue to entertain them in the same way from now on, providing packhorses and arranging everything necessary for them according to customary practice, so that they may come to or return from the palace properly and honorably. They shall provide two entertainments [Note: [Col. 0352D] “two banquets”] for them, and likewise provide packhorses and everything necessary for them according to customary practice [Note: [Col. 0351] the manuscript reads *soloto*].

28. We wish them every year, within Lent, on Palm Sunday, which is called *Hosanna*, according to our arrangement, to strive to bring silver from our production after we have learned how much our production in the present year amounts to [Note: [Col. 0351] the earlier reading is *deferendum*].

[Col. 0352D] 29. Concerning claimants from among our men, each judge shall take care that they do not need to come to us to make a complaint, and that through negligence he does not allow the days on which they must serve to be lost. If one of our servants has rights outside the district to pursue [Col. 0353A] [Note: [Col. 0353] the manuscript reads *adquirendum*], his master shall strive with all determination on behalf of his right. And if he has been entirely unable to obtain it in some place [Note: [Col. 0353] the earlier reading is plural, “they have been unable”], he shall nevertheless not allow that servant of ours to be wearied on this account; rather, his master himself, or his representative, shall strive to make this known to us.

30. We wish them to set aside from all their produce the service that they owe for our use; and whatever wagonloads they must transport to the army [Note: [Col. 0353] the earlier reading is *caregare*], they shall likewise set aside, both by households and by herdsmen, and they shall know how much they are sending for this purpose.

31. They are to arrange that what they are required to give to the provisioners or women’s quarters [Note: That is, the gynaecea.] is likewise separated each year, and that they give it in full at the appropriate time; they must also be able to tell us how they have handled it and where it comes from.

32. Each judge is to ensure that he always has good and excellent seed from what has been acquired [Note: “Acquired” (feminine plural); 1 has “acquired” (neuter plural).] or from elsewhere.

33. After all these things have been separated, sown, and completed, whatever remains from the entire produce [Note: “Added.”] is to be preserved, in accordance with our word, so that, according to our command, it may either be sold or set aside [Note: “Re” added.].

34. It must be provided for with the utmost care that whatever they have worked on or made by hand—that is, lard, dried meat [Note: Meat dried by smoke.], sausages [Note: Or salted meat.], salted fresh meat [Note: Fresh meat preserved with salt.], wine, vinegar, mulberry wine [Note: Wine made from mulberries.], cooked wine, garum [Note: A kind of fermented beverage.], mustard, cheese, butter, malt, beer, mead, honey, wax, and flour—all be made or prepared with the greatest cleanliness.

35. We wish that fat be made from fat sheep [Note: Fat prepared by fattening.] as well as from pigs [Note: 1 has *socia*]; moreover, they are to have at least two fattened oxen in each estate, either to be fattened there or brought to us.

36. Our woods and forests are to be well guarded. Wherever there is a place suitable for clearing, they are to have it cleared, and they are not to allow fields to become overgrown with forest. Where forests are supposed to remain, they are not to allow them to be excessively cut down and destroyed. They are to guard our game carefully within the forests; likewise they are to provide, for our benefit, for the falconers and sparrow-hawk keepers, and they are to collect our dues from these matters diligently. If the judges, or our officials or their men, have sent their pigs into our forest for fattening, they themselves are first to pay that tithe, so as to set a good example and show how the other men under them are thereafter to pay their tithe in full [Note: 1 has “may pay in full.”].

37. They are to put our fields and cultivated lands in good order, and to guard our meadows at the proper time.

38. They are always to have enough fed geese and fed chickens for our use whenever they are required to render service or to send them to us.

39. We wish them to receive each year the chickens and eggs that the servants or tenants deliver; and when they are not required for service, they are to have them sold.

40. Each judge is always to have in each of our estates, for reasons of status, *etlehas* [Note: Conring, Eccard, and the interpreters who followed them read *etlehas*; Bruns separated *et* and *lehas*, because he thought this produced a better sense and because there is no point before *etlehas*, although he says that a point is placed in similar cases elsewhere. But this reasoning is insufficient, since necessary punctuation is likewise absent in other cases. As for the meaning, the interpreters took *etlehas* to mean “swans,” but this is no more convincing than Bruns’s view that *lehas* here means “benefits,” for which one would look in vain for an example from the time of Charles.], peacocks, pheasants, ducks [Note: “Ducks.”], pigeons, partridges, and turtle-doves, and is by all means always to have them for the sake of rank.
