41. The buildings within our courtyards, and the fences around them, are to be well maintained. The stables, kitchens, bakeries [Note: 1 has *pistrima*.], and wine-presses are to be carefully prepared, so that our officials may properly and cleanly carry out their duties there.

42. Each estate is to have within its chamber: beds, bedclothes, feather mattresses [Note: 1 has *plumatias*.], *batlinias*, cloths, tablecloths, bench coverings, copper, lead, iron, and wooden vessels, door-bars, chains, hooks, axes, adzes [Note: French *coignée*, German *Spitzhauen*.], drills—that is, augers—chisels, and every other implement needed there, so that there is no need to seek or borrow such things elsewhere [Note: The manuscript adds *re* to *quaerere*.]. The iron tools that they take on campaign are likewise to be kept in their storehouse, in good condition; and when they return, they are to be put back in the chamber [Note: 1 has “are put back.”].

43. They are to deliver works to our women’s quarters at the appointed times, as has been established: namely, flax, wool, woad [Note: *Glastum*.], kermes-red dye [Note: According to Antonius, red wool.], *warentia*, wool combs [Note: 1 has “blades.”], cards, soap, grease, small vessels, and the other small items needed there.

44. Two parts of the Lenten provisions are to come each year for our service, both of legumes and of fish, cheese, butter, honey, mustard, vinegar, millet and panic grass [Note: 1 has “panic grass.”], dried or green herbs, roots, turnips as well, and wax [Note: 1 has “the rest.”], or soap, and the other small items. Whatever remains, they are to report to us in a written account, as we said above, and they are in no way to allow it to be omitted [Note: That is, “neglected.”], as they have done until now; for through those two parts we wish to know about the third that remains.

45. Each judge is to have good craftsmen in his jurisdiction: namely, blacksmiths, goldsmiths or silversmiths, shoemakers, turners, carpenters, shield-makers, fishermen, bird-catchers [Note: That is, fowlers.], soap-makers, brewers—that is, men who know how to make beer, cider, perry, or any other liquid suitable for drinking—bakers who can make fine flour for our use, net-makers who know how to make nets well, both for hunting and fishing and for catching birds, and the other officials whose enumeration would be lengthy.

46. They are to ensure that our enclosed preserves, which the common people call *brogili*, are well guarded and regularly repaired, and they are never to wait until it becomes necessary to rebuild them entirely. They are to do the same with every building.

47. Our huntsmen, falconers, and the other officials who constantly serve us at the palace are to have provision in our estates, according to what we or the queen have ordered by our letters, whenever we send them on some business of ours or the seneschal and cupbearer have ordered them, in our name, to do something [Note: Manuscript 1 has “our estates.”].

48. The wine-presses on our estates are to be well prepared. The judges are to ensure that no one dares to tread our grapes with his feet; everything is to be clean and respectable.

49. Our women’s quarters are to be properly organized: that is, they are to have good houses, ovens, sheds—that is, underground chambers [Note: Underground chambers; in French, *escrenes* and *ecraignes* in Champagne and Burgundy.]—and good fences around them, together with strong doors, so that they can carry out our work properly.

50. Each judge is to determine how many colts should stand in a single stable and how many keepers may be assigned to them. Those colt-keepers who are free and have benefits in that jurisdiction are to live from those benefits. Likewise, the royal tenants who hold manses are to live from them. Anyone who has none of these is to receive provisions from the demesne.

51. Each judge is to ensure that no wicked men can hide our seed underground or elsewhere, thereby causing the harvest to be poorer. They are likewise to guard against other misdeeds, so that such men may never be able to commit them.

52. We wish them to ensure that various persons receive full and complete justice, such as they are entitled to, concerning royal tenants, our slaves, or free persons who reside on our fisc lands or estates.

53. Each judge is to ensure that no thieves or wrongdoers of any kind can exist among the people under his jurisdiction.

54. Each judge is to ensure that our household works properly at its assigned tasks and does not go off idling in the marketplaces.

55. We wish the judges to have everything they have given or rendered for our use, or set aside, written down in one account, and everything they have distributed in another; whatever remains, they are to report to us in a written account.

56. Each judge is to hold hearings frequently in his jurisdiction, administer justice, and ensure that the members of our household live properly.

57. If any of our servants wishes to tell us something concerning our affairs against his master, he is not to be prevented from coming to us. If a judge learns that the younger men under him wish to come to the palace to complain against him, the judge himself is to make them come to the palace to present their arguments against him, so that their complaint may not cause displeasure in our ears. In this way we wish to learn whether they come from necessity or from some pretext.

58. When our puppies have been entrusted to judges, the judge is to feed them from his own resources, or have them entrusted to his subordinates—that is, to officials, deans, or cellarers—so that they may feed them properly from their own resources. Unless, perhaps, our command or the queen’s is that they be fed at our estate at our expense. In that case the judge is to send a man for this task who will feed them properly; he is to set aside the supplies from which they are to be fed, so that the man does not have to return daily to the storerooms.

59. Whenever each judge renders service, he is to arrange for three pounds of wax and eight sextarii of soap to be supplied each day. In addition, at the feast of Saint Andrew, wherever we may be with our household, he is to arrange for six pounds of wax to be supplied; likewise in the middle of Lent.

60. The chief officials are by no means to be chosen from the more powerful men, but from men of middling status who are faithful.

61. Whenever each judge renders service, he is to have his malt brought to the palace, and the masters who are to make good beer there are to come with it.

62. Each judge is to report every year, concerning our entire production—that which is cultivated with the oxen cared for by our oxherds [Note: Perhaps “how much?”]—what comes from the manses that are required to plough, what comes from the *sogales*, what from dues, what from paid compensation or fines, what from game captured in our forests without our permission, what from various compensations; what from mills, what from forests, what from fields [Note: This seems to be an error for *cambis*, “breweries.” See above, Col. 346, line 4.], what from bridges or ships; what from free men and from the hundred-courts that serve in the districts of our royal estate; what from markets; what from vineyards; what from those who pay in wine; what from hay; what from woodcutters and firewood; what from stakes or other timber; what from *proterarii* [Note: An obscure word. Cangius’s conjecture, *petrariis*, does not seem admissible from the connection of the sentences. Tresenreuter reads *petariis*, from *peta*; not implausibly.]; what from legumes; what from millet and panic grass; what from wool, flax, or hemp; what from tree crops; what from large and small nuts; what from grafts of various trees; what from gardens; what from turnips; what from fishponds [Note: The manuscript has *uuiuuariis*; compare chapter 65.]; what from hides; what from skins; what from horns; what from honey and wax; what from grease, tallow, or soap; what from mulberry wine, cooked wine, mead, and vinegar; what from beer; from new and old wine; from new and old grain; what from chickens and eggs, or geese—that is, ganders and geese; what from fishermen; from smiths; from shield-makers or shoemakers; what from *hutici* [Note: A large chest.], and from *con[lacuna]nis*, that is, chests; what from turners or saddle-makers; from ironworkers [Note: An ironworking shop.] and pits—that is, iron-mining pits [Note: The distinction here has already been erased.]—or other pits for lead; what from tributaries; what from colts and fillies. They are to report everything separated, distinguished, and ordered to us at Christmas, so that we may know what and how much we have of each thing.

63. None of these matters listed above should seem burdensome to our judges when we require them, because we wish them likewise to make every effort to require all these things from their subordinates without any resentment. Everything that a man ought to have in his own household or on his estates, our judges ought to have on our estates.

64. Our wagons that go on campaign, including the *basternae*, are to be well made, with good covers covered and sewn with leather, so that, if necessity arises, they can cross rivers by swimming, carrying the provisions inside, without water being able to enter, and so that our goods may cross safely, as we have said. We wish twelve modii of flour for our provisions to be placed in every wagon; and in those which carry wine, twelve modii according to our measure. Each wagon is to have a shield, a lance, a quiver, and a bow.

65. Fish from our fishponds are to be sold, and others are to be put in their place, so that there may always be fish. However, when we are not coming to the estates, they are to be sold, and our judges are to arrange that the proceeds be used for our benefit.

66. They are to give us an account of the goats, he-goats, their horns, and their skins, and each year they are to bring us from these sources well-fattened salted meat.

67. If, concerning vacant manses and acquired dependants, they have anything in addition for which they have no place where they can settle them, they are to arrange for us to be informed.

68. Each judge is always to have ready good small barrels [Note: Casks.] bound with iron, which can be sent on campaign and to the palace. They are not to make large barrels [Note: French *tonneau*, a cask.] out of leather.

69. At all times they are to report to us how many wolves each person has caught, and they are to have the skins themselves presented to us. In the month of May they are to search for and catch the wolf-cubs, both with poison [Note: Venom.] and hooks, and with pits and dogs.

70. We wish them to have in the garden all the herbs: namely, lilies, roses, fenugreek, costus, sage, rue, southernwood, cucumbers, melons, gourds, beans, cumin, rosemary, *careium*, Italian chickpeas, squill, gladiolus, dragonwort, anise, colocynths, *solsequium*, *ameum*, *silum*, lettuces, black cumin, white rocket, watercress, *parduna*, pennyroyal, alexanders, parsley, celery, lovage, savin, dill, fennel, endives, dittany, mustard, savory, *sisymbrium*, mint, wild mint, tansy, catmint, feverfew, poppy, beets, *vulgigina*, marsh mallow [*ibischa*, that is, *alteas* [Note: Added by a second hand.]], mallows, caraway, parsnips, *adripiae*, orache, *ravacauli*, cabbages, scallions, *britlae*, leeks, roots, shallots, onions, garlic, [Col. 0358C] madder, cardoons, broad beans, Moorish peas, coriander, chervil, *lacteridas*, and clary sage.

The gardener is to have Jupiter’s beard above his house.

Of trees, we wish them to have apple trees of various kinds; pear trees of various kinds; plum trees of various kinds; service trees, medlar trees, chestnut trees, and peach trees of various kinds; quince trees, hazelnut trees, almond trees, mulberry trees, laurels, pines, fig trees, walnut trees, and cherry trees of various kinds.

The names of apples are: *gozmaringa*, *geroldinga*, *crevedella*, *spirauca*, sweet ones, sharper ones—all varieties that keep through the winter [Note: Those that last through the winter.]—and early-eating ones; early varieties [Note: The following words have exercised the ingenuity of interpreters; they are certainly corrupt. It seems to me that they should be understood as specifying that pear trees bearing pears that keep through the winter are to be represented by three or four varieties, followed by sweeter, redder, and late varieties.]. Pear trees bearing keeping varieties, three or four kinds, sweeter, redder, and late.

The Royal Capitulary ends. [Note: The following glosses occur: *Hamedii*, that is, conspirators, whom we call *geidon*. *Metani*, that is, relatives. *Solsaticum*, that is, something cast away; *solsativit*, that is, he cast it away. “His *leudus* lies finished,” that is, his wergild. *Concapulavit*, that is, he cut down, *forheo*. *Livorasset*, that is, he had wounded.]

# THE CAPITULARY OF AACHEN (813, August–September)

[Col. 0359]

The annalist of Moissac (*Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, II) mentions this double capitulary, or its forty-six chapters concerning matters necessary for the Church of God and the Christian people. According to him, it was promulgated in September 813 at a great assembly of the nobles, although the annalist of Lorsch (*Monumenta Germaniae*, I, 121) indicates the month of August.

Our edition of the first part is based on: 1. the royal Paris manuscript, among the *Supplementa latina*, no. 164 bis, ninth century; 2. Paris, among the *Supplementa latina*, no. 75, tenth century; and 3. the edition of Baluze, who admits that he published it “from seven ancient manuscript codices: one Palatine manuscript in the Vatican Library, another of Saint-Remigius of Reims, a third of Saint Vincent of Metz, a fourth belonging to Pierre Pithou, a fifth to Jacques Sirmond, a sixth to Philibert de la Mare, senator of Dijon, and a seventh of Navarre.” Among these, the manuscript of Saint-Remigius is our manuscript 1; the Vatican and Saint Vincent of Metz manuscripts agree with our manuscript 2; and I would judge Sirmond’s manuscript to be none other than our manuscript 1.

Sirmond was the first to publish the second part, in volume II of the *Councils of Gaul*, p. 323, from the manuscripts of Saint Vincent of Metz and a certain manuscript of Ghent. Baluze reprinted it under the title “Chapters concerning the confirmation of the constitutions that the bishops had recently established in synods held by royal authority.” We have newly examined it with the aid of the following manuscripts: 1. the Palatine Library manuscript in the Vatican, no. 289, ninth century; and 2. the royal Paris manuscript among the *Supplementa latina*, no. 75. It contains the canons of the councils held this year at Mainz, Reims, Tours, Chalon, and Arles; according to Einhard, their constitutions were discussed in that assembly before the emperor.

## OF THE THIRTEENTH YEAR [Note: Thus in manuscript 2; manuscript 1 has no heading.]

[Col. 0359A]

Charles, most serene emperor Augustus, crowned by God, great and peaceable, together with the bishops, abbots, counts, dukes, and all the faithful of the Christian Church, established with their agreement and counsel these chapters, from the Salic, Roman, and Gundobadian laws, in the palace at Aachen [Note: Einhard records that Charles held a general assembly there in 813 and in it made Louis his partner in the empire and Bernard king of Italy. Baluze.], so that every faithful person might thus administer justice [Note: Manuscript 2 has *istas*.], which [Note: Manuscript 1 has *lege qui*.] he himself confirmed with his own hand, and so that all the faithful might strive to ratify these chapters with their hands [Note: Janus a Costa, speaking of the Salic, Gundobadian, and Roman laws in the title to book II of the *Decretals*, p. 358, says: “For it is clear that these three laws remained long untouched and inviolate in this kingdom, as is evident from the chapters excerpted by Charles the Great from the threefold law—that is, the Salic, Gundobadian, and Roman—which the most learned Jesuit, the priest Jacques Sirmond, possesses in manuscripts.” Baluze.] [Note: Sirmond’s old manuscript, as also those of Saint-Remigius at Reims and Dijon, have *Gombata*, which is the same thing. Agobard, archbishop of Lyons, wrote a book against this law—namely, against the part in which trial by combat is prescribed for deciding doubtful and obscure matters. Baluze.]

1. The bishops are to travel through the parishes entrusted to them and diligently investigate incest, parricide, fratricide, adultery, vainglory, and other evils [Note: The Dijon manuscript, with which agree corrections added in the hand of Jean Tilius in the Reims book, has “other evils.” The Palatine manuscript has the same reading, which also occurs in the ancient copies of Pithou and Sirmond. Baluze.] contrary to God that are mentioned in the sacred Scriptures [Note: In the Reims manuscript, the hand of Jean Tilius corrected this to “which Christians ought to avoid.” This indicates that Tilius’s corrections were copied from some ancient book unknown to us.], which Christians ought to avoid. Within those parishes they are also to take care of correcting the churches that require it. Likewise [Note: “S. tam n. B.”], they are to preside over both those churches that we have given as benefices and those of others where relics appear to be present [Note: The words “where relics” are absent from manuscript 2.]. Monks are to live according to the rule through the bishop’s word, the abbot’s governance, and their good example, in accordance with the way the establishments have been endowed. The provost and those who are outside the monasteries are not to keep hunters [Note: Manuscript 2 has “sellers”; manuscript B has “that is, if there are any.”], since we have frequently ordered that monks not live outside the monastery.

2. Churches, widows, and orphans are to have peace under the king’s ban. If this is not so, the matter is to be brought before us, if possible. If not, our envoys are to investigate how it occurred.

[Col. 0360A]

3. Draft animals likewise are to have peace under the king’s ban.

4. Those who hold our benefices are to strive to improve them well in every respect. Our envoys are to know about this.

5. Our vicars or centenarii are not to buy dependants from a royal servant. Any inheritance that belongs to the royal estate, if it has fallen outside the heirs, is to be received for our use by those same vicars, so that it is not defrauded.

6. If those who have been made free by the writing of a document die without a formal transfer, their inheritance is to be received for our use. Neither the count nor the vicar is to appropriate it for himself; it is to be reclaimed for our use. Likewise, we wish our officials to ensure that the dues they collect from such persons come to our use or wherever we command.

[Col. 0360B]

7. If, in an inheritance among seven heirs, they act contentiously and the king sends his envoy to carry out the division, the tenth dependant and the tenth rod of the inheritance are to be given to the king’s treasury.

8. The vicars are to have wolf-catchers, two in each jurisdiction [Note: For catching wolves, which at that time were greatly infesting the Frankish kingdom. Frothar, bishop of Toul, writes in letter 26: “We see Christian human lives suddenly destroyed by the wolves’ rabid infestation.”]. These men are not to be required to attend military expeditions or the count’s or vicar’s court, unless a complaint concerning them is brought forward. They are to strive to carry out this duty so that they may derive benefit from it, and the wolf skins themselves are to be given for our use. Each of those who serve in that jurisdiction as court attendants is to be given one measure of grain.

9. Concerning military service: in his county, each count is to strive, under a single ban, to order every man to go on campaign for sixty solidi, so that they come to the announced court at the place where they are ordered to appear. The count himself is to ensure that they are equipped: namely, with a lance, shield, or bow with two strings, and twelve arrows. Each of them is to have these things. The bishops, counts, and abbots are to have men who will provide properly for this, and who will come on the day of the announced court and show there how they are equipped. They are to have coats of mail or helmets and to perform seasonal military service, that is, in summer.

10. The king’s provisions are to be transported in wagons, together with those of the bishops, counts, abbots, and the king’s nobles: ample flour, wine, bacon, and food; millstones, adzes, axes, augers, slings, and the men who know how to cast with them properly. The king’s marshals are to bring them stones in twenty pack-loads, if needed. Everyone is to be prepared for campaign, and they are to have all the necessary equipment in sufficient quantity. Each count is to protect two parts of the pasture in his county for the use of that campaign [Note: Manuscript 1 has “for the campaigner.”], and is to have good bridges and good ships.

11. Each count is to have a prison in his county. The judges and vicars are to have gallows.

12. Men of good birth who act wickedly or unjustly within the county are to be brought into the king’s presence. The king is to exercise coercive authority over them by imprisoning or exiling them until they make amends.

13. Vicars are not to accept gifts on behalf of thieves who have previously been sentenced to death by the count [Col. 0361C]. If they do this, they are to undergo the same judgment as the thief was sentenced to undergo, because after the assessors have judged him, the count or vicar has no power to grant him life. But if a ban has been pronounced against him, after the ban has been completed he is to remain under it until he has satisfied the count and the person who brought the complaint or case against him [Note: The words “until he has satisfied” are absent.]; then he is to be outside the ban.

14. Bishops and abbots are to have advocates. These advocates are to have their own inheritance in that county. They are to be upright and good and willing to settle cases properly and justly.

15. Vicars are not to consent to those who wish to surrender themselves into service to avoid punishment for theft; the matter is to be settled according to a just judgment.

16. No one is to leave his lord after receiving from him something worth one solidus, except if he wishes to kill him, beat him with a stick, defile his wife or daughter [Note: Manuscript 1 has “to be defiled.”], or take his inheritance from him.

17. No one is to carry a club on campaign, but a bow.

18. Concerning forests: the forest wardens are to defend them properly and at the same time guard the animals and fish. If the king gives someone one or more animals from within the forest [Note: Manuscript 1 lacks “gives someone.”], he is not to take more than was given to him.

19. A good, wise, and prudent estate-manager is to be chosen for our use, one who knows how to render an account to our envoy and complete his service according to the way the establishments have been endowed; repair the buildings; feed the pigs, draft animals, and other livestock; tend the gardens, bees, geese, chickens, fishponds with fish [Note: That is, fisheries, as the distinguished Jean Mabillon interprets it in his notes to book I of the *Miracles of Saint Germanus*, bishop of Paris, pp. 106 and 118, citing Louis the Pious’s grant concerning Charles’s game preserve.], game preserves, mills, and clearings; and diligently fertilize the arable land. In the forests he is to maintain a royal manor, with fishponds there, and people are to live there. They are to plant vineyards and make orchards. Wherever they find useful men, woodland is to be given to them for clearing, so that our service may be improved. The women of our household who serve our interests are to receive wool and flax from our estates and make tunics [Note: Manuscript 1 has *sarcils* and *camisils*; manuscript 2 has *sarcillos* and *camisilos*.] and shirts, and these are to reach our chamber through an account rendered by our estate-managers or by envoys sent by them.

20. [Note: Baluze: “And if any of his faithful men …”] If any of our faithful men wishes to undertake a judicial combat or some other contest against his adversary, and summons one of his equals to assist him, but that man refuses and remains negligent in the matter, the benefice he held is to be taken away from him and given to the man who remained steadfast and faithful.

# EXCERPTS FROM THE CANONS

[Note: From the Council of Arles, chapters 3, 4, 5, and 6; Mainz 26 and 19; Arles 9; Mainz 53; Arles 12, 13, and 14; Tours 11; Arles 15; Mainz 25 and 17; Arles 17 and 18; Mainz 47; Arles 20 and Mainz 41; Mainz 52 and 40; Arles 23, 24, 25, and 26.]

1. Chapter: On baptism. Each archbishop is diligently and earnestly to admonish his suffragans [Note: Manuscript 1 lacks “his.”], so that each of them does not neglect to investigate carefully how his priests administer the sacrament of baptism; and all the bishops are earnestly to teach their priests this matter [Note: Manuscript 2 has: “They are to teach them earnestly so that it may be done in due order.”].

2. Laymen are not to expel priests from churches or presume to appoint them without the consent of the bishops [Note: Manuscript 2 lacks “without the consent of the bishops.”].

3. Laymen are absolutely not to dare to demand gifts from priests in return for entrusting a church to any priest.

4. It is necessary to provide for how canons and monks alike are to live, so that they strive to live according to the canonical or monastic rule.

[Col. 0363A]

5. [Note: When Dom Lucas Dacherius found in an old Corbie manuscript certain chapters prefaced with the name of Saint Boniface, archbishop, he thought them worthy of publication and for that reason published them in volume IX of his *Spicilegium*. The distinguished Charles Le Cointe, in the *Ecclesiastical Annals of the Franks*, volume VI, pp. 660 and following, declares that these chapters are later than the age of Boniface. Quite rightly. For we had long since discovered that they could not be Boniface’s, since most of the constitutions recorded there belong to later periods and almost all were taken from the books of the capitularies. In ancient manuscripts there are excerpts made by scholars from the capitularies of our kings, with this or a similar title: “From the council of the kings, which Boniface, legate of the Roman see, attended.” It would be easy to suppose that these were acts of some celebrated synod, were we not aware that the three later books of the capitularies, from which we have observed that these excerpts were for the most part taken, begin with two councils attended by Saint Boniface. But to return to the collection published by Dacherius: it begins with chapter 200 of book VI of the capitularies, from which most of the chapters in that collection were taken. Baluze.] Concerning convents of women: at a suitable time a priest is to be permitted to come there for the solemn celebration of Mass and then return to his own churches.

6. [Note: This chapter, as well as chapters 17, 23, and 26, is also found among the chapters published in volume IX of Dacherius’s *Spicilegium*. See the Council of Clovesho, chapter 29. Baluze.] No more people are to be placed in a convent of canons, monks, or women than it can support.

7. Concerning admonition about tithes.

8. Incestuous persons are to be investigated thoroughly, so that they may be expelled from the Church unless they have done penance.

9. There is to be peace and concord among bishops and counts, and among the other clergy [Note: Manuscript 2 adds “and monks and laymen.”] and laymen.

10. Counts, judges, and the rest of the people are to be obedient to the bishop and are to cooperate with one another in administering justice. They are not to accept gifts in exchange for judgments, nor false witnesses.

[Col. 0363B]

11. Each person is to strive to support his household and those dependent on him, so that they do not suffer from hunger.

12. Each bishop is to be permitted, in accordance with the canons and in the presence of witnesses, to distribute food from the church treasury to the poor.

13. Measures and weights are to be equal and just everywhere.

14. Concerning the office of preaching: it is to be carried out regularly, in accordance with what the common people are able to understand [Note: Manuscript 2 has: “So that the common people may be able to understand well.”].

15. No market or court is to be held on Sundays in which anyone is judged to death or to punishment; and concerning the work that must be avoided [Note: Manuscript 2 has: “No court is to be held, and no one is to be judged to punishment or death on these days; they are to be admonished concerning works that must be avoided.”].

16. Each bishop is meanwhile to travel through his parish and correct whatever matters require correction. If he cannot correct something [Note: Manuscript 2 has: “He is to strive, by teaching and admonishing, to correct whatever is necessary; and if he cannot correct something …”], he is to bring it before the aforesaid court.

[Col. 0363C]

17. Priests are to keep the chrism under seal and are not to presume to give it to anyone under the pretext of medicine or sorcery. If they do so, they are to be deprived of their office.

18. Each godparent or close relative is to instruct his spiritual godchildren in the Catholic faith, so that they may know how they will render an account before God [Note: On faith: “Each godfather or parent, or close relative, is to instruct his children so that they must give an account before God.”].

19. Churches established in ancient times are not to be deprived of tithes or any other possession so that these may be given to new churches [Note: Manuscript 1 has “to us.”].

20. The dead are not to be buried in a church unless they are bishops, abbots, or faithful priests [Note: Manuscript 2 adds “faithful and good priests.”].

21. Courts are not to be held in houses or atria of churches.

22. Counts, vicars [Note: Manuscript 2 has: “Vicars or judges, or counts.”], or centenarii are not to buy the property of the poor under some malicious pretext or stratagem, nor seize it by force. If anyone wishes to purchase such property, the transaction is to take place at a public court in the presence of the bishop.

23. Each bishop is diligently to investigate in his parish where the priests are from [Note: Manuscript 2 adds: “Priests or other clergy, and fugitives, and he is to make them return to their own places and to their own bishop.”]. If he finds a fugitive, he is to make him return to his own bishop.

Source/review notes: Corrupt oath grammar and damaged legal readings remain explicitly marked; all supplied witness forms and sigla are retained in the complete apparatus.

24. Whoever holds an ecclesiastical benefice shall provide every assistance for restoring the roofs of the church, or the churches themselves.

25. Let those who have been publicly convicted and found guilty of crimes be publicly judged and perform public penance according to the canons.

26. Let priests strive to live well and justly, and teach the people accordingly.

[Note: [Col. 0364D] Here Books 1 and 2 end. Thus far extend the chapters of this edict—or rather, the summary and abridgment of the Chapters. In another Codex of Ghent, however, from which we also transcribed the last two chapters (26 b and 26 c), which are not in the Metz Codex, two further chapters followed at this point, repeated from those above—namely, the fourth and fifth—in the following complete and integral form. SIRMOND.]

The Ghent Codex adds:

26 b. Let this be investigated: whether it is true, as they say in the regions of Austria, or not, that priests reveal robbers through confessions received for payment.

26 c. Let careful inquiry be made concerning factious men, who are accustomed to cause inappropriate disturbances both on Sundays and on other solemnities, as well as on ferial days. This must be prohibited altogether, so that they do not presume to do it.

26 f. Every provision must be made, and careful inquiry undertaken, into how the canons live, and likewise the monks, so that each of them may live according to his order, canonically and regularly, and not separately; that is, so that refectories and dormitories may be kept in common, as we long ago prescribed in our chapters.

26 g. Concerning convents of women: let priests be permitted at appointed times to come to them in the church to celebrate the solemnities of Mass, and immediately return to their own churches. Let all other clerics and laymen likewise be restrained, so that they dare not enter those same convents at all, unless necessity arising from the convent itself compels it. This, however, is to be done with the utmost care by the bishop or abbess. Likewise, this too is to be fully observed: women are not to wander about through the houses of clerics.

# LOMBARD CHAPTERS (A.D. 813)

[Col. 0365]

Among the Capitularies of Charles and Pepin, appended to the laws of the Lombards, several chapters are found that cannot be assigned with certainty to any particular time or place. We have thought it appropriate to report them here at the end of Charles’s capitularies. First, we present the chapters preserved at the beginning of the Capitularies in the Chisian Codex, fols. 59 and 60; in the Cavensis Codex, whose immediately preceding leaf has been cut away, only the final sentences survive in the first 210 lines of folio 210. Everyone can see that the text is very corrupt in several places. The first chapter concerns *alode* and refers to title 62, chapter 1, of the Salic Law.

The second chapter is of very doubtful authenticity. I therefore give here the judgment of our Blumius concerning it:

> “By that name, namely, Justinian’s *Novella*, nothing else can be designated except the Latin collection of Julian’s *Novels*, which at that time were in use in the West. Among these there is indeed a law prohibiting ecclesiastical persons from bringing actions before a civil judge (*Novella* 123, chapter 16), though it does not suggest such generality of prohibition that they were forbidden even to bring criminal actions. Nor does a certain constitution of Theodosius and Valentinian addressed to Albinus appear among Justinian’s eight *Novels* or in Julian’s additions; indeed, the collection mentioned above is completely silent concerning all the constitutions of Theodosius and Valentinian addressed to Albinus and issued from the year 443 to 448. Still more absent are two constitutions of theirs, one addressed to Firminus in the year 452 (*Novellae Valent.* book III, title 35; *Codex Theodosianus*, vol. VII, part II, p. 127), the other to Amatius, prefect of Gaul (Gothofred, chapter 1, part III, p. 7), although in neither of them is there found even the slightest indication from which one might infer an absolute prohibition against ecclesiastical men bringing criminal actions. Moreover, the latter of those constitutions is burdened by the strongest suspicion of forgery, which almost compels me to classify this entire Capitularium among the apocrypha.”

The chapters preserved in the remaining Codices follow.

[Col. 0365B]

1. Concerning *Alode*. If a man dies and leaves no son, but his father or mother survives, they shall succeed him in the inheritance. If neither father nor mother survives, but he has left brothers or sisters, they shall possess the inheritance. If none of these exist, the father’s sisters shall succeed to his inheritance. But if the father’s sisters do not exist, his mother’s sisters shall claim his inheritance for themselves. If none of them exists, whichever relatives are nearest in the paternal line shall succeed to the inheritance. But of Salic land no share of the inheritance shall come to a woman; rather, the whole land of the inheritance shall pass to the male sex.

2. When we were rereading certain chapters from the Roman laws, we found written in Justinian’s *Novella*, among other things, concerning a constitution of the emperor Theodosius and the Augustus Valentinian addressed to the prefect Albinus, that no one should dare to accuse bishops, priests, or deacons.

We do indeed dare to speak diligently—more at length in speech—of the holy and venerable priests and ministers, before whom all the earth bows its head; yet we have still heard of treachery in the City against the living God, or of an impious name being made. [The wording is corrupt and materially uncertain.]

But if anyone should presume, rashly or audaciously, to inflict an injury upon the law of the Church or its clergy, through whom the whole empire holds power, and if the accuser is a seditious person, he shall be required, after the penalty has been assigned to our treasury, to pay one hundred pounds of gold and one hundred pounds of silver; and thereafter he shall plead his case with the authorities of the Church.

But if he is a person of lesser standing, let him first consider in his treacherous mind whether he should accuse, commit an injury, or bring a criminal charge. Never, because of our rightful patrimony, has he been accustomed to attempt something through any such treachery; he leads those serving in Christ’s palace into the courts of the land. We have ordered that his hands be given to be plucked off. [The precise wording is corrupt.] But if he wishes to continue the life described above, let him have no concern for the Catholic Church.

3. From the judgment of the monks’ codex. If anyone strikes a priest, that is, a presbyter or deacon, it is decreed that he shall pay a penalty of ten pounds of gold, that is, 720 solidi. If anyone strikes a subdeacon and a defender of the Church, he shall pay a penalty of five pounds of gold, that is, 360 solidi. If anyone strikes a reader, he shall pay a penalty of three pounds of gold, that is, 216 solidi.

[Note: [Col. 0365] The following also occur in the Cavensis Codex, fol. 210.]

[Variant readings: *subdiacono et defensorem* (“a subdeacon and a defender”) in Cavensis; *penas* (“penalties”) in Cavensis; *pena* (“penalty”) in Cavensis; *libre* (“pounds”) in Cavensis; *sol. cc.* (“200 solidi”) in Cavensis, in place of the transmitted “216 solidi”; *lectores* (“readers”) in place of *lectorem* (“a reader”); and *XL* (“forty”) in place of “360.”]

Chapters preserved in the Ambrosian, Florentine, London, Viennese, Veronese, and Estense Codices.

[Col. 0366C]

1 [Note: [Col. 0365] Muratori, chapter 123.] If any provost or other official grants to anyone, under any written instrument, any property of the Church that he is responsible for overseeing, in a way that harms that Church, it shall be counted as sacrilege. Likewise, if a count or official of the public treasury grants to anyone any property belonging to the public treasury, it shall be counted as infidelity.

[The source reads *rem publicam*: property belonging to the commonwealth/public authority, not specifically the public treasury.]

2 [Note: [Col. 0365] Muratori, chapter 125; the Ambrosian and Florentine Codices, and, at the beginning, the London and Viennese Codices, repeat this among the laws of Lothar, chapter 68; below, under the general chapters of Louis I of 817, it is chapter 21.] Concerning women whom the law of the Lombards forbids, after their husbands’ death, to change their clothing to religious dress or assume the veil before a year has elapsed: they requested our permission that, as soon as divine piety should inspire them, they might be permitted to assume it without penalty.

But we considered that, because of this delay, many had even been abducted during that same period and carried away to another party. Therefore we accepted their petition, which we judged just, and grant permission for it to be done in this manner.

[Note: [Col. 0367] The Viennese, Veronese, and Estense Codices add: “with the counsel of the bishop or other priests, and so that she wait thirty days after the death of her husband.”]

3 [Note: [Col. 0367] Muratori, chapter 130.] It has pleased us, in accordance with the authority of the holy fathers, that if anyone has been justly excommunicated by his bishop, he be received by absolutely no one before he comes into the presence of his bishop to render satisfaction for his fault.

[Note: [Col. 0367] *deest V.*—absent in the Veronese Codex.]

4 [Note: [Col. 0367] Muratori, chapter 131.] Since there are some who live in our kingdom without property, evade the judgments of counts, and possess neither goods nor substance by which they can be constrained, and therefore do not cease to practice their wickedness everywhere, it has pleased us concerning them that those with whom they appear to reside either present them or render an account for their misdeeds.

[Note: [Col. 0367] The Viennese, Veronese, and Estense Codices add: “so that they are not their advocates.”]

5 [Note: [Col. 0367] Muratori, chapter 129.] Let the marriages of slaves not be dissolved if they have different masters; rather, the slaves, remaining in one marriage, shall serve their masters. This, however, is on condition that the marriage itself is lawful and accords with the Gospel: “What God has joined together, let no human being separate.”

[Note: [Col. 0367] “But where slaves have been joined together who belong not to one master but to different authorities, unless both masters agree, such a union shall not be valid; or, if it is recognized through negligence and not corrected with whatever power they possess, the person who negligently consents shall be responsible for this union. Much more could have been written concerning the crime of incest, such as mother, daughter, and stepmother, and almost innumerable other cases that do not come to mind for writing. Nevertheless, marital union is permanently withdrawn from such persons and those similar to them.” Viennese, Veronese, and Estense Codices.]

6. As is the custom among our people: if it happens that a Lombard or Roman has a case against another, we observe that the Roman people shall have their succession according to their own law. Likewise, let all written instruments be made according to their own law. When they swear, let them swear according to their own law.

When they pay compensation, let them pay according to the law of the person against whom they have committed the wrong.

[Variant: *iuxta suam ipsius legem*—“according to his own law”—in a corrector’s hand at the beginning of the twelfth century; the Florentine has *iuxta ipsius legem cui malum irrogatur componant*, “let them pay compensation according to the law of the person to whom the wrong is done.”]

It is likewise agreed that compensation should be made concerning the Lombards.

[Variants: *et langobardo* (“and concerning a Lombard”) in the Florentine; *et longobardus* (“and a Lombard”) in the Viennese; *et longobardos* (“and Lombards”) in the Muratorian witness; *observare* (“to observe”) in the Florentine, in place of *convenit componere* (“it is agreed to make compensation”).]

But in all other cases let us live under the common law which the lord Charles, most excellent king of the Franks and Lombards, added in his edict.

[Variants and glosses: *nostre* (“our”) in the Ambrosian and Florentine Codices; *convenit* (“it is agreed”) in one witness, in place of *evenerit* (“it happens”); *habuerint* (“have had”) in the London Codex, in place of *habeant* (“shall have”); *et alii homines ad alios similiter* (“and other men likewise with respect to others”) in the Estense Codex; *et alii similiter* (“and others likewise”) in another witness; *cetera* (“the remaining matters”) in the Ambrosian Codex; *vivamus scilicet nos Franci, Langobardi* (“let us live, that is, we Franks and Lombards”) as a gloss in the Viennese and Veronese Codices; *quam* (“which”) in the Florentine, in place of *quod* (“that”); *excellentissimus* (“most excellent”) in the London Codex and absent in the Ambrosian; *glossa scilicet retro posito* (“namely, a gloss referring to what was placed above”) in the Florentine.]

7 [Note: [Col. 0367] Muratori, chapter 134.] No limitation of ten, twenty, or thirty years shall be set up against religious houses; only the passage of forty years shall bring matters to an end, not only in other property but also in legacies.

[Note: [Col. 0367] Muratori, chapter 144.] In inheritances between two brothers, no term of years shall be counted; rather, they shall always divide equally, because they were born from one father and one mother. This same rule shall extend to the third degree.

[Variants: *donec poenitentiam acceperit*—“until he has received penance”—in the Ambrosian, Viennese, Veronese, and Estense Codices; *quae superius legitur*—“the matter read above”—in the Viennese Codex.]

[Col. 0368A]

Chapters from the Ambrosian, London, Viennese, Veronese, and Estense Codices.

8 [Note: [Col. 0367] The Ambrosian Codex places this among Pepin’s laws, the Florentine among Charles’s chapters, and the remaining Codices among the laws of Louis I. See Muratori, Pepin’s laws, chapter 49; Louis I, chapter 60.] If any woman deceitfully holds her son or daughter before a bishop for confirmation, she shall do penance for her deception, but shall not be separated from her husband.

9 [Note: [Col. 0367] Erased at this place in the Ambrosian Codex.] A false person has no power to accuse.

[Note: [Col. 0367] This text survives here and there in the Florentine, London, Viennese, Veronese, and Estense Codices.] If, in the first crime, he is seen to have given false testimony, in the second he shall not have the power to testify.

[Note: [Col. 0367] The remainder is absent in the Florentine Codex.]

From the Florentine and London Codices.

10 [Note: [Col. 0367] Florentine Codex, fol. 1041; London Codex, fol. 136.] We command that no one dare to exact usury on any account. Whoever does so shall pay the ban.

[Variant: *usuras* (“usuries”) in the London Codex.]

From the Florentine Codex.

11 [Note: [Col. 0367] Fol. 104.] Concerning the sacred vessels of the Church, which we have learned are given as pledges by certain persons in certain places: it is prohibited that anyone henceforth presume to do this, except when compelled by the sole necessity of redeeming captives.

12 [Note: [Col. 0367] Fol. 1041.] If anyone has promised to repay money on behalf of another’s debt, he shall be held to that promise.

[Variant: *qui* (“who”) is absent in the Codices.]

Concerning those men or priests, or any others throughout our kingdom, who, because of rewards or kinship, wish to obscure the truth from our envoys or faithful men who investigate our justice or administer justice, and who thereby expose themselves to perjury, we order and command that, if there is suspicion that a man has committed perjury, he shall afterward be judged either by combat or by the cross, so that the truth or the perjury itself may be revealed.

And if it is God’s will that the truth or perjury be revealed in that judgment, then we will and command that, if he is a priest or cleric, he pay our ban twice, as we decreed above, and afterward be judged according to the canons. But if he is a layman, he shall pay his *wergild* to our treasury.

[Note: [Col. 0367] Another chapter appears here in the Florentine Codex; see below, among the chapters of Emperor Louis II, chapter 22 (Muratori, *Additions* II, chapter 20).]

[Col. 0369A]

From the Florentine, Viennese, Veronese, and Estense Codices.

13 [Note: [Col. 0369] Florentine Codex, fol. 1291; Muratori, chapter 151.] Let the person who has committed perjury, after he has done penance, appear blameless.

[Variant: *p. aut infamis erit*—“or has become infamous”—in Georgisch.]

14 [Note: [Col. 0369] Muratori, chapter 79. In the later hand of the Florentine Codex, fol. 129, an addition is made. See chapter 803, Salic Law, chapter 6.] Whoever has transferred his property, for the sake of his soul, to the house of God, to his relatives, or to other men, and is going to war or into the service of God, or has been condemned to death, shall, if he dies on that journey or from that illness, leave the property to the person to whom it was transferred. But if he does not die on that journey or from that illness, he may, if he wishes, recover the property he transferred and hold it under his own right, as he held it before.

From the London, Viennese, Veronese, and Estense Codices.

[Col. 0369B]

15 [Note: [Col. 0369] Muratori, chapter 150.] Concerning a union that cannot exist according to the canons or the edict: it has pleased us that those who have been joined in it be separated from one another.

[Col. 0370A]

From the Viennese, Veronese, and Estense Codices.

16 [Note: [Col. 0369] Muratori, chapter 147.] Let neither bishops, nor abbots, nor counts, nor vicars, nor judges, nor anyone at all, under any evil pretext or through evil cunning, dare either to buy the property of the poor or of the less powerful, or to take it away by force. Rather, whoever among them wishes to purchase something shall do so publicly, before suitable witnesses and with proper accounts. Wherever anything is found to have been done contrary to this, let it be completely remedied by our command.

17 [Note: [Col. 0369] Muratori, chapter 148.] Let a long-standing custom that does not prejudice the public interest be observed as law, and let those practices that have long been observed remain in force.

From *Lombarda* II.50.4.

[Col. 0370B]

18 [Note: [Col. 0369] Muratori, chapter 152, from Goldast’s edition.] Let the person who has once committed perjury thereafter be neither a witness nor admitted to an oath, nor serve as a swearer in his own case or in another’s.

# CHAPTERS CONCERNING THE JEWS (A.D. 814)

[Col. 0369]

After the chapter concerning the Jews promulgated at the assembly of Nijmegen (above, col. 304), Charles and his son Louis enacted certain further provisions, preserved in the Codex of the Royal Library at Munich, formerly the Augsburg Codex, fol. 261. Since these were copied and sent to me by the distinguished Foringer, it is especially appropriate to report them here, because it cannot be determined which of them belong to Charles and which to his son. We add a second form of the Jews’ oath, found in the Blankenburg Codex of the Wolfenbüttel Library and written in a tenth-century hand. The other chapters that are transmitted under the name of Charlemagne in the Freising, Viennese, and Wolfenbüttel Codices are shown by the Council of Meaux of the year 845 to belong to Charles the Bald.

## CONCERNING THE CHAPTERS OF LORD EMPEROR CHARLES AND LOUIS

[Col. 0369C]

1. Let no Jew presume to receive anything from the Church of God, either as a pledge or for any debt, from any Christian, whether in gold or silver or in any other property. If he should presume to do so—which God forbid—let all his property be taken from him and his right hand be cut off.

2. Let no Jew presume to place any Christian in pledge to any Jew or to another Christian, lest his condition become worse. If he presumes to do so, let him restore according to his law, and lose both the debt and the pledge.

3. Let no Jew keep a mint in his house, and let him not presume to sell wine, grain, or any other thing. If this is discovered, let all his property be taken from him, and let him be confined in prison until he comes into our presence.

4. Concerning the oath of Jews against Christians. Make a circle twice around his feet with a *rumex* [the implement is uncertain]; he must stand there when he swears the oath. He must have on his right arm the five books of Moses according to his law; and if he cannot have them in Hebrew, let him nevertheless have them in Latin.

“If God help me—that God who gave the law to Moses on Mount Sinai—and if the leprosy of Naaman the Syrian does not come upon me as it came upon him, and if the earth does not swallow me as it swallowed Dathan and Abiron, I have not deserved evil against you in this matter.”

[Note: [Col. 0369] “Dathan” is written “Olathan” in the Codex.]

From the Blankenburg Codex, fol. 206.

## OATH OF THE JEWS

“I adjure you by the living and true God, and by that holy law which the Lord gave to blessed Moses on Mount Sinai, and by holy Adonai, and by the covenant of Abraham which God gave to the child Israel; and if the leprosy of Naaman the Syrian does not surround my body, and if the earth does not swallow me alive as it did Dathan and Abilon, and by the faithful bow that appeared from heaven to the children of men, and by that holy place where holy Moses stood, and by that holy [thing] which blessed Moses received there [printed *illam sanctum*, grammatically corrupt]: I am not guilty in this matter.”

[Note: [Col. 0369] The Codex corruptly writes “librana amansiro” in place of “the leprosy of Naaman the Syrian.”]

[Col. 0371]

# CAPITULARIES OF LOUIS I AND LOTHAR

## CAPITULARY (A.D. 816)

Formerly published by Eckhart from the Gudian Codex of the Ducal Library at Wolfenbüttel, this text is now presented again with the aid of that same ninth-century Codex, as well as the Chisian Codex of the tenth century and the Cavensis Codex of the eleventh century. In the latter two, however, following chapters 9, 10, and 11 published above under the year 801, pp. 84–85, the following chapters are numbered IV, V, and VI. We have also used the other Codices that exhibit the capitularies appended to the Lombard laws. We have assigned this capitulary to the assembly held by the emperor at Compiègne after Pope Stephen’s return, although some uncertainty remains because of another assembly held at Aachen in August. We shall examine this matter below.

## HERE BEGIN THE CHAPTERS THAT LORD EMPEROR LOUIS ORDERED TO BE ADDED IN THE THIRD YEAR

[Exact opening apparatus: the Gudian Codex has *INCIPIUNT* and *que* for *QUAE*. *In* is present in Chisian, Cavensis, and Ambrosian witnesses but absent in Gudian; Florentine, London, Viennese, Veronese, and Estense begin Louis’s capitularies with *Attulit ista pius divus nobis Lodoicus* (“the devout, divine Louis brought these things to us”). MS 1 reads *Hludowicus ... h. divino a Deo*; MS 2 reads *Loduicus imperator a Deo*. Ambrosian adds after *nostris*: *capitula composuit de causis opportunis. Haec sunt* (“he composed chapters concerning useful matters. These are they”).]

[Col. 0371A]

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Louis, most serene Augustus, crowned by God, to all our bishops, abbots, dukes, counts, and all our faithful. [The Chisian, Cavensis, Ambrosian, and other witnesses vary in the opening: “Louis, by God, crowned”; “Louis, by divine favor”; “Louis, emperor by God.” The Florentine, London, Viennese, Veronese, and Estense Codices add at the beginning: “The pious divine Louis brought these words to us.”]

These are the chapters that we have decided to add.

1 [Note: [Col. 0371] Here the Gudian Codex begins.] If two witnesses testify concerning any matter and disagree among themselves, then let the count choose one from each side, so that those two witnesses may fight with shields and clubs.

[Note: [Col. 0371B] The Florentine witness reads: “If the witnesses are not weaker.” The Viennese, Veronese, and Estense Codices, together with the London Codex, place this and what follows—except only the final sentence—in a gloss: “If the witnesses are not weaker. For if the witnesses are weaker, let them be examined by the cross. But if they are of advanced age and cannot contend at the cross, then let them send either sons, relatives, or whatever men can contend on their behalf.”]

[Exact chapter 1 readings: Gudian has *flibilioribus* for *flebiliores*, *Nam si* for *Quod si*, *possent* for *possunt*, *qualescumque homines* for *qualemcumque hominem*, *tendunt* for *contendunt*, *illa* for *ipsa*, and *dextera* (Gudian) or *dextra* (MS 1) for the right hand. The wording printed in italics is absent from Gudian.]

For if the witnesses themselves are weaker, then let them be examined by the cross. But if they are of advanced age and cannot stand at the cross, let them send either their sons, their relatives, or any man they can, who may contend on their behalf. And let the person who has been convicted of that falsehood lose his right hand.

[Note: [Col. 0371C] At this point the Viennese, Veronese, and Estense Codices add a fabricated law taken from the decretals of Pseudo-Isidore, from the Roman Council under Pope Sylvester, canon 16, which Muratori reports as number 4:

> “It has been decreed that no layman dare bring a charge against clerics. Let no one accept the testimony of a cleric against a layman. For no cleric, deacon, or presbyter may enter a court for any reason, nor presume to plead a case before a judge, since every court is said to derive from bloodshed and the sacrifice of idols. And if any cleric accusing another cleric enters a court, let him receive an anathema.”

The same text appears in the Ambrosian Codex after Muratori’s chapter 56, and in the London Codex before the law designated Muratori’s chapter 59.]

2 [Note: [Col. 0371] Found among Charles’s laws in Muratori, no. 76, and in the Ambrosian, Florentine, London, Viennese, Veronese, and Estense Codices.] Concerning all debts that must be paid: as was established in ancient times, let one solidus be paid throughout the whole Salic law by twelve denarii, except in the case of *leudes* [*leudes*, that is, compensations]. If a Saxon or Frisian kills a Salian, let one solidus be paid by forty denarii.

[Variant: Muratori reads “sixty” in place of “forty.” Another witness preserves only “let them pay two solidi.” The Viennese, Veronese, and Estense Codices continue: “Likewise concerning all disputes that these men have had against a Salian, for which they ought also to make compensation.”]

Among the Salian people, however, on both sides, let twelve denarii per solidus be paid for all debts, as we have said, whether for homicides or for all other matters.

3 [Note: [Col. 0371] Found among Charles’s laws in Muratori, chapter 67, and in the Ambrosian, Florentine, London, Viennese, Veronese, and Estense Codices.] Concerning a summons: no formal procedure is necessary except in a matter of freedom or inheritance. In all other investigations, let them come to the assembly through the count’s coercive authority, and let them be examined with a staff in order to administer justice. Counts, however, ought not always to oppress the poor through judicial proceedings.

[Variant: The Gudian Codex reads “let the count come to the assembly”; another witness reads “oppress.”]

# CONSTITUTION CONCERNING FREEMEN AND VASSALS

[Col. 0371]

These chapters now appear for the first time from the Chisian and Cavensis Codices. Previously only the first chapter had been published among Louis’s chapters appended to the Lombard laws. The precise year is not evident; nevertheless, since in both Codices they are read in one series with the chapters promulgated in 816—into which the *Marincense* capitulary has been inserted through some error—and before the capitularies of 817, we have thought it appropriate to assign them to the year 816.

[Col. 0373A]

1. If anyone has been released as a free man by a charter and is summoned by any person into servitude, let him first produce the lawful author of his freedom and remain in his freedom. [In one witness the text from “let him first produce the lawful author” through “let him remain in his freedom” is absent.] But if he lacks a lawful author, let him be permitted to defend himself by the testimony of good men who were present when he was released as a free man. If witnesses are lacking, let him establish that his charter, which is the third, is true and lawful by means of two other charters signed or subscribed by the hand of the same chancellor.

The chancellor, however, must be a person known and acceptable to the inhabitants of that place. But if the person who has been summoned can produce neither an author, nor witnesses, nor a comparison of charters, then let the person who entered him in the record prove according to law that the charter itself is false, and reclaim his slave. But if the one who issued the summons is defeated by the author, the witnesses, or the comparison of the charters, and cannot accomplish what he wished, let him be compelled to pay the fine contained in the charter of freedom itself.

[Variant readings: *ingenuitatis*—“of manumission”—in the Ambrosian Codex; *legitimum ... proferat*—“let him produce the lawful [author]”—absent in one witness; *est*—“is”—in the Ambrosian; *fuisset*—“had been”—in another; *interpellavit*—“summoned him”—in the Veronese.]

2. If anyone wishes to leave his lord and can prove against him one of these crimes, namely: first, if the lord wishes unjustly to reduce him to servitude; second, if he has plotted against his life; third, if the lord has committed adultery with his vassal’s wife; fourth, if he has deliberately attacked him with a drawn sword; fifth, if, after the vassal has placed his hands under the lord’s protection, the lord is able to provide protection for his vassal but has not done so—then let the vassal be permitted to leave him.

Whatever of these five offenses the lord has committed against his vassal, let the vassal be permitted to leave him.

[Variant readings: “second, if he has plotted against his life, and if the man perceiving this wishes, let him be permitted to leave him”; “if he wished to kill him”; “if the lord could have defended his vassal”; “after he himself has commended his hands to him.” See Charlemagne’s Aachen Capitular, A.D. 813, chapter 16, above, col. 362.]

# AACHEN CONSTITUTIONS (JULY, A.D. 817)

[Col. 0373]

In the year 817, after the rebellious Sorbs and Basques had been defeated, and ambassadors from the Saracens in Spain and from Godofrid’s sons in Denmark had come to Louis to seek peace, the emperor therefore judged that, in a time of peace, he should apply his hand to the affairs of the empire for the common benefit of the Church and all his people. After an assembly had been convened at Aachen, he divided the kingdom among his sons with the counsel of his nobles. He took Lothar as his associate in the empire and arranged for several laws to be promulgated.

These consisted of a rule for canons and religious women; chapters to be observed by regular clergy; chapters applying generally to bishops and the ecclesiastical orders; secular laws; and chapters. Of these, the first is assigned, from the inscriptions found in the Codices, to the year 816; the monastic chapters to the year 817, the fourth year of the empire, on the sixth day before the Ides of July; and, in one Wolfenbüttel Codex only, to the year 816, the third year of the empire, on the tenth day before the Kalends of September. The general chapters are assigned to the year 817.

Since the preface to the general capitulary and chapters 3, 5, 14, 15, and 19 show that all these matters belong together, and since the constitution concerning the payments owed by monasteries, promulgated at the same assembly, bears the year 817, I have judged that the entire body of these laws should be assigned to that year. The testimony of historians on this matter is certainly very divergent.

Einhard, whose authority we rank above that of all the others, is silent in his *Annals*. The Annals of Lorsch assign to August 816 an order that the monks sing the course of Saint Benedict and a book concerning the life of clerics and nuns. The Annals of Moissac assign to 815 laws for monks and canons, concerning the administration of justice and the restoration of inheritances or freedom unjustly taken away. The anonymous author of Louis’s *Life* assigns to 817 a book of canonical life, rules given to monks and religious women, and laws concerning slaves not being made clerics and concerning the dotal estate of churches. From Ermoldus it must be inferred that the sending of envoys to inquire into the life of regular clerics and monks occurred in 817.

The following therefore appear below:

1. The Division of the Empire.

2. The Rule of the Monks.

3. The General Capitular: namely, its preface; the capitular concerning the clergy; chapters to be added to the laws; chapters to be written separately; and chapters delivered to the envoys sent throughout the empire.

4. The Encyclical to the Archbishops, to be carried by the envoys.

5. The Constitution concerning the service owed by monasteries.

I. [Note: [Col. 0373C] Concerning this division of the Empire, Einhard says in his *Annals* that Louis carried it out in a general assembly of the people held at Aachen, where Lothar was crowned and established as his associate in name and empire, while the other sons of the emperor were called kings, one appointed over Aquitaine and the other over Bavaria. In letter 34 he likewise writes that, when Louis took Lothar into partnership in name and kingdom with the agreement of all his people, he charged him to care for Lothar and diligently admonish him concerning the correction of his conduct and the pursuit of honorable and useful things.

In the Annals of Aniane and in the Chronicle of Moissac the following is written concerning the division of the kingdom, and it is entirely relevant to our purpose:

> “In the year 817, the emperor Louis celebrated Easter at the palace at Aachen. In that same summer he ordered a great assembly of the people from his entire kingdom or empire to be held there at Aachen, the royal seat—that is, of bishops, abbots, counts, and the elders of the Franks. He revealed to them the secret of his plan, which he had conceived: to establish one of his sons as emperor. For he had three sons by his wife, Queen Ermengard: the name of one was Lothar, the name of the second Pepin, and the name of the third Louis.
>
> “Then all the people approved that he should, while still alive, establish one of his sons as emperor, just as his father Charles had done for him. Then all the people fasted for three days, and a litany was performed. After this, the emperor mentioned above chose Lothar, who was the elder by birth, as emperor, and by means of a golden crown handed the empire over to him, while the people acclaimed and said: ‘May Emperor Lothar live!’ Great joy arose among the people on that day. And the emperor himself blessed the Lord, saying: ‘Blessed are you, Lord our God, who have today granted that one descended from my line sit upon my throne, while my eyes behold it.’”

Later, in the year 821, at an assembly held at Nijmegen on the Kalends of May, Louis caused this division of the kingdom to be read aloud and confirmed by all the nobles who were present, as is recorded in Einhard’s *Annals* and in the *Life of Louis the Pious*. This arrangement remained in force for a long time, until Louis, after his sons’ affection for their father had been alienated because of Judith and her son Charles—who later acquired the surname “the Bald”—omitted Lothar’s name from his diplomas and edicts. Hence Lothar’s anger was aroused, as is clear from the plaintive letter of Agobard, archbishop of Lyon, to Louis himself. Hence those tragedies were inflicted upon the Pious ruler which, in the old Chronicle of Saint Gall, are rightly called a disgrace to the Franks. BALUZ.]

# DIVISION OF THE EMPIRE (JULY, A.D. 817)

[Col. 0373]

We present again the formula of this division, originally edited by Baluzius from the ninth-century Codex formerly belonging to Colbert and now Paris, Royal Library no. 2718, fols. 76–77, having collated it anew against that same Codex.

  **Exact apparatus:** Eginhardus de hac Imperii divisione agens in Annalibus ait eam a Ludovico peractam in generali [Col. 0374C] populi conventu apud Aquisgranum habito, ibique Lotharium coronatum ac nominis atque imperii socium [Col. 0375A] fuisse constitutum, caeteros imperatoris filios reges appellatos, unum Aquitaniae, alterum Bajoariae praefectum. Idem in epistola 34 scribit Ludovicum, cum Lotharium in societatem nominis et regni consensu totius populi sui assumpsit, sibi praecepisse [Col. 0375B] ut Lotharii curam gereret, ac illum de moribus corrigendis et honestis atque utilibus sectandis sedulo commoneret. In Annalibus Anianensibus et in Chronico Moyssiacensi ista de regni divisione leguntur, quae ad institutum nostrum omnino pertinent. «Anno 817, Ludovicus imp. apud Aquis palatium celebravit Pascha. Et in ipsa aestate jussit esse ibi conventum magnum populi de omni regno vel imperio suo apud Aquis sedem regiam, id est episcopos, abbates, comites, et majores natu Francorum. Et manifestavit eis mysterium consili sui, quod cogitaverat, ut constitueret unum de filiis suis imperatorem. Habebat enim tres filios ex uxore Ermengarda regina. Nomen uni Clotarius, nomen secundi Pipinus, et nomen tertii Ludovicus. Tunc omni populo placuit ut ipse, se vivente, constitueret unum ex filiis suis imperatorem, sicut Carolus pater ejus fecerat ipsum. Tunc tribus diebus jejunatum est ab omni populo, ac letania facta. Post haec jam dictus imperator Clotarium, [Col. 0375C] qui erat major natu, imperatorem elegit, ac per coronam auream tradidit ei imperium, populis acclamantibus et dicentibus: Vivat imperator Clotarius. Facta est autem laetitia magna in populo die illo. Et ipse imperator benedixit Dominum, dicens: Benedictus es, Domine Deus noster, qui dedisti hodie ex semine meo consedentem in solio meo, videntibus oculis meis.» Hanc regni divisionem postea Ludovicus anno 821 in conventu apud Noviomagum habito Kalendis Maii recitari fecit, et a cunctis proceribus qui tunc affuere confirmari, ut legitur in Annalibus Eginhardi et in Vita Ludovici Pii. Et haec quidem diu mansere, donec abalienatis a patre filiorum animis propter Juditham et filium ejus Carolum, cui postea Calvo cognomen haesit, Ludovicus nomen Lotharii omisit in diplomatibus et edictis. Hinc mota Lotharii ira, ut patet ex epistola flebili Agobardi archiepiscopi Lugdunensis ad Ludovicum eumdem. Hinc illae tragediae in Pium excitatae, quae in veteri Chronico S. Galli dedecus Francorum [Col. 0375D] merito dicuntur. BALUZ..  
  **English account:** Einhard and the cited annals describe Louis’s division of the empire, Lothar’s coronation, the other sons’ kingdoms, and the later confirmation and collapse of the settlement; this complete editorial note is translated in the body.

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ. [Note: [Col. 0373] “saluatoris,” etc.; manuscript 1 reads “Cum nos.” I have nevertheless adopted Baluze’s restoration, because the manuscript does not transmit the customary formula in full.] Hludowicus, by divine providence ordering all things, emperor augustus.

When, in the name of God, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 817, in the tenth indiction, and in the fourth year of our empire, in the month of July, at our palace of Aachen, according to customary practice, we had summoned a holy assembly and the generality of our people in order to deliberate matters concerning the churches and the interests of our whole empire [Col. 0375A], and were occupied with these matters, it suddenly came about through divine inspiration that our faithful men admonished us to deal, while our health remained intact and peace had been granted everywhere by God, with the condition of the whole kingdom and with the affairs of our sons, according to the custom of our ancestors.

Although this admonition was made devoutly and faithfully, it seemed in no way right either to us or to those who think soundly that, out of love or favor toward our sons, the unity of the empire preserved for us by God should be divided by human partition [Col. 0376A], lest perhaps on this occasion scandal should arise in the holy Church and we incur the displeasure of him in whose power rest the rights of all kingdoms.

Therefore we judged it necessary to obtain from him, through fasts, prayers, and generous almsgiving, what our weakness did not presume to undertake. When these observances had duly been carried out for three days, it came about, as we believe by the will of almighty God, that both our own [Note: In the Annals of Aniane, which we described above, it is stated that Lotharius was chosen emperor by Louis his father, with the acclamation of the people. See especially the sorrowful letter of Agobard, chapter 4. — Baluze.] and [Note: [Col. 0375D] This passage seems to require us to examine here the words of certain annals and old books, from which it may at first sight be inferred that the succession of our kings in their paternal kingdom anciently belonged to the votes of the people. For in the short chronicle by an unknown author, which Andreas Duchesne published from the library of Alexander Petau, it is quite expressly written in volume III of the *Scriptores historiae Francorum*, p. 350: “King Pippin dies, and his sons [read: his sons] Charles and Carloman are chosen in the kingdom.” Eginhard expressed this in other words, writing that they were made kings “by the consent of all the Franks.” Indeed, Flodoard, *History of Reims*, book IV, chapter 5, reports that Archbishop Fulk of Reims, when writing to Arnulf, king beyond the Rhine, about the election and coronation of Charles III, whom we commonly call the Simple, and explaining why the Franks had not made him king immediately after the death of the emperor Charles the Fat, said that he had then been very small both in body and learning and was not fit for the reins of government, “and, as the most savage persecution of the Normans was pressing, it was dangerous to elect him then.” A little later, in answering the same Arnulf, who complained that the Franks had elected Charles without his advice, he “maintains that they had followed the custom of the Franks, whose custom has always been that, when a king dies, they choose another from the royal stock or succession, without regard to or inquiry of any greater or more powerful king.” Moreover, in the order for ordaining a king of the Franks, published by Hugh Menard at the end of the book of sacramentaries, “two bishops address the people in the church, asking their will.” And the prayer for the king’s consecration reads: “Upon this thy servant, whom with suppliant devotion we jointly choose for the kingdom of the Franks, multiply the gifts of thy blessings.” Finally, the account of the coronation of Philip the First records that the election of the king of the Franks pertains especially to the archbishop of Reims, and that Philip was elected by Gervase, archbishop of Reims, with the assent of his father Henry. The acts of the coronations of Henry IV and Louis XIII show that this formula was retained down to these latter times. These, I think, are the arguments that may be advanced for establishing the people’s right in the election of the kings of the Franks. But against them there are read in ancient authors and records great and weighty arguments showing that the kingdom is owed to the sons of kings by right of succession so clearly that it is altogether necessary to interpret that election simply as consecration, when one who was already king is declared, in a solemn and public assembly of bishops and magnates, heir and successor to his father’s or grandfather’s kingdom. That this interpretation is legitimate is proved by the order for ordaining a king, in which the following is said to the king, corrected from an old manuscript of the Church of Reims: “Stand, and henceforth retain the estate which you have hitherto held by paternal succession, assigned to you by hereditary right.” For all the ancients teach that the kings of the Franks arise from a lineage. Agathias leads the line; writing about the Franks in book I, he says: “Sons succeed their fathers in the kingdom.” Speaking below of Theodebald, son of Theodebert, he says: “Thus Theodebald, his son, succeeds in the kingdom; and although he was very young and still under a master’s care and instruction, nevertheless the law of his country summoned him to the kingdom.” Saint Gregory, pope of Rome, writes the same; these are his words from the tenth homily on the Gospels: “In the lands of the Persians and the Franks also, kings arise from a lineage.” Charles the Bald cites this passage in his proclamation against Wenilo, as does Fulk, archbishop of Reims, in Flodoard. Charles the Great knew these things when he arranged the division of his kingdom among his sons. For although Eginhard writes that this was done in the assembly which the emperor held in 806 with the leading men and magnates of the Franks, and that the charter dividing the empire issued by Charles was confirmed by an oath from the magnates of the Franks, Charles himself nevertheless carried it out without votes of the people and without any mention of the consent of the magnates, by the same right by which a father leaves his property to his children as natural heirs. [Col. 0377D] This is confirmed by what Thegan writes at the beginning of chapter 6 of the *Deeds of Louis the Pious*. Thus Charles the Bald received his share of the kingdom by paternal gift, as the bishops of the provinces of Reims and Rouen write to Louis, king of Germany, in title XXVII, chapter 7, of the Chapters of Charles the Bald. And in title III, chapter 4, the bishops assembled at Theodon’s estate, addressing the same Charles, say that the kingdom had been left to him by inheritance. Therefore the note found in this place in the acts of the coronations of Henry IV and Louis XIII is entirely true: namely, that this consent of the people is not to be understood as election, but as the subjection, obedience, and fidelity which the people promise to the king according to the law of God. — Baluze.] the votes of all our people [Col. 0377A] converged in the election of our beloved firstborn Hlutharius.

Accordingly, since this had been manifested by divine dispensation, it pleased both us and all our people, by solemn custom, to establish him—crowned with the imperial diadem—as our colleague and, if the Lord so wills, successor in the empire, by common vote.

As for his other brothers, namely Pippin and Hludowicus, our namesake, it pleased us, by common counsel, to honor them with royal titles and to assign them the territories named below, in which, after our death, under their elder brother [Note: That is, so that there might be one kingdom, not three, as Agobard explains in his sorrowful letter: “You assigned portions of your kingdom to your other sons; but, so that there might be one kingdom and not three, you preferred that one whom you made sharer in your name with them.” The fact that Pippin and Louis took this badly is reported by Thegan, chapter 21, On the Deeds of Louis the Pious: “The emperor designated his son Lotharius so that after his death he might receive through his father’s hands all the kingdoms that God had entrusted to him, and might possess his father’s name and empire. For this reason the other sons were indignant.” — Baluze.] they may exercise royal power according to the chapters set out below, which contain the arrangement we have established among them.
