For the benefit of the empire, for preserving perpetual peace among them, and for the protection of the whole Church, we deemed it fitting to consider these chapters with all our faithful men, to commit to writing what had been considered, and to confirm what had been written with our own hands, so that, with God’s help, just as all had been enacted by common vote, so it might be inviolably preserved by all in common devotion, for the perpetual peace of them and of the entire Christian people; while in all things our imperial power over our sons and our people remains intact, together with all the submission that sons owe to a father and subjects owe to their emperor and king.

### Chapter 1

We wish Pippin to have Aquitaine and Wasconia, the whole March of Toulouse [Note: That is, the Toulouse district, which comprised everything lying between the Garonne and the Aude as far as Carcassonne; the old work on Aquitaine published by the distinguished Philip Labbe in volume two of his New Library of Manuscript Books places Carcassonne within the borders of Aquitaine, page 731. From that point onward Septimania, or Gothia, extended to the Pyrenees. Thus not only the Roussillon district belonged to Septimania, as is clear from the notice concerning the monasteries of the Frankish kingdom and from several monuments of the same period, but also Cerdanya and the city of Urgell, as stated in the notes on the Councils of Narbonnese Gaul, page 7, and on Agobard, page 92. Whatever belonged to the Frankish kingdom beyond the Pyrenees was called the Spanish March, whose extreme boundary was established at the River Llobregat. — Baluze.], and in addition four counties: in Septimania, Carcassonne; and in Burgundy, Autun, Avala [Note: The word is now erased.], and Nevers.

### 2

Likewise, we wish Hludowicus to have Bavaria, the Carentani, the Bohemians, the Avars, and the Slavs who are on the eastern side of Bavaria; and, in addition, two royal estates for his service in the district of Nordgau [Note: Today Lauterhofen.], namely Luttraof and Ingoldesstat, on the Danube.

### 3

We wish these two brothers, who are counted as kings, to exercise their own authority in distributing all honors within their power; only let ecclesiastical order be maintained in bishoprics and abbeys, and let propriety and usefulness be observed in the granting of other honors.

### 4

Likewise, we wish them once a year, at a suitable time, either together or separately, according as circumstances permit, to come to their elder brother with their gifts, in order to visit and see him and, with mutual fraternal affection, to discuss matters that are necessary and those that concern the common welfare or perpetual peace.

If one of them should happen to be prevented by some unavoidable necessity from coming at the customary and suitable time, let him inform his elder brother by sending messengers and gifts; but only on condition that, as soon as a suitable opportunity arises, he does not pretend that he cannot come through any sort of evasion.

### 5

We wish and admonish that, whenever either one or both of his brothers come to him with gifts, as stated above, the elder brother, in proportion to the greater power that has been granted to him with God’s approval, should himself repay them with a more generous gift, in pious and fraternal affection.

### 6

We wish and command that, whenever his younger brothers reasonably seek his help against foreign nations, the elder brother, as reason dictates and the opportunity of the time permits, should provide them with suitable assistance, either in person or through faithful messengers and his armies.

### 7

Likewise, we wish them not to presume to undertake either peace or war against foreign nations hostile to this empire preserved by God, without the counsel and consent of their elder brother.

They should, however, strive, according to their strength, to repel by themselves the sudden attack of enemies rising unexpectedly or sudden incursions.

### 8

Concerning envoys: if they are sent by foreign nations either to make peace, to undertake war, to surrender cities or fortresses, or for any other major matter, they must in no way answer them or send them away without the knowledge of their elder brother.

If envoys are sent to him from any quarter and first arrive with either of the younger brothers, that brother should escort them honorably, with faithful messengers, until they reach the elder brother’s presence [Col. 0379A]. In lesser matters, they may answer according to the nature of the embassy.

We nevertheless admonish them not to neglect, whatever the circumstances may be in their borderlands, always to report them to the knowledge of their elder brother, so that he may always be found vigilant and prepared for whatever necessity and benefit of the kingdom may require.

### 9

It also seems necessary to command that, after our death, each vassal should hold his benefice only under the power of his own lord, and not under another’s, in order to avoid disputes.

Each person should possess his own property and inheritance, wherever it may be, with justice preserved, honorably and securely according to his own law, without unjust harassment [Col. 0379B]. Every free man who has no superior should also have permission to commend himself to whichever of these three brothers he wishes.

### 10

If—and may God avert it, and may we in no way desire it—it should happen that one of them, through greed for earthly possessions, which is the root of all evils, becomes a despoiler or oppressor of churches or of the poor, or exercises tyranny, in which all cruelty consists, he should first be admonished privately, according to the Lord’s command, through faithful envoys, once, twice, and three times, to amend his conduct.

If he resists these admonitions, he should be summoned by his brother and admonished and corrected before the other brother, with paternal and fraternal affection.

If he completely disregards this salutary admonition, the common judgment of all should decide what is to be done with him [Col. 0379C], so that imperial power and the common judgment of all may restrain one whom salutary admonition could not turn back from wicked acts.

### 11

The rulers of the churches in Francia should have such power over the property belonging to them, whether in Aquitaine, Italy, or other regions and provinces subject to this empire, as they had in the time of our father or are known to have in our own time.

### 12

As for tributes, taxes, and mines, whatever can be exacted or possessed within their power, let them themselves have it, so that they may meet their needs from it and be better able to prepare the gifts to be brought to their elder brother.

### 13

We also wish that, if after our death the proper time for one of them to marry should arrive, he take a wife with the counsel and consent of his elder brother.

For the avoidance of disputes and the removal of harmful opportunities, however, we decree that none of them may presume to take a wife from foreign nations. Let all their people take wives wherever they choose among the territories, in order to bind peace more closely together.

### 14

If one of them should die leaving legitimate sons, the power itself should not be divided among them. Rather, let the people assemble together and choose one of them, whom the Lord wills; let the elder brother receive him in the place of his brother and son, and, once he has been elevated with his father’s honor, preserve this constitution toward him in every respect [Col. 0380B].

As for the other children, let them treat them with pious affection, arranging matters so that, according to the custom of our ancestors, they may preserve them and keep them under counsel.

### 15

If one of them dies without legitimate children, his power shall return to the elder brother. If it should happen that he has children by concubines, we admonish the elder brother to deal mercifully with them.

### 16

If, at the time of our death, one of them should not yet have reached the lawful age according to the law of the Ribuarians [Note: From this it is clear that Charlemagne’s ancestors were Ripuarians; the Merovingians had been Salian.], we wish that until he reaches the prescribed number of years, both he and his kingdom should be protected and governed by the elder brother, just as they are now by us.

When he has reached the lawful age, he shall exercise his own power in all things according to the stipulated arrangement.

### 17

The kingdom of Italy shall be subject in every respect to our aforesaid son, if God wills that he become our successor, just as it was subject to our father and, by God’s will, remains subject to us at the present time.

### 18

We also admonish the devotion of our entire people and the strength of their utterly sincere faith, renowned among nearly all nations, that if the son who succeeds us by divine will should die without legitimate children, then, for the salvation of all, the peace of the Church, and the unity of the empire, when choosing one of our children—if any survive their brother—they should imitate the arrangement we made in that brother’s election, so that in establishing him they may seek not a human will but the fulfillment of God’s will.

## II. THE CHAPTERS OF THE MONKS  
*(Year 817)*

[Note: This capitulary is explicitly mentioned in the Life of Saint Benedict, abbot of Aniane, where we read: “There were finally many monasteries that had once been established according to the rule, but gradually, as strictness grew lukewarm, the regular order had almost perished. Therefore, so that, just as all had one profession, all monasteries might also have one salutary custom, at the emperor’s command the fathers of the monasteries, together with very many monks, assembled and remained for several days. When all had been placed together, he examined the rule from the beginning, clarified everything obscure, disclosed what was doubtful, removed ancient errors, and confirmed useful customs and practices with the agreement of all. Thus, when the judgments of the rule and all doubtful matters had been brought to a profitable conclusion, he set forth, with everyone’s assent, the customs that the rule disclosed less fully; concerning these he also presented a capitulary to the emperor for confirmation, so that he might order all the monasteries in his kingdom to observe them. The emperor immediately gave his assent.” That these eighty chapters were customarily numbered among the Chapters of Louis the Pious is proved by an old catalogue of the library of Saint Gall, written under Louis the Pious. It contains the following: “The chapters of Emperor Hludowicus concerning the Rule of Saint Benedict.” — Baluze.]

We have revised the Baluze edition after examining the manuscripts, of which the first is:

1. Royal Library of Paris, manuscript no. 2826, ninth or tenth century, which presents the chapters in this order: 1–5, 8, 7, 6, 10–13, 15, 16, 14, 17–20, 23–32, 9, 33, 34, 38–52, 35, 53, 36, 54–56, 37, 57, 21, 58, 59, 60–69, 71, 70, 72, 73, 75–77, and two other chapters.

2. British Museum Library, among the Cotton manuscripts, Tiberius A. III, ninth or tenth century, whose chapter order is: 1–6, 11–13, 15, 16, 14, 17–20, 23–34, 38–53, 35, 36, 54, 55, 37, 57, 21, 58, 59–68, 72, 73, 70, 74, 75, 76.

3. Manuscript of the Ducal Library of Wolfenbüttel, Helmstedt collection, no. 532, parchment, ninth or tenth century, which presents the chapters in this order: 1–5, 8, 7, 6, 10–13, 15, 16, 14, 17–20, 22–32, 9, 33, 34, 38–40; all the rest are missing.

4. Manuscript of the Cassinese Library, no. 353, parchment, tenth century, edited by Angelo de Nuce in the appendix to Leo of Marsica [compare Muratori, Scriptores, IV, pp. 607–609]. It contains chapters 1–6, 11–13, 15, 16, 14, 17–20, 23–34, 39–49, 7, 50–53, 35, 36, 54, 55, 56, 57, 41, 58–69, 72, 73, 70, 74–76, 71, 79, 78.

5. Manuscript of the Paris Library, no. 1535, manuscript, tenth century, presents the chapters in an order closely approaching that of the Cassinese manuscript: chapters 1–6, 11–13, 15, 16, 14, 17–20, 23–34, 38–53, 35, 36, 54, 56, 55, 37, 57–69, 72, 73, 70, 74–77, 79, 78.

Here ends the text.

[Col. 0381A] In the year of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 817 [Note: 816 in manuscript 3.], and in the fourth year of the most glorious prince Hludowicus [Note: In the third year, on the tenth day before the Kalends of September, in manuscript 3.], on the sixth day before the Ides of July, when several abbots, together with their monks, had assembled and were seated in the house of the Aachen palace [Note: “Aachen” in one manuscript. “Of the palace” is absent from the editions.], which is called Lateranis [Note: This is the correct reading. It must nevertheless be admitted that the ancient copies—Dijon, Pithou, Paris, Saint Gall, and Cassinese—read: “when very many had sat together with their own,” while the Helmstedt manuscript reads: “when very many had sat together with their own,” and so forth. One of these abbots, and the principal one, was Benedict of Aniane, as we saw shortly above. Joshua, abbot of the monastery of Saint Vincent near Volturno in the province of Capua, also attended this assembly with him, as is read in the chronicle of that monastery preserved by André Duchesne. Apollinarius, abbot of Flavigny, also attended, as his successor Hugh writes in the Chronicle of Verdun; and Agiulf, abbot of Solignac, as is clear from Louis the Pious’s charter for the monastery of Solignac. Gabriel Bucelinus also reports that Ando, abbot of Stavelot, attended it. — Baluze.] they decreed, by common counsel and unanimous will, that the following chapters should be inviolably observed by those living under the rule.

### 1

When the abbots have returned to their monasteries, let them immediately read the Rule in full, examining it word by word, and, with the Lord’s help, strive to fulfill it effectively with their monks.

[Note: The Cassinese manuscript has “examining each sentence.”]

### 2

Let all the monks who are able learn the Rule by heart.

### 3

Let them celebrate the office according to what is contained in the Rule of Saint Benedict.

### 4

In the kitchen, the bakery, and the other workshops of the various crafts [Note: This is how it is read in the ancient Saint Gall, Dijon, Helmstedt, and Cassinese copies. The Magdeburg Centuriators also published it in this form. See the petition of the monks of Fulda presented to Charlemagne, chapter 16. Other manuscript copies simply read “in the other workshops.”], let them work with their own hands [Note: This and what follows are absent from the Centuriators’ edition.], and let them wash their clothing at the proper time.

### 5

At no time after the vigils should they return to their beds in order to sleep, unless it happens that they are to rise before the appointed hour.

### 6

During Lent, except on Holy Saturday [Note: Namely, as a sign of mourning and penitence. In later centuries the beard distinguished literate monks from the illiterate, whom we today call lay brothers, as is clear from the complaint of the monks of Lorsch against those of Hirsau and from chapter 10 of the Life of Blessed Berthold, abbot of Garsten. Among the Franciscans beards were once so rare that a friar who had one was thereby distinguished from the others. Marinus Sanutus Torsellus testifies to this in the preface to On the Secrets of the Faithful of the Cross: “James of Camerino of the Order of Friars Minor, who wears a beard.”], they shall not shave. At other times they shall shave once every fifteen days [Note: The remainder is missing in three manuscripts.], and during the octave of Easter [Note: This is absent from the Helmstedt manuscript.].

### 7

The use of baths shall depend on the prior’s discretion.

[Note: The second manuscript lacks this chapter. One manuscript reads: “They shall generally use baths only at Christmas and Easter, but separately.” Concerning the monks’ baths, the same Helmstedt manuscript shortly afterward contains the following, which is absent from the others: “They shall generally use baths only at Christmas and at the Lord’s Easter, but separately.” See the notes of Hugh Menard on the Harmony of the Rules, pp. 657, 831. — Baluze.]

### 8

They shall not eat poultry, indoors or outdoors, at any time except because of illness.

[Note: The second manuscript lacks this chapter.]

### 9

No bishop shall order monks to eat poultry.

[Note: The second manuscript lacks this chapter. See Menard’s notes, p. 720.]

### 10

Fruit and lettuce shall not be eaten unless some other food is being taken.

[Note: The second and third manuscripts lack this chapter.]

### 11

They shall not observe a fixed time for bloodletting [Note: In the Saint Gall manuscript, fleotomie; in another, fleutomie.]; rather, it shall be permitted to each according as necessity demands, and at that time special refreshment shall be provided in food and drink.

### 12

If necessity requires it because of the burden of work, they may drink after the evening meal, even during Lent, and also when the office for the dead is being celebrated, before the reading of Compline is given.

### 13

When one of them has been rebuked by his abbot or by any prior [Note: “By the abbot or by a prior,” in another manuscript.], he shall first say, “It is my fault”; then, prostrating himself at the prior’s feet in his cowl, if he has one, he shall ask forgiveness. At the prior’s command he shall then rise and humbly give an account of whatever he has been questioned about.

[Note: This chapter is read as follows in the Cassinese manuscript: “When one of them has been rebuked by the abbot or by any of his priors, he shall immediately, without delay, prostrate himself at his feet and first say, ‘It is my fault,’ just as he is clothed. Then, at the prior’s command, he shall rise and humbly give an account of what he has been questioned about.” See the Chapters of the Monks of Saint Gall, chapter 13, and Menard’s notes, p. 1089. — Baluze.]

### 14

They shall not be flogged naked before the eyes of the brothers for any fault.

[Note: The Pithou manuscript reads: “Monks shall not be flogged, whether naked or otherwise.” The other manuscripts and the Centuriators’ edition have the text printed here, except that that edition adds: “but modesty should always be covered.”]

### 15

They shall not be sent on a journey alone, that is, without another brother.

[Note: The Centuriators read: “Namely, alone and without…” The Helmstedt manuscript reads: “Namely, alone without…” The Cassinese manuscript reads: “He shall not be sent on a journey alone without another monk.” See Menard’s notes, p. 667.]

### 16

They shall not make one another godfathers or godmothers [Note: One manuscript adds: “and they shall not kiss any woman whatsoever.”], nor shall they kiss women.

[Note: The Centuriators read: “and they shall never kiss any woman whatsoever.” The Helmstedt manuscript reads: “And they shall not kiss any woman whatsoever.” The Cassinese manuscript reads: “nor shall they kiss women.”]

[Note: In addition to what Filesacus has observed on this subject in Book I, chapter 3, of his Select Discussions, I find that this prohibition was included in chapter 5 of the canons of Saint Leodegar, bishop of Autun; in the Council of London of 1102, chapter 19, under Archbishop Anselm; in the council said to have been held at Albi in 1254 under Zoen, legate of the apostolic see; and in the synod held by Cardinal and Archbishop of Palermo Giannettino Doria in 1615 in the church of Palermo. — Baluze.]

### 17

If necessity requires them to be occupied in gathering crops [Note: The Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 48: “But if the needs of the place or poverty require that they themselves be occupied in gathering the harvest, they should not be distressed.”], or in some other work [Note: The words “or in” are absent from four manuscripts.], let the appointed time for reading and resting at midday be omitted, and let those who are working [Note: These words are absent from the Pithou manuscript and another copy.] not murmur.

### 18

On Wednesdays and Fridays, when they are fasting, let them perform light work before None, or after None if necessity requires it, according to the prior’s discretion.

### 19

During Lent, after receiving books from the library according to the prior’s arrangement [Note: The Rule of Saint Benedict says in the same place: “During the days of Lent, let them each receive a book from the library.” In the letter of Theodemar, abbot of Monte Cassino, to Charlemagne, monks are permitted to have towels in which to wrap the books they take up for reading.], they shall not take others unless the prior has decided that this is expedient.

[Note: One manuscript reads “other books.”]

### 20

Let them be given clothing that is neither very poor nor very costly, but moderate.

### 21

Let the measure of the cowl [Note: Four manuscripts read “scapular” instead of “cowl.”] consist of two cubits.

[Note: This is the reading of all the ancient copies except the Cassinese, which has “scapular” in place of “cowl.” In chapter 55 of the Rule of Saint Benedict, the scapular appears to be distinguished from the cowl. In Theodemar’s letter, where he explains what the Italians and the Gauls then understood by cowl, a description of the cowl is first given and then of the scapular. Nevertheless, Sigebert, abbot of Gembloux, states in his book On the Unity of the Church, p. 120 of the Basel edition of 1566, that the scapular was customarily included under the general term “cowl”: “For work alone Saint Benedict established another cowl, which is called the scapular, because this kind of garment is suited only to cover the head and shoulders.” — Baluze.]

### 22

If the abbot should decide, for reasons of necessity, that something should be increased beyond the quantity set out below, it shall remain within his authority.

Otherwise, he shall take every precaution to ensure that each monk has two shirts, two tunics, two cowls, and two cloaks; those who need them shall also receive a third. They shall have four pairs of foot-coverings [Note: That is, coverings for the feet, as the same Menard has learnedly demonstrated, p. 889; consult him. In the chapters of Theodore, archbishop of Canterbury, published in volume nine of Dacheray’s Spicilegium, chapter 3, it is stated that the bishop must give the abbot whom he ordains a staff and foot-coverings. See Cujas, Book V of Observations, chapter 11. The ancient statutes of the monastery of Corbie, chapter 3, read: “Four shoes with new soles.” The distinguished editor conjectures that soleis should perhaps be read, meaning the foot-covering that the Gauls call a pantoufle. Louis the Pious’s precept concerning the annual allowances to be given in food and drink to the monks of Saint-Denis says: “for cordwainers and for repairing their soles.” In the Memorandum of Ansegisus, abbot of Fontenelle, published in volume three of Dacheray’s Spicilegium, p. 245, we read: “Five oxhides prepared for soles.” For this, solas should undoubtedly be read. The Basques and Occitans still call solas the part of a shoe that lies beneath the feet. — Baluze.], two pairs of trousers [Note: The letter of Theodemar to Charlemagne says: “Our brothers also have two pairs of trousers. Many of them, however, with God’s help, exercise such restraint that they have neither trousers nor more than two sets of clothing.”], one frock, two ankle-length fur garments [Note: Three manuscripts read “one fur garment.”], and two bandages; those who need them for travel shall have two more.

They shall have gloves, which are commonly called wantos [Note: This is the reading of the Helmstedt manuscript, and correctly so. For manicae are gloves, as Hugh Menard observes in his Notes on the Book of Sacraments, p. 361 at the end. The Life of Saint Basas, bishop of Chartres, says: “Gloves, which are commonly called wantos.” The Memorandum of Ansegisus, abbot of Fontenelle, in volume three of Dacheray’s Spicilegium, p. 246, has ubantos, where wantos should be read. In many manuscripts the words “gloves, which are commonly called…” are absent. — Baluze.], for summer, and in winter woolen mittens; two pairs of daily footwear; two pairs of slippers for summer nights, and in winter clogs.

They shall have sufficient soap and grease; fat for eating, except on Friday, during the twenty days before the Lord’s Nativity, and during the week called Quinquagesima [Note: One manuscript reads “that week,” while three omit the phrase].

Where there is no wine from which a hemina may be supplied, they shall receive twice the measure of a hemina of good beer.

And whatever else the Rule commands beyond these provisions, each of them shall receive without delay whenever necessity requires it.

[Note: That is, the Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 55, where it is additionally forbidden for a monk to have anything private or personal: “And if anyone is found to have something that he did not receive from the abbot, let him be subjected to the most severe discipline.” The Vision of Wetti, a monk of Reichenau, in the time of Louis the Pious, says: “There he also confessed that he had seen a certain structure, very disorderly and disfigured by soot, built of wood and stone in the form of a fortress, with smoke rising high from it like vapor. When he asked what it was, an angel replied that it was the dwelling of certain monks gathered from various places and regions for their purification. From their number he singled out one in particular, whom he said must await the day of the great judgment shut inside a leaden coffin because of his private possessions.” Hence the expression “the leprosy of ownership” in the Chronicle of Augsburg by the monk Sigismund, Book II, chapter 4, in Pistorius. The matter of monks who possessed private property has been treated fully in the notes on the Councils of Narbonnese Gaul, p. 28. — Baluze.]

### 23.

That during Lent, as also at other times, they wash one another’s feet in turn and sing antiphons appropriate to this service. On the Lord’s Supper, however, if he is able, the abbot shall wash and kiss the brothers’ feet and finally hand them the cup with his own hand.

[Note: [Col. 0385C] The Centuriators: “in the refectory let him hand them the cup with his own hand.” The Saint Gall, Pithoean, Paris, and Monte Cassino codices simply read, “and let him hand them the cup.”]

### 24.

[Note: [Col. 0385D] We have retained the reading of Sirmond and the Centuriators, confirmed by the third chapter of the instructions for the brothers addressed to Auva, which will be given below in its proper place, where it reads: “They also wash the feet of pilgrims every week.” The Supplication of the Fulda monks presented to Charlemagne, chapter 13: “Let the reception of pilgrims and the washing of their feet not be neglected, but, according to the Rule and according to the custom of our predecessors, whenever they come, let them be received mercifully, and let the washing of their feet be performed for them by all the brothers.” The ordinance of Charles the Bald by which he confirms the foundation of a hospice made by Hildradus, published by Hemeræus in *The Augusta Viromanduorum*: “Let up to twelve poor persons be received. Since they will be within the cloister and a suitable place will be available for them, let the brothers, assigned to the service of washing feet, take turns each day in religious observance.” The older copies of this Capitular likewise have only: “Let the Mandatum be performed after supper.” The author of the *Life of Alcuin*: “When you too used to go with me to the Mandatum, and I ordered you to drink wine, you would say with consummate cleverness: ‘I have drunk, lord Father, sufficiently with my uncle.’”]

Let the Mandatum, if it is supper time, for both the brothers and the pilgrims, be performed after supper.

[Note: [Col. 0385] The words “if it is supper time” through “of the pilgrims” are absent in four copies.]

### 25.

Let the abbots be content with the measure that their monks have, in eating, drinking, sleeping, dressing, and working, whenever they are not occupied with other useful duties.

### 26.

Let them not frequently travel around the estates, unless necessity compels them, nor entrust them to their own monks for safekeeping. If necessity requires them to go there, once the necessary business has been completed, let them return immediately to their own monasteries.

### 27.

Let the abbot, or any of the brothers, not eat with guests at the monastery gate.

[Note: [Col. 0386C] The Monte Cassino codex: “nor refresh himself, nor drink.”]

In the refectory, however, let him show them every courtesy in eating and drinking.

[Note: [Col. 0386C] These words and those that follow, through “If, however,” are absent from the Paris codex. They are also absent from the Saint Gall codex, which instead has, for the words found here in the other copies: “And he himself, with bishops, abbots, canons, and nobles, shall take of whatever is served to them.”]

Nevertheless, let he himself be content with the same measure of food and drink that the other brothers receive. If, however, on account of a guest he wishes to increase the customary measure for the brothers and for himself by something, let this remain within his authority.

### 28.

Let the servers eat not at one table but in their proper places, after the brothers have eaten; and let the same reading that was read to the brothers be read to them.

### 29.

Let nothing be given to the reader except what the Rule commands.

[Note: [Col. 0386C] Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 38: “The weekly reader shall receive a drink before he begins to read, for the sake of holy Communion, and lest it be too difficult for him to endure the fast. Afterwards let him eat with the kitchen servers and attendants.” See the fifth chapter of the instructions for the brothers addressed to Auva.]

### 30.

Let the Alleluia be discontinued at Septuagesima.

### 31.

[Note: [Col. 0386C] The provosts of monasteries, second after the abbots, as the frequently mentioned Hugh Menard proves at length in his notes on the *Concordia Regularum*, p. 169, 197, 414. For this reason the letter of Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims, to the monks of Corbie is addressed: “To Fulcrannus, provost, and the brothers of the monastery of Corbie”; and another to the monks of Centula: “To Magenardus, provost, and the brothers living in the monastery of Saint Riquier,” in Flodoard, *History of Rheims*, book III, chapter 25. At the Council of Mainz, chapter 11, it is prescribed “that a monastery, wherever possible, be organized through deans, because those provosts often fall into pride and into the devil’s snare.” The founders of this Canon had in view chapters 21 and 65 of the Rule of Saint Benedict. See the *Chapters of the Monks of Saint Gall*, chapter 30.]

Let the provost, within and outside the monastery, after the abbot, have greater authority over the other subjects of the abbot.

### 32.

Let no one but a monk be appointed provost over monks.

### 33.

[Note: [Col. 0386D] See the same *Chapters*, chapter 14.]

Let some of the elders who travel around the monastery go out with the brothers in obedience, while others remain in the monastery for its protection.

[Note: [Col. 0385] The words from “some” through “some” are absent in four copies.]

### 34.

[Note: [Col. 0386D] See the notes of the same Menard, pp. 936, 944, 977. See also the Council of Clofesho, chapter 24.]

Let entry into the monastery not be readily granted to a novice, and, for the purpose of testing him, let him serve the guests in the guesthouse for a few days.

[Note: [Col. 0386D] These words are not found in the Paris codex. Nevertheless, it is clear that they must be retained from chapter 58 of the Rule of Saint Benedict.]

Let him entrust whatever possessions he has to his parents.

[Note: [Col. 0387B] The Monte Cassino codex: “Let him entrust them to his parents or friends.” The Centuriators: “Let him entrust them to his parents or to the monastery.” In the Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 58, it reads: “If he has any possessions, let him either distribute them beforehand to the poor or, by a solemn donation, give them to the monastery.”]

After the year of his probation has been completed, let him do with them according to what the Rule prescribes. Let him neither be tonsured nor change his former clothing before he promises obedience.

[Note: [Col. 0387B] In the Centuriators’ edition the following is added: “that is, according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, let him make his profession in the church.”]

### 35.

Let a monk, after making his profession, keep his head covered with the cowl for three days.

[Note: [Col. 0387B] The Centuriators: “let him cover his head with the cowl.” See the notes of the same Menard, p. 943.]

### 36.

[Note: [Col. 0387B] Formerly, as we said in connection with Salvian, parents possessed such authority that they were permitted to vow their children to God even in childhood, so that the children were not allowed to abandon the discipline they had undertaken at their parents’ command. Indeed, they vowed not only children already born but also those not yet born and still in the mother’s womb. We have illustrated this with two notable examples. They vowed not only those already conceived, but also, in general, those who were yet to be born, as is clear from the testament of Louis VIII, king of the Franks, in André Duchesne, vol. V, p. 325: “Likewise, we wish and command that our fifth son be a cleric, and all the others who shall be born after him.” Menard, in his notes on the *Concordia Regularum*, pp. 985 and following, and Charles Le Cointe in the *Ecclesiastical Annals of the Franks* for the year 544, §74, confirm with many testimonies that children whom their parents had offered to God in monasteries were not permitted to leave for any reason, if the matter had been carried out in due order and according to the Rule. For the formula by which parents offer their children in monasteries, see the new collection of formulas, chapter 31, and our annotations there.]

Let the father or mother offer the child at the altar at the time of the offering.

[Note: [Col. 0387C] The Monte Cassino codex: “let them offer him according to the Rule of the offering.”]

Let them make a petition for him before lay witnesses, which the child himself shall confirm at the age of understanding, promising that he will observe the Rule.

[Note: [Col. 0387C] These words are absent from several copies.]

[Note: [Col. 0387] Four copies add: “let them offer him according to the Rule of the offering.”]

### 37.

Let children who have been offered eat meat only on account of illness.

### 38.

When the brothers sleep after Sext, if any of them wishes to read, let him read in the church or in his own bed.

[Note: [Col. 0387] Three copies: “in their beds.”]

### 39.

[Col. 0388A] Let the brothers work during Lent until None, so that, after Mass has been celebrated, they may eat at the proper time.

### 40.

[Note: [Col. 0387D] The Helmaestad codex: “Let there be a prison for those who flee,” etc. Monasteries have always had prisons in which criminal monks were confined to perform a more severe penance. There are many testimonies to this, especially in the statutes issued by Conrad, archbishop of Cologne, in the year 1260, concerning the life and conduct of monks. “We also decree,” he says, “that every monastery shall have its own prison, in which offenders shall be punished according to the Rule.” Later, however, this prison became so harsh that it moved Stephen, archbishop of Toulouse, to pity. The following is recorded in the manuscript *Chronological History of the Parliaments of the Occitan Country*, written two hundred years ago by Guillaume Bardin, clerical counselor in the parliament of Toulouse:

“In the year of the Lord 1350, on 27 January, when King John was staying at Villeneuve near Avignon, with the Rhône River between them, and the entire papal court in attendance at a contest of lances or spears, which we call a tournament, he devoted himself entirely to the affairs of the Occitan country and denied an audience to no one. Among them, the vicar-general of Stephen, archbishop of Toulouse, complained, at the command of that archbishop, about the horrible severity which the monks exercised against monks who had sinned gravely, throwing them into a perpetual, dark, and gloomy prison which they call *Vade in pace*—‘Go in peace.’ They had nothing for food except bread and water, and all fellowship with their companions was taken from them, so that those condemned to this punishment always perished in despair.

“Because of this complaint, the king decreed by his ordinance that henceforth abbots, priors, superiors, and all governors of monasteries and convents should visit twice a month and console the brothers who were being held in such distress, and that they should be permitted to request the companionship of one monk from the community twice a month. He therefore caused letters patent to be issued, entrusting and committing their execution to Olivarius de Saia, seneschal of Toulouse, and to the other future seneschals of the Occitan country.

“To revoke this ordinance, the Friars Minor and the Friars Preachers performed extraordinary acts and appealed to the authority of the pope; but the king persisted in his will and required them either to obey or to leave his kingdom. For this reason, although unwilling and resisting, they carried out the king’s will. For it is barbarous to deprive prisoners, already afflicted in this way, of every consolation and companionship of friends.”]

Let there be a detached house for those who wish to flee, or to fight one another with fists or clubs, or against whom regular disciplinary measures have been fully imposed, of such a kind that a fire can be lit there in winter and a courtyard is nearby where they can perform whatever work is imposed on them.

[Note: [Col. 0387] Three copies read “Let there be a prison.”]

[Note: [Col. 0387] Three copies lack the remainder.]

### 41.

If anyone negligently makes a noise, or commits any other excess in the refectory, let him immediately ask pardon from the prior.

[Note: [Col. 0388D] The Monte Cassino codex adds: “and, with the prior’s consent, let him rise. Nevertheless, silence shall be observed. When they have gone out, after completing the prayer, let him ask pardon and submit to judgment according to the measure of his fault. See the Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 71.”]

[Note: [Col. 0387] Four copies add: “and, with the prior’s consent, let him rise; nevertheless, silence shall be observed; and when they have gone out, after completing the prayer, let him ask pardon and submit to judgment according to the measure of his fault.”]

### 42.

Let no layman or secular cleric be received to live in the monastery unless he wishes to become a monk.

### 43.

Let no one be permitted to utter an expression of oath or affirmation except as the holy fathers were accustomed to speak.

[Note: [Col. 0388D] The Centuriators’ edition later adds: “that is, ‘Believe me, brother,’ or ‘As the Lord lives,’ or ‘The Lord knows.’”]

### 44.

[Col. 0389A] Let abbots be permitted to have cells in which there are either monks or canons. Let the abbot see to it that he permits no fewer than six monks to live there.

### 45.

[Note: [Col. 0389C] See the notes of the same Menard on the *Concordia Regularum*, p. 682.]

Let there be no school in the monastery except for those who have been offered.

### 46.

On the principal solemnities—that is, on the Nativity and the octave of the Lord, on the Epiphany, on Easter, on the Ascension of the Lord, and at Pentecost; on the feasts of the saints, namely Saint Stephen, blessed John the Evangelist, and the Nativity of the Infants; on the Purification and Assumption of Saint Mary; likewise on the feasts of the blessed Apostles; on the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist; and also on the feasts of Saint Lawrence, Saint Martin, and Saint Benedict; and on the birthdays of any saint whose honor is specially celebrated in any parish—let the full office be performed and let there be two meals.

[Note: [Col. 0389C] These words are not found in the Monte Cassino codex, nor does Theodomar’s letter mention them here.]

[Note: [Col. 0389] Four copies lack the words “let the full office be performed.”]

[Note: [Col. 0389C] Theodomar’s letter: “We also have them take food twice at midday.”]

### 47.

On Good Friday, let nothing other than bread and water be consumed.

### 48.

Let the blessing be said by the priest after Compline.

[Note: [Col. 0389C] The Centuriators’ edition later adds: “and then, before they enter the dormitory, let the prior sprinkle holy water over their heads.”]

### 49.

Of everything given as alms, whether to the church or to the brothers, let a tenth be given to the poor.

### 50.

Let the regular divisions of the Psalter be set aside, and let special psalms be sung for those who give alms and for the dead.

[Note: [Col. 0389C] That is, for all who grant us alms, as is read in the supplication that the Fulda monks presented to Charlemagne. It is preferable to quote the entire passage, since it greatly illuminates this chapter of Aachen. Thus the Fulda monks write:

“Likewise, on the second day of every week, let there be a prayer for all who grant us alms, namely, the same Psalm 50 which the entire congregation, prostrate together before the body of the blessed martyr, sang, with the Lord’s Prayer, verses, and a collect. For our deceased brothers, let that commemoration which we had daily twice—that is, after the celebration of Matins and of Vespers—be made: namely, the antiphon ‘Eternal rest,’ and the first part of the psalm ‘You are worthy of praise, O God,’ with a verse and collect.”]

### 51.

During the week of Pentecost, let them neither bend their knees nor fast, unless days of fasting have been appointed.

[Note: [Col. 0389D] The Centuriators’ edition adds: “On the Ember Days, however, let them fast, as on the vigil of Saint Mary, the Annunciation, the Assumption, and the Nativity. They likewise fast on the Nativity of all the Apostles, or of Saint John the Baptist, on his martyrdom, or on the Nativity of any saint in whose honor the place where the monks serve has been dedicated.”]

### 52.

Let laymen not be brought into the refectory for the purpose of eating and drinking.

[Note: [Col. 0389C] See the notes on the *Concordia Regularum*, p. 307.]

### 53.

Whenever necessity requires, let clothing, footwear, and all necessities be given to the brothers.

### 54.

Let those who are placed in authority be called nonni [“grandfathers”], out of paternal reverence.

[Note: [Col. 0389] Four copies lack the remainder.]

### 55.

[Note: [Col. 0390C] See the chapters of the monks of Saint Gall, chapter 30.]

Let the senior dean be placed above the other deans and, when the abbot or provost is present, let him retain his proper place.

[Note: [Col. 0389] Four copies read: “Let the dean, cellarer, and gatekeeper eat from their service only on account of illness.”]

### 56.

[Note: [Col. 0390C] The Centuriators’ edition has: “Let the provost, deans, cellarer, and gatekeeper, from their service, unless for a useful reason,” etc. The Saint Gall codex: “Let the provost, deans, cellarer, and gatekeeper, if they have been useful in their ministries, remain there as long as seems good to the abbot and the congregation.” The Monte Cassino codex: “Let the senior, dean, cellarer, and gatekeeper eat from their service only on account of illness.” But these last two words do not belong in this place. In the cartulary of Tulle, fols. 37 and 219, Otgerius the gatekeeper is listed among the principal monks of that monastery in the twelfth year of the reign of Louis the Transmarine.]

Let the provost, dean, and cellarer not be removed from their service except for a useful or necessary reason.

[Note: [Col. 0390D] Some codices have “cellarer”; the Paris codex has “cellarer.”]

[Note: [Col. 0389] Two copies lack the words “or provost.”]

### 57.

Let a pound of bread be measured at thirty solidi for twelve denarii.

[Note: [Col. 0389] Four copies read: “Let the scapular’s measure consist of two cubits.”]

### 58.

Let the dormitory be built beside the oratory, where monks who arrive from elsewhere may sleep.

### 59.

[Note: [Col. 0390D] In the ancient Monte Cassino and Saint Gall copies and in the Centuriators’ edition it reads: “Let abbots be canons.” On canonical abbots, see the Sixth Council of Paris, book III, chapter 18, and the Second Council of Aachen, chapter 2, §2, no. 1.]

Let abbots not take monks with them on a journey except to a general synod.

[Note: [Col. 0389] One copy, four, and five copies read: “Let canonical abbots not take monks with them.”]

[Note: [Col. 0390D] The Centuriators: “a general assembly.” This was the ancient rule, as appears from what was said above concerning the chapters of the Synod of Frankfurt, to which Benedict, abbot of Aniane, and Anianus, abbot of Caunes, brought their monks.]

### 60.

Let only two signals be sounded for Terce, Sext, and None.

### 61.

Let monks not have unsewn cloaks except shaggy ones.

[Note: [Col. 0389] Four copies read “woven” instead of “patched.”]

### 62.

[Col. 0391A] Let the abbot, provost, or dean, even if they are not priests, give the blessing to the readers.

### 63.

Let learned brothers be chosen who will speak with monks who arrive.

[Note: [Col. 0391C] The Centuriators simply have “with guests.”]

### 64.

[Note: [Col. 0391C] Here proof of an uncertain theft committed by the monks is ordered through excommunication from the body and blood of the Lord, contrary to the custom of that age. Canon 15 of the Council of Worms is a witness, and reads as follows:

“It often happens that thefts are committed in monasteries and those who commit them remain unknown. Therefore we decree that whenever the brothers must clear themselves concerning such matters, Mass shall be celebrated by the abbot or by someone whom the abbot has instructed, in the presence of the brothers; and at the final celebration of Mass they shall receive the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ for their purification, so that in this way they may show themselves innocent.”

Joachim Vadianus interpreted this passage—which is otherwise neither especially difficult nor obscure—in the following manner in book six of his work *On the Eucharist*, p. 218:

“Just as it is clear that in that Carolingian age there was error in communicating infants, so neither was it especially proper or pious that bishops and monks of that period were accustomed to receive the Eucharist as a testimony of innocence and purification from an alleged crime. Thus, when a theft had been committed in a monastery, all the monks participated in the body and blood of the Lord during the celebration of Mass, in order to free themselves from suspicion of the crime. This was done through a religious persuasion which was believed to keep the one conscious of guilt far from that sacred food, through fear of punishment.”

See Regino, book II, chapter 276, and our annotations there.]

In the case of an uncertain theft, let prayer first be made, and afterward excommunication from the body and blood of Christ, until the guilty person confesses.

### 65.

If a brother gives testimony against another brother concerning any fault, let belief be given to the more perfect brother.

### 66.

Let neither the invitatory psalm nor the Gloria be sung for the dead.

### 67.

Let the reader ask for the blessing while standing.

[Note: [Col. 0391D] The Monte Cassino codex: “standing in humility.”]

[Note: [Col. 0391] Four copies read: “standing in humility.”]

### 68.

[Note: [Col. 0391D] This word is understood in various ways, as Gretser explains at length in book two of *On Blessings*, chapters 24 and following. See also the notes on the *Concordia Regularum*, p. 875. This is called “the communion of broken bread” in the supplication of the Fulda monks to Charlemagne, chapter 4.]

Let blessed bread (eulogiae) be given to the brothers by the priests in the refectory.

### 69.

[Col. 0391B]

[Note: [Col. 0391] Two copies lack this chapter.]

At the chapter meeting, let the Martyrology first be read, and let the verse be said by which silence is broken; then let the Rule or any homily be read. Finally, let “But you, O Lord” be said.

### 70.

Let a reading be delivered at the chapter meeting; likewise at the conference, if the time is suitable.

[Note: [Col. 0392C] The Pithoean codex: “let what has been read be explained.”]

### 71.

[Col. 0392A]

[Note: [Col. 0391] Two and four copies lack this chapter.]

When the brothers fast in summer, let them sleep after Sext.

[Note: [Col. 0392C] This chapter reads as follows in the Centuriators’ edition: “When the brothers fast, let them sleep after Sext, that is, in summertime. After this let them celebrate Mass.”]

### 72.

If anyone is held by the guilt of an offense, let him have a more lenient observance on Sunday and not ask pardon.

### 73.

Let an anniversary office be performed for a deceased abbot.

### 74.

[Note: [Col. 0391] One copy lacks this chapter.]

At Mass, let them say the Sanctus standing, and the Lord’s Prayer kneeling.

[Note: [Col. 0391] Four copies read: “standing, bowed down.”]

[Note: [Col. 0392C] The Centuriators’ edition adds: “and let them say the other prayers kneeling, when the time is more suitable.”]

### 75.

Let no one be received into the monastery for a gift, unless good will and the integrity of his conduct commend him.

[Note: [Col. 0391] Four copies read: “unless his merits of character commend him.”]

### 76.

Let each brother be given his own separate measure of food and drink, and let him give nothing to anyone from the measure given to him.

[Note: [Col. 0392C] The Monte Cassino codex: “let him have no permission whatsoever to give.” A rule in the *Concordia Regularum*, p. 718: “We decree especially that no one presume to give to another from his measure or to receive from another, except the abbot or provost to whom the abbot has entrusted this responsibility.”]

### 77.

[Note: [Col. 0391] Two copies lack this chapter. In its place four copies have: “Let fats be put into the stew for eight days before the Nativity of the Lord, for eight days before Lent, and throughout every Friday.”]

Let the brothers have some fat in their daily food, except on Friday, during the eight days before the Nativity of the Lord, and from Quinquagesima until Easter.

[Note: [Col. 0391] The chapters that follow are absent from codex 1. In their place it has the following:

“LXXVI. Let five psalms be sung in summer before Prime, but in winter after the interval, every day for the king and all Catholics, household members, and almsgivers: namely, ‘Have mercy on me, O God’ [Psalm 50]; ‘O God, in your name’; ‘Have mercy on me, O God, have mercy’; ‘May God have mercy on us’; ‘O God, come to my aid’; and specifically for the king, ‘May the Lord answer you.’

“LXXVII. Let five psalms be sung for all deceased Catholics, namely, ‘Hear my words, O Lord; do not rebuke me in your anger’; ‘I love because he has heard’; ‘Out of the depths’; and for all the dead, whether monks or all faithful Christian Catholics, let five psalms be sung, namely, ‘The Lord shepherds me’; ‘To you, O Lord, I lift up’; ‘The Lord is my light’; ‘Lord, hear’; and ‘Praise the Lord, O my soul.’”]

### 78.

[Note: [Col. 0391] One and two copies lack this chapter.]

Let them eat poultry only at the Nativity of the Lord and at Easter, for four days, if there is any available. If there is none available, let it not be demanded as a due.

[Note: [Col. 0392C] This is the reading of the Pithoean and Paris codices. The Monte Cassino codex has “for three days”; the Saint Gall codex has “for six days only”; the Centuriators and the 1603 edition of the Capitularies have “for eight days.” The reading is supported by Theodomar’s letter, which says:

“We never eat poultry except on the day of the Nativity of the Lord, if there is any available, up to eight days. Likewise during the days of Easter.”

See Menard’s notes on the *Concordia Regularum*, p. 709.]

[Note: [Col. 0391] In the Saint Gall manuscript codex it reads “for six days only,” etc.; “at Easter, for three days,” according to four copies.]

[Note: [Col. 0392D] Theodomar likewise says: “Our most prudent father carefully prescribed in his Rule concerning the eating of poultry that, if the monks wish to eat it when it is available, they should not incur guilt. But if their abbot does not provide such food for them, they cannot demand it as though it were owed to them. Nevertheless, many of our brothers do not eat poultry,” and so forth.]

If the abbot or the monks wish to abstain, let it be within their discretion.

[Note: [Col. 0393] Four copies read “within their power.”]

### 79.

[Note: [Col. 0393] One, two, three, and four copies, as well as the Saint Gall codex, lack this chapter.]

Let mittens of wether-skin be given to the brothers.

[Note: [Col. 0393] Four copies read: “mittens, if resources permit, of wether-skin shall be given.”]

### 80.

[Note: [Col. 0393B] This chapter is absent from several codices and is taken word for word from the Rule of Saint Benedict, except that certain clauses found in the Rule are omitted here.]

In his teaching, the abbot must always observe that apostolic formula in which he says: “Reprove, entreat, rebuke.” That is, he ought to reprove the undisciplined and restless more harshly; but he ought to entreat the obedient, the gentle, and the patient, so that they may advance toward what is better. We admonish him to rebuke and correct the negligent and contemptuous, and not to overlook the sins of offenders; but as soon as they begin to arise, let him cut them out at the root as far as he is able, mindful of the danger of Eli the priest of Shiloh.

Let him restrain the wicked, the hard-hearted, the proud, or the disobedient by blows or bodily punishment at the very beginning of their sin, knowing that it is written: “A fool is not corrected by words”; and again: “Strike your son with the rod, and you will deliver his soul from death.”

[Note: [Col. 0393B] See Menard’s notes on the *Concordia Regularum*, p. 191.]

In all things, therefore, let everyone follow the Rule as mistress, and let no one rashly depart from it. Let no one in the monastery follow the will of his own heart, nor let anyone presume to contend insolently with his abbot within the monastery or outside it. If anyone presumes to do so, let him be subjected to regular discipline.

If anyone, frequently corrected for any fault, does not amend even after excommunication, let a harsher correction be applied to him—that is, let the punishment of blows proceed against him.

Likewise, anyone who presumes to leave the monastery’s enclosure, or to go anywhere, or to do anything, however small, without the abbot’s command, shall be subject to regular punishment.

Let offenders be rebuked before everyone, so that the others may have fear.

[Note: [Col. 0393B] In addition to the eighty chapters above, five others are found interspersed in the Centuriators’ edition, which we have judged should be added here:

“1. Let monks carry staffs when necessity or illness requires it.

“2. During the fast of the Four Ember Days, let no food be taken other than that prescribed by the holy fathers for Lent. Likewise on the first day of the fast.

“3. When the monks fast, let the Office of the Dead be celebrated before the reading before Compline is read. Then let them go to the refectory, drink, and afterward read the collect.

“4. During Easter week, let them not speak in the cloister, but let all observe divine reading. Likewise during Pentecost week, on all Sundays, on the Nativity of the Lord, and on all the principal feasts of the saints.

“5. Let them not eat in the house of the sick without the prior’s permission, nor drink.”

The first of these five chapters is greatly illuminated by the fifth chapter of the supplication that the Fulda monks presented to Charlemagne, in which they ask that the elderly and the sick be permitted to carry a staff for support.]

---

## III. GENERAL CAPITULARY OF AACHEN (Year 817)

[Col. 0393]

We present again the preface of the General Capitulary, written in Tironian notes in Codex 1 of the Royal Library of Paris, no. 2718, and formerly published by Baluze and Carpenter, having been deciphered with the aid of engraved copper plates under the guidance of the highly perceptive Ulrich Friedrich Kopp.

[Col. 0393C] **Note:** Thus manuscript 1. Baluzius, omitting these words, gives as the title: “In the year 816 of the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, Louis, most Christian and most pious emperor, assembled from throughout his empire a convention of bishops, abbots, counts, and the elders of the Franks, that they might enact chapters for the benefit of the whole Church. And so it was done.”

[Col. 0393C] In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ. Hludowicus, by the divinely ordained providence of God, august emperor.

Since, according to the Apostle, as long as we are in this world we are exiles from the Lord, and since nothing in the present is fixed or immovable, but everything passes swiftly onward, and since Scripture bears witness that whatever we can do we must do with diligence, because no one is promised tomorrow for doing good, and since, according to the Apostle, we shall all stand before the tribunal of Christ so that each may render an account for what he has done, we—who above all, although equal to other mortals by nature, surpass them only in the dignity of our rule—must act with watchful care and the full intention of our minds. For we shall render an account not only for a graver offense committed, but also for the deeds and words, and even the thoughts, of our sins, on the day of the strict judgment, according to sacred Scripture, which says that he will question our works and search out our thoughts.

We must therefore strive, by continually devoting ourselves to good works, to benefit in every possible way those over whom we appear to preside, insofar as divine grace has granted us the ability. But since every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, we ought humbly to beseech the Lord with continual prayers and to anticipate his presence with humble confession and suitable amendment, insofar as he grants us the power to do so, so that, just as it is his gift that we reign, it may also be his mercy through which we govern successfully. Thus, with his compassion, may we deserve both to hold the reins of the kingdom with the fairest balance and, with the manifold fruit of our administration—namely, justice, piety, and humility—to reach him who is King of kings and Lord of lords, so that we may reign with him without end.

And since he has deigned through his Apostle to call us his fellow workers, and since the holy Church, namely his bride, is called in the sacred Scriptures a field, it must be cultivated by daily labor with the hoe of good works. Just as harmful things continually spring up in it, as in a good field, so harmful growths must continually be rooted out through labor and good zeal, and useful things planted. We ought devotedly to attend to all its needs with whatever efforts we can make, so that, laboring with full devotion of mind for its correction insofar as the Lord grants us the ability, we may deserve to be fitted by its builder, the Lord Jesus Christ, into some part of his structure.

Therefore let it be known to all our faithful people of the holy Church of God, and to our successors whom God in his dispensation shall appoint, that when divine mercy, although we possessed no merits, had raised us to the summit of this empire after our father had been taken from human affairs, we considered how and in what manner, with the Lord’s assistance, we might bring to completion the desire for divine worship which, from the beginning of our life, Christ inspiring us, we had conceived; and we observed what zeal and labor our forebears, especially our father of pious memory, had displayed for the welfare of the holy Church of God. We wished, with the strength granted us by God, not only to preserve their pious deeds inviolate but also to imitate them, namely, so that if we perceived anything in ecclesiastical affairs or in the condition of the commonwealth that needed correction, we might correct it through our own efforts, insofar as the Lord granted us the ability.

Until now, however, hindered as we were by storms of worldly disturbances arising here and there and by the onset of many different occupations, we had been unable to accomplish this as we desired. For this reason, in the fourth year of our reign, having summoned certain bishops, abbots, canons, monks, faithful men, and our nobles, we undertook, with their counsel, to investigate with the keenest inquiry how, with God’s help, we might provide for each order—namely, canons, monks, and laymen—in accordance with reason and according to the resources available.

Although we had often previously issued arrangements concerning the condition of churches and the administration of justice, and had sent envoys to individual places, the devil’s envy had obstructed this through tyrannical wickedness. But since the Lord granted that he should be most opportunely defeated in these matters and gave peace everywhere, it was necessary for us to spend this time of granted peace for the common benefit of the holy Church of God and of all our people, in three ways: first, so that what had been begun well might, with God’s help, reach completion; second, so that anything begun with good will but without prudent discernment, and impeded by various causes, might be carefully examined and corrected prudently insofar as circumstances permitted; and third, so that if we saw that anything necessary was lacking, it might be sought out and, with God’s help, brought to completion. Thus thereafter no one could justly reproach our work, and it might benefit the salvation of many both in our own time and in the future, and, with God’s assistance, remain stable.

But how we acted in these matters, with divine cooperation and on the advice of our faithful, according to our ability and the brevity of the time—not as much as we ought and wished, but as much as God granted us the power to do—and what we endeavored, by common vote and common agreement, to provide for each order, we have recorded: what specifically the canons were to observe, what the monks were to observe, what was to be introduced into the secular laws, and what was to be inserted into the capitularies. We committed the several matters to the several groups for observance. Nevertheless, so that these provisions might remain valid in our time and in that of our successors and, with God’s approval, be preserved inviolate, we decided, for the sake of the firmness of memory and preservation, to gather together briefly into one body what had been collected, to record it in the capitularies that follow, and to deposit it in the public archive. Thus may our successors, by God’s dispensation, preserve our pious deeds and in turn teach their successors to preserve their own good deeds.

**End.**

[Col. 0395] The *Capitulare* pertaining to the ecclesiastical orders is transmitted through the following manuscripts: 1. Paris, Royal Library, no. 2718, ninth century; 2. Wolfenbüttel, Ducal Library, Blankenburg collection, tenth century; 3. Gotha, Ducal Library, eleventh century. Baluzius, however, had used: 4, 5, and 6, manuscripts of the Paris Library—no. 4626, the Bigotian manuscript; no. 4280 A, from Saint-Remi of Reims; and no. 4788, from Saint-Vincent of Laon—as well as another from the Thuani collection. It is also found in Paris, Royal Library, Fonds de Notre-Dame F. 4, tenth century; and chapters 1–4, 15, 16, 29, and 5 occur in manuscript no. 4628 A.

[Col. 0395D] **Note:** We had four copies of these capitularies: one from the Thuani Library, another from the Bigotian Library, a third which belonged to Saint-Remi of Reims, and a fourth from Saint-Vincent of Laon. The author of the *Life of Louis the Pious*, in Duchesne, vol. II, p. 298, mentions these capitularies. The eighth formula of Marculf’s appendix also refers to them. **Baluzius.**

These chapters, properly concerning bishops and the various ecclesiastical orders, are matters which they must not only observe themselves but also teach those subject or entrusted to them to carry out.

1. Since, according to the tradition of the holy Fathers, we know that the property of the Church is the votive offerings of the faithful, the price of sins, and the patrimony of the poor, we wish, with God’s help, not only to preserve what is possessed by each person but also to bestow much [upon the Church]. Nevertheless, so that we might entirely remove from ecclesiastics the suspicion formerly conceived concerning the division of that property, we decree that neither in our time nor in the time of our sons, nor, by God’s dispensation, in that of our successors who may wish to imitate our will or the example of our forebears, shall it suffer any division or loss whatsoever.

[Col. 0395D] **Note:** *nullam* (“none”) in manuscripts 2 and 3.

2. Not ignorant of the sacred canons, and so that the holy Church might more freely possess its honor in God’s name, we have given our assent to the ecclesiastical order: namely, that bishops be chosen from their own diocese through the election of clergy and people, according to the statutes of the canons, without regard to persons or acceptance of gifts, on account of the merit of their life and the gift of wisdom, so that by example and word they may be able to benefit those subject to them in every respect.

[Col. 0397] **Note:** *ignorari* (“to be ignored”) in manuscript 2.

[Col. 0397] **Note:** The words “so that the holy Church might more freely possess its honor” are absent from manuscript 2.

[Col. 0397D] **Note:** An example of such an election is provided by the *Address of the Envoys of Emperor Louis to the Clergy and People Gathered for the Purpose of an Election*, from the manuscript of Saint Michael at Massa, published by Sirmond and Baluzius, vol. II, cols. 601–605.

3. Since the canonical profession was being dishonored by many, partly through ignorance and partly through negligence, we thought it worthwhile, with God’s approval, at the sacred assembly to gather into one rule for canons and canonesses certain fresh flowers, as it were, picked from the words of the holy Fathers, from various meadows, and to hand it over for observance to canons and religious women, so that through it the canonical order might be observed without ambiguity.

And since the sacred assembly so extolled it in praise that it judged it should be observed down to a single iota, we decree that it be held without doubt by all who live under that profession and that henceforth it be observed in every respect both by canons and by religious women living canonically.

[Col. 0397] **Note:** *posset* (“might be able”) in manuscript 1.

[Col. 0397] **Note:** *seruetur* (“be preserved”) in manuscript 1.

4. It has been decreed that whatever is voluntarily contributed by the faithful to the Church during our reign shall, in richer places, be divided so that two parts go to the use of the poor and the third to the maintenance of the clergy or monks; but in poorer places it shall be divided equally between clergy and poor, unless the donors have specifically determined that it be given for particular purposes.

[Col. 0397C] 5. We have carefully ordered to be recorded in another document how, with God’s help, we have in part arranged the affairs of the monks; how we have granted them permission to choose abbots from among themselves; and how we have made provision so that, with God’s help, they might live in peace and guard their purpose tirelessly. And, so that this might remain valid with our successors and be preserved inviolate, we have confirmed it.

[Col. 0397] **Note:** *conservetur* (“be preserved”) in manuscript 2.

6. Concerning the ordination of slaves, who were indiscriminately promoted everywhere to ecclesiastical orders, it pleased everyone that the matter ought to be brought into agreement with the sacred canons. It has therefore been decreed that henceforth no bishop dare promote them to sacred orders unless they have first obtained freedom from their own masters.

If any slave, fleeing or hiding from his master, or by producing witnesses hired or bribed, or by any other cunning or fraud, should attain ecclesiastical orders, it has been decreed that he be deposed and that his master receive him.

But if a grandfather or father, migrating from one homeland to another, should beget a son in the latter province, and the son should be raised there and promoted to ecclesiastical orders, and should not know that he was a slave, and afterward his master should come and legally establish his claim to him, it has been decreed that, if his master wishes to grant him freedom, he may remain in his order. But if the master wishes to drag him out of the lord’s estate by the chain of slavery, he shall lose his order, because, according to the sacred canons, a person remaining in a lowly condition cannot exercise the dignity of the priesthood.

Concerning their property or peculium—those who are granted freedom by their own masters so that they may lawfully be promoted to ecclesiastical orders—it has been decreed that it shall remain in the power of the masters whether they wish to grant it to them or claim it for themselves. But if, after ordination, they acquire anything, the rule established in the canons concerning consecrated persons who possess nothing shall be observed.

[Col. 0397] **Notes:** *abstrahere* (“to drag away”) in manuscript 2 instead of *extrahere* (“to draw out”). *adquisiverit* (“he has acquired”) in manuscripts 2 and 3 instead of *adquisiverint* (“they have acquired”). *consecrantis* (“of the one consecrating”) in manuscripts 1, 2, and 3 instead of *consecratis* (“of the consecrated”).

[Col. 0397] **Note:** Manuscripts 1, 2, and 3 read *ita ordines* (“thus the orders”) instead of the transmitted wording.

Concerning the slaves of churches, it was decreed by common decision that the archbishops established in the several provinces should keep a copy of our authority, and their suffragans a copy of that authority. Whenever a useful person from the household of a church is found who is to be ordained, the authority itself shall be read aloud before the people from the ambo, and before priests or faithful laymen, before the altar’s horn, as is contained in our authority. After every form of cunning has been removed, he shall obtain freedom, and only then shall he be promoted to ecclesiastical orders.

The same procedure shall be followed concerning those whom laymen from the households of churches wish to promote to sacred orders. The same form shall also be observed concerning those whom the superiors of canons or monks request to be ordained.

[Col. 0397] **Notes:** *promoveantur* (“they be promoted”) in manuscripts 2 and 3. Manuscript 2 reads *et* (“and”) instead of the transmitted wording.

7. **Note:** This chapter appears in the manuscripts V, Vn., and Est. It is incorrectly cited by Muratori as chapter 5 among the laws of Hludowicus II.

It has been decreed that no ecclesiastic henceforth dare accept property from persons whose children or relatives might, through this ill-considered offering, be disinherited of their own property. If anyone thereafter attempts to do this, both the recipient shall be severely punished by synodal or imperial judgment, and the property shall return to the disinherited.

[Col. 0397] **Notes:** *inutili* (“useless”) in manuscript 1 instead of *inconsulta* (“ill-considered”). The words “and the property shall return to the disinherited” are absent from manuscript 3; according to some, manuscript Vn. has them in the margin. The words “so that also” are absent from manuscript 3. The words “by imperial judgment” are absent from manuscript 2.

8. It has also been decreed that no one established in a canonical or regular profession shall henceforth persuade anyone to receive the tonsure in order to obtain property; and whoever attempts to do this shall in every respect be punished by synodal or imperial judgment.

[Col. 0397] **Note:** *deest* (“is absent”) in manuscript 2.

9. It has been decreed that, without the authority or consent of the bishops, priests shall neither be appointed nor expelled from any churches. If laymen present to the bishops clerics of proven life and learning to be consecrated and appointed in their churches, the bishops shall not reject them on any pretext.

[Col. 0397] **Note:** Manuscript 2 reads *etiam si* (“even if”). The words “nor reject them on any pretext” are absent from manuscript 2.

10. It has been decreed that one complete *mansus* shall be assigned to each church, free from every other service, and that the priests appointed to them shall render no service from tithes, offerings of the faithful, houses, courtyards or gardens situated beside the church, or the aforesaid *mansus*, except ecclesiastical service. If they possess anything more, they shall render from it the service owed to their lords.

[Col. 0399] **Notes:** Baluzius reads *ullo* (“any”) instead of *alio* (“other”). Manuscript 2 reads *areas* (“plots of land”) instead of *atriis* (“courtyards”).

11. It has been decreed that, once this has been fulfilled, each church shall have its own priest wherever the bishop, taking account of circumstances, permits this to be done.

12. It has been decreed concerning new villages and the churches newly built in them that the tithes from those villages shall be assigned to those same churches.

13. Concerning the sacred vessels of the Church, which we have learned are pledged by certain people in certain places, it has been forbidden that anyone henceforth presume to do this, except when compelled by necessity to redeem captives.

[Col. 0399] **Note:** Compare above, p. 368, chapter 11; that passage should be deleted there.

14. Concerning destroyed churches, and concerning ninths and tithes, and the cloisters of canons, we have recorded below in other chapters how we have decided that they should be established and ordered.

15. Likewise, concerning the honor of the churches—how, with God’s help, it may flourish insofar as it depends on us—it is known to have been inserted in the chapters recorded below.

[Col. 0399] **Note:** *deest* (“is absent”) in manuscript 5.

16. Concerning the bishops established in Lombardy, who were accustomed, contrary to divine and canonical authority, to accept or demand oaths and gifts from those whom they ordained, it has been forbidden in every way that this should happen again, because, according to the sacred canons, both parties who do such things must be cast down from their proper rank.

17. The bishops have decreed concerning priests who indiscriminately permit women to live with them and who are therefore marked by suspicion of ill repute, that if, after being admonished, they do not correct themselves, they shall be punished by canonical censure as contemptors of the sacred canons.

18. Concerning priests who were accustomed to come to the cities on Maundy Thursday to receive chrism, it has been decreed that, among those who live at a distance, the bishop shall choose one out of eight or ten to carry the chrism he has received carefully to himself and his companions. Those who live no more than four or five miles from the city shall come in person, as usual, to receive the chrism. But for the sake of instruction they shall be summoned to the cities at another time, not during Lent.

[Col. 0399] **Note:** Manuscript 2 reads *non alio quam* (“at no other time than”) instead of *alio, non* (“at another time, not”).

19. So that bishops would not become a burden to the people on the pretext of preaching or confirming, after being admonished by us they promised henceforth to avoid this and to perform their ministry, insofar as opportunity allows, at a time when their journey, so far as it depends on them, would not be inconvenient or burdensome to those whom they can and ought to benefit.

[Col. 0399] **Notes:** Manuscript 2 reads *admot[i]* (“having been approached”) instead of *admoniti* (“having been admonished”); and *et* (“and”) instead of *vel* (“or”).

20. It has been forbidden in every way that boys be tonsured without the consent of their parents, or girls veiled; and whoever attempts to do this shall be compelled to pay the fine contained in the chapters of the secular law established by us.

[Col. 0399] **Note:** Manuscript 2 reads *et* (“and”) instead of *vel* (“or”).

21. **Note:** The first part of this chapter, up to *eligant* (“they should choose”), occurs in the Langobard laws manuscripts of Vienna, Verona, and Este, in Muratori, chapter 68, where it is incorrectly placed among the laws of Lothar. The Ambrosian and Florentine manuscripts write the chapter above, p. 366, no. 2. The London manuscript, close to the Florentine, has our chapter up to *eligant* in an erased passage.

Concerning women who lose their husbands, it is decreed that they should not veil themselves indiscriminately as they have hitherto done, but should wait thirty days after the death of their husbands. After the thirtieth day, they shall choose what they ought to choose with the advice of their bishop; or, if the bishop is absent, with the advice of other religious priests and of their relatives and friends.

And because we were asked by the sacred assembly that those who were performing public penance, and women who lost their husbands, should be protected by our authority until they had decided what they would do, we have decreed that special chapters be made concerning them and inserted into the chapters of the secular law.

[Col. 0399] **Note:** I supplied *supplevi* from manuscript 3; it is absent from the others.

22. Concerning abducted women and abductors, although we had specifically decreed what those who thereafter attempted to commit this abomination ought to suffer, we nevertheless thought it necessary to insert here what the sacred canons command concerning the matter, so that it might be clear to everyone how great an evil it is, and so that, constrained not only by human but also by divine authority, this evil might henceforth be avoided.

23. Concerning abducted girls who have not yet been betrothed, the Council of Chalcedon, at which 630 Fathers were present, states the following in chapter 38:

> “Those who abduct girls, and those who cooperate with and assist the abductors under the pretext of living together, the holy synod has decreed as follows: if they are clerics, they shall fall from their proper rank; if they are laymen, they shall be anathematized.”

[Col. 0399] **Notes:** Manuscript 2 reads “220” instead of “630,” and “chapter 27” instead of “chapter 38.”

These words clearly show how the perpetrators of this evil must be condemned, since those who participate and assist are struck with so great an anathema; and, according to canonical authority, abductors can in no way lawfully claim the abducted women for legitimate marriage.
