24. **Note:** This occurs among the Langobard laws in Muratori, chapter 124.

Concerning betrothed girls who are abducted by others, the Council of Ancyra, chapter 10, reads as follows:

> “Concerning betrothed girls who are afterward abducted by others, it has been decided that they be taken away and restored to those to whom they had previously been betrothed, even if it is established that violence was inflicted upon them by the abductors.”

Accordingly, it has been decreed by the sacred assembly that the abductor shall be punished with public penance. But if the betrothed girl’s fiancé refuses to receive her, and she did not consent to the same crime, she shall not be denied permission to marry another. If she herself consented, she shall be subject to the same judgment. If afterward they presume to unite with one another, both shall be anathematized.

[Col. 0399] **Notes:** Manuscript 1 reads *disponsatis* (“betrothed”) instead of *desponsatis*. Manuscript 1 reads *post* (“after”) instead of *postea* (“afterward”). Manuscripts 2 and 3 read *et in eis* (“and in them”) instead of *et* (“and”). Manuscript 1 reads *disponsatae* instead of *desponsatae*. Manuscript 2 reads *raptam* (“the abducted woman”) instead of *raptae* (“of the abducted woman”); and *eiusdem criminis* (“of the same crime”) instead of *eidem crimini* (“to the same crime”). Manuscripts 2 and 3 read *sententia* (“judgment”) instead of *sententiae* (“to the judgment”).

25. Concerning those who associate with consecrated virgins, the twentieth chapter of Pope Gelasius’s decrees contains the following:

> “We have learned that certain men rashly associate themselves with consecrated virgins and, after their purpose has been dedicated to God, mingle illicit and sacrilegious unions with them. It is right that such men should immediately be driven from sacred communion; and unless they perform public and approved penance, they should not be received at all. Or at least, if they have repented, the viaticum should not be denied to them as they pass from this life.”

But if those who have intercourse with consecrated virgins are punished so severely, how much more severely must those who abduct them be punished? Therefore, as stated above, it is necessary that this evil be cut out at the root by all who remain within the Christian religion, through the severity of divine or human authority.

[Col. 0401] **Note:** *non* (“not”) is absent from manuscript 2.

26. So that girls should not be veiled indiscriminately, we have also thought it appropriate to insert here what is to be observed from the sacred canons. Concerning the age at which girls are to be veiled, the Council of Carthage, chapter 16, states that they are not to be consecrated before the age of twenty-five.

Likewise, the same council, in chapter 93, states concerning the veiling of virgins:

> “It has also been decided that if any bishop, because the virgin’s chastity is endangered—when either a powerful suitor or an abductor is feared—or if she has been struck by some dangerous fear of death lest she die unveiled, or if her parents or those responsible for her care require it, veils a virgin, or has veiled her before the age of twenty-five, the council’s decree concerning that number of years shall not prejudice him.”

From this it follows that, according to the earlier sanction, virgins are properly to be consecrated in their twenty-fifth year. But if the necessities mentioned above compel this to be done earlier, it cannot prejudice the bishop who performs the consecration.

[Col. 0401] **Note:** The words “so that no one may be able to veil her” are absent from manuscript 5.

27. It has been decreed that no one henceforth presume to perform any trial by the cross, lest what has been glorified by Christ’s Passion be held in contempt through anyone’s rashness.

[Col. 0401] **Note:** Manuscript 2 reads *quod* (“which”) instead of *quae* (“which,” feminine).

28. We have carefully admonished the bishops to announce the nourishment of the divine word diligently to the peoples, either personally or through deputies, because, as blessed Gregory says, a priest provokes the anger of the hidden Judge against himself if he proceeds without the sound of preaching.

We have also admonished them to nourish the clergy entrusted to them in sobriety and chastity and to instruct them in the divine offices, so that those clergy may properly be promoted to the sacred ecclesiastical orders; to ensure that priests possess a well-corrected missal, lectionary, and other books necessary to them; and to repair, according to their ability, the ruined churches belonging to them.

We have admonished them also to instruct widows carefully; to teach them how they ought to live according to apostolic authority; to eradicate the superstitions which certain people practice in some places at the funerals of the dead; to urge others to live well by the example of their own innocence; and to strive with all their strength, insofar as the Lord helps them, to provide for all ecclesiastical affairs. So that they may be able to carry this out more freely, we wish in every way to offer them assistance, insofar as the Lord grants us the power to do so.

29. Certain chapters—for example, concerning incestuous marriages, and concerning churches divided among co-heirs and thereby deprived of their proper honor, or concerning churches which have been excessively reduced in their own property, or indeed concerning property recently taken away from certain churches under the pressure of necessity, as well as anything else in ecclesiastical or public affairs deserving correction—which, because of the brevity of time, we were unable to accomplish, we judged should be deferred until, with the Lord’s favor, the opportunity to accomplish them might be granted us through the counsel of the faithful.

We have nevertheless judged that the matters discovered should be inserted here so that, with God’s help, they may reach completion in due course.

[Col. 0401] **Notes:** Manuscript 2 reads *quoheredes* (“co-heirs”) instead of *coheredes*. Compare the *Capitulare Wormatiense* of the year 829, I, chapter 2. The words *in tantum differendum illud dignum* (“that worthy matter should be deferred to such an extent”) are absent from manuscript 1. Manuscript 4 continues: “so that, with God’s assistance, they may obtain their fulfillment through the times already amended, corrected, and restored, and so that we may confirm them in writing.” **Baluzius**, from the text of Ansegisus. In the Royal Paris manuscript, Fonds de Notre-Dame F. 4, the words *FINIUNT CAPITULA CANONICA* (“The canonical chapters end”) are found.

[Col. 0401] We have established the chapters added to the laws through the following manuscripts: A 1, Paris, Royal Library, no. 2718, ninth century; A 2, the same library, Fonds de Notre-Dame F. 4, tenth century; A 3, the same library, no. 4280 A, tenth century; A 4, Wolfenbüttel, Ducal Library, among the Augustan manuscripts, tenth century, although it contains only chapters 3, 4, 7, 9, and 18.

B 1, Saint-Paul’s, beginning of the ninth century; B 2, Corbie, tenth century; B 3, Paris, Royal Library, no. 4632, tenth century.

C 1, the same library, no. 4995, ninth century; C 2, the same library, no. 4628, tenth century; C 3, Wolfenbüttel, Ducal Library, Blankenburg collection, tenth century; C 4, the late jurist Ernst Spangenberg of Celle; and, in addition, all the manuscripts containing the *Capitularia* added to the Langobard laws, namely the Chisian and Cava manuscripts, which approach most closely the manuscripts of class B, and then the Gotha, Ambrosian, Florentine, London, Vienna, Verona, and Este manuscripts in Muratori. The Royal Paris manuscripts nos. 4626, 4628 A, 4631, 4788, and 4760 were also consulted.

[Col. 0403A] **Note:** These were corrected with the aid of seven ancient copies, two of which are in the Royal Library, the third in the Colbert Library, the fourth in the Thesan Library, and the fifth in the Bigotian Library. The sixth belonged to Saint-Vincent of Laon. The seventh was supplied to us by the distinguished man Hieronymus Bignonius, royal advocate in the Parliament of Paris.

In those copies the following title is prefixed:

> “Here begin the chapters which are to be added to the laws, which both the envoys and counts must possess and make known to the others.”

But in one royal copy, formerly belonging to the Mazarin Library, it reads:

> “This is the Salic law which is to be added to the laws,”

and so forth.

These are the chapters which Einhard writes that Louis added to the laws in the year 819:

> “An assembly was held at Aachen after the Nativity of the Lord, at which many matters concerning the condition of churches and monasteries were discussed and ordered. Certain necessary chapters were also written and added to the laws, because they were lacking.”

The following words from the author of the *Life of Louis the Pious* are also to be understood as referring to these chapters:

> “Meanwhile he added certain chapters to the laws, in which the legal cases that seemed to be limping were addressed; these chapters have hitherto been preserved as exceedingly necessary.”

**Baluzius.**

[Col. 0403A] Here begin the chapters which are to be added to the laws, which both the envoys and counts must possess and make known to the others.

[Col. 0403] **Note:** The remainder is absent from manuscripts 7 and 8. Manuscript B 1 begins: “Here begin the chapters of Lord Louis Augustus, emperor, and so forth.” Manuscript B 3 reads: “This is the Salic law which is to be added to the laws, and so forth.”

[Col. 0404D] **Note:** The whole inscription is absent from C 1. C 3 reads: “Likewise, of Emperor Louis.” Baluzius gave this inscription: “These chapters Lord Emperor Louis promulgated in the fifth year of his reign, with the entire assembly of the people, in the palace at Aachen, and ordered added to the Salic law. Afterwards, when he had held a general assembly at the estate of Theodon, he prohibited further chapters from being added, but wished them to be called simply law.”

1. **Concerning the honor of churches.** If anyone, either for a trivial reason or without cause, kills a man in a church, he shall pay with his life.

But if two men quarrel outside, and one flees into a church, and the other kills him there while defending himself, then, if he has no witnesses to this deed, he shall affirm under oath, together with twelve lawful compurgators, that he killed him in self-defense. After this, he shall be compelled to pay six hundred solidi to the church whose sanctuary he polluted by that homicide, and in addition our ban. The man who was killed shall lie without compensation being paid for him. Thereafter the killer shall receive, according to canonical judgment, suitable penance for the crime he committed.

If the offender was his own slave, he shall be examined by the judgment of boiling water to determine whether he did this voluntarily or in self-defense. If his hand is scalded, he shall be killed. If it is not, his master shall pay to the church according to the amount of his *wergild*, or, if he wishes, shall hand him over to that same church.

Concerning a church slave, a royal-fiscal slave, or a beneficiary’s slave, we wish his *wergild* to be paid in compensation for him once; the second time the slave himself shall be handed over to punishment. Nevertheless, the inheritance of a free man who has been sentenced to death because of such a crime shall pass to his lawful heirs.

[Col. 0404D] **Note:** Baronius cites this passage under 18 November to show that our ancestors were accustomed sometimes to consecrate the doors of churches or courtyards with sacred relics. **Baluzius.**

If such a homicide is committed in the courtyard of a church whose door has been consecrated with the relics of the saints, it shall be corrected or compensated in the same manner. But if the church door has not been consecrated, what is committed in the courtyard shall be compensated in the manner in which an offense committed in violated immunity ought to be compensated.

[Col. 0403] **Notes:** Manuscripts Cava, A, V, Vn., and Est. read *furore* (“in fury”) instead of *fuste* (“with a staff”). Manuscripts C 1, C 2, and C 3 add: “And if he is scalded, let him be killed. But if he is not scalded, the master…” Manuscript B 1 reads *noluerit* (“if he does not wish”) instead of *voluerit* (“if he wishes”). Manuscript C 3 writes *widrigildus*, while the Chisian manuscript writes *guidrigild*.

2. **Concerning injuries inflicted on priests in churches.** Bloodshed inflicted in churches with a staff shall be compensated threefold if the victim was a priest: two parts shall go to that priest, the third, as the *fred*, to the church, and in addition our ban.

Likewise, in the case of a deacon, it shall be compensated threefold according to his compensation, together with our ban. The same shall apply to a subdeacon, threefold according to his compensation. For a cleric of any order, three times his compensation shall be paid, and in addition our ban.

Likewise, for a blow without bloodshed inflicted on a cleric of any order, three times his compensation shall be paid, together with our ban. Whoever has nothing with which to pay the church shall surrender himself into the service of that church until he has paid the entire debt.

[Col. 0403] **Notes:** The Cava, A, Vienna, Verona, and Este manuscripts read *furore* (“in fury”) instead of *fuste* (“with a staff”). The Vienna, Verona, and Este manuscripts read *iuxta estimationem compositionem* (“according to the assessed compensation”) instead of *iuxta compositionem* (“according to the compensation”). The words from *haec* through *noster* (“this … our ban”) are absent from manuscripts V, Vn., and Est. Manuscript Vn. reads *vel aestimationem* (“or assessment”).

3. **Concerning widows, orphans, and the poor.** Whenever they come before the count in the *mallus*, their case shall first be heard and decided. If they are unable to find witnesses for themselves to pursue their cases, or if they do not know the law, the count shall assist them by giving them a suitable person to manage their case or speak on their behalf.

[Col. 0403] **Note:** Manuscript B 1 reads: “We command that whenever a widow, orphan, or poor person comes before the count…”

4. **Concerning the abduction of widows.** Whoever takes a widow as his partner within the first thirty days of her widowhood, whether against her will or with her consent, shall pay our ban—that is, sixty solidi—threefold.

[Col. 0403] **Note:** Manuscripts C 1, C 2, and C 3 read *componat* instead of *conponat* (“shall pay”) and add: “Nevertheless, the man who abducted her is not permitted to keep her.”

If he took her against her will, he shall pay her legal compensation, but shall not approach her thereafter.

5. **Concerning a man who is killed while performing public penance.** Whoever kills a man performing public penance shall pay our ban threefold and pay his *wergild* to his relatives.

[Col. 0403] **Note:** Manuscripts V, Vn., and Est. read: “If he did it in self-defense.”

[Col. 0404C] **6. That every free man shall have the power to give his property wherever he wishes for the salvation of his soul.** If anyone wishes to give his property for the salvation of his soul, either to some venerable place, or to a kinsman, or to anyone else, and at that time he is within the same county in which those properties are situated, let him take care to make a lawful transfer. But if, at the time when he wishes to transfer them, he is outside that county—that is, whether on campaign, at the palace, or in any other place—let him provide suitable witnesses, either from his own pagenses or from others who live under the same law as he does [Note: [Col. 0405] Here C 4 begins.]; or, if he cannot have such men, then others of the best who can be found there. In their presence let him make the transfer of his property and give sureties for the vestitura, who shall effect the vestitura for the person receiving that transfer.

After this transfer has been made in this manner, let his heir be unable to make any claim to the aforesaid property. Moreover, let he himself personally provide a surety for that same vestitura, so that no opportunity remains for the heir to alter this transfer, but rather that he be obliged to complete it. And if he has not yet divided his property with his coheirs, let this not be an impediment to him; but let his coheir, if unwilling voluntarily, be compelled by the count or by his messenger to make the division with the person to whom the deceased wished his inheritance to pass.

And if he asked that it be transferred to any church, let his coheir have with that church the same legal claim concerning the aforesaid inheritance that he ought to have had with another coheir. Let this also be observed with respect to father, son, and grandson [Note: [Col. 0405] Grandsons, B 1.] until the lawful ages. Thereafter let the properties themselves return to the immunity of that church.

**7. On preventing homicides.** Whoever kills a man either for a trivial reason or without cause shall pay his wergild in compensation to those to whom the deceased belongs. But he himself, because of such an act of presumption, shall be sent into exile for as long a time as we please; nevertheless, he shall not lose his property.

**8. What must not be given in payment of a wergild.** In payment of a wergild, we wish those things to be given which are contained in the law [Note: [Col. 0405] Namely, *robuaria* (sic; apparently the Ripuarian law), as the gloss of codex Vn. reads.], except a hawk and a sword, because perjury is sometimes committed on account of those two items, when men swear that they are of greater value than they really are.

**9. On the abduction of other men’s betrothed women.** If anyone abducts another man’s betrothed woman, let him return her [Note: [Col. 0405] Absent from C 1, 2, 3, 4.] to her father [Note: [Col. 0405] Absent from C 1, 2, 3, 4.], or to the person who by law ought to be her protector [Note: [Col. 0405] Absent from C 1, 2, 3, 4.], together with his legal compensation [Note: [Col. 0405] “Let him return her to the fiancé and pay her legal compensation to the protector,” V. Vn. E.]; and whatever he took away with her, let him return each item separately according to the law.

And if her protector consented to this act and therefore [Note: [Col. 0405] Absent from C 1, 2, 3, 4.] does not wish to seek anything from the abductor, let the count exact from him our *fredum* separately for each item [Col. 0405D]. Let him pay the fiancé his legal compensation and, in addition, pay our ban—that is, sixty solidi—or let the count cause him to come into our presence, and let him remain in exile for as long as we please; nor shall he be permitted to have that woman.

[Col. 0406A] **10. On convicting false witnesses.** If anyone has a dispute with another over any matter, and witnesses have been produced against him by judicial process, and he suspects that they are false, let him be permitted to set against them other witnesses, as good as he can obtain, so that by the testimony of truthful men the perversity of the false witnesses may be overcome.

But if the two groups of witnesses disagree with one another so completely that neither side is willing in any way to yield to the other [Note: [Col. 0405D] The Codex Thuaneus reads: “to believe.” Baluze.], let two of them be chosen—one from each side—to fight in the field with shields and clubs, so that it may be determined by their testimony which side follows falsehood and which follows truth. Let the champion who is defeated have his right hand cut off, because of the perjury he committed before the combat. Let the other witnesses of the same side, since they have appeared to be false, redeem their hands; two-thirds of this compensation shall be given to the person against whom they testified, and the third shall be paid as *fredum* [Note: [Col. 0405] “The third belongs to the count,” C 1, 2, 4.].

In a secular case, then, let such a disagreement among witnesses be proved by combat. In ecclesiastical cases, however, where one side concerns a secular matter and the other an ecclesiastical matter, let the same procedure be observed. But where the matter is ecclesiastical on both sides, let the heads of those churches have permission to reconcile themselves amicably, if they wish. If they cannot agree on such a reconciliation, let their advocates come into the public assembly before the count, and there let a lawful end be imposed upon their disputes.

Witnesses for any matter shall not be sought from elsewhere, but only from the county in which the property that is the subject of the dispute is situated; for it is not credible that the truth concerning either a man’s status or anyone’s possession can be known better through others than through those who live nearer [Col. 0406C] [Note: [Col. 0405] The Codex Thuaneus wrongly reads *regi veritas* (“truth to the king”); but this error was an easy one to make. ID.]. Nevertheless, if the dispute that has arisen between them is at the boundary of two counties, let them be permitted to have witnesses for their case from the neighboring *centena* of the adjacent county.

**11. On property placed under the ban.** If anyone’s property has been placed under the ban because of some crime committed by him, and, having learned of the matter, he delays coming so as not to do justice, and allows it to remain under the ban for a year and a day, let him not acquire it thereafter; rather, let it be joined to our fisc [Note: [Col. 0405] “But if, after returning within that period and after being summoned, he dies, even if he has not yet cleared himself, nevertheless let the property pass to his own heirs. But if he is unwilling to appear for judgment within the year, let him lose the property and clear his innocence. If he is unable to do so, let him undergo the legal penalty and nevertheless lose the property. The debt, etc.,” V. Vn. E.; “let him lose the property, unless …”].

But the debt which the person who owned it ought to have paid shall be discharged by the count and his officials, according to the assessment of the damage, from the movable property found in that estate, to those to whom the same debtor was indebted [Col. 0406D]. If the quantity of movable property found there is insufficient for the compensation, let it be supplemented from the immovable property; and whatever remains, let our fisc possess, as stated. If nothing can remain after the compensation, let everything be expended for it.

But if that man had not yet divided his property with his coheirs, let the count summon them and make a lawful division with them. Then, as has already been said, let him assign that man’s share to our fisc and pay the compensation from it, according to the amount set out above, to those to whom it legally belongs.

But if he was summoned not concerning another matter, but concerning the very property that had been placed under the ban and thereby reduced into our power, let the count in whose district it is established that the property lies take care to report this to us, so that by the authority of our order we may cause that property—which, according to the aforesaid procedure, has been reduced into our ownership—to pass into the right and possession of the man who was claiming it, if it ought to be his [Note: [Col. 0407] “If it ought to be his” is absent from C 1, 2, 3, 4.] [Note: [Col. 0407] “And if anyone has taken it into his own possession, let him be permitted to hold it by his oath; and if he is later convicted on that account, let his right hand be cut off.” Ch. C. A. and the other Lombard manuscripts.].

**12. On summonses.** If anyone is to be summoned concerning his status—that is, concerning his freedom—or concerning an inheritance, let him be summoned according to the provisions of the law. But concerning other matters for which someone must give an account, let him not be summoned in this manner, but let him be placed under the ban by the count. And [Note: [Col. 0407] “By the count”; “and” is absent from C 1, 2, 3, 4.] if, after one and another warning from the count [Note: [Col. 0407] “After the second warning of the count,” C 1, 2, 3, 4.], anyone is unwilling to come to the assembly, let him be compelled to come and do justice after his property has been placed under the ban.

**13. On restraining feuds.** If anyone commits homicide under the compulsion of some necessity, let the count in whose district the deed was committed cause both the compensation to be paid and the feud to be settled by oath.

But if one party refuses to consent to this—whether the person who committed the homicide or the person who ought to receive the compensation—let him cause the disobedient man [Note: [Col. 0407] “The count who …,” Baluze.] to come into our presence, so that we may send him into exile for as long as we please, until he is disciplined there and learns not thereafter to dare to be disobedient to his count, and so that greater harm may not arise from the matter.

**14. Where oaths are to be sworn.** Where it was formerly customary to undertake or swear oaths concerning freedom, let the assembly be held there [Note: [Col. 0407] “The oaths are to be sworn there,” C 3; “where …” Ch. C.] [Note: [Col. 0407] “Except in the church and its atrium, because according to the law it cannot be held elsewhere,” *Minora* C 1, 4.], and let the oaths be sworn there. Nevertheless, let the assembly be held neither in the church nor in its atrium [Note: [Col. 0407] “Let the assembly or judicial proceedings be held elsewhere, except in the church and its atrium, because according to the law it cannot be held otherwise,” *Minora* C 3.]. Let the count hold the lesser assemblies either within his own jurisdiction or wherever he is able to obtain permission.

We decree that a house be built by the count in the place where he ought to hold the assembly [Col. 0407D] [Note: [Col. 0407] “Established,” B 1, C 1, Lombard manuscripts.], so that public business may not be impeded by the heat of the sun or by rain.

**15. Concerning those accused of theft.** If a free man is accused of theft and possesses property of his own, let him give security for himself in the assembly before the count [Col. 0408A]. If he has no property, let him provide sureties who will give security for him and bring him to the hearing. Let him be permitted, on the first occasion, to clear himself according to the law by oath, if he is able.

But if, on another occasion, two or three men accuse him of theft [Note: [Col. 0407] “For,” C 1, 2, 3, 4.], let him be permitted to contend in the field against one of them with shield and club.

But if a slave is accused of theft, let his master make compensation for him or excuse him by oath [Note: [Col. 0407] “Let him cause compensation to be made, or …,” C 1, 2, 4.], unless he has committed such a theft that he ought to be handed over for punishment.

**16. On contempt of the king’s letters.** If anyone disregards our letters—that is, the *tractoria* sent for the reception of our messengers—let him either lose whatever honors he possesses, or sit for as long as it takes to satisfy our will in the place where he ought to have received the aforesaid messengers, receiving there, at his own expense, the embassies that come there [Col. 0408B].

But whoever disregards our letter in any way [Note: [Col. 0407] “Our written notice,” C 1, 2, 3, 4.] shall come to the palace at our command and receive, according to our will, a punishment appropriate to his foolishness. If a free man or a count’s official has done this, let him lose whatever honor or benefice he may have held. If he is a slave, let him be beaten naked at the stake and have his head shaved.

**17. On unjust tolls and customary exactions.** Wherever there was a custom in the time of our grandfather, lord Pippin, of paying a toll, let it continue to be paid there in the future [Note: [Col. 0407] “Previously,” C 1, 2, 3, 4.]; but where it was newly begun, let it not be continued.

Where it is not necessary to cross a river by a bridge [Note: [Col. 0407] “To the bridge,” C 1, 2, 3, 4.], or where a ship has gone through the middle of the water or under a bridge without approaching the bank, and nothing has been bought or sold there, let no toll be paid thereafter. Let no one compel another to go to the bridge where he can cross the water beside the bridge.

Whoever thereafter exacts a toll in such places, or from those going to the palace or to the army, shall return that toll with his legal compensation and pay our ban—that is, sixty solidi.

**18. On those unwilling to accept sound coins.** Whoever, being a free man, refuses to receive a pure and properly weighed coin shall pay our ban—that is, sixty solidi. If slaves of churches, counts, or our vassals presume to do this [Col. 0408D], let them receive sixty blows [Note: [Col. 0407] “Strikes,” C 1, 2, 3, 4.].

Or if their master or advocate, who is a free man, is unwilling, when ordered, to present them to the count or to our messenger, let him pay our aforesaid ban of sixty solidi [Note: [Col. 0407] “That is, …,” C 1, 2, 3; perhaps also C 4.].

[Col. 0409A] **19. On counterfeiters of coin** [Note: [Col. 0409] The entire chapter is absent from Ch. C.]. Concerning false coin, we order that whoever is proved to have struck it shall have his hand cut off [Note: [Col. 0409] “We order that,” B 1, 2.]. Whoever consented to this, if he is free, shall pay sixty solidi. If he is a slave, let him receive sixty blows [Note: [Col. 0409] “Strikes,” C 3.].

**20. On property belonging to the lord being returned without his order.** If anyone returns to someone seeking it any property of ours which was in the vestitura of our father [Note: [Col. 0409] “Without our order” is absent from C 4.], without our order, let him compensate us with an equal amount from his own property, together with his legal compensation [Note: [Col. 0409] Absent from C 1, 2, 3, and perhaps 4.].

Whoever knowingly attempts by evil cunning to acquire it shall be held faithless, because he has made void the oath of loyalty which he promised us; and therefore he is to be judged according to our will and power.

**21. On boys tonsured against their parents’ wishes, and on girls veiled.** If anyone tonsures a boy against the wishes of his parents [Note: [Col. 0409] Gloss: *salicis*, Vn.], or veils a girl [Note: [Col. 0409] “Apart from the knowledge of her bishop,” followed by a legal gloss in a fourteenth-century hand: “Otherwise, with his knowledge”; a similar provision concerns only one consecrated to the church in B 2.], let him pay his legal compensation threefold, either to the boy or girl themselves [Note: [Col. 0409] “The boy or girl” and everything following are expressed in the singular in C 3.] if they are already under their own authority, or to the person under whose authority they are [Note: [Col. 0409] “Was.” The preceding chapters are to be added to their law, C 1; “The preceding chapters are to be added in the law,” C 4.].

But let them have control over their own heads, so that they may remain in whatever appearance pleases them [Note: [Col. 0409] In codex B 3, the following chapter, chapter 2 of the capitulary cited below, is inserted here: “If anyone in another’s territory, whether on account of a benefice, etc.”].

[Note: [Col. 0409B] Lindenbrog adds the following chapter to those above: “But concerning summonses, except in matters of freedom or inheritance, there is no need for observance. In other matters, let them come to the assembly by the count’s compulsion and be examined justly, in order to do justice. Counts, however, ought not always to oppress the poor through assemblies.” Baluze.]

[Col. 0409] **Chapters to be written separately.** We have now reviewed, with the aid of the following five manuscripts, the chapters published separately by Baluze: A 1, Codex of the Royal Library of Paris, no. 2718; A 2, in the same library, Fonds de Notre-Dame F. 4; A 3, in the same library, no. 4280 A; B 1, Codex of Saint Paul; B 2, Codex of Corbie; B 3, Royal Library of Paris, no. 4628 A; B 4, in the same library, no. 4632, to which the Chisian and Cavensis codices are closely related; B 5, in the same library, no. 4626; C 1, Paris, no. 4995; C 2, in the same library, no. 4628; C 3, the ducal library of Wolfenbüttel, Blankenburg collection; C 4, the manuscript formerly belonging to Ernst Spangenberg. In addition, the Ambrosian, Florentine, London, Vienna, Veronese, and Este manuscripts in Muratori were consulted, as well as manuscript no. 4788 of the Royal Library of Paris.

[Col. 0409C] **Here begin other chapters** [Note: [Col. 0409] “Of the lord emperor Louis,” C 3.] **which are to be written separately and observed by all** [Note: [Col. 0409] The words “which … to be observed” are absent from C 3.].

The C manuscripts place this chapter first:

**1*. On not promoting slaves to sacred orders** [Note: [Col. 0409] This chapter has been edited from C 1, 2, 3, 4. It is absent from the remaining manuscripts and from the printed editions, and derives from Ecclesiastical Chapter 6 above, col. 397.] [Note: [Col. 0409] “To be sent,” 1.]. Let no bishop presume to promote slaves to sacred orders [Note: [Col. 0409] “Not to the sacred order,” 2.] unless they have first obtained freedom from their own masters. If thereafter any slave, fleeing or hiding from his master [Note: [Col. 0409] “Or” is absent from 2, 4; “hiding, with witnesses summoned,” 2.], or, by producing hired or bribed witnesses [Note: [Col. 0409] “With witnesses present,” 3.] [Note: [Col. 0409] “Summon,” 4.], or by any cunning or fraud, reaches ecclesiastical orders [Note: [Col. 0409] “To the ecclesiastical grades” is absent from 2; “orders,” 3.], let him be deposed, and let his master take him back.

**1. On *forcapii*** [Note: [Col. 0409] *Furcapiis*, B 1; *forcaphiis*, C 2.]. If slaves flee from their masters into another’s power, so that the person in whose power they are found receives no reward for this, whether he returns them or drives them out [Col. 0409D], not only this shall apply, but also, if he is unwilling either to return them or drive them out and refuses to surrender them to their lawful master, and they later flee from him, he shall be compelled to pay for them according to the law.

[Col. 0410C] **2. On tributary land.** Whoever transfers tributary land, from which tribute used to be paid for our account, either to a church or to anyone else, must ensure that the person who receives it pays to our account, in every respect, the tribute formerly paid from it—unless, perhaps, he has such a written guarantee from the royal domain [Note: [Col. 0409] “From our domain,” B 1, Ch. C., and the remaining Lombard manuscripts.] that he can demonstrate that this tribute has been remitted to him.

**3. On destroyed benefices** [Note: [Col. 0409] This chapter is taken from the Lombard capitulary of 803, chapter 24, above, col. 262; it is absent from B 1, Ch. C., and the remaining Lombard manuscripts.]. Whoever has allowed his benefice to be ruined through neglect of his own affairs and, within a year after it has been made known to him by the count or by our messenger, has not repaired it, shall lose that benefice [Note: [Col. 0409] “Forfeit it,” C 1, 2, 3, 4.].

**4. On census-land.** If anyone holds census-land which his predecessors gave either to a church or to one of our estates, he cannot lawfully retain it in any way unless the person to whose authority that church or estate belongs wishes him to do so [Col. 0410D] [Note: [Col. 0409D] These words are absent from the Laon manuscript. Baluze.], unless perhaps he is the son or grandson of the person who transferred it and that same land has been allotted to him to hold [Note: [Col. 0409] *Placita* corrected from *placitata*, A 1.].

But in this matter consideration must be given to whether the person who holds it is rich or poor, and whether he has another benefice or even property of his own. If he has neither of these, he must be treated mercifully, lest, completely stripped of resources, he fall into destitution; he should either pay from it the census that has been assigned to him, or receive some portion of it as a benefice from which he can support himself.

**5. On the ninths and tenths** [Note: [Col. 0411] The beginning of the chapter through *persolvantur* is absent from C 4.]. It has been determined that ninths and tenths shall be paid from the produce of the land and from the nourishment of animals [Note: [Col. 0411] “And from the nourishment of animals” is absent from C 1, 3.] [Note: [Col. 0411] The remainder of this chapter is absent from A, V, Vn., E., and the printed Lombard editions.].

Concerning the labor or restoration of churches, the count and the bishop or abbot, together with our messenger whom they themselves choose for this purpose, shall make an assessment, so that each of them may receive for work and restoration only as much as he is known to possess from the church’s property. Likewise, our vassals shall either collectively receive as much work as they possess of ecclesiastical property, or each individually according to the amount that he holds.

Or, if they agree to contribute silver in place of performing the work, let them pay in silver according to the assessed value of the work, so that with that price the rector of the church may hire workers and purchase materials for the aforesaid restoration.

Whoever neglects to give the ninths and tenths shall first restore them with the prescribed legal compensation and, in addition, pay our ban, so that, chastened in this way, he may beware of losing his benefice through repeated offenses [Note: [Col. 0411] The words “so that … loses” are absent from C 1, 3, 4.].

**6. On slaves fleeing to royal estates.** If anyone’s slaves flee to one of our estates, the administrator [Note: [Col. 0411] This word is written *auctor* in many manuscripts.] of that estate shall not refuse them to the master who seeks them [Col. 0411C], but shall immediately drive them out of the estate. If he thinks he has a legal right to reclaim them, let him make his claim and acquire them according to the law.

But if they fled to that estate during the time of our father, lord Charles, and their master seeks them, let the administrator of that estate either lawfully retain them or return them to the master who seeks them. The administrator must not dare to refuse them on account of the vestitura of our father, lord Charles, if they are known to be that master’s property.

**7. On newly established forests.** Whoever possesses newly established forests shall relinquish them, unless he can show by reliable evidence that he established them by the order or permission of our father, lord Charles—except those that pertain to our own use, concerning which we wish to decide whatever pleases us.

[Col. 0411D] **8** [Note: [Col. 0411] This chapter is absent from C 1, 3, 4.]. We wish our messengers, in each city, together with the bishop and count, to choose messengers [Note: [Col. 0411] “A messenger,” C 2; “or our men,” B 2, 3.] or our men who live there, whose responsibility it shall be to repair bridges in various places and, by our order, warn those who ought to repair them, so that each person may take care to repair them according to his ability and resources [Col. 0412A] [Note: [Col. 0411] “Remand them,” C 2; “remember them,” B 5.].

The C manuscripts add:

**9** [Note: [Col. 0411] Chapters 9–13 are here made public from the C manuscripts. Chapter 10 is also found in the Ambrosian, Florentine, London, Vienna, Veronese, and Este manuscripts and in Muratori (*Lombard Law* 81).] **On another man’s betrothed.** Whoever abducts another man’s betrothed without her consent, even if he has had intercourse with her [Note: [Col. 0411] “Her,” 1; “intercourse,” 2, 4; “restrained,” 3.], shall return her to the man whose betrothed she is, and he may marry her if he wishes, because she appears to have suffered force rather than violation [Note: [Col. 0411] “Is,” 2.].

But if he does not wish to marry her [Note: [Col. 0411] “Also,” 1.], let him take another woman. Nevertheless, if she herself wishes to marry, let her be lawfully joined to anyone else whom she chooses, except the abductor [Note: [Col. 0411] “Except the abductor” is absent from 2.]. Let the abductor, however, be held liable for adultery.

But if she also consented, let her likewise be forbidden from marriage thereafter, just as the abductor is [Note: [Col. 0411] “And,” 1, 2, 4; “from marriage,” 3; “thereafter” is absent from 3, 4.]. Let the man who was going to receive her take another woman whom he chooses.

**10. On proving a man’s status** [Note: [Col. 0411] “Concerning the foolish man who brings a charge,” 2; “Concerning one who brings a man into dispute over his status,” 4.]. If a man is challenged concerning his status, and the person who challenges him has a body of witnesses sufficient to convict him [Note: [Col. 0411] “To defeat him,” 1; “a body of witnesses,” 3.], let him provide eight lawful oath-helpers from the side from which he is challenged, whether paternal or maternal, and at least four lawful men from elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0411] “Named,” 1, 2.]; and by swearing let him vindicate his freedom.

But if he lacks such a body of witnesses [Note: [Col. 0411] “If the relatives are lacking,” 4.], let him take twelve free men from anywhere [Note: [Col. 0411] The remainder is absent from 1.] and defend his free status by oath [Note: [Col. 0411] “Twelve suitable free men,” 1.].

**11.** Every dispute may be settled before the centenarius, except the redemption of land and slaves, which can take place only before the count [Note: [Col. 0411] “The return,” 3, 4, V.].

Codex C 1 adds:

[Col. 0412C] **12. On a female slave made free by charter.** If a female slave is released into freedom by charter [Note: [Col. 0411] *Dimisa*, C.], and afterward marries a slave or a tenant, let the very master who previously owned her take her back after she has been so disgraced.

**13. On tenants.** Concerning how tenants or slaves of the church are to serve and what dues they are to pay: namely, the agrarian due according to the assessment of the judge. Let the judge attend to this; according to what he possesses, let him give: from thirty *modii*, let him give three *modii*. Let him pay the pasture due according to the custom of the province.

Let him perform the lawful *ancingae*—that is, a measure forty feet long and ten feet wide—plow, sow, enclose, gather, transport, and store. For a meadow, one *arpent*: enclose, mow, gather, and transport. For a *tremiss*, each tenant must work two *modii* of sowing land, gathering and storing the produce.

Let them plant, enclose, dig, layer, prune, and harvest vineyards. Let them pay ten bundles of flax and four fattened chickens [Col. 0412D]. Let them provide small horses, or go themselves wherever they are ordered. Let them perform transport service with a cart for up to fifty leagues; let no greater distance be imposed upon them.

For repairing the royal houses, stable, hayloft, granary, or vat, let them receive reasonable compensation for their labor, and whenever necessary let them make the whole structure sound [Note: [Col. 0413] *Necessesse*, C.].

Between chapters 5 and 6, Codex B 3 contains:

**14** [Note: [Col. 0413A] Compare chapter 7 of the following capitulary.] **On providing places for building canonical cloisters.** We wish places for building canonical cloisters—or, where they do not exist, places for those who lack them—to be transferred by our authority [Note: [Col. 0413] *Loci* corrected to *loca*; *tr iantur* in the margin, corrected to *tradantur*.].

That is, if the place is to be provided from the property of the same church, let it be assigned there by our messengers according to the suitability of the site and the quantity of the property. If it is from another church or from free men, let an exchange be made. But if it is from our fisc, let it be granted through our generosity, so that neither superiors nor subjects may have any excuse preventing them from living and conducting themselves communally according to their profession [Note: [Col. 0413] “Preserve,” the manuscript reading.].

**15** [Note: [Col. 0414A] Compare chapter 14 of the following capitulary.] **On how free men are to observe assemblies.** Concerning the assemblies which free men ought to observe, the constitution of our father must be observed and maintained in every respect: namely, that they come to the counts’ assemblies only three times a year, unless someone has been accused, has accused another, or has been summoned to give testimony.

For the other assemblies held by the centenarius, no one shall be compelled to come except the person who is litigating, judging, or testifying.

[Col. 0413] **Chapters for the royal messengers.** The chapters published by Baluze from Royal Library manuscripts 4626 and 4280 A, and from a third manuscript, are here issued again with the aid of those manuscripts: A 1, Royal Library of Paris, no. 2718; A 2, in the same library, Fonds de Notre-Dame F. 4; A 3, in the same library, no. 4280 A; B 1, the Saint Paul manuscript, with which the Chisian and Cavensis manuscripts agree. The Chisian manuscript repeats the entire capitulary among the laws of Lothar, fols. 106 and following; its readings are represented by the siglum Ch. B 2, the Codex of Corbie. C 1, Royal Library of Paris, no. 4628; also the Ambrosian, Florentine, London, Vienna, Veronese, and Este manuscripts, which contain capitularies appended to the Lombard laws in Muratori; and manuscripts of the Royal Library of Paris nos. 4626, 4628 A, 4613, 4631, and 4788 were also consulted.

[Col. 0413B] **These are** [Note: [Col. 0413] This heading occurs in A 3, B 2, C 1.] **the chapters especially pertaining, for the sake of remembrance, to the mission of our messengers, concerning which matters they ought to act** [Note: [Col. 0413] “Which Albwin and Wichald ought to undertake,” B 2.] [Note: [Col. 0413C–D] This should be understood as referring to chapter 13 of Thegan, which reads as follows: “At that same time the aforesaid prince sent his envoys throughout all his realms to inquire and investigate whether any injustice had been committed against anyone. If they found anyone who wished to report such a thing and could prove it with the most truthful witnesses, he immediately ordered them to come with him into his presence. When they went out, they found an innumerable multitude of oppressed people, either through the seizure of their patrimony or through the stripping away of their freedom. Wicked officials, counts, and men placed in authority carried this out by evil cunning. The aforesaid prince ordered all the deeds that had been wickedly carried out in his father’s days through the schemes of unjust officials to be destroyed.” In this passage I have restored *praesentiam* (“presence”) in place of *provinciam* (“province”), which is wrongly printed in the editions. Baluze.]

**1.** This is the mission of all our messengers. First, just as other messengers have already been instructed, they are to administer justice concerning property and freedoms unjustly taken away. If a bishop, abbot, vicar, advocate, or anyone from the common people is found to have done this, let it be restored immediately. But if a count, a royal administrator, or another palace messenger has committed this and brought the property into our power, let the matter, carefully investigated and recorded, be reserved for our judgment.

**2** [Note: [Col. 0413] This chapter is not separated from the preceding one in B 1, 2, C 1, Ch., V.]. We wish that, concerning the freedoms and property to be restored which are in our vestitura, inquiry first be made through the best men [Note: [Col. 0413] “Unless the claim was made through vestitura, and if …,” V. Vn. E.]. If the truth cannot be discovered through them, then let inquiry be made through those who are the next-best men in the neighborhood [Note: [Col. 0413] “So that the truth may be found,” V. Vn. E.].

If the truth of the matter cannot be found even through them [Col. 0414B], then let the litigants be permitted to produce witnesses from both sides. If they disagree, let them be examined according to the constitution promulgated by us [Note: [Col. 0414D] Above, col. 405, chapter 10.].

**3.** Concerning the poor, widows, and orphans who have been unjustly oppressed, so that they may be helped and relieved.

**4.** Concerning unjust new exactions and customs, such as tolls and tributes in the middle of a road where there is neither water, marsh, bridge, nor anything of the kind from which a charge could justly be exacted; or where ships customarily pass beneath bridges, or through the middle of a river where there is no obstruction: let these be removed. But let ancient exactions be reported to our knowledge [Note: [Col. 0413] “So that they may be removed before they come to our attention,” V. Vn. E. and the printed Lombard editions.].

**5.** Concerning the honor due to churches, so that it may be shown to them in every respect, just as we recently established with the consent of all our faithful [Note: [Col. 0414D] Above, col. 403, chapter 1.]—and so that our messengers may make this known to all those placed under their mission [Note: [Col. 0413] “Let them make known the matter of the ninths, etc.,” B 1.] [Col. 0414C] [Note: [Col. 0413] The remainder of the chapter is absent from V, Vn., E., and the printed Lombard editions.].

[Col. 0415A] **6.** Concerning the ninths and tenths, so that they may be given according to our command [Note: [Col. 0415D] Above, col. 411, chapter 5.].

**7** [Note: [Col. 0415D] Above, col. 413, chapter 14.] **Concerning places to be given for building canonical cloisters:** if the place is from the property of the same church [Note: [Col. 0415] Absent from A 1, 2, 3, C 1.], let it be assigned there; if it is from another church or from free men, let an exchange be made; but if it is from our fisc, let it be granted through our generosity [Note: [Col. 0415] “Through our liberty,” B 1, 2, C 1, Ch.].

**8.** Concerning the observance of our commands and immunities, so that they may be observed just as they were established by us and by our predecessors [Note: [Col. 0415] “Preserved just as they were previously granted by our predecessors,” C 1.].

**9.** Concerning those who, under cover of immunity, refuse to do justice, so that what we have established may be observed.

**10.** Concerning places that were formerly sacred but are now defiled by filth, so that, insofar as possible, they may be restored to their former condition.

[Col. 0415B] **11.** Concerning our benefices that are found to have been destroyed, so that what we recently established may be carried out [Note: [Col. 0415D] Above, col. 410, chapter 3.].

**12.** Concerning the new coinage, counterfeit coinage, contempt of our letters, the restraint or punishment of thieves, the pacification of feuds [Note: [Col. 0415] At this point a new chapter begins in A 2.], the prevention of homicides, and the suppression of perjuries and false witnesses: let what we have now established concerning all these matters and other similar matters [Note: [Col. 0415D] Above, col. 405 and following.] be announced to everyone and observed in the future.

### 13. [Note: This is connected with the preceding chapter in A 2, B 2, C, V, Vn., E, and Lang’s editions.]

We wish our envoys to observe the following: whatever they are able to correct, whether all these matters together or each separately, they are to correct; and whatever they have corrected, they are carefully to record in writing. They must take care to carry this out in such a way that no one can justly reproach them in any respect. They must in no way neglect what they ought or are able to do; rather, let them beware lest—God forbid—through favor toward anyone, or because of honor, fear, or hatred, they omit what they ought to carry out. Above all, let them strive to make known to us whatever they cannot accomplish by themselves. In every way, let them ensure that for each individual chapter they will be able to render us an account, both orally and in writing, of everything they have done there.

### 14. [Note: Above, col. 414, chapter 15.] Concerning the judicial assemblies that free men must attend

The constitution of our father [Note: Compare *Capitula Minora* of 803, chapter 20; *Capitularies of Aachen* of 809, chapter 5.] concerning the judicial assemblies that free men must observe is to be observed and maintained in full: namely, that they attend only three general assemblies each year, and that no one compel them to attend more assemblies, unless someone has been accused, has accused another, or has been summoned to give testimony. At the other assemblies, which the vicars or [Note: Absent in A 1, 2, 3, and C 1.] centenarii hold, no one is to be ordered to attend except one who is litigating, judging, or giving testimony [Note: “Giving testimony.” The editions of Langobardus add: “And whoever among our envoys is found to be a transgressor of this constitution shall pay our ban.” This, however, is absent from all the manuscripts.].

### 15. Concerning a debt secured by pledge (*rewadiatum*) for our benefit [Note: *Uudiatum* in Ch.]

Such consideration is to be made that he who sinned through ignorance is not compelled to pay the entire legal composition, but only what seems possible. He, however, who sinned solely through evil intent is to be compelled to pay the full legal composition.

### 16.

No one traveling to the palace or to the army, or returning from the palace or from the army, is to be compelled to pay the toll called *trasturae* [Note: *Transituras* in B 1 and Ch; *tracturias* in C 1; *transitura* in V.].

### 17.

The public bridges that were customarily built by the authority of the ban are to be restored everywhere during the present year.

### 18.

Clerics [Note: “And monks” is added in the Al. manuscript, Ch, V, and the editions of Langobardus and Ansegisus.] and monks, as well as fugitive serfs, are to be ordered to return to their own places.

### 19.

No bishop, abbot, count, or abbess is to have a centenarius as the count’s advocate.

### 20.

Vicars and centenarii who have either concealed or defended thieves and robbers are to be judged according to the sentence laid down for them.

### 21.

Counts, vicars, and centenarii [Note: “And centenarii” is absent from B 1, B 2, and Ch.] are to be reminded of the legal constitution that orders them not to accept gifts in order to pervert justice.

### 22.

Concerning our forests: wherever they exist, they are to make the most careful inquiry into how they are being kept safe [Note: *Salvi* in B 1, C 1, and Ch.] and defended [Note: *Defensi* in B 1 and Ch.]. They are to warn the counts not to establish any new forest; and wherever they find forests newly established without our command, they are to order that they be abandoned.

### 23.

Wherever these envoys themselves [Note: “Our envoys” in B 1 and C 1.] find a bishop, abbot, or anyone else endowed with any rank who either has refused to administer justice or has prevented it, they are to live from that person’s property for as long as they must administer justice in that place.

### 24.

In the county of a count who has had justice properly administered, these same envoys are not to remain for a long time, nor are they to cause a crowd to assemble there. They are to stay instead where justice has been administered either inadequately or negligently.

### 25.

In the jurisdiction of a count who has been dispatched on a *missaticum*, the same envoys are not to hold a judicial assembly until he has returned [Note: A new chapter begins here in A 2, B 1, B 2, and Ch.]. Thus, if a case has not previously been brought before the count, and the person making the complaint, through his own foolishness or defiance, has not wished to appeal to the count concerning it [Note: *Noluerit* in A 1 and A 2.], the matter is to be referred again to the count.

### 26.

Our envoys who are bishops, abbots, or counts, for as long as they remain near their own benefice, are to accept nothing from another person’s *coniectus* [Note: *Coniectu* in B 1; *collectu* in C 1.]. Once they have gone far away from it, they may then accept what is contained in their travel provision. Our vassals [Note: A new chapter begins here in A 2.] and officials who have been sent as envoys are to receive *coniectus* wherever they arrive.

### 27.

Our vassals and the vassals of bishops, abbots, abbesses, and counts who have not been in the army during the present year are to repay the military levy (*heribannum*) [Note: *Eribannum* in A 2; *aurebannum* in C 1; *aribannum* in Ch.], except those who were left at home for necessary reasons established by the lord and our father Charles [Note: “Our Louis” in C 1]. These include those dismissed by a count in order to preserve the peace [Note: The words “in order to preserve the peace” through their second occurrence are absent from B 1 and Ch.], to guard his wife and household, and those similarly dismissed by a bishop, abbot, or abbess in order to preserve the peace, gather the crops, restrain the household, and receive envoys.

### 28.

No bishop, abbot, or count, except on account of illness or by our command, is to have any excuse for failing to come to the judicial assembly of our envoys, or for not sending such a representative of his own who is able to render an account for him in every matter [Note: Here Goldastus adds a chapter from the later edition of Ansegisus, Book IV, chapter 72.].

### 29. [Note: This chapter is absent from B 1 and Ch.] Concerning the provisions of the royal envoys

Concerning the provisions of our envoys, what is to be given or received for each according to his rank [Note: In C 1 the manuscript ends at the following syllable because the leaf is cut away]—namely, for a bishop: forty loaves, three *friskingae*, three measures of drink, one pig, three chickens, fifteen eggs, and four measures of grain for the horses. For an abbot, count, and our official [Note: “Royal official” in A 3 and B 2.] let thirty loaves, two *friskingae*, two measures of drink [Note: Three measures in A 1 and A 3.], one pig, three chickens, fifteen eggs, and three measures of grain for the horses be given daily to each. For our vassal: seventeen loaves, one *friskinga*, one pig, one measure of drink, two chickens, ten eggs, and two measures of grain for the horses [Note: “Two. Here end the chapters of the lord Louis the great emperor, which are to be firmly guarded and observed” in A 2.].

### Codex of Saint Paul

#### 29b [Note: Chisianus also presents this chapter here, among the laws of Lothar.] Concerning abandoned benefices

Whoever has left a benefice deserted on account of his own property shall lose that benefice.

#### 30b

Whoever, being a free man, refuses to accept a pure and properly weighed denarius shall pay our ban, that is, sixty solidi. If, however, ecclesiastical serfs, or the serfs of counts or of our vassals, presume to do this, let them receive sixty blows; or if their master or advocate, who is a free man, refuses, when ordered, to present them either to the count or to our envoy, let him pay the aforesaid ban of sixty solidi.

## IV. ENCYCLICAL LETTER TO THE ARCHBISHOPS (A.D. 817)

Three copies of the encyclical letters by which the emperor sent the rule for canons to all the archbishops of his empire have been preserved in ancient manuscripts: (1) in Codex 1 of the ducal library at Wolfenbüttel, a parchment manuscript of the tenth century, a letter to Arno, archbishop of Salzburg, who had not attended the council; (2) in Codex 1537 of the Paris library, a parchment manuscript of the tenth century, a letter to Sicharius, archbishop of Bordeaux, who was likewise absent; (3) in an Aquitanian manuscript, a letter published by Sirmond to Magnus, archbishop of Sens, who had attended the council. Here we present both forms, revised after once again collating manuscripts 1 and 2.

### LETTER TO THE METROPOLITAN WHO HAD NOT ATTENDED THE ASSEMBLY

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ. Louis, by the divinely ordained providence of God august emperor, to the venerable Arno, archbishop of the church of Salzburg [Note: The words are missing in manuscript 1.] [Note: “To the venerable Sicharius, archbishop in Christ” in manuscript 2.], greeting in the Lord.

We believe that your Holiness is in no way unaware that a sacred and venerable [Note: “Memorable” in manuscript 1.] council, recently assembled at our palace in Aachen by divine direction and through our efforts, has carefully discussed and established many matters for the advancement of the dignity of the Church, with the grace of Christ going before and following after. But because it happened that your Paternity was not present at that holy and venerable council, we have resolved to send to your Beatitude, through our present envoy named Nothon [Note: “Adalhelm” in manuscript 2.], the formulas of canonical institution, collected and brought together from scattered statements of the holy fathers by that same sacred assembly [Note: “Collected” in manuscript 2.] [Note: “And brought together” in manuscript 2.].

For this reason we also ordered them to be carefully written out at our palace, so that they might reach you intact, containing no corruption or mutilation caused by the fault of the copyist. Therefore we wish and decree that, in accordance with the canonical dignity conferred upon you as holder of a metropolitan see and with the sanction of our authority, you summon the bishops of your diocese and the other ecclesiastical prelates to yourself at a suitable time and place; that you order the aforementioned formulas of institution to be read aloud before them, chapter by chapter [Note: *Memoratam* (singular) in manuscript 2.] [Note: *Formam* (singular) in manuscript 2.]; and that you clearly demonstrate what the sacred assembly established for the exaltation of the dignity of the ecclesiastical hierarchy and for the salvation of souls [Note: “It” in manuscript 2.]. You are also to review, before our aforesaid envoy, what must be held and observed by those who live canonically in one college [Note: “Confer” in manuscript 2.].

But if anyone’s dullness of mind should prevent him from understanding it, let it be soberly taught to him either by you or by other bishops—your comprovincial bishops, that is—who shine with the brilliance of learning. Your Prudence is likewise to be especially watchful that those who copy these texts [Note: “It” in manuscript 2.] copy them in such a way [Note: Singular “it is copied” in manuscript 2.] that they are neither corrupted through the copyist’s fault nor mutilated by anyone [Note: “By another” in manuscript 2.]; rather, they are to be copied without any corruption or mutilation, exactly as they have been shown to them by our aforesaid envoy [Note: The word “by” is absent from manuscript 1.].

Know also that a copy of the text has been kept in the archive of our palace so that it may clearly be possible to establish by comparison who copied it carelessly or who mutilated any part of it [Note: “It” in manuscript 2.]. [For, as we have learned, while it was being read aloud at that same sacred council, before it had been brought forth before us by the council and before the measure of food and drink had yet been established, certain people, mutilating a large part of it, unwisely copied some chapters from it. Therefore, if you discover that anyone in your diocese has done such a thing, you must nullify this deed before the assembly of your provincial bishops and before our aforesaid envoy; and you must order this authentic copy to be transcribed carefully, as we have stated, according to the instructions our envoy gives them.] [Note: The words from “For” through “order this authentic copy” are absent from manuscript 1.]

Therefore, let all the bishops of your diocese and the other prelates [Note: Absent from manuscript 1.] strive, aided by God, to copy these texts [Note: “It” in manuscript 2.] with vigilant care, to understand them with diligent effort, and to fulfill them in their works through the exercise of the most constant perseverance. Thus, when we send our envoys throughout the empire, by the authority conferred upon us by God, on the coming Kalends of September to investigate this matter—as we remember having said to that sacred and memorable council that we would do—the prelates and subjects alike [Note: “And prelates and subjects” is absent from manuscript 1.] of this saving institution may be found to be vigorous workers, insofar as the Lord grants them the ability.

For we shall order a diligent inquiry, while life lasts, into which of the prelates [Note: “Of the prelates” is absent from manuscript 1.] has vigorously carried out the office entrusted to him [Note: “Carries it out” in manuscript 2.], who has obeyed our sanction in building cloisters for canons and other dwellings, in supplying them with necessary stipends [Note: Absent from manuscript 2.], and in repairing houses as shelters for the poor; who has taken care to instruct his clergy in this same institution and in other spiritual teachings; and who, out of greed, has driven away those whom he could reasonably have supported in the service of Christ.

For we gave a period of one year so that what has been mentioned above [Note: “Promised” in manuscript 1.]—where it had not yet been done—could be completed with the greatest ease, without any excuse based on difficulty. Therefore, whoever during this year has neglected to obey our command very seriously, to the extent of his ability, in this matter [Note: “In that year” in manuscript 2.], will undoubtedly serve as a terror to the others, lest they presume to commit such a thing.

We have indeed sent you the formula of institution, which the common agreement [Note: “Common assent” in manuscript 2.] and equal zeal of that sacred council carefully extracted, item by item, from the sayings of the holy fathers, and which it established for observance by those devoted to chastity who live in one canonical community.

We wish you, or your comprovincial bishops, to order it to be diligently copied, and to have it presented for observance to the convents of women situated in your diocese in which a canonical life is lived. You must teach with complete clarity how it ought to be observed with the greatest religious devotion by the abbesses and the other nuns. For, unless we order one of the abbesses to come into our presence, we wish them to remain in their monasteries at other times, to lead their lives according to the form of this institution, and to bind those subject to them to the holy profession of religion.

None of them is to grant herself permission to wander outside, to reside in villages on any pretext, or to serve her own pleasures. Although some clerics possess monasteries of women, and some laymen possess monasteries of men and also of women, your most diligent care must nevertheless see to it that in every place under your diocese, wherever there are communities of clerics and nuns, they live according to the form of this institution, insofar as their resources and circumstances permit. For there is absolutely no church possessing resources in which it is impossible to govern so many and such persons as can perform the divine office, and in which hospitality cannot be practiced according to its means. [Note: The entire passage from “Therefore” through “according to its means” is absent from manuscript 1.]

We have also sent our aforesaid envoy to your Holiness for this reason: so that he might carefully and closely observe your zeal in this matter, as well as that of the other ecclesiastics residing in your diocese [Note: “Present in your diocese” in manuscript 2.], and assist you in admonishing the others [Note: “So that” in manuscript 1; “In warning them” in manuscript 2.]. He is also to report to us how willingly [Note: “Diligently” in manuscript 1.] the prelates, male and female, have received the institution, how diligently they have tried to copy it, and how devotedly they have taken care to fulfill it according to their ability.

We have ordered him to remain and travel about in your diocese, or in that of your comprovincial bishops, together with your envoy, for as long as the aforesaid formula is copied by everyone [Note: Manuscript 2 reads “to remain in the diocese”]. Thus, when he has carefully arranged and completed everything, and the time has allowed him to return to us after the work is finished, all that has been done is to be recorded in writing by both of you, and through him and your envoy it is to be reported to our knowledge [Note: “Diocese” in manuscript 2.]. In this way we shall know to whom we ought to return thanks and whom we ought to correct with appropriate reprimands [Note: “But if anyone…” in manuscript 2.].

But if anyone in your diocese should insolently resist this institution and your admonition, neglect with all his strength to observe what has been beneficially established by that sacred and venerable council, and, after being admonished, fail to correct himself [Note: Manuscript 2 reads: “And if he should contemptuously neglect to observe, insofar as the Lord grants him ability, what has been established and decreed by that sacred and venerable council.”], we command that, if he does not correct himself beforehand, whoever he may be, he hasten to come into our presence at the admonition of you or our envoy, so that he may be worthily corrected by us according to the measure of his fault.

We have also sent you [Note: “To you” is absent from manuscript 2.] the weight and measure according to which bread and drink are to be distributed equally to clerics and nuns. We decree that these measures be observed by everyone most firmly and inviolably, and we absolutely forbid anyone to increase or diminish them.

At the end of this letter, therefore, we admonish your Holiness that, according to the ministry conferred upon you by divine favor, you obey our most salutary admonition in this matter obediently and without excuse [Note: *Inexecrabiliter* in manuscript 2.], and provide the others with a good example by your obedience. It is fitting and just that, the more greatly you surpass others in the dignity of the priesthood and are held by us in venerable affection, the more devoted and ready you should show yourself to be in carrying out the will of God and of ourselves.

Farewell in the Lord, and pray for us.

### LETTER TO THE METROPOLITAN WHO HAD ATTENDED THE ASSEMBLY

The most glorious Louis, ever-victorious august emperor by heavenly favor, to the venerable Magnus, archbishop of the city of Sens, greeting in the Lord.

As we recently promised you at the sacred assembly that, with God’s assent, we convened at our palace in Aachen, where many things were carried out with Christ’s favor for the Church—indeed, in a catholic manner—we have sent to your venerable Paternity, through our present envoys, Ermenfred and Haymo, the formula of canonical institution that the same sacred assembly undertook to collect from the scattered statements of the holy fathers and bring together into one.

Because the narrowness of time denied you the opportunity to copy it, we took care to have it carefully copied, so that its text might reach you intact, without any corruption or mutilation. Therefore we have sent this letter to your Holiness, in which we order you, mindful of our admonition, to summon the suffragan bishops of your diocese to yourself at a suitable time and place; to have this institution read aloud chapter by chapter before the ecclesiastical orders; to make clearly known how the sacred assembly beneficially took care to establish it for the advantage of souls; and, in accordance with the ministry divinely conferred upon you and the command of our authority, to review before our aforesaid envoys that it is to be observed by those who are counted under the name of the canonical profession.

As for those whose understanding is slower and who perhaps cannot fully comprehend it, let its knowledge be poured into their minds through your efforts, or through those of your comprovincial bishops who are endowed with the gift of learning. We likewise wish your prudent Beatitude to ensure that all of them, as you instruct them, are warned by our aforesaid envoys to copy it carefully, without any corruption or mutilation. We have given them sufficient instruction as to how it should be copied carefully, diligently, distinctly, and clearly.

We had a copy of it placed in the archive of our palace for this reason: so that by means of it we might ascertain and investigate whether it had been copied carelessly by anyone. For, as we have learned, while it was being read aloud at that same sacred council, before it had been brought forth before us by the council and before the measure of food and drink had been clearly established, certain envious persons, mutilating a large part of it, unwisely copied some chapters from it.

Therefore, if you discover that anyone in your diocese has done such a thing, you must nullify the deed before the assembly of your provincial bishops and before our aforesaid envoys, and order this authentic copy to be transcribed carefully, as we have stated, according to the instructions our envoys give them.

We therefore wish all the prelates of the canons to copy it carefully, understand it diligently, and strive to fulfill it effectively in their works, insofar as the Lord grants them the ability, for the benefit of themselves and their subjects. Thus, when we send our envoys throughout our entire empire on the coming Kalends of September to investigate this matter, as we announced generally to everyone at their sacred and venerable council, all—prelates and subjects alike—may be found, according to their understanding and ability, informed and instructed by this same teaching and vigorous in carrying it out.

For we shall order a diligent inquiry, while life lasts, into how each of the prelates fulfills his ministry; how they have obeyed our command concerning cloisters and the other necessary dwellings of the canons, the provision of their stipends, and the preparation of shelters for the poor; and who has endeavored to instruct his clergy according to the rule of this institution and the other spiritual exercises; or whether anyone, out of greed, has cast out one of those whom he could reasonably have governed in the service of God.

Since, as you know, we wanted the matters mentioned above to be carried out as conveniently as possible, without opposition from any difficulty, in places where they had not yet been done, we allotted one year for their completion. Whoever during this year neglects to obey our command—or rather God’s command—to the extent of his ability will undoubtedly instill fear in the others, so that they will not dare to do such things.

We have therefore sent you the form of the institution that the same sacred and venerable council carefully extracted from the statements of the holy fathers and prescribed for observance by nuns living canonically in one community. We wish it to be carefully placed before all the women’s monasteries in your diocese in which a canonical life is lived, whether by you or by your comprovincial bishops.

We also decree that it be delivered by you both to the abbesses and to the other nuns, and that they be instructed through your efforts in how they ought to observe it. Except when we order one of the abbesses to come into our presence, we wish the abbesses at other times to remain in their own monasteries, strive to live according to this form of institution, and govern those subject to them. They are not to grant any of them permission to reside in villages, to wander outside on any pretext, or to serve their own pleasures.

Although some clerics possess monasteries of women, and some laymen possess monasteries of men and also of women, your most diligent care must nevertheless see to it that in all places situated under your diocese, wherever there are communities of clerics and nuns, they live according to the form of this institution, insofar as their resources and circumstances permit. For there is absolutely no church possessing resources in which it is impossible to govern so many and such persons as can perform the divine office, and in which hospitality cannot be practiced according to its means.

We have also sent our aforesaid envoys to your Holiness for this reason: so that they might carefully and closely observe your zeal in this matter and that of the other ecclesiastics residing in your diocese, and assist you in admonishing the others. They are also to report to us how willingly the prelates, male and female, have received the institution, how diligently they have tried to copy it, and how devotedly they have taken care to fulfill it according to their ability.

We have ordered them to remain and travel about in your diocese, or in that of your comprovincial bishops, together with your envoy, for as long as the aforesaid formula is copied by everyone. Thus, when they have arranged and carefully assessed everything, and the time has allowed them to return to us after the work is completed, all that has been done is to be recorded in writing by both sides, and through them and your envoy it is to be reported to our knowledge. In this way we shall know to whom we ought to return thanks and whom we ought to correct with appropriate reprimands.

But if anyone in your diocese should insolently resist this institution and our admonition, and contemptuously neglect to observe, insofar as the Lord grants him ability, what has been established and decreed by that sacred and venerable council, we command that, if he does not correct himself beforehand, whoever he may be, he hasten to come into our presence at the admonition of you or our envoys, so that he may be worthily corrected by us according to the measure of his fault.

We have also sent you the weight and measure according to which bread and drink are to be distributed equally to clerics and nuns. We decree that these measures be observed by everyone most firmly and inviolably, and we absolutely forbid anyone to increase or diminish them.

At the end of this letter, therefore, we admonish your Holiness that, according to the ministry conferred upon you by divine favor, you obey our most salutary admonition in this matter obediently and without excuse, and provide the others with a good example by your obedience. It is fitting that, the more greatly you surpass others in the dignity of the priesthood and are held by us in venerable affection, the more devoted and ready you should show yourself to be in carrying out the will of God and of ourselves.

Farewell in the Lord, and pray for us.

## V. CONSTITUTION CONCERNING THE SERVICE OF MONASTERIES (A.D. 817)
