Since the constitution itself has perished, it seemed appropriate first to recover its account from Sirmond, volume II of the *Councils of Gaul*, p. 685, and from Delalande, in the *Supplements to the Councils of Gaul*, where it was published from a manuscript of the monastery of Saint-Gilles in Septimania; it was also elucidated with notes by Baluze, Mabillon, and Bouquet, *Sacred Writers*, volume VI, p. 407. We have included some of those notes that concern the monasteries of Gaul.

In the year of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 817, Louis, most serene august emperor by the divinely ordained providence of God, held an assembly at Aachen, the royal seat, of the bishops, abbots, and the entire senate of the Franks. There, among the other arrangements of the empire, he established and ordered to be written which monasteries in his kingdom or empire could provide gifts and military service, which could provide gifts alone without military service, and which could provide neither gifts nor military service, but only prayers for the salvation of the emperor or his sons and for the stability of the empire.

[Note: The author of the *Annals of Aniane* writes: “There were also certain monasteries among them that were performing gifts and military service. Consequently, they had fallen into such poverty that the monks lacked food and clothing. Considering this, and at the suggestion of the aforesaid man Benedict, abbot of Aniane, the most pious king ordered that they should be able to serve in such a way that nothing would be lacking to those serving God, and that they might therefore pray eagerly to the most pious God for him, his offspring, and the stability of the whole kingdom.” From this, therefore, the *Life of the same Benedict*, published at the beginning of the *Concordia of the Rules*, should be emended. See the *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, fourth century, part I, p. 214. — Baluze.]

[Note: In addition to the monasteries listed here, which owed the king prayers alone, there were several others of this kind in Aquitaine, namely those of Tulle and Sarlat. The monastery of Régula on the Garonne owed the king nothing, as is clear from a charter of Count Bernard, part of which Marca published in Book III, chapter 6, of his *History of Béarn*. We found the charter complete among the papers of Arnold Oihenart, transcribed from the cartulary of Régula. The piety of later generations in Italy and England appears to have followed or imitated this constitution of Louis. In the cartulary of Casauria I find that the founders of the monastery of Saint Maurus of Amiternum retained no other census for themselves in the possessions given to that monastery “except only prayer for us and our parents.” The *Monasticon Anglicanum*, edited by the most diligent scholar William Dugdale, gives on page 208 an account of a certain deacon murdered inside a church by the retainers of a nobleman named Nogui. Later moved by repentance and making satisfaction to the church, he gave certain fields to the church of Lindau and decreed that the land thus given should be free from every form of lay service, except only daily prayer in perpetuity. — The editor.]

### THESE ARE THOSE THAT MUST PROVIDE GIFTS AND MILITARY SERVICE, NUMBER XIV

Monastery of Saint Benedict [Note: Probably Fleury, on the Loire, in the diocese of Orléans. — Baluze.].

Monastery of Ferrières [Note: Formerly called Bethlehem, according to the author of the *Life of Louis the Pious*. It is situated in the diocese of Sens. See the notes to Lupus of Ferrières, p. 341. — The editor.].

Monastery of Nigelles [Note: I think this refers to the monastery of Neauphle-le-Vieux, in the diocese of Chartres. — The editor. — In the district of Troyes. — Bouquet.].

Monastery of the Holy Cross [Note: Commonly Saint-Leufroy, in the diocese of Évreux: La Croix-Saint-Leufroy. — Baluze. — Alternatively Saint-Faron, near Meaux. — Bouquet.].

Monastery of Corbie [Note: In the diocese of Amiens. A celebrated monastery in which literary studies once flourished greatly. From it come so many good and ancient manuscript codices, through whose aid many passages in ancient authors have been corrected and emended, and many works that had previously remained hidden have been brought to public attention. — Baluze.].

Monastery of Saint Mary of Soissons [Note: A distinguished scholar, Michael Germanus, a Benedictine monk, recently supplied us with its history together with an appendix of ancient records. In an old parchment of the monastery of Canigou I find the names of certain abbesses and, as I think, of the more celebrated and noble nuns of that monastery: Frenburgis, abbess; Ermentrudis, abbess; Adelaidis, abbess; Adelaidis, treasurer; Ermena; Elisabeth; Hildeburgis; Fagela; Beringildis; Leuda; Eva; Mathildis; Lanscindis; Itisburgis; Richildis; Hildeburgis; and Rosmodis. — The editor.].

Monastery of Stabulaus [Note: Commonly Stavelot, in the Ardennes forest; its abbot at that time was Ando, according to Gabriel Bucelinus. In the agreements made in 870 between Charles the Bald, king of the Franks, and Louis, king of Germany, for the division of Lothar’s kingdom, it was agreed to add to Louis’s portion “the abbeys of Prüm and Stavelot, with all their royal estates and vassals,” as is read in the *Capitularies of Charles the Bald*, title 43, p. 223. The *Annals of Fulda* state that this monastery was devastated by the Normans in 881. Regino, however, reports that it was burned: “After this they reduced the palace at Aachen, Inda, Malmedy, and the monasteries of Stavelot to ashes.” Thus it is read in two very ancient manuscript codices, one belonging to the Colbert library and the other to Saint Arnulf of Metz. See the *Account of the Churches of Belgium*, p. 289 and following. — The editor.].

Monastery of Flavigny [Note: In the diocese of Autun. — The editor. — Now Flavigny; Bouquet, however, reads *Fariniacum* and interprets it as Favernay in the district of Besançon.].

Monastery of Saint Eugendus [Note: Saint-Oyend in the *Capitularies of Charles the Bald*, title 43, p. 224. It is situated on the Jura mountain in the diocese of Lyon. Today it is commonly called Saint-Claude. See Saint Bernard, letter 291.].

Monastery of Novalese [Note: At the foot of Mount Cenis, not far from the river Cenis, as Francis Augustine ab Ecclesia explains. They report that Hugh, son of Charlemagne, was a monk and abbot there. Andrew Duchesne published fragments of the *Chronicle of Novalese* in the third volume of the *Writers of the History of the Franks*, p. 635.].

### Beyond the Rhine [Note: That is, Francia on the right bank of the Rhine.]

Monastery of Saint Nazarius [Note: Lorsch, in the diocese of Mainz. — Baluze. — Now Lorsch.]

Offunwilarii [Note: Offonis villa is mentioned in the *Capitularies of Charles the Bald*, title 43, p. 223. Offonis cella, in the diocese of Strasbourg, is now called Schuttern, as Guillimannus explains in *The Bishops of Strasbourg*, pp. 67–73. Offonis villa, a monastery dedicated to Saint Leodegarius the martyr, is mentioned in a precept of Louis the Transmarine published by Perard in the *Monuments of Burgundian History*, p. 1165. — Baluze. — Now Schuttern.]

## IN BAVARIA
Monastery of Mananseo. [Note: I have thus corrected the corrupt readings *Manauser* [Delalande, *Mavauster*] and *Tognauser*; these are Monsee and Tegernsee.] Monastery of Tegerinseo.

## THESE ARE THOSE WHICH MUST GIVE GIFTS ONLY, WITHOUT MILITARY SERVICE, NUMBERING SIXTEEN

Monastery of Saint Michael of the First Marsh (*Maresci primi*). [Note: Hadrian Valesius believes that this refers to the monastery of Saint Michael “in danger of the sea” (*in periculo maris*), and that “of the first marsh” (*maresci primi*) was written in this notice, because it was situated in a marshy or swampy place—that is, on marshland. I do not find this view convincing. For the monastery of Saint Michael *maresci primi* is placed here among the monasteries of the Lyonnais region. Moreover, in the *Capitularies of Charles the Bald*, title 43, p. 224, a monastery, as I believe, of Saint Michael is mentioned together with the monastery of Saint Mary at Besançon. Chifflet, in *Vesontio*, part II, chapter 66, p. 279, notes that in the city of Besançon there is a church of Saint Michael on Saint Stephen’s Mount, certainly very ancient, although he had found no record anywhere of its foundation, despite discovering many and very ancient monuments relating to it; and he records its dedication in an old book of rites as follows: “The dedication of the basilica of Saint Michael, on the third day before the Kalends of October.” Baluze. — Mabillon has *Marsupium* in the county of Verdun; the reading should therefore be *the monastery of Saint Michael of Marsupium*. Delalande has *Saint Michael of the danger of the sea*.]

Monastery of Balma. [Note: In ancient times there were two monasteries of this name in the diocese of Besançon: one an old nunnery, the other a much more recent monastery for men, as the distinguished Charles Le Cointe demonstrates at length in the *Annals of the Church of the Franks* under the year 804. The men’s monastery is generally held to have been founded not long before Cluny, as Andrew Duchesne writes in his notes to the *Cluniac Library*, p. 22. See the *Capitularies of Charles the Bald*, title 43, p. 223; Saint Bernard, letter 251; and Innocent III, book I, letters 113 and following. Baluze.]

Monastery of Saint Sequanus. [Note: In the diocese of Langres. Ibid.]

Monastery of Natradis. [Note: I have no doubt that the reading supplied by the distinguished Hadrian Valesius’s *Description of Gaul* is the correct one; there he reads *Monasterium Nantuadis*. Nevertheless, lacking the support of ancient copies, I have not dared to alter the text. There is an old monastery in the diocese of Lyon whose last abbot was Hugh, abbot of Cluny, as Claudius Robert observes. Thereafter it was no longer an abbey but a priory. Today it is commonly called Nantua, almost halfway between Lyon and Geneva, in the county of Bugey. See the notes to Agobard, p. 18. Baluze. — Delalande has *Natuadis*; it should be *Nantuadis*.]

[Col. 0427A] Beyond the Rhine.

Monastery of Suarizaha. [Note: That is, Schuvarzach, as I believe, or Schwart­zach in the diocese of Strasbourg, formerly called Arnolfesau. See Guillimann, *On the Bishops of Strasbourg*, pp. 96, 120. Baluze. — Schwarzach on the Main, not far from Bamberg, founded in 816; for another monastery of this name was situated on the Rhine in Alamannia, and it was not transferred from Arnolfesau until 826.]

Monastery of Saint Boniface. [Note: That is, Fulda. Baluze.]

Monastery of Saint Wigbert. [Note: Hersfeld.]

## In Alamannia

Monastery of Elehenwanc. [Note: I have corrected the reading *Clehenwanc*; it is Ellwangen.]

Monastery of Fiuhctinwanc. [Note: I have corrected the reading *Fruhelinwanc*; today Feuchtwangen.]

Monastery of Nazaruda. [Note: Perhaps Hazarieda, Hasenried, or Herrieden on the Altmühl, not far from Feuchtwangen; for even after our Lang’s work on the districts of Bavaria, it may remain uncertain whether this belonged to Franconia or rather to Alamannia. Delalande: *Nazarecda*.]

Monastery of Campita. [Note: Kempten.]

## In Bavaria

Monastery of Altemburc. [Note: Altenmünster.]

Monastery of Altahe. [Note: I have corrected this and the following readings; the editions had *Alcabe, Creausa, Mathasco*, but the names are Altaich, Kremsmünster, and Mattsee. Delalande: *Alcane, Crenuza*.]

Monastery of Cremisa.

[Col. 0428A] Monastery of Mathaseo.

Monastery of Buria. [Note: Benedictbeuern.]

## THESE ARE THOSE WHICH MUST GIVE NEITHER GIFTS NOR MILITARY SERVICE, BUT ONLY PRAYERS FOR THE SALVATION OF THE EMPEROR OR HIS SONS AND FOR THE STABILITY OF THE EMPIRE, NUMBERING [Note: Read 54. The total number is therefore 84.] 18

Monastery of Melaredum. [Note: In the third volume of D’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, p. 244, it is written that Ansegisus, abbot of Fontenelle, gave “one pound to Saint Gregory, one pound to the monastery of Maurus, and one pound to Melundas.” Perhaps, therefore, *Melundam* should be read here instead of *Melaredum*. Baluze. — Saint-Germain of Auxerre. Bouquet.]

Monastery of Fossatus. [Note: That is, the monastery of Saint Peter of Fosses in the diocese of Paris, now called Saint-Maur-des-Fossés. Under Louis the Pious and Charles the Bald, the abbot of this monastery was Engelbert, who is mentioned in the charters of those princes concerning the privileges of the same monastery and in chapter 3 of the *Miracles of Saint Maurus*. During Engelbert’s time, the monastery of Glanfeuil, or Saint-Maur on the Loire, was subjected by the authority of Louis the Pious to the monastery of Fosses and thereafter governed by provosts sent by the abbot of Fosses, as may be gathered from the same book of the *Miracles of Saint Maurus*. Thus Gausbert, who governed the monastery of Glanfeuil during the reign of Charles the Bald, was not an abbot but a provost. This is shown to us by a charter of Anouvarech the Breton, mentioned in chapter 8 of the same *Miracles*, which we found at the end of the Holy Scriptures that Anouvarech himself presented to the monastery of Saint Maurus on the Loire. Carloman, son of Louis the Stammerer, subsequently confirmed this subjection of the monastery of Saint Maurus by his authority, as Charles the Simple teaches in Labbe, volume II of the *Historical Miscellanies*, p. 516: “Furthermore, we commend that the monastery of Saint Maurus in Glanfeuil, situated in the county of Anjou on the Loire and formerly subjected to the monastery of Fosses by our brother Carloman so that they might be one and be governed under one abbot, should continue in the same arrangement.” Finally, Urban II, at the Council of Tours, “restored the monastery of Saint Maurus at Glanfeuil, which had been torn away from the monks of Fosses by tyranny, to its former dignity and liberty, while it was to remain perpetually under the direction only of the monastery of Monte Cassino,” as is read in book IV, chapter 18 of the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*. Ivo of Chartres states in letter 159 that this was done at the urging of the count of Anjou, against the protests of the monks of Fosses and despite the contrary opinion of many who were present at the council. Baluze. — Fosses near Paris.]

Monastery of Luda. [Note: Delalande: *Lutra*. Lutra in the diocese of Besançon.]

Monastery of Saint Gregory. [Note: In the *Capitularies of Charles the Bald*, title 43, p. 223, in the portion of Lothair’s kingdom which Louis, king of Germany, received, Saint Gregory, the monastery of Maurus, and Ebersheim are listed in the same order as here. I therefore believe that the monastery of Saint Gregory mentioned in this notice is the one which, according to some accounts, was founded in the diocese of Strasbourg by Childeric II, king of the Franks, and which is now called Münster in Saint-Gregorienthal, in the diocese of Basel. Baluze.]

Monastery of Saint Maurus. [Note: Commonly called Marmoutier, in the diocese of Strasbourg. It was first founded by Saint Leobard, a disciple of Saint Benedict—or rather, according to others, by Maurus, a disciple of Saint Pirminius, bishop of Meaux—in honor of the holy apostles Peter and Paul and Saint Martin the bishop; it was subsequently enriched and endowed with privileges by Childebert, king of the Franks, around the year 553. The abbots of this monastery included John in 846 and Oswald in 879. Ibid.]

Monastery of Eborreheim. [Note: Ebersheim.]

Monastery of Clinga. [Note: In the diocese of Speyer. See Trithemius, *Chronicle of Sponheim*, under the year 991, and Brower’s notes to Hrabanus’s poems, chapter 109. Baluze.]

Monastery of Saviniciacum. [Note: In the diocese of Lyon; concerning it, see the charter of Lothair edited by de Marca in his dissertation *On Primates*, chapter 114, and our appendix, title 4. Ibid. — Now Savigny.]

Monastery of Crudatis. [Note: In the diocese of Viviers. King Boso mentions it in a charter edited by the distinguished Jean Columbi in book II of his *Deeds of the Bishops of Viviers*, p. 69, and by Catel in the *Memoirs of the History of Occitania*, p. 315. Baluze.]

[Col. 0429A] Monastery of Dusera. [Note: In the *Life of Louis the Pious* it is written *monastery of Dosora*. At that time this monastery, which was in the territory of Orange, had its own abbots, Dexter and Hildigysus, as is clear from charters of Louis the Pious and Lothair edited by Father Chifflet in the *Proofs of the History of Tournus*, p. 260 and following. Later it was given by the same Lothair to the bishops of Viviers; Jean Columbi edited the relevant charter on p. 66, in which we read: “We grant and confirm to the same holy see of blessed Vincent, the most glorious martyr, the abbey called Dozera, with its cells, situated in the county of Orange above the river Rhône.” The same grant was confirmed in identical words by Charles the Bald in the second year of his imperial reign. After the monastery was destroyed, the bishops consequently took pleasure in being called princes of Donzère. Baluze.]

Monastery of Lorwim. [Note: Unknown.]

Beyond the Rhine.

Monastery of Scewanc. [Note: Unknown.]

Monastery of Sculturbura. [Note: Perhaps Maulbronn. Delalande: *Scultzurburna*.]

## In Bavaria

Monastery of Berch. [Note: Haindlingberg in the prefecture of Mallersdorf. See our Lang’s *Registers* under the year 875.]

Monastery of Methema. [Note: The editions have *Mechema*, which I have corrected to *Methen*, Metten.]

Monastery of Sconenauva. [Note: The editions have *Scovenauva*, which I have corrected. Schönau.]

[Col. 0430A] Monastery of Moseburch. [Note: I have corrected the reading; the editions have *Aloseburch*. It is Moosburg on the Isar, dedicated to Saint Castulus.]

Monastery of Weizzenbrunno. [Note: The editions have *Weizzenbrunico*. Wessobrunn.]

## In Aquitania

Monastery of Saint Philibert. [Note: Founded on the island of Ré in the Pictonian Sea by Saint Philibert, after whom it was subsequently called the monastery of Saint Philibert, both here and in the *Life of Louis the Pious*. It appears to have been restored by Charlemagne. For Ademar of Chabannes, after saying that the island was burned by the Normans in 830 and left without a general monastic community, adds: “There the lord emperor Charles had built the monastery of Saint Philibert.” Today that monastery is not an abbey but only a priory, as Hadrian Valesius notes. Baluze.]

Monastery of Saint Maxentius. [Note: Commonly Saint-Maixent, in the diocese of Poitiers. It was restored by Louis the Pious, as the author of his *Life* testifies. Ibid.]

Monastery of Carroffinius. [Note: The monastery of Carroffi in the same *Life of Louis the Pious*. Commonly Charroux, in the diocese of Poitiers. An ancient monastery founded by Roger, count of Limoges, and his wife Euphrasia. Ibid.]

Monastery of Brantosmurii. [Note: Commonly Brantôme, in the diocese of Périgueux. It is commonly said that this monastery was founded by Charlemagne in 769, and some make Regino the author of this account. Wrongly. Regino recorded nothing of the kind. But in the Frankish *Annals* published from the Thuane Library—which some believe to be the annals Regino professes to have followed—we read that in the year mentioned above Charles established a basilica in Périgord in honor of blessed Peter, at a place called Brantosme. Duchesne, however, notes there that this account was written in the margin of an ancient manuscript by a somewhat later hand. In Ademar of Chabannes I find that Pippin, king of Aquitania, established the monastery of Brantôme at his father’s command. Ibid.]

Monastery of Saint Savinus. [Note: Commonly Saint-Savin, in the diocese of Poitiers. Baluze.]

Monastery of the Holy Cross of Nuns. [Note: Situated within the city of Poitiers, as is read in Gregory of Tours, book III, chapter 7, and in the title of the capitulary of 822 concerning this monastery; or, as in the charter of Louis the Stammerer published in volume IV of *Gallia Christiana*, within the walls of the city of Poitiers. It was founded by Saint Radegund the queen and for this reason is sometimes called the monastery of Saint Radegund, as in the *Life of Louis the Pious*: “the nunnery of Saint Radegund.” Indeed, Hincmar, archbishop of Reims, is said by Flodoard, book III, chapter 27, to have written to “Rothrude, consecrated to God, and the other sisters of the monastery of the Holy Cross and Saint Radegund, concerning the election of the abbess of that monastery.” But Louis the Stammerer, in the charter cited above, distinguishes the monastery of the Holy Cross from the monastery of Saint Radegund, placing the former “within the walls of the city of Poitiers,” and the latter “in the suburb of the aforesaid city.” These are his words, corrected and supplemented from an ancient manuscript: “Abbess Ava, from the monastery of the Holy Cross, which is situated within the walls of the city of Poitiers, approaching our clemency, presented before us the charters of our grandfather Louis and of our father, of pious memory, the glorious emperors Charles, in which it was inserted that not only they themselves, but also their predecessors, namely the kings of the Franks, had placed under their protection and the safeguard of immunity, together with the monastery of Saint Radegund, which is situated in the suburb of the aforesaid city,” and so forth. And below: “But for the security of the matter she requested us that, following the custom of our father and of our predecessors, namely the kings and emperors, we should decree that a charter of our immunity of this kind be made for the aforesaid monasteries, namely those of the Holy Cross and Saint Radegund, where she herself rests bodily. We gladly assented to her request and decreed that this charter of our authority be made concerning these monasteries for the love of divine worship,” and so forth.

These matters are to be understood as follows. The monastery of the Holy Cross is the nunnery in which that holy queen lived and died. The monastery of Saint Radegund is the monastery of monks founded by the same holy woman under the title of Saint Mary; it is clear from Gregory of Tours’ *Book of the Glory of the Confessors* that she was buried there. It was later given to canons and is now a collegiate church within the walls of the city of Poitiers. But because these two monasteries were close to one another, and both traced their origin to Saint Radegund, they were called by the same name at various times and were occasionally treated under the designation of a single monastery, as in Flodoard and in the capitulary of 822.

The passage in the *Life of Louis the Pious* stating that his wife Judith was ordered, in 829, to be confined in the monastery of Saint Radegund at the instigation of Pippin, king of Aquitania, must be understood of the nunnery. By contrast, Ademar of Chabannes, when he says that the same Pippin—whose death is known to have occurred in 838—was buried at Poitiers at Saint Radegund’s, must be understood to refer to the men’s monastery. I possess verses by Oliver, canon of Saint Radegund of Poitiers, on the death of Ebalus, abbot of Tulle.]

Monastery of Saint Mary at Limoges. [Note: The *Life of Louis the Pious* has “the nunnery of Saint Mary.” This is an ancient and distinguished monastery in the city of Limoges, commonly called La Règle. During the reign of Louis the Transmarine, its abbess was Deda, sister of Ademar, viscount of Ségur and lay abbot of the monastery of Tulle, as is read in the charter-book of that monastery, folio 130: “Deda, abbess of Saint Mary of La Règle, was the sister of Lord Ademar, viscount.” Likewise, folio 192: “Therefore, in the name of God, I, Deda, abbess, and Faucisburgis, a nun, and all the nuns of the same place, namely of Saint Mary of Limoges, sell to a certain man named Bernard, abbot, and to the whole congregation of the monastery of Saint Martin of Tulle, our holdings which are in the county of Limoges,” and so forth. The *Chronicle of Geoffrey, prior of Vigeois*, chapter 27, speaking of Pope Urban II, says: “On the tenth day before the Kalends of January he arrived at Limoges and celebrated the Christmas Mass at cockcrow in the church of the nuns of Saint Mary called La Règle.” The same work, chapter 41, mentions Mary, abbess of Saint Mary of La Règle, daughter of Archambaud the Bearded and Brunicendis, viscountess of Limoges, whose name was omitted by the writers of *Gallia Christiana*. Baluze.]

[Col. 0431A] Monastery of Mastracurii. [Note: Read *Masciacum*, as in the *Life of Louis the Pious*. This is a monastery in Auvergne, now called Mauzac. A charter of Brioude dated 854 says: “Lanfred, abbot of the monastery of Mauzac, which is in the land of Auvergne, in the vicariate of Riom.” Ibid. — Mauzac in Auvergne. Bouquet.]

Monastery of Menadinii. [Note: That is, the monastery of Menat in the *Life of Louis the Pious*. It is a monastery in Auvergne, commonly called Menat, founded by Saint Meneleus. Hence an old parchment of the monastery of Canigou reads: “The title of Saint Meneleus, monastery of Menat.” Baluze. — Perhaps Menat in Auvergne? Bouquet.]

Monastery of Magnilocum. [Note: The monastery of Magnus locus in the *Life of Louis the Pious*. “Heirradus, venerable abbot of the monastery called Magnus locus, situated in the county of Auvergne,” in a charter of Charles the Bald published among the *Proofs of the Liberties of the Gallican Church*, chapter 38, § 7. Baluze.]

Monastery of Conquas. [Note: In the diocese of Rodez, commonly Conques. In 819 its abbot was Medrald, who is mentioned in a charter of Louis the Pious, in which the monastery of Conques is said to be under royal protection and defense. During the reign of the same Louis, an exchange of holdings took place between this monastery and the church of Laon with his authority, as enacted in the *Capitularies of Charles the Bald*, title XI, chapter 12. Ibid.]

Monastery of Saint Antoninus. [Note: Read *Antonini*. In the Canigou parchment mentioned above there is a reference to the monastery “where the head of the martyr Antoninus, together with part of his body, rests in the valley called Nobilense, where a congregation of clerics appears to preside.” This concerns the monastery of Saint Antoninus in the diocese of Rodez, in which the venerable head of that martyr was deposited with the greatest honor; I have found it celebrated far and wide by signs and miracles in the most ancient records of the monastery. At that time it was a monastery of clerics, or canons; a bull of Urban II for the chapter of Saint Antoninus is still extant. Ibid.]

Monastery of Musciacum. [Note: It is written this way also in the *Life of Louis the Pious*. Commonly Moissac, in the region of Cahors. Ibid.]

## In Septimania

[Note: In those times, as we said above, Septimania included the counties extending from the river Aude and the city of Carcassonne as far as the Rhône and the Pyrenees; beyond them lay the Spanish March. Ibid.]

Monastery of Saint Giles in the Flavian Valley. [Note: An ancient and distinguished monastery in the diocese of Nîmes, commonly Saint-Gilles. Ibid.]

Monastery of Psalmodium. [Note: Likewise an ancient monastery in the diocese of Nîmes. In ancient records I find that its abbots included Regembald in 905 and Bernard in 1203. See Innocent III, book XV, letter 111, and Mabillon, book VI of *On Diplomatics*, chapter 205. Ibid.]

Monastery of Anianum. [Note: In the diocese of Maguelonne; its abbot at that time was Benedict. Ibid.]

Monastery of Saint Tiberius. [Note: Commonly Saint-Thibéry, in the diocese of Agde. It is situated on the river Hérault, in the village of Cesseron. A synod of the bishops of the province of Narbonne was held there in 907, at which it was decreed that the Church of Ausona should henceforth be free from the tribute which it paid to the Church of Narbonne. Another council was held there on the Ides of July 1050, presided over by Wifred, archbishop of Narbonne; at it the invaders of the estates of the monastery of Arles were excommunicated. Ibid.]

Monastery of Villamagna. [Note: In the diocese of Béziers. A consolatory letter from the monks of Villemagne to the monks of Canigou, concerning the death of Wifred, count of Cerdanya and a monk of Canigou, was written in 1025: “The bearer of your letter came to the threshold of blessed Martin, bishop of Villemagne, and of blessed Maianus the confessor, announcing to us the death of your father and of the other brothers,” and so forth. Shortly afterward they ask for prayers for the abbots of Villemagne: Abbot Guigrad, Abbot Richer, Abbot Poncius, and Abbot Gairald. Louis VII, king of the Franks, confirmed the rights and privileges of the monastery of Saint Martin of Villemagne at the request of Abbot Berengar, as is clear from his letters, which Philip Augustus copied into his charter issued at Paris in 1210. At that time a dispute arose between Berengar, abbot of Villemagne, and Stephen of Cervian over the *forcia*, that is, the castle or fortress of Cazouls. It was settled by arbitrators chosen by mutual agreement in 1205, on the fourth day before the Kalends of May, in the chapter-house of Villemagne. The arbitrators were Ermengaud, bishop of Béziers; Salomon of Falguières; Bernard, abbot of Saint Aphrodisius of Béziers; and Gerald Jordan, cantor of Béziers. The abbot of Villemagne attended the Council of Béziers in 1255. Ibid.]

Monastery of Saint Peter at Lunat. [Note: Guillelmus Catellus, in book I of his *Memoirs of the History of Occitania*, p. 35, suspects that this might refer to the church of Saint Peter in the city of Lodève; Hadrian Valesius, however, in the *Description of Gaul*, p. 351, identifies it with Lunel because of the similarity of the names. Yet, in my judgment, neither has reached the correct conclusion. The monastery of Saint Peter at Lunat is a monastery in the diocese of Béziers now called Juncelles, in the archdeaconry of Lunat, almost halfway between Lodève and the town of Saint-Pons. This is proved by an old charter mentioned by the distinguished Sainte-Marthe brothers in their catalogue of the bishops of Béziers, where they state that King Pippin, at the request of Benedict, abbot of the monastery of Juncelles, founded under the invocation of Saint Peter in the valley of Lunat, gave him the entire territory of Juncelles, “as is established by the instrument of donation preserved in the archives of the monastery.” Moreover, in a charter of Charles the Simple for the monastery of Psalmodium, I read that the monastery of Juncelles was situated “in the county of Juncelles, in the suburbs of the castle of Lunel.” I find that the abbot of this monastery attended the council held at Béziers in 1255. Likewise, G., abbot of Juncelles, attended the Council of Béziers in 1299. Peter, abbot of Juncelles, appeared at the Council of Narbonne in 1374 under Peter of Judicia, archbishop of Narbonne. Ibid.]

[Col. 0433A] Monastery of Caunas. [Note: Founded in the diocese of Narbonne by Milo, count of Narbonne, under Charlemagne, as is written in a letter of Gelasius II concerning the privileges of that monastery. This can be confirmed by what is read in the charter that the same Charles granted to the monastery of Caunes at the time of the Synod of Frankfurt. I find the following men recorded as abbots of the monastery of Caunes in ancient manuscripts:

Anianus, who attended the Synod of Frankfurt in 794.

John, in 826.

Hilderic, during the time of Charles the Bald.

Gondesalvius, in 853.

Egilkanes or Egiga, in 870.

Daniel, in 873.

Baldemar was abbot in the twenty-ninth year of the reign of Charles the king, after the death of Odo.

[Col. 0433B] Robert, son of Trudgardis, was abbot in the second year after the death of Charles the Simple and in the first year in which King Radulf died.

Aimeric, in the twenty-ninth year of King Lothair’s reign.

Radulf, in the first and second years of King Hugh’s reign.

Udalgarius, in the seventh year of King Hugh’s reign.

Isarnus, in 1095 and 1098.

Gerald, in 1101.

Isarnus, in 1103.

Peter, in 1136.

Casto, in 1165.

Berengar, in 1166 and 1171.

Peter, in 1177, 1183, and 1185.

Gerald, in 1228.

Peter, called Raymundi, in 1231, 1236, and 1240.

Peter, in 1262, 1268, 1269, 1270, 1275, and 1280.

William, in 1338, on 16 January. From the register of the royal archive at Carcassonne, folio 84.

[Col. 0433C] Embrinus. He attended the Council of Narbonne in 1374.

Solomon, in 1413.

Bertrand, in 1416.

Peter of Godiac, doctor of decrees, vicar and official of Narbonne, in 1432.

Guarinus of Tornello, in 1437.

Rigaldus of Albinhac, in 1450. Baluze.]

Monastery of the Castle of Malasci. [Note: Read “the castle of Malasci or Mallasti.” For so it is called in the charters of Louis the Pious, Pippin king of Aquitania, Charles the Bald, Odo, and Radulf, and in other ancient records. The monastery of the castle of Malasca is therefore the monastery now called Montolieu in the diocese of Carcassonne. I find the following men recorded as its abbots:

Olomundus, in 815.

Vilafredus, in 827.

Richimirus, in 854.

Ugobertus, in 883.

[Col. 0433D] Ramulfus, in the first and fourth years of the reign of King Charles—that is, I believe, Charles the Simple. See Mabillon, *Annals*, volume III, p. 696.

Arifonsus or Erifonsus, in the twenty-third, twenty-seventh, and twenty-eighth years of the reign of King Charles, son of Louis. At the same time Erifonsus, bishop, lived at Narbonne, as is clear from a charter of the same Charles preserved in the archive of the archbishop of Narbonne and in Catel; he is called bishop of Vendres in the charter-book of the Church of Elne.

Donadeus, in the fourth year of King Rodulf’s reign after the death of King Charles.

Tresmirus, in the thirteenth year of King Louis’s reign and in the fourth, fifth, twenty-first, twenty-third, and twenty-fifth years of King Lothair’s reign. A letter of Agapitus the Younger concerning the confirmation of the monastery’s privileges is extant to him.

Stephen, in the thirtieth, thirty-second, and thirty-third years of King Robert’s reign.

William, in 1054.

Peter, during the reign of King Philip.

[Col. 0434A] Berengar, in 1106.

Bernard, son of Ermengardis, in 1146 and 1147.

Sicard, son of Guillelma, in 1174.

Isarnus, in 1184–1188.

Bernard of Magaladz, in 1194.

Isarnus of Aragon, in 1205. I would not, however, assert that he was abbot, since he calls himself merely procurator of the monastery of Montolieu and avoids the title of abbot.

Ermengaudus, in 1229, 1230, 1231, 1232, 1234, 1236, 1242, 1243, and 1245.

Gerald, in 1249, 1259, 1270, and 1278. He was summoned by Gregory X to the Council of Lyon by letters issued at Lyon on the Ides of March in the second year of the pope’s reign.

Peter Bernardi, in 1297–1298.

[Col. 0434B] Bartholomew, in 1319. *Process of Bernard Delitiosi*, folio 183 verso; *Lives of the Popes of Avignon*, volume II, p. 355.

Ozilius, in 1327.

William, in 1334; Benedict XII made him cardinal-priest of the Four Holy Crowned Martyrs in 1337.

Raymund, in 1345.

G., in 1351 and 1358.

Bertrand of Pelaiano, formerly abbot of Saint-Sever, in 1365. Manuscript 2835, folio 95 verso.

Hilias Jacobi, formerly prior of Lingeville in the diocese of Rouen, nephew of Peter of Châlons, bishop of Montauban; he died in 1393.

Arnaldus.

Saxius, in 1429, made abbot by Martin V after the death of Arnold. He had been the monastery’s almoner.

John, in 1445–1461.

[Col. 0434C] William of La Roche, in 1465.

Simon of Bellosole, provost of Vaur and commendatory abbot of the monastery of Montolieu in 1505. Perhaps he was the same man who was bishop of Vaur.

John of Bellosole, succentor of the Church of Narbonne, commendatory abbot in 1515.

Sebastian of Bonne, major prior of the Church of Castres, made abbot in 1518, in accordance with the concordats.

Anthony of Bonne, nephew of the preceding through his full brother, chamberlain of the monastery of Montolieu, became abbot in 1540 through his uncle’s resignation. He was still in office in 1544.

Francis of Créqui, bishop of Thérouanne, was appointed abbot after the death of Anthony of Bonne, but renounced his appointment in favor of the next abbot.

James of Créqui, brother of the preceding, a monk of Saint-Denis, became abbot of Montolieu in 1550. — Ibid.]

Monastery of Saint Mary of Capariensis. [Note: In the county of Razès and the diocese of Narbonne. A charter of Charles the Simple published in the *Appendix to the Councils of Narbonne Gaul*, title 4, says: “We also add, from our royal liberality, to the aforesaid church of Saints Justus and Pastor, in the county of Razès, the abbey of Cubières.” The monastery of Saint Mary of Cubières, dependent on Cluny, is mentioned in a letter of Urban II to Hugh, abbot of Cluny. Ibid.]

[Col. 0434A] Monastery of Saint Mary at Orubion. [Note: On the boundary between the dioceses of Narbonne and Carcassonne, as is read in a charter of Charlemagne published in the same *Appendix to the Councils of Narbonne Gaul*. Commonly La Grasse. Ibid.]

Monastery of Saint Lawrence. [Note: An ancient abbey united to the Church of Narbonne by the authority of Louis the Stammerer, king of the Franks; eventually, in the eleventh century, it was reduced to a priory and subjected to the monastery of La Grasse. See the notes to the Councils of Narbonne Gaul, pp. 3, 20, 21. I believe this is the abbey meant here. I know, however, that there was once another monastery of this name in Cerdanya, which was then part of Septimania; it is mentioned in the Canigou parchment cited above: “To the lord fathers and likewise to the humble brothers, together with the elders residing in the monastery of the blessed Martin, bishop and confessor of Christ, of Canigou: John, though an unworthy monk and abbot, and the small flock of the monastery of Saint Lawrence of Cerdanya.” Before this John, the abbot of the same monastery had been Poncius, who died on the sixth day before the Kalends of June. Baluze. — Now Saint-Chinian.]

Monastery of Saint Eugenia. [Note: In the suburb of Narbonne.]

Monastery of Saint Hilary. [Note: In the diocese of Carcassonne. Formerly this monastery was dedicated to Saint Saturninus. Later Saint Hilary, bishop of Carcassonne, who was buried there, occasioned the change of name. Nevertheless, for several centuries it was called the monastery of Saint Hilary and Saint Saturninus. It had the following abbots:]

Nampius, in the time of Charlemagne. Monnellus, Egidonius, Leoninus, during the reign of Louis the Pious. Ana, during the reign of Charles the Bald. Castellanus, succeeded by Recamundus; Book VI of *On Diplomatic Matters*, p. 506. Benedictus, in the year 970 and in the twenty-seventh year of Lothair’s reign. Also in the second year of King Hugh’s reign. Gaufredus, in the sixth year of Robert’s reign. Benedictus, in the fifteenth year of Robert’s reign. Oliba, in the years 1020 and 1034. See volume IV of the *Benedictine Annals*, p. 711, chapter 38. Cono, in the year 1110. Udalgerius, 1117–1120. Pontius de Bravo, 1194–1202. Alboynus, in the years 1217, 1224, 1231, and 1235. [Col. 0435C] Guillelmus Petri, Alboynus’s successor, in the year 1253. Arnaldus, elected and confirmed in 1265. He was still in office in 1285. Pontius, in 1286. Jordanus, 1344–1350. Jacobus, 1385–1386. Bertrandus, in 1411. Guillelmus Babonis, in 1441. Gaubertus Augerii, elected and confirmed in 1451. Previously abbot of Saint Polycarp in the diocese of Narbonne. He was in office in 1453. Arnaldus Raymundus Roquete became abbot in 1481. — ID.] of Saint Hilary.

The monastery [Note: [Col. 0435C] That is, the monastery of Saint Mary of Arles in the county of Vallespir. The *Cartulary of the Church of Elne*, Book V, chapter 97: “I, Vusandus, abbot, and the entire congregation of the monastery of Saint Mary of Arles, which was founded in the county of Roussillon, in the valley of Asperia, above the bed of the Tech, that is, Endalecus, etc., [Col. 0435D] on the third day before the Nones of August, in the fifth year of King Radulf’s reign.” A charter of Charles the Bald, issued at the monastery of Saint-Denis on the seventh day before the Kalends of March in the year 869: “The monastery founded in honor of Saint Mary in the county of Roussillon, in the valley of Asperia.” The same statements occur in a charter of Louis the Stammerer issued at Troyes in 878. But Charles himself explicitly calls it the monastery of Saint Mary of Arles in the valley of Asperia in another charter issued at the monastery of Saint Saturninus while Toulouse was under siege, in 844: “Recisindus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary at Arles, coming to us, presented before us the charter of our lord and father, the Emperor Louis, which stated how the aforesaid monastery, built by Castellanus of old in the valley called Asperia, had been received under his immunity and protection.” This cannot, however, establish that the monastery was founded by Castellanus, only that it was restored by him. Louis the Pious makes this clear in a charter issued in the seventh year of his empire, fifteen days before the Kalends of October: “Castellanus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary, coming to us, informed us that he, together with his brothers, had built a monastery in the valley called Asperia, upon ancient foundations.” [Col. 0436A] At length this monastery was made subject to Cluny, as is clear from the bulls of Urban II and the subsequent Roman pontiffs. — ID.]

The entire county of Roussillon is divided into three parts: one is inhabited by the properly so-called Roussillonians, another by the Conflentines, and the third by the Vallespirians. This division is ancient. But, leaving the other matters aside for the present, our concern here is with the county of Vallespir, which this notice shows to have been in Septimania.

This is confirmed by many testimonies. A charter of Louis the Pious for Wimaro, a royal vassal: “We grant such a benefice that the properties which their father, by concession of our father, the most excellent Emperor Charles, brought from the wilderness in Septimania and built into a settlement called Vicus Sirisidum may remain, namely, in the valley of Asperia.” In the *Cartulary of the Church of Elne*, Book III, chapter 62, there is an ancient charter dated to the sixth year of the reign of Louis the Transmarine, in which we read: “I give you my allod which I possess in the county of Roussillon, in the valley of Asperia.” Another, in the fourteenth year of the same king, Book VI, chapter 82: “in the county of Roussillon, in the valley of Asperia, in the village of Corbaria.” Likewise another, Book IV, chapter 88, in the fifth year of the reign of Hugh Capet: “in the county of Roussillon or in the valley of Asperia.” Again another, Book I, chapter 99, dated 1095, on the fourth day before the Ides of February: “These, then, are the allods in the county of Roussillon, or in the valley of Asperia.”

Moreover, the charter of the Emperor Lothair for Wimaro, the vassal mentioned shortly before, shows that the county of Roussillon, in which Vallespir was situated, was in Septimania. It was issued in the twenty-first year of Louis the Pious’s reign and is preserved in the same cartulary, Book I, chapter 10: “Wimar, our vassal, fulfilling his loyalty, came to us and petitioned our clemency that we grant to him and his brother, named Rado, such a benefice that the properties which their father, by concession of our grandfather, the most excellent Emperor Charles, bringing them from the wilderness in Septimania, built into a settlement called Villanova, might remain, namely, in Roussillon.” A charter of Charles the Bald for Dodo, the vassal of Orgerius, preserved in the monastery of Saint Peter of Roda and issued in the twenty-ninth year of Charles’s reign: “certain properties of our right situated within the kingdom of Septimania, in the county of Roussillon.” See the notes to the *Councils of Narbonnese Gaul*, p. 6. — ID.] Valley of Asperia.

[Col. 0436A] [Note: [Col. 0436C] That is, in the Toulouse march, as stated above.] In Toulouse.

The monastery [Note: [Col. 0436D] Which Pope John XXII later elevated to episcopal dignity.] of Saint Papulus.

The monastery [Note: [Col. 0436D] Commonly called Sorèze, formerly in the county of Toulouse and now in that of Vaur. That the foundation of the monastery of Soricinium in the county of Toulouse is to be attributed to King Pippin is shown by a charter of his issued at Aachen, in which he states that this had been commanded to him by the Blessed Mother of God. Philippus, abbot of Soricinium, presided over the Council of Vaur of the Three Provinces in 868 in the name of Arnaldus, archbishop of Auch, as we stated in the notes to the *Councils of Narbonnese Gaul*, p. 56.] of Suricinium.

The monastery [Note: [Col. 0436D] Commonly called Mas d’Asil, formerly in the county of Toulouse and now in the diocese of Pamiers; dedicated to Saint Stephen. Isarnus, bishop of Toulouse, received it under his protection in 1075 at the request of Dalmatius, archbishop of Narbonne, as can be seen in the letters of Isarnus himself. From this it is clear that Dalmatius was extremely observant of the ancient law, which provides that each bishop should possess authority over his own parish and that a metropolitan should presume to do nothing in the parishes of his comprovincials without their authorization. — ID.] of Asilo.

[Col. 0437A] The monastery [Note: [Col. 0437A] Among the monasteries which the author of the *Life of Louis the Pious* says were restored by him is the monastery of Utera in the county of Toulouse. This may perhaps be the same as the monastery of Venercha. — ID. — Venerque near Toulouse.] of Venercha.

## In Gascony.

The monastery [Note: [Col. 0437A] It is certain that this monastery was situated in Gascony. Perhaps it was in the diocese of Auch, since it is placed before Cimorra. In the cartulary of the monastery of Cimorra [Col. 0437B] we read that Sansastrus of Cella Fraxili made an agreement “that Sansfurt of Argun should take his daughter, named Sancia, as his wife. When he wished to celebrate the wedding, Guillelmus of Beccava opposed him because he was his lord. On hearing this, Sansfurt gave him five solidi so that he might wholly relinquish her to him and establish Sansaster as his son-in-law, together with all the offspring descended from her.” The same cartulary mentions a certain knight named Fortonius of Cella Fraxili, who was living in 1134. Perhaps the monastery of Cella Fraxili is what is today called Cella-Medulphi, commonly Saramon, in the diocese of Auch. — BALUZ.] of Cella Fraxili.

The monastery [Note: [Col. 0437B]

All the ancient writers spell it this way; but in the fourth volume of *Gallia Christiana* it is written “Simorra.” An ancient monastery dedicated to the Blessed Virgin Mary, in which the relics of Saint Ceratius and Saint Saturninus are preserved. I find the following men recorded as abbots of this monastery in ancient documents:

Forto, or Fortunus, around the year 1020.

Otto, archbishop of Auch, around 1030.

Pontius, in 1055 and 1068.

Gastonus.

Astarus.

Laerus, Astarus’s successor, around 1070.

Bernardus, Laerus’s successor.

[Col. 0438B] Pontius, bishop of Bigorre, around 1076.

Petrus de Petiano, in 1080 and 1090.

Willelmus, in 1118 and 1122.

Petrus, 1143–1146.] of Cimorra.

The monastery [Note: [Col. 0438B] Commonly called Pessan, in the diocese of Auch. An ancient charter of the monastery of Cimorra: “And the inheritance remained to me: the monastery commonly called Pestiano, built in honor of Saint Michael the Archangel and situated in the monastery of Astariensis.” Mention is made of the abbot of Pezanum or Pessanum in the diocese of Auch by Gregory VII, Book VII, letter 18. — ID.] of Piciano.

The monastery [Note: [Col. 0438B] Saint Sixtus of Faget, diocese of Auch.] of Altum fragitum.

[Col. 0438A] The monastery [Note: [Col. 0438B] In the valley of Levitana and the diocese of Tarbes. See the *History of Béarn* by the most illustrious Peter de Marca, archbishop of Paris, Book IX, chapter 2. — BALUZ. — In the territory of Tarbes, near the Pyrenees. — BOUQ.] of Saint Savinus.

Here the aforesaid emperor, as stated above, ordered a statute concerning the aforesaid monasteries to be written, confirmed it with his own hand, and ordered it sealed with his imperial ring.

# ADDITIONAL CHAPTERS TO THE SALIC LAW (A.D. 819)

[Col. 0437]

In the year 819 after the birth of the Lord, according to Einhard’s testimony, an assembly was held at Aachen, at which many matters concerning the condition of churches and monasteries were discussed and regulated. Certain chapters, greatly needed because they were lacking, were also written down and added to the laws. Baluzius published them from two manuscript codices, one belonging to the Royal Library and the other to Saint Remigius of Rheims; they are now issued, revised with the aid of those same codices, namely: 1. the Royal Library of Paris, among the Latin Supplements, no. 164 bis, formerly of Saint Remigius; and 2. Codex C of the same library, no. 4632.

## IN THE NAME OF THE LORD. HERE BEGIN THE CHAPTERS OF THE SALIC LAW

[Note: [Col. 0437] The title is absent from manuscript 2.]

[Col. 0437C]

### 1. Concerning the first chapter [Note: [Col. 0437] of the Salic Law, that is, manuscript 2.]—concerning summons.

Regarding this chapter, it was ruled that the person who is summoned should have forty nights as the period of his summons. And if the count has not held his court within the aforesaid number of nights, that period shall be extended until the count’s court, and afterward he shall be granted a period of respite of seven nights. From then on, not a period of nights, but the count’s next court shall be granted to him.

### 2. Concerning the eleventh chapter [Note: [Col. 0437] XII. 1; XI. 2.] of the Salic Law.

If anyone kills another’s slave, sells him, or releases him as a free man, he shall be judged liable for 1,400 denarii, which amount to thirty-five solidi, apart from the principal value and the fine for concealment [Note: [Col. 0437] The rest of the chapter is lacking in manuscript 2.].

[Col. 0437D] Concerning this chapter, all judged that if the slave who had been unjustly sold or released as a free man appears, no other person should be restored in his place; for some said that the same slave who had been released as a free man should not be returned to servitude [Note: [Col. 0437] Manuscript 1 reads “restore.”] again. They judged instead that he should be restored to his former master and servile condition.

### 3. Concerning the fourteenth chapter [Note: [Col. 0437] XIV, manuscript 2.] of the Salic Law.

If a free man takes another’s female slave in marriage, he himself shall be placed in servitude with her [Note: [Col. 0437] Manuscript 1 reads “they shall be placed.”].

Concerning this chapter, all judged that if a free woman takes any slave in marriage, she should not only remain in servitude with that slave, but all the property she possesses, if she holds it divided from her parents, should pass to the master whose slave she took in marriage. And if she has not divided her paternal or maternal property with her parents, she may neither answer anyone who makes a claim nor, together with her heirs, enter further into the inheritance of the paternal property beyond the division [Note: [Col. 0437] Manuscript 1 reads “divided.”]. They likewise judged that the same should be done if a Frankish man takes another person’s female slave in marriage.

### 4. Also concerning the same chapter.

If anyone takes another man’s wife while her husband is alive, he shall be judged liable for 8,000 denarii, which amount to 200 solidi.

[Col. 0439A] Concerning this chapter, it was judged that, while the husband whose wife had been taken from him contrary to law was alive, she should be restored to him by the man who had unjustly taken her, together with the penalty prescribed above, namely 200 solidi [Note: [Col. 0439] Manuscript 2 reads 300.].

### 5. Concerning the twenty-sixth chapter [Note: [Col. 0439] XXXVI. 1.].

If a boy under twelve years of age commits any offense, the fredus shall not be demanded from him.

Concerning this chapter, it was judged that if a child under twelve unjustly seizes another person’s property, he shall make composition for it according to the law, except for the fredus, and shall be summoned in the same way [Note: [Col. 0439] Manuscript 1 reads “likewise.”] as the person against whom he acted contrary to law may be summoned [Note: [Col. 0439] The words “from … to …” are absent from manuscript 1.]. He shall likewise be brought by the count to his court in the same way as the person against whom he acted contrary to law may be brought [Note: [Col. 0439] The word has been supplied by the editor; it is absent from manuscripts 1 and 2.]. But if anyone wishes to bring a claim against him concerning paternal or maternal inheritance, it was judged that he should wait until the period of twelve years [Col. 0439B] has elapsed.

### 6.

All judged that if a Frankish man or a free woman voluntarily places himself or herself in servitude, then, if while remaining in freedom he or she had legally transferred his or her property to the Church of God or to anyone else, the person to whom it had been transferred should be able to possess and retain it [Note: [Col. 0439] The words “they themselves …” are missing in manuscript 2.]. And if he or she had begotten sons or daughters while remaining free, those children should remain free.

### 7. Concerning the thirty-seventh chapter [Note: [Col. 0439] XXXVI. 1, 2.].

If a slave kills a free man, the murderer himself shall be handed over to the parents of the slain man for half the compensation, and the slave’s master shall know that he must pay the other half [Note: [Col. 0439] Manuscript 1 reads “is handed over.”]. Or, if he understands the law, he may defend himself in court so that he does not pay the *leod* [Note: [Col. 0439] Manuscript 2 reads *lead*].

[Col. 0439C] Since the law makes no distinction between a slave of an ecclesiastic, a beneficiary, or another person, they wished to reserve for the lord emperor’s consideration whether slaves of ecclesiastics or beneficiaries can be handed over or released in the same way as slaves belonging to free persons [Note: [Col. 0439] The remainder of the chapter is lacking in manuscript 1.].

### 8. Concerning the forty-sixth chapter

That is, concerning the man who wishes to take a widow in marriage. All judged [Note: [Col. 0439] Manuscript 1 adds “men.”] that he should not take her as it is written in the Salic Law, but should marry her with the consent and approval of her relatives, just as their predecessors have done up to the present [Note: [Col. 0439] Manuscript 1 reads “husband.”].

### 9. Concerning the forty-seventh chapter

Concerning the person who has occupied another’s estate. Regarding this chapter, they judged that no one should be able to hold or possess another person’s estate or property for years under the pretext of moving there; rather, on whatever day the occupier of that property is summoned, he must either return the property to the claimant [Note: [Col. 0439] Manuscript 1 reads “of claiming”] or, if he can, defend his right to it according to law.

[Col. 0440B] ### 10. Concerning *affatomie* [Note: [Col. 0439C] Title 48 of the Salic Law.]

They said that it was a transfer [Note: [Col. 0439] Manuscript 1 reads “rejection.”]. Concerning this chapter, it was judged that just as their predecessors had possessed and practiced it through long custom, so all who live under the Salic Law should henceforth possess and practice it.

### 11.

They also judged that if a slave produces a charter of manumission, and the slave is unable to produce a legitimate author of that charter, the slave’s master may declare the charter forged.

### 12.

They also judged that everyone who makes a claim against another should have permission first to produce his own testimony against him. And if the person against whom the claim is made says that he holds what he possesses by law, and there are witnesses who can truthfully affirm this [Note: [Col. 0439] Manuscript 1 reads “can.”], [Col. 0440C] they judged that the truth of the matter should be established according to the chapters of the lord emperor [Note: [Col. 0439] Manuscript 1 reads “chapter”], which he had previously decreed should be observed as law.

# RESPONSES GIVEN TO A CERTAIN ENVOY (A.D. 819)

[Col. 0439]

First published by Baluzius, these responses have here been revised and corrected with the aid of the single codex, namely Royal Parisian Codex 2718, from the ninth century. It is clear that they were given to a certain envoy returning from an embassy. Since chapters 1, 2, and 6 appear to refer to the Aachen constitutions of the year 817, I have retained the date assigned to them by Baluzius, namely 819.

# CHAPTERS TO BE ADDED TO THE SALIC LAW

[Col. 0439D]

### Chapter 1

That the inhabitants of the counties should not investigate the cases of other men by oaths, except only the cases of the lord. Nevertheless, if the count has a case involving a poor or powerful person, that count should investigate it carefully, but without an oath, through the more truthful and better men of the county.

### 2 [Note: [Col. 0439] The codex omits the numbers and merely repeats the heading.]

The lord emperor wishes every count to come to such a court as he has now ordered and to bring with him twelve assessors, if that many are available. Otherwise, he shall make up the number of twelve from the better men of that county. The advocates of bishops, abbots, and abbesses are also to come with them [Note: [Col. 0439] The word has been supplied by the editor.].

### 3

It shall be established that everyone who owes the royal census must pay it in the same place where his father and grandfather were accustomed to pay it.

### 4

If, at a court or before the count of the palace, another person obstructs someone’s case [Note: [Col. 0439] The text apparently requires “when seeking” or a similar expression.], and unjustly impedes his case by arguing against it, we then wish the count of the palace, or the count himself in his county, to order that person to leave. If he refuses to obey, he shall pay the lord’s fine, namely 60 solidi, and shall give his pledge to the person whom he opposed, according to the law.

### 5

We wish the count to have the authority to do at his court what he ought to do, with no one contradicting him. But if he acts otherwise than justly, the person to whom that action pertains shall come into our presence, and we shall do justice for him concerning that count.

### 6

We wish the investiture of our lord and father to be maintained in the manner in which it is said to exist, wherever it may be, but only after the most careful investigation. If it is found to be just and legitimate, then let it be called an investiture; otherwise it must not be called an investiture, whether the property is ecclesiastical or palatine [Col. 0441B].

### 7

Concerning property in the castles acquired by our grandfather, it seems to us that the matter should be handled and distinguished as follows: only those should not have control of their own property who resisted for as long as they could and came under our grandfather’s power against their will. For whoever surrendered himself while his companions were stubbornly resisting, even if the castle had been taken by force, should nevertheless retain his own property in it [Col. 0442A] [Note: [Col. 0441] That is, “surrendered”; the codex reads “learned.”].

### 8

Concerning the properties over which the Emperor Charles had a legitimate grant, and which can be investigated in such a way that they ought by right to belong to us, we absolutely do not wish that, if our witnesses are good and suitable, others should rise against them in opposition to us. Nevertheless, it shall be your responsibility to ensure that the faithful men who are with you and who are to be our witnesses are good and truthful.

Furthermore, concerning ecclesiastical property, the same judgment shall remain in force which was issued in the time of our lord [Note: [Col. 0441] A word is missing; Baluzius supplied it as “and.”] and father: the defenders of the churches shall defend their property against their claimants [Note: [Col. 0441] A word is missing.] by the same law under which those who donated that property to the churches lived [Col. 0442B]. Likewise, the church shall have the same law against its claimants, with our justice preserved.

### 9

Concerning the fourth chapter, we have judged that the matter should be deferred until we discuss it with more of our faithful men.

# LOMBARD CHAPTERS (A.D. 819)

[Col. 0441]

Among the chapters added to the edicts of the Lombard kings, whose manuscript book identifies Louis as the author, these cannot be assigned with certainty to any particular year or place. Since, however, Louis appears after the assembly held at Attigny in August 822 to have left nearly all responsibility for Italy to Lothair, they should be assigned to the years 818–822, if Louis is indeed to be acknowledged as their author. They are not found in the Chisian, Cava, Blankenburg, or Gotha codices.

[Col. 0441B] From the Ambrosian, Florentine, London, Viennese, Veronese, and Este codices.

That the entire order of the churches should live according to Roman law, and that ecclesiastical property should be investigated and defended in such a way that the *emphyteusis* [Note: [Col. 0441] The editors read “the emphyteutic contract from which the church suffers harm.”] from which the church suffers damage should not be observed [Note: [Col. 0441] The editors read “should be observed … should be destroyed.”], but should be annulled according to Roman law, and no penalty should be paid.

From the Florentine, London, Viennese, Veronese, and Este codices.

### 2 [Note: [Col. 0441] In Muratori, chapter 58; compare Lothair’s capitulary of 832, chapter 12.]

It pleased us concerning those men [Note: [Col. 0441] Namely, free men, according to a gloss in manuscript V.] who say that they have been free for thirty years, that they should not be free by virtue of this possession unless they were born of a free father and mother [Note: [Col. 0441] The editors read “or.”] [Col. 0442B] or produce a charter of freedom.

### 3 [Note: [Col. 0441] In Muratori, chapter 56.]

Therefore, we absolutely command all bishops, abbots, and the entire clergy to have good—not cruel, greedy, perjured, or lovers of falsehood—but God-fearing men who diligently love justice in every respect [Note: [Col. 0441] The editors read “doing” or “diligently practicing it.”] as their deputies, provosts, advocates, or defenders.

Concerning judges, centenarii, tribunes, and vicars, we have considered it proper that, if they are found to be bad, they should be removed from their office [Note: [Col. 0441] At the end of the capitularies, the Ambrosian Codex adds the following: “[The text is corrupt: ‘We also wish and command, as the Apostle [says], [concerning] sons ... not, however, for this reason [are they] called free in the chapter ... slaves; for just as a slave [is] in the power of his master, a son [is] in the power of his father; therefore also sons, whether [of] an enslaved or a free father, as a slave [by] manumission, or otherwise according to law, [may] be free from their master.’]” Our Blume has already observed that this passage came from Roman law.].

# AACHEN CAPITULARY (A.D. 820, January, Aachen)

[Col. 0441]

Baluzius assigned this constitution, published from two copies in Royal Parisian Codex 2718 of the ninth century, to the assembly held at Thionville in 820. But since in that year—the year to which it unquestionably belongs from chapter 5—the general assembly was held not at the place indicated by Baluzius but at Aachen, while the other, autumnal assembly was held at Quierzy, we have judged that it should be assigned to the former. We publish it after revising it with the aid of: 1. Royal Library of Paris Codex 2718, folio 73; 2. another codex of the same library, folio 110; and 3. the Blankenburg codex of the Ducal Library of Wolfenbüttel.

[Col. 0443A] ### Chapter 1 [Note: [Col. 0443B] This chapter is also found in the Florentine Codex among Louis’s laws.]

Where tolls are and are not to be exacted.

We firmly wish it to be known to everyone throughout our empire, entrusted to us by God, that no one may exact a toll except in marketplaces where ordinary merchandise is bought and sold; nor at bridges, except where tolls were customarily exacted in ancient times; nor on the banks of rivers, where ships merely tend to remain for some nights; nor in forests, nor on roads, nor in fields, nor beneath a bridge from those passing through, nor anywhere else, unless something belonging to common use is bought or sold for any purpose [Note: [Col. 0443] Manuscript 2 reads “goods.”].

When a buyer uses the grass, wood, or other rural resources belonging to anyone, he shall deal with the person to whom the things he uses belong, according to the value of the use, and shall pay him what is just for such a thing. But if anyone, avoiding established markets so as not to be compelled to pay a toll, wishes to buy something outside the aforesaid places and is found doing so, he shall be restrained and compelled to pay the toll owed.

Anyone who receives or conceals a person avoiding the payment of such lawful tolls shall be compelled to make compensation according to his own law; the person whom he concealed, however, shall pay the toll owed. Otherwise, as stated above, no one may exact tolls from anyone except in the places mentioned. And if anyone acts against these commands of ours [Note: [Col. 0443] Manuscripts 1 and 2 omit “does so.”], let him know that he is to be condemned to a fine of 60 solidi.

### 2. Concerning the provisions of our faithful men

Whether with carts, pack animals [Note: [Col. 0443] Manuscript 3 reads “pack animals” with a variant spelling.], or [Col. 0443B] *friskingae*, or any other vehicles [Note: [Col. 0443B] It is certain that *friskingae* are here counted among the vehicles. They must have been some sort of vehicle of Frankish origin. — BALUZ.], no one may presume to exact toll from those who continually serve us in the palace, or from those who transport provisions to the palace, whether at bridges, on ships, or in any other places. If anyone does so, he shall know that he is likewise to be punished by a penalty of 60 solidi [Note: [Col. 0443] Manuscript 1 reads “a fine of sixty solidi.”].

But if anyone is found to have transported the things mentioned above not for his own provisions or personal use, but rather for the purpose of selling them, he shall know that he is to be condemned as set out above.

### 3

None of those who build bridges, whether from immunities, royal estates, or free men, shall be compelled to pay a bridge toll for the same bridge that he has built. And if someone should wish to repair or restore that bridge from his own resources, although he repairs or restores it from his own property, he must not presume to exact a greater payment for the same bridge than was customary and is recognized as just.

### 4

Let it be known to everyone that we do not wish a free man to be compelled to work on our royal preserves [Note: [Col. 0443] Manuscript 3 reads “royal preserves.”]. Nevertheless, no one may excuse himself on this account from the other public services which he was accustomed to perform according to ancient custom.

### 5

In general, we admonish everyone that the chapters which last year we judged, with universal agreement, should be added to the Salic Law [Note: [Col. 0443] Manuscripts 1, 2, and 3 read “of the law.”] should no longer be called chapters, but only law; indeed, they should be observed as law [Note: [Col. 0443] A marginal note in manuscript A adds: “that is, concerning the person who kills a subdeacon, a deacon, a priest, a bishop, or a monk.”].

# CAPITULARY OF THIONVILLE (A.D. 821, October)

[Col. 0443]

We owe this text to Book IV of Ansegisus, chapters 1–12, where its first chapter is preserved, as well as among the chapters added to the Lombard laws. That it was promulgated at the autumn assembly held at Thionville is stated in chapter 6. Since Louis the Emperor held a court at Compiègne after the first one celebrated there in November 816 only in the years 823 and 824, it is clear that those years cannot be intended here: when Ansegisus completed his work, namely in January 827, only three years had elapsed since then.

[Col. 0443C] ### 1

If slaves, having gathered a crowd through insubordination, use force against anyone—that is, if they commit murder, arson, or robbery of any kind—their masters, through whose negligence this has occurred, shall be compelled to pay our fine, namely 60 solidi, because they refused to restrain them so that they would not dare to do such things.

### 2

Concerning property or slaves said to have been seized by our royal estate, we wish our envoys to conduct an investigation without an oath, through the more truthful men living around that county, and to report to our knowledge whatever they are able to investigate more truly and certainly concerning the matter, so that we may then decide [Col. 0443D] whatever appears just to us.

[Col. 0444C] ### 3

If slaves belonging either to churches or to any free persons flee for refuge to our royal estate, and their masters or advocates reclaim them, then, if the administrator of our royal estate understands that he cannot justly retain them under our ownership, he shall expel them from that estate, and their masters shall receive them. But if it appears to that administrator that they ought to belong to our ownership, he shall expel them from that estate, and after they have been received by the same claimants, he shall bring a lawful action against them; and thus, if he can, he shall establish our right to possess them.

### 4 [Note: [Col. 0443D] Namely, the royal vassals. Indeed, in records of judgments conducted in those times we see the names of vassals placed after the names of royal envoys and counts, as in the charter concerning the dispute between Audmarus, archbishop of Vienne, and Wigericus, count. The *Acts of Saint Aldric*, bishop of Le Mans: “He ordered this justice to be investigated by Ebroinus, bishop of the city of Poitiers, and Morigonus, count, and Altmarus, seneschal of the Empress Judith and royal envoy, together with other royal vassals.” — BALUZ.]

Concerning our vassals who have been appointed to guard our march, or who have their benefices or private property in distant regions, or who serve us continually in our palace and therefore cannot regularly attend the courts: we wish our envoys or the count to make this known to us, and we shall arrange for them to come to their courts.

### 5

We wish the counts who are appointed to coastal defense [Note: [Col. 0445C] Beatus Rhenanus, Book II of *Germanic Matters*, p. 94: “There were also counts assigned to coastal defense, likewise to protect the march, whom we today call margraves.” Einhard, letter 22: “They were assigned to coastal defense.” — ID.]—whichever of them remains in his office—not to excuse himself from administering justice on account of that defense. But if he has his assessors with him there, he shall hold court there and administer justice.

### 6

Concerning those who say that they lost their own property through incest [Note: [Col. 0445C] This reading is consistent in all the ancient copies, except that the Rivipullian manuscript reads “uncertain.” Ancient scribes sometimes confused these words, as in chapter 5 of title 21 of Charles the Bald’s capitulary, and sometimes also wrote “his incestuous kinswoman”; in place of this, the Codex of Saint Vincent of Metz has “uncertain.” Likewise, in King Childebert’s decree, chapter 2, where the correct reading is “he joins an incestuous union to his marriage,” the ancient Rheims and Beauvais manuscripts read “uncertain.” But, returning to our subject, it is certain that here the reading should be the one we have printed. See F. Pithaeus’s glossary to the books of the capitularies under the word *reclamare*. — ID.], it has been established that if they lost those properties within the preceding five years, when we held our court at Compiègne [Note: [Col. 0446C] In November 816.], they shall not have them restored.

[Col. 0445B] ### 7 [Note: [Col. 0446C] Beatus Rhenanus, Book II of *Germanic Matters*, p. 94: “The laws of the Franks mention the conspiracy of slaves which took place in Flanders, the Menapian region, and other places along the sea.” — BALUZ.]

Concerning the conspiracies of slaves which take place in Flanders, Menapian territory, and the other maritime regions [Note: [Col. 0446C] A charter of Charles the Bald for the monastery of Saint Bavo, in Miraeus’s *Code of Pious Donations*, p. 73: “In the county of Menapia, in the village of Helsca,” where Miraeus conjectures that Helsca should perhaps be understood as the village of the territory of Aalst called Esche. Andreas Catullus, in *Tournai of the Nervians*, p. 18, argues that the Menapians, or Menapians of Menpiscus, were partly in the diocese of Tournai and partly in that of Thérouanne. — ID.], we wish our envoys to notify the masters of those slaves, so that they may restrain them and prevent them from daring to form such conspiracies again. And so that those masters of the same slaves may know that, if any of their slaves dares to form such a conspiracy after this command of ours has been communicated to them, the master himself must pay our fine, namely 60 solidi.

### 8

Concerning land on the seashore [Note: [Col. 0446C] Jeremiah, in his letter to Frotarius, bishop of Toul, which is the twenty-seventh among Frotarius’s letters: “It happened in our province in the present year that salt became very expensive because, owing to the rains, it could not be produced in the coastal saltworks where it used to be made.” — ID.], where salt is produced, we wish some of those concerned to come to our court and their case to be heard, so that we may then be able to decide the matter among them according to equity.

### 9

We wish the wives of deceased men, after their husbands’ deaths, to receive a third part of the improvements which they jointly made on the benefice [Note: [Col. 0446D] By this law the French king Louis XIV, after the death of Philip IV, king of Spain, seized Belgium as though by a right of devolution.]. And concerning the property which the person who held that benefice brought or acquired from elsewhere, or which was given to him by his friends, we wish it all to pass both to the orphans of the deceased and to their wives.

### 10

Concerning the embankments to be built beside the Loire: a good envoy is to be placed in charge of the work, and this is to be ordered to Pippin through our envoy [Note: [Col. 0446D] To the king of Aquitaine, the son of the Pious Emperor. — BALUZ.], so that he too may appoint an envoy for this purpose and the aforesaid work may be completed.

[Col. 0446B] 11. Concerning the twelve bridges over the Seine: we wish those inhabitants of the districts who are obliged to build them to be admonished by our envoys, so that they may restore them quickly and not consent to their vain contention when they say that they are obliged to build these same bridges nowhere except where they formerly stood; rather, they shall be ordered to build the same bridges wherever they are now necessary.

12. Concerning all bridges that must be built throughout our kingdom: let our envoys jointly admonish those who have customarily built them to restore them themselves.

# CAPITULARY OF ATIGNY (August 822)

[Col. 0445]

In August of the year 822, at Atigny, at a public assembly, the emperor Louis made a public confession before the entire people concerning the offenses he had committed against his brothers, his nephew Bernard, and Adalhard and Wala, and performed penance. Whatever similar matters he was able to discover had been done either by himself or by his father, he took care to correct with the utmost devotion [Note: [Col. 0445D] Einhard, *Annals*, p. 209.]. We now restore to the light the chapters issued concerning these matters, hitherto unpublished, from folios 105–106 of the Blankenburg manuscript of the ducal library of Wolfenbüttel.

## OTHER CHAPTERS OF THE LORD EMPEROR LOUIS

[Col. 0445D]

1. Therefore, admonished by the inspiration of almighty God and by your most devout zeal, and also stirred by your most salutary example, we confess that in many matters—more than reason or possibility now permits us to enumerate—we have been negligent both in our life and in doctrine and ecclesiastical ministries [Col. 0446D–0447A]. For this reason, just as we do not deny that until now we have been negligent in these matters, so from this time forward, with God’s help, once your kindness has granted us the appropriate ability or freedom, we profess that we wish to exercise more diligent care in all these things, according to the capacity of our understanding.

2. Since it is clearly established that the salvation of the people depends chiefly upon doctrine and preaching, and since preaching cannot be fulfilled as it ought to be except by learned men, it is necessary that such an arrangement be found in each see that will prepare both for the present correction and for the future benefit of the holy Church. How this ought and can be done will be demonstrated in the following chapter [Col. 0447B].

3. We desire to reform with the greatest diligence the schools, concerning which until now [Note: [Col. 0447] The manuscript reads *hocha hactenus*.] we have been less diligent than we ought to have been, so that every person—whether older or younger—who is being trained in order to be advanced to some ecclesiastical rank may have an appointed place and a suitable teacher. Let the parents or masters of each individual take care to provide food and bodily necessities by which they may subsist, so that they may have sufficient support and not withdraw from the study of doctrine because of lack of means [Col. 0448A]. If, however, necessity requires it because of the size of the parish, since they cannot be gathered in one place owing to the administration that their stewards must provide for them, let schools be established in two or three places, or wherever necessity and reason dictate.

4. But since instruction is in every way less useful if an opportunity for learning is not arranged for those who are to teach, it is necessary that provision be made by the lords of the property [Note: [Col. 0447] The manuscript reads *ad hominis*.] for those bishops who entirely or largely lack the ability to act in their dioceses, so that this may suitably be accomplished. Those who hold ecclesiastical property or baptismal churches by right and at their disposal are able to fulfill the office of preaching.

[Col. 0448B] 5. Concerning the powerful men who refuse to come to preaching, and for that reason keep many who imitate or follow them—people who ought to have come to hear the word of God—occupied in their own services [Note: [Col. 0447] A passage is absent from the manuscript.]. Some of these men also appoint or expel priests from churches without the bishop’s consent.

6.
