Let the Simoniac heresy be so carefully avoided that henceforth no one may confer an unstated benefit, whether because of the acceptance of gifts [Note: [Col. 0447] The manuscript reads *numerum* (“number”) for *munerum* (“gifts”).], or on account of kinship, familiarity, any kind of friendship, or service.

# CONSTITUTIONS OF THE EMPEROR LOTHAR I AT OLONNA (823)

[Col. 0447]

After the assembly at Atigny had been concluded, Lothar, having been sent to Italy with the counselors Wala and Gerungus, devoted several months to administering justice. At an assembly held at the estate of Olonna, either in the autumn of 822 or—what I consider more likely—in the spring of 823, he proposed laws that are now published complete for the first time. We have extracted them from several manuscripts, especially the Chisian, Cavense, Saint Paul’s in Carinthia, Blankenburg, Gotha, and Paris manuscripts, as well as from the edition of the Florentine fragment prepared by Charles in quarto in 1675. In publishing the general chapters, we used the Chisian and Cavense manuscripts, which alone among all the manuscripts preserve the complete text, no longer mutilated for the use of jurists. From chapter 11 onward we also used the Florentine fragment and the Blankenburg manuscript, together with the Ambrosian, Florentine, London, Vienna, Verona, and Este manuscripts as printed by Muratori, chapters 71–74.

We have published the chapters given to the counts on the authority of: 1. the Saint Paul’s manuscript and the Chisian manuscript, which most closely resembles it; 2. the Florentine fragment; 3. the Blankenburg manuscript; 4. Paris manuscript no. 4613, chapters 12 and 17; and also the Ambrosian, Florentine, London, Vienna, Verona, and Este manuscripts as printed by Muratori, chapters 1–14.

We present the third capitulary, perhaps given to the envoys, on the authority of: 1. the Blankenburg manuscript; 2. the Gotha manuscript; 3. the Modena manuscript as printed by Muratori, p. 151; and also the Ambrosian, Florentine, London, Vienna, Verona, and Este manuscripts as printed by Muratori, chapters 84–88.

The *Annals of Einhard* establish that, after completing the administration of justice and receiving the imperial crown at Saint Peter’s on Easter Day from the hands of Pope Paschal, Lothar returned to his father in June 823.

## HERE BEGIN THE CHAPTERS WHICH THE LORD EMPEROR LOTHAR, IN THE FIRST YEAR OF HIS EMPIRE, WHEN HE CAME TO ITALY, ESTABLISHED AT THE ESTATE OF HOLONNA

[Chisian manuscript: THOLONNA]

[Col. 0447C]

1. Let the elected chancellors, good and truthful men, draw up public documents before the count, his assessors, and his vicars; and let them under no circumstances presume to do this for money before the lawful price has been paid.

2. If any man commits adultery with another man’s wife, and they have been handed into his hands according to the law, and afterward are convicted, let them be received by the public authorities; and whoever has purchased them shall lose his purchase price.

3. We wish our counts to have permission to conduct investigations.

4. Concerning associations, we decree that no man shall form an association by oath or by any other obligation. If anyone presumes to do this, then the man who first began that conspiracy or who took part in this act shall be sent by the count himself into exile in Corsica, while the others shall pay the ban [Note: [Col. 0447] In the Cavense manuscript, *componant* through *componat* is lacking.]. If there is someone who has no means of paying that ban, let him receive sixty blows.

5. We wish no one to presume to come to the count’s assembly with a crowd or with shields; if anyone presumes to do so, let him pay the ban.

6 [Note: [Col. 0449] This chapter is absent from the Chisian manuscript.]. Concerning a consecrated woman, we decree that, if she commits adultery and this is discovered, the property she possesses shall be joined to the fisc; her person, however, shall be under the authority of the bishop in whose parish she is, so that she may be sent to a monastery.

7. We wish bishops, abbots, and abbesses to have their own advocates and to administer full justice before their count.

8. Concerning those men who have alienated their property anywhere and remain upon it: let the count constrain them through the public patrols (*scubia*), as the law provides [Col. 0449B].

9 [Note: [Col. 0449] This chapter is absent from the Cavense manuscript.]. Let the chancellors come to all sick people.

10. We decree that if a free man has bound himself into servitude for some reason, and has a free woman or children, they shall remain in their freedom. If that woman dies and he joins himself to another free woman who is serving, she shall remain in servitude.

11. If any free man is admonished by his count or by his officials to defend the homeland and neglects to go, and an army comes to devastate this kingdom or to oppose our faithful, let him be subject to capital judgment [Note: [Col. 0449] One witness reads *capitalem subeat sententiam* (“let him undergo a capital sentence”).]. The same is to be observed if they are summoned to hear of the arrival of our enemies [Note: [Col. 0449] Other witnesses read *audito adventu* (“after hearing of the arrival”).], and it happens that the enemy does not arrive [Note: [Col. 0449] One witness reads “if the enemy does not arrive.”]: those who have been summoned and do not wish to come shall each make amends according to his own law [Note: [Col. 0449] Other witnesses read “let him make amends according to his own law.”]. The second and third witnesses omit the word “go”; other readings have “those who have been summoned and do not wish to hear” or “those who have been summoned and do not wish to come.”

12. Since, in so short a period of time, we have labored with all our might, as far as we could, to ensure that your salvation [Note: [Col. 0449] The Cavense manuscript reads “our salvation.”] and that of this kingdom may endure in the future, we also desired to investigate how we might show ourselves generally benevolent toward you [Note: [Col. 0449] The Chisian and Cavense manuscripts read *venibolos* for *benivolos*.], together with all ecclesiastical and free persons, for their consolation and to strengthen their good will, so that they may preserve the fidelity [Col. 0449–0450A] toward us that they have always maintained [Note: [Col. 0449] *vocem inserui*—“I have inserted the word.”]. Nevertheless, we wish to grant this favor: if anyone’s slave joins himself in marriage to a free woman with her consent, and if within a year they have not been handed over for punishment [Note: [Col. 0449] This phrase is absent from the Chisian manuscript.], then, just as the law joins such persons to our fisc, so by our liberality [Note: [Col. 0449] Another witness reads “by our freedom.”] we grant that both shall return to the power and service of the master whose slave he was [Note: [Col. 0449] The Chisian manuscript inserts here the preface and chapter 2, concerning the *heribannus*, of the Lombard capitulary of 801; I have judged that these should be omitted.].

13. Similarly, we wish to grant to all free persons that no public judge or public official may dare to distrain them unlawfully through their oxen [Note: [Col. 0449] Other witnesses read “cattle.”], because we have heard that our people suffer many losses and afflictions on this account [Note: [Col. 0449] Other witnesses read “our peoples” or “our people.”]. Nor shall they be compelled to come to assemblies more than three times a year [Note: [Col. 0449] The Chisian manuscript reads *praeteriter*; the Cavense manuscript reads *praeter*; another witness reads “apart from a period of three days.”], as is contained in the capitulary, except for assessors, litigants, and necessary witnesses. For we wish to remove every hardship [Note: [Col. 0449] The phrase “I have received the reading” is editorial.] so that our people may live peacefully under our rule.

To those who have commended themselves to us, or who shall commend themselves in the future, we wish specially to grant this privilege of honor [Note: [Col. 0449] The Cavense manuscript reads *onori* (“to honor”); the Chisian manuscript reads *privilegio* (“by privilege”).] above other free persons: wherever they come, whether to an assembly or anywhere else [Note: [Col. 0449] The Cavense manuscript reads “whether at an assembly or in any place”; another reads “whether at an assembly or anywhere, let them be held worthy of honor.”], let them be regarded as worthy of every honor and be given precedence over others. Whatever claim they may have, let them be permitted to receive their justice without any delay [Note: [Col. 0449] Another witness reads “their justices.”].

As for their free men who have been or shall be commended to them, if the lord keeps them with him in service [Note: [Col. 0449] The Chisian and Cavense manuscripts omit “in service.”], they shall not be distrained or pledged on account of the administration of justice until they have returned from our service [Col. 0450C]. Then, if anything is claimed from them, their lords shall first be admonished [Note: [Col. 0449] The Chisian and Cavense manuscripts omit this phrase.] to render justice to those making the claim; and if they refuse to do so, they shall then be legally distrained [Note: [Col. 0449] Another witness reads “let them be distrained.”].

14. We also grant to our *castaldi* [Note: [Col. 0449] Other witnesses read *gastaldi*, “gastaldi.”], who oversee our estates, that if they purchase property with their own money [Note: [Col. 0449] The Chisian manuscript reads “with their property”; another witness reads “if they purchase property with their own money.”], or acquire it through any lawful transaction [Note: [Col. 0449] The Cavense manuscript reads “through a lawful and considered transaction.”], just as the law grants such property to our side, so we grant it to them, provided that they are found faithful in our service.

[Col. 0451A] ## Record of what the lord emperor ordered his counts

[Note: [Col. 0451] Manuscript 1 reads: “Here begin the chapters: how the lord emperor ordered his counts.” The Chisian manuscript has: “Here begin the chapters which the lord Emperor Lothar, in the first year of his empire, when he came into Italy, established at his general assembly at the estate of Olonna.” The Ambrosian manuscript reads: “Chapters which the lord Emperor Lothar established in the year of his empire in which he came into Italy, at the general assembly at the estate of Olonna.” The Vienna and Verona manuscripts read: “Reader, you will now see the writings of King Lothar.” The Vienna manuscript has the gloss: “Chapters composed at Olonna, and therefore they seem to be Lombard only.”]

1. First he decreed that, if a free man binds himself into servitude for some reason, and has a free woman or children, they shall remain in their freedom. If that woman dies and he joins himself to another free woman who is serving [Note: [Col. 0451] Other witnesses read “for the purpose of serving” or “a serving woman.”], she shall remain in servitude.

2 [Note: [Col. 0451] Chapters 2–8 are absent from the Chisian manuscript.]. If any man commits adultery with another man’s wife, and they have been handed into the hands [Note: [Col. 0451B] That is, into the hands of the adulteress’s husband.] according to the law, and afterward they are found together [Note: [Col. 0451] Other witnesses read “convicted” or “found guilty”], let them be delivered to the public authorities; and whoever has purchased them shall lose his purchase price [Note: [Col. 0451] One witness reads “whoever has purchased them shall lose his price.”].

3. We wish our counts to have permission to conduct investigations [Note: [Col. 0451] One witness adds: “to investigate the vicars and centenarii, who very often hold assemblies more because of greed than to administer justice and thereby oppress the people excessively. Let this be observed as it is contained in the capitulary of the lord Charles: no one shall be summoned to an assembly except someone who is pursuing his own case, or if another person must pursue it for him, except for the seven assessors who must attend every assembly.” The editors add: “to investigate that adulterous union.”].

[Col. 0451B] 4. Concerning associations, we decree that no man shall form an association by oath or by any other obligation. If anyone presumes to do this, then the one among them who first began that conspiracy or who took part in this act shall be sent by the count himself into exile in Corsica [Note: [Col. 0451] This clause is absent from witness 3.]; and the others shall pay the ban [Note: [Col. 0451] The ban is “our ban,” that is, sixty solidi. The Vienna, Verona, and Este witnesses add: “Unless the association was made or left uncorrected through the count’s negligence, and the author of the act is endowed with some rank”; they then continue, “And if such a person …”]. If there is someone who has no means of paying that ban, let him receive sixty blows [Note: [Col. 0451] One witness reads forty blows.].

5. We wish no one to presume to come to the count’s assembly with a crowd or with shields; if anyone presumes to do so, let him pay the ban [Note: [Col. 0451] Another witness reads “our ban.”].

6. Concerning consecrated women, we decree that if they commit adultery and this is discovered [Note: [Col. 0451] Other witnesses read “and if they are found”], the property they possess shall be joined to the fisc [Note: [Col. 0451] Another witness reads “to our fisc.”]; their person, however, shall be under the authority of the bishop in whose parish she is, and he shall place her in a monastery [Note: [Col. 0451] Other witnesses read “he shall send her to a monastery” or “she shall be admitted into a monastery.”].

7. We wish bishops, abbots, and abbesses [Note: [Col. 0451] One witness reads “abbesses” in a different form.] to have their own advocates and to administer justice fully [Note: [Col. 0451] Other witnesses read “full justice.”] before their count [Note: [Col. 0451] One witness reads “before the count.”].

8. Concerning men who alienate their property anywhere and remain upon it [Note: [Col. 0451] Other witnesses read “and remain upon those properties”], let the count constrain them through the public patrol [*scubia*], as the law provides [Note: [Col. 0451] Other witnesses read “through the public patrols” or “through the public watches (*excubiae*),” adding that they must observe the three general assemblies.].

9. We wish the bishop, together with his count [Note: [Col. 0451] One witness reads “his counts”], to choose an advocate.

10. It has pleased us that no burden be imposed upon free men [Note: [Col. 0451] One witness reads “free men”; the Chisian manuscript has: “It has pleased us concerning all free men that nothing be imposed upon them except…”], except as the law and justice provide [Note: [Col. 0451] Other witnesses specify: “that they make roads and bridges.”].

11. We wish the public patrol, which pertains to the benefit of our kingdom, not to offer an impediment to the commands of the immunities [Note: [Col. 0451] One witness reads “the command of the immunities”; the phrase concerns the protection granted by immunity charters.] but assistance [Col. 0452B].

12 [Note: [Col. 0451] Chapter 12 is absent from the Chisian manuscript.]. Let the elected chancellors, good and truthful men, draw up public charters before the count, his assessors, and his vicars; and under no circumstances let them presume to do this for money before the lawful price has been paid [Note: [Col. 0451] Other witnesses read “before the lawful price is given”; another reads “before the lawful price is added.”].

13 [Note: [Col. 0451] Chapters 13 and 14 are absent from manuscripts 2, A, Florentine, London, Vienna, Verona, and Este.]. Let the count be permitted to have excused persons, as the law of the Lombards provides [Note: [Col. 0451] One witness spells “Lombard” differently.].

14. We wish men to have the same custom as formerly existed among the Lombards [Note: [Col. 0451] One witness reads “the ancient Lombard custom.”] [Note: [Col. 0451] Another witness specifies: “concerning baptismal churches, regular monasteries of both men and women, and also hospitals and fines.”].

[Note: [Col. 0451] The following manuscript versions are printed in parallel in Migne.]

### Codex Sancti Pauli

15. [Note: [Col. 0451] This chapter is absent from witnesses 2, 3, and the others; in its place they contain other material, which we have printed alongside it.] Concerning the ninths and tenths: provision must be made for them to be paid from the fruits of the earth and the nourishment of animals.

Concerning the construction or restoration of churches, let the count and bishop, or the abbot, together with our envoy whom they themselves choose for this purpose, make an assessment, so that each of them may receive for construction and restoration only as much as he is known to possess from ecclesiastical property. Likewise, let our vassals jointly receive only as much work as they possess ecclesiastical property, or let each receive work individually according to the amount that he holds [Note: [Col. 0453] One witness reads “that they hold.”].

If they agree among themselves to give silver in place of the work, let them pay in silver according to the estimated value of the work. With this payment, the rector of the church may hire workers for the aforesaid restoration and purchase materials. Whoever neglects to pay the ninths and tenths shall first restore them with the legally prescribed penalty and shall moreover pay our ban, so that, chastised in this way, he may take care not to lose his benefices by repeating the offense.

### Codex Chisianus

16. Let no one presume to conduct his commerce at sea except at lawful ports, according to ancient custom [Col. 0453] [Note: [Col. 0453] The Chisian manuscript reads “according to ancient custom,” with the initial part of *more* absent.], for the sake of the justice of the lord emperor and of ourselves. If anyone acts otherwise, let him lose all his merchandise.

### Manuscripts 2, 3, 4, A, Florentine, Vienna, Verona, and Este

17. Let the chancellors who have been elected as truthful men come to sick persons and draw up documents according to the law [Col. 0454] [Note: [Col. 0453] The words “of charters” are absent from witnesses 3 and 4.]. Let these documents be confirmed by witnesses. As soon as the written charter has been completed [Note: [Col. 0453] Other witnesses place “the charter” before “has been completed.”], let it be shown before the bishop, the count, and the judges or vicars [Note: [Col. 0453] One witness reads “or the judge”; another “the bishop, count, judges, or vicars.”], or before the people [Note: [Col. 0453] Another witness reads “or the common people”], so that it may be recognized as genuine [Note: [Col. 0453] Witnesses vary between “may be recognized as genuine” and “may recognize it as genuine.”].

18. [Note: [Col. 0453] This chapter is not found in manuscript 4.] Let a Roman woman who has had a Lombard husband, once he has died, be released from her husband’s law and return to her own law [Note: [Col. 0453] Witnesses 2, Vienna, Verona, and Este have “Roman women” in the plural.]. In decreeing this, we also provide that the same arrangement shall be observed for women of other nations [Note: [Col. 0453] The words “and this” are absent from the Vienna and Verona manuscripts.].

# THIRD CAPITULARY

[Note: [Col. 0453] The manuscripts give the following titles: “Here begin the chapters which the lord Emperor Lothar established at Olonna in his time” (1); “Chapters established at Olonna in the first year of the empire of the most glorious lord Emperor Lothar” (2, 3).]

[Col. 0453A]

1. If any bishop, whether out of affection for a relative, desire for a gift, or friendship [Note: [Col. 0453] Manuscript 2 has “friendship and hospitals.”], gives hospitals, monasteries, baptismal churches, or churches belonging to anyone through a contract of *emphyteusis* [Note: [Col. 0453] Manuscript 1 has a corrupt form of *emphyteusis*, the long-term hereditary lease of property.], and has written that he and his successors are to be punished by a penalty, we grant the rectors of the churches authority to alter such arrangements without paying the stipulated penalty [Note: [Col. 0453] Manuscript 1 reads “to impose a penalty”; manuscript 2 has a corrected form corresponding to “to be punished.”].

2 [Note: [Col. 0453] Manuscripts 2 and 3 title this “Concerning a church built on private property.”]. It has been decreed that if any free man, with the consent of his bishop, builds a church on his own property and the fonts in it are consecrated by the bishop [Note: [Col. 0453] Manuscript 1 has the corrupt form “consecrate”], he shall not thereby lose his inheritance. But if the bishop wishes, the ministry of holy baptism may be transferred to his church [Note: [Col. 0453] Manuscript 2 reads “let him transfer it to his church.”]; the water itself that is transferred [Col. 0453B] shall remain under the builder’s legal ownership [Note: [Col. 0453] This clause is absent from manuscript 2.].

3 [Note: [Col. 0453] Manuscripts 2 and 3 title this “Concerning adulterers.”]. If an adulterer has been apprehended with an adulteress [Note: [Col. 0453] This phrase is absent from manuscript 2], and according to the edicts of the Lombard law both have been handed over to the adulteress’s husband for punishment [Note: [Col. 0453] Manuscript 2 has the singular “edict”], and if anyone purchases them and they are found to have been kept together in the same crime [Note: [Col. 0453] Manuscript 1 reads “found to have them convicted …”], the fisc shall acquire them.

4 [Note: [Col. 0453] Manuscripts 2 and 3 title this “Concerning a free man who falls into servitude.”]. If a free man who has a free wife subjects himself to another’s service because of some crime or debt [Note: [Col. 0453] Other witnesses read “because of a debt or for certain reasons.”], and that wife wishes to remain with him, the children born from such a marriage shall not lose their status of freedom [Note: [Col. 0453] Other witnesses read “born from such a marriage.”]. But if she dies and a second wife, who is nevertheless free, knowingly joins herself to such a marriage, their children shall be subjected to servitude.

5 [Note: [Col. 0453] Manuscripts 2 and 3 title this “Concerning changed clothing.”]. We decree that if a woman wearing a changed garment is discovered to be an adulteress, she shall not be handed over to her kin (*genitio*, a corrupt or uncertain reading) [Col. 0454A] as has been done until now, lest she perhaps find an opportunity to commit adultery first with one man and afterward with several. Rather, her property shall be reduced to the fisc, and she herself shall be subject to episcopal judgment.

6 [Note: [Col. 0453] Manuscripts 2 and 3 title this “Concerning witnesses.”]. We decree [Note: [Col. 0453] Manuscript 2 reads “We have decreed”] that if anyone cannot otherwise obtain witnesses, then, at the count’s command, those whom each person considers necessary for his testimony shall be brought to a public assembly to state the truth, so that through them the truth of the matter may be investigated under oath.

### The Blankenburg manuscript continues as follows:

7. The abbots who have been chosen by the bishops to inspect observance of the rule in monasteries must follow this procedure in the matters entrusted to them.

8. First, since they cannot immediately [Note: [Col. 0453] The manuscript reads *subdito* for *subito*.] and within a short time fully learn the conduct of the brothers in the monastery to which they have come unless they live with them for some days and nights, they should come to them with so few companions that they do not burden the monastery. Then, if they learn that the abbot is negligently carrying out his ministry, they should admonish him concerning himself or his brothers in accordance with the authority of the rule. They should do the same if any of the brothers are found to be negligent, admonishing them together with their abbot according to the authority of the rule.

If the fault is due to ignorance, they should correct them by teaching them through the same rule. But if they offend deliberately and amend their conduct after the admonition, all is well. If they refuse, they should first report the matter to the bishop of the place; and if further necessity arises, they should report it to the synodal assembly.

If some question arises concerning a chapter of the rule and they cannot settle it among themselves, they should report it to the synod. There, by the authority of the bishops, the more sacred meaning should be determined [Col. 0455A]. The person who has been sent should presume to do nothing by force. If customs are found to be harmful [Note: [Col. 0455] One witness reads “unless found”], they should report this as stated above [Col. 0456A].

# CAPITULARY GIVEN TO THE BISHOPS

[Col. 0455]

We have checked these chapters, which Baluzius published from manuscript no. 733 of the monastery of Saint Gall, ninth century, against that same manuscript. As is evident from chapters 6 and 8, they were given to bishops returning to their dioceses. They do not appear to have been promulgated, as Baluzius thought, in 819, but after the assembly at Atigny, from which Lothar reckons the beginning of his reign; therefore they seem to belong to 823 or one of the following years.

[Col. 0455A] 1. Concerning the condition of the Church and the honor of bishops: they ought to live and conduct themselves canonically according to the command of our lords [Note: [Col. 0455C] Louis and Lothar.] [Note: [Col. 0455C] The manuscript reads *conservare* (“to preserve”), as in Saint Gregory, book VII, indiction 2, letter 110, where *conservatione* occurs instead of *conversatione* in the old Orléans manuscript. The same error appears in Salvian, book VI, p. 146, in the editions of Brassicanus and Pithoeus, where one reads “for the joys of a new preservation” instead of “for the joys of a new conduct,” as the Roman and Nuremberg editions have it, or “conversion,” as in the Corbie manuscript. In the Fourth Council of Toledo, chapter 75, we find “by the preservation of royal safety,” for which an old book of the Church of Lyon has “by the conduct of royal safety.” Likewise, in book I of the Capitularies, chapter 35, most old copies read *conservationis*, whereas *conversationis* should be read. BALUZIUS.] [Note: [Col. 0455] One manuscript reads *conservare* (“to preserve”).].

2. Let priests and clerics live according to the rule of the earlier fathers.

[Col. 0455B] 3. Let both monks and nuns, wherever they may be, lead their lives according to the rule.

4. Concerning the restoration of churches, their lights, services, and Masses, as well as their roofs and repairs [Note: [Col. 0455] I have corrected the text in this way; the manuscript reads *sacritecta*.]: insofar as it is possible, let restorations and repairs be carried out, by command of our lords, wherever necessity requires.

5. Concerning the churches, monasteries, and hospitals that belong, or ought to belong, to the protection of the palace: let everyone acknowledge and consent to the justice and rightful authority of our lords the kings.

6. Concerning unlawful cases, all illicit unions, and every other detestable matter: let everyone in his parish, together with the consent and assistance of his count, strive to cut these off and correct them completely and promptly [Col. 0455C]. Whoever is unable to do this shall report it without delay to the ears of our most pious lord or to his nobles [Note: [Col. 0455] Baluzius already judged that this should be read thus; the manuscript has *posteribus*], so that the evil that has been perpetrated may be corrected canonically.

[Col. 0456A] 7. Concerning widows, orphans, the poor, and all those without power: let them receive their justice fully through the alms of our lords the kings.

8. Concerning homicides, perjuries, sacrileges, false testimonies, and whatever appears to be detestable or contrary to the sacred canons [Col. 0456B]: let these matters be fully corrected through your admonition and through the count’s judgment. Whoever refuses to do this shall disclose it without delay to the ears of our most excellent lord or to his nobles [Note: [Col. 0455] Baluzius already judged that this should be read thus; the manuscript has *posteribus*.].

9. Concerning tithes: let everyone offer his tithe to the church, as is recognized to be the custom or sacred practice.

10. Let those elected men who hold episcopal sees that can canonically be held be consecrated without delay.

We wish that everyone may undertake a good struggle concerning the matters reported above, and that other matters which we have not inserted in this capitulary but which must be addressed may be corrected through your most holy admonition. Whoever neglects to do this, if he is a priest or cleric, should know that he will be subject to canonical judgment [Note: [Col. 0455] The manuscript reads *servitium* (“service”).]; if he is a layman [Note: [Col. 0455] The manuscript reads *ladicus*], he will be subject to the judgment of our lords and their nobles.

*End.*

# REPORT OF THE BISHOPS TO THE EMPEROR LOUIS (824)

[Col. 0455]

We publish this from folios 104–105 of the Blankenburg manuscript of the ducal library of Wolfenbüttel. Since it was certainly issued after the death of Benedict, abbot of Aniane, on 11 February 821, we have assigned it chiefly to the year 824, when the emperor, concerned about the famine and other disasters afflicting the Frankish kingdom, resolved to investigate the condition of the empire.

# OTHER CHAPTERS OF THE LORD EMPEROR LOUIS

[Col. 0455D]

The wisdom of incomparable imperial glory [Note: [Col. 0455] The manuscript reads *In parabolis* (“In parables”) in place of *Incomparabilis*.], supported by heavenly reasoning, dispensing to its subjects the discipline of government as a due prerogative, presents the following chapters, grasped through salutary simplicity rather than through the difficulty of syllogisms [Col. 0456D].

## Source apparatus restoration

All printed witness readings, omissions, corrections, forms, sigla, and intervening column anchors in this supplied section are retained as source apparatus; where English cannot represent the distinction, the paired Latin forms are retained with concise glosses. The chapter order and parallel-manuscript notices follow the source.

[Col. 0457A] The order in which a bishop should be found. 1 [Note: [Col. 0457] The preceding codex has the number I; this one and the others have II, and only at chapter eight does it retain the numbering.]. The faith of the Holy Trinity is venerated by three orders altogether. Although reason declares that, once the canonical foundation of the Church’s faith has been established and a man chosen by the faithful men of the place, he should be advanced, necessity nevertheless admits even a monk, and authority does not exclude a layman. But when it is added what sort of man he must be, so many canonical and apostolic commands apply to this statement that what has been briefly indicated scarcely seems sufficient. Whether monogamous or a virgin, the Church requires a priest who is without reproach. Yet finally, if he speaks of what is permitted, let him make himself worthy of imitation in everything he does, so that he does not cease to water the hearts of his neighbors with the dew of doctrine, nor contradict by good works what he has taught.

[Col. 0457B] 2. We demonstrate, through the excellence of the word and the proper administration of affairs, in the sequence of sacred reading, that the office of a bishop consists in the care and zeal of ecclesiastical matters and in the strengthening of the faith. But his conduct then corresponds to his office when, because of the innocence of his life, he is foremost in action and, above all, elevated in contemplation.

3. Concerning the regulated conduct of clerics in the episcopate, what else is there to say except that they should live canonically? If they desire to be called, in accordance with the Apostle’s words, sons who are properly obedient [Note: [Col. 0457] “is one who,” codex I.], then, although they ought to be distinguished by varied forms of worship, they should strive to avoid usury and association with women.

4. Concerning the arrangement and office of priests, what their outward life should be is demonstrated by the bishop, who goes before them. These men, ordained for the oversight of the Church, should be seen to remain faithful to their calling when, with ready devotion, they habitually imitate, according to their ability, the footsteps of the energetic shepherd.

5. Concerning the administration of the bishopric’s property, let the statutes of our earlier fathers and of Roman law, properly preserved, suffice for us. Finally, they decreed that the revenues and patrimonies should be divided fourfold, partly to be distributed to the poor and partly assigned to the needs of the prelates and of the churches. Accordingly, let priests be chosen as guardians for the baptismal churches, in whom not only the name of the office but also the fitting practice of holiness may shine forth. Let the titular churches themselves, together with their rectors, who are equally set over them, be content with the order of subjection and humbly venerate the heights of the more exalted.

6. How the order of the hospices should be maintained is declared by the wills issued by their founders. For if, being clouded by errors of frivolity or perhaps simplicity, they lack a reasonable arrangement, let them await the judgment of a Catholic administrator.

[Col. 0458A] 7. Concerning the order of canons in their own places: the little florilegia excerpted from the decrees of the most glorious Caesar by their authors or from the ancient laws of the Church, compiled into one Codex and received by us, adorn their life by ordering it with most sweet grace.

8. Concerning regular monasteries, those which the rule of the blessed Benedict, of revered memory, gathered together and devoted to distinguished service in monastic meditation—let these suffice as having been uttered by the Holy Spirit.

9. Since it is plainly established that a congregation of monks cannot exist without an abbot of the same order, a modest and prudent man must be chosen from among them, with the consent of the bishop of the city, whose suffragans they are to recognize themselves as being. He must have already learned to live according to the rule, to devote himself zealously to the holy discipline as the regular order requires, and to be capable of correcting the faults of his subjects, if there are any.

[Col. 0458B] 10. As to how an abbot ought to conduct himself with his monks, instructed by the abundant testimonies of the same rule, let him pursue the exercises of virtue along the straight path by which he is led.

11. By whom and how an abbot who acts negligently ought to be corrected, the Council of Chalcedon, title 8, clearly explains, since it does not hesitate to exclude him from communion at the instance of the bishop of the place.

12. Concerning monasteries of women established in the canonical or regular order, the etymology of their very names demonstrates under which order they ought to be reckoned: canonical monasteries are instructed by canonical forms, and regular monasteries by regular forms.

13. Concerning this canonical institution, which is appropriate for religious women, we long ago learned of the instruments of august majesty. But some have already demonstrated by experience how the discipline of ecclesiastical office, excessively neglected, might be restored through effort: they assigned a school to teachers. Those who are slower in this undertaking, as though the dispensation of their offense had been postponed, should be held liable unless they correct themselves.

14. For the condition of the kingdom and of the commonwealth, lest it be humbled or weakened, divine mercy must first be entreated. Then, applying ourselves with all our strength, let us willingly determine with you such timely assistance as our ability permits.

[Col. 0458D] 15. Concerning how the regular order should be observed, we remember that we have indicated part of it above; after consulting further with your Highness, we shall strive to establish the remaining matters more fully.

# Roman Constitution of Lothar I (824, November)

[Col. 0457]

Lothar’s second journey into Italy, undertaken at the end of August 824, was undertaken chiefly with the purpose that, acting in his father’s place, he might establish and confirm Roman affairs with the new pope, Eugenius, and the Roman people. It succeeded according to his wishes. For Lothar, according to Einhard’s testimony, corrected the condition of the Roman people, which had long been corrupted by the perversity of certain prelates, with the benevolent assent of Eugenius, so that all who had been grievously desolated by the seizure of their property were magnificently consoled by the restoration of their goods, which had come about, by God’s favor, through his arrival. Here we present the constitution issued on this matter, revised according to the evidence chiefly of the Chisian, Cavensian, and Blankenburg codices, and also of the Ambrosian, Florentine, London, Viennese, Veronese, and Este codices, as recognized by Muratori, chapters 34–41. After examining Vatican Codex no. 3833, I readily understood that the edition derived from it and published by Chesnius, Baluze, and Bouquet possesses no authority. Cardinal Deusdedit, whose collection is read there toward the end of the first book, folio 49, clearly intended to provide only excerpts, as is already apparent from the title: “From the constitutions of the emperor Lothar, enacted under Pope Eugenius II in the atrium of blessed Peter the Apostle.” We append the formula of the oath rendered on that occasion by the Roman people, published by Chesnius, vol. II, p. 207.

# Chapters that the lord emperor Lothar established at the threshold of blessed Peter the Apostle, near the city of Rome, in the time of Eugenius, supreme pontiff [Note: [Col. 0459] “At the threshold of blessed Peter,” near the city of Rome, at the time of Pope Eugenius, the lord emperor’s chapters; Chisian. “At the threshold of blessed Peter the Apostle,” Cavensian.] [Note: [Col. 0459] “Near the city of Rome,” the lord emperor’s, at the time of Eugenius, supreme pontiff, Florentine and London codices.] [Note: [Col. 0459] The entire heading is absent from the Ambrosian, Vatican, and Viennese codices. In the Vatican and Viennese codices there is a gloss: “Chapters which the lord Lothar established near the city of Rome,” Vatican. “Concerning the pontiffs: these chapters of Lothar III,” that is, in the third year, Viennese. “Chapters made by Lothar near the city of Rome,” Este.]

[Col. 0459A]

1. We have established that all who have been received under the special protection of the lord apostolic or of us shall inviolably enjoy the just protection they have obtained. If anyone should presume to violate this in any way [Note: [Col. 0459] “in whatever manner,” Blankenburg.], let him know that he will incur danger to his life [Note: [Col. 0459] “Let him know that he is himself to be exposed to danger of his life,” Blankenburg.]. We also decree that they themselves shall observe proper obedience in all things to the lord apostolic [Note: [Col. 0459] “They shall observe his,” one witness.] and to his dukes and judges, for the administration of justice [Note: [Col. 0459] The following words are absent from Blankenburg and the printed editions.]. In this chapter let mention be made of the widows and orphans of Theodore [Note: [Col. 0459] “Theodorus,” Cavensian, Ambrosian, Vatican, Viennese, Este.], Floronus [Note: [Col. 0459] “Florinus,” Cavensian and Viennese.], and Sergius.

2. We prohibit the plundering that has hitherto customarily taken place from occurring, whether while the pontiff is alive or after his death. If anyone does this thereafter, let him know that he is to be condemned by legal judgment. As for what has been done in the past, we wish it to be legally corrected through our arrangement [Note: [Col. 0459] Absent from the Chisian.].

3. We wish no one to presume to interfere in the election of the pontiff—neither free person nor slave—who might cause any impediment to those Romans alone [Note: [Col. 0459] “Let him cause an impediment. Only those Roman [men],” Blankenburg.], to whom the custom was formerly granted [Note: [Col. 0459] “Let them not cease by,” Blankenburg.] by the constitution of the holy fathers to elect the pontiff [Note: [Col. 0459] “That they have the authority to elect the pontiff,” Vatican, Viennese, Este.]. If anyone presumes to act against this command of ours, let him be sent into exile.

4. We wish envoys to be appointed on behalf of the lord apostolic and on our behalf, who may report to us annually how each of the dukes and judges administers justice to the people [Note: [Col. 0459] “Among the people,” Cavensian.] and how they observe our constitution [Note: [Col. 0459] Absent from the Chisian, Cavensian, Vatican, Viennese, and Este codices.]. We decree that these envoys [Note: [Col. 0459] “To these envoys,” Blankenburg.] should first bring to the notice of the lord apostolic all the complaints that have been found to arise through the negligence of the dukes or judges [Note: [Col. 0459] Absent from the Chisian and Cavensian.], and that he should choose one of two courses: either those grievances should immediately be corrected by the same envoys, or, if not, the matter should be made known to us through our envoy, so that they may again be corrected by our envoys sent by us [Note: [Col. 0459] “So that it may be corrected,” Chisian.].

5. We wish the entire Roman people to be questioned [Col. 0460A] under which law they wish to live [Note: [Col. 0459] Absent from Blankenburg; “what law,” Cavensian; corrected to “what law,” Ambrosian; “under which law,” Vatican, Viennese, Este.], so that they may live according to the law which they profess that they wish to follow [Note: [Col. 0459] “According to which,” Ambrosian; “which,” Vatican, Viennese, Este.]. Let it also be announced to them, so that each person may know—dukes as well as judges and the rest of the people [Note: [Col. 0459] Absent from Ambrosian.]—that if, to their own offense, they act against that same law [Note: [Col. 0459] “If he acts,” Chisian, Ambrosian, Vatican, Viennese.], they will be subject to the same law which they profess, through the arrangement of the pontiff and of us [Note: [Col. 0459] “He will be subject,” Vatican, Viennese, Este.].

6. Concerning the property of churches unjustly seized under the pretext of having received permission from the pontiff, and concerning what has not yet been returned but was nevertheless unjustly seized by the power of the pontiffs, we wish it to be corrected through our envoys [Note: [Col. 0459] “Let it be corrected,” Blankenburg.].

7. We prohibit plundering from occurring any longer between our borders [Note: [Col. 0459] “Thus,” Blankenburg, Chisian, Cavensian; that is, “within the frontier.” In the Vatican codex the entire chapter is absent from the other witnesses.] [Note: [Col. 0459] Absent from Blankenburg and Cavensian.], and concerning what has occurred, we order that it be corrected according to the law on both sides. [Col. 0460B] Likewise, we wish the other injustices on both sides to be corrected [Note: [Col. 0459] “Justices,” Chisian.].

8. It has pleased us that all the judges, or those who ought to preside over all matters through whom judicial authority must be exercised in this Roman city [Note: [Col. 0459] “Judicial,” Chisian and Cavensian.], should come into our presence. We wish to know their number and names [Note: [Col. 0459] Absent from the Chisian, Cavensian, Vatican, Viennese, and Este codices.] and to give each of them an admonition concerning the office entrusted to him [Note: [Col. 0459] “To give them an admonition concerning the office entrusted to them,” Chisian and Cavensian.].

9. Finally, let every person be admonished that, just as he desires to have the grace of God and our favor, so he should offer obedience and reverence in all things to this pontiff.

# Oath of the Romans

I, so-and-so, promise by Almighty God, by these four holy Gospels, by this cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, and by the body of the most blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, that from this day forward I shall be faithful to our lords, the emperors Louis and Lothar, all the days of my life, according to my ability and understanding, without fraud or evil intent, while preserving the faith which I pledged to the lord apostolic [Note: [Col. 0459] “Lord … lords … lord,” Chisian.]. And I promise that I shall not consent that the election of a pontiff be conducted otherwise in this Roman see than canonically and justly, according to my ability and understanding. And the man who has been elected shall not, with my consent, be consecrated pontiff before he has taken an oath of this kind, in the presence of the envoy [Col. 0461A] of the lord emperor and of the people, with an oath such as Pope Eugenius has voluntarily made in writing for the preservation of all things [Col. 0462A].

# Constitutions of Lothar at Maringo (825, February 20) [printed: “525”]

[Col. 0461]

The constitutions promulgated at the royal estates of Maringo and Olonna in February and May of the year 825 belong to Lothar’s second journey. We make public the chapters issued at the estate of Maringo from the Chisian and Cavensian codices, where they occur after the laws of Louis I, following the Capitulary of the year 816, with only the heading “Likewise, other chapters.” From Einhard’s Annals we learn that in the summer of the preceding year, 824, the famine was still extremely severe. The Ambrosian codex, among the laws of Louis, presents chapter 1; among Lothar’s, chapter 4. The Florentine, London, Viennese, Veronese, and, as may be conjectured, Este codices present only chapter 1 among Louis’s laws (Muratori, chapter 5).

The chapters concerning the Corsican expedition have been preserved among Lothar’s laws only in the Chisian and Cavensian codices.

[Col. 0461B] 1 [Note: [Col. 0461] Compare the Lombard Capitulary of the year 806, promulgated after the time of famine.]. First of all, it pleased us that the written instruments of obligation made concerning individual persons who have handed themselves, their wives [Note: [Col. 0461] “Themselves and their wives and children,” Ambrosian.], sons, or daughters into servitude should be broken wherever they are found, and that those persons should be free, just as they were originally.

2. Whoever claims that he sold property for less than a just price, let both parties come together concerning the property he sold, together with appraisers; let them recall and value that property as it was worth at the time when the property had been fully restored, before we entered here with the army. If the property has then been appraised at a just price, as the instrument itself records—that he sold the property at its legitimate price, according to what it was worth at that time—let the sale remain valid. But if the appraisers judge that his property was worth more at that time than the price he received, and if the seller can show that he made the sale because of the necessity of famine, or if the instrument itself reveals that it was made during a time of famine, let the instrument be broken. Let him return the price according to what the instrument records, and let him receive his property back as he now finds it. [Anteposito, uncertain.] As for buildings or improvements made there afterward, let the person who made them remove them, or let them act as they have agreed among themselves [Note: [Col. 0461] Absent from the Chisian.]. In this matter of the sale, let the person who sold it, or his son, bring the action; no other relative [Note: [Col. 0461] Absent from the Chisian.].

3. Concerning an instrument that records a gift [Note: [Col. 0461] “Which,” Chisian.], we likewise wish the property to be appraised, if the property was worth more when it had been restored than the *launegild* [Note: [Col. 0461] “Launigild,” Cavensian.] which he had received, and if he made the gift under pressure and the necessity of famine. If he can prove this, let him return the *launegild* [Note: [Col. 0461] “Naudegild,” Chisian.] and receive his property back, and let the instrument itself be broken.

4. Concerning gifts or sales [Note: [Col. 0461] “Vindication,” Ambrosian.] made to holy places, we ordered that they be suspended until we have settled in a synod with the bishops and counts how they ought to be handled [Note: [Col. 0461] “A synod,” Ambrosian.]. We also order that a just judgment proceed for those parties where we or our host [Note: [Col. 0461] “Our hosts,” in a form “as above,” Ambrosian.] may be, concerning what has been written above. We further establish that those instruments which were made in the time of Desiderius [Note: [Col. 0461] “In the time of famine,” Cavensian.] under the compulsion of famine [Note: [Col. 0461] “Made,” Chisian, Cavensian.] or by any sort of device [Note: [Col. 0461] “Had been made,” Ambrosian.], should not be counted in this matter; rather, judgment concerning them should proceed according to their own law. And [Note: [Col. 0461] The words “And … law” are placed before this chapter in the Ambrosian codex as a separate chapter and are absent here.] we issue this order: whoever, from this present day, the twentieth of the month of February, wishes to sell [Note: [Col. 0461] Absent from the Chisian.] or alienate his property [Note: [Col. 0461] “To sell,” Ambrosian; “to alienate” is absent from the Chisian.], let it be entirely within his power, provided that he does so according to his law [Note: [Col. 0461] “If he is their judge,” Ambrosian.]. Therefore, since this pleased us [Note: [Col. 0461] “It pleased,” Chisian.], we ordered this notice of our present deliberation to be made for cutting off disputes [Note: [Col. 0461] “A notice of the present deliberation, for cutting off disputes, to be made,” Ambrosian.], and we had it read back to us [Note: [Col. 0461] “Had it read,” Chisian; “had it reread,” Ambrosian.]. We wish judgment to proceed accordingly [Note: [Col. 0461] “As the preceding judgment, if made,” Ambrosian.]. Notice made in the third year of our lords [Note: [Col. 0461] This phrase has been taken from the Ambrosian codex; it is absent from the Chisian and Cavensian.].

# Edict concerning the Corsican expedition (825, February 20)

[Col. 0461]

## In the name of the Lord

[Col. 0461D]

Here begin the chapters which the lord emperor Lothar established in the sixth year of his reign, in the third indiction, at the estate of Maringo [Note: [Col. 0461] Absent from the Chisian.] [Note: [Col. 0461] The Cavensian codex, led by some error, gives the heading of the capitulary concerning the threshold of Saint Peter here for the first time, and gives the other heading in its proper place.].

1. We wish each count to be held to this obligation among those who enter Corsica with him [Note: [Col. 0461] “Who entered,” Cavensian.] or who ought to remain there [Note: [Col. 0461] “Who ought to remain,” Cavensian.].

2. We wish the dominical vassals [Note: [Col. 0461] “Bassals,” Cavensian.] who are *austaldi* [Note: [Col. 0461] “Castaldi,” Cavensian.] and frequently serve in our court to leave behind the men whom they previously had [Note: [Col. 0461] “Whom they had before,” Cavensian.], who on this account have commended themselves to them [Note: [Col. 0463] “Who have commended themselves,” Chisian.], together with their lords [Note: [Col. 0463] “Let them remain with their lords. We wish to know,” Cavensian.]. As for those who remain in their own property, we wish to know who they are, and we also wish to consider who should go and who should remain. Those who hold our benefices but remain outside, we wish to go.

3. As for the men of bishops or abbots who remain outside, we wish them to go with their counts, except for two whom the count himself shall choose [Note: [Col. 0463] “Two dukes,” Cavensian.]. As for their free *austaldi* [Note: [Col. 0463] “Free castaldi,” Cavensian.], except for four, we wish them to be fully dispatched [Note: [Col. 0463] “Constrained,” Chisian.].

4. Concerning the other free men, whom they call *bharigildi* [Note: [Col. 0463] “Wadrildi,” Cavensian.], we wish each count to observe the following rule [Note: [Col. 0463] “Let the counts observe this arrangement,” Cavensian.]: namely, that those who possess sufficient resources to go on their own and whose health and strength prove them fit for this should go. Those who have resources but are nevertheless unable to go themselves should assist someone who is able and has fewer resources. According to the next order among the free men, those who cannot go by themselves because of their poverty, but who can go in part, should join together in groups of two, three, or four. If necessary, let the others, according to just consideration [Note: [Col. 0463] That is, “as far as just consideration permits.” The Chisian and Cavensian read “consideration.”], provide assistance to the man who is going, so that he can go [Note: [Col. 0463] “Let them provide assistance to the count who is going,” Chisian.]. Let this order be observed in this way down to those who, because of extreme poverty, can neither go themselves nor provide assistance to one who is going. Let them be excused by their counts, according to the ancient custom that is to be observed by faithful counts [Note: [Col. 0463] That is, “to be observed by faithful counts according to ancient custom.”].

[Note: [Col. 0463C] Browerus is mistaken in Book VIII of the *Annals of Trier* when he supposes that these chapters were enacted by Louis in the year 835. Since they exist in the Collection of Ansegisus, which he himself states was compiled in the year 827, it is clear that these chapters precede that year. Baluze.]

# Capitularies of Aachen (825)

[Col. 0463]

I have recognized these chapters, which truly form the foundations of the public law that continued to prevail in the Empire down to our own time, with the aid of Codex 1 of the ducal library of Wolfenbüttel, Blankenburg. I have assigned them to the year 825 and to the assembly held at Aachen in May, because chapter 6 clearly indicates that they were promulgated several years after the Capitulary of Attigny of 822, while chapter 15 seems to refer to the disaster of Aebli and Asinarii (824), since nothing else could have contributed more to the dishonor of the kingdom. Nor were they established after the year 825, as is clear from the fact that in that very year Archbishop Heistolf, who is listed among the envoys, must be considered to have died, according to the Xanten and Hildesheim annals.

# Preface of the lord emperor Louis to the bishops and the whole people [Note: [Col. 0463] Thus Codex 1.]

[Col. 0463B]

1. We do not doubt that it is known to all of you, either by sight or by hearing, that our father and our forefathers, after they were chosen by God for this purpose, devoted themselves above all to ensuring that the honor of the holy Church of God and the condition of the kingdom should remain worthy. We too, following their example according to our ability [Note: [Col. 0463] Absent from Codex 1.], have often taken care to admonish your devotion concerning these matters. By God’s mercy we now see that much has been amended [Note: [Col. 0463] “Amended,” singular, Codex 1.] and corrected. Therefore we ought both to offer fitting praises to God and to return manifold thanks for your good [Col. 0463C] intention [Note: [Col. 0463] Here Codex 1 continues.].

2. But since it has pleased divine providence to appoint our mediocrity for the purpose of caring for His holy [Note: [Col. 0464C] “The Church entrusted to you for governance,” *Capitularies of Charles the Bald*, title 2, chapter 1. A privilege of Louis the Pious for the monastery of Landevennec in Henschenius and Papebrochius, vol. I of March, p. 260, reads “with the universal Church entrusted to us by God’s dispensation.” See the notes to Agobard, p. 21. Editor.] Church and this kingdom, we and our sons [Note: [Col. 0463] “Son,” Codex 1.] and associates [Note: [Col. 0463] “Associate,” Codex 1.] wish to strive for this throughout the days of our lives: that, with God’s help, three particular matters may be specially preserved by both us and you in the administration of this kingdom [Note: [Col. 0463] Here the second chapter begins in Codex 2.] [Note: [Col. 0463] “And to,” … “to,” Codex 1.], namely, that the protection, exaltation, and appropriate honor of the holy Church of God and of His servants should remain, and that peace and justice should be preserved throughout the whole community of our people. We desire above all to devote ourselves to these matters and, in all the assemblies which, with God’s help, we shall hold with you, to admonish you concerning them, as we are bound to do [Note: [Col. 0463] Here Codex 1 continues.].

3. Although the entire burden of this ministry appears to rest in our person, it is nevertheless understood, by both divine authority and human arrangement, to have been divided into parts, so that each of you is understood to possess, in his own place and order, a share of our ministry. Hence it is evident that I must be the admonisher of all of you, while all of you must be our assistants. For we are not ignorant of what is appropriate to each of you in the portion entrusted to him; and therefore we cannot fail to admonish each one according to his order.

4 [Note: [Col. 0463] “III. 2.”]. But since we know that it particularly belongs to bishops to approach the sacred ministry justly in the first place, to live religiously in that ministry, to provide the peoples entrusted to them with the path of life both by living well and by preaching rightly, to ensure that holy religion is observed in the monasteries established in their dioceses, and to take care that each person truly lives according to his profession, we admonish and beseech all of you who are established in this sacred order and exercise pastoral office to strive especially in this matter. Through yourselves and through those subject to you, insofar as it belongs to your ministry, be true assistants to us in the administration of the ministry entrusted to us, so that in judgment we may not be condemned for our negligence and yours, but rather may deserve, because of the good endeavor of both, to be rewarded [Col. 0465B] for our good work. Wherever, through the negligence of an abbot or abbess, a count or one of our vassals, or any other person whatsoever, some obstacle or difficulty in this matter becomes apparent to you, do not delay in making it known to us in due time, so that, strengthened by our assistance and supported by our authority as is fitting, you may more easily accomplish what your authority requires.

5. Concerning the priests who belong to your care, apply great diligence so that, with great care, you may teach and admonish them how they ought to live and how they ought, by example and word, to benefit the people entrusted to their portion [Note: [Col. 0465] “And be taught and,” Codex 1.]. Compel them by your episcopal authority to strive to do this. Whatever is justly reproved in them by the people [Col. 0465D] [Note: In the Paris Codex one reads “the apostles,” certainly an error. We formerly corrected similar errors in Book III of Salvian’s *On the Government of God*, p. 48, and in Agobard, chapter 7 of the *Apologeticus*. Baluze.] your prudence must not neglect to correct through the example of your own conduct. Nor should your vigilance neglect to ensure that the churches entrusted to them are not neglected, according to the resources available, in repairs or in lamps. And just as you prohibit others from taking anything from the estates assigned to the lighting of the churches, so you and your archdeacons should set an example to others by taking nothing from those same estates. Rather, let them be allowed to serve the purpose for which they were given, so that everything, as has been said, may through your authority and zeal be directed to the repair of the churches and to their lamps [Note: [Col. 0465] Absent from Codex 1.].

6. In suitable places, do not neglect to establish schools for instructing and teaching the sons and servants of the Church, as you promised us previously at Attigny and as we enjoined upon you, wherever this has not yet been properly done, for the benefit and advancement of many.

[Col. 0466A] 7. To you counts we say, and we admonish you, that it belongs especially to your ministry to show reverence and honor to the holy Church of God, to live in harmony with your bishops, and to provide them with assistance in carrying out their ministry. See also that you yourselves administer peace and justice in your offices, and that whatever our authority publicly decrees should be done is diligently accomplished in your offices [Note: [Col. 0465] “Accomplished,” singular, Codex 1.].

8. Accordingly, we admonish your fidelity to remember the faith promised to us and, in the portion of our ministry entrusted to you—namely, the making of peace and justice—to present yourselves before God and human beings in such a way that you may justly be called and declared both our true assistants and protectors of the people. Let no matter whatsoever—whether the acceptance of gifts, anyone’s friendship, hatred, fear, or favor—compel you to depart from the state of righteousness, so that you always judge justly between neighbor and neighbor. Be helpers and defenders of orphans, widows, and the other poor, and, according to your ability, honorers of the holy Church and its servants. Those who, through recklessness and violence, endeavor to disturb the common peace by thefts and robberies [Note: [Col. 0465] “Theft and robbery,” Codex 1.] or plundering, restrain by your zeal and correction, as is fitting. If any person in any way impedes you so that you cannot do what we command, let this be made known to us at once [Note: [Col. 0465] “Who,” Codex 1.], so that, assisted by our authority, you may be able to fulfill your ministry worthily.

[Col. 0466C] 9 [Note: [Col. 0465] The division of the chapter in Codex 1 occurs only after “compel.”]. We admonish all laymen to preserve ecclesiastical honor, to show due veneration to bishops and the priests of God, and to attend devoutly with their households upon their preaching. Let them reverently observe the fasts commonly proclaimed by them, and teach and compel their own people to observe them. Let all also strive to ensure that the Lord’s Day is honored and observed as is fitting. And, so that this may be done more freely [Note: [Col. 0465D] That is, so that there may be complete freedom to pray to God, so that Christians may not be called away from prayer, markets and legal hearings should be prohibited on the Lord’s Day. An old gloss in one royal codex of the Lombard law reads: “So that people may observe Sundays more freely, markets and legal hearings are to be prohibited for them on those days.” Or alternatively: “And so that markets and legal hearings may be held more freely, let them be prohibited on Sunday.” Accordingly, in another royal codex, above the words “so that it may be done more freely,” there is written above the line: “namely, on other days.” Editor.], let markets and legal hearings be prohibited by the counts on that day, as has often been enjoined.

10. We also specially command abbots and laymen that, in the monasteries they possess through our generosity, they should carry out, with the counsel and instruction of the bishops, whatever pertains to the religion of canons, monks, and religious women, and that they should willingly hear and obey their beneficial admonition in this matter.

11. Again we say to bishops, abbots, our vassals, and all faithful laymen: be assistants to the counts in administering justice.

12. [Note: [Col. 0467D] Flodoard, Book III, chapter 23, concerning the letters of Hincmar: “He replies to Villebert of Châlons concerning his inquiries on behalf of Count Gangulf, saying that concerning certain matters which he denied having done against him and others which he confessed, he should act gently according to the apostolic command, so that in this he might fulfill the law of Christ, namely charity; and, enticing the same count as best he could by his skill toward satisfaction and affection for him, he should allow his kindness toward him to become clear.” Baluze.] Let bishops and counts live harmoniously with one another and with the other faithful, and let them provide one another with assistance in carrying out their ministries.

13. We also say generally to everyone that you should possess charity and peace toward one another, and that you should strive generally to observe our general command. To our envoys whom we have sent for any ecclesiastical or public utility or need whatsoever, show honor for the sake of our honor [Note: [Col. 0467] “Our,” Codex 1.], and, out of reverence for our authority, do not neglect to carry out what we enjoin through them [Note: [Col. 0467] Codex 1 continues.].

14. And since, as we have said, each of you is understood to possess a share of our ministry in his own portion, we wish to learn—through informers or any other reliable indications, or through our envoys whom we appoint for this purpose—how each person has striven in this matter. Through common testimony, that is, of bishops concerning counts and of counts concerning bishops, we wish to discover how diligently counts love and administer justice, how religiously bishops conduct themselves and preach, and, through the testimony of both, to learn about the equity, peace [Note: [Col. 0467] “Equity and peace,” Codex 1.], and concord [Note: [Col. 0467] “Concord,” Codex 1.] of the other faithful who remain in their respective ministries. Likewise, we wish that, when questioned by us concerning their common association and condition, all may be able to give true testimony about one another, and each about all [Note: [Col. 0467] Codex 1 continues.].

15. And if such a matter should arise in any province or county as concerns either the dishonoring of the kingdom or the common detriment, and which cannot be corrected without our authority, do not allow us, who by God’s help must correct everything, to remain long unaware of it. For whatever up to now has been neglected, whether by us or by you, in matters pertaining to the peace and justice of the whole people [Note: [Col. 0467] “pertains,” and h., 1.], to the honor of the kingdom, and to the common welfare, we must strive, with God’s help, to see that from now onward it is amended through our diligence and yours.

16. Concerning the peace to be maintained on a military expedition as far as the march, we wish this to be made known to all: whoever knows by name the author of the damage inflicted upon him in the past year [Note: [Col. 0467] “may know” (cognoscat), 1.], let him seek and obtain justice from him [Note: [Col. 0467] continues, 1.].

17. Nevertheless, we wish it henceforth to be known to all, so that each person may understand that he will be required to render an account for the deeds of all who travel on such an expedition in his service, whether they are his own men or others; and whatever they themselves commit in violation of the peace must be charged to his responsibility [Col. 0468A] [Note: [Col. 0467] thus, 1.]. The condition is specifically that the violator of the peace [Note: [Col. 0467] “violator” (vialator), 1.] shall first pay a fitting penalty according to the nature of his crime, either before us or before our envoy. And the lord who has taken such a man with him—one whom he either would not or could not compel to observe our command and who was not afraid, moreover, to commit plunder in our kingdom—if, because of that man’s negligence [Note: [Col. 0467] “negligence” through “until he warned” are absent in 1.], he did not warn him beforehand about these matters, and, after the negligence of the contemptuous man had come to his knowledge, neglected to correct him as was proper, shall be deprived of his honor; so that neither of them [Note: [Col. 0467] “neither of them” (neutrum), 1.] may remain without just punishment [Note: [Col. 0467] “may remain,” plural, 1.].

18. Concerning also the dishonoring of the king and the kingdom, and the evil reputation spread among foreign nations because of the negligence of those who either receive in their lodgings the envoys sent to us badly, or do not provide the expenses established by us, or refuse to provide transport animals, or steal something from them [Note: [Col. 0467] perhaps “by chance,” 1.], or—and this is the most intolerable—do not fear to perpetrate open violence against them by beating them and plundering their possessions: we wish this to be known to all. Whoever among those who hold our honors does not henceforth strive to correct this negligence, and does not instruct or compel his own men, who ought to perform this duty in his place, to carry it out properly and not presume to neglect it any longer, and who scorns to preserve both our honor and that of the kingdom entrusted to us—we no longer wish him to hold either our honor or that of our kingdom.

Rather, we wish each of our faithful men to instruct the stewards of his affairs specifically about these matters, so that whenever an embassy arrives from anywhere, and they see either our letters or our envoy, everyone may be able to receive him honorably in every place within our empire, for the sake of our honor and that of the whole kingdom [Col. 0468C] [Note: [Col. 0467] continues, 1.].

19. In those places where roads and lodging provisions have now been arranged by our father and by us through a capitulary, let them have envoys specially appointed for this purpose, who must continually oversee the matter [Note: [Col. 0467] “let them provide; let them have” is the reading of the edition.]. Thus our faithful men appointed for this purpose should strive to prepare in due time everything necessary for receiving these embassies, so that it is not then necessary to seek or bring things from afar when the time comes to provide or pay them. In all other places throughout our empire, let each of our faithful men, both personally and through his ministers [Col. 0468D], as we have said, exercise vigilant care.

20. Concerning the coinage, about which we have already issued admonitions for three years and have fixed the time when one type should be retained and all the others cease, we wish this also to be known to all: so that it may be corrected quickly and without any excuse, we have decided that the period shall extend until the feast of Saint Martin [Note: [Col. 0469D] That is, until Saint Martin’s feast day. This interpretation requires no proof. We frequently read in old books and authors of the Mass of Saint Martin, Saint John, the apostles Peter and Paul, Saint Andrew, Saint Michael, Saint Boniface, Saint Remigius, Saint Albinus, Saint Felix, Saint Marcellinus, Saint Balthild, Saint Nazarius, Saint Philibert, Saint Gall, Saint Clement, Saint Anianus, Saint Lambert, Saint Julian, Saint Maurice, Saint Bavo, and All Saints. Wormius, book III of the *Danish Fasti*, presents an old Runic Calendar, written three hundred years ago, with a Latin interpretation. In that Calendar the word *missa* is taken to mean a feast: thus *Paulus missa* in January, which Wormius rightly translates “Paul’s feast”; in February, *Matthias miss.*; in May, *crucis missa*; in June, *Joans missa* and *Petars missa*; in July, *Jacaubs missa* and *Olafs missa*. And likewise in the other months, not to mention them individually. BALUZ.]. Thus each count in his county may then be able to have fulfilled our command concerning this matter, so that from that day onward not another coin but that one alone shall be accepted throughout our kingdom by everyone, in accordance with the provision established in the capitularies that we gave concerning this matter to those counts in whose counties coinage is struck.

For at that time we intend to send our envoys through each county for this purpose, to investigate carefully how the counts have striven to fulfill our command in this matter. And whoever is found negligent in it shall, we wish, be ordered to come as quickly as possible into our presence [Col. 0469B] and render an account whether he was unwilling or unable to do what we commanded; or, if some obstacle prevented him from doing it, why he did not report that inability to us in due time [Note: [Col. 0469] “or,” 1.]. For if he was unwilling, or was unable because of his own negligence, we wish to find someone who is willing and able to observe what we command.

Moreover, so that our command in this matter may be fulfilled more quickly, we wish that whoever from that day onward brings out another denarius for the purpose of trade shall have it taken from him by the count and his ministers.

21. Likewise concerning unlawful tolls, about which we have both established in capitularies how they must be observed by everyone and issued very frequent admonitions [Col. 0469C], we wish our aforesaid envoys to investigate by whom our command in this matter has been fulfilled and by whom it has been neglected. Whoever has neglected or delayed to fulfill it shall, we wish, be ordered to come into our presence, so that he may quickly render an account of these matters, as we said above. And if he is found culpable, let him receive a fitting correction, so that it may provide the other negligent persons with an example of fear.

22. Wherever bridges formerly existed, and in those places where, during the time of our father and at his command, bridges were constructed for various necessities [Note: [Col. 0469] absent in 1.], we command that they be restored and renewed without any delay by those who then constructed them, so that they are repaired by the feast of Saint Andrew, unless perhaps the magnitude of the work itself or [Note: [Col. 0469] absent in 1.] a flood of waters in any place [Note: [Col. 0469] “in any place” through “none” is absent in 1.] prevents this [Col. 0470A]. Otherwise, no one is to presume, on any pretext, to neglect or delay this, but it must be completed by the appointed time.

And we wish our envoys, whom we mentioned above, to report in which places our command has been fulfilled, in which it has been neglected, and in which it has been delayed because of some impossibility or definite reason.

23. Concerning the ninths and tithes, about which both our father and we have frequently issued admonitions at various assemblies and have established through our capitularies how they should be observed, we wish and command that from all produce of labor, and from wine and hay, the ninth and the tithe be faithfully and fully paid by all. As for the tithe from livestock, let the custom that has prevailed up to now be observed by all. [Col. 0470B] If, however, there is a bishop who wishes to accept silver in place of this, the matter shall remain within his discretion, according to what he and the person who must pay it agree upon [Note: [Col. 0469] continues, 1.].

24. Likewise concerning labor for the restoration [Note: [Col. 0469] “work of rebuilding,” 1.] of churches, whether in constructing or redeeming them, the bishop’s will should rather be followed. Nevertheless, it must in no way be left undone that, as we have often commanded, this or that payment be made to the portions of the churches. And let this be known to all: whoever acts negligently in this matter and is found negligent in it before us shall, we insist, undergo precisely what we established concerning this matter in our capitulary with the common counsel of our faithful men [Note: [Col. 0469] continues, 1.].

25. Let the counts in every way become helpers of the ministers [Note: [Col. 0469] “ministers,” 1.] of the Church in their counties, so that they may be able to obtain this more fully from our men, from themselves, and from their own men. Whoever, after being admonished by the count once and twice concerning these matters, does not correct himself, we wish his negligence to be reported by that same count to our knowledge, so that by our authority he may be compelled to undergo what is contained in our capitulary.

26. We also wish the capitularies that have now or at another time been established by us with the counsel of our faithful men to be received from our chancellor by the archbishops and their counts [Note: [Col. 0469] “their own,” 1.] from their own cities, either personally or through their envoys. And [Note: [Col. 0470D] That is, each archbishop is to undertake within his province the responsibility of promulgating the capitularies established by the ruler. This was done so that at the next assembly they would be required to render an account whether the archbishops had obeyed the emperor’s command in this matter, as is clear from letter 28 of Frotharius of Toul. ID.] let each of them have these transcribed throughout his diocese for the other bishops, abbots, counts, and our other faithful men, and have them read aloud in their counties before everyone [Col. 0470D], so that our ordinance and will may become known to all [Col. 0471A]. Our chancellor, however, shall record the names of the bishops and counts who take care to receive them and shall report them to our knowledge, so that no one may presume to omit this.

We also wish our vassals [Note: [Col. 0471C] “and vassals,” Anseg.] serving us to receive fitting honor from everyone, as has often been commanded by our father and by us.

## CAPITULARY OF THE ENVOYS [Note: [Col. 0471C] These passages are taken from Ansegisus, book II, chapters 25–28; they are absent from the Blankenburg Codex and appear to have been given to the envoys.].

1. At Besançon, which is the diocese of Archbishop Bernoinus, Bishop Heiminus [Note: [Col. 0471C] Of Lausanne.] and Count Monogoldus. At Mainz, which is the diocese of Archbishop Heistulfus, the same Heistulfus as bishop and Ruodbertus as count. At Trier, Archbishop Hetti and Count Adalbertus [Note: [Col. 0471C] Frotharius, bishop of Toul, seems to discuss this mission of Hetti, archbishop of Trier, in letter 18. BALUZ.]. At Cologne, Archbishop Hadaboldus and Count Eemundus. At Reims, Archbishop Ebbo [Note: [Col. 0471C] Louis commands that Ebbo, archbishop of Reims, exercise this mission in the province of Reims whenever he can. Henschenius, in his notes on the *Life of Saint Anskar*, vol. I of the February volume, p. 404, interprets this clause as referring to Ebbo’s mission to the northern regions, for which he sometimes had to be absent from his province; at such times Bishop Rothadus was entrusted with the responsibility of fulfilling the mission in his absence [Col. 0471D]. I, however, think that the clause was simply added because Ebbo was frequently at the palace, and therefore substitutes had to be appointed to take his place during his absence.
