Flodoardus, book II, chapter 19: “Since Bishop Ebbo, therefore, was then frequently staying at the palace.” ID.], whenever he can, and, whenever he cannot, Bishop Ruothadus [Note: [Col. 0471D] Of Soissons. ID.] in his place, together with Count Hruotfridus, over the six counties, namely Reims, Châlons, Soissons, Senlis, Beauvais, and Laon.

Over the four bishoprics belonging to the same diocese—namely Noyon, Amiens, Thérouanne, and Cambrai—Bishop Ragnarius and Count Berengarius [Note: [Col. 0471D] Noyon, whose bishop attended the Council of Paris in 829. A letter of Amalarius to him is preserved in volume VII of D’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, p. 165. This may therefore help illuminate the catalogue of the bishops of Noyon. ID.].

At Sens, Archbishop Jeremiah and [Note: [Col. 0471D] Of Melun. Adrevaldus of Fleury, book I of *The Miracles of Saint Benedict*, chapter 25: “At that same assembly were present, sent from the king’s side, Bishop Jonas of Orléans and Donatus, count of the people of Melun.” Hincmarus, in his account of the estate of Noisy, chapter 4: “Lord Emperor Louis granted that estate of Noisy to Donatus as a benefice.” And below: “Donatus, convicted of his infidelity, swore to the emperor the required oath, and the emperor took away from him the county of Melun and the estate of Noisy with its dependencies.” The same man was sent to Hispania Tarraconensis in 827, which was then called the Spanish March, to settle the disturbances of that province. Einhardus: “The emperor sent the priest and abbot Helisachar, and with him the counts Hildetrandus and Donatus, to settle the disturbances of the Spanish March.” Then, in 837, he was sent again to the same province with Count Boniface and Adrebalus, abbot of the monastery of Flavigny [Col. 0472D], to hear the complaints brought against Bernard, duke of that region, as the author of the *Life of Louis the Pious* testifies. I think the same Donatus is mentioned in the *Capitularies of Charles the Bald*, title XIV, p. 70. ID.] Count Donatus.

At Rouen, Archbishop Willibertus and Count Ingobertus [Note: [Col. 0472D] Of Rouen. In an old manuscript of the Imperial Library, from which Gretser’s edition of the *Carolingian Codex* was produced, the following is written at the beginning in capital letters: “THE BOOK OF ARCHBISHOP WILLIBERTUS.” Peter Lambecius tells us this in book II of his *Commentaries on the Imperial Library*, p. 321, and immediately adds that he has no doubt that by Archbishop Willibertus—whose property this codex once was—Willibertus, archbishop of Rouen, must be understood, since he acquired it from Charlemagne’s library after Charlemagne’s death. ID.].

At Tours, Archbishop Landramnus and Count Hruodbertus. At Lyon, Tarentaise, and Vienne, Bishop Albericus and Count Rihhardus [Note: [Col. 0472D] Of Langres. His appears to be the thirtieth letter among those published under the name of Frotharius, bishop of Toul. ID.].

2. A statement of what pertains to the mission of the aforesaid envoys [Col. 0471C]. First, they are to assemble an assembly in two or three places, where all those concerned with their mission can gather; and they are to make generally known to everyone what their mission is—namely, that they have been appointed and sent by us for this purpose: if any bishop or count is unable, because of some impediment, to fulfill his office, he is to have recourse to them and, with their assistance, fulfill his office; and if there is some matter that cannot be corrected through their admonition, it is to be reported through them to our knowledge.

And if a bishop or count should act somewhat negligently in his office, he is to be corrected through their admonition. Let the whole people know that they have been appointed for this purpose: whoever, through the negligence, carelessness, or inability of a count, has been unable to obtain his justice may first bring his complaint to them and obtain justice through their assistance. And whenever anyone appeals to us out of necessity, we may refer the complainants’ reports to them [Col. 0472B] for resolution.

The envoys themselves are not to travel here and there without the most certain cause or necessity—unless perhaps they discover that something has arisen in the office of someone within their mission that requires their presence and cannot be corrected without their counsel or assistance. Nevertheless, they must be vigilant lest, through their negligence, anything remain uncorrected within their mission. Rather, whenever they recognize a definite and genuine necessity, they must not neglect to fulfill our command.

3. We also wish it to be known to all that they have been appointed for this purpose: that whatever we establish generally through our capitularies concerning any matters may be made known to everyone through them [Col. 0472C], and that these matters may lie within their charge, so that they are fulfilled by all. If, however, because of some obstacle that cannot be corrected through them, anything that we have established and commanded [Col. 0473A] remains incomplete, this is to be reported to us in due time through their account, so that we may correct what they were unable to correct.

4. We believe that you understand how weighty is the mission that we have entrusted to you, and how dangerous it is to neglect responsibility for so great a matter—responsibility that, for the common salvation of us all, you recognize that you have undertaken under our obligation.

When we questioned you about it, the answer given to us was not such as could have sufficed in that response for the same arrangement that the necessity of matters pertaining to the common welfare seemed to demand, or that could have provided us with any reassurance. We recognized that this happened because, last year, when we gave you the capitularies of your mission, we carefully commanded you to see that no injury was done without cause to those whom we wish to be honored [Col. 0473B].

Therefore, we wish to make known to you how, with God’s help, you must now fulfill this same command of ours. We wish our envoys—whom we have appointed for this purpose, that they may exercise care and concern so that each person whom we have appointed as governor of our people administers the office entrusted to him in his proper order, justly and in a manner pleasing to God, for our honor and the welfare of our people—to apply diligence in investigating whether the matters contained in our capitulary, which we gave them last year, are fulfilled according to the will of God and our command [Col. 0473C–0474A].

Accordingly, we wish these same envoys to meet in the middle of May, each in his own mission [Note: [Col. 0473C] I found in the Chartulary of the church of Vienne an old complaint brought by Archbishop Agilmarus against Count Wigericus at a solemn assembly of the royal envoys, at which Remigius, archbishop of Lyon [Col. 0474C], and four other bishops were present together with eleven counts and twenty royal vassals. This passage can therefore be greatly illuminated by it, and one can learn how such assemblies were held. BALUZ.], with all the bishops, abbots, counts, and our vassals, our advocates, and the deputies of the abbesses, as well as those who are unable to come themselves because of some unavoidable necessity, at one place.

And if it is necessary, for the convenience of assembling, to hold the same meeting in two or three places—especially for the sake of the poor among the people—let it be held in a manner suitable for everyone. Each count shall have his vicars and centenarii with him, and also three or four of his leading scabini.

At this assembly, first there shall be a discussion of the Christian religion and ecclesiastical order. Then our envoys shall inquire of everyone how each of those who have been appointed by us for this purpose [Col. 0474B] administers the office entrusted to him among the people according to the will of God and our command; whether they are sufficiently harmonious and united for this purpose; and how they mutually assist one another in carrying out their offices.

They are to conduct this investigation so carefully and diligently that through them we may be able to learn the whole truth of the matter. And if any matter is brought to their attention that requires their assistance, then, according to the nature of the cases contained in our capitulary, we wish them to go there and strive by our authority to correct it.

# THE CONSTITUTIONS OF LOTHAR AT OLONNA (A.D. 825)

[Col. 0473]

In May of the year 825, Lothar held a second assembly at the estate of Olonna, and it gave rise to the constitutions that we are able to present here in their proper order and in full, with the assistance of excellent manuscripts.

We have revised and enlarged the ecclesiastical capitularies published by Muratori, pp. 151–153, from the first Mutina Codex, with the aid of the following manuscripts: (1) the ducal library of Wolfenbüttel, the Blankenburg Codex; (2) the ducal library of Gotha; and also the Chisian, Cavensis, Ambrosian, Florentine, London, Vienna, Veronese, and Este manuscripts, published by Muratori in chapters 15–21; as well as a Florentine fragment published in 1675 by Carlo Dati. Only the Chisian manuscript preserved the date. Chapter 10 is also found in Vatican Codex no. 5359, appended to chapters 10 and 11 of the general capitularies and followed by chapters 2 and 3 of those capitularies.

We owe the shorter ecclesiastical capitularies to the Chisian, Cavensis, and Blankenburg manuscripts.

We have corrected the general capitularies—chapters 22–24 and 26–33 among Lothar’s Lombard laws, published by Baluze from the Paris Codex and by Muratori, p. 153, from the Mutina Codex—with the aid of the following: (1) Saint Paul’s manuscript, fols. 182–184; the Chisian and Cavensis manuscripts; (2) Royal Paris Codex no. 4613; (3) the Blankenburg manuscript; (4) the Gotha manuscript; (5) the Mutina manuscript published by Muratori at the cited place; and also the Ambrosian, Florentine, London, Vienna, Veronese, and Este manuscripts published by Muratori. The second chapter is also found in the Florentine Fragment published by Carlo Dati, in chapters 10 and 11, and chapters 2 and 3 are found in Vatican Codex no. 5359 (*Archiv.*, vol. V, p. 245).

## HERE BEGIN THE CHAPTERS [Note: [Col. 0473] Thus the Chisian manuscript. The heading is absent from the other manuscripts. The Blankenburg manuscript has: “Likewise, other chapters of Lord Lothar.” The Mutina manuscript has: “Likewise, chapters concerning the affairs of bishops.”] THAT THE LORD EMPEROR ESTABLISHED IN THE SIXTH YEAR OF HIS EMPIRE AT THE GENERAL ASSEMBLY HELD AT THE ESTATE OF HOLONNA [Note: [Col. 0473] “Holontna” in the Chisian manuscript.]

## ECCLESIASTICAL CHAPTERS

[Col. 0473D]

1. It has pleased us [Note: [Col. 0473] “First chapter, concerning bishops.” “It has pleased us, concerning bishops,” 2.] that if any person, because of whatever faults and crimes, has been corrected so many times that he is even judged deserving of episcopal excommunication for contempt [Note: [Col. 0473] “through contempt,” 1, 2.], the bishop shall associate his count with himself [Note: [Col. 0473] “count”; “bishop” in the Chisian and Cavensis manuscripts.], and by the consent of both, let such a contemptuous person be restrained, so that he may be obedient to the commands [Note: [Col. 0473] singular “command” in 1, Vatican, Vienna, Erfurt, and the Florentine Fragment; “in obedience to the command,” 2.] of his bishop.

If he does not give his assent, let him pay our ban to us [Note: [Col. 0473] “pay,” Florentine Fragment.]. But if he remains contumacious after this, then let him be excommunicated by the bishop [Col. 0475A]. If the excommunicated man cannot be corrected, let him be bound in chains by the count [Note: [Col. 0475] “restrained,” 2; “restrained” in the Vatican; “constrained” in the Florentine Fragment.], until that contemptuous person accepts our judgment [Note: [Col. 0475] “the same man,” 1.].

If the count is found guilty in such matters, let it be reported to us through his bishop. If our vassal should fall into this offense, let him be restrained by the count as above [Note: [Col. 0475] “constrained,” 1, 2.]. If he does not obey, let the matter be made known to us before he is sent into chains.

2. We wish all immunities of our forebears [Note: [Col. 0475] “by the favor of our forebear or by our own,” Florentine Fragment.], as well as our own, to be fully and justly preserved in every respect.

3. We wish that property given by free persons to places dedicated to God may remain as it was previously given, even if they reserve for themselves the usufruct and administration of that property, should they so desire [Note: [Col. 0475] After “if they should otherwise wish” something is absent in 1.]. If they do not otherwise arrange it, let it remain as it was previously given [Col. 0475B].

4. To each bishop, abbot, and abbess we grant two advocates [Note: [Col. 0475] “one who conducts the case and another who leads the oath, and for as long as they hold the advocacy, we release them from military service,” 1, Vatican, Vienna, Erfurt.], and for as long as they hold the advocacy, we release them from military service.

5. We prohibit anyone from presuming to practice usury after being admonished by his bishop. If anyone presumes to do so after his prohibition, he shall be restrained by the counts, as we commanded above concerning contemptuous persons [Note: [Col. 0475] “As was stated above concerning the counts, we command that they be restrained,” Fragment.].

6. [Note: [Col. 0475] Chapter 6 is present in 1, 2, and the Mutina manuscript; it is absent from the Chisian, Cavensis, Ambrosian, Florentine, London, Vienna, Veronese, Este, and Florentine Fragment manuscripts.] Concerning instruction, which through the excessive negligence and idleness of certain superiors has been utterly extinguished everywhere, it has pleased us that, as we have established, it be observed by all. Namely, those whom we have appointed by our arrangement in designated places to teach others [Note: [Col. 0475] “to the art,” 2 and Mutina.] are to devote the greatest effort to ensuring that the scholars entrusted to them [Note: [Col. 0475] “scholars thus,” 2 and Mutina.] make progress and apply themselves to learning, as the present necessity requires.

Nevertheless, for the convenience of all, we have designated suitable places for this exercise [Note: [Col. 0475] “exercises,” 2.], so that the distance of remote places and poverty might be an excuse for no one [Note: [Col. 0475] “might become,” 2 and Mutina.]. They are as follows:

First, at Pavia they shall assemble with Dungalus [Note: [Col. 0475] “Dungalus,” Mutina.]: from Milan [Note: [Col. 0475] “Mediolanio,” 1.], Brescia, Lodi, Bergamo, Novara, Vercelli [Note: [Col. 0475] “Vercelle,” 1.], Tortona [Note: [Col. 0475] “Tartona,” 2; “Artona,” Mutina.], Acqui, Genoa [Note: [Col. 0475] “Genua,” 2 and Mutina.], Asti [Note: [Col. 0475] “Haste,” Mutina.], and Como.

At Ivrea [Note: [Col. 0475] “Eboreia,” 2 and Mutina.] the bishop himself shall do this personally [Note: [Col. 0475] plural “shall do,” 1.].

At Turin they shall assemble from Ventimiglia [Note: [Col. 0475] “Twenty miles,” 2; “twenty miles,” Mutina.], Albenga [Note: [Col. 0475] “Albengano,” 2; “Albengano,” Mutina.], Vado, and Alba.

At Cremona they shall study: from Reggio, Piacenza, Parma [Note: [Col. 0475] “from Parma” is absent in 1.], and Modena.

At Florence [Note: [Col. 0475] “At Florence” is absent in 1.] those from Tuscany shall attend.

At Fermo and [Note: [Col. 0475] absent in 2 and Mutina.] from the cities of Spoleto [Note: [Col. 0475] “Spoleto,” 1; “Spoletini,” 2.] they shall assemble.

At Verona, those from Mantua and Trent [Note: [Col. 0475] “Tridendo,” 2; “Tridento,” Mutina.].

At Vicenza, those from Padua [Note: [Col. 0475] “Pactavi,” 2; “Patau,” Mutina.], Treviso, Feltre [Note: [Col. 0475] “Filtris,” 1.], Ceneda [Note: [Col. 0475] “Cenata,” 2; “Ceneta,” Mutina.], and Asolo [Note: [Col. 0475] “Asilio,” 1; “Asilo,” Mutina.].

The remaining cities of Friuli shall assemble at the school [Note: [Col. 0475] “shall gather,” 2 and Mutina.].

7. [Note: [Col. 0475] Chapter 7 is absent from the same manuscripts as chapter 6.] We wish each bishop to have the conduct and residences of the canons prepared by the Kalends of October of the coming year, without any negligence, as we have arranged [Col. 0476B].

8. We have commanded that each parish church be restored according to the ancient custom [Note: [Col. 0475] “Concerning the restoration of parish churches.” “To you,” 1.]. If the sons of that church are unwilling to restore them [Note: [Col. 0475] absent in 1.], let them be restrained by the ministers of the public authority, so that whether willingly or unwillingly they observe our command.

9. [Note: [Col. 0475] This chapter is absent from the Ambrosian, Florentine, London, Vienna, Veronese, Este, and Florentine Fragment manuscripts.] Concerning the giving of tithes [Note: [Col. 0475] “Concerning tithes, that they be given,” 2.], we establish that, just as it is contained in the capitulary enacted at Mantua [Note: [Col. 0475] “that it be observed, so that those who do not give them …,” Mutina.], those who refuse to give them shall be restrained and shall pay them [Note: [Col. 0475] “shall discharge,” 1; “shall be paid,” corrected to “shall pay,” 2; “shall be discharged by them,” Mutina.].

10. Concerning the *precariae* that were irrationally made by the rectors of churches and bound their successors to a severe penalty, so that the latter could not dissolve what the former had done [Note: [Col. 0475] “nor could the king dissolve it,” Mutina.], we command [Note: [Col. 0475] “we establish,” Chisian.] that no successor be bound by the penalty imposed by his predecessor [Note: [Col. 0475] “to his predecessor,” 2 and Vercelli.], but that it be entrusted to his discretion: if his predecessor distributed church property irrationally [Note: [Col. 0475] “fraudulently,” Chisian.], it may be recalled from him to be held under the right of the church [Note: [Col. 0475] “to be held,” 2, Chisian, Cavensis; “to be held,” Florentine Fragment.] [Note: [Col. 0475] The Vercelli Codex ends this chapter here and uses the heading: “From the capitulary of Lord Lothar established at Olonna, chapter X.”].

[Note: [Col. 0475] The following manuscript versions are printed in parallel in Migne.]

### The Blankenburg Codex continues

11. Concerning tithes: those unwilling to give them are to be compelled by the ministers of the public authority to do so, according to what was announced last year. That is, four or eight of the best men—or as many as may be necessary—from each parish are to be selected, according to the character of each parish [Col. 0477A], so that they themselves may serve as witnesses between the priest and the people as to where tithes have or have not been given. This is so that no necessity of taking an oath should arise there.

We do not, however, say that so many witnesses should be sent so that it is always necessary for all of them to be present together when the tithes are given; rather, when the responsibility is entrusted to several, they will be burdened less. If two are present, we believe that they are sufficient.

The negligent are to be admonished by the priests of the churches up to three times to give that tithe. If they despise this, they are to be barred from entering the church. And if they do not correct this at all, after being restrained by the ministers of the public authority, each of them is to pay six solidi to the church, and in addition is to be compelled to give the tithe.

For if they again prove contemptuous [Note: [Col. 0477] singular “proves contemptuous,” 1.], then by public authority their homes or houses are to be placed under *wifa*—that is, public seizure or forfeiture—until they make satisfaction for the tithe itself, as stated above. If they are again rebellious or defiant, and presume to enter their property under *wifa* by their own authority [Note: [Col. 0477] “their own,” 1.], then they are to be placed in custody by the ministers of the public authority until they are brought before the public court, and there, according to the law, they are to pay compensation to the count or to the public authority.

The remaining provisions are as stated above: they are to pay the tithes and make satisfaction of six solidi to the church.

### The Gotha Codex

11. It seems good to us, if it pleases our lord, that the oversight of our envoys be entrusted with ensuring that wherever monks or nuns now exist, they remain in that vocation, wherever the suitability of the place or the amount of property permits it.

12. But where they formerly existed and no longer do, let them live there—except if there were twelve or more. If twelve are found, and the place and property permit it, let them be monks. Where there is uncertainty whether they should be canonical clergy or monks, and the suitability of the place or the amount of property permits this, let them be given the choice whether they wish to live as monks or as canons.

13. But where they are now canons, let them remain canons. Where the institutions have been completely destroyed, let the number of canons there correspond to the amount of property.

## OTHER CHAPTERS [Note: [Col. 0477] “Likewise, other chapters of the emperor Lord Lothar,” Blankenburg.]

[Col. 0477B]

1. We command [Note: [Col. 0477] “We have found,” Blankenburg.] that the rectors of baptismal churches be priests, one for each individual church [Note: [Col. 0477] “of the individual churches,” Blankenburg; “one priest for each,” Cavensis; absent in the Chisian.], and not deacons [Note: [Col. 0477] “deacons,” Blankenburg.] or clerics of any lower order.

2. It has also pleased us [Note: [Col. 0477] absent in Blankenburg.] that the priests of baptismal churches, according to their ability, render the obedience due to the public authority [Note: [Col. 0477] absent in Blankenburg.] and show honor to their bishop [Note: [Col. 0477] “to their bishops,” Blankenburg.] without grievance [Note: [Col. 0477] “grievance,” Chisian; “burden,” Cavensis; “heaviness,” 3.], as necessity and order require [Note: [Col. 0477] “when necessity requires,” Blankenburg.].

3. We have also decreed that, if such public-service obedience is imposed upon bishops [Note: Ch. C. read episcopi talem; C. has tale.] that they cannot easily fulfill it unaided [Note: Ch. C. read “which … could not fulfill.”], they shall provide assistance from their subordinates according to the nature of the service imposed [Note: Ch. reads “may anticipate”; C. “may provide.”].

[Col. 0478B] 4. Concerning hospices, we decree [Note: C. reads “it pleased us”; Bl. “it seemed good to us”] that, according to the resources available or the fertility of the time, they shall follow the provisions written in the wills.

5. Concerning women living together with priests, it pleased us [Note: “that they be completely expelled” is absent in some witnesses] that they be entirely expelled, so that they may no longer associate in any way with those regarding whom they are suspected [Note: Ch. C. read “in any way to associate”; Bl. reads “to associate”]. And if, after the first warning [Note: Bl. reads “after the first warning”], she is convicted by her own bishop, through seven down to three suitable witnesses [Note: Ch. reads “with her bishop absent”; C. “by the seventh”], of having persisted in wrongdoing, she shall be subject to the penalty of her own rank [Note: Ch. has the plural “they shall be subject.”].

6. If a bishop has neglected such a warning [Note: V reads “warning”; Ch. “correction of this kind”] or correction, or if, after this synodal council, he has not corrected within forty days matters requiring correction [Note: Bl. reads “sixty”], he shall be subject to the judgment and sentence of his metropolitan [Note: Ch. reads “to the judgment”; C. “shall submit to the sentence”; Bl. “shall undergo the sentence.”].

[Note: The following manuscript versions are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0477B] 7. Concerning hospices, we decree that whoever possesses them shall administer everything connected with them according to God and according to the canons; and whatever was not given from them to the poor [Col. 0477C] [Note: C. reads “given to the poor”] after the death of lord Pippin [Note: Ch. reads “after the death”] shall in every respect be restored. But if anyone refuses to do this, he shall have no authority over those hospices until he comes with the royal envoys into our presence; and [Note: In Ch., “and until our presence” is absent] the envoys, together with that bishop, shall inventory them in our presence [Note: The words that follow are absent in C.].

Issued at Holonna, in the twelfth and sixth years of the reign of the emperors, lords Louis and Lothar, in the month of May, indiction 3.

[Col. 0478B] Codex Blankenburgensis.

7. Concerning monasteries and disordered or destroyed hospices belonging to the palace or to the rights of anyone whatsoever, which disregard the admonition of the bishops, it pleased our imperial foresight that judgment be reserved to us.

## GENERAL CAPITULARIES

[Note: “Another capitulary of lord Lothar” (3).]

[Col. 0477C]

1. [Note: “Chapter 1. Concerning counts” (4).] We decree that free men who possess enough property to be able to perform military service, but refuse to do so when ordered, shall, on the first occasion, according to their law, be subject to the prescribed penalty. If, however, he is found negligent a second time [Note: Some witnesses read “on the second occasion”], let him pay our ban, that is, sixty solidi. If anyone is found involved in the same fault a third time [Note: One witness reads “if anyone at all”], let him know that he will lose all his property or be sent into exile.

As for free men of middling means [Note: One witness reads “of middle rank”], who cannot perform military service on their own, we entrust them to the loyalty of the counts, so that two, three, or four of them—or more, if necessary—may provide assistance to one who seems the better man, in order to perform our service [Note: One witness reads “one person”; others “each person,” “each one,” or “to each.”]. As for those who, because of extreme poverty, can neither perform military service themselves nor provide assistance, let them be maintained until they are able to recover [Note: Witnesses read “to be recovered”].

2. [Note: “Concerning free men” (4).] It pleases us that free men who, not because of poverty but in order to evade public service, fraudulently and ingeniously donate their property to churches [Note: One witness reads “destroy”; others “transfer” or “assign”; the Florentine fragment omits the remainder], and then receive the same property back for use subject to a rent [Note: One witness reads “under incitement”], shall, for as long as they possess that property, perform military service [Note: Some witnesses read “military services”] and the other public duties. But if they neglect to carry out the orders, we grant the counts authority to distrain them through those properties [Note: One witness reads “our properties”; Ch. “their properties”; another “their property”], without our immunity resisting this, so that the condition [Note: One witness reads “statute and utility”] and usefulness of this kingdom may not be weakened by such devices.

3. [Note: “Concerning the lay order” (4).] We wish the same measure to be observed in the lay order concerning this matter; namely, if anyone has purchased another person’s property [Note: One witness reads “authority”] who is able to perform military service [Note: One fragment reads “who is able”; another “property”], or if it has come to him by any means, and he has left it to that person for use, then, if he is negligent concerning military service, he shall be distrained by the count through those properties [Note: One witness reads “distrained”], so that public usefulness may not be diminished in any respect [Note: One witness omits “public”; another reads “may not be diminished in usefulness.”].

4. [Note: “Concerning a brother’s inheritance” (4).] We decree concerning those brothers who, within our territories and those of Italy (Romania) [Note: One witness reads “romania”], succeed to their paternal or maternal inheritance: if it happens that one of them has been assigned to ecclesiastical service, and therefore the one who ought to serve in the secular sphere, in order to evade defending our kingdom, has declined to receive a share of the property within our territories [Col. 0479C] [Note: One witness reads “a share”], thereby avoiding compulsion, wherever his count finds him, we grant the count authority to distrain him.

The man must first provide sureties until his hearing, so that he may pay our ban [Note: One witness omits this; another reads “pay it”]. But if he cannot find a surety [Note: Other witnesses read “sureties”], he shall be held in the count’s custody until he finds sureties or has paid our ban [Note: One witness reads “until the ban has been paid”; another “has it paid.”].

5. Concerning free men who transfer their movable property into another’s power so that their plaintiff cannot pledge them, it pleases us that their property be confiscated until they come before the court and render justice. But if they refuse to come, their property shall be dealt with according to the capitulary of our lord and father [Note: One witness reads “this”]; for, after the property itself has been assessed [Note: One witness reads “the assessment”], compensation shall be made to the claimant for the loss [Note: One witness reads “the claimant’s loss”].

As for the person who received the movable property [Note: One witness reads merely “the movable property”; others “received”], if he cannot prove under oath [Note: One witness reads “prove the oath”] that he did not receive it in order to delay another’s justice, let him pay our ban [Note: One witness reads “pay it.”].

6. [Note: “Concerning brothers living in common” (4).] Concerning brothers who live together in their paternal or maternal inheritance [Note: One witness reads “or,” others “and”], unwilling to divide their property, on the pretext that only one of them should go on military campaign [Note: One witness reads “go”; another omits the phrase], we wish the following rule: if there is only one, let him go; if there are two, likewise; if there are three, let one remain; and if the number of brothers grows beyond three, let one always remain for the care of the household and the cultivation of their common property [Note: One witness reads “for domestic care”; another “for the improvement of the property”].

But if any dispute arises among them as to which of them ought to undertake the expedition [Note: One witness reads “which of them ought to undertake the expedition”; another “we prohibit anyone from remaining”], we prohibit any of them from remaining. Their own law shall likewise be observed concerning their age. The same condition shall also apply to their nephews [Note: One witness reads “and to their nephews”; another has a corrupt reading].

7. [Note: “Concerning witnesses” (4).] Let those who do not have the means from which, if convicted of giving false testimony, they can pay the full legal composition [Note: One witness omits “full”; another explains it as the wergild] be admitted as witnesses in none of these matters: concerning freedom, inheritance, or ownership of slaves and lands, or concerning homicide [Note: One witness spells this “omicide”] and arson [Note: V, Vn., and E. add “except forest fire”].

8. [Note: “Concerning oath-takers” (4).] We decree that all oath-takers shall swear individually [Note: One witness reads “together.”].

9. [Note: “Concerning an oath” (4).] Whoever pays an oath-penalty or a debt [Note: One witness has a corrupt reading] before sunset shall be secure thereafter.

10. [Note: “Concerning free men who surrender themselves into servitude” (4).] It seems good to us that if any free man deliberately gives himself into service, the person who receives him shall fulfill the public obligation which the man who surrendered himself into service ought, according to ancient custom [Note: One witness reads “ancient”], to have fulfilled.

11. [Note: “Concerning those who sell their property” (4).] Concerning those who possess their properties [Note: One witness has the singular], freely donate them to someone [Note: Other witnesses read “assign”], and afterward fraudulently take payment from some other unsuspecting person by selling those same properties [Note: One witness reads “the same property,” another “to another person”], if the person to whom the properties were first given, once he has learned of the transaction [Note: One witness reads “the transaction having been learned”], remains silent for a full year [Col. 0481A] and does not object, but by remaining silent out of a desire to deceive allows the purchaser to be deceived, then, if the stipulated period of one year within the country has elapsed [Note: Other witnesses read “within the year”], the earlier transfer shall be of no effect for him.

But the person who, after the first transfer, sold the properties, if he is proved while alive to have committed this deception [Note: One witness reads “to have intended this deception”], shall pay the lord’s ban [Note: One witness reads “the lord’s”], that is, sixty solidi. But if he has no ban with which to make payment [Note: One witness reads “if he does not have a ban”], he shall be flogged [Note: One witness has a corrupt reading].

12. [Note: “Concerning combatants” (4).] Those to whom combat has been adjudged by law because of some dispute [Note: One witness reads “contempt”], except in a matter of infidelity [Note: One witness adds “to the king”; Vn. gives a gloss “of the king”], shall fight with clubs [Note: V and E add “and shields”], as was previously established in the lord’s capitulary [Note: One witness reads “the lord’s capitulary.”].

13. [Note: “Concerning fugitives” (4).] Concerning fugitives, we decree that public officials shall receive nothing from the fugitive’s lord when they return him [Note: One witness reads “shall receive nothing”; another “when they have returned him”; other witnesses omit the final words].

14. It seems good to us concerning the half-free [aldiones] that the law provides, so shall it be [Note: Witnesses variously read “so shall they be,” “so shall it be done,” or “let him do so.”].

[Col. 0481A] In the Codex of Saint Paul there follow the names of Lombards assembled in the court of a certain count, who swore and subscribed that they would observe the promulgated laws.

Ortgrimo, gastald. He swore. [Col. 0481B] Peter, scabinus, likewise. Andrew, scabinus. Bruno. Urso, the child. Raginard. Urso, gastald. Grimoald. Audefred. Urso. Ambrose. Gauso. Likewise Aufred. Leo, son of Walprand. Arderig. Boso. Nordeman. Aldo. Ardeman. Leo, son of Andrew. Ardeman. Likewise another Andrew. [Col. 0481C] Landepert, notary. Urso, notary. Pertefus. Ladin. Sasprand. Leo. Bunia. Adalprand. Ando. Likewise Pertefus. Giso. Gaurentius. Arnigaus. Ripert. Landefred. …to [Note: Perhaps “...so,” “...co,” or “...io”; possibly Britcio, see below.] Gunfred. Ahistulf. Maring. [Col. 0481D] Peter. Adalluis. Froimund. Gausprand. Roipert. Ervig. Donesdei. Allold. Heldeprand. Alluid. Teudelas. Apolinar. Likewise Andrew. Ladin. Mauro. Peter. Anso, son of Andrew. Gaido. Landar. Guntul. Farag. Caterv. Ausar. Tragulf. Roprand. Ladin. Likewise Caterv. Heldebert. Peter. Andrew. Sax. Tarro. Leomall. Peter. Deusdedi. Liupald. Adalobald. Landepert. Manfred. Giselprand. Rachipert. Gunteramn. Liupand. [Col. 0482A] Rago. Pilich. Likewise Ladin. Gisulf. Urso. Wippil. [Col. 0482B] Zarald. Likewise Britcio. Hilpert. Honorific. Alprand. Anto. Christian. Andrew. Leo. Alfard. Peter. Roselm. Postfred. Berterig. Heldebert. Rotchild. Urso. Gumprand. Urso. [Col. 0482C] And another Urso. Stephen. Urso. Urso of Cornitulus. Anso. Adelmo. Teud. Tasprand. Lucian. Walprand. Ragimbod. Dono. Verbod. Tachiprand. Aderald. And Waning. Peter. Aripald. Garimar, notary. [Col. 0482D] Appo. Gudipert. Adalo. Walpul. Adelpert. Sindefred. Peredeo. Arauald. Lanfred. Peter. John. Leopr and. Peter. Ansegis. Tachipert. Lagipert. Graffilad. Peter. Almeprand. Lampul. Urso. Scelestine. Austrefus. Hildul. Ansepert. Peter. Raginald. Gauseprand. Heldeprand. Adrol. Leopert. Arduis. Urso. John. Ficaust. Ansol. Allo. Ardepert. Ardepert. Tagul. Landfred. Gumprand. Cano. Hermul. Adin. Liudefred. Heriand. John.

## EXCERPTED CAPITULARIES  
*(A.D. 826, June, Ingelheim)*

[Col. 0481]

From the capitularies reported by Ansegisus in Book II, beginning with chapter 29, and there followed by the capitulary of Aachen of A.D. 825, scarcely any place remains for these except the year 826 and the twofold assembly at Ingelheim, one held on the Kalends of June and the other in the middle of October. The chapters have been excerpted from the acts of the councils held by order of Charlemagne in the year 813—namely, the council of Mainz, canons 6, 7, 36, 41, and 47; Chalon, chapters 5, 18, 46, 51, and 52; Tours, chapters 41, 49, and 50; and Arles, chapters 19, 20, and 21. Chapters 1 and 2 of the seventh constitution of the emperor Julian were prefixed. The disasters and portents by which the Frankish kingdom had already been afflicted for several years, and by which the emperor’s mind had been terrified, may seem to have brought it about that these provisions acquired the force of law.

[Col. 0483A] 1. [Note: Burchard, who copied part of this chapter, says that he received it “from the council at Senlis, in the presence of King Louis, chapter 5.” Baluze.] No church established under Roman jurisdiction (Julian, Novel 7, chapter 1), nor hospice, nor house for the poor, nor hospital, nor orphanage, nor home for the aged, nor foundling home, nor monastery of either monks or holy women, having an abbot or abbess, may alienate immovable property—whether a house, field, garden, rustic slave, or civic bread [Note: Those elsewhere called “gradiles,” because they were openly received from the steps of the palace. See Cujacius, Book XXVI of the Observations, chapter 17, and Jacobus Gothofredus, Notes on Books 2, 4, and 6 of the Theodosian Code, concerning civic grain and gradile bread. ID.]—or bind it to creditors by way of a special mortgage.

The word “alienation” includes a sale, gift, exchange, and a perpetual emphyteutic lease [Note: Janus a Costa, on Book I of the Decretals, p. 261: “By the term alienation is understood every perpetual transfer, and every condition imposed upon ecclesiastical property. For I think that the passage which troubles learned men in the chapter ‘Nulli’ must be interpreted in this way: the word alienation includes a sale, etc.” ID.]. But all priests without exception must abstain from such alienation, fearing the penalties threatened by the Leonine constitution: namely, that the purchaser must restore the property to the venerable place to which it had previously belonged, together with the fruits and other profits produced in the intervening period; while the church’s steward must repay every gain he obtained from such prohibited alienation or by which he caused the church loss, so that thereafter he may no longer be steward.

Not only he himself but also his successors shall be bound by this, whether the chief steward himself alienated the property or, seeing the bishop alienating it, failed to prohibit him; all the more so if he consented. The notary who drew up such prohibited instruments must be sent into perpetual exile. The magistrates who admitted the same instruments, and the officials who assisted in having gifts or other alienations entered in the records and confirmed through legal proceedings [Col. 0483C], must surrender not only their magistracies but also their rank and possessions.

The constitution, however, remits what was done in the past; but it excepts certain contracts, which it explains in the following chapters, through which the immovable property of churches may also be alienated.

An exenodochium is a venerable place in which pilgrims are received. A ptochotrophium is a venerable place in which poor and infirm people are fed. A nosochomium is a venerable place in which sick people are treated. An orphanotrophium is a venerable place in which children deprived of their parents [Col. 0484A] are fed. A gerontochomium is a venerable place in which poor people who are infirm solely because of old age are cared for. A brephotrophium is a venerable place in which infants are nourished.

2. [Note: Burchard attributes this chapter to the same council of Senlis to which he had assigned the preceding chapter. His deception misled the author of the gloss on this chapter in Book III of the Decretals, under the title “Concerning the exchange of property,” where it is written: “It was asked in this council whether the Church could exchange immovable property with a prince. The council decreed [Col. 0484C] that if the prince should wish to exchange immovable property with holy places and receive another property from them, and make the exchange by common consent, this is lawful, provided that a reasonable cause demands it, that the property furnished by the prince is greater or at least equal, and that an imperial sanction be promulgated concerning this exchange.” See the notes of Antonius Augustinus on this passage in the First Collection of the Decretals. ID.] If a prince wishes to grant immovable property to a holy place (same source, chapter 2) and receive another immovable property from it, and in that manner conclude an exchange, he may do so by the divine pragmatic sanction promulgated by him [Note: “By a precept,” as people spoke in the age of the capitularies. Such a precept of the emperor Arnulf for the Church of Passau is found in volume I of the Salzburg Metropolis, p. 350. ID.].

3. Therefore, in order to preserve the harmony of this peace (Council of Mainz, chapter 6), it pleased us concerning orphans and poor people who are said, rightly or wrongly, to have lost the inheritance belonging to them by law through their paternal or maternal right: if anywhere such persons are found whose fathers or mothers made them disinherited through their transfers, whether at the persuasion or request of others or by any device, we wish and decree that the matter be wholly corrected, insofar as it belongs to us or to our authority, according to God’s will and your holy admonition and consideration. Thus, if anything of this kind should be found outside the sphere of our office, we may dare to call upon your clemency so that it may be corrected.

4. [Note: This constitution was repeated in the Council of Mainz of A.D. 847, chapter 18. ID.] For the provision of the poor (Council of Mainz, chapter 7), for whom we must take care, it pleased us that neither bishops, abbots, counts, vicars, judges, nor anyone at all should dare, under any evil pretext or through evil contrivance, to buy or forcibly take away the property of the poor or the less powerful. Whoever among them wishes to purchase anything must do so publicly in court, before suitable witnesses and with proper justification. Wherever the contrary is found to have occurred, the act shall be entirely corrected by our order.

5. We have decreed that the appointed feast days of the year be celebrated (Council of Mainz, chapter 36): namely, that the Lord’s day of Easter [Note: These words are not found in Regino. I think they imply that the faithful were to pass the Easter feast days without luxury and drunkenness, as he teaches Christians. But today everything has been changed in the opposite direction. See the notes on Agobard, p. 21. ID.] be venerated with all honor and sobriety; likewise, we have decreed that the whole of that week be observed; that the day of the Lord’s Ascension be fully celebrated; and Pentecost in the same manner as Easter.

We decree one day for the feast of the nativity of the apostles Peter and Paul; the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist; the Assumption of Saint Mary; the dedication of Saint Michael; the feast of Saint Remigius; Saint Martin; and Saint Andrew; four days for the Nativity of the Lord; the octave of the Lord; the Epiphany of the Lord; [Note: In former times this was the only feast of Saint Mary celebrated in the Church. The Assumption, Nativity, and then the Conception, Presentation, Annunciation, and Visitation were added later. The ingenious diligence of later generations went still further and discovered the feast of the Betrothal of Saint Mary, whose author was Peter Auratus, of the Dominican brotherhood. In 1546 he composed the office for this new feast and offered it to Paul III for approval, as Ferreolus Locrius testifies in Book VI, chapter 4, of Maria Augusta. Baluze.] and the Purification of Saint Mary. We have also decreed that the feasts of those martyrs or confessors be observed whose holy bodies rest in each parish.

6. Churches established in ancient times must not be deprived either of tithes or of their other possessions, nor may these be assigned to new oratories (Council of Mainz, chapter 41).

7. Then we commanded that each godfather or spiritual kinsman instruct his spiritual children in the Catholic faith (Council of Mainz, chapter 47).

8. In accordance with the Apostle’s words (Council of Chalon V), priests must be blameless, adorned with good conduct, and must by no means devote themselves to shameful profits, in accordance with what Scripture says: “No one serving as a soldier for God entangles himself in secular affairs, so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself.” They must abstain not only from shameful profits and usury themselves, but also instruct the peoples subject to them to abstain.

9. We have been told (Council of Chalon, chapter 18) that in some places bishops and counts receive pledges from incestuous persons and from those who do not pay tithes, and from priests for certain negligences, and divide the money among themselves. We have decreed that this be entirely abolished, lest an opportunity for avarice be created. We have established that incestuous persons be punished with penance according to the canonical sentence; and that those who, after repeated admonitions and preaching by priests, neglect to pay tithes be excommunicated. We do not wish them to be compelled by oath, because of the danger of perjury.

[Col. 0485C] 10. Great discernment must be exercised in receiving the body and blood of the Lord (Council of Chalon, chapter 46). Care must be taken lest, if reception is delayed excessively, this prove destructive to the soul, since the Lord says: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves.” But if it is received indiscriminately, we must fear what the Apostle says: “Whoever eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself.”

Therefore, according to that same Apostle’s instruction, a person must examine himself and then eat of that bread and drink from the cup. Specifically, abstaining for several days from the works of the flesh and purifying body and soul, he should prepare himself to receive so great a sacrament, following the example of David, who, unless he had declared that he had abstained from marital relations since yesterday and the day before yesterday, would certainly not have received the bread of the Presence from the priest.

[Col. 0486A] 11. Since it is evident that people of various conditions exist in the Church (Council of Chalon, chapter 51)—nobles and commoners, slaves, tenant farmers, inquilines, and other such classes—it is necessary that all clerics or laymen placed over them act toward them kindly and treat them mercifully, whether in exacting labor from them or in receiving taxes and certain dues. They should know that these people are their brothers and that, together with them, they have one Father, God, to whom they cry: “Our Father, who art in heaven”; and one mother, the holy Church, which gives them birth from the undefiled womb of the sacred font.

Therefore the most merciful discipline and suitable governance must be applied to them: discipline, so that by living without discipline they may not offend their creator; governance, so that, deprived of the assistance of their superiors in the daily necessities of life [Col. 0486B], they may not waste away.

12. Women and abbesses of such character ought to be placed over women’s monasteries and entrusted with them (Council of Chalon, chapter 52) that they know how to guard both themselves and the flock subject to them with great religious devotion and holiness. They must not cease to benefit those over whom they preside, but must watch over themselves and over them as holy vessels prepared for the Lord’s service.

She must present herself to her subjects in such a manner—in conduct, clothing, and every aspect of communal life—that she may provide guidance for them as they proceed toward the heavenly kingdoms. She must also know that, for those whom she has accepted under her governance, she will have to render an account in the sight of the Lord.

13. Incestuous persons, parricides, and homicides are found among us in great numbers—alas, for sorrow! (Council of Tours, chapter 41). Some of them, however, refuse to listen to the admonitions of priests and wish to persist in their former crimes. Those who refuse to be recalled by the life-giving warnings of priests ought to be restrained from such wicked conduct through the discipline of secular power. We have already excommunicated some of them, but, treating this lightly, they have persisted in the same crimes. Therefore let your gentleness determine what should henceforth be done with such people.

14. The lords of subjects must be admonished (Council of Tours, chapter 49) to act toward their dependents piously and mercifully; not to condemn them on any unjust pretext, oppress them by force, or unjustly take away their small possessions; nor to exact cruelly and impiously the very dues that ought to be returned to their subjects.

15. So that laypeople may receive communion at least three times a year, if not more frequently [Note: From this passage Vadianus inferred in Book VI of On the Eucharist, p. 216, that under Louis the Pious laypeople began to abstain from frequent communion in the body and blood of the Lord, whereas shortly before—namely, under Charlemagne—communion had been more frequent throughout the churches. He derives this abuse from the practice of private Masses and from the monks’ greed. His own words should be quoted:

“Under Louis, son of Charles, around the year 815 from the birth of Christ, the practice of private Mass became so widespread that, although shortly before—as we have said—communion had been more frequent throughout the churches, the prince was compelled to enact a law that laypeople should receive communion at least three times a year. So completely did each person shift onto another his own responsibility for receiving the Eucharist—while that other claimed that he could receive it on behalf of others—that what the faith and piety of all demanded was entrusted to the care of a few, as though they merited on behalf of others, and not without the addition of profit. This raised many monasteries, especially Benedictine ones, to the wealth which they now enjoy so splendidly and with such security.”

It is regrettable that this observation, which is false, escaped a learned man. Had he consulted the ancient Gallican canons, he would have found that the laity’s abstention from communion is much older than could be assigned to the time of Louis the Pious. For Canon 18 of the Council of Agde says expressly: “Laypeople who do not receive communion at Christmas, Easter, and Pentecost must not be believed to be Catholics or counted among Catholics.”

Moreover, the constitution of Louis reported by Vadianus is copied word for word from the Third Council of Tours, held under Charlemagne. Nor should this custom be thought to have arisen from a belief that had penetrated the minds of people of that age—that the faithful could receive the Eucharist through a substitute, namely, through the person who sacrifices for himself and the people and offers the oblations to God on the altar. Rather, it arose from the lukewarmness of Christians, whose bad consciences troubled them, as Bishop Fulbert of Chartres says in Letter 83, speaking of priests who do not communicate as often as they celebrate Mass.

John Aventinus, Annals of Bavaria, Book IV, p. 367, going astray in another direction, attributes this law to Charlemagne and thinks that it prohibited laypeople—whom he calls profane in Latin—from receiving the Eucharist more than three times a year. “He also decreed,” he says, “that it was not pleasing for the profane person to eat more than three times a year from the sacred banquet which we call the Eucharist.” Baluze.] or three times a year, laypeople receive communion (Council of Tours, chapter 50), unless perhaps someone is prevented by some more serious crime [Note: Regino adds: “that is, at Easter, the Nativity of the Lord, and Pentecost.” Burchard, Ivo, and Gratian do the same. But these words are not found in the Council of Tours, from which this chapter is taken. They are Regino’s interpretation, derived from an ancient synodal admonition, which reads: “Admonish all the faithful to approach communion of the body and blood of the Lord three times a year, that is, at the Nativity of the Lord, Easter, and Pentecost.” See also the inquiry concerning the life and conduct of laypeople, chapter 56, in Regino, at the beginning of Book II. Burchard, moreover, attributes this constitution to Pope Fabian. ID.].

16. Let parents instruct their children, and let the godparents diligently instruct those whom they receive from the baptismal font (Council of Arles, canon 19): the former, because they begot them and they were given to them by the Lord; the latter, because they stand as their guarantors in faith.

[Note: Godparents are those who present persons to be baptized and receive them, once baptized, from the sacred font, as Hugo Menard says in his Notes on the Book of Sacraments, p. 107. Jesse of Amiens, in his booklet On the Order of Baptism, chap. 1: “Let the men or women who receive the infants at their fonts sign them—that is, the godfathers or godmothers.” An anonymous-author homily for the Ascension of the Lord in the very old manuscript of the Church of Lyons: “What should be said about little children who, when they are baptized, have neither the understanding to believe nor the ability to answer for themselves? There is no question about adults, because they know how to answer for themselves. The solution is easy. Little children, who do not yet know how to speak, deserve to receive remission of sins through the faith of those who receive them from the sacred font. And certainly it is fitting that those who are stained by the sin of their carnal parents should be saved through the faith of their spiritual parents.” Amalarius, archbishop of Trier, in his letter to Charlemagne, chap. 2: “We teach the Lord’s Prayer to godfathers and godmothers, so that they may likewise teach those whom they are to receive for sacred baptism.” Chapter 4: “Let priests, acolytes, godfathers, or godmothers make that sign upon their foreheads.” Likewise chapter 15: “Then we examine the godfathers and godmothers to see whether they can sing the Lord’s Prayer and the Creed.” Council of Rheims, in Regino, book I, chap. 272: “Let the priest announce to all godfathers that they are indebted to their godchildren, and so forth.” In Ivo, part VI, chap. 158, *patrimis* is read. But it must be corrected from Regino and from the old manuscript exemplar of Saint Victor in Paris. In the same way, the first chapter of the Second Addition must be corrected, where *patroni* is read instead of *patrini*.]

[Col. 0488A] 17. That churches established in ancient times be deprived neither of tithes nor of any other possession (C. 20).

18. That, concerning the burial of the dead in basilicas, the constitution established by the ancient Fathers be observed (C. 21).

[Note: That is, as I think, in canon 6 of the Council of Nantes. For Regino, after reporting this chapter of ours, immediately transcribes that Nantian canon, as though he wished to show what is meant here by “the constitution of the ancient Fathers.”]

CAPITULARY OF LOUIS AND LOTHAIR  
(October 826)

[Col. 0487]

I have judged that these chapters, which Ansegisus reports last, namely in the third appendix, should be assigned to the year 826 and therefore to the assembly at Ingelheim, at which Ermoldus testifies that Lothair was present. This appears not far from the truth, as is indicated by the names of Heiminus and Manegoldus, royal envoys mentioned in the royal *missaticum* (district) of Besançon in 825.

[Col. 0487D] 1. Let Benedictus remain silent forever concerning his complaint.

2. Concerning the estate which Bishop Gehirfredus [Note: of Münster?] claims from Count Liutrigus: if our envoys find that he has justice on his side, let them not permit Liutrigus, by the investiture of Lord Charles, to obstruct his right.

3. Concerning the forest which Count Autharius wishes to possess, although it is said not previously to have existed there: we wish our envoys to investigate the truth of the matter and, according to what they find to be just, settle it by our authority.

[Col. 0488D] 4. Concerning the case of Count Rothmundus: let him be permitted to swear his oath here at the palace, since, because of the service assigned to him for us, he was unable to observe the appointed hearing within his homeland.

5. Concerning the two women who brought the documents: Heiminus and Monoaldus are to be questioned whether they belonged to the church or to the fisc.

6. Odo the cupbearer is to be questioned concerning his forest.

[Col. 0489A] 7. Concerning the property which the margrave transferred to Boso’s son or to other men: we wish those to whom it was transferred to receive their investiture and, in addition, confirmation.

8. Concerning the property which a certain woman transferred to Queen Hildegard, and the portion which she is said unjustly to have lost after reserving it for herself: we wish the charter of transfer to be sought and examined, and then let it be determined what she ought to possess.

9. Concerning the complaint which Helisachar and Heiminus have against Maginarius: we wish our envoys to settle it according to justice and equity.

10. Concerning the complaint of Count Hildebrand, that his men of the county refuse to provide post-horse service (*paravereda*): we wish our envoys to investigate this among those men who reside in that same county and are not liable to provide it, as well as among the neighboring counts; and if they find that those men are indeed liable to provide it, let them order them, by our command, to provide it.

[Col. 0489]

CAPITULARIES OF THE EMPERORS CHARLES THE GREAT, LOUIS, AND LOTHAIR, COLLECTED BY ANSEGISUS, ABBOT OF FONTENELLE

[Col. 0489]

Pertz’s Notice

[Col. 0489B] The capitularies of Charles, Louis, and Lothair, “written here and there on various little sheets over the course of different periods, as many as he could find,” Ansegisus, abbot of Fontenelle, an outstanding man and one of the highest authority among his people [Note: An account of his life and deeds survives in the *Deeds of the Abbots of Fontenelle*; cf. *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, *Scriptores*, vol. II, pp. 293–300.], proposed, as he himself says, “out of his great affection for the aforesaid most glorious princes and out of love for their most holy offspring, and also for the welfare of Holy Church, to gather into one little book.” His work, issued in January of the year 827, consists of four books.

In compiling them, Ansegisus used capitularies, most of which we find preserved down to our own time in books written in the age of Charles and Louis. Yet he omitted many of those which we have reported above, while including several that would have been consigned to oblivion without his work. His collection consisted of the following:

- Ecclesiastical capitulary of 789, with chapter 40 omitted.
- Capitularly of Pavia of 801, chapters 11 and 12.
- Chapters of 803 to be added to the Salic Law.
- Minor chapters of 803, with chapters 14, 18, and 19 omitted.
- Chapters 5, 7, and 8 of 803 to be added to the Ripuarian Law.
- The double capitulary at Thionville of 805, with ecclesiastical chapters 7 and 8 omitted, but with secular chapter 11 copied twice.
- Capitularly at Nijmegen of 806, with chapters 2, [lacuna], and 11 omitted.
- Capitularly of Aachen of 806, with chapters 5 and 6 omitted.
- Extracts from the canon of 806, with chapter 2 omitted and chapters 6–9 placed twice.
- Capitularly of Aachen of 809.
- Capitularly of the priests of 809.
- Capitularly of Aachen of 810.
- [Col. 0490B] Capitularly concerning military matters of 811.
- Capitularly of Boulogne of 811.
- Capitularly of Aachen of 812.
- General capitulary of Aachen of 817—namely, the ecclesiastical chapters, those to be added to the laws, those to be written separately, and those given to the envoys.
- Capitularly at Thionville of 821.
- Constitution of Aachen of 825, together with the chapters of the envoys.
- Extracted chapters of 826.
- Chapters of Louis and Lothair issued in 826.

Ansegisus distributed these materials among four books and appendices in the following manner: he placed chapters that seemed to possess some importance, preserving their chronological order, in the appropriate books; he placed smaller or less important chapters in a double appendix of ecclesiastical and secular laws. After the work had been completed, the recently issued edict of Louis and Lothair was added under the title of a third appendix.

He nevertheless erred by placing the capitularies of 803 in the first and third books and postponing them in both appendices to the chapters of 805 and 806; by placing Louis’s ecclesiastical capitulary of 817 in the first book among Charles’s laws; and by placing the capitulary at Thionville of 821 at the beginning of the fourth book. The chapters of the third book numbered 89 and 90, those of the fourth book numbered 71 and 72, chapters 33–35 of the first appendix, and chapter 38 of the second appendix also appear to have been added after the work had already been brought nearly to completion, since chronologically they should have been placed earlier. These additions, however, do not disturb the general arrangement of the work, which it will be useful to set out here.

APPENDIX III. Capitularly of October 826.

[Col. 0491B] Since chapters that had previously been joined together were separated by this arrangement of the work, it was inevitable that the wording of individual earlier chapters, once detached from its former connection, would require some correction. Ansegisus dealt with this matter chiefly by altering initial words where necessary—for example, in Book I, chapters 64, 67, 70, 73, 116, and 126, and Book IV, chapter 15.

He also went further, correcting or changing certain words with attention to grammatical usage—for example, *satagimini* in the preface, *eodem synodo* in Book I, chapter 3, *quae* in chapter 5, *vetent* in chapter 161, and *in utilitate nostra* in Book III, chapter 3; compare Book IV, chapter 23. For greater clarity, he supplied words or improved the connection of the sentences—for example in Book I, chapters 25, 71, 75, 113, 114, and 162, and Book III, chapters 1, 2, and 23.

Finally, he assumed the role of legislator and often removed from the laws material that had been proposed only temporarily and therefore lacked the force of permanent law, or that might already have appeared wholly inappropriate or superfluous for another reason. This applies to Book I, chapter 61, where he omitted the words “as the Guntbodingi do”; to Book I, chapters 126 and 135, where the words “in the present year” and “until now” were removed; and to Book III, chapter 6, where the collectors of tolls appointed by Charles—since by 827 they were no longer the same men as in 805—were omitted, along with the place-name Schesla, whose market right had perhaps already been withdrawn.

Moreover, in Book III, chapter 12, Ansegisus did not include the sentences “But if there should be something about which there is doubt, let it be inquired into at our next assembly, which we shall hold with those same envoys”; in chapter 13, “Nevertheless, those denarii which have now been minted, if they are of full weight and pure, are to be accepted”; in chapter 36, the words *foras mitio*; in chapter 56, the words *elegantur mansueti et boni*; and in chapter 83, he changed *quater in anno mense* into *quater in uno mense*.

When this work, established in this way, appeared to be extremely useful for administering the state, it was soon received with public approval. For scarcely two years had passed when, in 829, at the assembly of Worms, Louis and Lothair first began to commend it. From that time it acquired the force of law throughout the empire and gradually concentrated almost the whole authority of the older capitularies in itself. Thus, when later emperors—from Otto the Great and Frederick I to Otto IV—spoke of the capitularies of earlier kings, of the laws of the emperors Charles and Louis, and of the edicts of Charlemagne, we can scarcely doubt that they had Ansegisus’s books especially before their eyes and in their hands.

There is therefore no reason to wonder that a book supported by such endorsements was copied repeatedly during the succeeding centuries. Thirty-eight manuscripts survive today, copied in the ninth, tenth, eleventh, twelfth, and even fifteenth centuries: twelve in our Germany, together with Alsace and Switzerland; four in Italy, two of them seized from Germany; two recently purchased from the Dutch in Britain; and twenty in France. If one adds the lost Trier manuscript, the manuscript at Chiny-Werga, and the books cited by Baluzius whose later fate is unknown to us—namely, one in the Spanish March, one in Belgium, and four in France—the total rises to forty-six.

Although all of these generally agree with one another and with the genuine capitularies of the emperors, some diverge slightly from the others by adding or omitting one or another chapter. Thus, the formerly Corbie manuscript places, as a separate chapter in Book I, the canon of Pope Siricius from which chapter 51 of the ecclesiastical capitulary of 789 was taken. It has two followers in this respect, the Strasbourg manuscript and the second Herold manuscript.

The formerly Freising manuscript, now royal and Munich, inserted several chapters—especially of Lothair—into the text: after Book I, chapter 78, the chapters of Olonnus of 823, followed by Book III, chapters 1 and 2; after Book I, chapter 99, chapter 50 of the ecclesiastical capitulary of 789; after I, 101, the Olonnus capitulary of 823; then Book III, chapters 3, 4, and 5; after II, 15, the general Olonnus capitulary of 825, chapters 1, 2, 3, and 6; after III, 41, the chapter concerning false witnesses and chapter 2 of the Pavia capitulary of 832; after IV, 71, chapter 4 of the general Olonnus capitulary of 825; and after IV, 74, chapter 5 of that same capitulary.

The formerly Augsburg manuscript, now royal and Munich, contains nearly the same material. It refers these chapters, except Olonnus 825, chapter 4, in the rubrics of the books to the end of the text, adding after Book IV, 26, chapter 5 of the Salic capitulary of 803, together with many further chapters drawn from ecclesiastical canons and from the capitularies of Pippin, Charles, Louis, Lothair, and Charles the Bald.

Omitting the appendices, the Schaffhausen manuscript, after Book I, 77, and the Bonn manuscript, after I, 72, insert a chapter drawn from the canons of Pope Gelasius. The Vatican, Metz, Beauvais, and Cambron manuscripts add a chapter at the end of Book II which is found in the Dijon, Norman, Rheims, Bamberg, Pithoean, and Paris manuscripts after Book IV, 14.

The Bamberg and Paris manuscripts, no. 4628 A, place at the beginning of Book I a chapter beginning, “If a slave becomes a cleric.” These same manuscripts, together with the Norman, Pithoean, and Paris manuscripts, append one chapter absent from the other manuscripts to I, 99; two to II, 32; one to IV, 24; and one to IV, 69. Baluzius noted that the same chapters were added in more recent ink to the Rheims manuscript.

We have published I, 99b above under the year 817. II, 32b may appear to have dropped out among the laws of Louis II of 850, between chapters 9 and 10. We published IV, 24b above under the year 817. IV, 14b is cited by Benedictus in Book I, chapter 186. We have not discovered II, 32c or IV, 69b elsewhere.

Baluzius observed in his preface that manuscripts of this kind were cited in the years 864 and 873 by Charles, son of Louis I; in 868 by Hincmar, archbishop of Rheims; and in 909 by the Fathers of the Council of Trosly, and that they therefore enjoyed public authority in Gaul at that time. Yet that they depart from Ansegisus’s genuine work is shown by the chapter numbers cited at the assembly of Worms.

A still greater difference among the manuscripts of Ansegisus lies in the fact that while most of them recognize Charles, Louis, and Lothair as the legislators in the prefaces to the individual books, others, after deleting Lothair’s name, altered the text as far as seemed necessary as a result.

It is clear that such books could not have been produced before the end of 830, when it was again decided that Lothair’s name should be omitted from public documents. Nevertheless, the first exemplar of this second edition must have been produced in the immediately following years and before Louis’s death. It is entirely unclear to us whether its author should, with Baluzius, be identified as Ansegisus. We know only that this man, who rendered distinguished service concerning German affairs, died in the third year of that decade, namely on 20 July 833.

For a century and a half, learned men generally believed that the book of the first edition had been translated into German during the Middle Ages. If one examines the foundation of this belief, however, one finds that Browerus, who is said to have examined only one such manuscript, wrote only about a translation of Book IV, chapter 18.

The manuscript formerly preserved in the library of the cathedral church of Trier no longer existed even in Baluzius’s time; therefore the reliability of Brower’s edition cannot be tested. When I referred the matter to our Jacob Grimm, that outstanding man corrected Brower’s reading for our use and most willingly allowed it to be shared with scholars. We therefore present both editions of that translation, composed in the Trier dialect at the end of the ninth or beginning of the tenth century.

BROWER’S EDITION

[Note: The following two paragraphs are printed as a line-by-line translation in Migne.]

[Editorial note: The following are recorded variant readings in the Old High German text, rather than separate continuous text: *Selues/Thesselues*; *cebekerine/Cebeuuandelene*; *analige/anaualle*; *gesunduruth/nebaboda. neo.*; *Samithu/samidu*; *themo/himo*; *eruetha/eruida*; *vollacaman/voloquoman*; *vuizzut/vuizcut*; *vona/vane*; *vuizzethallikhen/ahter*; *ergeuen/vuitirigeuen*.]

### Translation of the Old High German text

That every free man may have the power to give his property wherever he wishes.

If anyone wishes to give his property for the salvation of his soul, to some venerable place, to a relative, or to anyone else, and at that time is within the county in which that property lies, let him strive to make a lawful transfer.

But if, at the time when he wishes to give it, he is outside that county—whether in the army, at the palace, or in any other place—let him obtain suitable witnesses, either from his own countrymen or from others who live under the same law as he does. If he cannot obtain them, let him use others of the best sort who can be found there. In their presence let him make the transfer of his property and give security for the investiture to the one who receives the transfer; let him make the investiture.

After this transfer has been made in this manner, the heir of the giver shall have no power to reclaim any of the aforesaid property. Moreover, the giver himself shall personally provide security for that same investiture, so that no opportunity remains to the heir to alter the transfer, but rather necessity compels him to complete it.

If he has not yet divided his property with his co-heirs, this shall not hinder him. If his co-heir is unwilling to do so voluntarily, let him be compelled, either by the count or by the count’s envoy, to make the division with the person to whom the deceased wished his inheritance to pass. And if he requested that it be transferred to any church, let his co-heir have from that inheritance, together with that church, the share which he ought to have had with his other co-heir.

Let this also be observed with respect to a father, a son, and a grandson, until they reach the lawful age. Afterward, the property itself shall return to the immunity of that church.

JACOB GRIMM’S RECENSION
