### Translation of the Old High German text

That every free man may have the power to give his property wherever he wishes.

If anyone wishes to transfer his property for the salvation of his soul, to a venerable place, to a relative, or to anyone else, and at that time is within the county in which the property lies, let him strive to make a lawful transfer. If, however, at the time when he wishes to give it, he is outside that county—whether in the army, at the palace, or in any other place—let him obtain suitable witnesses either from his own countrymen or from others who live under the same law as he does. If he cannot obtain them, let him use others of the best sort who can be found there, and in their presence let him make the transfer of his property. Let him give security for the investiture to the person who receives the transfer and make the investiture.

After this transfer has been made in this manner, the heir shall have no power to reclaim any of the aforesaid property. Moreover, the giver himself shall personally provide security for that same investiture, so that no opportunity remains to the heir to alter the transfer, but rather necessity compels him to complete it. If he has not yet divided his property with his co-heirs, this shall not hinder him. If his co-heir is unwilling to do so voluntarily, let him be compelled, either by the count or by the count’s envoy, to make the division with the person to whom the deceased wished his inheritance to pass. And if he requested that it be transferred to any church, let his co-heir have from that inheritance, together with that church, the share which he ought to have had with his other co-heir. Let this be observed with respect to a father, a son, and a grandson until they reach the lawful age. Afterward, the property itself shall return to the immunity of that church.

[Col. 0495C] After the invention of printing, the first to publish Ansegisus was Basilius Johannes Herold, on pp. 261–347 among the books of *Origins and German Antiquities*, Basel, September 1557, folio, under the title *Frankish Law*. He divided it into five books, stitched together from the manuscripts of Ansegisus, Amerbach’s book published in 1545, and the *Lombarda*.

He added the chapter mentioned above to Book I. Book III lacks chapters 64–68, 70, 72–75, 78, 79, 83, 89, and 90, except that chapters 67 and 68 and part of chapter 65 were placed in Book IV. Book IV does indeed present all the chapters of Ansegisus, but arranged according to the pattern of the second and first titles found in the Weissenau manuscript, pp. 183–200 and 173–183. It was enlarged not only by their chapters but also by many others, interspersed and added, taken from Amerbach’s edition of the capitularies and from the *Lombarda*, as well as by Ansegisus’s three appendices.

He omitted chapter 16 of the second appendix because it had already been presented once. In Book V, entitled “The Laws of King Pippin,” he presents chapters of Pippin and other kings gathered from the *Lombarda*.

In reproducing the text, he relied chiefly on the Weissenau manuscript, which we list below as number 4. In Book I, chapters 1–76, however, he followed Amerbach, only rarely correcting his readings with the help of the Weissenau manuscript. That he also used a second manuscript of Ansegisus is shown by the appendices, which are absent from the Weissenau manuscript, and by several readings found neither in Weissenau nor in Amerbach.

Witnesses to this are Book I, chapter 82, where he presents an entire line omitted by Weissenau; the chapter added at the end of Book I, which is likewise absent there; and the reading at the end of Book III, chapter 20, where the reading of the Weissenau manuscript, written by a later hand in an erased place, agrees with the Gotha, Cambron, Vatican, Colbert, and first St Gall manuscripts.

Which manuscript that other one was is not known. In several places it comes very close to the Strasbourg manuscript, although it was different from it.

[Col. 0497A] Several years before Herold, but without his knowledge—as is shown, for example, by a comparison of the appendices in both editions—Johannes Tilius undertook an edition of the capitularies, perhaps encouraged by Amerbach’s example.

He printed the whole work of Ansegisus together with Books I and II of Benedictus the Deacon, up to the words of chapter 289, “Who is found to have committed manifest violence, no longer banishment.” He did not add the rest of Benedictus and did not publish the incomplete book.

Nevertheless, a very few copies of his work appeared after Tilius’s death. One of these, which passed from the museum of Franciscus Orontius Fincius to Stephanus Baluzius and from him to M. Krusius, is now in the university library of Göttingen and was made available for examination by our V. S. Jacob Grimm.

[Note: The title of the book is: “In the name of Christ begin the Chapters of Kings and Bishops, and especially of all the Frankish nobles, for repressing the various inventions of the newly converted as though they were faithful. With privilege. Paris, at the shop of Jacob Bogardus, under the sign of Saint Christopher, opposite the college of the Cambrai men, 1548.”]

This extremely rare book was printed in the same format and with the same type as Tilius’s edition of the ancient laws in sextodecimo, which appeared without year or place. We preserve in the royal library at Hanover a copy of that edition, given by Tilius to Antonius Schonchovius and, in 1557, by Petrus Adurnus to Laurinus.

Tilius did not use the manuscript now designated in the royal library at Paris as no. 4635 in such a way that he thought its traces must be followed everywhere. Guided by Amerbach’s book, he attempted to restore the order of the chapters which he had learned belonged to the year 789 but which Ansegisus had rearranged according to his own plan. He removed chapters that he noticed had been included more than once both in Ansegisus and in Benedictus, leaving only certain similar ones, and consequently altered the chapter numbers.

Apparently supported by manuscripts of the royal library at Paris, nos. 4995 and by the manuscript of Saint Vincent at Metz, he also incorporated into the text, within brackets, certain sentences omitted by Ansegisus and headings prefixed or appended to the capitularies.

In Ansegisus’s Book I, after our chapters 38, 50, 64, 69, and 73, he inserted six other chapters taken from the ecclesiastical capitulary of 789, which he had read in Amerbach—namely, chapters 39, 52, 66, 67, 73, and 78 of our edition—so that the number of chapters in his book reached 168.

Moreover, to chapter 57 he added the address reported above; to chapter 76 he added, from Amerbach’s p. 35, an indication of the time when the capitulary was promulgated, the note “In the time of Hadrian,” and the heading of the following capitulary which we have published above.

[Note: “In the time of Pope Hadrian and the Emperor Charlemagne, when Bishop Paulinus held the place of the Apostolic See at Aachen, this chapter was made because laymen were accustomed to divide bishoprics and monasteries for their own use, so that no bishop, abbot, or abbess would remain with anything except that they should live like canons and monks.”]

He presents forty-seven chapters in Book II, inserting two after chapter 32 but omitting chapter 45, since it contains almost the same material as chapter 34.

Book III consists of eighty-nine chapters, with chapters 89 and 90—ecclesiastical 789, chapters 66 and 73—already received into Book I, and with a chapter added at the end concerning peace in the army or within the homeland: “We decree that if in the army …” Baluzius found this only in more recent ink in the Beauvais manuscript. He also added to chapters 12, 13, and 56 the passages noted above, and to chapter 76 its heading.

In Book IV, after chapters 14, 24, and 69, he inserts one chapter in each place, and before chapters 13 and 43 he inserts headings.

[Note: These differ slightly from those reported above: “Chapters which Lord Emperor Louis constituted to be added to the Salic laws, which both the envoys and the counts must possess and make known to the others.—These are the chapters belonging especially to the mission of our envoys, for the sake of remembrance.”]

He omits chapters 73 and 74, which were already found in that same book as chapters 24 and 23.

In the first appendix he omits chapters 33 and 34, and in the second appendix chapter 38—ecclesiastical 789, chapters 52, 78, and 67—because they had already been received into Book I. He also omits chapter 16 of the second appendix because it already occurs in Book III.

Having obtained a copy of the Tilius edition, Peter Pithoeus had it printed again at Paris in 1588, in octavo, with the text nowhere altered and only the headings of the books added. Nevertheless, he acted on his own initiative in the following respect: with the help of his own Codex and the Bellovacensis, he published Benedict’s capitula in full together with the additions; on pp. 416–424, the capitula of Charles the Bald issued at Sparnacum; and, in his preface, the capitula of King Pippin repeated above. He also added a glossary, or explanation, of several more obscure words.

The Codex which he principally used, now designated among the royal Parisian manuscripts as no. 4638, does not acknowledge the name of Emperor Lothar in the prefaces. Pithoeus therefore judged that it had been wrongly added by scribes during Lothar’s reign, and that nothing belonging specifically to Lothar was found among Ansegis’s books. He was evidently unaware of what is now very well known: that the names of both emperors, Louis and Lothar, are jointly placed at the head of public charters and records from the years 825–830 [Note: Beginning in the month of December. See our Boehmer’s excellent work, *Regesta Carolorum*, Frankfurt am Main, 1833, in quarto], and consequently also of Ansegis’s book published in the year 827. The error is not harmful to the edition, which, as I noted above, is identical with the Tilius edition.

[Col. 0498B] This same edition, corrected with no very fortunate pen under the supervision of Francis Pithoeus, Peter’s son, appeared again at Paris in 1603, in octavo, and was reprinted by Lindenbrog in his *Codex of Ancient Laws* in 1613. Goldast used both the Herold and Pithoeus editions in preparing his own works.

Nearly a century having elapsed after Pithoeus, Stephen Baluzius published his edition in folio in 1677. Having sought out Codices principally from Gaul, but also from Saint Gall, Rome, and Spain, he corrected and emended the Pithoean edition on the basis of these witnesses and illustrated his own edition with an extensive commentary.

Yet—may this be said with due respect for so great a man—he did not attain his aim. Following the example of Tilius, he presented Ansegisus joined to Benedict as though they constituted a single work, displaying seven books of capitularies, and allowing the very firm authority of Ansegisus to be touched by a certain suspicion because of his association with Benedict. Moreover, seduced by Pithoeus’s opinion, he not only deleted the name of Caesar Lothar from the prefaces of the individual books [Col. 0498C], but also, following Pithoeus’s example, admitted the five capitula inserted by Tilius into Books II and IV, although he himself had learned from the Capitularium of Worms of 829 that they were not present in the genuine book of Ansegisus, and had discovered that they were absent from many Codices.

The great name of Baluzius shielded these matters, so powerfully that for a century and a half afterward no scholar dared challenge or undermine the structure of the work. Georgisch, in the *Corpus of German Law* of 1738; de Chiniac, in the second edition of Baluzius’s *Capitularia* in 1780; Canciani, in volume III of his *Ancient Barbarian Laws* of 1785; and the distinguished Walter, the most penetrating investigator of native and Roman law, in the *Corpus of German Law* published in 1824, all thought it sufficient simply to reproduce Baluzius’s edition. What we have been permitted to accomplish in this matter remains to be stated.

As for the manuscript Codices on which the new edition of the book had to rest, we had neither the will [Col. 0498D] nor the opportunity to examine again those inspected by Baluzius. For Ansegisus’s work is a collection of capitula, the very great majority of which can be found among the capitularies edited above; consequently, neither did such collation seem necessary, nor did Baluzius’s skill in transcribing Codices [Col. 0499A] appear to require it.

We were therefore content to use those he had compared, and, together with those newly acquired by us, to establish a solid foundation for the work. How far this has succeeded according to our wishes may be inferred from the fact that we have used in our edition eleven Codices unknown to Baluzius, from the ninth, tenth, eleventh, and twelfth centuries, besides having at least inspected several others. The best of them is:

### 1. Hamburgensis

Formerly Corbeiensis, then belonging to Friedrich Lindenbrog (although he did not use it in editing Ansegisus), and now in the Hamburg Public Library, no. 83, in quarto, ninth century. Besides Ansegisus, it contains the Capitularium of Worms of 829 and the Salic, Ripuarian, and Alamannic laws. It was written with such care that I would copy it out entire as the foundation of the work. The following comes very close to it:

### 1*. Gothanus

A Codex of the ducal library at Gotha, eleventh century, in folio. From folios 375–395 the entire work is written in the following order, except for the appendices and chapters IV, 71–74:

IV, 24–41; [Col. 0499B] 42–70; I, 77–104; IV, 13–33; I, 1–76; I, 105–162; II, III, IV, 1–12.

Written with great care, it almost always confirms the authority of the Hamburgensis. The belief that it was copied either from that Codex or from the same exemplar is prevented, apart from the order of the chapters already indicated, by the fact that it sometimes contains readings absent from the Hamburgensis and, when it departs from that witness, usually has other Codices agreeing with it. All its readings were noted through the work of the highly learned young scholar L. C. Bethmann of Helmstedt.

### 2. Frisingensis

A Codex of the cathedral church of Freising, now in the Royal Library of Munich, H. N. 4 (234), parchment, in quarto, folio LXXXIX, eleventh century, written by two scribes. One hand wrote Ansegisus; the other added three appendices, then the first thirteen chapters of Book II—with the heading, “Here begin the chapters which are lacking above, though they had not been omitted there”—and finally added five chapters taken from *Benedict* I, 156; the Council of Arles VI, canon 22; the Council of Tours, addition III, 91; the Capitularium of 809, II, 13; and *Benedict* I, 279.

It inserts several chapters into Ansegisus: two after I, 78; one after 99; three after 101; four after II, 15; two after III, 41; one after IV, 71; and one after 74. It writes *ostis*, *ortus*, *sollers*, *conpendium*, and so forth.

Apart from the order of the chapters, all the indices and prefaces were collated. At my urgent request, and most readily granted by the distinguished Foringer, the following passages were collated: I, 140–158; II, 29–46; III, 64–66; IV, 1–12, 71–74.

### 2 b. Augustanus

A Codex of the cathedral church of Augsburg, now in the Royal Library of Munich, no. 153, parchment, in quarto, folio CCCXVIII, eleventh century. It contains a collection of penitential and synodal canons, the Alamannic law, Ansegisus, capitularies, a letter of Paulinus of Aquileia, and a synodal letter of the Council of Milan.

Folio 215 is missing, and with it Ansegisus II, 28–29. The appendices are absent; but in their place, immediately after the end of Book IV, another hand added those chapters which, as we said, are inserted here and there in the Freising Codex, joined in the same order as there. However, what the Freising Codex presents after I, 99, the Augsburg Codex places at the end of Book I; while it omits the fourth chapter placed by the Freising Codex after II, 15.

After IV, 71 and 74, the same second hand wrote in red the headings of the chapters inserted there from the Freising Codex; the chapters themselves are placed in that addition. Our Codex adds only one chapter after IV, 26, which the Freising Codex does not contain, taken from the Capitularium of 803, Salic law 5.

In its readings it generally comes close to the Freising Codex. The same passages were voluntarily collated by the distinguished Foringer.

### 3. Scafhusanus

A parchment Codex of the library of the church at Schaffhausen, in quarto, folio XCVII, compiled by several hands in the eleventh or at the beginning of the twelfth century. After a theological treatise and the Book of Baruch, it presents the Salic law—that is, Ansegisus—together with the Capitularium of 829, and then the *Life of Louis* by Thegan, mutilated at the end.

As regards Ansegisus, which D. Bethmann collated with the Hamburgensis and Gothanus, whose authority it confirms in many places, it is far inferior to them. Its divergences are almost always either worse or plainly false, and it more often seems to incline toward the second recension in individual passages.

It reverses the order of chapters I, 28 and 87, and inserts a new chapter after I, 77. It very often omits individual, indeed several, words, generally such as do not disturb the sense when omitted. Especially at the beginnings of chapters, it adds, omits, and changes words on its own initiative, so that it seems to have done all this deliberately. Consequently, it was neither always necessary to indicate these matters nor appropriate to print its plainly false readings everywhere; nevertheless, a very large proportion of them has been recorded.

### 3 b. Bonnensis

A parchment Codex of the Bonn Library, in octavo, twelfth century, which I examined in 1826 and described in *Rheinisches Museum* I.1 (1827), pp. 158–164. From that description it appears that in Ansegisus’s work it follows no. 3 so closely that it seems to be a copy of it. Its readings recorded there that are not shared with no. 3 are so constituted that I judged the Codex not worth collating with the printed editions. The following may belong to the same class:

### 3 c. Parisinus 4417

A Codex of the Royal Library of Paris, no. 4417, ninth century, formerly Aniciensis. Like the Schaffhausen and Bonn Codices, it lacks Appendices I and III and part of the chapters of Appendix II.

### 4. Weissenaugiensis

Formerly belonging to the monastery of Weissenau, now preserved in Lindenau Castle on Lake Constance; parchment, in quarto, from the end of the ninth or the tenth century. After Ansegisus’s Books I–IV it contains a Visigothic interpretation of the Theodosian Code, several Novels of Justinian [Savigny, *Zeitschrift* II, p. 160], Erchanbert’s *Breviary* [*Monumenta Germaniae*, II, 327–330], and, on pp. 173–200, two headings of chapters.

First, on pp. 173–183, chapters numbered 1–33: Ansegisus IV, 13–14; the Capitularium on advancing the army; and Ansegisus IV, 15–33.

Then, on pp. 183–200, chapters numbered 1, 2, 36–57, 59–65, 65–70, 77, 78, 70, 72–75, 78, 79, 83–88, 90–107: Ansegisus IV, 34–57, 59–70; III, 67, 68, 70, 72–75, 78, 79, 83, 86, 89, 90, 38, 39, 43–45, 47–49, 52, 53, 55, 61, 64–66; IV, 9; III, 11, 14, 16, 26, 27.

As far as Ansegisus is concerned, its three appendices are absent. The corrections made here and there seem to have come from the same hand. It writes *intellegere*, *negare* for *necare*, and *rettulit*; the letter *h* is often omitted.

The distinguished Dr. Maier, J.U.D. of Esslingen, most generously supplied us with its collation against the printed editions. This is the Codex on which Herold’s edition of the capitularies chiefly rests.

### 5. Vaticanus 4159

A parchment Codex of the Vatican Library, no. 4159, in octavo, folio CXII, from the end of the ninth or the tenth century, elegantly written but mutilated. The entire first quaternion is missing, and the Codex ends at Book IV, chapter 31.

Apart from all the prefaces, our Bluhmius collated I, 1–5, 140–159; II, 29–30; III, 45, 64; and IV, 1–11.

### 6. Schlettstadiensis

Formerly at Schlettstadt, now in the Public Library of Strasbourg; parchment, small folio, folio CXV, ninth century, collated by the highly learned Engelhardt. After the Alamannic law it presents first Ansegisus’s Book IV, then, in a somewhat different hand, supplements to Book IV, the three appendices of Ansegisus, Books I, II, and III, and certain theological material.

It departs most markedly from the others in Book IV. There countless individual words have been supplied, changed, or omitted; entire sentences, indeed chapters, are either greatly abridged or entirely absent, so that especially toward the end of the book Ansegisus can scarcely recognize himself. It did not seem necessary to record all these matters.

Chapters entirely omitted or excessively mutilated by the first scribe were supplied at the end of Book IV by another, who completed the remaining portion of the Codex. As a result, some chapters are read twice, indeed three times, and seven chapters of this book are also repeated at the end of Book III.

In the same fourth book there are also German glosses, at chapters 5, 17, 25, 26, and 29. Book I, chapter 19, is additionally omitted, and another chapter is added after I, 162.

The Codices belonging to the first recension, besides these, are the following.

### Vaticanus Palatinus

Baluzius’s Vaticanus 1, in the Palatine Library; the Codex of Saint Vincent at Metz; and the Royal Parisian Codex designated among the Latin Supplements as no. 75, from the tenth century and very closely related to them. The latter contains the four books and Appendices I and II.

### Divionensis

The Royal Parisian Codex no. 4761, Baluzius’s Divionensis, in which the following minor chapters from the year 803 are added to Appendix III: 16, 18, and 19, of which only the first is found earlier in Book I, chapter 138 [Col. 0501A].

Although these Codices were written in the tenth century, they insert into the genuine capitularies and Ansegisus several chapters excerpted from Benedict. The Codices named next—the Gothanus alter, Bellovacensis, Camberonensis, and Rivipullensis—present Ansegisus of the earlier edition, but joined to Benedict’s books.

### G. Gothanus

The Gothanus was written by a hand from the beginning of the eleventh century at the beginning of a large volume, whose gatherings 375–395 contain the Ansegisus mentioned above under no. 1*. The beginnings of the individual books are decorated with an illuminated initial. Between the index of the first book and the preface of Charles, there is an image of an emperor seated on a throne, holding a book and a scepter.

The text of Ansegisus has been slightly altered, just as Benedict not infrequently corrected the capitula he had adopted, especially by omitting words at the beginnings of chapters, including *quoque*, *vero*, *autem*, *quidem*, *etiam*, *itaque*, *ergo*, and *deinde*. It also makes more substantial changes, for example in II, 6 and 31, and III, 20. It omits chapters I, 24 and 86, and III, 66. It more often writes *annonas* for *nonas*, as noted by D. Bethmann, who recorded its variant readings.

### Bellovacensis

The Bellovacensis, like the Gothanus, contained Ansegisus with his appendices, Benedict’s three books and Additions II, III, and IV, and, according to Baluzius, certain capitularies of Charles the Bald.

### Camb.

The Camboronensis, a Codex of a monastery in Hainaut, like the Rivipullensis in Tarraconensian Spain, contained Ansegisus and Benedict’s first book.

### Riv.

The Rivipullensis also contained several capitula of Louis I and Charles the Bald, the capitula of Walter, bishop of Orléans, several letters of Hincmar, and finally the history of the translation of Saint Stephen. Baluzius recorded the readings of both, as well as those of the Bellovacensis.

### N. Normannicus

The Normannicus, of Mont Saint-Michel “in the danger of the sea,” acknowledges Lothar among the legislators; in all other respects it agrees almost entirely with the Babenbergensis, Pithoeanus, and Parisian Codices of the second recension. It presents Ansegisus and Benedict’s Book I, together with the first 363 chapters of Book II.

To these are added:

### Aurelianensis

Now preserved in the Public Library of that city; eleventh century, parchment, in folio; formerly belonging to Saint Benedict of Fleury [the distinguished Hanel, p. 274, no. 193]. It contains the four books and Appendices I and II.

### Wergatensis

The most ancient Wergatensis, cited by Chiniac in the second edition of Baluzius, vol. I, p. 698.

### Molinaeus

The Codex of Molinaeus, according to Baluzius’s preface, vol. I, pp. 32–33.

### Trevirensis

A Codex formerly belonging to the cathedral of Trier.

### Ottobonianus

The Ottobonianus, also cited by our Bluhmius [*Archiv* V, p. 583].

### Parisinus 4628 A

The Royal Parisian Codex no. 4628 A, manuscript, tenth century. After many of the capitularies mentioned above, it contains chapters II, 32b and 32c, numbered XXXIII and XXXIIII; the decree of Childebert with a catalogue of the Frankish kings; Ansegisus’s four books and Appendix III, preceded by a chapter on a slave made a cleric; capitularies from the years 828 and 829 and others; and finally Einhard’s *Life of Charlemagne* [Col. 0501D]. It also contains IV, 14b, 24b, and 69b.

Copied from it is:

### Parisinus 4631

The Royal Parisian Codex no. 4631, manuscript, fifteenth century.

### P. Parisinus 3878

The Royal Parisian Codex no. 3878, manuscript, tenth century. After a penitential work, it contains chapters excerpted from Ansegisus’s books and from the capitularies of Charles the Bald, a fragment of the synod of Trier of 895, and several other items. I examined it at Paris. A similar Codex seems to be:

### Trecensis

Formerly belonging to Francis Pithoeus. As Baluzius notes on p. 53, it contains only excerpts from the books of Ansegisus and Benedict; it is now preserved in the Library of Montpellier; parchment, eleventh century [Haenel, p. 235, H. 137].

## The second class

The second class consists of those Codices from which the name of Caesar Lothar has been erased. Three survive in Germany, one in Rome, and the remainder in Gaul. They are the following:

### a. Sang. 2

Codex of the Library of Saint Gall, no. 728, parchment, tenth century; see volume V of our annals, p. [Col. 0502A] 210. It contains Books III and IV and the three appendices. Baluzius gives only a few of its readings.

### b. Thu.

The Codex which Baluzius called the Thuaneus. It contains the four books and the three appendices. The following agree with it in almost everything:

### Sang. 1

Codex of the Library of Saint Gall, no. 727, parchment, tenth or eleventh century. It contains Ansegisus’s books with the appendices, Benedict’s Book I, and the first hundred chapters of Book II.

### Colb.

Baluzius’s Colbertinus, now designated in the Royal Library of Paris as no. 4637 [Colbert 467, Royal 4243 A], parchment, in folio, tenth century. It contains Ansegisus’s books and appendices, Benedict’s Book I, several chapters of Book II, and several of Book III.

### c. Vat. 2

The other Vatican Codex of the Palatine Library. It contains Ansegisus with the three appendices, Benedict’s Books I, II, and III, and Additions II, III, and IV. It agrees extensively with:

### Til.

Baluzius’s Tilianus, which contains the same material except for Addition III [Col. 0502B]. It was designated among the Mazarin Codices as no. 4243 and is now preserved in the Royal Library of Paris as no. 4635. It was written on parchment in the tenth century, in folio or large quarto.

### d. Rem.

The Codex of Saint Remigius at Reims, now designated in the Royal Library of Paris among the Latin Supplements as no. 164 bis, ninth century. It contains Ansegisus’s four books and Appendices I and II through chapter 37. In place of chapter 38 it presents another chapter, written in a different ink. In the same ink, the name of Lothar in the preface, two chapters before the beginning of Book I, and chapters peculiar to the Codices listed immediately below were entered into this Codex.

The most distinguished of these is:

### B. Babenbergensis

Codex of the Public Library of Bamberg, no. 60, parchment, in folio, ninth century. I was granted access to it by the steadfast supporter of our undertaking, the distinguished Jaeck, librarian at Bamberg. D. Bethmann recorded its readings.

After Childebert’s decree it contains an epilogue to the Salic law, a notice concerning the Frankish kings, Ansegisus’s books with Appendices I and II, the Aachen Capitularium of 813, chapters 1–20, the Capitularium of 828, and the Capitularium of Worms of 829; finally, in another hand, it contains chapters of Hincmar for priests.

In Ansegisus it adds one chapter after I, 99; one after II, 32; one after IV, 14; one after IV, 24; and one after IV, 69. The same chapters, and in general the same text of Ansegisus, are found in:

### Pith.

The Royal Parisian Codex no. 4638, parchment, tenth century, Baluzius’s Pithoeanus [purchased by P. Pithoeus on 18 June 1568; later belonging to Jacques-Auguste de Thou; Colbert no. 1597; Royal 4243, 1].

It contains Ansegisus’s four books; Appendices I and II through chapter 31, with the following page cut away, and, on a later page, the final words of chapter 9; then chapter 11 of the Bononian Capitularium of 811, mentioned above; chapter 67 of the ecclesiastical Capitularium of 789; the Aachen Capitularium of 813; capitularies from the years 828 and 829; Benedict’s Additions I, II, and III, chapters 7–124; Addition IV, chapters 1–94, 120–123, 125, and 138; five canons; and then capitularies of Charles the Bald.

Next to it stands:

### Par.

Baluzius’s Parisian Codex, formerly Sirmond’s. It contains Ansegisus’s books and Appendices I and II, Benedict’s four additions, and the Normannicus mentioned above.

### e. Notre-Dame 252

The Royal Library of Paris, Fonds de Notre-Dame, no. 252 (F. 9), manuscript, ninth century, formerly belonging to Anthony Loisel. Several pages are cut out. It now begins with the words of Book I, chapter 59: “Abbots, counts, judges, and everyone everywhere,” and ends at Book III, chapter 78. Another Codex bound in the same covering contains the Salic and Alamannic laws.

### Notre-Dame 247

The Royal Library of Paris, Fonds de Notre-Dame, no. 247 (F. 4), manuscript, ninth or tenth century. After the capitularies of Louis of Aachen from the year 817, it presents on folio 21 Ansegisus’s third book and the preface to the fourth book as far as the words “In the fourth, those things,” together with the Salic law.

### Parisinus 4636

The Royal Parisian Codex no. 4636, formerly Cangius’s no. 144 [Royal 4243], manuscript, from the end of the ninth or the tenth century. It is badly damaged at the beginning. Beginning in Book I, chapter 99, with the words “But if after these things he undertook,” it contains the four books—except for the preface of Book II—three appendices, Benedict’s three books, and Additions II, III, and IV.

### Parisinus 4634

The Royal Parisian Codex no. 4634 [Baluzius no. 202; Royal 4243, 2], formerly belonging to Saint Mary and Saint Stephen of Sens, manuscript, ninth or tenth century. It contains Ansegisus’s books and appendices, Benedict’s three books, and Additions II, III, and IV.

### Reg. and Bal.

The Codices Regius of the Royal Library of Paris, no. 3839, and Baluzianus, no. 3839 A, from the ninth or tenth century, contain excerpts from Ansegisus and Benedict, like the Trecensis.

We must now mention the Codices to which I do not know which class to assign. The following seems to come closest to our Babenbergensis:

### Gervasianus

Formerly belonging to Saints Gervasius and Protasius, afterward from the books of Gohier, and sold at auction in Paris several years ago; tenth century. It is said to have contained Ansegisus’s four books, the three appendices, and these capitularies of Charles the Bald:

“Chapters of Charles the Younger made in the monastery of Saint Medard. Chapters of Emperor Lothar and King Charles made in the palace at Valenciennes. Letters of King Charles to Bishop Unfrid and the counts … Chapters of Charles the Younger, made at Pistres in the year 863. Chapters of the same king, made at Pistres in the year 864. Sentences of Pope Gregory. Chapters of Charles the Younger, made at the public palace of Quierzy in the year 872.”

### Codices listed by Haenel

These are the Codices listed by the distinguished Haenel:

In England, in the possession of the distinguished Sir Thomas Phillipps at Middlehill:

- p. 854, no. 1737, 567: fragments of capitularies collected by Abbot Ansegisus, end of the tenth century, parchment, in folio;
- p. 856, no. 762, 605: Book IV of the capitularies collected by Ansegisus, together with other capitularies of Charlemagne and Louis the Pious, tenth century, parchment, in quarto, formerly belonging to Saint Remigius of Reims.

In Gaul:

- p. 63, no. 36, Library of Autun: a fragment of the capitularies of Charlemagne, parchment, in quarto, tenth century.

Equipped, therefore, with such resources—namely, having collated in full Codices 1, 1*, 3, 4, 6, G, and B; having collated in the three Codices 2, 2b, and 5 those passages which do not occur among the capitularies edited above; having examined eighteen Codices—3b, 3c, Paris, Latin Supplement 751, 4761, 3878, both Saint Gall Codices, Royal Parisian Codices 4637, 4635, Latin Supplement 1641, 4638, 3839, 4628 A, 4631, 4634, 4636, and Fonds de Notre-Dame nos. 247 and 252—and having also used the readings recorded by Baluzius in his edition—I established a new edition.

I proceeded in such a way that, relying chiefly on the Codices of the first class, above all the Hamburgensis and Gothanus, I nevertheless sought, with the aid of the remaining witnesses, to bring their readings into conformity with the standard of the book published in 827. I added readings that seemed important either because of the authority of the Codices or in themselves, and restored the genuine chapter numbers.

That I have not entirely failed in my purpose seems to be shown by the comparison of Ansegisus’s readings with the text of the individual capitularies edited above from the most ancient Codices themselves.

The book of Benedict, deacon of Mainz, who, a decade after Ansegisus’s death, attempted to attach spurious supplements to his work, will be discussed later.

## LEGILOQUUM

[Note: Codex 6 reads *Legiseloquium*. Codex G prefixes to this word: “In the name of Christ, here begin the chapters of bishops, kings, and especially all the nobles of the Franks.” Baluzius placed after the verses the title which Tilius prefixed to his edition of Ansegisus and Benedict [above, col. 497, note b]; but it is absent from every Codex of Ansegisus that I have inspected.]

Whoever recites this book, say to our princes: “Have mercy, O God.”

For they dictated [Note: *dictabunt*, 2. Codex 6 omits the words that follow *mente*. Four verses are absent from 1*, 2b, 3, 4, and B.] a good law with benevolent mind; therefore, I beg you, pray to God for them.

### The preface begins

[Note: 1: “The first preface of the Salic law”; 3: “Here begins the prologue of the Salic law”; 3b: “of the first book.” The entire preface is absent from 4.]

[Col. 0503]

[Col. 0503C] Under the rule throughout endless ages of Christ our Savior [Note: *and Savior*, 3], ruler of all and creator of every creature, in the year of his incarnation 827 [Note: 826 is written above it by a contemporary hand in 2b], in indiction 5 [Note: 2: “in the indiction”; G, B, and 4628 A: 6], but in the thirteenth year of the empire of the most glorious princes, our lord Louis Augustus [Note: B and G: *Chlodowicus*; 2: *Hluduwici* occasionally; 1*: *Hluduici* almost always], great propagator of the Christian religion [Note: absent from 2b], and of Lothar Caesar [Note: 2b, 3, and 6 consistently have *Hlotarii*], his son [Note: 1*, 2, 2b, 3, 6: *ipsius*; the second class of Codices and Baluzius: *and of his sons*], Ansegisus, abbot by no preceding merits but by the grace of almighty God [Note: 1*: “humble abbot of the monasteries of Luxeuil, Fontenelle, and Flavigny”], out of love for the good memory of the lord Charles the Great, emperor of the Christians [Note: 3: “of the lord emperor, the Christian Charles”], and out of sincere devotion to his most excellent and most devout lord Louis Augustus, his son [Note: B: *devotion*], as well as to the illustrious Lothar Caesar, son of the most devout Louis the emperor [Note: the words “as well as … emperor” are absent from B and G], gathered together the capitula written below.

Since they were undoubtedly made for the advancement [Note: G: *effect*] of the holy Church [Note: absent from 3], they are to be firmly observed as law for the common good [Note: 6: *for the usefulness*]. Formerly, in the time of the aforesaid great lord Charles the emperor, and also now, at this time, by the command of the aforesaid princes, the most devout lord Louis Augustus and the illustrious Lothar Caesar [Note: B, G, and Baluzius: “and of his most illustrious sons”], these enactments were issued at intervals of time [Note: B: “by his command”] for the preservation of the Christian religion and for maintaining peace and harmony of affection in the Catholic Church [Note: B: *Catholic*].

But because they had been written separately on various small pieces of parchment over the course of different periods, lest they be consigned to oblivion, on account of my excessive devotion, as I have said, to the aforesaid most glorious princes [Note: absent from 3], and out of love [Note: 6: *fear*] for their most holy offspring, as well as for the state of the holy Church, it pleased me to gather in this little book the capitula of the aforesaid princes which I was able to find, written at their command, so that they may contribute to preserving the condition of the holy Church for long ages and to increasing more gloriously in eternal life the merit of the aforesaid princes [Note: B and G: “so that they may contribute to the advancement of their merit in eternal life”]. Amen.

[Col. 0504D] Let this also be known to the reader: I have divided the aforesaid capitula, which were issued by the aforesaid princes at intervals of time, into four little books [Note: 6: *I divided*].

Those [Note: B: *that*] namely which the lord Charles the emperor enacted concerning ecclesiastical order, I gathered together in the first little book. But those ecclesiastical matters which the lord and most devout Emperor Louis and his son Lothar Caesar issued [Note: B, G, and Baluzius: “which the emperor issued”; the remaining words are absent], I set down in the second.

Those matters which the lord Charles enacted at various times [Col. 0506A] concerning secular law, I gathered together in the third. But those which the illustrious lord Louis the emperor and his son Lothar Caesar enacted [Note: B, G, and Baluzius: “which the emperor enacted, concerning”] for the augmentation of secular law, I collected in the fourth.

The preface ends.

## The Preface of the Lord Emperor Charles Begins

[Note: “Begins” is absent in 1 and 2; “the preface ends” in 1*. In the title, 1 lacks the words; 6 reads “of King Charles”; the whole title is absent in B.]

[Col. 0507]

[Col. 0507B] While our Lord Jesus Christ reigns forever [Note: All of the following is absent in 3.], I, Charles, by the grace of God and by his mercy, king and ruler of the kingdom of the Franks, devoted defender and humble helper of the holy Church, extend to all the orders of ecclesiastical piety and to the dignities of secular power, in Christ the Lord, eternal God, greetings of perpetual peace and blessedness.

Considering with the peaceful and devout contemplation of my mind, together with our priests and counselors, the abundant clemency of Christ the King toward us and toward our people, and how necessary it is not only continually to give thanks to his goodness with all our heart and mouth, but also to devote ourselves to his praises through the constant practice of good works, so that he who has bestowed such great honors upon our kingdom may deign by his protection to preserve us and our kingdom forever [Note: Absent in B.], we have therefore decided to ask your diligence, O shepherds of the churches of Christ and leaders [Note: “teachers” in 2b, 3, 4, B., G.] of his flock [Note: “of the law” in 3.], most illustrious lights of the world [Note: “lights of the moon” in B.], that with vigilant care and diligent admonition you strive to lead the people of God through the pastures of eternal life [Note: “to feed” in 2b.]; and strive to carry back the wandering sheep within the walls of ecclesiastical firmness upon your shoulders, by the example of good works [Note: G.: “by the examples of good works”] and by exhortation [Note: “exhortation” in 3, G.], lest a lurking wolf should find and devour anyone transgressing the canonical decrees or exceeding the traditions of the Fathers and the universal councils, which God forbid.

Therefore, with great devotion, they must be admonished and exhorted [Col. 0508B]—indeed, compelled—to keep themselves within the decrees of the Fathers with firm faith and tireless perseverance. In this work of devotion, let your holiness know with absolute certainty [Note: “with absolute certainty” in 3.] that our diligence cooperates with you [Note: B., G.: “cooperates with us”]. For this reason we have also sent our envoys to you [Note: “we have declared” in 5.], who, by the authority of our name, might correct together with you whatever needed correction. We have also appended certain chapters [Note: “other chapters” in 1.] from the canonical ordinances that seemed especially necessary [Col. 0508C] to you.

I ask that no one presume to judge this admonition of piety as presumptuous [Note: G.: “namely”], by which we endeavor to correct errors, cut away what is superfluous, and constrain what is right [Note: 1* and Bal.: “may strive”; the “a” is deleted in 1*]; rather, let him receive it with a kindly and charitable spirit. For we read in the books of the kingdoms how the holy Josiah [Note: Absent in 3.], going throughout the kingdom given to him by God [Note: “going throughout” is spelled differently in 2, 3, 4, 5, B.], by correcting [Note: “to correct” in 6.] and admonishing, strove to restore it to the worship of the true God. I do not make myself equal to his holiness; but since the examples of the saints must always be followed everywhere [Note: Absent in 4.], it is necessary for us to gather everyone whom we can toward the pursuit of a good life, to the praise and glory of our Lord Jesus Christ.

Therefore, as we have said, we ordered certain chapters to be noted, so that you might likewise strive to admonish them concerning these matters, and concerning whatever else you know to be necessary [Note: “may be necessary” in 6.] for you, so that you may preach both these and those with equal attention. Do not omit anything that seems useful to your holiness and to the people of God, so that with devout zeal you may not admonish [Note: “so that you may admonish” in 1*, 2, 6, G., Bal.; “to omit” in B.]; [Col. 0509A] in order that both your diligence and the obedience of those subject to you [Note: “of those subordinate to you” in 3.] may be rewarded by almighty God with eternal happiness [Note: “so that both your diligence and the obedience of those subject to you may be rewarded” in 1*, 3, 4, G.; the whole phrase is absent in B.].

[Col. 0510A] The preface of the most illustrious Lord Emperor Charles ends [Note: G. corrects “begins” to “ends”; “of the most illustrious Lord Emperor Charles” is abbreviated or absent in several witnesses, and the whole is absent in 3 and B.].

## The Chapters Written Above and Their Texts Begin

[Col. 0509]

[Col. 0509A] 1.

[Note: Before this chapter, the Rhem. codices B. and 4628 A present the following passage (Novella 123.17): “If a slave becomes a cleric. If a slave, with his master’s knowledge and without his objection, has entered the clerical order, by that very fact he shall become free and ingenuous. For if the consecration was performed without the master’s knowledge [Note: B.: “had been performed”], the master may, within one year only, prove his ownership and recover his own slave. But if, whether with the master’s knowledge or without it [Note: 4628 A adds “the slave”], according to what we have said, the slave has earned freedom through the dignity of the clerical order and thereafter abandons ecclesiastical service and passes over to the life of laymen, he shall be handed over to his master in servitude.”]

The Rhem. manuscript prefixes the following:

“If anyone brings a claim against someone concerning any agreement, the matter is to be treated not according to later or adjacent considerations, but according to the primary grounds, in accordance with how the matter originally occurred. But if legitimate witnesses were present at the agreement, it ought to be determined chiefly according to their testimony, and not according to later pretexts, since what was done through the first stipulation must be defined.”

### Concerning those who are excommunicated by their own bishop

There are some [Note: These three words are absent in 3.] who, because their offenses demand it, are excommunicated by their own bishop, yet are presumptuously admitted to communion by other ecclesiastical or lay persons [Note: 3: “through presumption”]. The holy Council of Nicaea [Note: 5 and 6: “Nicene”], as well as that of Chalcedon [Note: 3: “of Chalcedon”; 1*: “of Chalcedon of Constantinople”], and likewise those of Antioch and Sardica, altogether prohibit this [Note: 4: “prohibited”].

### 2. Concerning those who come to be ordained

For this is laid down in the same council [Note: “Likewise” in the Rhem. and Sangall. manuscripts and in the Paris manuscript]: the faith and life of those who come to be ordained must first be carefully examined by the bishop [Note: B., Bal.: “examined,” plural], and afterward they are to be ordained.

### 3. Concerning fugitive and foreign clerics

Likewise, in the same council, as also in the Council of Antioch [Note: Absent in 1* and B.; B. spells the name differently], and at the same time in the Council of Chalcedon, it is decreed that fugitive and foreign clerics are to be received or ordained by no one [Note: The words “or ordained” are absent in 3.] without letters of recommendation and the permission of their own bishop or abbot.

### 4. Concerning presbyters, deacons, or those who are in the clergy

Likewise, in the same synod [Note: 3 and 5 read “council”], presbyters, deacons, and all who are in the clergy are forbidden to have a woman in their house [Note: Absent in the Sangall. manuscript and in HLD.], on account of suspicion, except their mother or sister, or only those persons who avoid grounds for suspicion.

### 5. Concerning usury

Likewise, in the same council or in the decrees of Pope Leo, as well as in the canons called apostolic, just as the Lord himself commanded in the Law, it is altogether forbidden for anyone [Note: Absent in 3.] to lend anything at interest [Note: The words “at interest” are absent in 1*.].

### 6. Concerning presbyters when they celebrate Mass

It has been heard that some [Note: G.: “sometimes”] presbyters celebrate Mass without receiving Communion. This is expressly said to have been forbidden in the apostolic canons. Or how can he rightly say, if he has not received Communion [Note: 3 and B. read “if they have not received Communion”]: “We have received the sacraments, O Lord”?

### 7. Concerning those who are condemned by a synod or by their own bishop

You can read these matters individually in the statutes of the Council of Nicaea, or in the other synodal decrees of the holy Fathers, and in the Council of Antioch. Concerning those who have been condemned by a synod or by their own bishop and afterward presume to minister, it is commanded that no one dare communicate with them [Note: Absent in 6 and Bal.]. But if anyone does communicate with them, he shall be subject to a similar sentence [Note: 3, 6, and Bal.: “of a similar sentence”], just as the condemned person is [Note: The words “just as the condemned person” are absent in 6.].

### 8. Concerning suffragan bishops

Likewise, in the same council, it is decreed that suffragan bishops should look to the metropolitan bishop and dare to do nothing new in their parishes [Note: B. and often elsewhere spell the word differently] without the knowledge and counsel [Note: The words “and counsel” are absent in G., Colb., Thu., Sang., and Reg.] of their metropolitan [Note: Absent in 3.]; nor should the metropolitan act without their counsel.

### 9. Concerning chorepiscopi

Likewise, in the same council and also in the Council of Ancyra, it is decreed that chorepiscopi should know their proper limits and do nothing without the permission [Note: “without” in 4 and 6] of the bishop in whose parish they dwell.

### 10. Concerning bishops or any members of the clergy

Likewise, in the same council, a bishop or anyone from the clergy [Note: B.: “concerning business”] must not dare to appeal to the royal dignity concerning his own affairs without the counsel or letters of the bishops or of the metropolitan [Note: 1*: “must not dare”; 3: “to royal authority”]; rather, the matter is to be examined in the common council of the bishops [Note: 3 has a substantially different reading: “in the common council, by the counsel of the bishops”; B. reads “for communion”].

### 11. Concerning ordinations or any other business

Likewise, in the same council and also in that of Sardica [Note: 4 spells the name “Sardinica”], as well as in the decrees of Pope Innocent, no bishop is to dare to perform any ordinations in another’s parish or to conduct business that does not belong to him.

### 12. Concerning the care of bishops

Likewise, in the same council, it is decreed that a bishop is to care for the church to which he was ordained.

### 13. Concerning provincial bishops

Likewise, in the same council and also in that of Chalcedon, provincial bishops are to hold councils with their metropolitan twice a year on account of the affairs of the Church [Note: B. reads “hold councils.”]

### 14. Concerning monks and clerics

In the Council of Laodicea [Note: 1, 1*, and B. spell the name “Laudicea”], and also in the African council, it is commanded that monks and clerics [Note: 4 reads “or”] must not enter taverns for the purpose of eating or drinking.

### 15. Concerning Sunday, how it is to be observed

Likewise, in the same council, it is commanded that Sunday be observed from evening until evening [Note: 3 reads “celebrated.”].

### 16. Concerning unknown names of angels

Likewise, in the same council, it is commanded that unknown names of angels [Note: Const. 3 reads “of angels” differently] neither be invented nor uttered, except those whom we have by authoritative tradition. These are Michael, Gabriel, and Raphael [Note: 1*, 4, 6, B., and G. spell the names Michahel, Gabrihel, and Raphahel.].

### 17. Concerning women, whether they may approach the altar

Likewise, in the same council, it is stated that women ought not to enter the altar area [Note: Bal. reads “whether they may enter”; 3 has a different construction].

### 18. Concerning bishops, where it is not proper for them to be established

Likewise, in the same council and also in that of Sardica [Note: In 3, the statement is attributed to Sardica], it is stated that bishops ought not to be established in little villages or in rural fields [Note: B. and Bal. read “be established” in a different grammatical form].

### 19. Concerning the canonical books

Likewise, in the same council, only the canonical books are to be read in church [Note: This chapter is absent from 6. In the chapter lists of 1, 2, 2b, 3, and B., its heading is placed after the following chapter; Bal. places it after chapter 20.].

### 20. Concerning bishops to be ordained or any members of the clergy

Likewise, in the Council of Chalcedon, it is stated that bishops or anyone from the clergy ought not to be ordained for money [Note: 1 reads “so that”; 3, and nearly all witnesses with Bal., read “who, apart from…”]. For both are to be deposed: the one who ordains and the one who is ordained, as well as the person who acts as intermediary between them [Note: 3 and 6 have the plural “those who ordain”; the wording varies in B. and 4.].

Likewise, concerning the same matter, in the apostolic canons [Note: These words are taken from the canon itself, not from the chapter of the year 789]: “If any bishop, presbyter, or deacon has obtained this dignity for money, both he and his ordainer shall be deposed, and they shall be cut off from communion” [Note: 4 reads “he shall be cut off,” singular; 1*, 4, 6, and G. likewise vary in number].

### 21. Concerning sorcerers or enchanters

Likewise, in the same council, it is decreed that no one is to be allowed to become a *coclearius* [Note: 1 reads *cuclearius*; 4, *cocclearius*; 1* has “clerics” instead of “that”], sorcerer, enchanter, or enchantress. The Lord condemned such people terribly in the person of Simon Magus [Note: 1, 4, and B. omit “the Lord”; B. reads “it was condemned”; 1* reads: “because divine vengeance terribly condemned Simon Magus.”].

### 22. Concerning monks, clerics, and presbyters

Likewise, in the same council, two chapters below, and also in the decrees of Pope Leo, monks, clerics, and presbyters are not to enter into secular business.

[Col. 0512A] ### 23. Concerning another person’s slaves

Likewise, in the same council it is commanded [Note: Absent in 3 and 4] that no one solicit another person’s slave for the clerical or monastic order [Note: 1* reads “monastic”] without the will and permission of his master [Note: 3 reads “of his superior.”].

### 24. Concerning the stability of bishops or clerics

Likewise, in the same council [Note: This chapter is placed two chapters below in Bal.], and also in that of Sardica, neither a bishop nor clerics are to migrate from one city to another [Note: G. lacks this chapter but places its title before the following chapter.].

### 25. Concerning presbyters not to be ordained absolutely

Likewise, in the same synod [Note: B. and G. read “council”], no one is to be ordained absolutely and without a declaration of the stability of the place to which he is ordained [Note: G. reads “prior declaration”; 3: “to which he is to be ordained.”].

### 26. Concerning the profession of monks and clerics

Likewise, in the same council, clerics and monks [Note: 3 reverses the order] are to remain in the profession and vow [Note: Absent in 3] that they have promised to God.

[Col. 0512B] ### 27. Concerning monks who are advanced to the clerical order

Likewise, in the decrees of Pope Innocent concerning the same matter [Note: These words are absent in 3], if a monk is advanced to the clerical order, he is not to abandon the profession of monastic life [Note: B. reads “admit” instead of “abandon.”].

### 28. Concerning business among clerics themselves

Likewise, in the same council, if clerics [Note: G. reads “clerics and monks”] have any business dispute among themselves, they are to be judged by their own bishop, not by secular authorities [Note: This chapter is placed before the preceding one in 3, though not in its chapter list.].

### 29. Concerning conspiracy among clerics or monks

Likewise, in the same council, neither clerics nor monks are to form a conspiracy or lay snares against their pastor.

### 30. Concerning the accusation of bishops by laymen

Likewise, in the same council, laymen are not to accuse bishops or clerics unless their reputation has first been examined.

### 31. Concerning monasteries dedicated to God

Likewise, in the same council, places that have once been dedicated to God so that they may be monasteries [Note: 1* corrects *ut* from an earlier reading; 4 reads “or monasteries”; G. has a different form] are to remain monasteries forever [Note: The words “remain forever monasteries” are absent in 3; 1* reads “perpetual”], and may no longer be made into secular dwellings.

### 32. Concerning the faith of the holy Trinity that is to be preached

In the Council of Carthage [Note: 1* reads “Likewise, in the council”]: first of all, it is necessary that the faith of the holy Trinity, and of Christ’s incarnation, passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven, be carefully preached to everyone.

### 33. Concerning greed

Likewise, in the same council, concerning the prohibition of greed: no one is to usurp another’s boundaries or cross the limits established by the Fathers.

[Col. 0512D] ### 34. Concerning those who convert themselves to God

Likewise, in the same council [Note: 3 reads “in the same council”], concerning those who are in danger and convert themselves to God: they are to be canonically examined concerning reconciliation and canonically reconciled.

### 35. Concerning those who are not of good conduct

Likewise, in the same council [Note: 3 and 6 read “in the same council”], those who are not of good conduct and whose life is blameworthy must not dare to accuse bishops or persons of higher rank.

### 36. Concerning those who have communicated with an excommunicate

Likewise, in the same council, whoever presumptuously associates with an excommunicate [Note: Absent in 3] is himself to be excommunicated [Note: B. has the plural “associate.”].

### 37. Concerning the subjection of presbyters

Likewise, in the same council, two chapters below, no presbyter is to dare to act arrogantly against his bishop.

### 38. Concerning clerics of the ecclesiastical order

Likewise, in the same council, if clerics of the ecclesiastical order [Note: 3 reads “the orders of clerics”] incur guilt, they are to be judged before ecclesiastical authorities, not secular ones.

### 39. Concerning virgins dedicated to God

In the African council [Note: 3 reads “Likewise”], it is commanded that virgins consecrated to God be kept under careful protection by persons of higher standing.

### 40. Concerning the principal see of bishops

Likewise, in the same council, a bishop is not permitted to neglect the principal see of his parish [Note: 3 reads “to abandon”] and attend more frequently to another church in his diocese.

### 41. Concerning false names of saints

Likewise, in the same council, false names of martyrs [Note: 3 reads “of holy martyrs”] and uncertain memorials of saints are not to be venerated.

### 42. Concerning a wife dismissed by her husband

Likewise, in the same council, neither a wife dismissed by her husband is to take another husband while her husband is alive, nor is a husband to take another wife while his former wife is alive [Note: G. begins, “It has been decreed that…”].

[Col. 0513C] ### 43. Concerning judges approved by the metropolitan

Likewise, in the same council, judges approved by the metropolitan are not to be despised.

### 44. Concerning the accusation of low-status persons

Likewise, in the same council, two chapters below, persons of low status are not to have the power to accuse. And if they were defeated in the first charge for having spoken falsely, they are not to have the power to speak in the second [Note: The witnesses variously read “or,” “and,” “so that,” or “and if”; the exact connective is uncertain in the supplied apparatus.].

### 45. Concerning virgins who are to be veiled

Likewise, in the same council, virgins are not to be veiled before the years [not specified in the supplied text], unless reasonable necessity compels it [Note: The words “before the years” are absent in 1*.].

### 46. Concerning offerings intended for the poor

In the Council of Gangra [Note: 4 consistently spells the name “Gangarensis”], no one is permitted to seize or defraud offerings that belong to the poor [Note: 3 adds “Likewise.”].

### 47. Concerning fasts established by priests

Likewise, in the same council, ecclesiastical fasts established by priests are not to be relaxed without reasonable necessity [Note: G. reads “unless there is reasonable necessity.”].

### 48. Concerning those who sin against nature

In the Council of Ancyra [Note: 1* has an added introductory reading, “by whomever”]: “There have been found among you those who sin against nature with four-footed animals or with males [Note: G. reads “with relatives or with quadrupeds”]. They are to be restrained by harsh and strict penance [Note: The word “who” is absent in 1, 1*, and B.; 3 reads “these are to be restrained”]. Therefore bishops and presbyters, by whom the judgment of penance is imposed, should strive by every means to prohibit or cut away this evil from customary practice.”

### 49. Concerning presbyters: at what time they are to be ordained

In the Council of Neocaesarea [Note: 1* spells the name “Neocaesarea” differently], no presbyter is to be ordained before the thirtieth year of his age [Note: 3 reads “no one”], because the Lord Jesus Christ did not preach before the age of thirty.

### 50. Concerning the giving of peace

In the decretals of Pope Innocent, peace is to be given by everyone after the sacraments of Christ have been completed [Note: G. reads “after they have been received.”].

### 51. Concerning another man’s betrothed

In the decretals of Pope Siricius [Note: The name appears as Siricius, Syricius, or Ciricius in the witnesses], no one is to take another man’s betrothed.

### 52. Concerning names to be recited

Likewise, in the decretals of the same pope [Note: 3 identifies this as Innocent’s chapter; compare chapter 54 of the Ecclesiastical collection, above the year 789], names are not to be recited publicly before the priests’ prayers.

### 53. Concerning the canonical ordinances that presbyters must not disregard

Likewise, in the decretals of the same pope, no priest [Note: 3 and 4 read “of priests”; B. has a variant form] is permitted to be ignorant of the ordinances of the holy canons [Note: 1 reads “to be ignorant” in a variant form].

### 54. Concerning the cleric of another bishop

It is decreed in the decrees of Pope Leo and in the Council of Sardica that a bishop must not solicit or ordain another bishop’s cleric to himself [Note: The words “to himself” are absent in 3, and “not” is absent in B.].

### 55. Concerning another person’s slaves

Likewise, in the decretals of the same pope, no bishop is to presume to promote another person’s slave to clerical office without the will of his master. The Council of Gangra also prohibits this [Note: G. spells the council’s name differently; several witnesses omit the final clause].

### 56. Concerning priests acting against the decretals

Likewise, in the decretals of the same pope, if any priest presumptuously acts against the established decretals and, unwilling to be corrected, persists [Note: G. and Bal. read: “if, acting against them, he is unwilling to be corrected”], he is to be removed from his office.

### 57. Concerning widows who are not to be veiled

In the decrees of Pope Gelasius, no bishop is to presume to veil widows.

### 58. Concerning the Catholic faith and the first commandment of the Law

First of all, we admonish that the Catholic faith be carefully read by bishops and presbyters and preached to the whole people [Note: One witness corrects the text to “be preached,” explaining that the entire people is to hear it; other witnesses read “to be judged” or vary in the placement of “to the whole people.”]. This is the first commandment of the Lord God almighty in the Law: “Hear, Israel, the Lord your God is one God”; and that he be loved with all the heart, with all the mind, with all the soul, and with all one’s strength.

### 59. Concerning peace and concord to be maintained

There shall be peace, concord, and unanimity among the whole Christian people—among bishops, abbots, counts, judges, and all persons everywhere, whether higher or lower [Note: The final phrase is absent in 3.]—for nothing pleases God without peace, nor does the gift of holy offering upon the altar, as we read in the Gospel at the Lord’s own command.

And there is that second commandment in the Law: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” [Note: 1* reads “as yourself” with an additional intensifying syllable]. Likewise in the Gospel: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.” And again: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” [Note: 3 reads “if you are my disciples”; another witness has “if you are my disciples”; the preposition varies between “to” and “in” one another]. For by this commandment the sons of God and the sons of the devil are distinguished [Note: The words “in this” are absent in 4]: the sons of the devil always strive to stir up dissensions and discord, whereas the sons of God always devote themselves to peace and love.

### 60. Concerning judges

Those who have been given the power to judge are to judge justly [Note: Absent in 4], as it is written [Note: Absent in 1]: “Judge justly, sons of men.” Not for gifts, because gifts blind the hearts of the wise and overthrow the words [Note: G. reads “the hearts” rather than “the words”; 3 has a variant involving “words” or “hearts”] of the just. Not through flattery [Note: 1 reads a form corresponding to “thus”; B. has “flattery”; 1, 3, 4, 6, G. read a form corresponding to “offering”], nor with regard to a person’s status, as it is said in Deuteronomy: “Judge what is just,” whether he is a citizen or a foreigner; there is to be no distinction between persons, because it is God’s judgment.

First, then, let the law composed by the wise men of the people be carefully discerned in judgment, lest through ignorance one stray from the way of truth [Note: This differs from chapter 62 of the Ecclesiastical collection from the year 789.]. And when he understands the right judgment, let him beware lest he turn away [Note: 3 reads “and not turn away”] from just judgment either through the flattery of anyone, or through affection for any friend, or through fear of someone powerful [Note: 3 reads “of power”], or for the sake of a reward.

But it appears right and honorable that judges hear and decide cases while fasting.

[Col. 0516D] [Note: The closing wording differs from chapter 62 of the Ecclesiastical collection from the year 789.]

## Source apparatus restoration

All printed witness readings, omissions, corrections, forms, sigla, and intervening column anchors in this supplied section are retained as source apparatus; where English cannot represent the distinction, the paired Latin forms are retained with concise glosses. The chapter order and parallel-manuscript notices follow the source.

### 61. On Perjury

We have in the Law, by the Lord’s command: “You shall not swear falsely by my name, nor profane the name of your God,” and, “You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain” [Note: [Col. 0515] In 3 and 4, *nec* (“nor”) is erased; in 1, *c.* is erased after *in*.] [Note: [Col. 0515] G has *vacuum* (“empty”) instead of *vanum* (“in vain”).] Therefore everyone must be carefully admonished to avoid perjury—not only in the holy Gospel or at the altar, or in the relics of the saints, but also in ordinary speech [Note: [Col. 0515] *vel* (“or”) instead of *seu* (“or”) in 3.] [Note: [Col. 0515] *et* (“also”) is absent in 1, 4, and G.].

For there are some who swear by charity and truth and avoid swearing by the name of God [Note: [Col. 0515] *cavent* (“they avoid”) is represented in 1* by *non caveant* (“they do not avoid”); 1 has *ut caveant* (“that they avoid”); G has *i.*] [Note: [Col. 0515] *se* (“themselves”) is absent in 3.] [Note: [Col. 0515] *nominis* (“of the name”) is absent in B.], without knowing [Note: [Col. 0515] 3 has *dei nescientes* (“not knowing God”).] that God is the same as charity and truth, as the apostle John says—for the words *dicente Iohanne apostolo, quia Deus caritas est* (“the apostle John saying, because God is love”) are absent in 3 [Note: [Col. 0515] The words from *dicente* through *veritas* are absent in 3.]. The Lord himself likewise says in the Gospel: “I am the way and the truth.” Therefore whoever swears by truth and charity swears by God.

One must also beware, through Pharisaic superstition, of honoring gold more than the altar, lest the Lord say: “Fool and blind man, which is greater, the gold, or the altar that sanctifies the gold?” [Note: [Col. 0515] 1* omits *enim* (“for”); 4 has *stulte, ecce* (“fool, behold”); another manuscript has *quidem* (“indeed”) instead of *ecce*.]

It also seems proper to us that whoever dares to swear by holy things [Note: [Col. 0515] Vat. 1, Met. and Camb. have *audet* (“dares”) instead of *habet* (“has”).] should do so fasting, with all propriety and fear of God. And [Note: [Col. 0515] 3 has *ut* (“so that”) instead of *et* (“and”).] each one of you should know that he will render an account to God, wherever he may be, whether inside the church or outside the church. Little children who have not yet reached the age of reason must not be compelled to swear.

Whoever has once committed perjury must thereafter be neither a witness nor admitted to the sacrament, nor stand as one who swears in his own case or in another’s case [Note: [Col. 0515] 3 has *lege* (“in court”) instead of *sua causa* (“in his own case”).].

### 62. On Auguries and Other Magic Practices

We have the Lord’s command in the Law: “You shall not practice augury” [Note: [Col. 0515] 3 has *augurietis* (“you shall divine”).]; and in Deuteronomy: “Let no one be found who consults diviners” [Note: [Col. 0515] 3 has *s. homo* (“any person”).], observes dreams, or attends to auguries [Note: [Col. 0515] 1 has *ad auguria* (“to auguries”); B has *auguria* (“auguries”).] Likewise: “Let there be no magician, no enchanter, and no consulter of a pythoness” [Note: [Col. 0515] 1* has *inphitonis* (“of a pythoness”); 3, B, and G have *fitonis* (“of a soothsayer”); 4 has *phitonum* (“of pythons”).] [Note: [Col. 0515] 4, Reg., Trec., Til., Thu., and Sang. read *consulator* (“one who consults”) instead of *consultor*.]

Therefore we command that there be no diviners [Note: [Col. 0515] G, Reg., Trec., and Bal. have *auguriatores* (“augurists”).], enchanters, storm-makers [Note: [Col. 0515] G has *intempestarii* (“makers of unseasonable weather”).], or binders [*obligatores*]; and wherever such persons are found [Note: [Col. 0515] 1 has *sint* (“may be”) instead of *sunt* (“are”).], they must either make amends or be condemned [Note: [Col. 0515] *emendentur* means “let them be corrected/make amends”; *damnentur* means “let them be condemned.”].

Likewise, concerning trees, stones, and springs [Note: [Col. 0515] The words *vel petris vel fontibus* (“or stones or springs”) are absent in Bal.] where some foolish people place lights or perform other observances, we absolutely command that this most wicked practice, accursed by God, be removed and destroyed wherever it is found [Note: [Col. 0515] B has *extollatur* (“be lifted up”) instead of *tollatur* (“be removed”).].

### 63. On Hatred and Envy

It is necessary to preach how great an evil hatred and envy are [Note: [Col. 0515] 3, 4, and G have *praedicare* (“to preach”) instead of *praedicari* (“to be preached”).]. For it is written in the Law: “You shall not hate your brother in your heart, but openly reprove him” [Note: [Col. 0515] 1* and 3 have *ne* (“lest”) instead of *non* (“not”).] Likewise the evangelist John says: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer.” Likewise in the Gospel: “If your brother sins against you, go and reprove him between you and him alone,” and so forth [Note: [Col. 0515] The remainder is absent in 3 and Met.].

### 64. Likewise on Greed and Desire [Note: [Col. 0515] 4 has *Item de* (“Likewise on”) instead of *De* (“On”).]

Concerning greed, we read the apostle saying: “Greed, which is the service of idols” [Note: [Col. 0515] G has *s. est valde cavenda* (“which is very greatly to be avoided”).], must be avoided. Concerning desire, it is written that it is the root of all evils; and in the Law: “You shall not covet your neighbor’s property.”

### 65. On Honoring Parents

This [Note: [Col. 0515] B has *haec* (“these things”) instead of *hoc* (“this”).] must be earnestly urged, so that children honor their parents, because the Lord himself says: “Honor your father and your mother, so that you may live long upon the land which the Lord your God will give you.”

### 66. On the Faith of Priests, to Be Examined by Bishops

Bishops must carefully examine throughout their dioceses the faith of the priests, their Catholic baptism, and the celebration of Masses [Note: [Col. 0515] 3 has *sollemnia, si faciunt* (“the solemn rites, if they celebrate them”).], so that they hold the right faith, observe Catholic baptism, and properly understand the prayers of the Mass; and so that the psalms are worthily sung according to the divisions of the verses [Note: [Col. 0515] 3 has *ut psalmos digne modulentur* (“that they worthily sing the psalms”); G omits the words concerning understanding.], and so that they themselves understand the Lord’s Prayer and preach it to everyone so that it may be understood, in order that each person may know what he asks from God.

The “Glory be to the Father” must be sung among all with every honor [Note: [Col. 0515] The words are absent in 1 and G.]; and the priest himself, together with the holy angels and the people of God, must sing with one voice: “Holy, holy, holy” [Note: [Col. 0515] 1 and 1* have *una voce* (“with one voice”); 3 and B have *una* (“one”).].

Priests and deacons must be told in every way not to carry weapons, but rather to trust in God’s protection [Note: [Col. 0517] 6 and Bal. have *oratione* (“in prayer”) instead of *defensione* (“protection”).] than in weapons [Note: [Col. 0517] B has *armorum* (“of arms”) instead of *armis* (“weapons”).].

### 67. On the Honor of the Church

It has pleased us to admonish each bishop to see throughout his diocese [Note: [Col. 0517] G has *praevideat* (“take care beforehand”).] that the church of God receives its proper honor, and likewise that the altars are venerated according to their dignity [Note: [Col. 0517] 1* omits the words from *altaria* (“altars”) through *Dei* (“of God”); after *sacrata* (“consecrated”) it has written above the line: *non sint* (“they must not be”).]. The house of God and consecrated altars must not be accessible to dogs [Note: [Col. 0517] 6 omits the words from *non sit* through *sacrata*.].

The vessels consecrated to God must be held in great veneration. The consecrated offerings must be collected with great care by those who are worthy, and they must serve them with honor [Note: [Col. 0517] 3 has *cum omni* (“with every”); 3, 6, G, and Bal. have *serventur* (“be preserved”) instead of *serviant* (“serve”).].

Secular business and vain talk must not take place in churches, because the house of God ought to be a house of prayer, not a den of thieves. When people come to the solemn celebrations of Mass, let them have their minds attentive to God [Note: [Col. 0517] Pith., Rem., and Paris. have *homines* (“people”) instead of *animos* (“minds”).], and let them not leave before the completion of the priestly blessing [Note: [Col. 0517] 3 has *benedictionum* (“blessings”); the sacramentary omits *sacerdotalis* (“priestly”).].

### 68. On the Ministers of the Altar and on the School

We also earnestly request [Note: [Col. 0517] G omits *Sed et hoc* (“We also [request] this”).] your holiness [Note: [Col. 0517] 4 and 6 have *altitudinem* (“your highness”) instead of *almitatem* (“your holiness”).] that the ministers of God’s altar adorn their ministry with good morals, that the other canons observe their orders [Note: [Col. 0517] G has *et* (“and”) instead of *seu* (“or”).], and that monks observe the purpose of their consecration [Note: [Col. 0517] G has *atque* (“and”) instead of *vel* (“or”); G also has *regulam* (“rule”) instead of *propositum* (“purpose”).].

We beseech them to have a good and worthy manner of life, as the Lord himself commanded in the Gospel: “Let your light shine before men, so that they may see your good works” [Note: [Col. 0517] 3 omits *ut videant opera vestra bona* (“so that they may see your good works”); 1 and B omit *opera vestra bona* (“your good works”).] “and glorify your Father who is in heaven,” so that many may be drawn [Note: [Col. 0517] G has *adtrahantur* (“be attracted”).] to God’s service by their good conduct.

They should gather to themselves and associate with them not only children of servile condition but also the sons of free people. Schools for boys learning to read should be established; in every monastery or bishopric [Note: [Col. 0517] B has *monstrant ut episcopias* (“so that they may show monasteries and bishoprics”).] they should learn psalms, musical notation, singing, computation, and grammar [Note: [Col. 0517] G and Bal. add *discant* (“let them learn”).], and they should have carefully corrected Catholic books [Note: [Col. 0517] 3 and 6 have *emendatos* (“corrected”); B has *emendent* (“let them correct”); Bal. has *emendatos habeant* (“let them have corrected books”).]. For often, when some wish to pray properly to God, they pray wrongly because of uncorrected books.

Do not allow your boys to be corrupted by them either in reading or in writing [Note: [Col. 0517] The words are absent in 3.]. If it is necessary to write a Gospel-book, Psalter, or Missal [Note: [Col. 0517] 3 has *vel* (“or”) instead of *et* (“and”); B omits the word.], let men of mature age write them with every care.

### 69. On the Vow of Monks and on the Clerical Life

We have likewise taken care to request that all who everywhere have bound themselves by a vow to the monastic life [Note: [Col. 0517] 3, B, and Bal. have *constrinxerint* (“shall have bound themselves”).] live in every respect as monks and according to the rule [Note: [Col. 0517] 3 has *monastice* (“monastically”); 1* and 4 have *monachi* (“of monks”); G has *monastice*.], in accordance with their vow [Note: [Col. 0517] 4 and G have *ut* (“so that”) instead of *et* (“and”).], as it is written: “Pay your vows to the Lord your God.” And again: “It is better not to vow than to vow and not fulfill it” [Note: [Col. 0517] 3 omits *et* (“and”).].

Those coming to monasteries must first be tested in the place of probation according to the regular order, and then accepted. Those who come to monasteries from secular clothing must not immediately be sent outside to perform the monastery’s duties before they have been properly trained inside [Note: [Col. 0517] Sang. and 1 have *enutriantur* (“be nourished/trained”).].

Monks must not go to secular lawsuits [Note: [Col. 0517] 4 has *veniant* (“come”) instead of *vadant* (“go”).]. Similarly, concerning those who enter the clerical life—which we call the canonical life—we wish them to live in every respect canonically according to their rule [Note: [Col. 0517] *volumus* (“we wish”) is absent in 4; *ut illi* (“that they”) is absent in 3; B has *canonici* (“as canons”).]. Their bishop must govern their life, just as an abbot governs monks [Note: [Col. 0517] 3 has *ut* (“and so that”).].

### 70. On Receiving Guests
