81. On benefices and how they are *condricta*. [Note: The heading prints the corrupt form *qualiter condricta sint*; “how they are arranged” is a tentative sense.]  
82. On the benefices of bishops, abbots, and others, and on describing the royal fisc.  
83. On commissions concerning justice and when they are to be exercised.  
84. On a royal command not fulfilled in any commission.  
85. On investigating the royal census.  
86. On the things from which the census customarily went to the king’s share.  
87. On the counts being informed of courts by the royal envoys.  
88. On promising loyalty to the king.  
89. On killings committed within the country.  
90. On measures and weights.

[Note: In place of this heading, manuscript 3 has *expliciunt capitula que sunt salice legis addenda atque ab universis sancte Dei ecclesiae fidelibus observanda*, “Here end the chapters that are to be added to the Salic Law and observed by all the faithful of God’s holy Church.”]

# The aforesaid chapters and their text begin

[Col. 0551]

[Col. 0551B]

## 1. On maintaining the peace

Concerning peace, we admonish that all who are rebellious against him because of any crimes [Note: Col. 0551: *pro aliquo scelere*, “because of some crime,” 3.] be restrained. [Note: Col. 0551: *ei*, “against him,” is absent in 1 and Hild.; *eis*, “against them,” in 3 and 4.]

## 2. On general justice

Concerning the justice of the churches of God, widows, orphans, and wards, we command that at public courts those who complain not be despised but be heard carefully.

## 3. On royal justice

Concerning royal justice [Note: Col. 0551: *regularibus*, “regular,” 6.], we command that it be fully investigated.

## 4. On not carrying weapons

[Note: *non*, “not,” is absent from the heading in 3.]

Weapons are not [Note: *non*, “not,” is absent here in 3.] to be carried within the country—that is, shields, lances, and coats of mail. If someone is involved in a feud [Note: Col. 0551: *studiosus*, 1*; *faidiosus*, B.], let the matter be investigated: which of the two is at fault, so that they may be reconciled, and let them be compelled to make peace even if they do not wish it. [Note: Col. 0551: 3 adds: “If two have been opposed to one another, we command that it be investigated which of the two is at fault, so that they may be reconciled. If they do not wish it, let them be restrained. And if otherwise …”] If they will not otherwise reconcile themselves [Note: Col. 0551: *pacificari*, “be reconciled,” 4.], they are to be brought into our presence.

If, after reconciliation, one kills the other, he is to pay compensation for him [Note: Col. 0551: *conponant*, plural, 1*.], lose the hand by which he committed perjury [Note: Col. 0551: *qua*, “with which,” 6 and G.], and in addition pay the lord’s ban [Note: Col. 0551: *bannium*, 3.].

## 5. On the equipment to be taken to the army

The military equipment is to be maintained as we previously prescribed in another capitulary. [Note: Col. 0551: *ante*, “before,” 3, B.] In addition, every man holding twelve hides is to have a coat of mail. Whoever possesses a coat of mail but does not take it with him is to lose his entire benefice together with the coat of mail. [Note: Col. 0551: absent in 1*.]

## 6. On how far merchants may proceed

Merchants who travel to the regions of the Slavs [Note: Col. 0551: *clavorum*, B.] and Avars [Note: Col. 0551: the reading is *Avarorum* in 3 and Met.; *havarorum* in Bell., Til., R., B., Pith., Parm., and Norm.; *haurorum* in 1*; *arorum* in Div.; *bauuariorum* in 1 and 6, G, Riv., Thu., Sang. 1, and Colb.; *bauuarorum* in 4; *baiuvatorum* in Camb.; *baugariorum* in Sang. 2.] are to proceed with their goods only as far as the following places in Saxony: Bardenwih [Note: Col. 0551: *Bardenuuic*, 1* and 4; *Bardenuhuih*, 3; *Bardeuuuich*, G.], Magadoburg [Note: Col. 0551: *Magodoburg*, 1; *amodobruc*, 1*; *Magedoburg*, 6.], Erphesfurt [Note: Col. 0551: *Erpesfurd*, 1*, 3, 4, 6, B, G; *Herpffurth*, 3b.], Halaxstat [Note: Col. 0551: *Alaxstat*, 3; *Alaxastat*, 3b; *Laxta*, 1*; *Adalagastat*, G.], Forahheim [Note: Col. 0551: *Foratheim*, 3; *Foracheim*, B; *Forachen*, G.], Breemberg [Col. 0552B] [Note: Col. 0551: *Breemberg*, 1* and 3; *Breembirg*, B; *Breenpereg*, 4; *Breempereg*, 6; *Breemberht*, G.], Reganesburg [Note: Col. 0551: *Reginisburg*, 1*; *Reginesburg*, 3; *Raginisburg*, B and G; *Rageinispurg*, 4; *Ragesnisburg*, 6.], and Lauriacum.

They are not to carry weapons or coats of mail for sale. If they are found carrying them, all their property is to be taken from them: one half is to go to the palace, and the other half is to be divided between the aforesaid envoys and the person who discovered them.

## 7. On complainers or advocates

Concerning complainers or advocates who are unwilling either to accept the judgment of the *scabini* [Note: Col. 0551: *scabinorum* in 1*, 4, and consistently in G; *scabinearum* in B.] or to blaspheme [Note: The supplied text prints *nec blasphemare volunt*, literally “nor do they wish to blaspheme,” without an expected verb such as *desinere*, “to cease”; the syntax is problematic. Manuscript 1* reads *plasfemare*.], the ancient custom is to be observed: they are to be confined in custody until they do one of the two things [Note: Col. 0551: *fiat*, “one of the two is done,” 1*.].

If they cry out to the palace about this matter [Note: Col. 0551: *placitum*, “the court,” 3.] and bring letters [Note: *et litteras detulerint*, “and bring letters,” is absent in 3.], they are not to be believed merely on that account, but neither are they to be placed in prison [Note: Col. 0551: *carcerem*, “prison,” 4 and G.]. Instead, together with their custody and the letters themselves, they are to be sent back to our palace, so that the matter may be investigated there [Col. 0552C] as is proper.

## 8. On oaths

No one is to promise loyalty by oath to anyone else except to us and to his own lord, for our benefit and that of his lord. This does not apply to those oaths which, according to law, one person rightly owes to another. Boys who previously could not swear because of their youthful age [Note: Col. 0551: *potuerint*, “may have been able,” 1*.] are now to promise loyalty anew.

## 9. On conspiracies

Concerning conspiracies: whoever presumes to form one [Note: G and Baluze have the abbreviated *q. conspirationem f.*, “whoever presumes to form a conspiracy.”] and confirms any conspiracy by oath [Note: Col. 0551: *quicumque*, “whoever,” 1*.] is to be judged according to three distinctions.

First, wherever some evil has been perpetrated through it [Note: Col. 0551: *propter*, “because of,” Trec.; *pro*, “for,” Sang.], the authors of the deed are to be killed; their assistants are each to be flogged by the other, and they are to cut off one another’s noses.

Where no evil has been perpetrated, they are nevertheless to be flogged by one another and cut one another’s hair. [Note: Col. 0553: *detondeant*, “let them shear,” 1* and B.]

If some conspiracy has been confirmed by the joining of right hands, then, if those involved are free men, they must either swear with suitable oath-helpers that they did not do this for an evil purpose [Note: Col. 0553: *se non*, “that they did not,” G.], or, if they cannot do so, they must pay the composition prescribed by their law. If they are slaves, they are to be flogged.

In the future no such conspiracy is to be formed anywhere in our kingdom, whether by oath or without oath. [Note: Col. 0553: absent in 3 and G.]

## 10. On perjuries

[Note: G consistently reads *peiuriis* for *periuriis*, “perjuries.”]

Perjuries are to be carefully avoided [Note: Vat., Sang. 1, Colb., and Trec. add *Praecipimus ut periuria summopere caveantur*, “We command that perjuries be most carefully avoided.”], and witnesses are not to be admitted to swear before they have been examined. If they cannot otherwise be examined [Note: Col. 0553: *possunt*, “can,” 3.], they are to be separated from one another and questioned individually.

The accuser alone is not to be permitted to choose witnesses while the opposing litigant is absent. [Note: Col. 0553: *acusatore*, “accuser,” 3.] No one at all is to be admitted to an oath or to give testimony unless fasting.

If he is rejected, the person rejecting him must state and prove why he does not wish him to be admitted. [Note: Col. 0553: The printed reading *Si refutatur* (“if he is rejected”) is preserved in Camb., Riv., Vat., Pal., Sangall., Til., and Colb. Camb. also reads *Et ille qui ad testimonium adducitur, si refutatur* (“and if the one brought forward to testify is rejected”); Pith., Paris., and Norm. have the same, with *ducitur* for *adducitur*. Other manuscripts read *Si vero aliquis refutatur*, “if someone is rejected.” A critical note explains that the preserved reading is genuine but has lost several words, in place of which “if someone” was inserted by some witnesses; the Camb., Pith., Paris., and Norm. manuscripts eventually restore the genuine words of the *Capitulary*.]

Witnesses are to be chosen from that district or from neighboring hundreds, unless the case must be investigated farther outside the county. If anyone is convicted of perjury, he is to lose his hand or redeem it by payment.

## 11. On advocates, *vicedomini*, vicars, and centenaries

Corrupt advocates, *vicedomini*, vicars, and centenaries [Note: Col. 0553: *centenis*, “hundreds,” in B.] are to be removed [Note: Col. 0553: absent in 4.], and men are to be chosen who both know and are willing to discern and settle cases justly.

If any count is found to be corrupt [Note: G has the abbreviated *aliquis p.*, “if some [official] is found corrupt.”], this is to be reported to us. [Note: Col. 0553: *iniectus*, “introduced,” 4.]

## 12. On tolls

Concerning tolls, we are pleased that ancient and legitimate tolls be exacted from merchants, both at bridges and [Note: Manuscript 1* reads *et de*, “and from.”] from ships or at markets.

New or unjust tolls—where ropes are stretched, where one passes with ships beneath bridges, or in similar situations where no assistance is provided to travelers [Note: Sim., Met., Riv., and Baluze add the abbreviated *p. ut non exigantur*, “so that they are not to be exacted.”]—are not to be exacted.

Likewise, no toll whatsoever is to be demanded from those who, without the purpose of trading, transport their own property from one house of theirs [Note: Col. 0553: *domu*, “house,” 1*.] to another, to the palace, or to the army. [Note: Col. 0553: *ex*, “from,” 3.]

## 13. On counterfeit coins

Because counterfeit coins are produced in many places contrary to justice and contrary to the edict, we wish there to be no mint in any other place except our palace, unless we should again order otherwise.

### 14. Concerning the *haribannum* [Note: “airibannum” in 1*. The form *heribannum* is found throughout this chapter in the constitution, in 3, B, G, and most manuscripts; “haribannum” in H; *const.* 6; Vat., Riv.]

Concerning the *haribannum*, we wish our envoys to exact it faithfully, without favor, flattery [Note: “blanditia” in 1*. B. Hld. Bal.] or fear of any person, according to our command: namely, from a man possessing six pounds’ worth in gold, silver, mail-shirts [Note: “bruniis” in 4.], bronze, whole garments, horses, oxen [Note: “oxen, sheep, cows” in Ed. Til.], cows, or other livestock—and wives or children are not to be stripped, for this reason, of their clothing [Note: For “are not …” G. has: “for three [pounds’] worth of property”; the prescribed valuation is omitted.], but the lawful *haribannum*, that is, three pounds, is to be taken. But whoever has no more than three pounds’ worth in the aforesaid property [Note: The words “has no more … worth” are absent in G.], thirty solidi are to be exacted from him, that is, one and a half pounds [Note: “that is … one and a half pounds” is absent in G.]. Whoever has no more than two pounds is to pay ten solidi. If he has one pound, five solidi, so that he may again be able to prepare himself for God’s service and for our benefit. And our envoys must take care and investigate diligently lest, through any evil contrivance, they withhold our due by handing it over or entrusting it to another.

### 15. Concerning the royal census

Wherever the royal census was lawfully due [Note: “exigebat” (“was exacted”) in 3, 4, 6; “exibit” in B; “exigebatur” in G., Camb., Colb., Vat., Sang. 1; “exhibebatur” in 1*.], we wish it to be paid from there, whether from the person himself or from his property.

### 16. Concerning free men who have fiscal wives

Concerning free men who take royal fiscal wives, and free women who likewise take royal fiscal men [Note: “men” in 1, 3, B.], they are not to be disqualified from inheriting their parents’ property, from pursuing their own case, or from giving testimony on this account. Rather, the same honor is to be preserved toward us in this matter as is known to have been preserved toward our predecessors, kings or emperors [Note: After this chapter the Norman manuscript has: “Concerning children who have not sworn fidelity. Concerning those who were then children, and others besides who have not sworn fidelity to the lord emperor or to his children, let them now swear.” See above, chapter 8 of this book, Bal.].

### 17. Concerning the care of the royal envoys

Let each man in his assigned district take the greatest care to foresee, order and arrange matters according to God’s will [Note: Absent in 1*.] and according to our command.

### 18. Concerning the equality to be observed by the royal envoys [Note: Absent in 1, 1*. and 3.]

We wish our envoys to act equally in every case, whether concerning the *heribannum*, newcomers, or any other matters. Concerning newcomers, we wish those who have long been married in each locality to remain there [Note: “where” in 1.] and not to be expelled without cause or fault. Fugitive slaves and robbers, however, are to return to their proper places.

### 19. Concerning those who hold royal benefices

We have heard how both counts and other men who are seen to possess our benefices acquire properties for themselves from that very benefice, and make our dependants from their benefice serve those properties; consequently our estates remain deserted, and in some places the people living nearby suffer many wrongs.

### 20. Concerning those who commit fraud with royal benefices [Note: Absent in 1*.]

We have heard that some men transfer our benefice to other men as property and, after a price has been paid in that transaction, buy those same things back for themselves as allodial property [Note: “sell” in 3.]. This must be guarded against entirely, because those who do this [Note: “those who do these things” in 3.] do not faithfully observe the fidelity that they have promised us. And lest they perhaps be found in some act of infidelity [Note: The continuation, in a damaged place and written by a later hand, is given by G., Camb., Vat., Sang. 1 and Colb. as follows: “Let those who do this henceforth guard themselves entirely against such things, lest, by God’s grace and ours, they become exiles from their own honors and from their own land.”], for through their own will such deeds of theirs do not reach our ears.

### 21. Concerning those who are driven away because the rendering of their own justice is delayed [Note: “dilated” in 3.] [Note: “wearied” in 3. B.]

There are also others who ought to obtain justice according to the laws, but in certain places are harassed [Note: “driven away” in G., Thu., Vat., Sang. 1, Colb.] to such an extent that they surrender their right into the hands of sureties, so that they may retain at least something, while the more powerful take the larger share.

### 22. Concerning not carrying weapons to the court

No one is to carry weapons to the assembly or court within the realm, that is, a shield and a lance [Note: “that is, shield and lance” is absent in 4.].

### 23. Concerning robbers

Concerning robbers, we decree that whoever, after the feast of Saint John, gives lodging to a robber, if he is a Frank, is to swear with twelve other Franks that he did not know the man to be a robber [Note: “that he did not know him to be one” in 1*.], even if he is his father, brother or relative. If he cannot swear this, and is convicted by another of having received a robber as a guest, he is to be judged as a robber and traitor: for the robber is a robber and a traitor to us and to the Franks, and the man who received him is like him [Note: “like them” in 1*.].

But if he heard that the man was a robber [Note: Absent in 1*.], yet does not know this for certain [Note: B. reads “yet does not know it”; G. has “so that he does not know it firmly”; 3 has “firmly does not know.”], let him either swear alone that he had never heard him called a robber, whether truthfully or falsely, or be prepared, if the man is later convicted of robbery [Note: “convicted” in 4, 6, G., Bal.], to be condemned in the same way.

### 24. Concerning animals or other things from which purchases are made

No one is to buy a horse, ox, draft animal or anything else [Note: “or any other thing” in Rivip.] unless he knows the man who sells it, or knows from which district he is, where he lives, or who his lord is [Note: “who is his lord” in 1*. 4. G.].

### 25. Concerning the killing of clergy

Whoever kills a subdeacon is to pay a composition of three hundred solidi [Note: Four hundred in 1*.]; whoever kills a deacon, four hundred [Note: Six hundred in 1*, G., corrected]; whoever kills a priest, six hundred [Note: Nine hundred, corrected, in 1*, G.]; whoever kills a bishop, nine hundred [Note: “Whoever kills a bishop is to pay a composition for his life”; “eight hundred” in Hld.]; whoever kills a monk, four hundred solidi.

### 26. Concerning immunity, if any damage is done there

If anyone causes damage within an immunity [Note: “not” in 3.], he is to pay six hundred solidi [Note: Nine hundred, corrected, in 1*, G.]. But if a man commits theft, homicide or any other crime outside and flees within the immunity, let the count send word to the bishop, abbot, *vicedominus* [Note: “vicedominicus” in 3.], or whoever holds the place of the bishop or abbot [Note: “or” in 1*. B.], ordering him to hand over the accused.

If that man refuses and will not hand him over [Note: “him” in 1, 1*, 4.], let him be judged liable to fifteen solidi for the first refusal. If he refuses to hand him over at the second inquiry [Note: “another” in B.; the words “him at the inquiry” are absent in G.], let him be judged liable to thirty solidi. If he is unwilling to consent even at the third inquiry, the man who retains the accused within the immunity and will not hand him over [Note: “retains him within the immunity” is omitted in 1*.] is to be compelled to pay in full whatever damage the accused caused [Note: “has caused” in 1*. 6.]. The count himself, on coming, is to have permission to search for that man within the immunity wherever he can find him [Note: Absent in 1, 4.].

But if, at the first inquiry, the count is immediately answered that the accused had indeed been within the immunity but had escaped, the person concerned is to swear that he had not caused him to flee in order to evade anyone’s justice, and this is to satisfy the count.

If anyone attempts to resist the count as he enters the immunity with an armed band, the count is to report this to the king or prince [Note: “or to” in 6. G. Bal.], and judgment is to be rendered there: just as the man who caused damage within the immunity must pay six hundred solidi [Note: Nine hundred, correctly emended, in 1*, G.], so the man who dared to resist the count with an armed band [Note: “with an armed band” in 3.] is to be judged liable to six hundred solidi [Note: Nine hundred, corrected, in G.].

### 27. Concerning one who presumptuously assists another unjustly arguing in court

If anyone, through evil contrivance [Note: Absent in G., Thu., Vat., Sang. 1, Colb.], presumptuously assists a man who is unjustly arguing against another in court, and is rebuked for it before the judges or count [Note: Absent in 1*.], and cannot deny it, he is to be judged liable to fifteen solidi.

### 28. Concerning a man who has obtained freedom by a charter

If anyone has lawfully obtained freedom from his lord by a charter of emancipation, let him remain free. But if anyone unjustly attempts to enslave him [Note: “wishes to enslave him” in 4, 6.], and he produces his charter of emancipation and proves that his adversary wishes to enslave him [Note: The words “and he … proves” are absent in 6.], the man who attempted this is to be compelled to pay the fine specified in the charter.

But if the charter is not available because it has already been destroyed by the man who wished to enslave him [Note: “broken” in 1*. G.], let him pay his *wergeld* [Note: Also written *uuirdgildum*, *uurdgildum*, *uuidregildum*, *uuirgildum*, *uueregeldum*, and *uuerigeldi* in the various witnesses]: two parts to the man whom he wished to enslave and one third to the king; and let that man recover his freedom again by the king’s order.

### 29. Concerning a free man who gives himself into another’s power as a pledge [Note: “who has given himself” in 3; absent in 1*.]

A free man who has placed himself in another’s power as a pledge, and while held there causes damage to anyone, is to be dealt with as follows: the person who received him as a pledge must either pay the damage or produce the man in the assembly and release him, at the same time forfeiting the debt for which he received him as a pledge [Note: “power” in 3. B.].

The man who caused the damage, once released, is to be compelled to make amends according to the nature of the matter [Note: Absent in 1*.]. But if he has a free woman as wife, and they have children while he remains in pledge, they are to remain free [Note: “he has” in 4.].

### 30. How royal debts are to be paid [Note: “how each solidus is to be paid” in 3.]

All debts that are to be paid to the king’s share are to be paid in solidi of twelve denarii [Note: “in solidi, twelve denarii” in B.; “in solidi of twelve denarii” in 3.], except the *fredum* prescribed in the Salic Law. That is to be paid in the same solidus in which the other compositions are to be paid [Note: “are to be paid” in 1*.].

### 31. Concerning one who presumes to reopen a judged case [Note: Numbered 30 by mistake, and so numbered falsely thereafter in 3.]

If anyone presumes to reopen a case already judged in the assembly [Note: “in the assembly” in 1*, corrected], and is there convicted by witnesses, let him either pay fifteen solidi or receive fifteen blows from the *scabini* [Note: “scabinii” in 1*. 3.] who previously judged the case.

### 32. Concerning the qualities required of one summoned as a witness

The best men in each district or city are to be summoned as witnesses [Note: “of the district” is absent in 1.], and the person against whom he is to testify [Note: “or the person whom he must testify against” in 1*.] must be unable to bring any charge against him.

### 33. Concerning *scabini*, advocates and notaries to be chosen by the royal envoys

Our envoys are to choose *scabini* [Note: “scabinos” in 1*. 4. 6.; “scabineos” in 3.], advocates and notaries in each locality, and when they return they are to bring their names written with them.

### 34. Concerning those who disdain to observe the law

Those who have disdained to observe the law [Note: “disdain” in 1*.] are to be brought before the king by sureties.

### 35. Concerning the collection assigned to the *haribannum*-collector [Note: “airibannatoris” in 1*; *heribannatorii* in B.; “hairbannatoris” in 3.]

Those who owe the *haribannum* [Note: “hairibannum” in 3; the form *heribannum* is found in 1*, B., G.] are to make a contribution to the *haribannum*-collector [Note: “haribannator” in 1*. 6.].

### 36. Concerning coloni and fiscal dependants

Neither a colonus nor a fiscal dependant is to be able to make transfers anywhere [Note: “to anyone” in 6.].

### 37. Concerning not sending a man to court without cause

No one is to presume to send a man to court without cause, unless a judgment has been rendered [Note: “to judgment” in G.].

### 38. Concerning the case and testimony of a drunken man, and concerning the count’s court

No drunk man is to be able to pursue his own case in the assembly [Note: “in the assembly” in 1*, corrected.], nor give testimony; nor is a count to hold court unless he is fasting.

### 39. Concerning royal envoys and other men traveling on official business

Concerning our traveling envoys and other men journeying for our benefit, no one is to presume to deny them lodging.

### 40. Concerning those who are to be summoned to court

No one is to be summoned to court except a person who is pursuing his own case, or one from whom another must seek a case [Note: “who must seek it from another” in 1*. 4. G.]; except the seven *scabini*, who must preside at all courts [Note: “be present at” in G.].

### 41. Concerning false witnesses

Concerning false witnesses, we decree that they are not to be accepted [Note: Here 2 adds two chapters: 42, “That no witness is to be accepted beyond the vestiture of our grandfather and father”; and 43, from chapter 11 of Lothar’s Pavia capitulary.].

### 42. Concerning not swearing by the king’s life

No one is to presume to swear by the life of the king and his sons.

### 43. Concerning one who is free by charter, if he is summoned to servitude

If anyone has been released as a free man by charter and is summoned by any man to servitude, let him first produce the lawful author [Note: Throughout this chapter 6 uses *actor* instead of *auctor*.] of his freedom and remain in his freedom.

But if the lawful author is unavailable, let him be permitted to defend himself by the testimony of good men who were present when the free man was released. If witnesses are unavailable, let him confirm that his charter, which is the third, is genuine and lawful by means of two other charters signed or written by the hand of the same chancellor, whoever they may be [Note: “whoever” is deleted in 1*.].

The chancellor, however, must be someone known and accepted by the people of that locality [Note: “who was known to all the people of the place” in 3.]. But if the man who has been summoned to servitude has neither an author nor witnesses, and cannot find two other charters to confirm his own, then the man who summoned him is to establish, according to that very law, that the charter is false [Note: Absent in 4.] and claim him as a slave.

But if the accuser is defeated by the author, the witnesses, or the comparison of the charters, he is to be compelled to pay the fine contained in the charter of emancipation for having wished, but been unable, to carry out what he attempted [Note: “what he wishes” in 1. 4. G.; “what he will have wished” in 3.].

### 44. Concerning a slave who commits any damage

No one may abandon his slave because of damage inflicted by him on anyone [Note: “by any person” in 1*. B.], but the master is to answer for him according to the nature of the damage, or offer him to the claimant for composition or punishment [Note: “of the claimant” in 1* 4. B.; “of the plaintiff” in 3.].

But if the slave flees after committing the crime, so that his master cannot find him at all [Note: “has not been able to find him” in 1*.], the master is to strive to clear himself by oath [Note: Absent in 4.]—that this was neither his will nor his knowledge, and that his slave committed such a crime [Note: Absent in 4.].

### 45. Concerning legal summons to the assembly [Note: Absent in 3.] [Note: Absent in 3.]

If anyone has been legally summoned to the assembly and does not come, unless a lawful impediment (*sunnis*) has detained him [Note: “somnus” (“sleep”) in 3.], he is to be judged liable to fifteen solidi. The same applies to the second and third summons.

But if he refuses to come to the fourth, his property is to be placed under the ban until he comes and renders justice concerning the matter for which he was summoned [Note: “and concerning the remaining matter written above”; hence “concerning the matter about which” in Bal.]. If he does not come within a year, the king is to be consulted concerning the property placed under the ban [Note: “under the ban” in 6. G. Bal.], and whatever he decides concerning it is to be done.

The first summons is for seven nights, the second for fourteen nights, the third for twenty-one nights [Note: “eleven” in 3; “twenty-two” in 6.], and the fourth for forty-two [Note: The words “nights … and the fourth” are absent in 6.]. The same is to be done with a man’s benefice, if he happens not to possess property of his own: it is to be placed under the ban until the king is consulted [Note: “until the king has been consulted” in 6. B. G. Bal.; “until such time as” in 3.].

### 46. Concerning the author of the property [Note: “actor” in 6.]

If the author comes and refuses to receive the property that has been challenged [Note: “intertiam” in 6. B.; “intertiam” is a legal technical term.], let them contend by combat in the field or by the cross [Note: The words “by the field or by the cross” are absent in Met.].

### 47. Concerning men condemned to death and afterward granted life, if they seek justice [Note: “do justice” in G.]

Concerning those men who have been condemned to death because of their offenses and afterward granted life, if they themselves seek justice from others or wish to seek justice from them, this is how judgment is to be settled between them.

First of all, concerning the cases for which he was condemned to death [Note: “had been condemned” in 3.], he can make no claim [Note: “no petition” in B.], because all his property was publicly confiscated according to the judgment of the Franks [Note: “was confiscated” in 1.]. If afterward, once life has been granted to him, he can acquire anything lawfully, let him hold and defend it in his freedom according to the law.

He is not to be accepted as a witness, nor employed among the *scabini* [Note: “scabinos” in 1*. 4.] to judge according to the law. And if something is adjudged under oath that he must swear, and someone wishes to accuse him of giving a false oath, let them contend [Note: “let him contend” in G.; “let them contend with weapons” in Bal.].

### 48. Concerning a man granted life after judgment, if he refuses to render justice

If life has been granted to someone after the judgment of the *scabini*, and afterward he commits some wrongdoing and refuses to render justice, saying that he is dead and therefore ought not to render justice, it is decreed that he is to undergo the earlier judgment that he ought previously to have undergone.

If anyone commits some wrong against him, he is to have permission, according to the order of equity, to seek his justice concerning offenses committed after he was condemned to death [Note: Absent in 1*.]; concerning the earlier matters, let the previous judgment remain as above.

### 49. Concerning a free man who receives a robber under the ban

Concerning a robber placed under the ban, the free man who receives him is to pay fifteen solidi, and the slave is to be beaten with one hundred twenty blows [Note: “is to be beaten” in 6; “is to receive 120 blows” in G.].

### 50. Concerning a count who places a robber under the ban

A count who has placed a robber under the ban [Note: “holding a robber under the ban” in 3.] is to make known to his neighbors and to the other counts that the same robber has been banned by him, so that they do not receive him.

### 51. Concerning the free men who may be compelled to come to the assembly

No one else among free men is to be compelled to come to court or to the assembly, except the *scabini* or the counts’ vassals [Note: “the lord’s vassals” in 3. 3b.], unless they must pursue or answer a case [Note: “seek” in 1.].

### 52. Concerning how witnesses are to be brought forward to give testimony

Witnesses are not to be induced by reward to give testimony. No one is to give testimony or swear an oath unless fasting. Before they swear, witnesses are to be examined separately concerning what they intend to say about the matter regarding which they must give testimony.

### 53. Concerning no one delaying anyone’s justice [Note: “whatever” in 1*.]

No royal envoy, count, judge or *scabineus* is to presume to delay anyone’s justice if it can immediately be completed according to right, nor presume to accept rewards from anyone for this through any evil contrivance.

### 54. Concerning not compelling anyone to go to a bridge for the sake of a toll

No one is to be compelled to go to a bridge in order to cross a river for the sake of tolls [Note: “or” in 3.] when he can cross that river more directly elsewhere. Likewise, in an open plain where there is neither a bridge [Note: “nor a ford” in 3.] nor a crossing [Note: “traiectus” in 1*. G. Hld.; “triectus” in 4.], we strictly decree that no toll is to be exacted there.

### 55. Concerning a priest who gives holy chrism to overturn a judgment

A priest who gives holy chrism for the purpose of overturning a judgment, after he has been deposed from his rank, is to lose his hand [Note: Absent in 1*.].

### 56. Concerning the qualities required of judges, advocates, officials and other ministers

Judges, advocates, officials, centenarii, vicarii and *scabini* are to be appointed from among those who can be found to be the best [Note: “who can find the best” in 1. B.; “who may be able” in 3.] to exercise their offices [Note: “ministries” in 3.].

### 57. Concerning the public assembly

In places where public assemblies are customarily held, a roof is to be built of such a kind that it can be used both in winter [Note: “in winter” is absent in 4.] and in summer [Note: Absent in 1*. B.].

### 58. Concerning oaths assigned to the palace

Oaths that have been assigned to the palace [Note: “assigned” in 3. 4. B. G.] are to be completed at the palace. And if the compurgators refuse to come with the person concerned, they are to be compelled to come to the palace by a royal command, a written notice [Note: “indiluculo” in 3.], or a seal [Note: “and when the compurgators …” in G.].

### 59. Concerning the obstruction caused by complainants

Concerning complainants who cause great obstruction at the palace by reaching the ears of the lord emperor [Note: Absent in 4. 6.], let the envoys or counts send their own envoys against those who proceed by lying, so that they may convict them [Note: “so that they may communicate with them” in G.; “against them,” with *contra* erased, in 1, 1*.].

### 60. Concerning fugitives concealed contrary to the royal command [Note: “and robbers” in 4.]

Concerning fugitives who have been taken through various provinces and concealed contrary to the command of the lord emperor, whoever received or retained them after the time specified in the earlier command [Note: G. reads “the command”; 1* omits the words “who received them after the time.”] is to pay the royal ban [Note: “pay” in 3.].

### 61. Concerning excessively blasphemous robbers

Concerning robbers who are greatly blasphemous [Note: “blasphemia” in 3.], whoever captures one of them is to suffer no damage on that account.

### 62. Concerning peace within the realm

Concerning peace and justice within the realm, let this be fulfilled as we have often commanded in other chapters [Note: “we have commanded” in 6. B.].

### 63. Concerning restraining the juniors among the common people

Concerning the common people, let each man restrain his juniors, so that they may obey and comply more and more with imperial commands and [Note: Absent in 3.] orders.

### 64. Concerning one who comes against a royal envoy with an armed band

If anyone comes against a royal envoy with an armed band and weapons, and opposes or wishes to oppose the assignment given to him, and it is proved that he knowingly came to resist the royal envoy, let him pay with his life.

If he denies it, let him clear himself with twelve oath-helpers [Note: “and … clear himself” was added in the margin in 5.], and, because he came armed with an armed band to resist the royal envoy, let him pay the royal ban [Note: “pay” in 5.]. The lord emperor judged the same way concerning his own vassals. If a slave does this, let him be subjected to corporal discipline [Note: “discipline” in 3. 6. B.].

### 65. Concerning one who breaks into another person’s house

If anyone breaks into another person’s house, he is to pay triple compensation, according to the law and the *ewa* [Note: The witnesses give numerous variants: *ita*, *ewa*, *euuma*, *eam*, *eo iam*, *ea*, and *suam*. Some omit the words “according to the law and the ewa” entirely.], to the person whose house was broken into and plundered, for whatever he took away or seized or stole by force [Note: “by violence” in G., Camb., Thu., Vat., Sang. 1, Colb.], and in addition pay the royal ban.

If a slave does this, he is to receive the preceding sentence and in addition make composition according to his law. If a free man causes such damage to anyone that he is unable to make full compensation, he is to strive to give himself as a pledge in place of a slave until he completes the full compensation [Note: “to someone” in G.].

### 66. Concerning crops or grain seized or stolen on campaign [Note: The sentence concerning a free man is absent in G.; the entire chapter is absent there.]

If anyone on campaign, in defiance of the royal ban, seizes, grazes [Note: “blames” in 4.; the words concerning grazing are absent in 6; B., G. and Bal. place them after “or steals”], or steals crops or grain, or devastates them with horses [Note: “pannum” in 2b.], he is to pay triple compensation for the assessed damage according to the law [Note: “repay” in 4.].

If a free man does this, he is to be compelled to pay the royal ban for it [Note: “let him pay the royal ban”; the rest is absent in 3.]. A slave, however, is to restore the damage on the spot with triple legal compensation [Note: “if a slave” in 1*.], and is to be subjected to corporal discipline for the damage [Note: “for the ban” in 1.; “be subjected to” in 3.].

### 67. Concerning a free man summoned to the army under the ban [Note: “on campaign” in G.]

Whoever is a free man and has been summoned to the army under the ban [Note: “on campaign” in 3. G.] but refuses to come is to pay the full *heribannum*, that is, sixty solidi.

Or, if he does not have the means to pay that sum, let him give himself as a pledge into the service of the prince [Note: Absent in 6.] until, over time, the ban itself has been paid by him; then let him return again to his condition of freedom [Note: “return” in 3.].

If that man, who gave himself into service because of the *heribannum*, dies in that service, his heirs are not to lose the inheritance belonging to him [Note: “belonging to them” in 1*. 4. B.; “belonging to themselves” in 3.], nor their freedom [Note: “concerning freedom” in 3.], nor are they to become liable for the ban itself [Note: Absent in 1, 1*.].

### 68. Concerning the exacting of the *haribannum*

A count is not to presume to exact the *haribannum* on any pretext—not for *wacta* [Note: Also *wahcta* in 3 and *vacta* in G.], nor for the *scara*, nor for the *warda*, nor for lodging [Note: “herigare” in 3; “bergare” in G.], nor for any other ban—unless our envoy first receives the *haribannum* for our share and, by our command, gives him his third part from it.

The *haribannum* itself is not to be exacted in land or slaves, but in gold and silver, cloaks, weapons, animals, cattle, or such kinds of goods as are useful [Note: “and also” in 1.].

### 69. Concerning those who hold royal offices and, when summoned to the army, fail to come to the appointed court

Whoever among those holding our offices is summoned to the army and does not come to the appointed court is to abstain from meat and wine for as many days as he is proved to have arrived after the appointed court.

### 70. Concerning those who return from the army without permission

Whoever returns from the army without the permission or authorization of the prince—an act which the Franks call *heriscliz* [Note: Also *herisdiz* in 3 and *herisliz* in 4.]—we wish the ancient constitution, that is, the capital sentence, to be observed for punishing him [Note: The word “Franks” is absent in 4.].

### 71. Concerning those who hold princes’ benefices

Whoever among those who hold a prince’s benefice abandons his peer [Note: “father” in 6.] while he is marching against the common enemies in the army [Note: The words “marching … in the army” were accidentally omitted in the following chapter in 1*; no lacuna is marked.], and refuses to go or remain with him, is to lose his honor and benefice [Note: Absent in 4.].

### 72. Concerning not compelling anyone to drink on campaign

On campaign no one is to ask his peer or any other man to drink [Note: “compel” in Riv.]. Whoever is found drunk in the army is to be excommunicated in such a way that he may drink only water until he acknowledges that he has acted wrongly.

### 73. Concerning vassals who still serve in the palace but nevertheless hold benefices [Note: “have” in 1, 1*, B.; “do not have” in 4.]

Concerning the lord’s vassals who still serve within the household and are nevertheless known to hold benefices [Note: “know” in B.], it is decreed that whoever among them remains at home with the lord emperor is not to retain his settled vassals with him, but is to permit them to go with the count whose people they are.

### 74. Concerning preparation for the army according to ancient custom

It is decreed that preparation for the army is to be announced and observed according to ancient custom [Note: “is to be made” in 1*, corrected.], namely, provisions from the March for three months and weapons and clothing for half a year.

This was nevertheless arranged to be observed as follows: for those who travel from the Rhine [Note: Also *rehno*, *hreno*, and *reno* in the witnesses.] to the Loire [Note: “Ligeram” in 3; “Liger” in B.], the three months are to be reckoned in advance from the Loire [Note: The words “from the Loire onward” and the following phrase are absent in G.; B. has “carefully in advance from the Loire.”]; and those who travel from the Loire to the Rhine are to have provisions for three months reckoned in advance from the Rhine.

Those who are beyond the Rhine and travel to Saxony are to know that the March is at the Elbe [Note: “know that they are going to the March” in 3.]. Those who live beyond the Loire and must depart for Spain [Note: “travel to Spain” in 3; “who must proceed into Spain” in 4.] are to recognize the Pyrenees as their March.

### 75. Concerning giving or selling mail-shirts or swords to outsiders only with royal permission [Note: “selling” in 1*. 4. G.]

It is decreed that neither a bishop, nor an abbot or abbess, nor any ecclesiastical ruler is to presume, without our permission, either to give or sell a mail-shirt or sword to any outsider, except to his own vassals [Note: “vassals” in 3. B.].

If it happens that in any church or holy place there are more mail-shirts [Note: “mail-shirts are found” in 3.] than suffice for the men of that church’s ruler [Note: “rulers” in 1*.], then that ecclesiastical ruler is to ask the prince [Note: “the prince, that is, the ruler” in 1*. 3. Thu. Sang.] what he orders to be done with them [Note: “is to be asked” in 1*.].

Source/review notes: All supplied witness readings and sigla are retained; the uncertain phrase in rege continentur remains literal with its likely sense identified.

### 76. Concerning the limits of cases and lawsuits

Concerning the status of cases and lawsuits, we decree that, from the time when King Pippin, of blessed memory, died and we began to reign, cases or lawsuits made and arising between the parties shall be investigated and brought to an end by a judgment appropriate to them. But those cases brought before that time—that is, before the death of the aforesaid King Pippin—shall either not be pursued at all or shall be preserved until our inquiry.

[Note: Column 0563: one manuscript omits *from which*. Another reads “equal” instead of “between the parties.” For *preserved*, manuscripts read “reserved”; several witnesses have other variants.]

### 77. Concerning bishops, counts, and the more powerful, if they have a case among themselves

We order that if bishops, abbots, counts, and any other powerful persons have a case among themselves and are unwilling to make peace, they be commanded to come into our presence; nor shall their dispute be judged elsewhere, lest on this account justice be denied to the poor and less powerful. Nor shall any count of our palace presume to settle the cases of the powerful without our command; rather, he shall know that he is to devote himself only to administering justice to the poor and less powerful.

[Note: Column 0563: “counts” is absent in manuscript G.]

### 78. Concerning the selection of witnesses for investigating any matter

Whenever witnesses must be sought and selected for investigating any matter, let our envoy and the count in whose jurisdiction the matter is to be dealt with select such men as can be found to be the best in that county. Let it not be permitted to litigants to produce false witnesses through rewards, as has hitherto been customary.

[Note: Column 0563: manuscript G reads “to find.”]

### 79. Concerning the court of the hundred

Let no man be judged in the court of the hundred either to death, to the loss of his liberty, or to the return of property or slaves; but such matters shall be judged in the presence of a count or of our envoys.

[Note: Column 0563: manuscript 1 reads “counts.”]

### 80. Concerning the inquiry and description, by each envoy, within his assignment

Let each of our envoys diligently inquire and cause it to be recorded within his assignment what each man possesses in benefice, and how many settled men there are in that benefice.

[Note: Column 0563: manuscript 1 reads “cause him to record”; manuscript G reads “how many hides.”]

### 81. Concerning benefices, how they have been constricted

How those same benefices have been constricted, or who has acquired or constructed an allod from a benefice.

[Note: Column 0563: the word *condricta* is so written here, in the index, and in the text in manuscript 3; manuscript 4 has *constricte*, manuscript G *constructi*, and some codices *constructa*. One comparison of manuscript 3 reads “he destroyed an allod.” Manuscript B has “that is.”]

### 82. Concerning the benefices of bishops, abbots, and the rest, and concerning the recording of the royal estates

Let not only the benefices of bishops, abbots, abbesses, counts, and our vassals be recorded, but also our own royal estates, so that we may know how much of our property we possess in each envoy’s district.

[Note: Column 0563: the final words are absent in manuscript 3.]

### 83. Concerning the times when envoys’ circuits are to be carried out for the administration of justice

We wish our envoys to conduct their circuits for the sake of the justices that have hitherto remained outstanding on the counts’ side for only four months of the year: in winter, January; in spring, April; in summer, July; and in autumn, October. In the remaining months, each count shall hold his court and administer justice. Our envoys, however, shall hold their courts four times in one month and in four places with those counts for whom it is appropriate to be able to assemble at that place.

[Notes: Column 0563: “which have remained outstanding” is absent in manuscript 1. Manuscript 4 reads “from one side”; manuscript G reads “from the counts’ side.” One witness has *in March* corrected from an unclear reading; another reads “in winter, in March, in spring, in April, in summer, in July, in autumn”; other witnesses have variants. In another capitulary, from 812, chapter 8, the reading is “four times in one year.”]

### 84. Concerning failure to carry out the lord’s command in any envoy’s assignment

Whatever that envoy finds to have been done in that assignment contrary to our command, let him order not only that it be corrected, but also report the matter itself to us, exactly as he found it.

[Note: Column 0563: manuscripts 1, 3, B, and Bal read “let him correct it.”]

[Column 0565A]

### 85. Concerning the investigation of the royal census

Let our envoys diligently investigate our censuses, wherever payments have customarily been rendered from ancient times to the king’s share; and likewise the *freda*. Let them report to us, so that we may determine what ought to be done with these matters in the future.

[Notes: Column 0565: manuscripts 1, 3, and B read *census* rather than *censos*. Manuscripts 1 and B have the singular “customarily rendered.” Manuscript 3 reads “and let us arrange.”]

### 86. Concerning property from which the census was customarily rendered to the king’s share

If property from which the census was customarily rendered to the king’s share has been transferred to any church, let it either be returned to its rightful heirs, or let the person who has retained it pay that census.

[Notes: Column 0565: manuscript 1 reads “exacted” rather than “rendered”; manuscript 3 reads “something belonging to a church”; the words “or him” are absent in manuscripts 1, 3, and B.]

### 87. Concerning making the royal envoys’ courts known to the counts

Let each of our envoys make known at his court to the counts who belong to his assignment that, in those months in which he does not conduct his circuit, they are to meet among themselves and hold common courts, both for restraining robbers and for administering other forms of justice.

[Notes: Column 0565: manuscript 1 reads the feminine form “known”; manuscript G reads “which.” The word “known” is absent in manuscript B. Manuscript 1 reads “let them meet”; other witnesses have variants. Manuscript 1 reads “let them hold a court”; manuscript B has “jointly.”]

[Column 0566A]

### 88. Concerning the promise of loyalty to the king

Let our envoys cause our people once again to promise us loyalty, according to the custom established long ago; and let them themselves explain and interpret to those men how they ought to preserve that oath and loyalty toward us.

### 89. Concerning homicides committed within the country

Let homicides not be committed within the country, as they are forbidden by the law of God, neither for the sake of vengeance, nor out of greed, nor through robbery. Wherever such acts are found, let them be punished by our judges according to the law and by authority of our command. Let no man be killed except where the law commands it.

[Notes: Column 0565: the heading originally read “concerning men” and was corrected to “concerning homicides” in manuscript 3. Some witnesses place this chapter after chapter 64; others place it after chapter 69. Manuscript 1 reads “for the purpose of robbery.”]

### 90. Concerning measures and weights

Let everyone possess equal and accurate measures and just and equal weights, whether in cities, in monasteries, for giving to one another, or for receiving, just as we have been commanded in the law of God.

[Notes: Column 0565: manuscripts 1 and 4 have “in a monastery.” Manuscript 1 has “whether they are”; this is absent in B. Manuscripts 3 and 6, G, and Bal have other readings. Manuscript 1 reads “commands.”]

[Note: Column 0565B–C: After this, manuscript 6 adds here chapters 22–24 and 71–74, taken from the fourth book and placed there again. Til and Bal add one chapter taken from the Beauvais codex, where it is written in different ink but by the same hand. Since all the others omit it, we have placed it here:]

### 90b. Concerning peace in the army or within the country

We decree that if, in the army or within our kingdom, a dispute or disturbance arises between any persons whatsoever, whether great or small—as frequently happens when the devil lies in wait—so that the faithful of the holy Church of God and of us come there armed to resist the malice of wickedness, namely whoever is able to do so, with a coat of mail and shield, a two-edged weapon, and a club; and if any person wishes to bring any complaint against him, he may, according to the order of the law and with the oath that we have prescribed, personally establish each point by his own hand, showing that he would not have come there for any business or hatred, but only to bring concord and peace and to calm the dispute itself. If anyone refuses to come and is unable to establish his fitness in this way, let him pay our ban, namely sixty solidi, and render it to our share.

## BEGINNING OF THE FOURTH PREFACE TO THE LITTLE BOOK

[Column 0565]

Since above, in two booklets, I have set out the ecclesiastical chapters that the aforesaid princes, the lord Emperor Charles and the most pious Augustus Louis, and also Lothar Caesar, his son, issued, while in the third I collected the chapters pertaining to secular law that the lord Emperor Charles enacted, I have now gathered into a fourth booklet the chapters pertaining to the enlargement of secular law that the most illustrious lord Augustus Louis and Lothar, Caesar, enacted.

[Notes: Column 0565: one witness reads “the fourth.” In manuscripts B, G, and Bal, the words from “the most illustrious lord Louis” onward are absent; they instead have the singular “enacted.”]

## BEGIN THE CHAPTER HEADINGS

[Column 0565D]

1. Concerning slaves who, through defiance, inflict violence on someone.  
2. Concerning property or slaves seized by the royal treasury.  
3. Concerning slaves or ecclesiastical persons fleeing to the royal treasury.  
4. Concerning the king’s vassals appointed to guard the frontier.  
5. Concerning counts assigned to coastal defense.  
6. Concerning those who have lost their property because of incest.  
7. Concerning conspiracies of slaves in Flanders, in Mempiscus, and in other coastal regions.  
8. Concerning those who make salt on the seashore.  
9. Concerning the wives of the deceased: what share of the jointly cultivated land they ought to receive after their husbands’ deaths.  
10. Concerning embankments to be constructed beside the Loire.  
11. Concerning the restoration of twelve bridges over the Seine.  
12. Concerning the construction of all bridges.  
13. Concerning the honor of churches.

## THE AFORESAID CHAPTERS AND THEIR TEXT BEGIN

[Note: In this book codex 6 differs considerably from the others. Its chapters have been wholly altered and abridged in their individual places, and the entire order of the chapters has been confused. Since the scribe omitted and mutilated many chapters, while quite a few passages have been added and supplied at the end by another hand—and some have even been included twice—we have displayed their sequence here, preserving both the order and the numbers by which the chapters are marked in the codex:

Codex 6: 1–22, 23, 24, 25, 26–28, 29–32, 33, 34–37, 38–44, 45, 46–49. Edition: 1–22, 24, 25, 26, 29–31, 35–38, 41, 44–47, 49–55, 57, 59–62. Codex 6: 50–52, 53, 54, 27, 28 (a new hand begins), 32–34, 39, 40, 42, 43, 48, 56, 58, 63–69, 71–74. Edition: 65–67, 70, 23, 74, 27, 28, 32–34, 39, 40, 42, 43, 48, 56, 58, 63–69, 71–74.]

[Column 0567]

### 1. Concerning slaves who, through defiance, inflict violence on someone

If slaves, having gathered a crowd in defiance, inflict violence on someone—that is, if they commit homicide, arson, or the plunder of any kind of property—their masters, through whose negligence this has occurred because they were unwilling to restrain them so that they would not dare to do such things, shall be compelled to pay our ban, namely sixty solidi.

[Note: Column 0567: one manuscript has “on account of defiance” in the heading. Manuscript 3 has the singular “slave”; another reads “if he inflicts.” Several witnesses omit “them.” The readings for “their masters” include “of their masters,” “of the lord,” “if the masters,” and “if the lords.”]

### 2. Concerning property or slaves seized by the royal treasury

Concerning property or slaves said to have been seized by our treasury, we wish our envoys to conduct an inquiry without an oath, through the more truthful men who live around that county; and whatever they are able to investigate more truly and certainly concerning this matter, let them bring to our knowledge, so that we may then decide whatever seems just to us.

[Notes: Column 0567: an unclear reading was corrected to “truthful men.” Manuscript 4 reads “concerning the matter”; manuscript G adds “and.”]

### 3. Concerning slaves or ecclesiastical persons fleeing to the royal treasury

If slaves, ecclesiastical persons, or any free men flee to our treasury, and their masters or their advocates demand them back, and the agent of our treasury understands that he cannot justly retain them under our lordship, let him expel them from that treasury, and let their masters receive them. But if it seems to that agent that they ought to belong to our lordship, let him expel them from that treasury; and after they have been received by those who demanded them, let him bring a lawful action against them, and thus, if he can, establish his title to our possession.

[Notes: Several manuscripts vary between “agent” and “author.” One reads “commanded” rather than “seemed”; manuscript G has “ought not to belong.” Other witnesses have “will be able” rather than “can.”]

### 4. Concerning the king’s vassals appointed to guard the frontier

Concerning our vassals who have been appointed to guard our frontier, or who possess benefices or private property in distant regions, or who also serve us continually in our palace and therefore cannot hold regular courts: we wish our envoys or the count to make this known to us, and we shall arrange for them to come to their courts.

[Note: The words “who also serve us continually in our palace” were added recently in manuscript 2. Manuscripts 2, 2b, and 4 have “counts”; manuscript 1 has “known,” and manuscript B has another form of “known.”]

### 5. Concerning counts assigned to coastal defense

We wish counts who have been assigned to coastal defense—whoever among them remains in his jurisdiction—not to excuse himself from administering justice on account of that defense. Rather, if he has his own *scabini* with him, let him hold court there and administer justice.

[Notes: Manuscript 6 reads “we do not wish.” Manuscripts vary in the wording around “if he has”; one reads “but let him have with him,” another “but wherever.” The term *scabini* appears in several spellings; manuscript B has a superscript form apparently reading *scephenen*.]

### 6. Concerning those who have lost their property because of incest

Concerning those who say that they lost their property on account of incest, it has been established that if they lost those same properties before the most recent five-year period, when we held our court at Compiègne, they shall not have them restored.

[Note: One manuscript reads *incertum* (“uncertainty”) rather than *incestum*.]

### 7. Concerning conspiracies of slaves in Flanders, in Mempiscus, and in other coastal regions

Concerning the conspiracies of slaves that occur in Flanders, in Mempiscus, and in the other coastal regions, we wish our envoys to notify the masters of those slaves, so that they may restrain them and prevent them from presuming to form such conspiracies thereafter. Let those masters themselves know that, if any of their slaves presume to form such a conspiracy after this command of ours has been communicated to them, the master himself must pay our ban, namely sixty solidi.

[Notes: The place-name appears as *Menpiscus* and *Mempiscus* in different witnesses. The heading was mistakenly placed before the following chapter in manuscript 3 and was thereafter shifted through chapter 11. Another witness has “concerning conspirators in coastal regions.”]

### 8. Concerning those who make salt on the seashore

Concerning the land on the seashore where they make salt, we wish some of them to come to our court, so that their case may be heard and so that we may then be able to decide among them according to equity.

[Notes: One manuscript has another form of “salt.” Manuscripts 5 and B read “palace” rather than “court.”]

### 9. Concerning the wives of the deceased: what share of the jointly cultivated land they ought to receive after their husbands’ deaths

We wish the wives of deceased men, after their husbands’ deaths, to receive one-third of the jointly cultivated land that they cultivated together in the benefice. As for the property that the man who held that benefice brought or acquired from elsewhere, or that was bestowed on him by his friends, we wish it to pass both to the orphans of the deceased and to their wives.

[Note: One manuscript adds “what share they ought thereafter to have.”]

### 10. Concerning embankments to be constructed beside the Loire

Concerning the embankments to be constructed beside the Loire: let a good envoy be placed in charge of this work, and let this be entrusted through our envoy to Pippin, so that he too may appoint an envoy for the task, in order that the aforesaid work may be completed.

[Note: Manuscript 3 reads “so that.”]

### 11. Concerning the restoration of twelve bridges over the Seine

Concerning the twelve bridges over the Seine, we wish the men of the county who ought to construct them to be admonished by our envoys to restore them quickly. The envoys are not to agree to their empty contention when they say that they ought to construct those bridges nowhere else except where they had been in ancient times; rather, those men of the county shall be ordered to construct those same bridges where they are now necessary.

[Notes: Some manuscripts read “concerning the restoration of the Seine” or have the plural “bridges.” Manuscript 2 reads “somewhere” rather than “nowhere”; manuscript G omits “where”; manuscript 5 has another variant. The final words are absent in manuscript 6.]

### 12. Concerning the construction of all bridges

Concerning all bridges that are to be constructed throughout our kingdom, let our envoys jointly admonish those who used to construct them to restore them.

[Note: Manuscript 2 reads “so that they may be restored”; another reading is “who constructed them and used to construct them.”]

### 13. Concerning the honor of churches

If anyone, whether for a trivial reason or without reason, kills a man in a church, let him pay the compensation for his life. But if they have quarreled outside, and one flees from the other into a church and kills him there while defending himself—and if he has no witnesses to this deed—let him affirm under oath, with twelve legitimate oath-helpers, that he killed him while defending himself. Afterward he shall be compelled to pay six hundred solidi to the share of the church that he had polluted by that homicide, and in addition our ban. But let the man who was killed lie without compensation; and thereafter let the killer receive, according to canonical judgment, a penance appropriate to the crime he committed.

[Notes: Manuscript 6 gives the following expanded form from “if they have quarreled” through “in addition our ban”: “If they have quarreled outside, and one has fled into the church and then the other has killed him there while he was defending himself, let him pay six hundred solidi to the church that he polluted, and in addition our ban.” Another witness adds: “That is, for twenty-one years: for seven of these he shall do penance in bread and water at the church door, removed from the prayers and communion of the faithful; for the next seven he shall be associated with the prayers of the faithful; and after the remaining seven have passed, he shall fully follow communion. His abstinence shall be moderated by priestly discretion.”]

If the person who committed this deed was a personal slave, let him be tested by the judgment of boiling water, to determine whether he did it voluntarily or in self-defense. If his hand is burned, let him be killed; but if it is not, let his master pay to the church according to the man’s *wergild*, or, if he wishes, hand him over to that church. In the case of an ecclesiastical, royal-estate, or benefice slave, we decree that for the first offense his *wergild* shall be paid in compensation for him, while for a second offense the slave himself shall be handed over to punishment. Nevertheless, the inheritance of a free man who has been sentenced to death on account of such a crime shall pass to his lawful heirs. If a homicide of this kind is committed in the churchyard of a church whose door has been consecrated with the relics of saints, it shall be amended or compensated in the same manner. But if the church door has not been consecrated, let what is committed in the churchyard be compensated in the manner in which what is committed in violated immunity ought to be compensated.

[Notes: Several codices omit the words from “concerning an ecclesiastical, royal-estate, and benefice slave” through “let him be handed over.” Manuscripts differ in the forms of *wergild*, including *wirdgild*, *wergeldum*, *werigeldum*, and related spellings. One witness gives the following expanded form: “Let him be killed; and let his master, if he wishes, pay either the *wergeld* or hand him over to the church itself. For one ecclesiastical, royal-estate, or benefice slave, we wish one *wergeld* to be paid, or the slave himself to be handed over to punishment.”]

### 14. Concerning injuries inflicted in a church on priests or any members of the clergy

The shedding of blood in a church with a club, if the injured person is a priest, shall be compensated threefold: two parts to that priest and the third as *fredum* to the church; in addition, our ban shall be paid. Likewise, in the case of a deacon, let the compensation according to his status be paid threefold, together with our ban. The same shall apply to a subdeacon, threefold according to his compensation. For a cleric of any order, let the amount according to his compensation be paid threefold, and in addition our ban. Likewise, for a blow without bloodshed inflicted on a cleric of any order, let three times his compensation be paid, together with our ban. Whoever does not possess enough to pay the church shall give himself into the service of that church until he has paid the entire debt.

[Notes: Several codices omit portions of this chapter, including the words “and in addition our ban” and, in some witnesses, the material from “likewise” through “threefold.” The terms for deacon, cleric, and the forms of *wergild* vary among the witnesses.]

[Note: Various codices insert here a chapter reported by Regino from Book II of the Capitularies; manuscripts Vat. 1, Bell., Met., and Camb. place it at the end of Book II:

**14b. Concerning compensation for a slain priest.** Let the bishop to whose parish the slain priest belonged be paid according to the capitulary of our glorious father Charles, namely as follows: the bishop shall assign half of his *wergild* to the needs of the church over which he presided, and shall justly distribute the other half in alms for him; for no heir of his seems nearer to him than the one who joined him to the Lord.]

### 15. Concerning widows, orphans, and the poor

We command that whenever widows, orphans, and poor people come before the count in the public court, their case shall be heard and decided first. If they are unable to obtain witnesses for seeking their cases themselves, or if they do not know the law, the count shall assist them by giving them a suitable person to manage their case or speak on their behalf.

[Note: Manuscript 6 expands the final clause: “Let the count assist them and provide them with such an advocate as may speak only on their behalf.”]

### 16. Concerning the abduction of widows

Whoever takes a widow as his wife within the first thirty days of her widowhood, whether against her will or with her consent, shall pay our ban—namely sixty solidi—threefold. If he took her against her will, let him also pay her her legal compensation; but thereafter let him not touch her.

[Notes: The phrase “of her widowhood” is absent in manuscripts B and G. One manuscript omits “let him pay her her law.”]

### 17. Concerning a person killed while performing public penance

Whoever kills a person performing public penance shall pay our ban threefold and pay his *wergild* to his nearest relatives.

[Notes: One manuscript has a marginal gloss, “a man who performs public penance.” Other manuscripts vary in the spelling of *wergild* and in the form “let it be paid.”]

### 18. Concerning a free man, that he have the power to give his property wherever he wishes, and how he ought to do this

If anyone wishes to transfer his property for the salvation of his soul, either to some venerable place, to a relative, or to anyone else, and at that time is within the county in which those properties are situated, let him take care to make a lawful transfer. But if, at the time when he wishes to transfer them, he is outside that county—whether in the army, at the palace, or in any other place—let him obtain as suitable witnesses men from his own county or others who live under the same law as he does. If he cannot obtain them, let him obtain such other men as he can find there who are the best available; and before them let him make the transfer of his property, and give security for the investiture to the person who receives the transfer, so that he may perform the investiture.

After this transfer has been made in this way, let his heir be unable to bring any claim concerning the aforesaid property. Moreover, let he himself provide security for that investiture, so that no opportunity remains for the heir to alter the transfer, but rather that the necessity of completing it rests upon him. If he has not yet divided his property with his co-heirs, let this not impede him; but if his co-heir is unwilling, let him be compelled, either by the count or by his envoy, to divide it with the person to whom the deceased wished his inheritance to pass. If he requested that it be transferred to any church, let his co-heir have with that church the same legal claim concerning the aforesaid inheritance that he ought to have had with another co-heir. This shall be observed with respect to father, son, and grandson until they reach the lawful age; afterward the property itself shall return to the immunity of that church.

[Notes: One manuscript reads “whether he is within” and another has “three suitable witnesses.” Several witnesses omit portions from “and give security” through the end of the chapter. The readings for “performing” vary. One manuscript has “which he did not wish” rather than “which he wished.” Manuscript B omits the clause concerning the co-heir’s legal claim.]

### 19. Concerning the prohibition of homicides

Whoever kills a man either for a trivial reason or without reason shall pay his *wergild* to those to whom that man belongs. For such presumption, however, he shall be sent into exile for as long as we please; nevertheless, he shall not lose his property.

[Note: Manuscript 6 adds: “If he kills him, he shall pay twice the *wergild* to those to whom the man belongs.” Manuscripts 3, 4, and G omit the words “his *wergild*.”]

### 20. Concerning what ought to be given as compensation for a *wergild*

As compensation for a *wergild*, we wish those things to be given that are “contained in the king” (*in rege continentur*, apparently the royal tariff or list), except a hawk and a sword; for on account of those two, perjury is sometimes committed when men swear that they are worth more than they actually are.

[Notes: Manuscripts vary in the spelling of *wergild*. One reads “in the composition”; another “many times” rather than “sometimes.”]

### 21. Concerning the abduction of another man’s betrothed

If anyone abducts another man’s betrothed, let him return her, together with her legal compensation, either to her father or to the person who by her law ought to be her defender. Whatever he took with her, let him return each item separately according to the law. If her defender consented to this act and therefore does not wish to demand anything from the abductor, let the count cause our *freda* to be separately exacted from him for each item. Let him pay the fiancé his legal compensation, and in addition pay our ban, namely sixty solidi; or let the count cause him to come into our presence, where he shall remain in exile for as long as we please, and he shall not be permitted to keep that woman.

[Notes: Manuscript 6 has a different text from “if her defender” onward, including: “If her defender consented to this deed and does not wish to seek anything from the abductor, let the count separately exact our *freda* from him for each item.” Manuscript G reads “to the count.” Another manuscript omits the remainder after “let the count separately compensate each item.”]

Constituimus, ut si in hoste aut infra regnum nostrum litigatio aut scandalum inter quascumque personas, videlicet maiores et minores, ortum fuerit, quod frequenter, insidiante diabolo, contingere solet, ut ibi fideles sanctae Dei ecclesiae et nostri ob resistendam impietatis malitiam armati veniant, id est [Col. 0566B] qui potest habere, cum lorica et scuto, ancipite atque fuste. Et si aliquis quaelibet persona adversus eum quamlibet querelam habere voluerit, liceat ei secundum legis ordinem cum sacramento quod posuimus, manu propria singula se idoneum facere, ut propter [Col. 0566C] quodlibet negotium aut odium ibi non advenisset, nisi ob concordiam et pacem ferendam et ipsam litigationem mitigandam.
