## 22. Concerning the Conviction of False Witnesses

[Col. 0573] If anyone has had a dispute with another over any matter, and witnesses have been produced against him by judgment, and if he suspects them of being false, he may set against them other witnesses whom he can procure who are better, so that the perversity of the false witnesses may be overcome by the testimony of true ones. [Note: In one witness, this chapter is greatly abridged.]

But if the parties’ witnesses disagree with one another so completely that neither party is willing in any way to yield to the other, two of the witnesses themselves shall be selected—one from each side—and they shall contend in the field with shields and clubs, so that it may be determined which side follows falsehood and which truth in its testimony. [Note: One witness omits “in this way.” Another omits “which side follows falsehood and which follows truth.”]

The champion who is defeated shall, because of the perjury he committed before the combat, have his right hand cut off. The other witnesses of the same party who have appeared to be false shall redeem their hands by payment. [Note: One witness reads *shall have appeared*; another, *has appeared*.] Two-thirds of this composition shall be given to the person against whom they testified, and one-third shall be paid as the *fredum*.

In a secular case, such a dispute among witnesses shall indeed be proved by combat in the field. In ecclesiastical cases, however, where on one side the matter is secular and on the other ecclesiastical, the same procedure shall be observed. [Note: One witness inserts: “or the truth of the matter shall also be sought by the judgment of the cross. We have judged that this should likewise be done with the timid, the weak, and the infirm, who are unable to fight, lest they lose their justice for that reason.”]

Where the matter is ecclesiastical on both sides, the heads of those churches shall have permission to reconcile the parties amicably, if they wish. But if they cannot agree among themselves on such a reconciliation, their advocates shall come to the public court before the count, and there a lawful end shall be imposed upon their disputes. [Note: G omits the words from “Witnesses” through “shall be sought.”]

Witnesses in any case shall not be sought from elsewhere but from the very county in which the property at issue in the case is situated, since it is not credible that the truth of a matter concerning a man’s status or anyone’s possession could be known better through others than through those who live nearer. If, however, the dispute that has arisen between them is on the boundary of two counties, they may have witnesses for their case from the neighboring hundred of the adjoining county.

## 23. Concerning Property Placed under the Ban

If anyone’s property has been placed under the ban because of some crime that he himself has committed, and, once the matter has been made known, he has delayed coming to do justice and has allowed that property to remain under the ban for a year and a day, he shall not acquire it thereafter; rather, it shall be joined to our fisc. [Note: Some witnesses read “the king’s fisc.”]

The debt that the person to whom the property belonged ought to have paid shall, through the count and his officials, be paid to those to whom that debtor was indebted, according to the assessment of the loss, from the movable goods found on that property. [Note: Some witnesses read “noble goods” instead of “movable goods.”] If the quantity of the movable goods found there is insufficient for the composition, the deficiency shall be supplied from the immovable property; and whatever remains, as stated, shall belong to our fisc. [Note: One witness omits the words from “from the immovable property” through “whatever remains.”]

If nothing can remain after the composition, everything shall be expended upon it. [Note: One witness reads “if nothing can be found.”] But if that man had not yet divided his property with his coheirs, the count shall summon them and make a lawful division with them. Then, as has already been stated, he shall adjudicate that man’s share to our fisc and pay the composition from it, according to the amount explained above, to those to whom it belongs by law. [Note: One witness omits this sentence through the end of the chapter.]

But if the claim was made not concerning another matter but concerning the very property that had been placed under the ban and thereby brought into our power, the count in whose jurisdiction it is established shall take care to report the matter to us, so that we may cause that property—which, according to the method stated above, has been brought into our ownership—to pass, by the authority of our command, into the right and possession of the man who was claiming it, if it ought to be his.

## 24. Concerning Summoning

If anyone is to be summoned concerning his status—that is, concerning his freedom—or concerning an inheritance, he shall be summoned according to the provisions of the law. In other cases, for which a person is required to render an account, he shall not be summoned in this way, but shall be summoned by the count under the ban.

If, after one or two admonitions by the count, anyone is unwilling to come to court, he shall be compelled to come and do justice after his property has been placed under the ban. [Note: One witness reads “if anyone does not wish to come”; another, “to the other.”]

[Note: After this point, G, Bal., and B. insert a chapter taken from Louis, *Capitularies*, no. 817, and from the *Capitulary of Aachen*, written separately above: “26. How a person who has been challenged concerning his status shall vindicate his freedom. A man who has been challenged concerning his status, if the person challenging him has the means to prove the charge, shall take eight lawful compurgators from the side from which he is challenged, whether that side is paternal or maternal, and no fewer than four equally lawful men from elsewhere, and by swearing shall vindicate his freedom. But if the means of proof is lacking, he shall take twelve free men from whatever source and defend his free status by oath. Every dispute may be settled before the hundredman, except the restoration of land and slaves, which may take place only before the count.”]

## 25. Concerning the Restraint of Feuds

If anyone, compelled by some necessity, has committed homicide, the count in whose jurisdiction the deed was committed shall cause him both to pay the composition and to pacify the feud by oath. [Note: One witness reads “in whose power”; above *faidam* is written *frido* in the same hand.]

If either party is unwilling to consent to this—whether the person who committed the homicide or the one who ought to receive the composition—the count shall cause the person who has been obstinate toward him to come before us, so that we may send him into exile for as long a time as we please, until he is disciplined there, so that he will no longer dare to be disobedient to his count and so that greater harm may not arise from it. [Note: G reads “is willing” instead of “is unwilling”; Bal. reads “the count shall cause him.”]

## 26. Concerning Where Oaths Are to Be Sworn

Where it has traditionally been customary to claim (*adhramire*) or swear oaths concerning freedom, a court shall be held there and oaths shall be sworn there. A court, however, shall be held neither in a church nor in its atrium. [Note: The variants include *adramire* and *adrhamire*; glosses give “to enter upon” and “to swear,” and a German gloss above the word is *stabon*. Rivip. adds: “There the *scabini* and teachers of the law shall meet with the others and hold courts there.” One witness reads “where” for “there”; G, 4, and 6 abbreviate the clause. In one manuscript *ut* is deleted and supplied above; 6 has *neque* twice; 3 reads *teneatur* (“be maintained”) for *habeatur*.]

The count shall hold the lesser pleas either within his own jurisdiction or wherever he is able to obtain them. We certainly wish a house to be established by the count at the place where he ought to hold court, so that public business may not be neglected because of the heat of the sun or rain. [Note: One witness reads “a house” instead of “the house”; another omits “by the count.”]

## 27. Concerning Those Accused of Theft

If a free man is accused of theft and possesses property of his own, he shall claim himself at court before the count. If he has no property, he shall give sureties who shall cause him to be claimed and brought to the plea. He may, on the first occasion, if he is able, clear himself according to the law by oath. [Note: The witnesses variously read “if he can clear himself by oath according to the law,” “to redeem himself by oath according to the law,” and “to make himself acceptable.”]

But if, on another occasion, two or three persons accuse him of theft, he may contend in the field against one of them with shield and club. [Note: One witness omits the words “two or three accuse him of theft.”]

If a slave is accused of theft, his master shall make amends for him or excuse him by oath, unless he has committed such a theft that he ought to be handed over to punishment. [Note: One witness reads “shall cleanse him” instead of “shall make amends.”]

## 28. Concerning Disregard of Royal Letters

If anyone has disregarded our letters—that is, the *tractoria* sent for the reception of our envoys—he shall either lose the honors he holds [Note: One witness reads “shall relinquish”] or remain in the place where he ought to have received the aforementioned envoys, and receive there at his own expense the legations that come there, until our will has been satisfied.

Whoever in any way disregards our letter shall come to the palace at our command and, according to our will, receive a punishment appropriate to his folly. If a free man or a count’s official has done this, he shall lose whatever honor or benefice he may have held. [Note: One witness omits “or benefice.”] If he is a slave, he shall be beaten naked at the stake and his head shall be shaved. [Note: One witness reads “at the stakes”; another has “or to the palace” in the margin.]

## 29. Concerning Unjust Tolls and Customary Payments

Where it was customary in the time of our grandfather, the lord Pippin, to pay a toll, it shall be paid there in the future also. But where this was begun only recently, it shall no longer be done. [Note: One witness omits the words concerning a newly instituted toll.]

Where there is no necessity to cross a river by a bridge, or where a vessel has gone through the middle of the water or beneath a bridge without approaching the bank, and nothing has been bought or sold there, no toll shall henceforth be paid. No one shall compel another to go to a bridge where he can cross the water beside the bridge.

Whoever thereafter exacts a toll in such places, or from those who are traveling to the palace or to the army, shall restore that toll together with his legally prescribed composition and shall pay our ban, namely sixty solidi. [Note: The word *ferit* is written above the line. One witness omits the reference to those going to the palace or army.]

## 30. Concerning Those Unwilling to Accept Good Denarii

Any free man who is unwilling to receive a pure denarius of proper weight shall pay our ban, namely sixty solidi. [Note: One witness reads “who contradict the denarii.”]

If ecclesiastical slaves, or slaves of counts or of our vassals, presume to do this, they shall receive sixty strokes. But if their master or advocate, who is free, is unwilling, when ordered, to present them to the count or to our envoy, he shall pay the aforementioned ban of sixty solidi. [Note: One witness omits the words concerning ecclesiastical slaves and the presumption.]

## 31. Concerning Counterfeiters of Coin

Concerning false coin, we order that whoever is proved to have struck it shall have his hand cut off. Whoever consented to this, if he is free, shall pay sixty solidi; if he is a slave, he shall receive sixty strokes. [Note: Here codex 5 ends.]

[Note: Some witnesses introduce the chapter with: “Concerning false coin: whoever is proved to have struck it …”]

## 32. Concerning Our Private Property Returned Without Its Owner’s Command

If anyone returns to some claimant, without our command, property of ours that was in the possession of our father, he shall pay us an equal amount from his own property, together with the legally prescribed composition. [Note: One witness omits the words “to some claimant.”]

Whoever knowingly attempts to acquire it by evil deception shall be regarded as disloyal, because he has invalidated the oath of fidelity that he promised us. Therefore he shall be judged according to our will and power.

## 33. Concerning Boys Tonsured or Girls Veiled Against Their Parents’ Will

If anyone tonsures a boy against his parents’ will, or veils a girl, he shall pay his legal composition threefold, either to the boy or girl themselves, if they are already under their own authority, or to the person under whose authority they are. [Note: In 3, *que* is written above *suam*; 1* reads *forcapitis* at this point.]

They shall, however, have power over their own heads, so that they may remain in whatever such condition pleases them.

## 34. Concerning *Forcapiis* (Runaway Slaves)

[Note: 1* reads *potestatem* (“authority”) for *forcapiis*.]

If slaves flee from their masters into another person’s authority, the person under whose authority they are found shall receive no reward on that account, whether he returns them or drives them out. [Note: One witness has “authority” instead of “them”; another reads “believe.”]

Moreover, if he is unwilling either to return them or to drive them out, and refuses to surrender them to their lawful master, and they subsequently escape from there, he shall be compelled to pay for them according to the law. [Note: 1 reads *potestate* for *reddere*; 4 and Hld. omit *inde* (“from there”); G reads *exigere* (“exact”) for *solvere* (“pay”).]

## 35. Concerning Tributary Land

Whoever gives tributary land—from which tribute used to be paid to our share—to a church or to anyone else, the person who receives it shall in every respect pay to our share the tribute that was paid from it. [Note: One witness reads “which used to go out,” or “which used to be paid”; others read “the tribute that was paid as his own.”]

This shall not apply if he has such a grant from the royal property that he can demonstrate that the tribute itself has been remitted to him.

## 36. Concerning Destroyed Benefices

Whoever has allowed his benefice to lie abandoned on account of his own property, and within a year after it has been made known to him by the count or by our envoy has not had it repaired, shall lose that benefice. [Note: One witness reads “his benefice, once destroyed,” instead of “has allowed his benefice to lie abandoned.”]

## 37. Concerning Censual Land

If anyone holds censual land that his predecessors gave either to some church or to one of our estates, he cannot by any means hold it according to law unless the person under whose authority that church or estate falls is willing. [Note: One witness reads “before the assessors”; another has “or to some village.”]

This does not apply if he is the son or grandson of the person who gave it and the land is agreeable to him to hold. But in this matter consideration must be given to whether the person who holds it is rich or poor, and whether he has another benefice or even property of his own. [Note: One witness reads “or” and another “and”; one omits the clause concerning whether he has another benefice or property.]

If he has neither of these, he must be treated mercifully, lest, completely stripped of his possessions, he fall into poverty. He should either pay from it such a census as has been established for him, or receive some portion of it as a benefice, from which he may be able to support himself. [Note: One witness reads “by which he may be supported.”]

## 38. Concerning Ninths and Tithes

It has been determined that ninths and tithes shall be paid from the produce of the land and from the nourishment of animals. [Note: One witness reads “that ninths and tithes from the produce …”; other witnesses expand the phrase as “the produce of the land, ninths and tithes, and the nourishment of animals,” or “ninths and tithes beyond the other produce.”]

Concerning work on or restoration of churches, the count and the bishop or abbot, together with our envoy whom they themselves choose for this purpose, shall make an assessment, so that each receives from it for building and restoration only as much as he is known to possess in ecclesiastical property. [Note: One witness greatly abridges what follows.]

Likewise, our vassals shall either collectively undertake a share of the work proportionate to the ecclesiastical property they hold, or each shall do so individually according to the amount that he himself holds. [Note: One witness reads “may have.”]

Or, if they agree to give silver in place of performing the work, they shall pay in silver according to the assessed value of the work. With that money the head of the church may hire workers for the aforementioned restoration and purchase materials. [Note: One witness reads “the work” instead of “workers.”]

Whoever neglects to give ninths and tithes shall first restore them with the legally prescribed composition and, in addition, pay our ban, so that, chastened in this way, he may beware of losing his benefice by repeating the offense too often. [Note: One witness reads “lest he first lose his benefice.”]

## 39. Concerning Slaves Fleeing to Royal Estates

If anyone’s slaves flee to one of our estates, the manager of that estate shall not refuse them to the master who seeks them, but shall immediately drive them out of that estate. [Note: One witness reads “shall hand them over”; another omits a word after “immediately.”]

If the master thinks that he has a lawful right to reclaim them, let him reclaim them and acquire them according to law. But if they fled to that estate during the time of our father, the lord Charles, and their master seeks them, the manager of that estate shall either lawfully retain them or return them to the master who seeks them. [Note: One witness reads “shall have sought them”; another reads “shall contest them.”]

Because of the possession of our father, the lord Charles, the manager shall not dare to refuse those slaves if they are known to be his property. [Note: One witness omits “his property.”]

## 40. Concerning Newly Established Forests

Whoever holds such forests shall abandon them, unless he can show by a truthful indication [Note: One witness reads *indicione*; others read “by proof” or “by reason of truth”] that he established them by command or promise of our father, the lord Charles. [Note: One witness omits “by command or promise.”]

This does not apply to those forests that belong to our own use, concerning which we wish to decide whatever pleases us. [Note: One witness reads “on account of” instead of “except.”]

## 41. Concerning the Repair of Bridges in Various Places

We wish our envoys in each city, together with the bishop and count, to choose envoys or our men residing there whose responsibility it shall be to repair bridges in various places and to admonish, by our command, those who ought to repair them, so that each person may strive to repair them according to his ability and means. [Note: One witness omits the words from “and to admonish” through “repair them.”]

## 42. Concerning the Commission of All Our Envoys, Namely, the Matters with Which They Are to Deal

This is the commission of all our envoys. First, as has already been enjoined upon other envoys, they are to administer justice concerning property and freedoms unjustly taken away. If a bishop, abbot, vicar, advocate, or anyone from the common people is found to have done this, the property or freedom shall immediately be restored. [Note: One witness reads “it shall be restored.”]

But if a count, a royal estate manager, or another palace envoy has committed this and brought the matter into our jurisdiction, the matter, after careful investigation and written record, shall be reserved for our judgment. [Note: One witness omits “and brought the matter into our jurisdiction.”]

## 43. Concerning the Investigation of Freedoms and Property to Be Restored That Are in Our Possession

We wish that, concerning those freedoms and properties to be restored that are in our possession, inquiry should first be made through the best men available. If the matter cannot be discovered through them, then inquiry shall be made through those who are the best men in that neighborhood after them. If the truth of the matter cannot be discovered even through them, the litigants may then bring witnesses from both sides. If those witnesses disagree, they shall be examined according to the constitution promulgated by us. [Note: One witness reads “shall be investigated.”]

## 44. Concerning the Oppression of the Poor, Widows, and Orphans

Concerning the poor, widows, and orphans who have been unjustly oppressed: they are to be helped and relieved. [Note: One witness omits “widows and.”]

## 45. Concerning Newly Established Unjust Customs

Concerning newly established unjust exactions and customs, such as tributes and tolls in the middle of a road where there is neither water nor marsh nor bridge nor anything of that sort from which a charge could justly be exacted, or where ships customarily pass beneath bridges or through the middle of a river where there is no obstruction: these are to be removed. [Note: One witness reads “marshes”; another inserts: “so that they may be removed before the matter is brought to our notice.”]

Ancient customs, however, shall be reported to our notice. [Note: Witness 3 instead reads: “Those who exact such payments shall be brought into our presence.” G reads *aut* (“or”) for *autem* (“however”).]

## 46. Concerning the Honor of Churches

Concerning the honor of churches: it is to be shown to them in every respect, just as we recently established with the consent of all our faithful. Our envoys are to make this known to everyone within their commission. [Note: Several witnesses introduce the chapter with: “We command that the due honor of churches be shown in every respect.”]

## 47. Concerning Ninths and Tithes

Concerning ninths and tithes: they are to be given according to our command. [Note: Several witnesses introduce the chapter with: “We command that ninths and tithes be given.”]

## 48. Concerning Places to Be Given for Establishing Canonical Cloisters

Concerning places to be given for establishing canonical cloisters: if the land is from the property of that same church, it shall be granted there by our liberty. [Note: One witness begins: “For the establishment of canonical cloisters, we wish that, if a place from the property of that church is available, it be granted …”; another reads “if it is land.”]

If it is from the property of another church or of free men, it shall be exchanged. If it is from our fisc, it shall be granted by our liberality. [Note: Some witnesses read *libertate* (“by our permission”) instead of *liberalitate* (“by our liberality”).]

## 49. Concerning the Observance of Royal Commands

Concerning the observance of our commands and immunities: they are to be observed just as they were established by us and by our predecessors.

## 50. Concerning Those Who Refuse to Do Justice Under Pretext of Immunity

Concerning those who refuse to do justice under pretext of immunity: the provision established by us is to be observed. [Note: One witness reads “that those who refuse justice on account of immunity …”]

## 51. Concerning Places Once Sacred and Now Defiled by Filth

Concerning places that were formerly sacred and are now defiled by filth: they are to be restored, as far as possible, to their former condition. [Note: One witness omits “formerly sacred and now defiled by filth.”]

## 52. Concerning Destroyed Royal Benefices

Concerning our benefices that are found destroyed: the provision recently established by us is to be fulfilled. [Note: Some witnesses read “buildings” instead of “benefices.”]

## 53. Concerning False Coin and the Suppression of Various Other Offenses

Concerning new coinage and false coinage, disregard of our letters, the restraint or punishment of robbers, the pacification of feuds [German gloss: *geuehida*], the prevention of homicides, and the suppression of perjuries and false witnesses, and concerning all these matters and others like them: what we have now established is to be announced to everyone and observed in the future. [Note: One witness omits the words concerning the restraint or punishment of robbers and feuds. Another begins a new chapter here.]

## 54. Concerning the Observance of the Duties of the Royal Envoys

We wish our envoys to observe the following: whatever they are able to correct, whether together or individually, in these matters, they shall correct; and what they correct they shall carefully record in writing. They shall take care to carry this out in such a way that no one can justly criticize them.

What they ought or are able to do, they shall in no way omit. Rather, they shall beware lest—as God forbid—because of favor toward anyone, or because of honor, fear, or hatred, they omit what they ought to do. They shall make every effort to inform us of whatever they cannot accomplish by themselves.

They shall take every possible precaution so that, for each chapter, they may be able to render us an account, both orally and in writing, of everything they have done there. [Note: One witness reads “those things which” instead of “what.”]

## 55. Concerning the Pleas to Be Observed by Free Men

Concerning the pleas that free men ought to observe, the constitution of our father must be observed and maintained in every respect: namely, they shall attend only three general pleas in the year, and no one shall compel them to attend any additional pleas, unless someone has been accused, has accused another, or has been summoned to give testimony.

For the other pleas held by the hundredmen, no one shall be ordered to come except the person who is litigating, judging, or giving testimony. [Note: One witness reads “those” instead of “which”; another reads “others” instead of “no one else.”]

## 56. Concerning a Debt Assigned to the Royal Work

Concerning a debt that has been assigned to our work, an assessment shall be made such that the person who sinned unknowingly is not compelled to pay the whole legal composition, but only as much as seems possible. But the person who sinned with deliberate ill will shall be compelled to pay the entire legal composition. [Note: Witnesses variously read “who sinned only through bad will,” “the whole composition of the law,” and “the entire legal composition.”]

## 57. Concerning Those Traveling to or Returning from the Palace or the Army

No one traveling to the palace or to the army, or returning from the palace or the army, shall be compelled to pay the transport charge called *transtura*. [Note: The manuscripts offer the forms *tarensturas*, with a marginal gloss *heristiura*; *transituras*; *tristuras*; *tracturas*; *trasturas*; *straturas*; and *trexturas*.]

## 58. Concerning Public Bridges

Public bridges, which used to be built under the ban, are to be repaired everywhere during the present year. [Note: One witness reads “supplicatory bridges.”]

## 59. Concerning Fugitive Clerics, Monks, and Slaves

Clerics, monks, and fugitive slaves are to be ordered to return to their proper places.

## 60. Concerning the Advocates of Bishops, Abbots, Counts, and Abbesses

No bishop, abbot, count, or abbess shall have the count’s hundredman as advocate. [Note: One witness omits “counts.”]

## 61. Concerning Vicars or Hundredmen Who Conceal Robbers

Vicars or hundredmen who conceal or defend thieves and robbers are to be judged according to the sentence assigned to them. [Note: The source has *atrones*, evidently for “robbers”; the context may reflect an OCR or textual corruption.]

## 62. Concerning the Admonition of Counts and Vicars Regarding the Constitution of the Law

Counts and vicars are to be admonished concerning the constitution of the law, which orders that they are not to accept gifts in order to pervert justice. [Note: Some witnesses read “because they are ordered”; another reads “vicars and hundredmen.” One manuscript omits the entire chapter.]

## 63. Concerning Royal Forests

Concerning our forests: wherever they exist, the envoys are to investigate most carefully how they are preserved and defended. They are to warn the counts not to establish any forest anew. Wherever they find forests newly established without our command, they are to order that they be abandoned. [Note: A marginal gloss gives *vorst*—“forest.”]

## 64. Concerning the Royal Envoys and Those Who Refuse to Do Justice

Wherever our envoys find a bishop, abbot, or anyone else of whatever rank who either refuses to do justice or prevents it from being done, they shall live from that person’s property for as long as they must remain in that place to administer justice.

## 65. Concerning Where the Royal Envoys Should Not Remain for a Long Time

The same envoys shall not remain for a long time in the jurisdiction of a count who has properly administered justice. They shall not cause a crowd to assemble there. Rather, they shall remain where justice has been done inadequately or negligently. [Note: One witness reads “there” instead of “in that place”; another omits the words concerning where justice has been done.]

## 66. Concerning an Envoy and a Count Sent on Another Commission

The same envoys shall not hold a plea in the jurisdiction of a count who has been sent on another commission until that count has returned. Thus a case that has not yet been before the count, and the person who is bringing a complaint but, through folly or obstinacy, was unwilling to appeal to the count concerning it, shall be referred again to the count. [Note: One witness reads “petition the count” instead of “appeal to the count.”]

## 67. Concerning How the Royal Envoys Are to Receive Provisions

Our envoys who are bishops, abbots, or counts shall receive nothing from another person’s provision levy for as long as they are near their own benefice. Once they have gone far away from it, they shall then receive according to what is contained in their *tractoria*. [Note: One witness reads “their benefice allowance.”]

Our vassals and officials who have been sent as envoys shall receive provisions wherever they come.

## 68. Concerning Royal Vassals and Those of Bishops and Others Who Have Not Been in the Army

Our vassals, and the vassals of bishops, abbots, abbesses, and counts, who have not been in the army during the present year, shall pay the *heribannum*. [Note: Witnesses read *reuuadiant* for *rewadient*.]

This excludes those who were left at home for necessary reasons established by the lord and our father Charles: namely, those who were left by the count to preserve the peace and to guard his wife and household, and those who were similarly left by a bishop, abbot, or abbess to preserve the peace, gather the harvest, constrain the household, and receive envoys. [Note: One witness reads “constituted” instead of “established”; another omits the phrase “who were left at home.” One witness reads “by us” instead of “by the count.” Several witnesses omit the clause concerning guarding the wife and household and place it after chapter 73; some omit it altogether.]

## 69. Concerning Bishops, Abbots, and Counts, and the Plea of the Royal Envoys

Every bishop, abbot, and count—except in the case of illness or by our command—shall have no excuse for failing to come to the plea of our envoys, or for failing to send such a vicar of his own who can render an account for him in every matter. [Note: One witness reads “no one” instead of “every”; another reads “who does not” instead of “who can.” One witness reads “such vicars” and “for them.”]

### 69b. Concerning Not Exacting the *Heribannum* Before the Royal Command Has Been Made Known

[Note: This chapter is added in B, Pith., Paris., and Norm.; in Rheims it was added in the margin by a second hand.]

The envoys and each person in his own jurisdiction shall cause these chapters to be reread before the people, so that they may be known to everyone and no one may be able to claim an excuse. They shall not first exact the ban from anyone until these provisions have been made known to all.

[Col. 0583A] **70. On the provision for the royal envoys.** Concerning the provision for our envoys: how much ought to be given or received by each according to his rank [Note: [Col. 0583] “each person,” 1*; “according to his quantity,” 3. Copy 6 gives the following: for a bishop, 40 loaves, 3 urns of drink, 3 *frisgingae*, 15 eggs, and 4 *modii* of grain for the horses. For an abbot, a count, and others: 30 loaves, 2 *victimae*, 2 urns, 1 piglet, 3 chickens, 15 eggs, and 3 *modii* for the horses. For our vassal: 16 loaves, 1 *friskinge*, 1 piglet, 1 urn of drink, 10 eggs, and 2 *modii* for the horses.], namely, for a bishop: forty loaves, three *friskingae* [Note: [Col. 0583] *frisgingae*, 1, 6; *friskige* (below *friskingae*), 1*; *frissingae*, below *frixingiae*, 3; *frischinge*, B.], three [Note: [Col. 0583] four, B; *frisgingae*, 1, 6.] measures of drink, one piglet [Note: [Col. 0583] one piglet, 3, consistently G.], three chickens [Note: [Col. 0583] three chickens, 1* G.], fifteen eggs, and four measures of grain for the horses [Note: [Col. 0583] four measures, 3, 4, G.]. Abbots, counts, and each of our officials are to be given daily thirty loaves, two *friskingae*, two measures of drink [Note: [Col. 0583] two measures, 1*.], one piglet, three chickens [Note: [Col. 0583] three chickens, 1*.], fifteen eggs, and three measures of grain for the horses [Note: [Col. 0583] three measures, 1*; two measures, 3.]. To our vassal [Note: [Col. 0583] The following words are absent in 3.] seventeen loaves [Note: [Col. 0583] eighteen, 4; sixteen, 6, G.], one *friskinga* [Note: [Col. 0583] one *friskinga*, one piglet, one measure of drink, two chickens, 1*.], one piglet, one measure of drink, two chickens, ten eggs, and two measures of grain for the horses [Note: [Col. 0583] two measures of grain for the horses, 1*.].

**71. On a person who has been summoned for any matter in another country** [Note: [Col. 0583] Copy 3 omits the text from “there” through this heading; 1*, 5, Til., and Div. lack this and the following chapter. In 2b it appears elsewhere.]. If someone has been summoned for any matter in another country, where he is accustomed to reside continually either because of a benefice or for any other reason—for example, concerning his possessions or his slaves—he shall obtain justice there according to his own law, and shall swear a lawful oath with such oath-helpers as he can have with him in that region [Note: [Col. 0583] “in the same kingdom,” 2b.] or province. This does not apply if someone has brought a claim against him concerning his status, that is, his freedom, or concerning an inheritance that his father left him when he died. In these two matters he may offer to swear the oath in his own country, that is, at the lawful place of his oath [Note: [Col. 0583] “oath,” 4.]; and the person litigating against him, if he wishes, may follow him into his own country [Note: [Col. 0583] “his country,” G.] to receive that oath. Nevertheless, he must first, in the same place [Col. 0583C]—that is, where he was summoned [Note: [Col. 0583] Absent in 2b]—satisfy both the count and the judges and his adversary, proving by witnesses that the property [Note: [Col. 0583] “thing,” 3, B.] being claimed from him was left to him by his father [Note: [Col. 0583] Here 2 inserts chapter 4, a general chapter of the Capitula of Chalon, issued in May 825; after chapter 74 of the same Capitula it inserts chapter 5.].

**72. On payment and composition** [Note: [Col. 0583] The entire chapter is absent in 1*, 5, Til., and Div.]. Every payment and composition contained in the Salic Law is to be settled among the Franks by solidi of twelve denarii [Col. 0584A], except where a dispute has arisen against Saxons and Frisians [Note: [Col. 0583] “between,” 3, Bal.; “Frisians,” 3 consistently.]. In that case we wish the solidus to contain forty denarii, which either a Saxon or a Frisian must pay on behalf of the Salic Frank [Note: [Col. 0583] Absent in 3.] litigating with him [Note: [Col. 0583] “from one side to the other,” 3, Bal.] [Note: [Col. 0583] “and let him pay the composition for it, according to the measure set out above, to those to whom it belongs under the laws,” Met. (these are the final words of chapter 74).].

**73. On a person’s status** [Note: [Col. 0583] This chapter is nothing other than a repetition of chapter 24, doubtless derived from Ansegisus himself; it is absent in 1*, 5.]. Let him be summoned concerning his status, that is, concerning his freedom or inheritance, according to the provision of the law [Note: [Col. 0583] “that is, concerning” is absent in 3 and 4; “be admonished,” 3.]. But in all other matters for which someone is required to render an account, if, after the count’s second admonition, anyone refuses to come to the court, he shall be compelled to come and do justice, with his property placed under the ban.

**74. On a person’s property that has been placed under the ban on account of a crime** [Note: [Col. 0583] This too repeats chapter 23; absent in 1*, 5.]. If anyone’s property has been placed under the ban on account of a crime committed by him, and, once the matter has been established, he delays coming to do justice and allows it to remain under that ban for a year and a day, he shall not acquire it thereafter; rather, it shall be joined to the king’s fisc. But the debt that the person to whom it belonged was required to pay shall be paid, through the count and his officials, to those to whom the debtor owed it, according to the assessment of the damage, from the movable property found within that estate. If the quantity of movable property found there is insufficient for the composition, the deficiency shall be made up from immovable property; and whatever remains, as stated, shall be possessed by the king’s fisc. If nothing can remain after the composition, everything shall be expended on it. But if that person has not yet divided his own property [Col. 0584C] with his co-heirs, the count shall summon them and make a lawful division with them; then, as already stated, he shall add that person’s share to the king’s fisc and pay the composition from it, according to the procedure set out above, to those to whom it belongs under the laws.

# FIRST APPENDIX

[Col. 0583]

**Chapters** [Note: [Col. 0583] All three appendices are found in 1, 2, 6, and G. (G. combines the first and second into one); Bal. has the first and second. They are entirely absent in 1*, 2b, 4, and 5. Codex 3 contains nothing except chapters 1–3, 7, 8, 16, 17, 27, and 34–38 of the second appendix, attached to Book IV, so that its chapter 1 is our chapter 75, and so forth.] of the lord Emperor Charles concerning ecclesiastical matters. I have not joined them to the chapters written above [Note: [Col. 0583] “have been joined,” B; “I joined,” G.], because some of these seem to have been written almost as memoranda [Note: [Col. 0583] “had been written,” B.] and do not appear to express a complete sense, others are duplicated, being mixed with other chapters, while still others are entirely complete and brought to perfection.

[Col. 0583C] **1. On readings.** [Col. 0584C] **2. On chant.** [Col. 0585A] **3. On notaries.** **4. On the other disciplines** [Note: [Col. 0585] “disciples,” 1 (but “disciplines” is written above it in the same hand), 6.]. **5. On computation.** **6. On medical art.** **7. On churches that remain without dignity, services, and lights** [Note: [Col. 0585] “lamps,” B.]; and on those who take tithes but do not care for the churches; and on altars, so that they may not be excessive in the churches. **8. On laymen recently converted**, so that, before they have learned by living fully according to their law [Note: [Col. 0585] “fully according to the canonical [law],” G.], they are not sent to other business. **9. On those who abandon the world**, so that they must choose one of two alternatives: they must live either fully according to the canonical or according to the monastic [Note: [Col. 0585] “secular,” 1.] rule. **10. On recently discovered churches or saints without authorization**: they are not to be venerated unless approved by the bishop, while canonical authority concerning this matter and concerning all churches remains secure [Note: [Col. 0585] The words from “while” through “authority” are absent in Sang. 1, Colb., Thu., and Riv.]. **11. On bishops who have been ordained but not received.** **12. That it is not proper to absolve or ordain just anyone** [Note: [Col. 0585] “whomsoever,” as an absolute object; “that it is not proper to ordain,” G., Camb., Riv., Vat., Colb., Rem., B., Pith., Par., Norm.]. [Col. 0585B] **13. On a slave who has been ordained without his master’s knowledge** [Note: [Col. 0585] “a slave ordained without his master’s knowledge,” 6.]. **14. That a cleric may not minister in two cities, nor may abbots possess several monasteries or cells.** **15. On foreign bishops and clerics.** **16. On letters of foreigners and clerics traveling without letters.** **17. What sort of person, and for what offenses, is to be degraded from priestly office according to canonical rule.** **18. On one expelled from a church, excommunicated** [Note: [Col. 0585] “from communion,” 6, Hld.; “excommunication,” 1.] **or condemned from his office.** **19. On ecclesiastical order and the office of the Mass.** [Col. 0586A] **20. On the relics of the saints and village oratories.** **21. On not consecrating an altar unless it is made of stone.** **22. On confirmation with chrism.** **23. On baptism.** **24. On Easter, the Lord’s Day, and the remaining festivals.** **25. On fasting, Lent, and litanies.** **26. That the principal festivals are to be held only in cities or public settlements.** **27. On this office** [Note: [Col. 0585] Absent in G.]. **28. On repairing churches**: where there are more in one place than necessary, those that are unnecessary are to be demolished and others built. **29. On churches that are not properly built.** **30. On the judgment of penance**: we have left for inquiry by whom and in what manner penitents are to be judged through a penitential book [Note: [Col. 0585] “penitential sentence,” G.] and concerning incestuous unions, whom it is permissible to join [Note: [Col. 0585] “to impose [penance] on,” Bal.] and whom not. **31. On alms to be sent to Jerusalem for the restoration of God’s churches at the coming Nativity of the Lord** [Note: [Col. 0585] “at the coming [Nativity],” 6, Bal.]. [Col. 0586B] **32. That no one consent to wicked men but resist them as far as he can; and that the poor, orphans, widows, and the churches of God may have peace.** **33. That monks and virgins observe their profession in every respect.** **34. That these slave-dealers and *cotiones*** [Note: [Col. 0585] *cocliones*, Hld.], **who wander about without any law, are not permitted to roam through this land and deceive people; nor are those naked men with iron weapons, who say that, having been assigned penance, they go about as wanderers. It seems better that, if any have committed an unusual and capital crime, they should remain in one place, laboring, serving, and doing penance according to what has been canonically imposed upon them.** **35. On harmony among our faithful.**

# SECOND APPENDIX

Also the chapters of the lord Emperor Charles concerning secular matters [Note: [Col. 0585] “secular matters which are written above,” G.], which appear to have the same origin as those written above [Note: [Col. 0585] “Here begin the chapters of the lord Emperor Charles,” B. The entire heading in G. forms chapter 36; our chapter 1 there is chapter 37, and so forth.].

[Col. 0585]

[Col. 0585C] **1. On thieves:** let the rule remain as we previously commended it in another capitulary [Note: [Col. 0585] Absent in 3.], just as it is [Note: [Col. 0585] “let many things remain so,” B.].

**2. On adventitious persons:** when our envoys come to the assembly, they are to have a written statement of how many adventitious persons there are in their circuit, from which district they come, their names, and who their lords are.

**3.** If anyone has been challenged concerning his freedom and, fearing that he may fall into servitude, kills one of his relatives through whom he fears that he will fall into servitude [Note: [Col. 0585] “whom he recognizes,” G.], namely his father, mother, paternal uncle, maternal uncle, or any person of such kinship [Note: [Col. 0585] “any female person,” B., G.], the perpetrator himself shall die; his kinship [Note: [Col. 0585] “agnatic kin,” B., Bal.] and blood relationship [Note: [Col. 0585] “proximity” written above, or “blood relationship,” 3.] shall fall into servitude. If he denies that he killed him, he shall submit to the judgment of God by approaching nine heated plowshares.

**4. On fugitives and foreigners:** let them be restrained, so that we may know who they are and where they came from.

[Col. 0585D] **5** [Note: [Col. 0585] B joins this with the preceding chapter.]. Let *baugae* [Note: [Col. 0585] “small things,” 6; *bauca*, G.] and coats of mail not be given to merchants.

**6. On measures:** let them be made equal according to our command.

**7.** Let no testimony be brought concerning the investiture of the lord King Pippin.

**8** [Note: [Col. 0585] Joined with the preceding chapter by 3.]. Let everything that ought to be pledged [Note: [Col. 0585] “let the pledges be returned,” 1, 6, Hld.; “to pledge again,” 3; “to be repledged,” B.; “to pledge,” G.; “repledged,” 3, 6, B.] be fully repledged according to what is contained in the law, in accordance with that law; and afterward let either the lord king or the person whose case it is pardon it [Note: [Col. 0585] Absent in 1, 6, Hld.; “let him do it,” 3; “let him receive it,” B., Rem., Div., Pith., Par.], according to his pleasure.

**9.** We wish our envoys who have already carried written notices of the announcement to bring additional ones concerning the work.

**10.** How long they are to remain in each place, and how many men they are to have with them.

**11. On the prudence and steadfastness of our envoys.**

[Col. 0587A] **12. On false moneyers: an inquiry is to be made.**

**13. On those Saxons who have no wives.**

**14. On those who have been marked** [Note: [Col. 0587] “those who are to be sealed,” as the heading, G.], **who go about deceiving** [Note: [Col. 0587] “deception,” 6.].

**15.** If other circumstances do not intervene, we wish to hold a general assembly on 8 Kalends of July [Note: [Col. 0587] “8 Kalends,” 1; absent in B., G.], that is, at the Mass of Saint John the Baptist, at Mainz or Chalon [Note: [Col. 0587] *capillionem*, 1; *cabillonem*, Bal.; *capilionem*, B.].

**16** [Note: [Col. 0587] The entire chapter is absent in Hld.]. **On perjuries, so that they may be avoided.** Witnesses are not to be admitted to an oath before they have been examined [Note: [Col. 0587] “let them beware; that,” 1, 6; the words from “concerning perjuries” through “and” are absent in 3.]. If they cannot otherwise be examined, they are to be separated from one another and questioned individually. It is not to be permitted for the accuser alone to choose witnesses in the absence of his opponent. Absolutely no one is to be admitted to an oath or to give testimony unless fasting [Note: [Col. 0587] “added,” 1, 6; “brought forward,” 3.]. If the person brought as a witness is rejected, the person who rejects him shall state and prove why he does not wish to accept him [Note: [Col. 0587] “did not wish,” B.]. Witnesses are to be chosen from the same district, not another, unless perhaps the case must be investigated farther away [Col. 0587B] outside the county [Note: [Col. 0587] Absent in 3.]. If anyone is convicted of perjury, he shall lose his hand or redeem it.

**17.** Let no one, out of greed for money or avarice, pay the price in advance [Note: [Col. 0587] “pay in advance,” G.] or prepare a future agreement for himself [Note: [Col. 0587] “or,” 3, B.], so that he may receive double or triple [Note: [Col. 0587] “triple; then receive,” B., Bal.]; let him purchase them only when the produce is actually available [Note: [Col. 0587] “that,” G.].

**18. On cases that do not cease from arising each day.**

**19. On fugitives who do not cease receiving and concealing [others].**

**20. On wandering foreigners.**

**21. On homicides.**

**22. On the prescribed measures of *modii* and *sextarii*.**

**23. On our benefices that are not properly maintained.**

**24. On hospitality and receiving travelers, both our envoys [Col. 0587C] and other good men.**

**25. That we send envoys in our place** [Note: [Col. 0587] “your judgment,” G., Riv., Thu., Sang. 2, Colb., N.; “our judgment,” Camb., Vat. 1, Sang. 1.].

**26. On those who sell wine and grain before it has been gathered, and thereby become poor** [Note: [Col. 0587] Absent in 1, B., G., Hld.; G. and Bal. add: “so that they may be firmly restrained, lest this happen again.” Met., Rem., Bell., Div., Thu., Par., Til., and Pal. omit those words.].

**27.** Let no judgment concerning property or freedom be concluded or acquired before the deputy or centenarius, unless it is always in the presence of the imperial envoys or in the presence of the counts.

**28. On homicides committed in the present year among ordinary people, supposedly on account of mortal dust.**

[Col. 0588A] **29. On the military levy:** let the envoys diligently investigate who was able to perform military service but did not do so; let him pay our ban if he has the means to pay. If he has no means with which he can pay, let it be repledged and entered in a written record; and let nothing be exacted from this until it comes to the knowledge of the lord emperor.

**30.** Those who have committed *herisliz* [Note: [Col. 0587] *heresliz*, 6; *heriscliz*, “from which he is a fugitive,” B.; *hierisdat*, G.] are to be sent under sureties.

**31. On destroyed benefices and restored allods** [Note: [Col. 0587] “restored,” B., G., Hld.].

**32. On exacting the peace-fine** [Note: [Col. 0587] “peace,” B.].

**33. On timber for making ships.**

**34.** If a Saxon apprehends someone without theft or without any property of his own [Note: [Col. 0587] “property, some thing,” 6, Hld.], saying that the man has caused him damage [Note: [Col. 0587] “is permitted,” 1, 6, Hld.], and wishes to contest this in judgment, in the field, or at the cross [Note: [Col. 0587] The words “or at the cross” are absent from three codices: *Suppl. lat.* 75, Paris., Met., and Pal.], he shall have permission to do so [Note: [Col. 0587] Here B. begins a new chapter.]. If he does not wish this [Note: [Col. 0587] “wishes this,” Hld.], the free man himself shall establish his innocence with his oath-helpers. [Col. 0588B] If he apprehends another person’s slave without any proof [Note: [Col. 0587] “anyone’s slave,” 6, Hld.; “and a service belonging to anyone else,” B.], that slave himself shall establish his innocence by boiling water or another judgment.

**35.** If a Saxon finds horses in his crop and wishes to lead those horses away in order to prove his damage [Note: [Col. 0587] “a horse,” 3; “the horse from there,” 3.], and a free man opposes him in this or does him any harm on account of it [Note: [Col. 0587] Absent in 1, 6, G., Hld.; “to him,” Hld.; “to him,” G.; “does this to him,” 6, Bal.], he shall strive to compensate him threefold according to the law and according to the *ewam* [Note: [Col. 0587] *eouam*, corrected to *euuam*, with “that is, the law” written above, 1; *ea*, B.; “equitable,” G.; “according to his damage,” 3; the words “and according to the *ewam*” are absent in 6, Hld.], and shall additionally pay the lord’s ban and lose his hand, because he was disobedient to the command of the lord emperor, which he ordered to be established for the sake of peace [Note: [Col. 0587] “established. If,” 3.]. If a slave does this, he shall restore everything threefold according to his law [Note: [Col. 0587] “according to his lawful status, and in triplicate,” 3.] and shall undergo corporal punishment.

**36.** Every free man found not to have been with his lord in the army in the present year shall be compelled to pay the full military levy. If his lord or count left him at home, that lord or count shall pay the same military levy for him; and as many military levies shall be exacted from him as the number of men he left at home [Note: [Col. 0587] “the military levy from them,” 6.]. Since this year we granted each lord permission to leave two men at home [Note: [Col. 0587] “we grant each lord two men whom he might leave at home,” 3.], we wish them to show them to our envoys [Note: [Col. 0587] “our envoys,” G.], because we have granted only these men exemption from the military levy [Note: [Col. 0587] “who,” 1.].

**37.** Whenever we wish to send a ship, let the lords themselves travel in those ships and be prepared for this.

**38.** Diligently prohibit thefts, unlawful marriages, and also false testimony, as we have often requested, just as the law of the Lord also prohibits them [Note: [Col. 0587C]

In place of this chapter, Rhem. has the following: “We decree that in our palaces, for accusing, judging [Col. 0588C], and giving testimony, base and infamous persons are not to present themselves: namely, actors and buffoons [Col. 0589B], *manzeres* [Col. 0589C: Sons of prostitutes], jesters, men who keep concubines, nor those born from intercourse with disgraceful women, nor slaves, nor criminals. For such men frequently, because of the suspicion arising from their depraved conduct and nature, strive to assert whatever pleases them against more worthy persons, so that they may not appear inferior.”]

From the same codex Baluzius produces the following: “If any property belonging to a church has been defrauded by wicked administrators [Col. 0589C], whether by entreaty, payment, or the private favor of predecessors [Col. 0590B], it shall always be permitted to successors to bring a complaint, because at no time ought a church to lose its rightful property, except movable possessions such as gold, silver, clothing, animals, or houses. But estates, lands, villages, churches, and revenues, since great income can arise from them for the common good, may not under any exchange or agreement be transferred into anyone’s private property. Once this has been discovered [Col. 0590C], it shall be rescinded.”]

.

# THIRD APPENDIX

[Col. 0589]

Also the ecclesiastical and secular chapters of the most illustrious princes, the lord Augustus Hludowicus and Caesar Hlotharius [Note: [Col. 0589] “and Hlotharius Caesar” is absent in G.], which appear to have the same basis as those written above.

[Col. 0589A] **1.** Benedictus shall remain silent forever concerning his complaint.

**2. On the holding that Bishop Gehirfredus** [Note: [Col. 0589] *Geirfredus*, G.] **claims from Count Liutrigo** [Note: [Col. 0589] *Liutfrido*, Thu., Sang. 1.]: if our envoys find that he has justice on his side [Note: [Col. 0589] Absent in 1.], they are not to permit Liutrigo to obstruct his justice through the investiture of the lord Charles [Note: [Col. 0589] “to possess,” G.].

**3. On the forest that Count Autharius wishes to possess** [Note: [Col. 0589] “wished to possess,” 6.], where it is said not previously to have existed: we wish our envoys to investigate the truth of the matter and, according to what they find to be just, decide it by our authority [Note: [Col. 0589] “bring it to completion,” G.].

**4. On the case of Count Rothmundus** [Note: [Col. 0589] Thus 1, Hld.; *Ruohtmundus*, 6; *Hruotmundus*, G., Bal.]: let him be permitted to swear his oath here in the palace, because, because, on account of service owed to us, he was unable to attend the assembly within his own country.

**5. On the two women who brought written lists:** Heiminus and Monoaldus [Note: [Col. 0589] *Manoaldus*, G.] are to be questioned whether they had belonged to a church or to the fisc [Note: [Col. 0589] “fiscal,” Bell.] [Note: [Col. 0589] “had not been,” 1.].

**6.** Odo the cupbearer is to be questioned concerning his forest.

[Col. 0590A] **7.** Concerning the property that the margrave handed over to Boso’s son or to other men, we wish those to whom it was handed over to receive their investiture and, in addition, confirmation.

**8.** Concerning the property that a certain woman is said to have handed over to Queen Hildegard [Note: [Col. 0589] *Hildigard*, G., Bal.] and to have unjustly lost the portion she reserved for herself: we wish the charter of the transfer to be sought and examined, and then it is to be determined what she ought to have.

**9.** Concerning the complaint that Helisachar and Heiminus [Note: [Col. 0589] *Haiminus*, G.] have against Maginarius [Note: [Col. 0589] *Mainarius*, G.], we wish our envoys to decide it according to justice and equity.

**10.** Concerning the complaint of Count Hildebrand, that his people refuse to provide *paravereda* [Note: [Col. 0589] *Paravreda*, 6.], we wish our envoys to investigate among the men who live in that same county, as well as among the neighboring counts, whether they are obliged to provide it; and if they find that those men are indeed bound to provide it, let them order them, by our command, to provide it [Col. 0590B] [Note: [Col. 0589] “The text ends: ‘Thanks be to God; the eloquence of the law,’” 6.].

# CAPITULARIES OF AACHEN (December 828)

[Col. 0589]

We have revised and enlarged the capitularies of the years 828 and 829, after Amerpach’s editorial work, from the editions of Sirmondus and Baluzius, with the aid of twelve codices: 1. Codex of the library, formerly Corbie and now Hamburg, ninth century, in which the First Edition of Ansegisus is read; codex 1b agrees with it; and codex 1c of the same royal library, formerly Tegernsee, from which Amerpach’s first edition derives. 2. Codex of the Royal Library of Paris, no. 4417; and 3. a codex of the ecclesiastical library of Schaffhausen in Switzerland, twelfth century; 4. a codex of the University of Bonn, twelfth century; 5. Codex of the Royal Library of Paris among the Latin Supplements, no. 164 bis, formerly of Saint-Remigius at Rheims; 6. Codex of the Royal Library of Bamberg; 7. Codex of the Royal Library of Paris, no. 4628 A, which closely follows Codex 5; 8. Codex of the Royal Library of Paris, no. 4761; 9. a codex of the same library among the Latin Supplements, no. 75; 10. a codex of the same library, no. 4638, formerly belonging to Pierre Pithou. Nevertheless, we judged it sufficient to turn through and inspect only briefly codices 1b, 4, and 7, rather than collate them carefully.

Sirmondus, who used the papers of Pierre Pithou and was almost the first to publish these capitularies in nearly complete form, and Baluzius after him, established an order that you will find preserved neither in the codices nor entirely suited to the subject itself. Therefore, following our codices, especially the Corbie codex, I have attempted to restore the ancient order. First, then, we present the proceedings of the assembly held by Louis with several leading men in December of the year 828 [Note: [Col. 0589C] In the middle or toward the end of the month, after the death of Jeremiah, archbishop of Sens.], prefaced by the report of the speakers to the emperor, which appears here for the first time from the Blankenburg Codex, tenth century, fols. 96–97 [Note: [Col. 0589C] It is read there before the capitulary of the year 820, whose chapters, dealing with an entirely different subject, are attached to it in continuous numbering [Col. 0590C].]. We then present the proceedings of the general assembly held at Worms in August of the following year, prefaced by the report of the bishops from the Gotha Codex, eleventh century, folio format.

# REPORT OF THE SPEAKERS TO THE EMPEROR

[Col. 0591A]

## ALSO OF THE LORD EMPEROR HLUDOWICUS

**1.** On the necessity for bishops to meet with their metropolitan at suitable times each year, according to canonical authority. Both canonical and monastic abbots ought to attend this assembly without any exception. If possible, and if they are not detained by imperial service [Note: [Col. 0591] “if he is not detained,” 1.], counts should also be present; but if they are absent, envoys should attend in their place who are able to carry out whatever useful measures for correction may be found there according to the rule of Christianity. There are indeed many necessities that cannot otherwise be remedied except in such an assembly. The metropolitan must make known to your piety at what time this assembly ought to be held, so that, by your authority [Note: [Col. 0591] “authority,” 1.], people may gather to it more fully.

**2.** The ministry of holy baptism is not to be celebrated everywhere or at any time, except in the case of the sick, but exclusively at the times appointed by the holy fathers. For if it is performed otherwise, it is certain that the dignity of so great a sacrament, its proper reverence, care, diligence, and instruction will likewise be diminished.

**3.** It is indeed very necessary and worthy of the highest correction—and it must by no means be neglected, as it has until now been neglected by almost everyone, as though it were no less necessary—that which contains the salvation of our redemption and the fullness of salvation: namely, communion in the sacred body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ [Col. 0591C], who said: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves.” Therefore all the faithful must be admonished and instructed so that, cleansed and purified, they may communicate more frequently and approach that communion reverently, lest, according to the Apostle, they eat and drink judgment upon themselves.

**4.** The priests of the Lord, who are mediators between God and human beings and through whom human beings are reconciled to God, are not to be held in such contempt. Rather, out of love and reverence for God, the sacred ministry that the Church performs for God through them is to be honored in them; and they are not to be sent away from their own churches [Note: [Col. 0591] “to,” 1.] on such an unlawful pretext to carry out external business. For as a result the divine work is neglected, infants commonly die without the grace of baptism, and people without confession. The danger of this matter is lamentably turned both against those who summon them away from their churches and against the bishops whose representatives they ought to be.

**5.** Concerning the churches, let your most merciful piety command all people to observe what it established long ago at God’s inspiration. For many, after your sacred command [Col. 0592A] [Note: [Col. 0591] “our command,” 1.], have not only received the revenues that they used to exact from the church [Note: [Col. 0591] “what,” 1.], but have added even heavier exactions. Although many churches possess nothing, or very little, outside, the priests of those churches, who can scarcely live there, are compelled to provide revenues and various sustenance from the tithes and offerings of the faithful alone. Yet all these things that they customarily exact from them, they arrange to be given to themselves not from any property of their own, but solely from the altar and the walls of the church dedicated to God by the bishop.

**6.** Since in many places there are parricides [Note: [Col. 0591] “a parricide,” 1.] and other homicides, or persons involved in other capital crimes, who disdain to perform public penance and are therefore useless to the interests of the commonwealth, it is necessary for your Highness to command the counts to give assistance to the bishops, so that they may be able to subject such persons to canonical penance.

**7.** Let there be equal and just measures in all the provinces of your empire, according to the law of the Lord, which commands: “Let your *modius* be equal and your *sextarius* just.” Therefore the poor are greatly burdened by the diversity of measures in many places. Nevertheless, the anciently established revenue of each province must not be increased for the poor on this account.

**8.** Your speakers request and admonish you that, among the other things you worthily do for God, you should sometimes undertake the labor of hearing or examining the necessary cases of churches and the poor for the love of God, because the perfection of your office consists especially in such a duty. For it will be a labor worth undertaking to make all judges purer and better for this duty [Col. 0592C].

**9.** Concerning the institution of the life of canons, which your pious mercy, inspired and guided by God, has ordered: let everyone hold the same view, and let its care be entrusted to each metropolitan, so that wherever it has been completed according to your command, it may be perfectly observed, and wherever it has not yet been completed, it may be brought to completion through foresight and diligence. In this way each metropolitan can more appropriately and diligently admonish his suffragans by canonical authority than other envoys can; and both personally and through envoys whom he frequently sends, he can discover through careful investigation how it is observed in every place and where correction is needed.

# CONSTITUTION ON HOLDING ASSEMBLIES OF ARCHBISHOPS [Note: [Col. 0591D] From Codices 2, 3, and 5–10.]

[Col. 0592D]

# CHAPTERS ISSUED BY THE MOST PIOUS HLUDOWICUS [Note: [Col. 0591] Thus in 2 and 3 (*Hlothouuico*).]

In the sixteenth year of the reign of our lord Louis [Note: [Col. 0591] Extant in manuscripts 2–10.], a gathering of bishops is to be held in four places, namely at Mainz, where these archbishops are to assemble with their suffragans or vicars [Note: [Col. 0591] “Or vicars,” 6.]: [Note: [Col. 0591D] Archbishop of Mainz. Baluze.] Autcarius [Note: [Col. 0591] “Audgarius,” 3.], [Note: [Col. 0591D] Archbishop of Cologne. The same.] Hadebaldus, [Note: [Col. 0592D] Archbishop of Trier. The same.] Hetti, [Note: [Col. 0592D] Archbishop of Besançon. The same.] Bernoinus.

[Col. 0593A] At Paris [Note: [Col. 0593C] I suppose there will be some who will be pleased to know in which Parisian church that council was held, and to know the names of the bishops who attended that very celebrated gathering. It is therefore certain that the council was held in the church of Saint Stephen of Gressibus, Saint-Étienne-des-Grès, and that the following bishops attended it: Ebbo, archbishop of Reims; Aldric of Sens; Raginoard of Rouen; Landramnus of Tours; Jonas, bishop of Orléans; Jesse of Amiens; Rantgarius of Noyon; Rothadus of Soissons; Adalelmus of Châlons; Hildemannus of Beauvais; Godofredus of Senlis; Freculfus of Lisieux; Halitgarius of Cambrai; Franco of Le Mans; Haribaldus of Auxerre; Helias of Chartres or Troyes; Jonas of Nevers; Hubertus of Meaux; Inchadus of Paris. Moreover, Guiladus, Theodiselus, Amatheus, Bernoinus, Fulcharius, and Herbertus, bishops of unknown sees. Guiladus, however, may perhaps be the one called Wilardus in the published lists of the bishops of Coutances. Fulcharius, on the other hand, is perhaps the one called Flodegarius in the catalogue of the bishops of Angers; he held that see in the year 828, as is clear from the charter by which Louis the Pious confirmed the exchange made between him and Winneradus. From this, too, the gaps found in the catalogues of the bishops of Laon, Bayeux, Avranches, and Évreux may perhaps be filled. The same.] Ebo [Note: [Col. 0593D] Of Reims.], Ragnowardus [Note: [Col. 0593D] Of Rouen.] [Note: [Col. 0593] “Rainoardus,” 9.], Lantramnus [Note: [Col. 0593D] Of Tours.], who was to be archbishop of Sens [Note: [Col. 0593D] Jeremias died on 7 December 828. Aldric succeeded him.], with their suffragans.

At Lyons [Note: [Col. 0593D] Archbishop of Lyons. Baluze.] Agobardus, [Note: [Col. 0593D] Archbishop of Vienne. The same.] Bernardus, [Note: [Col. 0594C] Archbishop of Tarentaise. The same.] Andreas, [Note: [Col. 0594C] Of these, one was archbishop of Aix and the other of Embrun. The same.] Benedictus, [Note: [Col. 0594C] Of these, one was archbishop of Aix and the other of Embrun. The same.] Agaricus [Note: [Col. 0593] Absent in 3.], with their suffragans.

At [Note: [Col. 0593] “At Toulouse”: N. B. A. A. c. e. s. are absent in 9 and 10; before the words “At Lyons” they are found in 5, 6, 7, and 8.] Toulouse [Note: [Col. 0594C] Archbishop of Arles, the same, I think, who carried the Formula of the Canonical Institution, at the command of Louis the Pious, to Arno, archbishop of Salzburg. The same.] Noto, [Note: [Col. 0594C] Archbishop of Narbonne. See the Notes to Agobardus, p. 75. The same.] Bartholomaeus, [Note: [Col. 0594C] Archbishop of Bordeaux, that very man, I think, who, at the command of Louis the Pious, had carried the Formula of the Canonical Institution to Sicharius, archbishop of Bordeaux. The same.] Adalelmus, [Note: [Col. 0594C] Archbishop of Bourges. This passage proves that at that time the bishops of Bourges had not yet begun to think about primacy over the archbishops of Narbonne and Bordeaux. For here Agiulfus is placed after both of them, although Theodulfus calls him patriarch. This indicates that the title then conferred no prerogative over the other metropolitans even upon the archbishop of Bourges. Certainly Arno, archbishop of Salzburg, who possessed no extraordinary authority or jurisdiction, is nevertheless called patriarch by Alcuin in the ninth volume of Dacher’s *Spicilegium*, p. 116. Elusanus is missing from the metropolitans named here, as Sirmond rightly notes. The reason is that at that time the province of Novempopulania had no metropolitan of its own but was subject to Bordeaux, as stated above. Nevertheless, not long afterward it did have its own metropolitan, namely the archbishop of Auch. For there exists a letter of Pope John VIII to Airard, archbishop of Auch, and his suffragans, concerning the preservation of ecclesiastical discipline and the correction of the people’s corrupt morals. The same.] Aiulfus [Note: [Col. 0593] “Aiulfus,” 5, 6, 7, 8.], with their suffragans.

At these gatherings they are to discuss, investigate [Note: [Col. 0593] *Quaerere et investigare et* (“discuss and investigate, and”), 3.], and, with God’s help, discover matters concerning the Christian religion and entrusted to their care: what is observed by the rulers and the rest of the people, whether in accordance with divine authority or otherwise [Note: [Col. 0593] *Et ad*, 3.], and what has been partly or wholly abandoned so that it is no longer observed [Note: [Col. 0593] *Exinde* (“therefrom”), 3.]. Next, they are to discover what may be found in the morals, conduct, and actions of those appointed shepherds of the people that does not agree with divine rule and authority; and likewise [Note: [Col. 0593] *Ut* (“so that”), 3.] to discover what circumstances in either order caused them to deviate from the right path.

Whatever they discover concerning these matters is to be guarded with such careful diligence that they must not allow it to come to anyone else’s knowledge before the appointed time. Therefore, one notary is to be chosen from among them all; he is to record precisely whatever they discover [Note: [Col. 0593] *Describant* (“let them record”), 3.], and, bound by oath, faithfully preserve it.

We also wish their gathering to take place on the octave of Pentecost [Note: [Col. 0593] From “We wish” through “Easter” is absent in the royal Baluze manuscript.]. Our envoys, however, are to begin carrying out their mission on the octave of Easter [Note: [Col. 0593] Here manuscript 8 ends.].

These are the chapters to be considered by the bishops [Note: [Col. 0593] “Considered,” 3.].

1. Concerning the tithes given to the lord’s chapels [Note: [Col. 0593] “The lord’s chapel,” 3.] and the people who possess them and have converted them to their own use [Note: [Col. 0593] “And convert them to their own use,” 5; the rest, “converted,” 3.].

2. Concerning women who in certain places irrationally impose the sacred veil upon themselves.

3. Likewise concerning the small monasteries of girls in Autgar’s legation, in which no rule of good conduct is observed.

4. Also concerning the various small monasteries in the mission of Albricus [Sirmond’s edition: Albericus].

5. Concerning judgment by cold water.

6. Concerning those who engage in usury.

7. We wish and command that our envoys carefully [Col. 0594B] inquire how many free men remain in each county who are able to undertake an expedition on their own, and how many of those are such that one assists another [Note: [Col. 0593] The following through “is equipped” is absent in 2.], and how many are such that a third is assisted and equipped by two [Note: [Col. 0593] Added in 5, 6, 7, and 9.], and likewise how many are such that a fourth is assisted and equipped by three, or a fifth assisted and equipped by four, so that they may be able to undertake the same expedition and military service [Note: [Col. 0593] “The military expedition,” 5; the rest, “military service”]; and let them report their total to our knowledge.

# CONSTITUTION CONCERNING THE DISPATCH OF ENVOYS

[Note: [Col. 0595] Only the final sentences of this constitution are present in manuscripts 2, 3, and the others preserved there, where, after the chapters of the Worms assembly, they are read as laws to be added. Sirmond placed them first among the chapters given to the envoys at that assembly.]

1. We wish our envoys to receive such a provision when they travel through their assigned mission; namely, that each one receive forty loaves, two *friskingae*, one pig or lamb, four chickens, twenty eggs, eight *sextarii* of wine [Note: [Col. 0595] “Nine,” the edition], two *modii* of beer [Note: [Col. 0595] “Cider,” 3.], and two *modii* of grain [Note: [Col. 0595] From “chickens” through “two *modii*” is absent in 10.]. And when they are near their own homes, they are to accept no provision [Note: [Col. 0595] Here manuscript 10 ends.].

We also wish them to begin carrying out their mission on the octave of Easter. The bishops, however, are to hold their gathering on the octave of Pentecost.

# THESE ARE THE CHAPTERS CONCERNING THE INSTRUCTION OF THE ENVOYS

[Note: [Col. 0595] From a single manuscript, 5, and Sirmond’s edition.]

[Col. 0595B]

They must be told that we all need jointly to understand what danger threatens us, especially because through our negligence so many and such serious matters have occurred by which God could have been offended and the honor and dignity of the kingdom diminished [Note: [Col. 0595] Something seems to be missing: “or which we allowed or caused to happen.”]. We also understand another form of negligence arising from the previous circumstance: namely, that the mission itself was not carried out as the necessity demanded [Note: [Col. 0595] *Deposc[e]bat*, “demanded,” S.]; although in part you say that we ourselves provided the occasion, because we did not give you a full command in every respect to investigate this necessity.

Therefore, the utmost care must be taken concerning how, with the Lord’s help, the things that have been corrupted through negligence and carelessness may now be corrected, and how precautions may diligently be taken so that such things do not happen again. After this, the companions are to be designated, and then the nature of the mission to be assigned must be specified.

1. First, the envoys must be instructed above all to take care that they do not become a burden to the people during their journey, lest they inflict hardship upon those whom they ought to assist.

2. They are first to announce to the people, by our letter, our will and concern, and the purpose for which they have been sent by us. They must also be instructed concerning what they are to investigate.

3. Above all, they are to investigate how those who ought to govern the people each conduct themselves in his own office, so that we may recognize those who deserve thanksgiving for doing good, while those who deserve correction and rebuke for their negligence [Col. 0595D] may become known to us in every respect.

The investigation is to be conducted as follows. In each county, let those who are better and more truthful be chosen. If any of them is found not yet to possess the fidelity promised to us, let him make that promise. They are then to be instructed how they must preserve that faith toward us; namely, that if any one of them knows of any matter concerning those rulers and various officials who ought to govern and protect the people [Note: [Col. 0595] “Protect,” the edition.], and if, when questioned, it concerns harm and loss to the people and could thereby bring upon us danger to our souls and dishonor [Note: [Col. 0595] *Inoratio*, 5.], he must make it known without fail, if he wishes to keep his faith and promise intact.

If, after such admonition and formal warning [Note: [Col. 0595] “Constitution,” 5.], anyone is discovered to have spoken otherwise than the truth warrants, let him know that he is to be counted among the faithless.

These are the chapters which we wish them carefully to investigate [Note: [Col. 0595] Found only in manuscript 5 and the printed editions.].

First, concerning the bishops: how they perform their ministry, what their conduct is like, how they keep the churches and clergy entrusted to them ordered and arranged, and in what matters they chiefly devote themselves—spiritual matters, that is, or secular business.

Next, what kind of assistants they have in their ministry, namely chorepiscopi [Note: [Col. 0595] “Chorepiscopi, archpriests, archdeacons,” Sirmond.], archdeacons, and stewards, as well as the priests throughout their parishes; specifically, how devoted they are to instruction and what reputation they truthfully have among the people.

Likewise, let them investigate all monasteries according to the character and profession of each one. Likewise, let them investigate the other churches granted as benefices by our authority. Let them determine whether bishops, in traveling through their parishes, burden the other smaller churches or impose burdens upon the people, and whether improper *exsenia* are exacted from the priests by them or by their officials.

In the same way, let them investigate the counts: what diligence they show in their office, so that we may recognize anyone who performs it well. If someone acts otherwise, we absolutely wish to know this as well; namely, whether through his negligence and sloth the people lack justice and peace, or whether he has knowingly [Note: [Col. 0595] “Knowingly or unknowingly,” Sirmond.] allowed anything unjust to be done.
