Next, what sort of officials or envoys he has for governing the people, whether they act justly [Note: [Col. 0595] “Justly or unjustly,” Sirmond.] in those offices, or whether, with the count’s consent or through his negligence, they depart from truth and justice.

It must be determined which persons, and for what offenses, ought to come before our presence [Note: [Col. 0595] From “ought” through the second “ought” is absent from the manuscript; Sirmond printed it.]. Except for bishops, abbots, and counts, who must always come to our assemblies, let the others come if they are found guilty of such faults and crimes as are listed below.

# THESE ARE THE CHAPTERS

[Note: [Col. 0595] These chapters are absent from all manuscripts; I received them from Sirmond.]

# RESERVED FOR THE GENERAL ASSEMBLY, FOR THE KNOWLEDGE OF VERY MANY PEOPLE

1. Concerning priests bound and scourged by laymen.

2. Concerning a man who was sought for service and rescued by one heir, while the other heirs again try to summon him and acquire him.

3. Concerning counts and their vicars who in certain places receive from the people only as much provision for a minor mission as for a major one.

# LETTER TO BE READ GENERALLY TO THE PEOPLE OF GOD

[Note: [Col. 0597] The following manuscript versions are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0597]

[Col. 0597A] [Note: From Sirmond; absent from all manuscripts.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ. Louis and Lothar, august emperors by the providence of God’s ordinance, to all the faithful of God’s holy Church and to our own people.

We believe that you remember how this year, on the advice of the priests and our other faithful, we ordered a general fast to be observed throughout our entire kingdom, and that God be entreated with complete devotion [Col. 0597B] to be gracious to us, to reveal to us in what matters we had especially offended him, and to grant us a peaceful time for the correction we needed [Note: [Col. 0597] Absent in Sirmond.].

We had indeed wished to hold our general assembly at a suitable time and to deal there with our common correction. This would have happened by God’s mercy, had the uprising of our enemies, as you know, not prevented it. But since it could not then take place according to our will, it seemed good to us to hold the present assembly with some of our faithful and to consider there, with the Lord’s help, how those matters which had remained unfinished because of the aforesaid impediment might be brought to completion.

Therefore, we wish your diligence to know that at this present assembly we considered with our faithful that, first of all, the archbishops with their suffragans should assemble at a suitable time in appropriate places, and there, by investigating according to divine authority, should discover matters concerning both their own correction and amendment and that of all of us, and should announce their findings to us and to our faithful according to the ministry entrusted to them.

For who does not perceive that God has been offended and provoked to anger by our exceedingly wicked deeds, when he sees his anger raging for so many years in the kingdom entrusted to us by him through various scourges—namely, in continual famine, [Col. 0597D] in the mortality of animals, in pestilence among human beings, in the barrenness of nearly all crops, and, so to speak, in the most diverse disasters of disease and immense shortages—so that the people of this kingdom have been miserably harassed and afflicted, and in a certain manner stripped of every abundance of goods?

Nor do we doubt that this too occurs as a result of his just vengeance: that disturbances often arise in this kingdom through tyrants who by their wickedness strive to divide the peace of the Christian people and the unity of the empire. It must likewise be attributed to our sins that enemies of Christ’s name entered this kingdom in the previous year and boldly and with impunity—indeed, cruelly—carried out plunderings, burnings of churches, the capture of Christians, and the killing of the servants of God [Note: [Col. 0597D] Baluze reads thus; Sirmond has “by themselves.”].

For by God’s just judgment it is happening that, because we offend in all things, we are scourged both inwardly and outwardly. We are plainly ungrateful for God’s benefits, since we are found to use them not according to God’s will but according to our own carnal desire. And therefore the creatures of God, divinely granted to us, rightly fight for God against us ungrateful people, according to the saying: “The whole world will fight on his behalf against the senseless.”

But since we are afflicted and struck in so many ways, it is worthy and necessary that we return with our whole heart to him by whom we are struck, so that the prophetic saying may be fulfilled in us: “Affliction alone will give understanding to the hearing.”

Yet because the merciful and compassionate Lord moderates the scourge itself so that he appears to inflict it not for our destruction but rather for our correction, we ought truly to humble ourselves in his sight, to anticipate his face in confession, and to implore his mercy with bowed hearts. May he who in his most just governance has made us feel the scourges enable us to recognize our sins, for which we are justly scourged by him, and to understand more clearly in what matters we especially offended him and provoked his anger. Then, by his mercy, may we be able, through abandoning and correcting what is wrong, and through pursuing and carrying out good deeds with complete devotion, to offer God the sacrifice owed to him through a spirit of humility and a contrite soul, to escape his angry indignation, and, through worthy and appropriate correction and the performance of good works, to merit, though unworthy, his grace and favor.

But because we recognize that we have sinned more deeply in this matter—we who ought to have been an example of salvation to everyone, to care for all, and through imperial authority to correct the deeds of the wicked lest they increase—we desire, with the Lord’s favor, to obtain forgiveness in his merciful sight through worthy satisfaction, and through the most salutary correction, or through the good diligence that until now has been neglected through our laziness and ignorance, to correct with the utmost zeal, as far as lies within us, whatever can be corrected at the appropriate time on the advice of our faithful; and we wish to make our intention in this matter known to all.

Therefore, with the counsel of the priests and our other faithful, we have established and decreed, for this purpose—namely, to placate the Lord’s fury against us and those subject to us—that gatherings of the same bishops should be held most suitably at one and the same time in four places of our empire.

First, in the city of Mainz, where the archbishops Autgar, Hadebald, Hetti, and Bernuinus are to assemble with their suffragans.

Second, in the city of Paris, where the future bishop of Sens, Ebbo, Ragnoardus, and Landramnus are to assemble with their suffragans.

Third, at Lyons, where Agobardus, Bernardus, Andreas, Benedictus, and Agericus are likewise to assemble with their suffragans.

Fourth, at the city of Toulouse, where Nothus, Bartholomaeus, Adalelmus, and Agiulfus are to assemble together with their suffragans.

At these gatherings they are to discuss, investigate, and, with God’s help, discover matters concerning the Christian religion and entrusted to their care: what is observed by the rulers and the rest of the people, whether in accordance with divine authority or otherwise, and what has been partly or wholly abandoned so that it is no longer observed.

Next, they are to discover what may be found in the morals, conduct, and actions of those appointed shepherds of the people that does not agree with divine rule and authority; and likewise to discover what circumstances in either order caused deviation from the right path.

Whatever is discovered concerning these matters is to be guarded with such careful diligence that they must not allow it to come to anyone else’s knowledge before the appointed time. Therefore, one notary is to be chosen from among them all, who is to record what they discover; and, bound by oath, he is diligently and faithfully to preserve what has been found and arranged.

[Col. 0598A] [Note: From Sirmond; absent from all manuscripts.]

In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ. Louis and Lothar, august emperors by the providence of God’s ordinance, to all the faithful of God’s holy Church and to our own people.

We believe that you remember how this year, on the advice of the priests and our other faithful, we ordered a general fast to be observed throughout our entire kingdom, and that God be entreated with complete devotion [Col. 0598B] to be gracious to us and to reveal to us in what matters we had especially offended him [Note: [Col. 0597] “To be gracious and to reveal to us in what matters we had offended him,” Sirmond.], and to grant us a peaceful time for the correction we needed.

We had indeed wished to hold our general assembly at a suitable time and to deal there with our common correction. This would have happened by God’s mercy, had the uprising of our enemies, as you know, not prevented it. But since it could not then take place according to our will, it seemed good to us to hold the present assembly with some of our faithful and to consider there, with the Lord’s help, how those matters which had remained unfinished because of the aforesaid impediment might be brought to completion.

Therefore, we wish your diligence to know that at this present assembly we considered with our faithful that, first of all, the archbishops with their suffragans should assemble at a suitable time in appropriate places, and there, by investigating according to divine authority, should discover matters concerning both their own correction and amendment and that of all of us, and should announce their findings to us and to our faithful according to the ministry entrusted to them.

We likewise considered sending our envoys throughout our entire kingdom, so that they might strive with all the zeal they could muster concerning every matter that appeared to pertain to correction, and might immediately correct by our authority whatever they found possible [Col. 0598D] [Note: [Col. 0599C] “Goldast,” says Baluze, “understands Aizo, who had laid waste the kingdom of the Franks with Saracen forces.” Aizo’s defection and invasion of the kingdom with Saracen auxiliaries occurred in 826 and the following year, as Einhard relates in the Annals. Goldast’s opinion therefore cannot be true. It is better to interpret this of the Bulgars and Danes, whom the author of the Life of Louis the Pious reports to have entered Louis’s kingdom as enemies in 828 and burned some estates by setting fire to them. Baluze.]. If any difficulty opposed them in any matter, they were to take care to report it to our knowledge.

Therefore, we wish all of you, for the sake of the common salvation, the honor of the kingdom, and the people’s welfare, not to neglect to be obedient and helpful to our envoys in every way according to your strength. At the same time, you should know that for this reason we wish to sit in our palace on one day every week to hear cases, so that through this or that count, through the care of the envoys, and through the obedience of the people, it may become more clearly apparent to us.

And so that all these matters may succeed, we wish a general three-day fast to be proclaimed for the Monday after the octave of Pentecost and to be observed generally by everyone with the greatest devotion.

And because we know that the enemies of God’s holy Church are being stirred up everywhere and wish to attack the kingdom entrusted to us by God, we command and order that all men throughout our entire kingdom who are liable for military service be well prepared with horses, weapons, clothing, wagons, and provisions, so that whenever they are notified by us, they may depart without any delay and proceed in whatever direction necessity requires, and remain there for as long as necessity demands.

# THE CONSTITUTIONS OF WORMS

(Year 829, August)

[Col. 0601]

# THE REPORT OF THE BISHOPS TO THE EMPEROR

After four episcopal assemblies had been held in June and their proceedings written down by imperial decree, a general assembly was held at Worms in August. There, first, the acts of the four assemblies were combined into one document and presented by the bishops to the emperor.

This sufficiently extensive book, composed for the most part from the surviving acts of the Parisian assembly but with the order completely changed, is here published for the first time in its entirety through the benefit of the eleventh-century Gotha Manuscript. Previously, only its latter part had been published under the title “Second Addition to the Books of Benedict’s Capitularies.”

Since the bishops demanded many things, however, they obtained only a small part of them, as the chapters printed below demonstrate. Thus, even in the year 835, at the assembly of Aachen, they judged that many points of this petition had to be proposed again in the same words. Nevertheless, even the matters they did not obtain reveal the mind and plans of Ebo, then president of the Parisian synod and soon afterward standard-bearer of the rebellious faction, as well as those of Agobardus and the other bishops [Note: [Col. 0601D] For comparison, see Book II of the *Life of Wala*, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, vol. II.].

# RESPONSE [Note: *Resciptum*, manuscript.] TO THE CONSULTATION

## OR EXHORTATION OF THE BISHOPS TO LORD LOUIS THE EMPEROR

[Col. 0601A]

To the most distinguished and piety-endowed Louis, orthodox and unconquered Augustus [Note: [Col. 0601D] Compare the Sixth Council of Paris in Labbe, Book III, p. 1655, where Lothar’s name is nevertheless added.].

We, your servants, though unworthy, yet bishops, humbly render thanks to God and praise and proclaim his boundless piety and goodness. He makes you burn with such devoted love for him, his most devoted servant, that you continually think about the advancement and exaltation of his holy Church, and, like a faithful and beloved spiritual son, always strive to raise her to better and higher things.

For when the divine sword was rightly wearing down, within and without, the empire divinely entrusted to you with various disasters because of our iniquity [Note: [Col. 0601] *Atterreret claudibus*, “wear down with calamities,” manuscript c.], you wisely perceived that these events could only be taking place by God’s just judgment. Immediately, in a letter from your Serenity in the previous year, you admonished all [Note: [Col. 0601] “All,” manuscript c.] the shepherds of the churches: since it was certain that they were the Lord’s watchmen and that the divine sword was raging over the earth—that is, over sinners—they should remember their watchfulness; and after everyone had generally observed a three-day fast, each person in every order should carefully confront his own conscience and, wherever he recognized that he had offended God, should not delay in correcting himself through the satisfaction of penance.

In that letter [Note: [Col. 0601] *Apitibus*, manuscript c.] you were also pleased to insert that, if God granted you peace and leisure everywhere, you wished to complete your general assembly, so that first you might correct, with the Lord’s help, whatever was found to require correction in yourselves—that is, in your person and ministry—and then investigate anyone in every order of your empire who displeased God, and, according to God’s will and with the agreement of your faithful, restore them to the path of righteousness.

But since you did not obtain the desired time according to your wish, because external incursions intervened, it pleased your Serenity to hold an assembly during the previous winter with some of your faithful, to consider carefully the matters mentioned above, seek God’s will, and provide for the welfare of the Church entrusted to you.

Therefore, your Serenity arranged the chapters that seemed worthy of correction at that time and appointed energetic legates, so that through those chapters they might both punish the crimes of wicked men and make the praise of good men known to your Highness.

Among other things, you also established that assemblies of bishops should be held at one and the same time in four regions of your empire. At these assemblies they were to discuss, investigate, and, with God’s help, discover matters concerning the Christian religion and entrusted to their care, what was observed by the rulers and the rest of the people, whether in accordance with divine authority or otherwise, and what had been partly or wholly abandoned so that it was no longer observed; [Col. 0602B] next, what might be found in the morals, conduct, and actions of those appointed shepherds of the people that did not agree with divine rule and authority; and likewise what circumstances in either order had caused them to deviate from the right path. Whatever was discovered concerning these matters, they were to make known to your Highness.

We have taken care to do this, insofar as God granted us the ability, and have recorded our findings in the chapters that follow.

### Chapter 1. What properly belongs to the Christian religion

[Note: [Col. 0602D] See Labbe, cited work, Book I, chapter 1, p. 1599.]

The first foundation of the Christian religion is the Catholic faith: namely, to believe in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, one true God, three in persons and one in substance; also to believe that the Son alone assumed flesh for our salvation, in which he suffered, rose again, and ascended into heaven, and with which he will also come for judgment; and to believe that through the Holy Spirit the forgiveness of sins is granted in baptism, and that among the faithful in Christ’s Church the forgiveness of sins is undoubtedly bestowed through the gift of that same Holy Spirit, through the priestly ministry and through penance; and that there will be a general resurrection of all in true flesh at Christ’s coming.

Every believer must also know that this faith cannot be true and fruitful unless it is adorned with good works, namely hope, charity, humility, chastity, continence, sobriety, unanimity, concord, justice, piety, mercy, innocence, simplicity, and other things of this kind; all of these consist in love of God and of neighbor.

Without these, no one can please God or be saved, because, as the Apostle testifies, faith without works is dead in itself. Therefore, every Christian must carefully consider whether faith is alive in him through the practice of good works, or dead through the neglect of good works. And if, according to the Apostle’s teaching, faith without good works is dead, with what condemnation [Note: [Col. 0603] *Quadam*, manuscript c.] must those be punished who not only do not adorn that same faith with good works but also stain it with various crimes [Note: [Col. 0603] “Various,” manuscript c.]?

Among the other [Note: [Col. 0603] *Tertia*, manuscript c.] evils that stain that same faith, four spiritual vices seem rightly to us to require special emphasis; the more hidden they are, the more destructive they are: pride, through which the angel became the devil and was cast out of heaven; envy, through which that same devil cast man out of paradise; hatred and discord, which extinguish charity among neighbors, empty love of its force, overturn every good thing, and do not allow neighbors to remain in mutual love or even to choose the peaceful life that he had taught Christians.

We have called these vices more dangerous—even deadly—because their followers either do not understand them or disdain to understand them; and because, making light of them, they do not come to confession on account of them, they therefore do not merit correction.

[Col. 0603C]

### 2. That the universal holy Church of God is one body and that Christ is its head

[Note: [Col. 0603D] Cited work, p. 1599, Book I, chapter 2.]

First, then, we establish from the apostolic utterances that the universal holy Church of God is plainly one body and that Christ is its head. Thus Paul says: “You are the body of Christ and members individually.” Again: “For just as in one body we have many members, and not all the members have the same function [Note: [Col. 0603] *Actu*, “function,” manuscript c.], so we, though many, are one body in Christ.” Again: “Christ is its head, from whom the whole body, administered through connection and conjunction, grows into a holy temple in the Lord.”

There are countless other examples of this kind, which are omitted here to avoid prolixity. Therefore, whoever has made himself, through some unlawful act, a member of the devil from being a member of Christ—having been overcome by the devil’s cunning [Note: [Col. 0603] “Separated,” corrected to “overcome” in manuscript c.]—must not neglect to restore himself without hesitation while the time for penance is available.

## 3. That the body of the same Church is principally divided between two eminent persons

We know that the body of the entire holy Church of God is principally divided between two eminent persons, namely, the priestly and the royal, as we have received it as handed down by the holy fathers. On this subject Gelasius, venerable bishop of the Roman see, writes thus to the Emperor Anastasius:

> “There are indeed two powers, august emperor, by which this world is principally governed: the sacred authority of the pontiffs and the royal power. Of these, the burden of the priests is all the heavier, since they must also render an account before the divine tribunal on behalf of the kings themselves.”

Fulgentius likewise writes in his book *On the Truth of Predestination and Grace*:

> “As far as the life of the present age is concerned, no one in the Church is found superior to the pontiff, nor in the Christian world is anyone found higher than the emperor.”

Since these things are so, we have decided to speak first about the priestly person and afterward about the royal person.

## ON THE PRIESTLY PERSON

### Chapter 1. On the election and advancement of priests

The election and advancement of those who are to be placed over others as a model and example must be carefully provided for and guarded against, so that those through whom the Christian religion is to endure and the rest are to be preserved from offense may be chosen—once the simoniacal plague has been entirely removed—such as apostolic teaching, canonical order, and the pastoral rule of blessed Gregory instruct.

For if someone is chosen in return for some payment, whether of present or future reward, or for any other matter that may be contrary to the truth and to divine authority, it is plainly evident that the procedure is wholly different from what divine authority testifies; that God is offended by such an act; and that it is beyond doubt that scandal will arise both for the person so elected and for those over whom he is placed.

Therefore, in the election and ordination of a priest, the simoniacal heresy must be regarded as utterly detestable. It is demonstrably defiling the priestly dignity in the present age because of the avarice and ambition of certain people. Such greed contains no small amount of lawlessness deserving condemnation: at the beginning of the holy Church of God it was condemned, together with its author, by blessed Peter, chief of the apostles.

For in the second canon of the Council of Chalcedon it is also written:

> “If any bishop makes an ordination for money, reduces to a price a grace that cannot be sold, or ordains for money a bishop, presbyter, or deacon, or anyone else numbered among the clergy; or advances for money a steward, defender, or anyone subject to the rule, for the sake of his own most shameful gain, the person proved to have attempted this shall be subject to the danger of losing his own rank. The person who has been ordained shall gain nothing from this ordination or advancement made by financial dealing, but shall be deprived of the dignity or office that he acquired with money. If anyone acts as an intermediary in such shameful and wicked gifts or payments, then, if he is a cleric, let him fall from his own rank; but if he is a layman or a monk, let him be anathematized.”

### 2. That every effort must be made to advance to the priesthood men as learned and of such character as those described by blessed Gregory in the *Pastoral Rule*

Every effort must be made to advance to the priesthood men as learned and of such character as those whom blessed Gregory describes in the *Pastoral Rule*. There, among other things, he says:

> “No art is presumed to be taught unless it is first learned through attentive reflection. With what temerity, then, is pastoral leadership undertaken by the inexperienced, when it is the art of arts, the governance of souls?”

The Lord also speaks through the prophet Haggai concerning pastors:

> “Ask the priests about the law.”

Blessed Jerome explains this as follows:

> “Consider, he says, that it is the duty of priests, when questioned about the law, to give an answer. If he is a priest, let him know the law of the Lord; if he does not know the law, he himself proves that he is not the Lord’s priest. For it is the priest’s duty to know the law and to answer questions about the law.”

The following saying of blessed Gregory must also be placed especially before the eyes of all priests. Among other things, he says:

> “When the necessity of circumstances requires it, one must consider very carefully how each person comes to the height of governance, how he lives after duly attaining it, and how, living well, he teaches, and teaching rightly …”

[Note: Here, at the beginning, some words were written below and then deleted by the writer.]

### 3. That avarice must be corrected among members of the priestly order

Since we have learned that some members of our order shamefully pursue avarice and are rightly reproved by many, and that on this account the innocent are being defamed together with the guilty, we have decided that from now on we and our colleagues must correct one another through mutual exhortation. This is so that neither we may sin before God through this plague of avarice, nor give others an opportunity, through our evil example, to slander us and sin against us.

Since no Christian ought to store up treasures on earth but rather, according to the Lord’s saying, in heaven, priests must take the greatest care to restrain themselves from the plague of avarice, which is the root of all evils and excludes its followers from the kingdom of Christ. For they cannot rightly preach to their subjects that they should abstain from these things when they themselves have enslaved themselves to them—a great disgrace, indeed a dangerous one.

This pestilential disease is condemned more gravely and severely in them than in those who ought to be restrained from it by their words and examples.

Some people are accustomed to put forward various pretexts that flatter themselves under the name of necessity; and indeed, while necessity is alleged outwardly, avarice is concealed inwardly. Hence blessed Prosper says:

> “The priest who despises admonition cannot say to those who despise it that they should consider the judgment to come, when perhaps he himself does not consider it. He cannot say to lovers of the world, ‘Do not love the world,’ if the love of the world delights him; nor to the ambitious, ‘Now put an end to ambition,’ if destructive ambition is driving him to ruin.”

In the *Life of Blessed Ambrose* we also read:

> “For he groaned exceedingly when he saw avarice, the root of all evils—which can be diminished neither by abundance nor by want—increasing more and more among human beings, especially among those who held positions of power. Thus it was an extremely difficult task to intervene with them, since they sold everything for a price. This brought every evil upon neighboring Italy, and from then on everything turned for the worse. And what shall I say when they exercise their fury in such persons, who are accustomed to put forward either the affairs of their children or of their relatives as excuses for sins, when even a blind stain—or levity—began to seize many priests, for whom God is their portion, so that they too seek it? Woe to me in my misery, because we are not even moved by the end of the world to wish to be freed from so heavy a yoke of servitude, which plunges us to the depths of hell, so that we may make friends for ourselves from the mammon of iniquity who will receive us into eternal dwellings.”

### 4. That priests must practice hospitality

Since, therefore, for the sake of a common and necessary correction we have carefully investigated these matters and have demonstrated from divine revelations and the sayings of the holy fathers how one must enter pastoral leadership, how one must live in it, how one must teach, and how priests of the Lord—who ought to be a model and example for others—must avoid avarice, we considered it worthwhile to admonish ourselves by exhorting and to exhort by admonishing, so that priests of the Lord may remember especially to practice hospitality.

Until now some members of our order have acted in this matter less justly than they should, and for that reason many have marked with this reproach not only those who are negligent, but also those devoted to hospitality.

If hospitality is to be rewarded by the eternal Judge on the day of the dread examination—he who will say, “I was a stranger, and you welcomed me”—and if it must therefore be practiced with the greatest care by all Christians, then it must be carried out with far greater vigilance by those who, through words and examples, provide others with guidance toward eternal life. They must put aside the plague of avarice and every other pretext.

For among the other praises of virtue that ought to be present in a bishop, the Apostle also commends hospitality. The house of a bishop, as blessed Jerome writes, ought to be a common lodging for everyone; if a layman receives one, two, or a few people, he fulfills the duty of hospitality, but if a bishop does not receive everyone, he is described as inhuman.

### 5. That when bishops travel through their dioceses, they must take the greatest care not to be a burden to those whom they ought to benefit

We have learned from the report of certain people that some of our bishops, when traveling through their dioceses, become a burden not only to their fellow priests but also to certain other faithful whom they ought to have assisted. For this reason they drive many people into slander and hatred of them.

Therefore, we have collectively decreed that no bishop may henceforth do such a thing. We have also decreed that each bishop should travel through his diocese at a suitable time. Although canonical authority teaches that one quarter of the tithes and revenues from the offerings of the faithful should go to the use of bishops, nevertheless, wherever a bishop has his own resources, he should be content with them. Where he has no resources belonging to his own church, he may take from the aforesaid portion for himself and his household—not what avarice, God forbid, may have suggested, but what necessity has compelled.

If, however, no necessity for receiving anything presses upon him, he should take nothing from the aforesaid fourth part, but leave it, according to his disposition, for the use of the churches and for the poor of Christ.

### 6. That chorepiscopi must not exceed the measure of their authority established in the sacred canons

We have discovered that a reprehensible and highly unusual practice has arisen: certain chorepiscopi, going beyond the limits of their office, confer the gift of the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands and perform various other acts that belong solely to bishops, contrary to law.

This is especially improper since none of the seventy disciples, whose role they represent in the Church, is recorded as having conferred the gift of the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands. The Book of the Acts of the Apostles teaches that it is the particular duty of the apostles and their successors alone to confer the Holy Spirit.

The Council of Caesarea states the following concerning chorepiscopi:

> “Chorepiscopi also appear to correspond in example and form to the seventy; but they are honored as fellow ministers because of the zeal that they show toward the poor.”

Likewise, canon 10 of the Council of Antioch states:

> “Those who are called chorepiscopi in villages and rural estates, although they have received the laying on of hands from bishops and have been consecrated as bishops, nevertheless the holy synod has decreed that they should recognize their proper limits, govern the churches subject to them, and be content with the bishops’ oversight and care.”

### 7. That bishops must appoint ministers who hate avarice throughout their dioceses

We have learned that the ministers of certain bishops—namely chorepiscopi, archpriests, and archdeacons—practice avarice not only among the priests but also among the people of their dioceses, rather than serving the benefit of ecclesiastical dignity and caring for the salvation of the people. We have therefore collectively decreed that this negligence, or rather this execrable and condemnable vice of greed, must henceforth be avoided by everyone.

The downfall of Eli the priest must be feared and carefully avoided by the priests of the Lord. Eli’s sons acted unworthily, provoked the Lord to anger by their evil deeds, and inflicted injury upon the Lord’s sacrifice. Because he corrected them only with words and not with blows, he fell together with them when they fell through divine and just vengeance.

If, however—God forbid—any bishop henceforth appoints ministers who are followers of avarice in his diocese and refuses, by pastoral authority, to strike down their known wickedness severely, let him recognize that he is imitating the example of the negligent priest Eli, and let him know that he must submit in every way to synodal correction.

We have also decreed by common agreement that each bishop must henceforth exercise more vigilant care over his archdeacon, because many people are scandalized by their avarice and depravity of conduct, the priestly ministry is reviled, and many things in the churches are neglected by priests because of them.

### 8. On priests and their churches, from which many things are neglected and scandals arise

In our discussion, four dangers appeared to us concerning priests and their churches.

First, some priests, having acquired a certain sense of security, neither perform the duties belonging to worship nor show diligence in repairing and illuminating the church. They do not even display the reverence owed to their superiors. Moreover, they strip their churches and transfer their property to their own small estates. We have discovered that all these things result from the negligence of bishops.

Taking this as an opportunity, their superiors then boldly go so far as to presume to treat them unlawfully, dishonorably, and irreverently. Therefore, we have judged that all of us must henceforth take the greatest care that what the lord emperor has granted to the churches, with the consent of the bishops, for the honor and love of God, should not be diverted into the avarice of priests or the rapacity of episcopal ministers, but should be used for the benefit of the church and for the needs of the clergy and the poor.

### 9. That priests must not keep women in their houses contrary to the canons

We have learned that it is no less dangerous that, in the dioceses of certain bishops, some priests, contrary to the prohibitions of the holy canons, not only allow women to live in their houses but also make them serve them. We know that such women have often become a snare for priests and that many, on this account, have fallen into scandal and slander.

This transgression was prohibited, according to canonical authority, both in the assemblies of bishops during the time of your father and during your own time, but the matter has not yet been fully brought to completion.

Therefore, we have collectively decreed that those who until now have failed to correct such a great transgression, if henceforth they neglect to become its correctors, shall, according to the Apostle’s judgment, be restrained as though they were consenting to the wrongdoing of others.

### 10. On priests who become stewards, enter taverns, pursue shameful profits, and engage in other indecent conduct

Similarly, concerning those priests who, contrary to the statutes of the canons, become stewards, enter taverns, pursue shameful profits, serve usury in its various forms, visit other people’s houses dishonorably and immodestly, are not ashamed to devote themselves to feasting and drunkenness, and run indiscriminately through various markets, we have judged that the following must be observed: henceforth they must be restrained strictly and severely.

Their unlawful and unbecoming conduct must not cause the priestly ministry to be reviled, nor those who ought to be an example to others to become a cause of scandal.

### 11. That priestly conduct must have credible witnesses to their life

We have therefore agreed that bishops, following the examples of the holy fathers who have died, should have religious persons as witnesses to their conduct, so that they may leave no opening for those who wish to slander them.

The Apostle teaches in his letter to Titus that a priest must provide his disciples with a good example from his own life, saying:

> “In all things present yourself as an example of good works, in teaching, in integrity, in chastity,”

and so forth.

Blessed Gregory also says in his decrees:

> “A shameful custom has arisen: that secular lay boys should serve the pontiffs of this see in the private chambers of their bedrooms. Although the life of a pastor ought always to be an example to his disciples, often the clergy do not know what the life of their pontiff is like in private, while the secular boys know. Therefore, by this present decree I establish that certain clerics, or even monks, selected for the service of the pontifical chamber, should attend to it, so that the one who holds the position of governance may have such witnesses as see his conduct in private, and so that, through their constant observation, they may take from it an example of advancement.”

[Note: That is, so that they may derive progress from it.]

These, then, are the words of blessed Gregory. If anyone wishes to seek more extensive examples concerning this matter, let him read the lives of blessed Augustine and Ambrose and of the other saints and other distinguished men. He will clearly find that the life and conduct of a pontiff ought always to have credible witnesses to his life.

### 12. That bishops must avoid reproach and observe moderation when spending church resources on their relatives

Since many bishops, out of love for their relatives, purchase estates and dependents from the resources entrusted to them, either in their own name or in the name of some friend, and arrange that these should pass into the rights of their relatives, thereby undermining ecclesiastical rights and defiling the priestly ministry—or rather provoking subjects to slander and despise it—it has pleased everyone that this form of avarice be henceforth avoided.

We have firmly decreed, and intend this decree to remain permanently in force, that a bishop may dispose, according to canonical authority, of whatever property belonging to him he acquired either before his episcopate or during his episcopate by hereditary succession, and may give it to whomever he wishes.

After he has become a bishop, however, whatever property from the resources of the church he acquires, under any condition, either in his own name or in another’s, we have decreed that it must pass not into the rights of his relatives but into the rights of the church over which he presides.

We establish the same rule for priests and deacons who purchase estates in this manner from the property of the churches over which they preside. For we have discovered that many priests, through property acquired in this way, have stripped the churches over which they preside, departed from their ministry in many ways, enslaved themselves to the devil, and on this account driven many laypeople into scandal, condemnation, and ruin.

### 13. That bishops must not neglect the communities entrusted to them

We have learned that certain bishops have until now been extremely negligent in governing the communities entrusted to them, namely, canonical monks and nuns. For this reason they have provoked many people to slander and despise them. Thus certain other prelates established in their dioceses, following their evil examples, have likewise neglected their own communities.

We have judged it necessary to admonish them both through fraternal and through synodal assembly, so that henceforth they may restrain themselves from this negligence and present themselves as examples for others to imitate. Otherwise, through their carelessness, contempt for divine service and dangers to souls may arise; displeasure may be brought to the ears of Your Excellence; and our own modest standing may be subjected to weariness and disgrace in sacred assemblies.

### 14. That members of the order must not abandon their sees without necessity or definite usefulness

We have also discovered that certain members of our order, not for reasons of necessity or usefulness but rather out of avarice or pleasure, very often leave their own city and see and neglect their clergy in order to frequent more distant places.

As a result, divine worship is abandoned, preaching among the people and care for those subject to them are postponed, and hospitality is neglected. We have therefore unanimously forbidden anyone henceforth to do this without unavoidable necessity and definite usefulness.

### 15. On laymen’s clerics

Concerning the clergy of laypeople, about whom some of them seem to complain because certain bishops are unwilling to ordain them in their churches, even though they are useful, it seemed to us that peace and concord should be preserved on both sides. Useful and suitable men should be chosen with charity and reason. If a layman presents a suitable and useful cleric, the bishop must not reject him without a sound reason on any pretext whatsoever; and if he must be rejected, the reason must be made clear in order to avoid scandal.

### 16. On the correction of our own conduct

Since it is clear that the Christian religion must be administered beneficially by the successors of the apostles and that guidance toward eternal life must be provided to the peoples, we judged it necessary first of all to correct, with all our strength and with the Lord’s help, whatever in us appeared blameworthy, unsuitable, unbecoming, or contrary to the sacred ministries to which we have been unworthily devoted.

This means that henceforth we must exercise more diligent care and attention, with complete zeal and concern, in our life, teaching, conduct, moral integrity, and devotion to preaching, as well as in the correction of our fellow priests, ministers, and subjects.

We must devote ourselves not merely to worldly desires, cares, and anxieties, but rather to divine duties; we must also work at maintaining schools and educating the soldiers of the holy Church.

With God’s mercy, we desire to imitate and practice these things in every respect, as far as we are able, for the salvation of all of us, insofar as, with the favor of divine grace, priestly freedom and the leisure we desire are granted to us.

### 17. On the duties of bishops toward their people and toward the emperor

At our appointed assemblies, we first decreed unanimously and with one accord that each of us should strive, through words and examples, to encourage the people subject to him in his diocese toward better things. He should carefully admonish them to restrain themselves from evil and turn wholly to God; to strive to make God, whom they had made angry with themselves by sinning, favorable to them through worthy penitential satisfaction and generous almsgiving; and to implore God’s immeasurable mercy with bowed-down prayers for the life of our most pious and God-beloved emperors, for the safety of their wives and children, and for the stability of the empire entrusted to them.

After this, it seemed appropriate to us to insert here the chapters that we judged necessary to present to the lord emperor as a petition.

## PETITION

### 1. That the emperor’s sons and nobles should recognize the dignity and authority of the priesthood

We humbly ask Your Excellence that, through you, your sons and nobles may recognize the name, power, force, and dignity of the priesthood. You can easily understand this from the words of the Lord, who said to blessed Peter, whose place we unworthy men occupy:

> “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven.”

And elsewhere he says generally to the disciples:

> “Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them; whose sins you retain, they are retained.”

### 2. On the authority and dignity of priests

The following example should also be recalled. In ecclesiastical history, the Emperor Constantine says to the bishops:

> “God appointed you as priests and gave you authority to judge even us; therefore we are rightly judged by you. You, however, cannot be judged by human beings. For this reason, await among yourselves the judgment of God alone, so that whatever disputes you have may be reserved for that divine examination. For you, given to us by God, belong to God; and it is not fitting that a human being should judge gods, but only the one of whom it is written: ‘God stood in the assembly of gods; in the midst, God judges.’”

It should also be recalled how blessed Prosper, in the book that he wrote on the contemplative and active life, described the praise of priests:

> “To them—that is, to priests—the care of souls has been entrusted in a special way. They courageously bear the burden of the people committed to them and tirelessly pray to God for the sins of all as though they were their own. Like another Aaron, offering the incense of a contrite heart and humbled spirit by which God is appeased, they avert from the people the anger of future punishment. By God’s grace they become interpreters of the divine will; after the apostles, founders of the churches of Christ; leaders of the faithful people; defenders of the truth; enemies of wicked teaching; beloved by all who are good; and terrifying even by their appearance to those conscious of evil. They are avengers of the oppressed; fathers in the faith of those born again; preachers of heavenly rewards; examples of good conduct; lessons in virtue; and models for the faithful. They are the glory of the Church, in whom the Church shines more brightly; the strongest pillars, founded in Christ, upon which the whole multitude of believers rests; the gates of the eternal city, through whom all believers enter to Christ; the doorkeepers to whom the keys of the kingdom of heaven have been given; and stewards of the royal household, by whose judgment the ranks and duties of each person are distributed in the court of the eternal King.”

Although we are far inferior in life and merits to the holy priests who came before us, nevertheless the sacred ministry that we have unworthily undertaken possesses no less authority and dignity. Although we are unworthy of so great a ministry, it must not on that account be despised in us, for the sake of the one whose ministry we perform.

### 3. That the faithful should not form false suspicions about episcopal correction

We considered it especially necessary to bring this to the attention of Your Piety: through you, your faithful should be admonished and instructed that, whenever Your Highness entrusts us with some matter concerning our correction—or concerning your salvation and theirs—they should not, through empty and false suspicion, take scandal against us, offend God by slandering us without cause, and incur guilt in a matter from which they ought to have hoped for and obtained salvation.

We neither desire nor intend to pursue anything else—and it is not our duty to do so—except what belongs to our ministry and to their salvation. Therefore, we must not be judged beforehand through suspicion but patiently awaited, until the truth itself makes clear whether we ought rather to be heard or rejected.

If it should happen that rumor spreads some unfavorable opinion about us, we both can and must endure it with equanimity, with God’s help.

They themselves, however, cannot be free from guilt when they do not fear criticizing the intention of fathers and brothers without cause. For we and you must work with the greatest care to ensure that peace, concord, and unanimity always remain between the pastors of the churches and the flock of Christ. Unless they have charity, concord, and unity among themselves, they do not deserve to have God favorable to them as they ought.

Therefore, as has been stated above, when Your Piety, inspired by God, commands us to deliberate on something concerning the ecclesiastical and common good, it is not lawful for us to lie. At times it may be possible to conceal the truth temporarily without grave danger, but when questioned about the truth itself, we can never lie without serious peril.

Yet because truth often produces hatred, and because the word of God is described by the Lord as hostile to our carnal desires, nevertheless, on the way—that is, in the present life—we must consent to this: whenever we are questioned and speak the truth, even if certain weak people are scandalized without cause, we must still adhere to the truth itself.

For often, when we advise you that all the faithful should handle the property of the churches piously, reverently, and with fear of God, recognizing that it is dedicated to God, so that they may derive temporal benefit from it without suffering eternal loss through ignorance or negligence, some suspect that we offer this admonition out of greed rather than for the sake of salvation.

Yet we truly wish them to be deprived of none of the property entrusted to them. Rather, we wish to provide for their common salvation, because we take pleasure not, as many suppose, in the desire for property but rather in the salvation of souls, mindful of the Apostle’s saying:

> “For I do not seek what is yours, but you.”

### 4. On holding councils and establishing public schools

Since the sacred canons order councils to be held twice a year, we earnestly ask Your Piety to grant at least once a year the freedom to convene at a suitable time, so that these matters may appropriately and decently be carried out for the honor of God, of the holy Church of God, and for the correction of many.

If such councils are held once a year in each province, ecclesiastical honor will maintain the right of its own order; the insolence of certain proud clerics—who, trampling everywhere upon canonical authority, will not cease to bring trouble to imperial ears—will be restrained; the impunity of various crimes, which now provides a place for concealment, will no longer have such a place; and many other matters that have until now proceeded contrary to ecclesiastical teaching will, with the Lord’s help, be restored to their proper order.

Likewise, we earnestly and humbly urge Your Highness, following the custom of your father, to establish public schools by your authority in at least three highly suitable places in your empire, so that the labor of your father and of yourself may not, God forbid, perish through negligence. From this action will come great usefulness, honor for the holy Church of God, a great reward for you, and everlasting remembrance.

### 5. On restoring priests and clerics who have fled

Likewise, we considered it necessary to request this of Your Piety: that priests, Levites, and clerics of the lower orders who have fled to various parts of your empire, especially the regions of Italy, should be diligently sought out by your authority through your envoys, compelled to come into your presence, and restored through your clemency to the churches from which they withdrew through stubbornness.

[Note: That is, “to be requested from Your Piety …”]

### 6. That monks, priests, and clerics must not improperly approach the palace

We also humbly and earnestly ask this of Your Piety: that monks, priests, and clerics who, setting aside canonical authority, approach the palace indiscriminately and bring the most unwelcome disturbance to your sacred ears should be deterred by your authority and power and should not presume to do this.

For by such conduct ecclesiastical authority is despised, and the priestly religion and monastic profession are cheapened.

### 7. On restoring impoverished episcopal sees

We also humbly and earnestly request Your holy and most pious devotion that, for the love and honor of God and for the salvation of your soul, you should follow the custom of your father and, while you have time and opportunity offers itself, consider the relief and consolation of certain episcopal sees that appear to have been deprived—or rather completely stripped—of their own resources. Always remember how devoted your predecessors were to such most pious efforts.

### 8. On eliminating a grave evil in the dioceses of Alitgari and Rantgarii

We also ask Your Mercy to send your envoys to a certain part of the dioceses of Alitgari and Rantgarii, where we have heard that a most shameful, wicked, and—by the very description of it—foul deed is being perpetrated. Let trustworthy envoys of yours be present there and, through your imperial power, together with the authority of those whose dioceses they are, root out that evil from the place as quickly and completely as possible.

9. [Note: [Col. 0614D] Book III, 17.] Again, by humbly admonishing you, we suggest to your serenity that, through your most diligent care and by your imperial authority, such reckless shedding of Christian blood [Note: [Col. 0613] *sanguis* in c.] not be permitted to occur in your kingdom, always bearing in mind what the Lord said after [Note: [Col. 0613] omitted in c.] the Flood to his servant Noah:

> “From the hand of man and from the hand of a man and of his brother I will require the life of man. Whoever sheds human blood, his blood shall be shed; for man was made in the image of God.”

And in the Law:

> “Whoever kills a man shall be put to death.”

And the Apostle:

> “For rulers are not a terror to good conduct but to evil. Do you wish not to fear the authority? Do what is good, and you will receive praise from it, for it is God’s servant for your good. But if you do evil, be afraid; for he does not bear the sword without cause. For he is God’s servant, an avenger in wrath against the one who does evil.”

For divine authority says specifically of him:

> “He bears the sword of God for the punishment of evildoers,”

and not of anyone else. On the other hand, we know that, through a pernicious invention, some have usurped the practice whereby those who are supported by no public office, because of their own hatreds and their various worst intentions, improperly claim for themselves the ministry of vengeance in punishing their neighbors and killing people [Note: [Col. 0615] *interfaciendis* in c.]. What a king ought to exercise in a single case [Note: [Col. 0615] *exercuere* in c.], for the terror of many, they do not hesitate shamelessly to perpetrate in many cases because of hatred; and they think that, in avenging enmities, they are permitted to do what they do not want a king to do in carrying out God’s vengeance.

10. [Note: [Col. 0615D] Book III, 18.] Concerning abbots, both canonical and regular, and abbesses who appear to preside over communities of religious women, as well as laymen who possess monasteries, we ask your piety that, at the present assembly, they be expressly admonished by your serenity to provide a good example to others in their own conduct, to live religiously as is fitting, and altogether to avoid whatever is unsuitable to each person’s profession and prohibited by the sacred canons. Let them not, through negligence, allow the places granted to them by you [Note: The manuscript reads *nobis* (“by us”) instead of *vobis* (“by you”).] to be plundered and destroyed; and let them not neglect to govern the communities entrusted to them, whether spiritually or temporally, with paternal affection, nor to provide them with the necessary provisions, lest perhaps through some want the divine offices be neglected and the communities themselves be compelled to live less religiously. Let them also willingly hear our admonition, receive it kindly, and fulfill it obediently.

For if they obey our admonitions, we, with God’s help [Note: [Col. 0615] The manuscript reads *auxiante* instead of *adiuvante* (“with the help of”).], desire by our efforts to accomplish this to the best of our ability: that religion itself may always progress toward what is better, that your reward may thereby increase, that the peril of souls may be avoided as far as possible [Note: [Col. 0615] The manuscript reads *cauatur* instead of *caveatur* (“may be avoided”).], and that the weariness caused by complaints on this account may be removed from your ears.

11. [Note: [Col. 0615D] Book III, 19.] We also ask that your highness specifically instruct your representatives to be diligent and true helpers to us in carrying these matters out wherever necessity requires.

12. [Note: [Col. 0615D] Ibid.] Concerning priests and palatine chaplains [Note: [Col. 0615] The manuscript reads *capellis* instead of *capellanis* (“chaplains”).] who are kept contrary to canonical authority and ecclesiastical propriety, we admonish your diligence that they be restrained by your authority. For because of this ecclesiastical honor is made more contemptible, and your nobles and palatine ministers do not proceed with you to celebrate Mass on solemn days, as is fitting.

Indeed, we earnestly beseech you that, in observing the Lord’s Day, as we asked long ago, you apply due care, so that—unless great necessity compels it—you divest yourselves as far as you can on that day of worldly cares and anxieties, do what is appropriate to the veneration of so great a day, and by your sacred example teach and compel your own people to do likewise.

13. [Note: [Col. 0615D] Book III, 20.] Concerning the reception of the sacred body and blood of the Lord, we likewise admonish you to do what is beneficial to Christian religion, as our fathers admonished you at other assemblies, whenever it is possible; and by your example instruct those serving you to do the same.

14. [Note: [Col. 0615D] Book III, 21.] Concerning the chapter which your highness has decided should be established at a general assembly for the sake of ecclesiastical honor, we ask only this of your piety: that, in accordance with God’s will, you bring into effect whatever seems best to you in this matter.

## OF MATTERS TO BE ANNOUNCED TO THE PEOPLE

Likewise, chapter 1. [Note: [Col. 0616D] “Hinc inde Additio Benedicti II” (“From this point, the Addition of Benedict II”); Book I, 54, p. 1635.] We have judged it necessary to admonish or announce this to the faithful: those who seek the faith of Christ and are of mature age must, before approaching baptism, be instructed both in the faith and in the sacrament of baptism. Likewise, those who wish to receive infants from the sacred font must be instructed, so that they may understand both the force of that sacrament and what they have promised on behalf of others, or for whom they have stood as sponsors [Note: [Col. 0615] i.e. “and what they have promised on behalf of others, or for whom they have stood as sponsors.”].

We declare, however, that those who have been deprived of canonical communion and subjected to public penance must be expressly removed from these offices, so that they may not receive others from the baptismal font [Note: [Col. 0615] i.e. “from the baptismal font”], nor act as sponsors for others in receiving the gift of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0616C], until they merit reconciliation through the satisfaction of penance. For those whom divine law and canonical authority exclude from the thresholds of churches and from military camps [Note: [Col. 0615] corrected from “and from canonical [assemblies].”], lest they become a downfall to the people, must all the more be excluded from these sacred offices until the period of penance has been completed, as has been said [Note: [Col. 0615] The words “from military camps … sacred offices” are absent in c.].

2. [Note: [Col. 0616D] Book I, 8.] Baptisms are not to be celebrated outside the times established by the canons, because the sacred canons absolutely prohibit this unless some danger intervenes—so much so that they even exclude from ecclesiastical orders those who are baptized at another time.

3. [Note: [Col. 0616D] Book I, 9.] We have also judged it necessary that the faithful be instructed so that they may understand the covenant they made with God in baptism. The words “the covenant made with God in baptism” are absent in p. This covenant is violated by many completely and by many in part. It is violated completely when someone, after receiving the grace of baptism, falls either into unbelief, heresy, or schism; but in part when someone falls either into pride, envy, or the other spiritual vices that spring from the root of pride [Note: [Col. 0617] The codex reads *extradice* (“out of the root”).].

4. [Note: [Col. 0617D] Book I, 10.] All the faithful must understand very clearly what it means to renounce the devil, his works, and his pomp. Therefore preachers in admonishing, hearers in learning, and all in carrying this out by their conduct must henceforth apply greater diligence, so that they may be able to avoid their danger.

To renounce the devil, then, is to reject him utterly, despise him, cast him away, contradict him, and separate each person from him—or whatever else can be expressed by this word in this sense. His works are those that are contrary to the works of the Savior. First is pride, of which he is the author and which made him a demon from an angel; it is also the beginning of every sin. The other vices that spring from the root of pride [Col. 0617B] belong here as well.

The pomp of the devil is also the pomp of the world: ambition, arrogance, empty glory, and every kind of excess in human affairs, from which conceit grows—something that is often ascribed to respectability—and other things of this kind that are known to proceed from the fountain of pride. These and similar things are what each believer rejected from himself at the time of baptism, dedicated himself to Christ, and made a covenant with God not to return utterly to the things he had renounced [Note: [Col. 0617] The manuscript reads *redirediret*]. Yet if the obligations of a human agreement are firmly preserved, the obligations of so great a covenant made with God must be observed inviolably with still greater firmness and fervor.

5. [Note: [Col. 0617D] Book I, 30.] We unanimously decreed that henceforth each bishop should apply greater diligence to maintaining schools and preparing and educating soldiers of Christ for the benefit of the Church [Note: [Col. 0617] “Maintaining schools” is written in a space erased in the manuscript.]. In this matter we wish to test each person’s diligence: when the provincial council of bishops is held, each rector must ensure that his students are present at that council, so that they may be known to the other churches and so that everyone may see the diligent care devoted to divine worship [Note: [Col. 0617] This phrase is absent in c.].

6. [Note: [Col. 0617D] Book I, 33.] Bishops are to confer the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands only while fasting, except in the case of the sick and those in danger of death. Just as baptism is fittingly celebrated by fasting pontiffs at two times, namely Easter and Pentecost, so also should the bestowal of the Holy Spirit be celebrated by fasting bishops.

7. [Note: [Col. 0618D] Book III, 4.] Priests, as has been done until now, are not to be sent indiscriminately to various places, whether by bishops, other prelates, or even laymen, lest, because of their absence, souls be endangered and the offices of the churches in which they have been appointed be neglected.

8. [Note: [Col. 0618A, 0618D] Book I, 35.] It seemed good to us that each bishop should know, both personally and through his ministers, the life, conduct, and moral correction of those who lose their rank, and should not neglect to subject them canonically to penance, in accordance with what is written in the first title of the Council of Caesarea:

> “If a priest takes a wife, he shall be deposed from his order; but if he fornicates or commits adultery, he must be expelled still further and reduced to penance.”

For some, having lost their rank, become sons of Belial to such a degree that they are bound neither by public laws, since that is not permitted, nor by canonical laws, because of the negligence of certain bishops.

9. [Note: [Col. 0617] This number has fallen out of the codex.] It also seemed good to us that this should be prohibited: no priest should presume to celebrate Mass alone. For neither the words of the Lord and Savior, by which he handed over to his disciples the mysteries of the celebration of his body and blood [Col. 0618B], nor the instructions of the Apostle Paul indicate this; nor, if the Acts of the Apostles are read closely [Note: [Col. 0617] The manuscript reads *eucleatim*], is it found in any way that it ought to be done.

Therefore, it seems to us that the solitary consecrator of the Lord’s body and blood ought rather to be summoned and questioned: To whom does he say, “The Lord be with you”? And to whom is the response, “And with your spirit,” addressed? Or for whom does he say, among other supplications to the Lord, “Remember, Lord, all those standing around,” when no one is standing around? Since this custom conflicts with apostolic and ecclesiastical authority and appears to inflict a certain dishonor upon so great a mystery, it seemed good to all collectively that such a practice be prohibited from now on.

10. [Col. 0618C] It has often been established in other councils, and now in our assemblies, that each church, if it has the means, should have its own priest [Note: [Col. 0617] Absent in c.], and that each priest should be content with one church only.

11. [Note: [Col. 0618D] Compare Book III, 5.] Among the other duties of our admonition, this seemed sufficiently necessary to us: the faithful people must be solemnly warned to honor the Lord’s Day, on which the Author of life rose from the dead. For if pagans celebrate days in memory and reverence of their gods, and Jews, in a carnal manner, observe the Sabbath carnally, how much more should the devotion of the Christian religion, in memory of the Lord’s resurrection, venerate and honor that day?

We have learned, through the observation of our own people, of many cases, and through the reports of certain persons, of many others: some who worked at rural labor on this day were struck dead by lightning, some were punished by the contraction of their limbs [Note: [Col. 0617] The manuscript reads *contratcitione*], and some were consumed by visible fire, suddenly reduced to ashes and dying under punishment [Col. 0619A]. Therefore it is necessary that priests first, and kings and princes and all the faithful, most devotedly show observance and reverence toward this day.

12. [Note: [Col. 0619D] Book I, 47; compare Book III, 6.] Although this has often been admonished, it seemed to us once again most necessary to impress it upon the people and announce it to them: celebrations of Mass must absolutely not take place in unsuitable locations, and each bishop must entirely remove such a reckless custom from his parish.

If from now on any priest, except when traveling, when the place is far from a basilica, and necessity compels the celebration at altars consecrated by a bishop lest God’s people remain without the celebration of Mass and reception of the Lord’s body and blood, should attempt to celebrate Mass in such unlawful places [Col. 0619B] after so many and such great prohibitions, it is right that he incur the peril of losing his rank. It is therefore better not to hear Mass than for it to be celebrated or heard where it is neither lawful nor appropriate.

13. [Note: [Col. 0619D] Book I, 40; compare Book III, 7.] Since we have now learned that what has often been prohibited in your councils—that widows are not to be veiled without the advice of the bishops—is being violated by some, we have altogether forbidden it from happening henceforth [Note: [Col. 0619] The manuscript reads *deiceps*]. If any priest thereafter obstinately transgresses this constitution [Note: [Col. 0619] The manuscript reads *constitutiones*], namely, if he presumes to veil any widow without consulting the bishop, he shall incur the peril of losing his rank.

14. [Note: [Col. 0619D] Book I, 41.] Likewise, we have prohibited priests from veiling young unmarried girls. In this matter we have discovered that many priests have hitherto sinned, partly through ignorance [Note: [Col. 0619] The manuscript reads *ignoratia*] and partly through presumption.

15. [Note: [Col. 0619D] Book I, 41.] We have also discovered another negligence: certain women incautiously put a veil upon themselves without the consent of priests. We have likewise prohibited this from happening again.

16. [Note: [Col. 0620D] Book I, 43.] We have also found in certain places an unusual practice, full of folly and contrary to ecclesiastical authority: some abbesses and certain religious women presume, contrary to what is lawful, to place the veil upon widows and unmarried girls [Note: [Col. 0619] The manuscript reads *inponerere*]. Consequently, some who have thus been veiled think that they can devote themselves more freely to their carnal desires and fulfill their wishes [Note: [Col. 0619] The manuscript reads *aliter* (“otherwise”)]. Therefore we decree that if, after this definition, an abbess or any religious woman should proceed to such audacity as to presume to veil either a widow or an unmarried girl, she shall be subjected to canonical judgment until satisfaction is made.

17. [Note: [Col. 0620D] Book I, 44.] Concerning noblewomen who, after losing their husbands, are suddenly veiled and delight in remaining in their own homes while claiming various necessities [Col. 0620A]—a matter that was discussed and defined long ago in other assemblies before your serenity—we decree that they be admonished and instructed by the bishops with greater and diligent care, so that they may attend to their salvation and not, by living indiscriminately, using their own harmful freedom, and wandering about in various places, incur danger to their souls. Let them always keep before their eyes the apostolic saying:

> “The widow who lives in luxury is dead while she lives.” [Note: [Col. 0619] The manuscript reads *diliciis*.]

18. [Note: [Col. 0620D] Book I, 45.] We have prohibited in every possible way the unlawful access of women to the altar. For we have learned from the report of certain persons that in some provinces, contrary to divine law and canonical institution, women thrust themselves forward to the holy altars, shamelessly touch the consecrated vessels, and administer priestly vestments to priests; and, still more indecent and foolish than these acts, they present the body and blood of the Lord to the people [Note: [Col. 0619] “of the Lord” is absent in c.] and perform other acts that are disgraceful even to name. We have prohibited these things from being presumed henceforth. That women ought not to enter the altar is found in the Council of Chalcedon and in the decrees of Pope Gelasius.

19. [Note: [Col. 0620D] Book I, 46.] We have also learned that certain canons and monks, setting aside the modesty of their religious profession, shamelessly and irreverently visit the monasteries of religious women, both monastic and canonical [Note: [Col. 0619] The codex reads “of monks and canonical women,” corrected to “of monastic and canonical women”], without consulting their bishop. They usually allege that they go there for no other reason than kinship, friendship, or some sort of conversation.

Because this conduct is suitable neither to the canonical nor to the monastic profession, we altogether forbid it, unless the cause is preaching or some unavoidable necessity has compelled it; and even then it must never be presumed without the permission of the bishop or of the person acting in his place. If a sermon is to be preached, it must be delivered in a suitable place before everyone.

If, however, it is necessary to speak with one of the religious women, this must take place nowhere except in an appointed place, namely in an audience chamber, in the presence of religious men and women. When priests are to celebrate Mass in monasteries of girls, they must enter with the ministers assigned to them; once the rites have been duly completed, they must not in any way turn aside to secret conversations with the religious women, but must immediately leave with their ministers.

Moreover, if religious women wish to confess their sins to priests, they must do so only in the church before the holy altar, with witnesses standing nearby. If illness prevents the confession from taking place in the church and it must be made in any house whatsoever, it must likewise take place only with witnesses standing nearby. For it does not at all seem fitting to us that a monk should leave his monastery and visit monasteries of religious women for the purpose of imposing a measure of penance on those confessing their sins.

20. [Note: [Col. 0621] X c.] [Note: [Col. 0621D] Book I, 53.] Since we have learned that certain clerics and laymen, forgetting the Lord’s commandment, “You shall not lend your money at interest, and you shall not demand an excess of produce” [Note: [Col. 0621] The manuscript reads *exigies*.], have become inflamed with the stain of most shameful profit through various devices of usury, and, by their own invention and greed, have devised countless kinds of usury by which they afflict, oppress, and drain the poor, so that many, exhausted by hunger [Col. 0621B], perish, while many others, abandoning their own lands, seek those of others [Note: [Col. 0621] The manuscript reads *ternas*], wherever we learned that these things were being done, we absolutely prohibited them from happening again, with a solemn protestation.

We heeded what the Lord says through the legislators in the Book of Exodus:

> “If you lend money to my poor people who dwell with you, you shall not press them as an exactor, nor oppress them with usury.”

Also in the Book of Leviticus:

> “If your brother has become poor and weak in hand, and you receive him as a resident alien and sojourner, and he lives with you, do not take interest from him, nor receive more than you gave. Fear your God, so that your brother may live with you.”

And in the Book of Deuteronomy:

> “If one of your brothers who dwell within the gates of your city, in the land that the Lord your God will give you, should come into poverty, you shall not harden your heart or close your hand; instead, you shall open it to the poor and lend him whatever you perceive that he needs.”

Likewise in the same book:

> “Beware lest an impious thought secretly steal upon you and you say in your heart: ‘The seventh year of remission is approaching,’ and you turn your eyes away from your poor brother, unwilling to lend him what he asks, lest he cry out against you to the Lord and it become sin for you. But you shall give to him, and in relieving his needs you shall not act deceitfully, so that the Lord your God may bless you at all times and in everything to which you set your hand.”

The prophet Amos says:

> “Hear this, you who crush the poor and cause the needy to fail, saying: ‘When will the harvest pass, so that we may sell our goods, and the Sabbath, so that we may open the grain, diminish the measure, increase the shekel, and falsify the scales, so that we may buy the needy for silver and the poor for a pair of sandals, and sell the refuse of the grain?’” [Note: [Col. 0621] The manuscript reads *quis qualias*, corrected to *quis siliquas*.]

Jerome, in his exposition of the prophet Ezekiel, says:

> “Some think that usury exists only in money, whereas Scripture, anticipating this, removes the excess from every thing, so that you do not receive more than you gave. It is customary in the fields to demand usury in grain, millet, wine, oil, and other kinds of produce, or, as divine speech calls it, ‘excess.’ For example, in winter we give ten measures and at harvest receive fifteen—that is, half as much again. The person who thinks himself most just will take an additional quarter of the portion.
>
> “They are also accustomed to argue and say: ‘I gave one measure, which produced ten measures when sown. Is it not just that I receive an additional half-measure from what is mine, since through my generosity he has nine and a half measures of what is mine?’ ‘Do not be deceived,’ says the Apostle; ‘God is not mocked.’ Let the merciful lender answer us briefly: Did he give to someone who had, or to someone who did not have? He ought not to have given to someone who had, but he gave as though to someone who did not have; therefore why does he demand more, as though from someone who had?
>
> “Others customarily receive gifts of various kinds in return for money lent, and do not understand that whatever they receive beyond what they gave is called usury and excess.”

As to the inequality of measures, unjust measures, and sextarii, which the Lord’s law prohibits people from possessing, we do not see clearly enough how the matter can be brought to a definite correction, because in the various provinces they are held differently by almost everyone [Note: [Col. 0621] *poena* in c.]. Nevertheless, we absolutely desire and admonish this much: at least no one should possess or permit to be possessed in his domain double measures, for we have learned that on this pretext many poor people are afflicted in numerous places [Note: [Col. 0621] Book III, 2, p. 1658. Here chapter 21 of Addition II begins.].

There are indeed perpetrators of various evils whom divine law condemns and rejects; because of their different crimes and wickedness, the people are scourged by famine and pestilence, the condition of the churches is weakened, and the kingdom is endangered. Against them, while emphasizing their wickedness—even though it is sufficiently condemned in the sacred writings—we have judged it necessary that precautions once again be taken through our admonition and exhortation.

Such are the perpetrators of various forms of pollution, which some commit with males and with animals in many different ways.
