By provoking the incomparable sweetness of the most merciful Creator to bitterness, they sin all the more grievously because they sin against nature. For this crime five cities were consumed by heavenly fire and swallowed by the opening of the underworld; and forty thousand and more of the tribe of Benjamin were pierced by the fraternal sword. These judgments and evident acts of vengeance declare how detestable and abhorrent this vice is in the sight of the divine majesty.

There are also other most destructive evils that unquestionably remain from the rites of the pagans: magicians, diviners, sorcerers, poisoners, fortune-tellers, enchanters, and interpreters of dreams. Divine law orders that such people be punished without appeal. Of them it says in the Law:

> “The soul that turns to magicians and diviners and commits fornication with them, I will set my face against it and destroy it from the midst of its people. Sanctify yourselves and be holy [*dstote*, sic], for I am holy, the Lord your God. Keep my precepts and do them, for I am the Lord who sanctify you.”

And elsewhere:

> “You shall not permit magicians, diviners, or sorcerers of the land to live.”

For there is no doubt, as is known to many, that through certain tricks and demonic illusions some corrupt the minds of certain people with love potions, foods, or amulets, so that, turned to madness, they are judged by many while they do not perceive their own insults [Note: [Col. 0623] Text omitted.]. They are said to be able by their magic to disturb the air, send hail, predict the future, take away fruits and milk and give them to others, and perform countless other things of this kind. When men or women are found to be such, they must be corrected with all the greater severity by the discipline and power of the ruler, in proportion as they more openly and recklessly dare to serve the devil by their wicked audacity.

Concerning these matters it is also written in title 23 of the Council of Ancyra:

> “Those who seek divinations and follow them in the manner of the pagans, or introduce such people into their houses to inquire into something by magical art or for the purpose of purification, shall lie under the five-year rule, according to the prescribed degrees of penance.” [Note: [Col. 0623] The manuscript reads *subsequntur*.]

These matters must be admonished in every place, and especially in those places where many confidently believe that they can practice them lawfully and with impunity; there they must be admonished more earnestly and carefully and corrected more severely.

There are also other detestable vices which are treated almost as though they were naturally customary, so that those who commit them do not recognize the gravity of their crimes [Note: [Col. 0623D] Here chapter 22 of Addition II begins; [Col. 0623] the manuscript reads *usum*]. These include the vices that the Apostle openly lists: drunkenness, feasting, quarrels, anger, fights, dissensions, slander, envy, and hostility. According to the same Apostle, these exclude people from the kingdom of God, as he says:

> “Those who do such things shall not attain the kingdom of God.”

Some commit these acts so shamelessly and confidently that it can rightly be said of them:

> “They rejoice when they have done evil and exult in wicked things.”

Therefore all Christians must understand these matters carefully and avoid them most diligently, lest, by committing them, they lose the other good things they do and, because of these acts, make themselves strangers to the kingdom of God.

Likewise, they must understand and observe what concerns idle speech, for which, according to the Lord’s word, we shall all render an account on the day of judgment; concerning vulgarity, foolish talk, and curses, since according to the Apostle those who curse shall not possess the kingdom of God; concerning lying; concerning dangerous, harmful, and continual oath-taking; and concerning obscene and shameful songs. All Christians must understand and observe these things, so that they may guard themselves from them with the greatest care and, by pursuing them through negligence, suffer harm to their souls.

We therefore wish first, with divine grace assisting us, to renounce these things ourselves and provide a pattern and example to others. We judge it necessary to make them known humbly and announce them faithfully to your faithful people. We also wish to instruct all your parishes by admonition, lest, God forbid, through their ignorance and our negligence they become subject to such deadly dangers [Note: [Col. 0623] *sic*].

We have also collected in the work of our assembly several other chapters concerning the observance and salvation of the faithful laity [Note: [Col. 0623D] Here chapter 23 of Addition II begins]. Because of their great length, we merely mention them here: they ought to know that marriage was established by God and that it is to be sought not as a cause of lust but rather as a cause of children; that virginity, as our teachers teach, is to be preserved until marriage; and that those who have wives must have neither a concubine nor a mistress.

They should know how to love their wives chastely and, as though they were the weaker sex, give them their due honor. Sexual intercourse with wives should take place for the sake of offspring, not pleasure; men should abstain from intercourse with pregnant wives; and, except on account of fornication, as the Lord says, a wife is not to be dismissed but rather endured. Those who, after dismissing their wives on account of fornication, marry others are judged adulterers by the Lord’s sentence.

Likewise, Christians must avoid incest, and the places dedicated to God must be visited by the faithful more frequently and devoutly in order to pray to God and render him propitious. In basilicas dedicated to God, they must not devote themselves to idle, shameful, and obscene stories and conversations, nor conduct secular business or public hearings; those who do these things in the churches of God heap greater sins upon themselves.

They must judge with just judgment and beware of accepting gifts; avoid false testimony and slander; and observe the other matters that it would be lengthy to enumerate. There are also many other grave offenses that urgently require correction, which we have not thought it necessary to insert here because we know that they are sufficiently and clearly contained in your chapters, which you customarily correct through your authority and the advice of the faithful by means of your diligent representatives.

## OF THE ROYAL PERSON

Likewise, another matter. We, your faithful and most devoted servants and petitioners, according to the smallness of our understanding and as the brevity of time permitted, have drawn from the many matters dealt with in our assemblies and have concisely and orderly brought them together and set them down. In accordance with your holy ordinance, we have addressed those matters that we recognized as pertaining to the correction and amendment of ourselves, of the priests, and of our subjects, as well as those that we judged necessary to announce and recommend to the people; and we have included only what we judged necessary to request of your piety [Note: [Col. 0624D] Book III, from a letter, p. 1656, middle].

Although, in an inverted order, we chose first to satisfy your most ardent desire concerning the matters set forth above [Note: [Col. 0625] The manuscript reads *promissa*], we have by no means consigned to oblivion what ought first to have been placed at the head and what we recognized as pertaining especially to your person and office [Note: [Col. 0625] Absent in c.]. Rather, looking to your salvation, we have faithfully collected several necessary chapters and resolved to present them to you familiarly as an admonition, so that, by examining, reading, and hearing them openly and distinctly, your diligence may learn what we have faithfully undertaken, according to the measure of our abilities, in our aforementioned assemblies, and concerning which matters and for whose sake we have acted.

1. To explain why a king is so called, Isidore writes in the *Book of Sentences*: “For he is called a king from acting rightly; for if he rules piously, justly, and mercifully, he is rightly called a king. If he lacks these qualities, he is not a king but a tyrant.” [Col. 0625D: Compare II, 1, p. 1636.] The ancients, however, as the same Isidore writes in the *Book of Etymologies*, called all kings tyrants. But later, when those who ruled piously and mercifully acquired the name “king,” the name “tyrant” was applied to those who ruled impiously, unjustly, and cruelly. [Col. 0625D: That is, *ad*, “to.”] Hence blessed Gregory also says in the *Moralia*: “We have learned that holy men are therefore called kings in the sacred writings, because they act rightly, rule their own thoughts well, and order the impulses resisting them by rational discernment.” Those, therefore, are rightly called kings who know how to bring both themselves and their subjects to peace by governing well.

[Col. 0626D: That is, *ad*, “to.”] But to explain also what an emperor is constituted to be [Col. 0625: manuscript c reads *constit(us)*], Fulgentius writes in the *Book on the Truth of Predestination and Grace*: “Even the most clement emperor is not a vessel of mercy prepared for glory merely because he has received the summit of earthly rule, but only if, at the height of imperial power, he lives by right faith and, endowed with true humility of heart, submits the summit of royal dignity to holy religion; if he takes greater delight in serving God in fear than in ruling the people in fear; if gentleness tempers anger in him, goodness adorns his authority; if he shows himself more worthy of love than of fear to everyone; if he provides beneficially for his subjects; if he upholds justice in such a way that he does not abandon mercy; if, above all, he remembers that he is a son of holy mother Church, so that he makes his rule beneficial to her peace and tranquillity throughout the whole world. For the Christian empire is governed more truly when provision is made for the ecclesiastical order throughout the earth than when war is waged anywhere in the world for temporal security.” [Col. 0625D: The manuscript reads *purgatur*, “is purged,” instead of *pugnatur*, “war is waged.”]

Hence Isidore also writes: “Secular rulers sometimes hold within the Church the heights of the authority they have acquired, so that through that same authority they may fortify ecclesiastical discipline. Otherwise, the powers within the Church would not be necessary, except so that what a priest cannot accomplish through the teaching of his speech, authority may command through the terror of discipline.” [Col. 0625: The words between “the heights of the authority” and “within the Church” are absent in one manuscript.]

Solomon says in Proverbs: “Mercy and truth preserve the king, and his throne is strengthened by clemency.” [Col. 0625: One manuscript reads *regalem*, “royal,” instead of *regale*, “of the king.”]

[Col. 0626D: Compare II, 2, p. 1639.] The special ministry of a king is to govern and rule the people of God with equity and justice, and to strive that they may have peace and concord. He himself must first be the defender of churches, of the servants of God, of widows, orphans, and all other poor people, as well as of everyone in need. His power to inspire fear and his concern in such matters must, insofar as possible, be directed first to ensuring that no injustice is committed; then, if one occurs, to permitting it in no way to persist, and to leaving no one the hope of concealing wrongdoing or the audacity to act badly. Let everyone know that if anything evil they have committed comes to his attention, it will by no means remain uncorrected or unpunished; rather, the correction will be proportionate to the nature of the deed.

Therefore, he who is the judge of judges ought to cause the case of the poor to be brought before him and inquire into it carefully, lest perhaps some of those whom he has appointed and who ought to act in his place among the people allow the poor to suffer oppression unjustly or through negligence. [Col. 0625: One manuscript reads *incredi* instead of *ingredi*, “to enter.”]

Everyone, whatever his rank, ought to know that if he will have to give God an account for an idle word, all the more will he have to give an account for the ministry divinely entrusted to him. Hence blessed Job says:

“When I sat as a king with the army surrounding me, I was nevertheless a comforter of the afflicted. The ear that heard me blessed me, and the eye that saw me bore witness to me, because I had delivered the poor man who cried out and the orphan who had no helper. The blessing of the poor came upon me, and I comforted the widow’s heart. I put on justice and clothed myself; my judgment was like a garment and a diadem. I was eyes to the blind and feet to the lame. I was a father to the poor, and I investigated most carefully the case that I did not know. I crushed the jaws of the wicked and snatched the prey from his teeth.”

“A king who sits on the throne of judgment scatters all evil by his nod.”

Again, the same book says: “Love justice, you who judge the earth; think of the Lord in goodness, and seek him in simplicity of heart.”

And again there: “Listen, therefore, kings, and understand; learn, judges of the ends of the earth. Give ear, you who hold the multitudes and take pride in the crowds of nations, because power has been given to you by the Lord and strength by the Most High. Because you have not kept the law of justice and have not walked according to the will of God, he will appear to you terribly and suddenly, for the strictest judgment will be exercised against those who rule. To the lowly mercy is granted, but the powerful will suffer powerful torments. For the Lord will not exempt anyone on account of his person, nor will he respect anyone’s greatness. For he himself made both the small and the great, and he cares equally for all.”

There are also countless other testimonies of the holy Scriptures appropriate to the name and office of a king. Your holy devotion has spared us great labor in collecting them, because divine grace has so filled your mind with the prerogatives of many virtues and adorned your dignity that it is unnecessary for the priests of the Lord to burden your mind with more abundant examples or any exaggeration. [Col. 0627: One manuscript reads *s. in t.*, apparently “such in the text,” instead of the printed reading.]

Therefore we give fullest and manifold thanks to almighty God, who by his gracious goodness has so enriched you with pious religion, holy devotion, kindly humility, love of justice, works of mercy, and perfection in the other holy virtues that you are deservedly to be loved and imitated by all.

Yet if these qualities had not been bestowed upon you from heaven, we ought, even at the risk of our temporal safety, because of the authority of our ministry, to admonish you to undertake them—indeed, by admonishing you, to demand them from you in every possible way. You, on the other hand, most devotedly strive to offer us, for the love and honor of God, pious and timely assistance.

Accordingly, with the most humble prayers we especially urge your piety not to shrink from completing without ceasing, with God’s help, the good work you have begun, and not to fail in fulfilling works of justice, piety, and mercy in any way. For the reward of eternal life is given not to those who begin but to those who persevere, and, in the words of the Truth, “the one who perseveres to the end will be saved.”

[Col. 0627C] 2. [Col. 0627D: III, 22, p. 1665.] Again, by way of admonition, we humbly urge Your Greatness henceforth to apply great zeal and the most diligent care when appointing good pastors and rulers in the churches of God. For if this is done otherwise, the ecclesiastical order will not retain its dignity, the Christian religion will suffer loss and damage by being weakened in many ways, and—something we do not wish—danger will arise for your soul.

3. [Col. 0627D: III, 23.] Likewise we ask that, when appointing abbesses, you beware of endangering yourself, as you have often been admonished and as has been repeatedly made clear by divine authority.

4. [Col. 0627D: III, 23.] We also beseech you [Col. 0627: manuscript c reads *obseruamus*, “we observe”] to exercise the most diligent foresight in choosing your assistants and the servants of the state who, acting in your place, must rule, govern, and judge the people of God. Always attend to what is said to Moses in the Book of Exodus:

“Provide from the whole people,” he says, “and choose powerful men who fear God, in whom there is truth and who hate avarice; appoint them as tribunes, centurions, and commanders of fifty, to judge the people at all times. Whatever is greater, let them refer to you, while they judge only the lesser matters; thus the burden, divided among others, will be lighter for you. If you do this, you will fulfill the command of the Lord, and you will be able to bear his precepts.”

Hence also in the Book of Deuteronomy: “Judges and magistrates,” he says, “you shall appoint in all your gates which the Lord your God gives you, throughout your tribes, so that they may judge the people with just judgment and not incline to either side.” [Col. 0627: Manuscript variants include *tribuas* and *tribuus* for *tribus*, “tribes.”]

Again there: “And I said to you at that time: I cannot bear you alone, because the Lord your God has multiplied you, and today you are as numerous as the stars of heaven. May the Lord, the God of our fathers, add many thousands to this number and fulfill for you what he has spoken. I am not able alone to bear your affairs, your burdens, and your disputes. Give me from among yourselves wise and knowledgeable men whose conduct is approved in your tribes.”

But in the Book of Chronicles it is written:

“King Jehoshaphat appointed judges in the land, throughout all the fortified cities of Judah, in each locality, and he instructed the judges: ‘Consider what you are doing, for you are not exercising human judgment but the Lord’s, and whatever judgment you pronounce will rebound upon you. Let the fear of the Lord be with you, and perform everything diligently. For with the Lord your God there is no iniquity, no partiality, and no desire for gifts.’”

[Col. 0628D: III, 24.] We also ask your piety, for the sake of divine mercy, your salvation, the welfare of the whole people, and the honor and stability of the kingdom, to exercise the most diligent vigilance, so that your counselors, the ministers of your dignity, and the guardians of your soul and body—those who ought to be an ornament and example of goodness to others within the kingdom and a seasoning of good reputation among foreign nations—may have love, peace, and concord with one another, setting aside every pretense and cunning. Thus, in accordance with God’s will, your honor, and the advancement of the whole kingdom, they may strive together and exist in concord as your true helpers in all things.

For then they and the whole kingdom will be able to be truly and beneficially your counselors and helpers, if they are united in mind and possess mutual affection. It is fitting, moreover, that your sacred household appear worthy of respect and serve as an example for all, and that the reputation of its good name spread abundantly both among the subjects of your empire and among foreign nations. Since, therefore, all dissensions and disagreements must be resolved by imperial authority and every form of malice suppressed, it is necessary that the conduct which it decides to correct in others not be found in itself.

5. [Col. 0628D: III, 25.] We also humbly and earnestly admonish you to educate your children, whom divine goodness may grant you, continually and diligently in the fear of God, as you do. Impress upon them by attentive paternal admonition that they should remain in mutual love, fraternal affection, and the harmony of unity. With prudent and diligent watchfulness, take care that they do not offend their Creator through unlawful acts.

Attend to blessed Job, whose concern for educating children blessed Gregory describes in the *Moralia*: “He was such in the education of his children that he not only made them outwardly perfect in deed and speech, but also cleansed their hearts by the offering of sacrifice.”

Attend also to David instructing his son Solomon, concerning whom it is written in the First Book of Kings: “I am going,” he says, “by the way of all the earth. Take courage and be a man, and observe that you keep the commandments of the Lord your God, that you walk in his ways and keep his ceremonies, judgments, precepts, and testimonies, as it is written in the law of Moses and in the Book of Chronicles. But you, Solomon, my son, know the God of your father and serve him with a perfect heart and a willing mind.”

Attend also to Tobit, of whom it is written that, when he had become a man, he took Anna, a woman of his own tribe, as his wife, and begot a son by her, giving him his own name. From infancy he taught him to fear God and to abstain from every sin.

Again, addressing the same son, he says: “Have God in mind all the days of your life, and beware lest you ever consent to sin or neglect the precepts of our God. From your possessions give alms, and do not turn your face away from any poor person. For thus it will happen that the face of the Lord will not be turned away from you. Be merciful as far as you can, and so forth.”

A little later: “Beware, my son, of all fornication, and apart from your wife never permit yourself to know the crime. Never allow pride to rule in your mind or in your heart. For in it every destruction had its beginning.”

And soon afterward: “Always seek counsel from a wise person. Bless God at all times, and ask him to direct your ways, and let all your counsels remain in him.”

Again the same book says: “Listen, therefore, my sons, to your father. Serve the Lord in goodness, seek to do what is pleasing to him, and command your children to practice justice and almsgiving, to remember God, and to bless him at all times, in truth and with all their strength.”

[Col. 0629D] 6. [Col. 0629D: III, 25.] After setting forth all this, we make known to you that, concerning the matters which you entrusted to us for discussion in your capitularies—namely, what is held by the princes and the rest of the people either as divine authority teaches or otherwise, and what has been abandoned in part or altogether so that it is not observed [Col. 0629: manuscript c reads *quia* (“because”) for the first *quid* (“what”) and omits the second *quid*]—we confess that in the chapters set forth above, as well as in those which were written this year and sent throughout your empire by your envoys for the suppression of vices, many matters have been demonstrated that have hitherto been neglected by the pastors of the churches, by the princes, and by the rest of the people. We know that in these matters they have acted and are acting otherwise than divine authority prescribes. [Col. 0629: The words from “as well as” through “sent” are absent in one manuscript.] But if, through God’s working and your good zeal, this priestly admonition of ours obtains effect from now on, we believe that many things which many people have abandoned and failed to observe, contrary to the teaching of divine authority, will be corrected.

For the same capitularies also contain an inquiry into what caused priests and princes to stray from the right path. Apart from the chapters mentioned above, in which, as we have said, many things were being neglected, we have recognized that one particular obstacle has grown old through long usage: namely, that the ruling power, when various occasions arose, advanced into ecclesiastical cases in a way contrary to divine authority; while priests, partly through negligence, partly through ignorance, and partly through greed, occupied themselves in secular affairs and concerns beyond what they ought. There is no doubt that, for this reason, matters have been conducted differently on both sides from what divine authority teaches.

But since, by God’s mercy, many things have been corrected by your predecessors, your father, and yourself, we rejoice. If the matters we are admonishing you about have a favorable outcome, we believe that, with God’s cooperation, your intention and our devotion can bring this situation to a state of perfection. [Col. 0629: manuscript c has the uncertain reading *st. uestraque d.*; it reads *peruincere* (“to prevail”) for *pervenire* (“to reach”).]

Nevertheless, we know that the condition of this kingdom has been held, grown, and expanded under such circumstances, and that this matter was not completely corrected by our prudent and holy predecessors, whether bishops or princes, for reasons that may be stated in their proper place. The burden of such great deliberation exceeded our small strength, since we had neither the leisure nor sufficient time nor the full number of our fellow priests that the need itself required. Therefore, if God so wills, we have deferred treating and considering these matters until a more suitable and appropriate time, with life permitting.

For the perfection of so great a deliberation requires the agreement and assistance of the princes, the number, devotion, and zeal of the priests, the obedience and concord of the people, a suitable place, and an adequate span of time.

[Col. 0630D] 7. [Col. 0630D: II, 27.] Concerning the episcopal liberty which, with God’s favor and with your assistance and support, we desire to obtain in order to carry out the service of God, we have reserved for the proper time the matters that must be said to you and discussed with you. We desire this liberty so that we may be able both to save ourselves and to benefit usefully the people subject to us, and to pray more freely for you and for the stability of your empire. We also desire that the due assistance owed to your service and to the support of the kingdom not be diminished, but, if possible, rather increased.

# THE CAPITULARIES OF WORMS

[Col. 0631]

The threefold Capitularies of Worms were promulgated in the presence of Emperor Lothar and held a place among the Italian laws. Therefore, in editing them, we have taken into account not only the twelve manuscripts listed above but also those of Blankenburg, Gotha, Modena, Paris no. 4613, Milan, Florence, London, Vienna, Verona, and Este cited by Muratori. In none of them is a capitulary addressed to the envoys found.

## THESE ARE THE CHAPTERS WHICH SOME OF THE ENVOYS BROUGHT TO OUR ATTENTION IN THE TENTH YEAR OF OUR EMPIRE

[Col. 0631: Modena reads “some of **our** envoys.” From manuscripts 1, 1b, 1c, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, Gotha, and Modena.] [The wording is the same in all the manuscripts; Sirmond gives this heading instead: “These are the chapters which, in response to questions from certain envoys, were considered, written, or arranged, whether concerning ecclesiastical matters or other matters relating to the correction of the greater men and to public honor; they were arranged under three divisions.”]

## GENERAL CHAPTERS

[Col. 0631A]

1. Concerning those who establish priests in their churches or expel them without the consent of the bishop, and who, after being admonished by the bishop or by any royal envoy, refuse to obey: they are to be compelled to give security for our ban and ordered, through sureties, to come to our palace. Then we shall decide whether it pleases us that they pay that ban or undergo another *harmiscara* (a punitive service or penalty). [Manuscript 1 reads *iubeant*; Blankenburg and Gotha read plural forms, *persoluant … sustineant*. Blankenburg has *armiscaram*; Verona, Vienna, and Este have *ariscadam*.]

2. Concerning churches that have been divided among co-heirs: it has been decided that, if those co-heirs wish to retain and honor them according to the bishop’s provision and admonition, they are to do so. But if they oppose this, it is to remain within the bishop’s power either to permit them to remain in that condition or to remove the relics from them. Whenever churches belonging to our benefice are found divided in this way, the matter is to be recorded and reported to us. [Manuscript 3, 5, 7–10 read *considerandum*, “it is to be considered,” instead of *consideratum*, “it has been decided.” Manuscript 1 reads *uoluerunt*, “they wished,” instead of *uoluerint*, “they wish.” Manuscripts 3, 5, and the others read *describantur*, “that they be recorded,” instead of *describatur*, “that it be recorded”; Gotha reads *ut ubi scribetur*, “so that where it is written.”]

3. Concerning destroyed churches: let the bishops and envoys investigate whether they were destroyed through negligence or inability. Where negligence is found, those who ought to have restored them are to be compelled by episcopal authority to repair them. [Manuscripts 2, 3, and 5–10 add *hi qui eas*, “those who ought to restore them.”] If the destruction occurred through inability—whether because there are more churches than necessary or because they are larger than can be restored from the resources belonging to them—the bishop is to devise a means by which they can suitably be repaired and maintained.

4. [This chapter is absent from Gotha and Modena. Paris manuscript 4613 omits this chapter and all the following chapters of this capitulary.]

Concerning a single hide given to a church, from which certain men exact service for themselves contrary to the statutes: whoever is accused on this account, the count or the envoys are to compel him to restore what has been taken from it to the priests, together with the legally due payment. [One manuscript reads *siue*, “whether,” instead of *sibi*, “for themselves.” Manuscript 10 reads *contra canonum statuta*, “contrary to the statutes of the canons.” Blankenburg reads *presbytero*, “to the priest,” instead of *presbyteris*, “to the priests.” Compare above, chapter 10 of the capitulary of 817.]

5. [This chapter is absent from manuscript 2, Gotha, and Modena.]

Concerning those who for many years have neglected to pay the ninths and tithes, either in part or altogether: we wish them to be compelled by our envoys to pay, according to the earlier capitulary, the ninth and tithe of one year together with the legally due payment, and in addition our ban. They are also to be warned that whoever repeats this negligence is to know that he will lose the benefice from which this ninth and tithe ought to have been paid. [Manuscript 10 reads: “from which he ought to have paid this ninth and tithe,” and so forth.]

Thus it is contained in the first book of the capitulary of our father of blessed memory, chapter 157: “Let those who hold benefices of churches give from them the ninth and tithe to the church whose property they are. Those who hold such a benefice and work it in partnership are also to give tithes from their share to their own priest.” [Manuscripts 3 and 5–10 read *laborent*, “let them work,” instead of *laborant*, “they work”; manuscripts 3 and Blankenburg omit *et*, “and”; manuscripts 9 and 10 omit *ut*, “also”; manuscript 1 omits *de eorum portione proprio*, “from their own share.”]

Likewise, in the second book of our capitulary, chapter 21, concerning the same matter: “Concerning ninths and tithes, about which both our father and we have frequently given admonitions in various assemblies and have established through our capitularies how they are to be observed, we wish and command that from all produce cultivated jointly, and from wine and hay, everyone faithfully and fully pay the ninth and tithe. Concerning livestock, the customary arrangement hitherto observed by all in lieu of the tithe is to be maintained. If, however, any bishop wishes to accept money for this, it is to remain within his power, according to the agreement between him and the person who owes the payment.” [One manuscript adds *de annona*, “from grain”; Blankenburg reads *uel*, “or,” instead of *et*, “and.”]

6. [This chapter is absent from Gotha and Modena.]

Whoever removes a tithe from the church to which it ought by right to be given and presumptuously gives it to another church, whether because of gifts, friendship, or any other reason, is to be constrained by our count or envoy to restore the amount of that tithe together with the legally due payment. [Verona, Vienna, and Este add: “After three admonitions by priests, let him be excommunicated, and let him be brought by the count or envoy.” One note explains the legally due payment as six solidi.]

7. Concerning tithes which the people refuse to give unless they are redeemed from them in some manner: the bishops must prohibit this from happening. If anyone is found to be contemptuous and refuses to obey either the bishop or the count, then, if he is our man, he is to be compelled to come into our presence. The others are to be constrained so that, unwillingly, they restore to the church what they voluntarily neglected to give. [Blankenburg reads *quas*, “which,” instead of *quae*, “which”; manuscripts 3 and 5–10 read *quod*, “what,” instead of *qui*; Gotha has *quae*. Manuscript 10 adds “so that they restore them unwillingly.”]

8. [This chapter is absent from Gotha, Modena, Blankenburg, Florence, London, Vienna, and Este.]

Whoever has neglected to carry out repairs on the property of churches which he holds as a benefice is to be dealt with according to the earlier capitulary, in which provisions were made concerning labor, ninths, and tithes, namely, in the fourth book, chapter 38:

“Concerning the labor and restoration of churches: it has been decided that payment is to be made from the fruits of the earth and the nourishment of animals. Concerning the labor or restoration of churches, the count and the bishop or abbot, together with our envoy whom they themselves choose for this purpose, are to make an assessment, so that each of them receives for labor and restoration only as much as he is known to possess from the property of the churches. Likewise, our vassals are either jointly to undertake as much work as they hold ecclesiastical property, or each individually according to the amount he holds. Or, if they agree among themselves to give money in place of performing the work, they are to pay in money according to the assessed value of the work, so that with this payment the rector of the church may hire workers for the aforesaid restoration and purchase materials. Whoever has neglected to give ninths and tithes must first restore them together with the legally due payment and in addition pay our ban, so that, having been punished in this way, he may take care not to lose his benefice by repeating the offense too often.” [Manuscripts 1 and 1c read *considerandum*, “it is to be considered,” instead of *consideratum*, “it has been decided.” Manuscript 1 reads *accipiant*, “let them receive,” instead of *accipiat*, “let him receive.” Manuscript 1 reads *operis*, “of the work,” instead of *operarios*, “workers”; manuscripts 1 and 1c, and Blankenburg, read *materias*, “materials,” instead of *materiam*, “material.” Manuscript 1 reads *itarando*, an orthographic variant of *iterando*, “by repeating.”]

9. [This chapter is absent from Gotha, Modena, Blankenburg, Florence, London, Vienna, Este, and Rivipull.]

Concerning those who have neglected to cultivate the demesne lands for the purpose of avoiding payment of the ninth and tithe from them, and who therefore take other people’s lands to cultivate: we wish them to pay the ninth and tithe for three years, together with the legally due payment. [Manuscript 1 omits “and tithe”; manuscripts 2, 4, 8, and 10 read “the ninth with the tithe.” Blankenburg changes the forms to the plural: “those who have neglected … let them pay … take … let them pay.”] If anyone on this account proves contemptuous of the count or of our envoys, he is to be compelled through sureties to come to the palace.

10. [This chapter is absent from manuscripts 1, 1c, and 7, and from Blankenburg, Gotha, Modena, Florence, London, Vienna, and Este. In manuscripts 2, 3, 5, 6, 8, 9, and 10 it is counted as chapter eight; in manuscript 1c it occupies this place.]

Concerning the property of churches which has been possessed by them for a period of thirty years without any challenge: no testimony is to be accepted concerning it; rather, it is to be held in the same way as property belonging to the royal fisc is customarily held. [Manuscripts 3 and 6 read *ita*, “thus,” in place of *sunt*, “have been.”]

## OTHER CHAPTERS

1. [This chapter is absent from Blankenburg, Gotha, Modena, Florence, London, Vienna, Este, and Paris.]

Concerning destroyed benefices, let the provision contained in the earlier capitulary be observed, namely, in the fourth book, chapter 36: “Whoever has left his benefice deserted through his own fault, and has not repaired it within a year after the count or our envoy has made this known to him, is to lose that benefice.” [Manuscripts 1 and 1c read the words in a different order: “whoever has had his benefice deserted through his own fault.”]

2. Our envoys are to expel wicked *scabini* wherever they find them and, with the consent of the entire people, elect good men in their place. Once they have been elected, the envoys are to make them swear that they will not knowingly judge unjustly. [Manuscripts 2, 3, 8, and 9 read *scabin[i]os*, an orthographic variant; Blankenburg reads *inuenerint*, “they may have found,” and manuscript B reads *inueniunt*, “they find,” instead of *inveniant*, “let them find.” Manuscripts 1 and 1c read *scientes*, “knowingly,” instead of *scienter*.]

3. [This chapter is absent from Paris manuscript 4613.]

In every county, our envoys are to choose for conducting investigations and stating the truth of the matter those who can be found to be the best and most truthful, and they are to be assistants to the counts in carrying out justice. [Manuscript 1 omits “and”; it also omits “to” before “assistants.”]

[Col. 0634B] 4. We wish that whenever any *scabinus* is caught having judged unjustly because of gifts, friendship, or enmity, our envoy is to make him come under sureties into our presence. [Manuscripts 1c and 10, Gotha, and Paris 4613 omit “or enmity”; manuscript 3 omits “let him”; manuscripts 3, 5, 7, and Blankenburg read “let him come” instead of “make him come.”] From now on, all *scabini* are to be warned that no one may presume to sell even a just judgment.

5. [This chapter is absent from Gotha and Modena.]

Wherever exchanges have been lawfully, reasonably, and beneficially made for the churches of God, whether in our time or in the time of our father, let them stand. Wherever, however, they have been made uselessly, inconveniently, and unreasonably, let them be dissolved, and let each person receive back what he gave. Wherever a dead hand intervenes, or any other cause is found that appears reasonable, let the matter be carefully recorded and brought to our attention.

[Blankenburg, Florence, London, Vienna, and Este read: “Wherever unlawful, unreasonable, and useless exchanges have been made for the churches of God, let them be dissolved” (the intervening text is absent). Paris 4613 has a materially corrupt alternative: *ienitore nostro legitime et rationabiliter adque utiliter clesiis Dei facte sunt perteneat. Ubicumque vero inutiliter et incommodes adque rationabiles facte sunt*—apparently, “made in the time of our father, lawfully, reasonably, and beneficially for the churches of God, let them remain; wherever they were made uselessly, inconveniently, and [corrupt: ‘reasonably’]”—followed by *nostram iustitia*. The Royal, Metz, and Paris manuscripts read *rebellis* (“refractory”) in place of *rationabilis* (“reasonable”); Baluzianus, and manuscripts 5 and 9, have the same reading.]

6. [This chapter is absent from Paris manuscript 4613.]

Whoever is proved to have knowingly led witnesses into perjury is to be compelled under sureties to come to our assembly, [manuscripts 1, 1c, Gotha, and the others read “to our palace” instead of “to our assembly”] so that there, together with our faithful men, we may consider what should be done with such a person.

7. Concerning those who habitually pursue disagreements and contentions and refuse to live in peace: if they are convicted of this, we likewise wish them to come under sureties to our assembly, so that there, together with our faithful men, we may consider what should be done with such people. [Manuscript 10 reads “to come to peace”; Blankenburg reads “and refuse peace.”]

8. [This chapter is placed before the preceding chapter by manuscript 1 and is absent from Gotha, Modena, Paris 4613, Blankenburg, Florence, London, Vienna, and Este.]

Concerning good denarii which the people refuse to accept [Blankenburg reads *r. non uult*, “does not wish to accept”], we wish the provision established in our earlier capitulary to be observed and maintained, namely, in the fourth book, chapter 30 [manuscript 1 omits *id est*, “that is”]:

“Whoever, whether in a purchase or in payment of a debt, refuses to accept a pure and properly weighed denarius is to pay our ban, that is, sixty solidi. If ecclesiastical slaves, our fiscal slaves, or the slaves of our counts or vassals presume to do this, they are to be beaten with sixty blows. If our agents, or those of others, or advocates refuse to present them to our envoys or counts when ordered to do so, they are to pay the aforesaid ban, that is, sixty solidi.”

To fulfill this constitution of ours, bishops, abbots, and all others who hold our benefices are to assist the counts in constraining their own men. [Blankenburg reads *comites*, “the counts,” for *comitibus*, “the counts” in the dative.] If the counts neglect this constitution of ours, the matter is to be brought to our attention through our envoys. [Manuscript 1 has the variant *h. ad n.* (“this to us”).]

9. [Paris manuscript 4613 omits this chapter together with the remaining chapters of Capitularies II and III; in their place it gives chapters 12 and 17 of the Capitularies of Olonnus printed above.]

Concerning homicides and other injustices committed by our fiscal slaves—because they think they can commit such acts with impunity—we decree that our agents must be commanded to prevent them from henceforth being committed with impunity. Wherever such acts have been committed, we shall order that the perpetrators pay the penalty together with discipline. [Manuscript 1 reads *iniustis*, “unjust acts,” instead of *iniustitiis*, “injustices”; manuscripts 5, 9, and 10 omit “by our fiscal slaves”; Blankenburg and Gotha read *praecipimus*, “we command,” instead of *praecipiemus*, “we shall order.”]

10. Gatherings for wrongdoing are to be prohibited in every way. Wherever such presumptuous acts have occurred, they are to be corrected by an appropriate amends. If they have occurred through the negligence of a count or have remained uncorrected, the matter is to be brought to our attention. The author of the act, if he is a provost, advocate, centenarius, or any other free person of rank, is, after the legal amends have been made locally, to come under sureties into our presence. The multitude, whether composed of slaves or free people, is to be punished by a lawful amends. [Manuscripts 3, 5, 6, 7, 9, and 10 read “for doing evil” instead of “for wrongdoing”; manuscripts 1c, 2, and 8 have another form meaning “for doing evil”; manuscript 1 omits “whether.”]

11. [This chapter is absent from Blankenburg, Florence, London, Vienna, and Este.]

Concerning destroyed public bridges: it has pleased us, and we wish and command, that all our men who have disregarded our order concerning the repair of bridges come into our presence to give an account of why they dared to disregard our order. The counts are to give an account concerning their *pagenses*, explaining why they either did not compel them to do this or neglected to report it to us. Likewise, concerning unjust tolls, wherever they are collected, they are to know that they will give us an account for them. [Blankenburg adds that we have forbidden them to be collected any further.]

[Col. 0635D] 12. The ordeal of cold water which they have hitherto practiced is to be forbidden by all our envoys, so that it may not be practiced any longer. [Manuscript 1 omits *omnibus*, “all.”]

[Col. 0636A] **13** [Note: [Col. 0635] This chapter is missing in Goth., Mut., A., Fl., L., V., Vn., and E.]. Whoever among the vicars or other ministers of the counts has presumed to demand from the people a higher-value tax called the *inferenda* [Note: [Col. 0635] *inferendum*, Bl.] than was established by the envoys of our good-memory father—namely, two solidi for one cow—whatever he unjustly imposed and took away and retained for himself, he shall restore, with his legal compensation, to those from whom he took it; moreover, he shall pay our *fredus* [Note: [Col. 0635] “shall pay the composition”; 2, 3, 5, and 6 have variants.] and lose his office [Note: [Col. 0635] “and lose his office” is absent in 6.].

**14** [Note: [Col. 0635] This chapter is missing in Bl.]. After the count and the men of the county have returned from any military expedition, from that day onward the ban shall be revoked for forty nights [Note: [Col. 0635] *resisus*, 1 c.; *resisus*, 2, 3, 5, 6–10; Goth. has *recissus* in Amerbach’s edition.], a period which in the German language is called *scaftlegi* [Note: [Col. 0635] *scahft legi*, 9; *scaftleg*, Goth.; *scast legi*, 4, 8; *scat legii*, 3; *scat legi*, 1 c., 2, 6; *casolegi*, 10; *eriscild*, V., Vn., E.], that is, “the laying down of arms.”

**15** [Note: [Col. 0635] This chapter is missing in Bl., A., Fl., L., V., Vn., and E.]. Our envoys shall make known to the counts and the people [Note: [Col. 0635] From *hoc* through *volumus*, absent in Goth. and Mut.] that we wish to sit one day each week to hear and judge cases. The counts and our envoys, however, shall take great care lest, through their negligence [Note: [Col. 0635] From *eorum* through the second *eorum*, absent in Goth.], the poor should be oppressed and we should suffer annoyance because of their complaints, if they wish to have our favor. The people shall also be told to beware of bringing other cases to us in appeal, except those in which either our envoys or the counts have refused to render them justice.

## CHAPTERS TO BE HELD AS LAW

These are the chapters that are to be held as law [Note: [Col. 0635] Thus in 1, 2, and Goth. *Cap.* in 5. The entire rubric is absent in 3, 6, 7, 8, and 10.].

**1** [Note: [Col. 0635] This chapter is missing in Bl.]. Concerning homicides committed in churches or in their atria, the following shall be observed and upheld, as was established in the preceding capitulary [Note: [Col. 0635] In this manuscript, five pages have been erased, so that what follows can no longer be read.], namely, in Book [Col. 0636C] Four, Chapter 13:

> “If anyone kills a man in a church, either for a trivial reason or without cause, he shall pay the composition for his life. But if they have quarreled outside, and one has fled into a church and, defending himself there, killed the other, and if he has no witnesses to this deed, he shall affirm under oath, with twelve legitimate oath-helpers, that he killed him while defending himself. But if he himself was the author of the quarrel that arose between them, he shall be compelled to pay the *leud* [Note: [Col. 0635] *laud*, 1.] of the slain man and, in addition, our ban, and shall perform public penance [Note: [Col. 0635] *habet*, 1.]. But if it was not the man who killed the other, but the man who was killed, who provoked the same quarrel, let him lie without composition; and the man who killed him shall perform public penance according to canonical judgment. If anyone’s own slave commits this act, he shall be tested by the ordeal of boiling water to determine whether he did it voluntarily or in self-defense. If his hand is scalded, he shall be killed. If it is not, he shall be punished with public penance. Unless, perhaps, he too is found to have been the author of the quarrel that arose between them: then his master shall pay to the church according to his *wergild* [Note: [Col. 0637] *uuergeltus*, 1; *uuidregildus*, 6; *uuirgildus*, Goth.], or, if he wishes, surrender him to that same church. Concerning an ecclesiastical, fiscal, or beneficiary slave, we decree that his *wergild* shall be paid for him on the first occasion, but on the second occasion the slave himself shall be handed over to punishment. Nevertheless, the inheritance of a free man who has been sentenced to death for such a crime shall pass to his lawful heirs [Note: [Col. 0637] *illius*, Goth.]. If a homicide of this kind has been committed in the atrium of a church whose door has been consecrated with the relics of the saints, it shall be amended or compounded in the same manner. But if the church door has not been consecrated, what is committed in the atrium shall be compounded in the manner in which what is committed in violated sanctuary ought to be compounded [Note: [Col. 0637] Absent in 1.], as is contained in the preceding book [Note: [Col. 0637] As is stated in Book 8, Chapter 10.]”

**2.** Whoever, out of greed for property, kills his father or mother, brother or sister [Note: [Col. 0637] “or nephew,” Bl. and Goth.; “or nephew,” Fl.; “or nephew,” V. and Vn.], nephew, or any other relative, shall have the inheritance of the slain person pass to his other lawful heirs; but the killer’s inheritance shall be transferred to the fisc. He himself shall, at the bishop’s direction, be subjected to public penance.

**3** [Note: [Col. 0637] This chapter is missing in Bl. It occurs in the manuscripts Mut., A., Fl., L., V., Vn., and E. among the laws of Charlemagne (Muratori, chapter 133).] [Note: [Col. 0637D] Hincmar has preserved the history of this chapter in his book *On the Divorce of Lothar and Theutberga*, in his response to the fifth question, p. 509 in Sirmond’s edition:

> “The Augustus of our own age, Louis of blessed memory, at the synod and general assembly at Worms, while an envoy of the Apostolic See and of Pope Gregory was present, together with many others, concerning those matters which the bishops had recently and necessarily and usefully discovered at synods held in four places of his empire, regarding the case now under discussion, with the agreement of the wishes of all, bishops as well as faithful laymen, decreed as follows: ‘Whoever,’ he said, ‘having abandoned his own wife, or having killed her without fault on her part, takes another wife, shall perform public penance after laying down his arms. And if he is contumacious, let him be arrested by the count, bound with iron, and placed in custody until the matter is brought to our attention.’” BALUZ.]

Whoever, having abandoned his own wife or killed her without cause [Note: [Col. 0637] “or without fault,” 2, 3, and 5–10.] takes another [Note: [Col. 0637] *alium*, 1.] wife [Note: [Col. 0637] *uxorem*, 2, 3, and 5–10], shall perform public penance after laying down his arms. And if he is contumacious, he shall be arrested by the count, bound with iron, and placed in custody until the matter is brought to our attention.

[Col. 0637C] **4.** Whoever sells another person’s property to anyone, and that person gives or sells the same property to someone else [Note: [Col. 0637] From *sive* through *vendiderit*, absent in Goth.], and the person who then possesses the purchased property, through evil cunning, hands it over to his own son or to anyone else who has not yet reached the lawful age, in order to prevent justice from being obtained, we wish and firmly command that, if the father of that child is alive [Note: [Col. 0637] *vixerat*, 1.], he himself shall enter the case and give an account on behalf of his son. But if that father is dead, then his lawful relative, who appears rightly to be his guardian and defender, shall be compelled to give an account on his behalf. The same shall apply to all other matters of justice pertaining to him, [Col. 0638A] except his lawful inheritance, which ought lawfully to come to him by succession from his parents. But if anyone despises or neglects this command of ours, action shall be taken against him as against the other despisers [Note: [Col. 0637] *decogatur. Si vero*, 1.]. But the man who first seized and unjustly sold the same property, as well as the purchasers—except only the child [Note: [Col. 0637] “the child in this matter,” Bl. and Goth.]—shall be compelled to make reparation within the country for what they fraudulently did, and afterward, like despisers of our command, shall be compelled under sureties to come into our presence [Note: [Col. 0637] Absent in 1.].

**5** [Note: [Col. 0637] In the edition of the laws, Lugdunensis, this was incorrectly printed: “We wish our counts to have permission to conduct an inquiry concerning the vicars, etc.” This is found in no manuscript. See above, Lothar’s capitulary of 823, chapter 3.] Concerning vicars and centenarii who very often hold assemblies more from greed than for the administration of justice and consequently oppress the people excessively, the following rule shall be observed, as it is contained in the capitulary of the lord Emperor Charlemagne, Book 3 [Note: [Col. 0637] “4,” Bl. and G.], Chapter 40:

> “No one shall be summoned to an assembly unless he is pursuing his own case, or another must pursue a case against him, except for the seven *scabini*, who must be present at every assembly.”

Likewise, concerning the same matter, in our capitulary, Book 4, Chapter 55:

> “Concerning the assemblies which free men ought to attend, the constitution of our father must be observed and upheld in every respect: namely, that they attend only three general assemblies in the year, and that no one compel them to attend more assemblies, unless perhaps someone has been accused, has accused another, or has been summoned to give testimony. At the other proceedings held by the centenarii, no one shall be ordered to attend except one who is litigating, judging [Note: [Col. 0637] In this reading, *iudicat* is where manuscript 6 ends.], or giving testimony.”

And whoever is found by our envoys to be a transgressor of this constitution shall pay our ban.

**6** [Note: [Col. 0637] This chapter is missing in Goth. and Mut.]. Concerning free men who possess no property of their own but reside on a lord’s land: they shall not be received as witnesses on account of another person’s property. Nevertheless, they may be oath-helpers of other free men because they are free. Those, however, who possess property of their own and yet reside on a lord’s land shall not be rejected for the reason that they reside on a lord’s land; rather, they shall be received as witnesses because they possess property of their own [Note: [Col. 0637] Here manuscripts 2, 3, 5, 7, 8, 9, and 10 insert a chapter which certainly does not belong here—namely, among the chapters to be held as law—but should be assigned among the chapters given to the envoys. See below.].

**7** [Note: [Col. 0637] This chapter is missing in Bl., A., Fl., L., V., Vn., and E.]. Concerning the restraint of feuds [Note: [Col. 0637] “This chapter is observed,” Goth. and Mut.], let what is contained in our capitulary, Book 4, Chapter 25 [Note: [Col. 0637] “20,” 2, 3, 5, and 10.] be observed and upheld:

> “If anyone, compelled by some necessity, commits a homicide, the count in whose jurisdiction the deed was committed shall cause both the composition to be paid and the feud to be settled by oath. But if one party refuses to consent to this—whether the man who committed the homicide or the man who ought to receive the composition—he shall cause the person who is contumacious toward him to come into our presence, so that we may send him into exile for whatever period pleases us, until he is corrected there and no longer dares to disobey his count, and so that no greater harm may grow from the matter.”

## CHAPTERS GIVEN TO THE ENVOYS

### Other Chapters [Note: [Col. 0639] Taken from manuscripts 1 and 5; in 1 c. only chapters 1 and 2 are found. They are also absent in manuscripts Bl., Goth., and Mut.]

**1.** We wish all ecclesiastical property to be maintained in the same manner as property belonging to our fisc ordinarily is maintained, until we come to our general assembly with our faithful men and determine how these matters ought to be handled in the future.

**2.** Likewise, we wish every inquiry that must be made concerning property belonging to the right of our fisc to be conducted not through witnesses who have been produced, but through the testimony of those who are known to be the best and most truthful men in that county; and according to what they testify concerning the matter [Note: [Col. 0639] *de*, 1.], the property shall either be retained or restored.

**3.** Likewise, we wish that, concerning the property which Mahtfrid acquired in various places and through various persons, those who gave the same property to him should be questioned as to whether any of them wishes to reclaim it. Whoever declares that he wishes to do so shall be ordered to come to our general assembly, so that he may settle the matter with Mahtfrid [Note: [Col. 0639C] Mahtfrid, count of Orléans. See the notes on Agobard, p. 78. I think the same man is involved in the imperial privilege of Emperor Lothar, published among the proofs of the history of Tournus, p. 267, where he is called “Mahtfrid, illustrious count.” BALUZ.].

**4.** We wish our envoys, throughout their entire legation, first of all to inquire which free men have not yet promised us fidelity, and to make them promise it, as has always been customary; afterward they shall begin to carry out their legation through the remaining chapters.

[Col. 0639B] **5** [Note: [Col. 0639] From manuscript 1.]. We wish and command our envoys to inquire carefully how many free men remain in each county who are able to undertake a military expedition on their own, and how many can undertake such an expedition when a third man is assisted and equipped by two, when a fourth is assisted and equipped by three, and when a fifth or sixth is assisted and equipped by four; and they shall bring us a brief written summary of these numbers [Note: [Col. 0639] Manuscript 5 adds: “And they shall make those who have not yet promised fidelity promise fidelity to us with an oath.”].

[Col. 0640B] **5** [Note: [Col. 0639] From manuscript 5 and Sirmond’s edition, where it is inserted after Chapter 6 among the laws]. We wish and command our envoys to inquire carefully how many free men remain in each county. This diligence and this method shall be applied in each hundred, so that they may truthfully know and record those who can go on a military expedition; and afterward, in due order, concerning those who cannot go on their own, two shall prepare assistance for a third. And those who have not yet promised us fidelity shall be made to promise fidelity to us with an oath [Note: [Col. 0639] The edition reads *faciatis*.].

[Col. 0639C]

I found the following three chapters, which are taken from the book of Burgundian laws and from the Theodosian Code, transcribed in the Palatine manuscript and in that of Saint Vincent of Metz immediately after the preceding chapters of Louis the Pious. Regino, abbot of Prüm, likewise cites them from the capitularies of the same Louis. For that reason we did not wish to omit them here, and also because many things in them differ from the published editions of those laws. BALUZ.

We have compared them with Codex 9, where Chapters 1 and 2 are counted as one.

> **1. Concerning the limitation of periods.** Although it had long ago been ordered by us that, if a person of a barbarian nation in our people either remained on his own property, invited another person, or voluntarily assigned land for habitation, and had held it for fifteen years without third-party claims, it should remain in his possession, and the person who had given it should know that nothing thereafter was owed to him, nevertheless, without any exchange, the stated condition shall generally be preserved for all time. It has pleased us that this be established by the present law.

> **2. Likewise, concerning the limitation of periods.** If anyone says and proves that land handed over to him by another was violently taken away before the thirty-year period is complete, and it is established that the property was occupied, he may bring a claim and restore the matter to the parties who are reclaiming it. But if, once thirty years have elapsed, land said to have been seized by anyone has not been restored, he shall know that nothing is to be returned to him. Therefore all counts, whenever a dispute has arisen concerning private matters, shall take care to judge according to the order of this law [*istius*, Bal.]. And because the law properly provides for everything pertaining to the peace of all, no case concerning any property that has not been resolved within thirty years may afterward be brought in any legal proceeding; for it is clear that the number of years stated above ought to be sufficient for everyone to seek and receive whatever was owed to him.

> **3. Concerning tenants and coloni.** If anyone has held another man’s colonus on his property for thirty years, let him claim him as his own. If the colonus is found within the thirty-year period, he shall be reclaimed from the current holder by his master, together with the sons owed to him and all his peculium. But if he has died, his master shall reclaim his peculium. If a female colonus has remained under another’s lordship for twenty years, she shall not be claimed by her former master. Two parts of the offspring shall follow the male colonus, while one-third shall follow the female colonus. For if offspring was produced within thirty [Note: [Col. 0640D] “twenty,” Bal.] years, while the female colonus still belonged to the master, it shall not be denied to those reclaiming it, because this has been established in the Novels. Yet, so that the separation of the married couple may not occur, we command that the master of the colonus not be denied a substitute woman together with one-third of the offspring [Note: [Col. 0640D] Thus in the manuscript; corrected by a second hand to the reading adopted by Bal.: “so that the female partner may be received from the master of the colonus.”].

# ECCLESIASTICAL CONSTITUTION OF LOTHAR I  
*(Around the year 830)*

[Col. 0641]

[Col. 0641] Since these chapters are found in Codices 1, the Blankenburg manuscript, and 2, the Gothan manuscript, but are not assigned to a definite time, I have thought that they may be attributed to Lothar’s third journey and therefore to the final months of 829 or the first months of 830. They refer to the constitutions of Olonna of 825 and define more closely several matters prescribed there in the lesser chapters.

[Col. 0641A] **1.** It has pleased us that no bishop presume in any way to accept a payment for the consecration or dedication of baptismal churches, hospices [Note: [Col. 0641] *senodochiorum*, 2.], or oratories, contrary to the authority of the canonical fathers or contrary to ancient custom.

**2** [Note: [Col. 0641] This chapter is absent in Codex 1; it is found in the Florentine and London manuscripts.] [Note: [Col. 0641C] Compare the Constitution of Olonna of 825, Chapters 5 and 6, above.] Concerning women cohabiting with priests, it has pleased us that they be completely expelled and no longer associate with them in any manner. If, after the first admonition of his bishop [Note: [Col. 0641] “or second or third,” Fl.], a priest is convicted by three to seven suitable witnesses of having transgressed, he shall be subject to the peril of his own rank. But if the bishop neglects to issue such a summons for any reason, or after this synodal council does not correct the matter with an appropriate correction within fifty days, he shall be subject to the judgment of his metropolitan. Priests, however, shall have with them clerics of good reputation, who, because of the purity of their own lives, may become faithful witnesses concerning the lives of others.

**3** [Note: [Col. 0642C] Compare the same constitution, Chapter 7.] In hospices that have been rationally organized [Note: [Col. 0641] “and still remain in their original condition, the provisions entirely written down by the testator shall be observed.” In 2.], and [Note: [Col. 0641] Absent in 1.] still remain in their original condition, the testator’s will, exactly as written in the original testament [Note: [Col. 0641] *conscripta*, 1.], shall be preserved. But in those which from the beginning lacked a properly ordered arrangement [Note: [Col. 0641] “a disposition according to reason,” 1.], we wish one-fifth of the revenues to be given to the poor. Similarly, in those which had a rational [Note: [Col. 0641] *rationabiliter*, 2.] arrangement but through some negligence lack the ordering of their former condition, we wish the condition stated above [Note: [Col. 0641] “superscribed,” 2.] to be maintained until, through the provision of good administrators and an abundance of resources, they are able to return to their former arrangement.

**4** [Note: [Col. 0642C] Compare the same constitution, Chapters 2 and 3.] It has seemed good to us that the priests of baptismal churches, according to their ability, show due obedience and honor to their bishops without burden [Note: [Col. 0641] *grauitudine*, 2.], whenever necessity and order demand it. For if such obedience to the public interest is imposed upon bishops that they cannot perform it themselves, we wish them to provide assistance through their subordinates [Note: [Col. 0641] Absent in 2.] according to the nature of the service imposed. If anyone, apart from this necessity [Note: [Col. 0641] “If anyone, out of necessity, has churches burdened,” 1.], keeps churches burdened and ruined and presumes to burden them further in the future, such rectors, once this has been learned through the report of the envoys, shall be struck by the canonical penalty promulgated by us [Note: [Col. 0641] *promulgata*, 2.].

# DIVISION OF THE EMPIRE  
*(November 830)*

[Col. 0641]

[Col. 0641] Cointius and Pagius assigned the charter of this division, published by Pithoeus in *SS. Francorum* XII, pp. 330–336, from a “very ancient parchment,” to the year 835; Goldastus and Baluzius assigned it to the years 837 and 838. But the opinion of Goldastus and Baluzius cannot stand for several reasons, least of all because the divisions of the years 837 and 838, which differ greatly from this one, are found in the annals of Prudentius and in Nithard. Nor does anyone know of a division of the empire having been made at the assembly of Stremiacum in 835. It must certainly be assigned to the period when Louis was hostile to Lothar and did not think even Lothar’s name, or the prospect of his future authority over his brothers, worth mentioning; and when, favorably disposed toward Pippin and Louis, he decided that the kingdoms long assigned to them, Aquitaine and Bavaria, should be enlarged. Since Nithard, in the first book of his *Histories*, reports that the emperor fulfilled the condition of the assistance furnished by both brothers against Lothar in 830, the division appears to have been completed at the assembly held at Nijmegen in October and November, on the eleventh day of which we read Lothar’s name attached for the last time, in the customary manner, to his father’s name.

[Col. 0641D] In the name of the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ. Louis, by the divinely ordained providence of God, emperor augustus, to all the faithful of the holy Church of God and to the entire Catholic people, present and future, of the peoples and nations [Note: [Col. 0641] *nationi*, Pith.] established under our empire [Col. 0642D] and rule.

We wish it to be known to the understanding of all of you that, among our beloved sons Pippin, Louis, and Charles, we have decided to make the following division of the kingdom entrusted to us by God, so that after our departure from this mortality each of them may know—if divine mercy wills that they survive us—which portion has been assigned to him by us to hold and govern. We wish to describe and designate this division in such a way that each of them, according to our arrangement and the boundaries of his kingdom that extend among foreign peoples, may, with God’s help, determine and strive to defend them, and may be able to preserve peace and brotherly love among themselves. We have determined that the manner and arrangement of this division shall be as follows [Note: [Col. 0643D] Goldastus notes here: “The division and arrangement of the kingdoms is missing.” Nithard supplies this gap, to some extent, in Book I, where he describes the portion of the kingdom given to Charles the Bald:

> “That is, from the sea through the borders of Saxony as far as the borders of the Ripuarians, all Frisia, and through the borders of the Ripuarians the counties of Moilla, Halt, Trahammolant, and Masagobbi; then whatever lies between the Meuse and the Seine as far as Burgundy, together with Verdun; and from Burgundy, the counties of Toul, Odorn, Bed, Blois, Parthenay, both Barrois, Brienne, Troyes, Auxerre, Sens, the Gâtinais, Melun, Étampes, Chartres, Paris, [Col. 0644D] and then along the Seine as far as the Ocean Sea, and across that sea as far as Frisia—namely, all the bishoprics, abbeys, counties, fiscal estates, and everything situated within the aforesaid boundaries, together with everything belonging to them, wherever in any region they were situated and appeared to be under their jurisdiction—he gave to his aforesaid son Charles, with divine and paternal authority.” See also the *Annals of Saint-Bertin*, under the year 837. BALUZ.].

**1.** We have arranged everything according to the following order: if, after our departure from this light, one of them dies before his brothers and leaves such a son as his people wish to succeed his father in the inheritance of the kingdom, we wish his uncles to consent to this and permit their brother’s son to reign in the kingdom which his father, their brother, possessed. But if he has no such son, then we wish the portion of the kingdom which he possessed to be divided equally among the brothers who survive [Note: [Col. 0643] *remanserint*, B.].

**2.** We have also deemed it fitting to establish and command among the aforesaid sons, for the sake of the peace and harmony which we wish to endure among them forever, that none of them presume to invade his brother’s boundaries or the limits of his kingdom, nor fraudulently enter it to disturb his kingdom or diminish his marches. Rather, each of them shall assist his brother, as the opportunity of the time permits [Note: [Col. 0643] *opportunitas*, P.], and shall give him aid against his enemies according to reason [Col. 0643C] and ability.

**3.** Nor shall anyone receive any person who has fled to him from his brother for whatever causes or offenses, in order to make intercession for him. For we wish every sinful man who needs intercession to flee within the kingdom of his own lord, or to holy places or honored men, and from there to earn a just intercession.

**4.** Likewise, we command that [Note: [Col. 0644D] Thus the old parchment which we saw. Pithoeus published it in the same way; Duchesne has “any free man.” I think he borrowed this from Chapter 8 of Charlemagne’s division.] no one who has abandoned his lord against his will and gone from one kingdom to another be received by the king himself, nor shall he permit his men to receive such a person or presume unjustly to retain him. We decree that the same rule be observed not only concerning such men but also concerning fugitive slaves [Col. 0643D], so that no occasion for discord may remain [Col. 0644A]. We further command that, while we remain alive in the body, none of these three brothers shall make any man—whether our man or another man’s—promise fidelity to him by oath, and thereby turn him away from us or from his other lord through such an oath and draw him to himself.

**5.** Moreover, it seems necessary for us to command that, after our departure from this mortality, the men of each of them receive benefices, each in the kingdom of his own lord and not in another’s, lest this should at some time give rise to scandal. Each of those men shall have his inheritance without opposition in whatever kingdom he happens lawfully to possess it [Col. 0644B] [Note: [Col. 0643] Thus I have corrected it; the editions read *cognoverit*.].

**6.** And every free man, after the death of his lord, shall have permission to commend himself, among these three kingdoms, to whomever he wishes. The same shall apply to one who has not yet commended himself to anyone.

**7.** Concerning transfers and sales which ordinarily take place between the parties, we command that none of these three brothers accept from anyone in another’s kingdom a transfer or sale of immovable property—that is, lands, vineyards, woods, and slaves who are already settled in households, or other things reckoned as inheritance—except gold, silver, gems, weapons and clothing, as well as slaves who are not settled in households and those commodities known properly to belong to merchants. [Col. 0644C] We judge that this prohibition should by no means be imposed upon the other men.

**8.** If women, as commonly happens, are lawfully sought in marriage between the parties and kingdoms, they shall not be denied to those who ask justly. Rather, it shall be permitted for them to give and receive women in turn and to unite peoples with one another through kinship. The women themselves shall have power over their property in the kingdom from which they departed, although they must live in another kingdom because of their husband’s companionship.

**9.** Concerning hostages who were given on account of pledges and have been assigned by us to various places for safekeeping, we do not wish [Note: [Col. 0643] *volumus*, P.] the king in whose kingdom they are to permit them to return to their homeland without the consent of the brother from whose kingdom they were taken [Col. 0644D]. Rather, in the future, when hostages are received, each brother shall provide mutual assistance to the other, if one brother reasonably asks the other to do so. We command the same concerning those who have been sent, or are to be sent, into exile on account of their crimes.

**10.** If such a cause, intention, or dispute should arise between the parties concerning the boundaries or frontiers of the kingdoms that cannot be clarified or settled by human testimony, then we wish the will of God and the truth of the matter to be sought by displaying the standard of the cross, so that no battle or judicial combat of any kind may ever be decreed for such a cause to the destruction of anyone. But if anyone from one kingdom accuses a man from another kingdom before his lord of disloyalty toward his lord’s brother, his lord shall send him to his brother, so that there he may prove what he said concerning that man.

**11.** Above all, we command and order that the three brothers themselves jointly undertake the care and [Note: [Col. 0645C] Goldastus notes here: “Baronius, *Annals*, vol. IX, year 838, §2, unusually praises this entire passage, which he had corrupted, as usual, under the charge of falsehood in the constitution of Charlemagne, §16, inserting after the words ‘the Church of Saint Peter’ the following: ‘the defense of the holy pope also,’ contrary to the manuscript codices and to Pithoeus, from whom he copied, and to the editions of Mutianus. See Marca, Book I of *On the Harmony of the Priesthood and the Empire*, Chapter 12, §2 and following.”] defense of the Church of Saint Peter, just as it was once undertaken by our great-grandfather Charles, by our grandfather Pippin, by our father Charles the emperor of blessed memory, and afterward by us, so that with God’s help they may strive to defend it against its enemies and cause it to have its justice, insofar as this pertains to them and reason requires. Likewise, concerning the other churches that shall be under their authority, we command that they have their justice and honor, and that the shepherds and rectors of venerable places have power over the property belonging to those holy places, in whichever of the three brothers’ kingdoms the possessions of those churches may be found.

**12.** But if any of these statutes and agreements should, by any chance or through ignorance—which we do not desire—be violated [Note: [Col. 0645D] Thus precisely in the old parchment. Chapter 16 of Charles’s charter, from which this was apparently copied, has the same wording. Pithoeus, Duchesne, and Goldastus nevertheless printed *consentiis*.], we command that they strive to correct it as quickly as possible according to justice, lest greater harm should at some time grow through delay [Note: [Col. 0645] *inrutum*, P.].

**13.** We have arranged all these matters and decided to confirm them in the following order: for as long as it pleases the divine majesty that we live this bodily life, our power shall remain over this kingdom and empire, preserved by God, as it has been until now, in its government, ordering, and every royal and imperial dominion. We shall have the aforesaid sons obedient, and our people beloved by God, with all the submission that sons show to a father and peoples show to an emperor and king. And if one of these three sons, desiring above all to please almighty God and afterward us through greater obedience and good will, should earn by the uprightness of his conduct that we delight in conferring greater honor and power upon him [Note: [Col. 0645] Namely, “that we should confer it.”], we wish this to remain in our power, so that from the portion of his brother who has failed to take care to please us, we may increase his kingdom, honor, and power, and make him such as his own merits show him to deserve [Col. 0646B].

**14.** Finally, it seems necessary for us to establish that whatever we may still add to these decrees and commands of ours concerning matters and agreements relating to their advancement and welfare shall be observed and guarded by the aforesaid beloved sons in the same way as those matters already established and set down in these decrees, which we command them to guard and preserve.

[Note: [Col. 0645D] Goldastus omitted this and what follows in his edition. Certainly many errors are found there, and many passages are mutilated. Nevertheless, since Pithoeus found these materials in a very ancient parchment, and they were also found in the old parchment which we used, we thought they should not be passed over.]

For all Aquitaine between the Loire and the Seine, and beyond the Seine, twenty-eight counties, namely [Note: [Col. 0645D] Châlons, Meaux, Amiens, and Ponthieu]: the counties of Châlons, Meaux, Amiens, and Ponthieu [Note: [Col. 0645] *pontivus*, P.], as far as the sea.

[Col. 0646C] To Bavaria, all Thuringia [Note: [Col. 0645] t. T.
