P.], [Note: [Col. 0646C] Its duchy’s chief city is Cologne Agrippina.] the Ribuarian districts [Note: [Col. 0645] ribuarias P.; ripuarios B.] [Note: [Col. 0646C] In Guelders. *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, I, 6.], the Atuarian districts [Note: [Col. 0645] atoarias P.; atrarios B.], Saxony, Frisia, [Note: [Col. 0646C] Including Stavelot and Malmedy.] the Ardennes, Asbania [Note: [Col. 0645] hasbania B.], [Note: [Col. 0646C] Hainaut, Brabant, Flanders.] Bragmento, Franderes, [Note: [Col. 0646C] The Menapii, part of Flanders.] Menpiscon [Note: [Col. 0645] mempiscon B.], [Note: [Col. 0646D] Melantois.] Medenenti [Note: [Col. 0645] metunenti B.], [Note: [Col. 0646D] Aisne and Hainaut.] Ainau [Note: [Col. 0645] amau P. B.].

[Note: [Col. 0646D] Osterbant.] Austerban, [Note: [Col. 0646D] Districts around Arras, Thérouanne, and Boulogne.] Adertensis, Tervanensis [Note: [Col. 0645] teruunensis P.], Bolensis, [Note: [Col. 0646D] Saint-Josse-sur-Mer.] Quentovico, [Note: [Col. 0646D] Districts around Cambrai and Saint-Quentin.] Camalecensis, Virdomandensis [Note: [Col. 0645] virdomadensis P. B.].

To Alamannia [Note: [Col. 0646D] In the year 806 Charlemagne divided Burgundy into two parts, one of which he gave to Louis, king of Aquitaine, and the other to Charles. Here Louis wishes the whole of Burgundy to belong to Alamannia, except that part of Burgundy which had been given to Pippin. It is difficult to distinguish these matters. Anyone wishing to know more about the various divisions of Burgundy may consult the *Notice of Gaul* by the most learned Adrian Valesius.] all Burgundy, except what was given to Pippin [Col. 0647A] [Note: [Col. 0647A] That is, as I judge, the province properly so called and the Dauphiné, in which is Vienne, which the author of the *Annals of Saint-Bertin* for the year 834 says was a city of Provence.], the whole of Provence, and [Note: [Col. 0647A] That is, Septimania and the Spanish March. For at that time those provinces were included under the designation of Gothia, and for that reason they are often joined together in ancient documents. Charles the Simple’s charter in the *Cartulary of Elne*, book I, chapter 1: “We also command throughout our entire kingdom of Gothia or Hispania.” Another charter of the same king in the *Cartulary of the Church of Girona*: “We also command and order that whatever he has acquired or may thereafter be able to acquire within the boundaries of Gothia or Hispania …” Another charter of the same king in the *Cartulary of Saint Peter of Rodes*: “We also grant you throughout the whole kingdom of Gothia or Septimania.” The first capitulary of the year 806, chapter 1: “We have entrusted Septimania or Gothia to Louis, our beloved son”; and chapter 4: “Septimania or Gothia as far as Hispania.” Hence Charles the Simple is called “king of the Franks and Goths” in the *Cartulary of the Church of Elne*, book I, chapter 74. It must now be shown that the part of the province of Narbonne beginning at Carcassonne also belonged to the Gothic kingdom. This may first be proved by the authority of the *Life of Saint Benedict, abbot of Aniane*. Since its author says that Benedict was the son of a man who “held the county of Maguelonne for as long as he lived,” and that Benedict was a native of the regions of Gothia, it is clear that he understood that part of Narbonnese Gaul to have been included under the name of Gothia. This view is confirmed by the author of Alcuin’s *Life*, who says that the same Abbot Benedict often came to Alcuin from Gothia: “The man of God Benedict, joined to him above all the monks by intimacy, often hastened to him from the regions of Gothia in order to receive counsel for his own salvation and that of his people.” For he came from the monastery of Aniane, which was situated in the diocese of Maguelonne, a part of Septimania. In the archive of the monastery of Cuxa there is found, as I think, a charter of Bernard, count of Besalú, issued in the year 1000, in which it is written that he gave to that same monastery of Cuxa a monastery called Monisat, which is “in honor of the holy apostle Paul, in the province of Gothia, in the county of Fenouillèdes, in the diocese of the Church of Narbonne.” I also find in the *Cartulary of the monastery of Camprodon* that this monastery was situated in the county of Fenouillèdes. Hence the Gothic kingdom is mentioned in the charter which King Lothair granted to Abbot Sunyer in the diocese of Girona, preserved in the *Cartulary of the monastery of Saint Felix of Guíxols*. In the Gospel book of the monastery of Saint-Denis, which John Aventinus, book IV of the *Annals of Bavaria*, p. 462, relates to have been preserved in his time at Regensburg in the church of Saint Emmeram, these verses were read, inscribed for Charles the Bald, king of the Franks:

“Grateful France brings you gifts, illustrious king;

Gothia likewise begins with you, together with its lofty kingdoms.”

Nevertheless, although at that time both provinces were understood by the name Gothia [Col. 0648B], and although, under Louis the Pious, Count Bernard of Barcelona ruled Septimania and Gothia, it must not be supposed that Borrell—whom I find called duke of Gothia in the year of King Lothair in the *Cartulary of the monastery of Ripoll* and in the record of the foundation of the monastery of Saint Benedict of Bages in the diocese of Ausona—held the provinces of Tarraconensis and Septimania, since we know that he possessed only the counties of Barcelona and Urgell. Unless, that is, he wished to be called duke of Gothia because he held in his power part of the new Septimania, namely the district of Urgell. BALUZ.] all Gothia, and from that central Francia [Note: [Col. 0648B] Wavre, on the banks of the Alisontia. *Monumenta*, I, 489.] Warensis, [Col. 0648A] [Note: [Col. 0648B] Vongensis, around Vousi on the Aisne.] Vngensis, [Note: [Col. 0648B] On the Meuse and the Bar, including Donchery.] Castrensis, [Note: [Col. 0648B] Its chief place is Château-Porcien on the Aisne.] Portiano, [Note: [Col. 0648B] Around Reims, Laon, and Metz.] Remegensis, Laudunensis, Mosellis, [Note: [Col. 0648C] Pithou notes: “Here the oldest manuscript ends.” One might think that something has fallen out, either from Charles’s portion, to which Alamannia, together with the duchy of Chur and Alsace, had fallen in 829, or from the portion of King Louis of Bavaria, namely the districts of Worms and Speyer and the duchy of the Austrasians, together with the districts of Swalafeld, Nordgau, and Hesse. But since in the year 821, when the emperor reviewed the division established in 817, it is recorded in Einhard that these had been added to King Louis, I incline to this view, so that I believe Charles’s portion to have ended with the duchy of Trier.] Treveris.

# CONSTITUTIONS OF LOTHAIR I AT PAVIA

*(Year 832, February, Pavia.)*

[Col. 0647]

These chapters were promulgated during Lothair’s fourth journey, in which he visited Italy from the summer of the year 831 until the summer of the following year.

For the first constitution, excerpted from the capitularies of Charles and Louis, we used, after Amerbach had consulted the Tegernsee Codex, the edition of Labbe, who had published it among Sirmond’s papers, copied from Paris Codex no. 4613, in volume VII of the *Councils*, p. 1551; and, for its republication, the edition of Baluze, who used Codex 1. Chisianus, 2. Paris no. 4613, Vatican no. 5359, inspected by Blumius (*Archiv*, vol. V, p. 245), the Tegernsee Codex, now the Royal Munich Codex, the Florentine Fragment edited by Dati, the Blankenburg Codex in the ducal library of Wolfenbüttel, and the Ambrosian, Florentine, London, Vienna, Verona, and Este codices in Muratori, chapters 63–67, 95, 69, and 70. With their assistance it was possible both to revise and enlarge the text and, especially through the Chisianus, which I followed as my guide, to determine the place and time of its promulgation.

The second constitution now appears for the first time from the Chisianus Codex. It has been excerpted from the collection of the capitularies of Charlemagne, which we see surviving in the Codex of Saint Paul and reproduced here in the very order of the capitularies.

## THESE ARE THE CHAPTERS [Note: [Col. 0649] Begins in the Vatican Codex.] [Note: [Col. 0649] c.: “excerpted chapters, up to ‘it has pleased [us]’”; Vn. (the remainder is missing); c.: “excerpted chapters [u. p. unclear] by Emperor Lothair.” Est.] WHICH [Note: [Col. 0649] “whom,” in 1 and 2.] LORD LOTHAIR [Note: [Col. 0649] “Lotharius,” in 1.] THE KING [Note: [Col. 0649] “the king ordered to establish,” in 2; the remainder is missing.]

[Col. 0649A]

Together with the consent of his faithful, he excerpted [Note: [Col. 0649] “excersit,” 1; “excepit,” Vatican.] from the chapters of his grandfather, Lord Charles [Note: [Col. 0649] “auii,” 1.], and of the most serene Emperor Louis [Note: [Col. 0649] “ludouuici,” 1.], his father, at Pavia in the royal palace, under the tenth indiction, and commanded the entire people residing in the kingdom of Italy to preserve them [Note: [Col. 0649] “concepit,” 1; “praecipit,” Vatican.].

### 1. On the correction of churches

We wish that this be observed [Note: [Col. 0649] “you shall observe,” P.; “it shall be observed,” V.] as it is contained in our capitulary which we issued at Olonna [Note: [Col. 0649] “at Dolona,” P.; “Olonna,” Ch.]. And wherever there are more churches in one place than are necessary, let them be destroyed. But if perhaps a church has been built in some place [Note: [Col. 0649] “one place,” Ch.], which is nevertheless necessary and has no endowment, we wish that, in accordance with the command of our lord and father [Note: [Col. 0649] “our fathers,” Ch. P.], one mansus with [Note: [Col. 0649] omitted in P.] twelve bunuaria [Note: [Col. 0649] “bicharia,” Ch., Vatican, Vn., E.] of arable land [Note: [Col. 0649] “arable,” Ch.] be given there, together with two slaves [Note: [Col. 0649] “two female slaves, in addition,” Ch.] by free men [Col. 0649B] who ought to hear the service of God at that church, so that priests may be able to remain there and divine worship be conducted. But if the people refuse to do this, let the church be destroyed.

### 2. On bloodshed in a church

If blood is shed in a church with a staff, and the victim is a priest, let triple compensation be paid: two parts to the priest himself, the third as the *fredus* to the church, and, in addition, our ban. Likewise, in the case of a deacon, let compensation be paid at triple his composition, together with our ban. The same applies to a subdeacon, at triple his composition [Note: [Col. 0649] “composition … composition” is missing in both codices; I supplied it from Louis’s capitulary.]. For a cleric of any order, let triple his composition be paid, together with our ban. Likewise, for a blow without bloodshed against a cleric of any order, let triple his composition be paid, together with our ban. And whoever does not have the means to pay the church shall surrender himself into its service until he has paid the entire debt.

### 3

[Note: [Col. 0649] The heading is present in Blank.] We decree concerning priests and deacons deprived of ecclesiastical office that they be assigned to penance [Note: [Col. 0649] “under penance,” Bl.], as the canons prescribe. And if the bishop has a monastery in his diocese, let them be sent there. If he has no monastery, then let the bishop order that such men reside in the parish from which they come; and if they have property of their own, let them choose for themselves a patron who will provide them food and clothing [Col. 0650A] [Note: [Col. 0649] “clothing,” Blk.] from that property. They themselves, however, shall have no permission to wander or travel about, whether to legal assemblies, to the palace, or to the very property which they formerly possessed [Note: [Col. 0649] “may have possessed,” P.], without the permission of their bishop; but in the same place assigned to them they shall continually perform their penance. If they do not observe this [Note: [Col. 0649] “preserve,” Bl.], they shall first be restrained with blows; but if they are not corrected even so [Note: [Col. 0649] “if they have not been corrected,” Bl.], let them be confined in such a place where, willingly or unwillingly [Note: [Col. 0649] omitted in P.], they may live in penance [Note: [Col. 0649] “in penance,” above.].

### 4

No drunk man may prosecute his case in the court or give testimony; nor may a count hold a legal assembly unless he is fasting.

### 5. On complainants or pleaders

[Note: [Col. 0649D] That is, those who litigate. BALUZ.] Concerning complainants or pleaders who are unwilling either to accept the judgment of the assessors or to cease blaspheming (*blasfemare*), let the ancient custom be observed: that is, let them be confined in custody until they do one of the two things. And if they appeal to the palace on this matter and bring letters, they are not indeed to be believed; nevertheless, they are not to be placed in prison. Rather, together with the custody and the same letters, let them be sent back to our palace, so that the matter may there be examined as is proper.

[Note: [Col. 0649D] It may be inferred from letter 104 of Saint Boniface that Charlemagne was not the originator of this law. In it he writes to King Pippin as follows: “A certain servant of our Church, himself a most mendacious man, who was fleeing from us by trickery, named Anfrid, came to us with your little letter, asking us to do him justice. We sent him to you with those same letters and with our messenger, so that you might learn that he had lied to you. We ask you, for the sake of your reward, to defend us against such falsifiers and not to believe their lies.” ID.]

### 6. On conspiracies

Whoever presumes to form conspiracies and confirms any conspiracy by oath shall be judged in three ways. First, wherever some evil has been perpetrated through it, the authors of the deed shall be killed; their accomplices, however, shall be flogged by one another and cut off one another’s noses. [Note: [Col. 0650D] A marginal gloss in the Royal Codex reads: “If no evil has been perpetrated, the principal, according to some, must be sent to Corsica; according to others, both the principal and his followers must be flogged; according to others, the principal must die.” ID.] But where no evil has been perpetrated, let them likewise be flogged among themselves and cut off one another’s hair [Note: [Col. 0649] “noses.”]. If, however, a conspiracy has been confirmed by handshakes [Col. 0650C], then, if they are free men, let them either swear with suitable oath-helpers that they did not do this for an evil purpose, or, if they cannot do so, let them pay their legal composition; but if they are slaves [Note: [Col. 0649] “Ch. …” The remainder is missing in P.], let them be flogged. And so that no such conspiracy may henceforth occur in our kingdom, neither by oath nor without oath.

### 7

[Note: [Col. 0649] From 805 B, chapter 16; its final sentence is missing.] Concerning the oppression of poor free men: let it not happen that they are oppressed by the powerful through any evil contrivance against justice, so that they are compelled to sell or surrender their property. We have spoken here of free men lest perhaps parents should be unjustly disinherited, royal service be diminished, and the heirs themselves, through want, become beggars, robbers, or wrongdoers [Note: [Col. 0651] The following is added from a capitulary of Charlemagne in Mut., A., Fl., L., V., Vn., and Est.: “And so that they may not more frequently be summoned to legal assemblies, let it be observed as we prescribe in another chapter.”].

### 8

If anyone has disregarded our letters—that is, the *tractoria* sent for the reception of our envoys—let him either lose the honors he possesses, or remain in the place where he was required to receive the aforesaid envoys and there, at his own expense, receive the embassies coming thither until he has satisfied our will. Whoever, in any manner, disregards our letter shall come to the palace at our command and, according to our will, receive punishment appropriate to his folly. If a free man or a count’s ministerial has done this, let him lose whatever honor or benefice he may have held. If he is a slave, let him be beaten naked at the stake and have his head battered.

[Col. 0651B]

### 9

[Note: [Col. 0651] Missing in Paris.] Whoever, being a free man, refuses to accept a pure and properly weighed denarius [Note: [Col. 0651] At this word the Tegernsee Codex begins folio 87.], shall pay our ban, namely sixty solidi [Note: [Col. 0651] The remainder of this chapter is missing in Teg.]. If ecclesiastical slaves, or the slaves of counts or of our vassals, presume to do this, let them be beaten with sixty blows [Note: [Col. 0651] “blows,” Ch.]. Or if their master or advocate [Note: [Col. 0651] “advocates,” Ch.], who is free, refuses, when ordered, to present them to the count or to our envoy, let him pay the aforesaid ban, namely sixty solidi.

### 10. On false coinage

[Note: [Col. 0651] Missing in Paris. The Tegernsee Codex numbers it IX and continues likewise.] We order concerning false coinage that whoever is convicted of having struck it [Note: [Col. 0651] “whoever struck it or was convicted,” Teg.] shall have his hand cut off [Note: [Col. 0651] “his hand,” Ch.]. Whoever has consented to this, if he is free [Note: [Col. 0651] “hoc consibilis est,” Ch.], shall pay sixty solidi.

### 11

[Note: [Col. 0651] Present in Blank.] We decree that, if anyone is otherwise unable to produce witnesses, then, at the count’s command, those whom each person considers necessary for his testimony [Note: [Col. 0651] “quosque,” Bl.] [Col. 0651C] shall be brought into a public assembly, being about to establish the truth [Note: [Col. 0651] “praelaturi,” Ch., Blk.; “perlaturi,” Teg.; “prolaturi,” Vn., Est.] so that through them the truth of the matter may be investigated with an oath. If an inquiry has been made concerning two parties because neither of them is able to have witnesses, let the inquiry be conducted before they swear. If all the witnesses give testimony on one side, let them swear that they have given true testimony. If they disagree, and a certain part [Note: [Col. 0651] “quadam,” Ch., Bl.] of the witnesses [Note: [Col. 0651] “parte,” Bl.] gives testimony for one [Note: [Col. 0651] “omnium,” Bl.; “unum … alterum,” Ch., A., V., Vn., E.] party and the rest for the other, then let them be asked whether they dare to prove their testimony by combat. If neither party concedes to the other [Note: [Col. 0651] “concedes,” Ch.], let them swear, and let their testimony be proved by combat [Note: [Col. 0651] “the testimony, and then …”; the middle is missing in Bl.]. If one party withdraws [Note: [Col. 0651] “neither,” Ch.; “the party itself …” is missing in Ch.], then let the party that has dared to contend be admitted to give testimony.

### 12

[Note: [Col. 0651] This chapter is missing in the Vatican Codex.] A slave shall not be able to become free for thirty years if his father was a slave or his mother a female slave [Note: [Col. 0651] “and Mur.”]. The same [Note: [Col. 0651] “the same concerning aldiones” is missing in Teg.; “the same and concerning aldiones” in Bl.] is to apply to *aldiones* [Note: [Col. 0651] “we command,” P.].

### 13

[Note: [Col. 0651] The chapter is present in the Florentine Fragment, but in Blank at another place.] No chancellor shall dare to receive for any judgment or document more than half a pound of silver for longer documents; for shorter documents, however, he shall receive less than [Note: [Col. 0651] “the same half-pound,” Bl., Paris, Teg.] half a pound, as the matter requires [Note: [Col. 0651] “as the matter demands,” Teg., Bl., Paris (“king”).] and as seems right to the judges. [Col. 0652B] Concerning orphans and other poor people who cannot pay this, it shall be the count’s responsibility to ensure that he receives nothing from them. [As for little notes, he shall receive nothing except the parchment on which he can write the note itself. C. Blank.] Notaries, however, must swear that they will make no false document, and that no one shall make a document secretly [Note: [Col. 0651] “nor in secret”; “nor shall he make a document,” Teg.] [Note: [Col. 0651] “any document,” Florentine Fragment, Teg.] or make a false one [Note: [Col. 0651] “a false one, nor …,” Vatican, Vn.]; nor shall they make one in one county from another, except with the permission of the count in whose county [Note: [Col. 0651] “the county in which the document itself must stand,” Ch., P.; “the charter itself must stand,” Bl.] it is to remain [Note: [Col. 0651] “they must remain,” Florentine Fragment, Frg.]. But if the necessity of a journey compels someone [Note: [Col. 0651] “something,” Ch., Vatican, Vn.; “some matter,” Florentine Fragment, Frg. Fl.; “someone,” P., Teg.] to do so, or serious illness, let them act according to the capitulary of our lord and father [Note: [Col. 0651] “our lord and father” is missing in Ch., P., Teg., Frg. Fl., Bl.; the rest of the chapter is missing in Teg.]. But if he acts otherwise [Note: [Col. 0651] “if any notary acts otherwise,” Bl.; “if a notary acts otherwise,” Florentine Fragment, Frg.], let him appear empty and void [Note: [Col. 0651] “empty and void,” Vatican, Vn.; “empty,” Bl.]. [Note: [Col. 0651] Here the Vatican Codex ends. In the Florentine Fragment this chapter is preceded by a chapter of Louis II, “On women whose husbands have died,” and is followed by another chapter of the same king, “On charters falsified by certain persons, etc.”]

### 14

It has pleased us that these chapters, which we have excerpted [Col. 0652C] [Note: [Col. 0651] “excersimus,” Ch., P.] from the chapters of our grandfather of blessed memory, Charles, and of our lord and father, Emperor Louis [Note: [Col. 0651] “capitulary,” Florentine Fragment, Vatican, Vn.], be held and observed as law by everyone belonging to the holy Church of God and by our faithful residing in the kingdom of Italy. Whoever proves to be a contemptuous violator of these chapters shall pay a fine of sixty solidi [Note: [Col. 0651] “a fine of solidi denarii,” Blk.], as is contained in the chapters of the aforesaid lord [Note: [Col. 0651] omitted in Ch., Bl.] our grandfather [Note: [Col. 0651] “grandfather”; at this word Teg. ends.] Charles [Note: [Col. 0651D].

In place of what follows, Paris Codex 4613, fol. 961–97, adds the following; these should be compared with and used to correct the Olonna constitutions of the year 823 above:

“13. It has pleased us concerning free women who join themselves to slaves: since they belong to our royal power, we wish that henceforth they belong to those Lombards, both the woman herself and her sons and their daughters.

“14. It has been decreed that, if a free woman joins herself to another man’s slave, and her parents do not give her up for punishment within a year, we wish the royal court to acquire her. If the woman herself has remained with that slave for a year and a day, let the man whose slave he is have her, and let the children born from her be slaves just as their father is.

“15. It has been decreed that, if a free man who has a free wife submits himself to another in servitude on account of some crime or debt, and that wife is unwilling to remain with him, the offspring begotten from that marriage shall not lose the status of freedom. But if, after she has died, a second wife who is nevertheless free knowingly gives herself and joins herself to such a marriage, let their children be subjected to servitude.

“16. If anyone strikes a presbyter, that is, a priest [Leg. ‘a presbyter … a priest’], let him pay ten pounds of the finest gold.”

.

[Col. 0653A]

### 15

Let all who are rebellious on account of any crimes be restrained generally by everyone.

### 16

Concerning those who have scorned to observe the law: let them be brought into our presence through sureties [Note: [Col. 0653] “and,” Ch.].

### 17

Concerning measures: let them be made equal according to our command.

This capitulary was made in the nineteenth year of the empire of our lords Louis and the thirteenth of Lothair, in the month of February, in the tenth indiction [Note: [Col. 0653] “of the impious.”].

# OTHER CHAPTERS

### 1

Concerning wax-makers [Note: [Col. 0653] “wax-maker,” codex c.] and makers of boards and charters: let the practice that has existed for a long time be observed.

### 2

No one shall presume to make oaths through suitable oath-helpers against one another. In another manner, concerning their alms, or fires, or shipwrecks, however much agreements may be made, no one shall presume to swear in this matter.

### 3

No one shall presume to form a *trustis*.

### 4

When people travel to the palace or elsewhere, no one shall dare to attack them with a levy. No one shall presume to take another man’s grass during a time of defense, unless he is going to war or is our envoy. Whoever presumes to act otherwise shall make amends.

### 5

Concerning tolls that had previously been prohibited [Note: [Col. 0653] “prohibited,” c.]: no one shall collect them except where they existed from ancient times.

### 6

Concerning slaves who are sold: let them be sold in the presence of the bishop or count [Note: [Col. 0653] “sold in their presence” is missing in c.], or in the presence of the count’s deputy or judge [Note: [Col. 0653] “judge,” c.], or before witnesses of established reputation. No one shall sell slaves outside the march; [Col. 0653C] whoever does so shall pay the ban as many times as he sold slaves. If he does not have the price, let him give himself to the count as a pledge until he pays those bans.

### 7

No one shall presume to sell coats of mail outside our kingdom.

### 8

If a count has not administered justice in his office, let him cause a complaint concerning his household [Note: [Col. 0654D] That is, *casa* (“household”).] to be made to our envoy until justice has been carried out there. If our vassal has not administered justice, then let the count and the envoy sit in judgment over his case and live from his property until they administer justice.

[Col. 0654A]

### 9

If someone does not wish to accept a payment for a feud, let him be sent to us, and let us send him wherever he can cause the least harm.

### 10

Likewise, those who have refused to pay compensation for a feud and to administer justice concerning it: we wish to send them to such a place that no greater harm may thereby grow.

### 11

Concerning thieves, we command that this be observed: let them not be put to death for the first offense. For the second offense, let them lose their nose. For the third, if they have not made amends, let them die.

### 12

Concerning monasteries and hospices which are found in various counties and belong to the crown: whoever wishes to hold them shall hold them as a benefice from our lord the king.

[Col. 0654B]

### 13

Concerning the property delivered to Queen Hildegard: we wish it to be recorded in brief inventories, and we command that those inventories be brought to us.

### 14

It has pleased us concerning those documents made regarding individual persons who surrendered themselves, their wives, and their sons or daughters into servitude: wherever they are found, let them be returned, and let them be free as they originally were.

### 15

Concerning weapons for the army: let the rule stand as we previously stated it in another capitulary. In addition, every man possessing twelve manses [Note: [Col. 0653] “months,” c.] shall have a coat of mail. Whoever possesses a coat of mail but does not bring it with him shall lose the entire benefice together with the coat of mail.

### 16

No one shall promise fidelity to another by oath, except to us and to each man’s own lord, for our benefit and that of his own lord [Note: [Col. 0653] “their,” c.], except for those oaths which, according to law, one person ought to owe another. And the young men who previously could not swear because of their youthful age shall now promise fidelity to us.

### 17

Concerning perjuries: let precautions be taken, and let witnesses not be admitted to swear before they have been examined. If they cannot otherwise be examined, let them be separated from one another and questioned individually [Note: [Col. 0654D] Some codices read: “Let them be separated from one another.” Alcuin, in his *Book on Virtues and Vices* to Count Witto, chapter 20: “If false witnesses are separated, they are immediately found to be liars.” BALUZ.], so that the accuser alone [Note: [Col. 0654D] That is, the plaintiff, as an old interlinear gloss in one Royal Codex says. This was rightly observed so that no one might think that only criminal cases were meant here. ID.] may not be permitted [Note: [Col. 0654D] “That is, to bring witnesses so that they may swear,” says the same gloss. Hence another gloss in another Royal Codex says: “The defendant too is permitted to choose witnesses and to object, according to Lothair’s chapter: ‘If anyone with another …’” ID.] to choose witnesses while his opposing litigants are absent [Note: [Col. 0653] “licet ut,” c.]. No one at all shall be admitted to an oath [Note: [Col. 0653] “judgment,” c.] or to testimony unless fasting. And the person who is brought forward as a witness [Note: [Col. 0654D] A charter of King Louis VI for the monastery of Fosses: “But if anyone, through rash presumption, rejects their testimony in any matter.” The old history of Trier in volume XII of Dacher’s *Spicilegium*, p. 219: “He began altogether to reject charity from the brothers,” that is, to refuse it, as the distinguished editor notes in the margin. A rule of someone in the *Harmony of Rules*, p. 728: “Flesh and wine, or a drink in which there is drunkenness, are to be rejected by monks and not accepted.” See the notes of Hugh Menard there. BALUZ.]—if he is rejected, let the person who rejects him say and prove why he does not wish to accept him. Let witnesses be chosen from that same district, unless the case must be investigated farther outside the county. If anyone is convicted, let him lose his hand or redeem it.

[Col. 0655A]

### 18

Concerning advocates: corrupt advocates, deputy lords, deputies, or centenarii are to be removed, and such men are to be chosen [Note: [Col. 0655] “who …” is missing in c.] as know and wish to discern and determine cases justly. If a count is found to be corrupt, let this be reported to us.

### 19

It pleases us that just and ancient tolls be collected from merchants, both at bridges and from ships and markets. But new or unjust tolls—where ropes are stretched, or ships pass beneath bridges, or in similar circumstances in which no assistance is provided to travelers—are not to be collected. The same applies to Jews who, for purposes of trade, transport their property from one house of theirs to another, or to a legal assembly, or to the army [Note: [Col. 0655C] Or, “to supply their needs,” as it is written in a charter of Louis the Pious granting the monastery of Micy immunity from taxes on ships traveling along the rivers of the Frankish kingdom for any needs of the aforesaid monastery. This privilege was later confirmed by Charles the Bald. Pippin, king of Aquitaine, granted a similar privilege to the monastery of Saint-Philibert, as is clear from his charter, edited by R. P. Chifflet in his *History of the Monastery of Tournus*, p. 192. Likewise, Emperor Lothair granted a similar privilege to the monastery of Deûlémont, in the same Chifflet, p. 264. A similar privilege granted to the Church of Angers by Louis the Pious was published by the Sammarthani in volume II of *Gallia Christiana*; and another of Charlemagne for the monastery of Organo near Verona was published by Ferdinand Ughelli in volume V of *Italia Sacra*, p. 600. We also possess charters of Charlemagne and Pippin, king of Aquitaine, granting the monastery of Cormery immunity from tolls and other taxes for two ships traveling on various rivers. There is likewise a charter of Louis the Pious granting five ships to the Church of Vienne for transporting its business goods, and another concerning four ships of the monastery of Saint-Germain of Auxerre. Louis also granted the monastery of Saint-Aignan of Orléans the privilege of having six ships “which may travel wherever they wish, whether along the Loire River or along the other rivers within the jurisdiction of our empire, for the benefit and needs of the monastery,” as is recorded in letters of that same Louis edited by the distinguished Hubert, p. 75 of the *Proofs for the History of the Monastery of Saint-Aignan*. We have noted these matters so that readers might recognize that the general law now under discussion required the special authority of the ruler in order to be enforced in each individual place. ID.] If there is any matter about which doubt arises, let them be questioned at the nearest assembly of ours which we shall attend with those envoys [Note: [Col. 0655] “questioned,” c.].

### 20

Concerning various people who wish to give themselves to the service of God: let them not do so before requesting permission from us [Col. 0656A]. This is because we have heard that some of them do so not so much out of devotion as to flee military service or some other royal duty. We have also heard that some have been deceived, out of greed, by those who covet their property; for this reason we prohibit it from being done.

21. We wish our envoys to exact this faithfully, without favor, flattery, or intimidation toward anyone, according to our command; that is, from a man possessing six pounds in gold and silver, mail-shirts, bronze, whole cloths, camels, oxen, cows, or other property—[Note: [Col. 0656B] That is, livestock and animals. Hence *peculium* of either sex occurs in an old charter of the monastery of Schäftlarn in the third volume of the *Metropolis Salisburgensis*, [Col. 0656C] p. 321. The ancient statutes of Saint Peter of Corbie in the fourth volume of D’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, p. 20: “Likewise, whatever is acquired in any manner through various labors, or whatever is raised among various kinds of property.” The testament of Count Evrard in Aubertus Miraeus, *Codex donationum piarum*, p. 99, and in the twelfth volume of the same *Spicilegium*, p. 495: “Whether in labor or in property.” Moreover, in this passage of the present chapter, where *peculio* is read here, the Palatine and Beauvais manuscripts have *pecunio*. The meaning is the same. In the testament of Saint Aldric, bishop of Le Mans, we read that he decreed that whatever “of various kinds of money” and clothing should be found after his death in his workshop should be given to the monastery he founded beside the River Sarthe. A privilege of Charlemagne issued for the monastery of Aniane, edited by Mabillon, vol. V, p. 222: “For the pasture of herds and the feeding of livestock”; in place of this, Louis the Pious wrote in another privilege found there, p. 223: “For the pasture of herds [Col. 0656D] and the feeding of livestock.” A homily by an unknown author in a very ancient manuscript of Saint Gall: “When Abraham gave tithes from the spoils, how much more should every person give from his labor, from all his property, and from all his animals.” The Council of Douzy, p. 293 in Cellot’s edition, and p. 1655 in volume VIII of the latest edition of the Councils: “money of diverse kind and sex.” Cellotius, in his notes on this passage, since he did not understand it, explained *pecuniam* here as coined silver [ [Col. 0656D] See Servius, on Virgil’s First Eclogue.]; these are his words: “An unusual word, he says, and one I have read nowhere else. Nor can I imagine any other sex in money unless you take gold as the male and coined silver as the female.” Elsewhere, however, *pecunia* signifies any object that someone has purchased with his money, as in Book V of the *Capitularies*, chapter 347, and Book VI, chapter 11, and in the *Capitularies of Lothar*, title 3, chapter 12.] property; and wives or children are not to be stripped of their possessions on this account, from whose clothing and movable property the lawful *aribannum* is to be paid, or three pounds. But from one who possesses no more than property worth three pounds at the aforesaid valuation, let them exact thirty solidi. From one who possesses no more than two pounds, ten solidi; but if he possesses one pound, five solidi, so that he may again be able to prepare himself for the service of God and for our benefit. And let our envoys beware and inquire diligently lest, through any malicious contrivance, they divert our justice by transferring or entrusting it to another.

[Col. 0657A] 22. Whatever royal census was lawfully due from any source, we wish it to be paid, whether from the person himself or from his property.

23. Let each bishop and abbot carefully consider the custody of the church treasury, lest through treachery [Note: [Col. 0657] The manuscript reads *fidiam*.] or negligence anything from the gems, vessels, or the rest of the treasury be lost; for it has been reported to us that Jewish merchants, and others as well, boast that they can buy from them whatever pleases them.

24. We have heard that in some places they transfer our benefice to other men as property, and at the same assembly accept a price and buy the same property back for themselves as an allod [Note: [Col. 0657D] *Alodium* was formerly used for a free estate subject to no one’s jurisdiction, as Sirmondus says in his notes on Geoffrey of Vendôme, p. 5. Baluze.] . This must be avoided altogether, because those who do this do not faithfully preserve the loyalty they have promised us. And indeed we may perhaps discover some disloyalty, since those who do such things arrange matters so that such deeds of theirs do not reach our ears, as they wish.

25. Concerning beggars who roam through the country: we wish each of our faithful men to feed his own poor person from his benefice or from his household, and not permit him to go elsewhere begging. Wherever such people are found, unless they work with their hands, no one should dare give them anything [Note: [Col. 0657] The manuscript reads *nullum*.].

26. Concerning the ability of free men: they must perform military service according to the quality of their property.

27. Let no one consent to his men doing evil in the country. As for their claim that they cannot have men for the defense of the mark, they can do so if they properly constrain them.

28. Concerning the royal vassals: they are to be honored, and they are to remain personally attached to us or to our sons.

29. Free men are not to be outlawed for assemblies, except when a complaint has been brought against someone, or when there is no *scabinus* or judge, so that those poor men are not condemned on this account.

30. A free man who cannot pay whatever fine he owes, and has no surety, may place himself in pledge to the person to whom he is indebted, until he has paid the fine he owed. In the same chapter, concerning [an uncertain term, *soniste*; the manuscript reads *cles oniste*], let him either pay sixty solidi, or swear with twelve men; or, if the person pursuing the case is unwilling to accept the oath of twelve men, let them contend against him by the cross, or with shield and staff [Col. 0657D].

31. Concerning those who abandon the world: let them choose one of two alternatives, so that they must live wholly either according to canonical or according to monastic discipline [Note: [Col. 0657] The manuscript lacks the words “so that they must live wholly according to canonical discipline.”].

32. Concerning the justice owed to the churches of God, widows, orphans, and wards [Col. 0658A]: let them not be disregarded when they bring complaints before public judges, but let them be heard carefully.

33. If our slave is killed, let our royal estate take two parts of the composition, and the third part the parents of that deceased slave of ours, as we said above. We establish this for our own days and during the time of our reign, although our law cannot [Note: [Col. 0657] The manuscript reads *sit*.]. After our death, whoever is prince at that time shall act as God inspires him, or rightly, according to what he judges in his conscience. For we have learned, not once but many times, that when such cases have arisen, what our officials have taken from them has benefited neither the public treasury nor any department of the palace. Moreover, we have found and learned that many of our officials took from one person ten solidi, from another six, from another more, and granted such delay and respite that the person who had committed the homicide could plead that he should pay nothing for it. Therefore we have decided that our estate shall receive half of the composition for *aldiones*, and two parts for slaves [Note: [Col. 0657] The manuscript reads: “for slaves. As was said above, as this book has it.”], as we said above; while the close relatives themselves, since they suffer grief, should receive some consolation by way of recompense.

34. For the sake of God and his mercy, we command and establish, solely out of compassion, that if one of our *aldiones* is killed, our estate shall take half of the composition, and the other half the parents of the deceased, if the deceased, our *aldio*, has a living father, mother, brothers, or sons.

[Col. 0658C] 35. We command that no one dare buy anything from our slave or from our *aldio*. For the sake of security and for future times, we are having inventories made for all our estates of all the territories belonging to those estates. Therefore we command that whoever from now on is found to have bought anything from a slave, an *aldio* [Note: [Col. 0657] The manuscript reads *aldine*.], or even from our estate shall lose it, like one who unjustly seizes another’s property. And if an official has consented or had knowledge of it, let his property be seized and forfeited to the public. For everyone must consider, for God’s sake and for the sake of his soul, that we have released to him, as a free man [Note: [Col. 0657] Others read “but others”;], the *eremmannos* that belonged to us in our estates according to the ancient edict and the laws. Formerly, whoever left only one daughter inherited a third part of her father’s property [Note: [Col. 0657] The words “whoever left only one daughter” are lacking in the manuscript.], and two parts reverted to the public [Col. 0658D] if he had no close relatives [Note: [Col. 0657] The manuscript adds: “He inherited only a third part of his father’s property, and two parts reverted to the public.”]. And if someone had two daughters or more, they inherited only half from their father, and half went to the public. But now, behold, for the sake of God and his mercy [Note: [Col. 0657] “And for the sake of the reward of my soul” is found above.], we have released everything concerning such matters [Note: [Col. 0657] The manuscript reads *relavimus*.]. Therefore each person ought to be satisfied with his own property and ought not, contrary to reason, desire to purchase anything from our slave, *aldio*, or *abtin*. Whoever presumes to do this shall pay the composition prescribed in writing. Moreover, he appears to us to incur the guilt of perjury, since he has sworn to us that he is faithful to us. For what kind of loyalty is it when he conspires with judges, an official, an *aldio*, or a slave, and invades our property against our will? It has been established in the edict that whoever purchases anything from a slave or an *aldio* loses the price; and whatever law each Lombard wishes to have, he must preserve in our estate. Whoever from now on purchases anything, or gives it as a security, shall lose his price according to the force of the edict. Whoever presumes to act in this way shall lose both the price and, like one who unjustly invades another’s property without the owner’s knowledge, shall pay a composition. The official who has consented shall lose his property, as is stated above. For since we have released these things, each person should possess what we have commanded or shall command him to possess.

36. How the lord king commands all officials who have charge of his estates to act. First, concerning what has been confiscated in our time: each official is to swear and say on the Gospels: “Whatever I discover to have been taken from anyone contrary to justice, I will report to my lord the king [Col. 0660A], so that it may be released.” He must say in the oath, however, that he will do this neither out of favor toward a friend nor toward a relative, nor because he has been corrupted by a bribe, but only when he knows for certain that something was taken contrary to justice. Once it has been reported to us, it shall be released by our command.

37. Therefore we establish that possession of public property is to be investigated for sixty years. Since, because of pressing sins, no one remembers events from forty years ago, and few are found who live so many years, we establish that—except where something has already been confiscated through justice—if any seizure or fraud against public property occurred within thirty years, it is to be investigated and reported to us. It must not, however, be presumed beforehand that the property should be *wiffed* or distrained. For we wish to hear this case ourselves and order it according to God’s will. [Col. 0660B] For it has become clear to us that, if we ourselves hear the case, with God’s favor we can investigate it without sin and order it in such a way that we may gain merit; for neither our judges, nor our free men, nor our officials can enforce such discipline as we can. Whatever has been proved for thirty years, or has been in anyone’s possession for that period, he shall continue to hold from now on; no official may presume either to *wiff* it or molest him. Whoever presumes to do so, that official shall pay his own *wergeld*, except where a false privilege is discovered [Note: [Col. 0659] The manuscript reads *inuentur*.], which is plainly a matter requiring investigation [Note: [Col. 0659] The manuscript reads *opeta*.].

# The Assembly of Emperor Lothar at Compiègne (October 833)

[Col. 0659]

[Col. 0659] From the acts of the assembly at which Emperor Louis was deposed, there survive the report of the bishops and a document presented to Lothar by Agobard, archbishop of Lyon, as a model for the other bishops. We publish this document again, which is commonly circulated among the works of Agobard and has been collated with the unique manuscript in the Royal Library at Paris, no. 2853 m., ninth century; we present the bishops’ report from Sirmond’s *Councils of Gaul*, vol. II, p. 560.

## Report of the Bishops Concerning the Deposition of Emperor Louis

[Col. 0659C]

It is fitting that all who belong to the Christian religion should know what the ministry of bishops is, and what vigilance and care they must exercise concerning the salvation of all—bishops who are known to be Christ’s vicars and the key-bearers of the kingdom of heaven. Christ has bestowed such power upon them that whatever they bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever they loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven.

And how great is the danger in which they themselves stand if they neglect to administer the food of life to Christ’s sheep, and do not strive with all their strength to bring the straying back to the way of truth by rebuking and exhorting them, according to the prophetic saying: “If you do not announce his wickedness to the wicked man,” he says, “and he dies in his ungodliness, I will require his blood from your hand”—along with many similar passages concerning pastoral instruction that are scattered throughout the divine Scriptures.

Therefore these same shepherds of Christ must strive above all to maintain the most discerning moderation toward the faults of sinners, so that, according to the teaching and example of blessed Gregory, they may be companions in humility to those who act well, but, through zeal for justice, stand upright against the vices of sinners [Col. 0660C]. Thus, setting aside sluggishness and negligence, human favor and worldly fear, they must exercise their ministry in such a way that they may beneficially advise those living in the present and serve as examples of salvation to those who come after.

But because harmful growths never cease to spring up through the prompting of the ancient enemy in the field of God, which is the Church of Christ, and must be uprooted from their roots by the pastor’s hoe, and because certain malicious people either do not wish to understand good deeds or prefer, with malicious intent, to understand them in a sense contrary to the truth itself, these same shepherds ought, whenever they have decreed anything in their assemblies concerning the common good or public correction, to commit it to writing according to ecclesiastical custom. In this way they will completely remove from posterity every ambiguity and opportunity for legitimate disparagement or criticism [Col. 0660D].

Therefore we have thought it necessary to make known to all the sons of the holy Church of God, present and future, how we bishops, assembled under the rule of the lord and most glorious Emperor Lothar, met in general assembly at the palace called Compiègne in the year of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 833, in the twelfth indiction, and in the first year of that prince’s reign, specifically in the month of October; and how we humbly heard the aforesaid prince.

We took care, according to the ministry entrusted to us, to make clear to him, to his nobles, and to the entire body of people who had gathered there from every direction, what the force, power, and ministry of the priesthood are, and by what judgment he deserves to be condemned who refuses to obey priestly admonitions. Then we endeavored to warn both the aforesaid prince and all his people that they should strive most devoutly to please the Lord and should not delay appeasing him for the things by which they had offended him.

Many matters were examined that had occurred in this empire through negligence and that, by evident signs, concerned the scandal of the Church, the ruin of the people, or the destruction of the kingdom [Col. 0661B]. These matters had to be corrected quickly and avoided in every way in the future.

Among other things, we also recalled to everyone how God, through the administration of the Emperor Charles of blessed memory and through the labor of his predecessors, had made this kingdom peaceful, united, and nobly enlarged, and had entrusted it to the Emperor Louis to govern under great peace. Under the Lord’s protection, it remained in that same peace for as long as that prince strove to serve God, sought to follow his father’s examples, and was willing to heed the counsels of good men.

We also recalled how, as time went on, as was evident to everyone, through his lack of foresight and negligence it had fallen into such disgrace and low condition that it became not only a source of sorrow to its friends but also an object of ridicule to its enemies [Col. 0661C].

But because that prince had handled the ministry entrusted to him negligently, had done many things displeasing to God and to men, had compelled or permitted them to be done, had provoked God in many wicked counsels, and had scandalized the holy Church—and, to omit the countless other matters, had finally drawn the whole people subject to him into general destruction—the imperial power was suddenly taken from him by divine and just judgment.

Nevertheless, remembering God’s commands, our ministry, and his benefits, we judged it fitting, with the permission of the aforesaid Prince Lothar, to send a delegation to him by the authority of the sacred assembly. It was to warn him of his offenses so that he might adopt a definite plan for his salvation and, since he had been deprived of earthly power, might strive with all his strength, being in extremity, to save his soul according to divine counsel and ecclesiastical authority [Col. 0661D].

He willingly assented to the counsels and salutary admonitions of these envoys, asked for a period of time, and appointed a day on which he would give them a definite answer concerning their salutary admonitions.

When the appointed day arrived, the sacred assembly went unanimously to that venerable man, carefully admonished him concerning the ways in which he had offended God, scandalized the holy Church, and disturbed the people entrusted to him, and took care to recall all these matters to his memory [Col. 0662A]. He, gladly embracing their life-giving admonition and their appropriate and fittingly forceful reproach, promised that he would accept their salutary counsel in all things and undergo remedial judgment.

Then, joyful because of such a salutary admonition, he immediately begged that his beloved son, Lothar Augustus, should hasten to come to him, so that Lothar might, without any delay, come with his leading men. First, he wished a mutual reconciliation between them to take place according to Christian teaching, so that if any stain or discord existed in their hearts, a pure and humble request for forgiveness might cleanse it; and then, before the entire multitude, he wished to receive priestly judgment in the manner of a penitent. This was done not long afterward [Col. 0662B].

The lord Louis therefore came to the basilica of Saint Mary, Mother of God, where the bodies of the saints rest—namely, Medard, confessor and bishop of Christ, and the most outstanding martyr Sebastian. Priests, deacons, and a considerable number of clergy were present, as were the aforesaid lord Lothar, his son, his nobles, and the entire body of the people, as many as that church could contain within its enclosure.

Prostrated on the ground upon sackcloth before the most holy altar, he confessed before everyone that he had handled the ministry entrusted to him quite unworthily, had offended God in many ways through it, had scandalized the Church of Christ, and through his negligence had brought the people into disturbance in many different ways [Col. 0662C].

Therefore, he said that he wished to seek public and ecclesiastical penance for the expiation of such great offenses, so that, with the Lord’s mercy, through their ministry and assistance he might deserve to receive absolution from the many crimes over which God had bestowed upon them the power of binding and loosing.

The same bishops, as spiritual physicians, then gave him salutary admonitions. They asserted that true remission of sins followed a pure and simple confession, and instructed him openly to confess his errors—those in which he professed to have especially offended God—lest he conceal something within or deceitfully do anything in God’s sight. It was already known to everyone that formerly, at the palace of Compiègne, he had been corrected before the entire Church by another sacred assembly for having done this.

They warned him lest, as then, so now, by approaching God with a divided heart through pretense and cunning, he provoke anger rather than forgiveness for his sins [Col. 0662D], since Scripture testifies that hypocrites and the crafty provoke God’s anger.

After this admonition, he declared that he had especially sinned in all those matters concerning which the aforesaid priests had admonished and corrected him privately, whether by word or in writing, with deserved reproach. They gave him a summary document containing his offenses, identifying specifically the matters for which they rebuked him, and he carried it in his hands.

1. As the same document explains more fully, he incurred the guilt of sacrilege and homicide because he had not kept, according to his promise, the paternal admonition and terrible warning made to him under invocation of God before the holy altar, in the presence of priests and a very large crowd of people [Col. 0663A]. He had inflicted violence upon his brothers and relatives, and had permitted his nephew, whom he himself could have freed, to be killed. He had also, forgetful of his vow, later ordered the sign of holy religion to be made on account of his vengeful anger.

2. Since he had been the author of scandal, the disturber of peace, and the violator of oaths, he had corrupted, through unlawful power, the pact made for the peace and unity of the empire and the tranquility of the Church by the common counsel and agreement of all his faithful men, and confirmed by oath. He had also compelled his faithful men to swear another oath contrary to that first pact and oath, and by violating the oaths they had given had fallen under the guilt of perjury [Col. 0663B].

How displeasing this was to God is perfectly clear, because afterward neither he nor the people subject to him deserved to have peace; rather, by the just judgment of God, they were all subsequently brought into disturbance while suffering the punishment of sin.

3. Contrary to the Christian religion and to his own vow, without any public benefit or certain necessity, deceived by the counsel of wicked men, he ordered a general military expedition during the days of Lent. He also appointed a general assembly at the farthest boundaries of his empire on the Lord’s Supper, when all Christians ought properly to celebrate the Paschal mysteries.

In this expedition, insofar as it lay within his power, he drove the people into great murmuring, removed the priests of the Lord from their offices contrary to law, and inflicted the gravest oppression upon the poor [Col. 0663C].

4. He inflicted violence upon certain of his faithful men who had humbly approached him for the loyalty and safety of himself and his sons, and for the recovery of the wavering kingdom, and who had given him reliable information about the ambushes prepared by his enemies.

Contrary to every law, divine and human, he deprived these men of their property, ordered them to be driven into exile [*tradi* in manuscript S.], caused those who were absent to be condemned to death, and undoubtedly led those who judged them into a false judgment. He also inflicted prejudice upon the priests and monks of the Lord contrary to divine and canonical authority, condemned absent men, and in this way, by incurring the guilt of homicide, became a violator of divine and human laws [Col. 0663D].

5. He had repeatedly and irrationally caused various oaths, mutually contradictory and harmful, to be sworn by his sons or by the people, ordering and compelling them to do so. For this he had brought no small stain of sin upon the people entrusted to him and had likewise incurred the guilt of perjury, since such acts are rightly charged against the author through whom they were compelled.

As for the purgation of women, unjust judgments, false testimonies, and perjuries committed in his presence with his permission, he alone knows how greatly he offended God.

[Col. 0664A] 6. He undertook various military expeditions in the kingdom entrusted to him, not only uselessly but harmfully, without counsel or benefit. In them countless and innumerable crimes were perpetrated among the Christian people: homicides and perjuries, sacrileges, adulteries, robberies, and arsons committed both in the churches of God and in various other places; plundering and oppression of the poor were carried out in a lamentable manner, scarcely heard of among Christians. All these things, as stated above, rebound upon the author.

7. He arbitrarily and rashly made divisions of the empire contrary to the common peace and the welfare of the whole empire. He also compelled the entire people to swear an oath that they should act against his sons as against enemies, although he could have reconciled them through paternal authority and the counsel of his faithful men [Col. 0664B].

8. The many evils and crimes perpetrated through his negligence and lack of foresight in the kingdom entrusted to him—evils that cannot be enumerated, and from which the endangerment of the kingdom and the dishonor of the king had plainly arisen—were not enough for him. On top of all these miseries, he finally dragged the entire people subject to his power into common destruction, although he ought to have been a guide of salvation and peace to that people, at a time when divine mercy had resolved to have pity on its people in an unheard-of and invisible manner, one proclaimed to our age.

Therefore, concerning all these matters mentioned above and in relation to them, he confessed with tears before God, the priests, and the entire people that he was guilty, and declared that he had sinned in everything [*esset* in manuscript S.]. He sought public penance so that, by repenting, he might make satisfaction to the Church that he had scandalized by sinning. Just as he had been a source of scandal by neglecting many things, so he declared that he wished to become an example by undergoing worthy penance [Col. 0664C].

After this confession, he handed over to the priests, for future remembrance, the document containing his offenses and confession. They placed it upon the altar. Then he removed the belt of military service and placed it upon the altar; stripping off his worldly clothing, he received the clothing of a penitent through the laying on of the bishops’ hands, so that after such great and serious penance no one might return to secular military service.

After these matters had been completed, it seemed good that each bishop should insert in his own document an account of how this affair had been conducted, confirm it with his own writing, and offer the signed document to the aforesaid Prince Lothar as a memorial of the event. Finally, it seemed good to all of us who were present to gather briefly and concisely into one document the contents of all the documents—or rather, the substance of so great a matter—and to confirm what had been gathered by the subscriptions of our own hands, as the following demonstrates was done.

## Agobard’s Document

In the name of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ. In the year 833 of his incarnation, I, Agobard, unworthy bishop of the Church of Lyon, was present at the venerable assembly held at the palace called Compiègne.

This assembly consisted of most reverend bishops, most magnificent and illustrious men, a college of abbots and counts, and a people of diverse ages and dignities, under the presidency of the serene and most glorious Lothar, emperor and lover of Christ the Lord. Under his protection and with his assistance, the provisions written below were arranged in the first year of his reign, in the fourth month [Col. 0665A].

All these people were strongly compelled by true necessity to deliberate carefully about the danger facing the kingdom in the present and its future condition. For the kingdom had long been wavering and was being driven toward ruin through the negligence—or, to speak more truthfully, the cowardice—of the lord Louis [Note: [Col. 0665] The manuscript reads *luduuici*, but in what follows the initial *h* is present.] , once a venerable emperor. He had become entangled among corrupt minds and corrupters, who, according to the apostolic saying, were themselves wandering and leading others into error.

Whatever was discovered through useful and praiseworthy deliberation and consultation, whatever had necessarily to be established, I approved in judging and, by agreeing, judged myself. First came the matters that seemed to concern the welfare and stability of the kingdom and the king; then those that were clearly recognized as concerning the rescue and purification of the soul of the lord Louis.

These matters were diligently sought, truthfully discovered, and orderly carried out in the aforesaid assembly. The assembly determined that, through envoys and messengers, the lord Louis should be admonished concerning his errors and exhorted, according to the prophetic saying, to return to his heart and recognize his deeds, which he had carried out against God while running along the paths of wickedness and injustice [Col. 0665C]. He was then to accept counsel for his life and salvation, so that he might obtain indulgence and remission of his iniquities from the omnipotent Judge and Lord, who is most merciful in pardoning crimes.

Thus, although through repeated negligences he had lost the earthly kingdom, through humble confessions offered in prayer he might obtain the heavenly kingdom through him with whom there is mercy and abundant redemption [Col. 0666A].

For this reason a booklet was also produced by more diligent men and presented to him, setting out the disclosure of his crimes. In it, as in a mirror, he could plainly see the ugliness of his deeds, and the saying spoken by the perfect penitent might be fulfilled in him: “I acknowledge my iniquity; my sin is always before me.”

For this reason all the bishops who had been present at the aforesaid assembly approached him again, grieving and sympathizing with his weaknesses and miseries, exhorting, wishing, and asking that almighty God might, by the hand of his mercy, lead him out of the pit of misery and the mire of filth [Col. 0666A].

The most merciful Lord did not merely fail to take this away, but did not even delay it. As soon as contrition of humble heart had been revived in his mind, he prostrated himself before them—not once or twice, but three times or more—acknowledged his crimes, asked forgiveness, begged the assistance of their prayers, received counsel, requested penance, and promised that he would most willingly fulfill the humility imposed upon him.

The law and order of public penance were explained to him. He did not reject it but agreed to everything. Finally, he entered the church before the assembly of the faithful, before the altar and the tombs of the saints, and, prostrated upon sackcloth, confessed two, three, and four times, in a loud voice and with an abundant outpouring of tears. Having laid down his weapons with his own hand and thrown them at the foot of the altar [Note: [Col. 0665] This is the text; the corrected reading is “having laid down his weapons,” with the accusatives used absolutely, as was customary in that period.], he received public penance with a contrite heart through the laying on of the bishops’ hands, with psalms and prayers [Col. 0666B].

Having thus put off his former clothing and assumed the clothing of a penitent, he rejoiced and took confidence, and asked to be carried back upon the shoulders of the most pious shepherd into the unity of the sheep that had been found and redeemed.

After these events I, Agobard, unworthy bishop, was present; agreeing and consenting with the better judgment, I judged and subscribed by placing my own mark.

# The Assembly of Emperor Louis at Compiègne (835)

[Col. 0665]

[Col. 0665] From his acts, more fully described in the *Bertinian Annals*, there survives a document of Ebo, archbishop of Reims, by which he resigned his see. We present it here again from his apologetic booklet [Note: [Col. 0665D] Edited from manuscript no. 576 of the Palatine Library, in D’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, vol. VII, p. 175.] in a tenth-century manuscript of the ducal library at Wolfenbüttel, among the Helmstedt manuscripts, no. 32.

I, Ebo, unworthy bishop, recognizing my weakness and the weight of my sins, appointed as judges of my offenses my confessors and witnesses—namely, Archbishop Aiulf [Note: [Col. 0665D] Of Bourges.], and also the bishops Badarad [Note: [Col. 0666D] Of Paderborn.] and Modoin [Note: [Col. 0666D] Of Autun.]. I gave them a pure confession, seeking a remedy through penance and the salvation of my soul, so that I might withdraw from the episcopal office and ministry, of which I recognize myself to be unworthy, and make myself separate on account of my offenses, in which I secretly confessed to them that I had sinned.

I did this in such a way that they might be witnesses to another’s succeeding, being consecrated, and being substituted in my place—someone who could worthily preside over and benefit the church over which I had until then presided unworthily; and so that from that point I might be unable, by canonical authority, to make any claim or appeal. I have confirmed this by subscribing with my own hand.

# Fragments of Chapters

[Col. 0667]

[Col. 0667] The Gotha Codex, fol. 405, after the response to the bishops’ consultation of 829 and before proceeding to the capitularies of Emperor Lothar, presents several chapters, each marked with its own number: namely, chapter XXV, the chapter edited above, which the Gotha Codex had already presented at the end of the capitulary of 805 as number XXV; then the canon “If any brother” [Note: “If any brother” means, that is, a Christian, and he is a fornicator, or greedy, or serves idols, or is a slanderer, or a drunkard, or a robber, “with such a one do not even take food; remove the evil from among yourselves.”]; afterward chapter IX, which we edited above; chapter IV, concerning possession for thirty years; without a number, “Eight kinds”; chapters II and III, edited above from the Codex of Saint Paul. We have judged that those among these which do not appear above should be presented here.

[Col. 0667A] 1. Concerning possession for thirty years. If anyone has possessed houses, households, or lands for thirty years, and it has been established that the possession was his, after the completion of thirty years no legal contest shall arise—unless the possessor himself, according to the value of the property, defends it with his oath-compurgators. For, as has been said, this is not subject to a contest.

2. Tullius describes eight kinds of punishment as existing in the laws: the ban, bonds, blows, retaliation, disgrace, exile, death, and slavery. Whichever of these is appropriate to the degree of each person’s offense, when it is discovered to have been committed, should be imposed for a short period—except perhaps retaliation; for its purpose is that each person should suffer what he has done. Hence the legal maxim: “An eye for an eye; a tooth for a tooth.” For it can happen that, through the severity of vengeance, someone loses in so short a time the eye [Note: The codex reads *quae*, corrected to *quem*.] which he himself took from another through the wickedness of his offense. [Note: “According to the degree?”]

# THE LOMBARD CHAPTERS OF EMPEROR LOTHAR I

[Col. 0667]

[Col. 0667] These chapters, since they were not found in the Chisian, Cava, Paris, Blankenburg, or Gotha manuscripts of the laws of the Lombards, could not be assigned to any definite period; nevertheless, it is clear that they were issued between 832 and 840, since after that time Lothar, having been involved in wars in Gaul and Germany for three years and having raised his son Louis to be king of the Lombards in 844, did not return to Italy.

[Col. 0667B] From the Ambrosian, Florentine, London, Vienna, Veronese, and Este manuscripts.

1. [Note: In Muratori, chapter 78.] We wish that, if any person within the borders of our kingdom dares to kindle a fire in a forest [Note: So the manuscripts; that is, “to light” it; in Italian, *avvivare il fuoco*. Muratori reads “to threaten.”], diligent inquiry be made [Note: “Let inquiry be made,” V.]. If a slave is proved to have done this, either his master shall hand him over to be flogged and beaten on the head, or he shall be compelled to make good whatever damage he has caused. If, however, any free person is proved to have done this, he shall be compelled to make full restitution and shall additionally pay our ban; and if he has nothing with which to pay, he shall be flogged. When this has occurred, inquiry shall be made by the leading men of that place. If suspicion falls upon any person, then, if he is a slave, his master shall send him to judgment or shall swear an oath on his behalf; but if he is a free person, he shall establish his innocence by his own oath.

2. [Note: Muratori, chapter 79.] We have learned by report that in the territory of Tuscany documents have been issued which lack the month and day of the month [Col. 0668B]. We decree that, if any such documents are issued henceforth, they shall have no validity.

3. [Note: Muratori, chapter 91.] Each church shall have a defined territory from whose villages it is to receive the tithe [Note: “Receive,” V.].

4. [Note: Muratori, chapter 97.] Concerning notaries who receive charters for writing: if they do not write them, or if they lose them, they shall restore the property itself to the person whose charters had been entrusted to them. If they deny that it was entrusted to them, they shall swear together with their oath-compurgators [Note: Singular, “let him swear,” Vn.].

## From the London Codex

5. Anyone who comes to court as a possessor is not to be compelled to say from whom he holds the property, nor should the burden of proof be imposed upon him; rather, it is the duty of the claimant to show that the thing he claims belongs to him. [Note: From the London Codex, fol. 171.]

[Col. 0668C] From the *Lombarda*, book I, title 25, chapter 83.

6. [Note: Muratori, chapter 100.] We decree that no new condition be imposed by a lord upon an *aldio*.

# EXCERPTS OF CANONS OF LOTHAR I (A.D. 835)

[Col. 0667]

[Col. 0667] The canons numbered 36, 37, 19, 38, and 33 of the council held at Rome by Pope Eugene in November 826 are included among the laws of Lothar in the Ambrosian, Florentine, London, Vienna, Veronese, and Este manuscripts of the Lombard laws. Although they may appear to be of doubtful authority, since they are omitted from the Chisian, Cava, and Gotha manuscripts, we have nevertheless judged that they should be presented chiefly here, because in the Blankenburg manuscript that entire council is attributed to the laws of Lothar.

[Col. 0669A] 1. [Note: Muratori, chapter 92.] No one may dismiss a wife whom he has taken except on account of fornication and then marry another; otherwise, the transgressor must be restored to his former marriage. If husband and wife mutually agree to separate solely for the sake of religious life, this must in no way be done without the knowledge of the bishop, so that he may assign them individually to a place under his provision. But if the wife is unwilling, or either one of them is unwilling, the marriage is not to be dissolved even for such a reason.

2. [Note: Muratori, chapter 93.] No one may have two wives at the same time, or a wife and a concubine, because although this brings no gain to the household, it brings harm to the soul. For just as Christ keeps the Church chaste, so a husband ought to preserve his marriage chaste.

3. [Note: Muratori, chapter 96.] Bishops and the various priests are to have advocates, because bishops and all priests are appointed solely for the praise of God and the performance of good works. Therefore each of them ought to have an advocate both for ecclesiastical cases and for his own affairs, except, namely, in a public criminal matter [Note: “And for all hearings under oath,” c., h., V., Vn., E.]. The advocate should not be suspected of bad reputation, but should be of good repute and recognized for commendable skill, lest, while they attend to earthly profits, they lose eternal rewards.

[Col. 0670A] 4. [Note: “Of” is absent in A.] Concerning incestuous unions, this is decreed: henceforth no one shall take a close relative, nor a woman whom a close relative has had, as his wife; and the wife’s kinship shall be regarded by the husband as his own kinship. [Note: Muratori, chapter 98. This is almost an excerpt from canon 38 in the Blankenburg manuscript.]

5. [Note: Absent in A.] No one shall dare to marry a female cousin, a niece, a stepmother, his brother’s wife [Note: “Or fiancée,” V., Vn.], or even a woman from his own relationship, or one whom a kinsman has had. If anyone joins himself in such a wicked marriage and remains in it, let him know that by episcopal authority he is bound by the chain of anathema, so that no priest may grant him communion. But if he is converted and separated from the unlawful union, he shall be subjected to fitting penance, as the priests of the place shall determine. [Note: Muratori, chapter 99.]

6. [Note: Absent from the manuscripts.] Although the testimony of a priest is considered credible, nevertheless priests are not to be summoned in secular matters either to give testimony or to draw up documents, since it is not appropriate for them to be involved in such affairs. If, however, they happen to have heard or seen something in a case where no suitable lay persons can be found, lest the truth be concealed and evil be judged good, the matter shall rest upon the discretion of their own bishop, so that they may honorably bring the truth forward before him, before competent judges, or in another manner. [Note: Muratori, chapter 101.]

# DIVISION OF THE EMPIRE (A.D. 839, JUNE)

[Col. 0669]

[Col. 0669] Prudentius has preserved in his *Annals* the formula of the division of the empire instituted by Louis I at Worms in June 839 between his sons Lothar and Charles, in *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, *Scriptores*, volume I, pages 434–435. We present it here again, extracted from that source. [Note: Prudentius, p. 431, and Nithard, book I, chapter 6, *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, volume II, p. 653, record the portion assigned to Charles at Aachen in 837.]

[Col. 0669C] THE ONE PORTION INCLUDED:

The kingdom of Italy and part of Burgundy, namely the valley of Aosta, the county of Valais, the county of Vaud as far as the Rhône, and thereafter the eastern and northern bank of the Rhône as far as the county of Lyon; the county of Scuding, the county of Virasc, the county of Portois; the county of Sventis, the county of Calmont, the duchy of the Moselle, the county of Ardennes, the county of Condroz; thence along the course of the Meuse to the sea; the duchy of the Ripuarians, Wormsfield, Speyerland, the duchy of Alsace, the duchy of Alamannia, Chur, the duchy of the Austrasians with Swalafeld, Nordgau, and Hesse; the duchy of Thuringia [Col. 0670C] with its marches; the kingdom of Saxony with its marches; the duchy of Frisia as far as the Meuse; the county of Hamaland, the county of the Batavians, the county of Testrabent, and Dorestad.

THE OTHER PORTION INCLUDED:

The other part of Burgundy, namely the county of Geneva, the county of Lyon, the county of Chalon, the county of Amaous, the county of the Hattuarii, the county of Langres, the county of Toul; and so along the course of the Meuse to the sea; and the territory between the Meuse and the Seine, and between the Seine and the Loire, together with the Breton March; Aquitaine and Gascony with the marches belonging to them; Septimania with its marches; and Provence.

[Note: This capitulary, omitted from the first recension of the capitularies of Charlemagne, is presented here. EDITOR.]

# CAPITULARY OF CHARLEMAGNE’S MISSI IN AQUITAINE (A.D. 789, MARCH, AACHEN)

[Col. 0671]

[Col. 0671] I have assigned the document to the year 789 because of the oath of fidelity prescribed in the general capitulary of that year. The twenty years that had elapsed since the beginning of Charles’s reign, as well as chapters 2 and 3, agree very well with that date. The names of the *missi*, Mancio and Eucherius, indicate that they were Aquitanians by origin. The chapters refer to the constitution of Pippin edited above and to another promulgated by Charles in 779.

## THE SUMMARY BEGINS

[Col. 0671A]
