Concerning those chapters which the lord king ordered to be completed in Aquitaine by his *missi*, Mancio and Eucherius, in order to fulfill the oath of fidelity imposed upon them. [Note: The manuscript reads “Mancio Teugerius”; read “oath of fidelity imposed.”]

1. Concerning that edict which our lord and father Pippin established, and which we subsequently ordered our *missi* to preserve and fulfill; or concerning our edicts, how they have been observed.

2. Concerning the restoration of churches: what those who have held their property during these twenty years have done with it, or why it has not been restored.

3. Whether any of the property of the Church which they possessed at the time when God placed that country under our hands was afterward diminished or taken away.

[Col. 0671B] 4. Why bishops, abbots, or monasteries of saints, which ought to have been restored to holy order, have not been so restored.

5. Whether any new customary burden has subsequently been imposed upon the poor.

6. How those who hold benefices are to provide for their dependants, and for their own people.

[Col. 0672A] 7. How anyone who goes against us in hostile fashion is to act. [Note: Read “whoever goes against us.”]

8. When someone is in the army or on any service of ours, and has forcibly taken away or dispossessed any of his own property.

9. Concerning benefices held in dispute.

10. Concerning our *missi*: whatever they have agreed upon with their lords. [Note: That is, “whatever they may have agreed upon.”]

11. Tithes from everything are to be distributed according to the bishop’s command, and everyone is to contribute.

12. Concerning thieves and homicides [Note: That is, “homicides,” meaning murderers] from within the immunity.

13. Concerning punishment for thieves, or for some offense.

14. Concerning church property: from which ninths and tenths, or from how many holdings, precarial grants are to be renewed. [Note: So corrected; the codex reads *cansis censatis*.]

[Col. 0672B] 15. Concerning not forming a *trustis*. [Note: The codex reads *triste*.]

16. Concerning *gellonia*. [Note: That is, *geldonia*.]

17. Concerning levies imposed upon travelers [Note: So corrected; the codex reads *intrantibus*], and concerning bridges or ferries used by those who travel for the sake of prayer. [Note: The codex reads *clausa*.]

18. Concerning pasture during the time of defense. [Note: End of the page; the next passage, now cut away, appears possibly to have contained excerpts of chapters 18–23 of the capitulary of 779.]

The remainder is missing.

# APPENDIX TO THE CAPITULARIES

[Col. 0671]

# SPURIOUS CAPITULARIES

# CONSTITUTION OF CHARLEMAGNE AT SCAHINING (A.D. 784)

[Col. 0671] The Lorsch annals report that in 784 Charles advanced through Thuringia as far as Scahining and made an agreement with the Saxons. Johann Christoph Harenberg claimed to have published this very agreement, found in a certain chronicle of Gandersheim, in 1758 in the first fascicle of *Historical Monuments Not Yet Published*, p. 90. But since the reliability of the editor is not sufficiently established for what he published to claim unquestionable authority, and since suspicion of alterations in words or even in sentences, whether by the chronicler or by the editor, does not appear entirely groundless—for example, in the expressions “and an agreement was reached on many points,” “at the place of Seligenstadt, commonly called Sliestadt,” “tithes and ninths from every produce,” and “they shall make up gifts”—I have judged that this document, of doubtful authenticity, should not be admitted among the genuine capitularies of Charles.

[Col. 0671C] When, in eastern Saxony, an assembly had been held together with the leading men of the Franks and the East Saxons below the village of Scanigge in North Thuringia, with numerous bishops and abbots in attendance, and agreement had been reached on many points, we decreed that at the place of Seligenstadt, commonly called Sliestadt, between Oreheim and Scanigge, a town should be made from the village, and that the bishop of eastern Saxony should be able to reside there. If this cannot be accomplished, a larger and fortified place is to be selected as the bishop’s seat by our *missi* and counts, where the bishop will have nothing to fear from attacks by eastern enemies.

The Saxons shall give nothing to the bishop and priests who are to be obedient to him, whether for oaths, burial, or various services. They shall, however, give each church one holding, and to the bishop and priests tithes and ninths from every produce, so that the heads of the churches may live from them, the poor may be supported, and the utensils of each church may be procured.

The Saxons promised under oath that within a year they and all their people who had not yet been baptized would receive baptism; that they wished to add their own *scabini* to our counts when the latter administered judgment according to their laws; that they wished to abandon their pagan practices; that they would abandon human and animal sacrifices, the cremation of dead people, uncertain omens, and unreliable divinations; that they would remain faithful in all things to the kings of the Franks; and that before the Kalends of May they would make up gifts and afterward send them to us at our court at Eresburg. When they had sworn this with their fingers raised toward heaven, we, mercifully and with a reconciled mind, received them into our protection and that of our successors. The Ides of August (August 13).

# DECREE OF CHARLEMAGNE CONCERNING THE ROMAN EXPEDITION (A.D. 790)

[Col. 0673]

[Col. 0673] This fictitious charter, composed in the final years of the twelfth century, acquired a certain renown because several learned men thought that a major transformation in our German affairs, which they had persuaded themselves had occurred in the tenth or eleventh century, could be explained from it. But neither did that transformation—in which they had supposed that the order of free men had been reduced to servitude—occur in the Middle Ages, nor could it be explained by our constitution, since it speaks only of wars beyond the Alps and not of a transformation of the entire military system.

The charter’s falsity is demonstrated both by its form and by its content. It is plainly fabricated so that it might pass as a constitution of Charlemagne. The name of Charles, the year 790, the twenty-second year of his reign, the place Worms, and the sojourn there show that its author knew the histories and annals—for example, those of Metz for the year 790—and intended to compose a charter referring to that year. Consequently, the opinion of those who have tried to substitute Charles the Fat or Conrad II for Charlemagne collapses very easily, unsupported by any reason.

Now the fact that the charter did not proceed from Charlemagne is demonstrated most clearly by the formulae of invocation, title, and chancellorship, by the year “from the incarnation of the Lord,” by the wording redolent of twelfth-century charters, and by the plainly fictitious narrative: “while the time for our departure to the apostolic see for our consecration and reception of the crown was approaching … it happened that the princes and soldiers bitterly quarreled over the Roman expedition that was then imminent.”

It follows that the charter was not accidentally corrupted or altered, but fabricated by an author intending to deceive, and that no credence whatsoever should be given to it. It appears to have been composed when the frequent Italian expeditions of Frederick I—“for our crown or for some advantage or honor of the kingdom, a Roman expedition”—were already causing the Germans considerable annoyance, and perhaps to settle some dispute in favor of the abbot of Chiemsee in Bavaria. For its oldest copy, written around 1190, is found in the library of the monastery of Chiemsee, and all the others derive from it.

1. It is preserved in the Royal Library at Munich among the *Cimelia*, IV, 3, and was added to the twelfth-century codex already mentioned by us, in the same hand imitating the ductus of the charters. The *Monumenta Boica*, volume II, p. 375, attests that the same hand was responsible for the Codex of the Chiemsee traditions, extending to the year 1190. Two copies of this codex existed.

2. Codex of the Royal Library of Munich, *Cimelia* IV, 3–6, formerly of the city of Augsburg, parchment, twelfth century, octavo, first known to Marcus Welser. From it were derived the editions of Rittershausen (1598, quarto), Freher (1599), the insufficiently reliable facsimile of Johann Wilhelm Hoffmann, and Gebauer’s edition.

3. Another codex, copied from the Chiemsee manuscript in 1476 by Peter Sayn of Freising, on paper, was used by Senckenberg in his editions S I in the *Corpus of German Feudal Law* (1740 and 1772), and S II in the *New Collection of Imperial Recesses* (1747), while the Chiemsee manuscript itself was reproduced only in the *Monumenta Boica*, volume II, p. 372, and thence in Fischer’s *Literature of German Law*, with considerable negligence. Our most industrious assistant, the distinguished Foeringer, elucidated this history of the text by comparing the manuscripts and printed books with one another. At our request he not only placed both Munich codices at our disposal for examination but also sent us their readings with the greatest care. With their assistance we now present an edition established according to the Chiemsee codex.

[Col. 0673B] In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity, Charles, by the favor of divine grace king of the Franks and Romans. If we follow the custom of our predecessors, we strive to assist not only those living now but also those who will succeed them. For this reason, let everyone know how, while the time for our departure to the apostolic see for our consecration and reception of the crown was approaching, we spent a year with many princes at Worms [Note: *Wormaciae*, manuscript 2], and there resolved to confirm everything useful and honorable in the condition of the state and to eradicate from the roots everything harmful and contrary.

Meanwhile, while these matters were being conducted, it happened by chance that the princes and soldiers bitterly disputed about the Roman expedition then imminent, compelling them to provide from their benefices far more hauberks than they admitted they could or ought by right to provide. But since this had not been settled by any of our predecessors [Note: So manuscripts 1 and 2; A has *fuerat*.], we considered it appropriate [Note: Manuscript 2 and A reverse the order: “we considered appropriate.”] to put an end and a limit to their dispute and to grant a decree and a definite law concerning every Roman expedition.

Therefore, with the consent both of the spiritual and of the secular princes sitting with us there, we establish and decree that whenever a Roman expedition is prepared by us or by our successors for our crown or for some utility or honor of the kingdom, one year together with six weeks shall be granted as a period of preparation to all who are to go with us, and this shall be announced in such a way throughout the whole kingdom to our faithful. Whoever is ordered to undertake that expedition according to this law, if he does not accompany his lord to the court of the Gauls—that is, to the field commonly called Rungalle—and does not appear there with military equipment, shall be deprived before us of his fief, without hope of recovering it, except for those who remain with the grace of their lords.

Those who, whether free or servants, remain with their lords by homage shall, for every group of ten holdings they possess in benefice, bring one coat of mail with two shield-bearers; yet they shall receive three marks for each hauberk and one mark for each shield-bearer. Thus, going and returning, they shall faithfully serve with this stipend, without any loss or expense to their lords except whatever the lords themselves choose [Col. 0675B], [Note: “Stipend,” manuscript 1; “expense,” corrected from “stipend,” manuscript 2.]. If, however, which God forbid, it happens that the same soldiers acquire different lords on account of different benefices, so that no benefice remains without its due service, each shall pay each lord his due: namely, they shall understand that they are to give as much as they would have received from those lords had they gone, or else, at the aforesaid place, they shall lose their fief [Note: The words from “lose” through the second occurrence of “lose” are absent in A.]. Unless some have received benefices from us or from the kingdom: if these go with us, we do not wish them to lose their fiefs, but they are not to omit their services without the consent of their lords.

Likewise, concerning the sons or household members of churches—that is, ministerials—or the dependants of any princes who ought to be ready every day for service, we decree that whoever possesses five holdings in benefice shall bring to his lord, to whom he belongs, one coat of mail with one shield-bearer. It shall remain at the discretion of the lords whom they bring, from whom they receive their stipends, and to whom they grant the hauberks. They shall also be given five pounds of their own currency as a stipend for preparing the journey, together with two horses, one running and one walking; and a packhorse, well loaded with provisions, shall be assigned to two companions, who shall carefully maintain it for the use of their lords.

They too shall live at their lords’ expense for as long as they remain on the expedition they have undertaken [Note: “The undertaking,” M. B.]. Whatever they acquire by fighting from rebellious kingdoms [Note: “Of the kingdom,” A., S. I., S. II.], they shall bring two parts to their lords and retain a third for their consolation. Those whom their lords do not feed shall return to them a third part of what they have acquired.

Each prince shall have his own special officers: a marshal, steward, cupbearer, and chamberlain. The more these four are to labor, the more they are to be honored above the others in stipend, clothing, and mounts. Namely, each of them shall be given ten pounds with three horses; a fourth horse shall be added for the marshal—one for riding ahead, another for fighting, a third for traveling, and a fourth for carrying armor. [Note: Some manuscripts and editions give “ten pounds” for each; other witnesses omit the phrase.]

If such men, wishing to remain behind, are able to obtain permission from their lords [Note: *Aput*, manuscript 2; *inpetrare*, manuscript 2], they shall pay, for as many holdings as they possess, that many pounds of their own currency—or the entire yield of the fief for that year—as their stipend. [Note: The codex breaks off after “as many”; editions derived from it omit the remainder.]

But so that our command may receive support from everyone, we establish and firmly order that each *buringus* shall pay his lord ten solidi together with twelve hemp ropes, and in addition shall provide a packhorse with halter; if the lords wish, they shall lead it as far as the first navigable water [Note: Absent in M. B.]. The *mansionarius* shall provide five solidi, the *absarius* thirty denarii, the *bunuarius* fifteen, and the possessors of every *larus* shall provide six [Note: “*Larius*,” A., S. I., S. II.].

And so that the authority of this decree of ours may, in the name of God, obtain inviolable and incorruptible immunity among all our successors [Note: “Firmness” should have been written.], we have resolved, with all the princes who were present [Note: “Present,” M. B.] consenting, to strengthen it below with our own hand and have ordered it to be authenticated with the signet of our ring [Note: “Seal,” M. B.].

Sign of Charles, most glorious king. Hernustus the notary, in place of Lutward the chancellor, have examined and approved. Given on June 6, in the year 790 from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, and in the twenty-second year of his reign [Note: “Our reign,” S. I., S. II.], before his consecration [Note: “In the twenty-second year of the year of his consecration,” S. I.; “in the twenty-first year of the year of his consecration,” the reading of the Senckenbergian codex.]. Done happily at Worms. Amen.

# CAPITULARY OF CHARLEMAGNE AND LOUIS I AT THEODONIS VILLA

[Col. 0675]

[Col. 0675] These spurious chapters were first published under the name of Charlemagne in Crabbé’s *Collections of Councils*, Cologne, 1567, volume III, p. 269, and elsewhere; then they were taken by Goldast into his *Constitutions*, and by Sirmond into the *Councils of Gaul*, volume II, from Burchard and Ivo, and assigned to the years 820 and 821; afterward Baluze compared them with the Vatican Codex and assigned them to the year 822. Here they appear again from the eleventh-century Gotha Codex.

Since the manuscripts therefore place the name of Charles before them, they nevertheless cannot in any way be referred to his reign, since Haistulf and Hetti became archbishops in 813, while Hadabald and Ebo did not obtain archiepiscopal office until the years 819 and 822. Nor have they been assigned to Emperor Louis with greater success, since Ebo was elected archbishop after June 5, 822, and Haistulf died in 825 according to the Annals of Xanten, or in 826 according to others; the assembly must therefore have been held within these limits, although in that period no assembly was actually held either at Tribur or at Theodonis Villa.

After comparing the text with Baluze’s edition, we publish it again from the eleventh-century Gotha Codex and the Vatican Codex, whose readings Baluze reports, in nearly the same form as that first presented by the editors of the councils.

# FROM THE COUNCIL HELD AT THEODONIS VILLA IN THE TIME OF CHARLEMAGNE

[Col. 0677A]

At the council at Theodonis Villa, where thirty-two bishops were present—Aistulf, archbishop of Mainz, with his suffragans; Hadabald, archbishop of Cologne, with his suffragans; Hetti, archbishop of Trier, with his suffragans; Ebo, archbishop of Reims, with his suffragans, together with the messengers of the remaining bishops of Gaul and Germany—it was decreed, because of the excessive presumption of certain tyrants raging against the priests of the Lord [Note: “Raging,” B.], and because of what had recently occurred in Gascony, namely, that Bishop John had been dishonorably and unheard-ofly murdered, that by common agreement and humble devotion they should petition the ears of the prince, if it pleased his piety, so that the wrong committed against the priests of Christ might be fully determined according to the synodal statutes [Note: “Synodal,” manuscript 2]. It likewise pleased the judgment of the bishops that, if it could be entirely settled according to their authority, a canonical sentence should be imposed upon those who, setting aside the fear of the Lord, presume to rage against his ministers.

But if it pleased his piety, in accordance with the chapters of earlier kings, where their provision had mercifully introduced a monetary amount into offenses, for the lightening of the penance it was agreed that the aforesaid matters should be determined by money granted by the emperors and by their priests for defense, and by penance, according to the judgment of the bishops, if his piety wished to approve this; thus they agreed that the matter should be settled. [Note: “For the consolation of holy Church,” B.; the words “and by their priests” are absent in B.; “to be determined,” B.]

[Col. 0677C] 1. If anyone has brought a charge against a subdeacon, wounded him, or disabled him, and he recovers, he shall do penance for five Lents without the following years, and shall pay the bishop three hundred solidi, together with his composition and the episcopal fines [Note: Absent in manuscript 1.]. But if he dies, he shall do penance for each of the aforesaid Lents together with the subsequent years, and shall pay the bishop four hundred solidi, together with triple his composition and triple episcopal fines [Note: Absent in manuscript 1.].

2. If anyone has brought a charge against a deacon and he recovers, he shall do penance for six Lents without the following years, and shall pay the bishop four hundred solidi, together with his composition and the episcopal fines [Note: Absent in manuscript 1.]. But if he dies, he shall do penance for each of the aforesaid six Lents together with the subsequent years, and shall pay the bishop six hundred solidi, together with triple his composition and triple episcopal fines [Note: Absent in manuscript 1.].

3. If anyone has brought a charge against a priest and assaulted him [Col. 0678A], he shall do penance for seven Lents without the following years [Note: “Six,” B.], and shall pay the bishop six hundred solidi, together with triple his composition and triple episcopal fines. But if he dies, twelve years of penance shall be imposed upon the offender according to the canons, and he shall pay the bishop nine hundred solidi, together with triple his composition and triple episcopal fines.

4. If anyone has ambushed a bishop, seized him, or dishonored him in any way, he shall do penance for ten Lents without the following years [Note: “With,” B.] and shall pay triple the composition for a slain priest [Note: Absent in B.]. But if the bishop is killed accidentally and not willingly, the killer shall do penance with the counsel of the bishops of the province. If anyone kills him willingly, he shall not eat meat [Col. 0678B], shall not drink wine all the days of his life [Note: “All,” B.], shall lay aside the military belt, and shall remain forever without hope of marriage.

Aistulf, archbishop of Mainz, said: “If it pleases the princes and their other faithful men, let us ask that this be approved and subscribed.” And it was approved and subscribed both by the prince and by all the others.

# ECCLESIASTICAL CHAPTER

At Theodonis Villa [Note: “At Tribur, approved and subscribed by Charles and the leading men of Gaul and Germany,” Burchard and Ivo.], established by Charles [Note: “By the emperors Louis the Pious and Lothar, and approved and subscribed by the leading men of Gaul and Germany,” G.] the Great and Louis, and approved and subscribed by the leading men of Gaul.

It pleased us and our faithful men that, just as in another year at Tribur [Note: “In the year at Theodonis Villa,” B.] we had been admonished and petitioned by the bishops and the remaining priests and servants of God, so that the bishops and their ministers, whom God has reserved for his own, not human, judgment [Col. 0678C], might remain unharmed according to the statutes of the holy canons, the holy fathers, and the capitularies of earlier kings set forth before us—so that the priests of God and their assistants, through whose intercessions and supplications the holy Church of God is understood to endure—therefore we establish:

1. If anyone has brought a charge against a subdeacon and he recovers, he shall do canonical penance and shall pay the bishop three hundred solidi. If he dies, he shall do penance according to what the canons prescribe and shall pay the bishop four hundred solidi.

2. If anyone has brought a charge against a deacon [Note: “If anyone has brought a charge against a deacon,” B.], and he recovers, he shall do penance according to the canons and shall pay the bishop four hundred solidi [Note: Absent in manuscript 1.]. If he does not recover [Col. 0678D], he shall do penance according to the synodal precepts and shall pay the bishop six hundred solidi.

3. If anyone has mistreated a presbyter and he survives [Note: B: “if anyone has mistreated a presbyter”], let him do penance according to the judgment of the bishop in whose territorial jurisdiction he is known to be [Note: B: “let him do penance and pay 900 solidi to the bishop”]. But if he dies [Col. 0679A], let the offender do penance as the synod shall judge, and pay 900 solidi to the bishop [Note: B: “1,200 solidi to the bishop”].

4. And if anyone has laid an ambush for a bishop, seized him, or otherwise dishonored him, let him do penance according to the provisions of the canons, and let him pay threefold compensation for a presbyter who was not killed [Note: B omits “not killed”], together with the legal dues that appear to have been written and confirmed in the preceding chapter.

5. If anyone has deliberately killed a bishop, let him do penance according to what was decreed at Tribur [Note: B: “at Theodonis villa, by thirty-three”] by twenty bishops, and according to what was there commended and subscribed by us and by the leading men of all Gaul [Note: 1 omits “of Gaul,”] and Germany with benevolent acclaim, [and let him pay to the widowed church the money granted by us [Note: 1 and 2 omit this clause]].

[Col. 0679B] 6. We have also added this from our own authority: if anyone proves disobedient and obstinate toward the bishops in the sanctions of the holy canons and of our decree stated above [Col. 0680A], let him first be struck by canonical sentence; then let him have no benefice in our kingdom, and let his allod be placed under the ban. If he remains under our ban for a year and a day, let it be reduced to our fisc; let him be captured and confined in exile, and there be guarded and restrained until, compelled, he makes satisfaction to God and to the holy Church for what he had previously refused freely to do.

And if all of you approve these provisions, say so. And for the third time all cried out: “It is approved.” The emperors and nearly all the princes of Gaul [and Germany [Note: 1 omits “and Germany”]] subscribed, each making his own cross. The ecclesiastical order, offering praises to God and to the princes, sang the hymn *Te Deum laudamus*. [Col. 0680B] And thus the synod was dissolved.

# THE PACT OF EMPEROR LOUIS I WITH POPE PASCHAL (A.D. 817)

[Col. 0679]

[Col. 0679] This charter, which from the twelfth century onward was exceedingly famous and was regarded as genuine in subsequent centuries, no longer survives in an authentic exemplar—or in one regarded as authentic. For the distinguished Marinus Marini, prefect of the Vatican Archives, who in our own age again attempted to vindicate its authority, printed in his book *Nuovo Esame dell’autenticità de’ diplomi di Ludovico Pio, Ottone I, e Arrigo II, sul dominio temporale dei Romani pontefici* (Rome, 1822, octavo, p. 103) the text he had found in the thirteenth-century Codex Cencius of the Colonna family. Since, therefore, the question of the charter’s credibility receives very certain illumination from the condition of the papal territory in the time of Emperor Louis, something must briefly be said about its history.

In October 753, Pope Stephen II went to Aistulf, king of the Lombards, at the command of the emperor of Constantinople, intending to demand back the exarchate of Ravenna and the other places he had invaded. When this attempt proved fruitless, he approached King Pepin and, after receiving a promise of assistance at Ponthion on 6 January 754, concluded at the public assembly of Quierzy a pact concerning the defense of the Roman Church and the coronation of Pepin and his sons. By it Pepin promised that he would confer upon the Roman Church the territories that Aistulf had taken from the Greeks. The condition was expressed in these words [Note: *Life of Hadrian I*, ch. 52]:

“From Luna, together with the island of Corsica, then to Surianum, then to Mount Bardon, thence to Berceto, then to Parma, thereafter to Reggio, and from there to Mantua and Monte Silicis; likewise the whole exarchate of Ravenna as it had been in antiquity, and the provinces of Venetia and Istria, as well as the entire duchy of Spoleto and Benevento.”

The war was undertaken with great difficulty [Note: Einhard, *Life of Charlemagne*, ch. 6], and was waged only to the following end [Note: Continuation of Fredegar], being completed in 755: that the Lombards should restore Pentapolis, Narni [Note: “Narnia”], and Ceccano [Note: Ceccano lies south of Frosinone], the Roman cities of Tuscany and Campania that they themselves had invaded, and the other places over which the Roman people were complaining. When the war was renewed, Comacchio was added in 756.

Pepin’s donation, when drawn up, therefore included these cities [Note: *Life of Stephen II*, chs. 46–47]: Ravenna, Rimini, Pesaro, Conca, Fano, Cesena, Senigallia, Jesi, Forlimpopoli, Forlì with Sassofeltrio, Montefeltro, Acerra, Agiomonte, Monte Lucati, Serra, the castle of Saint Marino, Bobbio, Urbino, Calli, Lucioli, Gubbio, and Comacchio; and it is clear from what follows that Faenza, the duchy of Ferrara [Note: *Life of Hadrian I*, ch. 6], Imola, Bologna, and Gavello were also transferred at the same time [Note: *Codex Carolinus*, letter 54]. We do not find that the pope ever afterward obtained anything further from Pepin.

Eighteen years later, after Desiderius had first been defeated, the people of Spoleto and Rieti, the inhabitants of the duchies of Fermo, Osimo, and Ancona, and the inhabitants of the castle of Felicitas turned to Pope Hadrian [Note: *Life of Hadrian I*, chs. 32–33]. King Charles, having promised Hadrian at Rome to restore the exarchate seized by Desiderius, also confirmed Pepin’s donation at Quierzy [Note: ibid., ch. 42].

On the basis of these promises, Hadrian recovered part of the exarchate in 774 or 775 [Note: *Codex Carolinus*, letter 54]. The remainder—namely Imola, Bologna, Gavello, Faenza, the duchy of Ferrara, Comacchio, Forlì, Forlimpopoli, Cesena, Bobbio, the Tenth Tribunate, despite the resistance of the archbishop of Ravenna, and the castle of Felicitas, seized by the duke of Clusium—he could recover only in 775 or 776 [Note: “In 783 he held the whole exarchate”; letter 83].

Hadrian, however, advancing farther, began from 777 onward to demand lands that neither he nor Stephen or Paul had ever possessed, but which, he claimed, had formerly been wrested from the popes by the Lombard kings or others and were to be restored to him under the donation of Quierzy. First [Note: letter 59], from 777 onward, he sought several cities situated in Lombard Tuscany, the duchies of Spoleto and Benevento, Corsica [Col. 0681], and the Sabine patrimony; then [Note: letter 65] Terracina, which had been occupied and again lost, Gaeta, Naples, and the patrimonies in those regions. In 781, while Charles was present at Rome and his sons Pepin and Louis were consecrated kings of the Lombards and Aquitaine, he obtained from Charles a grant of the Sabine patrimony “for the furnishing of lamps and the support of the poor.” This, however, was not delivered to Saint Peter by Charles’s envoys until 783.

At the same time, or certainly in 787, the cities of Lombard Tuscany—Suana, Tuscania, Viterbo, Balneum Regis, and the others, namely the castle of Felicitas, Orvieto, Ferento, Orte, Marca—were restored [Note: letter 89]. In 787 and 787 [sic] he demanded that Populonia and Roselle, as well as the cities in the region of Benevento [Note: letters 88–89] and then Capua [Note: letter 90], be added. On Charles’s third journey to Rome he obtained a promise that Benevento would be handed over, but the promise proved void: influenced by the favor of Grimoald, duke of Benevento, the king permitted the pope to receive bishoprics, monasteries, royal estates, and uninhabited cities, while allowing their inhabitants to remain under Grimoald’s allegiance.

This was the end of Hadrian’s protests and of Charles’s favors. We find neither that Hadrian obtained anything further nor that his successor Leo III, who in 808 demanded the island of Corsica under the pact of Quierzy [Note: Leo III, letter 4], had any better fortune. It is therefore clear that Charles neither wished nor was able to preserve intact what, while Desiderius still held Pavia and the outcome of the war was uncertain, he had promised the pope in the renewal of the pact of Quierzy. He may have been led to this by the consideration that the popes could not prove their rights over the several territories situated south of the line described, in the form in which those rights appeared to be held and claimed [Note: *Codex Carolinus*, letter 59: Hadrian, seeking the cities in the regions of Tuscany, Spoleto, and Benevento, together with Corsica and the Sabine territory, proposes to the king documents from the Lateran archives that would prove Saint Peter’s rights. Letter 73 reports that Maginarius, Charles’s envoy, recognized the Church’s rights to the Sabine patrimony from documents and delivered the patrimony].

When Charles died, the situation was therefore this: under Frankish rule, the popes possessed:

1. By ancient right, the city of Rome with its duchy—that is, Campania with the Maritime region as far as Ceprano and Terracina—and Roman Tuscany, namely the cities of Porto, Centumcellae, Caere, Blera, Marturanum, Sutri, Nepi, Castellum, Gallese, Orte, Polimartium, Ameria, Todi, Perugia with its three islands, Narni, and Otricoli;

2. By the donations of Pepin and Charles, the exarchate of Ravenna, Pentapolis, and Emilia, with the cities mentioned above;

3. By the pact of Quierzy and by the rights acknowledged to the king Charles, the Sabine territory, the cities of Lombard Tuscany mentioned above—perhaps with the addition of Populonia and Roselle—and the rights transferred to them in the duchy of Benevento;

4. They claimed, but could not establish their claim to, many territories south of the line extending from Luna, with the island of Corsica, through Surianum, Mount Bardon, Berceto, Parma, Reggio, Mantua, and Monte Silicis—especially Corsica, Populonia and Roselle, the duchies of Spoleto and Benevento, Capua, Gaeta, Naples with the patrimonies located there—possessed partly by the Franks, partly by the dukes of Benevento, and partly by the Greeks.

To these Emperor Louis added nothing except a royal estate in Germany [Note: *Life of Stephen IV*, ch. 2]. It is therefore beyond doubt that the confirmation circulated under his name is spurious, not only because of its formal defects, but also because it is said to grant to the pope the islands of Sardinia and Sicily, part of Beneventan Campania with the cities of Sora, Arce, Aquino, Arpino, Teano, and Capua, and the Beneventan, Salernitan, Neapolitan, and Upper and Lower Calabrian patrimonies—territories that were not under Frankish control.

Having obtained the oldest surviving copy of the charter, namely that written at the beginning of the twelfth century in Vatican Codex no. 1984, we now present the text taken from it.

[Col. 0681A] In the name of the Lord God almighty, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit. I, Louis, emperor Augustus, establish and draw up by this pact of our confirmation, for you, blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, and through you for your vicar, Lord Paschal [Note: Marini: “Lord Paschal”], supreme pontiff and universal pope, and for his successors forever, all that your predecessors have held and administered in your power and jurisdiction down to the present: the city of Rome with its duchy, suburbs, and all its villages and territories, mountainous and maritime, its shores and harbors, and all the cities, castles, towns, and villages in the regions of Tuscany, namely [Note: M adds “likewise”] Porto, Centumcellae, Caere, Blera, Marturanum, Sutri, Nepi, Castellum, Gallese, Orte, Polimartium, Ameria, Todi, Perugia [Note: M: “Perusium”] with [Col. 0681B] its three islands [Note: M omits this], namely the greater and the lesser, Pulvensis [Note: L: “and the lake”; M: “Narmam”], Narni, and Otricoli, with all the boundaries and territories belonging to the cities written above.

Likewise, in the regions of Campania, Segni, Anagni, [Col. 0682A] Ferentino, Alatri, Patrica, Frusino, with the boundaries of Campania, and also [Note: M omits this] Tibur, with all the boundaries and territories belonging to those same cities; and also [Note: M omits this] the exarchate of Ravenna in its entirety, with its towns, cities, settlements, and castles, which the lord King Pepin, of blessed memory, and our father, Emperor Charles, of good memory, formerly restored by deed of donation to the blessed apostle Peter and your predecessors: namely the city of Ravenna and Emilia [Note: 1: “Entilia”], Bobbio, Cesena, Forlimpopoli, Forlì, Faenza, Imola, Bologna, Ferrara, Comacchio, Adrianis [Note: M: “and Adrianis, which is also Gavello”], and Gavello, with all the boundaries, territories, and islands on land [Note: M: “on land”] and sea belonging to the cities mentioned above.

Likewise [Note: M: “similarly”], Pentapolis, namely Rimini, [Col. 0682B] Pesaro [Note: M: “Pisaurum”], Fano, Senigallia [Note: M: “Senogallia”], Ancona, Osimo, Humana, Jesi, Forum Sempronii, Montefeltro, Urbino [Note: 1: “Ulbinum”], the Valvense territory [Note: M: “Balnense territory”], Calli, Lucioli, and Gubbio [Note: 1 and M: “Gubbio”], with all [Col. 0683A] boundaries and lands belonging to those same cities.

Likewise the Sabine territory, in its entirety, as it was granted by our father, Emperor Charles, to the blessed apostle Peter by deed of donation, in the manner in which it was delimited by Itherius and Maginarius, his envoys, between that same Sabine territory and the territory of Rieti.

Likewise, in the regions of Lombard Tuscany, the castle of Felicitas, Orvieto, Balneum Regis, Ferento, the castle of Viterbo [Note: M: “of Viterbo”], Orte, Marca [Note: 1: “Marta”], Tuscania, Suana, Populonia, Roselle, and the islands of Corsica, Sardinia, and Sicily, in their entirety, with all adjoining lands, territories, shores, coasts, and harbors belonging to the cities and islands mentioned above.

Likewise, in the regions of Campania, Sora, Arce, Aquino, Arpino, [Col. 0683B] Teano, and Capua, and the patrimonies belonging to your power and jurisdiction [Note: M: “belonging”], such as the Beneventan and Salernitan patrimonies, the patrimony of Lower and Upper Calabria, the Neapolitan patrimony, and wherever in the regions of the kingdom and empire entrusted to us by God your patrimonies are known to exist.

All these provinces, cities, towns, castles [Note: M: “fortifications”], villages, and territories written above, together with the patrimonies of your aforesaid church, blessed apostle Peter, and through you of your spiritual vicar, our father, Lord Paschal, supreme pontiff and universal pope, and of his successors until the end of the age, we confirm in the same manner, so that they may retain them in their right, principate, and jurisdiction.

[Col. 0683C] Likewise, by this decree of our confirmation we affirm the donations that Lord King Pepin, our grandfather, of blessed memory, and afterward our lord and father, Emperor Charles, freely granted to the blessed apostle Peter.

We also confirm the tribute, rent, and other payments [Note: M: “donations”] that were accustomed to be brought annually to the palace of the king of the Lombards, whether from Lombard Tuscany or from the duchy of Spoleto [Note: M: “Spoletan duchy”], as they are contained in the donations written above [Note: M: “as it is contained”] and as was agreed between Hadrian, the holy-memory pope, and our lord and father, Emperor Charles. For that same pontiff confirmed for him, by a decree of his authority, the aforesaid duchies, namely [Note: M: “the duchy of”] Tuscia and Spoleto [Note: M: “Spoletan”], [Note: 1: “or”], namely in such a manner that each year the aforesaid tribute should be paid to the church of the blessed apostle Peter, while our jurisdiction over those duchies in all respects and their subjection to our side remained intact.

Moreover, as we have said, we strengthen by this decree of our confirmation everything named above for your side [Note: M: “our side”], so that it may remain in your right, principate, and jurisdiction and that of your successors; so that neither by us nor by our sons or successors, [Col. 0684A] by any device or contrivance, may your power in any part be diminished, nor may anything be taken from you or your successors from all the aforesaid provinces, cities, towns, settlements, castles, villages [Note: M: “estates”], territories, and patrimonies, or from the rents and tributes.

Thus neither shall we withdraw them, nor shall we consent to anyone wishing to withdraw them; rather, we promise that, insofar as we are able, we shall defend everything written above—that is, the provinces, cities, towns, settlements, castles, territories, patrimonies, islands, tributes, and rents—belonging to the church of the blessed apostle Peter and to the pontiffs who reside forever in its most holy see.

This is so that all these may firmly remain in his jurisdiction for use, enjoyment, and administration. We claim no share or power in them to administer, judge, withdraw, or diminish, except insofar as we may be asked by him who at that time governs this holy Church.

And if any person from the aforesaid cities belonging to your church comes to us, wishing to withdraw himself from your jurisdiction and power, or fearing some unjust contrivance or fleeing a fault he has committed, we shall in no way receive him [Note: M: “otherwise receive him”], except to make a just intercession on his behalf—and only if the fault he committed is found to be pardonable. Otherwise, once he has been apprehended, we shall return him to your authority.

This does not apply to those who, having suffered violence or the oppression of powerful men, come to us so that through our intercession they may deserve to receive justice; their condition is different and very far removed from the one described above.

And when, by divine summons, the pontiff of this most holy see has departed from this world, no one from our kingdom—Frank, Lombard, or a member of any other people subject to our power—shall have permission to come against the Romans, publicly or privately, or to conduct an election [Note: M omits “against the Romans”]. Nor shall anyone presume to do any harm to a person in the cities or territories belonging to the jurisdiction of the church of the blessed apostle Peter [Note: M: “to do this because of a person”]. Rather, let the Romans be permitted, with all reverence and without any disturbance, to provide their pontiff with an honorable burial.

And let the man whom all the Romans, by divine inspiration [Note: M: “inspiration”] and through the intercession of blessed Peter, with one mind and concord, without any promise, have chosen to the pontifical office [Note: M: “may choose, without any promise”] be consecrated according to canonical custom, without any ambiguity or opposition [Note: M: “to consecrate”]. Once he has been consecrated, envoys shall be sent to us or to our successors, the kings of the Franks, to establish friendship, charity, and peace between us and him, as was customary in the time of Lord Charles, our great-grandfather, Lord Pepin, our grandfather, and also Charles, Emperor, our father.

We have strengthened this pact of our confirmation with the mark of our own hand and with the oaths, promises, and subscriptions of the venerable bishops, abbots, and also our leading men, so that it may be believed firm by all the faithful of God’s holy Church and guarded all the more firmly by future generations and ages to come. We have sent it through Theodore, nomenclator of the holy Roman Church, as our legate, to Lord Paschal [Note: M: “Paschal”], pope.

I, Louis, emperor by the mercy of God, have subscribed.

His three sons also subscribed, together with ten bishops, eight abbots, fifteen counts, one librarian, and one mansionarius [Note: M adds: “one doorkeeper also”].

# THE ROMAN COUNCIL OF EUGENE II (A.D. 826, November)

[Col. 0685]

[Col. 0685] We have already noted that its canons 36, 37, 19, 38, and 33 were received among the laws of Emperor Lothar. Since, therefore, the text of the council—of which only part had hitherto existed in the collections—presented itself in its entirety in the Blankenburg Codex of the ducal library at Wolfenbüttel, we decided that it ought to be copied out and set forth especially in this place.

The chapters are headed as follows: “These are the 104 chapters of Lord Emperor Lothar,” which is not read *in aere* [reading and sense uncertain]. It occurs on folios 113–115 of the codex; the text is read on folios 120–12 [pagination as printed].

[Col. 0685B] 1. That a bishop should be ordained who is approved by good works. In this chapter he advises that apostolic authority be observed in ordinations; he then adds the words of the *Pastoral Book*.

2. That no bishop or other priest should be ordained for gifts. In this chapter he warns that the simoniacal heresy must be avoided, because both the giver and the recipient ought to be deprived of their office.

3. How a bishop ought to teach and conduct himself. In this chapter he urges that superiors demonstrate to their subjects the path of good living by word and deed.

4. Concerning unlearned priests. Here a warning is given that unlearned ministers should be suspended from office until, once instructed, permission to minister is granted to them. If they cannot be taught, it will be for the bishop to decide how they are to be treated.

5. That the rule of the canons be observed in electing bishops. The rule of the canons is that no one is to be regarded as bishop who has not been elected by clergy and people.

[Col. 0685C] 6. That bishops should not remain outside their own parish. Here mention is made of the Council of Sardica, at which it was prescribed that bishops should not remain outside their own episcopate for more than three weeks, unless perhaps with the permission of the metropolitan.

7. Where clerics ought to reside. This chapter prescribes that a cloister be established beside the church, with a refectory, dormitory, and the other workshops or facilities suitable for the use of the clerics.

8. Concerning priests to be established in subject parishes. This chapter expresses the wish that the presbyters of the parishes be ordained with the consent of the faithful and with greater reverence.

9. That no more clerics than are sufficient should be ordained. For he warns that moderation must be observed in gathering clerics, so that no more are admitted than the resources canonically assigned to them can adequately support.

10. Concerning priests who do not live in churches or monasteries. Here it is prescribed that presbyters should not live in secular houses, but in a church [Col. 0685D] or in monasteries where there is no residence of women.

11. That a priest should not take pleasure in any game, so that he may be blessed and may meditate day and night on the law of the Lord.

12. That priests should not engage in lending at interest or rural work. Here he warns priests to abstain from hunting and agricultural labor, and he also warns them not to leave their houses without priestly dress.

[Col. 0686B] 13. Whether priests may give testimony. Here it is prescribed that priests should not be compelled to become witnesses; but if circumstances require it, they should be questioned by their own bishop, so that the truth may not be concealed.

14. Where a priest ought to be after condemnation. Here it is prescribed that a deposed priest be placed by the bishop in such a place that, while lamenting his sins, he may not sin again.

15. Concerning priests under suspicion. He therefore warns that if a priest who has twice or three times been corrected by the bishop because of his reputation concerning a certain woman is proved to have spoken with her, he is to be judged canonically.

16. That bishops may not take property from subject parishes and other pious places. This chapter prescribes that property may in no way be taken from parishes or from other pious places.

17. Concerning presbyters who refuse to receive one person’s offering on account of another. Here it is prescribed that a presbyter should not reject one person’s offering out of regard for another.

[Col. 0686C] 18. By what authority letters of dismissal are to be issued or accepted. Here it is prescribed that a bishop should grant a cleric permission to pass to another church only when requested to do so.

19. That bishops and all priests should have advocates, for the sake of priestly reverence, except in the case of a public crime.

20. Concerning those who cannot find an advocate. Concerning such persons it is prescribed that they be examined by the bishop before the people and, if they are of bad reputation, be judged canonically.

21. Concerning a monastery or oratory built by its own proprietor alone. This chapter prescribes that an oratory or monastery built by its own proprietor may not be taken away by force; rather, with the bishop’s consent, he may have a presbyter of good reputation.

22. Concerning an invasion committed as though on behalf of the Church. If an invader is proved to have said that he acted on behalf of the Church, let the invasion of private property belonging to him and his heir be paid for by him and his heir. Finally, if a priest is found poor in such a fault, let him be judged canonically by his own bishop, so that the church entrusted to him may not suffer loss.

23. Concerning guest-houses, poorhouses [Greek-derived *ptochotropheia*], hospitals [Note: 1: *nosocomia*], orphanages, homes for the aged [*gerontocomia*], foundling homes [*brephotropheia*; Note: 1: *brephotrophia*], and monasteries of both monks and nuns: it has been decreed that all these pious places are to be preserved through the bishop’s careful attention to the purpose of their founders.

24. Concerning pious places that exist without priests. [Col. 0687A] It has been decreed [Note: 1 omits this] that, if they belong to the rights of a church, they are to be provided with priests by the bishop; but if they pertain to secular persons, those persons are to be admonished by the bishop to provide priests within three weeks.

25. Concerning destroyed churches. Here it has been established that a destroyed church is to be restored from its own resources, or, if its resources are insufficient, repaired with the assistance of the people.

26. If a bishop demands payments from subject priests and clerics. Concerning this chapter it has been decreed that no bishop may demand more from presbyters or clerics than has been established.

27. What sort of men are to be appointed abbots. This chapter prescribes that they be instructed and supported by the dignity of the presbyterate [Note: 1: “presbyterate”].

28. It teaches how monks or abbots ought to conduct themselves. Although many things are to be observed by the various classes of monks and other things wholly rejected, nevertheless each bishop ought to strive with diligent care in his diocese concerning those who possess only the habit. Those who attempt to mock religion are to be restrained by the zeal of a good shepherd, so that they either return to their own monastery or are sent to another suitable one.

Those who have once vowed themselves to God and displayed the habit of monks, or have had their hair tonsured, must lead a regular life [Note: 1: “the life of the rule”], sleeping and residing together in one dormitory and refectory, as is appropriate, and doing everything in the likeness of the apostles. For no one said that anything he possessed was his own; rather, everything was common to them.

29. Concerning women who have assumed the religious habit. It has been decreed that women who have assumed the religious habit under the pretext of religious devotion be compelled to remain in it [Note: 1: “remain”] and be forced to live in monasteries according to the example of men.

30. Concerning the conduct of business and labor on Sunday. It has been decreed that anyone who acts against this sanction must be cleansed through penance.

[Col. 0687C] 31. Concerning criminal cases, thefts, and other similar matters discovered on Sunday. This chapter establishes that when persons are found to have committed such crimes on other days, it is permissible to seize and judge them. It is then prescribed that no one be punished on Sunday.

32. Concerning those who are detained unwillingly in monasteries without an accusation being shown. It has been decreed that, just as one who enters a monastery voluntarily has no permission to leave, so one who is brought in unwillingly is not to be detained unless he wishes it.

33. That laypeople should not stand in the presbyterium during Masses. Here he urges that, just as the places of clerics and laypeople are distinct, so those of men and women should be separate.

34. Concerning the restoration of schools for the study of letters. Here a warning is given that teachers of the liberal arts be appointed over schools in episcopal cities and parishes. If teachers of the liberal arts are lacking, teachers of the divine Scriptures are nevertheless to be sought by every means.

[Col. 0687D] 35. Concerning the holding of banquets on feast days. In this chapter dancing, shameful words, and the rites of the pagans are forbidden. Concerning those who have been warned but refuse to amend, it decrees that they are to be deprived of communion.

36. Concerning those who have abandoned a wife they had taken and joined themselves to another. Here the Lord’s judgment is recalled: no one may dismiss his wife except on account of fornication. If he dismisses her and takes another, he is afterward urged to return to the first. If both agree to separation for the sake of religion, he warns that it should not take place without the bishop’s counsel.

37. That it is not permitted to have two wives at the same time, or a wife and a concubine. Concerning the man who has a concubine in addition to his wife, it is prescribed that, if warned, he refuses to cast her away, he is to be deprived of communion.

38. Concerning incestuous unions. Here it is prescribed that no one take as wife a close relative, or a woman whom a close relative has had as wife.

39. Concerning foreign priests who are ordained by corrupt bishops. Here it is prescribed that henceforth no one be ordained presbyter without someone’s authorization.

40. That presbyters serving in different baptisteries or in any sacred oratories must, without excuse, attend the council of the bishop’s diocese.

41. That a layman who, by his own authority, installs another church’s presbyter without the consent of the bishop in whose parish the church is known to exist is to be separated from the communion of the faithful; but if the presbyter, when summoned by his own bishop, refuses to return, he is to lose his proper rank.

# HERE BEGIN THE CHAPTERS OF THE ADMONITION OF POPE EUGENE, MADE WITH THE COUNSEL AND SUBSCRIPTION OF THE BISHOPS

Brothers, fellow bishops, priests, and all members of the clergy: since this religious assembly, brought together by the Holy Spirit, urges us to deal with everything concerning ecclesiastical discipline [Col. 0688B] with more careful attention, if it pleases you, brothers, let us, with the Lord’s help, establish firmly for all ages those matters that concern the substance of our exhortations, in accordance with the precepts of divine law and the ordinances of the canons of Nicaea, so that no one may dare, at the peril of his own status, to violate either the divine constitutions or the decrees of the apostolic see.

For we who, as the chief priests, administer such offices will be answerable for the guilt of these transgressions if we are found negligent in the matters of God. We remember how the Lord threatens the negligence of priests. Indeed, the one who enjoys the greater honor commits the greater offense, and the eminence of dignities makes the vices of sinners more serious.

Therefore, above all, care must be taken that the provisions previously written concerning the sacred orders not be disregarded: whatever is found contrary to the law, the institutions of the holy canons, or the decrees of the fathers; whatever concerns individual chapters; those who are ignorant of letters and learning, yet are found to have been admitted to honor; those who are found acting against the statutes [Col. 0688C] that ought to be declared to your holiness; those who have suffered damage to some part of their members; and those who, after penance, have attained the sacred orders. Let every person who has acted as consecrator of such men take heed.

For we do not wish to exercise severity in anything. But anyone who has sinned through obstinacy or wrongdoing in the affairs of God, or who refuses to abolish what he himself has done wrongly, will find in himself whatever he failed to cut away in another. So that this may henceforth be guarded more tenaciously, if it pleases you, present all your causes and personal subscriptions, so that the hearing may be closed by synodal judgment against unlawful practices.

## Response of the Bishops

1. We truly recognize that, by the grace of the Holy Spirit, the heart of your apostolate has been set aflame, so that the squalor of such great misery may be wiped away from the minds of the faithful; and, as though a wound were fixed in the body, may be healed by applying to such misery a sealed and salutary antidote.

This has been wisely provided through the prohibition of contrary things, lest any person, governing two [objects or offices unclear] of whatever kind and washed in the water of sacred baptism, attempt this, so that, overwhelmed by the mass of so great a sacrilege—as has been heard—they fall into ruin; they must be avoided and uprooted from the very roots.

## Second Admonition of the Pontiff

**2.** We are constrained by the necessary ordering of affairs and are assembled in the governance of the apostolic see, so that we may weigh the decrees of the fathers’ canons and measure the precepts of our predecessors and forebears. Thus, whatever the necessity of the present times requires to be granted for the restoration of churches, we may, with careful consideration, regulate as far as we can—so that we may not seem entirely to exceed the form of the ancient rules, and so that the offices of the clerical militia, which appear to have been neglected throughout the various provinces, may be recovered for the better. We must not neglect the restoration of churches that have been abandoned in different places and that can be restored through the salutary assistance of aid, lest the salvation of our souls become a great guilt for us if, amid such a threatening danger, we neglect to offer whatever help lies within our power.

## Second Response of the Bishops

**3.** Even if there were no necessity requiring ecclesiastical discipline, that privilege of your see would truly have been sufficient for us: after receiving the keys of the kingdom following the Savior’s resurrection, the singular preaching of the most blessed Peter looked throughout the whole world toward the illumination of all. Just as the primacy of his representative stands eminent, so it must be feared and loved by everyone.

Therefore, worshiping God first of all in you, to whom we would return in faith without complaint—the faith praised by the apostolic mouth—we seek answers from that source. Thus nothing is prescribed through error or presumption, but everything through pontifical deliberation, so that we may be instructed by apostolic utterances concerning what you wish to be observed. In this way, with the brotherhood assembled and the decrees of the venerable synod brought forward, we may, supported by your authority against whatever is contrary to the law, understand, with God’s help, what order ought to be established among human beings.

Certainly, your triumph will be achieved if, in the time of your apostolate, the Catholic Church dares to retain what the chair of Saint Peter has obtained; if the new seeds of weeds are utterly uprooted; and if, while your holy apostolate prays for us, divine eternity preserves it forever.

*Hear, O Christ, the life of Pope Eugenius.*

**4.** We ask your holiness to strive to apply your ears more attentively, with the innermost affection of your heart, to each matter, so that our labor may in every respect advance the salvation of our souls. If it pleases you to hear them, let them be read before everyone.

All, responding, said: “Let them be read.”

The deacon Theodore read:

In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, which is the undivided Trinity.

First of all, concerning the churches of God that throughout the individual places in the parishes—whether villages or cities—lie in ruins and neglected, in which neither services nor lights are provided, and in which no provision for any ministry is found; and concerning the endowments that were given there from the time of their consecration, which have been taken away, so that no one even remembers what possessions they formerly held.

Therefore, brothers, foresee how the houses of God may be restored so that they may receive honor from faithful Christians, and so that the first fruits and revenues which God commanded the faithful to offer there may not be diminished. In this way priests and ministers of God, serving and living there according to God, may be able to observe their calling.

For it is written that priests should occupy themselves with nothing else except prayer, reading, and preaching. For who can safely announce the judge if the herald is silent? And, as the Lord threatens through the prophet, he says: “If you do not announce his iniquity to the wicked person, I will require his blood from your hand.” For if priests are poor or ignorant, how can they help others? Since “if a man is wicked to himself, to whom will he be good?” [Sirach 14:5]

Therefore, if the houses of God are found in poverty or destruction, how can they teach the people of God? Consider, brothers, what account we shall have to render before the tribunal of Christ. Let the Christian people see: if the houses of God suffer these things, what will be thought about the people themselves [Note: “re” in c.], their houses, and their descendants? For we shall render an account to God for all our actions and negligences at the fearful judgment.

**5.** Therefore priests and ministers of Christ who have been ordained among the clerical grades must be preserved in every respect in their proper office according to God and the teaching of the fathers. They must be learned in the divine books, so that they may be capable of examining themselves and teaching others by correcting them. Those entrusted with handling the divine mysteries must be able to fulfill their ministries wisely and properly [Note: “docenter” in c.], with the fear of God, so that they may truly please the God whom they serve.

**6.** It must certainly be guarded against that the unlearned or illiterate should approach the ministry of Christ in a manner that is unsuitable. Otherwise, God forbid, what the Lord says may happen: “If the blind lead the blind, both will fall into a pit.” They ought not to conduct secular business or behave improperly in other people’s houses; rather, living in the churches, they should strive to perform their proper offices.

**7.** Therefore monks and women religious who have voluntarily vowed and handed themselves over to God, and who have decided to display themselves before human eyes in the habit of religious devotion, should strive to remain in that life, religion, and work. For when they display themselves before human eyes, they are considered, especially in the sight of God, to have made an eternal profession.

Accordingly, they should take care not to be found hypocrites, existing under a false name and habit [Note: “hyporites” in the manuscript]. For it is impious for a human being to lie to God.

Therefore, let everyone strive to observe this and attend to the words of the wisest and best preacher, who says: “Let each person remain in the calling in which he was called.” For whoever changes his vow is bound by the guilt of his conscience and promise, and will appear guilty at God’s judgment if he entirely refuses to amend himself.

Finally, provision must be made, and every effort and vigilant care must be exercised by the person entrusted with the responsibility of governance, so that all these matters may be properly ordered with the fear of God, lest they be left undone through neglect and danger increase; for through negligence and sins both present dangers persist and further dangers grow.

If it pleases your holiness, abbots and abbesses in the monasteries that must be ordered should not be appointed through gifts, but should be sought out with greater diligence—those who know how to possess the fear of God and reverence for human beings, and who shine with good works. Thus, being thoroughly instructed, they may remain in those duties that belong to them and may teach all those subject to them, with right governance according to God and the holy Rule, fully and purely, so that at God’s judgment they may appear not rejected but rather unstained concerning the souls entrusted to them [Note: “judicio” is printed as “udicio”].

Then they may be able to hear that desirable voice: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your lord.”

**8.** We must consider this carefully, and the people must be warned most earnestly, so that no one may take as a wife, from his own kinship, either a veiled deaconess or a woman who has been abducted [Note: c reads “et” for “ex”]. Otherwise he may lose his soul through such acts and become condemned by the institutions of the princes.

These matters, brothers, must be diligently admonished by us to the sheep entrusted to us, lest the Christian people be found to have acted rashly through such presumption and both we and the people incur sin.

**9.** It is reported to us concerning certain regions that on the holy Lord’s Day various activities are carried out, as on other days, although they ought not to be done on that day. Therefore this matter must necessarily be admonished by us, and the people must be restrained with a serious warning, so that on this day, hearing the divine command, no one dares to perform servile work.

For God made heaven and earth and everything in them in six days, and on the seventh day he rested; he blessed and sanctified it, and, when giving the words of the Law to Moses, he said: “Remember the Sabbath day, to sanctify it; you shall rest, you and all that is yours.” And as the psalmist admonishes, saying: “Be still and know that I am the Lord.”

If the Hebrew people celebrate today with such devotion what was entrusted to them as a figure of the New Testament, how much more ought the Christian people to observe with great honor and fear the holy day of the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ and of our redemption, and occupy themselves with nothing else except prayer, hastening to the church of God, hearing the divine commandments with reverence, receiving them with all their heart, believing and practicing them, and diligently partaking of the consecrated body of Christ.

**10.** Therefore, my brothers, all people must be admonished and taught by your holiness so that, holding to the faith they promised at baptism, both men and women may keep the fear of God before their eyes. They must not neglect to learn and retain by heart the Lord’s Prayer and the Creed, so that what the heart believes may be expressed by the mouth.

They should recognize under what condition or religious commitment they received and professed holy baptism, and should strive to preserve Christ’s commandments in everything. By divine command they should love God and their neighbor, as it is written: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your strength, and your neighbor as yourself,” because love of one’s neighbor does no evil.

Hence the Lord also says: “Whoever loves me will keep my word, and I will love him and show myself to him.” And again: “Whoever does not love me does not keep my words; he has one who will judge him.”

For this reason James says: “If anyone observes the whole law but offends in one point, he has become guilty of all.” For what is this one thing except true and perfect charity, which each person ought to observe without deceit?

**11.** It is also necessary to admonish the brothers concerning this, so that each person may preserve a chaste marriage as is fitting, because it is written: “A woman shall be prepared by God for a man, and what God has joined together, let no human being separate.”

Let anyone who is such a person see and understand how he will be judged if he does not strive to amend himself. Whoever separates his own flesh contrary to the divine commandments deservedly becomes condemned.

Likewise, whoever joins himself to a prostitute seeks to defile the body of Christ and the temple of God. See, brothers, see, and attend with careful concern, lest anyone make the members of Christ members of a prostitute, as it is written: “Whoever clings to a prostitute becomes one body.”

For it is better that a man who is without a wife remain so, if he can; but if he cannot control himself, let him marry. Otherwise, God forbid, he may appear separated from God through the devil’s instigation and perish, as it is written: “Whoever separates himself from God will perish.”

Care must be taken lest anyone, pursuing the will of the flesh, lose this life—and the fellowship of the angels—for such a small and passing fault.

Beloved brothers, attend more diligently, for the love of God and through our apostolic admonition, to the things that have been read to you today, and strive to observe and teach them. Let the word of God pass through you in every respect without distinction, lest the enemy, who prowls like a roaring lion seeking someone to devour, find a place of devastation.

Thus both the matters already read and those that still remain to be confirmed through pious governance and your synodal council may benefit everyone toward salvation. For those who are known to have closed ears when admonished are undoubtedly in a state of despair.

Therefore, support everyone with the greatest care through preaching, lest, God forbid, they become alienated from the promised rewards through despair. By observing all these things, may they deserve to be found participants in the eternal kingdom at the divine banquet.

Although this is sufficient for the present in these few words, tomorrow, with God granting it, other matters must also be said for the sake of the affection of the whole people of Christ.

In the name of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, while our most pious lords, the august emperors, were ruling: Hludowic, crowned by God, great emperor, in the thirteenth year of his reign; and also Lothair, the new emperor, his son, in the tenth year of his reign; in the fourth indiction, in the month of November, on the twelfth day.

Eugenius, most holy and most blessed universal pope, with all his fellow bishops—namely: Petronacius, archbishop of the city of Ravenna [Note: “rarauennate” in c.]; Leopardus, bishop of Forosinfrae; Passivus, bishop of Herane; Runuald, bishop of Agnania; Lambert, bishop of Arezzo; John, bishop of Silva Candida; Stephen, bishop of Porto; Benedict, bishop of Aluana; Caesarius, bishop of Ostia; Georgius, bishop of Velletri; Constantine, bishop of Palestrina; Romanus, bishop of Cerveteri; Grasulfus, bishop of Fiesole; Paulinus, bishop of Sunogaul; Peredeus, bishop of Rieti; Auspertus, bishop of Populonia; Valerinus, bishop of Sutri; Stephen, bishop of Rimini; Germanus, bishop of Osimo; Pasivus, bishop of Gabi; Stephen, bishop of Orte; Andrew, bishop of Chiusi; Stabilis, bishop of Castellum Felicitatis; Walipertus, bishop of Urbino; Vestianus, bishop of Suana; Alifredus, bishop of Balneum Regiense; Paulinus, bishop of Trevi; Peter, bishop of Centumcellae; Agatho, bishop of Montefeltro; likewise Agatho, bishop of Polimartium; Magnus, bishop of Assisi; Liutardus, bishop of Nocera; Peter, bishop of Lucca [Note: “lucana”]; Bertoaldus, bishop of Luni; Agiprandus, bishop of Florence; Lomprandus, bishop of Pistoia; Theodoricus, bishop of Perugia; Donatus, bishop of Gabi; Codemundus, bishop of Tuscania; Ragipertus, bishop of Suelli; Tigrinus, bishop of Ancona; Agipertus, bishop of Fano; John, bishop of Pisa; Benenatus, bishop of Gubbio; Lupus, bishop of Fermo; Peter, bishop of Volterra; Sebastianus, bishop of Pavia; Dominicus, bishop of Pesaro; John, bishop of Jesi; Leoninus, bishop of Trevi; Gratiosus, bishop of Nepi; John, bishop of Todi; Eleutherius, bishop of Priverno; Benedict, bishop of Amelia; Theodosius, bishop of Mantua; Adrian, bishop of Salaria; Samuel, bishop of Sabina; Adrian, bishop of Segni; Cosmas, bishop of Humana; Maurinus, bishop of Urbino; Walane, bishop of Chieti—

and all the venerable priests, namely: John the archpriest; Dominic the priest; Georgius the priest; John the priest; Simeon the priest; Sergius the priest; Gregory the priest; Benedict the priest; Ursus the priest; Crescentius the priest; Simeon the priest; Lubianus the priest; Anastasius the priest; Benedict the priest; Maurinus the priest; Ursus the priest, seated before the most sacred body of the most blessed Peter, prince of the apostles;

and with the deacons also present, whose names are: Valentinus the archdeacon; Theodore the deacon; Leo the deacon; Faustinus the deacon; likewise Leo the deacon; Leontius the deacon; and various clergy—

The deacon Theodore read, and the pontiff said:

Since, through the heavenly mercy of God, we are rulers of the Lord’s people, it is especially fitting for us, relying on God’s protection, to think often about their salvation. Otherwise, God forbid, having been frustrated concerning the souls entrusted to us, we may be compelled to render a strict account before the Shepherd of all if, by failing to anticipate correction for offenses, the snares of the ancient enemy prevail.

When I consider and recall in my mind with what vigilance we ought to oppose the wickedness of each person’s crime, and, whenever it springs up to disturb the minds of the faithful, to resist it with the aid of the heavenly blow [Note: “resisterei” is printed in one witness], I am greatly shaken and exceedingly distressed, lest, God forbid, through serpentine cunning it deceive those who are too weak.

Yet, with God’s favor, we must show solicitude for souls with pious speech and mind, relying on divine assistance for the salvation of all people, so that we may not be deceived into a shamefaced appearance before the eternal Judge; the intervening phrase, “de cuiusquam perculsi asistere,” is corrupt and uncertain; rather, may we deserve to hear him say: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your Lord.”

For this reason I say with a groan that I hear that the Christian people living throughout the provinces and localities are rashly acting against the teachings of the Catholic faith and the statutes of the fathers. This must be cut away with a spiritual sword, lest the crop of the good farmer become soiled by weeds mixed with its dreadful fruits.

# Decrees of the Said Pontiff Concerning Ministers and Ecclesiastical Orders

**1. That a bishop be ordained who has been approved by his works.**

A bishop ought in every respect to be consecrated according to the discernment and admonition of the most blessed Paul: desirous of good works, blameless, and possessing all the other qualifications that follow, so that he may adorn the teaching of our God in everything and not be found worthy of contradiction, as is contained in the *Pastoral Book*.

“For,” says the *Pastoral Book*, “with what presumption is the teaching office received by the inexperienced, when the governance of souls is the art of arts?” And again: “That person, then—that person must by every means be led forward as an example—who, dying to all the passions of the flesh, lives spiritually; who has placed the prosperity of the world behind him; who fears no adversity; who desires only inward things; whose intention is so rightly ordered that neither the body entirely resists through weakness nor is excessively resistant through obstinacy [the printed *contumeliam* evidently represents *contumaciam*].

“He is not led by coveting what belongs to others, but gives away what is his. Through the compassion of mercy he is quickly inclined to forgive, yet, in forgiving no more than is proper [Note: “doceat” in c.], he is never bent away from the stronghold of righteousness. He commits no unlawful acts, but mourns as his own the acts committed by others. From the affection of his heart he sympathizes with another’s weakness, and rejoices in his neighbor’s goods as in his own advancement.

“He makes himself imitable by others in everything he does, so that among them he has nothing for which he would even blush concerning the past. He strives to live in this way and is able to irrigate the dryness of his neighbors with the streams of teaching. Through the practice of prayer he has already learned by experience that he can obtain from the Lord what he asks; to him the effect of his prayer is already, as it were, personally declared: ‘While you are still speaking, I will say, “Here I am.”’”

Therefore such things require such men: not unlearned men, lest they be found disgraceful at some opportunity, as the same book states. For when something spiritual is sought from a pastor by his subjects, it is exceedingly shameful if he then begins to seek or learn it at the moment when he ought to resolve the question.

**2. That no bishop or other priest be ordained through gifts.**

Each priest must therefore take care not to appear to be consecrated through rewards, lest, following the example of Simon Magus, he fall into condemnation and the devil’s snare. Both the person who is made through gifts and the person who makes him ought to be condemned, as is found in the Council of Chalcedon and in the councils of the other fathers. For the person ordained through gifts does not desire to contend for the remedy of souls, but to honor the profit of empty glory.

**3. How a bishop ought to teach and conduct himself.**

A bishop ought to be established in good works, so that he may shine not only through deeds that correspond to his office, but may also be an excellent observer of how the people, seeing the word of preaching demonstrated by his works, may undoubtedly attend to it and observe it, as the most blessed Pope Gregory teaches.

The speech of teachers must therefore be shaped according to the character of their hearers, so that it may suit each person individually and yet never depart from the art of common edification.

**4. Concerning unlearned priests.**

Although the admonitions of teachers and the statutes of the fathers prohibit unlearned priests from being consecrated, if a bishop is found to be unlearned, he must, at a suitable time and with due moderation, be admonished by his own metropolitan. Thereafter priests—that is, presbyters, deacons, and even subdeacons—must be admonished by their own bishop so that they may be taught.

Meanwhile, subordinate priests and such clerics must be suspended for a time from the celebration of the divine mysteries and offices, so that they may be able to undertake the ministry proper to them once they have been instructed. If they can be taught, the matter shall lie within the bishop’s authority.

**5. Concerning the canonical rule to be observed in electing bishops.**
