A bishop ought not to be consecrated unless he has been requested by the clergy and the people. Hence Pope Celestine [Note: “et lestinus” is printed in one witness] says: “Let no unwilling person be ordained bishop.” The consent and desire of the people, clergy, and order must plainly be sought.

And the most holy Pope Leo says: “No reason permits those to be counted among the bishops who have been neither elected by the clergy nor sought by the people.” If no worthy person is found in that same church, then another may be chosen from another church. Even if necessity should arise, no one who is unwilling may in any way be consecrated through coercion.

**6. That bishops not remain outside their own parish.**

Bishops ought frequently to be present for the cultivation of their own churches, because the absence of a bishop generally becomes a calamity for the people. Therefore, in accordance with the admonition of the Council of Sardica, they should not remain away from their own churches for more than three weeks, unless this occurs by the command of the metropolitan or the prince in a case of necessity. For subordinate priests likewise ought not to go farther away except by canonical authority.

**7. That clerics ought to live in community.**

It is necessary that cloisters be established beside the church, in which clerics may devote themselves to ecclesiastical disciplines. Therefore there should be one refectory and one dormitory for all, as well as the other workshops and facilities necessary for the use of clerics.

After the bishop, ministers should be chosen over these institutions whose life and teaching will adorn rather than disgrace them.

**8. Concerning priests to be established among dependent baptismal parishes.**

Bishops must diligently care for baptismal parishes as witnesses of their own churches. When the necessity arises for them to ordain priests there, they should, so that the arrangements may be more reverently observed, seek the consent of those who dwell there.

**9. That no more clerics than are sufficient be ordained.**

A measure of discernment must therefore be maintained in assembling clerics: no more should be admitted than the resources canonically assigned to them can adequately support.

**10. Concerning priests who do not live in churches or monasteries.**

Priests ought not to be appointed unless they are assigned to a church or a specific monastery, lest the necessity arise for them to live in secular houses. Otherwise their own bishops should assign them to live and conduct themselves either in the episcopal residence or in monasteries, so that they may perform their office. Women must not be permitted to live in these places under any circumstances.

**11. That a priest not take pleasure in games.**

A priest must diligently search out and proclaim the divine utterances, so that he may be found blessed, of whom the psalmist says: “He will meditate on his law day and night.” Therefore he should not take pleasure in having any game played before him.

If he is found to be a transgressor, he must cease such conduct after the bishop’s admonition, or be judged canonically [Note: c reads “desint au.”].

**12. That priests not engage in moneylending or rustic occupations.**

Priests, who ought without distinction to be present at the churches’ proper and necessary offices, must not be occupied at all with moneylending, hunting, or any other occupation or rustic labor. For it is not fitting for them to appear outside their houses without priestly dress.

They should not expose themselves to the injuries of certain secular people, but observe only those things that appear to have been established by the fathers. Anyone found acting contrary to this must either cease or submit to canonical discipline.

**13. If a priest gives testimony.**

Although the testimony of priests is considered more credible, they themselves should not be summoned to give testimony in secular affairs or to produce documents. For it is not fitting for them to be involved in such matters.

If, while a case is proceeding, they have seen or heard something, and no suitable secular persons can be found, then, so that the truth may not be concealed and the wicked and the good may not be judged alike, it shall lie within the bishop’s discretion to bring the truth honorably forward, either before himself and competent judges or in some other manner.

**14. Where priests should be placed after condemnation.**

If a priest, or anyone else advanced in an ecclesiastical order, is found in a crime for which he ought to be cast out, he must, after deposition, be placed through the bishop’s care in a suitable location, where he may mourn his sins and not commit them again [Note: “eo” is printed as “eos” in one witness].

**15. Concerning suspected priests.**

If any priest—that is, a presbyter, deacon, or even subdeacon—is suspected by reason of the crime of fornication with any woman, and after a first and even a second admonition by the metropolitan, another bishop, or the person to whom he appears subject, is found speaking with her or associating with her in any way, he must be judged canonically.

Therefore each bishop must devote careful and diligent attention to this matter, lest the Church of Christ be defiled by its own ministers. Since a priest is not permitted to have his own wife, he must especially abstain from every woman.

**16. That a bishop may not take away property from dependent parishes and other religious places.**

No bishop may hold immovable property from dependent parishes or other religious places for his own use, lest the greater be enriched excessively and the lesser be found impoverished through such an act.

Anyone acting contrary to this must be restrained by canonical authority [Note: “enormititur” is printed in one witness].

**17. Concerning presbyters who refuse to receive one person’s offering for another.**

No presbyters should be flattered or persuaded by speeches not to receive, for the solemn celebration of Masses, the offerings of all who come to them in any sacred place.

Since they are mediators between God and human beings, they ought to offer the most abundant prayer in carrying out vows and releasing sins. If anyone acts rashly against this rule, he must either cease or be restrained by the judgment of his own teacher.

For our Redeemer, although he is almighty and full of immeasurable mercy, does not receive the vows of countless peoples or loosen the bonds of sins in any way!

**18. Why letters of dismissal should be issued or accepted.**

A bishop should not issue a letter of dismissal for a priest or another cleric subject to him unless the person has been requested by another bishop, lest the sheep be found as though lost or wandering. Rather, the consent of one sheepfold should be found in the other.

And, so that false letters may not be believed as true, nor true ones suspected as false, they must be confirmed by the seal of the universal pontiff, the emperor, or the metropolitan.

**19. That bishops and all priests have advocates** [Note: one witness numbers this as XX].

Since bishops and all priests are appointed solely for the praise of God and the performance of good works, each of them ought to have an advocate for both ecclesiastical and personal affairs, except, of course, in a public crime. The advocate must not be of suspected ill repute, but of good reputation and proven skill, lest, while they attend to human profits, they lose eternal rewards.

**20. Concerning those unable to find advocates.**

If a priest is found unable to produce an advocate in court, his bishop ought finally to examine the priest before his own people, determining whether he has lived a good or bad life, or for what reason he cannot have an advocate for the matter in question [Note: “cura” may mean “causa,” “case”].

If he is found to be bad, care must be taken to correct him according to the nature of his fault and the canonical rule.

**21. Concerning a monastery or oratory built solely through its founder’s ownership.**

A monastery or oratory canonically constructed must not be taken away against the will of its founder. He may entrust it to whichever presbyter he wishes for sacred service in that diocese, with the bishop’s consent and with a letter of dismissal from a person of good authority, lest an unworthy man be appointed.

The priest must obediently return to the bishop for assemblies and according to the reverence due to that bishop.

**22. Concerning an invasion committed as though on behalf of a church.**

If an invader is convicted and says that he acted on behalf of a church concerning private property belonging to him, the invasion must be paid for by him and his heir.

If a priest is found poor in such a fault, he must be judged canonically by his own bishop, so that the church entrusted to him may not suffer loss.

**23. Concerning hospitals and similar places.**

Through the care of the bishops in whose dioceses these places exist, they must be ordered toward the same purposes for which they were established, so that the proper provisions and care may be directed to those who need them.

**24. Concerning religious places that exist without priests.**

There are, it is said, certain religious places found in various regions that, through such impious neglect and deprivation of priests, have no proper services resounding or being performed there. Although they were established solely for the praise of God, as the divine oracle testifies, “My house is a house of prayer,” they are now found to be defiled like other houses by the utility of secular people.

Therefore, if such a place is subject by its own right to a church, the bishop must establish there without interruption a priest together with resources sufficient for its needs. If the places have been established under the authority of secular people, they must be admonished by the bishop of that diocese. If, after being admonished, they neglect to establish a priest there within three months, the bishop responsible for the matter must thereafter report it to the prince without neglect, so that the matter may be corrected by his judgment.

**25. Concerning destroyed churches.**

Churches and all religious places lying in ruins must be restored at the expense of those who made and accepted the promise of their establishment. If their resources are insufficient, the people of the parish must necessarily assist, so that the houses of God may be seen to exist honorably.

**26. If a bishop demands gifts from subordinate priests of churches.**

No bishop may demand from a priest subject to him, or from any other cleric or religious place, gifts beyond those established by the fathers, nor impose them through forced labor.

Since he is to be an excellent observer, he should observe carefully that all the sheep entrusted to him are nourished by him above all and assisted in their necessities, rather than oppressed through unlawful exactions.

**27. What kind of abbots should be appointed.**

Abbés must be appointed in monasteries (*coenobia*, as they are called at the present time) who can undoubtedly fulfill worthily the ministry signified by that name.

They must be so learned that, whenever negligence among the brothers occurs, they can fully recognize and correct it. They should also possess priestly honor, so that they may restrain and cut away in every respect the neglected matters and offenses of the sinful brothers subject to them.

They must observe the Rule in such a way that they are not found to transgress its statutes in any respect.

**28. Concerning monks who possess only the habit and do not live that life.**

Although there are many kinds of monks that ought to be observed, and others that must be rejected in every respect, each bishop must nevertheless labor with careful concern in his diocese concerning those who possess only the habit.

Those who attempt to deceive people through an appearance of religious devotion must be restrained through the zeal of a good shepherd, so that they either return to their own monastery, from which they have been absent, or are sent to another suitable monastery that has been examined.

Those who have once vowed themselves to God and displayed the monastic habit must maintain a regular life, sleeping and living together in one dormitory and refectory, as is fitting, and doing everything in the likeness of the apostles. For no one said that anything he possessed was his own; rather, everything was held in common among them.

**29. Concerning women living under a religious habit.**

Women who receive a religious habit or veil under the pretext of religious devotion, although they had previously been powerful, must thereafter not be permitted to join themselves to men. Instead, they must choose a monastery and live according to its rule, or observe chastely the habit they have received in their own homes.

Those found acting disgracefully must be corrected through the bishop’s care.

**30. Concerning businesses and labor not to be conducted on Sunday.**

It is established that everyone must observe absolutely that on Sunday no one dares to carry on work or commerce, except in matters of food for travelers, so that all may freely and properly be able, according to their means, to hurry to church on that day and devote themselves solely to prayer to almighty God.

Thus those who are called by the Christian name may be seen to perform works fitting to it.

**31. Concerning criminal cases, thefts, and similar matters found on Sunday.**

There are people who, on Sunday—the day on which they ought to cleanse away crimes through prayer—take pleasure in committing other crimes.

Therefore, matters committed on other days must be settled by the authority of the judge. On that day, a person suspected and infamous for guilt should be placed either upon satisfactory surety or in custody, so that he may be judged on lawful days.

**32. Concerning those who have been brought into a monastery against their will without an evident offense.**

Just as those who have chosen a monastery are not permitted to leave monasteries, so those who have been brought into a monastery unwillingly and without the just demonstration of an offense must not be held there unless they wish to remain; for they do not observe what they have not sought.

Such people must therefore be considered especially likely to commit sins rather than mourn them, as is stated most clearly in the decree of the most holy Pope Leo.

**33. That laypeople not stand in the presbytery during Masses.**

Laypeople ought to appear separately, out of respect for priests and the other clerics serving the churches. Therefore no layperson may stand, when Mass is being celebrated, in the place where priests and the remaining clerics stand, which is called the presbytery, so that they may perform the sacred offices freely and honorably.

**34. Concerning the repair of schools for the study of letters.**

It is reported to us concerning certain places that neither teachers nor care are available for the study of letters. Therefore, in all episcopal residences, among dependent parishes, and in other places where necessity arises, every care and diligence must be applied so that teachers and instructors may be appointed.

They must be learned in letters and the liberal arts and must continually teach their doctrines, because through these things the divine commandments are especially revealed and made clear.

35. Concerning not holding banquets on feast days. There are some—and especially women—who on feast days, sacred days, and the birthdays of the saints do not come for the pleasures in which they ought to delight, but contrive to come while holding and teaching choruses, singing seductive and shameful words, and acting in the manner of pagans. [Note: [Col. 0697] *ac venire* (“and to come”), C.] Such people, when they come to church with lesser sins, return with greater sins. In such a matter every priest ought most diligently to admonish the people, so that on these days they may come to church for prayer alone, because those who do such things not only destroy themselves but also take care that others perish.

36. [Note: [Col. 0697C] Among the Capitularies of Lothar, above.] Concerning those who abandon a wife taken in marriage and take another. No one may abandon a wife taken in marriage, except on account of fornication, and then join himself to another; otherwise the transgressor ought to be reunited with his first marriage. But [Note: [Col. 0697] *si*, V, Vn.] if husband and wife should agree to separate from one another solely for religion, [Note: [Col. 0697] *dimittere* (“to dismiss”), V, Vn.] this must in no way be done without the knowledge of the bishop, so that, after he has provided for it individually, a place may be assigned to them. [Note: [Col. 0697] *s. vitae r.*, “for religious life,” V, Vn, E.] For if the wife is unwilling, or either one of them is unwilling, even for such a reason the marriage must not be dissolved. [Note: [Col. 0697] *consenserint* (“they should agree”), V, Vn, E.; *vita* (“life”) is absent in V, Vn, E.; *matrimonium non soluatur* (“the marriage should not be dissolved”), V, Vn, E.]

37. [Note: [Col. 0697C] Among the Capitularies of Lothar, above.] That it is not permitted to have two wives at one time, or a wife and a concubine. No one may have two wives at one time, or a wife and a concubine, because when there is no gain for the household, there is harm to the soul. For just as Christ keeps the Church chaste, so a husband ought to preserve a chaste marriage.

38. Concerning incestuous and unlawful unions. No one should dare to join in marriage with a cousin, a niece, a stepmother, a brother’s wife, or anyone from his own kinship, or one whom a relative has had. If anyone should enter into such a wicked marriage and remain in it, let him know that he is bound by the bond of anathema imposed by apostolic authority; and no priest shall give him Communion. But if he turns away and separates from the unlawful union, let them be subjected to fitting penance, as the priest of the place shall have determined.

I, Eugenius, by the grace of God bishop of the holy catholic and apostolic Roman Church, have subscribed to this decree promulgated by us.

[Col. 0697]

BENEDICT THE DEACON’S COLLECTION OF CAPITULARIES

Pertz’s notice.

(From the *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, volume IV.)

[Col. 0697] This work, appended to the editions of Ansegisus—of which we gave notice in the preface placed before his Collection, excepting the Heroldine edition—is found in the manuscripts listed there: the Gotha, Beauvais, Cambrai, Ripoll, Norman, Troyes, St. Gall no. 727, Colbert, the other Vatican manuscript, the Tilian, Pithou, Paris, and the royal Paris manuscripts 4636, 4634, 3839, and 3839 A. Since Stephanus Baluzius had used most of these, except the Gotha and Paris 4636 and 4634, for his edition, we decided that the text of Baluzius needed only a light revision, using especially the assistance of the very learned young D. Bethmann. The Gotha manuscript immediately appends Benedict’s work, understood as books V, VI, and VII, so that after Ansegisus one reads the words *De Conglutinatione istorum*, etc., written in red ink. Here and there a second hand made corrections, added notes in the margin, and placed two transverse strokes over joined letters *ii*; but only rarely—at two or three points—did it restore words that had been wrongly placed to their proper order by means of the letters *a* and *b*. Very often, where passages useful to the clergy are read, it added in the margin the sign *NOTA*, sometimes with additions such as: “Note carefully”; “Note: a chapter most useful for bishops”; “A very useful note concerning immunity”; and similar remarks. Wherever the scribe of the manuscript indicated that he could not read the exemplar from which he was copying, he marked this in the margin by adding the letter *r*.

[Col. 0699] Of the remaining manuscripts, only the Beauvais manuscript and the other Vatican manuscript present three complete books with Additions II, III, and IV; they resemble the Gotha manuscript also in that, in place of the first Addition, they display only the chapter headings in red at the end of the third book. The royal Paris manuscripts 4634, 4636, and 4635 omit even these headings, although the last is very incomplete and defective. The royal Paris manuscript 4637 contains the three books with Additions I, II, and III; Paris 4635 contains only Additions II and IV. The Ripoll and Cambrai manuscripts present only Benedict’s first book; St. Gall no. 727, books I and II, chapters 1–100; the Norman manuscript, book I and II, chapters 1–363; the Colbert manuscript, book I and excerpts from II and III; and St. Arnulf of Metz, excerpts only from books I–III. The Thuaneus manuscript, formerly Pithou’s, and the Clermont manuscript, lacking three books, contain only the four Additions.

These manuscripts, so far as can be inferred from Baluzius’s annotations, do not differ greatly from one another. Our edition therefore follows the Gotha manuscript chiefly, since in the quality of its readings it is generally preferable to Baluzius’s edition. We have carefully recorded in the margin those readings of Baluzius that ought not to be accepted, together with the more significant variants of Baluzius’s text, and any readings from other manuscripts that Baluzius added and that are worth knowing.

We have already noted that the royal Paris manuscript no. 4761, formerly from Dijon, contains chapters excerpted by Benedict and treated by Baluzius as the second and third Capitularies of Charlemagne of uncertain date. In nearly the same way, the royal Paris manuscript no. 1455—a ninth-century parchment manuscript in folio, from the library of Jacob Tavelli of Sens, later Colbert 3368, royal 3887, 1, 1, A—has, on the page prefixed to the manuscript, book I, chapters 35 and 36, marked as follows: “Concerning accused priests: how they are to clear themselves.” It also contains chapter XLV, likewise wrongly treated by Baluzius as a separate Capitulary. It may also be found in the royal Paris manuscript no. 4376, at the end of the collection of canons, under the title: “From the council of the kings Charles, Louis, and Lothar, which Boniface, legate of the Roman See, attended,” Benedict, book II, chapter 291.

BEGINNING OF THE PREFACE TO THE FOLLOWING CAPITULARIES

[Col. 0699]

[Col. 0699A] Concerning the joining together and communication [Note: [Col. 0699] *communione* (“communion”), G.] of these seven books—namely, the royal capitularies—and how, for whom, and by whom they are shown to have been collected, arranged, and written: the following reading indicates this, as do also the verses appended to them.

Four little books having been completed, venerable reader,

which sufficiently recount the laws of the canons that must be observed,

and which the noble father once suitably collected,

Ansegisus, rejoicing and led by the love of God,

at last, when the pious Autcarius, whom Mainz then held as its chief

bishop, gave the command,

I, Benedict the levite, appended three little books,

in which the work of the law is recounted.

That these were found is clear, as the preface itself reveals,

distinctly, with their titles and headings placed beneath.

Reading these books again, drink them with devoted heart;

I ask you to strive gratefully to pour forth prayers,

so that those who piously enacted these pious laws

may be granted an eternal reward in heaven.

[Col. 0699B] The preceding four little books contain several chapters of the most glorious emperors Charles and Louis, which were collected in their time by Abbot Ansegisus and brought together in the aforesaid little books, as is stated in their preface. But since perhaps not even half of them, as we have thought, was found or collected by him, [Note: [Col. 0699] “more truthfully, half,” G.] it was necessary that they should be sought from the faithful wherever they could be found, and that, for the remembrance of such great rulers and for the usefulness of those same chapters, they should be gathered together, inserted into parchment, and entrusted to the memory of the faithful.

Therefore, whatever he was unable to find or perhaps did not wish to insert, and whatever we later learned from the faithful of the holy Church of God and from Pippin, Charles, and Louis, which was by no means inserted in the aforesaid books, we diligently sought to investigate, for the love of almighty God, of the holy Church of God and its servants, and for the benefit of the whole people. We gathered these things distinctly under their titles in the three following books and did not delay writing them for Louis, Lothar, and Charles, the most noble kings, sons of Louis, the most pious emperor, and for transmission to all faithful Christians. Thus they might know how, according to the pattern of their grandfather, great-grandfather, and father, and in accordance with the will of the Lord—as those rulers also did—they might, with the Lord’s help, deserve to govern the clergy and people entrusted to them.

We found the chapters that we have tried to gather in the following three books scattered in different places and on different sheets, just as they had been issued in different synods and general assemblies. We found them especially stored in the archive of the holy metropolitan church of Mainz by Riculfus, metropolitan of that holy see, and afterward discovered by Autgarius, his successor and kinsman, secondly [in succession]. We preferred to insert them into this little work in the form stated above.

We therefore warn readers that, if they should find the same chapters duplicated or triplicated, they should not attribute this to our incompetence, because, as we have said, we found them on different sheets and for that reason could not correct them so quickly; rather, we have left them to be corrected by readers filled with knowledge. Moreover, we found some having matching beginnings but unequal endings, and others having matching endings but unequal beginnings; in some there was less, and in others more. For that reason we have left them just as we found them.

We also ask everyone that, if hereafter they should discover more of these materials which the aforementioned Ansegisus did not insert and which we have so far been unable to find, they should not hesitate to insert them distinctly in a fourth or fifth book, so that they themselves may thereby have God’s grace and the clergy and people may not lack their benefits. For these chapters are exceedingly useful and will greatly benefit those who wish to know them; they must be held as law, both ecclesiastical and secular, with the firmest authority.

Therefore, first of all we placed several verses composed metrically in praise of the aforesaid rulers. Then follow the chapters of the first book, with their numbers appended, so that the desired provision may be found more easily. After this had been done, a letter of Pope Zacharias was placed at the beginning of the first book, addressed to all bishops and the remaining ranks of the ecclesiastical order, and to all dukes, counts, and all those who fear God throughout Gaul and the provinces of the Franks, as it is contained in that letter.

Two synodal assemblies follow it, which Boniface, legate of the holy Roman and apostolic Church and archbishop of the aforementioned church of Mainz, held canonically in the place of the aforesaid Pope Zacharias, together with Karlomannus, prince of the Franks, so that all might recognize that the chapters of the aforementioned rulers had been especially confirmed by apostolic authority. The matters that follow these, likewise, as we have said, were established in large part by that same authority and were strengthened by the assent of men of both orders throughout the Franks.

In the second book, after the numbering of the chapters, several chapters excerpted from divine law have been placed at the beginning, just as we found them scattered and mixed among their chapters, so that everyone might know that these chapters agree with the divine laws and canonical regulations.

In the third book, after the numbering of that book’s chapters, certain chapters from the canons, collected here and there by Bishop Paulinus, Master Albinus, and the other teachers at the command of Charles, the unconquered prince, have been inserted. After some intervening material, other provisions consistent with the monastic rule follow; finally come the chapters that follow, written for the benefit of the holy Church of God, its servants, and the entire Christian people, as they are contained in that same book.

We also ask all readers, and all judges and wise men, never to interpret these matters maliciously, or to judge anyone unjustly, or to criticize them because some of them have not been composed according to the rules of grammatical art. Rather, they should strive to pray for the rulers themselves, for their faithful and for the faithful of the holy Church of God who deliberated over these matters together with them, and for us, who labored to collect and copy them. With us and with them they should strive equally to embrace, venerate, love, and uphold these chapters as laws, with the Lord’s approval, so that we may all deserve to receive an equal reward from this work. Amen.

BEGIN THE VERSES ON THE AFORESAID RULERS

A golden offspring, powerful in a fortunate lineage,

the strength of the Franks and their perpetual glory,

once Pippin shone sublimely, and

Karlomannus acted in ways pleasing to God.

For, as true guardians moved by love of piety,

they established the sacred laws of the Church.

While the rejoicing reader reads them written here,

let him read no less the laws that follow.

From this point the emperor Charles, relying on divine favor,

nobly ruled his nobles throughout the world.

Guiding their scepters with pious reins as one ruler,

he surpassed the renowned deeds of all his fathers.

Following David and the others with the jewels of his virtues,

he shone everywhere with the distinguished fame of his name.

Why should I recount the many nations that he finally subdued,

from which, returning, he carried away splendid trophies?

Nor is it surprising: while he honored the commands of the heavenly King,

he decreed laws that holy men must observe.

For this he deserved to ascend the heavenly kingdoms,

where he also received abundant rewards.

[Col. 0702A] From there Louis succeeded to his ancestral kingdom,

an exceptional ruler, divine summit of the world.

Under him Germany shone with Augustan splendor,

granting many benefits to her cultivator.

For the emperor, a lover of peace and piety,

cared for his peoples and his communities.

Naturally, renewing the sanctions of earlier kings,

he prudently added pious titles of his own.

Therefore, when he died, he entered the stars of heaven,

singing worthy songs to the exalted God.

From there too follows offspring worthy of veneration throughout the world,

worthy, in his distinguished name, of his father.

[Note: [Col. 0701C] For the following four couplets, the Beauvais manuscript has:

“Lothar first received his ancestral kingdom,

and, made a dweller of the forest of Ardennes, he rejoices.

From there Louis, the hero, rules the people on this side of the banks

of the Rhine and crushes the savage necks of the people.

Then Charles, the beloved image of his dear father,

orders and subdues the assembly of the Gauls.

To them, who hold the fates and the lands in equal portions,

we offer these writings, always to be held by them.”]

For Louis rules on this side of the banks of the Rhine,

and behold, he subdues the fierce peoples.

Lothar too, having obtained an equal dominion,

carries the fearsome scepters of the Frankish emperor.

Then Charles again holds the kingdom of the Franks by lot,

bearing the name of his grandfather, with God’s help.

We, to whom those laws belong which the three books contain,

have offered these writings, always to be held by them.

[Col. 0702B] Their rule teaches us continually to live rightly

and properly to please the Lord through pious pursuits.

These things cut away wicked customs with fair moderation,

granting the pious a rule for living.

For many often commit deadly robberies,

and some violate temples dedicated to God.

Others are defiled by the stain of their crimes,

which no pipe could recount in its entirety.

But the judgment of the sacred laws restrains such people

and forbids them to commit these acts by its pious decrees.

Therefore it is fitting to praise the strong rulers in verse,

who shone through the sacred gift of virtues.

Under whose scepters Francia remained most secure,

flourishing in freedom and trampling proud necks,

whom various peoples feared as a stern mistress,

since she seized them by force of arms in triumph.

Hence she earned for herself a name and everlasting glory,

bringing lofty trophies from conquered peoples.

The kings who were granted the gift of the heavenly homeland

rejoice continually and sing without end.

Gladly they have entered the lofty heights of the heavens,

whom the devoted lyre has already resounded in triumph.

Exceedingly happy are those whom the blessed court receives

and willingly joins to the citizens of heaven.

There they no longer fear dark and harmful shadows;

rather, they behold the delights of the true light.

Thus the Gospel page bears witness,

that the God who thunders on high is the light of the world.

This radiance makes the hearts of the men above rejoice,

and, shining forth, drives away the gloomy clouds from afar.

A certain poet also sang this most beautifully long ago:

that the Lord God is the light to be loved. [Note: [Col. 0701] *luxit* (“he shone”), G; *lusit* (“he played”), Baluzius.] [Note: [Col. 0701] *amando* (“by loving”), G, Baluzius.]

To him belong glory and power, praise and veneration always,

and sacred dominion throughout all ages.

May he grant you a long period of peace,

who bear the talents entrusted to you for the people.

BOOK ONE

[Col. 0701]

[Col. 0701D] 1. Letter of Pope Zacharias addressed to the Franks and Gauls. Pope Zacharias to all bishops, priests, deacons, abbots, and also to all dukes, counts, and all who fear God throughout Gaul and the provinces of the Franks.

Our most reverend and most holy brother, Bishop Boniface, reported to us that, when a synod had been assembled in your province in accordance with our admonition, with our sons Pippin and Karlomannus, your princes, taking part, and the metropolitan Boniface also acting in our place, the Lord enlightened your hearts, together with those of your princes, for his preaching, so that you obeyed all his admonitions and expelled from among you false, schismatic, murderous, and fornicating priests. We have therefore given thanks to our almighty God and are unceasingly praying for you, so that he who began a good work in you may bring it to completion.

For we beseech all of you before God to obey his admonitions firmly. We have appointed him in our place to preach in those regions, so that, with God’s favor, he may lead you to the way of righteousness and you may be saved from all crimes.

Until now, through the agency of sins, you have had false and erring priests. Consequently all the pagan peoples prevailed over you in battle, because there was no distinction between laymen and priests, though priests are not permitted to fight. What sort of victory is given where priests, at one hour, perform the Lord’s mysteries and offer the Lord’s body to Christians for the redemption of their souls, and afterward kill with their own sacrilegious hands the Christians to whom they ought to have administered it, or the pagans to whom they ought to have preached Christ? Especially since the Lord says to them: “You are the salt of the earth. But if the salt has lost its savor, with what shall it be salted? It is good for nothing any longer except to be thrown outside and trampled underfoot by people.”

Since these things are so, and such priests are found among you, how will you be able to be victorious against your enemies? But if you have priests who are clean and chaste, free from all fornication and murder, as the sacred canons command and our aforesaid brother Boniface preaches in our place, and if you obey him in everything, no people will stand before you. All the pagan peoples will fall before your face, and you will be victorious; moreover, by doing good, you will possess eternal life.

But you, dearest brothers, who are true priests or are placed under royal discipline, present yourselves in such a way that you may be known as ministers of God and stewards of the mysteries of God, so that your ministry may not be reproached. [Note: [Col. 0703] *nostrum* (“our”), G.] Let it not happen among you as it is written: “As is the people, so is the priest.” And if this should happen, what praise from people will you have, or what recompense may be expected from God?

Correct yourselves, therefore, as true priests. Promote such men to the priesthood that a good testimony may remain for both you and them from those who are outside, so that you may gain praise from people and deserve to receive from God the reward of eternal blessedness, because through you they have been led to the right faith of Christ, having innocent priests.

Come together for a synod every year to deliberate concerning the unity of the Church, so that, if anything adverse should occur, it may be cut out by the roots and the Church of God may remain unshaken.

Farewell.

2. The synod begins, with its proceedings, held by Saint Boniface and the bishops of the Franks under Duke Karlomannus in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 742, by apostolic command. [Note: [Col. 0703] 762, G.]

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ.

I, Karlomannus, duke and prince of the Franks, in the year 742 from the incarnation of Christ, namely on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May, [Note: [Col. 0703] “March,” G.] with the counsel of the servants of God and my nobles, summoned to a council and synod the bishops who are in my kingdom, together with the priests: namely Boniface the archbishop, Burchard, Regenfrid, Wiztanus, [Note: [Col. 0703] Guntharius, G.] Witbald, Dadanus, Eddanus, and the remaining bishops with their priests. I did this so that they might give me counsel on how the law of God and ecclesiastical religion—which had been scattered and had collapsed in the days of earlier rulers—might be restored, and how the Christian people might attain the salvation of the soul and not perish after being deceived by false priests.

By the counsel of my priests and nobles, we appointed bishops in the cities and established over them the archbishop Boniface, who is the legate of Saint Peter. We also decreed that every year a synod should be assembled, so that, in our presence, the decrees of the canons and the laws of the Church might be restored and the Christian religion corrected.

We restored and returned to the churches the revenues that had been defrauded from them. But we removed and degraded false priests, adulterers, and fornicators, deacons, and clerics from the revenues of the churches, and compelled them to do penance.

We entirely forbid all servants of God to carry weapons, fight, or go on campaign or to war, except only those who have been chosen for divine service, namely to fulfill the solemnities of Mass and carry the patronage of the saints. That is, let the prince have with him one or two bishops [Note: [Col. 0703] “priests,” Tilian and Troyes.] together with priest-chaplains, and let each prefect have one priest who can judge and assign penance to people confessing their sins.

We also forbade all servants of God to hunt or wander through the forests with dogs; likewise, they may not have hawks [Note: [Col. 0703] “or falcons,” G., in the margin.] or falcons.

We also decreed, in accordance with the canons of the saints, that every priest residing in a parish should be subject to the bishop in whose parish he lives, and should always, during Lent, render and demonstrate to the bishop an account and order of his ministry, whether concerning baptism, the Catholic faith, prayers, or the order of Masses.

Whenever a bishop canonically visits his parish and the peoples in order to confirm them, the priest must always be ready to receive the bishop with the assembly and assistance of the people who are to be confirmed there. On the Lord’s Supper, he must always request new chrism from the bishop, so that he may stand as a witness to the bishop’s chastity, life, faith, and teaching.

We also decreed that, as a precaution, no unknown bishops or priests arriving from anywhere should be admitted to ecclesiastical ministry before synodal examination.

We further decreed that, according to the canons, every bishop should exercise care in his parish, with the assistance of the *grafio*, who is the defender of the Church, so that the people of God may not practice pagan rites but may cast away and reject all the filth of heathenism: whether profane sacrifices for the dead; sorcerers or diviners; amulets and auguries; incantations; or sacrificial offerings which foolish people make near churches according to pagan custom under the name of the holy martyrs or confessors of the Lord, provoking their saints to anger; or those sacrilegious fires which they call *Nedfratres*; or any other pagan observances whatsoever. [Note: [Col. 0703] *c.* (“and so on”), Deum and Colbert-Ripoll, Baluzius.]

We likewise decreed that, if after this synod—which was held on the eleventh day before the Kalends of May—any servant of God or handmaid of Christ should fall into the crime of fornication, he should do penance in prison on bread and water. If he is an ordained priest, he should remain in prison for two years and should first be seen to have been scourged and flayed; afterward the bishop should increase the penance.

If a cleric or monk should fall into this sin, after the third beating he should be put in prison and do penance there for a full year. Likewise, veiled nuns [Latin *nonnanes*; G: *nonanes*] should be held to the same penance, and all the hair of their heads should be shaved.

We further decreed that priests and deacons should not wear cloaks in the manner of laymen, but *casulae*, according to the custom of the servants of God. No one should permit a woman to live in his house. Monks and monastic handmaids of God should strive to order, govern, and live in their monasteries or hospices according to the rule of Saint Benedict, and should not neglect to lead their own lives according to the ordering of the aforesaid father.

3. Likewise, another synod held by the aforesaid bishops and prince at Liptinas on the Kalends of March by apostolic authority. [Note: [Col. 0703] “of Charles,” G.]

Now, at this synodal assembly, which was gathered on the Kalends of March at the place called Liptinas, all the venerable priests of God, counts, and prefects, agreeing with the decrees of the former synod, confirmed them and promised that they wished to fulfill and observe them.

The entire clergy of the ecclesiastical order—bishops, priests, and deacons together with the remaining clerics—received the canons of the ancient fathers and promised that they wished to restore ecclesiastical laws in conduct, teaching, and ministry.

The abbots and monks received the rule of the holy father Benedict, in order to restore the standard of regular life.

We command that fornicating and adulterous clerics, who, while previously holding holy places or monasteries, have polluted them, be removed from them and brought to penance. [Note: [Col. 0705] *clericos* (“clerics”) is absent in Baluzius.] [Note: [Col. 0705] *redire* (“to return”), G.] If after this determination they fall into the crime of fornication or adultery, they shall undergo the judgment of the former synod. The same applies to monks and nuns. [Note: [Col. 0705] *nona* (“nun”), written above the line, and *nec*, G.]

We also decreed, with the counsel of the servants of God and the Christian people, because of the wars and persecutions of the other peoples who surround us, that, under a precarious tenure and a census, we may retain for some time a portion of the Church’s property for the assistance of our army, with God’s indulgence, on the condition that each year one solidus—that is, twelve denarii—be paid from each household to the church or monastery. The arrangement shall be such that, if the person to whom the property was lent should die, the Church will be restored to possession of its own property; and again, if necessity compels or the prince orders it, the precarious grant shall be renewed and a new document written. It must be observed absolutely that the churches or monasteries whose property has been granted on precarious tenure do not suffer want or poverty. But if poverty compels it, the full possession must be returned to the church and the house of God.

Likewise, we command that, in accordance with the decrees of the canons, adulteries and incestuous marriages which are not legitimate be prohibited and corrected by the judgment of the bishops, and that Christian slaves not be handed over to pagans.

We also decreed—as my father had previously commanded—that anyone who practices pagan observances in any matter should be fined and condemned to fifteen solidi.

4. Concerning the Catholic faith and the first commandment of the law. First of all we admonish that the Catholic faith be carefully read by bishops and priests and preached to the entire people. For this is the first commandment of the Lord God almighty in the Law: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God.” And he is to be loved with the whole heart, the whole mind, the whole soul, and the whole strength.

5. Concerning the preservation of peace and harmony. Let there be peace, concord, and unanimity among bishops, abbots, counts, judges, and all Christian people everywhere, whether greater or lesser persons, because nothing pleases God without peace, nor does the gift of holy offering at the altar, as we read in the Gospel itself at the Lord’s command.

And there is that second commandment in the Law: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” Likewise in the Gospel: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.” [Col. 0705D] And again: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.”

By this commandment the sons of God and the sons of the devil are distinguished, because the sons of the devil always strive to stir up dissensions and discord, whereas the sons of God always devote themselves to peace and love.

6. Concerning one baptized by a priest who had not been baptized. If someone was baptized by a priest who had not been baptized, and the Holy Trinity was invoked in that baptism, he has been baptized, as Pope Sergius said. But he needs the imposition of hands. Bishop George of Rome and John the *sacellarius* held this opinion. [Note: [Col. 0705] Baluzius conjectured “Stephen.”]

[Col. 0706A] 7. Concerning one who has held his stepson or stepdaughter before the bishop. If anyone has held his stepson or stepdaughter before the bishop for confirmation, he shall separate from his wife and shall not take another. Likewise, the woman shall not take another. George held this opinion.

8. Concerning those who flee to other countries because of a feud. Those who flee to other countries because of a feud and leave their wives behind—neither that man nor that woman shall enter another marriage.

George held this opinion.

9. Concerning incest. If a man has committed incest with a woman consecrated to God, or with his mother, or with his godmother from the font or confirmation, or with a mother and daughter, with two sisters, or with his mother’s daughter, or with his sister’s daughter, or with a niece, or with a cousin, or with a *subrina* (a female cousin), or with an aunt on his father’s or mother’s side, or with those whom the canons prohibit him from marrying, [Note: [Col. 0705] “or to join with them” is absent in Capp. 757, 19.] [Note: [Col. 0705] *copulare* (“to join”), G.] he shall lose his property for these crimes, if he has any.

[Col. 0706B] If he is unwilling to correct these things, no one shall receive him or give him food. If anyone does so, he shall pay sixty solidi to the lord king until that man corrects himself.

If he has no property, then, if he is free, he shall be sent to prison until satisfaction is made; but if he is a slave or freedman, he shall be beaten with many blows.

If his master permits him to fall again into such wrongdoing, the master himself shall pay sixty solidi to the lord king. [Note: [Col. 0705] The remainder is absent in 757, 19.]

Concerning the other relatives, judgment shall be given according to the enactments of the holy fathers and the decrees of the canons.

10. Concerning ecclesiastical men. If ecclesiastical men commit the aforesaid crimes, then, if the person is honorable, he shall lose his honor; lesser persons shall either be beaten or sent to prison.

11. Concerning priests and clerics, that the archdeacon should summon them to the synod. We have ordained concerning priests and clerics that the archdeacon of the bishop should summon them to the synod. [Note: [Col. 0705] “together with the count,” *Capitula incerti anni* 3.] If anyone refuses to go, then, on the bishop’s order, the count, after being warned, shall have him compelled, so that the priest himself or his defender shall pay sixty solidi, and afterward, whether he wishes or not, he shall come to the synod. The bishop shall then have that priest or cleric judged according to canonical authority. The sixty solidi shall be paid from this matter into the lord king’s treasury.

12. Concerning one who resists the bishop’s envoy, or a priest or cleric, in the case of an incestuous person. If anyone violently opposes a priest, cleric, or bishop’s envoy concerning an incestuous person, [Note: [Col. 0705] *v. m. e.* is absent there in book 3.] then the count shall have that person brought before the king under sureties, together with the bishop’s envoys. [Note: [Col. 0705] *ut*, “so that,” G.] The lord king shall then compel them in such a way that the others may be corrected.

13. Concerning those who hold Church property by word of the lord king. The men who hold Church property by word of the lord king are to be so ordered that they must make restitution for the churches from which the property comes, or for the houses of the bishopric or monastery to which they are known to belong, in proportion to the property they hold. They must fully pay there the rents, tithes, and ninths. [Note: [Col. 0705] *annonae* (“grain payments”), G.] This is how we have ordered them at Verneuil. Whoever does not do this shall lose the property itself.

14. That presbyters who hold villages or churches shall pay wax or other dues to the cathedral church of the city, as has been customary. Let those who hold these villages or churches pay the dues or the wax which for a long time they have rendered to that bishopric; we have now ordered that they continue to do so. Whoever does not do this shall pay sixty solidi.

[Col. 0707A] 15. On preserving immunities. Let immunities be preserved in their entirety.

16. On administering justice. Let everyone administer justice, both public officials and ecclesiastical persons. If anyone comes to the palace on account of his case, and has not disclosed before his bishop and his ministers matters that are ecclesiastical, or before his count matters that are secular, in the court before the *rachinburgii*; or if his case has been heard before the count in court and before the *rachinburgii*, and he refuses to accept what they have lawfully judged; if he comes to the palace on account of these matters, let him be beaten. If he is a person of higher rank, let him undergo the legal penalty on that account.  
[Note: [Col. 0707] “his ... secular matters” is lacking in C.; beginning at 9.]

17. On ecclesiastical men who come to the palace to lodge complaints. If ecclesiastical men come to the palace to complain about their cases, let them be beaten unless their complaint is against their superior, or unless their superior has sent them on account of their case.  
[Note: [Col. 0707] This differs in the same manuscript, beginning at 10.]  
[Note: [Col. 0707] *vapulenter* in G.]

18. On a woman who, without her husband’s permission, puts a veil on her head. If a woman has put a veil on her head without her husband’s permission, she may be received again into the marriage if her husband wishes.  
[Note: [Col. 0707] *comiato*: *commeatu* in Normann. and Cap.; *licentia* in Trec., Camb., Pal., Colb., Reg., and in Regino, Burchard, Ivo, and Gratian.]

19. On a man who gives his stepdaughter against her will to a freeborn man or a slave. If anyone gives his stepdaughter, against her will and that of her mother and relatives, to a freeborn man, or to an ecclesiastical person, or to a slave, and she refuses to have him and leaves him, her parents shall have authority to give her another husband. But if she already has a husband, she shall not be separated from him.  
[Note: [Col. 0707] “a slave or an ecclesiastical person” in 757, 4.]

20. On a freeborn woman who takes a slave. If a freeborn woman takes a slave, knowing that he is a slave, let her keep him. For there shall be one law for the man and the woman.  
[Note: [Col. 0707] “and knowing” in G.]

21. On a man who has a lawful wife, if his brother commits adultery with her. If a man has a lawful wife, and his brother commits adultery with her, that brother and that woman who committed the adultery shall never, as long as they live, have another marriage. The man whose wife she was, however, has the right to take another wife if he wishes.

22. That priests and clerics, leaving their bishop, shall not rush to secular courts. Priests and clerics who have cases against one another ought not to leave their own bishop and rush to secular judgments.  
[Note: [Col. 0707] “cases” in G.]

23. That presbyters and deacons shall do nothing apart from the bishop. Let presbyters and deacons attempt to do nothing apart from the bishop.

24. On one who gives or receives offerings without the bishop’s order. If anyone gives or receives offerings apart from the bishop, or apart from the person appointed by him to distribute mercy to the poor, both the giver and the receiver shall be anathema.

25. That it is not permitted to communicate with the excommunicated. It is not permitted to communicate with the excommunicated. Nor is it permitted to pray together with those who meet in private houses while avoiding the prayers of the church. A person who does not assemble in one church is not to be received by another church.

26. On one who disturbs the Church of God. If anyone persists in disturbing and troubling the Church of God, let him be suppressed by external authorities as a seditious person.

27. On monks, that in every city or region they shall be subject to their bishop. Let monks in every city or region be subject to their bishop, love quiet, and devote themselves solely to fasting and prayer while remaining in the places where they have renounced the world. Let them not engage in ecclesiastical or secular business, or be troublesome in any way, by abandoning their own monasteries—unless perhaps the bishop of the city commands them to do so for some necessary work.

28. That a cleric shall remain in the church to which he was assigned. A cleric ought to remain in the church to which, at the beginning, he was assigned and allotted by the bishop, and to which he fled as though to a more important one. We decree that those who reject this arrangement must be recalled to their own church, in which they were first ordained, and serve only there. If anyone transgresses this definition, the holy synod has decreed that he must withdraw from his own rank.  
[Note: [Col. 0707] The text is lacking in G.]

29. That the bishop shall oversee the monasteries. It is fitting that the bishop of the city provide suitable oversight of the monasteries.

30. On one who has been excommunicated for his negligence. If anyone has been excommunicated for his negligence and, during his excommunication, presumes to receive communion before being heard, he shall be judged to have pronounced the sentence of condemnation against himself.

31. That presbyters shall not sell church property. It has been decided that presbyters shall not sell the property of the church in which they have been appointed without the knowledge of their bishops.

32. That manumissions shall be celebrated in the church. Manumissions shall be celebrated in the church.

33. On seeking defenders of the churches from the emperor. Defenders of the churches against the power of secular persons or the wealthy are to be sought from the emperor.

34. That no priest shall be ignorant of the canons. No priest may be ignorant of the canons.

35. What is to be done concerning criminal presbyters against whom there is no proof. We must also consider with great care what is to be done concerning those criminal presbyters against whom there is no proof and who always deny the charges. This matter has very often been discussed by us, our progenitors, and our predecessors, but until now it has not been definitively settled. Therefore, to seek counsel, we are sending our priests to our father, Pope Leo; and whatever we learn from him or his representatives, we shall not delay reporting to you together with those whom we are sending. Meanwhile, consider carefully among yourselves what we should establish concerning these matters, together with the instructions of the aforesaid holy father, so that the people’s murmuring may cease and, satisfying them in these matters, we may remain unharmed on both sides, with the Lord’s help. The constitution in question follows.  
[Note: [Col. 0707] *vobiscum* in Baluz., p. 327.]  
[Note: [Col. 0707] *consulandum* in G.]

36. On the purgation of priests.  
[Note: [Col. 0707] *furcatione* in G.]  
From the capitula of Lord Charles.

We do not doubt that it is known to all of you, by sight or hearing, that, very often, at the prompting of the ancient enemy, various crimes are brought against priests. Although, during the time of our good-memory father Pippin, and in ancient times by the holy fathers and other people of good devotion, this matter was very often discussed—namely, how reasonable examination and satisfaction should be obtained from the accused—we have nevertheless been unable to find it fully and definitively settled.

In our own time, the same matter has very often been discussed by the holy bishops, the other priests, and the remaining ministers of ecclesiastical rank, both those living in our kingdoms or elsewhere for God’s sake and those acting together with us, because many and excessive complaints about this matter have come to us from various regions.

But, after consultation with our lord and father, Leo the apostolic bishop, with the other bishops and priests of the Roman Church, with the patriarchs and other priests of the East and of the Greeks, with many holy bishops and priests, and also with all our bishops, the other priests and deacons, the remaining faithful, and all our counselors, we wish all of you ministers of both orders to know what has been determined.

It has been established, for the reasons, necessity, and authority stated above, after consultation with everyone, that whenever a crime is brought against any priest, if the accuser himself is such a person as ought to be admitted—for the canons fully specify what persons may be admitted to accuse priests—and if that accuser, who is canonically admissible, can prove the charge against him before the bishops with the lawful number of true and good witnesses, then let the case be judged canonically; and if he is found guilty, let him be condemned canonically.

But if the accuser is entirely unable to prove the charge against him on the grounds stated above, let that too be determined canonically. If, therefore, that priest is regarded as suspect or untrustworthy by his bishop, by his fellow priests, or by good and just men of his people or congregation, then, so that he may not remain under accusation or the suspicion mentioned above, let him, following the example of Pope Leo, with three, five, or seven good and neighboring priests—or more, if it seems right to his bishop or if he sees that more are necessary because of the people’s tumult—and with other good and just men, clear himself by an oath sworn before the people upon the four Gospels, and restore himself to the Church.  
[Note: [Col. 0709] Baluz. inserted here, from a few manuscripts: “who had twelve presbyters for his purgation.”]  
[Note: [Col. 0709] *prospexerit* in G.]
[Note: [Col. 0709] *datum* in G.]

If anyone wishes to know what sort of witnesses ought to be admitted for the accusation of priests, and what should be done with the accuser, he can find the matter fully stated in the canons.

37. On one who confesses a crime. It is evident that the person who confesses a crime is the one who does not take advantage of the opportunity granted and assigned for clearing himself by judgment. For it makes no difference whether, in a present examination, all the things said about him are proved, since his very absence is established as a confession.

38. On usury. Not only clerics, but Christian laypeople as well, ought not to exact usury.

39. On counts, that they shall assist the ministers of the Church in their ministries. Let counts become helpers in every respect to the ministers of the Church and to their ministries, so that they may be able to obtain this more fully both from our men, from themselves, and from their own people. Whoever, after being admonished by the count a first and a second time concerning these matters, does not correct himself, we wish his negligence to be reported to our knowledge by that same count, so that by our authority he may be compelled to undergo what is contained in our capitulary.  
[Note: [Col. 0709] “in their ministries” in 825, 23, and II. 23.]  
[Note: [Col. 0709] *continet* in G.]

40. On the ordination of presbyters. Let presbyters not be ordained before they have been examined. Before ordination, let them be fully and diligently instructed in how they ought to avoid vices and how they ought to teach their subjects, lest through their negligence they become sluggish or dull in sacred doctrine, or be stained by the vice of an evil reputation or by any evil resemblance—God forbid.

For the disparagement of priests concerns Christ, whose ministers and messengers they are known to be.  
[Note: [Col. 0709] *dicuntur* (“are said”) in Baluz.] Those who disparage priests and Christ’s ministers sin exceedingly gravely, for, as the evangelical trumpet testifies, it is better for each person that a millstone be hung around his neck and he be cast into the depth of the sea than that he should scandalize one of the little ones, namely Christ’s ministers.

And elsewhere: “Whoever receives you receives me; and whoever despises you despises me.” We earnestly admonish all to avoid this sin of disparagement and scandal, and, bearing witness before God, we beseech God’s faithful not to disparage Christ’s ministers.

Likewise, we admonish the ministers and priests of Christ our Lord, and our teachers, not to give their subjects an opportunity to disparage them, because “whoever disparages his brother is a murderer,” and disparagement is said to be worse than fornication. Therefore we admonish and especially beseech everyone not to act in such a way that anyone is found to be a murderer without a sword or any bodily wound.

And just as we have decreed judgment concerning persons physically killed, so, with the Lord’s consent, we decree that judgment be carried out concerning those who are exposed before us as guilty of this crime of disparagement, so that, insofar as the Lord grants assistance, the peace of the churches in the lands and regions entrusted to us by God may not be disturbed by any storm of disparagement or war.

41. On how presbyters are to obtain entry into churches. Let no presbyter give a gift for entry into a church.

42. On not compelling anyone to drink. Let no one be permitted to compel another to drink.

43. On the persons by whom presbyters are to be appointed to churches. Let no layperson presume to install or expel a presbyter in a church except with the consent of the bishop.  
[Note: [Col. 0709] “from the church” is lacking in I. 141.]

44. On giving an honorarium for churches. Let bishops determine what honorarium presbyters shall give to their superiors for their churches.

45. On the distribution of tithes. Let tithes be under the authority of the bishop, so that he may determine how they are to be distributed by presbyters.

46. On improving churches or altars. Let churches and altars be established in better condition. Let no presbyter presume to store grain or hay in a church.

47. On churches or altars of uncertain consecration. Let churches or altars whose consecration is uncertain be consecrated.

48. On preparing altar linens. Let presbyters preach throughout their parishes to women that they should prepare linens for the altars.

49. On another presbyter’s parishioners. Let no presbyter receive another presbyter’s parishioner for Mass, unless he is traveling or has a legal hearing there.

[Col. 0710C] 50. On another presbyter’s parish. Let no presbyter presume to celebrate Mass in another presbyter’s parish without consulting him, unless he is traveling; nor may he dare to receive a tithe belonging to another.  
[Note: [Col. 0709] *eo* is lacking in I. 148.]

51. On the boundaries of churches. Let every church have a defined territory from whose villages it is to receive tithes.

52. On the property of presbyters. Let every presbyter leave to his own church the property he acquires after the day of his consecration.

53. On not compelling penitents to drink wine. Let no presbyter or layperson compel a penitent to drink wine or eat meat, unless, for the present occasion, he gives one or two denarii on the penitent’s behalf, according to the severity of the penance.  
[Note: [Col. 0709] “invite” in I. 151.]

54. On presbyters from whom people should beware. Let no presbyter write documents or act as his superior’s steward.

[Col. 0710D] 55. On presbyters who celebrate ecclesiastical services in private residences. It has been decreed that if any presbyter celebrates ecclesiastical services in private residences without the permission and counsel of his bishop, he shall be deprived of priestly rank.

56. On preaching and the presbyters’ capitula. Let every presbyter have capitula concerning greater and lesser vices, by which he may be able to recognize and preach to his subjects how they should guard themselves against the devil’s snares.

57. On the Eucharist. Let the presbyter have the Eucharist prepared, so that whenever someone becomes ill, or a small child becomes ill, he may immediately give him communion, lest he die without communion.

58. On having three ampullae on the Lord’s Supper.  
[Col. 0711A] Let a presbyter carry three ampullae with him on the Lord’s Supper: one for chrism, another for oil with which catechumens are to be anointed, and a third for anointing the sick, according to the apostolic teaching. Whenever someone becomes ill, let the presbyter bring in the priests of the church, so that they may pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord.  
[Note: [Col. 0711] *inunguendos* (“to be anointed”) inserted below in G.; compare Anseg.]

59. That all clerics shall be subject to their bishops. Let all presbyters, deacons, and subdeacons remain under the authority of the bishop.  
[Note: [Col. 0711] “deacons and” is lacking in 755, 8.]

60. On the order of priests. Let no presbyter presume to baptize or celebrate Mass in another parish without the order of the bishop in whose parish he is. Let all presbyters assemble at the bishop’s council. If they disdain to do what has been set out above, both they and their defenders shall be judged according to canonical regulation.

61. On one who does not confess that the Word of God suffered in the flesh. If anyone does not confess that the Word of God suffered in the flesh, was crucified in the flesh, tasted death in the flesh, and became the firstborn from the dead, according to the fact that he is life and giver of life as God, let him be anathema.  
[Note: [Col. 0711] “is made alive” (*vivificatur*) in G.]

62. On the forms of excommunication, both of clerics and of laypeople. If a presbyter has been degraded or excommunicated by his bishop and afterward, in contempt, presumes to perform any part of his office without permission, and is then corrected and excommunicated by the bishop, anyone who knowingly communicates with him shall know that he is likewise excommunicated.

If any cleric, layperson, or woman commits incest and, after being corrected by the bishop, refuses to amend, and is excommunicated by him, anyone who afterward communicates with that person shall likewise be excommunicated.

So that you may know what the form of this excommunication is: the person may not enter a church, take food or drink with any Christian, or receive gifts from anyone; no one may offer that person a kiss, join him in prayer, or greet him, until he has been reconciled by his bishop.

If anyone complains that he has been unjustly excommunicated, he shall have permission to come to the metropolitan bishop, so that he may be judged there according to canonical regulation; meanwhile, he shall observe his excommunication.

If anyone despises all these provisions and the bishop is entirely unable to correct the matter, let him be condemned to exile by the king’s judgment.

63. On those condemned by a synod or by their bishop. You can read these matters individually in the statutes of the Council of Nicaea, in the synodal decrees of other holy fathers, and in the Council of Antioch. It is prescribed there that those who have been condemned by a synod or by their bishop and afterward presume to minister are not to be received into communion by anyone. Whoever communicates with them shall likewise be subject to the same sentence as the condemned person.

64. On bishops or any members of the clergy. Likewise, in the same council, it is provided that a bishop or any member of the clergy shall not dare to bring a complaint before the royal dignity concerning his own cases without the counsel or letters of the bishops or of the metropolitan; instead, their case shall be examined in a common council of bishops.

65. On how Sunday is to be observed. Likewise, in the same council, it is prescribed that Sunday be observed from evening to evening.

66. On unknown names of angels. Likewise, in the same council, it is prescribed that unknown names of angels neither be invented nor spoken, except those whom we have on authoritative testimony. These are Michael, Gabriel, and Raphael.

67. On women, that they shall not approach the altar. Likewise, in the same council, it is provided that women ought not to enter the altar area.

[Col. 0712A] 68. On ordaining bishops or other members of the clergy. Likewise, in the Council of Chalcedon, it is provided that a bishop or any member of the clergy ought not to be ordained for money, because both are to be deposed: the one who ordains and the one who is ordained, as well as the person who acts as mediator between them.

The canons of the apostles state the same concerning this matter: If any bishop, presbyter, or deacon obtains this dignity for money, let him and his ordainer be deposed, and let them be cut off from communion.

69. On sorcerers and enchanters. Likewise, in the same council, it is provided that spoon-makers, sorcerers, enchanters, and enchantresses shall not be permitted to practice their arts, which the Lord condemned terribly in Simon Magus.

70. On clerics’ cases among themselves. Likewise, in the same council, it is provided that if clerics have any case against one another, they shall be judged by their bishop, not by secular authorities.

71. On conspiracies of clerics, monks, or laypeople. Likewise, in the same council, it is provided that neither clerics, monks, nor laypeople shall form conspiracies or lay snares against their pastor.

72. On preaching the faith of the holy Trinity. In the Council of Carthage: First of all, it is necessary that the faith of the holy Trinity, and of Christ’s incarnation, passion, resurrection, and ascension into heaven, be carefully preached to everyone.

73. On those who turn to God. Likewise, in the same council, concerning those who are in danger and turn to God: let them be examined canonically concerning reconciliation, and let them be reconciled canonically.

74. On those who do not lead a good life. Likewise, in the same council, it is provided that those who do not lead a good life and whose conduct is blameworthy shall not dare to accuse bishops or persons of higher rank.

75. On those who communicate with an excommunicated person. Likewise, in the same council, it is provided that whoever presumptuously communicates with an excommunicated person shall himself be excommunicated.

76. On the subjection of presbyters. Likewise, in the same council, in the following two chapters, it is provided that no presbyter shall dare to act arrogantly against his bishop.

77. On clerics of the ecclesiastical order. Likewise, in the same council, it is provided that if clerics of the ecclesiastical order incur guilt, they shall be judged by ecclesiastical persons and not by secular authorities.  
[Note: [Col. 0711] “in the council” in G.]

78. On false names of saints. Likewise, in the same council, it is provided that false names of martyrs and uncertain memorials of saints shall not be venerated.

79. On a wife dismissed by her husband. Likewise, in the same council, it is provided that neither a wife dismissed by her husband shall take another husband while her own husband lives, nor shall a husband take another wife while his former wife lives.

80. On the offerings of the poor. In the Council of Gangra, it is provided that no one may seize or defraud offerings intended for the poor.

81. On fasts established by priests. Likewise, in the same council, it is provided that ecclesiastical fasts established by priests shall not be broken without a reasonable necessity.

82. On those who sin against nature. In the Council of Ancyra: If there are found among you people who sin with quadrupeds, or with blood relatives as far as the seventh generation, or with males against nature, they are to be restrained by severe and strict penance. Therefore, the bishops and presbyters who impose the judgment of penance should strive by every means to prohibit or eradicate this evil from customary practice.  
[Note: [Col. 0711] *quicumque* in G.]

83. On names being recited. Likewise, in the same council, it is provided that names shall not be recited publicly before the priests’ prayers.

84. On priests not being ignorant of the canonical ordinances. Likewise, in the same council, it is provided that no priest may be ignorant of the ordinances of the holy canons.

85. On priests acting against decretal provisions.  
[Col. 0713A] Likewise, in the same council, it is provided that if any priest presumptuously acts against the constitutions of the decretals and refuses to be corrected, he shall be removed from his office.

86. On bishops examining the faith of presbyters. Let bishops carefully examine throughout their parishes the faith of the presbyters, Catholic baptism, and the celebration of Masses, so that they hold the right faith, observe Catholic baptism, and properly understand the prayers of the Mass; and so that they chant the psalms worthily according to the divisions of the verses, understand the Lord’s Prayer themselves and preach it so that all may understand it, so that each person may know what he asks from God.

Let “Glory be to the Father” (*Gloria Patri*) also be sung among all with full honor, and let the priest himself, together with the holy angels and the people of God, sing with one voice: “Holy, Holy, Holy.”

Presbyters and deacons must be told in every way not to carry weapons, but to place their confidence more in God’s protection than in arms.  
[Note: [Col. 0713] “among all people” in G.]

87. On presbyters being appointed to churches by bishops and by no others. It has been decreed that presbyters shall neither be appointed nor expelled from any churches without the authority or consent of the bishops. If laypeople present to the bishops clerics of commendable life and teaching to be ordained and appointed to their churches, let the bishops reject them on no pretext.

88. On new villages and churches newly established in them. It has been decreed concerning new villages and the churches newly established in them that the tithes from those villages shall be assigned to those same churches.

89. On presbyters who keep women in their houses. The bishops have decreed concerning presbyters who indiscreetly permit women to live with them and thereby become marked by suspicion of bad repute: if, after being admonished, they do not correct themselves, they shall be struck with canonical punishment as despisers of the sacred canons.

90. On scribes. Let scribes not write incorrectly.

[Col. 0713C] 91. On incestuous persons. Concerning incestuous persons: let them be examined canonically, and let neither some be released nor others constrained because of anyone’s friendship.

92. On the communion of the faithful. Let all the faithful receive communion and attend Masses without any excuse.  
[Note: [Col. 0713] *perexpectent* in I. 132.]  
[Note: [Col. 0713] “without any plea” (*deprecatione*) in I. 132.]

93. On taking refuge in a church. If anyone takes refuge in a church, let him have peace in the church’s atrium, and let it not be necessary for him to enter the church. No one may presume to drag him away from there by force. He may confess what he has done, and from there he shall be brought by the hands of good men into the public hearing for examination.

94. On the admonition of priests. Let priests admonish the people to give alms and pray for the various afflictions which we continually suffer on account of our sins.

95. On preaching to the people. Let each priest strive, according to his order, to preach and teach the people entrusted to him.

[Col. 0713D] 96. On parents’ and godparents’ instruction of children. Let parents diligently strive to instruct their children, and let godparents instruct those whom they receive from the baptismal font: the parents, because they have begotten them and they have been given to them by the Lord; the godparents, because they stand as guarantors for them.

97. On churches established in ancient times. Let churches established in ancient times be deprived neither of tithes nor of any possession.

98. On those who appoint or expel presbyters without the bishop’s consent.
