Concerning those who appoint presbyters in their churches or expel them from their churches without the bishop’s consent, and who, after being admonished by the bishop or by any royal envoy, refuse to obey: let them be compelled to pay our ban, and ordered to come to our palace through sureties. Then let us decide whether it pleases us that they pay that ban or suffer another *harmiscara* (penalty).  
[Note: [Col. 0713] *persolvat* in G.]  
[Note: [Col. 0713] *sustineat* in G.]

99. On churches divided among coheirs. Concerning churches that have been divided among coheirs, it has been determined that, if the coheirs wish to hold and honor them according to the oversight and admonition of the bishop, they may do so. If they oppose this, let it remain in the bishop’s power to decide whether he permits them to remain in that condition or removes the relics from them. Wherever churches belonging to our benefice are found to have been divided in this way, let them be recorded and reported to us.  
[Note: [Col. 0713] The word is lacking in G.]

100. On a hide given to a church. Concerning a single hide given to a church, from which certain people, contrary to the statutes, exact service for themselves: whoever is accused on this account, let the count or our envoys compel him to restore to the presbyters what was taken from it, together with its lawful due.

101. On those who refuse to give tithes unless they are redeemed from them. Concerning tithes which the people refuse to give unless they are redeemed from them in some way: the bishops must prohibit this. If anyone is found to be contemptuous and refuses to heed either the bishop or the count, if he is our man, let him be compelled to come into our presence. Let the others be constrained so that, unwillingly, they restore to the church what they voluntarily neglected to give.  
[Note: [Col. 0713] *qui* or *quod* has been written above it in G.]

102. On witnesses for examining any matter. Whenever witnesses must be sought and chosen to examine any matter, let our envoy and the count in whose jurisdiction the matter is to be handled choose people of the kind who can be found to be the best in that district. Let litigants not be permitted to bring false witnesses through rewards, as has until now been customary.

103. On the case of a drunken man, his testimony, and the count’s court. Let no drunk man be able to pursue his case in court or give testimony. Nor may a count hold court unless he is fasting.  
[Note: [Col. 0713] “of the name” in G.]

104. On whether presbyters have given holy chrism to subvert a judgment. Let a presbyter who has given holy chrism to subvert a judgment, after he has been deposed from his rank, lose his hand.

105. On the court of the hundred. Let no one be judged in the court of the hundred concerning death, the loss of his freedom, the return of property, or the return of slaves. These matters are to be judged in the presence of the count or our envoys.  
[Note: [Col. 0713] “these” in Bal.]

106. On the abduction of widows. Whoever takes a widow in marriage, whether unwilling or willing, within the first thirty days of her widowhood shall pay our ban—sixty solidi—in triple amount. If he took her unwillingly, he shall pay her legal compensation, but shall not approach her thereafter.  
[Note: [Col. 0713] “or” in Bal.]

107. On one who kills a person doing public penance. Whoever kills a person performing public penance shall pay our ban in triple amount and pay his *wergild* to his relatives.  
[Note: [Col. 0713] “his” in Bal.]

108. On observing the lord’s commands. Concerning the observance of our commands and immunities, we order that they be observed just as they were established by us and by our predecessors.  
[Note: [Col. 0713] “immunity” in Bal.]

109. On places that were once sacred and are now polluted with filth. Concerning places that were once sacred and are now polluted with filth: let them be restored, insofar as possible, to their former condition.

110. On retaining useful exchanges and abolishing useless ones. Wherever exchanges made in our time or in the time of our father are lawful, reasonable, and useful to the churches of God, let them remain. Wherever they were useless, inconvenient, or unreasonable, let them be dissolved, and let each person receive back what he gave. But wherever a dead hand intervenes, or any other cause is found that does not appear reasonable, let the matter be carefully recorded and reported to our knowledge.  
[Note: [Col. 0715] *inter* in Bal.]

111. On consecrating a church in which the bodies of unbelievers have been buried. It is not permitted to consecrate a church in which the bodies of unbelievers have been buried. But if it appears suitable for consecration, let the bodies be removed and the church rebuilt after its wood has been scraped or washed. If it had previously been consecrated, it is permitted to celebrate Masses in it, provided that those buried there were faithful.

112. On the office of laypeople. A layperson ought not to recite a reading in church or say the *Alleluia*, but only a psalm or responsories without the *Alleluia*.

[Col. 0715B] 113. On releasing the vow of fools. A bishop may release a vow if he wishes.

114. That presbyters shall not disclose a bishop’s crime. A presbyter may not disclose the sin of a bishop, because the bishop is above him.

115. On another presbyter’s parishioners. Let no presbyter receive another presbyter’s parishioner, unless he is traveling; nor may he dare to receive a tithe belonging to another.

116. On the imposition of hands and canonical absolution. Let no priest presume to judge, without the authority of the canons, the sins of people who confess them to him.

Whenever a priest, according to the canonical procedure stated above, assigns penance to someone confessing his crimes to him, if that person lets his hair grow long or changes his clothing, let the priest impose hands on him, with the prayers contained in the sacramentary for the imposition of penance, according to canonical authority. If he has confessed secretly and voluntarily, let it be done secretly. If he has been convicted or has confessed publicly and openly, let it be done publicly and openly, and let him perform penance publicly before the church according to the canonical degrees.

After he has completed his penance, whether secretly or openly, according to canonical regulation, let him be reconciled canonically, and let hands be imposed on him with the prayers contained in the sacramentary for reconciling a penitent, so that through divine prayers and mercies he may deserve to be absolved from his crimes. For no bound person is absolved without the imposition of hands.

Therefore our Lord and Master gave his disciples and their successors the power of binding and loosing, so that they might have the power to bind sinners, and so that those who worthily perform penance might be absolved and their sins forgiven through invocation of God.

This is not surprising. For if human beings give their servants authority over their subjects to bind and loose, harm and help, how much more has the Lord of all human beings given this authoritative power to the leaders of the holy Church, saying: “Receive the Holy Spirit. Whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them; and whose sins you retain, they are retained.” And the rest.

### 117. Concerning a penitent whose crime has become widely known

The Council of Carthage prescribes concerning this matter that, if the public and notorious crime of some penitent has disturbed the whole Church [Note: [Col. 0715] “in the council”: “which the whole Church has known.”], hands are to be imposed upon him before the apse. Elsewhere, in the canons or in the decretals of Pope Leo, the same matter is prescribed: that the absolution of penitents is to be effected through the imposition of the bishops’ hands and their supplications; and many other things of this kind and similar things.

### 118. Concerning penitents who have received the Eucharist while ill

Penitents who, while ill, have received the Eucharist as viaticum are not to consider themselves absolved without the imposition of hands if they survive.

### 119. Concerning the remedy of penance, and that the absolution of penitents is to be effected through the imposition of the bishops’ hands and their supplications

For this reason it is necessary that the guilt of sins be loosed before the final day through priestly supplication, even if, when the danger of death is pressing, reconciliation follows immediately after the acceptance of penance.

From [Note: [Col. 0715] G and Bal.’s manuscripts read “copy.”] a letter of Pope Leo to Theodore, bishop of Fréjus. The manifold mercy of God so comes to the aid of fallen humanity that hope of eternal life is restored not only through the grace of baptism but also through the medicine of penance. Those who have violated the gifts of regeneration, condemning themselves by their own judgment, attain the remission of their crimes through remedies arranged by the divine will, so that they cannot obtain God’s pardon except through the supplications of priests [Note: [Col. 0715] G reads “be obtained.”].

For the mediator between God and human beings, the Lord Jesus Christ, has handed this power over to the leaders of the Church, so that they may impose the discipline of penance upon those who confess and admit those cleansed by that saving satisfaction to communion in the sacraments through the door of reconciliation. The Savior himself continually intervenes in this work, and is never absent from them, as he himself says: “Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age.”

By this it is indicated that, if anything is accomplished through our ministry in good order and with an acceptable result, we should not doubt that it has been granted to us through the Holy Spirit. But if one of those for whom we supplicate the Lord, being overtaken by some obstacle, should fall away from the benefit of the present indulgence and, before reaching the remedies established for him, should end his temporal life in accordance with human nature, what he did not receive while remaining in the body [Note: [Col. 0715] G reads “receives.”] he will not be able to obtain after being stripped of the flesh.

Therefore it is necessary for us to examine the merits and deeds of those who have died, since our Lord, whose judgments cannot be comprehended, has reserved for his own justice what he did not allow to be fulfilled through the ministry of priests [Note: [Col. 0715] G reads “will reserve.”]. He wished his power to be feared, so that this fear might benefit everyone [Note: [Col. 0715] G reads “error”], and so that no one might fail to fear what some lukewarm or negligent persons accept.

For it is greatly useful and necessary that the guilt of sins be loosed before the final day through priestly supplication. Yet to those who, in a time of necessity and under the pressure of dangers, implore the protection of penance and immediately afterward reconciliation, neither satisfaction is to be forbidden nor reconciliation denied. For we can impose neither measures nor times upon the mercy of God, with whom conversion suffers no delay, as the Spirit of God says through the prophet: “When you have turned and groaned, you will be saved.” And elsewhere: “First declare your iniquities, that you may be justified.” Again: “For with the Lord there is mercy, and with him abundant redemption.”

In administering God’s gifts, therefore, we must not be difficult, nor must we neglect accusations against oneself, groans, and tears, since we believe that the disposition to repent is conceived through God’s inspiration. The Apostle says: “Lest perhaps God may grant them repentance, so that they may recover from the snares of the devil, by whom they are held captive for his will.”

### 120. Likewise concerning the absolution of penitents, that it is to be effected through the prayers of bishops or priests with the imposition of hands

If someone has received penance in danger, in peace, or while ill, and it is believed that he is immediately going to die, he is to be reconciled through the imposition of hands, and the Eucharist is to be poured into his mouth.

### 121. That a penitent is to be admitted to communion after displaying the fruits of penance

A penitent, after displaying the necessary fruits of penance, is to receive legitimate communion with the reconciliatory imposition of hands.

### 122. That penitents are to receive a hair shirt from the priest on their heads at the time when they seek penance

At the time when penitents seek penance, they are to receive from the priest the imposition of hands upon their heads and a hair shirt, as has been established everywhere.

### 123. That during the whole time of fasting hands are to be imposed upon penitents by priests

Throughout the whole time of fasting, hands are to be imposed upon penitents by priests.

### 124. That those who have fallen away are to be absolved through the imposition of the bishop’s hands

We are not to believe that those who have fallen away in faith are to be absolved except through the imposition of the bishop’s hands.

### 125. That penitents who die before reconciliation are to receive communion

It has been decided that those who, having accepted penance, depart to the Lord before reconciliation are to receive communion, because they honored penance. If they survive, they are to remain in the order of penitents, so that at the appointed time they may receive legitimate communion through reconciliation and the imposition of the bishop’s hands [Note: [Col. 0717] Added by Benedictus: “or, at his command, by the hands of a priest.”].

### 126. Concerning those who have taken part in the feasts of the pagans

Those who have taken part only in the feasts of pagans and have eaten sacrificial foods can be cleansed through fasts and the imposition of hands.

### 127. That criminal sins are to be cleansed by priests through many fasts and frequent impositions of hands

It has been decided that criminal sins are to be cleansed through many fasts, frequent impositions of the priests’ hands, and their supplications, in accordance with the statutes of the canons, so that no one may consider himself absolved from his crimes without the imposition of the bishop’s hands or, at his command, those of a priest.

It is not to be wondered at if the absolution of sins is effected through the imposition of hands and the prayers of priests, since in the old law the Lord commanded the priest’s hand to be placed upon the head of the victim. For just as then it was through that victim, so now it is through the invocation of the Holy Spirit, through whom remission of sins takes place [Note: [Col. 0717] G reads: “who is remission”], that sins are remitted through the imposition of the bishops’ hands, or through the imposition of the hands of other priests by their authority, together with their supplications.

For when the Lord raised Lazarus, he said to his disciples: “Take away the stone”—that is understood to mean, so that the dead man might rise. He gave an example: just as they themselves remove the stone with their hands so that the dead man may rise, so they and their successors are to impose hands upon penitents, so that through the imposition of hands and their prayers they may cause the dead man to rise from the grave—that is, the sinner to rise from his vices—and raise him up.

And just as they loosened the aforementioned Lazarus, bound with grave-cloths—that is, with ropes—at the Lord’s command when he said, “Unbind him and let him go” [Note: [Col. 0717] G omits “who says, ‘Unbind him and let him go’”], so these priests, with the Lord’s help and the accompanying Holy Spirit, who always works in them, are to loosen sinners’ bonds through the imposition of hands and, at the time established by the holy fathers, admit them to communion in the sacred Eucharist. Having been absolved, they are to permit them to depart.

### 128. That penance is to be given to penitents according to canonical authority, and that before their suspension from communion they are to keep vigil at the church’s office

Penance is to be given to penitents according to the form of the canons. First, having suspended them from communion, they are to make them keep vigil at the church’s office and frequently return among the other penitents for the imposition of hands. When the time of satisfaction has been completed and priestly prayer has been offered [Note: [Col. 0717] G reads: “after receiving the imposition of hands”], the penitents are to be reconciled through the imposition of hands according to the order of the sacraments and the canons, and they are to be strengthened with holy communion.

### 129. Concerning penitents who have been separated from communion

Those who are separated from communion are to be received back into communion in the places in which they had been secluded, through the imposition of hands. No one is to consider himself absolved from sins without the reconciliatory imposition of hands; rather, through the imposition of hands and the prayers of priests he is to be reconciled, as ecclesiastical authority prescribes.

### 130. That a penitent is not to be suspended from reconciliation for too long when death is near

The offering of one who, still a penitent and not yet reconciled, has departed this life is to be received by the Church [Note: [Col. 0717] G reads “is to be accepted.”]. One who is doing penance in danger of death is not to be delayed long from the grace of reconciliation. But if the danger of death is plainly pressing, penance having been accepted through the imposition of hands [Note: [Col. 0717] G reads “the penance previously accepted through the imposition of hands”], reconciliation is immediately to be provided, lest the sick man depart from human affairs before receiving the gift of reconciliation. Otherwise, for those who survive, it may somehow appear to be a perpetual cause of grief if the nature of death should suddenly remove from the present life one who, cut off from the members of the Church, had not obtained the grace of reconciliation.

Therefore, in accordance with the decree of Pope Leo, to those who in a time of necessity and under the pressure of imminent danger implore the protection of penance [Note: [Col. 0717] G reads “the remedy of penance and, as is customary, the remedy of reconciliation”] and immediately afterward the remedy of reconciliation, neither satisfaction is to be forbidden nor reconciliation denied, because we can impose neither measures nor times upon the mercy of God.

Concerning those who, having accepted penance, have departed this life before being reconciled, although there is a diversity of prescriptions concerning this matter, the opinion of those who have decreed more humanely and in considerable number has nevertheless pleased us: that the memory of such persons be commended in the churches and that an offering dedicated for their spirits be accepted.

### 131. Concerning priests or deacons convicted of a more serious offense

It has also been confirmed that, whenever priests or deacons have been convicted of some more serious fault for which it is necessary to remove them from ministry, hands are not to be imposed upon them as upon penitents or as upon faithful laypeople. Nor is it to be permitted that those who have been rebaptized be promoted to the clerical rank.

### 132. Concerning penitents who perform penance for more serious or lesser offenses

Concerning penitents who perform penance either for more serious offenses or for lesser ones: if no illness intervenes, the custom of the Roman Church shows that they are to be released on the Thursday before Easter. In other matters, it is the priest’s responsibility to assess the weight of the offenses, attending to the penitent’s confession and to the tears and weeping of the one who is correcting himself, and to command his release when he has seen suitable satisfaction [Note: [Col. 0717] G reads “as much as he has judged.”].

But if someone falls ill and reaches the point of despair, release is to be granted to him before the time of Easter, lest he depart from the world without communion.

### 133. Concerning those who have taken part only in the feasts of pagans and eaten sacrificial foods

Those who have taken part only in the feasts of pagans and have eaten sacrificial foods can be cleansed through fasts and frequent impositions of hands, so that thereafter, abstaining from sacrificial foods, they may be able to participate in Christ’s sacraments.

But if they have either worshiped idols or been defiled by murder or fornication, they ought not to be admitted to communion unless they have been reconciled through public penance and the imposition of hands accompanied by priestly prayer.

The periods of repentance are to be established with moderation, according as the priests see the dispositions of the converts to be devout, while also taking account of old age and considering the needs arising from every kind of danger or illness. If someone is so severely afflicted that, while he is still doing penance, hope for his salvation is despaired of, priestly care must come to his aid through absolution by priestly prayers—that is, through the imposition of hands—and through the grace of communion.

### 134. That penitents who perform penance for more serious sins are to be among the hearers for three years if they have truly repented

Penitents who perform penance for more serious sins, if they repent from the heart, are to be among the hearers for three years, as the Council of Nicaea established concerning those who had fallen away. For five or seven years they are to remain among the penitents under the hands of priests. For two years they are in every way forbidden to offer oblations; they are only to join the people in prayer.

Nor are they to be ashamed to bow their necks to God, since they did not fear to deny him. But if, as mortal beings, the end of life should begin to press upon them within the limits of the prescribed time, aid is to be given to those who implore it—whether by the bishop who imposed the penance, or by another who has verified that it was imposed, or likewise by a priest, but only at the command or with the permission of their own bishop. Through the imposition of hands and absolution by priestly prayers, viaticum is not to be denied to those departing from the world.

To children, however—those whose name derives from purity—or to clerics, laypeople, or likewise to young girls, for whom the ignorance of their age provides an excuse, communion is to be restored after they have been held for some time under the imposition of hands.

But if, before the appointed time of penance, persons who had received the grace of communion recover, whether because physicians had despaired of them or because they had been oppressed by evident signs of death [Note: [Col. 0719] G reads “indeed”], we are to observe in their case what the Nicene canons ordained: that they be counted among those who communicate only in prayer, until the period of time granted to them has been completed.

### 135. Concerning catechumens, who are not to be passed over

Catechumens are not to be passed over, since the case is not dissimilar, as the same holy canons have ordained. Those who in any way have renounced Christ, whom they had once confessed, are to be among the hearers for three years. Afterward they are to be permitted to pray with the catechumens and are to receive the grace of Catholic communion through the imposition of hands.

### 136. That those who perform public penance are to remain among the hearers for one year in a hair shirt

Those who perform public penance are to remain for one year in a hair shirt among the hearers, or until the great day. When the people enter the church, they are to ask forgiveness with streaming tears and humbly pray the people to deign to pray for them.

For three years they are to remain among the penitents under the hands of priests, in the place established for penitents behind the church door. Apart from the people, yet still within the church, no longer prostrate on the ground but with face and head bowed, they are humbly and sincerely to ask forgiveness, as stated above, and request that prayers be offered for them.

For two years they are in every way forbidden to offer oblations; they are only to join the people in prayer. Thus, in the seventh year, at the Lord’s Supper, they are to attain perfection and receive the grace of Catholic communion through the imposition of the hands of the bishop—or, if he is absent, at his command, of other priests—together with absolution through priestly prayers.

#### How the seven years of penance are to be carried out

Throughout these seven years they are to persevere in many fasts, prayers, tears, almsgiving to the best of their ability, and weeping [Col. 0719D]. They must take the greatest care that such things do not happen to them again, as the Lord says: “Go, and do not sin again.”

### 137. Concerning penitents who transgress

Those who repeatedly commit sins or repeat penance through frequent transgression are to be restrained or condemned by repeated sentence unless they attempt to correct through satisfaction what they have transgressed, so that what they did not voluntarily purge they may correct unwillingly.

If anyone refuses to comply with this and proves disobedient to the commands of his priest, he is to be excommunicated according to the measure of his fault. But if anyone presumes to communicate with such persons before their reconciliation and satisfaction, without the permission of their own bishop, he is to undergo the same excommunication.

The priests to whom such persons are known to belong are likewise to be punished by the same sentence if, whether because of some gift, favor, or negligence, they are unwilling to admonish them; if they do not receive those returning through satisfaction; or if, out of contempt, they do not expel them from the Church—until either a sentence of correction or a sentence of condemnation concerning them has been promulgated.

### 138. That penance is to be given to penitents without respect of persons

The priest is to impose the laws of penance upon anyone who implores penance, without respect of persons.

### 139. Concerning more negligent penitents

More negligent penitents are to be received more slowly.

### 140. Concerning one who requests penance while ill

If someone requests penance while ill, and, by chance, while the priest who has been summoned is coming to him, he is overcome by illness, becomes speechless, or falls into delirium, those who heard him are to give testimony, and he is to receive penance.

If he is believed to be immediately dying, he is to be reconciled through the imposition of hands, and the Eucharist is to be poured into his mouth. If he survives, the aforementioned witnesses are to remind him of the satisfaction he requested, and he is to be subjected to the prescribed period of penance for as long as the priest who imposed the penance has determined.

### 141. That penitents are not to consider themselves absolved except through the imposition of hands

Penitents who have received the Eucharist as viaticum while ill [Note: [Col. 0719] B reads “received”] are not to consider themselves absolved without the imposition of hands if they survive.

### 142. Concerning penitents who die by chance on a journey or at sea before fulfilling the laws of penance

Penitents who, before fulfilling the laws of penance, happen to die on a journey or at sea, where a priest could not come to their aid, are to be commended in memory, prayers, and offerings.

### 143. Concerning the location and buildings of monasteries to be provided

It is worthy and necessary that our envoys sent through the various regions, together with the bishops of each diocese, inspect the sites of monasteries of canons, monks, and likewise women, to see whether they have been established in a suitable and appropriate place where the necessary convenience can be obtained [Note: [Col. 0719] G reads “could be obtained”], which contributes to the usefulness of the monasteries. As it is said in the holy Rule: “A monastery ought to be established in such a way that all necessities may be carried on within the monastery, so that the monks or clerics have no need to wander outside, because this is altogether unprofitable for their souls” [Note: [Col. 0719D] “Or clerics”: Benedict added this from his own text].

Likewise, the aforesaid envoys and the bishops with them are to inspect the buildings of monasteries in different places, to see whether they are suitable and appropriately arranged for the holy profession, and whether they have a strong enclosure in which the souls of those dwelling there can be preserved under canonical or regular discipline.

Wherever they are found to be otherwise, the bishop of that place is in every way to have the matter corrected, so that the canons, monks, and nuns may have a custody worthy of their profession, and so that no opportunity for wrongdoing may be given to them—God forbid.

### 144. That bishops are to know how canons who are with abbots live

We command that each bishop know, in each monastery, how many canons each abbot has in his monastery. The two of them are altogether to ensure that, if the canons wish to become monks, they live according to the Rule; but if not, that they live entirely according to canonical discipline [Note: [Col. 0719] G omits this].

### 145. That priests carefully guard the chrism

Priests are to guard the chrism under seal and are not to presume to give any of it to anyone under the pretext of medicine or sorcery. If they do so, they are to be deprived of their office.

### 146. That priests regularly use oraria

Priests are continually to use oraria, because of the distinction of priestly dignity.

### 147. That laypeople neither expel priests from churches nor install them there without the consent of their own bishops

Laypeople are not to expel priests from churches, nor install them without the consent of their bishops.

### 148. That laypeople are not to demand gifts from priests

Laypeople are in no way to demand unjust gifts from priests in connection with assigning a church to any priest [Note: [Col. 0721] Bal. reads “from any priest.”].

### 149. Concerning fugitive clerics

Each bishop is carefully to inquire in his parish where the priests or clerics are from. If he finds a fugitive, he is to make him return to his own bishop.

### 150. Concerning the Greater Litany

It has pleased us that the Greater Litany be observed by all Christians for three days.

### 151. Concerning the observance of the Ember seasons

We decree that the four seasons of the year be observed by everyone with fasting. That is, in the month of March, during the first week, on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday, everyone is to come to the church at the ninth hour with litanies for the solemn celebration of Mass.

Likewise, in the month of June, during the second week, there is to be fasting on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday until the ninth hour, and everyone is to abstain from meat. Likewise, in the month of September, during the third week. In December, it is to be observed during the week that is complete before the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity, as has been handed down in the Roman Church.

### 152. Concerning an imposed fast

If anyone, in pride, despises an imposed fast and refuses to observe it with the other Christians, the Council of Gangra prescribes that he be anathematized unless he strives to correct himself.

### 153. Concerning Sundays

We have decreed that all Sundays be observed with complete reverence and that people abstain from servile work. There is to be no market on those days, nor any court session at which someone is judged [Note: [Col. 0721] Bal. reads “handed over”] to death or punishment.

### 154. Concerning tithes

We admonish and command that the tithe not be neglected but be given entirely to God [Note: [Col. 0721] G reads “to give”; likewise below], since God himself established that it be given to him. For it is to be feared that, if anyone withholds from God what is owed to him, God may perhaps take away from that person what is necessary because of his sin; and whoever neglects to give the tithe to God will have the nine parts taken away from him [Note: [Col. 0721] The following material is taken by Benedict from the synodal letter of the Second Council of Tours, A.D. 567].

### 155. That churches are to have peace

No one is to dare to drag a defendant who has fled to a church away from it, or hand him over from there to punishment or death, so that the honor of God and his saints may be preserved. Rather, the rulers of the churches are to strive to obtain peace, life, and bodily safety for such persons. Nevertheless, they are to make legal settlement for what they have done unjustly.

### 156. Again concerning the peace of churches

We command that secular court sessions be held neither in churches nor in church buildings or atria.

### 157. That ancient churches are to retain their privileges

Churches established in ancient times are not to be deprived either of tithes or of their other possessions so that these may be assigned to new oratories.

### 158. Concerning ecclesiastical benefices

All who hold an ecclesiastical benefice are to contribute fully toward repairing the church roofs and restoring the churches themselves, and are to render the ninth and the tenth [Note: [Col. 0721] The words “and the ninth and the tenth are to be rendered” are absent from manuscripts 813 and 24; G reads “or provisions.”].

### 159. That a priest is not to sing Mass alone

No priest, as it seems to us, can properly celebrate Mass alone. For how will he say, “The Lord be with you,” or exhort them to have their hearts lifted up, and perform the many other things similar to these, when no one else is with him?

### 160. Concerning making the offering and peace in the church

The Christian people are also continually to be admonished to make the offering and peace in the church, because that offering is a great remedy for the souls of the offerer and his own people, and in that peace true unanimity and concord are demonstrated [Note: [Col. 0721] G reads “are to be demonstrated.”].

### 161. Concerning the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer

Priests are always to admonish the Christian people to learn the Creed, which is the seal of faith, and the Lord’s Prayer. We also wish those who neglect to learn these things to receive fitting discipline, whether through fasting or through some other correction.

Therefore it is fitting that they send their sons to school, either to monasteries or elsewhere to priests, so that they may properly learn the Catholic faith and the Lord’s Prayer and be able to teach others at home. Whoever cannot do this otherwise is to learn it in his own language.

### 162. That the evil of drunkenness is to be avoided entirely

We command that the great evil of drunkenness, from which all vices spring, be avoided in every way. We have decreed that anyone unwilling to avoid it is to be excommunicated until he makes suitable correction.

### 163. Concerning spiritual godchildren

We command that each godfather and spiritual kinsman instruct his spiritual children in the Catholic faith.

### 164. That lustful singing is to be abandoned around churches

We entirely prohibit the performance of shameful and lustful songs around churches; such conduct is also to be avoided everywhere.

### 165. Concerning those who commit incest

We command that bishops diligently investigate those who commit incest [Note: [Col. 0721] Camb. reads “punish”]. If they are unwilling to repent, they are to be expelled from the Church until they return to penance.

### 166. That marriage is not to be contracted in the fourth, fifth, or sixth degree

We also prohibit anyone from contracting marriage in the fourth, fifth, or sixth degree [Note: [Col. 0721] The words “in the fifth, fourth, and sixth” are absent from the Council of Mainz]. Wherever such a union is found after the prohibition has been made, it is to be dissolved.

### 167. That one may not take one’s own child from the baptismal font or hold the child at confirmation

Therefore no one is to take his own son or daughter from the baptismal font, nor is anyone to marry his goddaughter or godmother, nor a woman whose son or daughter he has held at confirmation. Wherever this has occurred, the parties are to separate.

### 168. Concerning condemned marriages

If someone has married a widow and afterward committed fornication with her daughter, or has married two sisters, or if a woman has married two brothers, or a father and son, such unions are to be anathematized. They are never again to be joined in marriage, but are to be punished under severe discipline [Note: [Col. 0721] Trec. and Camb. read “struck down.”].

### 169. Concerning the care and preaching of priests toward the people entrusted to them, and that they are to expel criminals from the Church

Priests are to care for the people entrusted to them and are to preach diligently concerning the salvation of their souls. They are also to rebuke criminals according to evangelical instruction [Note: [Col. 0721] G reads “of the priest.”].

### 170. That all priests are to teach their subjects the Lord’s Prayer and the Creed

The priest is to ensure that all who are counted by the name of Christian know the Lord’s Prayer and the Creed by heart and understand them.

### 171. At what times baptism is to be administered

Baptism is not to be administered except at the appointed times, namely Easter and Pentecost, unless illness intervenes. Nor is baptism to be administered elsewhere except in public villages, unless, as has already been said, illness makes it necessary.

### 172. That no payment is to be accepted for baptism

No priest is to presume to accept payment for baptism. If he does so, he is to know that he is to be condemned according to canonical rule.

### 173. Concerning tithes, that they are faithfully given by the faithful and canonically distributed by priests

Tithes are to be faithfully rendered to the holy Church, and priests are faithfully to distribute them according to canonical rule.

### 174. Concerning priests, that they are not to undertake secular offices or become village judges

Priests are in no way to undertake secular offices; that is, they are not to become judges or village officials [Note: [Col. 0723] G omits “or village officials”].

### 175. That priests ordained for titular churches are to promise stability before their promotion

Priests who are ordained for titular churches are, in accordance with the canons, to make a promise of stability in that place before they are ordained.

### 176. That women are not to live with priests

Priests are not to have permission for women to live with them, so that they may avoid suspicion.

### 177. Concerning fugitive priests or clerics

Canonical authority is to be observed concerning fugitive priests or clerics. That is, no one of us is to ordain a cleric belonging to another parish, nor receive one who has been ordained, without the permission of his bishop [Note: [Col. 0723] Bal. reads “pontiff.”]. It is also to be considered what is to be done concerning such persons.

### 178. That Mass is in no way to be celebrated in unconsecrated houses

It has been decreed that no priest is in any way to presume to offer the oblation in houses that have not been consecrated by bishops.

### 179. That priests, deacons, and subdeacons are neither to carry weapons nor to engage in hunting

Care must also be taken that priests, deacons, and subdeacons do not presume to carry weapons or engage in any hunting.

### 180. That a woman may not abandon the holy veil once she has received it

In whatever manner a woman, with canonical permission from her husband or after his death, has received the holy veil upon her head—whether willingly or unwillingly—she is to remain in it entirely and is not to abandon it.

### 181. That the property of the poor or less powerful is not to be purchased under an evil pretext

For the sake of provisions for the poor, for whom we ought to care, it has pleased us that neither bishops, abbots, counts, vicars, judges, nor anyone else at all dare, under an evil pretext or through evil intent, either purchase the property of the poor or less powerful or take it from them by force.

But whoever among them wishes to purchase something is to do so in a public court, before suitable witnesses, and with proper legal justification [Note: [Col. 0723] G reads “if anyone.”]. Wherever the contrary is found to have occurred, it is to be completely corrected by our command.

### 182. Concerning the power of bishops over ecclesiastical property, and concerning the agreement of bishops with laypeople

Bishops are to have the power to oversee, direct, govern, and administer ecclesiastical property according to canonical authority.

We wish laypeople to obey bishops in their ministry, in the governing of the churches of God and the defense of widows and orphans [Note: [Col. 0723] The remainder is omitted by the Metz manuscript, which offers the following in its place: “And Pope Nicholas says in that passage that, in accordance with the sanction of the sacred canons, all the property of the Church is to remain in the power of the bishop, and that he is to distribute it, according to the fear of God, to whomever and in whatever manner he wishes. In the book written above, this chapter is likewise found taken from canonical authority: ‘If anyone’ (cf. chapter 24).”], defend widows and orphans, and obey them in preserving their Christian faith.

The bishops are also to cooperate with counts and judges in administering justice. Under no circumstances is a just law to be corrupted in any matter through anyone’s lie, false testimony, perjury, or payment.

### 183. Concerning one who presumes to reopen a case that has been judged

If anyone presumes to reopen a case that has been judged in the public court and is there convicted by witnesses, he is either to pay fifteen solidi or receive fifteen blows from the scabini who previously judged the case.

### 184. Concerning coloni and fiscalini

Neither a colonus nor a fiscalinus is to be able to make transfers anywhere.

### 185. Concerning the life of canons

Therefore, as far as human frailty permits, we have decreed in every respect that canonical clerics live canonically, observing the teaching of divine Scripture and the instructions of the holy fathers. They are not to presume to do anything disorderly without the permission of their bishop or their superior.

In each bishopric they are to eat and sleep together wherever they have the means to do so. Or those who receive stipends from ecclesiastical property are to remain in their cloister and come every day early in the morning to the reading, where they are to hear what is commanded them. At table likewise they are to listen to a reading and render obedience to their superiors according to the canons.

### 186. Concerning priests who have been killed

For priests who have been killed, payment is to be made to the bishop to whose parish they belong, according to the capitulary of our glorious father Charles. Specifically, the bishop is to give half of the priest’s wergild for the needs of the church over which he presided, and distribute the other half justly as alms for him, because no heir of his appears closer to us than the one who joined him to the Lord.

### 187. Concerning the accusation of a bishop

No criminal is to be permitted to accuse a bishop.

### 188. That monasteries dedicated to God are not to become secular lodging places

Henceforth, monasteries known to have been consecrated to God are, in accordance with canonical institution and insofar as we can prevent it, not to be made secular lodging places. Instead, they are to be assigned to religious people who fear God and to consecrated persons.

### 189. That conspiracies or confederacies are not to be formed

Conspiracies or confederacies are not to be formed, because the sacred canons severely condemn those who do such things.

### 190. Concerning those who hold Church property

If anyone holds ecclesiastical property and, after being admonished, evades judgment, then, until he comes to an investigation, he is either to restore the ecclesiastical property or be deprived of communion.

### 191. Concerning a Church slave caught in theft

If a Church slave is caught in theft, he is to be disciplined by the public judge, just like the others. If a public judge presumes, without a theft having been committed [Note: [Col. 0723] G reads: “without presuming that a theft has been committed by the Church slave”], either to detain or to injure a Church slave without the hearing of the vice-lord or archdeacon, he is to be barred from the thresholds of the Church for an entire year [Note: [Col. 0723] G reads “they are to be barred.”].

192. Concerning those who have inflicted injury on a cleric. From the Council of Auxerre. Whoever, whether a judge or a layman, presumes to inflict injury on a priest or deacon, or on anyone of the clergy or of the junior clergy, without the hearing of the bishop, archdeacon, or archpriest, shall be held excommunicated from the fellowship of all Christians.

193. That murderers and other accused persons who ought to die according to the laws, if they flee to a church, are to be given no food. Murderers and other accused persons who ought to die according to the laws, if they flee to a church [Note: G. omits “they are not to be excused”], are to be given no food. [Note: G. has instead: “From the capitularies enacted by Lord King Charles in the eleventh year of his reign.”]

194. Concerning tithes to be distributed at the bishop’s command. Let each person give his tithe and distribute it at the bishop’s command.

195. How thieves are to be dealt with. Let thieves from within the immunity [Note: G.: “from the immunity”] be brought before the judge of that immunity at the count’s placitum. Whoever fails to do this shall lose his benefice and honor. Likewise, if our vassals do not fulfill this, let them lose their benefice and honor. Those who have no benefice shall pay the bann.

196. Concerning perjury. Concerning one who commits perjury: let him pay no redemption, but lose his hand. If the accuser wishes to contest the matter of that perjury, let them stand at the cross. If the swearer prevails, let the accuser make compensation according to his law. This is to be observed in lesser cases. In greater matters, or concerning the status of free birth, let them observe the law.

197. Concerning thieves justly put to death and men unjustly punished. The bishops testify that vengeance and a just judgment carried out against thieves entail no sin for the count, provided that this is done without envy or malicious pretext, and that nothing else is introduced there except true justice brought to completion. But whoever punishes a man out of hatred or evil intent, and not for the sake of carrying out justice, shall lose his honor and make compensation under the laws to the one against whom he acted unjustly, according to the penalty he inflicted.

198. Concerning nones [Note: G. consistently has “annones,” provisions] and tithes, or the census, of churches. From the properties of churches from which a census is now paid, let the tithe and the ninth be paid together with the census. From those from which they were not formerly paid [Note: G. has “exacted”], let the ninths and tithes likewise be given. From holdings of fifty casati, one solidus; from thirty, half a solidus; from twenty, one tremissis [the text reads *transmissus*]. Let the precariae also be renewed in the customary manner [Note: the remainder differs in the year 779, chapter 13]. Where they are not written down, let a record be made among the *conventores* on the basis of our word.

199. Concerning the tributaries of churches. Let it be done with regard to wax-payers, tablet-holders, and charter-holders as it was decreed long ago.

200. That no oath be made for a guild. Concerning oaths sworn mutually for a guild: let no one presume to make such an oath. In another matter, concerning their almsgiving, or fires, or shipwrecks, although they may make an agreement, let no one presume to swear in this connection.

201. That no one obstruct travelers. Concerning travelers who are going to the palace or elsewhere: let no one dare to attack them by a levy [Note: G.: “levy”]. Let no one presume to take fodder during the time of defense [Note: G.: “in time of defense”], unless he is going to war or is our envoy.

202. Concerning prohibited tolls. Concerning tolls, as they were formerly prohibited, let the rule be observed: no one shall collect anything except what had been established from ancient times [Note: Bal.: “had been established”].

203. That slaves not be sold without witnesses. Concerning slaves: let them not be sold except either in the presence of the bishop or count, or in the presence of the archdeacon, centenarius, count’s vicedominus, or count’s judge, or before well-known witnesses. Let no one sell slaves outside the march; whoever does so shall pay the bann as many times as he sold slaves. If he does not have the price, let him hand himself over to the count as a pledge for the price until he pays the bann itself.

204. How counts or royal vassals who do not administer justice are to be dealt with. If a count does not administer justice in his ministry, let him serve our envoys from his own property or from his gifts [Note: absent in the year 779] until justice has been done there. If our vassal does not administer justice, then both the count and our envoy shall sit at his house and live from his resources until they administer justice.

205. Concerning those who refuse to receive the price for a feud and to administer justice. If someone does not wish to receive the price for a feud and to administer justice on that account, we wish to send him to such a place that greater harm may not increase.

206. Concerning thieves to be punished twice through their limbs and a third time through their life. Concerning thieves, we order this to be observed: for the first offense, he shall not die, but shall lose one eye; for a second offense, the thief’s nose shall be cut off; for a third offense, if he has not amended himself, he shall die.

207. A decree of prayers requested from certain bishops. A capitulary was established at this assembly of the bishops as follows: each bishop is to celebrate three masses and three psalters—one for the lord king, another for the Frankish army, and a third for the present tribulation. Priests are to celebrate three masses. Monks and nuns [Note: G.: “nuns”] and canons are each to recite three psalters. All are to observe two-day fasts, both bishops and monks and nuns and canons, as well as their dependent people holding casati [Note: G.: “chaste men”], and those who are able to do so.

Each bishop, abbot, and abbess who is able is to give a pound of silver, or its value, as alms; those of moderate means, half a pound; the poorer, five solidi. Bishops, abbots, and abbesses are to feed four poor and hungry people during this period of distress until harvest time. Those who cannot do so for that many are to support three, two, or one, according to their means.

The more powerful counts are to give a pound of silver, or its value, as alms; those of moderate means, half a pound [Note: Bal.: “half a pound”]. A royal vassal with two hundred casati [Note: omitted by Bal.] is to give half a pound; with one hundred casati, five solidi; with fifty, one ounce. Let them observe two-day fasts, and let their people, their dependents, and those who are able to do so observe them as well [Note: the decree has a different wording].

Whoever wishes to redeem the three-day fast is to give: the more powerful counts, three ounces; those of moderate means, thirty denarii; the poorer, one solidus. With regard to poor and hungry people, let them do as is written above. May all these things, if it pleases the Lord, be completed by the Mass of Saint John for the lord king, the Frankish army, and the present tribulation.

208. That the properties of churches are the vows of the faithful, the prices of sinners, and the patrimonies of the poor; and that not only must those things be preserved which have been entrusted to them, but other things must also be added. Since, according to the tradition of the holy fathers, we know that church property is the vows of the faithful, the prices of sinners, and the patrimonies of the poor, we desire not only to preserve what it possesses but also, with God’s help, to contribute many things to it. Nevertheless, in order completely to remove from ecclesiastics the suspicion that had long since arisen concerning the division of the property of that church, we decree that neither in our time, nor in the time of our sons, nor—by God’s dispensation—in the time of our successors who may wish to imitate our will or that of our ancestors, shall they suffer any division [Note: G.: “let them make no division, so that he may suffer”] or loss whatsoever.

209. Concerning gifts made to the church that are to be divided. It has been decreed that whatever is freely given by the faithful to the church during our imperial rule shall, in richer places, be divided into two thirds for the use of the poor and one third for the support of the clergy or monks. In poorer places, however, it is to be divided equally between the clergy and the poor, unless it has been specifically given by the donors for some particular purpose.

210. Concerning the ordination of slaves. Concerning the ordination of slaves, who were being indiscriminately advanced everywhere to ecclesiastical orders, it has pleased all that agreement must be maintained with the sacred canons. It has therefore been decreed that henceforth no bishop shall presume to promote them to sacred orders unless they have first obtained freedom from their own masters.

If any slave, fleeing or hiding from his master, or by using hired or bribed witnesses, or by any craft or fraud, has reached ecclesiastical orders, it is decreed that he be deposed and that his master receive him. But if his father or mother, migrating from one homeland to another, has begotten a son in the same province, and the son has been raised there and promoted to ecclesiastical orders, unaware that he was a slave, and afterward his master comes and legally claims him, it has been decreed that, if his master wishes to grant him freedom, he may remain in his order. But if the master wishes to remove him from the royal estates by the chain of slavery, he shall lose his order, because a person remaining of servile condition cannot exercise the dignity of the priesthood in accordance with the sacred orders.

Concerning the property or peculium of those who are granted freedom by their own masters so that they may lawfully be promoted to ecclesiastical orders, it has been decreed that it remains in the power of the masters whether they wish to grant it to them or claim it for themselves. If they acquire anything after ordination, the rule established in the canons concerning consecrated persons who possess nothing is to be observed.

With regard to the slaves of churches, it has been decreed by common agreement that the archbishops appointed in each province shall possess our authority, while the suffragans shall carry a copy of it with them. Whenever someone useful from the household of the church is found who is to be ordained [Note: G.: “a useful woman”], this authority is to be read aloud before the people in the ambo and before the priests or faithful laymen, and before the altar horn. As our authority states, he is to obtain freedom, with every form of deceit removed, and only then is he to be promoted to ecclesiastical orders.

The same procedure is to be followed concerning those whom laymen wish to promote from the households of churches to sacred orders. The same form is also to be observed concerning those whom the superiors of canons or monks request for ordination.

211. Concerning persons from whom property is not to be accepted. It has been decreed that no ecclesiastic shall henceforth presume to accept property from persons whose children or relatives might, through this ill-considered offering, be disinherited from their own property. If anyone thereafter attempts to do this, let him be strictly punished by synodal judgment, and let the property return to those who were disinherited.

212. That no priest persuade anyone to receive the tonsure out of greed. It has been decreed that no one established in a canonical or regular profession shall henceforth persuade anyone to receive the tonsure in order to obtain property [Note: G.: “strive to do so”]. Whoever attempts this shall in every way be punished by synodal or imperial judgment.

213. Concerning the appointment of priests. It has been decreed that priests shall neither be appointed nor removed in any church without the authority or consent of the bishops. If laymen present to the bishops clerics of commendable life and learning, to be ordained and established in their churches, the bishops shall reject them on no pretext whatsoever.

214. Concerning the mansus of each church. It has been decreed that one complete mansus be assigned to each church without any service obligation. The priests established in them are not to perform any service other than ecclesiastical from the tithes or offerings of the faithful, from the houses, courtyards, or gardens situated beside the church, or from the aforesaid mansus. If they possess anything more, let them render the service owed from it to their superiors.

215. Concerning the priests of each church. It has been decreed that, once this has been fulfilled, each church shall have its own priest wherever, with the bishop’s provision, circumstances permit this to be done.

216. Concerning sacred church vessels given as pledges. Concerning the sacred vessels of churches, which we have learned are given as pledges by some people in certain places, it has been prohibited that anyone henceforth presume to do this, unless they are compelled by the sole necessity of redeeming captives.

217. Concerning destroyed churches, and concerning nones [Note: G. consistently has “annones”] and tithes. Concerning destroyed churches, and concerning nones and tithes, as well as the cloisters of canons, how we wish them to be established and ordered, we have noted in other chapters.

218. Concerning priests who keep women in their houses. The bishops have decreed concerning priests who indiscreetly permit women to live with them and thereby become marked by the suspicion of a bad reputation: if, after being admonished, they do not correct themselves, they are to be punished by canonical censure as despisers of the sacred canons.

219. Concerning priests who came for chrism on the Lord’s Supper. Concerning the priests who used to come to the cities on the Lord’s Supper to receive chrism, it has been decreed that, from those who live far away, the bishop select one out of eight or ten to carry the chrism he has received carefully to himself and his companions. Those who live no farther than four or five miles from the city are to come in the customary manner to receive chrism. They are to be summoned to the cities for instruction at another time, not during Lent [Note: Bal.: “for instruction, therefore”].

220. Concerning the preaching and confirmation of bishops. So that bishops would not become burdensome to the people under the pretext of preaching or confirmation, they have promised, after being admonished by us, that henceforth they wish to avoid this and to carry out their ministry at such a time, insofar as circumstances permit, that their journey, as far as depends on them, will not be unwelcome or burdensome to those whom they can and ought to benefit.

221. Concerning tonsuring boys and veiling girls. It has been prohibited in every way that boys be tonsured without their parents’ consent or that girls be veiled [Note: G. omits “or that”]. Whoever attempts this shall be compelled to pay the fine contained in the capitularies of the secular law established by us.

222. Concerning women who lose their husbands. Concerning women who lose their husbands, it pleases us that they not veil themselves indiscriminately as they have done until now, but that they wait thirty days after their husband’s death. After the thirtieth day [Note: G.: “thirty days”], with the advice of their bishop—or, if the bishop is absent, with the advice of their other religious priests and of their relatives and friends—let them choose what they ought to choose.

Since we were asked by the sacred assembly to protect, by our authority, those who are performing public penance and women who lose their husbands until they deliberate what they should do, we have decreed that special chapters be made concerning them and inserted into the capitularies of the secular law.

223. Concerning abducted women and their abductors. Although we had specifically decreed what those who thereafter attempt this wickedness ought to suffer, we have nevertheless thought it necessary to insert here what the sacred canons prescribe concerning such persons, so that it may be clear to all how great an evil this is and so that, constrained not only by human but also by divine authority, this evil may henceforth be avoided.

224. Concerning girls abducted before they were betrothed. Concerning girls abducted before they were betrothed, the Council of Chalcedon, at which 630 fathers were present, states in chapter 38:

“The holy synod decreed that those who abduct girls under the pretext of living together, as well as those who cooperate with and assist the abductors, if they are clerics, shall be deprived of their own order; if they are laymen, they shall be anathematized.”

These words clearly show how the authors of this evil are to be condemned, since those who participate and assist are struck by so great an anathema. They also show that, according to canonical authority, the abductors can in no way lawfully claim the abducted women for legitimate marriage.

225. Concerning betrothed girls abducted by others. Concerning betrothed girls who are afterward abducted by others, the tenth chapter of the Council of Ancyra states:

“It has pleased us that betrothed girls who are afterward abducted by others be rescued and returned to those to whom they had previously been betrothed, even if it is established that violence was inflicted on them by the abductors.” [Note: The variant reads “violence inflicted on them” / “an injury inflicted by their own [men]”; C.]

Accordingly, it has been decreed by the sacred assembly that the abductor is to be punished with public penance. If the abducted woman’s fiancé refuses to receive her, and she did not consent to the same crime, she is not to be denied permission to marry another. If she consented, however, she is to be subject to the same judgment. If afterward they presume to unite, let both be anathematized.

226. Concerning those who unite themselves to virgins dedicated to God. Concerning those who unite themselves to sacred virgins, the twentieth chapter of the decrees of Pope Gelasius states:

“We have learned that certain men rashly unite themselves to sacred virgins and, after a purpose dedicated to God, mingle incestuous and sacrilegious unions. It is immediately right that such men be expelled from sacred communion, and unless they perform public and approved penance, they are not to be received at all. Yet if they have repented, the viaticum is not to be denied them as they depart from this world.”

If those who unite themselves to sacred virgins are punished so severely, how much more severely must those who abduct them be punished? Therefore, as was stated above, it is necessary that this evil be utterly cut out by the force of divine or human authority from all who belong to the Christian religion.

227. At what age girls are to be veiled. So that girls not be veiled indiscriminately, we have also thought it appropriate to insert here what is to be observed from the sacred canons. Concerning the time for veiling girls, the African Council states in chapter 16 that they are not to be consecrated before the age of twenty-five.

Likewise, in the same council, chapter 93, concerning the veiling of virgins, it states:

“It has also pleased us that, whenever any bishop, because of the danger to a virgin, whether a powerful suitor or some abductor is feared, or if she has been troubled by some perilous anxiety concerning death [Note: The text originally had the masculine *conpunctus*; the final two letters were deleted by a transverse line and replaced above, but all of this was immediately erased with a finger], veils or has veiled a virgin before the age of twenty-five, lest she die unveiled, whether at the insistence of her parents or of those entrusted with her care, this shall not prejudice him, because of the council’s provision concerning that number of years.”

From this it is gathered that, according to the earlier sanction, virgins are properly to be consecrated in the twenty-fifth year of their age. If the necessities mentioned above compel this to be done earlier, they cannot cause any prejudice to the bishop who performs the consecration [Note: G.: “they can cause no prejudice”].

228. That an examination by the holy cross is not to be made. It has been decreed that no one henceforth presume to conduct any examination by the holy cross, lest the passion or glorification of Christ be held in contempt through anyone’s rashness.

229. Concerning the proclamation of the nourishment of the divine word. Let the bishop, either personally or through vicars, diligently announce the nourishment of the divine word to the people, because, as blessed Gregory says, a priest provokes the anger of the hidden Judge against himself if he goes about without the sound of preaching.

Let him nourish the clergy entrusted to him in sobriety and chastity and instruct them in the divine offices, so that they may properly be promoted to the sacred ecclesiastical orders. Let them take care that priests have well-corrected missals, lectionaries, and other books necessary to them. Let them teach them how, according to their ability, to repair the churches belonging to them that have been destroyed; how to instruct widows diligently; how they ought to conduct themselves according to apostolic authority; and how to eradicate the superstitions that certain people practice in some places at the funerals of the dead.

Let them summon others to live well by the example of their own innocence, and let them strive with all their strength, insofar as the Lord helps them, to care for all ecclesiastical business. We have diligently admonished them concerning these matters. So that they may carry them out more freely, we desire by every means to give them assistance, insofar as the Lord grants us power.

230. Concerning homicides committed in churches or in their atria. If anyone kills a man in a church, either for a trivial reason or without cause, let him make composition for the life. But if they have quarreled outside and one has fled into the church and there killed the other while defending himself, and he has no witnesses to this act, let him be compelled to swear with twelve legitimate compurgators [Note: This differs in Book IV, chapter 13]. Let the one who was killed lie without composition; afterward, according to canonical judgment, let the killer receive a penance appropriate to the crime he committed.

If his own slave committed this act, let the slave be examined by the judgment of boiling water as to whether he did it willingly or in self-defense. If his hand is burned, let him be killed; if it is not, let his master pay his *wergild* to the church according to its amount, or, if he wishes, hand him over to that same church.

Concerning an ecclesiastical, fiscal, or beneficiary slave, we decree that for the first offense his *wergild* be paid as composition for him; for the second, the slave himself shall be handed over to punishment. Nevertheless, the inheritance of the free man who has been sentenced to death for such a crime shall pass to his legitimate heirs.

If a homicide of this kind is committed in the atrium of a church whose door has been consecrated with the relics of the saints, let it be amended or composed in the same manner. If the church door has not been consecrated, let the matter committed in the atrium be composed in the manner in which a violation committed in an infringed immunity ought to be composed.

231. Concerning injuries inflicted on priests in churches. If blood is shed in a church with a club, and the victim is a priest, let three times the composition be paid: two parts to that priest, the third as *fredus* to the church, and, in addition, our bann. Likewise, for a deacon, let three times his composition be paid, together with our bann.

Likewise, for a blow without the shedding of blood [Note: G.: “with the shedding of blood”], for each order of the clergy, let three times his composition be paid according to its amount, together with our bann [Note: Read differently in Book IV, chapter 14]. Whoever does not have the means to pay the church shall hand himself over to the service of that church until he has paid the entire debt.

232. Concerning widows, orphans, and the poor. Whenever widows, orphans, or poor people come before the count in the court, let their case be heard and settled first. If they cannot obtain witnesses for themselves to pursue their cases, or if they do not know the law, let the count help them by providing someone who will manage their case or speak for them.

233. Concerning the abduction of widows. Whoever takes a widow as his wife during the first thirty days of her widowhood, whether against her will or with her consent, shall pay triple our bann, that is, sixty solidi. If he took her against her will, let him make composition according to her law, but let him not touch her again.

234. Concerning the killing of a man performing public penance. Whoever kills a man performing public penance shall pay triple our bann and pay his *wergild* to his relatives.

235. That every free man have the power to give his property wherever he wishes for the salvation of his soul. If anyone wishes to transfer his property for the salvation of his soul, whether to some venerable place, to a relative, or to anyone else, and at that time is within the county in which the property is located, let him strive to make a lawful transfer.

If, at the time when he wishes to transfer it, he is outside that county—whether in the army, at the palace, or in any other place—let him provide suitable witnesses either from his own pagenses or from others who live under the same law as he does. If he cannot obtain such witnesses, let him use whatever better witnesses can be found there [Note: G. corrects *possunt* to *possit*, “he can find for himself”]. Before them, let him make the transfer of his property and give sureties for the investiture to the one who receives the transfer, so that they may perform the investiture.

After the transfer has been made in this manner, let his heir never be able to make a claim concerning the aforesaid property. Moreover, let he himself provide a surety for that same investiture, so that no opportunity remains for the heir to alter the transfer, but rather necessity compels him to complete it.

If he has not yet divided his property with his co-heirs, this is not to be an impediment. If his co-heir unwillingly refuses, let him be compelled, either by the count or by his envoy, to make the division with him, so that the inheritance may come to the person to whom the deceased wished it to pass [Note: G.: “or to whomever he wished it to come”].

If he requested that it be transferred to a church, let his co-heir have the same legal standing with that church concerning the aforesaid inheritance as he ought to have with another co-heir [Note: Bal.: “with that co-heir”]. Let this also be observed with regard to a father, son, and grandson until they reach the lawful age. Afterward, the property itself shall return to the immunity of that church.

236. Concerning the prohibition of homicides. Whoever kills a man, either for a trivial reason or without cause, shall pay his *wergild* in composition to those to whom the dead man belongs. He himself, however, shall be sent into exile for as long a time as we wish because of such presumption. Nevertheless, he shall not lose his property.

237. What is not to be given as composition for a *wergild*. We wish those things to be given in composition for a *wergild* that are contained in the law, except a hawk and a sword, because perjury is sometimes committed on account of those two things when people swear that they are worth more than they are.

238. Concerning the abduction of another man’s betrothed. If anyone abducts another man’s betrothed, let him return her, together with her law, either to her father or to the one who according to law ought to be her protector. Whatever he took with her, let him return each item separately according to the law.

If her protector consented to this being done and therefore does not wish to seek anything from the abductor, let the count exact from him a *fredus* for each item, one by one, on our behalf [Note: G.: “the abductor”]. Let him make composition according to his law to the fiancé and, in addition, pay our bann, that is, sixty solidi. Alternatively, let the count bring him into our presence; let him remain in exile for as long as we wish, and let him not be permitted to keep that woman.

239. Concerning the conviction of false witnesses. If anyone has a dispute with another over any matter, and witnesses have been produced against him by judgment, and he suspects them of being false, he may oppose them with other witnesses whom he can obtain who are better, so that by the testimony of truthful witnesses the perversity of false witnesses may be overcome.

If the two groups of witnesses disagree with one another so completely that neither side wishes in any way to yield to the other [Note: Bal.: “believe the other”], let two of them be selected, one from each side, to fight one another in the field with shields and clubs [Note: Bened. omits a great deal here].

240. Concerning concord between bishops and counts. Let bishops stand with counts, and counts with bishops, so that each may be fully able to carry out his own ministry [Note: G.: “and so that”].

241. Concerning thieves, homicides, adulterers, and incestuous persons to be restrained under great discipline. Let thieves, homicides, adulterers, and incestuous persons be corrected under strict restraint and discipline [Note: Some material is missing here].

242. Concerning the invasion of another’s property. Concerning their own property [Note: *propresis* in the 803 text; Bai. 6], let them come before our envoys, counts, and judges and there receive a final judgment. Beforehand, no one shall presume to seize another’s property [Note: The text corrects *proprindere* to *propria invadere*, “invade another’s property”]. Rather, as we have said, let him pursue his own case before our judges and there receive what is just.

243. For what matter one ought to come into the king’s presence. If anyone wishes to say that judgment has not been rendered justly for him, then let him come into our presence. Otherwise, let him not presume to come into our presence in order to delay another person’s justice.

244. That recent converts not quickly be sent to undertake other business. Concerning laymen who have recently converted: let them not be sent to other business before they learn to live fully according to their law.

245. What is to be done with those who abandon the world in order to evade due service. Concerning those who abandon the world in order to avoid service, and then do neither of the two things, let them choose one of them: either let them live fully according to canonical law or according to the rule, or let them perform royal service.

246. What is to be done in a time of famine and every kind of tribulation. If famine, devastation, unseasonable weather, or any other kind of tribulation occurs, let no one await a royal edict, but let the mercy of God immediately be entreated. In the present year of famine and scarcity, let each person help his own people as he is able. Let no one sell his grain at an excessive price, and let no foodstuff be sold outside our realm.

247. That weapons not be carried within the homeland, and how those at feud are to be compelled to return to peace. Concerning the carrying of weapons within the homeland—that is, shields, lances, or coats of mail [Note: Bal. omits the variant readings]: if someone is engaged in a feud, let it then be investigated which of the two is at fault, so that they may be at peace. Let them be compelled to make peace, even if they do not wish it. If they refuse to make peace in any other way, let them be brought into our presence.

If, after making peace, one kills the other, let him make composition for him and, without any redemption, lose the hand by which he violated his oath [Note: Absent in the capitulary of 805 and in Book III, chapter 4]; in addition, let him pay the royal bann.

Let slaves also not carry lances [Note: cf. the capitulary of 805]. Whoever is found doing so after the bann has been issued shall have the spear broken across his back.

248. Concerning the possession of armor and coats of mail. With regard to armor in the army, let what we previously commanded in another capitulary be observed. In addition, every man with twelve manses is to have a coat of mail. Whoever has a coat of mail and does not bring it with him shall lose his entire benefice together with the coat of mail.

249. Concerning those who refuse to accept the judgments of the scabini [Note: Bal.: “the judgment of the judge”]. Concerning claimants or litigants who neither wish to accept the judgment of the scabini nor wish to blaspheme, let the ancient custom be observed: they are to be confined in custody until they do one of the two things [Note: G.: “or”].

If they complain to the palace about this matter and bring letters, they are not to be believed simply because of them. Nevertheless, they are not then to be put in prison; rather, they are to be sent to our palace under guard, together with the letters themselves, and there their case is to be examined as is proper.

250. That fidelity by oath is to be promised only to the king and one’s lords. And that other oaths are to be made lawfully. Concerning the oath: let fidelity not be promised by oath to anyone else except us and each man’s own lord, for the benefit of us and of his lord. This excludes those oaths that one person justly owes another according to the law.

Let the children who previously could not swear because of their youthful age now promise fidelity.
