251. That conspiracies, if they are made, are to be judged in three ways. Whoever presumes to form conspiracies and confirms any conspiracy by oath shall be judged in three ways.

First, wherever any evil has been committed on account of it, let the authors of the deed be killed. Let their helpers be flogged one by one by one another and cut off one another’s noses [Note: G.: “let their noses be cut off”]. Where no evil has been committed, let them likewise flog one another and cut off one another’s hair.

If a conspiracy has been confirmed by right hands, then, if they are free men, let them either swear with suitable compurgators that they did not do this for an evil purpose, or, if they cannot do so, let them make composition according to their law. If they are slaves, let them be flogged, so that henceforth no such conspiracy may occur in our kingdom, whether by oath or without an oath.

252. How witnesses are to be dealt with and what sort are to be brought for testimony. Perjuries are to be guarded against, and witnesses are not to be admitted to an oath before they have been examined. If they cannot be examined in another way, let them be separated from one another and questioned individually.

The accuser alone is not to be permitted to choose witnesses in the absence of his opponent in the case. Absolutely no one is to be admitted to an oath or to give testimony unless he is fasting.

If the person brought forward as a witness is rejected, let the person rejecting him state and prove why he does not wish him to be accepted. Witnesses are to be chosen from that same *pagus*, not from another, unless the matter must be investigated at a considerable distance outside the county.

If anyone is convicted of perjury, let him lose his hand or redeem it.

[Col. 0733A] **253. What persons should be chosen to investigate and settle cases.** Concerning corrupt advocates, *vicedomini*, vicars, and centenarii: let them be removed, and let such men be chosen as both know and wish to investigate and settle cases justly. And whoever is found to be corrupt must certainly be reported to us. [Note: [Col. 0733] *discutiendas* (“to investigate”) Bal.; *si comes* (“if [it is] the count”) III. 11.]

**254. Concerning tolls collected from markets, ships, and elsewhere, and what should be done about any that are unjustly exacted.** Concerning tolls, our pleasure is that the ancient and just tolls be exacted from merchants, both at bridges and from ships or markets. But new or unjust tolls—where ropes are stretched, or where ships pass beneath bridges, or in similar places where no assistance is provided to travelers—are not to be exacted. Likewise, nothing is to be exacted from those who, without intending to trade, transport their property from one of their houses to another, or to the palace, or to the army. If anything arises about which there is doubt, it is to be referred for inquiry at our assembly [Note: [Col. 0733] *palace* G.] which we shall hold with our envoys.

[Col. 0733B] **255. Concerning those who wish to turn from the world to monasteries.** Free men who wish to give themselves to the service of God must not do so before requesting permission from us. We issue this order because we have heard that some of them do this not so much out of devotion as while fleeing military service or another royal obligation; and we have heard that others have been deceived, out of greed, by those who covet their property. For this reason we prohibit it.

**256. Concerning poor free men, so that they are not unjustly oppressed by the powerful.** Regarding the oppression of poor free men: let them not be oppressed by the powerful through any evil contrivance against justice, so that they are compelled to sell or surrender their property. This is why we have spoken of free men above and here as well: lest their parents should perhaps be disinherited contrary to justice, royal service be diminished [Note: [Col. 0733] *minuetur* (“will be diminished”) G.], and the heirs themselves, through want, become beggars, thieves, or criminals. And let them not be summoned to an assembly more frequently than we prescribed in another capitulary.

[Col. 0733C] **257. Concerning churches or saints newly discovered.** Churches or saints newly established without authority are not to be venerated unless approved by the bishop; while canonical authority concerning this matter and concerning all churches remains intact.

**258. So that the military levy is faithfully exacted from everyone without regard to persons.** Concerning the military levy, we wish our envoys to exact it faithfully, without favor, flattery, or intimidation toward any person, according to our command. That is, from a man possessing property worth six pounds in gold, silver, armor, copper, complete garments, horses, oxen, sheep, cows, or other livestock—yet in such a way that his wife or children are not stripped of their clothing for this reason—they are to take the lawful military levy, namely three pounds. But from one who possesses no more than property worth three pounds, thirty solidi are to be exacted. One who possesses no more than two pounds is to pay ten solidi. If he possesses only one pound, he is to pay five solidi, so that he may again be able to prepare himself for the service of God and for our benefit. And our envoys must take care and investigate diligently lest, through any evil contrivance, they withdraw our due from one person by handing it over or assigning it to another.

[Col. 0733D] **259. Concerning free men or women who join themselves to fiscal dependants.** Free men who take wives from the royal fiscal estates, and women who are free and either have or take royal fiscal dependants as husbands, are not for this reason to be excluded from inheriting their parents’ property, from pursuing their own case, or from giving testimony. Rather, in this matter the same honor is to be shown to us as is known to have been shown previously to our royal or imperial predecessors.

[Col. 0734A] **260. So that the Lord’s Prayer, the Creed, and the law or capitularies of the kings may be carefully understood.** Let laymen fully learn the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer. Counts, centenarii, and other noblemen likewise are to learn their law fully [Note: [Col. 0733] *deest* (“is absent”) G.], as has been decreed elsewhere. We command our envoys to ensure that the things which for many years we have ordered throughout our kingdom by our capitularies—things which they ought to do, learn, observe, or make customary—are now carefully investigated, and that they earnestly strive to renew all these things completely for the service of God, for our benefit, and for the perfection of all Christian people; and, insofar as the Lord grants them strength, to bring them fully to completion. They must report to us specifically who has undertaken this good struggle and fulfilled it, so that he may receive grace from God and from us. But whoever has been negligent in this matter is to receive such discipline [Col. 0734B] as a contemptuous person of this kind deserves to receive, so that the others may be afraid to act henceforth.

**261. Concerning the killing of clerics, priests, and monks.** Whoever kills a subdeacon is to pay three hundred solidi in compensation. Whoever kills a deacon, four hundred solidi [Note: [Col. 0733] *DC* (“600”) in an erased place G.]. Whoever kills a priest, six hundred [Note: [Col. 0733] *DCCCC* (“900”) in an erased place G.]. Whoever kills a bishop, nine hundred [Note: [Col. 0733] *e. de uita conponat* (“he is to pay compensation for his life”) in an erased place G.]. Whoever kills a monk is to be judged liable for four hundred.

**262. Concerning damages committed within immunities.** If anyone causes any damage within an immunity, he is to pay six hundred [Note: [Col. 0733] *DCCCC* (“900”) in an erased place C.] solidi in compensation.

**263. What is to be done concerning thieves detained within an immunity.** If a man commits theft, homicide, or any other crime outside and then flees into an immunity, the count is to command the bishop, abbot, *vicedominus*, or whoever holds the bishop’s or abbot’s place, to hand the culprit over to him. If that person resists and refuses to hand him over, he is to pay fifteen solidi for the first refusal. If he is unwilling to agree even on the third demand, whatever damage the culprit has caused is to be paid in full by the person who detains him within the immunity and refuses to hand him over. The count himself, when he comes [Note: [Col. 0733] *veniat* (“let him come”) G., corrected form.], is to have permission to search for the man within the immunity, wherever he is able to find him.

If, during the first inquiry, the count is told that the culprit was indeed within the immunity but escaped, the person concerned is immediately to swear that he did not allow him to flee in order to defeat anyone’s justice; and this oath is to be accepted as satisfaction. But if anyone attempts to resist the count, who enters the immunity with an assembled force, the count is to refer the matter to the king or prince, so that it may be judged there. And just as the person who caused damage within the immunity must pay six hundred solidi in compensation, so the person who presumes to resist the count with an assembled force is to be judged liable for six hundred solidi.

[Col. 0734D] **264. Concerning places for establishing canonical houses.** If places for establishing canonical houses are to be granted from the property of that same church, they are to be granted there by our generosity. If they are exchanged from the property of another church or of free men, this is to be done by exchange. But if the property is from our fisc, it is to be granted by our generosity.

**265. Concerning buying during harvest-time out of greed and shameful profit.** Whoever, at harvest time or during the vintage, buys grain or wine not from necessity but out of greed—for example, buys one modius for two denarii and stores it until he can sell it for four or six denarii, or more—we call this shameful profit. But if he buys it out of necessity, so that he may keep some for himself and give some to others, we call it commerce.

[Col. 0735A] **266. Concerning the stability of bishops and clerics.** A bishop is not to move from one place to another without a decree of the bishops, nor a cleric without the command of his own bishop.

**267. Concerning churches or altars of uncertain consecration.** Churches or altars whose consecration is uncertain are to be consecrated.

**268. Concerning drunkenness.** Above all, let the elders guard themselves against drunkenness and set a good example of sobriety for their juniors.

**269. An admonition to counts concerning the welfare of the holy Church of God.** To you counts we speak, and we admonish you, because it pertains especially to your office to show reverence and honor to the holy Church of God, to live in harmony with your bishops, and to provide them assistance in carrying out their office. You yourselves are also to establish peace and justice in your offices, and you are to ensure that whatever our authority publicly decrees is diligently carried out in your offices.

[Col. 0735B] **270. An admonition to laymen concerning the preservation of ecclesiastical honor.** We admonish all laymen to preserve ecclesiastical honor, to show due reverence to bishops and the priests of God, to attend devoutly with their households when those priests preach, and to observe the fasts which they jointly proclaim, teaching and compelling their dependants to observe them. Let everyone strive above all that Sunday be honored and celebrated as is proper. And so that this may be done more freely, markets and assemblies are to be prohibited by the counts on that day, as has often been admonished.

**271. An admonition to bishops and counts concerning harmony with one another and with the other faithful.** Let bishops and counts live in harmony with one another and with the other faithful, and let them mutually assist one another in carrying out their offices.

**272. Concerning works to be completed for the restoration of churches.** In works for the restoration of churches, whether by carrying them out or by redeeming the obligation with payment, the bishop’s will is to be followed above all. Nevertheless, it must in no way be left undone that this or that be paid to the churches, as we have often ordered [Note: [Col. 0735] *haec* (“this”) G.]. Let everyone know that whoever acts negligently in this matter and is found negligent before us is to undergo precisely what we ordered, with the common counsel of our faithful, in our capitulary concerning this matter.

[Col. 0735C] **273. That counts should assist the ministers of the Church in their offices.** Let counts become helpers in every respect to the ministers of the Church and to their offices, so that they may obtain this more fully from our resources, from themselves, and from their own people [Note: [Col. 0735] *et* (“and”) G.]. Whoever does not correct himself after being admonished by the count once and then a second time is to have his negligence reported by that same count to our attention, so that by our authority he may be compelled to undergo what is contained in our capitulary.

**274. That bishops and priests are not to accept sureties from incestuous persons, from those who do not pay tithes, or from those living negligently.** It has been reported to us that in certain places bishops and counts accept sureties from incestuous persons and from those who do not pay tithes, and that certain priests divide money among themselves as a penalty for negligence. We have decided that this must be abolished completely, lest an opportunity be given to avarice. We decree that incestuous persons are to be punished with penance according to the canonical judgment. Those who, after frequent admonitions and preaching by the priests, neglect to pay tithes are to be excommunicated. But we do not wish to bind them by oath, because of the danger of perjury.

**275. Concerning destroyed churches.** Regarding destroyed churches, let bishops and envoys investigate whether they were destroyed through negligence or through inability. Wherever negligence is found, those who were obliged to restore them are to be compelled by episcopal authority [Col. 0736A] to repair them [Note: [Col. 0735] *emendare* (“to repair”) Bal.]. But if this happened through inability—for example, if there are more churches than necessary, or if they are larger than can be restored from the property belonging to them—the bishop is to devise a way in which they can suitably be repaired and maintained.

**276. Concerning those who have neglected to pay ninths and tithes.** Regarding those who for many years have neglected to pay ninths and tithes, either in part or entirely, we wish them to be compelled by our envoys to pay the ninths and tithes according to the earlier capitulary, together with their lawful obligation and, in addition, our ban. It is also to be announced to them that whoever repeats this negligence is to know that he will lose the benefice from which this ninth and tithe ought to have been paid.

For this is contained in the capitulary of our father, of blessed memory, in Book One, chapter 57: “Whoever withholds the tithe from the church to which it ought in justice to be given, and presumptuously gives it to another church, whether because of gifts, friendship, or any other pretext, is to be constrained by the count or by our envoy to restore the amount of that tithe together with his lawful obligation.”

[Col. 0736B] **277. Concerning those who neglect to carry out the restoration of churches.** Whoever, from the property of churches which he holds as a benefice, neglects to carry out their restoration is to be dealt with according to our authoritative capitulary in which provisions were made concerning works, ninths, and tithes, as it is stated in Book Four, chapter 38 [Note: [Col. 0735] *XXXVIIII* (“39”) G.]:

“Concerning work and the restoration of churches, it has been established that payments are to be made from the produce of the land, from the nourishment of animals, and from all revenues, except military provisions [Note: [Col. 0735] *et . . . hostilienibus* was interpolated by Benedictus.]. Concerning the work or restoration of churches, the count, bishop, or abbot, together with our envoy whom they themselves choose for this purpose, is to make an assessment, so that each person receives for work and restoration as much as he is known to possess from the property of the churches. Likewise, our vassals are either to contribute jointly as much work as they hold ecclesiastical property, or each individually according to the amount which he himself holds. Or, if they agree to give silver in place of performing the work, they are to pay in silver according to the estimated value of the work, so that with this price the rector of the church may hire workers and purchase materials for the aforesaid restoration. Whoever neglects to pay ninths and tithes is first to restore them together with his lawful obligation, and in addition is to pay our ban, so that, chastened in this way, he may take care not to lose his benefice by repeating the offense too often.”

[Col. 0736C] **278. Concerning those who neglect the lord’s fields so that they will not pay the ninths from them.** Regarding those who have neglected to cultivate the lord’s fields for the purpose of avoiding payment of the ninths from them, and for this reason take other people’s land to cultivate, we wish them to pay for three years the ninth itself together with its lawful obligation. If anyone has for this reason shown contempt either toward our counts or toward our vassals, he is to be compelled through sureties to come to the palace.

[Col. 0736D] **279. So that it may be understood in what act an immunity is violated.** It has come to our attention that certain churches or monasteries possessing our immunities [Note: [Col. 0735] *nostram* (“our”) G.] and those of our predecessors suffer many injuries and disturbances from certain persons, and are unable to obtain any protection or defense from those same immunities, because the violators of the immunities claim that the name of immunity encompasses nothing more than the enclosure of the monastery; while everything else, although belonging to those churches or monasteries, lies outside the immunity.

Therefore we wish and decree that everyone understand that not only the monastery’s or church’s enclosure and the fortifications [Col. 0737A] of the churches are protected by the defense of the immunity, but also houses, estates, the enclosures of estates, artificial fishponds, and everything enclosed by ditches, hedges, or any other kind of barrier are included under the same name of immunity. Whatever, within such defenses and belonging by right to those churches or monasteries, anyone voluntarily commits for the purpose of harming or inflicting damage is to be judged an act by which the immunity has been violated.

But if, by chance—as commonly happens—some damage is done by any persons to fields, open land, or woods which are uncultivated [Note: [Col. 0737] *aborantibus* (“by those laboring”) Bal.] and in no way enclosed by a fortification, then, even if that field, open land, or wood belongs to a church or monastery possessing a written grant of immunity, the immunity is not to be judged violated on that account. The person convicted of causing scandal or damage in such a place is therefore not to be punished by a composition of six hundred solidi, but according to the law observed in that locality. [Note: [Col. 0737] *conuinctus* (“convicted”) G.]

[Col. 0737B] **280. Concerning general claims to justice.** Concerning the rights of the churches of God, widows, orphans, and wards, we order that in public courts those who cry out for justice are not to be despised, but are first to be heard carefully.

**281. Concerning animals and other property from whom they are to be purchased.** No one is to buy a horse, ox, beast of burden, or anything else unless he knows the man who sells it, or knows from what district he comes, or where he lives, or who his lord is.

**282. Concerning the person taken as a witness, what sort of person he should be.** The best person in the district or city is to be taken as a witness, and no crime should be capable of being brought against him by the person against whom he is to testify. [Note: [Col. 0737] *testimoniare*, corrected to *testimoniari* in G.]

**283. Concerning the contribution of those liable for the military levy.** Let those who are required to pay the military levy make a contribution to the collector of the levy.

**284. Concerning coloni and fiscal dependants.** Neither a colonus nor a fiscal dependant is to presume to make transfers anywhere.

**285. Concerning false witnesses.** We order that false witnesses not be admitted.

[Col. 0737C] **286. Concerning men condemned to death and afterward granted life, if they seek justice.** Those men who have been condemned to death because of their crimes and afterward have been granted life, if they themselves seek justice from others, or if others wish to seek justice from them, are to have judgment settled between them as follows.

First, regarding the cases for which he was condemned to death, he can make no claim at all, because all his property was publicly confiscated according to the judgment of the Franks. But if afterward, once life has been granted to him, he is able to acquire anything lawfully, he is to hold and defend it in freedom according to the law. He is not to be accepted as a witness, nor is he to serve among the *scabini* in judging according to law. If judgment has been given concerning an oath which he is required to swear, and someone wishes to declare that oath false, he is to contest it.

[Col. 0737D] **287. Concerning a man who has been granted life after judgment, if he refuses to render justice.** If, after the judgment of the *scabini*, life has been granted to someone, and afterward he commits some evil and refuses to render justice, saying that he is dead and therefore ought not to render justice, it is established that he is to undergo the earlier judgment which he should previously have undergone. If anyone commits any wrong against him, he is nevertheless to have permission, according to the order of equity, to seek his justice concerning acts committed after he was condemned to death. As for earlier matters, the judgment is to remain as stated above.

**288. Concerning free men who may be compelled to come to the assembly.** No one else among free men is to be compelled to come to an assembly or court, except *scabini* or the counts’ vassals, unless he must pursue his own case or answer a claim.

[Col. 0738A] **289. How witnesses are to be used for giving testimony.** Witnesses are not to be hired by reward to give testimony. No one is to give testimony or swear an oath unless fasting. Before they swear, witnesses are to be examined separately concerning what they intend to say about the matter on which they must testify.

**290. That no one may delay anyone’s justice.** Let no one—whether our envoy, count, judge, or *scabinus*—presume to delay anyone’s justice if it can immediately be completed according to right; nor may he presume to accept rewards from anyone for this through any evil contrivance.

**291. Concerning excessively blasphemous [Note: [Col. 0737] *plasphemis* (“blasphemous”), G., consistently.] thieves.** Concerning thieves who are greatly blasphemous: whoever apprehends one of them is not to suffer any loss because of it.

[Col. 0738B] **292. Concerning the selection of witnesses to investigate any matter.** Whenever witnesses must be sought and chosen to investigate any matter, our envoy and the count in whose office the matter is to be handled are to choose such persons as can be found to be the best in that district. Litigants are not to be permitted to produce false witnesses by means of rewards, as has hitherto customarily been done.

**293. Concerning the court of the centenarius.** No man is to be judged in the court of a centenarius either to death, to the loss of his freedom, or to the return of property or slaves. Such matters are to be judged in the presence of the count or of our envoys.

**294. Concerning assemblies to be made known by royal envoys to the counts.** Each of our envoys is to make known at his court to the counts who belong to his assigned district that, during the months in which he does not conduct his mission, they are to meet among themselves and hold common assemblies, both to constrain thieves and to administer other forms of justice.

[Col. 0738C] **295. Concerning the wives of deceased men, and what share of the joint labor they should receive after their husbands’ death.** We wish the wives of deceased men, after their husbands’ death, to receive one-third of the jointly cultivated work which they cultivated together in the benefice. Concerning the property which the holder of that benefice brought or purchased from elsewhere, or which was contributed to him by his friends, we wish it to pass both to the deceased man’s orphans and to his wives.

**296. Concerning proving false witnesses.** If someone has a dispute with another over any matter, and witnesses have been produced against him by judgment, then, if he suspects that they are false, he is permitted to bring against them other witnesses whom he can obtain who are better, so that through the testimony of truthful witnesses the perversity of the false witnesses may be overcome.

But if the two groups of witnesses disagree with one another so completely that neither side is willing in any way to yield to the other, let two be chosen from among them—one from each side—to fight in the field with shields and clubs, so that it may be established by which side’s testimony falsehood or truth is being followed. The champion who is defeated is to have his right hand cut off because of the perjury he committed before the combat. The other witnesses of that same side who are proved false are to redeem their hands. Two-thirds of this composition is to be paid to the person against whom they testified, and one-third is to be paid as *fredum*.

In a secular case, therefore, such a dispute among witnesses is to be settled in the field. In ecclesiastical cases, where one side concerns a secular matter and the other an ecclesiastical matter, the same procedure is to be observed. But where the matter is ecclesiastical on both sides, the rectors of the churches concerned may reconcile themselves amicably if they wish. If they cannot agree on such a reconciliation [Col. 0739A] [Note: [Col. 0739] *possit* (“may be able”) Bal.], their advocates are to come to the public court before the count, and there a lawful end is to be imposed on their disputes.

Witnesses for any case are not to be sought from elsewhere, but from the very county in which the property at issue is situated. For it is not credible that the truth concerning a man’s status or anyone’s possession can be known better through others than through those who live nearer. If, however, the dispute that has arisen between them is located on the boundary of two counties, they may have witnesses for their case from the neighboring hundred of the adjoining county.

**297. Concerning tributary land.** Whoever transfers tributary land—from which tribute used to be paid to our treasury—to a church or to anyone else, the person who receives it must in every way pay to our treasury the tribute which was paid from it, unless he happens to possess a grant from the lord’s treasury by which he can demonstrate that this tribute has been remitted to him.

[Col. 0739B] **298. Concerning rent-bearing land.** If someone possesses rent-bearing land which his predecessors gave either to a church or to one of our estates, he cannot in any way hold it according to law unless the person to whose authority that church or estate belongs is willing, unless he is the son or grandson of the person who transferred it, or unless that same land has been formally assigned to him for holding [Note: [Col. 0739] *placitata* (“formally assigned”) Bal.].

In this matter, however, consideration must be given to whether the person who holds it is rich or poor, and whether he has another benefice or property of his own. If he has neither, he is to be treated mercifully, lest, completely stripped of his possessions, he fall into poverty. He is either to pay from it the rent that has been established for him, or receive some portion of it as a benefice from which he can support himself.

**299. Concerning observance of the lord’s commands.** Concerning observance of our commands and immunities, we order that they be observed as established by us and by our predecessors.

[Col. 0739C] **300. Concerning one who abandons his own wife or kills her without fault and takes another.** Whoever, after abandoning his own wife or killing her without fault, takes another wife is to lay aside his arms and perform public penance. If he is obstinate, he is to be apprehended by the count, bound in irons, and placed in custody until the matter is brought to our attention.

**301. Concerning free men who possess no property of their own but reside on the lord’s land, and are not to be admitted as witnesses.** Free men who possess no property of their own but reside on the lord’s land are not to be admitted as witnesses because of another person’s property. Nevertheless, they may serve as compurgators for other men because they are free. Those who both possess property of their own and reside on the lord’s land are not to be rejected for the reason that they reside on the lord’s land; rather, they are to be admitted as witnesses because they possess property of their own.

[Col. 0739D] **302. Concerning priests, deacons, and the rest of the clergy.** The canons of Saint Sylvester and of the other 284 bishops.

“These ranks were established within the bosom of the synod, so that no priest may bring an accusation against a bishop, no deacon against a priest, no subdeacon against a deacon, no acolyte against a subdeacon, no exorcist against an acolyte, no lector against an exorcist, and no doorkeeper against a lector. A prelate is not to be condemned without seventy-two witnesses, nor is the supreme prelate to be judged by anyone, since it is written: ‘The disciple is not above his teacher.’ A priest, moreover, is not to be condemned without forty-four witnesses. A deacon established in office in the city of Rome is not to be condemned without thirty-six. A subdeacon, acolyte, exorcist, or lector is not to be condemned except, as it is written, on the testimony of seven persons who have children and wives and who openly preach Christ. Thus the mystical truth is given.”

[Col. 0740A] **303. From the capitularies of Lord Charles: how service, labor, rents, taxes, and other obligations are to be exacted from holdings, manses, or quarters.** Because of the excessive complaint which has reached us concerning ecclesiastical or fiscal dependants who were not assigned a fixed work duty when we were in the county of Le Mans, it seemed good to us, together with the counsel of our faithful, to establish the following.

Whoever among the aforesaid men holds a quarter of a holding [Note: [Col. 0739] *teneret* (“would hold”), and thus throughout the whole passage; Bal. conjectures the imperfect *teneret*.] is to plow one full day with his animals for his lord, with his plow, in the lord’s field, and afterward no annual service is to be demanded from him by his lord during that week. Whoever does not have enough animals to complete this in one day is to complete the aforesaid work in two days.

Whoever has only four animals, so weak that he cannot plow by himself [Note: [Col. 0739] *possent* (“could”), Bal.], is to plow with them, joined to other animals, for one day in the lord’s field, and afterward during that week is to perform one day of manual labor.

Whoever can do none of these things and has no animals is to work for his lord with his hands for three days, from morning until evening, and his lord is to demand nothing more from him [Note: [Col. 0739] *deest* (“is absent”) G.; *s. ei* (“so that he may not demand it from him”) Bal.]. For these things were being done in different ways: some worked the whole week, others half a week, and others two days. We therefore establish this, so that the household may neither be able to withdraw from the aforesaid work nor be required by its lords to do more.

Whoever possesses less than the best quarter of land is to perform work according to the assessment of his land. We have ordered this to be announced publicly and in our name by Count Adalard, our palace count, for their satisfaction, together with our other faithful.

[Col. 0740C] **304. That bishops should correct and reform incestuous persons.** Let bishops reform and correct incestuous persons and show great diligence concerning them. They are likewise to have authority to correct widows within their parish.

**305. That what King Pippin established in assemblies and synods be preserved.** We order that the things which our father, of blessed memory, established in his assemblies and synods be preserved [Note: [Col. 0739] *conservari* (“to be preserved”) Bal.].

**306. Concerning one who buys something from another person’s slave.** If anyone buys something from another person’s slave without the knowledge of his master, and the master does not wish the sale to be valid, he is to return the price to the buyer, so that the purchase has no validity. If he does not possess the thing itself, he is to return an equivalent.

**307. That the affairs of churches be heard immediately by the judge.** It has pleased us that the affairs of churches be heard immediately by the judge without any delay and be advanced effectively.

[Col. 0740D] **308. That a judge investigating a criminal should not pronounce a capital sentence before the accused confesses or is convicted by innocent witnesses.** It has pleased us that a judge investigating a criminal should not pronounce a capital sentence before the accused himself confesses or is clearly convicted by innocent and truthful witnesses. In the case of the greater persons, the judgment of us or of our successors is to be awaited.

**309. That those who are accomplices in a crime not be admitted as witnesses.** It has pleased us that witnesses who are accomplices in a crime not be admitted, nor infamous persons, slanderers, or others whom canon law and secular law prohibit.

**310. Concerning the prohibition of incestuous marriages.** We prohibit incestuous marriages: that is, persons are not to be joined together up to the degree of affinity [Col. 0741A], or for as long as they could inherit from one another, because such unions are to be judged incestuous rather than marriages.

**311. That judgment not be given against absent persons.** It has pleased us that judgment not be given against absent persons. If this is done, the sentence pronounced is to have no validity.

**312. That the more lenient sentence be preferred to the harsher.** It has pleased us that, between equal sentences, the more lenient always be preferred to the harsher.

**313. That one who has confessed concerning himself not be believed against another.** It has pleased us that one who has confessed a crime concerning himself not be believed against another person.

**314. Concerning not accepting the testimony of one man.** The testimony of one man is not to be accepted. For if there are several on both sides, the more truthful, religious, and honorable are to be chosen, and they are to confirm by their oath that they will say nothing false. [Note: [Col. 0741] *inter se* (“among themselves”) G.]

### 315. That no one should act harshly or mildly against bishops

[Note: In the margin, G: “a heading most useful to bishops.”]

We command and order that no one—God forbid—should act either mildly or harshly toward bishops, since this concerns the danger of our entire empire. And so that everyone may recognize the name, authority, power, and dignity of the priestly office, this can easily be understood from the words of the Lord, by which he said to blessed Peter, whose place bishops occupy: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven; and whatever you loose on earth will be loosed also in heaven.” And elsewhere he says generally to the disciples: “Receive the Holy Spirit: whose sins you forgive, they are forgiven them; and whose sins you retain, they are retained.”

That statement also ought to be recalled as an example which Emperor Constantine addressed to the bishops, as recorded in ecclesiastical history:

> “God,” he said, “appointed you priests and gave you the power to judge even us. And therefore we are rightly judged by you, while you cannot be judged by human beings. For this reason, await judgment among yourselves from God alone, so that your disputes, whatever they may be, may be reserved for that divine examination. For you have been given to us by God as gods. It is not fitting, however, that a human being should judge gods, but only the one of whom it is written: ‘God stood in the assembly of the gods; in the midst, God distinguishes among the gods.’”  
> [Note: G adds *diiudicat* (“judges”) instead of *discernit* (“distinguishes”).]

This also ought to be brought back to their memory: how blessed Prosper, in the book he wrote on the contemplative and active life, comprehended the praise of priests:

> “To them,” he says—that is, to priests—“the special care of tending souls has been entrusted. Bearing manfully the burden of the people entrusted to them, they tirelessly plead with God for the sins of human beings as for their own; and, like another Aaron, offering the incense of a contrite heart and humbled spirit, by which God is appeased, they turn away from the people the anger of the punishment to come. By God’s grace they become judges of the divine will, founders of the churches of Christ after the apostles, leaders of the faithful people, defenders of truth, enemies of wicked doctrine, lovable to all good people and terrifying even by their very appearance to those conscious of evil, avengers of the oppressed, fathers in the Catholic faith of those reborn, preachers of heavenly rewards, examples of goodness, lessons in virtue, and models for the faithful. They are the glory of the Church, in whom the Church shines; they are the strongest pillars, upon which the whole multitude of believers, founded in Christ, rests; they are the gates of the eternal city, through whom all who believe enter to Christ; they are the gatekeepers to whom the keys of the kingdom of heaven have been given. They are also administrators of the royal household, at whose discretion the ranks and duties of each person are distributed in the court of the eternal King.”

[Note: G reads *instigabiliter* (“urgently”) for *infatigabiliter* (“tirelessly”).]

### 316. That the forgiveness of sins occurs through the Holy Spirit

All must know and believe that, through the Holy Spirit, the forgiveness of sins is conferred in baptism, and that, by the gift of that same Holy Spirit, forgiveness of sins is unquestionably granted to the faithful in the Church of Christ through priestly ministry, repentance, absolution, and the laying on of hands.

### 317. On the four vices that stain the Catholic faith

It has seemed good that everyone should know that there are four vices which, among other evils, stain our faith. The more hidden they are, the more harmful they are: namely, pride, through which the angel became the devil and was cast out of heaven; envy, through which that same devil cast the human being out of paradise; hatred and discord, which extinguish charity among neighbors, empty love of its content, overturn all good things, and do not allow neighbors to remain in mutual love or to lead the quiet and peaceful life appropriate to Christians. And so forth.

### 318. That the universal holy Church of God is one body and Christ is its head

First, therefore, that the universal holy Church of God is plainly believed to be one body, and Christ its head, is confirmed by apostolic declarations. Thus Paul says: “You are the body of Christ, and individually members of it.” Likewise: “For just as in one body we have many members, and all the members do not have the same function, so we, though many, are one body in Christ.” Again: “Christ is the head, from whom the whole body, administered through bonds and connections, grows into a holy temple in the Lord.”

[Note: G, corrected, reads *administratuum* for *administratum*.] There are countless other examples of this kind, which are omitted here in order to avoid prolixity.

Whoever, therefore, through some illicit act has made himself, from a member of Christ, a member of the devil, must know that he is not in the body of Christ but in the body of the devil. Accordingly, he must not neglect to restore himself without delay to the body of Christ, from which he has been separated by diabolical cunning, while the time for repentance is readily available.

### 319. That the body of the same Church is principally divided between two eminent persons

We know, therefore, as we have received it handed down from the holy Fathers, that the body of the entire holy Church of God is principally divided between two eminent persons: namely, the priestly and the royal.

Concerning this, Gelasius, the venerable bishop of the Roman See, writes to the Emperor Anastasius:

> “There are indeed two august powers by which this world is principally ruled: the consecrated authority of the pontiffs and the royal power. Among these, the burden of the priests is so much heavier, inasmuch as they must render an account before the divine tribunal even for the kings themselves.”

Fulgentius likewise writes in his book *On the Truth of Predestination and Grace*:

> “As far as the life of this present age is concerned, no one in the Church is superior to the pontiff, and in the Christian world no one is found higher than the emperor.”

### 320. That corepiscopi should not exceed the measure prescribed in the sacred canons

We have learned that a reprehensible and highly novel practice has arisen: certain corepiscopi, advancing beyond their proper limit, confer the gift of the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands and perform other acts that belong exclusively to pontiffs, contrary to law. This is especially improper since none of the seventy disciples, whose role they represent in the Church, is read to have conferred the gift of the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands. That the duty of conferring the Holy Spirit belongs exclusively to the apostles and their successors is taught by the Book of the Acts of the Apostles.

In the Council of Caesarea, however, the following is written concerning corepiscopi:

> “Corepiscopi also appear to be, as an example and representation, the seventy; but as fellow ministers, on account of the zeal they show toward the poor, they are to be honored.”  
> [Note: G omits *ut* (“as”); Bal. reads *nullus* (“no one”) for *nullum* (“none”).]

### 321. Concerning corepiscopi who reside in villages, as stated in the Council of Antioch

Those who in villages or estates are called corepiscopi, although they have received the laying on of hands from bishops and have been consecrated as bishops, nevertheless the holy synod has decreed that they recognize their proper limits and govern the churches subject to them, being content with the direction and care of those churches.

### 322. On the honor and obedience owed to bishops and the other priests

Since it is evident that the Christian religion is beneficially administered through the successors of the apostles and that guidance toward eternal life ought to be provided to peoples, we first judged it necessary to command everyone that they should reverently show bishops the honor owed to them, without any pretense or disparagement, and obey them in all things as fathers. They should strive to carry out, as best they can, whatever they advise for the salvation of souls, if they wish to have the favor of God and of us.

For the Lord says: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever rejects you rejects me.” And again: “If he does not listen to you, tell it to the Church. And if he does not listen even to the Church, let him be to you as a gentile and a tax collector.” Elsewhere: “If anyone causes one of these little ones”—that is, my disciples or apostles, whose place bishops now hold in the Church—to stumble, it would be better for him that a millstone be hung around his neck and that he be drowned in the depth of the sea than that he should cause one of these least ones to stumble.”

All these things must be brought to the attention of the faithful and carefully considered, lest, God forbid, they fall into this scandal. Rather, by obeying them, let them become not children of destruction but children of God, and let them receive not punishment with the foolish but eternal rewards with the just.

[Note: Bal. omits “into scandal.”]

We urge everyone to honor and venerate bishops and priests exceedingly, before whom the whole earth bows its head and through whom our own rule also flourishes. We do not wish them to be attacked, blasphemed, or disparaged by anyone, because disparagement of priests concerns Christ, whose embassy they exercise in the Church. If someone disparages another human being, he will be considered a murderer; what, then, will become of those who disparage priests, since they kill themselves and destroy those who listen?

Those who double their crimes are worthy of double punishment. Those who prove rebellious or disobedient to these holy admonitions should know that they will be excluded from the thresholds of the holy Church.

[Note: G has “A note on the honor of priests” in the margin.]

### 323. On the four negligences of priests

Concerning priests and their churches, from which many things are neglected and scandals arise, four dangers have appeared in our investigation.

First, some of our priests, having acquired a certain sense of security, neither perform what pertains to divine worship nor show zeal for the restoration and lighting of the church. They do not even show due reverence to their superiors; moreover, they strip their churches and transfer their possessions to their own small estates. We have determined that all these matters belong to the negligence of bishops.

Taking this as an occasion, their superiors then break out into such audacity that they even presume to treat them unlawfully, dishonorably, and irreverently. Therefore we have judged that all of us must henceforth take the greatest care that those things which, with the consent of the bishops, have been granted by the lord emperor to the churches for the honor and love of God do not turn to the greed of priests or the rapacity of episcopal officials, but come instead to the benefit of the Church and to the uses of clerics and the poor.

[Note: Bal. has *permoti* (“moved,” “stirred”) instead of *eorum* (“their”).]

### 324. On priests who keep women in their houses

We have learned that it is no less dangerous that, in the parishes of certain bishops, some priests, contrary to the prohibitions of the holy canons, not only allow women to live in their houses but also have them serve there. We know that such women have very often become a snare to priests and that many, on this account, have fallen into scandal and disparagement.

This transgression was prohibited, according to canonical authority, both in the time of our father and in our own time at assemblies of bishops, but it has not yet been fully brought to correction. Therefore we have decreed jointly that those who until now have failed to correct such a great transgression, if henceforth they neglect to become correctors of this matter, shall, in accordance with the apostle’s judgment, be restrained as if they were consenting to the evils.

[Note: G has *correptionem* (“correction”) instead of *correctionem*.]

### 325. On priests who become stewards contrary to the statutes of the canons

Likewise, concerning those priests who, contrary to the statutes of the canons, become stewards, enter taverns, pursue disgraceful profits, serve usury in various ways, visit other people’s houses dishonorably and immodestly, are not ashamed to devote themselves to banquets and drunkenness, and run indiscriminately through various markets, we have judged that care must be taken that they henceforth be restrained strictly and severely. Otherwise, through their unlawful and indecent conduct, the priestly ministry will be discredited, and those who ought to have been examples to others will become a cause of scandal.

### 326. That priestly conduct should have credible witnesses to its life

Therefore, with equal agreement, it has seemed good to us that bishops, following the examples of the holy Fathers who preceded them, should have religious witnesses to their manner of life, so that they may provide no opportunity at all to those who wish to disparage them.

To show that a priest ought to provide his disciples with a good example from his own person, the apostle teaches when writing to Titus: “In everything, show yourself an example of good works, in teaching, in love, in purity,” and so forth.

Blessed Gregory likewise says in his decrees:

> “A shameful custom has arisen: that, for the bishops of this See, secular lay boys should attend to the private services of their bedchamber. Yet since the life of a shepherd ought always to be an example to his disciples, often the clerics do not know what the life of their bishop is like in private, while, as has been said, secular boys do know. Therefore, by the present decree, I establish that certain clerics, or even monks, chosen for this ministry, should attend to the episcopal bedchamber, so that the one who occupies the place of governance may have such witnesses as see his private conduct and, from their attentive observation, take an example of progress.”

This, then, is what blessed Gregory wrote. Moreover, if anyone wishes to seek more abundant examples concerning this matter, let him read the lives of blessed Augustine and Ambrose and of the other holy men. He will plainly find that the life and conduct of a bishop ought always to have credible witnesses to his life.

[Note: Bal. omits “if.”]

### 327. That bishops should avoid reproach when assigning church property to their relatives and should observe the proper measure of discretion

Since many bishops, out of love for their relatives, purchase estates and slaves from the property entrusted to them, in their own name or in that of some friend, and determine that these should pass into the rights of their relatives, thereby both ecclesiastical rights are shaken and the priestly ministry is darkened—indeed, it is disparaged and despised by those subject to them—it has seemed good to everyone that this kind of greed should henceforth be avoided.

We have decreed that the following shall be fixed and remain in force perpetually: regarding property over which he has his own legal right, which a bishop acquired either before the episcopate or, certainly, during his episcopate by hereditary succession, he may, in accordance with canonical authority, do whatever he wishes with it and give it to whomever he wishes.

After he has become a bishop, however, whatever property from the resources of the Church he acquires under any condition, whether in his own name or in another’s, we have decreed that it shall pass not into the rights of his relatives but into the rights of the Church over which he presides.

We establish that the same rule is to be followed concerning priests who, from the property of the churches over which they preside, purchase estates in this manner. For we have learned that many priests, on account of such purchases, have stripped the churches over which they preside, deviated from their ministry in many ways, enslaved themselves to the devil, and, on this account, caused many laypeople to rush into the scandal of condemnation and destruction.

[Note: Bal. omits “whatever he wishes.”]

### 328. That certain bishops neglect the canons, monks, and nuns subject to them

We have learned that some bishops have until now been very negligent in governing the communities subject to them—namely, canons, monks, and nuns—and that, on this account, they have provoked many to disparage and despise them. As a result, some other prelates established in their parishes, following their wicked examples, have likewise neglected their own communities.

We have decreed that these bishops must necessarily be admonished in a fraternal and synodal assembly, so that henceforth they restrain themselves from this negligence and present themselves as examples for the others to imitate. Otherwise, through their carelessness, contempt for divine service and dangers to souls may arise; the ears of our Excellency may be troubled; and weariness and disgrace may be brought upon the priestly order in sacred assemblies.

[Note: Bal. has “we judged it necessary” instead of “we decreed that they must necessarily be admonished.”]

### 329. On bishops, abbots, and priests who abandon their own places

We have learned that certain bishops, abbots, and priests, not for reasons of necessity or usefulness but rather out of greed and personal pleasure, very often abandon the seat of their own city, the enclosure of their monastery, or their own church, neglect their clergy, and frequent more distant places.

As a result, divine worship is abandoned, preaching to the people and care for those subject to them are postponed, and hospitality is neglected. To prevent anyone from doing this in the future without unavoidable necessity or some useful purpose, we prohibit it by common agreement.

### 330. On the clerics of laypeople

Concerning laypeople’s clerics, concerning whom some appear to make complaint because certain bishops, at their request, do not wish to ordain them in their churches although they are useful, it has seemed good to us that peace and harmony should be preserved on both sides, and that useful and suitable men should be chosen with charity and reason.

If a layperson presents a suitable and useful cleric, the bishop should not reject him for any reason without a definite cause. If he is to be rejected, the evident reason should be made known in order to avoid scandal.

### 331. On monks, priests, and clerics who indiscriminately visit the palace

It has seemed good that monks, priests, and likewise clerics who, disregarding canonical authority, indiscriminately visit the palace and cause the greatest annoyance to our sacred ears should not presume to do this. For in such conduct ecclesiastical authority is despised, priestly religion and the monastic profession are made less honorable.

### 332. That there should be no rash shedding of Christian blood

We wish and command that it be announced by our authority to everyone, and indeed preached by the priests, that such rash shedding of Christian blood must not be permitted in our kingdom.

[Note: G reads “in our kingdom of heaven.”] Everyone should always bear in mind what the Lord said after the Flood to his servant Noah:

> “From the hand of a human being, and from the hand of a man and his brother, I will require his life. Whoever sheds human blood, his blood shall be shed. For the human being was made in the image of God.”

And in the Law:

> “Whoever kills a human being shall be put to death.”

And the apostle says:

> “For rulers are not a terror to good conduct, but to evil. Would you have no fear of the authority? Do what is good, and you will receive praise from it, for it is God’s servant for your good. But if you do what is evil, be afraid, for it does not bear the sword without cause. It is God’s servant, an avenger for wrath against the one who does evil.”

For divine authority speaks specifically of that servant:

> “He bears the sword of God for the punishment of evildoers,”

and not of just anyone else.

On the other hand, we do not know by what pernicious invention some have usurped the practice whereby those who are supported by no public office, because of their hatreds and their very diverse evil desires, unlawfully claim for themselves the ministry of vengeance in avenging their neighbors and killing human beings. What a king ought to exercise against one person, because of the fear of many, they shamelessly do not hesitate to perpetrate against many out of hatred. They think that, for the sake of avenging enmities, they may do what they do not want the king to do in the exercise of God’s vengeance.

[Note: G omits “It is God’s servant.”]

### 333. On canonical and regular abbots, and on abbesses

We absolutely command canonical and regular abbots, abbesses who preside over nuns, and laypeople who possess monasteries to take great care of them, provide a good example to the others, conduct themselves religiously as is fitting, and entirely avoid whatever is inappropriate to each person’s profession and prohibited by the sacred canons.

They must not, through negligence, allow the places granted to them by us for some necessity to perish or be destroyed. They must govern the communities entrusted to them, both spiritually and materially, with paternal affection, and must not neglect to provide them with the necessary stipends. Otherwise, because of some deprivation, divine offices may be neglected and the communities themselves may be compelled to live less religiously.

Those who neglect to do these things should know that we will take them away from them and give them to more religious persons.

### 334. That chapels must not be established without the order or permission of the proper bishop

It has seemed good to us that, as we have been admonished by bishops, the other priests, and the servants of God, no chapels should be established in our palace or anywhere else without the permission or order of the bishop in whose parish they are located.

We also decree that everyone should receive Holy Eucharist on Sundays and on the chief festivals, except those who have been ordered to abstain. The observance of every Sunday, from morning until evening, must likewise be maintained by everyone according to canonical authority.

[Note: Bal. has “without that of ours”; these words have been deleted in G.]

### 335. That all who are suspected in the Catholic faith should be regarded as doubtful witnesses

All who are suspected in the faith of Christ or in the Catholic faith should be regarded as doubtful in human testimony. The testimony of those who are taught to be false in faith must therefore be weakened, and no credence should be given to those who are ignorant of the faith of truth.

### 336. That anyone who injures a church minister must pay threefold compensation

If anyone injures, strikes, or wounds a minister of the Church—that is, a subdeacon, lector, exorcist, acolyte, or doorkeeper—he shall pay threefold compensation, as their relatives customarily pay compensation.

An injury to a deacon, priest, or bishop shall be compensated fourfold. An injury to other clerics shall be compensated according to the law of their relatives.

An injury to monks who live in a monastery according to the Rule shall be compensated according to their family status, so that reverence may be shown to God and the Church and peace may be maintained for those who serve it.

[Note: G omits “who live in a monastery according to the Rule.”]

### 337. That a contumacious person who has no reverence for churches must pay 500 solidi

If any contumacious or arrogant person has no fear of God or reverence for churches, and has forcibly dragged from a church or its portico a fleeing slave of his own or anyone else whom he was pursuing, and has not shown honor to God, he shall pay 500 solidi to that church for his neglect and 200 solidi to the treasury as the *fredus*.

He shall also be punished by public penance according to the judgment of the bishop, so that there may be honor for God and reverence for the saints, and so that the Church of God may always remain inviolable.

[Note: Colb. adds: “If a layman is murdered in a church, the altar shall be destroyed until it is restored at the discretion of the proper bishop. But if a priest is killed there or before the altar, the altar together with the church shall be destroyed until it is reconciled with the consent of the apostolic [authority].”]

### 338. That everything which holy antiquity established concerning churches and their ministers should remain inviolate

We now command that everything which holy antiquity once established concerning the sacred places of churches and their ministers, which the religious authority of our predecessors established, or which our serenity has confirmed, be preserved intact both now and in the future.

### 339. On estates dedicated to God

It has seemed good that estates dedicated to the heavenly mysteries and handed over to God should not be harassed or seized by anyone on any pretext, but should remain permanently secure under the protection of immunity. The same applies to their people and to everything known to be subject to them.

If anyone acts against these provisions, he shall pay compensation according to what we have established concerning immunity and shall be punished by public penance imposed by the priests until satisfaction has been made.

[Note: Bal. has “and handed over to God,” instead of “which are handed over to God.”]

### 340. Concerning one who performs servile work on Sunday

If a free man performs servile work on Sunday, and yokes an ox and travels with a wagon, he shall lose the right-hand ox. If he performs other servile work prohibited by canonical authority, he shall make amends to the priests, as other negligences are customarily corrected by judges, and he shall receive penance from the priests according to the measure of his fault.

The same rule is to be observed concerning the principal festivals. If the priests are unable to correct such people, they shall then be brought by the judges to the priests and compelled to obey them in all things.

### 341. Concerning those who forcibly seize anything within the kingdom

If anyone in the army, within the kingdom, wishes without royal authorization to plunder anything by hostile force—to take hay, grain, large or small livestock, or to break into or burn houses—we entirely prohibit such acts.

If anything of this kind is done by a presumptuous person, he shall, if free, be liable to a penalty of sixty solidi and shall restore everything equivalent, or purge himself by the testimony of twelve witnesses.

If a slave does this, he shall be subject to capital punishment, and his master shall restore everything equivalent, because he did not correct or guard his slave so that he would not perpetrate such acts. For if we consume one another, we shall quickly perish.

Nevertheless, everyone must guard his army so that no plundering takes place within the kingdom.

[Note: G corrects *praesumptiosum* to *praesumptuosum* (“presumptuous”).]

### 342. Concerning one who incites another’s slave to theft

If anyone incites another’s slave to theft, or to anything harmful, in order to defraud his master and thereby be able to accuse him, and the fraud is exposed through the investigation of the judge, the master shall neither lose his slave nor make any compensation on this account.

The person through whose plotting or urging the act was committed shall be punished as a thief. The slave shall return what he took and, in addition, receive 120 lashes.

### 343. Concerning a thief caught at night

If a thief is caught at night in the act of theft while carrying stolen goods with him, and is killed, no legal complaint shall arise from that killing.

### 344. Concerning one who unknowingly buys something from a thief

If anyone unknowingly buys something from a thief, he shall, after a period has been granted, seek out the seller. If he cannot find him, he shall prove by oath and by his clothing that he is innocent, restore what is found in his possession, and not cease seeking the thief.

If he wishes to conceal the thief and is later discovered after swearing falsely, he shall be condemned in the crime just as that thief would be.

### 345. Concerning one who secretly kills another’s animal by night or by day

If anyone secretly, by night or by day, kills another person’s horse, ox, or any animal, denies it, and is later proved responsible, he shall pay compensation as for a stolen animal.

### 346. Concerning one who kills another’s animal and does not deny it

If anyone, for a reason that arises, kills another person’s animal and does not deny it, he shall not delay in giving an equivalent animal and shall take the carcass of the dead one.

### 347. Concerning one who knowingly buys stolen property

If anyone knowingly presumes to buy stolen property and is proved responsible for it, he shall return an equivalent item to the person whose money he used to make the purchase, without prejudice, of course, to that person’s legal claim against someone else.

[Note: G corrects “whose money” to “which money.”]

### 348. Concerning one who knowingly receives stolen property from a robber for safekeeping

If anyone knowingly receives stolen property from a robber for safekeeping, he shall pay compensation as a thief.

### 349. On not swearing oaths lightly

We wish oaths not to be taken hastily. Each judge should first ascertain the case truthfully, so that the truth cannot remain hidden from him, and people should not come easily to the taking of oaths.

[Note: G has “judging” written above *swearing*, or alternatively “swearing.”]

### 350. Concerning one who makes a false accusation against another’s life

If anyone makes a false accusation against another’s life, or incites someone through envy or an unjust accusation, he himself shall suffer the penalty or loss which he inflicted upon the other.

Do not condemn anyone before you investigate the truth, because it is written: “Test everything; hold fast to what is good.”

### 351. Concerning one who, through envy or deceit, burns the house of a free person or a slave

If anyone, through some envy or deceit, sets fire by night or by day to the house of a free person or a slave and burns it, he shall restore all the buildings and pay compensation for everything that burned there.

In addition, he shall be liable to sixty solidi and be punished by public penance according to the judgment of the priests. For each person who escaped from that fire, he shall pay compensation according to the law, and he shall restore everything they lost there.

### 352. That if anyone unjustly accuses another’s slave, he must return a similar slave to the master

If anyone unjustly accuses another’s slave, and the slave, though innocent, undergoes torture, he shall return to the master a similar slave for this act.

If the innocent slave dies under torture, he shall without delay restore to the master two slaves of equal worth.

### 353. On a public road

If anyone, contrary to the law, blocks a public road, a paved road, or a common road belonging to someone, he shall pay compensation according to his law and remove the obstruction he placed there.

If he wishes to deny it, he shall swear with twelve oath-helpers.

### 354. On a neighborhood road

If anyone blocks a neighborhood road or a herdsmen’s road, he shall pay compensation according to his law and open the road again. The same must be done concerning a path.

### 355. Concerning one who pollutes a spring

If anyone, out of any envy, pollutes or defiles a spring, he shall first cleanse it so that no suspicion of pollution remains in it, and he shall make compensation to the neighbors according to his law.

If the well belonged to several people in the neighborhood, they shall be punished by compensation among themselves.

### 356. Concerning one to whom gold, silver, ornaments, or other goods have been entrusted

If gold, silver, ornaments, or any other goods have been entrusted to someone, whether handed over for safekeeping or for sale, and they happen to be burned in his house together with his own property, the person who received the entrusted goods shall take an oath with witnesses that none of them benefited his own resources, and he shall not be compelled to pay anything—except for gold and silver, which could not burn.

If, however, the entrusted goods are proved to have been taken by theft, a period shall be granted to the person who lost them so that he may seek out the thief through his own investigation. If he finds him, he shall ensure that the entrusted owner recovers only his own property; the compensation for the theft, however, shall belong to the person who held the entrusted goods.

If the thief is not found within the established period, half of the entrusted goods shall be returned to the owner, while both parties shall bear half the loss. If afterward the owner finds that any of the goods had been concealed with the person to whom he entrusted them, they shall be exacted from him as stolen property.

[Note: Bal. reads *qui* (“who”) for *cui* (“to whom”).]

### 357. That a thing involved in a dispute may not be sold

A thing involved in a dispute may not be given away or sold.

### 358. Concerning one who sells his slave

If anyone sells his slave, perhaps without knowing the slave’s property, the master who sold him shall have the right to seek out the slave’s possessions wherever he is able to find them.

[Note: G has “are able to be found.”]

### 359. Concerning one who has been redeemed with his own peculium

If a slave has been redeemed from his own peculium, and his master happens not to know this, he does not thereby leave the master’s power, because, while unaware, the master received not the price but the property of his slave.

[Note: B has “who” instead of “because.”]

### 360. Concerning one who removes another person’s property from its place

If anyone removes another person’s *causam* (“case”; an uncertain reading, since L. and Baiuv. read *navem*, “ship”) from its place, he shall return it unharmed or return an equivalent. If he has dragged anything outside, concealed it, and denied it when questioned, he shall pay compensation as for stolen property.

[Note: L. and Baiuv. read “a ship”; G. deletes the *u* from *causam*. G omits “as for.”]

### 361. Concerning one who finds another person’s dead body

If anyone finds another person’s dead body and, out of human kindness, buries it so that it is not defiled by pigs or torn apart by wild beasts or dogs, whether the dead person is free or a slave, he shall suffer no accusation on this account. Rather, he should receive suitable remuneration from the person’s relatives.

If he does not wish to accept payment from the relatives, he shall receive it from the Lord, who commanded that the dead be buried.

[Note: G has *recipiat* (“let him receive”) instead of *recipiet* (“he will receive”).]

### 362. On sales withdrawn because of a low price or a defect

It has seemed good that the following rule be observed in a sale: whether a thing, a slave, or any kind of animal is sold, no one may break the validity of the sale by saying that he sold it for too low a price. Once the transaction has been completed, it must not be changed unless he happens to discover a defect concealed from him by the seller.

If the seller disclosed the defect, the sale shall stand and shall not be altered. If he did not disclose it, the sale may be changed on that day, or on the next day, or on the third day. If he has kept it for more than three nights, he may no longer change the transaction, unless he was unable to find the seller within three days.

When he finds him, the person who sold the defective item shall take it back. If he refuses to take it back, he shall swear with his oath-helpers that he knew of no defect in it on the day when he made the transaction; and the transaction shall stand.

[Note: Bal. has “because” instead of G’s “who.”]

### 363. That whoever gives earnest money for anything must be compelled to pay the price

Whoever gives earnest money for anything must be compelled to complete the price agreed upon by the buyer.

### 364. That no one molest passing pilgrims

It has been decreed that no one should presume to molest passing pilgrims or dare to harm them, since some travel for God’s sake and others because of their own necessities. If, however, there should be some presumptuous person who harms, attacks, strips, wounds, strikes, binds, sells, or kills a pilgrim, he shall make compensation to that pilgrim individually at twice the rate ordinarily paid for another person; or he shall make compensation according to his law to the pilgrim’s lord or companion. If the pilgrim has died and has no lord or companion there, then the bishop or priests of that district shall, with the judge enforcing it, collect the compensation itself at double the rate, as for a native, and give it as alms. In addition, he shall be compelled to pay sixty solidi to the fisc. If he has left the pilgrim alive, he shall compensate him individually, as stated above, for every injury inflicted upon him and for everything taken from him, at twice the rate ordinarily paid for someone from within the province. But if he has killed him, he shall pay double compensation as for a free man from that province; and the said money shall be given by the aforesaid priests as alms, since the Lord says: “You shall not grieve a stranger or sojourner.”

### 365. Concerning one who has sold another’s property

If anyone sells another person’s property without the consent of its owner—whether a male slave, a female slave, or any other thing—he shall restore that property according to law and add another similar one. If he cannot find the original, he shall restore two similar items of equal value.

### 366. Concerning one who knocks out one eye of another person’s quadruped

If anyone knocks out one eye of another person’s horse, ox, or any other quadruped, the animal shall be assessed at its value, and he shall pay one-third of that amount.

[Note: [Col. 0749] “horse,” or “ox,” or “quadruped”: Bal.]

### 367. Concerning one who kills someone by order of the king or duke

If anyone kills a man by order of the king or of the duke who governs that province, no claim shall be brought against him, nor shall he thereby become liable to a feud, since the law and the lord’s command killed the man, and he himself could not resist. The prince and his successors, however, shall defend him and all his descendants, so that they do not perish or suffer harm on this account. If, nevertheless, he himself or his descendants suffer any harm or are killed for this reason, double compensation shall be paid.

[Note: [Col. 0749] “they shall be compensated”: Bal.]

### 368. Concerning one who produces a written document, so that he may prove its truth by witnesses

If anyone produces a written document, he must prove its authenticity by witnesses, since it has been established in all cases that the person producing the document must affirm it.

### 369. That whatever has been remitted to provincials through the prince’s favor shall not be demanded by the collector

Whatever has been remitted to provincials through the prince’s favor in respect of taxes shall not be demanded by the collector.

### 370. That criminal priests who come to the synod shall be placed in the middle

We order that priests accused of crimes who canonically come to the synod shall be placed in the middle, in accordance with the decrees of Pope Innocent, chapter 33. After the objections brought against those priests have been examined, if they can be convicted, they shall be removed from the priestly office, since those who are not holy cannot handle holy things, and they shall be excluded from the ministry which they polluted by living unlawfully. If they cannot be convicted, then, according to the statute previously established with the advice of Pope Leo and many bishops, they shall satisfy their own bishop and people together with the other priests, the faithful, and upright men.

### 371. That every priest celebrate Mass with sandals

Every priest shall celebrate Mass according to the Roman order wearing sandals.

[Note: [Col. 0749] *scandaliis* for *sandaliis*: G.]

This shall also be announced to the people: on every Sunday they are to offer oblations to God, and the oblation itself is to be received outside the enclosure of the altar.

### 372. That on Sunday the priest go in procession with blessed water

Every priest shall go around his church on Sunday with psalm-singing, together with the people, and shall carry blessed water with him. The scrutiny shall also be conducted in due order, at its appointed time, according to Roman custom.

### 373. Concerning the provision of monastery sites and buildings

It is proper and necessary that the envoys sent to the various localities, together with the bishops of each diocese, inspect the sites of monasteries, of canons, and likewise of monks and of women, to see whether they are situated in a suitable and appropriate place where the necessary conveniences can be obtained for the benefit of the monastery, as the holy Rule says:

> “The monastery ought to be so established that everything necessary may be carried on within the monastery, so that the monks or clerics have no need to wander outside; for this is altogether not expedient for their souls.”

### 374. Concerning hospitality and care for the poor

Be mindful of hospitality and of the care of the poor, and of the reason why ecclesiastical goods have been offered by the faithful and received by the Church. Distribute them in such a way that from the one to whom you will have to render an account of these things you may deserve to receive not condemnation, but the reward of eternal joy.

### 375. That assistance from the king be provided to those who fulfill the ecclesiastical ministry

We wish you to know our will: we are prepared to assist you wherever necessary, so that you may be able to fulfill your ministry. At the same time, we admonish you to preserve the honor granted to us by God, out of respect for our humility and for the obedience that, through fear of God, we show toward your admonitions, just as your predecessors did for our predecessors.

### 376. That no bishop or abbot give or take away benefices from his men for bribes

We also admonish bishops and abbots not to take away or give benefices to their men for bribes, since many complaints and grievances concerning this matter customarily reach our ears.

### 377. That the king’s counselors not accept a gift for obtaining a benefice from him for someone else

No one of our counselors shall accept gifts for obtaining from us a benefice for anyone, since we wish to give a benefice to the person who has served us well.

### 378. That a cleric, monk, or nun not be accused before a civil court

No one shall dare accuse a cleric, monk, or nun before a civil court, but rather before the bishop. He shall pronounce a sentence consonant with the law or the canons and just.
