Let all bishops and all the faithful of the holy Church of God observe this. Let our provincial governors also see to it that the lawsuits of any clerics, monks, or nuns are settled.

If anyone in an official position violates this constitution, he shall be fined ten pounds of gold. If he is an executor, he shall be confined in the chains of the churches to undergo punishment, and he shall lose his office.

### 379. Concerning a monk who abandons his monastery

If a monk abandons his monastery, all his possessions—both what he brought into the monastery and what he did not bring into it—shall belong to the ownership of the monastery, and he himself shall be compelled to serve the office of governor. If, however, a monk moves to another monastery, his substance shall be possessed by the first monastery, and he himself shall not be received in the other monastery.

### 380. Concerning a slave received into a monastery

If an unknown person wishes to enter a monastery, the monastic habit shall not be given to him before three years have passed. If, within three years, he is sought as a slave, freedman, or tenant, he shall be returned to his master together with everything he brought, provided that an assurance of immunity has been received. If he has not been sought within three years, he may not afterward be sought; only the things that he brought into the monastery shall be received by the slave’s master.

### 381. Concerning monks who become laymen

If a monk becomes a layman, he shall be stripped of his honor and belt, and his possessions shall be added to the monastery. If he abandons the monastic life, the governor of the province shall seize him and enroll him in his court.

### 382. Concerning the building of a church

No one shall build a church before the bishop of the city comes and publicly plants a cross there. Beforehand, the person who wishes to build shall specify what will suffice for the lights, the custody, and the stipends of the guards; and after making the donation, he may build the house.

### 383. Concerning one who establishes an oratory in his house

Anyone who has an oratory in his house may pray there. Nevertheless, he shall not dare celebrate sacred Masses in it without the permission of the bishop of that place. If he does so, his house shall be assigned to the rights of the fisc.

[Note: [Col. 0751] “powers” instead of “rights”: G.]

The count and his envoys who knew of this and did not prevent it shall be fined a pound of gold and shall receive canonical excommunication or exclusion from the bishop of that place.

### 384. Concerning the election of an abbess

The abbess shall be elected by the entire congregation, not according to rank, but as the one who is established to have the better reputation and whom the better persons have chosen. Those who elect her shall present her before the holy Gospels, saying that they have chosen her not because of friendship or human favor, but because they know her to be sound in faith, chaste in life, worthy in administration, and useful for every condition of the monastery. Then she shall be confirmed by the bishop to whom the monastery is subject.

### 385. Concerning a deaconess or woman devoted to God

If anyone abducts, solicits, or corrupts a religious woman, the Church shall claim the property of both of them, in which such a woman lived; nevertheless, both shall be subjected to capital punishment. If the woman did not consent, she shall be entrusted, together with her property, to the protection of the monastery. If she has children, their lawful portion shall be reserved for them.

[Note: [Col. 0751] “to the protection of the monastery” is the first hand in G.; but the scribe himself corrected it to “to the more secure monastery.”]

If such a crime is not punished by religious institutions within a year after it has become known,

[Note: [Col. 0751] “after,” corrected from “because of”: G.]

the count of that place shall assign these goods to our fisc. If the count of the province neglects to impose punishment for such a crime, he shall lose his honor and shall be compelled to pay two pounds of gold to the power of the fisc.

### 386. Concerning the restoration of a monastery

No king or any other person may lawfully transfer a monastery into private ownership, exchange it, or sell it by any device whatsoever. Divine, apostolic, and canonical authority has also sanctioned this under penalty of anathema. If it has been done, it shall have no validity; the person who received it shall lose the price, while the person who disposed of it shall lose in the monastery itself the price he received and, together with the price, shall lose the monastery. The monastery itself shall be restored to its former condition.

### 387. Concerning litigants

In cities in which governors preside, they themselves, or the defenders, shall hear cases. Nor do we permit those who prefer to judge a bishop, priests, or clerics to do so.

[Note: [Col. 0751] The words “this to be done” are absent in Julian.]

### 388. Concerning actors

If any actor wears priestly, monastic, religious-woman’s, or any other garment resembling an ecclesiastical status, he shall undergo corporal punishment and be handed over to exile.

### 389. Concerning a forty-year prescription

No prescription of ten, twenty, or thirty years shall be set against religious houses, but only the passage of forty years; and this applies not only to other things, but also to legacies and inheritances.

[Note: [Col. 0751] “Ten,” corrected from “six”: G.]

### 390. That no one dare accuse a bishop, priest, or cleric before public judges

It has been decreed that no one shall presume to accuse a bishop, priest, or cleric before public judges, but rather before bishops.

### 391. Concerning the prohibition against judging the absent

It has been decreed that judgment shall not be rendered against absent persons. If this is done, the sentence pronounced shall have no validity.

### 392. That no priest be judged unless his accusers, and lawful ones, are present

It was formerly established by the holy Roman and apostolic Church, and has been confirmed by us in synodal judgment, that no one from the priestly order shall be judged or condemned unless, when accused, he has lawful accusers present and is given an opportunity to defend himself and clear away the charges.

### 393. That the life of the accusers be examined first

It was likewise sanctioned by the aforesaid holy Roman and apostolic Church and decreed by all with synodal authority that first the person, faith, life, and conduct of the accusers must always be carefully investigated, and afterward the charges brought must be faithfully examined; for nothing ought to be done otherwise unless the life of the complainants has first been investigated.

### 394. Concerning witnesses to be required in an accusation against clerics

It has been decreed that if anyone brings an accusation of fornication against a cleric, lawful testimony shall be required from him according to the command of the apostle Paul. If he cannot prove by the testimony given what he has said, the accuser shall receive the excommunication of the accused.

### 395. That a culpable person not be admitted

If the person of the accuser appears culpable in the judgment of the bishops, he shall not be admitted to bring a charge except concerning his own cases.

### 396. Concerning the prohibition against judging anyone before the case has been examined

It is not just to judge or condemn a man whose case has not been thoroughly examined.

### 397. Concerning the prohibition against a lesser judging a greater

A lesser person cannot judge a greater.

### 398. Concerning the prohibition against judging anyone without a lawful accuser

It is not the judge’s prerogative to judge or condemn anyone without a lawful accuser. For the Lord knew that Judas was a thief, but because he was not accused, he was not expelled.

### 399. Concerning one who litigates frequently, so that he is not received without examination

No one shall receive the accusation of a person who litigates frequently and is quick to accuse without a serious examination.

### 400. Concerning examining a case minutely in court and repeatedly discussing it

A judge ought to investigate everything and examine the order of events through a full inquiry, granting time for questioning, presenting, and adding to the case, so that the action of the parties may be completely delimited there. He should not hasten to confront litigants with his sentence before they have completed everything and have nothing further to present in the matter. The case should be discussed until the truth of the matter is reached. It is necessary to question the parties frequently, lest something that ought to be added remain overlooked.

### 401. Concerning those who think that, through bribed witnesses, they should be admitted to accuse priests, so that they are not admitted unless free from every suspicion

There are some who appear to fight against ecclesiastical rule and think that they ought to be admitted to an accusation through bribed witnesses. Such persons shall not be admitted at all unless they show by public records that they are free from every suspicion.

### 402. That no one act against religion

The emperor, or anyone who preserves piety, shall not presume to do anything contrary to the divine commandments.

### 403. That laymen must not presume to dispose of religious matters

Although they may be religious, no laymen shall be granted the authority to dispose of ecclesiastical resources or of persons devoted to God.

### 404. That it be permitted to appeal to higher judges whenever necessity arises

Whenever anyone appeals from ecclesiastical judges to other ecclesiastical judges where there is greater authority, this shall not be denied to those who have made the appeal.

### 405. Concerning the annulment of an unjust judgment settled through fear of or by order of the prince

An unjust judgment and an unjust decision arranged by judges through fear of the king or by royal command shall have no validity.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0753]

## SOME CHAPTERS OF THE DIVINE LAW BEGIN

### 1. Concerning the shedding of blood

Whoever sheds human blood, his blood shall be shed.

### 2. That those who take the Lord’s name in vain be severely punished

You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain; nor will the Lord hold innocent the one who takes the name of the Lord his God in vain.

### 3. Concerning honoring father and mother

Honor your father and your mother, so that you may live long upon the earth.

### 4. That one who sells his daughter as a maidservant shall not go out as a female slave does

If anyone sells his daughter as a maidservant, she shall not leave as maidservants customarily leave. If she pleases her master to whom she was sold, let him admit her as free; and it is not permitted to sell her to another people.

[Note: [Col. 0753] The words “she shall not” are absent in G.]

### 5. That one who strikes a man shall die

Whoever strikes a man intending to kill him shall die.

### 6. Concerning one who deliberately wishes to kill his neighbor

If anyone deliberately kills his neighbor and by treachery, you shall drag him away from my altar so that he may die.

### 7. Concerning one who strikes his father or mother

Whoever strikes his father or mother shall die.

### 8. That one must not curse father and mother

Whoever curses his father and mother shall die.

### 9. Concerning one who steals and sells a man

Whoever steals a man and sells him, once convicted of the offense, shall die.

[Note: [Col. 0753] “and, after being admonished”; “he shall die”: G.]

### 10. Concerning men who quarrel among themselves and one strikes the other

If men quarrel and one strikes his neighbor with a stone or fist, and the latter does not die but lies in bed; if he rises and walks outside leaning on his staff, the one who struck him shall be innocent, provided that he compensates him for his lost work and medical expenses.

[Note: [Col. 0753] *operas et impensas eius in medicos* (“his lost work and medical expenses”): Bal.]

### 11. Concerning one who strikes his male or female slave with a stone or rod and the slave dies

Whoever strikes his male slave or female slave with a stone or rod, and the slave dies in his hands, shall be liable. But if the slave survives for a day or two, he shall not be subject to punishment, because the slave is his property.

### 12. That if some people quarrel among themselves and one of them strikes a pregnant woman

If men quarrel and someone strikes a pregnant woman, causing her to miscarry, then, if she survives, he shall be subject to the compensation demanded by the woman’s husband and determined by the arbitrators.

### 13. But if the woman dies, the striker shall pay life for life

If her death follows, he shall pay life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth, hand for hand, foot for foot, burn for burn, wound for wound, bruise for bruise.

### 14. That whoever puts out the eye of a male or female slave shall set them free

If anyone strikes the eye of his male slave or female slave and makes them one-eyed, he shall set them free in exchange for the eye that he put out. If he knocks out the tooth of his male or female slave, he shall likewise be subject to the same judgment.

### 15. Concerning an ox that butts and wounds a man or woman, and its owner

If a goring ox kills a man or woman, it shall be stoned and shall not be eaten. The owner of the ox shall be innocent. But if the ox was a goring ox yesterday and the day before yesterday, and its owner was warned, and he did not restrain it, and it killed a man or woman, the ox shall be stoned and its owner shall be killed.

[Note: [Col. 0755] *domino* for *dominum*: Bal.]

If a ransom is imposed upon him, he shall give for his life whatever is demanded of him.

### 16. Concerning one who opens and digs a cistern

If anyone opens and digs a cistern and does not cover it, and an ox or donkey falls into it, the owner of the cistern shall repay the value of the animals. But what has died shall belong to him.

### 17. Concerning another person’s ox, if it wounds someone else’s ox

If someone’s ox wounds another person’s ox and it dies, they shall sell the living ox and divide the price and the carcass. But if its owner knew that the ox was vicious and did not wish to guard it, he shall give ox for ox and shall receive the entire carcass.

### 18. Concerning one who steals an ox or sheep

Whoever steals an ox or sheep shall restore five oxen for one ox and four sheep for one sheep.

### 19. Concerning a thief found breaking into a house

If a thief breaks into a house, or is found digging into it, and, after receiving a wound, dies, the one who struck him shall not be liable for bloodshed. But if he does this after sunrise, he has committed homicide and shall himself die. If what he stole is found alive with him, whether ox or donkey, it shall be restored.

### 20. Concerning one who damages a field or vineyard

If anyone damages a field or vineyard and lets his animal loose to graze another person’s property, he shall restore, as an assessment of the damage, whatever is best that he has in the field or vineyard.

[Note: [Col. 0755] *obtime* for *optimum*: G.]

### 21. Concerning one who kindles a fire in the fields, so that he must restore the damage

If a fire spreads and reaches sheaves and catches piles of grain or standing crops in the fields, the person who kindled the fire shall repay the damage.

### 22. Concerning one who entrusts money to a friend

If anyone entrusts money or a vessel to a friend for safekeeping, and it is stolen from the person who received it, then, if the thief is found, he shall repay double. If he is not found, the master of the house shall be brought before the gods,

[Note: [Col. 0755] *adeos*: G.]

and shall swear that he did not extend his hand to his neighbor’s property in order to commit fraud, whether involving an ox, donkey, sheep, or garment. In every matter that can occasion loss, the case of both parties shall come before him. If the arbitrators judge him liable, he shall restore double to his neighbor.

### 23. Concerning an ass, ox, or any animal entrusted for safekeeping

If anyone entrusts to a friend an ass, ox, sheep, or any animal for safekeeping, and it dies, is crippled, or is captured by enemies, with no one having seen what happened, there shall be an oath in the midst,

[Note: [Col. 0755] *medium* for *medio*: Bal.]

that he did not extend his hand to his neighbor’s property. The owner shall accept the oath, and the person who received the animal shall not be compelled to make restitution. If it was stolen, he shall restore the damage to its owner. If it was eaten by a wild beast, he shall bring to him what was killed, and no restitution shall be made.

Anyone who borrows any of these things from his neighbor, and the animal is crippled or dies while the owner is absent, shall be compelled to make restitution.

[Note: [Col. 0755] *non* is absent in G.]

But if the owner is present, no restitution shall be made, especially if it was hired for the wage of its work.

### 24. Concerning one who seduces a betrothed virgin or sleeps with her

If anyone seduces a betrothed virgin and sleeps with her, he shall endow her and have her as his wife.

### 25. Concerning the girl’s father, if he refuses to give her, so that he must pay money according to the custom of the dowry

If the father refuses to give the virgin, he shall pay money according to the custom of the dowry ordinarily received by virgins.

### 26. Concerning sorcerers

You shall not allow sorcerers to live.

### 27. Concerning those who have intercourse with an animal

Whoever has intercourse with an animal shall die.

### 28. Concerning those who sacrifice to gods or afflict strangers

Whoever sacrifices to gods shall be killed. You shall not grieve or afflict a stranger.

### 29. Concerning tithes and firstfruits to be offered to the Lord

You shall not delay offering your tithes and firstfruits to the Lord from your firstborn sons. You shall do likewise with oxen and sheep. Let it remain seven days with its mother; on the eighth day give the offspring to the Lord.

### 30. Concerning a deposit or pledge given

Your deposit or pledge,

[Note: [Col. 0755] “deposit, that is, pledge”: B.]

or if someone conceals what has been entrusted to him, or if he finds a lost item and swears that he did not find it, once convicted of the offense he shall return everything he sought to obtain by fraud, and in addition a third and a fifth part to the owner whom he defrauded.

### 31. Concerning not revealing the shame of one’s neighbor

No one shall approach the blood of his neighbor in order to reveal his shame. Nor shall you uncover the shame of any woman, because it is your own shame.

### 32. Concerning a man who sleeps with a female slave

If a man sleeps with a woman in sexual intercourse, and she is a slave, even if she is of marriageable age but has neither been redeemed by a price nor granted freedom, both shall be beaten but shall not die.

### 33. That one must not practice divination or consult magicians and soothsayers

You shall not practice divination or consult magicians or soothsayers, nor inquire of anything through them.

[Note: [Col. 0755] *augurari* for *auguriemini*: G.]

[Note: [Col. 0755] *sciatis* for *sciscitetis*: B.]

I am your God.

### 34. Concerning honoring an old man

Rise before a gray head and honor the person of an old man, and fear God.

### 35. That nothing be done contrary to equity

You shall not do anything unjust in judgment, in rule, in weight, or in measure. Let the balance be just and the weights equal; let the measure be just and the sextarius equal.

### 36. Concerning one who commits adultery with his neighbor’s wife

Whoever commits adultery with another man’s wife and commits adultery with his neighbor’s spouse shall die—the adulterer and the adulteress.

### 37. Concerning one who sleeps with his stepmother

Whoever sleeps with his stepmother and uncovers the disgrace of his father, both shall die. Their blood shall be upon them.

### 38. Concerning one who confesses a theft for God’s sake

If a man confesses, for God’s sake, the theft he committed, he shall return the principal and an additional fifth to the one against whom he sinned.

### 39. Concerning one who strikes a man with iron

If anyone strikes a man with iron and he dies, the one who struck him shall be guilty of homicide and shall himself die.

[Note: [Col. 0755] “of judgment”: B.]

### 40. That no one be condemned on the testimony of one person

No one shall be condemned on the testimony of a single person.

### 41. Concerning setting aside tithes

You shall set aside tithes from everything that is produced for you at that time and store them within your gates. You shall lend them to priests and Levites, to strangers and pilgrims, to orphans and widows; and the Lord your God will bless you all the days of your life.

### 42. Concerning one who, walking along the road, finds a bird’s nest

If you are walking along the road and find a bird’s nest in a tree or on the ground, with the mother sitting above the chicks, you shall not take her together with her young, but shall let her go while keeping the chicks, so that the Lord may bless you.

### 43. That when a new house is built, a wall be made around the house

When you build a new house, you shall make a wall around the roof, lest blood be shed in your house and you become liable when someone falls and plunges down.

### 44. Concerning not sowing a vineyard with another seed

You shall not sow your vineyard with another seed, lest both what you sowed and what grows from the vineyard be consecrated together.

### 45. That an ox and a donkey not be yoked together for plowing

You shall not plow with an ox and a donkey together.

### 46. That one must not wear a garment woven from wool and linen

You shall not wear a garment woven from wool and linen.

### 47. Concerning a betrothed virgin girl

If anyone betroths a virgin girl, and another man finds her in the city and has intercourse with her, you shall bring both of them to the gate of that city, and they shall be stoned: the girl, because she did not cry out although she was in the city; and the man, because he humbled her.

### 48. Concerning a betrothed virgin found in the field

But if a man finds in the field a girl who is betrothed and sleeps with her, he alone shall die. The girl shall suffer nothing.

### 49. That a eunuch with crushed testicles not enter the Church of God

A eunuch whose testicles have been crushed or amputated and whose penis has been cut off shall not enter the Church of the Lord. Nor shall a *manzer* enter it—that is, one born of a prostitute.

### 50. Concerning not lending money at interest

You shall not lend money, grain, or any other thing to your brother at interest.

### 51. Concerning not delaying the fulfillment of a vow

When you make a vow to the Lord your God, you shall not delay fulfilling it, because the Lord your God will require it of you. If you delay, it will be counted as sin against you until you do what you promised the Lord with your own mouth.

### 52. That a man who has taken a wife not go to war

When a man has taken a wife, he shall not go to war, nor shall any public obligation be imposed upon him. He shall remain free of blame in his own house, and he shall rejoice with his wife for one year.

### 53. That fathers not be killed for sons, nor sons for fathers

Fathers shall not be killed for their sons, nor sons for their fathers; each person shall die for his own sin.

### 54. Concerning one who suffers violence from persecutors, so that he is to be received

If anyone has suffered violence from persecutors, he shall be received and find rest in whatever church he comes to.

### 55. Concerning a woman who cannot marry her husband

If a man and woman have joined themselves in marriage and afterward the woman says concerning the man that he cannot marry her, and she can prove that this is true, she shall take another.

[Note: [Col. 0757] *illum* (“him”) is absent in G.]

### 56. That offerings not be accepted without the bishop’s consent

No one shall dare either to give or to receive, without the knowledge of the bishop, the offerings of produce owed to the Church.

### 57. That the priests of a city order nothing without the command of their bishop

The priests of a city shall order nothing without the command of their bishop, nor shall they do anything in any parish.

### 58. That priests not sell church property without their bishop’s permission

Priests shall not sell church property or give it to anyone without the permission or knowledge of their bishop.

### 59. If a priest or deacon abandons his church, let him be deposed

A priest or deacon who abandons his church and goes over to another shall be deposed.

### 60. Concerning priests, deacons, or subdeacons deprived of office by their own bishops

If a priest, deacon, or subdeacon who has been deprived of office by his own bishop presumes to resume his ministry, he shall have no hope of restoration.

[Note: [Col. 0757] *sancti ministerii officium ... praeripere* (“to seize the office of the holy ministry”) for *suum ministerium incipiat praesumere*: G.]

### 61. If a bishop, priest, deacon, or subdeacon goes to war, let him be deposed

If any bishop, priest, deacon, or subdeacon goes to war and puts on military arms for fighting, he shall be deposed from every office, to such an extent that he shall not even have lay communion.

### 62. That priests of another region not celebrate in the presence of the priests of that region

Priests from another region shall not celebrate in the presence of the priests of that region.

### 63. Concerning husbands and wives who leave one another

Those who leave their wives or husbands shall not marry; instead, they shall either remain continent or be reconciled to one another.

### 64. Concerning bishops who litigate or have been judged

If a bishop has a dispute with another bishop, he shall seek judges not from another province but from his own. A bishop who has been judged in some case shall also be permitted to seek a new judgment, and, if necessary, to approach the Roman bishop freely.

### 65. No one shall receive a blessing from a heretic

No one shall receive a blessing from a heretic.

### 66. Concerning prayers directed to the Father

No one shall direct prayer in supplication to anyone except the Father; he should first discuss these prayers with people who are more instructed or learned.

### 67. Concerning a cleric ordained by another bishop

A cleric ordained by another bishop, without his own bishop requesting or consenting to it, shall not remain in the clergy.

### 68. Concerning those priests who do not know how to baptize according to the Savior’s command

We order that all those whom the priests baptized who did not know how to baptize according to the command of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, or to invoke the mystical words of the Holy Trinity, be baptized again, because they were baptized without faith in the Holy Trinity.

[Note: [Col. 0757] “all the people”: Colbert and Tilianus.]

### 69. Concerning how our envoys, together with the bishops of the individual regions, are to act regarding the churches of God and their priests

Our envoys, together with the respective bishops, shall take great care that ruined churches be completely restored and adorned, and that those which have not been endowed, or which have lost or had their endowment taken away, be fully and canonically endowed, so that they may justly recover what they unjustly lost.

#### Concerning those who neither wish to endow their churches nor restore their endowment

If those to whom the churches belong refuse to endow them, or refuse to return what has been taken away, the bishop of the place shall reclaim the churches for the ownership of his see, to possess them in future times. If any of the free men resist this, the bishop of that place shall remove the relics from them and place them in a better location, while the churches themselves shall be destroyed or burned.

### 70. Concerning one who kills himself or hangs himself by a noose

Concerning one who kills himself or hangs himself by a noose, it has been determined that, if anyone wishes out of compassion to give alms, he may give them and offer prayer in the psalms. Nevertheless, such persons shall be deprived of offerings and Masses, since the judgments of God are incomprehensible and no one can investigate the depth of his counsel.

### 71. That incestuous persons and parricides be restrained canonically

Concerning incestuous persons and parricides: they are to be restrained canonically. Thus it was judged concerning the man who violated his maternal aunt’s daughter: he was not to take up the marriage again, he was to abandon the military belt, and he was either to seek a monastery or, if he wished to remain outside, fully fulfill the periods of penance according to the canons.

### 72. That phylacteries be made neither by a cleric nor by any Christian

Clerics or laymen shall in no way make phylacteries, false inscriptions, or amulets, which the foolish think will help against fevers or other diseases, whether made by them or by any Christian, because they are signs of magical art. Instead, for illness let that which the apostles and the canons have sanctioned be provided—that is, prayers and anointing with holy oil.

[Note: [Col. 0757] “so that neither by a cleric nor by any Christian they be made”: G.]

[Note: [Col. 0757] “inscriptions”: G.]

### 73. That no priest claim more than one church for himself

It has pleased the entire synodal assembly that no priest presume to claim more than one church for himself.

### 74. Concerning the Greater Litany, that it be celebrated according to Roman custom

The Greater Litany shall be celebrated by all according to Roman custom on the seventh day before the Kalends of May.

75. That no one should end his life without Communion or be deprived of anointing with blessed oil. If anyone is weighed down by illness, he should not end his life without Communion, nor be deprived of anointing with consecrated oil. And if he foresees the end, the priest should commend his soul to God by prayers and with the most holy Body.

Therefore it pleased all that no presbyter should presume to claim more than one church for himself; for just as every layman ought to have no more than one wife, so also every presbyter ought to have no more than one church.

76. On presbyters degraded and afterward involved in many crimes. Presbyters who have been degraded and, after their degradation, become involved in many crimes are to be reduced to public penance according to the canons.

77. If anyone wishes to receive consecrated water. On Holy Saturday of Easter or on the Saturday of Pentecost, if anyone wishes to receive consecrated water for sprinkling in his house, let him receive it before the infusion of chrism.

78. On clerics and presbyters who refuse to obey their bishops, that they be excommunicated. Clerics and laypeople who refuse to obey their bishops canonically are to be excommunicated.

79. On the metropolitan bishop. It is fitting that the metropolitan, who has been exalted by the pallium, be honored and admonish the others.

80. That each person should observe his lineage down to the seventh generation. We decree that each person must observe his lineage down to the seventh generation, and that, for as long as they recognize themselves as related by affinity, they must not enter into the union of this marriage.

81. On presbyters ordained by unknown bishops. If each bishop finds in his own parish presbyters whose ordainers are unknown, and it is doubtful whether those who ordained them were bishops or not, then, provided that the presbyters themselves are men of good conduct and Catholic faith, educated in the ministry of Christ and in every holy law and suitably qualified, they shall receive from their own bishop the blessing of the presbyterate, be consecrated, and thus exercise the sacred ministry.

[Note: “incogniti” corrected to “cogniti” in G.]

82. That whoever forbids a traveler lodging must pay sixty solidi. If anyone forbids a person traveling along the road a place to stay, he shall pay sixty solidi publicly.

83. That everyone should take the greatest care that no one ends his life without episcopal confirmation. Let everyone take the greatest care that no one ends his life without episcopal confirmation and that his soul does not perish.

84. On those who remove or devastate the offerings of the faithful, or give or receive them without the command of their own bishop. Those who remove offerings of the faithful from churches or from the authority of priests, or receive offerings that have been removed, not only violate the vows of others but also commit sacrilege and prove themselves defrauders of the church of God; for the ancients establish that to defraud or remove anything is sacrilege.

85. That presbyters should not move from place to place without the command of their own bishop. Presbyters who move without the command of their own bishop from one church to other churches are to be held excluded from Communion until they return to the same churches in which they were first established.

86. On visiting bishops and clerics, that they should be content with the hospitality offered. Visiting bishops and clerics are to be content with the hospitality offered, and none of them may perform any priestly office without the permission of the bishop in whose parish he is known to be staying.

87. That no one should have a marriage except a lawful one. No one may have a marriage except a lawful one. No one shall commit incest. No one shall leave his own spouse except, as the holy Gospel teaches, on account of fornication. If anyone expels his own spouse, joined to him in a lawful marriage, then, if he wishes rightly to remain a Christian, he may not join himself to anyone else; instead, he must either remain in that condition or be reconciled to his own spouse.

88. On those who despise the summons or correction of bishops. If any layperson, whether of higher or lower rank, commits a sin and, summoned by the authority of his bishop to correction and penance, delays in coming, let him remain an exile from the church and separated from the fellowship of Catholics until he corrects what he has committed, canonically washes away his guilt through satisfaction, and obtains pardon and forgiveness through the prayers of his own bishop. After satisfaction has been made, let that bishop, having improved him, restore him canonically to the bosom of the church, from whose womb he had strayed.

89. That no layperson should receive anything from the estates of bishops. We command that no layperson or cleric should seek, covet, or receive anything from the estates or possessions belonging to the sees of bishops, or from those church properties known to be situated in their parishes, without the command or consent of the bishops whose care they belong to; otherwise, may the covetous fire for sacred things that is within them burn them more fiercely to ashes. Likewise, we admonish everyone to restrain and curb, with all their strength, themselves and their people from every devastation of all churches. For what else do we understand those who devastate churches to be doing than stirring up conflict against the God of eternal dominion and majesty, when those buildings serve him day and night and have been consecrated to him? Let those who devastate them beware, we declare, lest they be devastated by him if he is angered—the one whose stroke the backs of mountains cannot withstand.

90. On one who kills a monk or cleric, that he should lay down his arms. Whoever kills a monk or cleric shall lay down his arms and serve God in a monastery all the days of his life, never to return to the secular world, and shall perform public penance for seven years.

91. On a man and woman joined in marriage, when afterward she says that he cannot marry her. If a man and woman have joined themselves in marriage and afterward the woman says of the man that he cannot marry her, then, if she can prove that this is true, she may take another, because, according to the Apostle, her husband could not render her the marital due.

92. That a betrothed girl should not be given to another man. Parents may not give a betrothed girl to another man. Nevertheless, she may go to a monastery if she wishes.

93. That the baptized should not eat with catechumens. The baptized may not eat with catechumens, give them a kiss, or say “Ave” to them. How much less, then, with those excommunicated by the bishop or with pagans?

94. On an ordained presbyter who discovers that he has not been baptized. If an ordained presbyter discovers that he has not been baptized, he is to be baptized [Note: Absent in some manuscripts, Bal.] and ordained again, together with all those whom he previously baptized.

95. If a free man has taken a female slave in marriage. If a free man has taken a female slave in marriage, he does not have the right to dismiss her if they were previously joined with the consent of both.

96. On abductors and abducted virgins or widows. If anyone abducts or steals another man’s betrothed—a virgin or a widow not yet betrothed—it has been decided that, whether he subsequently betroths or endows her or not, and whether he has been able to take or retain her by any device with the consent of her parents or not, he may never have her as his wife. Instead, she is to be taken away from the abductor or thief and, at a suitable time, if she herself did not consent to this evil, returned to her relatives so that she may marry another man according to law.

The abductor or thief, however, and all who consented to them are to be punished with public penance according to canonical authority. They shall pay her relatives three times whatever they unjustly did in this abominable crime, and they shall restore each individual item separately threefold according to law.

But if the woman who was abducted, whether at first or afterward, willingly consented to so abominable a crime, she may never marry afterward. She is to be punished with public penance and placed under such custody that she may in no way indulge in sexual relations with anyone.

Thus are the aforesaid crimes to be punished, so that everyone may know that neither the laws of the world consent to such abominable unions nor do the sacred canons offer any counsel for them; rather, the laws of the world command that such persons and their accomplices be struck down by death. The sacred canons, composed by the Spirit of God, strike not only abductors but also all their accomplices and those who consent to them with anathema, as is clear to all readers in chapter 28 of the Council of Chalcedon, at which 630 fathers were present.

97. On those who commit robberies within the kingdom. If anyone commits robbery within the kingdom or forcibly takes anything from any of our faithful or from his dependent, he shall pay threefold by law to the person from whom he took it. In addition, he shall pay us our ban, that is, sixty solidi. Afterward he is to be brought before us by the count, so that, shut up in the bastonicon, he may suffer punishment until it pleases us.

If the act was public, let him perform public penance for it according to the sanction of the holy canons; if it was secret, let him perform penance for it on the advice of priests. For robbers, as the Apostle says, will not possess the kingdom of God unless they truly repent.

Whoever takes anything from church property is to be judged more severely, because the removal of sacred things is sacrilege, and anyone who removes or carries off anything from them is called sacrilegious. Such persons are also to be held infamous until they have made satisfaction to the church they injured.

98. On priests, Levites, and monks who are killed or disabled. If anyone kills or disables a priest, Levite, or monk, he shall pay compensation according to the provisions of the earlier capitularies added to the Salic Law. In addition, he shall pay us our ban, that is, sixty solidi, lay down his arms, and serve God in a monastery under arduous penance all the days of his life, never afterward serving the secular world or secular persons, nor joining himself to a wife.

99. On those who inflict injury or dishonor upon a bishop. If anyone inflicts any injury or unjust dishonor upon a bishop, he shall pay compensation for the life, and everything he appears to possess shall be assigned in full to the church over which he is known to preside. He shall also pay us our ban threefold, that is, sixty solidi; or he himself shall be assigned permanently to service in our fisc until he can redeem himself threefold according to his wergild.

The holy church consists in its priests [Note: Codex Theodosianus, Constitutions of Theodosius and Valentinian, chapter 20; Pseudo-Pius, letter 2.]. Therefore those who inflict injury or insult upon bishops or other priests must be punished with a great penalty; for detraction of priests concerns Christ, in whose place they perform the ministry of ambassadors in the church.

100. On a religious woman who has been deceived—that is, whose clothing has been changed or who has professed religion. If anyone abducts, solicits, or corrupts a religious woman, the church in which such a woman lived shall claim the property of both; they themselves, however, shall be subjected to capital danger. If the woman did not consent to this, she is to be handed over, with her possessions, to the authority of the monastery.

But if the count of that district, together with the counsel of his bishop, in whose parish such a crime was committed, neglects to avenge it, he shall lose his office and surrender his belt of office, be punished with public penance, and, in addition, be compelled to give his wergild to the rights of the fisc.

101. On blasphemy against God. If anyone in any way utters blasphemy against God, he is to be handed over by the bishop or the count of that district to prison until satisfaction has been made and punished with public penance, until he is publicly reconciled to the church through the prayers of his own bishop and canonically restored to the church’s bosom.

102. On those who establish an oratory in their house. Whoever has an oratory in his house may pray there. Nevertheless, he must not dare to celebrate Mass there or permit anyone else to do so without the permission or dedication of the bishop of that place. Whoever does this shall have his house assigned to the rights of the fisc. The count who learns of this and does not prohibit it is to be punished with public penance or deprived of his office.

[Note: Bal. reads “if” for “whoever.”]

103. On preserving the privileges of churches and clerics from violation. The privileges granted to churches and clerics by our predecessors or by us are always to remain inviolate.

104. That the lives of bishops and other clerics should not be disturbed. Let no excesses disturb the lives of prelates, for it is most unworthy that those who are called the thrones of God should be disturbed by any agitation or treated unjustly. Hence the saying: “Whoever touches you touches the pupil of my eye” [Note: G. reads “as if.”] And this: “Whoever hears you hears me; and whoever despises you despises me.” And again: “Whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble, it would be better for him that an ass’s millstone be hung around his neck and that he be plunged into the depths of the sea”; and so forth.

105. On clerics or priests who accept churches without the permission of their bishop, or move from one to another. No one may accept a church within a parish without the consent of his bishop, nor may anyone move from one church to another.

106. On incestuous and criminal persons, and on the sick and penitents, and on the fast of the four seasons. Let priests take great care concerning incestuous and criminal persons, lest they perish in their crimes and their souls be required of them by Christ, the strict judge. Likewise, let them take care concerning the sick and penitents, so that the dying do not depart without reconciliation and the viaticum. And let the fasts of the four seasons be carefully observed by the faithful.

107. That bishops should admonish public judges to release prisoners at the Nativity of the Lord, Easter, and Pentecost, and that they should hear Mass on those days and be given refreshment. Let bishops admonish public judges that on the most solemn days—that is, the Nativity of our Lord Jesus Christ, the holy Resurrection, and Pentecost—those held in chains, whoever they may be, must be released, and that, out of reverence for our Lord Jesus Christ himself, they ought to merit release.

If a judge despises the shepherd who admonishes him, he is to be barred from the thresholds of the church for as long as the bishop of that place sees fit.

108. On a monk who abandons his monastery. If a monk abandons his monastery, all his property—both what he brought into the monastery and what he did not bring into it—shall belong to the monastery, and he himself shall be compelled to serve the fisc.

If the monk moves to another monastery, his former monastery shall possess his property, and he himself shall not be received in the other monastery without the permission of his abbot and his own bishop.

109. On possessions belonging to religious places. Possessions belonging to religious places are not to be subject to any assessment, except for the construction of roads or bridges, provided that those places have possessions within them. In all other matters they shall have complete immunity.

110. On a monk or nun. Whatever monk or nun has entered a monastery shall have no power to dispose of his or her property, even if they have children; rather, all the property they lawfully possessed on the day they entered the monastery shall belong to the monastery.

111. On what has been granted to churches by individual rulers and what individual bishops have obtained, and that those who remove these things commit sacrilege. Also, concerning clerics, that they should not be accused before secular judges but before their own bishops. Whatever individual kings have established concerning the most holy churches, or whatever individual bishops have obtained for ecclesiastical causes, is to be preserved under the penalty of sacrilege with perpetual and solid permanence [Note: G. reads “joined.”]. Clerics, moreover, are to be reserved not for secular judges but for episcopal judgment. For it is not right that ministers of the divine gift should be subjected to the judgment of temporal powers.

112. On the privileges of churches. The privileges granted to churches and clerics by individual kings or bishops and by other governors are always to remain inviolate.

113. That matters pertaining to religion should be heard in their proper places and by the synods of their own diocese. Whatever pertains to the observance of religion is to be heard in its proper places and by the synods of its own diocese.

114. That the privileges of churches should always remain inviolate. Whatever different rulers have established concerning the most holy churches, we command shall remain inviolable.

115. That it is sacrilege to remove anything from a church or to inflict injury upon priests, ministers, the sacred worship itself, or the place. If anyone breaks into this kind of sacrilege—namely, if he assaults churches and their property and inflicts upon priests, ministers, the worship itself, or the place any injury that ought not to be inflicted—let him know that, once convicted or having confessed, he is to be punished for the injury to divine worship by a capital sentence.

Nor should it be awaited that the bishop refrain from avenging his own injury, to whom the holiness of forgiveness alone leaves the glory. Let it be not only permitted but even praiseworthy for everyone to prosecute as a public crime the atrocious injuries inflicted upon priests or ministers and to obtain vengeance against such guilty persons.

116. On those who violate or disregard the privileges of churches. If the venerable privileges of a church are violated through anyone’s rashness or neglected through disregard, the offender shall, according to the sanction of the laws, make threefold compensation to the church against which it was done. He shall also pay us our ban threefold—that is, three times sixty solidi.

117. That those who plunder or devastate church estates are sacrilegious and should be condemned to exile. Every insult of such usurpation must be driven away, lest estates dedicated to the heavenly mysteries be harassed by the assaults of certain persons. If anyone presumes to do this, then, after the severity of the deserved punishment that must lawfully be exacted against sacrilegious persons, he is to be condemned to perpetual exile and deportation.

118. That bishops and the other priests should be free from all bonds. Consecration always makes bishops and the other priests of the Lord free both from servile obligations and from all other attached conditions. Therefore we command that no one demand from them any services other than divine ones.

119. That Christians should not attach themselves to or serve Jews. It has been decided that Christian slaves should neither serve Jews nor attach themselves to them.

120. On the offerings to be received by those celebrating at each Mass. It has been decided that whenever the celebrant sacrifices the Body and Blood of Christ Jesus our Lord upon the altar, he should each time present himself as a participant in the reception of the Body and Blood of Christ.

121. On chorepiscopi, that they should no longer be made. It has been decided that no chorepiscopi should henceforth be made, since up to now they have been created by people ignorant of the decrees of the holy fathers, especially the apostolic decrees, and attached to their own repose and pleasures. For this reason they have often been prohibited in former times and, in our time, by the holy apostolic see. So that henceforth no one, whether ordaining such a person or desiring to be ordained as one, may undertake such presumption, this has been canonically prohibited by all the bishops of our kingdom in synod.

122. That Jews should not be placed over Christians as masters or officials. Jews must not dare to govern a Christian household in an administrative capacity under the rank of stewards and agents, nor may anyone order this to be done by them. If anyone presumes to act against these provisions, then, if he is a bishop, presbyter, or deacon, he shall be removed from his own rank; if he is a monk or layperson, he shall be deprived of Communion. If they persist in disobedience, let them be anathematized.

[Note: From Trec. [Troyes?], Chalcedon 27.]

123. On clerical falsifiers. If a presbyter or deacon gives false testimony in a financial case, he shall be separated from the sacred ministry for three years. If he gives false testimony in a criminal case, he shall be deposed and subjected to the lawful penalties. Other clerics convicted of any falsity are to be degraded and subjected to the lawful disciplines.

124. That clerics should not undertake secular affairs. A cleric or monk must not become a collector of public revenues, a tenant or master of taxes, a manager of a household, a legal agent [Note: G. reads “management”], or a guarantor in such cases.

If anyone acts against these statutes, then, if he is a bishop, we decree that all the property that has come to him from any cause or person, whether before or after his episcopate, is to be claimed for his church. If other clerics have done this, the monetary penalty that the bishop judges should be exacted is to be claimed for the church.

Those who entrusted their affairs to such persons or accepted them as guarantors in the aforesaid cases shall have no action against the church, its administrators, or the persons whom they trusted. But if anyone has trusted them or accepted them as guarantors for a public debt or legal action, he shall be compelled to pay the debt owed to the fisc from his own property.

125. On clerics who abandon the church. If clerics abandon the church and others are called in their place, and the former later return, nothing is to be provided for them. What those departing left behind shall not go for the use of the administrators but shall pass to their successors.

126. What clerics should be like. No one is to become a cleric unless he has a good reputation and is educated.

127. On the number of clerics. Let a bishop not create a multitude of clerics indiscriminately, but let their number be regulated according to the resources or revenues of the churches.

128. On sacred ordinations. If a lector, subdeacon, deacon, or presbyter despises the honor of the clerical state, he shall, together with his property, be subjected to curial status.

129. On injury to a bishop and the subversion of a litany. If anyone inflicts injury upon a bishop or other ministers within a church, we order that he be subjected to torture and die in exile. If he disturbs the holy oratories themselves or the divine ministries, or overturns a litany, he shall be subjected to capital danger. If, however, he has inflicted only an insult, he shall be handed over to torture and exile.

130. That the faithful should not marry within their own blood relationship, and that those who have previously remained unmarried should not presume to marry without a priest’s blessing. Christians [Note: “Jews” in the title in the Visigothic Law.] are not to contract marriages within their blood relationship down to the seventh degree [Note: “sixth” in the Visigothic Law.]. Nor may those who were previously unmarried dare to marry without the blessing of a priest.

131. On not receiving the penitents of others. Those who are separated from Communion because of their offense are, it has been decided, to receive Communion in whatever places they were excluded—in those same places.

132. That a cleric or monk may not travel without a letter from his bishop. Clerics and monks are not to have permission to wander about without letters of recommendation from their bishop.

133. On dowries and public weddings. No marriage is to take place without a dowry, nor may anyone presume to marry without a public wedding.

134. On church property that has been removed, defrauded, or withheld. If anyone, through wicked cunning, removes, defrauds, seizes, withholds, or suppresses any small gift belonging to the church and bestowed under the titles of the holy Scriptures [Note: Bal. reads “snatched away”], and, immediately admonished by the priest, does not return what was given to God, let him be expelled from communion with the Catholic Church.

135. That no one should dare to claim or hold church property lying in any region unless it is lawfully owed to him. Let no bishop, cleric of any rank, or any other person, under any pretext, whether in one kingdom or another, seek or presume to receive property belonging to another church, wherever it may be situated. If anyone does so, he shall be suspended from the Communion of the church and from the affection of all the brothers and children until he restores by law to the church, whose property it is by direct legal right, what was taken away.

136. On those who remove or retain property entrusted to churches. No one may retain, alienate, or remove property or resources justly entrusted to churches, monasteries, or hospices for any charitable purpose. If anyone does so, he shall be excluded from the thresholds of the church as a killer of the poor, bound by the judgments of the ancient canons, for as long as he fails to return what he removed or retained.

137. That he should name his accomplices when part of the robbery is found with him. Whoever is recognized as having committed the crime and with whom part of the stolen property is found must immediately be compelled to name his accomplices. If he refuses to name them, he shall be held liable to punishment.

138. On those found to have indicated what was to be plundered. Whoever, free or slave, indicates something to be plundered so that someone’s property may be destroyed or cattle or pack animals carried off, and is publicly found convicted of this by certain proofs, shall, for what he indicated, receive 120 lashes while stretched out publicly.

139. That abbots should remain under the authority of the bishop in whose parish they are. Out of respect for religious humility, abbots are to remain under the authority of the bishops. If they do anything outside the rule, they are to be corrected by the bishops. Once a year they are to assemble at the place chosen by the bishop, after receiving his summons.

140. That no monk should leave his monastery and build cells without the permission of his bishop or abbot. No monk, abandoning the monastery’s congregation through ambition or vanity, should presume to build a cell without the permission of his bishop or the consent of his abbot.

141. On apostates. Whoever, after professing holy religion, apostatizes, returns to the secular world, and afterward does not seek the remedies of penance is not to receive Communion at all. We also order that such persons not be admitted to clerical office.

142. On the excommunicated. If anyone has been suspended from Communion by priestly authority, it has been decided that he is to be excluded not only from conversation and table fellowship with clerics but also from those with the entire people, until, coming to his senses, he hastens to return to soundness.

143. That judges should not judge the offenses of faithless persons without the counsel of their own priests. Let judges not presume to judge anything concerning the offenses of faithless persons outside the restraint of priests.

144. On exposed infants and their collection. If an exposed child is compassionately taken up before any church, let the person who takes it up deposit a letter of declaration. If the child who has been taken up is not sought out and recognized within ten days, let the person who collected it hold it securely. But whoever becomes its claimant after the aforesaid period shall be condemned by ecclesiastical discipline as a homicide, just as the authority of the fathers decreed.

145. On clerics who abandon their office and flee to secular persons. It has been decided that if a cleric, having abandoned his office because of discipline, should perhaps flee to a secular person, and that person provides him the support of protection, both are to be expelled from the Communion of the church.

146. That a slave should not be believed if he brings a charge against his master or another free person. A slave is not to be believed at all if he brings a charge against anyone, or even accuses his own master of a crime. For even if, placed under torture, he discloses what he alleges, he must in no way be believed.

147. That witnesses should testify only to what they know occurred in their presence. Witnesses must not give testimony in absentia or by letter; rather, those who are present must not conceal the truth that they know and have seen. Nor may they testify about other matters [Note: Bal. reads “other cases”], but only about those things known to have been done in their presence.

148. What writings should be considered valid. Writings that clearly express the day and year, are known to have been drawn up according to the order of the law, and have been confirmed by the signs or subscriptions of the author or witnesses are to be regarded as wholly firm and valid.

149. On preserving agreements and settlements. Agreements or settlements lawfully and justly made in writing, provided that the day or year is clearly expressed in them, are in no way to be altered.

150. That a son or heir may not act against an earlier determination. A son or heir may not act against a previous just or lawful determination, because the presumption of one who unjustly attempts to overturn the acts of his elders is rightly rejected.

151. That no one should be accused or punished unless the crime has been revealed by manifest evidence. We do not indiscriminately grant permission to accuse or punish unless either the crime has been revealed by manifest evidence or that same wrongdoing has been lawfully accused and proved, so that it may not appear that we are in any respect or manner transgressing the commands of the holy fathers or opposing the sacred rules of the ancients.

152. That an exchange should have the same validity as a sale. If an exchange has not been extorted by force or fear, it shall have the same validity as a sale [Note: G. reads “exemption.”].

153. If anyone, compelled by fear, declares himself a slave. Whoever, compelled by fear, declares outside court that he is a slave shall incur no prejudice to his freedom until he is brought before a court; or, if he proves his freedom in the presence of the judge, he shall obtain it [Note: G. reads “so that.”]. But if he is proved to be a slave, he shall immediately be restored to his master.

154. On presbyters or deacons traveling without letters from their bishop. No one is to grant Communion to a presbyter or deacon traveling without letters from his bishop.

155. That one abbot should by no means preside over two monasteries. We forbid one abbot to preside over two monasteries.

156. On presbyters and other clerics not being subjected to coercion by secular judges but by their own bishops. Let no judge presume, without the permission of the proper bishop, to coerce or condemn presbyters, deacons, other clerics, or the younger members of the church [Note: G. reads “to despise,” by correction]. If anyone does so, he shall be deprived of Communion for as long as he acknowledges his guilt and, through satisfaction, makes amends to the church for what he committed.

157. That clerics should not go to secular judges. No one of the clerical order may, without consulting his own bishop, go to a secular judge. Without his bishop’s permission, he must not presume before that judge to bring an action against anyone, answer anyone, or present anything; nor may he dare to bring a criminal matter before a secular court.

158. On secular persons who presume through false accusation to harass the church or clerics. If any secular person attempts through false accusation to harass the church, its property, or clerics of any rank, and is convicted of this, he shall be expelled from the thresholds of the church and from Catholic Communion unless he performs worthy penance and makes amends through satisfaction to the church.

159. That freedmen and freedwomen should not testify. A freedman or freedwoman is not to be admitted to give testimony in any case against anyone, except in certain cases where freeborn persons are known to be lacking, as has also been permitted concerning slaves; for our clemency considers it unworthy that damages should be inflicted upon freeborn persons by the testimony of freedmen [Note: G. corrects this to: “that testimonies should shake freeborn persons.”]. Those born from them, however, are to be admitted as witnesses.

160. On those who are accomplices with thieves. Not only the person who commits a theft, but also anyone who is an accomplice or knowingly receives what has been taken by theft, is to be counted among the thieves and subjected to the same punishment.

161. If a possessor is expelled by force. Whoever violently expels a possessor before a judicial sentence has been issued concerning him, even if he has the better case, shall lose the case in question. The person who suffered the violence shall recover everything in the condition in which it was and shall securely retain what he possessed.

But if someone invades what he could have obtained by judgment, let him lose the case and return to the expelled person as much again as he invaded.

162. That the faithful should learn the faith of the Holy Trinity. Let the faithful learn the faith of the Holy Trinity. Among other things, they ought to believe in it that, through the Holy Spirit, the remission of sins is conferred in baptism, confirmation, penance, and the other canonical decrees, as it is written; and that, in the church, remission of sins is unquestionably granted to the faithful through Christ, by the gift of that same Holy Spirit, through the priestly ministry and through penance; and that there will be a resurrection of all peoples in true flesh at Christ’s coming; and so forth.

Let them retain this faith by heart and recite and explain it word for word to their priests. The priests themselves are to teach it faithfully, fully, and truthfully to the people, since the first foundation of the Christian religion is the Catholic faith.

This faith is true and fruitful when it is adorned with good works, namely hope, charity, humility, chastity, continence, sobriety, unanimity, harmony, justice, piety, mercy, innocence, simplicity, and other virtues of this kind. All these consist in love of God and neighbor. Without them no one can please God or be saved.

[Col. 0768A] **163. Concerning contumacious presbyters or clerics.** If any presbyter, deacon, or other cleric proves contumacious, proud, disobedient, or rebellious toward his bishop, those who hold an ecclesiastical rank shall lose their respective rank; the remaining clerics, monks, or laymen shall be deprived of communion until they make satisfaction.

**164. Concerning judges who inflict calumny or injury upon clerics.** If a judge of any rank presumes, without the permission of the cleric’s bishop, to subject, constrain, accuse, or injure a cleric through public proceedings, he shall be deprived of communion, together with all who assist in or perpetrate such crimes, until satisfaction has been made to the Church. Nevertheless, the bishop must not fail canonically to render full justice to those who have suffered injury from the aforesaid clerics.

**165. That all the faithful learn the Lord’s Prayer.** The faithful shall learn the Lord’s Prayer and understand it, recite it word for word to their priests, and teach it to other faithful who do not know it.

**166. That no bishop invade another bishop’s parish, nor any presbyter another presbyter’s parish.** No bishop or presbyter shall invade another’s parish, but shall be content with the governance of the people entrusted to him.

**167. That property not be taken from monasteries or other churches, nor they themselves disturbed by anyone.** No one shall be permitted to disturb in any way monasteries consecrated to God, or to take anything forcibly from their property.  
[Note: [Col. 0767] *quemquam*, “anyone,” according to Bal.]

**168. That traveling clerics be content with the offering of hospitality, and that none of them perform priestly office in another’s parish without the bishop’s permission.** Bishops and traveling clerics shall be content with the hospitality offered; none of them may perform any priestly office without the permission of the bishop in whose parish he is known to be staying.

**169. That no bishop prefer himself to another without the consent of the others.** No bishop shall, through ambition, place himself before another, but all shall acknowledge the time and order of their ordination.

**170. That the people offer their oblations to the priests in church, and communicate every Sunday.** It has been decreed that the faithful offer oblations to the priests in church every day, if possible. If this cannot be done daily, it shall at least be done on Sunday, without any excuse. They shall hear preaching and, if possible, communicate every Sunday, unless they are prevented by a criminal and manifest sin; for otherwise they cannot be saved, since the Lord said: “Whoever eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me, and I in him. And whoever eats me will live because of me.” And there are other examples, which would be lengthy to write here.  
[Note: [Col. 0767] *vivit*, “lives,” according to G.]  
[Note: [Col. 0767] *essent*, “would be,” according to G.]

**171. That priests ring the signals at the canonical hours.** Priests shall ring the signals at the canonical hours and perform their office, whether by day or by night; for it is written: “Pray without ceasing.” Therefore they shall not omit the canonical hours.

**172. Concerning the wearing of stoles.** Priests shall wear stoles as a sign of chastity, as has been decreed.

**173. That the Secret not be begun until the hymn has ended.** Priests shall not begin *Te igitur* until the angelic hymn has ended.

**174. That priests announce the Creed to the faithful.** Presbyters shall announce the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer to all the faithful subject to them, so that, with the Holy Spirit enlightening them, they may be set free.

**175. That presbyters instruct men and women not to receive boys or girls from the sacred font unless they have memorized the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer.** Presbyters shall announce that neither men nor women may receive boys or girls from the sacred font unless they have memorized the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer.  
[Note: [Col. 0767] *suscipiantur*, “are received,” according to G.]

**176. That silence be maintained in church and the word of God heard devoutly.** It has been decreed that the faithful maintain silence in church, devoutly hear the word of God, confess truthfully all their crimes to their priests, and cleanse their bodies and hearts, in which God may deign worthily to dwell; for it has been said to them: “You are God’s temple, in whom I desire to dwell.” They shall obey their priest in all things and be instructed as to why the Mass and priests have been established; and they shall understand the power and mystery of the Lord’s body and blood, and of the Mass and the prayers performed in it by the priest. For it is said in the prayer itself:

> “Remember, Lord, your servants and handmaids, and all who stand around, whose faith is known to you and whose devotion is acknowledged; they offer you this sacrifice of praise for themselves and all their own, for the redemption of their souls, and for the hope of their salvation and security. To you they render their vows, eternal, living, and true God.”

And the rest. They shall also be instructed to understand the power of bishops in binding and loosing, and the other matters pertaining to them, as well as those pertaining to the other priests. They shall fear and honor their priests according to the Lord’s command, and they shall be told in what ways they are accustomed to offend against them.  
[Note: [Col. 0769] *ministerium*, “ministry,” according to G.]  
[Note: [Col. 0769] *tibique*, “and to you,” according to Bal.]

**177. That infants be presented to the bishop for confirmation.** Presbyters shall announce to the people that, as soon as they are able, they should have their infants presented to the bishop for confirmation.

**178. That presbyters not depart without holy chrism, blessed oil, and the saving Eucharist of Christ.** Presbyters shall not depart anywhere without holy chrism, blessed oil, and the saving Eucharist of Christ; but wherever they are summoned, even unexpectedly, to perform their office, they shall be found ready to discharge their obligation.

**179. That presbyters request the oil of the sick from the bishop.** All presbyters shall request the oil of the sick from the bishop, keep it with them, and urge the sick faithful to seek it, so that, anointed with that oil, they may be healed by the grace of God, since the prayer of faith poured out by presbyters will save the sick.

**180. That no parish presbyter presume to receive chrism elsewhere except from his own bishop.** No parish presbyter shall presume to receive chrism anywhere except from his own bishop on Maundy Thursday.

**181. That baptism not be administered except on the vigils of Easter and Pentecost.** No one shall presume to baptize except at the two appointed times, namely the vigil of Easter and the vigil of Pentecost, except in danger of death.

**182. That the faithful who wish to receive children from the sacred font be instructed.** It has been decreed that the faithful who wish to receive children from the sacred font be instructed, so that they may understand the power of that sacrament and what they have promised on behalf of others, or for what they have become sureties; and they shall know that in no way may they become fathers to others before they have learned, understood, and recited the foregoing. If sureties are accustomed to be condemned for earthly profit, how much more must care be taken that they not be condemned for divine law. Those, however, who have been deprived of canonical communion and subjected to public penance shall be removed from these offices, so that they may neither receive others from the sacred font in baptism nor act as godparents for others in receiving the gift of the Holy Spirit, until through penance they merit reconciliation by satisfaction. The same applies to those who have committed such a sin as requires them to be punished and bound by public penance.

**183. That no payment be demanded for baptizing and signing the faithful.** No payments shall be demanded for baptizing or signing the faithful. Whoever does so shall risk his honor.

[Col. 0770A] **184. Concerning those whose baptism is doubted, who are commanded to be baptized without concealment.** Those about whom there is doubt whether they have been baptized or not shall be baptized in every case, without any scruple, after these words have first been spoken: “I am not rebaptizing you; but if you have not yet been baptized, I baptize you in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.”

**185. That presbyters teach the faith of the Holy Trinity in church.** It is known to all that it is impossible to please God without faith. Therefore there shall be no presbyter who does not publicly teach in church, in a language that his hearers understand, that the faith of almighty God is to be believed simply in unity and Trinity, together with those matters that must generally be proclaimed to all concerning the avoidance of evils, the performance of good works, and the judgment that will occur at the resurrection. If he himself cannot clearly explain these matters in words, he shall ask a more learned man to write them out for him, so that he may read them plainly and those who hear may understand. If he can do no more, let him at least admonish them with these words: “Do penance, for the kingdom of heaven is near.”  
[Note: [Col. 0769] *adpropinquavit*, “has drawn near,” according to Bal.]

**186. That presbyters announce to the people the four appointed seasonal fasts.** Presbyters shall teach the people to observe the four appointed seasonal fasts, namely in March, July, September, and December, when the sacred orders are distributed according to the statutes of the canons.

**187. That the three appointed fasts be observed in the year.** Again, priests shall admonish the people to observe the three appointed fasts in the year: forty days before the Nativity of the Lord; forty days before Easter, when we pay the tithes of the year; and forty days after Pentecost. Although some of these fasts lack canonical authority, it is nevertheless fitting for all of us together to observe them, as stated above, on account of the custom of the people and the practice of our ancestors. And although it is fitting to pray and abstain on every day, at these times one ought to devote oneself more fully to fasting and penance. Apart from these appointed times, every Friday shall be observed as a fast on account of the Lord’s Passion. Saturday also is regarded by many as consecrated to fasting because Christ lay in the tomb on that day.

**188. That the people not present their infants for baptism except at the two appointed times.** It has been decreed that the people not present their infants for baptism except at the two appointed times, unless illness has intervened; and they shall be instructed concerning the ways in which they offend in this matter.

**189. That Sunday be reverently observed.** Observe Sunday with reverence. Do not perform servile work on it—that is, work in the field, meadow, vineyard, or any other heavier labor—nor bring legal actions or accusations against one another; but serve only in divine worship, and keep Sunday from evening to evening. Presbyters shall announce these principal feasts, so that they may be observed like Sundays:

- the Nativity of the Lord, for four days, beginning on the eighth day before the Kalends of January;
- the Circumcision of the Lord, on the Kalends of January, for one day;
- the Epiphany, on the eighth day before the Ides of January, for one day;
- the Purification of Saint Mary, on the fourth day before the Nones of February, for one day;
- the Lord’s Easter until the octave of Easter, for three days after Sunday;
- the Ascension of the Lord, for one day;
- the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, on the eighth day before the Kalends of July, for one day;
- the Passion of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, on the third day before the Kalends of July, for one day;
- the Assumption of Saint Mary, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of September, for one day;
- the passing of Saint Martin, on the third day before the Ides of November, for one day;
- the Passion of Saint Andrew the Apostle, on the second day before the Kalends of December, for one day.

[Note: [Col. 0769] *aut*, “or,” according to G.]

**190. That presbyters announce that the Saturday of Easter, with its Easter, and the Saturday of Pentecost, with its Sunday, are to be observed in the same manner.** Presbyters shall announce that, just as holy Easter is celebrated when Saturday evening comes, so the day of Pentecost shall likewise be held in the highest honor, with holy Easter, fasting, Mass, and baptism.

**191. That presbyters announce to the people that they must abstain from illicit marriages.** Every presbyter shall publicly announce to the people that they must abstain from illicit marriages, and that, according to the Lord’s command, a lawful marriage can in no way be separated for any reason except fornication, unless both parties consent—and even then only for the service of God.

**192. That presbyters publicly announce to the people that tithes and first fruits of all crops are to be offered for blessing.** Presbyters shall publicly announce to the people that they bring the first fruits of all the earth’s crops to the priests’ houses for blessing and afterward eat from them; and that every year they render tithes from all the fruits and livestock of the earth to the churches, give alms from the nine parts that remain, and redeem their sins from them, as it is written: “Almsgiving delivers from death.” It also cleanses sins, as is read in Wisdom: “Just as water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin.”  
[Note: [Col. 0771] The witness G. lacks *et* (“and”).]

**193. That the faithful understand the pact they made with God in baptism.** It has been decreed that the faithful understand the pact they made with God in baptism.
