Many transgress it completely, and many in part. The faithful shall be instructed concerning what it means to renounce the works and pomps of the devil and all his works. If human agreements are firmly observed, how much more fervently must the obligations of so great a pact, made with God, be observed irrevocably!

**194. That priests admonish men and women to carry lights to the basilicas.** Priests shall admonish men and women to bring lights, incense, small loaves, and first fruits to the basilicas, as it is written: “Honor the Lord from your substance, and give to the poor from the first fruits of your crops.”

[Col. 0771C] **195. That presbyters admonish the people not to engage in disputes and excessive talking in church.** Presbyters shall admonish the people not to presume to chatter in churches, but with weeping and contrition of heart to implore God’s help both for themselves and for their neighbors. When the presbyter celebrates Mass, they shall always direct their hearts toward heavenly things. When sacred readings or the Gospels have been recited, they shall listen together in silence and with devoted minds, as God said through Moses: “Hear, Israel, and be silent.” They shall offer oblations and cause the people to communicate.

**196. That presbyters diligently ensure that nothing dishonorable or shameful occurs in churches.** When the people come to churches, both on Sundays and on the feasts of the saints, they shall do nothing there except what pertains to the service of God. They shall not perform those dances, jumping dances, shameful and lustful songs, or those demonic games, either in the streets, in houses, or anywhere else, since these things have remained from pagan custom. Whoever does such things shall receive canonical judgment.  
[Note: [Col. 0771] *et illusa*, “and mockeries,” according to G.]  
[Note: [Col. 0771] *cum*, “with,” according to Bal.]

[Col. 0771D] **197. That nothing be done at the funerals of the dead according to pagan custom.** The faithful shall be admonished not to perform for their dead the things that have remained from pagan ritual. Rather, each person shall devoutly and contritely implore God’s mercy for the soul of the deceased. When they carry the dead to burial, they shall not make that loud wailing; instead, as we said above, they shall, with a devout mind and contrition of heart, implore God’s mercy for the soul, insofar as they have understanding. Those who do not know the psalms shall strive to sing in a loud voice, for the soul of the deceased, “Lord, have mercy; Christ, have mercy” (*Kyrie eleison, Christe eleison*), with the men beginning and the women responding in a loud voice. They shall presume neither to eat nor to drink upon the tombs. If they do so, they shall receive canonical judgment.

**198. That the faithful cause thirty days to be completed for the dead of their friends and relatives.** For the dead of their friends and relatives, the faithful shall complete thirty days of fasts and oblations, and they shall not place one dead person upon another, nor leave the bones of the dead upon the ground. If they do so, they shall be subject to canonical judgment.

**199. Concerning those whom a bishop or priest has excommunicated, that the faithful not receive them.** It has been decreed that the faithful not receive those whom a bishop or priest has excommunicated on account of their sins, until they have accepted penance and come to confession.

**200. That no presbyter abandon his church without the consent of his bishop.** We are compelled also to observe the statutes of the canons in this matter: no presbyter shall abandon the church entrusted to him without the consent of his bishop and transfer to another at the persuasion of laymen.

**201. That no presbyter perform the sacred mysteries except in a consecrated place.** No presbyter shall presume to perform the sacred mysteries except in places consecrated by the bishop.

**202. That no presbyter erect another altar in a consecrated church except one consecrated by the bishop.** No presbyter shall erect another altar in a consecrated church except one sanctified by the bishop, so that there may be a distinction between what is consecrated and what is not consecrated.

**203. That a bishop, presbyter, or deacon not be a gambler or drunkard.** A bishop, presbyter, or deacon must not be a gambler or drunkard. Likewise, if clerics or laymen persist in gambling, they shall be deprived of communion.

**204. That no cleric accept interest.** Since the venerable canons and divine authority prohibit the taking of interest, no cleric shall presume to do so; and insofar as they are able, they shall strive to forbid it to laymen.

[Col. 0772C] **205. That all reverently observe Sunday, on which the Lord rose.** It has been decreed that the faithful reverently observe Sunday, on which the Lord rose. If pagans observe certain days in memory and honor of their gods, and Jews, in a carnal manner, observe the Sabbath carnally, how much more ought Christians to honor this day, lest on that holy day they devote themselves, as is customary, to vain stories, conversations, songs, or dances while standing at crossroads and in the streets. Rather, they should go to a priest or to some wise and good person and make use of their preaching and good instruction concerning the soul. On that day, or on Saturday, they should all come to vespers and matins or to Mass, if possible with their oblations, singing “Kyrie eleison,” and sing “Kyrie eleison” both on their way there and on their return. Likewise, shepherds of livestock shall do the same while going out to the fields and returning home, so that everyone may truly recognize them as Christians and devout people.

[Col. 0772D] **206. Concerning the reconciliation of penitents.** Since genuine necessity prevents us from fully observing the statutes of the canons concerning the reconciliation of penitents, this must nevertheless by no means be omitted: by order of the bishop, each presbyter shall immediately reconcile individual penitents, after they have received the penance of confession and a prayer has been given, but only in cases of hidden sins, since bishops should always be consulted concerning manifest sins. The dying, however, shall receive communion and reconciliation without delay.

**207. How many days constitute a woman’s purification.** When a woman has given birth, we have learned from the precept of the Old Testament after how many days she should enter the church: she must abstain for thirty-three days in the case of a male child, but sixty-six in the case of a female child.

> “This, however,” as Saint Gregory says, “must be understood mystically; for if, in the very hour in which she has given birth, she enters the church to give thanks, she is burdened by no weight of sin. It is the pleasure of the flesh, not the pain, that is culpable. In the joining of flesh there is pleasure, but in the bringing forth of offspring there is groaning. Hence it is said even to the first marriage: ‘In pain you shall give birth.’ If, therefore, we forbid a woman who has given birth to enter the church, we impute her punishment to her as guilt.”

**208. That Masses not be celebrated in unsuitable places.** It has been decreed that the faithful absolutely must not celebrate Masses in unconsecrated or unsuitable places, except because of hostile circumstances or a lengthy journey; and, if necessity compels it, this shall be done at altars consecrated by the bishop. Priests who presume to sing Masses in illicit and unconsecrated places shall know that they will lose their rank. For it is better that Mass not be heard than that it be celebrated or heard where it is neither permitted nor appropriate. Everyone shall also be admonished that usury must not be practiced.  
[Note: [Col. 0773] *fieri*, “be celebrated,” according to G.]  
[Note: [Col. 0773] The witness G. lacks *si* (“if”).]  
[Note: [Col. 0773] *amissurum*, “that he will lose,” according to G.]

**209. Concerning kinship.** Marriage is not permitted within the fourth degree of blood relationship, nor in the fifth or sixth, as it is written in the law: “No man shall approach a near female relative of his blood to uncover her nakedness”—that is, as far as the seventh degree. A lawful marriage may not be separated without the consent of both, provided that both remain unmarried in order to serve God. One may give the other permission to enter God’s service, provided that the one who gives permission remains unmarried. In the Old Testament it is thus written concerning intercourse with animals: “A woman who has lain with any beast shall be killed together with it.” In the New Testament, the woman, like the man who has had intercourse with animals, shall do penance for fifteen years; others say eleven.  
[Note: [Col. 0773] *XII*, “twelve,” according to G.]

Animals polluted by human intercourse shall be killed and their flesh thrown to the dogs, but their hides may be taken. Where there is doubt, they shall not be killed.

**210. Concerning what is to be done with a slave who has inflicted damage on anyone.** No one may abandon his slave on account of damage inflicted by him upon anyone; rather, according to the nature of the damage, the master shall answer for him or offer him to the claimant for composition or punishment. If the slave flees after committing the crime, so that he cannot be found at all by his master, the master shall strive to clear himself by oath, declaring that it was neither by his will nor with his knowledge that his slave committed such a crime. As they requested, so the lord emperor consented.

**211. Concerning one who has been summoned by law to the mallus and has not come.** If anyone has been summoned by law to the mallus and has not come, and no legitimate hindrance has detained him, he shall be judged liable for fifteen solidi. The same shall apply at the second and third summons. If he contemptuously refuses to come at the fourth, his property shall be placed under the ban until he comes and renders justice concerning the matter over which he was summoned. If he does not come within a year, the king shall be consulted concerning the property placed under the ban, and whatever he judges concerning it shall be done. The first summons shall allow seven nights, the second fourteen, the third twenty-one, and the fourth forty-two. The same shall be done with a man’s benefice if he happens not to possess property of his own: it shall be placed under the ban until the king is consulted.  
[Note: [Col. 0773] *sonnis*, “lawful hindrance,” according to Bal.]  
[Note: [Col. 0773] Bal lacks *pro* (“concerning/on account of”).]  
[Note: [Col. 0773] *bannum*, “under the ban,” according to Bal.]

**212. Concerning one who has no children and wishes to make another his heir in their place.** Anyone who has no children and wishes to make someone else his heir shall make the transfer before the king, or before the count and the assessors, or before the royal envoys who have been appointed by him in the province to administer justice.

**213. Concerning denarial persons, how they can inherit.** A *denarial* man may not inherit within his own kindred until the third generation has been reached. A *cartolarius* man shall do likewise.  
[Note: Bal reads *chartularius*, “chartular.”]

**214. That every oath be sworn in a church.** Every oath shall be sworn in a church and over relics; and whatever is to be sworn in church shall be sworn either with six chosen men, or, if twelve are required, with as many suitable men as he can find. May God and the saints whose relics these are so help him that he may speak the truth. If a disputed thing has been taken away by theft, the person against whom the disputed thing has been brought may clear himself by oath concerning the theft, declaring that what was taken was neither by his will nor with his knowledge; and an equal amount shall be restored without damage.  
[Note: Bal reads *si*, “if,” instead of *sic*, “thus.”]

**215. That the faithful beware of vices remaining from pagan practice.** It has been decreed that the faithful beware of the vices that remain from pagan ritual: magicians, diviners, practitioners of lots, poisoners, fortune-tellers, enchanters, interpreters of dreams—those whom divine law commands to be punished without revocation. Care must be taken that they not be allowed to remain among the faithful.

**216. Concerning the restoration of churches.** Concerning the repair of churches, and concerning places where there are more churches than necessary: those that are not needed shall be demolished, and others shall be built.

**217. That presbyters not be ordained before they have been examined.** Presbyters shall not be ordained before they have been examined. Excommunication also shall not be imposed suddenly and without cause.

**218. That the royal envoys choose assessors, advocates, and notaries.** Our envoys shall choose assessors, advocates, and notaries in each locality, and when they return they shall bring with them a written list of their names.

**219. Concerning those who despise keeping the law.** Those who refuse to keep the law shall be brought before the king by sureties.

**220. That the faithful abstain from vices treated as though they were natural customs.** It has been decreed that the faithful abstain from detestable vices that are regarded as though they were naturally customary, which the Apostle plainly enumerates: drunkenness, feasting, quarrels, anger, strife, dissensions, slander, envy, and enmity. Concerning these the Apostle says: “Those who do such things shall not inherit the kingdom of God.” And elsewhere: “Not only those who do them, but also those who consent to those who do them.” Of such people it can also be said: “They rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst things.”  
[Note: [Col. 0773] The words *Et . . . facientibus*, “And . . . those who do them,” were inserted by Benedict.]

**221. Concerning those who must pay the army levy.** Those who must pay the army levy shall make a contribution to the levy collectors, and shall render no other service to counts or vicars.

**222. Concerning fugitives and travelers, that they be constrained.** Fugitives and travelers shall be subject to inspection, so that we may know who they are and where they have come from.

**223. That arm-rings and mail coats not be given to merchants.** Arm-rings and mail coats shall not be given to merchants.

**224. That measures be made equal.** Concerning measures: they shall be made equal according to our command.

**225. That Christians beware of idle speech and other vices.** It has been decreed that all the faithful firmly beware of idle speech, for which, according to the Lord’s judgment, we shall all render an account on the day of judgment; of buffoonery, foolish talk, and curses, since according to the Apostle those who curse shall not possess the kingdom of God; of harmful lies; of dangerous, habitual, and persistent oaths; and of obscene and shameful songs. All Christians must strongly avoid all these things, lest by devoting themselves to them through negligence they suffer harm to their souls.  
[Note: [Col. 0773] *debeant*, “should,” according to Bal.]

**226. That no testimony be offered concerning King Pippin’s investiture.** No testimony shall be offered concerning the investiture of the lord King Pippin.

**227. That neither colonus nor fiscalinus make transfers.** Neither a *colonus* nor a *fiscalinus* may make transfers anywhere.

**228. That no one presume to bring a man to judgment without cause.** No one shall presume to bring a man to judgment without cause, unless judgment has been rendered.

**229. If a free man cuts his hair in a regular monastery.** If a free man cuts his hair in a regular monastery and transfers his property there, he shall firmly keep the promise he has made according to the Rule.

**230. Concerning marriage, which was established by God and is to be desired not for the sake of lust but rather for the sake of children.** It has been decreed that the faithful know that marriage was established by God, and that it is to be desired not for the sake of lust but rather for the sake of children. Virginity shall be faithfully preserved until marriage. Married men must have neither a mistress nor a concubine; they must love their wives in chastity and render them, as the weaker vessel, their due honor. Carnal intercourse with wives ought to take place for the sake of offspring, not pleasure.

**231. That everything which must be pledged be repledged according to the law.** Everything that must be pledged shall, according to what is contained in the law, be fully repledged in accordance with that law. Thereafter either the lord king or the person whose case it is shall show mercy as he sees fit.  
[Note: [Col. 0775] *wadiari*, “to be pledged,” according to Bal.]

**232. That no drunkard be able to prosecute his case in the mallus.** No drunkard shall be able to prosecute his case in the mallus or give testimony. Nor shall the count hold a hearing unless he is fasting.

**233. Concerning compelling no one to drink.** No one shall be permitted to compel another to drink.

**234. Concerning the royal envoys traveling about.** Concerning our traveling envoys and other men journeying on our business: no one shall presume to deny them lodging or pasture, except in his own meadow.

**235. That the faithful abstain from intercourse with pregnant women.** It has been decreed that the faithful abstain from intercourse with pregnant wives, and likewise during the time of menstruation. A wife is not to be dismissed on account of fornication, according to the Lord’s judgment, but rather is to be endured. Those who, after dismissing their wives on account of fornication, take other wives are declared adulterers by the Lord’s judgment.

**236. Concerning dogs shorn on the right shoulder.** Concerning dogs whose right shoulder has been shorn: the person who has such a dog shall come with it into the presence of the king.

**237. Concerning the chapters newly added to the law.** The people shall be questioned concerning the chapters recently added to the law. After all have agreed, they shall make their formal confirmations concerning those chapters.

**238. That no one be summoned to a hearing except the seven assessors and those who must prosecute a case.** No one shall be summoned to a hearing unless he wishes to prosecute a case or knows that another wishes to prosecute him, except for the seven assessors, who must be present at all hearings.

**239. Concerning the rejection of false witnesses.** False witnesses shall not be admitted at all.

**240. How incestuous unions must be avoided by faithful Christians.** It has been decreed that the faithful recognize how incestuous unions must be avoided by Christians, and that they visit places dedicated to God more frequently and more devoutly than they have done until now, to pray to God and make him favorable to themselves. In basilicas dedicated to God they must not devote themselves to idle, shameful, and obscene stories or conversations, nor conduct secular business or public hearings. Those who do these things in churches heap greater sins upon themselves.  
[Note: [Col. 0775] *ibique*, “and there,” according to G.]

**241. That no one swear by the life of the king.** No one shall presume to swear by the life of the king or his sons.

**242. That the royal envoys bring written reports not only concerning announcements but also concerning actions.** Our envoys who have already brought written reports concerning announcements shall also bring reports concerning actions.

**243. That no one presume to collect tolls, road dues, or dust dues.** No one shall presume to collect a toll on the roads, a road due in the villages, or a dust due.

**244. That the faithful render just judgments.** It has been decreed that the faithful render just judgments and accept no gifts for doing so; that they avoid false testimony and abstain from slander, as well as from the other evils that would take too long to enumerate.

**245. That churches obtain their rights.** Above all, it must be commanded that churches possess their rights, both over the lives of those who dwell in them and, after their death, over their money and property.  
[Note: [Col. 0775] *tam in pecuniis quam et*, “both in money and also,” according to Bal.]

**246. That all understand the bishop’s authority and be instructed how they must live according to either the canonical or monastic Rule.** All bishops shall understand their authority and shall be instructed so that they may govern their ministries—both in men’s monasteries and in those of women, as well as among external presbyters and the rest of God’s people—according either to the canonical or the monastic Rule.  
[Note: [Col. 0775] *regantur eorum ministerio*, “be governed by their ministry,” according to Bal.]

**247. Concerning widows, orphans, and the less powerful.** Widows, orphans, and the less powerful shall have peace under God’s protection and under our *mundeburdium*, and shall obtain their rights.  
[Note: [Col. 0775] Bal reads *nostro mundeburdo*, “under our protection”; G. reads *nostrae*, “of our.”]

**248. Concerning not treating the priests’ excommunication as insignificant.** It has been decreed that the faithful not regard the excommunication imposed by their priests as insignificant; for if they do so, they will rightly be separated from the assembly of Christians.  
[Note: [Col. 0775] G. reads *iustae* for *iuste* (“rightly/justly”).]

**249. Concerning bishops and counts, that they mutually provide one another with support.** Bishops shall stand with the counts and the counts with the bishops, so that both may fully perform their respective ministry.

**250. That thieves, homicides, adulterers, and incestuous persons be constrained under severe correction.** Thieves, homicides, adulterers, and incestuous persons shall be corrected under severe constraint and discipline, according to the Bavarians’ [uncertain reading: *eduam*] or the law.  
[Note: [Col. 0775] *beuuariorum*, “of the Bavarians,” according to G.]

**251. Concerning seized property.** Concerning private property: those who have done such a thing shall come before our envoys, counts, and judges, and there receive a final judgment, so that no one thereafter presume to seize another’s property. Rather, let them pursue their own case before our judges, as we have said, and there receive what is just.  
[Note: [Col. 0775] *proprindere*, “to seize,” according to Bal.]

**252. Concerning pride, through which the devil fell.** It has been decreed that the faithful be instructed concerning pride, through which the angel chosen from heaven became the devil.

253. **Concerning the person whose case is not judged rightly.** If anyone wishes to say that judgment has not been rendered justly for him, let him then come into our presence. Otherwise, however, he must not presume to come into our presence in order to delay another person’s justice.

[Col. 0776D] 254. **Concerning envy, through which the devil cast man out of paradise.** It was decided that the faithful should be admonished concerning envy, through which the devil cast man out of paradise.

255. **Concerning hatred and discord.** It was decided that the faithful should be admonished concerning hatred and discord, which extinguish charity among neighbors, empty out love, overturn every good thing, and do not allow neighbors to remain in mutual love.

256. **This chapter, issued in the year 806 of the Lord’s incarnation, at Teodon’s estate, in the sixth year of the reign of the lord Charles.**

1. That the readings in church be read distinctly.  
2. Concerning song: that singing be performed according to the order and custom of the Roman Church.  
3. Concerning notaries: that each bishop, abbot, and each of the counts have his own notary.  
4. Concerning the other disciplines of the Church: that they be carried out according to the canons or the rule.  
5. Concerning the medical art: that children be sent to learn it.  
6. Concerning churches that remain without honor, offices, and lights; and concerning those who take the tithes and do not care for the churches: that this be corrected in every way; and concerning altars: that they not be superfluous in the churches.

257. **Concerning laymen who have recently been converted.** Concerning laymen recently converted: they should not be sent to other business before they have fully learned their own law by living according to it.

258. **That scribes not write falsely.** Concerning scribes: that they not write defectively.

259. **That the computation be learned.** Concerning the computation: that everyone learn it accurately. [Note: [Col. 0777] Bal. reads *de compoto veraciter illum discant*, “that they learn the computation accurately.”]

260. **Concerning those who abandon the world for the service of God.** Concerning those who leave the world in order to evade service and then do neither: let them choose one of two things—either live fully according to the canonical way or according to the institution of the rule, or perform the service of the Lord.

261. **That personal male slaves not be tonsured, nor female slaves veiled, except according to measure.** Concerning personal male slaves and female slaves: that they not be tonsured or veiled beyond what is proper. And let provision be made there, so that the estates not be desolated. [Note: [Col. 0777] G. omits *vel ancillae non*, “nor female slaves.”]

262. **That superfluous gatherings in no way be held.** Concerning superfluous gatherings: that they in no way be held; rather, let each person gather as many as he is able to advise.

263. **Concerning those who are not summoned according to the rule.** Concerning those who are not summoned according to the rule: let this be corrected henceforth.

264. **That young girls not be veiled.** Let little girls of tender age not be veiled before they know how to choose what they wish, without prejudice to canonical authority.

265. **Concerning laymen: that they not be placed over monks.** Let laymen not be placed over monks within a monastery, nor let archdeacons be laymen.

[Col. 0777C] 266. **That incestuous persons be examined canonically.** Concerning incestuous persons: let them be examined canonically; and on account of anyone’s friendship, let some not be released while others are constrained.

267. **Concerning those who become rebellious through some crime.** Let everyone strive for peace; and let those who are rebellious on account of some crime be constrained.

268. **Concerning the justice of the churches of God, of orphans, minors, and widows.** Let the rights of the churches of God, of widows, orphans, and minors not be disregarded in public courts when they cry out, but let them be heard diligently.

269. **Concerning royal justice.** Let royal justice be fully investigated and administered.

270. **Concerning famine and other tribulations.** If famine, devastation, an irregularity of the weather, or any kind of tribulation should come, let no royal edict be awaited; rather, let God’s mercy immediately be implored. And in the present year, concerning the shortage caused by famine, let each person help as he is able, and let no one sell his provisions at an excessively high price. And let no foodstuff be sold outside our realm.

271. **That weapons not be carried within the country.** Concerning not carrying weapons within the country—that is, shields, lances, or coats of mail: if anyone is involved in a feud, let it then be investigated which of the two is at fault; and let them be compelled to peace, even if they are unwilling. If they refuse to make peace in any other way, let them be brought into our presence. If, after the reconciliation, one kills the other, let him pay the composition for him and lose the hand with which he violated his oath, without any redemption; moreover, let him pay the royal penalty. And let slaves not carry lances. Whoever is found doing so after the ban has been proclaimed shall have the shaft broken over his back.

272. **That every man with twelve holdings have a coat of mail.** Concerning military equipment, let the order that we previously issued in another capitulary be observed. In addition, every man with twelve holdings shall have a coat of mail. Whoever has a coat of mail but does not bring it with him shall lose the entire benefice together with the coat of mail.

273. **Concerning merchants who travel to the regions of the Slavs or other peoples.** Concerning merchants who go to the regions of the Slavs and Avars, how far they ought to proceed: in the regions of Saxony, as far as Bardowick, where Herti shall supervise; and at Cesla, where Madalgaud shall supervise; at Magdeburg, Atto shall supervise; at Erfurt, Madalgaud shall supervise; and at Alagastat, likewise at Forchheim and at Brehembret and at Regensburg, Ottulf shall supervise; at Lavarioca, Warnarius shall supervise—so that they do not take weapons or coats of mail there to sell. If they are found transporting them, let all their property be taken from them; one half shall go to the palace, and the other half shall be divided among the aforesaid royal agents and those who discovered the offense.  
[Note: [Col. 0777] Bal. reads *Ceslic* for *Cesla*; *Madegaudus* for *Madalgaudus*; G. reads *Otto* for *Atto*; *Forhcem* for *Forachem*; *et in ad herehembret* for *et ad Brehembret*; and *Gragenesburc* for *Ragenesburc*.]

[Col. 0778B] 274. **That claimants who refuse to submit be confined.** Concerning accusers or legal pleaders who are willing neither to accept the judgment of the scabini nor to refrain from blasphemy, let the ancient custom be observed: namely, that they be confined in custody until they do one of the two things. If they appeal to the palace on this account and bring letters, they are not to be believed; nevertheless, they are not then to be put in prison. Rather, let them be sent to our palace under guard, together with those very letters, and let the matter be investigated there as is fitting.

275. **Concerning the oath: that fidelity be promised by oath to no one other than one’s own lord.** Concerning the oath: let fidelity by oath be promised to no one other than us and each person’s own lord, for the benefit of us and of his lord, except for those oaths which, according to justice and law, one person owes another. And let the children who previously could not swear because of their youthful age now promise fidelity.

276. **Concerning those who make a conspiracy: that they be judged in three ways.** Whoever has presumed to make conspiracies and has confirmed a conspiracy by any oath shall be judged in three ways. First, wherever any evil has been perpetrated on account of it, let the authors of the deed be killed; but let their accomplices be flogged one by one by one another and cut off one another’s noses. Where no evil has been perpetrated, let them likewise be flogged among themselves and shear one another’s hair. But if a conspiracy has been confirmed by joined right hands, then, if they are free men, let them either swear with suitable oath-helpers that they would not have done this for an evil purpose, or, if they cannot do this, let them pay compensation according to their law. If they are slaves, let them be flogged, so that thereafter no conspiracy of this kind, by oath or without an oath, may take place in our kingdom.

277. **Concerning perjury: that it be avoided.** We command that perjury be avoided and that witnesses not be admitted to an oath before they have been examined. If they cannot otherwise be examined, let them be separated from one another and questioned individually. Accusers must not be permitted to choose witnesses in the absence of their opponent. Absolutely no one is to be admitted to an oath or testimony unless fasting. If the person brought forward as a witness is rejected, let the person rejecting him state and prove why he does not wish him to be accepted. Let witnesses be chosen from that same district, not another, unless perhaps the matter must be investigated farther outside the county. If anyone is convicted of perjury, let him lose his hand or redeem it.

278. **That wicked royal stewards, advocates, and centenarii be removed.** Concerning wicked advocates, royal stewards, vicars, and centenarii: let them be removed, and let such men be chosen as both know and wish to discern and settle cases justly. Whoever is found to be wicked must certainly be reported to us.

[Col. 0779A] 279. **That ancient and just tolls be exacted from merchants, but new and unjust ones be rejected.** It pleases us that ancient and just tolls be exacted from merchants, both at bridges and on boats or at markets. But new or unjust tolls—where ropes are stretched, or where boats pass beneath bridges, or anything similar is done, in which no assistance is provided to travelers—are not to be exacted. Likewise, no toll is to be exacted from those who, without commercial purpose, transport their property from one of their houses to another, or to the palace, or to the army. If there is anything about which doubt arises, let it be brought before our assembly, which we shall hold with our agents, for examination.

280. **Concerning fugitive clerics and laymen: the provision contained in the royal capitulary is to be observed.** Concerning fugitive clerics, laymen, or even women: let the provision stand as we already commanded in another capitulary.

281. **That those who wish to enter God’s service not do so without royal permission, if they are free men.** We command that free men who wish to give themselves to the service of God not do so before first requesting permission from us. For we have heard that some of them do this not so much out of devotion as while fleeing military service or another royal duty; and we have heard that others have been deceived for the sake of greed by those who covet their property. For this reason we forbid it.

282. **That the powerful not oppress the poor.** Concerning the oppression of poor free men: let them not be oppressed by the powerful through any evil device contrary to justice, so that they are compelled to sell or surrender their property. We speak of free men in this matter so that their parents might not perhaps be disinherited contrary to justice, royal service be diminished, and the heirs themselves, through want, become beggars, robbers, or wrongdoers. And let them not be summoned so frequently to the assembly, except as we commanded in another capitulary.  
[Note: [Col. 0779] G. reads *palatium*, “the palace,” for *placitum*, “the assembly.”]

283. **That newly discovered churches not be venerated without the bishop’s approval.** Concerning churches or saints newly discovered without authority: let them by no means be venerated unless the bishop approves, while canonical authority concerning this and concerning all churches remains intact.

284. **Concerning false coinage made contrary to justice.** Concerning false coins, since they are being produced in many places contrary to justice and contrary to the edict, we wish there to be no mint in any place except at our palace, unless we should order otherwise again. Nevertheless, let those denarii that have now been minted be accepted if they are of proper weight and pure.

285. **That the royal military levy be faithfully exacted.** Concerning the military levy, we wish our agents to exact it faithfully, without favor, flattery, or fear of any person, according to our command. That is, from a man possessing six pounds’ worth in gold, silver, coats of mail, copper, complete garments, horses, sheep, cows, or other livestock, they shall take from his clothing the lawful military levy—namely, three pounds—so that his wife and children are not stripped of their possessions on this account. Whoever has no more than property worth three pounds in the aforesaid categories shall pay thirty solidi. Whoever has no more than two pounds shall pay ten solidi. If he has only one pound, he shall pay five solidi, so that he may again be able to restore himself for the service of God and our benefit. Let our agents take care to investigate diligently, lest through any evil device they withhold our due by handing it over or entrusting it to another.  
[Note: [Col. 0779] G. reads *v. minus n.*, “or less,” for *nisi*, “unless/only.”]

286. **That the royal census be paid from the place where it was formerly lawfully exacted.** Wherever the royal census was formerly lawfully exacted, we wish it to be paid from there, whether from the person of the man himself or from his property.

287. **What is to be done concerning robbers.** Concerning robbers: let matters remain as we previously set forth in another capitulary.

288. **What is to be done concerning those who have royal fiscal women as wives.** Concerning free men who have wives from the royal fisc, and concerning free women who likewise have or take men belonging to the royal fisc: let them not be rejected from seeking their parental inheritance or their own case, nor from giving testimony on this account. Rather, let the honor shown to us in this matter be such as is known to have been shown previously to our predecessors, the kings and emperors.

289. **Concerning the canonical books: that they be kept accurate.** We wish—and therefore command our agents—that accurate canonical books be kept in the churches, as we have often already commanded in another capitulary.

290. **That laymen learn the Lord’s Prayer by heart.** Let laymen fully learn the Creed and the Lord’s Prayer. Let the counts and centenarii, noble men, also fully learn their own law, as has been decreed elsewhere. We command our agents concerning the things which for many years we have commanded throughout our kingdom in our capitularies to be done, learned, observed, or made customary: let them now investigate all these matters diligently and strive to renew them entirely for the service of God, for our benefit, and for the advancement of all Christian people; and, insofar as they prevail with the Lord’s gift, let them bring them to perfection and report fully to us who among them has undertaken this good struggle to fulfill them, so that he may have grace from God and from us. But whoever has been negligent in this matter shall receive such discipline as such a contemptuous person deserves, so that the others may also be afraid to act thus again.  
[Note: [Col. 0779] G. reads *fuerat*, “had been,” for *fuerit*, “has been.”]

291. **Capitula to be sent concerning the Salic Law regarding the killing of clerics [Bal. reads “deacons”] and other cases.** Whoever kills a subdeacon shall pay a composition of three hundred solidi; whoever kills a deacon, four hundred solidi; whoever kills a priest, six hundred; whoever kills a bishop, nine hundred; whoever kills a monk shall be judged liable for four hundred solidi. [Notes: [Col. 0779] G. has corrections reading four hundred for the first amount, six hundred for the second, and nine hundred for the third; for the bishop, G. adds “let him pay a composition for his life.” For the monk, G. gives: “four hundred, and in addition the royal penalty, that is, sixty solidi, and let him surrender his arms and serve God in a monastery under severe penance for the days of his life. If anyone causes harm within an immunity, etc.” Paris, Bibliothèque nationale, Codex Regius no. 4376.]

If anyone causes any damage within an immunity, he shall pay a composition of six hundred solidi. But if a man commits theft, homicide, or any crime elsewhere and, after committing it, flees within an immunity, let the count order the bishop, abbot, royal steward, or whoever holds the place of the bishop or abbot to surrender the accused to him. If that person objects and refuses to surrender him, on the first objection he shall pay fifteen solidi. If, upon a second demand, he refuses to surrender him, he shall pay thirty solidi. If he is unwilling to consent even at the third demand, whatever damage the accused has caused, the entire amount shall be exacted from the person who retains him within the immunity and refuses to surrender him. The count himself, when he comes, shall have permission to seek that man within the immunity wherever he is able to find him.

But if, upon the count’s first inquiry, he is told that the accused had indeed been within the immunity but had escaped by flight, let the person in charge immediately swear that he did not cause him to flee in order to obstruct anyone’s justice, and let this suffice for him. If, however, when the count enters the immunity, anyone attempts to resist him with an assembled force, let the count report this to the king or prince, so that it may be judged there. And just as the person who caused harm within an immunity ought to pay a composition of six hundred solidi, so the person who presumes to resist the count with an assembled force shall pay six hundred solidi.  
[Note: [Col. 0779] G. corrects the amount to nine hundred solidi.]

292. **Capitula established by the lord Emperor Charles.** Let no one carry weapons within the country to the assembly.

[Col. 0781A] 293. **Concerning robbers.** Whoever, since the Mass of Saint John on the previous year, has given lodging to a robber, if he is a Frank, shall swear with twelve other Franks like himself that he did not know the man to be a robber—even if he is his father, brother, or some other relative. If he cannot swear this and is convicted by another that he received a robber as a guest, let him be treated as a robber, since he is disloyal to us and to the Franks; and the person who received him is like him. But if he heard that the man was a robber and yet does not know it with certainty, let him swear alone that he had never heard, either truthfully or falsely, that the man was a robber; otherwise, let him be prepared to be punished in the same way if that man is later convicted of robbery.

294. **That no one buy a horse, ox, or other animal from an unknown man.** Let no one buy a horse, ox, beast of burden, or any other animal unless he knows the man who sold it, what district he is from, where he lives, and who his lord is.  
[Note: [Col. 0781] G. reads *maneat*, “where he remains/lives,” for *manet*.]

[Col. 0781B] 295. **Concerning those who have been condemned to death for their crimes and afterward granted life: how judgment is to be settled if they seek justice from others or someone wishes to seek justice from them.** First of all, concerning the cases for which a person was condemned to death, he can make no claim, because all his property was confiscated publicly according to Frankish judgment. If afterward, once life has been granted to him, he is able to acquire anything lawfully, let him hold and defend it in his freedom according to the law. But let him not be received as a witness, nor hold a place among the scabini in judging the law. If something has been judged against him under oath, which he must swear, and someone wishes to declare that oath false, let him contest it with arms.  
[Note: [Col. 0781] Bal. omits *quis*, “someone,” in the phrase “for which someone was judged.”]

296. **Concerning a man judged by the judgment of the scabini.** If life has been granted to anyone after the judgment of the scabini, and he subsequently commits some evil and refuses to render justice, saying that he is dead and therefore ought not to render justice, it is established that he shall undergo the higher judgment which he ought previously to have undergone. If anyone does something evil against him, he shall have permission, according to the order of equity, to seek his justice for the matter committed after he was condemned to death. As for earlier matters, let them remain as was judged above.

297. **Concerning the person who receives an outlawed robber, whether slave or free.** Concerning an outlawed robber: a free man who receives him shall pay fifteen solidi; a slave shall receive one hundred and twenty blows.  
[Note: [Col. 0781] Bal. omits *ut*, “so that.”]

298. **Concerning the count who places a robber under outlawry: that he make it known to the neighboring counts.** Let the count who has placed a robber under outlawry inform his neighboring counts that the same robber has been outlawed by him, so that they do not receive him.

299. **Concerning those who devote themselves to earthly commerce: that they do so more from desire for heavenly life than from human ambition.** It was decided that all the faithful who are occupied with business and the buying and selling of goods should be admonished not to desire earthly profits more than eternal life. For whoever thinks more about earthly possessions than about the salvation of his soul strays far from the way of truth and, according to a certain wise man, loses his innermost self during his life. In this matter, as in others, the apostolic word must be followed, for it says: “Let no one overreach or defraud his brother in business, for God is the avenger of all such things.” Just as tithes and alms are to be given by those who eagerly labor at cultivating fields and at other work to acquire food, clothing, and the necessities of human use, so too must this be done by those who devote themselves to commerce for the sake of necessary needs. God has given every person an art by which he is nourished; and everyone ought, from the art by which he obtains the necessities or support of the body, to provide support also for the soul, which is more necessary.  
[Note: [Col. 0781] Bal. reads *anhiantes*, “eagerly striving,” for *inhiantes*.]

300. **That an appeal by those seeking recourse in ecclesiastical matters not be denied a hearing.** It was decided that whenever an appeal has been made from any ecclesiastical judges to other ecclesiastical judges possessing greater authority, the appeal must not be denied to those who have made it.

301. **That no bishop usurp another bishop’s people or boundaries.** Let no bishop usurp the people or boundaries of another bishop.

302. **Concerning proud clerics: that they be restrained.** Let clerics who are proud or stubborn be restrained, so that inferiors who have inflicted an injury on their superiors may be afraid; for it is clear that those who despise humility are not of God but of the devil, who is the inventor and prince of pride. Therefore, if anyone is swollen with pride or insulting toward an older man, his contemptuous stubbornness and pride ought in every respect to be broken.

303. **Concerning those who violate the ordinances of the fathers: if a layman, let him be deprived of communion; if a cleric, of his rank.** If anyone transgresses and corrupts the ordinances, or considers them to be of no account, then, if he is a layman, let him be deprived of communion; if he is a cleric, of his rank.

304. **Concerning those who act against their profession or subscription.** Whoever acts against his profession or subscription shall be deposed in council.

305. **Concerning a priest who separates himself from his bishop.** If any priest, puffed up against his bishop, makes a schism, let him be anathema. If, God forbid, puffed up by pride, he decides to separate himself from communion with his bishop and, making a schism with certain others, offers sacrifice to God separately, let him be regarded as anathema, having lost his position. Nevertheless, let him also be driven far from the city and congregation in which he was, lest he deceive the ignorant or those living simply by serpent-like fraud.  
[Note: [Col. 0781] The phrase *scisma ... inflatus* is absent at the end of the line in the manuscript, but the same hand has added it in the margin with the note: “What is absent in this line through the scribe’s error is written in the eighth [line/page].”]

306. **Concerning priests who celebrate the service without the knowledge of their bishop.** If any priest wishes to celebrate the service (*agenda*) in any place without consulting his bishop, he has acted contrary to his own honor.

307. **That a fallen bishop, if he cannot gather many, be heard by twelve.** If any bishop, which we do not wish, should fall into some offense, and extreme necessity prevents him from gathering a larger number, let him be heard by twelve bishops, so that he does not remain under accusation.  
[Notes: [Col. 0781] G. reads *incurrit*, “falls into,” for *incurrerit*, “should fall into”; Bal. omits *ei*, “for him.”]

308. **That bishops not usurp other bishops’ people, and that none of them overreach his colleague in a diocese or elsewhere.** It was decided that no bishop should usurp the people of another, and that no bishop should overreach his colleague in a diocese.  
[Note: [Col. 0781] G. reads “his colleague’s diocese” for “in a diocese.”]

309. **Concerning a bishop who is accused by someone, or if he himself brings forward a dispute: that the case be settled by episcopal judges.** If any bishop is accused by anyone, or if he himself brings forward some dispute, let the case be settled by episcopal judges, whether those whom their primates appoint for them or those whom they themselves, by common agreement, choose from among their neighbors.

310. **That no bishop trample upon, overreach, or hinder another bishop.** Let no bishop trample upon or overreach another bishop, or cause him any harm.

311. **That priests or deacons do nothing without the knowledge of their bishops.** Let priests or deacons do nothing without the knowledge of their bishops.

312. **Concerning giving a place to a visiting bishop in which he may celebrate.** Let a visiting bishop be given a place in which to celebrate, and let him be received kindly.

[Col. 0783A] 313. **Concerning not condemning the person whose case has not been carefully examined.** It is not just to condemn a man whose case has not been examined fully.  
[Note: [Col. 0783] G. reads *contempnendo*, “despising,” for *condempnando*, “condemning”; Bal. reads *eum*, “him,” for *virum*, “a man.”]

314. **Concerning those who falsely bring capital charges against brothers.** It was decided that those who are convicted of having brought false capital charges against their brothers shall not receive communion until the end of their life.

315. **Concerning deposing a priest or Levite if he confesses a crime concerning himself.** Let a priest or Levite who confesses a crime concerning himself be deposed.

316. **That those found to have placed defamatory pamphlets in a church be anathematized.** If anyone is found placing defamatory pamphlets in a church, let him be anathematized.  
[Note: [Col. 0783] G. reads *fuisse*, “to have been,” for *posuisse*, “to have placed.”]

317. **That an informer not receive communion even at the end of his life if anyone is proscribed or killed through his informing.** If any faithful person acts as an informer, and someone is proscribed or killed through his informing, it was decided that he shall not receive communion even at the end of his life.

[Col. 0783B] 318. **That no bishop or person of a lower rank presume to judge anyone on the Lord’s Day.** Let no bishop or anyone of a lower rank presume to hear cases on Sunday. On the other days, with the appropriate persons present, they shall have permission to judge what is just, except in criminal cases.  
[Note: [Col. 0783] Bal. reads “except in a criminal case.”]

319. **Concerning a powerful man who strips a poor man and does not restore what he took when admonished by the bishop: that he be excommunicated.** If any powerful man strips anyone of his property and does not restore it when admonished by the bishop, let him be excommunicated.

320. **That no cleric presume to depart from his bishop and transfer to another.** Let no cleric depart from his bishop and transfer himself to another.

321. **That clerics who presume to take up arms be delivered to a monastery to do penance.** Let clerics who, in any disturbance, deliberately presume to take up arms, when discovered, be stripped of their clerical rank and delivered to a monastery for penance.

322. **That no king permit the sanction of this canon to be violated in any respect.** Let the form of this constitution be preserved, so that whoever among the kings henceforth believes or permits the sanction of this canon to be violated in any respect shall become an accursed anathema and, as a transgressor of the Catholic faith, shall always stand guilty before the Lord.  
[Note: [Col. 0783] G. corrects *execrandum*, “to be execrated,” to *execrando*, “by execration”; G. omits *huius canonis*, “of this canon.”]

323. **That each person succor another’s ruin and remove God’s anger from himself through compassion.** Certainly, each person ought to come to the aid of the miserable in their ruin, insofar as he is able, and by relieving another’s punishment remove God’s punishment from himself. For he offers the Lord prosperity who drives adversity away from the afflicted.  
[Note: [Col. 0783] *et* is corrected from another reading in G.; Bal. has *et ex*, “and from.”]

324. **That the law instituted by the earlier king be confirmed with equal authority by his successor.** We strengthen with firm authority the law issued by our prince, and we decree with equal authority that it be observed in future times.

325. **That all bishops assemble at the metropolitan see to hold a synod.** It was decided to decree that, obeying the institutions of the fathers, we should assemble at the metropolitan see with devoted zeal at the time when all the provincial bishops have chosen to hold a synod.

326. **That all who do not go on military expedition or flee from the army lose their dignity.** It was decided that everyone who either does not advance on a military expedition without serious necessity or flees from the army shall irrevocably lack the testimony of his dignity, so that in certain little estates, territories, or villages the inhabitants of those places may be degraded by this disgrace and have no permission to give testimony or bring accusations.  
[Note: [Col. 0783] Bal. reads *pestus* for *pestis*, “plague/disgrace.”]

327. **That Christians not marry within the proximity of their blood relationship.** Let Christians not enter marriages within the proximity of their blood relationship, nor presume to marry without the blessing of a priest.

328. **That institutions established for the common good not be altered.** Let what has been established for perpetual benefit not be altered by any change; and let what has been set down for the common good not be drawn toward private advantage. While the boundaries established by the fathers remain, let no one condemn another; rather, within his own proper and lawful limits, let each person exercise himself broadly in charity, as he wishes.

329. **Concerning the preservation of the Nicene faith.** And that the privileges of the churches remain intact. Let the Nicene faith be preserved, and let the privileges of the churches remain unimpaired.

330. **That nothing be done against the head.** Even when something must be done against the head, we do not willingly admit it.

331. **Concerning priests who wish to go to the assembly contrary to the canons, and who are decreed by royal ordinance to be excluded from communion when received.** From the report of certain persons we have learned how priests who, contrary to the canons, wished to go against us to the assembly with some unknown and audacious recklessness were received. Therefore we send this letter to you, in which by our decree we sanction that the aforesaid disturbers ought to be excluded from communion. As for those who wished to lend their support by counsel to this unbridled act, it belongs to your charity to determine how they should be treated. You ought to point out to them that, in accordance with the canons, they have attempted to incur grave penalties and that it was unfitting for priests to try to become rebels. We admonish you, however, to remain watchful and not to descend to the rash audacity of those whom the holy and apostolic Church knows to have been anathematized.  
[Note: [Col. 0783] G. reads *prorupta audatia*, “rash audacity,” for *proruptam audaciam*. Bal. omits *decreto*, “by decree.”]

332. **Concerning not settling the cases of the Lord’s priests before they have been faithfully heard on both sides and examined equally and carefully.** We, who by nature wish to uphold the rights of the Lord’s priests, can determine nothing in an unknown matter by judgment against either party before we faithfully hear everything that has taken place.

333. **That the Lord, who saves human souls, wishes us to be imitators of his mercy.** The Lord, who came to save human souls, not to destroy them, wishes us to be imitators of his mercy, so that justice may indeed restrain sinners, but may not drive the converted away from mercy.

334. **Concerning removing the danger to religion from each person’s pious conscience.** We ask you to remove from the conscience of your piety the danger to religion and faith. In the handling of divine matters, show the fairness that is granted to you in secular affairs, so that presumption does not do violence to the Gospel of Christ.

335. **That those whose case remains to be settled be content for the time being with their own property and with that of all the churches.** We approve what was established by our predecessors: that, for the time being, they be content with communion in their own goods and in all the churches, until the case is settled by us.

[Col. 0784D] 336. **That people not be allowed to fall into matters whose status is uncertain.** Do not allow anyone, through the shameless and insolent cunning of pretending that it is uncertain what ought to be followed, to fall into such things, since it is not permissible to depart even in a single word from evangelical and apostolic teaching, or to understand the divine Scriptures otherwise than our blessed apostles and fathers learned and taught.

337. **Concerning those who were driven from their sees and others were substituted in their place.** We have heard that very many brothers were driven from their sees and deported into exile, while others were substituted in the place of those who survived. Let the medicine of justice first be applied to these wounds, so that no one may be deprived of what belongs to him while another uses what belongs to someone else. Let everyone abandon this error. No one’s honor ought to perish. But for those who have labored for the faith, their own right must first be restored together with all their privileges.

338. **Concerning those who ought not to return to secular military service.** No one ought to return to secular military service after penance; nor should those have any legitimate complaint who have voluntarily withdrawn from disputes already begun.

339. **Concerning those who ought to be corrected with greater authority.** If there should be some sluggish or negligent brothers who ought to be corrected with greater authority, correction must nevertheless be applied in such a way that love is always preserved. Therefore the apostle, instructing Timothy, says: “Do not rebuke an older man, but entreat him as a father.” If this moderation is owed by apostolic instruction to any inferior members, how much more must it be shown to our brothers and fellow bishops?

340. **That no one impose on another a burden that he is unable to bear himself.** Just as no one wishes to carry a burden of great weight, so let him not presume to impose a heavy burden on another.

341. **That no one presume to violate apostolic decrees.** Serve the divine apostolic constitutions with such unanimity that you permit the pious decrees of the canons to be violated in no respect. Let no one be permitted, at the peril of his own status, to violate either the divine constitutions or the decrees of the apostolic see.

### 342. On preserving friendship and familiarity, which those who do not quarrel easily preserve

Let friendship protect everyone from quarreling. For the Apostle also writes to the Corinthians: “Since there are rivalries and quarrels among you, are you not carnal and walking according to human ways?” Do nothing through quarrel or empty glory; but, in humility of mind, each should regard the others as superior to himself, and let no one look to his own interests individually, but to those of others.

### 343. That people of a foreign nation should be instructed in the laws for practical use

We both permit and desire people of a foreign nation to be instructed in the laws for practical purposes. But we reject and prohibit them from handling legal disputes; for although they may be powerful in eloquence, they nevertheless become entangled in difficulties. [Col. 0785C]

### 344. That a slave should not be believed if he has accused anyone of a crime

A slave is never at all to be believed if he has accused anyone of a crime, or even if he has charged his own master with a crime. For even if, placed under torture, he discloses what he alleges, he nevertheless ought in no way to be believed. [Note: [Col. 0785] *oportebat* in G.]

### 345. That witnesses should not give testimony unless they are present

Witnesses should not give testimony in their absence or by letter; rather, being present, they should not conceal the truth they have known and seen. Nor should they give testimony concerning other matters, but only concerning those which they know were conducted in their presence.

Holy Scripture bears witness to this, saying: “The Pharisees said to the soldiers, ‘We give you money, and say that his disciples came while you were sleeping and stole him.’” [Col. 0785D] Hence Augustine says: “You produce sleeping witnesses! Truly you yourself have fallen asleep, since you failed while investigating such matters. If they were sleeping, what could they see? If they saw nothing, how are they witnesses? But they failed while making their investigations.”

### 346. On preserving agreements and settlements

We permit agreements or settlements that have been made lawfully and most justly in writing to be changed in no way, provided that a day or year is clearly expressed in them.

### 347. That this is true charity, by which God and one’s neighbor are loved

All the faithful should therefore be admonished to take care to observe this. It has been decided that all the faithful should be warned that this is true charity: a person loves God more than himself and his neighbor as himself, and wishes to do nothing to another except what he wishes to be done to himself, along with many other matters whose enumeration would be lengthy. [Col. 0786A]

For all who think that charity consists in eating and drinking and in giving and receiving things are gravely mistaken, as the Apostle says: “The kingdom of God is not food and drink.” Yet these things themselves, when done with charity, are good and are to be counted among the virtues. [Note: [Col. 0785] *fiant* in G.]

### 348. That relatives or kindred should in no way testify against outsiders

We do not permit brothers, sisters, uterine siblings, paternal uncles, maternal uncles, maternal aunts, or their children, nor a nephew, niece, cousins, or other members of one’s own blood relationship, to give testimony in court against outsiders—unless perhaps parents of the same kinship have a dispute among themselves, or it is completely established that in the case under consideration no other freeborn person is available.

### 349. That a son or heir may not act against the decision of his predecessors

A son or heir may not act against the just or legitimate decision of his predecessors, because the presumption of one who unjustly attempts to violate the acts of his elders is justly rejected.

[Col. 0786B]

### 350. Permission to accuse or punish is not to be granted indiscriminately

We do not grant permission to accuse or punish indiscriminately, unless either the crime has become evident through clear indications or that same evil has been lawfully accused and proven; so that no one may appear, in any intention or procedure, to transgress the commands of the holy fathers or oppose the sacred rules of the ancients. [Note: [Col. 0785] *obviari* in G.]

### 351. If someone unknowingly buys something from a thief

No freeborn person may buy any property from an unknown person unless he certainly provides a guarantor who can be trusted, so that the excuse of ignorance may be removed. If the buyer acts otherwise, he must, under compulsion from the judge, produce the seller within a sufficient period established by the judge. [Note: [Col. 0785] *sic* in G. and the Visigothic Law; Bal.: *aut repraesentet*, “or produce.”] [Note: [Col. 0785] *quam* in Bal.]

If he cannot find him, he must prove himself innocent either by oath or by witnesses: that he did not know him to be a thief. Whatever is recognized as being in his possession he must restore, after receiving half the price. [Note: [Col. 0785] G.: “after receiving half the price.”] Both parties shall promise by mutual oaths that they will diligently seek the thief.

If they are entirely unable to find the thief, the buyer shall restore to the owner the purchased property in full. [Col. 0786C] [Note: [Col. 0785] Bal.: “the property in the amount for which it was purchased.”] But if the owner of the property knows the thief and does not wish to make him public, he shall lose the property altogether, and the buyer shall possess it undisturbed. The same procedure shall also be observed concerning slaves.

### 352. That freedmen should not testify

A freedman or freedwoman shall not be admitted to give testimony against anyone in any matter, except in certain cases where no freeborn person is known to be available, as was stated above concerning slaves. For our clemency considers it unworthy that the testimony of freedmen should bring harm upon freeborn people.

Those born from such persons shall be admitted as witnesses in the third generation.

### 353. If a possessor is expelled by violence

[Col. 0786D] Whoever violently expels a possessor, before a judicial sentence has been issued in his favor, shall lose the case itself—even if he had the better claim. The person who suffered the violence shall receive back everything in the condition in which it had been, and shall securely retain what he possessed.

But if the aggressor seizes something which he could have obtained through judgment, he shall both lose the case and return to the expelled person as much again as he seized.

### 354. If someone is found to have invited others to plunder

If someone invites others to plunder, so as to overturn anyone’s property [Note: [Col. 0785] Bal.: *evertant*], or to seize livestock or any animals [Note: [Col. 0785] Bal.: *diripiant*], he shall restore sevenfold to the person whose property was plundered what was taken.

Those who were with him, if they are freeborn, shall be compelled to pay five solidi each. If they do not have the means to pay, they shall receive one hundred and fifty lashes. [Note: [Col. 0785] The number is absent in the source of this chapter; see the Visigothic Law.]

But if slaves commit this without their master’s consent, they shall be beaten with one hundred and fifty lashes, and all the property shall be restored by them intact.

### 355. That he should name his accomplices when part of the plunder [Col. 0787A] has been found with him

When a crime has been established against someone and part of the plunder has been found with him, he shall immediately be compelled to name his accomplices. If he refuses to name them, he shall be held for punishment.

If he is a person of higher status, he shall both give an account of the crime and restore what was taken or destroyed by a fourfold payment. [Note: [Col. 0787] Bal.: “four times”; the Visigothic Law: “elevenfold.”]

But if part of the plunder is found with a slave, he shall be publicly stretched out and receive one hundred and fifty lashes [Note: [Col. 0787] The Visigothic Law: two hundred], and he shall not delay naming his accomplices.

### 356. Concerning those who are found to have disclosed where something could be plundered

Whoever, freeborn or slave, discloses that something may be plundered, so that someone’s property may be destroyed or livestock or draft animals seized, and is found publicly convicted of this by certain proofs, shall be punished for what he disclosed.

If he is freeborn, he shall restore by law double what was destroyed or taken and shall pay us our fine, that is, sixty solidi. [Note: [Col. 0787] The Visigothic Law lacks what follows.]

But if he is a slave or tenant, he shall be publicly stretched out and receive one hundred and fifty well-impressed lashes. [Note: [Col. 0787] G.: “pressed lashes.”] [Col. 0787B] In addition, he shall restore what was taken according to his law.

### 357. That no accusation against a teacher should be accepted, nor an accuser against him heard

Let no one accept or hear accusations against a teacher, because it is unworthy that those who are called the thrones of God should be disturbed by any agitation.

### 358. That one bishop should not claim jurisdiction for himself

It has been decided that one bishop should not claim jurisdiction for himself.

### 359. That those whose faith, life, and free status are unknown should in no way accuse priests

Those whose faith, life, and free status are unknown must not be allowed to accuse priests.

### 360. That absent persons should not be judged

No judgment shall be rendered against absent persons. If this is done, the sentence issued shall have no validity.

### 361. Concerning those who bring false charges against others

Everyone who has brought false charges against others shall be punished and shall bear disgrace for his falsehood. [Note: [Col. 0787] The words “and shall bear” are absent in G.]

### 362. That low-status persons should not be admitted to accuse priests [Col. 0787C]

Persons of low status shall in no way be admitted to accuse priests.

### 363. That judges should not presume to decide the case of an absent person by their own judgment

Let the judges of the Church beware lest they issue a sentence while the person whose case is being disputed is absent, for it will be void; indeed, they will give an account in the synod for the deed. [Note: [Col. 0787] G.: *facito*, “you shall do it.”]

### 364. That no criminal should accuse a bishop

No criminal person may accuse a bishop.

### 365. That whoever accuses a bishop accuses God’s ordinance

Whoever accuses or condemns bishops accuses God’s ordinance, by which they are appointed, while pursuing spiritual matters less than earthly ones. [Note: [Col. 0787] Bal.: singular *episcopum*; G. corrects *contempnat* to *contempnit*.]

### 366. That litigants, whether claimants or possessors, should be directed to bishops if they choose episcopal judgment

We wish and command that all who, with God’s help, are subject to our authority—Romans, Franks, Alamanni, Bavarians, Saxons, Thuringians, Frisians, Gauls, Burgundians, Bretons, Lombards, Basques, [Col. 0787D] Beneventans, Goths, Spaniards, and all the rest subject to us—although they may appear to be bound by whatever bond of law or connected by customary practice, should observe this judgment as a law perpetually binding on all.

We have taken it from book 16 of the Emperor Theodosius, specifically chapter 11, as a rescript issued to Duke Ablavius in response to his inquiry; and, with the advice of all our faithful, both clergy and laity, we have placed it among our chapters as a law to be observed. [Note: [Col. 0787] Bal.: “as a perpetual law to be observed”; G. first wrote this similarly but later corrected it.]

That is:

[Col. 0788A] “Whoever has a lawsuit, whether he is a possessor or a claimant, whether at the beginning of the lawsuit or after the passage of time, whether while the case is being pleaded or when the sentence has already begun to be pronounced, if he chooses the judgment of the bishop of the sacred law, shall immediately and without any hesitation be directed to the judgment of the bishops with the pleadings of the litigants, even if the opposing party resists.

For the authority of the sacred religion investigates and brings forth many things which the deceptive bonds of legal prescription do not allow to be brought forth in court. Therefore all cases, whether handled under praetorian or civil law, shall be confirmed by the law of perpetual stability once settled by the judgments of bishops; nor shall it be lawful thereafter to reopen a judgment decided by the judgments of bishops.

All judges shall also accept without hesitation the testimony given even by one bishop, and no other witness shall be heard when the testimony of a bishop has been offered by either party. For that is confirmed by the authority of truth; that is incorrupt which a holy man has uttered from a conscience undefiled in mind.

We once decreed this in a salutary edict; by this perpetual law we confirm it, suppressing the malicious seeds of litigation, so that wretched people entangled in the long and almost perpetual snares of legal actions may withdraw at a timely end from wicked claims or premature greed. [Col. 0788B]

Whatever, therefore, our clemency had decreed concerning the judgments of bishops, we have also included in this law. It is fitting that Your Gravity and the others should observe it perpetually for the benefit of all.”

### 367. That those things established by the authority of the Catholic fathers should be preserved inviolate

We command that those matters which antiquity once ordained concerning the Catholic law, which the religious authority of our fathers established, or which our serenity strengthened, be preserved whole and inviolate, with novel superstition removed. [Note: [Col. 0787] Bal.: “preserved.”]

### 368. That privileges established for the sake of religion should not be mutilated by any new threat

We do not command anything new in the present decree, but confirm those things which appear to have been granted long ago. Therefore we prohibit, even under threat of punishment, the mutilation of the privileges which religious reverence obtained in former times. [Col. 0788C] Likewise, those who obey the Church should enjoy those benefits with which the Church [is associated; the construction is defective]. [Note: [Col. 0787] G.: *mutuari*, “to borrow/exchange”; Bal.: *ecclesiae beneficiis*, “the benefits of the Church.”]

### 369. That if chorepiscopi have performed any consecration or confirmation, it should be canonically corrected by bishops

The confirmation of persons, and the consecrations of churches, altars, virgins, chrism, presbyters, deacons, and subdeacons performed by chorepiscopi are to be canonically corrected and canonically carried out by bishops ordained according to the canons. [Note: [Col. 0787] Bal.: “The acts performed by chorepiscopi are to be canonically corrected and carried out by bishops who have been canonically ordained.”]

For chorepiscopi ought not and could not have undertaken or performed these matters. They could not confer what they do not possess. [Note: [Col. 0787] Bal. places the words “nor can they perform what they do not possess” in brackets after *invalid*, omitting there the words “such an ordination” and “and consecration.”]

Such an ordination or consecration is by no means considered by the prudent and rightly minded to be a repetition; rather, it is undoubtedly recognized that such ordination, confirmation, and consecration are invalid.

If any chorepiscopus attempts to perform any of the aforesaid acts, they shall not be validly performed but shall remain incomplete and invalid, [Col. 0788D] and he himself shall irrevocably lose every ecclesiastical rank.

### 370. On the general supplication of the whole people before the ruler on behalf of the priests, that they should not go to the army or battle, and on the danger which consequently threatens them all

[Col. 0788D] From the chapters generally decreed at Worms by the lord Emperor Charles, confirmed by all and handed down for everyone to observe as law. [Note: [Col. 0787] G.: “by all people.”]

We all beseech Your Majesty on bended knees that bishops henceforth, as until now, should not be harassed by military expeditions; [Col. 0789A] but when you and we go to the army, let them remain in their own dioceses, strive to serve God faithfully, perform their sacred mysteries canonically and in a manner pleasing to God, and labor earnestly to pray courageously for you and your whole army, together with all entrusted to them, and to sing Masses, litanies, and perform almsgiving.

We have seen some of them wounded in military expeditions and battles, and we have learned that others have perished. These things are exceedingly dangerous and must be strongly avoided. We therefore bring this forward lest you and we perish together because of such matters.

The Lord knows that when we see them in such circumstances, terror seizes us, and some of our men, overcome by fear because of this, are accustomed to flee and turn their backs to the enemy. For you can have more combatants if they remain in their own dioceses than if they go with you, since then all those who watch over them will fight, whereas now they merely guard them.

[Col. 0789B] Without doubt they can benefit you and us more if they remain behind than if they go on a military expedition or to battle, because then we are helped by their prayers, while now we are burdened by their hardships.

When Moses prayed with his hands stretched toward heaven, Israel prevailed; and when he ceased praying and his hands grew heavy, before they were supported and he resumed his prayers, Israel was defeated and turned its back.

Supported, therefore, by such and many other examples, whose length we now avoid mentioning, [Note: [Col. 0789] Bal.: “overcome by their length”] since one statement is sufficient for the wise, we all earnestly beseech and request that this be granted. We absolutely do not wish to consent to their going with us on such expeditions, except for two or three well-instructed men, chosen by the others, to give blessings and reconcile those in danger, lest you and we perish together with many others, but rather be supported by their prayers, as has already been said.

We also wish this rule to be observed concerning priests: they should not go on a military expedition unless they are well instructed and chosen [Col. 0789C] and permitted by their own bishops, and unless they are such men that all of us can be confident in their knowledge, life, and conduct.

We also wish you and everyone to know that we do not make these requests because we desire to seize their property or any of their money—unless they themselves willingly wish to give us something—or because we wish to deprive their churches of their goods. Rather, if the Lord grants us the ability, we desire to increase them, so that they, you, and we may be safer and, with God himself assisting, may deserve to please him more fully.

For we know that the goods of the Church are consecrated to God; we know that they are the offerings of the faithful and the prices of sinners. [Note: [Col. 0789] Bal. omits: “For we know … the prices of sinners.”]
