Therefore, if anyone removes these goods from the churches to which they have been given by the faithful and consecrated to God, he undoubtedly commits sacrilege. He is blind who does not see this.

Whoever among us, then, gives his goods to the Church offers and dedicates them to the Lord God and to his saints, and not to anyone else, by saying and acting as follows. He makes a written document concerning the goods which he desires to give to God, and [Col. 0789D] holds that document in his hand before or upon the altar, saying to the priests and guardians of that place:

“I offer and dedicate to God all the goods contained in this document, for the remission of my sins and those of my parents and children—or for whomever he may wish to offer them to God—to serve God from them in sacrifices and the solemn rites of Masses, in prayers, lights, almsgiving to the poor and clergy, and other divine services and for the uses of that church. If anyone removes them from there—which I absolutely do not believe will happen—let him render the strictest account for this under the penalty of sacrilege to the Lord God, [Col. 0790A] to whom I offer and dedicate them.”

He also inserts other curses in it, whose enumeration would be lengthy. [Note: [Col. 0789] G. has “he places penance in it, and other things.”] For what does the person who later removes them from there do except commit sacrilege?

If, then, stealing something from a friend is theft, defrauding or removing something from a church is unquestionably sacrilege. Hence the sacred canons, composed by the Spirit of God, state:

“If anyone wishes to receive or give the offerings of the Church outside the Church without the knowledge of the bishop or of the person entrusted with such duties, and does not wish to act with his counsel, let him be anathema.”

Far be it from us that we should become sacrilegious or accursed through desire for or removal of ecclesiastical goods, or ever be bound by such snares. For we know—and do not doubt—that people under anathema or sacrilegious are not only infamous and excluded from the fellowship of the faithful until they amend these matters through public satisfaction to the Church, reconciliation by the bishops, and the laying on of hands, but also become exiles from the kingdom of God if they fail in such matters.

[Col. 0790B] Therefore, so that every suspicion may be entirely removed from all of us priests and from all the faithful of Christ and of the holy Church of God, we all profess, holding straws in our right hands and throwing them away with our own hands, before God and his angels, before you, and before all the priests and peoples standing around, that we will neither do such things nor consent to those who wish to do them, but rather, with God’s help, resist them.

We also wish this to be known to you and to all the faithful of the holy Church and to our own people: with those who, without the will, consent, or grant of the ruler of that church to which the property rightly belongs—and especially without the consent of its own bishop—presume to request ecclesiastical property from kings, retain it, remove it, seize it, or lay waste to it, we must never knowingly or willingly have any association before public correction and satisfaction have been made to the Church.

We must neither go to the army nor to battle with them, nor take food, nor go to a church, palace, or elsewhere on a journey; nor may our people go with their people, nor our horses or other livestock go to pasture with their animals, nor may we dwell [Col. 0790C] or remain together with them, nor have any participation with them except for the purpose of correction, lest we and our people perish together with them because of their iniquities and crimes, which God forbid.

For we know that the righteous perish on account of the wicked.

If you wish us to regard such people as faithful, separate them from us and confine them under public penance in a prison, and grant what has been requested.

Therefore command that all these matters be inserted into the ecclesiastical writings and ordered to be included among your chapters, so that they may be preserved in future times without any concealment by you and us, or by your and our successors. It is clear to everyone that this has been done.

### 371. That bishops should not go to war

[Col. 0790D] Grant of the lord Emperor Charles.

We wish it to be known to all that we desire to grant not only those things which you have requested concerning the harassment of bishops and priests by military expeditions, and which you have asked to be done for our benefit and yours, but also whatever you may find beneficial for the holy Church of God, for the priests, for the whole people, and for you.

At present, as you have requested, we grant these matters. When, with God’s help and while life endures, we come to the general assembly, we desire, with the counsel of all our faithful, to confirm them in writing, so that they may remain inviolable through the firm assistance of the Lord for our times, for the times of our successors, and for the future.

[Col. 0791A] For now we are ready to establish those things which are general and appropriate to all orders, and to transmit them to all the faithful of the holy Church of God and to our own people for the love and remembrance of almighty God. At our next synodal assembly and general meeting, where many bishops and counts will have gathered, we shall confirm these matters as you have requested. [Note: [Col. 0791] G.: *synodale*, “synodal.”]

### 372. From the foregoing: concerning all priests

First of all we admonish that the Catholic faith be carefully read by presbyters and bishops and preached to all the people, because this is the first commandment of the almighty Lord in the Law, which says: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God.” And he is to be loved with all the heart, with all the mind, and with all the strength. [Note: [Col. 0791] G.: “From the foregoing, concerning all priests.”]

### 573. From the foregoing: concerning everyone generally

Let there be peace, concord, and unanimity with all the Christian people. Let bishops, abbots, counts, judges, and all persons everywhere, greater or lesser, maintain peace. [Note: [Col. 0791] G.: *personas*, “persons.”]

For nothing is pleasing to God without peace, nor is the offering of the holy sacrifice pleasing at the altar, as is read in the Gospel at the Lord’s own command. For this is also the second commandment: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”

Likewise in the Gospel: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God.” [Col. 0791B] And again: “By this everyone will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.”

By this commandment the sons of God and the sons of the devil are distinguished: for the sons of the devil always strive to stir up dissensions and discord, while the sons of God always devote themselves to peace and love.

### 374. From the foregoing: concerning everyone generally

We also have this commandment in the Law of the Lord: “You shall not practice divination.” [Note: [Col. 0791] Bal.: “You shall not augur.”] And in Deuteronomy: “Let no one inquire of diviners, observe dreams, or attend to omens.” Likewise: “Let no one be a sorcerer, enchanter, or consulter of the pythoness.” [Note: [Col. 0791] G.: “consulter.”]

Therefore we command that there be no lot-casters (*cauculatores*), enchanters, storm-makers, [Note: [Col. 0791] G. has “or those who cast spells or enchanters”; G. also has “or storm-makers” written above the line.] or spellbinders, and wherever they are found, they must be corrected or condemned. [Note: [Col. 0791] These words are absent in G.]

Likewise, concerning trees, stones, or springs where foolish people perform illuminations or other observances, we absolutely command that this most wicked practice, abominable to God, be removed and destroyed wherever it is found.

### 375. From the foregoing: concerning everyone generally

Likewise, let homicides not be committed within the country, as they are forbidden by the Law of the Lord, whether for the sake of vengeance, greed, or robbery. Wherever such acts are found, let them be punished by our judges according to the law and by our command. Let no one be killed except when the law commands it. [Note: [Col. 0791] G.: *inventi*, “they are found.”]

### 376. From the foregoing: concerning all priests

Let bishops carefully examine the presbyters throughout their dioceses, so that they know well their faith, baptism, and celebration of Masses; so that they hold the correct faith and observe Catholic baptism; so that they understand the prayers of the Mass well; so that they chant the psalms suitably according to the divisions of the verses; and so that they themselves understand the Lord’s Prayer and preach it to everyone in an intelligible manner, so that each person may know what he asks of God.

Let “Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit” be sung among all with complete honor, and let the priest himself, with all the angels and peoples of God, sing with one voice: “Holy, Holy, Holy.” [Note: [Col. 0791] G. originally had *communa*, corrected by the same hand to *communi*; Bal.: *cum una*, “with one.”]

Presbyters and deacons must also be told in every way not to carry weapons, but rather to trust in God’s protection [Note: [Col. 0791] B.: “in prayer”] more than in weapons.

### 377. From the foregoing: partly concerning priests, partly concerning the people

We have also decided to admonish Your Reverence that each of you should see to it throughout his diocese that the Church of God receives its honor, and that the altars likewise be venerated according to their dignity. Let neither the house of God nor the consecrated altars be accessible to dogs.

Let the vessels consecrated to God be kept with great reverence, and let the consecrated sacrifices [Col. 0792A] be collected with great care by those who are worthy, or be preserved with honor. Let no secular business or empty glory be pursued in churches, because the house of God ought to be a house of prayer, not a den of thieves.

Let them keep their minds attentive to God when they come to the solemn celebrations of Mass, and let them not leave before the completion of the priestly blessing.

“There are six things which the Lord hates, and the seventh his soul detests: haughty eyes, a lying tongue, hands that shed innocent blood, a heart devising wicked plans, feet swift to run into evil, a deceitful witness, and one who sows discord among brothers.”

Whoever is wise according to God is blessed according to God. It is better to see what you desire than to desire what you do not know. Where there is pride, there will also be insult; but where there is humility, there is wisdom. Where there is no governor, the people will fall into ruin. It is better where there are many counsels; for God is in heaven, and you are upon earth. Therefore let your words be few. Many cares produce dreams, and in many words folly is found.

We beseech everyone to maintain good and exemplary conduct, as the Lord himself commanded in the Gospel: “Let your light shine before people, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.” Thus, through their good conduct, many may be drawn to the service of God.

Let them gather and associate with themselves not only children of servile condition but also the sons of freeborn people. [Note: [Col. 0791] G.: “let them be gathered.”] Let schools for the children of the Gentiles be established.

Let every monastery and bishopric possess psalms, musical notation, chant, computation, grammar, and carefully corrected Catholic books. For often, when they wish to pray properly to God, they pray wrongly because of corrupt books.

Do not allow your boys to be corrupted either by reading or by writing. [Note: [Col. 0791] Bal.: “Do not allow them [*eos* is absent] …”] If it is necessary to write a Gospel book, Psalter, or Missal, [Note: [Col. 0791] Bal.: *missalem*] let men of mature age write it [Col. 0792C] with complete care.

### 378. From the foregoing: concerning everyone generally

Let everyone possess equal, correct measures and just and equal weights, whether in cities or monasteries, whether for giving or receiving, as we have the commandment in the Law of the Lord.

Likewise in Solomon, with the Lord saying: “A weight and a weight, a measure and a measure, my soul hates.”

This also seems fitting and worthy to us: that guests, pilgrims, and the poor should have regular and canonical hospitality at various places. For the Lord himself will say at the recompense of the great day: “I was a guest, and you received me.”

And the Apostle, praising hospitality, said: “Through this some pleased God, receiving angels as guests.”

### 379. From the foregoing: partly concerning priests, partly concerning the people

Likewise, let these dealers (*mangones*) and brokers or auctioneers (*cociones*), who wander about without any law through this land, not be permitted to wander and deceive people. They go about naked, carrying iron, saying that a penance has been imposed upon them somewhere. [Note: [Col. 0791] G. has a difficult reading: “who, naked with iron, roam about saying that penance was given to them somewhere.”]

It seems better that if they have committed some unusual and capital crime, they should remain in one place, laboring, serving, and performing penance according to what has been canonically imposed upon them.

### 380. From the foregoing: concerning everyone generally

We establish, according to what the Lord commanded in the Law, that servile labor not be performed on Sundays, just as our father of good memory commanded in his synodal edicts that men should not engage in such work: neither gathering in the vineyard, nor plowing, reaping, or cutting hay in the fields, nor building a fence, nor uprooting thorns, nor cutting trees, nor working in stone, nor constructing houses; nor should they work in the garden, assemble for a public meeting, or go hunting.

But if extreme necessity arises, let them perform only three tasks and no others: that is, transporting military supplies, transporting provisions, or, if it should happen to be necessary, carrying someone’s body to the grave.

Likewise, women should not perform textile work [Note: [Col. 0793] absent in Bal.], nor cut, sew, or perform combing work; they should not card wool, beat flax, wash clothing in public, or shear sheep. Thus Sunday may be honored in every way and rest observed, so that people may freely come from everywhere to the solemn celebrations of Mass and to the church and praise God for all the good things he did for us on that day.

For we read, as the Apostle says: “The works of the flesh are manifest: fornication, impurity, licentiousness, idolatry, sorcery, enmities, quarrels, rivalries, animosities, anger, strife, dissensions, heresies, sects, envy, murders, drunkenness, revelries, and things like these. I warn you, as I warned you before, that those who do such things will not possess the kingdom of God.”

Therefore prohibit with zeal these very things which the great preacher individually named in the Church of God, understanding how dreadful is what he said: “Those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God.”

With every diligence preach the faith that must be held in the Lord. Concerning humility and patience, chastity and self-restraint, kindness and mercy, almsgiving and confession of one’s sins, admonish everyone also to forgive all their debtors their debts according to the Lord’s Prayer.

### 381. From the foregoing: concerning all priests

Bishops must strive to encourage dissenting brothers toward peace rather than toward litigation.

Ecclesiastical and canonical authority teaches that councils should not be celebrated without the authorization of the Roman pontiff. [Col. 0793C]

Let bishops provide intercession for those who are oppressed by unjust force.

No bishop who has been summoned concerning certain crimes should be heard except in a legitimate synod, assembled at the proper time by apostolic and canonical summons.

Let no one presume to accuse a bishop before secular judges, but before his own primates.

Canonical authority completely rejects accusers and accusations which the laws of the world do not accept. [Note: [Col. 0793] “or of God” is written above the line in G.]

It is not fitting that a primate be weakened by various slanders and accusations, but rather that he be strengthened by the rules of the fathers. For Pope Liberius was also driven into exile for two years on behalf of Athanasius, and many other bishops who refused to condemn him were condemned to exile. All priests ought to follow their example.

Detraction carries great weight when the detractor is believed worthy of credence. Therefore not everyone is to be admitted, but only men of the highest probity. First, the person, credibility, life, and conduct of the accusers must always be investigated. Afterwards, the matters brought forward must be carefully examined; for nothing ought to be done otherwise unless the life of those who bring the charge has first been scrutinized.

No one has authority to judge or condemn any cleric before he has the accusers present and grants him an opportunity to defend himself [Note: [Col. 0793] *l. se d.* Bal.] and clear himself of the charges.

Every accusation is to be heard within the province and decided by the bishops of that province. The permission to accuse must not extend beyond the boundaries of the province.

A bishop must not litigate, even when challenged, over transitory matters.

It is not right to judge or condemn a man whose case has not been fully investigated.

[Col. 0794A] A greater cannot be judged by a lesser.

It is not the function of a judge to judge or condemn anyone without a legitimate accuser; for the Lord knew that Judas was a thief, but because he was not accused, he was not expelled.

The holy canons have decreed that bishops who have been expelled and stripped of their possessions are to be received back into their own sees, and that everything belonging to them must first be lawfully restored to them. Afterwards, if anyone wished to accuse them, they established that he must do so at equal risk, decreeing that the judges should be bishops who rightly understood the matter, assembled in the church, where witnesses would be present for each of those who appeared to have been oppressed.

It was resolved that if any person believes that he has a private claim against a bishop or against the administrators of a church, he should first have recourse to him in a spirit of charity, so that, having been admonished in a friendly conversation, he may remedy the matters brought forward as complaints. If he wishes to delay this matter [Note: [Col. 0793] G. reads *deferre*, “to defer,” for *differre*, “to delay”], let him receive the sentence of excommunication.

[Col. 0794B] If any cases or disputes arise between clerics and laymen, whether of higher or lower rank, it was resolved that, in accordance with the Nicene Council, the dispute should be settled after all the bishops of the same province have assembled. No one may, to the prejudice of the Roman Church—whose reverence is owed and must be preserved in every case—abandon those priests who, by divine appointment, govern the churches of God in the same province and hasten to other provinces, or seek or submit to the judgment of bishops from other provinces, unless an appeal has been made. If anyone should presume to do so, he is to be judged by all as both deposed from the clerical office and guilty of injury.

But if more important cases have arisen, they are to be referred by episcopal judgment to the Apostolic See, as the holy synod has decreed and venerable custom requires.

The decrees of the Council of Nicaea and of the African Council very wisely and justly determined that all cases should be concluded in their own places, where they arose—especially since everyone has been granted the right, if offended by the judgment of those who heard the case, to appeal to the councils of his province or even to a universal council.

When the rule written concerning the administration of government is observed, it is clear that matters belonging to each province are administered by the synod of that province, as is established by the decree of the Council of Nicaea.

If any bishop is accused of specific crimes, he is to be heard or judged by all the bishops who are in the province.

Whatever pertains to the observance of religion is to be heard in its proper places and by the synods of its own diocese.

Each province is to be content with its metropolitan and its fellow-provincial bishops.

“Cursed is everyone who moves his neighbor’s boundary markers.” And all the people shall say: “Amen.” And so forth.

Those who are bishops beyond the diocese [Note: [Col. 0793] G. reads *quae*, “which,” for *qui*, “who”] must by no means approach churches that lie outside the boundaries assigned to them, nor disturb them by any presumption.

The boundaries established by the Fathers must not be transferred, so that one person may invade another’s parish and presume to celebrate the divine mysteries there without the knowledge of the bishop [Note: [Col. 0793] *eo* G.; “to him”] to whom it has been entrusted.

### 382. From the capitularies enacted by Lord King Charles in the eleventh year of his reign. Concerning those who, within the kingdom, seize anything by force without royal command

If anyone in the army, within the kingdom, wishes to plunder anything by hostile force without royal command, whether to take hay or grain, larger or smaller cattle, or to break into or burn houses, we absolutely prohibit these things from being done. If any presumptuous person does this, let him, if he is free, be liable to sixty solidi [Col. 0795A] and restore all similar property, or purge himself with twelve witnesses [Note: [Col. 0795] *t. depurget* G.; “let him purge himself completely,” from *depurget*]. But if a slave does this, let him be subject to capital punishment, and let his master restore all similar property, because he neither corrected nor guarded his slave so that he would not commit such acts—for if we consume ourselves, we shall quickly perish. Nevertheless, let each man guard his own army, so that no plundering may take place within the kingdom, if he does not wish to amend by law whatever those entrusted to him have done unjustly [Note: [Col. 0795] *fecerint* Bal.; “they have done”]. For it is right that masters or commanders render an account for those entrusted to them, if they have carried out any plunder or acted unjustly, because they have not corrected them in such a way that they would not dare to commit such acts.

### 383. From the capitularies of Lord Louis at Ingelheim [Note: [Col. 0795] *Ingilinum* G.; “at Ingelheim”], enacted by apostolic authority and synodal decree, with the general consent and exhortation of all, both clerics and laymen

If anyone commits robbery within the kingdom or forcibly takes anything from one of our faithful or from his man, let him pay legally three times the value of what he took, and in addition pay our ban, that is, sixty solidi, to us. Afterwards let him be brought before us by the count, so that, shut up in the prison, he may suffer punishment until it pleases us. If the act was committed publicly, let him perform public penance for it according to the decree of the holy canons; but if secretly, let him perform penance for it on the advice of the priests. For, as the Apostle says, robbers will not possess the kingdom of God unless they perform true penance. Whoever takes anything belonging to churches is to be judged more severely for it, because the taking of sacred things is sacrilege, and one who takes or steals anything from them is called a sacrilegious person. Such persons are to be kept away from the thresholds of holy Mother Church until they have made satisfaction to the church they injured, and they are to be branded with infamy.

### 384. Concerning one who, by a malicious conspiracy, grants permission for plunder, so that he is burned alive

If anyone, by a criminal conspiracy, grants permission for plunder, or if anyone divides what has been plundered, let him be burned alive.

[Col. 0795C] ### 385. That the presumptuous harassment of church estates be removed by all

The insult of such usurpation must be removed by everyone, so that estates dedicated to heavenly sacred purposes are not harassed by certain intruders. If anyone should presume to do so, after the severity of the due punishment that must lawfully be inflicted upon sacrilegious persons, let him be punished by public deportation into exile.

### 386. That one who is found to have committed violence receive capital punishment

One who is discovered to have committed manifest violence is no longer to be punished by relegation or deportation to an island, but is to receive capital punishment. The sentence pronounced against him is not to be suspended by an intervening appeal [Note: [Col. 0795] *fuerit* Bal.; “has been”], because many crimes are contained under the single name of violence: when some attempt to inflict force on others, while others resist indignantly, beatings and killings are frequently found to have been committed. Therefore it was resolved that if someone should happen to be killed, whether from the side of the possessor or from that of the person who attempted to violate the possession, punishment is to be inflicted upon the one who attempted to use force and gave either party the cause of the evils [Note: [Col. 0795] *exeri*; G. has *exequi*, “to carry out,” superscribed by the same hand].

[Col. 0795D] ### 387. Concerning one who usurps a position not owed to him

If anyone usurps a position not owed to him, let him not defend himself by claiming ignorance; and let the one who attempts this be fully liable for sacrilege.

### 388. That whatever different rulers have established concerning the holy churches remain inviolate

Whatever different rulers have established concerning the most holy churches, we command to remain inviolate.

### 389. That if anyone’s rashness corrupts the privileges of a church, he be punished by a penalty of five pounds of gold

If anyone’s rashness violates the venerable privileges of a church, or neglects them through dissimulation, let him be punished for the offense by a condemnation of five pounds of gold [Note: [Col. 0795] *deest* G.; “is lacking” in G.].

[Col. 0796A] ### 390. That what different rulers have established, or individual bishops have obtained for ecclesiastical causes, be preserved perpetually and unshaken

Whatever has been established by different rulers, or whatever individual bishops have obtained for ecclesiastical causes, is to be preserved under the penalty of perpetual sacrilege and with enduring permanence. Clerics are to be reserved not for secular judges but for episcopal judgment; for it is not right that ministers of the divine office be subjected to the discretion of temporal powers.

### 391. Concerning the privileges of churches, that they remain uncorrupted

We command that the privileges granted by law to churches and clerics remain uncorrupted.

### 392. That what has been given to the holy churches of God ought to be preserved rather than taken away

It is unjust and akin to sacrilege that what anyone has given or certainly left to a venerable church for the salvation or repose of his soul should be taken away and transferred elsewhere by those who above all ought to have preserved it.

[Col. 0796B] ### 393. That laymen, even if religious, have no authority granted to them to dispose of church property

It is nowhere recorded that laymen, even if religious, have ever been granted any authority to dispose of ecclesiastical possessions.

### 394. That plunderers of a church are sacrilegious, as is proved by the testimony of Scripture

Plunderers of a church are sacrilegious. Thus it is also decreed in the Council of Agde, under its fourth chapter, as follows: “To steal something from a friend is theft; but to defraud, remove, or secretly take something from a church is sacrilege.” For all who act against the laws, and who plunder the property of the church or harass churches and priests contrary to divine decrees, are called sacrilegious and must undoubtedly be regarded as infamous and sacrilegious.

### 395. That what is consecrated to the Lord belongs to ecclesiastical jurisdiction

What is offered or consecrated to the Lord belongs to the jurisdiction of the priests. All who take these things away or transfer them elsewhere are sacrilegious.

[Col. 0796C] ### 396. That if anyone presumes to claim a dignity he has not deserved from a ruler or a just elder, he be regarded as sacrilegious

If anyone presumes to claim a dignity he has not deserved from a ruler or an elder, let him be regarded as sacrilegious.

### 397. That those implicated in various crimes not be admitted as witnesses

Murderers, evil-doers, thieves, sacrilegious persons, robbers, poisoners, adulterers, those who have committed abduction or given false testimony, and those who have resorted to diviners and magicians are in no way to be admitted either for accusation or as witnesses.

### 398. That a judge not hurl a sentence against an accused person before he confesses or his associates convict him

A judge investigating a criminal must not pronounce a capital sentence before either the accused himself confesses or he is clearly convicted by innocent witnesses or by his associates in the crime.

### 399. That absent persons are not to be judged

No judgment is to be made against absent persons. If this is done, the sentence pronounced shall have no validity.

[Col. 0796D] ### 400. That no bishop oppress another bishop

No bishop is to oppress another bishop, overstep him, or cause him any harm in his parish.

### 401. Concerning a deposed bishop who appeals to the Roman pontiff

If a deposed bishop proclaims in the city of Rome that his case is to be heard, no other bishop is to be ordained to his see after the appeal of the one who appears to have been deposed, unless the case has been determined by the judgment of the Roman bishop.

### 402. That detractors or revilers not attack the preachers of the church; this is condemned by canonical Scripture

All the faithful and all orders must take the greatest care not to tear apart, secretly or publicly, the Lord’s anointed by detraction and reviling, considering the example of Mary, who, because she spoke against Moses, the servant of the Lord, on account of the Ethiopian woman, was punished with the uncleanness of leprosy. And consider the Psalmist’s words: “Do not touch my anointed ones, and do not act wickedly against my prophets.” And the Lord says through Moses: “You shall not speak evil of the gods, nor curse the ruler of your people.” If David, the most just of kings, did not presume to lay a hand upon Saul, although it was already established that he had been rejected and cast off by the Lord, how much more must care be taken lest anyone lay the hand of detraction, reviling, indiscretion, or dishonor upon the Lord’s anointed and upon the preachers of the holy church of God.

### 403. That bishops ought to correct one another if anything should arise among them

The emperor Constantine said concerning accusations against bishops: “These accusations have their proper time, namely, the day of the great judgment, and their judge is the one who will then judge everyone. Therefore, since I am a man appointed to this office, it is not permitted for me to hold a hearing concerning such matters—that is, concerning priests who are both accusers and accused—for it is wholly unfitting that such men should be shown to be judged by others.” The emperor Valentinian likewise said concerning the cases of bishops: “Your affair,” he said, “is above us. Therefore conduct your cases among yourselves, because you are above us.” And so forth.

### 404. Concerning sacrilegious persons, that they are thieves, as Scripture bears witness

Everyone must know that all who plunder, devastate, invade, and harass the property of the church, or unjustly alienate it from the jurisdiction of the churches to which it had been entrusted, are sacrilegious thieves. Thus the most blessed Augustine says in the forty-eighth homily on the Gospel of John:

“Behold, Judas is among the holy ones; behold, Judas is a thief. And do not despise him: he is a sacrilegious thief, not an ordinary thief, a thief of purses, but of the Lord’s purses, of sacred purses. If crimes are distinguished in court between ordinary theft and embezzlement—for *peculatus* [Note: [Col. 0797] *peculator* G.; G. reads “embezzler,” while *peculatus* means “embezzlement from public property”] means theft from public property, and theft from private property is not judged in the same way as theft from public property—how much more severely must the sacrilegious thief be judged, who dared not to take something from just anywhere, but to take it from the church? Whoever takes or steals anything from the church is compared with the lost Judas.”

Note that blessed Augustine affirms that taking anything from the church is theft [Note: [Col. 0797] *n. aliquid quod* G.; G. reads *aliquid quod*, “something that”], calls the perpetrator of so great a theft a sacrilegious thief, and even compares him with the lost Judas. And shortly afterwards:

“Why,” he says, “did he have purses, when angels ministered to him, unless it was because his church was going to have its own purses?”

See by the teachings of so great a doctor how we are instructed: what went before in the Head appears to have been fulfilled in his Body, which is the church. Moreover, we know that Christ and the church are one person. Therefore what belongs to the church belongs to Christ; what is offered to the church is offered to Christ; and what is taken away from his church is unquestionably taken away from Christ.

Suppose it was destined that the church of Christ would have money. If money, then certainly also estates, slaves, and countless ornaments of various kinds. And because it is unlawful to take away what is given to the church, the words of blessed Jerome, writing in his exposition of the Gospel of Matthew, bear witness as follows:

“All who misuse the temple offerings and those things that are contributed for the uses of the church in other matters, so as to fulfill their own will, are like the scribes and priests who purchased the lie and the blood of the Savior.”

### 405. That whatever is offered to the Lord is the holy of holies and belongs to the jurisdiction of the priests [Note: [Col. 0797] *deest* G.; “is lacking” in G.]

No one may be ignorant that everything consecrated to the Lord—whether it is a human being, an animal, a field, or anything whatever—once it has been consecrated, will be the holy of holies to the Lord and belongs to the jurisdiction of the priests. Therefore everyone who takes away, devastates, invades, or plunders these things from the Lord and from the church to which they belong will be without excuse [Col. 0798A] until he has made correction and satisfaction to the church [Note: [Col. 0797] *ecclesiae. que* corrected to *et* G.; “and to the church”]. He is a sacrilegious person, and not merely sacrilegious but also a sacrilegious thief [Note: [Col. 0797] *et quod* Bal.; “and that”].

### 406. Concerning those sacrilegious persons who inflict injuries upon the church and its priests

If anyone breaks out into this kind of sacrilege, invading churches and their property and inflicting or imposing any injury upon priests, ministers, the worship itself, or the place, to the injury of divine worship, he must know that, once convicted or confessed, he is to be punished by capital sentence. The bishop need not be expected to demand vengeance for his own injury; holiness leaves to him alone the glory of forgiveness [Note: [Col. 0797] *dereliquit* Bal.; “has left”]. Let it be not only permitted but even praiseworthy for everyone to prosecute as a public crime the atrocious injuries inflicted upon priests or ministers and to obtain vengeance against such criminals.

### 407. That everything offered to God is unquestionably also consecrated

Everything that is offered to the Lord is unquestionably consecrated to the Lord. It is not only the sacrifices that priests consecrate to the Lord upon the altar that are called the offerings of the faithful; whatever is offered to him by the faithful [Note: [Col. 0797] *quaecunque ei a f. offeruntur* Bal.; “whatever is offered to him by the faithful”]—whether slaves, fields, vineyards, woods, meadows, waters or watercourses, crafts, books, utensils, stones, buildings, clothing, skins, woolen goods, livestock, pastures, parchment, movable or immovable property, or anything whatever among these things that is made for the praise of God or can provide support for the holy church of God, its priests, and its adornment—when voluntarily offered by anyone to the Lord and his church [Note: [Col. 0797] Bal. reads *sine*; G. corrects *siue* to *suae*, “his”], is unquestionably consecrated to the Lord and belongs to the jurisdiction of the priests.

And because we truly acknowledge that Christ and the church are one person, whatever belongs to the church belongs to Christ. Whatever is offered to the church, whether among the things mentioned above or in any other form, whether by promises, pledges, writings, or bodily goods, is offered to Christ [Col. 0798C]. Whatever is alienated or taken away from his church by any device—whether by alienating, devastating, invading, diminishing, or plundering—is taken away from Christ.

If stealing something from a friend is theft, then especially taking, alienating, secretly appropriating, or devastating anything from Christ our Lord, who is King of kings and Lord of lords, is sacrilege. For all plunderers of the church are manifestly sacrilegious. No one who commits sacrilege will possess the kingdom of God except through pure, proven, and public penance, satisfaction to the church, and reconciliation through the laying on of the bishops’ hands, according to the canonical decrees. Such a person is not only alienated from the kingdom of God but also, until the aforesaid satisfaction, is excluded from the thresholds of the holy church, especially from the church he injured.

Until the aforesaid satisfaction, we must in no way communicate with the perpetrators of such crimes, whether living or dead. For one who steals his neighbor’s money commits iniquity; but one who takes away the church’s money commits sacrilege. Such persons are not only sacrilegious but also sacrilegious thieves, wolves, and murderers—killers of the poor [Note: [Col. 0797] absent in Bal.—*deest*; “is lacking”]—and, moreover, are condemned before God and his saints by the bond of anathema.

### 408. That Christians not contract marriages within the closeness of their own blood relationship [Note: [Col. 0797] *c. conducant* G.; G. reads *conducant*, “let them contract”]

Christians are not to contract marriages within the closeness of their own blood relationship. Nor may they dare to marry virgins without the blessing of a priest, or presume to take widows without the consent and approval of their priests and the people.

### 409. Concerning one who joins himself in an incestuous relationship to persons whom the divine decrees prohibit

If anyone, without regard to the proper degree [Note: [Col. 0797] *q. non eo gradu sed i.* G.; “not in that degree but in an incestuous one”], joins himself in an incestuous relationship to persons whom the divine decrees prohibit, let both be deprived of communion until they demonstrate their repentance by separation. They shall have neither the right to hold military service in the palace nor permission to conduct lawsuits in the courts.

For bishops or priests in whose diocese or district the act occurred are to announce to the king or judges the crime committed by those who have joined themselves in incest in the manner described above [Note: [Col. 0799] *nam quomodo predicti* G.; “for in the manner described above”], so that, once it has been reported to them [Note: [Col. 0799] *epis* G.; an abbreviation or corrupt reading, apparently referring to “bishops”], they may separate themselves from their communion or cohabitation.

Their property is to pass to their nearest relatives until the separation, under this condition: before they are separated, it must not reach their own possession by any device—neither through relatives, purchase, nor royal authority—unless they acknowledge the aforementioned crime by separation and penance [Note: [Col. 0799] *separationem et poenitentiam* G.; “separation and penance”].

### 410. From Book 3, chapter 11, of the laws of Theodosius, concerning incest

Incestuous persons are not legitimate heirs, but both persons are to be branded with infamy.

[Col. 0799B] ### 411. That no one take as a spouse a virgin or widow devoted to God

Henceforth, as the ecclesiastical canons prohibit, no one may take as a wife in an unlawful marriage—whether by force or consent—a virgin devoted to God, anyone living under a religious habit, a woman who has professed continence in widowhood, a near relative, or even a woman through whose union he could incur the mark of incestuous infamy. For a marriage cannot be genuine if it is led from a better purpose to a worse and consummated under a union bearing a false name, with incestuous pollution [Note: [Col. 0799] *c. incestiva, p.* Bal.] and the uncleanness of fornication.

If people of any nation, of either sex, attempt to commit this abomination from now on, let them, upon the intervention of a priest or judge, be separated in every way and relegated into perpetual exile [Note: [Col. 0799] *redigentur* G.; “they shall be reduced/relegated”], even if no one makes an accusation [Note: [Col. 0799] *accusator sit* Bal.; “there is an accuser”]. Nor, so long as they live, may they be excused by any prescribed time limit or by lapse of time [Note: [Col. 0799] Bal. reads *indefinitione*, “without limitation”].

### 412. That one who defiles himself with a woman consecrated to God commits blasphemy against God

You ought to know that one who defiles himself with a woman consecrated to God or with a veiled woman inflicts blasphemy upon God.

### 413. That a cleric be deprived of his proper honor if he has intercourse with a woman consecrated or veiled [Note: [Col. 0799] *D. s. v. v. s. c.* is omitted in G.; the abbreviated wording is absent there]

If a cleric defiles himself with a veiled woman or with a woman consecrated to God, let him be deprived of his proper honor.

### 414. That those who violate the bodies of consecrated women are sacrilegious and, according to the Apostle, sons of perdition

Everyone must know that the bodies of women consecrated to God are shown by the testimonies of Scripture to be temples consecrated to God through the vow of their own pledge and the words of the priest. Therefore those who violate them are recognized as sacrilegious and, according to the Apostle, sons of perdition.

### 415. That fornication is declared to be more dangerous than all other sins

Fornication is more serious and worse than almost all sins, and it can truly be called the snare of death, the pit of hell, and the abyss of destruction, because adulterers and lustful persons, through the poverty of their hearts, lose their souls. For, as Scripture says, the price of a prostitute is scarcely that of a loaf of bread; and whoever joins himself to a prostitute becomes one body with her; and whoever indulges in lust is dead in a living body.

### 416. What kinds of documents should have validity

Documents that clearly express the day and year and are known to have been written according to the order of the law, or that have been confirmed by the marks or subscriptions of their author or witnesses, are to be regarded as fully valid.

### 417. That an exchange have the same validity as a sale

An exchange, provided it has not been extorted by force or fear, is to have the same validity as a sale.

[Col. 0800A] ### 418. Concerning the excommunication of judges and powerful men who do not amend their conduct

Judges or powerful men who oppress the poor are to be excommunicated if, after being admonished by their bishop, they do not amend their conduct.

### 419. That incestuous marriages be corrected by the judgment of bishops

We command that, according to the decrees of the canons, adulteries and incestuous marriages that are not legitimate be prohibited and corrected by the judgment of the bishops.

### 420. That everyone remain in the place where he has vowed to remain [Note: [Col. 0799] *voverunt* G.; “they vowed”]

Let everyone remain in the place where he was established and where he made his vow, and there let him fulfill his vows.

### 421. That union with a spiritual co-mother is a grave sin

Everyone must know that union with a spiritual co-mother is a grave sin, to be dissolved by divorce and punished by capital sentence, or removed by perpetual pilgrimage.

### 422. Concerning one who practices pagan observances

We have decreed, as our predecessors or ancestors once decreed, that anyone who practices pagan observances in any matter be fined and condemned to fifteen solidi.

### 423. An order that Christian slaves not be handed over to pagans or Jews [Note: [Col. 0799] *precipio* G.; “I command”]

We command everyone generally that Christian slaves not be handed over to pagans or Jews.

### 424. That everyone know how great an evil it is to defile those consecrated to God

We command everyone to know, and all priests to preach and denounce under penalty of sacrilege, how great an evil and how enormous a crime it is to have intercourse with women devoted to God—widows or virgins—whether veiled or consecrated to God, and especially with nuns and virgins or widows consecrated to God, both in monasteries and outside them.

For there is no doubt that this sin is twofold. To give an example: what punishment would a servant deserve before his master if he violated his master’s wife by adultery? How much more the man who has defiled by the corruption of his lust the bride of Christ, the Creator of heaven and earth, when blessed Paul the Apostle says: “Do you not know that your bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit?” And elsewhere: “Do you not know that you are the temple of God and that the Spirit of God dwells in you? If anyone violates the temple of God, God will destroy him; for the temple of God is holy, and that is what you are.”

Again, he joins adulterers and fornicators with the service of idolatry in his enumeration of sins, saying: “Do you not know that the unrighteous will not possess the kingdom of God? Do not be deceived: neither fornicators, nor those who serve idols, nor adulterers, nor the effeminate, nor men who lie with males, nor thieves, nor the greedy, nor drunkards, nor revilers, nor robbers will possess the kingdom of God.”

### 425. That, because the necessity of wars compels it, a portion of the money owed to the church be retained for a certain time under a precarious grant and an annual rent

With the counsel of the servants of God and the Christian people, on account of the imminent wars and persecutions of the other nations that surround us [Note: [Col. 0799] *qui* G.; “which,” where the source has *quae*, “which” feminine], we agree that, under a precarious grant and an annual rent, we may retain for a certain time a portion of the church’s property for the assistance of our army, with God’s permission. The condition is that each year one solidus—that is, twelve denarii—be returned to the church or monastery from each household [*casata*]. This is to be done in such a way that, if the person to whom the property was lent dies, the church receives back its own property; and, if necessity again compels it and the ruler commands, the precarious grant is renewed and a new document is written [Note: [Col. 0799] *et* Bal.; “and”].

This must be observed absolutely, so that the churches or monasteries whose property has been granted under a precarious grant do not suffer want and poverty. But if poverty compels it, the full possession is to be restored to the church and the house of God.

### 426. That no one presume to invade the privileges or possessions of churches, or anything belonging to them [Note: [Col. 0801] *In* G.; “that”]

We command all subject to our authority that no one presume to violate the privileges of churches or monasteries, invade, devastate, or alienate church property, plunder their possessions, or attempt to possess them without a precarious grant [Note: [Col. 0801] *precario* G.; “under a precarious grant”]. For, as we have been instructed by the holy Fathers, this is known to be a very grave sin, as the sacred Scripture testifies, saying: “Whoever takes anything from his father or mother and says that this is not a sin is a participant in murder.”

Our Father is undoubtedly God, who created us; our mother is the church, which spiritually regenerated us in baptism [Note: [Col. 0801] *sic etiam* G.; “likewise” in G., with the letter *u* written above]. Therefore whoever defrauds, steals, devastates, or alienates the money of Christ and of the church will be judged a murderer in the sight of the just Judge. Concerning this, one of the wise says: “Whoever steals his neighbor’s money commits iniquity; but whoever takes away the church’s money commits sacrilege.”

### 427. That neither the king nor any secular person seize by force the estates of churches governed by bishops, abbots, or abbesses [Note: [Col. 0801] *quae* Bal.; “which”]

Correcting ourselves and giving an example to our successors, we generally forbid any layman, emperor, king, prefect, or count, supported by secular power, to seize for himself by violence, to claim from us as due to himself, or in any way presume to invade a monastery, estates, or any property under the authority of a bishop, abbot, or abbess. Nor may he begin to govern in place of the abbot, keep monks under his authority, or possess property that was purchased by the blood of Christ.

The ancient Fathers called such a man a robber, a sacrilegious person, a murderer of the poor, and a wolf of the devil entering the sheepfold of Christ; he is especially to be condemned by the bond of anathema before the tribunal of Christ.

Concerning such men, remember the words of the holy Apostle Paul to Timothy [Col. 0801C]: “Command those who are rich in this world not to be arrogant or to set their hope on uncertain riches, but on God, who provides everything.”

If such persons do not accept the church’s correction, they are like the pagans and publicans, with whom the church of God communicates neither in life nor in death. Against such persons, who are found both here and there [Note: [Col. 0801] *t. et hic quiedbi r.* G.; the wording is corrupt or abbreviated and remains materially uncertain], let us sound the trumpet of God [Note: [Col. 0801] omitted in G.], lest by remaining silent we be condemned and perish together with them.

If the man who acts impiously is horrible to God, then such a person is certainly separated from God and is justly subjected to anathema. For anathema signifies nothing other than separation from God, just as judgment concerning anathema signifies in the Old and New Testaments.

### 428. Concerning those who not only contribute something of their own property to the church but also unjustly possess what has been contributed by others

It has pleased us, and it is fitting that all observe, that since some people, mindful of themselves, are proved by various documents to have contributed something from their possessions to churches for the remedy of their souls, while this property is now held by various people who fear God less with deadly cunning [Col. 0801D], so that another’s offering becomes their ruin—and they cannot contemplate in their hearts the day of the Lord’s judgment—anyone who, forgetful of his own death, presumes unjustly to possess and retain property assigned to churches, as we said above [Note: [Col. 0801] *possederit* Bal.; “has possessed”], and, having learned the truth, refuses to restore God’s property to his servants, is to be regarded by all the churches as separated from holy communion and as an outsider. He is to receive no other remedy unless he purges his guilt by making restitution of the property itself [Note: [Col. 0801] *n. cum culpam propriam v.* Bal.; “unless he has purged his own guilt”].

For one who dares to seize or unjustly possess ecclesiastical property is not worthy to be permitted to approach the altar of the Lord. Those who persist in this wicked defense are all to be judged murderers of the poor, because they have thus deprived them of their sustenance.

Nevertheless, priestly provision must be made so that clear admonition precedes punishment, and so that the one who unjustly took the usurped property restores it with equity [Note: [Col. 0801] *et* Bal.; “and”]. If he neglects this, and necessity afterwards compels it, let the priestly discipline, once prepared, strike the plunderer.

No one should attempt to administer property throughout the kingdoms [Note: [Col. 0801] *interregna* G.; “interregna,” literally “interregnums,” rather than *regna*, “kingdoms”] without the authority of his own bishop, because the power of God encloses the boundaries of all kingdoms under his singular dominion.

Whoever acts contrary to these our decrees, delays in correcting by law what he has neglected, or thereafter wishes to persist in the aforesaid wickedness, is to lose all the honors he appeared to possess, and is to be punished by us secularly and legally, strictly, firmly, and forcefully; and by the priests he is to be struck with the heavenly sword. If he does not correct himself, let him die not only excommunicated but also anathematized.

429. Concerning ecclesiastical property that is owed to it by right, so that it is not transferred elsewhere. All must know that it is sacrilege for ecclesiastical property to be unjustly removed in any way from the churches to which it rightfully belongs and transferred elsewhere. [Col. 0802B]

430. That those who devastate ecclesiastical property are reckoned before God as murderers. We wish everyone to know that those who take away the monies of Christ and the Church, and defraud, seize, devastate, or plunder His property, are reckoned before God as murderers, because they plunder the property of the poor, whom the Church ought to feed.

431. That those who commit sacrilege, adultery, predation, or devastation be punished by capital penalty. We prohibit sacrilege, adultery, predation, and devastation from being committed by anyone in our kingdom under penalty of death, so that if anyone voluntarily commits one of these offenses, or anything of this kind, he shall pay with his life, and all his property, both movable and immovable, shall be joined to our treasury or handed over to the Church whose property he has devastated, alienated, or taken away. For it is the greatest sacrilege to take away, devastate, alienate, invade, or steal the offerings of the faithful, which are the property of the churches [Note: [Col. 0801] G. has “or to steal”]. For, as Holy Scripture says, neither sacrilegious persons, nor adulterers, nor predators or devastators, who are robbers, shall possess the kingdom of God. And if those who plunder the property of their brothers are excluded from the kingdom of God, what do you think should be done to those who plunder or take away property dedicated to God? For the more gravely someone sins in the present age, the more gravely he will be tormented in hell. [Col. 0802C]

432. Concerning men: that they ought to love their wives in chastity and provide them, as the weaker vessel, with protection and every necessity. We wish everyone to know that, at the Lord’s command, men ought to love their wives in chastity; and, as the weaker vessel, each man ought faithfully to provide them with honor, protection, and everything necessary, insofar as he is able. This we also, who are the Lord’s ministers and do not carry God’s sword without cause, command all to do to the best of our ability, by episcopal authority in the place of all the bishops and by royal authority. [Note: [Col. 0801] Bal. has “all” instead of “everyone”].

[Col. 0802D]

433. Concerning preserving faith between husband and wife. We wish everyone to know—as we have also often been admonished by the Lord’s bishops and the other servants of God—that husbands ought truly to preserve faith and love toward their wives, and wives likewise toward their husbands, and not deviate from them in any way; and that married persons are not permitted to have either a paramour or a concubine.

434. That clerics of any order be not injured by laymen, nor accused before anyone other than bishops [Note: [Col. 0801] G. reads “of whatever orders, by any laymen”]. Neither a presbyter, nor a deacon, nor a subdeacon is to be dragged from the churches or suffer any injury without the knowledge of his bishop. Rather, whatever anyone has against them, let him bring it to the notice of their own bishop; and let the bishop, examining the case with justice leading the way, satisfy the mind of the person accusing the clerics. [Col. 0803A]

435. That those who accuse the innocent before the ruler or others be condemned [Note: [Col. 0803] Bal. reads “Concerning those”; Bal. omits “be condemned”]. Concerning those who are convicted of accusing innocent persons before rulers or judges: if the accuser is a cleric of higher rank, let him be degraded from the order of his office; but if he is a layman, let him suffer the penalty which the accused would have suffered had they been convicted. Moreover, if it is such a case that they ought to live [the transmitted wording is obscure], let them be subjected by the priests to public penance, so that their spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord. [Col. 0804A]

436. That clerics not be sued concerning cases which the secular laws do not admit [Note: [Col. 0803] G. reads “concerning cases which the secular laws dismiss”]. No cases are to be heard by ecclesiastical judges that are not contained in the laws or are known to be prohibited.

# BOOK THREE

[Col. 0803]

Some of these chapters, for the sake of the brevity and concision of the book of canons, have been excerpted by the lord Charles and by his most learned bishops—some from the beginning of a sentence, some from the middle, and some from the end. They are to be regarded as extremely necessary and retained in memory. The remaining chapters were enlarged both by those same men and later by the lord Hludowic, his son, and his nobles. [Note: [Col. 0803] omitted by Bal.]

[Col. 0803B]

1. Concerning the primacy of churches and priests. Let each church and each priest retain his own primacy, as has been established in the ancient canons.

2. That the entire order of clerics remain subject to its bishop. Clerics who are appointed in poorhouses [Note: [Col. 0803] G. reads “who are appointed in [uncertain reading]”], or who are ordained in monasteries or basilicas of martyrs, are to remain under the authority of the bishops who are in each city, according to the traditions of the holy fathers, and are not to break away from their own bishop through defiance. Whoever dares to overturn this arrangement in any way and does not submit to his own bishop is to be subjected to canonical correction if he is a cleric; but if he is a layman or monk, let him be deprived of communion.

3. That no cleric, abandoning his own bishop, migrate to secular affairs. It is not proper for a priest or cleric who has business against another to leave his own bishop and rush into secular affairs.

[Col. 0803C]

4. That presbyters or deacons presume nothing without the consent of their own bishop. Presbyters [Note: [Col. 0803] G. omits the actual words of the chapter] and deacons are not to attempt to do anything apart from the bishop.

5. That the period of penitence depend upon the bishop’s consideration. The power will belong to the bishops, after examining the conduct of penitents, either to deal with them more humanely or to add further time. Above all, however, their former and subsequent life is to be investigated, and humanity is to be shown to them accordingly.

6. Concerning the conduct and faith of penitents. The conduct and faith of penitents shorten the period.

7. Concerning offerings of produce bestowed upon the ministers of the Church. If anyone wishes to receive or give the Church’s offerings outside the church without the knowledge of the bishop or of the person entrusted with such duties, and does not wish to act with his advice, let him be anathema.

8. Concerning those things which are bestowed for the use of the poor [Note: [Col. 0803] G. omits this entire chapter]. If anyone gives or receives an offering apart from the bishop, or apart from the person appointed by him to distribute mercy to the poor, let both the giver and the receiver be anathema. [Col. 0803D]

9. That whoever violates a synodal excommunication have no hope of recovery in another synod. If any bishop condemned by a synod, or any presbyter or deacon condemned by his own bishop, should dare to touch anything belonging to the sacred ministry—whether a bishop according to the preceding custom, or a presbyter or deacon—he is in no way to be permitted to have hope of restoration or a place for satisfaction in another synod [Note: [Col. 0803] Bal. has “in another”]. Moreover, all who communicate with him are to be cast out of the Church [Note: [Col. 0803] Bal. and G. have “cast out,” but the text here immediately corrects it], especially if, after learning that this has happened, they attempt to communicate with him. [Col. 0804B]

10. That no one communicate with excommunicated persons or with those who abandon the churches. It is not permitted to communicate with excommunicated persons; nor is it permitted to pray together with those who meet in houses while avoiding the prayers of the Church. A person who does not assemble in one church is not to be received by another church.

11. Concerning suppressing disturbers of the Church. If anyone persists in disturbing and troubling the Church of God, let him, as a seditious person, be suppressed by external authorities.

12. That monks everywhere remain subject to their bishops. Monks in each city or region are to be subject to the bishop, love quiet, and devote themselves solely to fasting and prayer, remaining in the places where they have renounced the world. They are not to participate in either ecclesiastical or secular affairs, nor cause any disturbance by abandoning their own monasteries, unless perhaps they are ordered by the bishop of the city to do so for some necessary work. [Col. 0804C]

13. That each person minister in the church to which he has been ordained. A cleric ought to remain in the church to which he was first assigned by the bishop and to which he fled as to the superior one. Those who reject this are to be recalled to their own church, in which they were originally ordained, and minister there alone. If anyone transgresses this definition, the holy synod has decreed that he is to withdraw from his own rank.

14. Concerning receiving those who suffer persecution. We establish in every respect that those who suffer persecution from wicked or faithless persons are to be received by the just and faithful.

15. Concerning law and custom. Some matters are upheld by canon and order; others have been confirmed by custom.

16. Concerning not usurping another’s boundaries. It is forbidden for anyone to usurp another’s boundaries or, through payment or someone’s favor, to cross the limits established by the fathers. Nevertheless, new allegations, whether obscure or concealed under some category, when examined by us, are to be given their proper form; and what is censured in laymen ought much more to be condemned beforehand in clerics. The whole council said: “No one does anything against the prophets, no one against the Gospel or against the Apostle, without danger.” [Col. 0804D]

17. That transgressors of the canons be excommunicated. We command that whoever transgresses the definition of the canons be excommunicated.

18. That the bishop care for the monasteries. It is fitting for the competent bishop of the city to exercise oversight of the monasteries.

[Col. 0805A]

19. Concerning admonishing those who are ordained. If anyone is ordained a cleric, he ought to be admonished to observe the established rules.

20. Concerning satisfaction for penance. The satisfaction of penance is to be assessed not so much by the length of time as by contrition of heart.

21. Concerning the measure of penance. The periods of penance are to be established with moderation according to episcopal judgment [Note: [Col. 0805] Bal. has “of the bishop”], as the bishop sees the dispositions of those examined to be devoted; likewise, taking into consideration those of advanced age and the needs arising from any dangers or illnesses. [Note: [Col. 0805] G. has “fatherly consideration”].

22. Concerning avoiding the ordination of wicked men. Whoever ordains as priests men who ought not to be priests does not provide for the people but harm them; he does not furnish governance but increase danger.

23. Concerning bishops who have ordained unsuitable men. Those who, in ordaining priests, have neglected the statutes of the holy fathers and consecrated those whom they ought to have rejected—if any bishops have ordained such a priest as it is not permitted to be—although they may in some way have escaped damage to their own honors, they shall henceforth have no power deriving from the ordination, nor shall they ever take part in that sacrament which they conferred while neglecting judgment [Note: [Col. 0805] G. has “without judgment”]. [Col. 0805B]

24. Concerning avoiding illicit ordinations. Illicit ordinations are to be avoided. And if any illicit ordinations have been performed, let them be removed. Nor should we think the petitions of the people so powerful that, when we wish to comply with them, we do anything against the will of our Lord God, who forbids us to sin.

25. Concerning not ordaining the rebaptized. It must not be permitted that the rebaptized be promoted to the clerical rank.

26. That one who communicates without permission after excommunication be condemned. If anyone has been excommunicated for his negligence and, during the time of excommunication and before a hearing, has presumed to communicate, he is to be judged to have pronounced the sentence of condemnation upon himself.

27. Concerning not selling ecclesiastical property. It has been decided that presbyters are not to sell the property of the church in which they have been appointed without the knowledge of their bishops. [Col. 0805C]

28. That clerics not approach virgins or widows without the bishop’s permission. Clerics or continent persons are not to approach widows or virgins except at the command of bishops or presbyters. Nor are they to do this alone, but with fellow clerics [Note: [Col. 0805] G. has “clerics”] or with those whom the bishop or presbyter has ordered. Nor are the bishops or presbyters themselves to have access to such women alone, but when clerics or some reputable Christians are present.

29. Concerning the title of the first see. Let the bishop of the first see not be called prince of priests, or supreme priest, or anything of this kind, but only bishop of the first see.

30. Concerning the bishop’s discretion toward penitents. According to the difference among sins, let bishops determine the periods of penance at their discretion.

31. Concerning manumissions. Manumissions are to be celebrated in the Church. [Note: [Col. 0805] omitted by Bal.]

[Col. 0805D]

32. That no one have the power, after leaving the principal see, to reside longer in another church in his diocese or on his own property. It has been decided that no one have the power, after leaving the principal see, to transfer himself to another church established in the diocese, or, while established on his own property, to devote himself to its administration or attendance longer than is proper, thereby neglecting his own people.

33. Concerning requesting defenders of the Church from the king. Defenders of the churches against the power of secular persons or the wealthy are to be requested from the emperor.

34. Concerning clerics’ attendance at the council. It has been decided that whenever a council is to be assembled, bishops and presbyters who are hindered neither by age, illness, nor some other more serious necessity shall attend suitably. If they cannot attend, let them subscribe their excuses in the letter of summons [Note: [Col. 0805] Bal. has “summons”]. [Col. 0806A]

35. Concerning not promoting a reader of one church in another church. It has been decided that one who has once read in a church is not to be retained or promoted into the clergy by another church. And there is to be no appeal from elected judges.

36. Concerning the remission of penance. All penitents who are doing penance for either serious or lesser faults are to be released on the Thursday before Easter, provided no illness intervenes. In other matters, it belongs to the priest to determine the gravity of the offenses.

37. Concerning not invading another’s parish. The boundaries established by the fathers ought not to be moved, so that one person invades another’s parish and presumes to celebrate the divine mysteries there without consulting the person to whom it has been entrusted.

38. Concerning not repeating a valid baptism. Those who have been rightly baptized cannot have that gift repeated. But provision must be made to baptize those washed with water alone in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. [Col. 0806B]

39. Concerning punishment of sins. Sins of the people ought not to remain unpunished in the Church.

40. Concerning not despising prohibitions. If anyone despises prohibitions, he shall be subject to the danger of his rank.

41. Concerning removing transgressors of the canons. Whoever among the priests acts contrary to the prohibitions of the canons is to be removed from his office and is to know that pardon will henceforth be denied him.

42. Concerning delaying the advancement of those promoted to sacred orders. Whoever desires to be enrolled in the divine service is to remain for five years among the readers or exorcists. Thereafter, he is to be an acolyte or subdeacon for four years. Then, if he deserves it, let him approach the blessing of the diaconate; in that order he ought to remain for five years if he has performed his duties blamelessly. Afterward, if he has proved worthy, let him become a priest.

43. Concerning confession of crimes. It is clear that a person confesses a crime when, after a hearing has been granted and assigned for his purification, he does not use the opportunity to clear himself. For [Note: [Col. 0805] G. omits “For”] it makes no difference whether everything said about him is proven in the present examination, since his very absence stands as a confession. [Col. 0806C]

44. That nothing contrary to teachers be taught. No one ought to uphold doctrine to the injury of its teachers, for I fear that to keep silent about this is to suppress it. And elsewhere: “The matter rightly concerns us if we favor error by our silence.”

45. Concerning deeper questions. Deeper questions are neither to be despised nor asserted absolutely.

46. Concerning not neglecting the commands of the canons but practicing them vigorously. He who gave us things to be practiced, not neglected, does not permit them to be idle for us.

47. Concerning not pursuing novelty. If we begin to pursue novelty, we shall trample upon the order handed down to us by the fathers [Note: [Col. 0805] G. has an uncertain reading, “cal cauimus”].

48. That no priest presume anything in another’s parish. Let each priest be content with the boundaries granted to him, and presume nothing in another’s parish, lest through usurpation a place be granted to one priest to the injury of another [Note: [Col. 0805] Bal. reads “the place of someone else”]. [Col. 0806D]

49. Concerning not being ignorant of the canons. No priest is permitted to be ignorant of the canons.

50. Concerning teaching the people. The people are to be taught, not followed.

51. That a person bound by some condition not be ordained without his master’s request. Those who are bound by an original status or by the condition of another ought not to be ordained by bishops unless, perhaps, the request or consent of those who claim some power over them has been given; for the person who is to be enrolled in the divine service must be free from others. [Col. 0807A]

52. Concerning uprooting evil things completely. Let whatever grows evilly be torn out by the roots, and let no weeds corrupt the Lord’s harvest.

53. Concerning not exacting interest. Not only clerics, but neither should lay Christians exact interest [Note: [Col. 0807] G. adds “also”; G. omits “should not”].

54. Concerning persecuting the wicked. We cannot govern those entrusted to us in any other way than by pursuing with zeal for the Lord’s faith those who are destroyers or destroyed, and cutting them off from sound minds with whatever severity we can, lest this plague spread more widely.

55. Concerning guarding the people against sacrilegious persons. Before the Lord’s tribunal, the person who refuses to guard his people against the authors of sacrilegious persuasion will not be able to excuse himself from the guilt of negligence.

56. Concerning the welfare of the flock and the shepherd. We are not otherwise one flock and one shepherd unless, as the Apostle teaches when he says: “Let us be perfect in the same understanding and in the same wisdom.” [Col. 0807B]

57. Concerning lukewarm teachers [Note: [Col. 0807] G. has “of the teacher”]. The faults of those in the inner orders are to be attributed to no one more than to sluggish and negligent teachers, who often foster a great pestilence while they pretend not to apply the necessary medicine. [Note: [Col. 0807] Bal. conjectures “of those in the lower orders”].

58. How doubtful or obscure matters are to be held. In matters that are doubtful or obscure, let us know that we must follow what is found to be neither contrary to the evangelical commands nor opposed to the decrees of the saints [Note: [Col. 0807] G. omits this].

59. Concerning wives and concubines. Not every woman joined to a man is the man’s wife, nor is every son the heir of his father. Thus, a wife is one thing and a concubine another; likewise, a slave woman is one thing and a free woman another. And elsewhere: “There is no doubt that the woman in whom it is shown that there was no nuptial mystery does not belong to marriage.”

60. Concerning abandoning concubines. It is not a duplication of marriage when, after a slave woman has been abandoned, a wife is taken; rather, it is an advance in honor.

61. Concerning abstaining from what is lawful. One who asks pardon for unlawful acts ought also to abstain from many lawful acts [Note: [Col. 0807] G. omits this]. [Col. 0807C]

62. That penitents ought not to engage in the profits of commerce. It is not fitting for penitents to pursue any commercial profits, because it is difficult for sin not to intervene in the transaction between seller and buyer.

63. Concerning the guilt of the powerful. A person who enjoys greater honor commits a greater offense; and the eminence of dignities makes the vices of offenses greater. [Note: [Col. 0807] G. omits “greater honor”].

64. That wicked men not be consecrated. Whoever has acted as the consecrator of wicked priests must undo his own action; and whatever he illicitly committed or found committed by his predecessors, he must condemn if he wishes to avoid danger to himself.

65. That an unjust petition of the people be without effect. Nor should we think the petitions of the people so powerful that, when we wish to comply with them, we do anything against the will of our Lord God, who forbids us to sin.

66. Concerning not abusing authority that has been granted. Whoever abuses the authority permitted to him deserves to lose the privilege.

[Col. 0807D]

67. That no one absolve a penitent from another parish. No priest in another’s city or diocese is to receive, without the consent and letters of the bishop or presbyter, a penitent, or one placed under a priest’s hand, or one who says that he has been reconciled—whether a presbyter in a parish or a bishop in a city.

68. Concerning not promoting criminals. Criminals may not be promoted into the clergy; and if those placed in the clergy are found guilty of any crimes, let them be barred from their offices.

69. Concerning those entangled in various passions. It is not permitted for those entangled in *moniis* [probably *daemoniis*, “demons”] and other afflictions to handle the sacred ministries.

[Col. 0808A]

70. Concerning not judging the dead rashly. One must not rashly judge those who have departed to God.

71. Concerning avoiding contention. Contention is to be avoided with the greatest care.

72. That wicked men harm themselves by administering good things. Wicked men harm only themselves by administering good things; they do not defile the sacraments of the Church.

73. That while a husband or wife lives, neither may be joined to another marriage. It is clear that those who, after a divorce, have joined themselves to another marriage are adulterers on both sides. But those who, while their wife is alive—even if the marriage appears to have been dissolved—have hastened to another union cannot fail to be regarded as adulterers, to such an extent that even the persons to whom they have joined themselves are shown to be adulterers.

74. Concerning the bishop’s authority in his parish. Let each bishop have authority over his own parish, govern it according to the reverence appropriate to each person, and exercise oversight of every possession that is under his authority. [Col. 0808B]

75. That no cleric approach the ruler without the bishop’s consent. If anyone requests to approach the ruler for a necessary reason, this is to be done with the counsel and deliberation of the metropolitan and the other bishops of that province.

76. Concerning the bishop’s authority over ecclesiastical property. Let the bishop have authority over ecclesiastical property, to distribute it to all who are in need, with the greatest reverence and fear of God. He too is to share in whatever he needs, if indeed he is in need.

77. That a cleric not travel outside his parish without his bishop’s permission. It is not proper for a priest or cleric to depart without the command of his bishop.

78. How bishops are to be advanced. Bishops are to be advanced to ecclesiastical authority by the judgment of the metropolitans and of the bishops who are situated around them.

79. That elections of bishops not be entrusted to mobs. It must not be permitted for mobs to conduct the elections of those who are to be promoted to the priesthood. [Col. 0808C]
