80. That bishops not cross the boundaries of their parishes. Bishops who are over dioceses are in no way to approach churches that are outside the boundaries assigned to them, nor cross them through any presumption. [Note: [Col. 0807] omitted by G.]

81. That bishops, unless summoned, perform no ordinations outside their own diocese. Bishops are not to go outside their diocese, unless summoned, to perform ordinations or other ecclesiastical administrations.

82. That the synod of the province administer matters to be conducted in the province. Once the rule written concerning governance has been preserved, it is clear that matters belonging to each province are to be administered by the synod of that province, as it is established that the Council of Nicaea decreed.

83. Concerning the authority of the primate of a diocese. If anyone is injured by the metropolitan, let him be judged before the primate of the diocese. [Col. 0808D]

84. That accusers of clerics not be received without proof. Clerics or laymen accusing bishops or clerics are not to be admitted indiscriminately and without proof to an accusation, unless their reputation or suspicion concerning them has first been examined.

85. That a criminal have no right to accuse. A person entangled in any crimes shall have no right to accuse an elder. It was said by all the bishops: “If he is a criminal, let him not be admitted.” Approved.

86. That the accused be granted a place from which he comes, where he can have witnesses. It has been decided that the accused or the accuser is to choose for himself a place in the locality from which the accused comes, if he fears some violence from a reckless crowd—a nearby place to which it will not be difficult to bring his witnesses—where the case may be concluded. [Col. 0809A]

87. That a bishop not be deprived of his authority before a just judgment. No Christian can rightly think that a bishop may be deprived of his episcopate before the outcome of his case has become known.

88. That no criminal be permitted to accuse a bishop. No criminal is permitted to accuse a bishop.

89. Concerning seeking the primate in the accusation of a bishop. If a bishop is accused, the accuser is to bring his case before the primates of that province.

90. That a culpable accuser not be received. If the person of the accuser appears culpable in the judgment of the bishops, he is not to be admitted to bring an accusation except concerning his own cases.

91. That no ecclesiastical person be compelled to testify. No ecclesiastical person is to be compelled to give testimony.

92. Concerning a universal council. A universal council is to be held only out of necessity.

[Col. 0809B]

93. Concerning special cases. Cases that are not common are to be judged in their own provinces.

94. That a metropolitan presume nothing in another province. Let each province be content with its own metropolitan and its own provincial bishops, and let no one presume anything within the boundaries of another province.

95. That a bishop not be ordained against opposition. No one is to be ordained bishop against the will of the clerics or the people. Let the clerics have the right to resist if they see themselves overburdened; and those whom they recognize to be intruders, let them not fear to reject.

96. That three bishops can ordain a bishop at the command of an archbishop [Note: [Col. 0809] Bal. has “can”]. If necessity arises, three bishops, wherever they may be, can ordain a bishop at the command of the archbishop.

97. Concerning opposition to the ordination of a bishop. If opposition arises concerning the ordination of a bishop, they are not to presume to purify the person who is to be ordained by means of the three already present; rather, one or two more are to be requested from the same people for whom he is to be ordained [Note: [Col. 0809] Bal. reads “the person who has been ordained”]. First, therefore, let the persons who offer the opposition be examined; afterward, let the matters they allege be investigated. And when he has been cleared in public view, only then is he to be ordained bishop. [Col. 0809C]

98. That chorepiscopi not exceed the measure prescribed in the sacred canons. We have discovered that a blameworthy and very entrenched practice has arisen: certain chorepiscopi, advancing beyond the measure of their office, both confer the gift of the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands and perform other acts that belong only to bishops, contrary to right—especially since no one of the seventy disciples, whose role they represent in the Church, is read to have conferred the gift of the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands. But that it belongs as a proper duty only to the Apostles and their successors to confer the Holy Spirit is taught by the Book of the Acts of the Apostles.

In the Council of Caesarea, the following is written concerning chorepiscopi: “Chorepiscopi also appear to be modeled on and patterned after the seventy. But as fellow ministers, they are to be honored because of the zeal they show toward the poor.”

Likewise, in the tenth canon of the Council of Antioch: “Those who are called chorepiscopi in villages or estates, although they have received the laying on of hands from bishops and have been consecrated as bishops, nevertheless the holy synod has decided that they should recognize their proper measure and govern the churches subject to them, content with their administration, care, and oversight.”

99. What persons are not to be admitted to an accusation. It has been decided that all slaves or freedpersons (*liberti*) [Note: [Col. 0809] G. has “free persons” (*liberi*)], and all disreputable persons, are not to be admitted to an accusation, nor anyone whom the public laws do not admit to accusing persons of public crimes. [Col. 0810A]

100. That if accusers cannot prove one crime, they not be admitted concerning the others. It has been decided that whenever many crimes are brought against clerics by accusers, and they are unable to prove one of those crimes, the one with which they first dealt, they are not to be admitted concerning the remaining charges.

101. That witnesses under fourteen years of age not be received. Witnesses are not to be admitted to give testimony if they are not ordered to be admitted even for an accusation, or if the accuser has produced them from his own household. No one under fourteen years of age is to be admitted to give testimony.

102. That clerics or bishops be heard by their metropolitans or fellow provincial bishops. The canons of the African province and also the decrees of Nicaea have entrusted clerics of lower rank and the bishops themselves most explicitly to their metropolitans [Note: [Col. 0809] the text has *suis*; G. has *suos*]. For they most prudently and justly determined that all cases be concluded in the places where they arose, especially since everyone has been granted the right, if offended by the judgment of those hearing the case, to appeal to the councils of his province or even to a universal council. [Col. 0810B]

103. If a deposed bishop appeals to the Roman pontiff, his case is to be determined by the judgment of the Roman bishop. If a bishop has been deposed by the judgment of bishops who reside in nearby places, and he declares that his case ought to be heard in the city of Rome, no other bishop is to be ordained to his see after the appeal of the one who appears to have been deposed, unless the case has been determined by the judgment of the Roman bishop.

104. That an accused bishop be heard or judged by all his fellow provincial bishops. If any bishop is accused concerning specific crimes, he is to be heard by all the bishops who are in the province.

105. That a legitimate wife is to be taken in a nuptial marriage [Note: [Col. 0809] G. reads “is to be called”]. There is no doubt that the woman in whom it is shown that there was no nuptial mystery does not belong to marriage. Therefore, whoever gives his daughter in marriage to a man who has a concubine, this is not to be understood as giving her to a married man, unless perhaps that woman appears to have been made free, lawfully endowed with a dowry, and honored by a public wedding. Women joined to men by paternal decision are without guilt if the women who were kept by the men were not wives in marriage, because a married woman is one thing and a concubine another. [Col. 0810C]

106. Concerning metropolitans: that they neither hear the cases of fellow provincials without their own bishop nor presume to examine the complaint or accusation of any fellow bishop without the presence of all the other fellow provincial bishops. Let no metropolitan hear the cases of anyone without the attendance of all the other fellow provincial bishops, while the trumpet of the canons cries out: “Let the metropolitan do nothing without the knowledge of all”—that is, of the fellow provincial bishops—“except insofar as it concerns his own parish” [Note: [Col. 0809] omitted by G.]. [Col. 0810D]

107. Concerning slanderous or suspect accusers of priests. Let no one receive or hear slanderous or suspect accusers.

108. Concerning removing accusers and accusations that the secular laws do not admit. We also remove accusers and accusations that the secular laws do not admit.

109. Concerning cases of bishops or other priests to be settled by fellow provincials within their own province, and not by others unless an appeal has been made to the primates or the apostolic see [Note: [Col. 0809] Bal. omits “to the primates … apostolic see”]. If any cases or disputes arise among clerics and laymen, or among clerics of either the higher or the lower order, it has been decided that, according to the Council of Nicaea, the dispute be settled after all the bishops of that same province have assembled. Nor is anyone permitted—without prejudice, however, to the Roman Church, whose reverence must be preserved in all cases [Note: [Col. 0811] Bal. has *cui* for *quae* (“whose/which”); G. has *debetur* for *debet* (“is owed” for “must be”); G. has *custodire* for *custodiri* (“to preserve” for “to be preserved”)]—after abandoning those priests who by divine will govern the Churches of God in the same province, to rush into other provinces or seek or submit to the judgment of other fellow provincial bishops, unless these men are suspect [Note: [Col. 0811] omitted by Bal.]. If anyone presumes to do so, let him be judged by all both deposed from the clerical office and guilty of injury. [Col. 0811A]

110. Concerning examining accusers in the judgment of their elders. It must be examined in court what sort of conduct and faith belong both to the person who accuses and to the person who is accused [Note: [Col. 0811] G. omits “It must be examined” and “and to the person who is accused”].

111. Concerning not admitting accusers of bad conduct or whose life is open to accusation in a case against priests. Those who are not of good conduct, or whose life is open to accusation, are not to be permitted to accuse their elders.

112. Concerning not admitting accusers whose faith, life, and freedom are unknown in proceedings against priests. Those whose faith, life, and freedom are unknown cannot accuse priests. [Col. 0811B]

113. Concerning priests’ not being ignorant of the canons. It has been decided that no priest is permitted to be ignorant of the canons.

114. Concerning a bishop presuming to claim jurisdiction for himself alone. It has been decided that one bishop not claim jurisdiction for himself alone.

### 115. On bishops wishing to condemn those by whom they were consecrated

Bishops can bring no prejudice against the pontiff by whom they are proven to have been consecrated. If this is known to have been attempted, it is beyond doubt that it has no force and cannot in any way be regarded as an ecclesiastical statute.

### 116. On bishops who have been expelled or stripped of their possessions, so that they are not accused before being fully restored according to the law

If a bishop has been stripped of his possessions and brought under accusation, he ought at the outset to yield to the order of the pontiffs, so that everything which he had lost through the suggestions of his enemies [Note: [Col. 0811] *super*—“over,” in Bal.] may be legally restored to his authority by an honorable council [Col. 0811C], and the prelate first be returned to his former status. [Note: [Col. 0811] *ipsequem*, in G.] Only then, after his affairs have been arranged and put in order—not suddenly, but with due deliberation—should he come at the appointed time to the case; and, if it seems just, he should answer the accusers’ charges.

### 117. On excluding from clerical cases those whom the laws of the world do not admit

Those whom the laws of the world do not admit must be denied permission to speak in a judicial inquiry or to obtain anything.

### 118. On not compelling clerics to give public testimony

Clerics must not be compelled to give public testimony concerning a judicial inquiry of their own.

### 119. On not admitting to the accusation of priests an accuser whose person is stained by crimes

If the person of the accuser appears in the judgment of the bishops to be culpable—that is, entangled in crimes—he is not to be admitted to bring an accusation, except in matters concerning himself.

### 120. That an intervening bishop not sit on the see [Note: [Col. 0811] *in cathedram*—“on the see,” in Bal.] where he is acting as intercessor

It has likewise been decreed that no intervening bishop may retain the see to which he has been appointed as intercessor, on account of any popular faction or sedition [Col. 0811D]. [Note: [Col. 0811] *interventorum*—“of intervening bishops,” in Bal.]

### 121. Whenever an appeal is made from lesser ecclesiastical judges to greater ecclesiastical judges, it must not be denied to those who have appealed

It has been decreed that whenever an appeal has been made from any ecclesiastical judges to other ecclesiastical judges where greater authority resides, it must not be denied to those who have appealed.

### 122. On not violating apostolic and canonical decrees in the least

Care must be taken in all things that apostolic or canonical decrees be violated in no respect.

### 123. Decree of lord Charles, king of the Franks, that the servants of God neither go to war nor carry arms [Col. 0812A]

Charles, by the grace of God king and ruler of the kingdom of the Franks, and devoted defender and helper of the holy Church in all things.

At the urging of the Apostolic See, and with the counsel of all our faithful, especially the bishops and the other priests, we absolutely forbid the servants of God to carry arms, fight, or go to the army or to war in any way, except only those who have been chosen for divine ministry [Note: [Col. 0811] *mysterium*—“mystery,” in G.]—namely, to fulfill the solemn rites of the Mass and to carry the protections of the saints. That is, the prince may have with him one or two bishops together with chaplain-priests, and each prefect one priest, who can judge and assign penance to those confessing their sins.

### 124. That priests must not shed the blood of Christians or pagans

Priests must shed the blood neither of Christians nor of pagans.

[Col. 0812B] ### 125. That the servants of God must not engage in hunting

We forbid all servants of God to engage in hunting or woodland roaming with dogs, and to keep hawks or falcons.

### 126. That unknown bishops or priests are not admitted to ecclesiastical ministry before synodal examination

We decree, in accordance with canonical precaution, that all unknown bishops or priests arriving from anywhere are not to be admitted to ecclesiastical ministry before synodal examination.

### 127. On priests who have had several wives

If priests have had several wives, or have shed the blood of Christians or pagans, or have acted against the canons, let them be deprived of the priesthood, because they are worse than laymen.

### 128. That each person, with the help of the church’s defender, be vigilant lest the people practice diabolical works in his parish

We have decreed that, in accordance with the canons, each bishop must exercise vigilance in his parish, with the help of the count [*grafio*], who is the defender of the Church [Col. 0812C], so that the people of God do not practice pagan rites [Note: [Col. 0811] *paganicas*—“pagan,” in G.], but cast away and reject every impurity of heathenism: whether profane sacrifices for the dead, or diviners and soothsayers, or amulets and auguries, or incantations, or sacrificial offerings which foolish people make beside churches according to pagan custom under the name of the holy martyrs or confessors of the Lord. These offerings provoke their saints to anger rather than to mercy. [Note: [Col. 0811] *qui*—“who,” in Bal.]

### 129. That each bishop visit his parish every year

We decree that each bishop diligently visit his parish every year, and strive to confirm the people, teach the congregations, investigate and prohibit pagan observances and diviners or soothsayers, auguries, amulets, incantations, and every impurity of the heathen.

### 130. That priests be subject to their bishops and render an account of their ministry during Lent

We have decreed, in accordance with the canons of the saints, that every priest residing in a parish be subject to the bishop in whose parish he lives, and that every Lent he render and display to the bishop an account and order of his ministry, whether concerning baptism, the Catholic faith, prayers, or the order of the Masses.

Whenever, according to canon law, the bishop visits the parish to confirm the people, the priest must always be ready to receive the bishop with the assembly and assistance of the people who are to be confirmed there. On the Lord’s Supper, that is, Maundy Thursday, he must always request new chrism from his bishop. No one should presume to baptize with old chrism; rather, he should not delay burning the old chrism in the lamps of the church. [Note: [Col. 0811] “is absent” in G.]

[Col. 0813A] ### 131. That no one accept a church within a parish without the consent of his bishop

No one is to accept a church within a parish without the consent of his bishop, nor transfer from one church to another.

### 132. That priests care for the incestuous, the sick, and penitents

Priests must exercise great care for the incestuous and criminals. Likewise for the sick and penitents, so that the dying do not depart without the anointing with consecrated oil, reconciliation, and the viaticum. And [Note: [Col. 0813] this material is misplaced.] concerning the fast of the four seasons.

### 133. That all free men come to the assembly twice a year

No one should delay coming to the assembly: once around summer and once around autumn. For other assemblies, if necessity or a royal summons requires it, no one who is called should delay coming.

### 134. That no one be negligent when prayers are to be offered for the king or his faithful

Whenever it is announced that prayers are to be offered for the king or his faithful for any reason, no one should thereby appear negligent.

[Col. 0813B] ### 135. On the fast of the four seasons, which the priest must announce to the people and which all must observe [Note: [Col. 0813] “that,” in G.]

The priest himself must observe the fast of the four seasons and announce that it is to be observed by the people.

### 136. That a priest celebrate Mass only in consecrated places

No priest may presume to celebrate Mass except in places dedicated to God, or while traveling in tents and on stone altars consecrated by bishops. Whoever presumes to do so will be subject to the peril of his rank.

### 137. On priests unable to fulfill their ministry

Priests who do not know how to fulfill their ministry properly, and who do not strive with all their strength to learn according to the instruction of their bishops [Note: [Col. 0813] *praecepta*—“instructions,” in Bal.], or who are despisers of the canons, must be removed from their office until these matters have been fully corrected. [Note: [Col. 0813] “this matter corrected,” in Bal.]

### 138. On those who die after receiving penance [Note: Chapter 16 of the Capitulary of the year 769 could have followed here; however, because it was very dangerous for uneducated clerics, Benedict judged that this other text should be written in its place.]

Concerning those who depart from the body after receiving penance [Col. 0813C], it has been decreed that they are to receive communion without the laying on of the hand of reconciliation. This is sufficient consolation for the dying, according to the definitions of the fathers, who appropriately called this kind of communion the viaticum. If they survive, they are to remain in the order of penitents, so that, after demonstrating the necessary fruits of penance, they may receive legitimate communion with the laying on of the hand of reconciliation. [Note: [Col. 0813] *morienti*—“for the dying person,” in G.]

### 139. That no judge distrain a priest, deacon, or cleric without the consent of his bishop

No judge may presume on his own authority to distrain or condemn a priest, deacon, cleric, or junior member of the Church without the knowledge of the pontiff [Note: [Col. 0813] “is absent” in G.]. If he does so, he is to be separated from the Church to which he is known to have inflicted injury, until he acknowledges and corrects his offense.

### 140. That no bishop or layman presume to retain the property of another bishop

No bishop or layman may presume to claim or retain the property of any other bishop, church, or private person [Note: [Col. 0813] “private possessions,” in G.], whether through the division of kingdoms or the separation of provinces. If anyone attempts to do this, let him be suspended from the charity of all and separated from the grace of communion until he restores the property taken, together with compensation for its fruits.

### 141. On war, fighting, and arms forbidden to priests

For the second time, instructed by apostolic authority for the sake of more complete observance, and by the many admonitions of holy bishops and the rules of the sacred canons, and having taken counsel with all our nobles, we wish—correcting ourselves and giving an example to those who come after us—that no priest go to war, except only two or three bishops, chosen by the others for the sake of blessing, preaching, and the reconciliation of the people, together with the priests chosen with them who know well how to assign penances to the people, celebrate Masses, care for the sick, and administer anointing with consecrated oil and sacred prayers. Above all, they must take care that no one depart from the world without the viaticum.

These men must neither carry arms nor go to battle nor become shedder of blood or instigator of bloodshed. They must carry only the relics of the saints and the sacred ministries, and devote themselves earnestly to prayers, so that the people who must fight may, with the Lord’s help, be victorious, and so that the priest may not be like the people.

The others, who remain at their churches, are to send their well-armed men with us or with whomever we command [Col. 0814B]. They themselves are to offer Masses, litanies, and alms for us and for our entire army, praying to the God of heaven that we may prosper on the journey on which we are proceeding and, with God’s assistance, emerge victorious.

For we have learned that the nations and their kings [Note: [Col. 0813] *quae*, in Bal.] who allowed priests to fight beside them neither prevailed in war nor emerged victorious, because there was no distinction between laymen and priests, for whom fighting is not permitted. We know that the peoples and kings of Gaul, Spain, the Lombards, and certain others did this; and because of that most abominable crime they were neither victorious nor able to retain their homelands. [Note: [Col. 0813] “the aforesaid,” in Bal.]

Avoiding this pitfall, we prefer, with the Lord’s help, to be victorious with the few who are permitted rather than, with many who are forbidden, to turn our backs [Note: [Col. 0813] *terga*—“backs,” in Bal.]—which God forbid—and perish together with the peoples mentioned above.

For what kind of victory is granted when priests, at one hour, handle the Lord’s mysteries and offer the Lord’s body to Christians for the redemption of their souls [Col. 0814C], and afterward kill Christians whom they ought to serve with this sacrament, or pagans to whom they ought to preach Christ [Note: [Col. 0813] Bal. places this after *ministrare* (“serve”); G. inserts it here where it has been erased.], with their own sacrilegious hands—especially when the Lord says to them: “You are the salt of the earth. But if the salt loses its savor, with what will it be salted? It is no longer useful for anything except to be thrown outside and trampled by people”?

Since these things are so, we have chosen instead—with the Lord’s assistance and with his help extended to us, to them [Note: [Col. 0813] absent in G.], and to all their churches, and without anyone diminishing their honors or the property of their churches on this account—that they should preserve their rank and the decrees of the holy canons. If, however, they do these things contrary to the canons, whether we command or consent to it [Note: [Col. 0813] *consequentibus*—“following,” in G.], let them either lose their rank or perish, and let us likewise, God forbid, lose victory or perish with them.

For, because of our sins, we fear that if we command or permit such unlawful acts, we may perish together with them, since not only those who commit such acts but also those who consent to their perpetrators are guilty before God and his saints of an equal offense [Col. 0814D].

But if these things are faithfully observed by both sides, we believe that, with God’s help, all [Note: [Col. 0813] absent in G.] pagan peoples will fall before us and we shall be victorious; moreover, by doing good, we shall possess everlasting life with the Lord’s assistance.

### 142. On those who have thought that priests were forbidden to go to battle in order to diminish their honor

Because, at the instigation of the ancient enemy, we have heard that some suspect us on the grounds that, as stated in our earlier capitularies, we permitted bishops, priests, and the other servants of God to go to war only if two or three chosen from the others, and likewise a very few priests chosen by them, went; and that they should not hasten to battle, carry arms, kill either Christians or pagans, become instigators of bloodshed [Note: [Col. 0815] *sanguinem*—“blood,” in Bal.], or do anything contrary to the canons—thinking that we wished to take away or diminish the honors of priests and the property of the churches: we wish everyone to know that we neither intended to do this nor to consent to anyone wishing to do it. Rather, the more any one of them observes his rule and serves God, the more we wish to honor him and hold him dear.

So that these things may be believed more certainly and preserved for future times, we command that no one possess church property except by precarious tenure. When these precarious grants have ended, let the church’s officials determine authoritatively whether they choose either [Note: [Col. 0815] absent in G.] to recover the property itself or to permit their heirs to hold it under precarious tenure and a rent. This must be done, however, so that they legally transfer to the same churches—whose right the property is understood to be—their own proper and useful possessions; and if the rectors of those churches are to renew the precarious grants, let them renew them canonically. [Note: [Col. 0815] “thus, if the precarious grants are to be renewed by the rectors of those churches, let them be renewed,” in Bal.]

We know, then, that many kingdoms and their kings have fallen because they stripped the churches and devastated, removed, alienated, or plundered their property, and took property away from bishops, priests, and—what is more important—from their churches and gave it to men who fought.

For this reason they were neither strong in war nor steadfast in faith, nor did they emerge victorious. Many turned their backs wounded, and more were killed; they lost their kingdoms and regions and, what is worse, the heavenly kingdom, and they were deprived of their own inheritances and remain so to this day.

Avoiding all these things, we wish neither to do such things nor consent to them, nor set an example for our children [Note: [Col. 0815] *inuantibus*, corrected to *inventibus* in G.] or successors. Rather, as far as we are able and capable, joining to our spirit the spirit of Pope Leo and all the bishops, whose counsel we used in carrying out this action [Col. 0815C], we forbid and solemnly adjure them, by God and by the merits of all the saints, not to do such things or consent to those who wish to do them. Instead, let them be helpers, defenders, and enhancers, as far as they can, of the churches and of all the servants of God, lest they fall into the pit into which the kings and kingdoms mentioned above fell, or be plunged, God forbid, into the depths of hell.

And so that these matters may be preserved more devotedly for future times, we command that neither now nor at any time in the future may anyone, without the consent and will of the bishops in whose parishes the church properties are known to be located, request, invade, devastate, or alienate them by any device.

If anyone does so, whether in our time or in the time of our successors, let him be subject to the penalties for sacrilege. He is to be legally punished by us, our successors, and our judges or counts as a sacrilegious man, a homicide, or a sacrilegious thief, and he is to be anathematized by our bishops, so that even after death he is deprived of burial and of all the prayers and offerings of the Church of God, and no one may receive his alms.

All divine Scripture especially testifies that it is the greatest sacrilege to take away, invade, alienate, devastate, or steal the property of the Church. Blessed Pope Symmachus, striking all such persons with a synodal sentence, says:

> “It is unjust,” he says, “and equivalent to sacrilege that what each person has contributed or certainly left to the venerable Church, either for the salvation or for the repose of his soul, for the sake of the poor, should be taken away or transferred elsewhere by those by whom it was especially fitting that it be preserved.”

Many decrees of the holy canons and edicts of the holy fathers likewise testify to these same matters. They lie fully open to those who wish to investigate and know them.

[Col. 0816A] ### 143. On abominable crimes because of which kingdoms have been struck down, so that they may be wholly avoided

Under penalty of sacrilege, we absolutely and generally forbid everyone to invade, devastate, or alienate the property of any church, or to oppress, harass, or injure priests and the other servants of God in any way. We likewise forbid people of either sex to commit adultery, fornication, sodomitical lust, incest, or any unlawful marriage; unjust homicide, perjury, false testimony, and every other unlawful act, because we know that on account of these things not only kingdoms and kings but also the people living in them have perished.

But since, with God’s help and through the merits and intercession of the holy servants of God whom we have taken care to exalt and honor and whom we continue to exalt and honor, we and our successors have so far acquired kingdoms and regions and have enjoyed many victories, we must henceforth take the greatest care that, because of the unlawful acts and most filthy lusts mentioned above [Note: [Col. 0815] “the said,” in Bal.], we do not, God forbid, lose these things.

For many regions that pursued the invasion, devastation, alienation, and harassment of church property, the oppression of priests and the other servants of God, or any kind of injury, as well as the unlawful acts and adulteries mentioned above, or sodomitical lust or intercourse with prostitutes [Col. 0816B], remained neither strong in secular war nor steadfast in faith.

How the Lord permitted avenging punishments for such crimes to come upon the perpetrators through the Saracens and other peoples, and permitted them to serve them, is clear to all who read the histories of those peoples. [Note: [Col. 0815] *promisit*—“promised,” in G.]

Unless we guard ourselves against these things, we do not doubt that similar calamities will come upon us, because God is an avenger of all these matters.

Therefore let everyone subject to us know that whoever is found and convicted of one of these offenses will lose all honors, if he has any; be sent to prison until he makes just correction and satisfaction through public penance; and be made alien from the fellowship of all the faithful.

That pit into which we know that others have fallen must be avoided with the greatest care.

[Col. 0816C] ### 144. On priests who are known to have secular protectors against their bishops

Those priests who, living according to their own judgment without their own bishop, have secular protectors against their bishops, gather people separately, conduct their erroneous ministry not in a church but through rural places and little dwellings, and disturb the churches must be avoided and deprived of their proper honor. They are to be handed over to prisons or to monastic life under penance for the days of their lives, so that they may pay for the evils they have committed.

### 145. That no cleric of any rank presume to bring anyone before a secular court without the permission of his pontiff

No cleric of any rank may presume to bring anyone before a secular court without the permission of his pontiff. Nor may a layman accuse any cleric in a secular court, since the Apostle rather commands that the cases of private Christians be brought before the churches and settled there.

### 146. That clerics not hunt with birds or dogs

Clerics must not hunt, nor keep hawks [Note: [Col. 0815] *accipitres*—“hawks,” in G.] or falcons.

### 147. That priests render an account of their ministry to their bishop every year

Every priest must render to his bishop each year an account of his ministry, concerning the Catholic faith, baptism, and the entire order of his ministry.

### 148. That all bishops visit their parishes every year

Each bishop must visit his parish every year, confirm and teach the people, prohibit what must be avoided, and usefully urge the performance of what ought to be done.

### 149. On one who transgresses the statutes without compulsion

If anyone knowingly violates the statutes or considers them worthless [Col. 0817A], if he is a layman, let him be deprived of communion; if he is a cleric, let him be deprived of his honor.

### 150. That church affairs always be heard first in legal cases

Cases concerning church affairs are to be heard immediately by the judge, without any delay.

### 151. That no bishop usurp another bishop’s boundaries

A bishop must not usurp the congregations or boundaries of another bishop.

### 152. On neither judging nor testifying in one’s own case

No one may judge in his own case or give testimony in it.

### 153. That an expelled bishop or one deprived of his property not be accused before full restoration; nor one freely and completely enjoying his goods before being privately admonished; and that he not be compelled to answer unless canonically summoned

The canonical trumpet has taught us that an expelled bishop or one stripped of his property must in no way be accused or judged before he has been legally and fully restored.

But if someone freely and completely enjoying his own property and that of the church entrusted to him, as well as his honors, is accused of definite crimes [Col. 0817B], it is not permissible to proceed against him until the accusers have privately admonished him that he must correct the matters at issue.

If they have not first made peace with one another [Note: [Col. 0817] *minare*; G. has *peccaverint*, “have sinned”], they are to be canonically summoned to a synod [Note: [Col. 0817] *convocetur*—“let him be summoned,” in G.], so that all who have neglected these matters may publicly rebuke and correct both parties [Note: [Col. 0817] *arguatur*—“let him be rebuked,” corrected form]. Those who were unwilling to be corrected privately and confidentially are to be corrected there.

If, whether voluntarily or compelled by some necessity, he has been canonically summoned in an assembly of the brethren or in any other place, but has not come after having previously been privately admonished, no one may compel him to answer before these things have taken place. Rather, as has been said, he must first be privately approached [Note: [Col. 0817] *conventus*—“approached,” in Bal.] so that he may remedy in himself and in his affairs the matters about which complaint is being made.

Then, at the time fixed in the Nicene canons, he is to be summoned to a synodal assembly to answer canonically.

No one may dare accuse a bishop before public judges, but only before the primates of the dioceses or before the Apostolic See. Nor may he seek or accept the judgment of anyone other than his own judges or judges who have been chosen [Note: [Col. 0817] *iudicium*—“judgment,” in G.].

Certainly, if anything contrary to these provisions is done, there is no doubt that it is entirely without force.

[Col. 0817C] ### 154. On restraining proud or contumacious clerics or laymen

Clerics who are proud or contumacious must be restrained, so that inferiors who have inflicted injuries on their superiors may have fear. For it is manifest that one who despises humility is not of God but of the devil, who is the inventor and prince of pride.

Therefore, if anyone proves himself arrogant or insulting toward a superior, his contempt, contumacy, and pride must be broken in every respect.

### 155. That no cleric or abbot presume to go to secular courts without the command of his own bishop; and that no one be contumacious or disobedient to his bishop

It has been established in synods by the holy fathers that no cleric may appear before the public courts of laymen except at the command of his bishop or abbot, according to chapter nine of the canons of Carthage, where it is written:

> “He who, abandoning ecclesiastical judgment, wishes to clear himself in public courts, even if a judgment has been pronounced in his favor, is to lose his place. This applies in a criminal case. In a civil case, however, he is to lose what he wins if he wishes to retain his place. Since the authority of the Church is open everywhere for the selection of judges, the man who, thinking ill of the universal Church, seeks help from a secular judgment thereby judges himself unworthy of the fellowship of his brethren, although the Apostle commands that the cases of private Christians rather be brought before the Church and settled there.”

It has likewise been established that no priest, deacon, subdeacon, faithful layman, or anyone subject to a rule may, puffed up against his bishop, create a schism, or appear contumacious [Col. 0817D] or disobedient. For it is written in the canons: “Let priests and deacons presume to do nothing apart from the bishop.”

And the first man fell through disobedience. Whoever dares in any way to overturn this arrangement and does not submit to his own bishop, if he is a cleric, shall be subject to the corrections of the canons; but if he is a layman or monk, he shall be deprived of communion.

### 156. That bishops are not to be accused except before the highest primates, since not all metropolitans are highest primates; and that this be especially guarded against lest it occur through greed or envy

If a bishop is accused, the accuser must bring the case before the highest primates, who are to examine carefully whether the matter is being undertaken out of piety or not.

If it has been brought forward through someone’s envy, hostility, wicked greed, or ill will, the case must in no way be admitted. For it is unfitting that those who are called the thrones of God and ought to be immovable should be moved or disturbed by the accusations of wicked men.

If, however, it is found that the case has been brought forward out of piety, let them be heard patiently [Note: [Col. 0817] *audiatur*—“let him be heard,” in Bal.]; if not, let them be rejected and corrected canonically. [Note: [Col. 0817] G. repeats the preceding text here instead of this heading.]

[Col. 0818B] ### 157. What is to be done with an advocate found guilty of deceit or fraud

If an advocate is found to have acted in a case undertaken by him out of wicked greed, he is to be separated from the assembly of honorable men and from participation in judicial proceedings. He must take care not to assume the role of both judge and advocate.

### 158. On those who act contrary to their profession or subscription

Whoever acts contrary to his profession or subscription is to be deposed in council. [Note: [Col. 0817] *venerunt*—“came,” in Bal.]

### 159. On clerics, monks, or laymen forming conspiracies

Neither clerics, monks, nor laymen may make a conspiracy or lay an ambush against their shepherd. If they do so, they shall be subject to canonical rebukes. [Note: [Col. 0817] “nor laymen” is absent in Anseg. I. 29.]

### 160. On usurpers of the boundaries of others

If anyone is proved to be an invader of another’s boundaries, he must restore as much land as he presumed to invade, together with double the fruits. [Note: [Col. 0817] *horum*—“of these,” in Bal.]

### 161. On priests who are puffed up or create a schism

If any priest, puffed up against his bishop, creates a schism [Col. 0818C], let him be anathema.

If, puffed up by pride—which God forbid—he thinks he must separate himself from communion with his bishop and, creating a schism with some others, offers sacrifice to God separately, let him be regarded as anathema after losing his position. Moreover, he is to be driven far from the city and the congregation in which he was, lest he deceive either the ignorant or those living simply through everlasting fraud.

### 162. That priests not be sent indiscriminately by bishops, others in authority, or laymen

It has been established that priests must not, as has hitherto been done, be sent indiscriminately to various places, whether by bishops, other prelates, or even laymen, lest through their absence both the danger to souls and the duties of the churches in which they have been appointed be neglected.

### 163. On not reopening settled crimes

An accusation cannot be reopened concerning crimes of which the accused has been acquitted.

### 164. On proving an accusation

If anyone believes that his adversary should be accused before a judge in such a way that he claims to have suffered violence [Col. 0818D], he must be held to proving the matter.

### 165. On priests who celebrate Masses in unconsecrated places without consulting their own bishops

If any priest wishes to celebrate Mass in any place without consulting his bishop [Note: [Col. 0817] G. inserts *missam*, “Mass,” above the line], he acts contrary to his own honor.

### 166. That priests neither be appointed to nor expelled from churches without consulting the bishop

It has been decreed that priests may neither be appointed to nor expelled from any churches without the authority or consent of the bishops.

If anyone thereafter attempts to do this, he is to be strictly punished by synodal judgment. [Note: [Col. 0817] The following material is absent in Anseg. I. 84.]

[Col. 0819A] ### 167. Whoever disparages or accuses bishops accuses God’s ordinance [Note: [Col. 0819] *episcopo*—“the bishop,” in Bal.]

Whoever accuses or condemns bishops accuses God’s ordinance by which they have been established. A bishop is therefore not to be accused by the people, or by men of bad conduct or wicked life; rather, the rulers of the Church are to be judged by God.

### 168. On the murder of infants [Note: [Col. 0819] “murderers,” in Bal.]

If anyone kills an infant, he is to be held as a murderer.

### 169. On what is to be done with those who commit robbery, attack travelers, or plunder houses by night

If anyone sets out to commit robbery, attacks a traveler on landed estates [Note: [Col. 0819] *assederit*—“has beset,” in G.; with a marginal note: “otherwise, has overcome him by ambush”], or enters another’s house as a nocturnal plunderer, and is killed, no one is to seek an account of the robber’s death. [Note: [Col. 0819] “of the robber’s soul,” in G.]

### 170. That judges not pronounce a capital sentence before the accused confesses or is convicted by innocent witnesses

A judge examining a criminal must not pronounce a capital sentence before the accused himself confesses or is convicted by innocent witnesses.

If a crime has been alleged against persons of higher rank, the prince’s judgment must be awaited.

[Col. 0819B] ### 171. What is to be done if bishops incur guilt

If any bishop is accused by anyone, or if he has raised some question, the case is to be concluded by episcopal judges, whether those whom the primates assign to them or those whom they themselves choose by common agreement from among their neighbors.

### 172. On those who presume to veil widows or virgins without consulting the bishop

It has been established that widows must not be veiled without consulting the bishops.

It has likewise been established that if any priest thereafter contumaciously transgresses this rule—namely, if he presumes to veil any widows without consulting the bishop—he will incur the peril of his rank.

The same has been established concerning girls who are virgins: priests must not veil them, and if anyone attempts to do so, he is to be condemned as a transgressor of the canons.

### 173. On an accused bishop who regards his comprovincials as suspect, so that he may appeal to the Roman pontiff

It has been decreed that whenever a bishop is accused, if he regards his comprovincials or neighbors as suspect, he may appeal to the pontiff of the holy and universal Roman Church, so that he may settle through him whatever is just and pleasing to God.

### 174. On defendants who flee to churches or their altars, so that they are not dragged out

Those who flee must lay down their arms. Otherwise, let them know that they will be dragged out by armed force, so that the necessity of fear does not compel them to remain around the altar and pollute places worthy of veneration.

Whoever presumes to drag them out from the porticoes, atria, little gardens, baths, or adjoining areas of the churches is to be punished by death.

### 175. On not usurping the congregations of others and not oppressing a bishop

No bishop may usurp the congregations of another bishop, trample upon or overreach another bishop, or cause him any harm in his parish or anywhere else.

### 176. On not admitting to the accusation or testimony against priests those suspected of unsound faith

All who are suspected of holding an unsound position concerning the Catholic faith of Christ are to be regarded as doubtful in accusations against priests or in human testimony, and are not to be admitted.

### 177. What informers are, and what is to be done with them

Informers are those who either expose another person’s property or seek another person’s life. If they are convicted, they shall immediately be strangled. If a slave informs against his master, even if he proves the charge brought, he shall be punished.

### 178. That the case of bishops is to be settled by judges who are bishops

[Col. 0820A] If anyone brings a charge against a bishop [Note: [Col. 0819] *inpetitur* (“is charged”), G.], or if he brings forward some question, the case shall be concluded by judges who are bishops—whether those whom their primates assign to them, or those whom they themselves, with mutual agreement, choose from among their neighbors.

### 179. That no one shall contract a secret marriage or commit abduction, nor marry a woman whom his relative has had; rather, whoever wishes to marry shall take as his wife a woman endowed with a dowry and given by her parents through the blessing [Note: [Col. 0819] “in place of the blessing,” G.] of priests

It has been decreed that public marriages shall be entered into by those who desire to marry, because in marriages contracted secretly [Note: [Col. 0819] “in” is absent in G.] serious sins often increase or accumulate, both among the betrothed of others and among relatives, or in adulterous unions—and, what is worse to say, among blood relatives. From such unions the offspring are commonly blind, lame, hunchbacked, squinting [Note: [Col. 0819] “bleary-eyed,” G.], or marked with other shameful blemishes. Everyone must take care that this not happen thereafter.

First, however, the priest in whose parish the marriage is to take place must be consulted, in the church before the people. There the priest himself, together with the people, must inquire whether she is his relative, or another man’s wife or betrothed [Col. 0820B], or an adulteress. If he finds that everything is lawful and honorable, then, with the counsel and blessing of the priest and after consulting other good men, he must betroth and lawfully endow her.

For blessed Augustine writes as follows concerning a lawful marriage:

> “The woman who is to be taken as a wife must be such that, according to the law, she is chaste in virginity, lawfully endowed with a dowry, handed over to the bridegroom by her parents, and received from the bridesmen. Thus, according to the law and the Gospel, she is honorably joined in a public marriage and may lawfully be taken as a wife; and throughout all the days of her life she must never be separated on account of a man, except by mutual consent and for the purpose of devoting herself to God [Note: [Col. 0819] In the margin G.: “or to God.”]. If she has committed fornication and her husband wishes it, she is to be dismissed; but while she lives, another woman is not to be taken, because adulterers will not possess the kingdom of God; and she must be assigned penance. Do not, men, take wives whose former husbands are alive, for such marriages are adulterous.”

And, as we have said, it must be carefully determined that she is not his relative, because it is written: “No man shall approach a near relative of his blood, to uncover her nakedness.” Likewise it is written: “You shall not lie with your neighbor’s wife, nor defile yourself by mingling your seed with hers.”

And in the decretals of Pope Gregory it is read:

> “If anyone takes as his wife a deaconess, or a nun, or a spiritual godmother, or his brother’s wife, or his niece, or his stepmother, or his daughter-in-law, or his cousin, or a woman from his own family, or one whom his relative has had, let him be anathema.” And they all answered three times: “Let him be anathema.”
>
> “Again: if anyone carries off or steals a widow as a wife, or those who consent to him, let him be anathema.” And they all answered three times: “Let him be anathema.”
>
> “If anyone carries off or steals a virgin as a wife without having betrothed her, or those who consent to him, let him be anathema.” And they all answered three times: “Let him be anathema.”

And elsewhere in the canons it is written [Note: [Col. 0819] “commanded,” Bal.] that no one shall contract marriage within the degree of affinity arising from his blood relationship, nor shall anyone presume to marry a virgin without the blessing of a priest. All these things must be strictly avoided.

But [Col. 0820D] after all these matters have been investigated and nothing has obstructed the marriage, then, if she is a virgin, she is to be taken as a wife with the blessing of the priest, as contained in the sacramentary, and publicly rather than secretly, with the counsel of many good men, so that, by the Lord’s mercy, good children may be born from them, and not such as were mentioned above.

### 180. That those excommunicated by a priest may not accuse elders before they have been canonically reconciled

An excommunicated person shall not presume to accuse elders or bishops for as long as he remains under that excommunication [Note: [Col. 0819] Bal. places “while he is in excommunication” after “by a priest.”]. If he presumes to do so, he shall not be received; rather, he shall either incur a greater excommunication or be expelled from the church.

### 181. Those convicted of homicide, sorcery, or poisoning who wish to appeal are not to be heard

[Col. 0821A] In civil cases or lesser crimes, a delay is to be granted according to the laws. Convicted murderers, adulterers, sorcerers, and poisoners are not to be heard if they wish to appeal.

### 182. That priests, deacons, and the other clergy must do nothing without the command of their bishop

Priests or deacons shall do nothing without the knowledge of their bishops.

### 183. Concerning those who violate or abduct virgins, and concerning the abduction of others’ betrothed women

It has been decreed that no one shall violate virgins or widows, or abduct girls or widows. For it is written in the canons, in the Council of Chalcedon:

> “Concerning those who abduct girls under the pretext of living together, the holy synod decreed that those who cooperate with or assist the abductors, if they are clergy, shall be removed from their rank; if they are laymen, they shall be anathematized.”

These words clearly show how the authors of this evil are to be condemned, since those who participate and assist are struck with so great an anathema; and, according to canonical authority, abducted women can in no way be claimed by their abductors as lawful wives.

Concerning girls who have been betrothed and afterward abducted by others, the canons of the Council of Ancyra state:

> “It has been decided that betrothed girls who are afterward abducted by others shall be rescued and restored to those to whom they had previously been betrothed, even if it is established that violence was inflicted upon them by their abductors.”

Accordingly, the holy assembly has decreed that the abductor shall be punished with public penance. But if the abducted woman’s fiancé refuses to receive her, and she did not in any way consent to the crime, she shall not be denied permission to marry another. If she consented, she shall be subject to the same sentence. If afterward the two presume to unite, both shall be anathematized.

### 184. That accusers must be brought before the court, and that the accused must be given sufficient time to clear themselves of the charges

No one should be judged or condemned before the accuser is present; and the accused must be given a considerable period in which to defend himself and clear himself of the charges.

### 185. That clergy are not to be subjected to fiscal or public office

Clergy shall not be subjected to any fiscal or public office, but, free from every human service, shall serve the church.

### 186. That no priest shall permit women to live with him or presume to associate with them

It has been decreed concerning priests who indiscreetly permit women to live with them and thereby incur the stigma of a bad reputation, that if, after being admonished, they do not correct themselves, they shall be struck with canonical punishment as contemptors of the sacred canons.

### 187. That witnesses or accusers who live with enemies are not to be admitted in accusations against priests

Those witnesses or accusers are not to be admitted who live with the enemies, or whom the enemies themselves have brought from their household, because evil conversations corrupt good morals.

[Col. 0821D]

### 188. That witnesses are not to be admitted if they have been hostile to the Christian religion

Permission to testify shall be denied to those who have disregarded the dignity of the Christian religion and name.

### 189. That visiting bishops are to be received piously

A visiting bishop shall be given a place from which to celebrate the sacrifice.

### 190. That women shall not make unlawful access to the altar, nor presume to handle sacred vessels or the body and blood of the Lord

It has been decreed that women shall not make unlawful access to the altar, because it is contrary to all divine authority and canonical institution for women voluntarily to intrude upon holy altars, to touch sacred vessels immodestly, to minister priestly vestments to priests, or to touch and distribute to the people the body and blood of the Lord [Col. 0822A]. This has no support in any reason or authority, and it is altogether prohibited from happening henceforth.

Any women who thereafter presume to do this shall be subjected to canonical judgment until they have made satisfaction. That women ought not to enter the altar area is found at considerable length in the Council of Chalcedon and in the decrees of Pope Gelasius.

### 191. Concerning accused priests, that they are not to be brought to trial before their accusers have been fully investigated according to canonical and regular sanctions

If anyone is accused, he shall not be thrust into judgment [Note: [Col. 0821] “shall not be condemned in judgment,” Bal.] before the accuser has been tested [Note: [Col. 0821] “presented,” G.] and investigated according to the law and canonical judgment. If the person is found unworthy to accuse, he shall not be admitted to the accusation, because it is unworthy that the life of an innocent person should be stained by any harmful danger.

### 192. Concerning violators of tombs

Those who violate tombs, whether freeborn or slaves, shall be punished. If a person of higher rank is caught in this crime, he shall, after losing half his property, be branded with perpetual infamy [Col. 0822B]. If he is a cleric, he shall be stripped of all clerical honor and assigned to perpetual exile. If a judge delays prosecuting or carrying out the matter, he shall be deprived of his property and honor. Anyone who wishes to bring an accusation of this crime shall be granted permission [Note: [Col. 0821] “they wish,” Bal.].

### 193. That priests shall not abandon their church

No one shall abandon his church for any reason whatsoever.

### 194. Concerning priests who lose their rank and become so degraded [Note: [Col. 0821] “because concerning him,” Bal.] that they become sons of Belial; what is to be done

It has been decreed concerning priests who lose their rank that each bishop, both personally and through his ministers, shall ascertain their life, conduct, and moral reform, and shall not neglect to subject them to canonical penance, in accordance with what is written in the first title of the Council of Caesarea:

> “If a priest takes a wife, he shall be removed from the order. But if he commits fornication or adultery, he must be expelled entirely and brought to penance.”

For some, after losing their rank, become so thoroughly sons of Belial that, because of the carelessness and negligence of their rulers, they are bound neither by public laws—for that is not permitted—nor by canonical laws [Col. 0822C].

### 195. Concerning laymen who presume to debate religion

No avenue of opportunity shall be open to anyone who comes forward publicly to dispute or discuss religion, to bring forward any matter for deliberation, or to accuse elders. If anyone thereafter believes that he ought to act contrary to this, or attempts to persist under the impulse of a pestilential persuasion [Note: [Col. 0821] “persuasion,” G.; “by an earthquake,” G.], he shall be restrained by an appropriate penalty and a deserved punishment [Note: [Col. 0821] “undeserved,” G.].

### 196. Concerning those who bring false rescripts of rulers, and concerning several other matters

Those who bring false rescripts of rulers shall be punished as forgers [Note: [Col. 0821] “false rescripts,” G.]. Whoever unknowingly alleges something false shall not be held under the penalty for forgery. Neither a slave nor a freedman may be interrogated concerning the life of his master or patron. No one shall torture a pregnant woman. Whoever has confessed concerning himself cannot be believed against another [Col. 0822D].

### 197. What is to be done concerning those who bring false capital charges against their brothers

It has been decided that those who are convicted of having brought false capital charges against their brothers shall not receive communion until death and shall remain infamous forever.

### 198. That no one shall dare persuade the people of another priest’s parish to leave their own parish, gather at his church, or give him their tithes

It has been decreed that no priest shall persuade the faithful of the holy church of God from another priest’s parish to leave their own church and gather at his church or give him their tithes [Note: [Col. 0821] “to the other parish,” G.]. Rather, let each person be content with his own church and people, and let him never do to another what he does not wish done to himself, in accordance with the Gospel saying: “Whatever you wish people to do to you, do the same to them.”

Whoever acts contrary to these ordinances or attempts to violate them shall, as a contemptor of his rank, be subject to danger.

### 199. That laymen have no authority to dispose of persons dedicated to God or of ecclesiastical property

No authority is ever recorded as having been granted to laymen, however religious, to dispose of persons dedicated to God or of ecclesiastical property.

### 200. Concerning those who compose or sing writings or songs in blasphemy against another

The person who composes songs in blasphemy against another [Note: [Col. 0823] “they,” Bal.], or who sings them, shall be punished outside the ordinary procedure [Note: [Col. 0823] “he,” G.]. For the law orders those who devise or publish defamatory libels to be exiled. Whoever, when appealing to a judge, utters an insult shall be branded with infamy. Not only does the person who utters a curse or insult become infamous, but so does the person whose counsel is shown to have caused it.

[Col. 0823B]

### 201. What is to be done concerning priests or Levites who confess a crime against themselves

A priest or Levite who confesses any crime concerning himself shall be deposed.

### 202. That no priest shall dare reconcile public penitents without consulting the bishop; and that all public penitents must come to their own bishop on the Lord’s Supper

It has been decreed and prohibited in the holy canons that no priest shall presume to reconcile a public penitent without consulting the bishop, except perhaps someone endangered by death. Rather, on the fifth day before Easter, which is the Lord’s Supper, all public penitents shall come to the city, in ashes and sackcloth, prostrate before their bishop. There they shall be reconciled and judged canonically and in due order by the bishop, as contained in the sacramentary [Note: [Col. 0823] “sacramentary,” G.] and the Roman order; they shall be comforted, preached to, and instructed concerning what they ought thereafter to do and what they ought to avoid, and they shall be healed through divine prayers by the laying on of the bishop’s hands [Note: [Col. 0823] “layings-on,” G.].

At no time has permission been granted to a priest to reconcile a penitent in a public Mass without the bishop’s authorization. If anyone presumes to do this, he shall be punished by canonical correction.

### 203. Concerning clergy or laymen who become accusers of their bishop

If any cleric or layman becomes a reproacher or slanderer of his bishop, he shall be regarded as a murderer.

### 204. Concerning cases to be proved in court, and the invalidation of a sentence against an absent party; concerning cases not to be reopened; and that absent persons are not to be condemned or permitted to accuse or be accused through another

No one can be convicted in court without witnesses or a document. A sentence given by a judge while one party is absent has no validity. A case judged between persons present cannot be reopened after ten years, nor a case between absent persons after twenty years. In a capital case no absent person shall be condemned. Nor can an absent person be accused through another accuser.

[Col. 0823D]

### 205. What is to be done concerning faithful informers

If an informer is a member of the faithful, and through his information someone has been proscribed or killed, it has been decided that he shall not receive communion even at the end [Note: [Col. 0823] “for the end,” Bal.].

### 206. Concerning priests or clergy who, through the money of other priests, seize or overturn churches or benefices

It has been decreed and prohibited to all that if a priest is caught giving gifts or paying money to a cleric or layman so that he may seize another priest’s church, he shall, on account of this greed or robbery for the sake of shameful profit, be expelled from the clergy and remain outside the rule.

If, however, the bishop, out of mercy, wishes to confine him for a long period in the misery of prison, doing penance for what he has done and keeping him there until satisfaction [Note: [Col. 0823] “by the bishop,” G.], this shall be permitted. Later, if he corrects himself and promises not to do such things again, the bishop may treat him more humanely if he wishes and if the man is found worthy.

[Col. 0824A]

### 207. That secular people should consider themselves to have no authority over persons dedicated to God or the church’s property, except for reverence

By synodal decree it has been sanctioned that laymen or secular persons shall not consider or presume that they have any authority over persons dedicated to God or over the church’s property, except for reverence. The care of disposing of these matters is taught to have been indisputably entrusted by God to the priests.

If anyone presumes to act contrary to this, he shall be struck with anathema.

### 208. That slaves who confess their masters’ crimes are not to be heard

If slaves have confessed their masters’ crimes, they shall in no way be heard, unless perhaps they report them as guilty of treason.

### 209. What is to be done concerning people who strip the poor and do not make restitution when admonished by the bishop

If any powerful person strips anyone of his property and, when admonished by the bishop, does not restore it [Col. 0824B], he shall be excommunicated.

### 210. Concerning those who approach secular judges without the bishop’s command or travel without their bishop’s permission and letters; and concerning laymen who bring accusations against churches or clergy

It has been decreed that a priest, deacon, or any cleric subject to the rule shall not go to a secular judge without consulting his bishop. It has likewise been decreed that a cleric or monk may not travel without a letter from his bishop.

And elsewhere the canons read as follows:

> “Let no one grant communion to a priest, deacon, or cleric traveling without letters from his bishop.”

It has also been decreed that if any secular person attempts, through slander, to harass a church or cleric, and is convicted, he shall be restrained from the thresholds of the church and from Catholic communion unless he performs worthy penance.

### 211. That vicious laymen are not to be received by clergy unless they voluntarily wish it

All the bishops acclaimed in the third session [Col. 0824C]:

> “It is certainly right that, just as laymen do not receive priests or clergy for their own accusation or in secular courts, so the clergy themselves should not receive these laymen for accusations against priests or clergy, or for ecclesiastical affairs, unless the laymen voluntarily wish it; for it is inappropriate that those who reject them should be received by them.”

### 212. That those who voluntarily wish to kill a person but are unable to carry it out are to be regarded as murderers

Whoever wishes voluntarily to kill a person but is unable to carry it out shall be punished as a murderer.

### 213. Concerning clergy who withdraw from their own bishops

No cleric shall withdraw from his own bishop and transfer himself to another.

### 214. That no priest shall presume to sell his tithes or anything belonging to the church without the permission of his own bishop

It has been decreed that no priest or deacon shall irreverently presume to sell his tithes or anything belonging to the church without the counsel of his own bishop [Note: [Col. 0823] “irreverently,” G.], because it has been decreed in the canons as follows:

> “It has been decided that priests or deacons shall not sell church property where they have been appointed, without the knowledge of their bishops.”

Care must be taken that this not happen again, as we have heard that certain priests in some places have shamelessly attempted to sell their tithes before the harvests had ripened or been collected, for the sake of drunkenness. We all forbid this from happening again. Rather, the tithes are first to be received by the priests with thanksgiving.

If there is a necessity to sell them for the restoration of churches or the redemption of captives, they shall do so with the counsel of their own bishop and of other good priests. They must ensure that, under any pretext, the offerings of the faithful are not secretly and without witnesses defrauded [Col. 0825A], and that what ought to refresh the poor, restore churches [Note: [Col. 0825] “church,” G.], support clergy, provide for bishops, or feed and honor guests and pilgrims is not diverted by priests, deacons, or any of the faithful to excessive drinking, feasting, or carnal desires, which are pursued in many ways. Rather, they must faithfully apply these offerings to the purposes mentioned above, and know that they are stewards not of their own property but of the Lord’s.

Therefore the Lord’s priests ought faithfully to preserve and usefully administer them as the Lord’s property. If, God forbid, they act otherwise, they shall be strictly punished by canonical censure.

### 215. Concerning the exclusion of those under anathema

The voice of anyone under anathema shall be entirely disregarded in accusation, testimony, or human judgment, and such persons shall not be permitted to accuse anyone. But if anyone treats the penalty of anathema lightly, he shall either be confined on an island or assigned to exile, so that he cannot disturb the church of God and its servants [Col. 0825B].

### 216. That a sentence judged against absent persons or minors has no validity

A sentence judged against absent persons or minors shall have no force.

### 217. What is to be done concerning clergy who carry weapons in a sedition

Clergy who are found to have deliberately taken up weapons in any sedition [Note: [Col. 0825] “are found to have taken up weapons,” Bal.] shall, after losing their rank, be handed over to penance in a monastery.

### 218. Concerning those who become drunk, that they are to be suspended from communion unless they correct themselves, or subjected to corporal punishment

It has been decreed that priests, deacons, and all other clergy must avoid drunkenness in every way, because it is the fuel and nurse of all vices. Accordingly, a person who is established to have been drunk shall, as the order permits, either be removed from communion for forty days or subjected to corporal punishment.

### 219. What is to be done concerning ecclesiastical judges who presume to judge absent persons

Let ecclesiastical judges beware [Col. 0825C] of pronouncing a sentence while the person whose case is being heard is absent, because the sentence will be void; indeed, they will have to answer for the case in the synod as though for an accomplished offense [Note: [Col. 0825] “the case will certainly be brought before the synod,” Bal.].

### 220. Concerning those who bring their case before foreign judges; those who have not first litigated in their own court; and judges who delay cases through negligence

If anyone believes another should be accused, he shall bring his case before the judge of that province. Whoever has not first litigated in his own court shall incur the entire loss of the suit.

If the case is not concluded through the judge’s negligence, we order him to pay to our treasury as much as the value of the matter in question is found to have been. Those who adhere to his counsels shall be assigned to exile.

### 221. That the ruin of the wretched must be greatly relieved

Certainly everyone ought to come to the aid of the ruin of the wretched, so that, by relieving another’s distress [Note: [Col. 0825] “by disclosure,” corrected to “by relief,” G.], he may remove God’s punishment from himself. For the person who drives adversities from the afflicted makes a propitious offering to the Lord.

[Col. 0825D]

### 222. What is to be done concerning false diviners

Diviners who claim to know the future shall be beaten and expelled from the city.

### 223. That, at the time chosen by all the provincial bishops, they must assemble at the metropolitan see to hold a synod

It has pleased us to decree that, obeying the institutions of the fathers, they shall assemble at the metropolitan see [Note: [Col. 0825] “the metropolitan see,” Bal.] with devoted zeal, at the time when all the provincial bishops [Note: [Col. 0825] “provincially,” Bal.] have chosen, to hold a synod.

### 224. What is to be done concerning a bishop who presumes to trample upon, slander, or injure another bishop

No bishop shall trample upon another bishop or presume to slander or injure him [Col. 0826A]. If he does so, he shall be subject to the danger of losing his rank.

### 225. That no priest shall presume to pour public blessings over the people in a church or consecrate or reconcile an altar

It has been decreed that priests shall not presume in any way to pour a blessing over the people in a church, consecrate or reconcile an altar, remove it, or set it in place.

It has likewise been decreed that priests shall not attempt, without the permission or counsel of their bishop, to erect an altar or move it from one place to another, as we have heard some have done. The bishop is the one whose office it is to consecrate the altar and, after its removal or violation, to reconcile it.

If they act otherwise, they shall be subject to the danger of losing their rank.

### 226. That what has been taken from absent persons must be fully restored

Concerning absent persons, we wish to repeat the law: whatever has been taken from them by anyone must be returned without delay to their friends, relatives, or slaves when they have appealed to the judge [Col. 0826B], so that the property which the master left behind as his own when he departed may be fully reclaimed from his agents wherever he resides [Note: [Col. 0825] “the property,” G.].

Whatever has been seized from those serving in the army or from absent persons, we order to be restored without any delay.

### 227. That measures established for perpetual benefit must remain unchanged

Measures established for perpetual benefit shall not be altered by any change; nor shall what has been established for the common good be diverted to private advantage. While the boundaries established by the fathers remain in force, no one shall damage what belongs to another. Within his own proper and lawful limits, however, each person may exercise himself as broadly as he wishes in charity.

### 228. Concerning those who neglect the divine offices and do not attend the morning, evening, or other divine offices

It has been decreed that if a priest, deacon, or any cleric assigned to a church is within the city, or in any place where there is a church, and does not come to the church for the daily service of psalmody at the morning or evening hours, he shall be deposed from the clergy, unless, after being disciplined, he wishes to earn pardon from the bishop through satisfaction.

### 229. What is to be done concerning those who have been led into captivity

Whoever has been led into captivity by necessity, and has passed to the enemy not by his own will but through hostile plunder, shall, when he returns, reclaim and take possession without opposition from anyone of whatever he previously held in fields or slaves, whether it is possessed by the treasury or whether any of it has been given by the ruler to someone else—provided that he was with the enemy not voluntarily but proves that he was held in captivity.

### 230. That one must not rise against one’s head

We do not willingly permit anyone to rise against his head, even if it ought to be done.

### 231. That priests shall assemble in the city each week, as they are summoned by the bishop or by one appointed by him, without delay, for the sake of learning

It has been decreed that all parish priests shall assemble in the city in groups, during the weeks assigned to them by the bishop, for the sake of learning. Some portion of the priests shall remain in the parishes, so that the peoples and churches of God are not without ministry; others shall learn useful things in the city, so that they may eventually return to their parishes better, wiser, and more useful to the people [Note: [Col. 0825] “to the peoples,” Bal.].

There, in the city, they shall be instructed in good spirit by the bishop or by his well-taught ministers [Note: [Col. 0825] “blessed,” G.] concerning the sacred readings, divine worship, and the holy canons; concerning the sacrament of baptism [Note: [Col. 0825] “the sacraments,” Bal., from the Bellovacensis codex.], the solemn rites and prayers of the Mass [Col. 0827A], and all the other offices necessary for them. They shall be taught fully, distinctly, and individually.

The bishop and his well-taught ministers shall truthfully and prudently teach them everything they must teach, preach, and do in the parishes, so that they may know what they ought to do and what they ought to avoid; so that they may lead their lives well, suitably, and blamelessly; by living well, provide a good example to others and cause no offense; and fulfill their ministries wisely and reasonably, so that, God forbid, they do not fall into any offense but may deserve the grace of God.

### 232. What is to be done concerning those convicted in court of evident violence

A person convicted in court of the crime of evident violence shall be punished by death.

### 233. That priests shall not presume to judge matters they do not know

We, who desire the judgments of the Lord’s priests to be mature, cannot decide anything concerning unknown matters to the prejudice of either party [Col. 0827B] before we have truthfully heard everything that happened.

### 234. Concerning those who abandon ecclesiastical offices and flee to secular persons; concerning clergy who steal from the church; and concerning clergy who grow their hair or change their habit or clerical clothing

It has been decreed that if any cleric, having abandoned his office because of discipline, flees to some secular person, and the person to whom he has fled offers him protection, both he and the cleric shall be expelled from communion with the church [Note: [Col. 0827] “from the church’s communion,” Bal.].

It has likewise been decreed that if any cleric commits theft from the church, he shall be granted foreign communion.
