Similarly, it has been decreed that clerics who grow their hair shall be forcibly tonsured by the archdeacon, even if they refuse. They shall not be permitted to use or possess clothing or footwear except what is becoming to religion.

### 235. Concerning slaves who commit violence with or without their masters’ knowledge, and how these matters are to be corrected

If slaves are convicted or confess, without their master’s knowledge, that they have committed violence [Col. 0827C], they shall be punished by being subjected to severe tortures. If they committed the crime of violence at their masters’ command, the masters who gave the unlawful orders shall be branded with infamy and shall not be permitted to retain the dignity of their nobility or honor.

The slaves who obeyed such commands of their masters shall be condemned to the mines. Moreover, judges shall not be permitted to delay, dismiss, or pardon the investigation of violence. If they establish that violence occurred and do not immediately punish it, they shall know that they will incur danger. Base persons who are frequently proved to have committed violence shall in every way be struck with the penalty prescribed above by the laws.

### 236. How sluggish or negligent brothers are to be cared for

If there are any sluggish or negligent brothers who ought to be corrected with greater authority, correction must nevertheless be applied in such a way that love is always preserved.

### 237. That clergy shall not be rebellious or arrogant toward their bishop, nor despise his excommunication; and how those who do these things are to recover their dignity

It has been decreed that rebellious clerics shall be corrected by bishops according to what the order of their dignity permits. If some who hold a higher rank, lifted up by pride, happen to despise communion, or neglect to attend the church or fulfill their office, they shall be granted foreign communion. When penance has corrected them, they shall be re-entered in the register and shall receive their rank and dignity.

### 238. That accusers are not to be believed before both parties have been heard

Whenever any accuser makes a statement about his adversary while the latter is absent, he must not be believed at all before both parties have been heard [Note: [Col. 0827] “he must not be believed beforehand,” Bal.; “he” erased, G.].

[Col. 0828A]

### 239. Concerning priests who are not to be removed [Note: [Col. 0827] G. placed the heading of the following chapter before this one.]

We command that no priest accused of no crime or of a false crime be dragged away [Note: [Col. 0827] “be disparaged,” Bal., here and in the heading.].

### 240. That those who regard judges as suspect shall make an appeal

If anyone feels that a judge is hostile to him for any reason, or happens to regard him as suspect, he shall make an appeal, so that, when this has been granted to him, he may be heard before another judge, with the entire case intact and without delay.

### 241. That everyone should take care, as far as possible, not to do to another what he does not wish to suffer himself

Just as no one wishes to carry a burden of grievous weight, so let him not presume to impose a heavy burden on another.

### 242. That people in discord shall not approach the altar or receive the grace of holy communion; and what is to be done if one of them corrects himself while the other remains in discord

It has been decreed that none of the persons in discord shall presume to approach the Lord’s altar or receive the grace of holy communion before they have been reconciled [Note: [Col. 0827] “before he has been reconciled,” Bal.]. Rather, they shall compensate through penance for twice the time during which they served discord [Col. 0828B] [Note: [Col. 0827] “the time during which it will be compensated,” Bal.].

But if one of them, while the other remains contemptuous, comes forward to make satisfaction in charity, then from the moment at which he is shown to have hastened toward reconciliation, he shall be received into the church as a peacemaker.

### 243. That penitents must abstain from banquets, ornaments, and white clothing

A person who mourns must abstain from banquets, ornaments, and white clothing.

### 244. Concerning the divine, apostolic, and canonical decrees, which must not be violated

We command that all of you serve the divine and apostolic constitutions in such a way that you permit the pious decrees of the canons to be violated in nothing. We also command that no one presume to violate either the divine constitutions or the decrees of the Apostolic See under penalty of endangering his status.

245. On priests who irrationally move from one church to another, and on those ordained in their place. It has been decreed that those priests who migrate, or have migrated, from church to church and abandon, or have abandoned, their titles without the permission and consent of the bishop shall be held excluded from communion for as long as they have not returned to the churches in which they were first established. But if, while one was migrating, another was ordained in the place of the living man, he who abandoned his church shall lack the dignity of the priesthood for as long as his successor rests in the Lord.

246. That actions for injuries may be brought only by those who are present. Actions for injuries may be brought only by those who are present. For a charge that awaits judgment of vengeance or calumny cannot be brought by others.

247. That everyone who does not quarrel protects friendship. Everyone who does not quarrel protects friendship. For the Apostle also writes to the Corinthians: “Since there are jealousies and quarrels among you, are you not carnal and walking according to human ways?” “Do nothing through quarrelling or empty glory, but in humility of mind regard one another as superior to yourselves, each looking not to his own interests but to those of others.” [Col. 0828D]

248. That no one may thereafter appeal concerning what the church has possessed by thirty-year right; and concerning abductors of widows or virgins; and that women should not minister at sacred altars. It has been established that the properties of the church, and likewise the dioceses possessed by certain priests, shall claim for themselves whatever the thirty-year law has secured; and after thirty years no one may appeal concerning that which the statutory period has excluded. It has likewise been decreed that abductors of widows or virgins shall be expelled from communion with the church, and that women shall not minister at sacred altars or presume to undertake anything assigned to the offices of men.

[Col. 0829A] 249. On judges who judge contrary to law and refuse to hear the law. Whoever, when laws or legal principles have been presented to him in court, refuses to hear them and judges contrary to them, if convicted of this, shall be deported to prison [Note: [Col. 0829] “assigned to prison,” Bal.].

250. On the unskilled, that they should not be preferred to the skilled. It is utterly unjust that the unskilled should be preferred to masters, newcomers to the old, or the inexperienced to those proven by service.

251. That litigants may remedy a defective case by the remedy of appeal, and that appellants should not be placed in custody [Note: [Col. 0829] “is lacking,” Bal.]. Judges must ensure that a litigant may remedy a defective case by the remedy of appeal, and that appellants are neither confined in prison nor kept under military guard [Note: [Col. 0829] Bal. and G. read “to guard”; here the text has been corrected], but may freely attend to their business. The voice of appeal must not even be denied to those destined for punishment.

252. That no one should give false testimony; and concerning the danger, penance, or rejection of false witnesses. We wish and command that all abstain from false testimony, knowing both that this is a most serious crime and that it was prohibited by the Lord himself on Mount Sinai, when he said: “You shall not bear false witness.” Or: “A false witness shall not go unpunished.” Let everyone who has committed this know that he must be cleansed by such penance as is prescribed for perjury, or struck by such condemnation and excommunication as are prescribed for homicide or perjury. For it is the height of folly and wickedness that someone counted by the Christian name should, from desire for silver and gold, clothing, land, or any other thing—as often happens—or because of drunkenness or gluttony, fall into so great a crime that he must either remain for seven years in severe hardship or be rejected by the church, the Lord saying: “What does it profit a man if he gains the whole world but suffers the loss of his soul?” [Col. 0829B]

253. That the accuser shall suffer the same penalty which the accused would have suffered if he cannot convict him. Let the accuser undergo the penalty which the accused would have suffered if he cannot convict him. No one can recognize a debtor more fully than the person who has endured the wrongdoer’s wickedness.

254. That the person producing a document must affirm it. It has been established that the person producing a document must affirm it. For if the person who produced the document does not establish its truth, he must be held guilty of falsification.

255. That all the faithful should faithfully obey their bishops. Whoever refuses to hear his bishop, is excommunicated, and persists in his refusal shall endure perpetual condemnation before God from the bishops; moreover, he shall be entirely excluded from our palace, and all his property shall pass to his legitimate relatives.

256. What should be done concerning murderers. We have ordered that the following rule be observed concerning murderers: whoever, in reckless daring, kills another without cause shall be struck with the penalty of death and shall never be able to ransom himself for any price. If it is agreed that someone shall submit to composition, none of his relatives or friends may assist him in any way. If anyone does so, he shall pay his own wergild in full.

257. What should be done concerning thieves and criminals. We have decreed that the following be observed concerning thieves and criminals: if five or seven men of good faith, without a declared enmity, affirm under oath that a certain criminal perpetrated a theft contrary to the law, he shall die according to the law [Note: [Col. 0829] G. inserted this in the margin; it is absent in Bal.]. If a judge releases an apprehended robber, he shall lose his life, so that the others may observe discipline in all things [Note: [Col. 0829] “and so that,” Bal.; [Col. 0829] absent in Bal.].

[Col. 0830A] 258. What should be done concerning incest. No one shall ever join himself in marriage to a close relative. If this happens, let them be separated by the bishop of that place, and let both perform public penance for seven years according to the canonical degrees. Those unwilling to do this shall be regarded by everyone as accursed [Note: [Col. 0829] Bal. reads: “let him who is unwilling … be regarded”].

259. On not readily admitting accusers, and on judging or condemning anyone without certain proof. First of all, everyone must be investigated carefully, so that matters may be settled justly. Let no one condemn anyone before a just judgment or judge anyone on the basis of suspicion. Let the matter first be proved, and then let judgment be given; for it is not the one accused but the one convicted who is guilty. It is most wicked and dangerous to judge anyone on suspicion. In doubtful matters, let the decision be reserved for God’s judgment: let them entrust to their own judgment what they certainly know, and to divine judgment what they do not know. For no human examination may condemn one whom God has reserved for his own judgment. We ought not to judge uncertain matters until the Lord comes, who will bring hidden things to light, illuminate the things concealed in darkness, and reveal the purposes of hearts [Col. 0830B] [Note: [Col. 0829] G. reads “brings … to light”; the present text has “will bring”]. Although matters may be true, nevertheless they are not to be believed unless they are established by certain indications, unless they are proved by manifest judgment, unless they are made public according to judicial procedure.

260. On the superstition and condemnation of the chorepiscopi. We wish it to be known to all the faithful of God’s holy church and to our own people that the question of the superstition of the chorepiscopi did not come before us once, twice, or three times, but very frequently troubled our ears. The question itself was discussed repeatedly not only among clerics but also among laymen. Priests, deacons, and subdeacons ordained by regular bishops said, therefore, that those who appeared to have been as if consecrated by chorepiscopi were not priests, deacons, or subdeacons, and ought not to perform priestly office unless they had been completed by canonically ordained bishops. Drawing their sanction from canonical authority, they also asserted that those ordained by chorepiscopi had received through that laying on of hands a head that was wounded rather than episcopally sanctified. Where a wound has been inflicted, medicine must be applied so that health may be restored.

The laymen likewise said that they did not wish to hear the offices of such ministers or priests—that is, of those who had been as if ordained by chorepiscopi—and that they would nowhere allow their children, whether older or younger, or their household, to be signed or confirmed through the laying on of their hands, lest they receive a wound rather than a blessing.

When we wished to examine this quarrel more thoroughly, it seemed good to us to consult the apostolic see concerning it, as canonical authority commands and says: “If greater matters have arisen, let them be referred without hesitation to the apostolic see, as the holy synod has decreed and pious custom demands” [Note: [Col. 0829] “After episcopal judgment” has been omitted here, as in the second letter of Pope Pelagius, chapter 8].

Therefore we sent Archbishop Arno to the apostolic Leo, so that, among the other matters he was carrying, he might also question him about this, and so that whatever had to be decided concerning these matters might be regularly settled by our bishops with apostolic authority. He reported to us, by word and letter, that it was not necessary to discuss or define these things again, because they had very often been prohibited and condemned by his predecessors, by many holy bishops, and by synodal decrees; therefore, it was not necessary to debate them but to uphold what had already been defined.

For he said that no priest, deacon, or subdeacon ordained by them existed; no church dedicated by them; no virgin consecrated; no one confirmed; and no act belonging to episcopal ministry performed by them. Whatever of these things they had illicitly presumed to do had to be properly performed by canonically ordained bishops and reformed into a better condition [Col. 0831A] [Note: [Col. 0831] G., from a correction, reads “to perform and reform into a better condition”; Bal. reads “to perform and to reform into a better condition”], because reason does not allow something to be regarded as repeated when it is not shown to have been done.

He ordered that all the aforesaid chorepiscopi be condemned and driven into exile. But all these persons, especially the bishops of the kingdom entrusted to us by God, dealing more mildly with the aforesaid apostolic bishop’s permission and together with Arno, placed the aforementioned village bishops among the priests, on the condition that they presume nothing further in episcopal ministry and that thereafter no one who wished to avoid endangering his rank should be made such a bishop.

For this was decreed in the synod which we held at Regensburg by apostolic authority, for this same reason and for other matters: no one should consent to any of the aforesaid acts being done by any of them; whatever they have presumed to do episcopally must be performed by canonically ordained bishops; and no one anywhere should be regarded as having received anything belonging to episcopal ministry from chorepiscopi, because there was nothing in the giver which any of these people could have received [Note: [Col. 0831] G. reads “in the one giving”; Bal. reads “in the giver”]. Since none of them possessed what he could give, he could not give it.

For they were not bishops, since they were neither assigned a title at an episcopal see of any city nor canonically ordained by three bishops. Therefore they could perform nothing belonging to episcopal ministry. For this reason what they thought they had done is not shown to have been done: what they did not possess they could in no way give. Thus no principle permits what is known to have been regularly performed by canonically ordained bishops in the aforementioned matters to be regarded as repeated.

Hence, when the question of honor wrongly received often arises, who could doubt that what ought not to have been conferred must in no way be granted? For we know, as we also read in the ancient decrees of the fathers, that the true and just blessing of a legitimate bishop can remove every defect [Note: [Col. 0831] Bal. reads “by a true and just blessing of a legitimate bishop”] that had been imposed by a corrupt person. [Col. 0831C]

261. On not administering church property without the command of one’s own bishop. It has seemed good that bishops should always possess full authority over ecclesiastical property in every respect, according to the decrees of the holy canons. No one may dare to give or receive such property without the command of his own bishop; no one may presume to invade, devastate, or in any way damage it.

For concerning those who devastate churches and their property, we understand nothing other than that they are waging war against the God of eternal dominion and against his majesty, since those buildings serve him day and night and are consecrated to him. Let those who devastate and invade them beware—we foretell it [Note: [Col. 0831] G. deletes this phrase; Bal. includes it]—lest, if he is angered, they be devastated and destroyed by him whose blow the backs of mountains cannot endure.

We neither wish to do these things ourselves nor to consent to those who wish to do them, lest, God forbid, we destroy ourselves or consent to those who wish to destroy themselves. Therefore we command that if anyone has until now possessed something from ecclesiastical property by our grant, and wishes to retain it thereafter, he must come to his own bishops and strive to obtain it from them and from the heads of the churches from which such property appears to derive, in whatever just manner he can; and he must not seek, desire, or receive anything from it in any other way, lest the fire of greed for holy things, which is present in them, burn them more fiercely [Note: [Col. 0831] “the greedy,” Bal.; [Col. 0831] “them” is absent in Bal.].

Accordingly, the following decree is found in the sacred canons, composed by the Spirit of God: “If anyone gives or receives an offering apart from the bishop or the person appointed by him to distribute mercy to the poor, let both the giver and the receiver be accursed.”

For we know that accursed people are infamous and ruined even in the present age, are entirely excluded from the fellowship of the faithful without bread or water, and, if they depart this life without satisfaction to the church, will be exiles from the kingdom of God. Whoever pretends not to see or refuses to avoid this pit, let him know that he will be deprived in every respect of our fellowship, because not only those who do such things but also those who consent to wrongdoing are guilty.

For it is better for us not to possess an earthly kingdom than to lose the eternal one. I believe that God can help me more through the merits of his saints than through the entire secular army. Therefore we wish all to know that, even if we could gain the whole world through the good things we enjoy, we would not wish to lose our souls or yours, nor consent to those who wish to destroy themselves for the aforementioned desires.

For we have learned from the trumpet of the Gospel that it profits a man nothing to gain the whole world if he suffers the loss of his soul. And again: “What exchange will a man give for his soul?” And again: “These shall go into everlasting punishment, but the righteous into eternal life.” [Col. 0832B]

262. That women should not enter the altar; and that those to be baptized [Note: [Col. 0831] G. reads “the baptized”] should be instructed in the sacrament of faith and, after baptism, receive the heavenly chrism through the laying on of bishops’ hands. Women must not enter the altar. Those to be baptized must learn the symbol of faith and recite it to the bishop or priests on Thursday of Holy Week. Those who receive baptism while ill must, once recovered, be taught the symbol of faith, so that they may know how great a status of birth they have been deemed worthy of. Those who have been baptized must also receive the heavenly chrism after baptism and become participants in the kingdom of Christ.

263. That catechumens or penitents should not be given baptism or the sacrament of the Lord’s body at Easter, Pentecost, or the Nativity of the Lord, or before canonical reconciliation, but only blessed salt. During the most solemn days of Easter, the sacrament must not be given to catechumens, to those excluded from the church’s doors, or to those performing public penance before canonical reconciliation [Col. 0832C]; only blessed salt shall be given by priests in place of communion. Since the faithful do not change the sacraments during those days [Note: [Col. 0831] Bal. reads “among the faithful”], neither ought catechumens [Note: [Col. 0831] Bal. reads “among catechumens”] or public penitents to be changed [Note: [Col. 0831] Bal. reads “are changed”].

264. That general matters belonging to the order of the church should first be settled in synod, and particular matters discussed afterward. It has seemed good that whenever a synod is convened according to the statutes of the fathers, no bishop or priest should dare to bring forward any particular matter before the matters concerning the amendment of life, the strictness of the rule, and the remedies of souls have been settled.

265. Concerning those who seek church property from rulers, so that what they obtain may be considered void and they themselves deprived of communion. Those who seek church property from kings and, driven by dreadful greed, seize the substance of the needy shall have what they obtain declared void and shall be excluded from communion with the church whose property they desire to take [Col. 0832D] [Note: [Col. 0831] “a small thing,” Gal.].

266. That no bishop should presume to take anything from another bishop’s diocese. Let no bishop of another city, violating the canons, invade the parishes of any bishop and, inflamed by the torches of mad greed, seize what belongs to others because he is not content with his own [Note: [Col. 0831] Bal. and the Council of Clermont I, 10 read “his own and in the same way”; the Lyon and Paris manuscripts read “his own in some way”].

267. That those who invade, devastate, or plunder church property should be deprived of communion if they do not correct themselves when warned by the bishop. If anyone, by wicked cunning, removes, defrauds, invades, retains, or suppresses any small gift of whatever kind conferred upon the church by written titles, and, once admonished by the priest, does not immediately return it with God’s help, let him be expelled from communion with the Catholic church. [Col. 0833A]

268. That later bishops should not place themselves before earlier ones. Let no bishop dare to place himself before his predecessors.

269. That clerics who travel outside their own parish without letters from their bishop should be deprived of communion; and, if they prove incorrigible, restrained by flogging [Note: [Col. 0833] Bal. reads “restrained”]. Clerics must not have permission to wander without letters of recommendation from their bishop [Note: [Col. 0833] G. corrects “clerics” to “clerics to whom,” written in paler ink]. In every place to which they come without their bishop’s letters, as stated, they shall be held excluded from communion. The same rule shall be observed for monks. If they are not corrected by verbal rebuke, we decree that they too be restrained by flogging [Note: [Col. 0833] Bal. reads “when verbal rebuke has not corrected them, they too…”].

270. Concerning clerics, that they should be excommunicated or flogged if they do not avoid drunkenness. Above all, clerics must avoid drunkenness, which is the fuel and nurse of every vice [Note: [Col. 0833] absent in Bal.]. No one can possess sound judgment of body and mind if, overcome by wine, he is shown to be alienated from his senses. A mind weakened in this way is led more readily toward judgment, so that it can often incur sin or crime without knowing it [Note: [Col. 0833] G. reads “so that it may be led, and more readily…”]. Such ignorance cannot escape the punishment which is shown to have arisen from voluntary madness. Therefore, whoever is proved to have been drunk shall, as the order permits, either be removed from communion for forty days or subjected to bodily punishment.

271. Concerning those who attempt to harass the church or a cleric through calumny. If anyone attempts through calumny to harass the church or a cleric and is convicted, let him be barred from the church’s doors and from communion with Catholics, unless he performs worthy penance.

272. That laymen should not be ordained without prior religious commitment; and that men of proven character should be appointed over women’s monasteries [Note: [Col. 0833] G. reads “appointed over”; Bal. reads “assigned”]. We command that no layman become a cleric without first embracing the religious life. Men of proven character and mature age may enter a monastery of girls only for their necessities or services. Clerics who enter to celebrate Mass must hasten to return as soon as the ministry has been completed. Otherwise, neither a cleric nor a young monk may have access to the community of girls, unless either paternal or sibling relationship is proved to justify admission [Note: [Col. 0833] absent in Gal.].

273. What should be done concerning those who consider their bishop’s discipline toward them too severe. If any cleric considers his bishop’s discipline or correction toward him unjust, let him appeal to a synod according to the ancient constitutions [Note: [Col. 0833] G. reads “retraction”].

274. Concerning conspiracy among clerics, monks, or laymen. If any clerics, as has plainly occurred in many places at the devil’s instigation, unite in rebellion against authority through a conspiracy, and it becomes clear that oaths have been exchanged among them or a written document has been composed, this presumption must not be overcome by any excuses. Once the matter has been discovered and the case brought before a synod, the bishops then assembled shall punish the presumptuous according to the rank and status of the persons involved [Col. 0833D]. For just as charity is to be displayed in the heart according to the Lord’s commands, not through the writing of a document or by conspiracy, so whatever is admitted against the sacred Scriptures must be suppressed by episcopal authority and discipline.

275. What should be done concerning those who invade or devastate church property entrusted to them, or accept it without the consent of their own bishop. If anyone, driven by dreadful greed, seizes or retains property due to the church or to a priest, or obtains it from an authority through a dispute, he shall not excuse himself by any means if he does not restore it. If, after recognizing the ecclesiastical right, he does not immediately restore it to the church or priest, or delays bringing the matter before the chosen judges so that he may ascertain the right itself, let him be suspended from ecclesiastical communion until, after restoring the property, he makes both the church and the priest whole [Note: [Col. 0833] G. has “after ‘recognized’—the letter following t is erased—‘or’ deleted and written in the margin”].

The same form of ecclesiastical discipline prescribed by the earlier canons shall apply to those who delay assigning, in any manner, or presume to retain offerings legally left by the dead to churches or priests. The same judgment shall also affect anyone who presumes to reclaim, by any means, what he gave to churches out of devotion.

Let abbots, priests, and the other ministers have no power to alienate or pledge anything from church property or from the sacred ministry entrusted to them without the permission and subscription of their bishop. If they presume to do so, let them be deposed, with communion granted; and whatever has been rashly presumed or alienated shall be recovered by order of the bishop.

276. Concerning what is forbidden or permitted to be done on Sunday. We have heard that the people have been persuaded that on Sunday one ought not to travel with horses, oxen, or vehicles, nor repair anything needed for food, nor undertake any work pertaining to the cleanliness of a house or person. This is shown to belong more to Jewish superstition than to Christian observance. Therefore we decree that on Sunday whatever was previously permitted shall remain permitted [Note: [Col. 0833] absent in Bal.]. Nevertheless, we have judged that people should abstain from rural labor—that is, plowing, work in the vineyard, cutting the harvest, threshing, clearing land [Note: [Col. 0833] G. reads “arising from the clearing”], or hedge-work [Note: [Col. 0833] G. reads “which”]—so that they may come more easily to church and devote themselves to prayer. If anyone is found engaged in the works listed above or presumes to undertake what is forbidden, the manner in which he must correct this shall rest not with lay discipline but with the priest’s correction. [Col. 0834C]

277. Concerning those who presume to leave the church before Mass has ended. No layman shall leave Mass before the Lord’s Prayer has been said. If a bishop is present, his blessing must be awaited. No one may presume to leave before Mass has been completed.

278. Concerning those who presume to enter the church with weapons. No one may attend the morning or evening Masses with weapons intended for warfare. Whoever does so shall be subject to the priest’s authority as to the severity with which he should be corrected.

279. That laymen should not presume to stand inside the chancel rail in the church. Laymen must not presume to stand beside the altar where the holy mysteries are celebrated, among the clerics, either at vigils or at Masses. That area which is divided from the rail toward the altar shall be open only to the choirs of clerics singing psalms [Note: [Col. 0833] G. reads “that area”; G. also reads “turned toward”]. But the holy of holies shall be open to laymen and women for prayer and communion, as is customary. [Col. 0834D]

280. Concerning those who break the fast at the ninth hour on Holy Saturday of Easter. Some break the fast at the ninth hour on Holy Saturday and use banquets. Although on that very day the sun, shrouded in darkness, withdraws its light, and the elements themselves, thrown into confusion, display the grief of the whole world, they nevertheless profane the day’s fast and devote themselves to feasting. Since the universal church spends that entire day in mourning and abstinence because of the Lord’s Passion, whoever breaks the fast on it—apart from children, the old, and the sick—before the prayers of indulgence have been completed shall be excluded from Easter joy. Nor shall anyone receive the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood on that day who does not honor the day of his Passion through abstinence. [Col. 0835A]

281. Concerning the purgation of priests, and how the matter was treated and settled for the second time at Worms by Lord Charles and his men. We wish all of you, both present and future, to know that we undertook such extensive deliberation concerning the purgation of accused priests, after consulting the apostolic see, all our bishops, the other priests, and especially all our faithful, and decreed that it be carried out with witnesses, as is contained in our earlier capitulary, because we did not know that the blessed Pope Gregory had already settled this case.

When we had held a general assembly at Worms [Note: [Col. 0835] Bal. has “at Wormatia” here and in the heading], a letter of the blessed Pope Gregory was brought to us by Rihulf [Note: [Col. 0835] Bal. reads “Riculf”], metropolitan of Mainz, in which, among other things, these words were contained: “Concerning a priest or any other cleric accused by the people: if there are no certain witnesses who speak the truth concerning the crime brought forward [Note: [Col. 0835] Bal. reads “prove the truth”], an oath shall be required, and let him produce that witness of the purity of his innocence to whom all things are naked and open; thus let him remain in his own rank.”

Since all these matters exceed our powers, we leave them to be decided by the judgment of the bishops according to canonical sanction. When such matters arise, let the bishops strive to decide them in such a way that the accused win neither just reproach before the world nor, God forbid, condemnation before God, but, with the help of him who grants all things without stain, the rewards of eternal blessedness.

282. That everyone should judge with right judgment; and concerning the avoidance of lawsuits and quarrels. We exhort everyone to strive to bear wrongly judged lawsuits or quarrels with the summit of patience, as our Lord Jesus Christ admonishes us in his commands, saying: “Judge justly, children of men.” And: “With whatever judgment you judge, you shall be judged.” And again: “Gifts blind the eyes of the wise and remove the words of the righteous.” Whoever consents does not judge rightly. Thus the Lord’s command teaches: “What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do.” “Woe to you, judges and rulers, who accept gifts from the wicked and take justice away from the righteous.” And remember what is said: “God will repay each person according to his works or according to his righteousness.” [Col. 0835C]

283. That witnesses should be bound by an oath before they are questioned about a case. Before they are questioned about a case, witnesses must be bound by an oath [Note: [Col. 0835] G. corrects *debere* to *debent*], so that they swear they will say nothing false [Note: [Col. 0835] Bal. adds “against the truth”]. We also command that belief be granted more readily to witnesses of honorable standing than to those of low standing. The testimony of a single person, however distinguished and suitable his character may appear, must in no way be heard.

284. That no one should accuse bishops, priests, or clerics in secular courts. By the law of our gentleness we prohibit bishops from being accused in courts, lest, while their future impunity is thought to be assured by their benefit [Note: [Col. 0835] G. reads “benefits”], free opportunity be given to furious minds to attack them. If anyone has a complaint, therefore, which he brings forward, it should preferably be explained before other bishops, so that suitable and convenient hearing may be provided for everyone’s questions.

285. Concerning the privileges of churches and clerics, which must not be violated. We prohibit, even under threat of punishment, the mutilation of privileges which religious reverence obtained in former times, so that those who obey the church may also enjoy the benefits belonging to those to whom the church belongs [Note: [Col. 0835] G. reads “those,” rather than “these”].

286. That servants whom Jews have bought or circumcised should be removed from their power. If any Jew buys and circumcises a Christian slave or one belonging to any other sect, he shall be removed from that Jew’s power and remain free.

287. Concerning what earlier rulers established for the advantage of churches, so that it should always remain unmoved [Note: [Col. 0835] G. reads “or”]. We command that whatever antiquity formerly established concerning catholic law, whatever the pious authority of our forefathers decreed, and whatever our serenity has confirmed, be guarded whole and inviolate, with novel superstition removed [Note: [Col. 0835] G. reads “what is certain concerning catholic law”].

288. Concerning complete restoration. Complete restoration is said to occur whenever a thing or case that had perished is restored to its former condition, or what was taken from someone is restored, so that the cases or property of those who are known to have been compelled by fear of someone’s power, deceived by fraud or error, or deprived of their property or free status through captivity or any unjust necessity may be restored in full; or when some, because of the necessity of a long journey, are absent; or when matters shown to have been undertaken to the detriment of minors are to be restored. [Col. 0836B]

289. Concerning things unjustly taken, so that they may be justly restored in full according to the laws. Whenever the benefit of complete restoration is sought for the recovery of a thing or case, proceedings must be brought either concerning the thing or against the person, so that the thing itself which was taken may be recovered. When an action against the person has begun, the one proved to have taken the thing wrongfully shall restore within a year fourfold what was taken [Note: [Col. 0835] G. reads “shall be restored”]; after a year, it shall be returned twofold [Note: [Col. 0835] G. reads “fourfold”].

290. That judges may not harass the servants of churches or clerics. By divine authority we command that the servants of churches and of bishops or of any clerics not be worn down by judges or public officials through various compulsory services. Therefore the whole council asked the piety of our most glorious lord [Note: [Col. 0835] G. reads “the whole council was asked”] to restrain such presumptions from now on [Note: [Col. 0835] G. reads “that they should not have such presumptions”], so that the servants of the offices mentioned above may labor for their masters or for the church. If any judge or official wishes to occupy a cleric, or the servant of a cleric or church, in public or private business, let him be made an outsider to the church’s communion, which he obstructs.

291. That no further contest may be raised concerning crimes once decided. Concerning crimes of which someone has been acquitted, the accuser may not revive the accusation against him.

292. That the endowments of churches, together with the churches themselves, should always remain under the administration of their own bishop. Many people, contrary to the canonical decrees, ask that churches they have built be consecrated in such a way that they do not consider the endowment they have bestowed on the church to belong to the bishop’s administration. This practice displeased us in the past and is prohibited for the future. Everything must instead belong to the bishop’s administration and authority according to the ancient constitution.

[Col. 0836D] 293. That bishops should always see how judges act with all those entrusted to them. In accordance with the king’s admonition, bishops must always be observers of how judges deal with the people [Note: [Col. 0835] Bal. reads “bishops must always be observers”]. They must either correct the judges after warning them, or make their insolence known to the ears of the rulers [Note: [Col. 0835] Bal. reads “ears,” from the Beauvais manuscript and Ivo; the Troyes manuscript reads “to the judges”]. If they are unable to correct those who have been reproved, they shall suspend them both from the church and from communion.

294. Concerning devout women who sin and are not to be received unless they cease sinning. A devout woman who sins is not to be received into the church unless she ceases to sin. And if, after ceasing, she performs suitable penance for ten years, let her be admitted to communion. Before she is admitted to prayer in the church, however, she is not to approach the table of any Christian woman. If she is admitted, let the woman who received her also be regarded as absent. The corrupter likewise is to be bound by an equal penalty. A woman who has taken a husband is not to be admitted to penance unless, while that husband is still alive, she begins to live chastely, or unless she does so after he has died.

295. Concerning those who are excommunicated by priests, so that no one may approach them. If any layman is under excommunication [Note: [Col. 0837] an erased word, G.], no cleric or religious person is to approach his house. Likewise, if a cleric is under censure, he is to be avoided by clerics. If anyone is discovered conversing or dining with him [Note: [Col. 0837] “being entertained at table,” Bal.], he too is to be placed under censure. But this is to apply to those clerics who belong to his bishop and to all who have been notified about the person under censure, whether layman or cleric.

296. Concerning what is to be done with wandering and frivolous priests and clerics. It has also been decided that if a wandering and unstable cleric, whether established in the diaconal ministry [Col. 0837B] or in the presbyteral office, does not obey the commands of the bishop by whom he was ordained, so that he may perform his ministry continuously in the church entrusted to him, he is to be deprived both of communion and of honor for as long as he persists in his fault.

297. Concerning those who promise to pay a debt, that they are to be detained until payment [Note: [Col. 0837] “until absolution,” G.]. If anyone has promised to repay money on behalf of another’s debt, he is to be held to the fulfillment of the established promise.

298. Concerning what is to be done with those who have received another’s property for sale. If, after a price has been agreed [Note: [Col. 0837] “facto pterio,” G.; but these words have been deleted by a transverse line.], someone entrusts property to anyone for sale, and while it is being offered for sale by that person it perishes for whatever reason, the loss falls upon the person who gave it to him to sell. But if, without being requested by the owner, the recipient himself promised to sell the property and lost it while wishing to sell it, he incurs the loss of the property himself.

299. That a creditor is not to sell a debtor’s property before summoning him three times concerning payment. If a creditor, holding a pledge deposited with him without condition, has summoned the debtor three times so that, once the debt has been paid, he may recover his pledge, and the debtor has refused, after three warnings, to recover his pledge upon payment of the debt, the creditor shall have free power to sell the pledge.

300. That the faithful are not to share food with the rebaptized. Religious believers are not to share food with those who have been rebaptized.

301. Concerning what is to be done with those who, when ordered by a priest to leave the church, contemptuously refuse. Those who, when ordered by a priest to leave the church for any fault, contemptuously refuse are to be received to pardon more slowly, because of the offense of contumacy.

302. Concerning clerics disobedient to admonition, who are to be flogged. Clerics whom admonition has not corrected are to be restrained by flogging [Note: [Col. 0837] “admonitions,” G.].

303. Concerning those who owe something to others, while something is also owed to them by those same persons, so that the amounts are to be set off in payment. If anyone owes another ten solidi, and the person who owes them is owed five solidi by his creditor for whatever reason [Note: [Col. 0837] corrected to “to him,” G.; “are owed to him” is deleted in G.], and the creditor comes and demands the full ten solidi from the debtor, if that debtor proves that five solidi are owed to him by the creditor, let the one who refused to set off the debt lose the case in which he sued for the full ten solidi [Note: [Col. 0837] “loses,” G.]. The same rule applies to grain and other commodities.

304. Concerning what is to be done with those who have lent something to a son under paternal authority. Whoever, contrary to the prohibitions of the laws, lends money to a son under paternal authority without the father’s knowledge cannot claim it from the son either while the father is alive or after he has died [Note: [Col. 0837] “to a son under paternal authority,” Bal.].

305. Concerning laymen who abandon their wives. [Col. 0838A] Those laymen who abandon or have abandoned the marital union without serious fault, and who, without putting forward any plausible grounds for their disagreement, abandon their marriages in order to presume upon unlawful or alien relationships—if, before they have stated the causes of their disagreement before the bishops of their province [Note: [Col. 0837] “before the bishop,” G.], and before their wives have been condemned by judgment, they cast them off—are to be excluded from communion with the church and from the assembly of the holy people, because they stain faith and marriage [Note: [Col. 0837] “so that no causes,” G.].

306. That stipends are to be distributed to clerics according to merit. All clerics who faithfully and diligently serve the church are to receive from the priests the stipends due for their holy labors, according to the merit of their service and the order of the canons [Note: [Col. 0837] “or they are to be bound to maintain the order”; the remainder is lacking, Bal.].

307. Concerning the rejection from clerical cases of accusers and accusations that the laws of the world do not admit. We decree by divine and synodal authority that accusations, accusers, and the proceedings connected with them, which secular laws do not admit [Note: [Col. 0837] “by law,” G.], are to be completely rejected from the cases of clerics; for it is unworthy that superiors should suffer from inferiors what inferiors disdain to undergo from them.

308. Concerning a bishop who presumes to retain, ordain, or judge another’s parishioner. No bishop is to presume to retain, ordain, or judge another’s parishioner without the consent of his own bishop; for just as his ordination will be invalid, so also will his judgment [Note: [Col. 0837] “judicial decision,” Bal.], since we hold that no one is bound by the sentence of any judge except his own. For the one who could not ordain him will in no way be able to judge him.

309. Concerning foreign judgments, which are not to be accepted. We prohibit foreign judgments by a general sanction; for it is unworthy that a person who ought to have provincial judges chosen by himself should be judged by outsiders.

310. Concerning penitents, how they ought to receive penance. At the time when penitents seek penance, they are to receive from the priest the imposition of hands and sackcloth. If they have not cut their hair or changed their clothing, they are to be rejected. Unless they have performed penance worthily, they are not to be received. It is also not to be entrusted readily to young people, because of the weakness of their age. Nevertheless, the viaticum is not to be denied to anyone lying at the point of death.

311. Concerning contumacious clerics and those slow to perform their office. Contumacious clerics are to be corrected by the bishops insofar as the order of their dignity permits. If any, lifted up by the pride of their former rank, should perhaps despise communion, or neglect to attend the church or fulfill their office, let them be granted communion among strangers; so that, when penance has corrected them, they may be entered again in the register and recover their rank and dignity.

312. Concerning those who presume to use another’s money entrusted to them as a loan. If anyone deposits a purse or sealed silver, and the person with whom it was deposited handles it against the depositor’s will, an action both for breach of deposit and for theft lies against him [Note: [Col. 0837] lacking in Bal.].

313. Concerning a creditor who, when the debtor delays payment, sells the pledge retained by him, and must return to the debtor whatever was received in excess. If a creditor sells a thing given to him as security for a debt because the debtor delays payment, whatever more was received than was owed [Note: [Col. 0837] lacking in Bal.; “is owed,” G.] he must return to the debtor [Note: [Col. 0837] “let it be returned,” Bal.; “more,” G.].

314. That a bishop is not at all to be summoned to judgment outside his own province unless he has appealed; but he is to be heard within his province by all his provincial bishops. No bishop is to be summoned to judgment outside his own province. Rather, once he has been canonically summoned to a place suitable for all, at the time of a synod he is to be heard by all the provincial bishops [Note: [Col. 0837] “co-provincial bishops,” Bal.], who must deliver a concordant and canonical sentence concerning him. For if this has been granted to lesser persons, both clerics and laymen, how much more ought it to be observed in the case of bishops? But if he himself regards the metropolitan or the judges as suspect or finds them hostile, let him be judged before the primate of the diocese or before the pontiff of the Roman see.

315. Concerning bishops who appeal to the Roman pontiff. It has been decided that if an accused bishop appeals to the Roman pontiff [Note: [Col. 0839] “a condemned bishop,” in Hadrian, from whom this chapter has been taken], that which he himself decrees is to be established.

316. Concerning presbyters who permit pagans to perform pagan practices [Note: [Col. 0839] “paganism,” Bal.] in their parishes, and concerning what is to be done with the fields in which such acts are known to have occurred. If, in the parish of any presbyter, unbelievers light torches [Note: [Col. 0839] “kindle them,” Bal.], or worship trees, springs, or stones, and he neglects to remove this [Note: [Col. 0839] a second hand adds “someone” above the line in G.], let him know that he is sacrilegious [Note: [Col. 0839] “sacrilege” corrected to “sacrilegious,” G.; “guilty of sacrilege,” Bal.]. If the lord or organizer of the matter itself [Note: [Col. 0839] “exhorter,” corrected from “ortator,” G.] refuses to correct it after being warned, let him be deprived of communion.

[Col. 0839B] 317. Concerning penitents who presume to marry other men after their husbands have died. A woman doing penance who presumes to marry another man after her husband has died, and a woman who has lived with an outsider in either a suspect or forbidden intimacy, are both to be kept away from the thresholds of the church with that man. It has also been decided that the same rule is to be observed concerning a man placed under penance [Note: [Col. 0839] “to be observed,” Bal.].

318. Concerning those who have received another’s property for sale and, having sold it for less, are compelled to pay the price entrusted to them. If anyone instructs another to sell his property for ten solidi, and the latter sells it for eight, he is to be compelled to make up to the person who gave the commission the price that had been instructed, whatever less he received from the buyer. The sale, however, cannot be rescinded.

319. Concerning one who has bought a slave in good faith, if the slave flees because of an earlier fault. If a slave bought in good faith flees because of an old fault, the owner is compelled to return not only the price but also whatever the slave took away in his flight.

[Col. 0839C] 320. Concerning those who presume to condemn people without investigation by tyrannical power. And concerning bishops and priests, that they ought not to be judged by anyone except those by whom they may also be ordained. There are some who condemn people without investigation by tyrannical power rather than by canonical authority. Just as they elevate some through the favor of partiality, so, moved by hatred and envy, they humble others and condemn them on the light breath of opinion, although they do not establish their crimes. Therefore, by common decree we decree that whenever any bishop is accused, his case is to be heard after all the bishops of the same province have assembled, so that he may not be secretly judged or condemned; for he cannot first be judged by others except by those by whom he could have been ordained. If this is done otherwise, it shall have no force.

321. Concerning those who have cases against their own bishops or against others, to be heard before the synod of the province; except those who have a complaint against their metropolitan. If a cleric or layman has a case against his own bishop or against another, or if a bishop has a case against anyone, let him be judged before the synod of the province. But if a bishop or cleric has a complaint against the metropolitan of that same province, let him seek the primate of the diocese, and let him be judged before him or before the apostolic see.

322. Concerning silencing in accusation or testimony the mouths of those who are known to be dead by divine utterances. It has been decided to close the voice of those whom we know to be dead, not by human but by divine utterances, so that they may neither accuse priests nor testify against them; for a deadly voice ought rather to be cut off than heard.

[Col. 0840A] 323. Concerning not denying an appeal to the accused. It has been decided that if the accused regards the judges as suspect, he may appeal; for a hearing ought not to be denied to one who requests it [Note: [Col. 0839] “ought not to be denied,” G.].

324. That the confessions of defendants who have confessed concerning themselves are not to be believed against others [Note: [Col. 0839] corrected in G. from “from them”; Bal. likewise has this reading]. The confession of those involved in crimes is not to be believed against others unless they have first proved themselves innocent [Note: [Col. 0839] “what they are,” G.]; for the declaration of a defendant against anyone is dangerous and must not be admitted.

325. Concerning usurpers of boundaries, before the hearing of the case has been concluded. If anyone is proved to be a usurper of boundaries, because, before anything had been settled by judgment, he invaded what another had held, he is not only to lose what he wrongfully presumed to take, but, so that no one may seize another’s property, once the usurper of another’s right has been defeated in the case, he is to restore as much ground as he presumed to invade [Note: [Col. 0839] “the cause has been concluded” corrected to “the matter has been judged,” G.].

326. Concerning those who act against the will of the deceased and are therefore to lose the inheritance. An inheritance is to be taken away from all who act against the will of the deceased, as unworthy persons.

327. Concerning those to whom something has been left by testament, who are not permitted to do anything against the will of the deceased. Whoever has received and claimed something left to him by testament, and wishes to act against the will of the deceased, shall have no permission whatsoever to do so.

328. That the will of the deceased is to be carried out in all things by the heirs. No one has been granted permission to usurp the property of men or to divide it contrary to good morals. But if a father has ordered a division made by him, it is to remain in force, provided that it is shown that the same will persisted until the end of his life [Note: [Col. 0839] “by the synod,” G.].

329. Concerning sons who have injured their father, and are to be deprived of gifts. If a son has obtained something by his father’s gift and afterward injures him, once the causes of the injury have been proved in court, the father, if he wishes, is to have the gift restored to him in full.

330. Concerning a gift made by a father to his son, if the father has been injured by him, which is to be revoked. A gift made by a father to his son is to be revoked if the father proves that he has been injured by him.

331. Concerning detraction from rulers and elders, which is to be avoided by all [Note: [Col. 0839] “by all people,” G.]. All the faithful and people of every rank must take the greatest care not secretly or publicly to tear apart the Lord’s anointed with detraction and abuse, considering the example of Mary, who, because she had spoken against Moses, the Lord’s servant, on account of the Ethiopian woman, was punished with the uncleanness of leprosy. And also the psalmist’s words: “Do not touch my anointed ones, and do not speak wickedly against my prophets.”

332. That all who have been summoned in a dispute must plead nowhere except in their own court. If a cleric or layman has been summoned on a charge or in a dispute, he is to be heard nowhere except in his own court, once summoned there.

333. That appellants are not to be hindered by any detention. An appellant ought not to be injured by any harsh treatment or custody in prison or detention. The appellant is also to be allowed to remedy a defective case by means of an appeal.

334. Concerning those who, disregarding a guarantor, have chosen to pursue the debtor for payment. If anyone, disregarding the guarantor, prefers to hold his debtor, the guarantor or his heir is released from the obligation of the guarantee. But if the representative in the litigation has been defeated, his principal is liable for payment.

335. That free men can worsen or improve their status. A free man who has control over his own status can make it worse or better; and therefore he may hire out his services by day and by night.

[Col. 0841A] 336. Concerning not keeping concubines. A man who has a wife cannot have a concubine during that time, lest affection for the concubine separate him from his wife [Note: [Col. 0841] “and lest,” G.].

337. Concerning monks who despise their [Note: [Col. 0841] lacking in Bal.] monasteries and are to be recalled by the bishop. It has also been agreed by unanimous consent that if any monks or nuns, having been placed in a community, choose a religious way of life and afterward withdraw from that community either to their parents or to any private property, and, after being admonished by their bishop by letter, delay returning to the enclosure of their monastery, they are to be suspended from communion until the end of their life. They are not to be admitted to the grace of the Eucharist before they return, with the most humble supplication and satisfaction, to their own fold, from which they appear to have withdrawn through the insolence of wandering [Note: [Col. 0841] The following material is not found in the Council of Chalcedon, the source of this chapter.][Note: [Col. 0841] lacking in Bal.].

338. Concerning women who have changed into religious dress in their own homes, and afterward choose sexual intercourse, and what is to be done. Concerning widows and girls who, in their own homes, have changed their clothing into the habit of religion, whether by their parents [Col. 0841B] or by themselves, and afterward believe that they may enter into marriage contrary to the institutions of the Fathers or the commands of the canons: both are to be regarded as suspended from communion until they amend what they have unlawfully done. If they neglect to amend it, they are to be permanently separated from communion and from the table of all Christians [Note: [Col. 0841] “separated,” feminine, Bal., who shortly before did not alter “both.”].

339. That four persons must always be present in trials. What persons are normally present in trials? Four: the accuser in the case, the defender in the case, the witnesses, and the judge. What function does each perform? The judge uses equity, the witnesses truth, the accuser intent to enlarge the case, and the defender mitigation to diminish the case. For a case often arises from calculation, fear, glory, or money—that is, from the desire to obtain some advantage or to avoid some disadvantage.

340. That not only those who commit theft, but also those who give assistance or advice for carrying it out, are liable to an action for theft. Not only the person who commits the theft, but also the person through whose work or advice the theft was committed, is liable to an action for theft.

341. Who are agnates and who are cognates [Note: [Col. 0841] “are,” Bal.]. Agnates are those who descend through the male line; cognates are those who descend through the female line. Therefore paternal uncles and the sons of paternal uncles are both agnates and cognates; maternal uncles, however, and the sons of maternal uncles are cognates, not agnates.

342. Concerning those who have falsely claimed under fear or terror that they were slaves. Whoever, through fear and the pressure of someone’s terror, has falsely declared in the official record before the governor that he is a slave [Note: [Col. 0841] added above the line in G.] is not thereby prejudiced in defending his status afterward.

343. Concerning those who break into houses, plunder or storm estates, or commit robberies, and what is to be done. Those who plunder, break into [Note: [Col. 0841] lacking in G.], or storm houses or estates, if they have done so as an assembled crowd bearing weapons, are to be punished by death. The term “weapons,” however, includes everything by which harm can be done to a person’s safety.

344. Concerning those who receive robbers or other criminals. Those who receive attackers and likewise robbers are subjected to the same penalty as the robbers themselves; for once the receivers of marauders have been removed, the desire of the ravagers falls silent.

345. Concerning those who cause arson. If anyone sets a fire out of malicious intent, he is ordered to be killed after being convicted of this crime by the most severe penalties. But if it is established that the fire was caused through negligence, whatever damage was inflicted on anyone, and whatever property perished in the fire, is to be repaired by double compensation.

[Col. 0842A] 346. Concerning constitutions enacted against the canons, the decrees of prelates, or good morals, which have no validity. Constitutions enacted against the canons, the decrees of the Roman or other pontiffs, or good morals have no force.

347. That a cleric is not to be bound by a sentence pronounced by a judge other than his own. In cases involving clerics, this rule is to be observed: none of them is to be bound by a sentence pronounced by anyone other than his own judge [Note: [Col. 0841] “and not,” Bal.].

348. That those who have inflicted false charges on others are to be punished and made infamous for their falsehood. Everyone who has inflicted false charges on others is to be punished and, because of his falsehood, bear infamy [Note: [Col. 0841] “bring forth,” G.].

349. Concerning the reconsideration of a provincial synod through the vicars of the bishop of the city of Rome. A provincial synod is to be reconsidered through the vicars of the bishop of the city of Rome, if he has decreed it [Note: [Col. 0841] “if they have decreed it,” G.].

350. That no one is to accuse a bishop or the agents of a church before others until he has first approached him privately and requested justice from him in private. If anyone has a case against a bishop, he is not first to go to other bishops or other judges to accuse him until he has privately stated his complaint to him and received from him either a just correction or a reasonable explanation. Truth itself instructs us: “If your brother sins against you, go and rebuke him between you and him alone. If he does not listen to you, take with you two or three others. And if he does not listen to you, tell it to the Church”; that is, accuse him publicly then and not before. And so forth.

351. Concerning infamous persons or sacrilegious persons, who cannot accuse the religious [Note: [Col. 0841] “the infamous person,” as G. corrects it; “infants,” Bal.]. No infamous or sacrilegious person is ever permitted, in any matter whatsoever, to give testimony against a religious Christian, even if he is a humble and servile person, nor to bring an action or formal charge against a Christian concerning anything [Note: [Col. 0841] “although … Christian” is lacking in Bal.].

352. That cases which secular laws do not admit are not to be heard by ecclesiastical judges [Note: [Col. 0841] “are not to be admitted,” G.]. No cases are to be heard by ecclesiastical judges that are not contained in the laws or are known to be prohibited.

[Col. 0842C] 353. That those who are compelled to suffer damages for a moderate injury are to be made infamous. Whoever is compelled to suffer damages for an injury judged moderate, although he may appear to have been condemned in a civil action, is nevertheless made infamous.

354. Concerning those who are not to be condemned in their absence. In a capital case no one is to be condemned in his absence. Nor can an absent person accuse or be accused through another.

355. That those who violently occupy another’s property must fully restore to its rightful owners whatever has been lost or alienated there. If, from property that someone has violently occupied, anything perishes or burns for any reason, or if slaves who were violently seized die, even if it does not appear that this occurred through any fraud of the person who occupied it, nevertheless everything that has perished is to be restored by that person, since he is seen to have violently occupied property belonging to another.

356. Concerning those who have engaged in intercourse with animals, or have committed incest with blood relatives up to the degree of affinity in the manner of animals, or have had intercourse with males. In this title Greek words are given, namely, περὶ τῶν ἀλογευσαμένων, ἤ καὶ ἀλογευομένων [Note: [Col. 0841] “periton. alegeus. alle. non. ecce alogio. me. con.”, G.]. This can be rendered in Latin: “Concerning those who have behaved or are behaving irrationally.” In this sentence there is a threefold meaning: namely, concerning those who have had intercourse with animals, or who, in the manner of animals, have committed incest with blood relatives up to the degree of affinity, or who have had intercourse with males. Whoever has committed any one of these acts is either to be punished with death, or, if life is granted to him, is to perform true penance according to the decision of the Council of Ancyra, contained in chapters fifteen and sixteen [Note: [Col. 0843] “and [chapter] six” is lacking in Bal.].

357. That in a capital case or a case concerning status the parties themselves, not advocates, are to act. Whenever a matter has been brought forward in a capital case or a case concerning status, it is to be conducted not through representatives but by the parties themselves [Note: [Col. 0843] another hand has written “advocates” in the margin, B.].

358. That metropolitans are not to presume to hear the cases of their provincial bishops unless all the provincial bishops are present. If any metropolitan bishop attempts to do anything outside what pertains solely to his own parish without the counsel and consent of all the provincial bishops [Note: [Col. 0843] “co-provincial bishops,” Bal.], he shall be subject to the danger of his rank; and what he has done is to be considered invalid and void. But whatever it is necessary to do or arrange concerning the cases of the provincial co-bishops and concerning the needs of their churches, clerics, and laypeople, is to be done with the consent of all the provincial bishops [Col. 0843B], not with any arrogance of domination, but with the most humble and harmonious administration, as the Lord says: “I did not come to be served, but to serve.” And elsewhere: “The one who is greater among you will be your servant”; and so forth. Likewise, the provincial bishops themselves are to act with his counsel, except insofar as matters pertain to their own parishes, according to the constitutions of the holy Fathers [Note: [Col. 0843] “all this is added in the margin,” G.], so that with one mind and one voice the holy Trinity may be glorified harmoniously forever.

359. That clerics are to reject the reproach by which laypeople are accused. Let it be known to all that whatever is reproved in laypeople ought much more to be condemned beforehand in clerics.

360. Concerning what is to be done with informers, and who informers are. Let the informer’s tongue be cut out, or, once convicted, let his head be cut off. Informers are those who betray others out of envy.

361. Concerning those who fabricate a written or verbal insult against another’s reputation [Note: [Col. 0843] “fama,” G.] in public. Whoever fabricates in public a written or verbal insult against another’s reputation, and is discovered but cannot prove what he wrote, is to be flogged. Whoever first finds such writings is to tear them up, if he does not wish to incur the charge of having committed the act himself [Note: [Col. 0843] “fabricated,” Bal., here and in the text].

362. Concerning those who give the same thing to two owners. If anyone gives one thing to two people by lawful written instruments, to one first and to the other afterward, it is not to be investigated in these gifts who was first and who later. Rather, the person who possessed the thing when the donor handed it over is to possess it, as it was handed over to him. Nor does it matter whether such a gift was made to relatives or to outsiders.

363. Concerning slaves, who are not to be interrogated against their master by anyone. Slaves cannot be interrogated against their master either by the governor or by an administrator, whether in minor cases or in capital cases.

364. Concerning those who, in anger, have accused someone of a crime and afterward, coming to their senses, refuse to pursue it, and what is to be done. If anyone, in anger, rashly brings a criminal charge against someone, the insult is not to be regarded as an accusation. But, after time has been allowed for reflection, let him declare in writing that he will prove what he said in anger, so that, if after his anger he comes to his senses and refuses to repeat and write it, he is not to be held guilty of the crime.

365. That those who bring a criminal charge must write that they will prove it; and that the case is to be heard where the crime is known to have been committed. Whoever brings a criminal charge must write that he will prove it. In truth, the case is to be heard where the crime was committed; and whoever does not prove what he has charged is to suffer the penalty that he himself imposed [Note: [Col. 0843] G. reads “and,” corrected from “so that,” which Bal. likewise has. Another contemporary hand has written in the margin: “otherwise: so that if he does not prove the charge, he suffers the penalty that he himself imposed.”].

366. That no one is to leave his church without unavoidable necessity. No one is to leave his own church for any reason while he is able to remain in it.

367. Concerning what is to be done with those who have been summoned before another’s judge. A person summoned before his own judge is to state his case; one who has not been summoned before his own judge may remain silent if he wishes. And whenever the person summoned appeals, a period of delay is to be granted.

368. Concerning those who presume to read notorious writings or sing notorious songs. Those who are found reading or singing infamous books are to be excommunicated.

369. Concerning those who are to be excluded from accusing clerics. Homicides, criminals, thieves, sacrilegious persons, plunderers, poisoners, adulterers, those who have committed abduction, those who have given false testimony, and those who have resorted to diviners and magicians are in no way to be admitted either to accusation or to testimony.

370. Concerning those who presume to consult diviners or astrologers. Whoever consults astrologers, soothsayers, haruspices, or prophets concerning the safety of the ruler or the highest interests of the state is to be punished by death together with the person who gives the response.

371. Concerning the authors or instigators of seditions or riots. The authors or instigators of sedition and riot among the people are, according to the quality of their rank, either to be crucified, thrown to wild beasts, or deported to an island.

372. Concerning the danger facing judges and their duty of caution. The danger facing the one who judges is greater than that facing the one who is judged. Therefore each person must take care not to judge or punish anyone unjustly.

373. Concerning suppressing accusations against a teacher. No one is to undertake accusations against a teacher, because a person whom God has reserved for his own judgment cannot be condemned by human examination.

374. That those who take up arms against fathers are hateful to God. God hates those who take up arms against fathers in such a way that invaders of their fathers are branded with infamy throughout the whole world.

[Col. 0844C] 375. How the tithes and offerings of the faithful are to be distributed by priests. Presbyters are to be instructed and likewise admonished, so that they understand that the tithes and offerings they receive from the faithful are the support of the poor, guests, and travelers [Note: [Col. 0843] “to these,” Bal.], and that they must use them not as their own but as entrusted to them. They must know that they will render an account of all these things in the presence of the divine majesty, and that, unless they faithfully administer them to the poor and to those mentioned above, they will suffer condemnation. The sacred canons establish how they are to be distributed: namely, that four portions are to be made from the whole—one to support the fabric of the church, another to be distributed to the poor, a third to be held by the presbyter with his clerics, and a fourth to be reserved for the bishop. Whatever the pontiff orders from these things is to be done with prudent counsel.

376. That women are not to live with presbyters or other clerics, serve them, stand within the chancel, or approach the altar. It must be prohibited and observed by every means that any priest keep in his house those women concerning whom there may be suspicion, as is stated in the canons. He must not keep not only those women, but even those whom the ancient canons permit; for, at the instigation of the devil, wickedness is frequently found to have been committed even with those women, or with their female attendants. If any woman among them has such a need that the support of a presbyter is necessary for her, she is to have a house in a village or settlement far from the presbyter’s dwelling, and there he is to provide her with what is necessary. But this too is to be prohibited in every way according to the authority of the canons: no woman is to presume to approach the altar, serve the presbyter, or stand or sit within the chancel.

377. That incestuous persons are to be diligently sought out by priests through truthful and God-fearing men and punished canonically. Priests are to seek out incestuous persons with every diligence, through truthful men who keep the fear of God before their eyes. If any are found, they are immediately to strive either to correct them personally or, with the assistance of their archdeacon or bishop, to eradicate this very evil; lest, through such a great disgrace and crime, the priests themselves be polluted and perish, and others in their neighborhood incur the wrath of almighty God.

378. That presbyters and other clerics are to guard themselves from every vice, faithfully instruct those subject to them, and lead them in every good work [Note: [Col. 0845] lacking in G.]. Clerics are to be admonished and instructed so that, first, they themselves may be free from all fornication, impurity, luxury, and every pollution of the flesh. Then they are to preach in words and display examples to the people subject to them [Note: [Col. 0845] “the people subject to them,” Bal.], teaching them to abstain from all fornication and from every irrational or useless animal lust and pollution, and to prepare themselves for God with body and mind made pure.

### 379. On receiving and judging the confessions of the faithful, and on giving counsel as to what penance should be imposed according to the nature and extent of the sin

When a priest receives the confession of sins from any member of the faithful, he must inquire first how the sin was committed, whether it was repeated afterward or done frequently, and whether it was done voluntarily, under compulsion, through drunkenness, or by any other contrivance. When he has discovered [Note: [Col. 0845] Bal. reads *viderit*, “has seen,” instead of *invenerit*, “has discovered.”] from what source the root of that sin proceeded, he should then apply an appropriate remedy. What remedy is to be applied for each sin must be understood according to the ordinances of the authentic canons and of the holy fathers [Note: [Col. 0845] G. reads *intelligi*; Bal. reads *intelligi debet*, “must be understood.”], and not according to human preference, but according to the will of God. In this matter, neither human will nor favor is to be pursued; rather, the will of God must be sought in all things, so that by worthy prayers and worthy repentance [Col. 0845C] the vengeance of almighty God, provoked by sin, may be appeased [Note: [Col. 0845] Bal. reads *suo*, “by his own,” instead of *cum*.].

### 380. Concerning those who, previously bearing no hatred but defending themselves, have killed someone; how the prescribed period is to be corrected

If anyone, walking quietly along a road, or even being in his own house, in a city street, or in a village, suddenly kills a man because another has attacked him or because, when a quarrel has arisen, he wished to defend himself—having previously borne no hatred toward that man—let him do penance for seven years according to canonical regulation. For three years he is to be deprived of communion; for the remaining four, while admitted to communion and to the reception of prayers and offerings [Note: [Col. 0845] omitted by Bal.], it shall depend upon the priest’s judgment whether he is worthy to receive the body of Christ or should be separated from it until the completion of his penance. Abstinence from food shall be determined by the priest according to the penitent’s ability, devotion, and disposition to shed tears [Note: [Col. 0845] Bal. reads “according to the devotion and feeling of his tears.”].

### 381. Concerning a woman who has married two brothers, and concerning her husband: what is to be done

A woman who has married two brothers must be cast off until the day of her death.
