Yet, out of consideration for human frailty, she ought to be reconciled through the sacraments at the end of her life, provided that the marriage is first dissolved, that she remain unmarried, and that her husband [Note: [Col. 0845] A gloss is written above the line in G.: “that is, the later husband, if he knew.”] live without a wife and submit to a similar penance.

But if two brothers have committed fornication with one woman, each not knowing of the other’s fornication, then, as soon as they learn of the adultery, the one who has her as his wife must dismiss her. After doing penance, he may be joined to another woman if his wife has died; while she is alive, he may not. She, however, may never afterward be taken in marriage, but, subjected to perpetual penance [Note: [Col. 0845] G. reads *poenitentia*, “penance.”], let her receive the grace of communion until the end of her life [Note: [Col. 0845] Bal. begins a new chapter here: “Concerning women and men who crush infants.”].

A woman who, while sleeping, has crushed her son, so that he died, shall do penance for six years. If her husband was in the house, he shall do penance for four years; if he was in the same bed, he shall likewise do penance—two years on bread and water, and the remaining four according to what the priest judges them able to bear—and shall impose abstinence from food.

### 382. Concerning a woman who has committed adultery against her husband, and likewise a man who has committed adultery against his wife: how both are to be treated

If a married woman has committed adultery and comes secretly to confession, she shall do penance for seven years, three on bread and water; for the remaining four, it shall be left to the priest’s judgment how he considers her able to bear it, and abstinence from food shall accordingly be imposed upon her.

Likewise, if a married man has committed adultery, he shall do the same; that is, he shall not receive communion for three years.

If a man’s wife has committed adultery, and this has been discovered and made public by the husband, he may dismiss his wife, if he wishes, on account of fornication. She, however, shall perform public penance according to what has been set forth above. While she lives, her husband may in no way have permission to take another wife.

But if he wishes to reconcile the adulteress to himself, he shall have permission to do so, provided that he performs penance together with her; and, when the penance has been completed, both shall approach the grace of communion, as was stated above.

The same rule shall be observed in the case of a woman. If her husband has committed adultery against her, she has the power to dismiss him on account of fornication. Nevertheless, she shall remain unmarried as long as her husband lives, because neither does he have the power to take another wife while the first is alive [Note: [Col. 0845] G. omits this; written in the margin: “otherwise, unless the first remains; nor may she take another except the first.”], nor does she have the power to take another man. They do, however, have permission to reconcile with one another.

### 383. That all should devoutly assemble for the bishop’s confirmation and not neglect to provide him with what is necessary

We command that all should diligently and devoutly come together to receive, through the laying on of the hands of the bishop [Col. 0846C], the gift of the Holy Spirit [Note: [Col. 0845] Bal. reads *domum*, “house,” instead of *donum*, “gift.”], and that they faithfully supply their bishop [Note: [Col. 0845] Bal. reads *sua*, “her,” instead of *suo*, “their.”] with whatever is necessary; and that everyone obey him in all things.

### 384. Concerning the instruction of children, both in the mystery of faith and baptism and in the gift of the Holy Spirit

Everyone must know that children, when they have reached an age capable of understanding, are to be instructed concerning the sacrament of faith, the mystery of baptism, and the gift of the sevenfold grace of the Holy Spirit.

### 385. Concerning frequent confession of sins

We wish it to be known to everyone that, except for the confession made to priests in order to receive counsel and to appease God, confession of sins is to be made frequently to God in prayer.

### 386. Concerning the disclosure of other people’s sins, and that concealing them is itself a sin

We desire it to be known to all the faithful that those who are aware of the sins of others commit sin unless they disclose them for the sake of correction and salvation [Col. 0846D]. Hence it is written: “It does no good for the person who does not share in another’s error if he gives consent to the one who errs.” And elsewhere: “Not only those who do such things, but also those who consent to those who do them, are guilty.”

### 387. That those who have received the faith offend more grievously than others if they nevertheless persist in evil works

Everyone must know and remember without forgetting that those who have received the faith of Christ and ended their lives in evil deeds will be punished more severely than those who died without faith and nevertheless performed good works; for it is better not to receive the faith than, after receiving it, to turn backward.

### 388. Concerning marriage, which was instituted by God

Let it be known to everyone that marriage was established by God, and that it is not to be desired for the sake of lust but for the procreation of children; and that the life of good married people has been portrayed by Job [printed *lob*].

### 389. Concerning the chastity of those who are to be joined in marriage

Everyone must know and firmly retain that those who wish to take wives, just as they desire to find them chaste and undefiled, must likewise approach them chaste and undefiled, and receive them with the blessing of the priest, as is contained in the sacramentary. But first they must bind them by a deed of dowry.

### 390. That everyone, from the least to the greatest, should obey his priests as he obeys the Lord, in whose place they exercise an embassy in the Church

From the chapters confirmed at Theodon’s villa by Lord Charles.

We wish and command that everyone, of both the higher and lower orders, from the least to the greatest, should obey his priests, just as they obey the Most High God, in whose place the priests exercise an embassy in the Church [Col. 0847B]. For by no means can we recognize how those can be faithful to us who appear unfaithful to God and disobedient to their priests [Note: [Col. 0847] Bal. reads *infideles*, “unfaithful,” instead of *infidi*.]; nor how those will obey us and submit to our ministers and legates who do not obey their priests in matters concerning God and the interests of the churches.

Indeed, according to the word of truth, the one who can destroy soul and body in Gehenna is more to be feared than the one who can torture the body and take away temporal honors. Of the former it is said: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever rejects you rejects me.” And elsewhere: “Whoever touches you touches the pupil of my eye.” And again: “Whoever causes one of these little ones to stumble, it is better for him that an ass’s millstone be hung around his neck and that he be drowned in the depths [Note: [Col. 0847] Bal. reads “the depth”] of the sea.” And again: “Whoever receives you receives me; and whoever receives me receives him who sent me.” And there are many other sayings like these [Note: [Col. 0847] Bal. reads *horumque*, “and of these,” instead of *horum*].

Supported, therefore, by these declarations [Col. 0847C], we command that everyone, to the best of his ability, be supremely obedient to them both in carrying out their ministries and in restraining wicked, sinful, and negligent people.

But those who, God forbid, are found negligent in these matters or disobedient to them must know that they will retain neither honors in our realm—even if they are our sons—nor a place in the palace, nor any association or communion with us or with our people. Rather, under severe constraint and hardship, they shall suffer punishment [Note: [Col. 0847] G. reads *lui*, “let him pay,” instead of *luere*, “suffer.”].

For in these matters we wish to recognize the faith and goodwill of all our faithful; for if they faithfully and usefully fulfill these obligations, they will be faithful to God and to us. But if, God forbid, they act otherwise, they will openly be marked as not only unfaithful but also infamous and rejected; their houses will be confiscated, and they themselves will be exiled.

### 391. Concerning the baptism of infants and uncertainty about the consecration of churches or altars and the confirmation of the faithful: what is to be done

It has been decided that when trustworthy witnesses cannot be found who testify without doubt that infants have been baptized, and when the infants themselves are not old enough to answer concerning the sacraments entrusted to them, they are to be baptized at the lawful time without any scruple.

The same is to be done concerning churches, altars, and the confirmation of the faithful whenever there is doubt about them: they are to be consecrated and the faithful confirmed without any hesitation. For reason does not permit something that is not shown to have been done to be considered repeated.

### 392. Concerning advocates or defenders of churches to be requested from the prince

For the causes and needs of churches and of their servants of God [Col. 0848A], advocates or defenders are to be requested from the prince whenever necessity arises, and he is to provide the most trustworthy men faithfully and willingly, in accordance with the canonical decrees.

### 393. That wherever anyone is ordained, there he is to belong [Note: [Col. 0847] Bal. reads “remain”]

Clerics of whatever rank, wherever they have been ordained as ministers, are to belong to those same places and remain in them.

### 394. Concerning priests and ministers of the Church: that they should seek or receive chrism from their own bishops and not from others; and concerning the abolition of the superstition of chorepiscopi

In each bishop’s diocese, the priests and their ministers are to seek or receive chrism not from any bishops whatsoever but from their own bishops. At no other time, in accordance with the holy canons and Roman custom, is holy chrism to be prepared except on the Lord’s Supper. On those days also it is to be distributed canonically to priests or their ministers, but not handed over to others, except solely to faithful priests, deacons, or subdeacons [Col. 0848B]. For it is unworthy that anyone else should receive it except those who will use it in administering it.

It has likewise been decreed that neither the consecration of virgins, nor the imparting of the Holy Spirit, nor the consecration of churches or altars, nor any of those acts reserved to bishops, is to be performed by chorepiscopi—who, according to the decrees of the holy fathers, occupy the place of the seventy disciples, that is, of priests—or by the priests themselves.

For if a bishop cannot be consecrated by two bishops, how can that man be a bishop, or perform anything belonging to the episcopal ministry, except insofar as a priest, whose place he holds in the Church, could perform it? Therefore, everything that these men presumptuously performed in the episcopal ministry [Note: [Col. 0847] Bal. reads *praesumptiosi*, “presumptuous,” instead of *praesumptiose*] is shown to be invalid and without effect. It has been judged and repeatedly prohibited, both by the decree of the apostolic see and by that of all the bishops, to be invalid in every respect [Note: [Col. 0847] G. omits the words from *comprobantur* through *esse*, leaping from the first *irrita* immediately to the second.], and rather harmful than beneficial.

Therefore, we absolutely prohibit such things from being done under the bond of anathema [Note: [Col. 0847] omitted by Bal.]. Those who have been polluted rather than sanctified by them are to be canonically restored to a better condition—that is, by three duly ordained bishops—because restoration is not repetition but ecclesiastical and canonical perfection.

### 395. Concerning those who abduct women, so that they may not have them as wives

It has been decided that those who abduct, steal, or seduce women are in no way to have them as wives, even if afterward they reach an agreement with them, endow them, or receive them in marriage with the consent of their parents.

If anyone wishes to have a wife, let him take her canonically and lawfully, and not abduct her. Whoever abducts, steals, or seduces a woman shall never have her as his wife; rather, he shall return her to her lawful relatives, pay the full lord’s fine threefold, and in addition perform public canonical penance.

At this they all cried out with one voice, saying: “We all firmly wish to uphold this and desire that it be preserved by everyone forever.”

### 396. That God is to be prayed to in every place, but that Mass is to be celebrated only in places dedicated to God by bishops

Everyone must know that prayer to God and confession of sins should and may be made in other suitable places if the site of a basilica is far away. The celebration of Mass, however, may and should properly take place only in places dedicated to God by bishops—except in time of hostility, and even then only on altars and in tabernacles dedicated to God by bishops [Note: [Col. 0847] Bal. reads *ullatenus*, “in no way,” instead of *nullatenus*].

### 397. Concerning laymen who are disobedient to their bishops and delay coming to correct themselves: what is to be done

If any layman, whether of higher or lower rank [Col. 0849A], has committed a sin and, summoned by the authority of his bishop, has delayed coming for correction and penance, let him remain expelled from the Church and separated from the company of Catholics until he corrects what he unlawfully committed and canonically washes away his guilt through satisfaction. Through reconciliation with his own bishop, let him obtain pardon and forgiveness through prayers, and, after completing his satisfaction and having been corrected by that bishop, let him be canonically restored to the embrace of the Church, from whose womb he had strayed.

### 398. Concerning clerics, that they are not to use weapons or military cloaks

Clerics are not to use display, military cloaks, or weapons.

### 399. That what a bishop cannot correct in his diocese he should refer to other prelates, or, if necessary, report to the king

Whatever a bishop cannot correct or reform in his diocese by himself and through his own men, he must bring before the other bishops for correction, or not delay reporting it to the king, so that whoever appears disobedient to ecclesiastical regulations may be corrected by external authorities [Col. 0849B].

### 400. Concerning those who serve God, if they fall into the abyss of fornication: how they are to be corrected [Note: Bal. reads *sunt*, “are,” instead of *sint*, “are to be”]

We decree that any male or female servant of God who falls into the crime of fornication shall do penance in prison on bread and water. If he is an ordained priest, he shall remain in prison for two years and shall first be flogged [Note: [Col. 0849] G. corrects *flagelletur*, “let him be flogged,” to *flagellatur*, “he is flogged”; the printed reading is *flagelletur*.] and skinned [Note: [Col. 0849] G. reads *corticatus*, “cut,” instead of *scorticatus*, “skinned.”]; afterward the bishop shall increase the penance.

If a cleric or monk falls into this sin, after the third beating he shall be put into prison and do penance there for a full year [Note: [Col. 0849] Bal. reads “when the year has passed.”]. Likewise, veiled nuns shall be held to the same penance, and all the hair of their heads shall be shaved.

### 401. Concerning those who have been baptized by pagans

We command that those who have been baptized by pagans be baptized again by the priests of Christ in the name of the Holy Trinity, and afterward be confirmed with chrism by bishops, because otherwise they can neither be called nor be Christians [Note: [Col. 0849] G. reads *qui*, “who,” instead of *quia*, “because.”].

### 402. Concerning those who have been confirmed by chorepiscopi [Note: [Col. 0849] G. reads *in*, “by,” instead of *a*, “by/from.”]

If anyone has been confirmed by a bishop and not by a chorepiscopus [Note: [Col. 0849] G. reads “by a chorepiscopus” instead of “by a bishop.”], who was and was called not a bishop but a bishop’s vicar [Note: [Col. 0849] G. reads “who, because he was not a bishop but a bishop’s vicar”], before they were prohibited, such confirmation is not to be repeated.

For before the apostolic and synodal prohibition, chorepiscopi belonged not to the order of the apostles but to that of the seventy disciples, as the sacred canons testify; and we know that the latter never imparted the Paraclete Spirit. But because, as has been said, those chorepiscopi were long ago prohibited, they are now nothing, and they could never at any time impart the Paraclete Spirit [Note: [Col. 0849] Bal. adds *sanctum*, “Holy”], nor can they do so now.

Therefore, what was not formerly recognized as having been canonically performed does not appear to be repeated.

### 403. That anyone baptized by heretics in the name of the Holy Trinity is not to be rebaptized, but perfected by the laying on of hands alone

Whoever has been baptized by heretics in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit [Col. 0849D] must not be baptized again in any way, but is to be cleansed solely through the laying on of hands.

### 404. That those who are to be baptized learn the creed of the faith

Those who are to be baptized must learn the creed of the faith and recite it to the bishop or priests on the Thursday of the final week. Those who receive baptism while suffering from illness are, once they have recovered, to be taught the creed of the faith, so that they may know how great a dignity [the text reads *quanta natione*, literally “of what nation,” apparently corrupt] they have been considered worthy to receive.

Those who have been baptized must also receive heavenly chrism after baptism and become participants in the kingdom of Christ.

### 405. That those whose baptism is uncertain, or who were baptized by a priest sacrificing to gods or eating sacrificial meat, are to be rebaptized

It has been commanded that those concerning whom there is doubt whether they have been baptized or not, or who were baptized by a priest sacrificing to gods or eating sacrificial meat, are to be baptized [Note: [Col. 0849] G. reads *ante*, “before,” instead of *an*, “or whether.”].

### 406. That no one is to take more than two wives

No one is to take more than two wives, because a third is already excessive.

### 407. Concerning prayers, almsgiving, and the faithful celebration of Masses for the faithful departed; from these the impious are to be excluded, since neither their alms are to be accepted by priests or by the remaining faithful

For the Catholic dead, commemorations are to be made and offerings and prayers are to be presented to God. Nothing of this, however, may be done for the impious, even if they are Christians.

### 408. That no bishop or priest should introduce another matter at a synod before matters concerning correction of life have been completed

No bishop or priest should dare to bring forward any other matter [Col. 0850B] before the matters pertaining to the correction of life, the strictness of the rule, and the remedies of the soul and of life have been completed [Note: [Col. 0849] G. has mistakenly altered this heading together with the following one. Bal. omits “and of life.”].

### 409. Concerning those who, seduced by wicked greed, seek the property of the Church from kings: what is to be done

Those who seek the property of the Church from kings and, driven by horrifying greed, seize the possessions of the needy shall have their acquisitions considered invalid, and shall be excluded from communion with the Church whose property they desire to take [Note: [Col. 0849] G. reads *reicolam*, apparently corrupt, instead of *reculam*.].

### 410. That no bishop should devastate the possessions of another bishop or invade his people

Let no bishop of another city invade the parish of any bishop, in violation of the canons, or, inflamed by the torches of insane greed and not sufficiently content with his own possessions, seize what belongs to another.

### 411. Concerning one who has defrauded or invaded the Church’s gifts, that he is to be excluded from the Church’s communion

If anyone, through wicked deceit, has removed, defrauded, invaded, retained, or concealed gifts of any kind belonging to a church and bestowed in the titles of the holy Scriptures [Col. 0850C], and, after being immediately admonished by the priest, does not restore what was given to God, let him be expelled from the communion of the Catholic Church.

### 412. Concerning a bishop who has been judged, if he wishes to appeal to the apostolic see

A bishop who has been judged may appeal, if he wishes, to the apostolic see. From the fifth title [Note: [Col. 0849] Bal. reads “chapter”] of the Council of Sardica. If he appeals, no one else is to be ordained to his chair [Note: [Col. 0849] Bal. reads *cathedra*, “chair,” instead of *in cathedram*, “to the chair”].

### 413. Concerning those who appeal from judges appointed by the primate: what is to be done

If anyone appeals from the judges appointed by the primate, other judges of greater number are to be appointed. If he appeals from these as well, the case is to be referred to the judgment of the council.

### 414. Concerning priests, that they should not presume to celebrate the liturgy without consulting the bishop [Note: [Col. 0849] Bal. reads *agenda* twice]

Priests are not to dare to celebrate the liturgy in any place without consulting the bishop.

### 415. That no priest of a city should do anything without the bishop’s command

A priest of a city is to command nothing and do nothing in any parish without the order of his bishop.

### 416. That priests should not sell Church property without the bishop’s consent

Priests are not to sell Church property without the consent of their bishop.

### 417. Concerning a cleric rejected by another church, that he is not to be received

A church is not to admit a cleric rejected by another church [Note: [Col. 0849] omitted by G.].

### 418. That prayer should always be directed to the Father

No one is to direct prayer to anyone other than the Father [Col. 0851A]. He should first discuss such prayers with those more learned.

### 419. Concerning Church property, which no one is to unjustly retain or seize

No one is permitted to retain, alienate, or take away property or resources lawfully assigned to churches, monasteries, or hospices [Note: [Col. 0851] G. reads *sinodochiis*, “hospices,” instead of *xenodochiis*] for any almsgiving.

If anyone does so, let him be excluded from the thresholds of the Church, bound by the judgments of the ancient canons as a murderer of the poor, until what has been taken away or retained is restored.

### 420. That whoever causes harm to a church’s property is to be regarded as expelled from the Church’s fellowship

No bishop, cleric of any order, or any other person, under any pretext whatsoever, whether in one kingdom or another, is to seek or presume to take the property of any other church.

If anyone does so, let him be suspended from communion at the altar and from the love of all the brothers and sons until he himself restores what was taken to the church to which it belongs by direct legal right [Note: [Col. 0851] G. corrects *ipse* to *ipsi*].

### 421. Concerning the privileges of churches, which are to be preserved inviolate [Note: [Col. 0851] G. reads “are preserved”]

We command that the privileges and charters of churches always remain uncorrupted. Whatever our predecessors or parents established for the benefit of the holy churches, or whatever individual bishops have obtained for ecclesiastical causes, is to be preserved, strengthened by perpetual permanence, under penalty of sacrilege.

### 422. Concerning clerics who are to be corrected by their own bishops

It has been decided that clerics are not to be disciplined or judged except by their own bishops. For it is not lawful that ministers of the divine office be subjected to the judgment of temporal authorities.

If they prove disobedient to the commands of their own bishops, then, in accordance with canonical decrees, they are to be brought before external authorities—that is, secular judges.

### 423. That no chorepiscopus should impart the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands or perform consecration [Note: [Col. 0851] Bal. reads “pontifical consecration”]

It has been decided, as we decreed through the general and synodal counsel of Pope Leo, all our bishops [Col. 0851C], and the remaining faithful, that no chorepiscopus should presume through the laying on of hands to impart the Holy Spirit; to consecrate priests, deacons, or subdeacons; to veil virgins; to prepare holy chrism; to consecrate churches or altars; or to give the people a blessing in a public Mass.

All these things belong to the highest pontiffs, that is, cathedral bishops, and not to chorepiscopi or priests, whose form the chorepiscopi hold according to the decrees of the holy canons.

If they attempt to perform any of these acts, what they perform shall be invalid [Note: [Col. 0851] Bal. reads “what they will perform”], and they themselves shall be entirely deprived of every ecclesiastical honor.

### 424. Concerning those ordained as priests, deacons, or subdeacons by chorepiscopi

Those who have been ordained as priests, deacons, or subdeacons by chorepiscopi are in no way to presume to minister in the office of priest, deacon, or subdeacon.

Likewise, people who appear to have been confirmed by them in their ignorance [Note: [Col. 0851] G. has erased the word; compare the immediately following context], as well as virgins, churches, chrism, or altars consecrated by them, are not to be regarded as confirmed, consecrated, or dedicated. For what they did not possess they could not give, since they have no license to perform any of these acts; all of them belong to the highest pontiffs and not to chorepiscopi, who were neither highest pontiffs nor bishops and can never afterward become such.

For we neither read nor know that anyone from among the seventy ever performed any of these acts. We recognize that priests and chorepiscopi held their place and form according to their example, before the chorepiscopi themselves were prohibited.

All these acts [Col. 0852A] are to be performed by cathedral bishops, who are known to have been consecrated either in the presence of provincial bishops or by their judgment and that of the metropolitan; not by priests or chorepiscopi, who both appear to belong to the same form.

If any of these acts were performed by them, whether through ignorance [Note: [Col. 0851] G. has *a. p. i.*, apparently an abbreviated or corrupt reading] or presumption, and are therefore considered to have been performed by unqualified men, they are nevertheless to be reformed or performed anew by cathedral bishops. For what they intended to do in these matters remained incomplete; and, as has already been stated, what they did not possess they could not give.

They were not bishops, since they were ordained neither by three bishops nor to any episcopal chair; therefore they could perform none of these acts.

And lest anyone think that such ordination, confirmation, or consecration constitutes a repetition, let him consider what is written: “What is not shown to have been done, reason does not permit to be considered repeated.” And other statements of this kind and similar ones.

### 425. That judges should not judge anything concerning the offenses of wicked men outside the restraint of priests

Judges are not to presume to judge anything concerning the offenses of the faithless [Col. 0852B] outside the restraint of the priests.

### 426. Concerning priests of bishops who are to be sent to correct matters where the bishops themselves cannot go

Bishops are then to be regarded as free from blame when they send their priests to correct those matters which they themselves have not corrected.

### 427. Concerning one who is found to be false in the faith

If a lie discovered among human beings makes a person infamous and subjects him to penalties [Note: [Col. 0851] G. reads *affixit*, “has afflicted,” instead of *affligit*, “afflicts”], how much more will someone caught being false in the divine faith be entirely excluded from accusation or testimony.

Therefore, those whose orthodoxy is suspect are rightly prohibited from accusing or giving testimony.

### 428. That not only sins are to be mourned, but also eradicated through the bitter tears of penance [Note: [Col. 0851] G. reads *fluctibus*, “waves,” instead of *fletibus*, “tears”]

Just as Christians must mourn the crime of those who prove themselves transgressors against Christ, so it must be decreed by every means that no one who is convicted of having turned from a better purpose to a worse one should obtain pardon without satisfaction to the Church. For cruel and shocking presumption must be eradicated by a still harsher punishment.

### 429. Concerning one who has not only committed theft but has also consented to a thief

Not only the person who has committed theft, but also anyone who was privy to it or knowingly received stolen goods, is to be counted among thieves and subjected to a similar punishment.

### 430. That Masses are not to be celebrated on Good Friday or Holy Saturday

On Holy Saturday, that is, the vigil of Easter, the fast is not to be broken before the beginning of the night except by children or the sick. Nor is Mass to be celebrated on Good Friday or on that same Holy Saturday, nor are the divine mysteries to be celebrated on either of those two days.

For since the canons command it, these sacraments must by no means be celebrated during those two days.

431. Concerning those who presume to celebrate or hear Masses in illicit and wholly unconsecrated places, contrary to canonical authority. [Col. 0852D] It has very often been decreed and prohibited that the celebration of Masses must not take place at all in unsuitable locations. It has likewise been decreed that if any priest—except when one is traveling, the place of a basilica is far away, and necessity compels this to be done at altars consecrated by a bishop, lest God’s people remain without the celebration of Mass and reception of the Lord’s body and blood—after so many and such great prohibitions should dare to celebrate Masses in such illicit places, he shall incur the danger of his rank. The people too must be warned not to urge priests to sing Masses in the aforesaid illicit places, or to beg priests to do these illicit things; for it is written: “See that you do not offer your burnt offerings in every place that you see, but in the place that the Lord will choose, so that he may place his name there.” It is therefore preferable not to hear Mass than to celebrate or hear it where it is neither lawful nor proper to do so.

It is also read in the canons that no priest should dare to celebrate Masses in houses or in other places, except in dedicated churches. If anyone acts against these decrees, let him be struck with canonical correction. It has likewise been decreed that no priest should presume to minister or celebrate Masses in vessels other than those dedicated to God and consecrated by bishops. For just as it is not permitted that anyone other than those consecrated by bishops should sing Masses and consecrate sacrifices, so it is not lawful for priests to presume to celebrate Masses in houses, altars, or vessels other than those consecrated by bishops.

[Col. 0853] G omits text at this point. The corporal cloths and other priestly vestments must also be consecrated and blessed by bishops, as well as everything that is included for the use of a basilica or altar, or in the ministry of priests for the completion of the divine mysteries, so that with these things they may minister to God more sacredly and more acceptably.

Hence in other decrees of the holy fathers we read:

> “Although it is permitted to pray to God everywhere in true faith, we nowhere read, nor do we truly know, that sacrifices may be offered or the Lord’s body consecrated justly in any other places than those dedicated to God by a bishop—except in a case of hostile attack or the greatest necessity. Even then, it is not in lodgings or unconsecrated houses, but in tents dedicated by bishops, and at altars anointed with sacred unction by pontiffs and consecrated with divine prayers; and this only in the greatest necessity and while traveling far from a church, so that the people may not remain without the solemnities of Mass and reception of the sacrament of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ.”  
> [Col. 0853] *solemnia* (“solemnities”), Bal.

We read that our ancient fathers and predecessors granted this on no other occasion, and neither from laziness nor presumption, but for the aforesaid necessity. [Col. 0853] Bal. reads *propter dictam necessitatem* (“on account of the said necessity”). Otherwise, except as prescribed, it is not lawful to celebrate the solemnities of Mass in unconsecrated places. Nor is it in any way lawful to do this except under the greatest necessity and for the necessities already mentioned. For the divine law, commanding with the utmost force, says: “Let everyone beware of offering his burnt offerings in every place that the Lord has chosen.” And elsewhere: “He offers rightly who, prevented by necessity or illness from coming to the church, prays to God elsewhere. But he does not divide rightly who celebrates Masses in illicit places and at wholly unconsecrated altars.”

It is far better not to sing or hear Masses than to sing or hear Masses in illicit places. For whoever does what is illicit and commits what is prohibited errs greatly and sins exceedingly; and unless he performs canonical and just penance for this in the present life, he will undoubtedly receive the greatest condemnation for it at the future judgment.

Many examples, indeed innumerable examples, of these matters are found in the legal books mentioned above and in other canonical and divine books. We have postponed inserting them here because of their length, and have not inserted them here to avoid weariness and labor for the scribe or reader. [Col. 0853] *scriptorum sive lectorum* (“of scribes or readers”), Bal. [Col. 0853] G omits text at this point. For if anyone desires to find more and better examples from these sources, he will be able to find them sufficiently by reading the books mentioned above and searching diligently.

If, therefore, after so many prohibitions anyone should presume to violate these decrees, renewed and confirmed by apostolic, synodal, and imperial authority—and especially written and established with the consent and at the urging of all the peoples of our empire and our leading men—then, if he is a cleric, he shall be subject to the danger of his rank. If he is a monk or layman, he shall be excluded from the threshold of the church until the church is satisfied.

If, however—God forbid—he proves disobedient or contumacious toward his own bishop or the other priests, he shall be seized by our counts or envoys and confined in prison under great hardship until satisfaction has been rendered to us, to his own bishop, and to the church.

432. That he commits incest who unites himself to his female relative as far as the line of affinity. No member of the faithful shall take his female relative as a wife as far as the line of affinity—that is, through the seventh generation—or pollute her in any way with the stain of incest. If anyone knowingly presumes to violate this rule, then, if he is free, he shall pay our ban, namely sixty solidi, into our treasury; and in addition he shall undergo the canonical penalty for incest and perform public penance according to the canonical degrees.

If he is a slave or a member of the clergy, he shall be publicly scourged and have his hair shaved off, and he shall perform public and canonical penance according to the command of his own bishop. If anyone—whether free, enslaved, a cleric, or a fiscal dependent—proves disobedient or contumacious toward his own bishop, his priest, or his archdeacon, whether in this matter or in any other crime, all his property shall be seized by the count and the bishop’s envoy until he obeys his bishop and performs canonical penance.

If he does not correct himself in this way and delays coming to the bishop and to canonical penance, he shall be seized by the count and held in prison under great hardship, and he shall have no control over his property until the bishop orders otherwise. If the count or his officials delay carrying these provisions out, he shall be excommunicated canonically by the bishop or by his minister, and until he fully carries them out he shall always be deprived of communion with Catholics, until the bishop himself decides to deal more humanely with him.

If, however—which we do not wish—the count himself proves disobedient or negligent either in the aforesaid matters or in the excommunication itself, he shall be deprived both of his comital office and of communion until both men come into our presence, so that we may correct him with episcopal authority and imperial fear in such a way that the others may be afraid and never again dare to commit such things. [Col. 0853] Bal. reads *ut et* (“so that also”).

433. That incestuous persons, so long as they remain in their crime, are to occupy not the place of faithful Christians but only that of pagans, catechumens, or possessed persons. While incestuous persons remain in that detestable and unspeakable crime, they are not to be counted among faithful Christians but among pagans, catechumens, or possessed persons. That is, they are not to eat or drink with Christians, nor eat or drink from the same vessel; they must do these things alone. They are not to be kissed or greeted by them.

But if they prove disobedient to their priests and refuse to separate themselves from so abominable a crime and return to public penance, they are to be counted among those who are endangered by an unclean spirit, or even among those of whom Truth itself says: “If he does not listen to you, let him be to you as a pagan and a tax collector.” [Col. 0853] G reads *per se* (“by itself” or “in itself”).

For they must not pray with the faithful or enter the church, but keep watch at the church door, asking pardon from those who enter and leave it with their faces prostrate on the ground, and begging them not to disdain to pray for them. Drenched in tears, with contrite faces and humbled spirits, they must always appear before everyone, remain until the church is satisfied and their own bishop grants canonical reconciliation, and never return to their former incest. They must not conduct secular business, nor take part in lawsuits, accusations, or testimony. Rather, through the frequent prayers of priests, the laying on of the hands of their own bishop, the distribution of alms, and the good works of other people, they ought to be cleansed and healed. [Col. 0853] Bal. thinks *bonorum hominum* should be read as *bonorum operum*, “of good works.”

434. Concerning incestuous persons, who are not to prevail under any designation of marriage. We judge that incestuous persons are not to prevail under any designation of marriage.

435. Concerning incestuous unions. If anyone unites himself in an incestuous relationship at a degree forbidden by divine regulations with persons with whom such union is prohibited, both parties shall be deprived of communion until they demonstrate their penance by separation; nor shall they have the right to hold military office at the palace or to litigate cases in court.

For, in whatever manner they have joined themselves in the aforesaid incest, the bishops or priests in whose diocese or district the act occurred shall announce the crime to the king or to the judges, so that, once it has been reported to them, the offenders may separate themselves from their communion and cohabitation. [Col. 0855] The words *aut cohabitatione* (“or cohabitation”) are absent in G.

Their property shall pass to their nearest parents until the separation, under this condition: before they are separated, it shall not reach their own estates by any device—neither through relatives, purchase, nor royal authority—unless they confess the aforesaid crime through separation and penance.

[Col. 0855B] 436. Concerning the order of canonical accusation. We command that the order of accusation established long ago by canonical rules be observed. If any cleric is accused in a criminal or lesser case, or summoned in a capital matter, he must not immediately be considered guilty merely because he could be accused, lest we make innocence subject to accusation.

Rather, whoever brings the charge must come into episcopal judgment, state the accused person’s name, undertake the bond of written accusation, and observe the prescribed form; yet, with due regard for rank, he must submit to the consequences. Let him know that he has no license to lie, since the likeness of the penalty demands vengeance upon slanderers.

437. Concerning slaves, freedmen, or infamous persons who are not to be admitted. No slaves or freedmen, and no infamous persons, are to be permitted to accuse persons of higher standing, nor are any of those whom the public laws do not admit to the accusation of public crimes to be permitted to do so. Infamous are all whom canonical decrees, ecclesiastical decrees, and secular laws declare to be infamous.

[Col. 0855C] 438. Concerning bishops, other priests, and clerics, who are not at all to be accused before secular judges. If any bishop, priest, deacon, or any other cleric is accused before bishops—as elsewhere this ought not to occur—by any person whatsoever, whoever has undertaken this kind of blameworthy accusation, whether he is a man of lofty rank or of any other dignity, must understand [Col. 0855] G reads *ulterius* (“further”) for *ullius* (“of any”), that he is required to present what is to be proved by evidence and demonstrated by documents.

If anyone brings forward matters concerning such persons that cannot be proved, let him understand by the authority of this sanction that he will suffer damage to his own reputation. Through the loss of honor and diminution of esteem, he is to learn that from now on he may not attack another’s modesty with impunity.

For just as it is right that bishops, priests, deacons, and others, if they can be proved guilty of the charges brought against them, should be removed from their ecclesiastical ranks, so a similar measure of justice must be seen in the moderate punishment that we have ordered to be inflicted upon threatened innocence. Therefore bishops alone are to hear such cases, with the testimony of many persons recorded in the proceedings.

439. Concerning the distinction between primates and metropolitans. No other metropolitans are to be called primates except those who hold the principal sees and whom the holy fathers, by synodal and apostolic authority, decreed to be primates. The rest, who have acquired other metropolitan sees, are to be called not primates but metropolitans.

440. What is to be done concerning household members or persons, both free and enslaved, who accuse their master or reveal his secrets. If anyone from the household or slaves of any house emerges as an informer and accuser of any crime, intending to attack the reputation, life, and property of the person whose household or authority he has served, he is to be struck down by the avenging sword at the very beginning of the disclosure of the crimes and accusation, before witnesses are produced and before the case is examined in judgment.

A deadly voice ought to be cut off rather than heard. We close the mouths of those whom we know to be dead—not by human but by divine voices—from accusing or testifying against priests.

441. That bishops are to be judged, accused, or condemned by God, whose servants they are, since, according to the Apostle, no one ought to judge another’s servant; and that they are not to be torn apart by human beings or by men of wicked life, since the Lord himself provides the rule. Bishops are to be judged by God; they are not to be torn apart by human beings or by men of wicked life, since the Lord himself gives the example. For through him, and not through others, he expelled from the temple the buyers and sellers and overturned with his own whip the tables of the money changers and cast them out of the temple.

And as he says elsewhere: “God stood in the assembly of gods; in the midst, however, he distinguishes gods.”

[Col. 0856B] 442. Concerning those who kill themselves in any manner. Whoever, by his own will, throws himself into water, hangs himself by the neck, casts himself from a tree, strikes himself with iron, or in any way gives himself over to voluntary death—an offering for such persons is not to be received. [Col. 0855] Bal. reads *recipietur*, “will be received.”

443. Concerning those who injure a cleric. Any judge or layman who presumes, without a hearing before the bishop, archdeacon, or archpriest, to inflict injury upon a priest, deacon, any member of the clergy, or any of the younger members of Mother Church is to be regarded as anathema and excluded from the fellowship of all Christians. [Col. 0855] The words *matris ecclesiae* (“of Mother Church”) are absent in G.

444. That laypeople are not to be present when canonical rights are litigated or matters governed by the rule are examined, unless they themselves are accused. When matters that are canonical are litigated or certain matters governed by the rule are examined, neither secular judges nor any laypeople ought to be present, except only those who are accused in their own persons.

[Col. 0856C] 445. That ecclesiastical rights should always remain inviolate. We admonish that the rights of churches, as they were ordained by fathers divinely inspired, should remain inviolate. [Col. 0855] Bal. reads *inlibata* (“unimpaired”) for *inviolata* (“inviolate”). Let no shameless ambition covet anything belonging to another, nor let anyone seek his own advancement by imitating another.

446. A petition from the people to the emperor Charles and the bishops. God appointed your religious authority for this purpose: that you remove injustices, cut off presumption, assist priests who labor, and give no occasion for many reproaches. After recognizing the injured party, provide him assistance; but cut off the one who causes the accusation, if he truly is an accuser.

447. Concerning the rejection of outside judges and the refusal of foreign judgments or examinations. Let it be the concern of the bishops of each place to order the cases and interests of all who live under their governance. It is highly inappropriate that, while neglecting their own bishops, any others should interfere in their affairs. Rather, those who can canonically ordain them, or by whom they were ordained, and who are compelled to give an account for their conduct and for their souls, ought to order their lives with suitable and regular moderation.

448. What is to be done concerning a bishop who has a case against his own metropolitan or against anyone else. If it should happen—which we do not wish—that a bishop has some case against his own metropolitan or against anyone else, we have decreed that those who hasten to seek it may have recourse to the judgment of the Apostolic See, which you know was permitted even by the institution of the ancient fathers’ canons.

[Col. 0857A] 449. That Christ Jesus is the foundation of all goodness, and how one must enter the sheepfold through the door. No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, and that is Christ. Whoever therefore, with love of God and neighbor, holds firm to the faith that is in Christ has laid Jesus Christ, the Son of God and man, as his foundation.

It is therefore to be hoped that where Christ is the foundation, the practice of good works will also follow. Truth itself says: “Whoever does not enter the sheepfold through the door, but climbs in by another way, is a thief and a robber. But whoever enters through the door is the shepherd of the sheep.” A little later he adds: “I am the door.”

Therefore the one who enters the sheepfold through the door is the one who enters through Christ. He enters through Christ who thinks and preaches the truth concerning that same Creator and Redeemer of the human race, and guards what he has preached; who undertakes the summit of rule in order to bear its burden, not from desire for the glory of passing honor; and who diligently watches over the care of the flock entrusted to him, lest either wicked people, speaking perversely, tear God’s sheep apart, or evil spirits, urging the delights of vices, lay them waste. [Col. 0857] Bal. reads *oblectamenta*, “delights,” instead of *delectamenta*.

450. Concerning cases that have been settled and are not to be reopened. Judgment must not be demanded concerning a case that has been settled or adjudicated.

451. Concerning those who rise up against their superiors, and what is to be done concerning hostile accusers or witnesses. Those who rise up against their superiors clearly show that they scorn to be servants of God.

The Son of God says in the holy Gospel: “I neither accuse nor judge anyone.” For the Son does nothing without the Father, because their operation is common and their will united. In this passage he speaks as a judge, showing what kind of judge and what kind of witnesses ought to belong to God, so that people may understand that, in judging, they must form a sentence not according to their own will and power but according to equity.

Justice, not power, must be manifested in judgment.

452. Concerning the rules for clerics. Clerics are admonished by the law of the fathers to keep themselves apart from ordinary life and abstain from the pleasures of the world. They must not attend spectacles or public celebrations; they must avoid public banquets and cultivate private ones that are not only modest but also sober. They must by no means engage in usury, nor eagerly pursue shameful profit-making occupations or anyone’s frauds. [Col. 0857] The words *qui nec turpium occupationes lucrorum fraudesque cuiusquam studiose appetant* (“nor eagerly pursue shameful profit-making occupations or anyone’s frauds”) are absent in the Council of Mainz, 813.

They must shun love of money as the source of every crime; cast aside secular offices and business; not seek positions of honor through ambition; not accept gifts in exchange for the benefits of God’s healing; beware of deceit and conspiracies; flee hatred, rivalry, detraction, and envy.

They must not walk with wandering eyes, an unrestrained tongue, or an impudent and arrogant bearing. [Col. 0857] Bal. reads *infrenata*, “unrestrained,” instead of *infreni*. Rather, they must display modesty and shame through simple dress and demeanor. They must utterly detest obscenity both of words and of deeds.

They must avoid visiting and frequenting widows and virgins, and must in no way seek companionship with unrelated women. They must also strive to preserve perpetual chastity of an undefiled body, or at least be joined in the bond of a single marriage.

They must offer due obedience to their elders and not exalt themselves through any desire for boasting. Finally, they must devote themselves continually to teaching, reading, psalms, hymns, spiritual songs, and discipline. For such ought those to be who strive to dedicate themselves to divine worship, so that, while they devote themselves to knowledge, they may administer the grace of instruction to the people. [Col. 0857] The words *qui divinis cultibus sese mancipandos studeant* (“who strive to dedicate themselves to divine worship”) are absent in Bal.; G. reads *student*, “strive.” Bal. reads *do* (“give”) instead of *dum* (“while”).

453. Concerning the denial of permission to accusers to bring charges before they have cleared themselves of the matters alleged against them. The accused are not to be granted permission to bring charges until they have freed themselves from the crime by which they are oppressed.

454. What is to be done concerning false witnesses and perjurers. If anyone is convicted of having induced or solicited anyone to give false testimony or commit perjury, or of having solicited anyone through any kind of bribery, he is not to receive communion until his death.

455. Concerning the status of a virgin in marriage. It must be inquired whether the virgin’s father wishes it, since the man is the head of the woman. The father’s will concerning the virgins must be sought, since God leaves a person in the hands of his own counsel.

456. That clerics or laypeople are not to receive communion in another church without letters from their bishop. It has been decreed that no cleric or layperson is to receive communion in another parish without letters from his own bishop.

457. That laypeople who despise the canons are to be excommunicated, while clerics are to be deprived of their rank. If anyone transgresses and violates these statutes, or considers them worthless, then, if he is a layman, he shall be deprived of communion; if he is a cleric, of his rank.

458. That whoever tries to defend another’s cleric is to be deprived of communion. If any cleric, evading the rule of ecclesiastical discipline, should wander away, whoever receives him and does not reconcile him with his own bishop, but rather presumes to defend him, shall be deprived of communion with the Church.

459. Concerning accusations in clerical cases that are not to be accepted when prohibited by the laws of the world; and concerning clerics condemned by no one being defended. It has been decreed that ecclesiastical judges are to hear no accusations that are prohibited by secular laws.

It has also been decreed that if any cleric of whatever rank is condemned by the judgment of bishops for any crime, no one may defend him, whether from the churches over which he presided or from any other person. A penalty involving loss of money and honor is to be imposed; and we decree that neither age nor sex is to constitute an excuse. [Col. 0857] G. reads *clericum si iudicio* (“if a cleric by the judgment”) instead of *cuiuslibet honoris clericus* (“a cleric of whatever rank”).

460. That no other metropolitans are to be called primates except those who hold the principal sees, since no others can form three groups of bishops except those who hold the principal sees, who are required to form three groups as this decree orders. It has been decided that whenever a council is to be convened, bishops who are not prevented by age, illness, or some other serious necessity should attend suitably.

The primates of their provinces are to be informed that all the bishops are to be divided into either two or three groups, and that from each group, in turn, as many as are chosen are to attend the day of the council with the utmost urgency.

461. That one must not speak with those to whom a bishop does not speak, nor communicate with the excommunicated, so that they may humble themselves and be reconciled more quickly. Useful passages from the letter of Saint Clement, necessary for the churches in the present time, are to be brought forward honorably and received with reverence by all the faithful, especially clerics. Of these, because of their venerable antiquity, we have especially approved the following and strengthen it by the present statutes. The blessed martyr mentioned above recalls it as an ordinance of the most blessed apostle Peter, saying:

> “You ought also to understand from among yourselves if there are matters that he cannot state more clearly and openly because of the snares of evil people. For example, he is hostile to someone on account of his actions. You must not wait for him to say to you, ‘Do not be friends with that person.’ Rather, you must prudently observe his will—namely, the will of the one who governs the church—and obey without agitation. You must turn away from the one toward whom you perceive him to be hostile, and you must not speak with those to whom he does not speak.
>
> “Thus, when someone who is at fault desires to regain the favor of all of you, he may hasten more quickly to be reconciled with the one who presides over all, so that he may return to salvation when he begins to obey the admonitions of his superior.”

And the other matters marked out in what follows concerning the friends of those who are enemies of the truth.

Let the clergy therefore know that guilt is to be attributed to them, and the people of the faithful likewise to be charged with blame, if anyone is counted among the evil in this vice and is recognized as a subverter of discipline. [Col. 0857] Bal. reads *quidam* (“certain matters”) for *quae* (“which things”). The words *vel vestrarum* (“or of your [feminine plural]”) are a correction of *vestrorum* in G.; Bal. reads *vel vestram* (“or your [singular feminine]”).

462. Concerning bishops, who are not to be injured or torn apart but rather endured. A bishop ought to teach his church opportunely and inopportunely and without interruption, and prudently govern and admonish it, so that it may abstain from vices and attain eternal salvation.

The church, for its part, ought to receive his teaching with such great reverence and love and cherish him as God’s legate and herald of truth. For, as Truth testifies, “Whatever he binds on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever he looses on earth will be loosed in heaven.” [Col. 0859] Bal. supplies a longer version: “Whatever he has bound on earth will be bound in heaven, and whatever he has loosed on earth will be loosed in heaven.”

This sentence must be greatly feared, and you must take care not to offend those to whom the Lord has granted such power. Therefore they are rather to be obeyed, loved, and held in the highest reverence—not slandered, torn apart, or expelled, but supported and loved. For the Lord himself says: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you despises me.”

Therefore we command you and all the faithful to guard yourselves against such things and to leave your descendants not a bad example but a good one, because an injury done to bishops concerns Christ, whose office they perform.

Accordingly, you who are disciples of the true God must first cast discord and dissension of spirit from your hearts, for from these every evil work proceeds, and preserve kindness and simplicity with your whole mind.

Nevertheless, let everyone know that the bishop labors above all of you, because each one of you bears his own labor, whereas the bishop bears both his own and that of each individual. Therefore, just as he labors for all of you, so you all ought to labor for him with the utmost effort, even to the point that, if necessary, you should lay down your lives for him, just as he ought, if necessary, to lay down his life for you. For the Savior himself says: “The good shepherd gives his life for his sheep.”

You, for your part, obey them and keep watch for them, because they keep watch as those who will have to render an account for your souls, so that they may do this with joy and not with groaning. [Col. 0859] G. corrects *et* to *ut* (“so that”); G. reads *faciunt* (“they do”) instead of *faciant* (“they may do”). Bal. omits *diligendi*, “loved.”

463. Concerning lawful marriage. It has been decreed that a wife is to be joined lawfully to a husband. For, as we have received from the fathers and found handed down by the holy apostles and their successors, marriage is not lawful in any other way than when the woman is sought from those who appear to hold authority over her and by whom she is guarded; when she is betrothed by her nearer relatives and endowed according to law; and, at the proper time, blessed priestly, as is customary, by a priest with prayers and offerings.

She is to be guarded and accompanied by her nearest relatives and by *paranymphi*, as custom teaches; and, when the proper time has come, she is to be given according to law and solemnly received. Let them devote two or three days to prayers and preserve chastity, so that good offspring may be generated and they may please the Lord in their actions. [Col. 0859] Bal. reads *boni* (“good,” masculine) instead of *bonae* (“good,” feminine).

In this way they will please the Lord and produce children who are not illegitimate but legitimate and entitled to inherit. [Col. 0859] G. corrects *qui* to *et* (“and”); Bal. reads *quae* (“which”).

464. Concerning those who presume to judge anyone on suspicion or without a legitimate accuser. It has been decided that no one should presume to judge any cleric or layperson on the basis of some suspicion. Likewise, no one is to be condemned without a legitimate accuser, because it is exceedingly bad and dangerous to judge anyone on suspicion or condemn anyone without a legitimate accuser.

465. That bishops should visit their parishes every year. It has been decided that each bishop should not neglect to visit all his dioceses and parishes every year, but should strive, by teaching, strengthening, restoring whatever is necessary in each place, and correcting matters as best he can, to reform them.

466. That priests and deacons, when appointed in the parishes, should make a promise to their bishop concerning their stability, obedience, and observance of the statutes. When priests or deacons are appointed throughout the parishes, they ought to make a profession to their own bishop.

467. That judges should not presume to occupy clerics or church slaves in their own forced services or in any other matters. It is not permitted for judges to occupy clerics or church slaves in their own forced services. [Col. 0859] G. lacks the words “or in any matters.”

468. Concerning churches and their endowments, which are always to remain subject to the bishop’s disposition. It has been decided that all churches, with their endowments and all their possessions, are to remain under the authority of their own bishop and always belong to his administration or disposition.

469. That clerics ought not to resort to secular judges. Clerics who seek secular judges are to be excommunicated.

270. Concerning those who use force against widows or take women against their will. It has been decided that no one should use force against widows on account of their chastity, and that a woman should not be taken by a man against her will. If anyone does so, he shall pay our ban to us threefold, and he shall be compelled by the bishop—and, if necessary, by the count applying force—to perform public penance according to the canonical degrees.

If he proves disobedient, he shall be presented to us under the guarantee of the strongest sureties, so that he may either be confined in prison or deported into exile, and so that the others may fear and never presume to do such things.

471. Concerning powerful men who strip anyone of his property. It has been decided that if any powerful person strips anyone of his property and, after being admonished by the bishop, does not restore it, he shall be excommunicated.

472. Concerning those who enter a church but do not receive communion. It has been decided that all who enter a church are to receive communion, unless they have been excommunicated by their own priest. [Col. 0859] G. adds in the margin: “Alternatively, if they have been excommunicated by their own priest, they are not to receive communion.”

If some refuse to do this, they are to be regarded as separated from communion and from the fellowship of Christians for as long as it takes them, through satisfaction rendered to the church, to merit reconciliation with their own bishop by the laying on of hands and restoration to holy communion.

473. Concerning those who receive the Eucharist but do not consume it. It has been decided that all who receive the holy Eucharist but do not consume it are to be rejected as sacrilegious. [Col. 0859] Bal. omits *placuit ut* (“it has been decided that”).

474. That those who are excommunicated by priests are always to be avoided by the faithful until reconciliation, except by those to whom permission has been granted. It has been decided that none of the faithful is to communicate with those who have been excommunicated by their own priests, except those to whom permission has been granted by the priests; nor is anyone to approach them before they have been canonically reconciled. Whoever attempts to do so shall be subject to the same sentence.

475. Concerning those who suppress justice for a gift or someone’s favor. If an outsider to the rule of the Christian faith, who claims to be a defender of truth, pollutes truth itself by accepting gifts, let him hear the prophet speaking against him: “Because you sold the righteous for silver and the poor for a pair of sandals, behold, I will creak over you as a wagon creaks when loaded with hay; and flight shall perish from the swift, the strong man shall not retain his strength, and the mighty in heart shall escape naked.”

476. How these statutes are to be observed, and what is to be done concerning clerics or laypeople who despise them. We sanction that all these ecclesiastical constitutions, which we have summarized and briefly touched upon, shall remain with enduring stability, as they are more fully contained in the canon.

If any cleric or layperson refuses to obey these sanctions, then, if he is a cleric, he shall be subject to excommunication. If he is a layperson of higher rank, he shall lose half his property, which is to benefit the treasury. If he is a person of lower rank, he shall be punished by the loss of his property and assigned to exile.

477. Concerning the statutes established by our predecessors regarding divine worship, which are always to remain unimpaired. Whatever our forefathers established at different times, we command to remain inviolate and uncorrupted concerning the most holy churches. Therefore, let nothing be altered from the privileges. Let protection be extended to all who serve the churches, because in our times we desire rather to add to their reverence than to alter anything that was formerly granted. [Col. 0861] G reads *tui id* instead of *tuitio*; Bal. omits *ex* (“from”).

[Col. 0862A] **478. On the chapters confirmed by apostolic authority.** Above all, the chapters of the last three of these books have all been confirmed by apostolic authority, since an apostolic legation was especially involved in their composition [Note: [Col. 0861] “in forging,” Bal.]. For we have not inserted their names here, apart from the three—namely Leo, Sergius, and Georgius—even though we had found them inserted in each individual assembly, avoiding the tedium of readers and copyists. If anyone wishes to know them more fully, let him read their authentic copies, in which he will find them inserted. Meanwhile, let him not neglect to learn these things, love them, and fulfill them in practice [Note: [Col. 0861] “by dictating,” Bal.]; for, as the Lord knows, they have been collected and inserted here for love of and the usefulness of the holy Church of God, as was stated at the beginning of this work. We pray that peace may be granted to those who read them, glory to those who observe them, and eternal life to those who fulfill them in their works [Note: [Col. 0861] read “may be attributed,” Bal.].

## FIRST ADDITION

[Col. 0861]

For the chapters of this first addition, see above among the Constitutions of Aachen of the year 817, col. 393.

## SECOND ADDITION

[Col. 0861]

The chapters that follow were not collected, arranged, and inserted here at the time when they are found written down, as in the following sections; rather, they were subsequently discovered by faithful men and inserted in this document just as they had been enacted, so that they might more easily be found by the faithful whenever necessary.

## HERE BEGIN THE CHAPTERS

[Col. 0861B]

**WHICH ARE GENERALLY TO BE ANNOUNCED TO THE PEOPLE THROUGHOUT THE PARISHES**

### 1. That those to be baptized should be instructed in the sacrament of faith; and that infants should not be received from the sacred font, nor persons held for confirmation, by those who remain canonically unreconciled in public penance.

We have judged it necessary to admonish or announce this to the faithful, so that those who seek the faith of Christ and are of mature age may, before approaching baptism, be instructed both in the sacrament of faith and in that of baptism. Likewise, those who wish to receive infants from the sacred font must be instructed, so that they may understand both the force of that sacrament and what they have promised on behalf of others, or for whom they have stood as sponsors.

We judge that those who have been deprived of canonical communion and subjected to public penance must be specially removed from these offices, so that they may neither receive others from the most holy font of baptism nor serve as sponsors for others in receiving the gift of the Holy Spirit, until by the satisfaction of penance they have merited reconciliation. For those whom divine law and canonical authority separate from the thresholds of churches and from military camps, lest they become a ruin to the people, must all the more be separated from these sacred offices until the period of penance has been completed, as has already been said.

### 2. At what time baptism ought to be celebrated.

Baptisms are not to be celebrated outside the times established by the canons, since the sacred canons absolutely prohibit this unless some danger is pressing—so much so that they even bar from ecclesiastical orders those who are baptized at another time.

### 3. That the covenant made with God in baptism should be observed by the baptized.

We have also judged it necessary to ensure that the faithful are instructed about this, so that they may understand the covenant they made with God in baptism. The covenant made with God in baptism is violated completely by many and partially by many others. It is violated completely when someone, after receiving the grace of baptism, falls into unbelief, heresy, or schism; but partially when someone falls into pride, envy, or the other spiritual vices that proceed from the root of pride.

### 4. What renunciation in baptism means, and how it should be observed.

All the faithful must understand very clearly what it means to renounce the devil, his works, and his pomps. Therefore preachers in admonishing, and hearers in learning and fulfilling these things in practice, must henceforth apply great diligence, so that they may be able to avoid their own peril.

To renounce the devil, then, is entirely to reject, despise, cast him away, and oppose him, and for each person to separate himself from him—or whatever else can be expressed by this word in this sense.

His works are those that are contrary to the works of the Savior. First among them is pride, of which he is the author and which changed him from an angel into a demon; pride is also the beginning of every sin, together with the other vices that proceed from its root.

The devil’s pomp is that which is also the pomp of the world: ambition, arrogance, empty glory, and every kind of excess in human affairs. From these grows self-exaltation, which is often customarily attributed to honor, along with other things of this kind that are known to proceed from the fountain of pride.

These and similar things are what every believer rejected from himself at the time of baptism, devoted himself to Christ, and made a covenant with God not to return entirely to the things he had renounced. Yet if the rights of a human agreement are carefully preserved, the rights of so great a covenant, made with God, must be observed inviolate with still greater firmness and fervor.

### 5. On schools to be maintained in each city [Note: [Col. 0861] “to be conducted,” G.].

By common agreement we have decreed among ourselves that henceforth each bishop should apply greater diligence to maintaining schools and preparing and educating soldiers of Christ for the usefulness of the Church. In this matter we wish to test the diligence of each one, so that, when the provincial council of bishops is convened, each rector may have his scholars present at that council, so that they may be known to the other churches and his diligent concern for divine worship may be made evident to all.

### 6. That bishops ought to confer the laying on of hands while fasting.

Bishops are to transmit the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands only while fasting, except in the case of the sick and those in danger of death. Just as baptism is appropriately celebrated by fasting bishops at the two seasons, namely Easter and Pentecost, so too ought the conferral of the Holy Spirit to be celebrated by fasting bishops [Note: [Col. 0863] “to be celebrated,” Bal.].

### 7. On not sending priests indiscriminately to various places.

As has been done until now, priests are not to be sent indiscriminately to various places, either by bishops, by other prelates, or even by laymen, lest, because of their absence, the dangers to souls and the duties of the churches in which they have been appointed be neglected [Note: [Col. 0863] “or,” G.].

### 8. That priests who have lost their rank should be subjected to canonical penance.

Regarding priests who lose their rank, it has seemed good to us that each bishop should himself, and through his ministers, ascertain the life, conduct, and moral reform of those who lose their rank, and should not neglect to subject them to canonical penance, according to what is written in the first title of the Council of Caesarea:

> “If a priest takes a wife, he is to be deposed from the order; but if he commits fornication or adultery, he must be expelled further and reduced to penance.”

For some, after losing their rank, become sons of Belial to such an extent that, because it is unlawful, they are constrained neither by public laws, nor, through the negligence of certain bishops, by canonical laws.

### 9. That no priest should presume to celebrate Mass alone.

It has also seemed good to us that this should be prohibited: no priest should presume to celebrate Mass alone. For neither do the words of the Lord and Savior, by which he delivered the mysteries of his body and blood to be celebrated by his disciples, indicate this; nor do the instructions of the apostle Paul; nor, if the Acts of the Apostles are read carefully, is it found in any way that this ought to be done.

Therefore such a solitary consecrator of the Lord’s body and blood seems to us deserving of being summoned, indeed questioned: to whom does he say, “The Lord be with you,” and from whom does he receive the response, “and with your spirit”? Or for whom, among other things, does he pray to the Lord, saying, “Remember, Lord” [Note: [Col. 0863] “of your male and female servants and of all those present,” Bal.], when no one is present?

Since this practice is contrary to apostolic and ecclesiastical authority and seems to inflict a certain dishonor on so great a mystery, it has seemed good to all of us collectively that such a practice be prohibited henceforth.

### 10. That each church should have its own priest.

It has often been decreed in other councils, and now in our own assemblies, that each church, if it has the means, should have its own priest, and that each priest should be content with one church only.

### 11. That rural work should not be done on the Lord’s Day.

Among the other duties of our admonition, this has seemed sufficiently necessary: it must be solemnly announced to the faithful peoples that they should honor and venerate the Lord’s Day, on which the author of life [Note: [Col. 0863] “victor,” G.] rose from the dead.

For if pagans take pains to honor days in memory and reverence of their gods, and Jews, in a carnal manner, observe the Sabbath carnally, how much more should the devotion of the Christian religion, in memory of the Lord’s resurrection, honor and venerate that same day!

We have learned, from the sight of many among us and from the report of many others, that some who were engaged in rural work on this day were struck down by lightning, some were punished by the contraction of their limbs, and some were suddenly consumed by visible fire, being reduced to ashes and dying under punishment.

Therefore it is necessary that priests first, then kings and princes, and all the faithful, most devoutly exhibit to this day the observance and reverence that are its due.

### 12. On not celebrating Masses at unsuitable places.

Although this has often been urged, it has seemed to us [Note: [Col. 0863] omitted in Bal.] extremely necessary to impress it again upon the people and announce it to them: celebrations of Mass must in no way take place in unsuitable places, and each bishop must entirely remove such a rash custom from his parish.

If from now on any priest attempts, after so many and such great prohibitions, to celebrate Mass in such unlawful places—except when traveling, when a basilica is far away and necessity compels the celebration on altars consecrated by a bishop, lest the people of God remain without the celebration of Mass and reception of the Lord’s body and blood—it is right that he incur the danger of losing his rank.

It is therefore better not to hear Mass than to celebrate or hear it where it is neither permitted nor proper.

### 13. That priests should not veil widows without consulting the bishops.

Since it has often been prohibited in our councils that widows should not be veiled without consulting the bishops, and since we now know that this same constitution is being transgressed by some, we have absolutely forbidden it to happen henceforth.

If thereafter any priest obstinately transgresses this constitution—namely, if he presumes to veil a widow without consulting the bishop—he shall incur the danger of losing his rank.

### 14. On priests not veiling virgin girls.

Likewise, we have prohibited priests from veiling virgin girls. In this matter we have found that many priests have hitherto transgressed, partly through ignorance and partly through rashness.

### 15. That certain women place the veil upon themselves without the consent of priests.

We have also discovered another negligence: certain women imprudently place the veil upon themselves without the consent of priests. We have likewise prohibited this from happening any further.

### 16. On abbesses and nuns who place the veil upon widows and girls contrary to the canons.
