Moreover, in certain places we have found an established practice full of folly and contrary to ecclesiastical authority: namely, that certain abbesses and some of the nuns presume, contrary to law, to place the veil upon widows and virgin girls, and [Note: [Col. 0863] omitted in G.] consequently some of those so veiled think that they can more freely devote themselves to their carnal desires and fulfill their wishes.

Therefore we decree that if, after this definition, either an abbess or any nun proceeds to such audacity that she presumes to veil either a widow or a virgin girl, she is to be subjected to canonical judgment until satisfaction has been made.

### 17. On noble women who veil their heads immediately after the death of their husbands.

Regarding noble women who, after losing their husbands, are suddenly veiled and take pleasure in remaining in their own homes while alleging various necessities—an issue that was discussed and settled long ago in other assemblies before your serenity—we decree that bishops must admonish and instruct them with greater and more diligent care, so that they may provide for their salvation and not, by living so indiscriminately, using their own harmful freedom, and wandering about in various places, incur danger to their souls [Note: [Col. 0863] Bal. reads “nor thus” (nec sic)].

Let them always keep before their eyes the apostolic saying:

> “The widow who lives in pleasures is dead while she lives.”

### 18. On the unlawful access of women to the altar.

We have prohibited in every way the unlawful access of women to the altar. For we have learned from the report of certain persons that in some provinces, contrary to divine law and canonical institution, women thrust themselves forward to the holy altars, touch the sacred vessels immodestly, and hand the priestly vestments to priests; and, which is more indecent and absurd than these acts, distribute the body and blood of the Lord to the people [Col. 0865A] and perform other things that are shameful even to mention. We have prohibited these practices [Note: [Col. 0865] “we prohibit,” Bal.], so that no one may presume to do them in future [Note: [Col. 0865] “may presume,” G.].

That women ought not to enter the altar area is found at length in the Council of Chalcedon and in the decretals of Pope Gelasius.

### 19. That no canon or monk should presume to visit a monastery of nuns or canonesses except for preaching or [Note: [Col. 0865] the words that follow are absent in G.] some definite necessity, and then only with the bishop’s permission or that of his representative.

We have also discovered that certain canons and monks, having set aside the modesty proper to their religious state, visit the monasteries of holy women—both nuns and canonesses—immodestly and irreverently, without consulting their bishop. They commonly allege that they go there for no other reason than kinship, friendship, or some sort of conversation.

Because this conduct is suitable neither to the canonical nor to the monastic way of life, we absolutely forbid it, unless perhaps the cause of preaching or some unavoidable necessity compels it [Note: [Col. 0865] “may have compelled it,” Bal.]. Even then, no one is to presume to do this without the permission of the bishop or of the person who acts in his place.

If a sermon is to be preached, it must be delivered in a suitable place before everyone. If there is reason to speak with one of the nuns, this must take place nowhere else [Note: [Col. 0865] “elsewhere,” G.] but in an appointed place, namely, in the audience room, in the presence of religious men and religious women as witnesses.

When priests must celebrate Mass in monasteries of girls, they are to enter with the ministers assigned to them. After the rites have been properly completed, they must not in any way turn aside to secret conversations with the nuns, but must immediately depart with their ministers.

Furthermore, if nuns wish to confess their sins to priests, they must do so only in the church, before the holy altar, with witnesses standing nearby [Note: [Col. 0865] “or,” G.]. If illness prevents the confession from being made in the church, it must be made in any house whatsoever, but not [Note: [Col. 0865] Bal. reads “but not” (sed non)] unless witnesses likewise stand not far off [Note: [Col. 0865] G. reads quid, “what”].

For it does not seem at all proper to us that a monk should leave his monastery and visit a monastery of nuns for the purpose of imposing a form of penance on those confessing their sins.

### 20. That money must not be exacted from the poor with interest.

We have learned that certain clerics and laymen, forgetful of the Lord’s command—“You shall not lend your money at interest, and you shall not exact an excess of produce; I am the Lord your God”—have become inflamed with such a frenzy for the most shameful profit that, through the many and countless kinds of interest invented by their ingenuity and greed [Note: [Col. 0865] Bal. reads ut, “so that”], they afflict, oppress, and drain the poor. Many perish, exhausted by hunger; many others abandon their own possessions and seek foreign lands.

Wherever we have learned that this is being done, we have absolutely prohibited it, with an emphatic protest, so that it should not happen again. We have taken account of what the Lord says through the lawgiver in the Book of Exodus:

> “If you lend money to my poor people who dwell with you, you shall not press them as an exactor, nor oppress them with interest.”

In the Book of Leviticus [Note: [Col. 0865] the text has levitici; G. has levitico, both meaning “Leviticus”]:

> “If your brother has become poor and weak in hand, and you receive him as a resident alien and sojourner, and he lives with you, do not take interest from him, nor more than you gave. Fear the Lord your God, so that your brother may live with you.”

And in the Book of Deuteronomy:

> “If one of your brothers who dwell within the gates of your city, in the land that the Lord your God will give you, should fall into poverty, you shall not harden your heart or close your hand; rather, you shall open it to the poor and lend him whatever you see that he needs.”

Again, in the same book:

> “Beware lest an impious thought steal upon you and you say in your heart, ‘The seventh year of remission is approaching,’ and you turn your eyes away from your poor brother, unwilling to lend him what he asks, lest he cry out against you to the Lord and it become sin for you. Instead, you shall give to him and do nothing deceitful in relieving his needs, so that the Lord your God may bless you at all times in all the works to which you put your hand.”

The prophet Amos says:

> “Hear this, you who crush the poor and destroy the needy of the land, saying: ‘When will the harvest pass, so that we may sell our merchandise, and the Sabbath, so that we may open the grain stores, diminish the measure, increase the shekel, and falsify the scales, so that we may possess the needy for silver and the poor for a pair of sandals, and sell the refuse of the grain?’”

Jerome, in his exposition of the prophet Ezekiel, says:

> “Some think that interest exists only in money. Scripture, foreseeing this, removes the excess from every thing, so that you receive no more than you gave. Interest is commonly exacted in the fields in grain, millet, wine, oil, and other kinds of produce—or, as divine speech calls it, ‘excess’: for example, that in winter we give ten measures and at harvest receive fifteen. This is more than half again as much; someone who considers himself most just will take a quarter more. They commonly increase the amount and say: ‘I gave one measure which, when sown (satus; G. rasos, “levelled”), produced ten measures. Is it not just that I receive half a measure more of mine, since by my generosity he has nine and a half measures of mine?’ ‘Do not be deceived,’ says the Apostle; ‘God is not mocked.’ Let the merciful moneylender answer us briefly: did he give to one who possessed, or to one who did not possess? He ought not to have given to one who possessed, but he gave as though to one who did not possess. Why, then, does he demand more as though from one who possessed? [Note: [Col. 0865] G. omits ab, “from.”] Others, after lending money, commonly receive gifts of various kinds, and do not understand that whatever it is is called interest and excess if they receive more from the person to whom they gave than they gave.”

As to inequality of measures, unjust bushels, and sextarii, which the law of the Lord prohibits from being possessed or used [Note: [Col. 0865] the text has habere, “to possess”; Bal. haberi, “to be possessed”], we do not see clearly enough how the matter can be brought to a definite correction, since in almost all the various provinces they are held differently by everyone. Nevertheless, we strongly desire and admonish this above all: let no one have, or permit to be had, double measures within his domain, since we have learned that on this pretext many poor people are afflicted in numerous places [Note: [Col. 0865] the words “above all we desire and admonish” are absent in G.].

### 21. On various wicked crimes.

There are indeed perpetrators of various evils, whom divine law condemns and rejects. On account of their various crimes and outrages, the people are scourged by famine and pestilence, the condition of the churches is weakened, and the kingdom is endangered.

Against such persons, while emphasizing their wickedness—which is sufficiently accursed in the sacred writings—we have judged it necessary to take precautions once again through our admonition and exhortation, as these people do who perpetrate various pollutions, which some commit in the most diverse ways with males and with animals. By provoking to bitterness the incomparable sweetness of the most merciful Creator, they sin all the more grievously because they sin against nature.

For this crime five cities were consumed by heavenly fire and swallowed by the opening of hell [Note: [Col. 0865] omitted in Bal.]; likewise, forty thousand and more of the tribe of Benjamin were pierced by the sword of their brothers. These examples and manifest punishments show how detestable and abominable this vice is in the sight of the divine Majesty.

There are also other most destructive evils that undoubtedly remain from the rites of the gentiles: magicians, diviners, practitioners of lots, poisoners, soothsayers, enchanters, and interpreters of dreams. Divine law commands that such people be punished without retracting or exception.

Of them it is said in the law:

> “The soul that turns to magicians and diviners and fornicates with them, I will set my face against it and destroy it from the midst of its people. Sanctify yourselves and be holy, for I am the Lord your God. Keep my commandments and perform them, for I am the Lord who sanctifies you.”

And elsewhere:

> “Do not allow magicians, diviners, and sorcerers of the land to live.”

For it is beyond doubt, as many know, that through certain deceptions and diabolical illusions they infect the minds of some with love potions, foods, or amulets [Note: [Col. 0867] “peoples,” G.], so that, turned insane, they are judged by many not to perceive their own humiliations.

They are said by their magic to be able to disturb the air and send hail, foretell the future, take away fruits and milk and give them to others, and perform innumerable other things of this sort. Men or women, whoever they may be, who are found engaged in such practices [Note: [Col. 0867] the text has qui, “who”; G. quae, “which”] must be corrected with the greater severity through the discipline and authority of the ruler, in proportion as they more openly and fearlessly serve the devil with wicked and rash audacity.

Regarding them, the Council of Ancyra, title 23, also states:

> “Those who seek divinations and follow the custom of the gentiles, or introduce such persons into their houses to inquire into something by magical art or for the purpose of purification, shall lie under the rule of five years, according to the established degrees of penance.”

These matters must be admonished and corrected more diligently and more severely in every place, and especially where many trust that they can lawfully and with impunity practice or commit them.

### 22. On other vices that are treated as though naturally customary.

There are also other detestable vices that are so commonly practiced as though naturally customary that those who commit them do not notice the peril in which they stand. These include the things that the Apostle openly lists: drunkenness, revelries, quarrels, anger, brawls, dissensions, slanders, envy, and enmity. According to the same Apostle, these exclude people from the kingdom of God, as he says [Note: [Col. 0867] the text has inquiens, “saying”; Bal. prints inquietem, apparently a typographical error]:

> “Those who do such things will not obtain the kingdom of God.”

Some commit these acts so shamelessly and confidently that it can rightly be said of them:

> “They rejoice when they have done evil and exult in the worst things.”

Therefore all Christians must understand these matters carefully and avoid them with the greatest diligence, lest, by committing them, they lose the other good things they do and make themselves strangers to the kingdom of God because of them.

Likewise, in accordance with the Lord’s word, we shall all give an account on the day of judgment for idle speech; concerning buffoonery, foolish talk, and curses—for, according to the Apostle, those who curse will not possess the kingdom of God; concerning lies; concerning dangerous, harmful, and habitual oaths; and concerning obscene and shameful songs. All Christians must understand and observe these matters, and take the greatest care to avoid them, lest by devoting themselves to such things through negligence they suffer damage to their souls [Note: [Col. 0867] omitted in G.].

We therefore wish first, with the help of divine grace, to renounce these matters ourselves and provide a pattern and example to others. We have judged it necessary humbly to make them known and faithfully announce them to your faithful [Note: [Col. 0867] G. corrects this to “our faithful”]. We also wish to instruct all the people throughout our parishes by admonition, lest—God forbid—through their ignorance and our negligence they become subject to such deadly vices.

### 23. That laymen should have wives only for the sake of children, and that marriage was instituted by God.

In the work of our assembly we have also collected several other chapters pertaining to the observance and salvation of the lay faithful. Here we mention them only briefly, omitting their length: namely, that they should know that marriage was established by God, and that it is not to be sought for the sake of lust but rather for the sake of children; that virginity, as our teachers instruct, is to be preserved until marriage; and that those who have wives must not have either a concubine or a mistress.

They must also learn how to love their wives chastely and, as a weaker vessel, to render them their proper honor; that intercourse with their wives should take place for the sake of offspring, not pleasure; and how men must abstain from intercourse with pregnant wives; likewise [Note: [Col. 0867] “these matters do not occur in the bishops’ report.”] how men must abstain from their wives during menstruation [Note: [Col. 0867] “these matters do not occur in the bishops’ report.”].

Unless it is on account of fornication, as the Lord says, a wife is not to be dismissed but rather endured. Those who, after dismissing their wives on account of fornication, marry others are to be regarded, according to the Lord’s judgment, as adulterers.

They must also learn how incestuous unions are to be avoided by Christians; that places dedicated to God are to be visited by the faithful more frequently and devoutly, in order to pray to God and render him propitious; that in basilicas dedicated to God they must not devote themselves to idle, shameful, or obscene stories and conversations, nor conduct secular business or public lawsuits; and that those who do these things in the churches of God heap greater sins upon themselves.

[Col. 0868B] They must learn to judge with just judgment, to avoid accepting gifts, to avoid false testimony and detraction, and many other matters that it would be too long to enumerate.

There are also many other crimes that urgently require correction. We have not thought it necessary to insert them here, because we know that they are sufficiently clearly included in your capitularies, which you have judged must be corrected through your authority and with the counsel of the faithful by means of your energetic envoys.

We, your faithful and most devoted servants and intercessors, according to the smallness of our understanding and as the shortness of time permitted, have gathered together, condensed, and arranged in order the matters that, according to your holy ordinance, we recognized as pertaining to the correction and reform of ourselves, of our fellow priests, and of our subjects, as well as those that we foresaw must necessarily be announced and taught to the peoples. We have also included what we have now judged should be requested from your piety, extracting a few things from the many matters conducted in our assemblies.

Although, in an inverted order, we chose first to satisfy your most ardent desire concerning the matters set forth above, we have by no means consigned to oblivion what ought first to have been placed at the beginning and what we recognized as pertaining especially to your person and office. Rather, looking to your salvation, we have faithfully collected several necessary chapters and devoted ourselves to presenting them to you familiarly as an admonition.

Thus, by looking at, reading, and hearing them openly and distinctly, your discernment may recognize the matters about which, and on behalf of whom, we have faithfully acted in the assemblies mentioned above, according to the measure of our strength.

### 24. On the title “king,” and what the king himself ought to be.

Isidore writes in the Book of Sentences about why someone is called a king:

> “For ‘king,’ he says, is so called from acting rightly. If he acts piously, justly, and mercifully, he is rightly called a king. If he lacks these qualities, he is not a king but a tyrant.”

As the same Isidore writes in the Book of Etymologies, the ancients called all kings tyrants. Later, however, those who ruled piously, justly, and mercifully acquired the name of king; but for those who ruled impiously, unjustly, and cruelly, the name “tyrannical,” rather than “kingly,” was applied.

Hence blessed Gregory also says in the *Moralia*:

> “We have learned from the sacred writings that holy men are called kings because they act rightly, govern their own thoughts well, and compose the movements resisting them through rational discernment. Those, therefore, are rightly called kings who know how to pacify both themselves and their subjects by governing them well.”

Fulgentius writes in the Book on the Truth of Predestination and Grace concerning the purpose for which an emperor is established:

> “The most merciful emperor is not a vessel prepared for mercy and appointed to glory merely because he has received the summit of earthly rule, but if, while occupying the imperial height, he lives by right faith [Note: [Col. 0869] “S. in i.,” Bal.] and, endowed with true humility of heart, subjects the height of royal dignity to holy religion; if he takes greater pleasure in serving God in fear than in ruling the people in pride [Note: [Col. 0869] “in fear,” G.]; if gentleness in him moderates anger [Note: [Col. 0869] “moderates,” G.; “mitigates,” Bal.], and kindness adorns power [Note: [Col. 0869] “adorns,” Bal.]; if he shows himself to all as more worthy of love than of fear; if he provides salutary care for his subjects; if he holds fast to justice without abandoning mercy; if, above all, he remembers himself to be a son of the holy mother Catholic Church in such a way that he makes his rule beneficial to her peace and tranquility throughout the whole world.

> “For the Christian empire is more truly governed and extended when care is provided for the ecclesiastical order throughout the whole earth than when war is waged in any part of the world for the sake of temporal security.”

Hence Isidore also writes:

> “The princes of the world sometimes hold within the Church the heights of the power they have acquired, so that through that same power they may strengthen ecclesiastical discipline [Note: [Col. 0869] ut, “so that,” added by a second hand; G. reads nisi ut, “unless so that”]. Otherwise, powers would not be necessary within the Church, except so that what the priest cannot accomplish through the word of teaching, power may command through the terror of discipline.

> “Often the heavenly kingdom is advanced through an earthly kingdom: those who, placed within the Church, act against the faith and discipline of the Church are crushed by the severity of rulers, and the ruling power imposes upon the necks of the proud that discipline which the usefulness of the Church cannot enforce.”

Solomon says in Proverbs:

> “Mercy and truth preserve the king, and his throne will be strengthened by clemency.”

### 25. What the royal ministry consists of

The royal ministry consists especially in governing and ruling the people of God with equity and justice, and in striving that they may have peace and concord. He himself ought first to be the defender of churches and of the servants of God, widows, orphans, and all other poor people, as well as all those in need. His vigilance and concern ought, insofar as possible, to be directed to this end: first, that no injustice be done; then, if one occurs, that he in no way permit it to persist, nor leave anyone the hope of concealing himself [Note: [Col. 0869] G. has *vel latendi* (“or of hiding”) in the margin.] or the boldness to do wrong. Rather, let everyone know that if anything evil they have committed comes to his attention, it will by no means remain uncorrected or unpunished; instead, the nature and measure of a just correction [Note: [Col. 0869] G. lacks *iustae* (“just”).] will correspond to the character of the deed. Therefore, he who is the judge of judges ought to ensure that the cases of the poor come before him and to investigate them carefully, lest those whom he has appointed and who ought to act in his place among the people permit the poor to suffer oppression unjustly or negligently [Note: [Col. 0869] G. has *oppressionem* (“oppression”) instead of *oppressiones*.].

Everyone, whatever his rank, ought also to know that if he will have to render an account to God for an idle word, much more will he have to render one for the ministry divinely entrusted to him.

Job speaks as follows concerning the king’s ministry:

> When I sat as a king, with the army standing around me, I was nevertheless a comforter of the afflicted. The ear that heard me called me blessed, and the eye that saw me bore witness for me, because I delivered the poor man who cried out, and the orphan girl who had no helper. The blessing of the perishing came upon me, and I consoled the widow’s heart. I clothed myself with justice, and it clothed me as with a garment and a diadem—with my judgment. I was an eye to the blind and a foot to the lame. I was a father to the poor, and I investigated most diligently the case that I did not know. I crushed the jaws of the wicked and snatched the prey from his teeth.

Solomon [Note: [Col. 0869] Bal. has “Solomon says”] says: “The king who sits on the throne of judgment scatters every evil by his gaze.”

Likewise, the same author says in the Book of Wisdom:

> Love justice, you who judge the earth; think of the Lord with goodness, and seek him in simplicity of heart.

And there:

> Hear therefore, O kings, and understand; learn, you judges of the ends of the earth. Give ear, you who rule the multitudes and take pride in the crowds of nations, for authority has been given to you by the Lord, and power by the Most High, who will examine your works and scrutinize your thoughts. For although you were his ministers, you did not judge rightly, nor did you keep the law of justice, nor did you walk according to the will of God. He will appear to you terribly and swiftly, because a very severe judgment will be held against those who rule. For mercy is granted to the lowly, but the powerful will suffer powerful torments. The Lord will show partiality toward no one, nor will he be awed by anyone’s greatness, because he himself made the small and the great, and he cares equally for all.

There are also countless other testimonies of the holy Scriptures appropriate to the royal name and office. Your holy devotion has thereby spared us great labor in collecting them, because divine grace has so filled your spirit and adorned your dignity with the prerogatives of so many virtues that it is unnecessary for the Lord’s priests to burden your mind with more abundant examples or any exaggeration.

Therefore, we offer the almighty God the fullest and manifold thanks: by his gratuitous goodness he has enriched you with pious religion, holy devotion, kindly humility, love of justice, works of mercy, and perfection in the other holy virtues, so that you rightly deserve to be loved and imitated by all.

Indeed, if these gifts had not been bestowed upon you from heaven, we [Note: [Col. 0869] This sentence is missing in Bal.] ought, despite the temporal danger, on account of the authority of our ministry, to admonish you—or rather, by admonishing you, to compel you—to undertake them in some fashion. You, on the contrary, because of divine love and honor, both urge us toward greater things by your admonitions and take the greatest care to bring us pious and timely assistance [Note: [Col. 0869] G. has *quomodo* (“how”) instead of *quoquo modo* (“in some fashion”).].

Accordingly, with the most humble prayers we specially urge Your Piety not to find it burdensome, with God’s help, to complete without ceasing the good that you have begun, and not in any way to fail in fulfilling works of justice and mercy. For the reward of eternal life is given not to those who begin, but to those who complete. And according to the word of Truth: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved.”

### 26. That the king ought to exercise great vigilance in choosing and appointing the rulers of the Church

Again, by way of admonition, we humbly urge Your Greatness henceforth to apply great zeal and the most diligent care in appointing good pastors and rulers in the churches of God. For if this is done otherwise, the ecclesiastical order will not retain its dignity; the Christian religion, being weakened in many respects, will suffer the damage of its decline; and danger to your soul will arise—which we do not desire.

### 27. On appointing abbesses

Likewise, we ask that in appointing abbesses you take special care for your own danger, as you have often been admonished and as divine authority has repeatedly made clear to you.

### 28. On choosing assistants for public affairs and ministers

We also earnestly beseech you to exercise the most diligent foresight in choosing your assistants and the ministers of public affairs, who ought, in your place, to rule, govern, and judge the people of God. Always bear in mind what is said to Moses in the Book of Exodus:

> Therefore, he said, from the whole people choose prudent men who fear God, in whom there is truth and who hate avarice; and appoint them as tribunes, centurions, and commanders of fifty, so that they may judge the people at all times. Whatever is greater, let them refer to you, and let them judge only the lesser matters; thus the burden, divided among others, will be lighter for you. If you do this, you will fulfill the Lord’s command, and you will be able to bear his precepts.

Hence also in the Book of Deuteronomy:

> You shall appoint judges and magistrates in all your gates, which the Lord your God will give you throughout each of your tribes, so that they may judge the people with a just judgment and incline toward no side.

And there:

> I said to you at that time: I alone cannot bear you, because the Lord your God has multiplied you, and today you are as numerous as the stars of heaven [Note: [Col. 0871] *et* is superscripted in G., yielding *ut sitis* (“so that you may be”)]. May the Lord, the God of your fathers, add many thousands to this number and deal with you as he has spoken. I am not able alone to bear your affairs, your burden, and your disputes. Provide from among yourselves wise and knowledgeable men whose conduct has been tested in your tribes.

Likewise, it is read in the Book of Chronicles:

> King Jehoshaphat appointed judges over the land in all the fortified cities of Judah, in each place. And he commanded the judges, saying: “See what you are doing, for you do not exercise the judgment of man, but of the Lord; and whatever judgment you pronounce will rebound upon you. Let the fear of the Lord be with you, and act with diligence in all things, for there is no iniquity with the Lord our God, no partiality, and no desire for gifts.”

We also ask Your Piety, for the sake of divine mercy, your salvation, the usefulness of the whole people, and the honor and stability of the kingdom, to exercise the most diligent vigilance, so that your counselors, ministers of your dignity, and guardians of your soul and body—who ought within the kingdom to be for others an ornament and example of goodness, and among foreign nations a seasoning of good reputation—may, putting aside every pretense and every cunning, have charity, peace, and concord with one another. Thus, according to the will of God, your honor, and the advancement of the whole kingdom, let them strive together and be your true assistants in all things, concordantly.

They will be able to be true counselors and true assistants of yours and of the whole kingdom for its welfare only if they are united in mind and have mutual affection. For it is fitting that your sacred household should appear worthy of respect to all and exist as an example to all, and that the reputation of its good name should abundantly spread among both the subjects of your empire [Note: [Col. 0871] G. has *aliis* (“to others”) instead of *sive alios* (“whether the others”).] [Note: [Col. 0871] G. has feminine *subiectas* instead of *subiectos*.] and foreign nations.

Since, therefore, all dissensions and disagreements must be settled by imperial authority, and every wickedness must be suppressed, it is necessary that what it decides to correct in others be found in it least of all.

We also humbly beseech and admonish you to educate your children—whom divine goodness has chosen to grant you—continually and diligently in the fear of God, as you indeed do; and to urge them by attentive paternal admonition to remain with one another in the charity of mutual affection, in brotherly love, and in the harmony of unity. Take no less care, with watchful and prudent circumspection, that they do not incur the offense of their Creator through unlawful acts. Bear in mind the blessed Job, whose concern for educating his children, as blessed Gregory wrote in his *Moral Works*, was such that he not only made them perfect outwardly in deed and word, but also cleansed their hearts through the offering of sacrifice.

Consider also David [Note: [Col. 0871] G. has *ad* (“to”) instead of *et* (“also”).] instructing his son Solomon, concerning whom it is read in the First Book of Kings [*Malachim*]:

> I am entering the way of all the earth. Be strong and be a man, and observe the observances of the Lord your God, so that you may walk in his ways and keep his ceremonies, judgments, commandments, and testimonies, as it is written in the law of Moses.

And in the Book of Chronicles:

> But you, Solomon my son, know the God of your father, and serve him with a perfect heart and a willing spirit.

Consider also Tobit, of whom it is written that, when he had become a man, he took Anna as his wife from his own tribe and begot a son by her, giving him his own name. From infancy he taught him to fear God and to abstain from every sin.

Likewise, addressing this same son, he says:

> Throughout all the days of your life keep God in mind, and beware lest you ever consent to sin or neglect the commandments of our God. Give alms from your substance, and do not turn your face away from any poor person; for then it will happen that the face of the Lord will not be turned away from you. Be merciful as you are able.

And so forth.

Likewise, shortly afterward:

> Guard yourself, my son, against every fornication, and apart from your wife never permit yourself to know guilt. Never allow pride to dominate your mind or your heart, for every destruction took its beginning from it [Note: [Col. 0871] *in* (“in/from it”) is supplied from Bal.].

And again, not long afterward:

> Always seek counsel from a wise person; bless God at all times, and ask him to direct your ways, so that all your plans may remain in him.

Likewise:

> Hear therefore, my sons, your father. Serve the Lord in fear [Note: [Col. 0871] Bal. has *veritate* (“truth”) instead of *timore* (“fear”).], and seek to do what is pleasing to him. Command your children to practice justice and almsgiving, to remember God, and to bless him at all times in truth and with all their strength.

Having set all these matters before you, we make known to you that, concerning the matters you entrusted to us to consider in your capitularies—namely, what is held by rulers and by the rest of the people according to divine authority or otherwise, and what has been abandoned, in part or entirely, so that it is not observed—we acknowledge that in the capitularies set out above, as well as in those which you ordered written in the present year and sent throughout your empire by your envoys in order to suppress vices, many things have been pointed out that have until now been neglected by the pastors of the churches, by the rulers, and by the rest of the people. We know that in these matters they have acted and are acting otherwise than divine authority requires.

But if, through God’s working, this priestly admonition of ours achieves its effect through your good zeal from now on, we believe that many things which many have abandoned and failed to observe contrary to divine authority will be corrected.

For in those same capitularies it is also stated that it should become clear what causes led priests and rulers to deviate from the right path. Apart from the capitularies mentioned above, in which, as we said, many things were being neglected, we have specifically recognized that one obstacle has grown deeply rooted over a long period: namely, that the ruling power, intervening on various pretexts, has rushed into ecclesiastical cases contrary to the rule of divine authority; while the priests, partly through negligence and partly through ignorance, have occupied themselves with greed, secular affairs, and worldly concerns beyond what they ought. It is beyond doubt that, on this account, matters have been conducted differently on both sides from what divine authority teaches.

But since, through God’s mercy, we rejoice that many things have been corrected by our predecessors, by your father, and by you, we believe that, if the matters we urge meet with favorable success, your intention and our devotion may, with God’s cooperation, reach a state of perfection.

Nevertheless, because we know that the condition of this kingdom has grown and expanded under such circumstances and conditions, and that this matter was not completely corrected by our most prudent and holy predecessors [Note: [Col. 0871] Bal. has *vestris* (“your”) instead of *nostris* (“our”).”—whether bishops or rulers—for reasons that may be stated in their own time; and because the burden of so great a consideration exceeded the strength of our smallness, since we had neither the leisure nor the time nor the full number of our fellow priests that the necessity itself demanded, we have deferred treating and considering these matters to a more suitable and appropriate time, if God so wills.

For the perfection of so great a consideration requires the agreement and assistance of the rulers, the number, devotion, and zeal of the priests, the obedience—or concord—of the people, and the appropriateness of place and the span of time.

As for the episcopal liberty which, God granting and your assistance supporting us, we desire to attain in order to perform God’s service, we have reserved it to be discussed and considered with you at its proper time. Thus may it be possible both for us to save ourselves, to benefit usefully the people entrusted to us, and to pray more freely for you and for the stability of your empire; and may the due support arising from your service and from the aid of the kingdom not be withdrawn from us, but, if possible, rather increased.

## THIRD ADDITION [Note: [Col. 0873] *Haec capitula proprie sunt* (“These capitularies properly are”) is absent in G.]

These capitularies properly concern bishops and the various ecclesiastical orders. They ought not only to observe them but also to teach those subject or entrusted to them to carry them out.

### 1 [Note: [Col. 0873] All chapter numbers are lacking from this point in G.]. On the property of the Church [Note: [Col. 0873] The heading is absent in G.]

Since, according to the tradition of the holy Fathers, we know that the property of the Church consists of the vows of the faithful, the prices of sins, and the patrimonies of the poor—and since we desire, with God’s help, not only to preserve what has been acquired but also to contribute much—we have nevertheless determined, in order to remove completely from ecclesiastical persons the suspicion long ago conceived concerning the division of the property of any church, that neither in our times nor in the times of our sons and, God disposing, of our successors who may wish to imitate the will or example of us or our predecessors, such property shall suffer any division or loss whatsoever [Note: [Col. 0873] G. has *patiatur* (“let it suffer”) instead of *patiantur* (“let they suffer”).].

### 2. That bishops be chosen through the election of the clergy and people, for merit of life and wisdom

Not ignorant of the sacred canons, and desiring that the holy Church might more freely enjoy its honor in the name of God, we have given our consent to the ecclesiastical order: namely, that bishops be chosen through the election of the clergy and people, according to the provisions of the canons, from their own diocese, without regard to the acceptance of persons or gifts, on account of merit of life and the gift of wisdom, so that they may everywhere benefit those subject to them by example and word.

### 3. On the canonical profession, disfigured by many

Since the canonical profession was being dishonored by many, partly through ignorance and partly through laziness, we considered it worthwhile, with God’s approval, at the holy assembly, to gather into one rule for canons and canonesses, selecting and arranging them from the sayings of the holy Fathers as though from various meadows and gathering certain blooming flowers, and to hand it over to canons and nuns for observance, so that through it the canonical order might be maintained without ambiguity.

And since the holy assembly so highly praised it that it judged it ought to be observed down to one iota, we decree that all who live under this profession must unquestionably hold to it, and that henceforth it must in every respect be observed both by canons and by canonically living nuns.

The matter of the honor of churches—how, with God’s help, it may flourish as far as lies within us—is likewise known to have been included in the capitularies noted below.

[Note: [Col. 0873] The following is absent from the source of Ansegisus I, 79.]

### 4. On bishops in Lombardy who customarily demand oaths and gifts from those whom they ordain [Note: [Col. 0873] Bal. has *solerent* (“were accustomed”) instead of *soliti erant* (“had been accustomed”).]

Concerning the bishops established in Lombardy, who had been accustomed to receive or demand from those whom they ordained oaths and gifts contrary to divine and canonical authority, it is forbidden in every way that this should happen any longer, because according to the sacred canons both persons who do such things ought to be removed from their own rank [Note: [Col. 0873] Bal. has *deici* (“be cast down”); Ansegisus I, 91, has *decidi* (“be cut off”).].

### 5. On capitularies concerning incestuous marriages and other matters that ought to be addressed

Certain capitularies—such as those concerning incestuous marriages; churches which are divided among co-heirs and thereby deprived of their proper dignity; churches whose own resources have been excessively reduced; and property recently taken from certain churches under the pressure of necessity—as well as any other matters, whether ecclesiastical or public, deserving correction, which we cannot accomplish because of the brevity of time, we judged ought to be deferred until, with the Lord’s favor, the opportunity to accomplish this is granted to us through the counsel [Note: [Col. 0873] Bal. has *consulto* (“deliberately,” or “by deliberation”) instead of *consultu* (“through counsel”).] of the faithful.

We have nevertheless judged that the matters discovered, so that they may obtain their effect over time with God’s help, ought to be inserted here.

### 6. On the case of monks who have been granted permission to choose abbots from among themselves

As for how, with God’s help, we have in part arranged the case of the monks; how it was determined that we should grant them permission to choose an abbot for themselves from among themselves; and how we have ordered matters so that, with God’s help, they may live in peace and indefatigably preserve their way of life and purpose—we have had all this carefully noted in another document and have confirmed it so that it might be valid among our successors and preserved inviolate.

### 7. On those who do not receive chrism from their own bishop [Note: [Col. 0873] Bal. has *accipiunt* (“receive”) instead of *accipiant* (“may receive”).]

If anyone attempts to baptize using chrism other than the new chrism which he receives through the gift or permission of his own bishop—unless death has intervened beforehand—it is clear that by this reckless act he has pronounced upon himself the sentence of his own condemnation.

### 8. That no one be despoiled except by a just judgment

There is no privilege by which someone already stripped may be stripped again. Therefore, unless a just judgment so decides, no one is to be despoiled.

### 9. On one who disputes anything further after the truth has been found

Whoever, after the truth has been found, continues to dispute anything further is seeking falsehood. Therefore, everyone must proceed with caution.

### 10. On cases not contained in the law, which ecclesiastical judges must not judge

No cases are to be heard by ecclesiastical judges which are not contained in the laws or which are known to be prohibited.

### 11. On the conduct of the accused and the accuser

In court, inquiry must be made into the conduct and faith both of the one who accuses and of the one who is accused.

### 12. On those who have neglected the honor of the Christian name

The right to accuse or to give testimony is to be denied to those who have neglected the dignity of the Christian religion and name.

### 13. That offerings not be celebrated in private houses by bishops or priests

Offerings ought not to be celebrated in private houses by bishops or priests.

### 14. That every agreement be dissolved by a later agreement

Every agreement is dissolved by a later agreement. A free man, however, can either worsen or improve his status.

### 15. On accusers who come from the house of an enemy

Accusers who come from the house of an enemy are not to be believed.

### 16. On providing for brothers, so that it is not done irrationally

Brothers must be provided for in such a way that we do not seem to destroy what has been built. For if I destroy what I have built, I make myself a transgressor.

### 17. On clerics who willingly take up arms during a revolt

If clerics are found to have willingly taken up arms in any revolt, they are to be deprived of their ecclesiastical rank and handed over to a monastery for penance.

### 18. That the law of emperors is not above the law of God

The law of emperors is not above the law of God, but beneath it.

### 19. On confessing sins to God daily in prayer

Apart from the confession made to priests in order to receive counsel and to appease God, confession of sins ought frequently to be made to God in prayer.

### 20. That the spiritual person examines everything and is himself examined by no one

“The spiritual person judges all things, but he himself is judged by no one.”

### 21. That husbands abstain from their wives during menstruation

During menstruation, husbands must abstain entirely from their wives.

### 22. On those who have a just complaint against bishops or church administrators

If anyone believes that he has a just complaint against a bishop or church administrators [Note: [Col. 0875] Bal. has *i. se cr.*—an abbreviation or correction in the margin], he must not approach primates or other judges before first approaching the persons themselves privately—not once, but very often—so that he may receive from them either his justice or a just explanation.

If they act otherwise, they are to be deprived of communion both by those persons and by others, as despisers of the apostles and the other Fathers, concerning whom the prophet says: “They will be as though they did not exist, and the men who oppose you will perish.”

### 23. On the power of binding and loosing granted to priests by Christ

Laypeople ought to know that the Lord has granted priests the power of binding and loosing, and that they must obey their admonitions and humbly submit to excommunication.

### 24. That priests who go to external churches without the bishops’ command be suspended from communion

Priests who migrate from one church to another without the order of their own bishop are to be held excluded from communion until they return to the same churches in which they were originally established.

### 25. On one who finds or considers his judge opposed to him

If anyone finds or happens to regard a judge as opposed or suspect in any case, let him present an appeal.

### 26. On peace, concord, and unity

There must be peace, concord, and unity among the Christian people. Since we have one God the Father in heaven, one mother, the Church, one faith, and one baptism, we ought to live together in one peace and in unity if we desire to reach the one true inheritance of the heavenly kingdom. For God is not a God of dissension but of peace, as he himself says: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called sons of God.”

### 27. On the authority of bishops regarding church property, and on agreement between bishops and laypeople

Bishops are to have the authority to oversee, rule, govern, and administer church property according to the authority of the canons.

We wish laypeople also to obey bishops in their ministry, for governing the churches of God, defending widows and orphans, and preserving their Christianity. Bishops, too, are to cooperate with counts and judges in carrying out justice, so that a just law is in no way distorted by anyone’s falsehood or false testimony, perjury, or bribe.

### 28. On injury to a bishop and the overturning of a litany

If anyone injures a bishop or other ministers within a church, we order that he be subjected to torments and die in exile. If he disturbs the holy oratories themselves or the divine ministries, or overturns a litany, he is to incur capital punishment. But if he has committed only an insult, he is to be handed over to torments and exile.

### 29. On tithes

We admonish and command that the payment of tithes to God not be neglected at all [Note: [Col. 0875] Bal. has singular *decima* (“the tithe”) instead of plural *decimas* (“tithes”).]. God himself established that they be given to him [Note: [Col. 0875] Bal. has *dari* (“be given”) instead of *dare* (“to give”)]. For it is to be feared that whoever withholds from God what is owed to him may perhaps cause God, through his sin, to take away from him what he needs.

### 30. That churches have peace

No one may dare to drag an accused person who has fled to a church out of it, or surrender him from there to punishment or death, so that the honor of God and his saints may be preserved. Rather, the rulers of the churches must strive to obtain peace, life, and bodily safety for such persons [Note: [Col. 0875] Bal. has singular *ei* (“for him”) instead of plural *eis* (“for them”)]. Nevertheless, they must make lawful compensation for what they have done unjustly [Note: [Col. 0875] Bal. has *fecerit* (“he has done”) instead of *fecerunt* (“they have done”).].

### 31. On a bishop who dies intestate

If anyone from the ecclesiastical order dies without a testament and without cognizance [*cognitione*, a legal term whose precise force is uncertain], his inheritance is to devolve upon the church in which he served. The same applies to nuns.

### 32. Again, on the peace of churches

We command that secular lawsuits not be held in churches, in church houses, or in church courtyards.

### 33. On ecclesiastical benefices

All who hold an ecclesiastical benefice must provide full assistance for restoring the roofs of churches and repairing the churches themselves, and must pay the ninth and the tenth.

### 34. On the sacred orders

If a lector, subdeacon, deacon, or priest despises the honor of the clerical state, he is to be subjected, together with his property, to curial status.

### 35. On making offerings and peace in the church

The Christian people must also be continually admonished to make an offering and the sign of peace in church. For the offering itself is a great remedy for the souls of the giver and his household, and true unity and concord are demonstrated in the peace.

### 36. That the evil of drunkenness be entirely avoided

We command that the great evil of drunkenness, from which all vices spring, be avoided in every way. Whoever refuses to avoid it is to be excommunicated until he makes a suitable amendment.

### 37. On the number of clerics

A bishop must not create a multitude of clerics indiscriminately; rather, their number is to be regulated according to the merit or income of the churches [Note: [Col. 0875] G. has *demoretur* instead of *moderetur*.].

### 38. On spiritual godchildren

We command that every godfather and spiritual relative instruct his godchildren in the Catholic faith.

### 39. That licentious songs be abandoned around churches

We entirely prohibit the performance of shameful and licentious songs around churches. This must be avoided everywhere.

### 40. What clerics should be like

No one is to become a cleric unless he has a good reputation and is educated.

### 41. On bishops and abbots not permitting shameful jokes in their presence

Bishops and abbots [Note: [Col. 0875] The word is absent in G.] must not permit shameful jokes to be made in their presence. Rather, they should have poor and needy people at table with them; divine reading should resound there; and they should take food with blessing and praise of God, according to the Apostle: “Whether you eat or drink, do everything for the praise of God.”

### 42. On bishops conducting just judgments

Bishops and judges [Note: [Col. 0875] The words *e et i.* are found in Tilianus, the Council of Rheims, and Burchard.] must discern just judgments, because some matters are to be judged now, while others are to be reserved for God’s judgment.

For it is written:

> Do not judge before the appointed time, until the Lord comes, who will both bring to light the hidden things of darkness and disclose the counsels of hearts; and then each person’s praise will come from God.

And they should remember this:

> For with the judgment by which you judge, you will be judged.

### 43. On clerics who abandon the church

When clerics abandon a church and others are recalled to take their place, if they return after their departure, nothing is to be provided for them. What those who depart have left behind is not to go for the use of the rulers, but is to pass to their successors.

### 44. On monks’ and canons’ service being usefully carried out with counsel

Monks and canons must have full counsel concerning how they may serve God and guard their souls better, so that they do not seek an occasion for wandering on account of any necessity [Note: [Col. 0875] Bal. has *nec* (“nor”) instead of *ne* (“so that not”)], and so that an opportunity is not thereby given to the devil to tempt them.

### 45. That widows ought not to live in luxury

Widows must not live in luxury, but, according to the Apostle, must live under the authority of the bishop, as is fitting.

### 46. That clerics not undertake secular business

A cleric or monk must not become a collector of public revenues, a contractor of taxes or of household management [Note: [Col. 0877] *aut* (“or”) is deleted in G.], a representative in litigation, or a guarantor in such matters.

### 47. On one who acts contrary to canonical statutes

If anyone acts contrary to these statutes, and he is a bishop, we decree that his church may claim all his property, whatever its source or from whatever person it came to him, whether before or after his episcopate.

If clerics there have done this, the church is to claim the monetary penalty which the bishop judges should be exacted.

Those who have entrusted their business to such persons or accepted them as guarantors in the matters mentioned above are to have no action against the church, its administrators, or the persons whom they trusted [Note: [Col. 0877] G. has *creaverunt* (“created” or “appointed”) written above *crediderunt* (“trusted”).].

But if anyone has trusted them or accepted them as guarantors for a public debt or collection, he is to be compelled to pay the debt from the property of the fisc.

### 48. On one who acquires church property through a false precaria or fraud

If any person wishes to acquire and hold church property for himself through lies or fraudulent devices by means of a *precaria*, and after the *precariae* have been made those same lies are reported to the ears of the church’s ruler, that church is to recover in full, without any opposition whatsoever, the property that was deceitfully taken from it.

But the man who, through those same lies, handed over his own property to that church out of desire for the *precaria* is likewise to receive it back under his own control.

### 49. That the ancient practice of penance, which ought to be carried out according to canonical authority, has fallen out of use

The manner of performing penance according to the ancient institution of the canons has fallen out of use in most places, and the ancient order of excommunicating and reconciling is not observed. Assistance is therefore to be sought from the lord emperor, so that if anyone sins publicly, he may be punished with public penance, and so that, according to the order of the canons, each person may be excommunicated and reconciled according to his merit.

### 50. On a cleric summoned to guardianship

If a bishop, priest, deacon, or subdeacon is summoned to guardianship or administration, he may undertake only such an office of administration. This is permitted provided that, within four months, he has declared in writing before the competent judge that he accepted such an office voluntarily [Note: [Col. 0877] Bal. has *conceditur* (“is permitted”) instead of *concedetur* (“will be permitted”).]. He is then not to suffer prejudice with regard to another guardianship.

### 51. On churches established on private property and divided among heirs

It has been reported to us that churches established on private property are divided among heirs, and that such hostility arises from this division that one altar becomes four parts, with each part having its own priest. This cannot be carried out in any way without discord and hostility.

Therefore, it seemed good to us that churches of this kind ought not to be divided among heirs. If they come into dispute and hostility arises among them, so that the priest cannot perform his office there, the bishop of the city is to order that the solemn celebration of Mass not take place there in any way until they return to concord and, by common vote and counsel, that church canonically has a priest who can freely perform his ministry there.

### 52. On those who are confirmed twice or three times, without the bishops’ knowledge

It has been reported to us that certain people from the common people are confirmed twice or three times, although the bishops themselves are unaware of it. Therefore, it seemed good to us that confirmation, like baptism, must not be repeated in any way. Those who are baptized or confirmed twice or more are decreed to serve not the world but the Lord alone, in the most religious manner, under a monastic or clerical habit.

### 53. On clerics who play at tables

If any cleric plays at tables or attends spectacles, he is to be prohibited from sacred ministry for three years. If he performs worthy penance, he is to be reconciled.

54. Concerning those who dissolve the marriages of slaves. It has been reported to us that certain persons, with a presumptuous exercise of authority, dissolve the lawful marriages of slaves, paying no attention to the Gospel saying: “What God has joined together, let no human being separate.” Therefore it has seemed good to us that the marriages of slaves not be dissolved, even if they have different masters; rather, while remaining in one marriage, they shall serve their masters. This is to be observed in cases where there was a lawful union and it took place with the consent of the masters.

55. Concerning those who do not confess their sins fully. We have also recognized that this requires correction: certain people, when confessing their sins to priests, do not do so fully. Since it is established that the human being consists of two substances, namely soul and body, and since one sins sometimes through the movement of the mind and sometimes through the weakness of the flesh, the sins themselves must be investigated with careful inquiry, so that a full confession may be made concerning both. That is, they must confess what has been done through the body and what is committed in thought alone. The confessor of sins must therefore be instructed to require confession concerning the eight principal vices, without which it is difficult to live in this life, since a person sins through thought or, more seriously, through action at their prompting. Hatred, envy, pride, and other such diseases of the soul cause harm all the more dangerously the more subtly they spread.

56. Concerning holy churches. No rector of a church, hospice, or monastery established under Roman jurisdiction may in any way alienate its immovable property—that is, a field, house, slave, civic bread, or anything similar—nor may he pledge it to a creditor. (Alienation is a sale, gift, exchange, or perpetual emphyteutic contract.) Everyone is altogether obliged to abstain from such alienation. A notary who draws up such instruments shall be handed over to perpetual exile. Magistrates and judges who approve such instruments shall lose both their office and their possessions. [Note: [Col. 0877] G. lacks the passage.] [Note: [Col. 0877] *consenserint*; G. corrects it to *censuerint*.]

57. Concerning those who say that sins ought to be confessed only to God. Some say that sins ought to be confessed only to God, while others judge that they must be confessed to priests. Both practices are carried out within the holy Church, not without great benefit, provided that we confess our sins both to God, from whom forgiveness of sins comes, and, with David, say: “I made my sin known to you, and I did not hide my iniquity. I said, ‘I will confess my iniquities against myself to the Lord’; and you forgave the wickedness of my sin.” In accordance with the apostle’s instruction, let us also confess our sins to one another and pray for one another, so that we may be saved.

The confession made to God purifies sins; the confession made to a priest teaches how those sins are purified. For God, the author and giver of salvation and healing, often provides this through the invisible working of his power, and often through the ministry of physicians. [Note: [Col. 0877] G. lacks the heading.]

58. That respect of persons must be avoided in all judgments. Since, as the apostle testifies, there is no respect of persons with God, and it must be avoided in every judgment, it must be guarded against all the more in this judgment of penance, so that no priest may ever judge a person otherwise through favor or hatred than what he has found in the sacred canons, or what has appeared more correct to him according to the authority of the holy Scriptures and ecclesiastical custom. If physicians, who endeavor to apply medicine to bodies, do not spare those whom they desire to heal—on account of respect for any person—from the cautery, the knife, or any other harsh treatment, how much more must this be observed by those who are physicians not of bodies but of souls.

Penance is not to be measured by the length of time, but by fervor of mind and mortification of the body. “A contrite and humbled heart God does not despise.”

59. Concerning monks and nuns. No one shall dare to accuse a monk or nun before a secular court, but rather before the bishop; and he himself shall issue a judgment consonant with the law or the canons. Let all bishops, and all Roman prefects, urban praetors, and provincial governors, observe this, so that they may take care to settle the disputes of monks and nuns promptly. If anyone holding public office violates this constitution, he shall be fined ten pounds of gold. [Note: [Col. 0879] G. reads twelve.] If he is an enforcement officer, he shall be confined in the chains of the churches to undergo punishment, and shall lose his office.

[Col. 0879B] 60. That many indulge in luxuries during penance. Many people—and this must be said with sorrow—while doing penance await not so much the remission of sin as the completion of the appointed period. If the use of meat and wine has been forbidden them, they change not their will but merely their consumption of the same food or drink, and indulge their pleasures to such an extent that they are known to live more luxuriously through their desire for other foods and beverages forbidden to them. Spiritual abstinence, however, which ought especially to flourish among penitents, must avoid both the consumption and the desire for certain foods and drinks. That person, I say, is to be considered more devoted to frugality who forbids himself entirely not only the consumption of certain things but also bodily pleasures.

61. Concerning those who sin deliberately. Nor do we think that this should be passed over: certain people who sin deliberately promise themselves a certain impunity on account of their generosity in almsgiving. Almsgiving extinguishes sins, according to the saying: “Water extinguishes a burning fire, and almsgiving extinguishes sins.” But this applies to sins committed either from necessity, by chance, or through any weakness. Those sins, however, which are deliberately committed to satisfy anyone’s lust and for the very purpose of redeeming them through almsgiving can in no way be redeemed by it, because those who do this appear to hire God for a payment, so that they may be permitted to sin with impunity. Therefore no one ought to sin in order to give alms; rather, one ought to give alms because one has sinned. The mind and body that lust has drawn into guilt must be brought back to forgiveness through affliction and contrition.

62. Concerning the monk who abandons his monastery. If a monk abandons his monastery, all his possessions—both those he brought into the monastery and those he did not bring into it—shall belong to the monastery, and he himself shall be compelled to serve in the office of a magistrate. If, however, a monk moves to another monastery, let his substance be possessed by the first monastery, and let him not be received in the other monastery.

[Col. 0879D] 63. That penance must be performed according to the provisions of the canons. The measure of penance imposed on those who confess their sins must be established either by the teaching of the ancient canons, by the authority of the holy Scriptures, or by ecclesiastical custom, as stated above. Booklets that are called “penitentials” are to be rejected and entirely eliminated, since they contain certain errors and have uncertain authors. Of them it can rightly be said: “They were killing souls that were not dying, and reviving souls that were not living.” By imposing certain light and unusual forms of penance on those burdened with serious sins, they sew cushions beneath every elbow, according to the prophetic saying, and make pillows beneath the heads of people of every age, to capture souls.

[Col. 0880A] 64. That certain people give or take churches from priests without the consent of bishops. It has been discovered that many people, through the rashness of their own will and, more seriously, driven by greed, give churches to whatever priests they please or take them away from them without the consent of the bishops. Therefore, while preserving the canonical rule, no one is to give a church to any priest without the bishop’s consent. If someone has acquired it unjustly, he shall lose it before the bishop with canonical severity, and not without his own guilt.

65. Concerning the Scots who claim to be bishops and ordain certain people without their masters’ permission. In certain places there are Scots who claim to be bishops and ordain many negligent priests and deacons without the permission of their masters or superiors. Since their ordination generally falls into the heresy of simony and is subject to many errors, we have unanimously decreed that it must be declared invalid in every respect.

66. Concerning lay monks. If a monk becomes a layman, he shall be stripped of his rank and belt, and his possessions shall be added to those of the monastery. If he abandons the monastic life, the governor of the province shall take charge of him and enroll him among the tax collectors or among those of his court.

[Col. 0880B] 67. Concerning those who neglect the Eucharist on the Lord’s Supper. On the Lord’s Supper some people neglect to receive the Eucharist. Ecclesiastical practice shows that it must be received on that same day by all the faithful except those to whom it has been forbidden on account of serious crimes, since penitents too are reconciled on that day in order to receive the sacraments of the Lord’s body and blood. [Note: [Col. 0879] *reconciliat*; Baluze reads *reconciliat* as well.]

68. That the sick and infirm are to be anointed with blessed oil. According to the teaching of the blessed apostle James, with which the decrees of the Fathers also agree, the sick are to be anointed by priests with oil blessed by bishops. For he says: “Is anyone among you sick? Let him summon the priests of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord; and the prayer of faith will save the sick person, and the Lord will raise him up; and if he is in sins, they will be forgiven him.” Such medicine, which heals the illnesses of soul and body, must not therefore be held in little regard.

69. Concerning a betrothed man or woman who enters a monastery. If a betrothed man or woman enters a monastery, whatever has been given as a pledge shall be returned only in the original amount.

70. Concerning the places in which Masses are to be celebrated. In what places and with what equipment the solemnities of Mass are to be celebrated outside basilicas, and whether they ought to be celebrated at all, the Council of Laodicea states as follows: “It is not proper for bishops or priests to celebrate offerings in houses.” [Note: [Col. 0879] G. deleted “and whether they ought to be celebrated.”]

71. Concerning things that pertain to the delight of the ears and eyes, which priests ought to avoid. Whatever pertains to the allurements of the ears and eyes, whereby the strength of the mind may be thought capable of being softened—as may be perceived concerning certain kinds of music and several other matters—all the priests of God ought to avoid, because through the allurements of the ears and eyes a multitude of vices usually enters the mind. They must also flee from the disgraceful insolence of actors and obscene, shameless jokes, and proclaim to the other priests that these too must be avoided.

72. Concerning the building of a church. No one shall build a church before the bishop of the city comes and publicly fixes a cross there. Beforehand, the person who wishes to build must specify what will suffice for the lights, the upkeep, and the stipends of the custodians. After making the donation, he may build the house in this manner.

73. That priests must beware of secular entertainments. It is not fitting for priests to attend secular entertainments or any shameful jokes. They must also by no means pursue the hunting of wild animals or birds.

[Col. 0881A] 74. Concerning priests and deacons, that they should follow the example of their bishops in good works. Priests and deacons should follow the example of their bishop in every display of good works, and should recognize that the same integrity of good conduct that must be observed by the bishop must also be observed by themselves.

75. Concerning the person who has built an oratory in his house. Whoever has an oratory in his house may pray there; nevertheless, he must not dare to celebrate sacred Masses there without the permission of the bishop of that place. If he does so, his house shall be assigned to the rights of the fisc. The prefect of the praetorium who learned of this and did not prohibit it shall be fined one pound of gold. [Note: [Col. 0881] G. reads *librarum*; corrected to *libra* in G.; Baluze reads “by payment of a pound of gold.”]

76. How much care bishops ought to have concerning the needy. Bishops must show the greatest care and concern for the poor, and must distribute ecclesiastical property entrusted to the churches with prudent circumspection, as ministers of God and not as followers of shameful profit. Let them use these things not as their own, but as goods entrusted to them for distribution.

[Col. 0881B] 77. Concerning the bishop’s expenditure for the poor and the church’s household. Bishops may, in the presence of priests and deacons, distribute from the church’s treasury to the household and the poor of that same church according to canonical instruction and in proportion to their needs.

78. Concerning deaconesses. If a deaconess marries, she shall be struck down by the sword of the avenger, and her property shall be assigned to the church where she served. Those who corrupt them shall likewise be punished; their goods, however, shall be claimed for the rights of the fisc. [Note: [Col. 0881] G. reads: “If deaconesses marry, let them be struck down … let their … be …”; corrected by a later hand.]

79. Concerning not ordaining a priest before the lawful time. A priest must not be ordained before the lawful time, that is, before his thirtieth year. Before approaching the consecration to the priesthood, he must remain in the bishop’s residence for the purpose of learning his office, for as long as his character and conduct can be observed. Then, if he is worthy, he shall be promoted to the priesthood.

80. Concerning how bishops should diligently examine their parishes. Each bishop must strive diligently to examine his parish; and no priest moving from another priest’s parish into his own shall presume to celebrate the office without letters of recommendation, as has been found to have been done in many places in former times.

81. Concerning a religious woman who has been deceived. If anyone abducts, solicits, or corrupts a religious woman, the church in which such a woman lived shall claim the property of both; they themselves, however, shall be subjected to capital punishment. If the woman did not consent, she shall be entrusted, together with her possessions, to the protection of the monastery. If she has children, their lawful share shall be reserved for them. If within a year after such a crime has become known it is not avenged by the religious laymen, the count of private affairs [Note: [Col. 0881] G. reads “of first affairs.”] shall assign it to our fisc. If the governor of the province neglects to impose punishment for such a crime, he shall lose his belt of office and shall be compelled to pay five pounds of gold to the fisc.

82. [Note: [Col. 0881] In Baluze this chapter is placed later. It should be read as Tours 14.16.] That no priest should pass from a lesser title to a greater one. No priest may move from a lesser title to a greater one, but must remain in the title to which he was ordained. If anyone is found to have done this contrary to the statutes, he shall receive the same sentence as a bishop who has moved from a lesser to a greater see.

83. That tithes should always be distributed with the bishops’ approval. The tithes given to each church are to be distributed by the priests, with the bishops’ approval, for the use of the church and the poor, with the greatest diligence.

84. Concerning blasphemy against God. If anyone in any way utters blasphemy against God, he shall be subjected by the prefect of the city to the ultimate penalty. Whoever, knowing of such a person, does not reveal him shall likewise be punished. If the prefect of the city neglects to punish these offenses, after God’s judgment he shall incur our indignation. [Note: [Col. 0881] G. reads *Deo* (“to God”).]

85. Concerning young widows, that they should not be veiled quickly. Young widows are by no means to be veiled quickly, until their religious commitment has been tested and their good conduct is known, lest the apostle’s saying perhaps be applied to them: “Those who live in luxury are dead even while they live.”

86. That counts and judges should agree with their bishops and receive them honorably. It is beneficial for counts, judges, and the rest of the people to be agreeing and obedient to their bishops, for the love of God and the honor of their rank. They should always seek useful counsel from them and not despise their salutary admonitions, but listen to them with the attentive ear of the heart. Likewise, bishops should receive the aforementioned persons humbly and treat them honorably in every respect, and should strive to support one another through mutual consolations.

87. Concerning an heir who does not fulfill something by disposition. [Col. 0882B] If heirs do not fulfill the instructions of a testator, the bishop of that place shall take away from them all the property left to them, together with its produce and other profits, so that the wishes of the deceased may be fulfilled.

88. That counts and judges should not admit base persons as witnesses. Counts and judges must be admonished most earnestly not to permit base and unworthy persons to appear as witnesses before them, since many consider perjury a trivial matter, to such an extent that they can be hired to swear an oath for the satisfaction of a single day or for any small payment, and do not fear destroying their souls through perjury. For this reason such persons must never be admitted to any testimony. It must also be noted that not only those who swear falsely, but also those who consent to perjurers, must be punished with a similar condemnation. [Note: [Col. 0881] G. reads *formidant*; the text has *formident*.]

89. That no Christian should demand gifts for any legal proceeding. No Christian ought to demand or accept gifts from anyone for any legal proceeding or judgment, since divine Scripture expressly forbids this in many places, as Scripture testifies when it says: “Gifts blind the eyes of the wise and overturn the words of the righteous.”

90. Concerning property that is not permitted to pagans. Christians may not hold the property of Jews, pagans, or heretics under a title of emphyteusis or lease, nor may they similarly lend their own property to such persons.

91. Concerning secular legal proceedings, that they should not take place in a church. Secular legal proceedings, which until now have been held in many places by counts and vicars in churches or in the courtyards of churches, must henceforth be prohibited, by the authority of the Lord who, after driving the merchants from the temple, declared that the house of God must be a house of prayer. [Note: [Col. 0881] Baluze reads *adserit* for *asseruit*.]

92. Concerning incestuous persons, parricides, and murderers. Incestuous persons, parricides, and murderers are found among us in great numbers—alas, with grievous sorrow. But some of them refuse to heed the admonitions of priests, wishing to persist in their former crimes. Those who will not be recalled from such wicked behavior by the life-giving admonitions of priests ought to be restrained by the discipline of secular power. We have already excommunicated some of them, but, disregarding this, they have persisted in the same crimes. Therefore let your gentleness determine what should henceforth be done with such people.

93. Concerning magical arts and incantations. Priests must admonish the faithful people to understand that magical arts and incantations can provide no remedy for any human illness, nor can they heal sick, lame, or even dying animals. Nor are cords or bindings made of bones or herbs beneficial when applied to anyone; rather, these are snares and ambushes of the ancient enemy, by which that treacherous one strives to deceive the human race. [Note: [Col. 0883] G. reads *iudicandas*.] [Note: [Col. 0883] G. corrects *meredii* to *remedii* and gives an alternative marginal reading: “that they can provide no remedy for any human illness, nor for sick or dying animals.”]

94. That the name of God should not be taken in vain by swearing. We admonish all people not to take the Lord’s name in vain in every sentence, as though to confirm their assertion. The Lord himself forbids this when he says: “You shall not take the name of your God in vain.” The name of God is taken in vain when someone, in every statement by which he wishes another person to believe him, invokes almighty God as a witness to the matter about which he speaks and asks God to be his helper in the same way that the things he says are true. [Note: [Col. 0883] The passage is absent in Baluze; G. added it in the margin.] The Lord himself, forbidding every kind of oath in this manner in the Gospel, says: “Do not swear at all, neither by heaven nor by earth nor by your head,” and so forth.
