[Col. 0883B] 95. Concerning laymen, that they should not demand gifts from priests. Laymen must not dare to demand gifts from priests for the advancement of the church, because, on account of greed, churches are often given by laymen to such priests as are unworthy to perform the priestly office.

96. Concerning peace and concord. Concerning the good of peace and concord: it must be preserved unbroken by everyone, between bishops and counts, between clerics and monks, and among the entire Christian people, as the blessed apostle Paul taught when he said: “Pursue charity and holiness, without which no one will see God.” Therefore, whatever summons us to pursue true peace and perfect charity must be followed with all our strength; but whatever separates us from them must be avoided by us like deadly poison.

97. Concerning counts and judges, that they should be obedient to their bishop. Counts, judges, and the rest of the people must be obedient to the bishop and agree with one another in administering justice. They must not accept gifts for a judgment or produce false witnesses, lest through this they pervert the judgments of the righteous, because it is written: “Justice exalts a nation, but injustice makes peoples wretched.” And the psalmist says: “Blessed are those who keep judgment and do justice at all times.” [Note: [Col. 0883] G. has the phrase in the margin; Baluze omits it.]

98. That bishops should visit their parishes once a year. Each bishop must visit his parish once a year. They should know that responsibility for the people and the poor has been imposed upon them, for their protection and defense. Therefore, when they see judges and powerful persons acting as oppressors of the poor, they must first rebuke them through priestly admonition. If they refuse to amend their conduct, their insolence must be reported to the ears of the king, so that those whom priestly admonition does not move to justice may be restrained from wickedness by royal power. [Note: [Col. 0883] Baluze correctly conjectured *pupillorum*—“orphans”—for *populorum*.]

99. Concerning priests keeping chrism under seal. Priests must keep the chrism under seal and must not presume to give it to anyone under the pretext of medicine or for any other purpose. For it is a kind of sacrament and may be touched only by priests. If they do so, they shall be deprived of their rank.

100. Concerning those who hold a benefice from church property. Whoever holds a benefice from church property must give full assistance toward restoring the roofs of that church or building the churches themselves.

101. Concerning the person who becomes infamous through theft. Anyone condemned for any kind of theft becomes infamous.

102. Concerning not condemning a person who is absent. We order that no one be condemned in a capital case while absent, because an absent person can neither accuse nor be accused through another.

[Col. 0884A] 103. Concerning all possessions being returned by the preceptor to the possessor. The preceptor shall restore to the possessor all possessions, everything taken from him, and all the produce obtained before the case was formally joined. [Note: [Col. 0883] The wording is printed thus by Baluze and G.; in this manuscript an *r* is written above the *c*.]

104. Concerning incestuous persons, that they are not legitimate heirs. We wish everyone to know that incestuous persons are not legitimate heirs, but that both persons are marked with infamy. Therefore intercourse with relatives or sexual violation of them must be avoided as a particularly shameful plague, because incestuous persons, until canonical separation and ecclesiastical satisfaction through public penance, are to be regarded with all their belongings more among those afflicted by an unclean spirit or among hearers than among Catholic Christians.

105. That a litigant may remedy a defective case through the remedy of appeal. Judges must observe that a litigant may remedy a defective case through the remedy of appeal. They must neither throw appellants into prison nor have them guarded by soldiers; rather, they must allow them to attend freely to their business. Nor may the right of appeal be denied even to those destined for punishment.

[Col. 0884B] 106. Concerning the prayer of an obedient person. Everyone must know that the prayer of one obedient person is heard more quickly than that of ten thousand contemptuous persons.

107. That each province should be judged by its own judges. We decree that no province be degraded, but that each have its own bishop-judges within itself. Whoever has a case must be judged by his own judges and not by those of another place—that is, by the proper judges of his own province and not by outsiders, unless an appeal has been made.

108. That everyone ought to live justly and piously. We wish everyone to know how justly, soberly, and piously they ought to live. One ought to live justly according to the Lord’s command, which says: “Let your light shine before human beings, so that they may see your good works and glorify your Father who is in heaven.” This means: Live so justly that you may be worthy to be called children of light. [Note: [Col. 0883] G. has *quid*; in the margin, “or *in quo*.”] The Gospel also teaches how each person ought to live soberly, saying: “See that your hearts are not weighed down by gluttony, drunkenness, and the cares of this life.” Paul likewise teaches that one should live piously and patiently, exhorting us: “With all patience and teaching.” He also teaches that one should govern one’s household with piety; and, lest this piety appear undiscerning, he first gives the instruction: “Reprove with all authority.”

109. Concerning the presenter of a written document, that he should affirm it. It has been decreed that the presenter affirm the written document. For if the person who presented the document had not established its truth, he must be held liable for falsification.

110. That a priest ought to persevere in the religious habit. Everyone must earnestly strive for each priest to remain in the religious habit and to consider himself instructed by the prophetic word, which says: “Cry out; do not cease; raise your voice like a trumpet.” When it says, “Cry out; do not cease,” it excludes every limitation of time, which no one can evade as an excuse. For, as we know, the meaning is clear from the books of the offices: these things were by no means to be sought through bodily practice from those who lived spiritually, as the psalmist says: “My vows to you, O God, are upon me; I will render praises to you.” [Note: [Col. 0883] Baluze reads *graphopsalmo*—“the psalm-writing author”—instead of *psalmigrapho*.]

We, however, who are placed in the midst—that is, between spiritual and bodily understanding—must in everything present ourselves as ministers of God, so that our ministry may not be blamed, and fulfill the prophetic word: “Learn justice, you who inhabit the earth.” And, God forbid it of us, the same prophet says: “Zeal has seized an uninstructed people.” Again another prophet says: “The priests did not understand.” The same prophet also says: “The priests did not say, ‘Where is the Lord?’ and those who held my laws did not know me.” With what face, then, and with what conscience does a person claim to be called a priest whom the Lord, through the prophet, declares that he does not know?

[Col. 0885A] 111. Concerning the person who has a case, that he should be judged by his own judges. Whoever has a case must be judged by his own judges and must not leave his homeland and go to strangers out of a desire to roam about or through arrogance; rather, he must be judged before the metropolitan and the other bishops of his province.

112. Concerning canonical clerics who live in cities or monasteries. We wish and command, as we have been very frequently admonished by the pastors of the holy Church through synodal and canonical authority, that canonical clerics who live in cities or monasteries and have benefices from which they can obtain food and clothing should be content with these, according to the apostle. They must not take or convert to their own uses the stipends of their brothers, from which the poorer brothers and those who, serving the Lord continually in the places mentioned above, keep watch there and perform the divine office without interruption, are maintained. For we know that they cannot do this without danger and loss to their souls. If anyone disregards these statutes, he shall lose both things—that is, both the benefice and the prebend; and if he enjoys ecclesiastical orders, he shall be deprived of them. [Note: [Col. 0885] The word *hoc* is supplied by Baluze.]

113. Concerning the Church’s sharing with those who have nothing. Whatever the Church possesses, it possesses in common with all who have nothing. It is not proper to distribute any of it to those who are self-sufficient from their own resources, since to give anything to those who have means is nothing other than to waste it.

114. Concerning those who possess their own property and nevertheless wish something to be given to them. Nor may those who possess their own property and nevertheless wish something to be given to them take, without great sin, what a poor person would have lived on.

115. Concerning condemned marriages. If a man marries a widow and afterward commits fornication with her stepdaughter, or marries two sisters, or if a woman marries two brothers, or a father and son, we command that such unions be anathematized and that the parties never again be joined in marriage, but that this be carried out under severe discipline. [Note: [Col. 0885] Baluze lacks the final phrase.] [Note: [Col. 0885] G. reads “with the daughter of her mother’s daughter” in place of “with her stepdaughter.”]

[Col. 0885C] 116. That one should not receive one’s own child from the baptismal font. Therefore no one shall receive his own son or daughter from the baptismal font; nor shall anyone marry his goddaughter or godmother, or the woman whose son or daughter he has held at confirmation. Whenever this has occurred, the parties shall be separated.

117. Concerning women introduced into the household. It is therefore to be firmly prohibited to all clerics to have a woman living with them in their houses beyond what the canons permit.

118. Again concerning the peace of the churches. We command that secular legal proceedings by no means take place in churches, in the houses of churches, or in their courtyards.

119. Concerning fugitive clerics. [Note: [Col. 0885] Baluze lacks the opening.] Each bishop must diligently inquire in his parish where priests or clerics are from. If he finds a fugitive, he must make him return to his own bishop.

120. What litanies are. Litanies are called by a Greek name; in Latin they are called *rogationes*, “supplications.” The difference between litanies and *exhomologesis*—Greek *ἐξομολόγησις*, “confession”—is that *exhomologesis* is performed solely for the confession of sins, whereas litanies are designated as such because they are performed to ask God and obtain his mercy in some matter. But now both terms are used under a single designation. [Note: [Col. 0885] G. reads *exhomolegisin*.]

[Col. 0885D] 121. Concerning clerics tonsured unjustly. We decree concerning clerics that those who have hitherto been found tonsured against their will, whether in the canonical or monastic order, shall remain as they are if they are free. Henceforth care must be taken that no one be tonsured except at a lawful age and by his own free will, or with the permission of his master.

122. Concerning what it means to leave the world. To leave the world means, as Gregory said, to oppose the pleasures of the world. Hence Paul admonishes us, saying: “Those who buy, as though they did not possess; and those who use this world, as though they did not use it.” And Gregory, in the *Book of Pastoral Care*, says: “Let the things supplied to you outwardly serve you in such a way that they do not turn your mind away from the pursuit of heavenly love.”

123. That the person who unites himself to a blood relative as far as the line of affinity commits incest. No member of the faithful may marry a blood relative as far as the line of affinity—that is, through the seventh generation—or pollute her in any way with the stain of incest. If anyone knowingly presumes to violate this, then, if he is free, he shall pay our ban, that is, sixty solidi, to our fisc; in addition, he shall suffer the canonical penalty for incest and perform public penance according to the canonical degrees.

If he is a slave or an ecclesiastical dependent, he shall be publicly scourged and tonsured, and, according to the command of his own bishop, shall perform penance publicly and canonically. If anyone, whether free, slave, ecclesiastical dependent, or fiscalinus, is disobedient or obstinate toward his own bishop, his priest, or archdeacon, whether concerning this or any other crime, all his property shall be seized by the count and the bishop’s envoy until he obeys his bishop and performs canonical penance. [Note: [Col. 0885] Baluze reads “the royal envoy.”]

If he does not correct himself in this way and delays coming to the bishop and to canonical penance, he shall be arrested by the count and kept confined in prison under severe hardship; nor shall he have control over his property until the bishop orders it. If the count or his officer delays carrying this out, he shall be excommunicated canonically by his bishop or by the bishop’s officer; and until he fully fulfills these requirements, he shall always be deprived of communion with Catholics, unless the bishop himself should decide to act more mercifully toward him.

If, however—and may this not happen—the count himself proves disobedient or negligent, whether concerning the matters mentioned above or concerning the excommunication itself, he shall lose both the honor of the countship and communion until both parties come into our presence, so that we may correct him through episcopal authority and imperial fear in such a way that the others may be afraid and never again dare to commit such acts.

124. That incestuous persons, so long as they remain in their crime, should occupy not the place of faithful Christians but only that of pagans, catechumens, or the possessed. While incestuous persons remain in that detestable and abominable crime, they are to be regarded not among the faithful Christians but among pagans, catechumens, or the possessed—that is, they are not to take food or drink with Christians, nor eat or drink from the same vessel, but are to do these things alone; they are not to be kissed or greeted by them. But if they prove disobedient to their priests and are unwilling to separate themselves from so utterly abominable a crime and return to public penance, they are to be counted among those who are endangered by an unclean spirit, or even among those of whom Truth itself says: “If he does not listen to you, let him be to you as a heathen and a tax collector.” [Col. 0886D] For they must neither pray with the faithful nor enter the church; rather, they must keep watch before the church door and, with their face prostrate on the ground, ask pardon from those entering and leaving it, and beg them not to disdain to pray for them. They must always appear before everyone drenched in tears, with contrite face and humbled spirit, until they have obtained the church’s satisfaction and the canonical reconciliation of their own bishop, and they must never return to their former incest, conduct secular business, or take part in legal hearings, accusations, or testimony. Rather, by the frequent prayers of priests, the laying-on of the hands of their own bishop, the distribution of alms, and the performance of other good works, they ought to be cleansed and healed.

## FOURTH ADDITION

We have taken care to collect the following chapters from the decrees of the holy fathers and the edicts of emperors, and have ordered them, by general counsel, to be inserted among our chapters for observance under the firmest force of law by Erchembald, our chancellor. Some chapters found in other books are missing here; we omitted them because they are already inserted above, at the end of the third book.

[Col. 0887]

### 1. From the Institution of Sacred Laws, book 12, chapter 10

Let the one who calls himself a defender of the truth hear how far he is a stranger to the rule of the Christian faith when he stains truth itself by accepting gifts. Against him the prophet says: “Because you sold the righteous for silver and the poor man for a pair of sandals, behold, I will creak over you as a wagon creaks when loaded with hay; and flight shall perish from the swift, and the strong shall not retain his strength, and the mighty shall not save his life, and the stouthearted among the strong shall flee naked.”

### 2. From the same book, title three, chapter 15

[Note: G reads *titulo lationis* (“title of presentation”); the chapter heading is absent in the Visigothic Law, the source of this chapter.]

We permit no Christian or Jew, of either sex, to marry within the degree of blood relationship to himself or herself, or to his or her spouse, and likewise within the relationship of the males, according to the law enacted among Christians, as far as the seventh degree [L. Wisig.: sixth degree], or to incur the stain of incest. This temptation to such intermixture shall therefore be punished by the following penalty: after being separated from one another, they shall, after being publicly shorn, each receive a hundred lashes and, bound in exile, remain under public penance; their property shall pass to the sons whom they had from a previous marriage, provided that those sons themselves have not been stained either by any Jewish transgression or by the stain of incestuous birth.

But if they have no sons, or if the sons they have, as stated, are involved in Jewish error or stained by incestuous birth, then the entire property of the persons mentioned shall remain in the power of the ruler, so that, by princely discretion, it may either remain granted to Christians or to their heirs. If heirs of this status are lacking, it shall be joined to our treasury and serve it.

Nevertheless, we order that the following be observed in every respect: if any Christian man or woman, or Jew or Jewess, wishes newly to celebrate a wedding feast, we permit none of these persons to enter marriage except after the title of the dowry has first been established, as salutary institution has prescribed among Christians, or after receiving the priest’s blessing within the bosom of the holy Church of God.

But if any Christian or Hebrew contracts a new marriage [the words “or Hebrew” are absent in the Visigothic Law] without the priest’s blessing, or transgresses anywhere the solemnity of the law concerning the dowry, he shall either be compelled to pay a hundred solidi to the ruler [Bal. and the Visigothic Law read “a hundred”; G reads “sixty”], or, publicly beaten, receive a hundred lashes [the Visigothic Law and Bal. read “a hundred”; G omits this]. Each person shall suffer these penalties or blows individually: namely, both the man who married and the woman who married, and likewise their consenting parents; each shall personally bear the loss imposed by the law [Bal. and the Visigothic Law: “of this law”].

### 3. In book 7 of the Tripartite History, chapter 12

Thus, since Valentinian held the same views as the Nicene fathers [G: “the Nicaean fathers”], he was helpful to those who professed similar opinions, but was not troublesome to those who thought otherwise. When, at the beginning of his reign, he was travelling from Constantinople through Thrace [G: “Tragias”] toward Rome, the bishops who held the correct faith sent the bishop Hicpaucianus as an embassy, so that he might deign to take part in correcting the doctrine.

When he approached the emperor and announced the bishops’ embassy, the emperor replied: “Since I am merely one of the people [Col. 0887: the Colbertinus manuscript reads ‘the least’], it is not lawful for me to investigate such matters. Rather, let the priests, whose responsibility this is, assemble among themselves wherever they wish.”

When the ruler had answered thus, the bishops assembled at Lampsacus. After they had deliberated for two months, among other things, in accordance with the earlier canons, they decreed that bishops who had been expelled and stripped of their possessions should be restored to their own sees [G adds in the margin; Bal. omits this] and that all their property should first be returned to them [Bal.: “to receive”]. If anyone thereafter wished to accuse them, they decreed that he should do so at his peril, determining that the bishops who held the correct faith, assembled in the church, should be judges, with the witnesses to each of the matters alleged present there. And so forth.

### 4. From Pope Leo’s letter [G: “examples”] addressed to the Council of Chalcedon

We have heard that very many brothers have been driven from their sees and deported into exile, while others have been substituted in the place of those who survived. Let the medicine of justice first be applied to these wounds, so that no one may be deprived of his own while another makes use of what belongs to someone else. Let all priests therefore abandon this error in such a way that no one’s honor should perish; rather, for those who labored for the faith, their rightful position ought first to be restored with all its privileges. And so forth.

### 5. From a letter of Pope Stephen written generally to all bishops

Whatever is unjustly done concerning things consecrated to God and concerning bishops shall be counted sacrilege, because they are sacred and must not be violated by anyone. No bishop, once he has been stripped of his possessions or expelled from his own see for any reason, ought to be accused, nor may any crime be brought against him by anyone, until he has been completely restored and everything taken from him by whatever means has been restored to him according to the laws, and he himself has been regularly returned to his own see and former status. Thus all possessions, everything unjustly taken from him, and all revenues preceding the beginning of the accusation must be restored in full to the bishop concerned by the primates and the synod [Bal.: “by the primate and the bishops of the synod, in full,” omitting “concerning whom the matter is”]; for not only ecclesiastical but also secular laws teach that this must be done.

[Col. 0888C]

### 6. Augustine to Boniface, concerning the restoration of those who have fallen

When it was established in the Church that no one, after performing penance for a crime, should receive clerical office, return to clerical office, or remain in clerical office, this was done not from despair of forgiveness but through the rigor of discipline. Otherwise one would argue against the keys given to the Church, concerning which it was said: “Whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven.”

But lest perhaps, because of hope of ecclesiastical honor, a mind swollen with pride should perform penance for other crimes, it was most rigorously resolved that after performing penance for a condemnable crime no one should remain a cleric, so that, through despair of temporal elevation, humility might become a greater and truer medicine.

For holy David also performed penance for deadly crimes, yet remained in honor; and blessed Peter, when he shed the bitterest tears, certainly repented of having denied God, yet remained an apostle. But this does not mean that the diligence of those who came later should be thought superfluous, for where nothing was taken away from salvation, they added something to humility, by which salvation might be more securely protected. I believe they had learned this from the feigned repentance of some, motivated by their desire for positions of honor and power. The experience of many diseases compels people to discover many medicines.

### 7. From a letter of Pope Leo addressed to the bishop of Aquileia

We admonish you to restore that part of ecclesiastical discipline which was formerly decreed by the holy fathers and often by us [G: *que*; its second hand corrects *decretum* to *decreta*]: no one is free to pass from the rank of presbyter, or deacon, or any subsequent clerical order to another church. Each person must remain where he was ordained, not enticed by ambition, not led astray by greed, and not corrupted by human persuasion. Thus, if anyone seeks his own interests rather than those of Jesus Christ and neglects to return to his people and his church, he is to be regarded as an outsider both to the privilege of honor and to the bond of communion.

### 8. That no bishop be disparaged or rashly accused, and that his accusation not easily be received by the primates, because injury to bishops concerns Christ, in whose place they serve as legates

From the decrees of Pope Anastasius.

It was resolved that no one should rashly accuse a bishop, nor should he be heard by the primates indiscriminately or without distinction concerning any sort of petition, since the Lord says: “You shall not receive a false report.” Truth itself says: “What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another”; and so forth.

Elsewhere it is written: “What does it profit one who is not defiled by his own error, if he gives his consent to one who errs?” Without doubt, the one who has his own sin and follows another’s [G’s second hand corrected “follows” to “follow”] abandons the commandments [G’s second hand corrected “abandons” to “admits”]; and so forth.

But if anyone has a case against a bishop, he must first approach him charitably and either point out the injury done to himself or correct the bishop, as the Lord says: “If your brother sins against you, go and rebuke him between you and him alone. But if he does not listen to you, take with you two or three others”; and so forth.

Before this has been done, therefore, no one should presume to accuse a bishop publicly, because no one acts against the Gospel, the Apostle, or the decrees of the fathers without danger. The Apostle Paul also commands, saying: “Do not rebuke an elder, but entreat him as a father.” Elsewhere it is written: “If anyone is faithful, let him see that he does not speak falsely or harmfully, or set an ambush for anyone”; and elsewhere: “He is not wise who harms.” The Lord says in the Law: “You shall not slander your neighbor”; and likewise: “You shall not be an accuser or a whisperer among the peoples; you shall not stand against the blood of your neighbor. Keep my laws; I am the Lord.”

If these things were said concerning all human beings, how much more must they be observed concerning bishops, of whom the Savior says: “Whoever has grieved you has grieved me” [G: “has touched”]; “whoever touches you touches the pupil of my eye”; and so forth. Likewise: “Whoever does them an injury shall receive what he has done unjustly.”

And in Daniel it is read: “Let all who show evil to your servants be confounded; let them be confounded in the presence of the Almighty, and let their strength be broken, so that they may know that you alone are the Lord God, glorious over all the earth” [Bal.: “over the whole world”].

According to the ordinance of ancient institution, benevolence ought to do more toward correcting people than severity; exhortation more than agitation; charity more than power. The Lord also admonishes through the prophet, saying: “Restrain your tongue from evil, and let your lips not speak deceit. Turn away from evil and do good.” No one who does good wishes to harm another by word or deed.

If anyone does not observe these things, he is the enemy of his own soul. If they are clerics, let them fall from their own rank; but if they are laymen or monks, they must be expelled still more, or become outcasts.

### 9. That whoever has a complaint against a bishop or the administrators of a church must not first approach their judges before approaching in private those against whom he brings an accusation, so that he may receive from them, charitably, either correction or a reasonable excuse

It was resolved that if any person believes he has a matter against a bishop or the administrators of a church, he should first return to him in a spirit of charity, so that, admonished in a private conversation, he may repair the matters brought forward as complaints. If he wishes to delay doing this, let him receive the sentence of excommunication, and so forth [Bal. omits “and so forth”].

### 10. That a bishop not be accused before a secular judge

No one shall presume to accuse a bishop before secular judges, but only before the highest primates.

### 11. That if anyone thinks himself oppressed, he may present a right of appeal

It was resolved that an accused person who regards the judge as suspect may appeal, since a hearing ought not to be denied to one who requests it [G: *gravare* (“to oppress”) for *gravari* (“to be oppressed”)].

### 12. Concerning the reconsideration of a provincial synod by apostolic legates

A provincial synod is to be reconsidered by the vicars of the bishop of the city of Rome, if he himself so decrees [Bal.: “by apostolic legates”].

### 13. That no criminal accuse a bishop

Concerning those who bring an accusation against a senior, it was resolved that no criminal may accuse a bishop.

### 14. That criminal cases be conducted not through representatives but by the parties themselves

Whenever someone is summoned in a capital case or in a case concerning status, the matter must be conducted not through representatives but by the parties themselves [Bal.: “must be conducted”].

### 15. Concerning appeal from the higher judges

It was resolved that whenever an appeal is made from any ecclesiastical judges to other ecclesiastical judges of greater authority, a hearing must not be denied.

### 16. That no metropolitan presume to act without the presence or counsel of all the other bishops of his province, except in matters belonging to his own parish

The other bishops likewise shall act with regard to him.

From the fifth Roman synod.

If any metropolitan bishop attempts to act outside what belongs solely to his own parish without the counsel and consent of all the bishops of his province, he shall be subject to the danger of losing his rank, and what he has done shall be considered invalid and void.

But whatever it is necessary to do or arrange concerning the cases of fellow bishops of the province and the needs of their churches, clerics, and laypeople must be undertaken with the consent of all the bishops of the province—not with any arrogance of domination, but with the most humble and harmonious administration, as the Lord says: “I did not come to be served, but to serve.” Elsewhere: “The one who is greatest among you shall be your servant” [Bal. omits this]; and so forth.

The bishops of the province themselves likewise shall act with his counsel, except in matters belonging to their own parishes, according to the constitutions of the holy fathers, so that the holy Trinity may be glorified harmoniously forever, with one mind and one voice.

### 17. How a bishop is to be summoned to a synod and how the case is to be handled there

The holy Roman synod said:

These are the provisions that, because of the plots of evil men who indiscriminately rage against the Church and ecclesiastical men, we wish to be preserved most firmly forever.

If a bishop is accused by accusers who are admissible, then, after those accusers have first approached him charitably so that he might correct and amend the matter itself, and he has refused to correct it, his case is to be canonically referred—not earlier, but then—to the highest primates. They must canonically convene a council in a suitable place within that province, at the time fixed by the canons of Nicaea, so that he may be heard there by all the bishops of the same province. He himself, having been canonically summoned, must attend, unless illness or some other serious necessity prevents him; for no one may be accused beyond the boundaries of the province before a hearing has been requested.

[Col. 0891A] If, God forbid, he has been stripped of his possessions, or—something that ought to be foreign to all the faithful—expelled from his own see, or separated from his own sheep by some detention, then he may neither be summoned nor judged canonically until he has been restored to his former honor and all that was taken from him through the plots of his enemies has been restored. He may come voluntarily if his necessity requires it, but not for the purpose of being judged.

He must not be required to answer anyone at all before everything he lost through the suggestions of his enemies has been completely restored to his control by an honorable council, and the prelate has been returned to his former status [Bal. omits “as before”]. Once he has freely and securely arranged and ordered his affairs, he is then to be canonically summoned and come at the proper time to the synod, in a legitimate and canonical manner, to answer the case.

If it seems just, he may respond to the charges of the accusers. For it must be provided above all that he not be compelled to answer before all these things have occurred, since contention must always be avoided. No Christian can rightly think that a bishop’s episcopate may be taken away before the outcome of his case is known.

If the bishop is ill or some serious necessity prevents him, let him send a representative to the synod. The person against whom the charge is directed must not be suspended from communion unless, having been summoned by letter on the appointed day by the chosen judges to state his case, he entirely fails to appear—that is, unless some other necessity intervenes for a period of two or three months, or longer, as the case may require.

If both parties come to state their case—for one must not be heard without the other—the court must investigate the character, faith, and reputation of the accusers, and the intention with which they act. They must not be admitted to this process unless they are men of good conduct and right faith, free from every suspicion, distinguished by good lives, and not infamous.

If the persons of the accusers appear blameworthy in the judgment of the bishops, they must not be admitted to bring charges [unless they have raised their own cases, but not criminal or ecclesiastical cases]. An infamous person can be neither a representative nor a legal advocate.

When the opposing party is absent, the accuser must not be heard; nor shall a sentence pronounced by a judge in the absence of the other party possess any validity. An absent person may neither accuse nor be accused through another, and a related witness may not be admitted.

No one should therefore be brought from one province to another or to the county court except at the report of the judge to whom an appeal has been made—that is, the plaintiff must always follow the defendant’s forum.

If anyone finds that the judge is hostile to him, let him present a right of appeal, which ought to be denied to no one. And so forth.

### 18. That the accusation of clerics take place within the province, unless the accused has appealed to a higher authority

If any cleric is charged with any crimes, his accuser must bring his action in the province where the person charged resides, and must not suppose that he can drag him elsewhere or farther away to judgment. The person who has been charged [Bal.: “to whom the charge has been brought”], if he regards the judge as suspect, may appeal.

### 19. That foreign judgments not be held

We prohibit foreign judgments by general sanction [Bal.: “we forbid them”], because it is unworthy that one who ought to have provincial judges chosen by himself should be judged by outsiders.

### 20. That no metropolitan [G: *metropolitanorum*, “of metropolitans”] hear the cases of any of his bishops, clerics, or churches without the presence of all the bishops of his province

From the third Roman synod.

No metropolitan bishop may hear the cases of any bishops without the attendance of all the other bishops of his province [G: “their cases”], for the judgments will be invalid. Indeed, he may not [G corrects *et* (“and”) to *nec* (“nor”)] hear the cases of his own priests without the presence of his own clerics, because the bishop’s sentence will be invalid unless confirmed by the presence of the clerics.

### 21. Concerning the investigation of the accuser’s person

From Pope Sixtus’s decree, chapter 8.

It was resolved that in the accusation of clerics the person, faith, conduct, and life of the slanderers must always be investigated first [G: *persona*, corrected to *personae*]. For faith ought to precede all a person’s actions, because one who is uncertain in faith is an unbeliever. No trust at all is to be placed in those who do not know the faith of truth and do not lead a life of upright conduct, because such people easily and indiscriminately tear apart [I. and Bal.: *quousque*, “until”] and accuse those who live rightly and piously. Their suspicion must therefore first be examined and corrected [G: the reading “suspicion” was originally written with an additional word, later corrected].

### 22. Concerning persons and accusations that are not to be received

From the sixth Roman synod, chapter 11, with which the Nicene synod [G: *sinodo*], the decrees of Popes Julius and Symmachus, and other synodal decisions agree.

We also reject accusers and accusations that the laws of the world do not admit.

[Col. 0892B]

### 23. That no bishop presume to retain, ordain, or judge another bishop’s parishioner

From the tenth Roman synod, chapter 7, with which the Council of Antioch also agrees in chapter 22 [Bal. omits the references].

No bishop may presume to retain or ordain another bishop’s parishioner without his consent, or to judge him; for just as his ordination will be invalid, so also will his judgment, since we hold that no one is bound by the sentence of any judge except his own. For the one who could not ordain him will in no way be able to judge him.

### 24. Concerning the primacy of the apostolic see, to which final judgments concerning bishops and the privilege of convening synods are reserved; and concerning the canonical summons of a bishop

From the Roman synods, chapter 49, and from the decrees of Pope Julius.

No bishop may be charged—that is, judged, heard, or prosecuted—for any crimes unless he has been canonically summoned and called to a legitimate synod at the proper time by apostolic authority. By the Lord’s command and through the merits of the blessed apostle Peter, singular authority to convene councils has been entrusted to this see, together with a power repeatedly confirmed by the decrees of the holy and venerable fathers and the canons.

If anyone presumes to act otherwise, what they have done shall be brought to nothing; it shall in no way be reckoned among ecclesiastical acts, and whatever has been undertaken against him shall have no force. For this same see, as the voice of Truth testifies, obtained the first primacy. It would not be first if it had another see above it. It is also the head of all the churches, from which they all took their origin.

It did not earn its primacy through synodal decisions or any contrived institutions, but through the gift of the Lord, who said: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my church”; and other such passages and similar ones.

If anyone opposes these commands in a proud spirit, he must not go unpunished but shall be subject to the danger of losing his rank.

### 25. That if anyone regards his metropolitan as suspect, he be heard before the primate

From the Council of Chalcedon, chapter 17.

If anyone thinks himself oppressed by his own metropolitan, let him conduct his case before the primate of the diocese or before the see of the city of Constantinople. And so forth.

### 26. Concerning the order of accusation, and that no one be easily accused

From the sixth Roman synod, chapter 9, with which other enactments of emperors and synodal bishops also agree.

We order that the order of accusation established long ago by canonical decrees be observed. If any cleric is charged in a civil or criminal case, or summoned in a capital crime, he must not immediately be considered guilty merely because he could be accused, lest we make innocence subject to accusation.

But whoever brings the charge must come into court, state the name of the accused, take up the bond of written accusation, and preserve the proper form. He must nevertheless be required to endure with due regard for his rank. Let him know that he has no license to lie, since the similarity of the punishment demands that false accusers be punished.

### 27. That an accused bishop [G omits “accused bishop”] may appeal to the apostolic see, if he wishes

From the synodal edicts decreed under the emperor Theodosius and confirmed by his authority. If anyone seeks these, he will find them in the books of his letters.

It was resolved that if an accused bishop appeals to the Roman pontiff, whatever the pontiff himself determines shall be established.

### 28. Concerning an accused or judged bishop who thinks he has a good case [G: *potuerit* (“may be able”), corrected from *patuerit* (“will be apparent”)] and wishes to be heard by the Roman pontiff

No one may prevent him; this must be granted to him freely and without any impediment.

From the foregoing sources [G: “above”; Bal. reads “with these”], with which the Council of Sardica and other decrees of the canons and holy fathers also agree.

An accused or judged bishop in any case may renew the judgment and, if necessary or if he himself wishes, approach the Roman pontiff without any detention or impediment. While the pontiff is hearing his case in a renewed judgment, he must not be deprived of his see or dignity, since the holy fathers long ago established that no one may usurp the see of an accused bishop.

Elsewhere: “No Christian can rightly think that a bishop’s episcopate may be taken away before the outcome of his case is known.” And so forth.

### 29. That while an accused or judged bishop has appealed to the Roman pontiff, no injury be done to him, nor anyone seize his see or be ordained in his place before the Roman pope has ended his case by judgment

From the foregoing, with which many decrees of the holy fathers and the canons agree [G: “the canonical decrees”].

It was resolved that a bishop accused or judged by the bishops of his province may freely appeal to and approach the pontiff of the apostolic see. The pontiff shall arrange for his case to be reconsidered either personally or through his vicars.

While the pontiff is hearing his case in the renewed judgment, no one else may be placed or ordained in his position. Although the bishops of the province may investigate the case of an accused bishop, they are not permitted to decide it without consulting the Roman pontiff, since the blessed apostle Peter was told by the Lord himself and no other: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven.”

### 30. Concerning the appeal of bishops to the Roman Church whenever necessity demands it, since the authority of the fathers has reserved to it, by singular privilege, the affairs of bishops and the most important cases

From the foregoing sources, with which all the decrees of the canons and holy fathers, above all, agree.

All bishops who are charged or accused in certain more serious cases may, whenever necessary, freely appeal to the apostolic see and flee to it as to a mother, so that they may be supported, defended, and liberated by it, as has always been the case. The authority of the ancient apostles, their successors, and the canons has reserved to its disposition all major ecclesiastical cases and the judgments of bishops [G omits “all major”].

Bishops are condemned if they act toward their brothers otherwise than the pope of that see wishes. For the canons command that in such matters nothing be decided without the Roman pontiff and that a bishop not be summoned to a synod; whatever is undertaken in these matters without consulting him shall have no force.

### 31. Concerning the case of Bishop Lupicinus

From a letter of Pope Leo addressed to the African bishops.

We order that the case of Bishop Lupicinus be heard there, because this is our wish [Bal. and Leo’s Letter 87 read “there”; G reads “to him”]. We restored communion to him, who had asked for it greatly and repeatedly, for this reason: after he had appealed to our judgment [G: “after being appealed”], we saw that he had been suspended from communion unjustly while the case was pending [G: “we see”].

It has also been established that the man who was rashly placed over him was one who ought not to have been ordained before Lupicinus, present in the matter, had either been refuted or certainly confessed, so that he could properly be subjected to a just sentence. Then the person being consecrated could receive the vacant place, as ecclesiastical discipline requires.

If any other case should arise concerning the condition of the churches and the harmony of the priests [Bal.: “cases should arise”; G: “pertain”], we wish, for fear of the Lord, that it be examined there, and that a full report be sent to us concerning all matters, both those to be settled and those already settled. Thus whatever has been determined justly and reasonably according to ecclesiastical custom may also be confirmed by our judgment.

From these matters we can learn how the others are to be handled, and how we may have no regret that we have done anything contrary to the statutes of our predecessors [Bal. adds: “Written on the fourth day before the Ides of August”; the remainder is mutilated].

### 32. Concerning laymen who presume to dispute about religion

From synodal statutes and the edicts of emperors, from book 16 of the emperor Theodosius, concerning those who contend about religion [G omits “about religion”].

The emperors Valentinian, Theodosius, and Arcadius, Augusti, together with the decree of Tatianus, prefect of the praetorium [Bal.: “the emperors”; G: “Tratiano”]:

No opportunity shall be open to anyone who goes out in public to debate religion, discuss it, or bring forward any proposal [G: “defer”]. If thereafter anyone should believe that he may violate such a law with grave and condemnable boldness, or dare to persist in doing so through the impulse of a pestilential obstinacy [G: *usu*, “use”], he shall be restrained by a suitable penalty and deserved punishment.

Issued on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of July, during the consulship of Theodosius Augustus for the second time and of Quinegius [G: “who was concerned with the matter”].

### 33. From a letter of Pope Leo addressed to Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus

[Bal. adds at the beginning: “No monk, except the priests of the Lord, should presume to preach.”]

We establish, confirming especially the statutes of the fathers mentioned above, the matter that you reported to us verbally concerning the insolence of certain monks: apart from the priests of the Lord chosen by the bishop of that particular place, no one may presume to preach, whether he is a monk or a layman who boasts in the name of any kind of learning [G: “judgment”; G’s “decrees” corrected to “addressed”].

### 34. Concerning informers

From the Council of Elvira.

If any informer is a member of the faithful, and through his informing someone is proscribed or killed, it was resolved that he should not receive communion even at the end of his life [Bal.: “at the end”]. If the case is lighter, he may receive communion within five years. If he is a catechumen, let him be admitted to baptism after the period of five years.

### 35. Clerical accusers of their brothers are to be received to communion, not to the clergy

From the Council of Carthage.

Bishops are to excommunicate those who accuse their brothers. If they correct their fault, they may receive them to communion, but not to the clergy.

### 36. Concerning governors and others who wish to administer public affairs, so that they may not share in communion without letters from their bishop; and that, when they act against discipline, they be excommunicated

From the Council of Arles.

Concerning governors who, as members of the faithful, advance to public office, it was resolved that when they have been promoted they receive ecclesiastical letters, namely letters of communion. This is to be done in such a way that, in whatever places they exercise office, the bishop of that place takes responsibility for them; and when they begin to act against discipline [G: *erint*, “have acted”; Bal.: “public discipline”], only then are they to be excluded from communion.

The same rule applies to those who wish to administer public affairs.

### 37. That clerics or laymen not share in communion in another church without letters from their own bishop

From the Council of Carthage.

Cassius, bishop of Velenensis [G: “Cassianus”], said: “Let your gravity decree that no cleric or layman share in communion in another parish without letters from his own bishop.”

38. Also in the chapter [Note: [Col. 0895] “from the chapters of Bal.”]. If any person among the secular order, whether of higher or lower rank, commits a sin and, when summoned by the authority of his bishop, delays coming for correction and penance, let him remain banished from the Church and separated from the company of Catholics until he corrects what he unlawfully committed, canonically washes away his guilt through satisfaction, and obtains pardon and remission through divine prayers and the reconciliation of his own bishop; after he has made satisfaction, let that bishop canonically restore him, corrected through satisfaction, to the bosom of the Church from whose womb he had strayed [Note: [Col. 0895] “by that satisfaction,” G.].

39. Concerning the honor and peace of the holy Church. Let the honor and peace, together with the justice, of the holy Church of God and of its servants [Col. 0895B] be preserved unharmed by everyone.

40. Concerning the priests of God and the ministers of the altar. Let no one inflict any injury upon the priests of God or the ministers of the altar contrary to canonical authority.

41. Concerning harmony between bishops and counts. Let bishops and counts be in harmony, and let the counts and their ministers be helpers in all things to the bishops and their ministers.

42. [Note: [Col. 0895] Together with chapters 42–45, compare the *Capitulare de banno dominico*, above.] Concerning arson and robbery. Let no one commit arson or robbery in our kingdom. Let thieves and robbers be firmly restrained, so that they dare not take away anyone’s property unless it is freely given or exacted by a lawful levy [Note: [Col. 0895] “no one,” corrected to “anyone,” G.; “not to anyone,” Bal.].

43. Concerning the preservation of peace. Let peace be preserved for everyone in our kingdom according to the custom of our forefathers.

44. Concerning a maiden or widow. Let no one carry off a maiden or widow, nor consent to those wishing to do so.

45. [Col. 0895C] Concerning payment of the ban. Let our ban be paid for each of these matters if anyone violates them [Note: [Col. 0895] “have done,” G.]; and let each of those who violate them provide to the counts or our envoys sureties fully trustworthy up to our presence, so that [Note: [Col. 0895] “and,” G.] these matters may be corrected according to Roman law [Note: [Col. 0895] “may correct,” G.].

46. Concerning secular business. It has pleased us that the ministers of the Lord’s altar and monks abstain altogether from secular business. There are therefore many kinds of secular business [Note: [Col. 0895] “singular matters,” G.]; nevertheless, we have touched briefly upon a few of them. To these belongs every form of lust, not only in the uncleanness of the flesh but also in every carnal desire. Whatever a person desires beyond what is just is called shameful gain. To receive or give unjust gifts; to hire someone for a price for some secular lawsuit; to love disputes, lawsuits, or quarrels; to argue in secular courts, except in defense of orphans or widows; to be contractors or agents in secular affairs; to be a jester in obscene words or deeds, or to delight in secular amusement; [Col. 0895D] to love dice; to seek adornment unsuitable to one’s profession; to live in luxury or [Note: [Col. 0895] “to wish to live,” G., Bal.] to pursue gluttony and drunkenness; to possess unjust weights or measures; to conduct an unjust business—although a just business is not to be forbidden on account of various necessities, since we read that the holy apostles engaged in business, and in the Rule of Saint Benedict it is prescribed that care be taken through whose hands the business of the monastery passes; to pursue hunting with dogs and birds; and, whatever the circumstances, to engage in anything superfluous. Behold, such things and the like we altogether forbid the ministers of the Lord’s altar and likewise monks. Of these the apostle says [Col. 0896A]: “No one serving God entangles himself in secular business.”

47. Concerning apostolic imitation. The apostle says: “Be imitators of me, and observe those who walk in this way, as you have our example”; do not observe those who are enemies of the cross of Christ, whose end is destruction, whose god is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame, who set their minds on earthly things. But our citizenship is in heaven. As Jerome says in his letter to the Galatians: “Those who imitate well are those who, when they see or hear that graces, gifts, and virtues exist in some persons, desire to be such themselves and strive to imitate their faith, life, and diligence, through which they earned those things, so that they too may attain those goods worthy of emulation” [Note: [Col. 0895] “he says,” Bal.; “whoever,” Bal.], seeking spiritual things rather than carnal ones, so that they may reach the end of good works with steadfast progress.

Augustine, interpreting this saying in the first book [Note: [Col. 0895] Bal. adds “first,” although Augustine wrote only one book.] *On the Christian Contest*, says: “Be imitators of me, just as I also am of Christ.” We must therefore understand that the apostle himself also triumphed in himself [Col. 0896B] over the powers of this world, just as he had said of the Lord, whose imitator he professes to be. Let us therefore imitate him also, as he exhorts us, and chastise our body and bring it into servitude, if we wish to conquer the world.

At one time he commands us to become imitators of Christ by his own example, saying: “Be imitators of me, just as I also am of Christ.” At another time, turning from himself toward God, he exhorts us to imitate God himself, saying: “Be imitators of God, as beloved children.” Then, showing that nothing produces this imitation so much as for a person to live in such a way that his goodness benefits the community and he foresees what is useful to everyone, he added: “Walk in love.” Therefore, when he had said, “Be imitators of me,” he immediately discoursed on love, because this virtue above all makes human beings close to God.

48. Concerning canonical clerics, that they should live canonically. Therefore, as far as human frailty permits, we have decreed that canonical clerics live canonically, [Col. 0896C] observing the teaching of sacred Scripture and the instructions of the holy Fathers, and that they dare to undertake nothing in an orderly manner without the permission of their bishop or their superior [Note: [Col. 0895] “and,” Bal.].

49. Concerning those who kill their own servants without a judge. If anyone kills his own servant without the knowledge of the judge, let him cleanse his guilt of bloodshed by excommunication or by two years of penance.

50. Concerning those who do not return to peace. It has pleased us that, as often happens, whenever people have separated from one another through hatred or a prolonged lawsuit and cannot be recalled to peace despite persistent efforts, they should first be rebuked by the priests of the city. If they refuse with destructive resolve to lay aside their enmities, let them be expelled from the assembly of the Church by the most just excommunication.

51. Concerning those who enter the church but, because of excessive indulgence, abstain from the sacrament. If anyone enters the church of God, does not listen to the sacred Scriptures, and because of his luxury turns away from communion in the sacrament and avoids the established rule of discipline in observing the mysteries, we decree that such a person must be cast out of the Catholic Church until he performs penance and shows the fruit of his penance, so that, having received communion, he may merit forgiveness.

52. Concerning clerics or laypeople. Bishops are not to receive clerics or laypeople removed from communion by other bishops.

53. Concerning clerics who have lawsuits against one another. Clerics who have personal disputes against one another ought not to abandon their own bishop and rush to secular courts.

54. [Col. 0897A] Concerning one who dares to communicate before a hearing after excommunication. If anyone who has been excommunicated dares to receive communion before a hearing, he has brought condemnation upon himself.

55. Concerning a powerful person who despoils someone. If any powerful person despoils anyone and does not restore what was taken when admonished by the bishop, let him be excommunicated.

56. That the endowments of all churches ought to belong to the bishop’s administration. Many people, contrary to the decrees of the canons, ask that the churches they have built be consecrated in such a way that they judge the endowment they have given to those churches not to belong to the bishop’s administration. This practice displeased us in the past and is forbidden in the future; rather, everything shall belong to the bishop’s administration and authority according to the ancient constitution.

57. Concerning what the faithful offer in parish basilicas. With regard to the lands, vineyards, slaves, and livestock that any faithful person offers to parish churches [Note: [Col. 0897] “whatever,” Bal.], let the institutions of the ancient canons be observed, [Col. 0897B] and let everything remain in the bishop’s power. Of what is added to the altar, however, one third is to be faithfully brought to the bishops [Note: [Col. 0897] omitted, G.].

58. Concerning the four ecclesiastical portions. In every church governed by a bishop, four portions are to be made both from revenues and from the offerings of the faithful [Note: [Col. 0897] “offerings,” Bal.]: one for the bishop, another for the clergy, a third for the poor, and a fourth to be applied to the repair of the churches.

59. Concerning one who has treated the penalty of anathema lightly. From a letter of Pope Gelasius. If anyone treats the penalty of anathema lightly, let even the document by which he thinks he possesses an estate fail him; and let any ecclesiastical person be permitted to raise an objection and to reclaim, together with the fruits of past time, those estates that have been alienated.

60. Concerning those among the laity who have been contemptuous of the canons. Let laypeople who despise the canons be excommunicated, and let clerics be deprived of their office.

61. [Col. 0897C] That the people should not presume to leave before the Mass is completed and the blessing received. When people assemble in God’s name to celebrate Masses, they shall not depart before the solemnity of the Mass has been completed. Where a bishop is present, let them receive the priest’s blessing. If anyone leaves the congregation while the priest is delivering the word in the church, let him be excommunicated.

62. Concerning those who break the ecclesiastical fasts without necessity. If any of those who practice continence, driven by the impulse of his own thoughts and in arrogance, breaks without bodily necessity the fasts handed down in common and guarded by the Church, let him be anathema.

63. That the sacrament not be given to catechumens. It has likewise been decreed that, even during the most solemn Paschal days, the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood not be given to catechumens, except for the customary sacrament of salt; for if the faithful do not change the sacraments during those days, neither ought the catechumens to change. This rule is also to be followed altogether by those who are publicly performing penance.

64. Concerning what is to be done with those who have been rebaptized or reconfirmed. Concerning those who have fallen into rebaptism without any necessity or compulsion, it has been decided that the statutes of the Nicene Synod known to have been established concerning transgressors be observed for them: namely, that they pray among the catechumens for seven years and among the Catholics for two; afterward, through the bishop’s moderation and mercy, let them communicate with the faithful in the offering and the Eucharist. Those who have been reconfirmed shall follow the same rule.

65. Concerning clerics who flee to secular protection because of the bishop’s severity. It has been decreed that if a cleric, abandoning his office because of severity, [Col. 0898A] should perhaps flee to a secular authority [Note: [Col. 0897] “secular person,” G.] and the person to whom he flees gives him the support of protection [Note: [Col. 0897] “gives him protection,” Bal.], both he and that person shall be expelled from communion with the Church.

66. Concerning shameful speech. Scurrilous clerics and those who jest with obscene words are to be removed from office.

67. Concerning clerics who presume to sing at a banquet. Clerics who sing during meals are to be restrained with the severity of the sentence stated above.

68. That a cleric should not swear by created things. A cleric who swears by created things is to be sharply rebuked; if he persists in the fault, he is to be excommunicated.

69. That no one should go to a banquet before the third hour of the day or eat before the blessing. Religious clerics or laypeople ought not to begin banquets before the sacred third hour of the day; nor should clerics ever eat bread unless a hymn has been said, and after meals they should give thanks to God the author.

70. That a priest who celebrates the *agenda* without consulting the bishop should be deprived of his honor. From the Council of Carthage. Numidius, bishop of Massilita [Note: [Col. 0897] “Maxilita,” G.], said: “In some places there are priests who, either through simple ignorance or through bold concealment, conduct the *agenda* in private houses with several people while the bishop is present but has not been consulted. Your Holiness recognizes that this is contrary to discipline.”

Bishop Genilius said: “Brothers and our fellow bishops do not delay responding to your worthy proposal on account of ignorance.” All the bishops said: “Any priest who wishes to celebrate the *agenda* in any place without consulting the bishop is acting against his own honor.”

71. That a priest should not presume to give a blessing over the people or bless a penitent in a church. A priest is altogether forbidden to pour a blessing over the people in the church or to bless a penitent in the church.

72. That ordinations should not be made by the judgment of the multitude. It must not be permitted that mobs make the choice of those who are to be advanced to the priesthood.

73. If certain clerics promoted by their bishops contend [Note: [Col. 0897] “despise,” Bal.] and do not remain there from which they refuse to depart. [Col. 0898C] From the Council of Carthage. It has been decided that whatever clerics or deacons, because of the needs of the churches, do not obey their bishops when the bishops wish to promote them in their own church to a higher honor, shall not minister in their rank in the place from which they refused to depart.

74. From the decrees of Pope Gregory the Younger, concerning incest. If anyone takes his cousin in marriage, let him be anathema. Shortly afterward he adds and says: “If anyone takes as a wife a woman from his own kinship or one whom his kinsman had possessed, let him be anathema.” And the Lord says in the divine law: “No man shall approach his nearest blood relation to uncover her nakedness.” Shortly afterward: “Nor shall he approach the wife of one who is joined to him by affinity.”

Likewise, as stated above: “Let no one take a blood relative of any specified degree in marriage or desire to be joined to her in wicked wedlock.” Likewise, from the statements of bishops and of the emperors Theodosius and others: “All the names of kinship are contained within seven degrees; beyond these neither affinity is found nor can succession be extended any further.” [Note: [Col. 0897] The words “and shortly afterward,” “and in the divine law,” “and a little later,” “likewise, as stated above,” and finally “likewise from the statements of … others” were written in red by G., making six headings out of one.]

75. Likewise concerning incest. From letters sent by Pope Gregory to the holy [Note: [Col. 0897] omitted by Bal.] Boniface, archbishop of Mainz. We decree that everyone observe his lineage up to the seventh generation, and that, for as long as they recognize themselves as related by affinity [Note: [Col. 0897] “those whom they recognize as related by kinship” (or “them,” written above the line), G.], they not enter into the union of this relationship.

And in the holy canons composed by the Spirit of God it is inserted concerning incestuous unions: “For incestuous unions we reserve absolutely no pardon, unless they heal the adultery by separation.” We decree, however, that incestuous persons are not to be called by any name of marriage; but those to whom an illicit union is forbidden, unless they are among those whom the decrees of the holy Fathers prohibit from being joined in marriage, shall have the freedom to enter into a better marriage.

76. Concerning not giving the sacrament to catechumens during the solemn days of Easter. Let the sacrament not be given during the most solemn Paschal days to catechumens, nor to those who have been excluded from the doors of the church, nor, before canonical reconciliation, to those performing public penance, except the blessing of salt.

77. Concerning those who have used only the banquets of the pagans or sacrificial foods [Note: [Col. 0899] “their own,” G.] [Note: [Col. 0899] Bal. adds in red: “Or, that those who commit homicide or other capital crimes cannot be healed except through public penance.”]. Those who have merely taken part in pagan banquets and eaten sacrificial foods may be cleansed through fasting and the laying on of hands, provided that thereafter they abstain from food sacrificed to idols and may participate in Christ’s sacraments. But if they have either worshiped idols or been defiled by homicide or fornication, they ought not to be admitted to communion except through public penance.

78. Concerning intimacy with strange women. Let no one presume to maintain intimacy with strange women. Whoever is found doing so is to be corrected more severely [Note: [Col. 0899] “more strictly,” Bal.].

79. That women should not enter a monastery of monks. Let women under no circumstances enter a monastery of monks.

80. That the Lord’s Prayer should be said at all evening and morning hours. It has been decided that every day, after Matins and Vespers, the priest shall recite the Lord’s Prayer [Note: [Col. 0899] “and the prayer,” G.].

81. Concerning those who inflict death upon themselves by any means, and concerning those who are punished for their crimes [Note: [Col. 0899] “Concerning those who inflict death upon themselves through any negligence, so that no commemoration of them is made in the offering. Likewise, concerning those who die violently,” G.]. It has been decided that those who violently inflict death upon themselves by sword, poison, jumping, hanging, or any other means are not to be commemorated in the offering [Note: [Col. 0899] omitted, G.], nor are their bodies to be led to burial with psalms; for many have taken this upon themselves through ignorance [Note: [Col. 0899] “through lack of understanding,” Bal.]. The same has been decided concerning those who are punished for their crimes.

82. Concerning idle words. “For every idle word that people speak, they will give an account on the day of judgment” [Note: [Col. 0899] “they will give an account to God on the day of judgment,” Bal.]; much more are those who speak harmful words condemned. An idle word is one that lacks either the usefulness of righteousness or the reason of a just necessity; nevertheless, they will give an account of it on the day of judgment [Note: [Col. 0899] “an account will be given,” Bal.].

83. Concerning one who has killed a person. Whoever kills a person shall perform penance according to canonical sanction and shall first be cast out of the Church. There, lying prostrate on the ground in ashes and sackcloth, [Note: [Col. 0899] omitted, G.] he shall always lie humbly at the entrance and exit of the people, asking that they not disdain to pray for him. He shall do this until the satisfaction of the Church and the priests, living only on bread and water, unless the bishop under whose authority he exists decides to act more humanely toward him.

84. Concerning the repairs of churches, which are made from gifts contributed to those churches, so that whatever has been gathered may be recalled under the bishop’s authority [Note: [Col. 0899] “may be recalled,” Bal.]. Whatever has been collected for the repair of churches [Note: [Col. 0899] “for the church’s fabric,” G.] must be recalled, according to the will of the donor, by the bishop, priest, or servants of the holy places. If anyone removes, carries off, or steals these things, or defrauds, devastates, or alienates them by any device [Note: [Col. 0899] “by any circumstance,” G.], let him know that he is canonically excommunicated until he takes care to restore what he removed [Note: [Col. 0899] “until,” Bal.].

85. That no secular judge should constrain a priest, deacon, or any cleric without the consent of his bishop. Let no judge presume on his own authority to constrain or condemn a priest, deacon, cleric, or junior member of the Church without the knowledge of the bishop [Col. 0900A].

86. Concerning freedmen, that they should be defended by priests. Let the freedmen of any free persons [Note: [Col. 0899] “of anyone,” G.] be defended by priests and never be recalled to public service [Note: [Col. 0899] “public penance,” G.].

87. That no cleric should, on any pretext, keep a strange woman in his house. Therefore, from now on, let no cleric presume to keep a strange woman in his house on the pretext of necessity for making clothing [Note: [Col. 0899] “of making a garment,” corrected to “of making clothing,” G.] or for arranging the household.

88. From a letter of blessed Pope Gregory sent to Boniface the archbishop [Note: [Col. 0899] “examples,” G.], in which, among other matters, a decree concerning widows is read [Note: [Col. 0899] The words “concerning widows” are omitted in Bal., who places them at the beginning of the heading.].

“My dearest brother, I believe that your affection, which wished to consult us concerning widows departing from their purpose of widowhood, knows from the holy apostle Paul and from many holy Fathers that such women were long ago condemned unless they convert. We too judge, by apostolic authority, that they must be condemned and kept away from the communion of the faithful and from the doors of the church until they obey their bishops and return, whether unwillingly or willingly, to the good undertaking they began.

“Concerning virgins who are not veiled, if they have strayed, we have the following decree from our predecessor of holy memory, Pope Innocent: ‘Those women who, although not yet covered by the sacred veil, have always pretended to remain in the purpose of virginity—although they were not veiled—if they marry, must perform penance for some time, because their pledge was held by the Lord. For if among human beings a contract of good faith is ordinarily dissolved for no reason, how much more will this promise, which she made with God, not be dissolved without punishment?’” And so forth.

For if virgins not yet veiled are punished by public penance in this way and excluded from the company of the faithful until satisfaction, how much more must widows—who are of more mature age, possess more mature wisdom and judgment, have often experienced the company of men, allowed themselves to be veiled, and assumed the religious habit—who afterward apostatized and returned to their former vomit [Note: [Col. 0899] “vow,” G.] be expelled by us and by all the faithful from the doors of the church and from the company of the faithful until satisfaction, and handed over to prisons.

In this way, following the blessed apostle Paul, we hand such a person over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh [Note: [Col. 0899] “so that the spirit may be saved,” omitted in G.], so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord. Concerning such people the Lord also speaks through Moses, saying: “Remove the evil from your midst.” Of them the prophet also says: “The righteous man will rejoice when he sees vengeance; he will wash his hands in the blood of the sinner.”

Concerning such people, their likenesses, and those who consent to them—for not only those who do such things but also those who consent to those doing them are guilty—the Lord speaks through that same prophet David, saying: “You saw a thief, and you ran with him, and you placed your portion with adulterers”; and many similar things.

Such persons are undoubtedly shown to be adulteresses, because, abandoning their immortal spouse, they have returned like dogs to their former vomit [Col. 0900D] and, having become apostates and polluting themselves with illicit and sacrilegious contagion, have joined themselves to mortal men. Also, according to the same apostle Paul, because they abandoned the purpose of widowhood, dared to break the faith they had pledged to God, and violated their first faith, they are to be condemned. By us, by you, and by the other men of our order—each within his own diocese—they are to be expelled from the doors of the church and from the company of the faithful until satisfaction, as has been stated.

We command all the faithful to abstain in every way from the company and association of such women. Concerning them it has also been decided that, for as long as they persist in that detestable, illicit, and sacrilegious union of the flesh, no Christian may communicate with them in any respect or approach the house in which they live, except those to whom their own bishop, for the purpose of correction, has specifically ordered it. With them, moreover, as the aforesaid holy apostle commands, no faithful person may eat food. If anyone presumes to attempt or rashly undertake any of these things, let him be struck with the same sentence of excommunication as they.

89. Concerning tithes given to churches, which priests must not presume to sell. Let priests not presume to sell the tithes [Note: [Col. 0901] “from the tithes,” G.] that are given for the use of the poor and the churches [Note: [Col. 0901] omitted, G.], as—strange to say—they have until now grown old in granaries for the accumulation of treasures [Note: [Col. 0901] omitted, Bal.]. As a result, many of the poor die having to demand them from the hands of priests. But when, by God’s generosity, they become abundant, let them be prepared for the support of the poor at the appropriate time.

90. Concerning priests gathering the poor. Let priests gather two or three poor people every day to wash their feet.

91. Concerning estates that priests purchase after their ordination. Let priests who acquire estates from their own means after ordination confirm their testaments to the churches. Otherwise, let them be removed as fraudsters [Note: [Col. 0901] “let them promote,” G.].

92. That priests should come to the cities to administer their ministries. Let priests come individually to the cities under the direction of the bishop to administer their ministries [Note: [Col. 0901] “mysteries,” G.].

93. Concerning those who have received communion, that they should abstain for three hours because of the mixing of food. Let communicants be instructed to abstain for two or three hours because of the admixture of food.

94. Concerning the daily satisfaction of priests. Just as no one exists daily without fault [Col. 0901C] [Note: [Col. 0901] omitted, G.], so no one, whether priest or Christian, ought to exist without daily satisfaction.

95. Concerning one who, without the bishop’s consent, expels or appoints a priest in a church. Concerning those who appoint priests in their churches or expel them from churches without the bishop’s consent, and who, when admonished by the bishop or by any royal envoy, refuse to obey: let them be compelled to give a pledge for our ban and be ordered to come to our court through sureties. Then we shall decide whether it pleases us that they pay that ban [Note: [Col. 0901] “they pay,” Bal.] or undergo another penalty [Note: [Col. 0901] “they undergo,” Bal.].

96. Concerning churches divided among heirs. Regarding churches that have been divided among co-heirs [Note: [Col. 0901] “who,” G.], it has been determined that, if the co-heirs wish to retain and honor them according to the foresight [Note: [Col. 0901] “province,” G.] and admonition of the bishop [Note: [Col. 0901] omitted, G.], they shall do so. But if they oppose this, let it remain in the bishop’s power to decide whether he permits them to remain in that condition or removes the relics from them. [Col. 0901D] Wherever churches belonging to our benefice are found divided in this way, let the matter be recorded and reported to us.

97. Concerning the destruction of churches. Concerning destroyed churches, let bishops and royal envoys investigate whether they were destroyed through negligence or inability. Where negligence is found, let those who ought to have restored them be compelled by episcopal authority to make amends [Note: [Col. 0901] “to them,” G.]. But if it happened through inability [Note: [Col. 0901] omitted, G.]—whether because there are more churches than necessary or because they are larger than can be restored from the resources belonging to them—let the bishop find a way [Col. 0902A] by which they can suitably be repaired and maintained.

98. That service should not be exacted contrary to the decrees from a church mansus that has been given. Concerning a single mansus given to a church, from which certain people exact service for themselves contrary to the statutes: whoever is accused on this account, the count or our envoys shall cause what was taken from the priests to be restored with its legal compensation.

99. Concerning nones and tithes, which some neglect to give.
