Concerning those who for many years have neglected to give nones [Note: [Col. 0901] “annonae,” G.] and tithes, either in part or entirely, we wish them to be compelled by our envoys to pay, according to the earlier capitulary, the ninth and tithe of one year with their legal compensation and, in addition, our ban. Let it also be announced to them that whoever repeats this negligence shall know that he will lose the benefice from which that ninth and tithe ought to have been paid.

For it is contained in the capitulary of our good-memory father, in Book I [Note: [Col. 0901] “part, chapter 157,” Bal.]: “Let those who possess benefices of churches give from them a ninth and a tithe to the church whose property they are. And those who possess such a benefice and cultivate it on a half-share shall give tithes from their portion to their own priest.”

Likewise, in our capitulary, Book II, chapter 21, concerning the same matter: “Concerning nones and tithes, about which both our father and we have frequently given admonition at various courts and have arranged through our capitularies how they should be observed, we wish and command that from every cultivated field, from wine, and from hay, the ninth and tithe be faithfully [Note: [Col. 0901] “happily,” G.] and fully paid by everyone. Regarding the increase of livestock, everyone shall observe the custom that has existed until now concerning the tithe. If, however, there is a bishop who wishes to accept money for this, it shall remain in his power, according to what he and the person who must pay it agree.”

100. Concerning one who neglects to give the tithe to the church to which it is owed and gives it to another church. Whoever removes a tithe from the church to which it ought by right to be given and presumptuously gives it to another church, whether because of gifts, friendship, [Col. 0902C] or any other pretext, shall be constrained by the count or our envoy to restore the amount of that tithe together with its legal compensation.

101. Concerning tithes to be given by the people. Concerning tithes that the people refuse to give unless they are redeemed from them by some means: bishops must forbid this from happening. If anyone is found to be contemptuous and unwilling to obey either the bishop or the count, then, if he is one of our men, he shall be compelled to come into our presence; the others shall be constrained to restore unwillingly to the church what they neglected to give voluntarily.

102. Concerning those who neglect to restore churches from the resources they hold as benefices. Whoever neglects to carry out repairs from the property of churches that he holds as a benefice shall be dealt with according to the earlier capitulary, in which provision was made concerning works, nones, and tithes—namely, Book IV, chapter 38:

“Concerning the work and restoration [Col. 0902D] of churches, it has been determined that from the produce of the earth and the increase of animals, together with all other resources, the full amount shall be paid, so that it may be done according to the Gospel command, where it says: ‘I give tithes of everything I possess’; and so forth.

“Concerning the work or restoration of churches, the count and the bishop or abbot, together with our envoy whom they themselves choose for this purpose, shall make an assessment, so that each of them receives for construction and restoration only as much as he is known to possess from the property of the churches. Likewise, our vassals shall receive, either collectively, only as much work as corresponds to the church property they possess, or individually according to the amount that each one holds.

“Or, if they agree among themselves to give money for the work to be done, they shall pay in money according to the value of the work. With that price, the rector of the church may hire laborers and buy materials for the aforesaid restoration. Whoever neglects to give nones and tithes shall first restore them with their legal compensation and, in addition, pay our ban, so that, chastised in this way, he may beware of repeating the offense and losing his benefice.”

103. Concerning those who neglect to cultivate demesne lands [Note: [Col. 0903] “neglect,” Bal.] so that they may not pay nones from them [Note: [Col. 0903] omitted, G.]. Concerning the person [Note: [Col. 0903] “persons,” G.] who neglects to cultivate demesne lands for the purpose of not paying nones and tithes from them, and for this reason takes other people’s lands to cultivate, we wish him to pay for three years the ninth itself together with its legal compensation. If anyone on this account proves contemptuous of either our counts or our envoys, let him be compelled through sureties to come to the palace.

104. Likewise, other chapters [Note: [Col. 0903] Bal.: “Concerning destroyed benefices.”]. Concerning destroyed benefices, let the provision contained in the earlier capitulary be observed—namely, Book IV, chapter 36, concerning one who has left his benefice deserted [Note: [Col. 0903] The words “concerning one who has left his benefice deserted” are the heading of a new chapter in red, G.]:

“Whoever has left his benefice deserted on account of his own affairs and, within a year after it has been made known to him by the count or our envoy, has not repaired it shall lose that benefice.”

105. Concerning bad scabini, that they should be expelled. Let our envoys, wherever they find bad scabini, expel them and, with the consent of the entire people, choose good men in their place. When they have been chosen, let them make them swear that they must not knowingly judge unjustly.

### 106. On choosing the better and more truthful

In every county, those who can be found to be better and more truthful are to be chosen by our envoys to conduct inquiries and state the truth of the matter; and they are to assist the counts in administering justice.

### 107. On scabini who have judged unjustly because of gifts or friendship

We wish that any scabinus who is discovered to have judged unjustly because of gifts, friendship, or enmity be compelled, under sureties, to come before our presence through an envoy. Henceforth it is to be announced to all scabini that no one may presume to sell even a just judgment.

### 108. On lawful and reasonable exchanges of the churches of God

Where exchanges made in our time or in that of our father were lawful, reasonable, and beneficial to the churches, let them remain. Wherever, however, they were made uselessly, disadvantageously, or unreasonably, let them be dissolved, and let each person receive back what he gave. But wherever a dead hand intervenes, or any other cause is found that appears reasonable, let it be carefully recorded and brought to our attention.

### 109. On one who is proved knowingly to have led witnesses into perjury

Whoever is proved to have knowingly led witnesses into perjury is to be compelled under surety to come to our palace, so that there [Note: G. reads *sic*; it is corrected from *ubi*, the reading found in Bal.] we may consider with our faithful men what should be done with such a man [Note: From “what should be done with such a man” onward, the text is lacking in G.].

### 110. That no one refuse good coins

Concerning the good denarii that the people refuse to accept, we wish the provision written in our earlier capitulary to be observed and maintained, namely, in Book Four [Note: Bal. adds “chapter 30”]:

> Whoever, whether in a purchase or in payment of a debt, refuses to accept a pure and properly weighed denarius shall pay our bann, that is, sixty solidi. But if ecclesiastical slaves, or our fiscal slaves, or those of counts or of our vassals, presume to do this, let them be beaten with sixty blows. And if our agents, or those of others, or advocates, when ordered by our envoys or by counts, refuse to present them, let them pay the aforesaid bann, that is, sixty solidi.

And to fulfill this ordinance of ours, bishops and abbots, or the other holders of our benefices, are to assist the counts in coercing their men. If the counts neglect this ordinance of ours, let it be reported to our attention through our envoys.

### 111. That harmful assemblies be prohibited in every way

Assemblies held for wrongdoing are to be prohibited in every way; and wherever such presumptuous acts have occurred, let them be corrected by an appropriate amends. If they have occurred through a count’s negligence or have remained uncorrected, let this be reported to our attention.

But if the instigator of the act is a provost, advocate, centenarius, or any other free person holding an office [Note: G. reads *praedicta*, “the aforesaid,” instead of *praedita*, “holding office”], let him, after the lawful amends have been made locally, come before our presence under sureties. The multitude, whether composed of slaves or free persons, is to be punished by a lawful amends.

### 112. That public bridges which have been destroyed be rebuilt

[Note: In G. this is not marked as a rubric but is written continuously with the rest, the two chapters being joined in this way.]

Concerning destroyed public bridges, it has seemed good to us that those who have despised our order regarding the repair of bridges should be dealt with as follows: we wish and command that all our men come before our presence to give an account of why they dared to despise our order.

The counts, however, shall give an account of their pagenses: why they either did not compel them to do this or neglected to report it to us [Note: Bal. reads *reddant*, “shall give,” instead of *reddent*, “will give”]. Likewise, concerning unjust tolls, wherever they are collected, let them know that they will have to give us an account of them.

### 113. On the ordeal of cold water

Our envoys are all to prohibit the ordeal of cold water, which they have hitherto practiced, so that it may not be performed any longer [Note: G. reads *faciat*, “he may perform,” instead of *fiat*, “it may be performed”].

### 114. On the return of the count and the pagenses from a military expedition, so that from that day the bann be suspended for forty days

After the count and the pagenses have returned from any military expedition, from that day onward the bann is to be suspended for forty nights [Note: G. has in the margin: “or revoked”], which in the German language is called *scatslegi* [Note: G. reads *scatflegi*], that is, “the laying down of arms.”

### 115. On the king’s audience

[Note: The words “On the king’s audience” and the opening *et* are absent from G., where the earlier words of the chapter, up to *volumus* at the end, are placed at the end of the preceding chapter.]

And let the counts and the royal envoys take the greatest care of the poor. Let our envoys make this known to the counts and the people: we wish to sit for one day every week to hear and judge cases.

The counts and our envoys, however, are to show great diligence, lest through their negligence the poor be tormented and we suffer annoyance because of their complaints, if they wish to retain our favor. Let it also be said to the people that they should take care not to bring other cases before us in complaint, except those in which either our envoys or the counts have been unwilling to do them justice.

### 116. On the *inferenda* to be exacted by vicarii or other ministers of counts

If any vicarius or other minister of a count presumes to exact from the people a levy called *inferenda* at a higher value than was established by the envoys of our father of blessed memory [Note: G. reads *praesumpsit*, “presumed,” instead of *praesumpserit*, “presumes”], namely, two solidi for one cow [Col. 0904D], let him restore to those from whom he took it, together with its lawful compensation, whatever he unjustly added and took away for himself; moreover, let him pay our *fredus* and lose his office.

### 117. On one who kills a relative out of greed for property

Whoever, out of greed for property, kills his father, mother, brother, sister, nephew, or any other relative, let the inheritance of the slain pass to his other lawful heirs; but let the killer’s inheritance be confiscated to the fisc. The killer himself, at the direction of the bishop, is to be subjected to public penance.

### 118. On one who dismisses or kills his own wife without cause

Whoever, after abandoning his own wife or killing her without cause, takes another wife is to lay down his arms and perform public penance. If he is obstinate, let the count seize him, bind him in irons, and place him in custody until the matter is brought to our attention [Note: Bal. lacks the words “until the matter”].

### 119. On one who sells another person’s property to anyone

Whoever sells another person’s property to anyone, and that person gives or sells the same property to someone else, and the person who then possesses the purchased property, by malicious deception, hands it over to his own son or to any other person who has not yet reached the lawful age, in order to deprive justice of its course, we firmly wish and command that, if the father of that child is alive, he himself enter the case and give an account on behalf of his son.

But if the father is dead, then his lawful relative, who appears justly to be his guardian or defender, is to be compelled to give an account on his behalf. The same applies to all other legal matters pertaining to him, except his lawful inheritance, which he was legally due to receive through succession from his parents.

If anyone despises or neglects this command of ours, let him be treated as are other despisers of our commands. But the person who first seized and unjustly sold the property, as well as the purchasers—with the sole exception of the child himself—are to be compelled to make amends within the country for what they fraudulently did. Afterwards, as despisers of our command, they are to be compelled under sureties to come before our presence.

In the eleventh year of the reign of our lord Charles, the most glorious king, in the month of March, when bishops gathered together in a synodal council, together with abbots, illustrious men, and counts, decrees were judged, in accordance with the will of God, to be appropriate for the relevant matters [Note: Bal. reads “to be useful”].

### 120. On metropolitans

[Note: The heading “On metropolitans” is absent from G.]

Concerning metropolitans: the suffragan bishops are to be their assistants, and whatever they recognize as requiring correction with regard to their ministry, they are to correct and amend willingly [Note: “Subordinate,” from the Capitulary of the year 779].

### 121. On bishops to be ordained

Concerning bishops: wherever bishops have not at present been ordained, let them be ordained without delay.

### 122. On monasteries established under a rule

Let monasteries that are under a rule live under that rule. Likewise, let monasteries of women observe the holy order. Let each abbess reside continually in her own monastery.

### 123. On the authority of bishops over priests and clerics

Let bishops have authority over priests and clerics within their diocese, according to the canons.

### 124. On incestuous persons

Let bishops correct incestuous persons and take great care concerning them. They are likewise to have authority within their diocese to correct widows.

### 125. On neither receiving nor ordaining another bishop’s cleric

No one is to be permitted to receive another bishop’s cleric or to ordain him to any rank.

### 126. On homicides who ought to die according to the law

Let homicides and other guilty persons who ought to die according to the laws not be excused if they flee to a church. If they are unwilling to make amends, let no food be given to them [Note: G. reads “if they are unwilling to give amends”].

### 127. On giving tithes

Concerning tithes: let each person give his tithe, and let it be distributed by order of the bishop.

### 128. On presenting thieves at the count’s court

Let judges present thieves from within the immunity at the count’s court. Whoever fails to do this shall lose his benefice and honor. Likewise, if our vassals fail to fulfill this, let them lose their benefice and honor; and whoever has no benefice shall pay the bann [Note: Bal. reads “whoever has a benefice shall pay the bann”].

### 129. That one who commits perjury lose his hand

Concerning one who commits perjury: let him pay no redemption but lose his hand. If the accuser wishes to press the charge of perjury, let them stand at the cross; and if the swearer prevails, let the accuser make amends according to his law. This is to be observed in lesser cases. In greater matters, or concerning the status of free birth, let them observe the law.

### 130. On punishment and judgment concerning thieves

They declare that punishment and judgment carried out against thieves on the testimony of bishops are to be without sin on the part of the count, provided that, without hatred or malicious pretext, nothing else is introduced there except true justice brought to completion.

Whoever punishes a person out of hatred or malicious deception, and not for the administration of justice, shall lose his honor and shall make amends under the law to the person against whom he acted unjustly, according to the penalty he inflicted.

### 131. That royal enactments be observed inviolate

We wish to preserve whatever our father of blessed memory established in his courts and synods.

### 132. On the payment of tithes and ninths from church properties from which dues are owed

From church properties from which dues are now owed, let tithes and ninths be paid together with the dues; and from those from which they were not previously paid, let ninths and tithes likewise be given.

From sixty *casati*, five solidi; from thirty, two and a half solidi; from fifteen, four *transmissi* [Note: G. reads *transmissus*, singular]. Let the *precariae* be renewed only in the prescribed manner. Wherever they are not written down, let a record be made among the contracting parties on the basis of our word.

Whoever is unwilling to do the aforesaid, and voluntarily delays paying these three obligations and accepting the *precariae*, let him very quickly lose the benefices he held. Nevertheless, let the church from which they came claim them for itself in perpetuity, without anyone’s opposition or hindrance.

### 133. That the provision concerning wax-makers be followed as established

[Col. 0906C] Let the matter of wax-makers, board-makers, and charter-writers be handled as it was decreed long ago [Note: G. reads *cartallariis*, “cartallarii,” instead of *cartelariis*].

### 134. That no one dare swear an oath for a guild-association

Concerning those who swear together by oath on behalf of a guild-association, let no one presume to do this. In another way, concerning their alms, or fires, or shipwrecks, even if they make an agreement, let no one presume to swear an oath in this matter.

### 135. That no one dare attack those traveling to the palace

Concerning travelers who are going to the palace or elsewhere: let no one dare attack them through an assembly. Nor may anyone presume to take another person’s fodder during a time of defense, unless he is going to war or is our envoy.

### 136. That tolls be observed as decreed long ago

Concerning tolls, let the previous regulations be observed, as they were formerly prohibited: no one is to take anything except what was established in ancient times.

### 137. On not selling slaves except in the presence of authorities

Concerning slaves: let them not be sold except in the presence of a bishop or count, or in the presence of an archdeacon, centenarius, vicedominus, or the count’s judge, or before reliable and well-known witnesses.

Let no one sell slaves outside the mark. Whoever does so shall pay the bann as many times as the number of slaves he sold. If he has no means to pay, let him give himself to the count as a pledge as a slave, until he pays the bann.

### 138. On not selling coats of mail outside the kingdom

Concerning coats of mail, let no one presume to sell them outside our kingdom.

### 139. On a count who does not administer justice

If a count does not administer justice in his jurisdiction, let him serve our envoys from his own gifts until justice has been done there.

If our vassal does not administer justice, then the count and our envoy are to sit at his house and live at his expense until he administers justice.

### 140. On one who refuses to accept a payment because of a feud

If anyone does not wish to accept a payment for a feud [Note: Bal. reads “because of the feud”], let him be sent to us [Note: G. reads “let them be sent”], so that we may direct him [Note: G. corrects *ipsum*, “him,” to *ipsos*, “them”] to a place where he can harm no one [Note: G. corrects *possit*, “he can,” to *possint*, “they can”].

### 141. On one who refuses to pay the compensation for a feud

Likewise, if anyone does not wish to pay the compensation for a feud and do justice concerning it, we wish to send him to such a place that no greater harm may arise from the same matter.

### 142. What is to be done with thieves

Concerning thieves, we command the following to be observed: for the first offense, the thief is not to die but is to lose one eye; for a second offense, the thief’s nose is to be cut off; for a third offense, if he has not made amends, he is to die.

### 143. How the faithful are to supplicate God in prayers and almsgiving for the king and his army in this present tribulation

A capitulary has been established with the agreement of the bishops as follows: each bishop is to celebrate three Masses and recite three psalters—one for our lord the king, another for the Frankish army, and a third for the present tribulation. Each priest is to celebrate three Masses. Monks, nuns, and canons are each to recite three psalters.

All are also to perform two-day fasts, both bishops and monks, nuns, and canons, as well as the people belonging to their *casati* or those who are able to do this. Each bishop, abbot, and abbess who is able is to give a pound of silver, or its value, as alms; those of moderate means, half a pound; those of lesser means, five solidi.

Bishops, abbots, and abbesses are to nourish four poor and hungry persons during this hardship until the harvest season. Those who cannot support that many are to support three, two, or one, according to their ability [Note: Bal. reads *ut*, “or,” in this place].

The more powerful counts are to give a pound of silver, or its value, as alms; those of moderate means, half a pound; from one hundred *casati*, five solidi; from fifty, one ounce [Note: G. reads *untia*, “ounce”]. Let them perform two-day fasts, as are their men and their *casati*, or those who are able to do this.

Whoever wishes to redeem the two-day fast is to give three ounces if he is a more powerful count, thirty denarii if of moderate means [Note: Bal. notes that this is how the text should now be written; G. and Bal. read “those of lesser means”], and one solidus if of lesser means. Concerning the poor and hungry, let them act as it is written.

If it pleases the Lord, let all these things be completed by the Mass of Saint John, for our lord the king, the Frankish army, and the present tribulation.

### 144. That no priest, other cleric, or any of the faithful presume to sell, give, pledge, or otherwise alienate tithes belonging to the church

No priest, deacon, cleric, or layperson is to presume to sell, give, pledge, or otherwise encumber tithes before he has faithfully collected them in their entirety and gathered them for use in his granaries within the precincts of the church to which they are lawfully due [Note: Bal. reads *debeat*, “to which they ought to belong,” and omits the following words through *habeat*].

Afterwards, in accordance with the command of his own bishop and according to the canonical sanctions and decrees of blessed Pope Gelasius, he is to distribute them. If anyone disregards or attempts to violate this, then, if he is a cleric, he shall be subject to the danger of losing his rank; but if he is a monk or layperson, let him be deprived of communion.

### 145. On the bishop’s supervision concerning archdeacons

Let bishops take care that the greed of archdeacons does not foster the faults of priests, since iniquity deceives itself in many ways.

### 146. On not removing the bones of the dead from graves

Let no one rashly remove the bones of the dead from their graves [Note: G. reads *ossa*, “bones,” instead of *ossibus*, “from the bones”].

### 147. On not swearing oaths

Let each person take care not to swear, because perjurers will not possess the kingdom of God, just as adulterers will not.

### 148. On confirming in their own churches estates purchased by priests

Let priests ordained from among the poor, when they purchase estates, confirm them to their churches.

### 149. On satisfaction for daily offenses

Just as no one is without fault every day, so no one—including priests—ought to be without daily satisfaction.

### 150. On the suspension of communicants

Let communicants be taught to abstain for two or three hours because of the admixture of food.

### 151. On priests assembling in the city for the sake of learning

Let priests come individually to the cities under the direction of the bishop to discuss their ministries [Note: G. reads *mysteria*, “sacred mysteries,” instead of *ministeria*, “ministries”].

### 152. On priests gathering the poor

Let priests gather two or three poor persons every day in order to wash their feet.

### 153. On not selling the tithes of churches

Let priests henceforth not presume to sell tithes, which are given for the use of the poor and the churches. Until now, incredibly, they have grown old in storehouses for the accumulation of treasures; as evidence of this, many poor people die demanding them from the hands of priests.

But wherever, by God’s generosity, there is an abundance, let provisions be prepared for the support of the poor during a time of famine.

### 154. On issuing *formatae*

Let no cleric depart without a *formata*. From the Council of Africa or Milevis, chapter 30:

> Let no one depart for the count’s court without a *formata*, or concerning how *formatae* are to be issued. It has been decided that whenever a cleric wishes to go somewhere to the count’s court because of his own necessity, he is to receive a *formata* from his bishop. If he wishes to go without a *formata*, let him be excluded from communion. If an unexpected necessity arises requiring him to go to the count’s court, let him present that necessity to the bishop of the place and carry with him a written statement from that bishop.
>
> The *formatae* issued by primates or by any bishops to their own clerics are to bear the date of Easter. If the date of Easter for that year is still uncertain, let the preceding Easter be added, as is customary when “after the consulship” is entered in public documents.

### 155. On negligent clerics

From the Council of Agde, chapter 2. Concerning contumacious clerics and those slow to perform their office:

Let contumacious clerics be corrected by the bishops as the order of their rank permits. If any clerics, puffed up with the pride of a higher rank, should perhaps despise communion, neglect to attend church, or fail to perform their office, let them be given an external communion, so that when repentance has corrected them, they may be entered again in the register and recover their rank and dignity.

### 156. That clerics not go to secular judges without the bishop’s permission

From the Council of Agde, chapter 32. Let a cleric not go to a secular judge without consulting his bishop.

Let no cleric presume to bring a case before a secular judge without the bishop’s permission [Note: G. reads *pulsari*, “to be summoned,” instead of *pulsare*, “to bring a case”]. If he is summoned [Note: G. reads *qui*, “who,” instead of *si*, “if”], let him not answer; nor may he dare to bring a criminal case before a secular court.

If any secular person attempts to harass a church or cleric through false accusation and is defeated, let him be excluded from the church’s threshold and from Catholic communion, unless he performs worthy penance.

### 157. That no cleric or monk depart without the permission of his bishop

From the Council of Agde, chapter 38. Let no cleric or monk be permitted to depart without a letter from his bishop.

Clerics are not to have permission to wander about without letters of recommendation from their bishop. Let the form of this present judgment likewise be observed for monks. If he is not corrected by verbal rebuke, we also decree that he be restrained by beatings.

### 158. That no cleric depart without the permission of his bishop

From the Council of Agde, chapter 52. Concerning clerics who depart without a letter from their bishop:

Let no one grant communion to a priest, deacon, or cleric traveling without letters from his bishop.

### 159. On those who do not receive communion in their own provinces

From the Council of Africa, chapter 18:

It has been decided that anyone who, while not receiving communion in his own province, secretly goes to other provinces or overseas regions to receive communion shall suffer the loss of communion or of his clerical status.

### 160. On perpetrators of various evils

There are indeed perpetrators of various evils whom divine law condemns and rejects. Because of their various crimes and offenses, the people are scourged by famine and pestilence, the condition of the churches is weakened, and the kingdom is endangered.

Although these matters have been sufficiently condemned in the sacred writings, we have judged it necessary to take precautions against them again through our warning, exhortation, and prohibition.

Such are the perpetrators of various pollutions, which some commit in the most diverse ways with males and with animals. By provoking the incomparable sweetness of the most merciful Creator to bitterness, they sin all the more gravely because they sin against nature. Because of this crime, five cities were consumed by heavenly fire and swallowed by the opening of hell; moreover, forty thousand and more of the stock of Benjamin were pierced by the brotherly sword.

These examples and evident punishments show how detestable and abominable this vice is in the sight of the divine majesty. For we know that the Roman law, which is the mother of all human laws, commands that the perpetrators of such crimes be burned by fire.

Therefore we solemnly announce to all of you, and by the strict judgment of God and by our fidelity command all your people, all who serve you, and all who are subject to you together with you, to beware of these things and in no way to consent, by word or deed, to those who commit them; for, as the apostle promises, those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God.

It is now time for you to spare the multitude of the perishing people, who, by following the examples of a sinful ruler, were falling into the pit of death. For without doubt we shall receive from the eternal Judge either punishments or rewards for all those whom we draw toward the life of the heavenly homeland through good examples, or whom we lead ahead toward destruction as they follow bad examples [Note: Bal. reads *praeimus*, “we lead ahead”; G. reads *praeveimus*, “we lead forward”; “or carry across” is written in the margin].

For if our people, as has been spread through these provinces and reproached to us in Francia and Italy—and is even a reproach among the pagans themselves—should, scorning lawful marriages and living adulterously and luxuriously after the manner of the Sodomite people, lead a shameful life, then from such intercourse with prostitutes it must be expected that degenerate, ignoble, and lust-maddened peoples will be born; that in the end the whole common people will incline toward what is worse and more ignoble; and finally that it will be neither strong in secular war, nor steadfast in faith, nor honorable among human beings, nor beloved by God.

The same happened to the other peoples of Spain, Provence, and Burgundy: having withdrawn from God in this way, they fornicated until the omnipotent Judge permitted the avenging punishments for such crimes to come upon them through their ignorance of God’s law and through the Saracens, and permitted them to become subject to them.

It must also be noted that another monstrous crime lies hidden beneath that offense, namely, homicide. For when those prostitutes—whether monastic or secular—bore offspring conceived in sin, they often killed them, for the most part, filling not Christ’s churches with adopted sons but tombs with bodies and hell with wretched souls [Note: G., correcting an earlier reading also found in Bal., reads “with bodies”; the earlier reading was “with animals”].

Far be it that you should perish because of such people [Note: Bal. conjectures “for such sins”], and that we should fall together with the kingdom and the glory of the entire kingdom perish. From what has gone before we have learned what may happen in the future unless it is anticipated.

It is also better for us to be without such people than to fall with them, and for the kingdom in the future to be annihilated or possessed by heathens and their peoples.

We wish you to know that whoever is found either committing such acts or willingly consenting to them shall be punished by us according to the aforesaid Roman law [Note: G. adds in the margin: “we wish”].

### 161. On one who takes another wife after abandoning or killing his own wife without cause

Whoever, after abandoning his own wife or killing her without cause, takes another wife is to lay down his arms and perform public penance. If he is obstinate, let the count seize him, bind him in irons, and place him in custody until the matter is brought to our attention.

### 162. On one who hands over property unlawfully acquired to his son or to any person who has not reached the lawful age

Whoever sells another person’s property, and the person who possesses the purchased property, by malicious deception, hands it over to his own son or to any other person who has not yet reached the lawful age, in order to deprive justice of its course, we wish and firmly command that, if the father of that child is alive, he himself enter the case and give an account on behalf of his son.

But if the father himself is dead, then his lawful relative, who appears justly to be his guardian or defender, is to be compelled to give an account on his behalf. The same applies to all other legal matters pertaining to him, except his lawful inheritance, which he was legally due to receive through succession from his parents.

If anyone despises or neglects this command of ours, let him be treated as are other despisers of our commands. But the person who first seized and unjustly sold the property, as well as the purchasers—with the sole exception of the child himself—are to be compelled to make amends within the country for what they fraudulently did. Afterwards, as despisers of our command, they are to be compelled under sureties to come before our presence.

### 163. That no human service be exacted from a *mansus* given to a church; whoever does so shall make amends according to his law

Concerning a *mansus* given to a church, from which certain people exact service contrary to the established provisions: whoever is accused on this account, the count or the envoys are to have the priests restored whatever was taken from it, together with its lawful compensation.

Whoever exacts from a *mansus* given to a church any service beyond ecclesiastical service is to make amends according to the law, under the coercion of the bishop or count.

### 164. On those who neglect to give ninths, tithes, restorations, or dues, so that they make amends according to the law and moreover pay our bann

Concerning those who for many years have neglected to give ninths and tithes, either in part or entirely, we wish them to be compelled by our envoys to pay, according to the earlier capitulary, the ninth and tithe for one year together with their lawful compensation, and in addition our bann.

Let it also be announced to them that whoever repeats this negligence shall know that he will lose the benefice from which this ninth and tithe ought to have been paid.

For this is contained in the capitulary of our father of blessed memory, Book One, chapter 157:

> Let the ninths and tithes be restored according to the law, and let the lord’s bann moreover be paid by the negligent person [Note: Bal. includes these words in the text; G. wrote them in red ink, apparently because he was uncertain where to divide the passage. They are not found in the capitulary itself.]. Let those who hold the benefices of churches give from them the ninth and tithe to the church whose property they are [Note: From these words Bal. made a rubric for a new chapter 165, adding to it: “And let ninths and tithes not be redeemed unless the bishop approves”; G., writing the words in red ink, inserts them immediately below in the middle of the chapter before “we wish and command.”]. Those who hold such a benefice and cultivate it jointly are to give tithes from their portion to their own priest.

Likewise, in our capitulary, Book Two, chapter 21, concerning the same matter [Note: G. wrote this passage in red ink]:

> Concerning ninths and tithes, about which both our father and we have frequently issued admonitions in various courts and have established through our capitularies how they are to be observed, we wish and command that from all produce cultivated jointly, and from wine and hay, the ninth and tithe be paid fully and faithfully by everyone. Concerning the nourishment that is to be given as a tithe, let the custom hitherto observed be maintained by everyone. If, however, any bishop wishes to accept silver for this, let it remain within his authority, according to whatever agreement he and the person who ought to pay it reach.

### 165. (166 in Bal.) On those who unjustly take away a church’s tithe, instead of giving it according to the disposition of the bishop to whom it belongs, and presume to give it elsewhere because of friendship or gifts

Whoever takes a tithe away from the church to which it ought rightfully to be given, and presumptuously gives it to another church because of gifts, friendship, or any other pretext, is to be coerced by the count or our envoy to restore the amount of that tithe together with its lawful compensation.

### 166. (167 in Bal.) On those who neglect to give tithes unless the tithes are redeemed from them in some manner, so that they are firmly compelled to make amends, willingly or unwillingly

Bishops are to prohibit the practice whereby people who do not wish to give tithes have the tithes redeemed from them in some manner [Note: Bal. reads “unless they wish to redeem themselves from them in some manner”].

If anyone is found to be contemptuous and unwilling to listen either to the bishop or to the count, then, if he is our man, he is to be compelled to come before our presence. Others are to be coerced so that, unwillingly, they restore to the church what they voluntarily neglected to give [Note: G. corrects *quod*, “what,” to *qui*, “those who”].

[Col. 0911C] **167. (168 BAL.) Concerning those who neglect to carry out repairs to churches and their buildings, or to pay the tithes and ninths; and, if they do not reform, are to lose their benefices.**

Whoever, from the property of churches which they hold as a benefice, neglects to carry out repairs to them, let the earlier capitulary be fulfilled in their case—the one in which provisions were made concerning works, ninths, and tithes—namely, Book IV, chapter 38:

> “With regard to the work or repair of churches, the count and the bishop or abbot, together with our envoy whom they themselves shall choose for this purpose, are to conduct an assessment, so that each of them may receive from it for work and restoration as much as he is known to hold from the property of the churches. Likewise, our vassals, either jointly or individually, are to undertake as much work as corresponds to the amount of ecclesiastical property they possess, or each according to the quantity which he himself holds. Or, if they agree among themselves to give money for carrying out the work, they are to pay in silver according to the estimated value of the work, so that with this payment the rector of the church may hire laborers for the aforesaid restoration and purchase materials. And whoever neglects to pay the ninths and tithes must first restore them together with the legally prescribed penalty; moreover, he must pay our ban, so that, chastened in this way, he may take care not to lose his benefice by repeating the offense too often.”

**168. (169 BAL.) So that those who refuse to cultivate demesne lands for the purpose of avoiding payment of the ninths and tithes from them may be thoroughly compelled to pay these dues for three years according to law.**

Concerning those who neglect to cultivate demesne fields for the purpose of not paying the ninths and tithes from them, and for this reason accept other people’s lands to cultivate, we decree that they pay the ninth and tithe for three years, together with the legally prescribed penalty. And if anyone on this account proves contemptuous either of the count or of our envoys, he is to be compelled, through sureties [Cod. G: “through sureties”], to come to the palace.

**169. (170 BAL.) Concerning tolls, where they are not to be exacted.**

It has been decreed that wherever, in the time of our grandfather, lord Pippin, it was customary to pay a toll, it is to be paid there in the future as well; but where the practice was only recently begun, it is not to continue any further. And wherever it is not necessary to cross a river by a bridge, or wherever a ship passes through the middle of the water and under the bridge without approaching the bank, and where nothing has been bought or sold, no toll is to be paid thereafter. And no one is to compel another to go to the bridge where he can cross the water beside the bridge. Whoever thereafter exacts a toll in such places, or from those traveling to the palace or to the army, must restore the toll with the legally prescribed penalty and pay our ban, namely, sixty solidi.

**170. (171 BAL.) Concerning church property that has been possessed by the same church for thirty years without any claim being brought against it, so that no testimony concerning that possession is henceforth to be admitted.**

With regard to church property that has been possessed by the churches for periods of thirty years without any interruption, no testimony is to be admitted against it; rather, it is to be maintained in the same manner as property belonging to our fisc is ordinarily maintained.

# B. SECTION TWO OF THE DIPLOMATIC CODE OF CHARLES THE GREAT—PRIVILEGES

[Col. 0913]

## DIPLOMAS, FOUNDATIONS, PRIVILEGES, AND PIOUS DONATIONS CONCERNING ECCLESIASTICAL PROPERTY

### I. PRIVILEGES RELATING TO THE REGIONS OF GAUL

### I. Diploma of Charles the Great for the Monastery of Gorze (768)

*(From Calmet, History of Lorraine.)*

[Col. 0913A]

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks, illustrious man, to all bishops, abbots, counts, and also envoys, and to all our faithful subjects, present and future.

If we bring to fulfillment the petitions of priests and servants of God which they have brought to our ears, we exercise royal clemency; and, so that they may pray for the salvation of our soul and the stability of our kingdom, we encourage their hearts to do so. Therefore let your diligence know that the venerable man Theomar, abbot, came into our presence and brought us the privilege of Chrodegang, of blessed memory, archbishop of the city of Metz, which he had drawn up concerning the monastery of Gorze, where those dwelling there are to remain until the end of the age. It contained the statement that, with the consent and will of our lord and father, Pippin, formerly king, and also with the consent of his priests and clerics, the aforesaid monastery had been built in the names of the apostles Peter and Paul; and that afterward he had deposited there the body of the most holy Gorgonius, brought from Rome. This was done on the condition that monks should live in that monastery perpetually according to the order and rule of Saint Benedict, and should unceasingly implore the mercy of the Lord for themselves and for others.

Yet, in order to confirm the undertaking of this good work, we have learned that the aforesaid bishop assigned various properties to the same holy place and confirmed them in such a way that thereafter neither he himself, their bishop, nor his successors and archdeacons, nor any other assistants of the church, should at any time violate them. Accordingly, the aforesaid abbot Theomar and his monks assert that this privilege has been confirmed and that they possess all these things peacefully. But, out of devotion, he asked our Highness that we might draw up and confirm our own confirmation concerning the aforesaid monastery and its rectors, thereby increasing our reward. We could not refuse his petition; rather, know that we granted and confirmed it willingly.

Therefore, having examined the aforesaid privilege, we command that, just as it declares, and just as it was made by the bishop himself with the consent and will of our lord and father and of the priests and clerics, and as the most holy bishops confirmed it in a public synod, so it shall be confirmed in every respect by the grace of God and of ourselves. Let neither the bishops of Metz nor the other rectors of that church violate what is contained in this privilege, nor let it in any way ever be broken. Rather, just as the aforesaid bishop arranged it for the praise and service of the Almighty, for the common reward of himself, of the kingdom, and of the Franks, so let it endure in our time and in that of our successors, so that the rectors of that church, together with the holy company of monks, may be more eager to pray to the mercy of the Lord for the salvation of the fatherland and the stability of our kingdom.

[Col. 0914B] Sign of Charles, most glorious king.

### II. Diploma by which Charles the Great grants the Priory of Saint Deodatus to the Monastery of Saint-Denis (769)

*(From D. Bouquet, Collection of Historians.)*

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks, illustrious man.

Whatever we grant to the benevolent places of the churches of God, we believe contributes to the salvation of our soul; especially do we strive to fulfill this with regard to those places where our parents appear to rest. Therefore let it be known to all our faithful subjects, present and future, that, for the love of God and the increase of our reward, we give to the house of the holy lord Dionysius the martyr, where that precious lord rests bodily with his holy companions, and where our lord and father, King Pippin, appears to rest, and where we too, if it pleases God, desire to be buried—and we wish the gift to belong there to that holy place—namely, a monastery called Saint Deodatus, within the Vosges forest, which our lord and father Pippin is proved to have held in his grant.

This is on the condition that ten and fifteen brothers, in turn, must always guard that place, and that there they must not cease, day and night, to implore the Lord in psalms, Masses, and the other prayers of supplication, as well as in particular prayers for us and for our lord and glorious father.

For this reason we ordered this decree of ours to be written for the house of the holy lord Dionysius, so that from this day the rectors of that monastery may receive and possess, by our indulgence, the aforesaid monastery with everything belonging to it, so that thereafter they may have and hold that place without anyone’s opposition or legal claim. And so that this decree or confirmation of ours may remain firm and stable in our time and in that of our successors, we have ordered it to be strengthened below by our own hand and sealed with our ring.

Sign of Charles, most glorious king.

Hitherius recognized it.

Given on the Ides of January, in the first year of our reign. Done at the public palace of Aachen, prosperously, in the name of God. Amen.

### III. Diploma of Charles the Great for the Monastery of Corbie (769)

*(From D. Bouquet, ibid.)*

[Col. 0915B]

Charles, king of the Franks, illustrious man.

If we affirm by our decrees what was once granted and conceded by our former predecessor kings to holy places or for the benefit of the servants of God, we exercise the custom of kings, and we trust that this contributes to our reward and to the stability of our kingdom.

Therefore the venerable Hado, of the monastery of Corbie, situated in the county of Amiens, which our predecessors, formerly King Clothar and Queen Balthehild, ordered to be built from its foundations through their efforts, brought to the clemency of our kingdom the report that the aforesaid rulers had granted that monastery, through their decrees, permission to possess peacefully and perpetually, under complete immunity and without the entry of judges or claims by the public fisc, all property which they themselves had appeared to establish there for their reward, as well as whatever had been added or granted by succeeding kings or by any God-fearing persons, or had been acquired by the custodians of the aforesaid monastery by any means, in whatever counties or territories.

Accordingly, the abbot himself brought before us to be read the decrees of our predecessors, as well as the confirmations of Childeric, Theuderic, Clovis, Childebert, Dagobert, and Pippin, formerly kings, and also of our father; and he asserts that this benefit has been preserved from that time until now. But, in the interest of firm security, he asked our Highness that our authority should more fully confirm this same arrangement for the aforesaid monastery. Know that we granted and confirmed his petition with a joyful heart and conceded everything in every respect.

Therefore, by this present decree we order and determine that whatever was granted and conceded by our predecessors to the aforesaid monastery in any places or territories, or is known to have been added or granted by those who fear the Lord, or was acquired by any means by the abbots themselves who serve God there, or may henceforth, with God’s help, be improved or increased there by any persons—both what the monastery now appears to possess or control and what may hereafter, with the Lord’s assistance, be granted or acquired there by any written charters—after examination of the decrees of the aforesaid rulers, they may hold and possess peacefully under complete immunity and without the entry of judges.

Thus no public judge is ever to presume to enter the courts of that monastery or the lands where the people mentioned above appear to dwell, whether to hear cases, exact fines, demand provisions or lodging, or seek or receive any payments belonging to our fisc. Rather, under complete immunity, as we have said, and with all fines granted, they may possess or control these things peacefully in our time and in that of our successors, so that the servants of God may be more eager to pray to the mercy of God for the stability of our kingdom. And, so that this decree may be held more firmly and preserved in every respect through the ages, we have ordered it to be strengthened below by the subscriptions of our hand.

Itherius recognized and subscribed it.

Given on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of April, in the first year from the beginning of my reign. Done at Andriaca villa, in the name of the Lord.

### IV. [Note: Among the Sammarthani, who published the same decree in volume IV of *Gallia Christiana*, p. 24: Mauronius, Clementiniacus, Papionis, Pinnarius, Sabracus.] Diploma of Charles the Great for the Monastery of Saint Albinus at Angers (769)

*(From D. Bouquet, ibid.)*

[Col. 0916C]

Charles, king of the Franks, illustrious man, to all our officials, etc.

Therefore the magnificent man Gunthar, rector of the monastery of Saint Albinus, which is built near the walls of Angers, and the clerics of the church of our special patron, came into our presence and brought to the clemency of our kingdom the report that our predecessors, and also our lord and father Pippin, of blessed memory, formerly king, through their authorities and written signatures, had ordered … that certain estates of the same abbey, assigned to the canons of that place, should once again be confirmed by a written authority of our Highness for the same uses, to be held by perpetual right. The names of these estates are as follows: Maironnus, Clementiniacus, Papirius, Prunarius, Sabiacus, Multonacus, Monasteriolum, and the vineyard situated within Monasterium; and the fishing from the gate of Canciacum [Note: Among the same authorities, Crotiense.] to the island called Virelista.

And he established that every year one hundred modii of salt should be given to the aforesaid brothers from the estate of Vistiniacum [Note: Among the same authorities, Justiniacum]. Therefore, as has been indicated above, we ordered this decree of our Highness to be made, by which we command that the aforesaid properties, in their entirety and without diminution by any rector of that place, be assigned to the uses and support of the servants of God serving Christ in that place.

We also establish that the number of brothers may never be increased by any abbot beyond fifty. And so that this decree of our authority may be held more firmly, better believed by his successors and the faithful of the holy Church of God in times to come, and preserved more carefully, we ordered it to be sealed below with our ring.

Sign of Charles, most glorious king.

Hiterius recognized it.

Given in the month of May, in the first year of Charles, most glorious king of the Franks. Done at Murnacum [Note: A place commonly called Mornai among the Santones.]

### V. Diploma of Charles the Great for the Immunity of the Monastery of Sithiu (769)

*(In Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*.)*

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks, illustrious man.

If we confirm by our decrees the deeds of our predecessor kings, which they performed or granted for holy places, we exercise the royal custom and trust that, in the name of God, this contributes to our praise and to the stability of our kingdom.

Therefore the venerable man Hardrad, abbot of the monastery of Sithiu, situated in the county of Tervana, built in honor of Saint Mary, mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, and also of the holy apostles Peter and Paul and the other holy lords, came into our presence and brought to the clemency of our kingdom the report that the kings, our predecessors, had granted complete immunity to all the courts and estates of that monastery: whatever they possessed at that time, or whatever had thereafter been added or granted there in any counties or territories from royal gifts, from the gifts of the people, by purchase, or by any acquisition.

They had granted it to his predecessors and to the monastery of Sithiu in such a way that no public judge might ever presume to enter there to hear cases, exact fines, take sureties, demand lodging or provisions, or distrain the people of the monastery, both free men and servants, who dwell upon its lands; nor might judicial authority enter there to seek or exact any payments. Rather, under the grant of immunity, together with all fines and bans conceded, the monastery was perpetually to possess everything.

Accordingly, he asserts that he has the decree of our predecessors in his hands and that the benefits granted by it appear to have been preserved from that time until now. But, for complete security, the aforesaid abbot asked our Highness that we should confirm this more fully for that place by our authority. Know that, for the increase of our reward and out of reverence for that holy place, we have granted his request and confirmed everything in every respect.

Therefore we command that whatever our predecessors justly and reasonably granted or confirmed concerning this immunity, as set forth above, and which has been preserved in a direct course from that time until now, shall likewise, by our decree, be preserved more fully in the name of God hereafter. After examination of the decrees of the aforesaid rulers, as they themselves make clear, let the benefits granted to the abbot Hardrad and to his successors at the monastery of Sithiu be preserved in every respect for all time; and let them have no fear of suffering any opposition or impediment from public judges on this account. Therefore the community must continually implore the mercy of the Lord for the stability of our kingdom and the salvation of the fatherland.

And so that this authority may be held more firmly and preserved in every respect, we have ordered it to be strengthened by the subscriptions of our hand.

Sign of Charles, most glorious king.

Given in the month of July, in the first year of our reign. Done at Andiaco.  
[Note: Audiacum was a palace of the county of Angoulême; but Mabillon doubts that Charles the Great was at this place in the first year of his reign. He believes that he resided at the palace of Andriacum, at Alteia, not far from the monastery of Sithiu. For in that very year he was staying at the villa of Andriaca, where he granted the privilege to Hado, or Chado, abbot of Corbie.]

### VI. Diploma of Charles the Great for the Church of Saint Stephen at Angers (770)

[Note: Which monastery or little monastery of Saint Stephen this was is unclear. Nor does it seem that it should be understood as the monastery of Saint Albinus, formerly situated outside the city, which is said to have been dedicated at its beginning to Saint Mary or to Saint Germanus of Auxerre, not to Saint Stephen.]

*(From D. Bouquet, ibid.)*

[Col. 0918C]

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks, illustrious man, to all officials, present and future.

Our Highness strengthens the foundations of its authority when we heed the petitions of priests and servants of God concerning what pertains to their peace or assistance, and bring this to fulfillment in the name of God; we trust that this contributes to our reward and to the stability of our kingdom.

Therefore let your greatness and usefulness know that the apostolic man Mauriolus, bishop of the city of Angers, concerning the monastery of Saint Stephen, which is built beneath that city near its wall, reported to us that our predecessor kings had granted that little monastery to the church of Saint Mauritius, and asked that we should now grant it such a benefit, for the increase of our reward, that in the little estates of that monastery, wherever they appear to possess them in any counties or territories, no public judge should dare to enter either to hear cases, exact fines or penalties, demand hostile services, lodging, or provisions, or seek any payments.

Rather, what had long been customary to exact for the fisc we should, for the increase of our favor, grant under the name of immunity for the lights of Saint Mauritius, the glorious martyr. We have done so.

Therefore by this present decree we determine and absolutely command that neither you, nor your subordinates, nor their successors, nor any official of the judges of our fisc, in whatever counties or territories the little church of Saint Stephen appears to hold its estates, as we have said above, may demand or offer any fines or penalties, hospitality, lodging, provisions, or payments, nor exact them from their subordinates, except that, as we have said, they are to benefit the lights of Saint Mauritius, under the name of immunity, for the increase of our reward, where Mauriolus the bishop appears to be custodian.

And so that this decree may be held more firmly and preserved better through the ages, we have ordered it to be strengthened below by the subscriptions of our own hand.

Sign of Charles, most glorious king.

Hitherius recognized it.

Given in the month of March, in the eleventh year of our reign. Done happily at the public palace of Herstal. Amen.

### VII. Diploma of Carloman for the Monastery of Honau (770)

*(From Mabillon, volume II of the Benedictine Annals.)*

Carloman, by the grace of God king of the Franks, illustrious man, to all bishops, abbots, dukes, counts, household officers, vicars, centenarii, and all our envoys traveling about, present and future.

Know that we believe the fortification of our kingdom is greatly increased if, with benevolent deliberation, we grant suitable benefits to the places of the churches, and trust, with the protection of the Lord, that they will endure securely.

Therefore let your diligence know that, at the petition of the venerable man Stephen, abbot, we appear to have granted the following benefit for eternal reward: in the estates or properties of the church of Saint Michael the Archangel, of the monastery built on the Rhine island called Honau, whatever it now appears to possess by our gift or that of anyone else, or whatever divine piety may thereafter wish to enlarge in the right of that holy place, no public judge may ever presume to enter to hear cases or exact fines from anywhere.

Rather, the aforesaid Stephen and his successors, and no public judicial authority, shall be able to control those properties under the name of complete immunity, for the sake of the Lord and Saint Michael.

Therefore we command that neither you, nor your subordinates or successors, nor any public judicial authority, may ever presume to enter the estates, wherever in our kingdom they may be, which have been granted to that church by royal generosity, by private persons, or by good men, or which may thereafter be granted by those who fear God, to hear disputes, exact fines for any cause, or take lodging, provisions, or sureties.

Rather, whatever from the servants who are within the fields or vineyards or upon the lands of the aforesaid church, through the hands of their officials, may benefit that church, let it belong to it forever. What we have granted with full devotion for the sake of the Lord’s name, for the remedy of our soul, and for our descendants who follow us, let neither royal eminence nor the grave cupidity of any judges attempt to oppose.

And so that this present authority may remain inviolate, with God’s help, in the present and future, we have ordered it to be confirmed below by our own hand.

Sign of Carloman, most glorious king.

Maginarius recognized and subscribed it.

Given in the month of March, in the eleventh year of our reign. Done at the palace of Theudone-villa, prosperously, in the name of God.

### VIII. Charter of King Carloman by which he grants the Estates of Faberola and Norontes to the Dionysian Monastery (771)

*(From the new appendix to the second edition of the second book of *De re diplomatica*, p. 645.)*

[Col. 0920B]

Carloman, by the grace of God king of the Franks, illustrious man.

Since Scripture admonishes us that each person ought to prepare himself steadfastly so that, when he comes into the presence of the heavenly Judge, he may deserve to hear that gracious word of the Lord at which all the righteous will rejoice because of their good deeds, we therefore, as we rightly believe, consider how from the earthly possessions which heavenly grace has deigned abundantly to bestow upon us in this age we ought at least to give something to the poor, so that we may be able to obtain the mercy of the Most High.

Accordingly, for the remedy of our soul and for our father, formerly Pippin, we cede and give to the monastery of Saint Dionysius the martyr, where the precious lord rests bodily with his companions, and we wish the gift to belong to that holy place—namely, the estates which that father of ours had formerly assigned through our hands to the house of God, called Faberola, situated in the county of Meaux, and Norontes, in the county of Chartres, together with all their appurtenances and in their entirety, to that monastery and to the monks dwelling there, and for providing lights for that church and support for the poor, so that the aforesaid estates may contribute to its increase, just as they were possessed by our vassal Audegarius; and so that the monks may be more eager to pray attentively, day and night, to the mercy of the Lord for us and for our father.

Therefore we cede and give the aforesaid estates of Faberola and Norontes to that holy place, together with their lands, houses, buildings, inhabitants, slaves, vineyards, woods, fields, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, movable and immovable property, mills, flocks with their shepherds—everything in every respect, as we have said, with complete integrity. Whatever appears at the present time to be our possession there, let the aforesaid monastery and its rectors have, hold, and possess perpetually, in our time and in that of our successors; and let it remain fully confirmed in right to that house of God, as our alms, forever, without anyone’s claim being brought against it.

And so that this authority may remain firm and unshaken, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with our ring.

Sign of Carloman, most glorious king.

Maginarius recognized and subscribed it.

Given in the month of December, in the fourth year of our reign. Done at the public palace of Salmunciacum, in the name of God, prosperously.  
[Note: Salmonciacum, commonly Samoncy, below Laon toward the east, on the road leading to Notre-Dame de Liesse.]

### IX. Decree of Charles the Great concerning the Freedom of the Monastery of Saint Michael (772)

[Note: The monastery of Saint Michael, or Old Monastery—Vieux-Moutier—was in the county of Verdun, at the Massoupe. In 819 Abbot Smaragdus transferred this monastery to the bank of the Meuse; around it grew the town called Saint-Mihiel after the monastery.]

*(From Mabillon, volume II of the old *Analecta*, p. 401.)*

[Col. 0921B]

Charles, by the grace of God illustrious man, king of the Franks.

Royal Highness strengthens the foundations of its authority when it strives to heed the petitions of priests for their peace or assistance and to bring them to fulfillment in the name of God.

Therefore, when the venerable man Hermengaud, abbot or bishop of the monastery of Châtillon, in the county of Verdun, at the edge of Vindemiaca, where the river Marsupia rises—the monastery which the illustrious Volfaudus and his wife Adalsina are known to have built on their own property in honor of Saint Michael the archangel and the other holy lords, where he appears to live with a numerous community—came before us, we appeared to have granted, for the sake of our reward, complete immunity for all the property, estates, and resources of that monastery, and for everything which at the present time it appears to possess in any counties and territories in our kingdom, with God’s favor, whether from its allodial property, from purchases, from any acquisition, or from royal gifts, as well as for whatever it may thereafter be able to acquire or improve, and whatever good men who fear God may add or grant there.

This was done just as our lord and father, Pippin, formerly king, of good memory, had done, so that no public judge might presume to enter there to hear cases, exact fines, demand lodging or provisions, investigate or exact any payments, distrain the people belonging to it, whether free men or servants, who appear to dwell upon the land of that monastery, or take sureties.

Rather, the aforesaid Hermengaud, bishop, or the monastery itself, must possess and control all its property and resources under the name of immunity, together with all fines granted.

Therefore by this present decree we determine and order what we wish to remain in perpetuity: neither we, nor our subordinate officials or successors, nor anyone exercising judicial authority, nor anyone on the part of the bishops, nor any other person, may presume to enter the property or resources of that abbot or bishop or of his monastery—whatever it appears at present to possess, whether from allodial property, purchase, any acquisition, or royal gifts, whatever it may thereafter be able to acquire or improve, and whatever good people who fear God may add or grant there.

Rather, as we have said, by our indulgence the aforesaid abbot or bishop Hermengaud, or his monastery, or the entire community dwelling there, or his successors, must possess and control, under complete immunity, all the fines granted. Thus, with God’s help, these things may contribute there, in that holy place, to the increase of the lights in our time and in that of our successors; and therefore the community must continually pray to the mercy of the Lord for the stability of our kingdom and for the prosperity and salvation of the fatherland.

Nor is it to fear that at any time it will suffer any claims or impediment from public judges, from us, from succeeding kings, from any part of our fisc, or from anyone else on this account.

And so that this decree of ours may be held more firmly and preserved better through the ages, we have subscribed it with our own hand and decreed that it be sealed with our ring.

Sign of Charles, most glorious king.

Given in the month of May, in the fourth year of our reign. Done at Drippo, in the public royal palace.

### X. Decree of Charles the Great for the Monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés (772)

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks, illustrious man. [Col. 0922C] Royal serenity ought always to establish those things which contribute in many ways to eternal gains, so that it may be able to ascend from present rule to heavenly life. Therefore it is fitting and proper for us to carry out everything with sound deliberation, especially to put into effect, in God’s name, the petitions of priests when they have been brought to our ears.

Accordingly, let it be known to us and to many others how the basilica of Saint Vincent and Saint Germanus, built below the town of Paris, where that precious lord rests bodily, appears to have been granted by our earlier royal ancestors, and by us, with complete immunity, all the villas, fields, and lands which it possesses. But for the increase of our reward, at the petition of the venerable man Lantfred, abbot who appears to preside there as custodian, and out of reverence for that holy companion, we confirm by our precept the villas with fields and lands which it possesses both beyond the Loire and in its vicinity, as well as wherever, with God’s favor, its possessions are known to exist in our kingdom; likewise, its immunities and all the other instruments belonging to that basilica of Saint Vincent and Saint Germanus, and whatever has been assigned to it from every direction, or may hereafter be added or granted there by God-fearing men. We grant anew, with complete immunity, that whatever our fisc could in any way have from all those known to dwell upon the lands of that Saint Vincent or Saint Germanus, and all dues, shall be held by them without the intervention or demand of any judge.

Therefore we command that neither we, nor our juniors or successors, nor anyone invested with judicial authority, under any pretext whatsoever, presume to enter any of the lands of the aforesaid basilica, or anything which it appears to possess at the present time, or which may hereafter be added or granted there by God-fearing persons, in order to hear cases, exact rightful dues [*recta* (sic)], impose distraints or lodgings, demand any minor goods, or reject men from their testimony in court on account of their status. And, setting aside the claims which they were accustomed to demand on behalf of us or our predecessors, let everything written above remain undisturbed for all time, with God’s help. Thus, as has been said, concerning all the men known to dwell upon the lands of the aforesaid basilica of Saint Vincent and Lord Germanus, and concerning their status—for we grant them permission to give testimony against free men in every court—and concerning whatever you might have been able to exact or hope to exact from them, we strive entirely to remove and set aside such claims at the present time.

Moreover, because these immunities may have been interrupted where they existed through the cunning of judges, we decree them anew, so that no one may presume to do this, unless he wishes to suffer the loss of many possessions. Rather, what is known to have been granted by our ancient parents, the earlier kings, to that holy basilica of Lord Vincent and Saint Germanus, after examining their precepts, we strengthen anew by our indulgence. With the fullest and readiest will, for the sake of faith, we grant to the aforesaid abbot Lantfred and his successors that no one presume to oppose, diminish, or tear away any part of it on any pretext.

And if our fisc appears to possess anything anywhere in the kingdom, with God’s favor, from the aforesaid villas of Saint Vincent or Lord Germanus, or if anything belonging to them can be increased, let it contribute perpetually to the increase of that basilica. We have also decreed that this authority, so that it may endure perpetually in inviolable permanence in our times and those to come, with God’s help, from us and our successors, be strengthened below by our own subscription and sealed below with our ring.

**Sign of Charles, the most glorious king.**

Rado, acting in the place of Hitherius.

Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of November, in the fifth year of our reign. Done at the public palace of Aristallium, happily, in God’s name.

## XI. Charles the Great’s precept for the monastery of Morbach (772)

*(From Martène, Anecdota, volume I.)*

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks, illustrious man. [Col. 0924A] It is proper for princely clemency to lend a kindly ear to everyone, and especially for the benefit of souls, etc. Accordingly, the venerable man Faribert, by God’s gift abbot of the monastery of the Pilgrims’ Dwelling, situated in the Alsatian district beside the Morbach stream, constructed in honor of Saint Leodegarius, Saint Peter the apostle, Saint Mary, and the other saints, where he is known to serve with a very numerous company of monks, brought before the clemency of our kingdom that our predecessors had once granted, by their authorities subscribed with their own hands, complete immunity for the villas of that monastery, and for whatever it presently possessed, both from the immunities of princes—including Eberhard, who founded that monastery as his alms—and from the generosity of the people, or whatever might thereafter have been assigned there by God-fearing men. Thus no public judge was to enter the villas or possessions of that monastery to hear cases, exact dues, impose lodgings or provisions, take sureties, distrain the monastery’s men for any causes, or demand any payment there.

Indeed, the aforesaid abbot Faribert, rector of that monastery, also showed us the very precept and confirmation of our aforementioned predecessors for rereading, and asserts that this benefit has been preserved to that monastery and the aforesaid church until now. But, for the sake of secure permanence, he asked our Highness that our authority should once again confirm this generally for that monastery and those monks. We appeared, out of reverence for that place and so that we might share in its reward, to have granted his petition with the fullest goodwill and to have confirmed everything.

Therefore we command that no public judge enter the possessions or resources of that church to hear cases, exact dues, impose lodgings or provisions, take sureties, distrain the men of that church and monastery—both free and unfree—who appear to dwell upon their lands and who belong there, for any causes, or demand any payment there. Rather, let what has been preserved for the aforesaid monastery until now from the benefits of our earlier predecessors, after their former authorities have been examined, remain likewise undisturbed generally and henceforth by our authority. Whatever our fisc could exact from it shall perpetually contribute to the lights of that Lord Leodegarius and Saint Mary, for the stability of our kingdom.

And so that these authorities may remain valid both in the present and future times, we ordered them to be strengthened below by our hand and sealed with our ring.

**Sign of Charles, the most glorious king.**

Given on the Ides of January, in the fourth year of our reign, at our public palace, happily, in God’s name.

## XII. [Note: [Col. 0925D] This Carolingian diploma was printed in Martène, *Thesaurus anecdotorum*, volume I, p. 10; Eccard, *Origines Habsburgo-Austriacae*, p. 119; and Lunig, *Spicilegium ecclesiasticum*, continuation I, p. 955, but from corrupt copies.] Charles the Great’s charter of immunity granted to the abbey of Murbach under Abbot Haribert (772)

*(From Schoepflin, *Alsatia diplomatica*.)*

[Col. 0925A]

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks, illustrious man. The principle of clemency teaches everyone to lend a kindly ear, and especially, when the benefit of souls is concerned, we ought with devoted mind to weigh what we know was granted by earlier kings, our predecessors, to ecclesiastical places, and, so that we may share in their reward, not refuse suitable benefits but confirm them with the strongest legal force.

Accordingly, the venerable man Haribert, by God’s gift abbot of the monastery of the Pilgrims’ Dwelling, situated in the Alsatian district beside the Morbach River, constructed in honor of Saint Leodegarius, Saint Peter the apostle, Saint Mary, and the other saints, where he is known to serve with a very numerous company of monks, brought before the clemency of our kingdom that our predecessors had once granted, by their authorities subscribed with their own hands, complete immunity for the villas of that monastery which it presently possessed, both from the gifts of princes—including Eberhard, who founded that monastery as his alms—and from the generosity of the people, or whatever might thereafter have been assigned there by God-fearing men.

Thus no public judge was to enter the villas or possessions of that monastery to hear cases, exact dues, impose lodgings or provisions, take sureties, distrain the monastery’s men for any causes, or demand any payment there. The aforesaid abbot Haribert, rector of that monastery, therefore showed us the very precept and confirmation of our aforementioned predecessors for rereading, and asserts that this benefit has been preserved for that monastery and its aforesaid church until now. But, for the sake of security, he asked our Highness that our authority should once again confirm this generally for that monastery and those monks. Know that, out of reverence for that place and so that we might share in its reward, we appeared to have granted his petition with the fullest goodwill and confirmed it in every respect.
