Therefore we command that no public judge enter the possessions or resources of that church to hear cases, exact dues, impose lodgings or provisions, take sureties, or distrain the men of that church or monastery, both free and unfree, who appear to dwell upon their lands or *mitio* and who belong there, for any causes, or demand any payment there. [Note: [Col. 0925D] *Mitio.* This word appears to be placed in the ablative case and to mean the same as *dominium*, legitimate possession. The word occurs rarely, and only, indeed, in the charters of Pepin and Charles the Great. See the latest edition of Du Cange’s *Glossary*, under *Mitium*.]

Rather, just as this benefit has been preserved for the aforesaid monastery until now by our aforementioned predecessors, after the authorities of earlier princes have been examined, so let it remain generally undisturbed henceforth by our authority. Whatever our fisc could exact from it shall perpetually contribute to the lights of Lord Leodegarius and Saint Mary, for the stability of our kingdom. And so that this authority may remain valid both in the present and future times, we have strengthened it below by our hand and ordered it sealed with our ring.

**Sign of Charles, the most glorious king.**

Lutherius: I have reviewed and subscribed.

Given on the Ides of January, in the fourth year of our reign, at the public palace of Blanciacum, happily, in God’s name.

## XIII. Diploma of Charles the Great granted to Eddo, bishop of Strasbourg, by which he confirms to the Church of Strasbourg the entire territorial jurisdiction in the Brusch valley (773)

*(From Grandidier, *History of Strasbourg*.)*

[Note: [Col. 0925D] Most authors testify, following Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*, p. 75, that Charles the Great consistently signed his name with the letter C before he had been crowned emperor; they add that, after being elevated to the imperial dignity, he always called himself *Karolus*, changing C into K. Several French authors of the new *Diplomatics*, volume II, pp. 218–222, discuss this at length and judge that the opinion is not sufficiently consistent with the truth.]

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks, illustrious man. [Col. 0926C] We believe without doubt that the following pertains to the stability of our kingdom, in God’s name: that we bring to completion the petitions of priests or churches which have been brought before our ears. Therefore let it be known to all our faithful, present and future, that the venerable man Eddo, bishop of the Church of Strasbourg, which is constructed in honor of holy Mary, God’s mother and ever-virgin, petitioned the clemency of our kingdom concerning a certain little place called Stilla.

[Note: [Col. 0926D] Today the village of Still, situated in the Brusch valley and the Schirmeck bailiwick, still belonging to the bishop of Strasbourg.]

The aforesaid church has possessed it for a long time through royal confirmations, and the rectors of that church have possessed the aforesaid place within the following named boundaries: along the royal road,

[Note: [Col. 0926D] This is the royal road which leads through the Brusch valley from Alsace into Gaul; it still exists today and was renewed some years ago.]

which runs above the stream called Stilla,

[Note: [Col. 0926D] Today the Still stream, whose sources are in the part of the Vosges called Welfersthal, two leagues from Ochsenstein Castle. From there it descends into the Schirmeck valley and shortly afterward joins the Brusch.]

above the house of Rummald,

[Note: [Col. 0926D] Today the village of Urmatt, half a league distant from Haslach, lying on the royal road and belonging to the bishop of Strasbourg.]

then to the place called Paphinisnaida,

[Note: [Col. 0926D] A place in the Brusch valley whose location is unknown.]

from there across the whole mountain called Arlegisberg,

[Note: [Col. 0927C] Today the village of Heiligenberg, a quarter of an hour distant from Still and belonging to the bishop of Strasbourg.]

as far as the place where the stream called Hasla rises,

[Note: [Col. 0927C] Today the Hasel stream, whose sources are seen not far from those of the Still, between the Still and Wich streams, and which plunges into the Brusch near the collegiate church of Haslach.]

then to the place where Wichia rises,

[Note: [Col. 0927D] Today the Wich stream near the village of the same name, rising in the same region as the Hasel and likewise flowing into the Brusch.]

as far as it enters the Brusch,

[Note: [Col. 0927D] The Brusch River rises among the highest and most rugged peaks of the Vosges near the village of Sell, flows through the entire Schirmeck valley, which takes its name from it and is called Breuschthal. This valley, six leagues long, belongs wholly to the bishop of Strasbourg and joins Alsace to the principality of Salm and to Lorraine.]

and from there again along the Brusch for a long distance until the Stilla enters it—these lands they acquired for the benefit of the aforesaid church.

Therefore he asked that, for the security of the property, we should once again grant and confirm this by our authority to that church. Know that we granted and confirmed his petition with a willing heart and conceded everything in every respect.

Accordingly, we ordered this precept of ours to be written, so that the aforesaid church and its rectors may from this day forward have, hold, and possess perpetually all the things named above, with their boundaries, limits, and appurtenances. Let no one invested with judicial authority, or any other person, at any time presume to disturb the aforesaid Bishop Eddo, his successors, or their agents concerning the aforesaid possessions, or to raise any claim against them contrary to the order of justice. Rather, let this gift of our authority remain there under the firmest legal right.

And so that this authority of ours may remain inviolate and be better preserved in our times and those to come, we have decreed that it be strengthened below by our subscriptions and sealed below with our ring.

**Sign of Charles, the most glorious king.** Hitherius: I have reviewed.

Given on the Nones of March, in the fifth year of our reign.

[Note: [Col. 0927D] Charles the Great succeeded to the kingdom of Gaul after his father Pepin’s death on 24 September 768; he was proclaimed king at Noviomagus on the following 9 October.]

[Note: [Col. 0927D] The Metz Annals testify that King Charles wintered at the villa called Theodonis in the year 773; see Bouquet, volume V, p. 341.]

Done at the villa of Theodonis, at the public palace, happily, in God’s name.

## XIV. Precept of Charles the Great, king of the Franks, concerning the restoration of what had been taken from the Church of Honau (about 773)

[Note: [Col. 0927D] This precept has neither date nor year. It should be placed between the year 772, when, after Carloman’s death, Charles the Great united Austrasia with the kingdoms of Neustria and Burgundy, and the year 774, when, after the conquest of Pavia and the capture of King Desiderius, he inserted the title “king of the Lombards” in his charters. Mabillon, *Annales Benedictini*, volume II, p. 699, first published it, followed by Eccard, *Origines Habsburgo-Austriacae*, p. 105.]

*(From Grandidier, same work.)*

[Col. 0927C]

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks, illustrious man. He commends to everyone who has taken anything from the Church of the Scots, which is on the island of Honau, that he return again everything he has received or seized without the permission of Abbot Beatus. If anyone retains even a small amount, he commands all the judges of that land to seek out all the church’s possessions for him lawfully, according to Frankish law, because the possessions of foreigners properly belong to the king.

Therefore let all the aforesaid things be restored to the Church of the Scots without any impediment—whether land, vineyard, money, people, silver, or gold. If any of them does not do this, let him acknowledge that he has disobeyed the king’s precept, because the kings of the Franks have granted liberty to all the foreign Scots, so that no one may seize anything from their possessions, nor may any lineage except their own lineage possess their churches. Act accordingly if you wish to have our favor.

## XV. Diploma of Charles the Great establishing, among other things, that no one may enter the Church of Strasbourg by simony, and issuing regulations concerning the election of the bishop and the division of revenues (774, 3 April)

[Note: [Col. 0928D] This charter, though corruptly, was published by Schilter in his notes to the *Chronicon Koenigshovii*, p. 495; by Lunig, *Reichsarchiv*, continuation I, fascicle 3, p. 275; and by La Guille, *History of Alsace: Documents*, p. 18. Koenigshovius had copied it from an authentic document which at that time, and still in Wimpheling’s day, existed in the archives of the high chapter of Strasbourg, but which is no longer extant.]

*(From Grandidier, same work.)*

[Col. 0928B]

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks, illustrious man. Since the Lord has made us princes and defenders of the churches, so that we may not appear ungrateful for his grace, we ought to increase his service, confirm what has been well and suitably established, reform what needs correction, and, after putting discord to rest everywhere, restore peace, concord, and tranquility.

Therefore let it be known to all our faithful, present and future, that the venerable Etto, bishop of the holy Church of Strasbourg, came before our Highness, bringing with him the apostolic men Lullus, metropolitan of Mainz, and John, bishop of Constance,

[Note: [Col. 0928D] On Lullus of Mainz, see Serrarius, *Rerum Moguntinarum*, book IV, p. 604 in the first edition and p. 371 in the second; and on John, bishop of Constance, see *Gallia christiana*, volume V, p. 895.]

and, before many people, made a tearful complaint that certain of his predecessors, bishops namely, together with certain canons of theirs—provosts, deans, custodians, chamberlains, cantors, and scholars—had abused ecclesiastical authority so greatly that, although they ought to have been true destroyers of the simoniacal heresy, they had imprudently become its unjust defenders.

For in the granting of prebends, under the name of an offering and as though for the common good, they demanded an unlimited amount of money, which they secretly divided among themselves, not according to what was needed by the brothers, but according to the will of a few of those mentioned above, providing only for themselves. [Col. 0929A]

[Note: [Col. 0929C] In Pope Hadrian’s letter 34, addressed to Lord King Charles, in Bouquet, volume V, p. 579—letter 85 in the *Carolingian Code*—we read: “Having pastoral care of all the churches, we do not permit the divine commandments to be preached concerning the offense of consecration which is committed in the regions of Italy and Tuscany through the simoniacal heresy, etc.”]

But since we know that every form of simony was condemned and utterly abolished by Pope Hadrian and his predecessors, it seemed appropriate to our deliberation and that of those present to regulate the complaint of the aforesaid Bishop Etto moderately and usefully, lest we appear entirely to destroy the interests of the Church or rashly oppose the decrees of the Fathers.

Therefore, at the request of the brothers of that bishopric, with the counsel of many who desired peace and concord, and with the prudent agreement of the bishops—namely Lullus of Mainz, Etto, and John—we established and confirmed by our royal authority that those entering the Church, if they are judged worthy in knowledge, morals, and birth, should not appear empty-handed in the sight of the Lord. From their hereditary property, they shall devoutly give to the mother Church as much as they wish under God’s inspiration; or, if this is lacking, they shall voluntarily offer seven pounds of that currency for charity and the common benefit of the brothers, so that, remembering us on that account, they may be consoled more cheerfully.

The bishop and provost, however, so that they may not be considered exempt from this charity, since they are lords and masters, shall make a gift of three ounces of gold.

We also decree that, when the former bishop has died, no one coming from elsewhere shall be chosen; rather, if a suitable bishop is found within that Church, he shall be elected from its own body. But if no worthy man is found there—which we scarcely believe—then only afterward may another be taken from elsewhere, yet in such a way that neither Roman majesty nor royal honor is offended.

We consider such a man to be one who possesses merit of life, instruction in wisdom, chastity, and sobriety; who is not turbulent or wrathful; and who, the more he is an outsider, is all the better behaved, prudent, and thoughtful, so that, by destroying the traditions of the Fathers, he may not offend or trouble anyone.

We further wish the possessions of the present bishop and his successors to be separated from all the possessions of the brothers and not to be disturbed by them anywhere in their lodgings or overnight stays. Rather, without any future contradiction, let the cloister’s possessions remain undisturbed under the disposition of the provost and the brothers.

But if any bishop, duke, judge, powerful or powerless person, spiritual or secular, should presume to alter or violate this decree of our disposition and confirmation, or attempt to diminish the possessions of the aforesaid bishop, or initiate any violence or disturbance on account of these provisions of ours, let him pay one hundred pounds of the finest gold: half to our fisc, thirty to the archimandrite of Mainz,

[Note: [Col. 0929C] The Greeks formerly called general abbots, or heads of monks, *archimandrites*; the title was later extended to archbishops. Dagobert, bishop of Bourges, calls himself *archimandrite* of the Church of Bourges in a charter of the year 9[.....]0. In the archive of the Church of Grenoble, Amblard of Lyon is called *archimandrite*. See other examples cited by Du Cange in his *Glossary*, volume I, p. 657.]

and twenty to the Church of Strasbourg.

And so that this authority of our firmness may be more carefully observed, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with our ring.

[Col. 0930B] **Sign of Charles, the most glorious king.** Gilbert, chancellor, acting in the place of Hitherius, reviewed and subscribed.

[Note: [Col. 0929D] Charles then celebrated Easter at Rome with Pope Hadrian, as the *Annals of Fulda of the Franks* testify, in Bouquet, volume V, p. 328; likewise the *Metz Annals*, in Duchesne, volume II; and others. At the same place he also made the solemn donation to the Roman Church which Charles gave, as Anastasius relates in the *Life of Pope Hadrian*, in Bouquet, volume V, p. 461.]

Given on the holy day of Easter, on the third day before the Nones of April, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 774, in the twelfth indiction, in the sixth year of the reign of our lord Charles, the most glorious king, while Pope Hadrian was seated in his see. Done at Rome, happily, in God’s name. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 0929D] This is the first of the Alsatian charters to contain the indiction and the year of the Incarnation. Papebrochius and others consider all diplomas before the year 800 which bear the Christian era and the indiction either false or interpolated. “At this period,” says Eckhart, *Commentaries on the Affairs of Eastern Francia*, volume II, p. 28, “the settled opinion is that the year of the Incarnation is not found in genuine charters of Charles.” Schatenus has already refuted all of them. It is true that the Dionysian era, composed in 533, was not immediately admitted into charters but was introduced only after a long interval; yet, since it is prefixed to the German, Leptine, and Soissons councils of the years 743 and 744, why could Charles not have used it in a diploma of 774? He used it in 783 in an authentic diploma for the monastery of Saint Arnulf at Metz, in Meurisse, *History of the Bishops of Metz*, p. 179, and Bouquet, volume V, p. 748. The same may be said of the indiction. Therefore a charter cannot be called false merely because, nine years earlier, it used the same formulas. In fact, almost all diplomas concerning monasteries and private persons in the second royal dynasty lack the years of the Incarnation and the indiction. But Mabillon notes, *De re diplomatica*, p. 189, that some solemn documents concerning the Church or the kingdom, in addition to the regnal years, contain the years of the Incarnation. Besselius makes the same observation, *Chronicon Gotwicense*, volume I, book II, p. 133; and the French authors of the new *Diplomatics*, volume VI, p. 442, clearly state the same: “The diplomas of Charlemagne dated by the indiction and the years of the Incarnation, both before and after he became emperor, should not be rejected if, in other respects, they are unobjectionable.” Whatever the truth of this controversy, which supports the year of the Incarnation, every difficulty disappears if we say that the Christian era and the indiction were inserted by a later hand in the copy, since all the other formulas indicate a Carolingian diploma.]

## XVI. Precept of Charles the Great for the monastery of Anisolum (774)

*(From D. Bouquet, *Collection of Histories*.)*

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks, illustrious man, to all our faithful, present and future. If we confirm by our decrees those exchanges which the rectors of churches make among themselves for the benefit of venerable places, we exercise royal custom and believe that the transaction will thereafter remain established by the firmest right.

Therefore let it be known to all your dignities how the venerable men Merold, bishop of the city of Le Mans, and Rabigaud, abbot of the monastery of Anisolum, came into our presence, asserting that, for the benefit of both parties, they wished to exchange church possessions among themselves. They presented in our presence the exchanges, strengthened by the hands of good men, for reading. From them we learned that the aforesaid bishop had given to Rabigaud the abbot, for the benefit of Saint Carilefus and from the estate of Saint Gervasius, the villa called Sabonarias in the district of Le Mans, in the territory of Labrocinus, which Lord Senard constructed anew through his own work and where he rests, with all the possessions belonging or pertaining to it: namely, all lands, houses, buildings, resident inhabitants, slaves, *liti*, freedmen, and the benefits of free men; vineyards and woods; fields, meadows, pastures; waters and their courses; movable and immovable property; mills; herds with shepherds—in short, everything, together with the entire household property, whatever can be said or named.

Likewise, in exchange, the aforementioned Rabigaud gave from the possessions of Saint Carilefus to Bishop Merold, for the benefit of Saint Gervasius, the villas called Curte-Bosane and Monte-Ebretramno in the district of Le Mans, in the territory of Siliacum, with all their appurtenances: lands, houses, buildings, slaves, *liti*, freedmen, the benefits of free men, vineyards, woods, fields, meadows, pastures, waters and their courses, movable and immovable property, livestock of both sexes, greater and lesser—in short, everything, whatever can be said or named, in its entirety.

But the aforesaid men asked our Highness, for complete security, that we should confirm this by our authority. Know that we granted and confirmed their petition with a willing heart.

Therefore we command that whatever one party has transferred to the other, or received in exchange, shall from this day, by this authority and after the exchanges themselves have been examined as they are set out in them, be held by both parties with full and most secure power in every respect: to have, hold, exchange, or otherwise fully administer within the same Church whatever each has received from his counterpart. Neither the aforesaid men nor their successors shall ever violate these exchanges.

Accordingly, we ordered two documents of the same wording to be made, which we confirmed with our own hand and ordered sealed with our ring.

**Sign of Charles, the most glorious king.**

Idherius: I have reviewed.

Given on the eleventh day before the Kalends of March, in the sixth year of our reign, publicly at the city of Pavia.

## XVII. Precept of Charles the Great, king of the Franks, for the monastery of Saint Martin at Tours (774)

*(From D. Bouquet, same work.)*

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards, and patrician of the Romans.

[Note: [Col. 0931] Mabillon observes that in original documents the second letter of the name *Langobardorum* is consistently represented by *a*, not by *o*, as often appears in printed editions.]

For if, from what divine piety has abundantly granted us, we make suitable concessions to venerable places for the benefit of God’s servants, we trust that this contributes to the increase of our reward and the stability of our kingdom.

Therefore let it be known to all the dignity of our faithful how we and our wife, Queen Hildegard, for the love of God and for the common increase of our reward, give to the sacred church of the most blessed confessor Saint Martin, our patron, constructed in the city of Tours, where that precious lord rests bodily, and where the venerable man Gulfard appears to preside as abbot; and we wish what has been given to remain perpetually with that holy place and its congregation for the purpose of providing vestments.

This is: the island with the castle of Sermionum, situated in Lake Mincio, and the fishery estate, together with Liona and all its boundaries and limits, as it was seen publicly and at the palace to belong there, and whatever may thereafter have fallen within our fisc, both within that boundary and outside it, with everything belonging to it in its entirety: estates, churches, villas, manses, slaves, tenant farmers, buildings, vineyards, olive groves, fields, woods, meadows, pastures, waters and their courses, movable and immovable property, everything in every respect. Also included is that little monastery within the castle, which Ansa constructed as a new work, in honor of Saint Saviour, with all its substance.

We also give to the aforesaid place the valley called Camonia, with Salto and Caudino, as far as Judalanias, with the mountains and Alps from the boundary of Tridentum called Tonale as far as the boundary of Brixia, and around the Bergamasque region—whatever within those boundaries, or belonging to or appearing to pertain to that valley from ancient times and at present, was seen to have rendered public revenues and revenues to the palace, or may thereafter have fallen within our fisc.

In the same manner, with its entirety, just as we have written concerning the boundary of Sermionum, we have handed over all these things as well.

In addition, we attach to the aforesaid holy place the hospice situated between the Po and the Ticino, constructed in honor of Saint Mary near the city of Pavia, at the place called Wahan, together with the villa of Solarium and all their appurtenances, as well as one small house within Pavia—that is, with lands, houses, churches, buildings, resident inhabitants, slaves, tenant farmers, vineyards, woods, fields, meadows, pastures, waters and their courses, movable and immovable property, everything in every respect.

All the things named above, with their boundaries, limits, and appurtenances, we have from the present day granted perpetually to the aforesaid basilica of Saint Martin and its rectors, and with the fullest goodwill bestowed them as an increase. Therefore we ordered this precept of our authority to be written, so that from this day the party of the aforesaid basilica of Saint Martin and its rector may have, hold, and possess the things stated above, and so that they may contribute to that house of God as an increase from the alms of our reward.

Let no one invested with judicial authority, or any other person, at any time presume to disturb the aforesaid Abbot Gulfard, his successors, or their agents concerning the aforesaid possessions, or to raise any claim against them contrary to the order of justice. Rather, let this gift of our authority remain there under the firmest legal right.

And so that this authority of ours may be held more securely and be better preserved in our times and those to come, we have decreed that it be strengthened below by our own hand.

**Sign of Charles, the most glorious king.**

Hitherius: I have reviewed.

Data 17 Kalends of August, in the sixth year and the first of our reign. Done at the city of Pavia, prosperously in God’s name. Amen.

## XVIII. Charter of Charlemagne for the Dionysian monastery (774)

*(From D. Bouquet, same work.)*

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards, and patrician of the Romans, illustrious man.

Since, as Scripture admonishes, each person ought to prepare himself steadfastly so that, when he comes before the heavenly Judge, he may deserve to hear that gracious voice of the Lord: “Come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25:34)—whereat all the righteous will rejoice—therefore, wisely, as we believe, considering how, from the earthly goods which heavenly grace has generously deigned to bestow upon us in this age, we ought at least to give something to God’s saints and to Christ’s poor, so that we may obtain the mercy of the Most High, for this reason we cede, for the remedy of our soul and for our father of good memory, the late Pippin, to the monastery of the lord martyr Dionysius, where that precious lord rests bodily with his companions, and where our aforesaid lord and father is seen to be buried, and where Folleradus is known to be abbot.

We wish the following to be ceded to the aforesaid holy place: namely, the estates which that same lord, our father, formerly transferred through our hands to that house of God, called Faverolas, situated in the county of Madriacum, and Noronte in the county of Chartres, with their entirety and appurtenances, for that monastery and the monks dwelling there, and for providing lights and the support of the poor. We establish this as it was possessed by our vassal Audegarius.

Moreover, [we cede] the forest belonging to them, called Equalina, with its forest-keepers and the definite boundaries marked within it: namely, toward the county of Madriacum, the boundary runs from *Lemma* to Petra Ficta, then to the Molariae above Victriacum, then to Mons Presbyteri, then to Condatum, as far as Cuculosa.

**Note:** Leuwa is read by Dubletus, who interprets the word as meaning a boundary; Mabillon reads *Lemnia*, that is, “forest.” See Du Cange under this word.

The second boundary, toward the county of Pinciacum, runs to Condonaria, to the Vennas as far as Aureum Vallum, then to Levicia.

The third boundary, toward the county of Paris, runs from Ulfarciaca to Campus Dominicus, then to Campus Wilgeverti, then to Sarnetum as far as the cell of Saint Germanus; then, along the road that leads to the old monastery toward the county of Stampes, the boundary runs to Rosbacium, then to Frumenterilis; from there, toward the county of Chartres, the boundary runs to Putioli, then to Pucilitti, then to Hitlini-villare, then to Wadastivilla at the pear tree, then to the Frona that belonged to Stephanus, then to Calmons; then, along the road that leads to Helmoretum, to Longus-lucus and Senone-valle above Nivigella.

All the aforesaid, with its entire substance and integrity, as it is known to have been possessed until now by our fisc, including animals of both sexes, deer, and roe deer—whose hides we order to be used for covering the books of that sacred place. We also establish that the bodies of the sick brothers are to be restored and strengthened for a time from the aforesaid hunting.

Therefore we cede and donate to that holy place the aforesaid estates, Faverolas and Norontes, together with the forest Equalina and the things mentioned above, with lands, houses, buildings, inhabitants, slaves, vineyards, woods, fields, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, movable and immovable property, mills established upon that lordship or wishing to be established there; likewise, with the markets held in those estates and with those gathering there for the sake of trading.

Thus no count, viscount, vicar, centenarius, or any collector exercising judicial power may dare to exact tolls or fines, seize game without the abbot’s permission, set snares or traps, or impose or add any customary charge. Rather, with every obstacle of disturbance removed, and with the boldness of hostile persons kept away from the estates and markets, everything in its entirety, as stated, shall remain for the aforesaid holy place with complete integrity and immunity. Whatever at the present time appears to be our possession or lordship there shall belong to the aforesaid monastery and its rectors, who shall have, hold, and possess it in our time and in future times.

And so that they may be more pleased diligently to implore the Lord’s mercy for us and for our lord and father, we have confirmed this authority below with our own hand and ordered it sealed below with our ring.

**Sign of Charles, most glorious king.**

Wigbaldus, in the place of Hitherius, recognized and subscribed.

Given in the month of December, in the first year of our reign.

**Note:** Charles the Great was already king of the Lombards, as the title of this charter indicates; hence the first year of the reign must be understood as the first year of his Italian kingdom. Ruinart, who prepared the second edition of *De Re Diplomatica*, says that he transcribed this diploma from the original. Mabillon, however, in book 24 of the *Benedictine Annals*, no. 52, testifies that among the genuine examples of his diplomas it reads “in the seventh year and the first.”  

Done at the public palace of Salmimciacum, prosperously in God’s name. Amen.

## XIX. Diploma of Charlemagne for the monastery of Leprah, in the diocese of Strasbourg, founded by Fulrad, abbot of Saint Dionysius (774, 14 September)

**Note:** This diploma was previously published by Dubletus, *Antiquités de Saint-Denis*, book 3, p. 707; Cointius, *Ecclesiastical Annals of the Franks*, vol. 6, p. 84; Félibien, *History of Saint-Denis*, *Proofs*, no. 50, p. 34; Bouquet, in *Writers of Frankish History*, vol. 5, p. 725; and Hartzheim, *Councils of Germany*, vol. 1, p. 235, but everywhere it is found incorrectly. Here we give the charter as it was communicated by D. La Forcade, transcribed from the original. Besides ours, another copy of the same diploma exists in the archive of Saint-Denis; in certain respects it differs from the original. We indicate its principal variant readings in the notes.

*(From Grandidier, History of Strasbourg.)*

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards, illustrious man.

**Note:** The authors of the new *Diplomatica*, vol. 4, p. 627 and following, demonstrate that it was customary to begin diplomas with such expressions as “for,” “therefore,” “accordingly,” and so forth.

Whatever we appropriately grant or confirm to venerable holy places out of love for God, we confidently believe, without doubt, will redound to us, under the Lord’s protection, for eternal blessedness. Therefore let your greatness or usefulness know how the venerable man Folradus, abbot, represented to the clemency of our reign that, in love and reverence for the most blessed saints Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius, he had built, or constructed anew from its foundations, a cell on his own property in the county of Alsace, at a place called Fulradovilare, within the boundaries of Audoldovilare.

**Note:** A second copy of this diploma has, instead of “Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius,” “Dionysius, or Privatus.”

**Note:** Fulradovilare is the ancient name of the village now called Leberau or Lièvre, in Lorraine, in the territory of Saint-Dié, about three leagues from Sélestat. It received the name Fulradovilare from Fulrad himself, who, as his testament shows, possessed extensive estates in Alsace.

**Note:** Audoldovilare is the ancient name of the present small town in Lorraine which, because of the relics of Saint Hippolytus brought there from Rome by Fulrad, is called Saint-Hippolyte, contracted as Sant-Bilt. Fulradovilare is said to lie within the boundaries of Audoldovilare, for Lebraha is only a mile from Saint-Hippolyte.

He had built the cell, or constructed it anew, and intended thereafter, with the Lord’s help and the assistance of good men, to continue building it, so that the most blessed martyr Hippolytus might lie buried there in body.

**Note:** This cell of Fulrad is the priory of Saint Alexander, which Alexander VI united in 1502 to the collegiate church of Saint George at Nancy; its revenues now belong to the primatial church.

**Note:** The body of Saint Hippolytus, first buried at Audoldovilare by Saint Fulrad, had already many years earlier been transferred to the abbey of Saint-Denis.

**Note:** A second copy of this diploma reads as follows: “The martyr Hippolytus rests there bodily, and so that the monks may live there and appropriately observe their rule and order. Therefore we…”  

Therefore, for the Lord’s name and the salvation of our soul, so that our reward may remain eternal, and also at the petition of our faithful Fulradus, we donate to the aforesaid place certain wooded lands from our fisc in the county of Alsace, at Qwningirhaim, for the use and support of the servants of God dwelling there, in love of the blessed saints Dionysius and Privatus, and also Saint Hippolytus; and we wish the donation to remain perpetual.

That is, our forest and woodland mentioned above:

**Note:** The names of places in this diploma are read with considerable corruption. They are expressed more distinctly in the original charter of Emperor Lothar, from the year 854.

**Note:** Or Lebraha, French *Lièvre*, German *Leber*: a stream whose waters join those of the Scara (Scher).

On one side, from the Laimaha, where the cell of Bobolinus is situated, and from there along the place where the Aetsinisbach enters the Laimaha; then along the Aetsinisbach to the place where it rises; then to Nannents; thereafter across the mountain to Rumbach.

**Note:** Now a Lorraine village called l’Allemand-Rombach, in the royal bailiwick of Saint-Dié and the parish of Leborau. The primatial church of Nancy enjoys one-third of the tithes there; the remainder was granted to the parish priest of Leborau.

Then to Tludimisberch, then to the other Rumbach, then to Bureberch; from there to the third Rumbach.

**Note:** Now a Lorraine village called Petit-Rombach, in the parish of Sainte-Croix, whose parish priest receives one half of the tithes; the aforesaid primatial church receives the other half.

**Note:** Now Grand-Rombach, a small village in the bailiwick of Saint-Dié and the parish of Sainte-Croix; concerning it, see the note above on Petit-Rombach.

Then it proceeds to Achinis regni.

**Note:** Now the village of La Hingrie, situated in the parish of Leborau, a league from l’Allemand-Rombach.

From there into the forest, through Ducias and the boundaries; then along the Laimaha river into the valley of the Two Banks, through the territories of Gasmaringa and Odeldinga, as far as Ophanpol; from there along the Laimaha river on the other bank to where the Audenbach flows into the Laimaha; then along that little river to the foot of Stophanberch, through the valley.

**Note:** Perhaps Stemberg or Stampemont, an Alsatian village in the parish of Colroy.

Along the entirety of that mountain as far as Stagnbah; from there through Rivadmarca, Odeldinga, and Gasmaringa; and from there along the boundaries as far as Ophampol.

All these places named above, territories, and boundaries, wholly and entirely within the aforesaid limits, together with fishing and the capture of whatever birds, we grant to that holy place; and for the needs of the church we wish this to be granted. We order that throughout that entire forest, outside the boundaries specified, they shall have pasture for their livestock by our indulgence.

For we command and order that none of our faithful, nor anyone exercising judicial power, presume to disturb or condemn that house of God or its rectors concerning the places specified, or to act against the order of justice—neither you, nor your juniors, nor your successors. Rather, for the increase of our reward and the stability of our reign, let this grant increase in the lights of that church and in the support of the servants of God dwelling there in future times, so that the congregation may be more pleased diligently to implore the Lord’s mercy for us, for our wife, and for our offspring.

**Note:** Hildegard, whom Charles married in 771 after repudiating Harmengarde. See Einhard in Bouquet, vol. 5, p. 96.

**Note:** Charles the son was born in 772; Rotrude the daughter in 773; Adélaïde the daughter in 774.

And so that this authority may be firmer and better preserved through the ages, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with our ring.

**Sign of Charles, most glorious king.**

Wigbaldus, in the place of Hitherius, recognized.

Given on 18 Kalends of October, in the sixth year, while our lord Charles, most glorious king, was reigning.

**Note:** In the same year and month, Charlemagne issued a diploma for the monastery of Fulda, “given on 8 Kalends of October, in the sixth year of his reign; done at the public palace of Düren,” as Schannat reports in the *Proofs of the Diocese of Fulda*, no. 4.

Done at Düren, at the public palace.

## XX. Diploma of Charlemagne granted to Heddon, bishop of Strasbourg, by which he declares the people of the Church of Strasbourg exempt from all tolls (775, December)

*(From Grandidier, History of Strasbourg.)*

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards, and patrician of the Romans, to all bishops, abbots, dukes, counts, household officers, vicars, centenarii, all our envoys traveling about, and everyone endowed with judicial power.

It ought to be the greatest care and concern of kings diligently to examine what is requested for the needs of the churches of God and not to deny them suitable and opportune benefits, but to put into effect, in God’s name, whatever is undertaken for God’s sake.

Therefore let your greatness or usefulness know how the venerable man Etto, bishop of Strasbourg, came and petitioned the clemency of our reign that, wherever the people of the aforesaid church—which was built in honor of holy Mary, Mother of God and ever-virgin—might travel or return through cities, villages, castles, crossings, or ports, by water or by land, that is, with carts and pack animals, for the sake of trade, no administrator of the public treasury should exact any toll from them.

**Note:** *Carra*, or wagon, in French *chariot* or *charrette*. *Saumaria*, that is, pack horses, in French *chevaux de somme*. See Du Cange, *Glossary*, vol. 2, p. 346, and vol. 6, p. 55.

Therefore, by this precept of our authority, we have decreed—and order it to remain perpetual—that none of you may exact from the goods which the people of the Church of Strasbourg, by God’s favor, transport throughout our kingdoms for purposes of trade, whether by water or by land, with carts and pack animals, wherever they may go through cities, villages, castles, crossings, or ports—except at Quentowicus, Dorestad, and Sclusas—any toll, bank toll, port toll, bridge toll, greeting toll, turf toll, wheel toll, meal toll, pasture toll, laud toll, timber toll, dust toll, any other exaction, any census, or any return-payment; nor may anyone presume to cause disturbance or hindrance to the people who conduct that trade.

**Note:** Quentowicus, that is, the settlement at Quentum, which Baluzius, in his notes on the letter of Lupus, abbot of Ferrières, concludes to be identical with the monastery of Saint Josse, commonly called Saint-Josse-sur-Mer, in Picardy. The *Chronicle of Fontenelle*, chapter 15, for the year 788, says: “Geroldus was appointed administrator of royal affairs by Charlemagne for many years, exacting tributes and tolls in various ports and cities, especially at Quentawich.” Quentowicus no longer exists, and no ruins remain by which its true and certain location can be identified. Some say it was Quent-le-Vieil, others Saint-Josse-sur-Mer, and others Berck. It is probable, according to a dissertation inserted in the *Verdun Journal* for January 1758, pp. 35–39, that Quentowicus was ancient Britain, which Nicolas Sanson suspects to have been the present Abbeville.

**Note:** Dorestad, now Batavodurum, a town in Holland in the duchy of Guelders, called by the Dutch Batenburg or Wijk bij Duurstede. See Ortelius, *Geographical Thesaurus*, and Vosgien, *Portable Geographical Dictionary*.

**Note:** A port of Flanders called l’Écluse or Sluis.

**Note:** *Ripaticum*, “bank duty,” was a tax paid on riverbanks, either for maintaining the embankments, for goods displayed on the banks, or for permission to use the banks to transport boats. Du Cange, *Glossary*, vol. 5, p. 14[lacuna]3.

**Note:** *Portaticum*, “portage,” was a toll exacted at the passage of gates. Du Cange, vol. 5, p. 674.

**Note:** *Pontaticum*, “bridge duty,” was a tax on bridges, according to Du Cange, vol. 5, p. 664; Bouquet, in *Writers of Frankish History*, vol. 6, p. 755, also explains it as a toll on ships passing under bridges.

**Note:** *Salutaticum*, in French *droit d’heureux abord*, was the right to exact greetings, gifts, or payments made beyond the ordinary census or customary payment. Du Cange, vol. 6, p. 107. I would call *salutaticum*, if one may speak so, “a sol per livre.”

**Note:** *Cespitaticum* was a tax for maintaining a road with turf. Du Cange, *Glossary*, vol. 2, p. 525. The same name was also given to a tax assessed on turf or rented lands. Bouquet, vol. 4, p. 765.

**Note:** *Rotaticum*, “cartage or wheel duty,” was a tax paid for the damage which wagons usually caused on public roads. See Du Cange, vol. 5, p. 1511, and Eckart, *Commentaries on the Affairs of Eastern France*, vol. 1, p. 569.

**Note:** *Cenaticum*, perhaps corresponding to the French *étapes*, was food or refreshment which soldiers demanded from their hosts while traveling to their stations. Du Cange, vol. 2, p. 724.

**Note:** *Pastio* was a levy for pannage and the right of pasture. The same, vol. 5, p. 241.

**Note:** *Laudaticum*, perhaps from *Lode*, was a type of tax imposed on ships; Du Cange does not specify its nature. The same, vol. 4, p. 77.

**Note:** *Trabaticum* was a type of tax, perhaps for transporting or supplying beams for public works. The same, vol. 6, p. 1207.

**Note:** A kind of tax unknown to Du Cange, vol. 5, p. 979. Goldastus thinks it was a tax paid for road labor and for dust brought onto the royal road.

**Note:** Or “any exaction.” Du Cange, vol. 4, p. 1313.

**Note:** By this term every tax or toll in general is designated, whether census or payment. The same, vol. 2, p. 485, and vol. 5, pp. 1207 and 1215.

Rather, by this authority of ours, let them be permitted, without opposition or hindrance from anyone, to travel and return freely and safely throughout our entire kingdom, by God’s favor, wherever it may be necessary for them, with ships and other vehicles. And if they spend time in any place, or buy or sell there, absolutely no toll is to be exacted from them, as stated above.

And so that this authority may be firmer and better preserved through the ages, we have decreed that it be strengthened below with our own hand and ordered it sealed below with our ring.

**Sign of Charles, most glorious king.**

**Note:** Wencker believes this Rado the chancellor to be the same as Rachio, who later became bishop of Strasbourg; see his *Collections of the Archive*, p. 228. We have already stated that his opinion is unproven.

Rado, in the place of Hitherius, recognized.

Given in the month of December, in the eighth year and the second of our reign. Done at the villa of Scalistatum, at the public palace, prosperously in God’s name. Amen.

**Note:** Now the town of Sélestat in Alsace; Charlemagne was staying at Sélestat at that time. Regino, under the year 775, says: “Charles celebrated the Nativity of the Lord in a villa called Sélestat in Alsace.” The annals known as the Loisellian Annals, in Bouquet, vol. 5, p. 39, and the Frankish annals known as the Tilian Annals, in Duchesne, vol. 2, p. 14, say the same.

## XXI. Precept of Charlemagne by which he donates the estate of Luzarches to the Dionysian monks (775)

*(From D. Bouquet, same work.)*

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards, to all our faithful, present and future.

Since, as Scripture admonishes, each person ought to prepare himself steadfastly so that, when he comes before the heavenly Judge, he may deserve to hear that gracious voice of the Lord, at which all the righteous will rejoice because of their good works, therefore, wisely, as we believe, considering how, from the earthly goods which heavenly grace has generously deigned to bestow upon us in this age, we ought at least to give something to the poor, so that we may obtain the mercy of the Most High, for this reason we donate, for the remedy of our soul, to the church of Saint Dionysius—where that precious lord rests bodily with his companions and where the venerable man Fulradus appears to preside, and which, by Christ’s favor, we have newly built and have now ordered to be dedicated with great splendor—the following, wishing it to be donated perpetually to that holy place:

Our estates called Luzarcha, situated in the county of Paris on the river called … [lacuna], together with the church in honor of Saints Cosmas and Damian; and another estate of ours called Masciacum, situated in the county of Meaux, with all their boundaries and appurtenances.

They are to benefit that monastery and the monks serving there in their entirety, for the provision of lights for that church and for the support of the poor. The aforesaid estates shall increase in benefit, namely with lands, houses, buildings, inhabitants, slaves, vineyards, woods, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, mills, movable and immovable property, as stated above. The aforesaid monastery and its rectors shall have, hold, and possess everything in its entirety, and shall have the liberty in our time and in future times to do with it whatever they wish, so that the servants of God may be more pleased to pray day and night more earnestly to the Lord’s mercy for us and for our descendants.

And so that this authority may be firmer and better preserved through the ages, we have decreed that it be strengthened below with our own hand and ordered it sealed below with our ring.

**Sign of Charles, most glorious king.**

Wigbaldus, in the place of Hitherius, recognized.

Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of March, in the seventh year and the first of our reign. Done in the monastery of Saint Dionysius.

## XXII. Diploma of Charlemagne concerning the immunity of the Dionysian monastery (775)

*(From D. Bouquet, Collection of Histories.)*

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards, to all our faithful, present and future.

Let your greatness or industry know that Fulradus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Dionysius the martyr, where that precious lord rests bodily, brought before us grants or confirmations of earlier kings, and of our lord and father, the late King Pippin, showing that for a long time they had granted to that house of God all tolls from the estates of the aforesaid church, from the people who appear to dwell upon its lands, and from its merchants who are known to travel under the protection of that house of God.

When we found in their confirmations or precepts that this had been granted for a long time, we therefore renew and confirm it by this present authority of ours: throughout our kingdoms, by God’s favor—France and Italy—whether concerning ships traveling up or down all rivers, or carts and their pack animals, or their people and merchants who appear to travel under the protection of that house of God, wherever and in whatever county they arrive, whether in cities, castles, villages, ports, public bridges, or other markets; and whether concerning their people who appear to dwell upon their lands, or their estates and fields, or people who come from outside to their estates to trade or buy wine—no toll, exclusion duty, tithe, bargaining duty, wheel duty, weighing duty, turf duty, dust duty, greeting duty, transfer duty, or any other charge shall be exacted.

Nor shall anything be exacted from their ships or carts, their pack animals, or what their people carry on their backs; nor from their merchants who are known to travel under the protection of that house of God; nor in their estates or fields; nor from people who come from outside to their estates to trade or buy wine. Neither for our work, nor yours, nor that of your juniors or successors, shall any toll or exclusion duty be exacted in any way within the kingdoms of France and Italy or anywhere else; nor shall you demand or exact the tithe, except, as we have said, according to what they appear to possess in their documents, within our kingdoms, by God’s favor, as it has been granted and bestowed.

And so that this precept may be firmer, we have decreed that it be strengthened below and ordered it sealed with our ring.

**Sign of Charles, most glorious king.**

Wigbaldus, in the place of Hitherius, recognized.

Given on the day before the Ides of March, in the seventh year and the first of our reign. Done at the public palace of Carisiacum, prosperously in God’s name. Amen.

## XXIII. Precept of Charlemagne concerning the immunity of the monastery of Saint-Denis (775)

*(From D. Bouquet, same work.)*

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards, and patrician of the Romans.

At the beginning of our reign, with the Lord’s help wholly aiding our exaltation, we have kept watch with devotion; and, for that good work, with the counsel of the bishops, elders, and nobles of ours, we ought to renew immunity for the confirmation of our kingdom, for reward, and for the attainment of eternal life—and so we have done.

It is therefore fitting that royal clemency, among other petitions, receive with gracious hearing what is written for salvation and requested for the divine name, and without doubt bring it to fulfillment, so that eternal things may be acquired from the perishable goods of the present age, according to the Lord’s command: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of unrighteousness” (Luke 16:9). Therefore, according to that saying, we ought to purchase heavenly things with earthly things from the mammon of unrighteousness; and while we bestow suitable benefits upon holy places, we trust that the Lord will be our rewarder for this.

Therefore the venerable man Fulradus, abbot of the church of our personal patron, the lord martyr Dionysius, where that precious lord rests bodily, petitioned the clemency of our reign. He stated that, from the earlier kings and for a long time, complete immunity had been granted to the estates of the aforesaid holy church; he affirmed that he held those precepts in his hands and that this immunity had remained inviolably preserved until now.

For this reason he asked that, by our authority, for the security of the matter, we should renew and confirm this immunity concerning that holy place and the people who, together with their property, entrust or donate themselves to that church, according to what the earlier kings had granted or confirmed for that church through their authorities.

Therefore let your greatness or usefulness know that, out of reverence for that holy place and for the peace of those serving God there, we have willingly granted this anew and confirmed it in every respect.

Accordingly, by this precept, which we specifically decree and wish to remain perpetual, we order that neither we, nor our juniors or successors, nor anyone equipped with judicial authority, may at any time presume to enter the estates of the aforesaid church of Saint Dionysius—wherever they may be, in whatever counties, within the kingdoms which by God’s favor we have acquired in Italy, namely Lombardy, or the Val Tellina, which in our own time we have transferred to that house of God, and which the portion of that monastery appears to possess or control, or which has been granted there by God-fearing people through lawful documents, or may thereafter be added and transferred there—for the hearing of cases, the taking of sureties, the exaction of fines, the provision of lodgings or requisitions, or the demanding of any payments.

Rather, whatever our fisc could hope to receive from it, we have granted in its entirety, together with all fines, for the increase of our reward.

**[Editorial correction in the source: “concessis” for “concessimus.”]**

Thus, as stated, having examined the precepts of the earlier kings and what our present authority appears to contain, whatever that holy place is proved to possess from the present day onward, as we have said, and whatever may later be added or donated there by God-fearing people or by us, or whoever may justly and reasonably hand himself over with all his property and transfer or confirm his possessions through lawful documents, shall remain from the present day under complete immunity, quiet and secure.

And, as stated, whatever our fisc might perhaps have hoped to receive from it shall, for the lights, support, or nourishment of the poor of that monastery, be wholly and entirely granted and bestowed forever by our royal decree, so that they may be more pleased to pray earnestly for the stability of our reign and our peace, and for all our peoples, to the mercy of the Lord.

And so that this authority may remain perpetually firm and inviolable concerning that holy place in our time and in future times, may be preserved and maintained unharmed through the ages, and may be more readily believed by all judges, we have taken care to outline it by the notation of our own hand.

**Sign of Charles, most glorious king.**

Wigbaldus, in the place of Hitherius, recognized.

**Note:** A similar precept was issued in October, in the eleventh year and the fifth of his reign, that is, in the year 778.

Given on the day before the Ides of March, in the seventh year and the first of our reign. Done at the palace of Carisiacum, prosperously in God’s name. Amen.

## XXIV. Precept of Charlemagne by which he confirms to the Dionysian monastery various possessions recovered under King Pippin (775)

*(From Mabillon, *De Re Diplomatica*.)*

[Col. 0943A]

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards, to all bishops, abbots, dukes, counts, household officers, royal officials, vicars, centenarii, and all our envoys traveling about, as well as to all who possess judicial authority:

It is the supreme care and concern of kings to examine diligently whatever priests request for the benefit of the churches of God, and not to deny them appropriate and suitable benefits, but to bring to fulfillment, in God’s name, whatever is undertaken for the sake of God. [Col. 0943B]

Let your greatness—that is, all of you—therefore know that the venerable man Fulrad, abbot of the monastery of our special patron, Saint Dionysius the martyr, where that precious lord rests bodily, presented to the clemency of our reign a petition and showed us, for rereading, a decree of our lord and father, the late King Pippin. It contained an account of the possessions of Saint Dionysius which, over a long period, had been acquired or donated through the munificence of kings and through the contributions of Christian-minded and good men, but which had been taken away or removed from that estate by wicked or evil men through unjust greed, malicious contrivance, the negligence or lukewarmness of abbots, or a failure of judgment.

Accordingly, the monks and the estate’s agents, together with the royal decrees and other written instruments concerning these possessions, had repeatedly appeared before our father in the palace and before his dukes to state their case, accompanied by several men who were holding those possessions improperly. Out of reverence for Saint Dionysius the martyr and from love of God, our father ordered their charters to be carefully reread. At their request he sent his envoys Wiching and Ludion through various districts, together with those instruments, to inquire and investigate the matter. Wherever they found their justice established, wherever the monks and agents produced lawful documents, wherever the estate of Saint Dionysius had thereby been endowed, or wherever possessions had been given or contributed there by God-fearing men, and wherever the estate had been lawfully and reasonably endowed under the law, but had afterward been taken from it by malicious contrivance, they were to restore them to the monks. This they indeed did.

These were the places identified in various districts: in the district of Fanmart, the cell called Cruce, which belongs to the fisc of Solemnio, and which the late King Hildbert granted to the estate of Saint Dionysius by his decree; and Avisinas, which Vassus held from our father; likewise, in the district of Brabant, the places called Scancia and Cambrione; likewise, in the district of Brie, the place called Linariolas; and in Melcianus, the places named Nartiliago and Coconiago; and in the Beauvais district, the places called Pitito-villare, Masciago, Saciago, Ansino-villare, Thedegario-villare, Ambrico-curte, Ebroaldo-curte, and Gellis; likewise, in the district of Camliacum, the place called Boderovillo and Nialla; likewise, in the district of Vexin, Upper and Lower Bacivus and Madriu, which Gabbifrisio held as a benefice; likewise, in the district of Madriacum, Vinias, Camapio and Niventis, Villa-nova, Rosbacio, Sigrancio, and Berane-curte; likewise, in the district of Telleau, the places named Pictus, Macerias, Verno, Fircera, Potio, Bodalca, Brittene-valle, Artiliaco, Agusta, Rausero, Crisonarias, and Uvariaco.

Likewise, in the district of Vimnau, the places named Marca, Malcha, Malchis, Avisinas, Rodeno, Rodalca, Sodicola, Vidriaco, Horona, and Arcas; likewise, in the district of Paris, Tabernas; likewise, in the district of Amiens, the places called Pisciago and Adsalto; and various other places in various districts, both greater and lesser, which it was unnecessary to list individually.

Thus that estate now appears to have been endowed, so that, just as the possessions were found and investigated by them, and the monks and agents received them on behalf of Saint Dionysius, from that time onward, to the present day, the estate of God, together with its monks and agents, may hold those possessions vindicated and secured for the present and future ages. [Col. 0944B]

Accordingly, the aforesaid Abbot Fulrad and the monks of that holy monastery, who are known to reside and lead their lives in that estate of God, asked us to confirm them anew in these matters for the future by a decree sealed with our own hand. We have done so. Since it is established that they vindicated and received those possessions lawfully and justly in the palace before our father, we decree that both the abbot and his successors shall always hold them, for the benefit described above, as belonging to that holy estate, for providing lamps, clothing for the monks, and other benefits, as well as receiving the poor and pilgrims. May this always give them greater pleasure to pray unceasingly, day and night, for us, for our sons, and for the stability of the Frankish kingdom, and to implore the mercy of the Lord. And, as they promised us, each day they shall recite our name both in the Masses and in their private prayers at the tomb of Saint Dionysius. If thereafter we are able to discover further rights belonging to them, we shall willingly restore them.

And so that this our authority and decree, which they requested from us concerning that estate of God, may benefit it and remain unshaken and firm for the present and future ages, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Charles, the most glorious king.

Wigbald, acting in place of Hitherius, examined and subscribed.

Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of July, in the seventh year and the second of our reign. Issued at the public palace of Carisiac, successfully, in the name of God.

## XXV. Judgment of Charles the Great, by which the monastery of Placicium in the district of Pincerais is assigned to the monastery of Saint-Denis against Herchenrad, the elder bishop of Paris (775)

*(From D. Bouquet, Collection of Histories.)*

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards, illustrious man.

Royal dignity is elevated to its summit when, according to the words of accusation and response, it wisely deliberates the disputes of all parties against one another, so that, under God, power remains with the king to order all things that must be ordered with awe.

Accordingly, when, in God’s name, we had taken our seat at the villa of Dury in our palace to hear everyone’s cases and to determine just judgments, the apostolic father in Christ, Herchenrad, bishop of the city of Paris, came there and brought a complaint against Abbot Fulrad. He claimed that Fulrad was unjustly and improperly retaining for the monastery of Saint Dionysius the monastery of Placicium, constructed in honor of Saint Mary and Saint Peter in the district of Pincerais. A Frankish man named Aderald had donated it by his written instrument to the estate of Saint Mary, Saint Stephen, and Saint Germanus.

But Abbot Fulrad was present and answered as follows: he had never retained the monastery of Placicium improperly or unjustly for the monastery of Saint Dionysius, because, he said, a Frankish man named Hagadeus had donated the monastery of Placicium by his written instrument, with full legal title, to the monastery of Saint Dionysius. By that transfer, the monastery of Placicium had a stronger claim to adhere to the estate of Saint Dionysius than to be restored by Bishop Herchenrad to the estate of Saint Mary, Saint Stephen, and Saint Germanus.

They affirmed that they had the written instruments in their hands and produced them in our presence for examination. We also learned with certainty from both parties the facts of this case. With the mercy of Christ cooperating in divine matters, and in accordance with longstanding custom—which they themselves willingly accepted—we ordered judgment to be rendered: since the dispute between the two parties could not be resolved by those written instruments, their men were to go to the judgment of God and stand at the cross by the proper procedure. These were Aderamnus, on behalf of Saint Dionysius and Abbot Fulrad, and Corellus, on behalf of Saint Mary, Saint Stephen, and Saint Germanus, and of Bishop Herchenrad.

They were seen to stand in our chapel, while the Mass was being celebrated by the presbyter Harnaldus. At that hour, under the protection of God’s divine right hand, almighty God revealed his just judgment: Corellus, the man of the aforesaid Bishop Herchenrad, appeared fearful and defeated at that judgment of God, at the cross. Then Bishop Herchenrad, in our presence and that of our nobles, acknowledged and conceded that neither he nor his church of Saint Mary, Saint Stephen, or Saint Germanus possessed any right by which they could have the monastery of Placicium.

Therefore, together with our faithful men—namely the counts Ghaerard, Bernard, Radulf, Hilderad, Ermenald, Hebroin, Theudoald, and Agmo; and Haltbert, Laumbert, Haerteric, and Count Anselm of our palace, as well as many others—we judged as follows: since the aforesaid man of Saint Dionysius and Abbot Fulrad, named Adelramnus, had defeated at that judgment of God, at the cross, the aforementioned man of Saint Mary, Saint Stephen, and Saint Germanus, namely Corellus, and since Corellus had appeared fearful and defeated at that judgment of God, we therefore order that, since we know this case to have been conducted and completed in this manner, the aforesaid Abbot Fulrad shall hold the aforesaid monastery of Placicium, together with its dependencies and whatever appears to belong to it, vindicated and secured by firmest right for the monastery of Saint Dionysius against the aforementioned Bishop Herchenrad, his church of Saint Mary, Saint Stephen, and Saint Germanus, and their successors. Henceforth, without any further claim by Bishop Herchenrad or his successors, it shall remain settled, defined, and granted to them forever.

[Note: [Col. 0945D] This judgment is especially noteworthy because it mentions proof by the cross. The procedure was as follows: during the time of Mass, or while the Psalms and the Lord’s Prayer were being recited, two men appointed for the purpose stood at the cross with their arms extended. The side of the man who first became tired and lowered his arms, or whose arms began to tremble, was considered defeated. An excellent example of this rite appears in volume V of *Italia sacra*, column 611. See also other examples in Cange’s *Glossary* under the entry *Crucis*. Observe further from this passage that, in the time of Charles the Great, the church of Paris had, besides Saint Stephen, Saint Mary and Saint Germanus as patrons—the latter undoubtedly the bishop of Paris, who, after the solemn translation of his body from the tomb, was admitted among the patrons of his church. The same is read in the charter of Count Stephen for Bishop Inchadus, under Charles the Great, in the work of the distinguished Stephen Baluze, in his notes to the *Capitularies*, column 1061. Placicium, Plaisir, is a village not far from the town of Saint-Germain, in the forest of Ledia. See Dublet, p. 713. The notary has omitted here the regnal formula for the Lombard kingdom; such omissions occur occasionally, though rarely. Nor should it be omitted that two bishops of Paris named Ercanradus must be admitted, rather than one alone, as in the fuller *Gallia Christiana*: one the elder, reigning under Charles the Great and mentioned in this diploma; the other the younger, under Charles the Bald before Aeneas.]

Theudegarius examined and subscribed.

Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of August, in the seventh year of our reign, at the villa of Dury in the public palace, successfully, in the name of God. Amen.

## XXVI. Decree of Charles the Great donating certain estates to the monastery of Saint-Denis (775)

*(From D. Bouquet, Collection of Histories.)*

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards, and also patrician of the Romans.

Whatever we grant or confirm to the venerable places of the saints out of love for God, we trust will contribute to our reward and to the stability of our kingdom. [Col. 0947A] Therefore let all our faithful know that, for the name of the Lord and for the salvation of our soul, so that our reward may endure forever, we give to the estate of Saint Dionysius and Saint Privatus, where those precious saints rest bodily, Eadallago and Salona in the district of Salminis; the possessions of my property at Wastingas, which Adalbald handed over to my father, insofar as they appear to belong to that place; likewise, those manses which our father granted as a benefice to Fulrad; the estate of Infilicio, and the land and forest of one mansus at Abduxium; likewise another mansus in the villa of Ermerago, and the mansus at Almingas, and the manses at Carisiac, insofar as anything appears to belong to those manses.

I wish this donation to be perpetual, namely with lands, inhabitants, houses, buildings, manses, slaves, fields, forests, meadows, pastures, vineyards, waters and watercourses, movable and immovable property—in full and entirely, whatever appears to belong to the places named above. We give and hand over all of it to Saint Dionysius and Saint Privatus, and wish it to be granted to them in every respect.

Therefore we command and order that none of our faithful, nor anyone exercising judicial authority, presume in any way to disturb the aforesaid estates of God or their rectors concerning the possessions entered above, or to raise any claim against them. Rather, as we have said, may this benefit those holy places as an increase in the present and future ages. And so that this authority may be held more firmly and better preserved through the ages, we have decreed that it be strengthened below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with our ring.

Sign of Charles, the most glorious king.

Rado, acting in place of Hitherius, examined.

Given in the month of November, in the eighth year and the second of our reign. Issued at Theodone-villa, successfully, in the name of God. Amen.

## XXVII. Decree of Charles the Great for the monastery of Morbach

*(From D. Bouquet, same work.)*

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards.

It is fitting for royal clemency to lend a kindly ear to all, and especially to consider with devoted mind, for the benefit of souls, what we find to have been granted by preceding kings, our ancestors, to the places of the churches. We ought not to deny such benefits, by which we may deserve to share in the reward, but to confirm them with the strongest legal force through our decrees.

Accordingly, the venerable Amico, abbot by God’s gift of the monastery of the Pilgrims’ Dwelling, situated in the district of Alsace on the river Morbe, constructed in honor of Saint Leodegarius, Saint Peter the apostle, Saint Mary, and the other saints, where he is known to serve together with a great multitude of monks, presented to the clemency of our reign the following petition.

Our predecessors, he said, had once granted, through their charters subscribed by their own hands, full immunity for the villages of that holy church which it then possessed (the text reads *quod*; variant: *quas*)—both from the gifts of princes, including Eberhard, who founded that monastery as his alms, and from the generosity of the people of the district, as well as from whatever had previously been assigned there by God-fearing men. Thus no public judge might dare enter those villages or possessions of that church, either to hear cases, exact fines, make lodgings or requisitions, take sureties, distrain the church’s men for any cause, or demand any payment.

The aforesaid abbot Baldebertus, rector of that monastery, showed us that decree of our aforesaid predecessors (variant reading: *antecessorum, etc.*, “of predecessors, etc.”) and their confirmation for rereading, and asserted that this benefit had until now been preserved for that church. For the sake of firmness, he therefore asked our highness to confirm this anew, in general terms, for that monastery and its monks.

We have willingly granted and confirmed his petition in every respect, out of reverence for that place and so that we may deserve to share in its reward. Know, therefore, that we command that no public judge enter the possessions or resources of that church to hear cases, exact fines, make lodgings or requisitions, take sureties, distrain the church’s men—whether free or enslaved—who are seen to dwell on their (*eorum*) lands [variant: its (*ejus*) lands], or to reside there from the beginning (*initio*, reading uncertain), for any cause, or demand any payments.

Just as this benefit, granted to that church by the aforesaid predecessors of ours, has until now been preserved by the authority of earlier rulers, so henceforth, through our authority, it shall remain generally undisturbed. Whatever our fisc might otherwise have hoped to receive from it shall contribute to the increase of the lights of Saint Leodegarius, Saint Peter, and Saint Mary, and to the stability of our kingdom.

And so that this authority may remain valid for the present and future ages, we have strengthened it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with our ring.

Sign of Charles, the most glorious king.

Wigbald, acting in place of Hitherius, examined.

Given on the day before the Nones of April, in the seventh year and the first of our reign. Issued publicly at the palace of Carisiac, successfully, in the name of God. Amen.

## XXVIII. Decree of Charles the Great for the monastery of Flavigny (775)

*(From D. Bouquet, same work.)*

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards, and patrician of the Romans, illustrious man.

If we grant with devoted mind the requests of priests that concern the advancement of the churches, we trust that we thereby possess Jesus Christ, the recompense of all good things, as our reward.

The venerable Manasses, abbot of the monastery called Flavigny, in the district of Alsace, constructed in honor of our Lord Jesus Christ, Saint Peter, and Saint Praejectus, asked our highness that all toll throughout our kingdom from their merchants, and from all their men who appear to travel on behalf of that estate, should be exempt, so that they should not have to pay any toll in cities, markets, villages, settlements, bridges, or ports—neither the monks, nor their merchants, nor their men who appear to travel on behalf of that estate.

They shall pay neither *teloneum* (toll), nor *pontaticum* (bridge toll), *rodaticum* (road toll), *barganaticum* (market or trading toll), *pulveraticum* (dust or road toll), *mutaticum* (customs toll), *rivaticum* (river toll), *salutaticum*, *laudaticum*, or *tranaticum*, nor any toll on what their men appear to carry on their backs. Whatever should thereby be rendered to our fisc, we have granted entirely to that estate of God, for the lights, the support of the monks, and the reception of the poor, as an act of our almsgiving. We now wish it to be granted and remitted from the present time onward.

Thus, as we have said, we have granted and remitted perpetually to that estate of God, Saint Peter, and Saint Praejectus all tolls in cities, settlements, villages, bridges, and ports; bridge, road, market, dust, customs, river, *salutaticum*, *laudaticum*, and *tranaticum* tolls; the toll on what their men carry on their backs; and the tolls from their merchants and all their men.

Likewise, we grant to that estate of God all toll in their villages, on their lands, and within or outside their enclosures, whenever they come there, and on whatever is traded there, as described above, through our decree.

And so that this decree may be held more firmly and better preserved through the ages, we have decreed that it be confirmed below with our own hand.

Charles.

Given on the fifth day before the Nones of May, written by Rado at the palace of Theodone-villa, in the seventh year of the aforesaid lord Charles.

## XXIX. Decree of Charles the Great for the monastery of Saint Martin of Tours (775)

*(From D. Bouquet, same work.)*

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards, and patrician of the Romans.

It is fitting for the dignity of royal clemency to examine with diligent care all reasonable requests made by priests and not to deny them suitable or appropriate benefits, especially when they have been fully confirmed for the sake of God by the protective authority of earlier kings.

Therefore let all our faithful know that the venerable Hitherius, abbot of the monastery of Saint Martin, the distinguished confessor of Christ and our special patron of the city of Tours, where that precious saint rests bodily, made known to the serenity of our reign that his predecessor, Abbot Auttandus, had established certain villas which were to provide for the brothers each month throughout the entire year.

He asked the dignity of our excellence to confirm this very arrangement by a decree of our authority, for God’s sake and out of reverence for that saint, following the custom of his predecessors. We have consented to his petition and, venerating the patronage of Saint Martin, have granted this gift of indulgence with gratitude, just as the preceding kings had specially fulfilled it.

Accordingly, by this present decree we order and decree that the following places, with their dependencies, shall serve the brothers according to the assessments established for them:

Luggogalus, Curciacus, Lupiacus, Magittus, Catuntius, Tauciacus, Loona, Nobridius, Albiniacus, Mazoyalus, Podentiniacus, Castanelus, Camiliacus, Brionnus, Novientus, Genestolalus, Caniacus, Alnetus, Cadriacus, Merila, Delfiacus, Parriciacus, Prisciniacus, Cassiacus, Sadobria, Membriolas, Spicarias, Ortlucas, Sereonas, Salustriacus, Lausiacus, Axedus, Belcontus, Trinierobrus, Baion-villare, Nova-villa, Noëntus, Blasina, Pociacus, Talsiniacus, Brigogalus, Crucilia, Bladalaicus, Dociacus, Melciacus, Angularis Portus, Restis, and Antoniacus.

Likewise, by this decree of our gentleness we establish that the monastery’s cellarer shall be supplied for the brothers as arranged, so that at the appointed time he may provide fully for them. The porter, however, shall perform his service from his office in the month of December.

From the other villas, let firewood, grain, and birds be supplied in the customary manner, so that this may benefit us for the salvation of our soul and the growth of our kingdom, and so that those servants of God may thereafter serve God more freely and more effectively and pour out diligent prayers for the condition of the holy Church of God.

We therefore admonish all who will succeed us in the kingdom entrusted to us by God that, just as they wish their own ordinances to be preserved by their successors, so they should strive to preserve this constitution of our privilege inviolate, for the common salvation of us all.

And so that this authority may be held more firmly and better preserved in our present and future ages, we have strengthened it with our own hand and sealed it with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Charles, the most glorious king.

Rado, acting in place of Hitherius, examined.

Issued at the palace of Theodone-villa, successfully, in the name of God. Amen.

## XXX. Decree of Charles the Great for Bishop Angilram of Metz (775)

*(From the History of Metz, vol. III.)*

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards, illustrious man, to the dukes, counts, household officers, and all agents residing both beyond and this side of the Rhine, the Rhône, and the Loire, both present and future.

With the help of the Lord, who established us on the throne of the kingdom, we unquestionably believe that the growth and stability of our kingdom are advanced in God’s name if we bring to fulfillment the petitions of priests and the churches of God, when they disclose in our hearing just requests.

Therefore the apostolic man, our lord and father, Angilram, bishop of the holy church of Metz, produced for our examination decrees of our royal predecessors, strengthened by their own hands.
