We learned that they generally contained the following provision: for a long time his predecessors had enjoyed the benefit that no public judge should presume to enter the estates of the church of Metz and of Saint Stephen, our patron, or the basilicas constructed within that city, or within that diocese—including the monasteries, villages, and castles belonging or subject to it—or cause any harm there.

No one was to summon their men before public courts or hearings, or presume to condemn them by any malicious device, exact fines or tolls, or impose any requisitions. Rather, in their private courts, the agents of that church were to render justice to each person according to the conditions of his case, and were to receive the truth from the others as well. Wherever those agents or the other men of the aforesaid church received fines, those fines were to benefit the holy places of Christ the bishop as an increase.

Likewise, if their men paid any fine for any offense, the fine that could thereby have been expected by the public treasury had been granted to those churches.

The aforesaid bishop therefore asked that our authority confirm this matter more fully, in God’s name, for himself and his church, and for the monasteries, castles, and villages belonging or subject to it. Know that we have granted and confirmed his petition with a willing heart, for the sake of God, out of reverence for those holy places, in consideration of his faith, and for the increase of our reward, and that we have granted it anew.

We command that whatever is known to belong to those churches—villages, houses, buildings, slaves, vineyards, forests, fields, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, inhabitants of either sex and every age, with their complete boundaries and their property intact—whether granted through the munificence of kings and queens, or assigned to the church of Saint Stephen, or to the other churches constructed under the city of Metz or in the dioceses of that bishop, through sales, donations, exchanges, transfers, written instruments, or any lawful means, and whatever the churches are presently seen to possess or control, shall by this our authority be fully confirmed and granted in God’s name to those churches, to the aforesaid bishop, to his abbots, and to their successors. [Col. 0951C]

We therefore command that neither you, nor your juniors or successors, enter the estates of that church, of the aforesaid bishop, or of his abbots; their monasteries, castles, and villages, whether beyond or this side of the Rhine, the Rhône, and the Loire; the aforesaid city of Metz; or their districts and dioceses, monasteries, or cells, with all the churches belonging or subject to them, to impose fines, tolls, *conjectos* (requisitions), *summutas* [variant: *sunniatas*] (transport requisitions), or other requisitions, to make any arrangements, or to cause any kind of harm by any device whatsoever—if you wish to have my favor graciously extended to you in all things.

It has pleased us to add the following in writing: concerning three matters—public military service, that is, our ban when it is publicly proclaimed, and the repair of watch-posts or bridges—those genuinely free men who are free and exempt in their own right, and who are known to dwell on the lands of that church, of that bishop, or of his abbot, if they should appear negligent in any respect concerning these three matters, shall answer for them before our judges, neither more nor less.

In all other respects, however, let them be preserved entirely under immunity, for the increase of our reward, so that they may benefit that estate of God.

And let the immunity granted by us or by our ancestral predecessors to the church of Saint Stephen, and to the aforesaid monasteries, castles, villages, districts, dioceses, and abbeys which appear to belong to that bishop, remain perpetually undisturbed and preserved. Thus may the bishop, the clergy, and the poor who hope for sustenance there be moved more fully to entreat the mercy of the Lord.

Since this immunity had always been preserved for a long time around that church, its basilicas, monasteries, villages, and dioceses under preceding kings, we have now, for the remedy of our soul and for eternal recompense, confirmed and granted it by our decree to the church of Saint Stephen, where his most sacred blood is seen to be alive. Whoever among our judges or anyone else should wish to oppose, violate, or alter this decree shall incur the wrath of the Triune Majesty and of all the saints whom that bishop and his abbots serve, and shall never be able to possess our favor.

Rather, let it be preserved in every way, at all times, under complete immunity by you and your successors, so that you may possess our favor, as we have said, graciously extended to you.

For the complete security of this matter, and so that it may remain unshaken forever, we have decreed that this authority be strengthened below with the marks of our hand, in God’s name.

Given on the eleventh day before the Kalends of February, in the seventh year and the first of our reign.

Issued at Carisiac, etc.

## XXXI. Diploma of Charles the Great confirming the privilege of Salona against the bishop of Metz (775)

*(From Mabillon, On Diplomatics.)*

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards, and patrician of the Romans.

Our serenity ought to grant justly and reasonably whatever our faithful request, in return for the service and loyalty which they have shown toward my father, King Pippin, and toward me.

Let all our faithful, present and future, know that Fulrad, chaplain of our palace and abbot of Saint Dionysius, came and reported to us a privilege issued on behalf of Saint Dionysius. A synodal council established it in the ninth year at Patris-Brunna, following the undertaking of Bishop Angilram and Archbishop Wilharius, concerning his property at the place called Salona, which is constructed in honor of the holy Mother of God and of the blessed martyrs, confessors, and virgins, where Saint Privatus the martyr and Saint Hilary the confessor are seen to rest.

We found it inserted in the privilege that neither Bishop Angilram nor his successors, nor the archdeacon, nor any envoy of his church of Metz, should exercise episcopal authority in that monastery, unless the abbot of Saint Dionysius requested that they conduct ordinations, administer chrism, or bless tablets.

We asked Bishop Angilram whether he ought to consent to this privilege. He did not deny it in any way; rather, just as his fellow bishops had established in the synodal council, so he consented, as the privilege itself clearly indicates.

Therefore we order that this decree and confirmation remain in force on behalf of Saint Dionysius, so that after this day no bishop—neither Angilram nor his successors—may interfere with that monastery. It shall remain regularly under the immunity and privilege of Saint Dionysius, like the other churches that appear to belong to the estate of Saint Dionysius. And the small plots which Angilram and Fulrad exchanged within the territory and boundaries of Salona [lacuna].

Likewise, by our permission and confirmation, without interference from the bishops of the church of Metz, Saint Dionysius, together with the monastery of Salona, shall remain under our protection and defense and under that of our nobles, on behalf of Saint Dionysius. Whatever was added or assessed there through royal exchanges, donations, or contributions from the people, and whatever Fulrad added to enrich that monastery from his own possessions, shall remain at all times under the immunity and defense of Saint Dionysius, confirmed by our authority.

May this give the congregation of Saint Dionysius, Saint Privatus, and Saint Hilary greater pleasure to implore attentively the mercy of the Lord for us, for them, and for our wife.

And so that this authority may be held more firmly and better preserved through the ages, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and sealed it with our ring.

Sign of Charles, the most glorious king.

The name and sign of the chancellor have been omitted.

Given on the [lacuna] day of December, in the tenth year of the reign of our lord Charles the king.

Issued at the public palace of Aachen, successfully, in the name of God. Amen.

## XXXII. Diploma of Charles the Great for the monastery of Prüm (775)

*(From D. Calmet, History of Lorraine.)*
Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards, and also patrician of the Romans.

To all bishops, abbots, dukes, counts, vicars, centenarians, [Col. 0954A] and our other faithful, both present and future, let it be known how our lord and father, Pippin, formerly king of blessed memory, appears to have built from new foundations the monastery called Prüm, in honor of the holy Savior; how he appears to have assigned fiscal and proprietary possessions to that holy place and to have confirmed them in every respect; and how he appointed the venerable man Asuerus abbot, together with a [troop] of monks, to govern it, commanding him to administer that holy place according to its rule.

Therefore the aforesaid abbot and the monks residing in that monastery petitioned the clemency of our kingdom that the men whom our lord and father, Pippin, formerly king of blessed memory, granted or assigned to that monastery should remain at the aforesaid place, without anyone’s opposition, under the same tenure and custom as before, and as our other fiscal dependents are held—both with respect to their legal cases and their obligations, and with respect to every other law or custom, as the other fiscal dependents throughout our kingdoms have held them, and as they formerly observed in each county.

We could not deny their petitions, for the sake of the Lord’s name and the remedy of our soul; rather, know that we have granted and confirmed everything. Therefore we order and command that no one whatsoever among our faithful, nor any person exercising judicial authority, presume in any way to disturb the aforesaid house of God, its rectors, or the men serving that holy place whom our lord and father granted to it, or to bring any legal claim against them in this matter, except that, as we have said, in our own times and in those of our successors they shall serve that place in the same manner as they served their former masters before our lord and father assigned them to the aforesaid house of God.

In the same way, therefore, they shall serve that holy place under the same tenure, both by rendering their legal obligations and by observing the remaining law and custom, as the other fiscal dependents appear to do. And so that this decree may be held more firmly and preserved better through the ages, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with our ring.

Sign of Charles, most glorious king.

Given in the month of November, in the eighth year and the sixth year of our reign.

Issued publicly at the royal estate of Thionville, happily, in the name of God. Amen.

### XXXIII. Judicial ruling of Charles the Great, king of the Franks, by which he assigns to the monastery of Honau the estates at Osthoven and Hohgoefft claimed by the Corbie monastery  
*(issued at the end of the year 775).*

[Note: [Col. 0953D] This is a record of a judicial proceeding without day or year. Since Charles uses in it the title “king of the Lombards,” it must unquestionably be assigned to a date after the year 774. Schoepflin, from Urstisius’s corrupt manuscript, read the chronological note: “Given in the tenth year of the reign of King Charles,” which corresponds to the year 778. But the manuscript gives us no trace of this; indeed, the circumstances altogether exclude Charles’s having been in Alsace at that time, since he was occupied with his arduous Spanish expedition.]

[Note: [Col. 0954D] This charter, corrupt and mutilated, was published by Mabillon, *Annals of the Order of Saint Benedict*, vol. II, p. 699, and by Eccard, *Origins of Habsburg*, p. 105; and in a much more corrupt form by Schoepflin, *Alsatian Diplomatic Documents*, vol. I, p. 51, from a manuscript of Christian Urstisius.]

*(From Grandidier, History of the Church of Strasbourg.)*

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards, patrician of the Romans, illustrious man.

Royal majesty is then raised to the summit of its dignity when, in accordance with the statements of claim and reply, it wisely deliberates the disputes of all parties against one another, so that under God there remains in the king the power to arrange all things of a grave nature.

When, in the name of God, we had taken our seat at the estate of Selestat in our palace to hear everyone’s cases and bring them to an end by a just judgment.

[Note: [Col. 0955C] On the ancient royal palace of Sélestat, consult Schoepflin, *Alsatia Illustrated*, vol. I, p. 699.]

There came there the advocate of Saint Michael, or of Abbot Beatus, named Othbertus, and brought a claim against certain men named Agissericus and Aldradus, advocates of the monastery of Corbie. He demanded from them the estates at the place called Osthova and Gehfida, which Immo had transferred to the monastery of Saint Michael by his charter, alleging that they had unjustly retained them in their possession.

[Note: [Col. 0955C] Beatus was then abbot of the monastery of Saint Michael at Hohenaugia.]

[Note: [Col. 0955C] Today the village of Osthofen, three miles from Strasbourg, a fief of the bishopric of Strasbourg granted to the lords of Zuckmantel.]

[Note: [Col. 0955C] Today the village of Pohgaefft, a fief of the bishopric of Strasbourg, possessed by the counts of Leiningen.]

Agissericus and Aldradus themselves were also present and replied as follows: they had never taken away the aforesaid estates unjustly or by wrongful means, because, they said, Gerbriga had granted them by her charter. They affirmed that they had that charter in their hands and produced it before us for examination.

Yet concerning this matter we learned nothing certain from either side. Therefore, with the mercy of Christ cooperating, and in accordance with the long-established custom, since the parties themselves willingly consented, we ordered a judgment to be issued: since the dispute could not be decided by the charters produced by either side, the parties were to proceed in the proper manner to the judgment of God, namely, to the cross. Othbertus, on behalf of Saint Michael and Abbot Beatus, and Agissericus, on behalf of the monastery of Corbie, were to come forth and stand at the cross.

[Note: [Col. 0955C] This was the ordeal of the cross, which they called the judgment of God and which took place during Mass. Two adversaries stood at the cross with their arms extended. The one who first lowered his arms, or whose arms began to tremble, was judged defeated. Gretzer, *On the Cross*, book II, chapter 21; Ebeling, *On Appeal to the Judgment of God*, chapter 7; and Schilter, *Teutonic Glossary*, p. 190, contain much on this subject. There is also a historical-political dissertation by Georgius Althammer, *On the Judgment of the Cross*, printed at Ulm in 1677.]

They were accordingly seen to stand as ordered. At that hour, however, under the protection of God’s divine right hand, almighty God revealed his just judgment: Agissericus, the man of the aforesaid monastery of Corbie, appeared at that divine judgment before the cross trembling and convicted.

Then he and Aldradus, in our presence and that of our nobles, were seen to have returned and restored the aforesaid estates at the places named Osthova and Gehlida, by their pledges and sworn guarantees, to Othbertus, the advocate of Saint Michael and of Abbot Beatus, and thereafter, by means of their tokens of transfer, to have withdrawn from the matter in every respect.

[Note: [Col. 0955D] Namely, pledges, *gages* in French. See Du Cange, *Glossary*, vol. VI, p. 1379.]

[Note: [Col. 0955D] A *festuca* is a sign and symbol of delivery or transferred possession. A seller handed it to the buyer, or anyone transferring possession of property in any manner handed it to the recipient. In such charters, in order that they might be legally valid, a straw or *festuca* was inserted; such objects may still be seen inserted in certain original documents. Du Cange, *Glossary*, vol. III, p. 410.]

Accordingly, together with our faithful—namely, the counts Windringo, Odrigo, Theodericus, Bernhardus, Albuinus, Gherardus, and Berngarius, and Anshelmus, count of our palace, as well as many others—we were seen to have rendered judgment as follows:

[Note: [Col. 0955D] Count Theodericus is mentioned in the Frankish annals called the Loiselian Annals, in Bouquet, vol. V, p. 60, under the year 811, among the leading Franks who confirmed by oath the peace agreed between Charles and Hemming.]

[Note: [Col. 0955D] Count Bernhardus is likewise mentioned among them.]

[Note: [Col. 0956C] A certain Albinus is mentioned; Anastasius, in his life of Pope Hadrian, calls him one who was beloved by King Charles. See Bouquet, vol. V, p. 460.]

[Note: [Col. 0956C] Count Beringarius is mentioned under the year 768 in the continuator of Fredegar’s Chronicle. See Bouquet, vol. V, p. 8.]

[Note: [Col. 0956C] Count Anselmus, count of the palace, is said by Einhard, *Life of Charles the Great*, chapter 9, to have been killed in the Pyrenees in the year 778 while returning from Spain. See Bouquet, vol. V, p. 93.]

Since Agissericus and Aldradus were present and could in no way deny the case, and since Agissericus himself appeared trembling and convicted at the divine judgment before the cross, and since they were seen to have returned and restored the property immediately, by their pledges and sworn guarantees, to Othbertus, the advocate of Saint Michael and of Abbot Beatus, and by their token of transfer to have withdrawn from the matter in every respect, we therefore order that, since we have learned that this case was conducted and completed in this manner, Abbot Beatus, or the monastery of Honau, shall possess the aforesaid estates at Osthova and Gehfida, free from Agissericus and Aldradus, their heirs, and all others attempting unjustly to retain them, as adjudicated and vindicated property for all time. Henceforth, every claim between them shall be removed, settled, and concluded forever.

Theudegarius recognized this document.

[Note: [Col. 0956D] It is preserved in Mabillon, *On Diplomatics*, p. 498; Bouquet, vol. V, p. 734; and Hartzheim, *Councils of Germany*, vol. I, p. 236. A judicial ruling of Charles the Great, in almost the same style, for the monastery of Saint-Denis, issued at the estate of Düren in the seventh year of his reign—that is, 775—also survives. Theudegarius likewise recognized that charter, and there too Count Anselmus of the palace appears with Counts Gherardus, Bernardus, and others who were in the king’s entourage. It is therefore again clear that the judicial ruling at Selestat must also be assigned to the year 775.]

### XXXIV. Decree of Charles the Great for Paulinus, teacher of grammar (year 776)

*(From D. Bouquet, Historical Collection.)*

[Col. 0957A]

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards, and patrician of the Romans, to all bishops, abbots, dukes, counts, *castaldi*, and all our faithful, present and future.

Those who faithfully serve us are rightly raised by gifts from us. Therefore, if we bring to fulfillment the petitions with which they have addressed our ears, we exercise royal custom and encourage their devotion to us through service.

Let it therefore be known to all your greatness how we have ceded and granted to the highly venerable man Paulinus, teacher of the art of grammar, the following properties and possessions, formerly belonging to Waldandius, son of the late Mimo of Laberiano, which came to our palace because he was killed in battle by our faithful together with Forticausus, our enemy:

namely, the estate at Laberiano, with all its entirety and substance—that is, with lands, houses, buildings, resident tenants, slaves, cottages, farmsteads, servants and *aldiones*, vineyards, woods, fields, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, movable and immovable property—in every respect and altogether, whatever the aforesaid Waldandius appears to have possessed there or anywhere else, whether by gift of kings or judges, by purchase, or by any other acquisition.

From this present day we permanently transfer and cede all this to the aforesaid Paulinus for possession, so that from this day forward the aforesaid Paulinus may hold and possess the aforementioned properties peacefully, and may enjoy unrestricted freedom in every respect to do with them whatever he wishes.

Therefore we order and command that no one whatsoever among our faithful or successors presume at any time to disturb the aforesaid Paulinus concerning the aforesaid properties or bring any legal claim against him. Rather, by the gift of our generosity, he shall be able to possess those properties with the firmest proprietary right for all time.

And so that this grant may be held more firmly and better preserved in our times and those to come, we have decreed that it be strengthened forever by our own hand and ordered it sealed with our ring.

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of July, in the eighth year of our reign, at the city of Loreia, happily, in the name of God.

[Note: [Col. 0957D] Loreia, commonly Loredo, in the duchy of Venetia on the Adige.]

### XXXV. Decree of Charles the Great renewing the lost charter instruments of the monastery of Honau (year 776, 9 June)

[Note: [Col. 0957D] This charter is preserved in Mabillon, *Annals of the Order of Saint Benedict*, vol. II, p. 698, and Eccard, *Origins of Habsburg Austria*, p. 104, but corruptly; more correctly in Schoepflin, *Alsatian Diplomatic Documents*, vol. I, p. 49.]

*(From Grandidier, same work.)*

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards, [Col. 0958A] to all our faithful, present and future.

Those who have suffered loss through injustice must necessarily be relieved by royal clemency. Therefore the venerable man Beatus, abbot of the monastery of the Scots called Honau, which Bishop Benedict built anew in honor of Saint Michael, where the most venerable father rests bodily, brought before the clemency of our kingdom the following matter:

The charter instruments of that monastery, by which it possessed property throughout the kingdoms of the Franks, whether property granted and confirmed there by decrees of kings and queens or by other God-fearing men, had been lost in earlier years through negligence. The abbot himself asserts that he now possesses those properties peacefully on behalf of the aforesaid monastery, as he did before.

For the sake of security, therefore, he petitioned our majesty that, since this had happened through negligence, it might be known to all that by our authority we ought to confirm anew all the properties of that church, whatever it appears to possess lawfully and equitably.

We did not wish to deny his petition; rather, know that we have granted and confirmed it as follows. We order that whatever the monastery of Saint Michael just mentioned now lawfully possesses, by which that house of God is endowed, together with whatever was granted and confirmed there by decrees of kings and queens or by other God-fearing men, shall henceforth be held and possessed by the aforesaid Abbot Beatus, by his future successors, and by the rectors of that holy church. May they also cause the possessions of that house of God to increase throughout the ages.

And so that this authority may be held more firmly, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with our ring.

Sign of Charles, most glorious king.

Wigbaldus recognized it in the place of Hitherius.

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of June, in the eighth year of our reign. Issued publicly at the palace of Carisiacum, happily, in the name of God.

[Note: [Col. 0957D] Mabillon reads “the thirteenth year” instead of “the eighth,” which falls in the year 781. Since Hitherius—whom Schoepflin incorrectly writes as Ritherius—is not found as chancellor in charters after the year 776, but Rado is, we have preferred the reading “eighth.”]

[Note: [Col. 0958D] Carisiacum, a village on the Oise that has retained the name Chiersi or Kiersi. On Carisiacum and its true location, see the extensive investigation by Michael Germanus in Mabillon, *On Diplomatics*, book V, pp. 258–268.]

### XXXVI. Diploma of Charles the Great for the monastery of Salona (year 777)

*(From D. Calmet, History of Lorraine.)*

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards, and patrician of the Romans.

Our serenity ought justly and reasonably to grant to our faithful what they request, in return for the service and loyalty that they appear to have shown toward my father, King Pippin, and toward me.

Let it be known to all our faithful, present and future, how Folradus, our palace chaplain and abbot of Saint-Denis, came and reported to us a privilege issued by the fathers of Saint-Denis, which a synodal council in the ninth year, at the urging of Bishop Angilramnus and Archbishop Wilharius, established concerning their proprietary possessions at the place called Salona. That monastery was built in honor of the holy Mother of God, and of the blessed martyrs, confessors, and virgins; Saint Privatus and Saint Hilary the confessor appear to rest there.

In the privilege we found inserted that neither Bishop Angilramnus nor his successors, nor the archdeacon nor envoy of his church of Metz, should have episcopal authority in that monastery, unless the abbot of Saint-Denis requested it—for ordinations, the conferring of chrism, and the blessing of tablets.

We asked Bishop Angilramnus whether he ought to consent to that privilege. He in no way denied it; rather, just as his fellow bishops had established it by synodal council, so he consented, as the privilege itself clearly declares.

Therefore we order that this decree and confirmation remain on behalf of Saint-Denis: after this day, no bishop whatsoever, neither Angilramnus nor his successors, shall interfere with that monastery, which shall remain under the immunity and privilege of Saint-Denis, like the other churches that appear to belong to that house of Saint-Denis.

And concerning the small plots of land that Angilramnus and Folradus exchanged within the estate and boundary of Salona, [lacuna]

In the same way, by our permission and confirmation, and without obstruction from the bishops of the church of Metz, the portion of Saint-Denis, together with the monastery of Salona, shall remain under our protection and defense and that of our nobles, and shall belong to Saint-Denis.

Whatever was added there through royal exchanges, gifts, or donations made by the people, whatever was assessed there, and whatever Folradus enriched that monastery with from his own possessions, shall remain under the immunity and defense of Saint-Denis for all time, confirmed by our authority. Thus the congregation of Saint-Denis, Saint Privatus, and Saint Hilary may be more pleased to pray earnestly for us, for them, and for our wife for the mercy of the Lord.

And so that this authority may be held more firmly and better preserved through the ages, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and sealed it with our ring.

Sign of Charles, most glorious king.

The name and sign of the chancellor are omitted.

Given in December, on the [day omitted], in the tenth year, while our lord Charles was reigning. Issued at the public palace of Aachen, happily, in the name of God. Amen.

### XXXVII. Decree of Charles the Great confirming all the immunities of the monastery of Saint-Denis (year 778)

[Note: [Col. 0959D] Observe that in this diploma Charles the Great confirms the donations of those who either vowed themselves as servants of the Church or, entering the monastic institution, devoted themselves and all their possessions to it. Thus the resources of monasteries increased above all. Note also the expression “my father,” which Charles uses, as in another diploma extracted from the archive of Saint Michael on the Meuse, although in the text he speaks in the plural.]

*(From Mabillon, On Diplomatics.)*

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards, [Col. 0960A] and patrician of the Romans.

At the beginning of our reign I watched over the advancement of our elevation, with the Lord’s help, and for the sake of good works we deliberated, together with the counsel of bishops and our senior nobles, to confirm immunity for the strengthening of our kingdom and, through reward, to renew and obtain eternal life; and so we acted.

It is therefore fitting that royal clemency, among other petitions, receive with favorable hearing whatever is written for salvation and requested for the divine name, and unquestionably bring it to fulfillment. Thus, from the fleeting things of the present age, eternal things are acquired, in accordance with the Lord’s command: “Make friends for yourselves from the mammon of iniquity.”

Therefore, according to that saying, we ought to purchase heavenly eternity with the mammon of iniquity, so that when we grant suitable benefits to priests, we may deserve to have the Lord as our recompense in the eternal tabernacles.

The venerable man Folradus, abbot of the basilica of our special patron, the lord martyr Dionysius, where that precious lord rests bodily, petitioned the clemency of our kingdom. He stated that from ancient times all immunity concerning the estates of the aforesaid holy basilica had been granted by earlier kings. He also affirms that he has at hand those decrees, strengthened by the hands of the kings, and those of my father Pippin, king of blessed memory, and that this has remained inviolably preserved until now.

He therefore requested that, for the sake of security, we should again grant and confirm by our authority the immunity concerning that holy place and the people who hand themselves over to that basilica, together with their possessions, according to what earlier kings had granted and confirmed for that basilica by their authorities.

Therefore let your greatness and prudence know that, out of reverence for that holy place and for the peace of those serving the Lord, we have again granted this with the readiest will and confirmed it in every respect.

Accordingly, by this decree, which we specially establish and wish to remain perpetual, we order that neither you nor your subordinates or successors, nor anyone invested with judicial authority, presume at any time to enter the estates of the aforesaid basilica of Saint Dionysius, wherever they may be and in whatever counties of our kingdom, with God’s favor, they may lie—whether the portion of that monastery appears to possess or control them today, or whether they were granted there by God-fearing men through lawful instruments, or may hereafter be added and assigned—for the purpose of hearing cases, taking sureties, collecting fines, imposing lodging, requisitioning provisions, or demanding any payments.

[Col. 0960D] Whatever our treasury might hope to obtain from them shall instead, in every respect, for the benefit of our reward, be granted entirely to the monastery, together with all fines, as stated above, in view of the decrees of earlier kings and of what this present authority contains.

Whatever that holy place appears to possess at the present day, as we have said, and whatever may thereafter be added or granted there by God-fearing men or by us, or whatever persons may justly and reasonably hand themselves over to that monastery with all their possessions and assign their property there by lawful instruments, shall remain from this day forward under complete immunity, peacefully and securely.

Whatever our treasury might perhaps have hoped to obtain from these things shall be granted entirely and in every respect, forever, for the lamps, provisions, and alms of the poor of that monastery, for our prayers.

Thus may it please them more fully to pray earnestly to the mercy of the Lord for the stability of our kingdom and for the peace of all our people.

And so that this authority may remain firm and inviolate forever, in our times and those to come, concerning that holy place, and may be preserved unharmed through the ages and believed more readily by all judges, we have taken care to outline it with an annotation in our own hand.

Sign of Charles, most glorious king.

Giltbertus recognized and subscribed in the place of Rado.

Given in the month of October, in the eleventh year and the fifth year of our reign.

Issued at the estate of Goddinga, happily, in the name of God.

### XXXVIII. Diploma of Charles the Great confirming the property and possessions of the monastery of Honau (January 778)

[Note: [Col. 0961D] This charter was already published by Mabillon, *Annals of the Order of Saint Benedict*, vol. II, p. 699; Eccard, *Origins of Habsburg Austria*, p. 103; Bouquet, *Writers on Frankish Affairs*, vol. V, p. 739; and Schoepflin, *Alsatian Diplomatic Documents*, vol. I, p. 50, but incorrectly.]

*(From Grandidier, History of the Church of Strasbourg.)*

[Col. 0961C]

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards, and patrician of the Romans, to all bishops, abbots, dukes, counts, household officials, vicars, centenarians, and all our envoys traveling about, both present and future.

We believe that the protection of our kingdom is greatly increased if, through benevolent deliberation, we grant suitable benefits to churches and their establishments, and, with the Lord’s protection, trust that they will endure securely.

Therefore let your prudence know that, at the petition of the venerable man Abbot Beatus, we appear to have granted the following benefit for eternal reward: in the estates or possessions of the church of the archangel Saint Michael, belonging to the monastery built on the island of the Rhine called Hohenaugia, whatever it appears to possess at the present time by our gift or that of anyone else, or whatever divine piety may thereafter enlarge in the right of that holy place, no public judge shall ever presume to enter for the purpose of hearing cases or collecting fines from any source.

Rather, the aforesaid Beatus and his successors shall be able to exercise authority over those possessions under the complete title of immunity, for the sake of the Lord’s name and of Saint Michael.

Therefore we order and command that neither you nor your subordinates or successors, nor any public judicial authority, presume at any time to enter the estates anywhere in our kingdom that have been granted to that church by royal or private generosity or by the gifts of good men, or that may hereafter be granted by God-fearing men, in order to hear disputes, collect fines for any case, impose lodging or provisions, or take sureties.

Whatever our treasury might hope to obtain from those who serve within the fields or vineyards, or who dwell on the lands of the aforesaid church of Saint Michael, or who dwell elsewhere and appear lawfully to belong there, whether in fines or from any other source, shall, by our indulgence and for the sake of future salvation, be devoted forever to the lamps of that church through the hands of its agents.

What we have granted with full devotion for the sake of the Lord’s name, the remedy of our soul, and our succeeding offspring, let neither royal majesty nor the belated greed of any judges attempt to oppose.

And so that this authority may be held more firmly and better preserved through the ages, we have decreed that it be strengthened below by our own hand and ordered it sealed with our ring.

Sign of Charles, most glorious king.

Erchambaldus recognized and subscribed in the place of Rado.

Given in the month of January, in the tenth year of our reign. Issued at the public palace of Herstal, happily, in the name of God. Amen.

[Note: [Col. 0961D] Today Herstal on the Meuse, near Liège. Germanus in Mabillon, *On Diplomatics*, book IV, p. 286, and Paullinus, *On the Counties of Germany*, p. 84, have provided much information about it.]

### XXXIX. Decree of Charles the Great for Nimfridius, abbot of the monastery of Crassus (year 779)

*(From D. Bouquet, Historical Collection.)*

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards, and patrician of the Romans.

To all bishops, abbots, dukes, counts, vicars, centenarians, and all the faithful of the holy Church of God and of our own realm, present and future, let it be known how the venerable man Nimfridius, abbot, brought before our serenity the following matter:

Together with his monks, in the wilderness of the territory of Narbonne, on the river Orobio, at a place called Novalias, he had built a monastery as a new foundation in honor of the holy Mother of God, ever-virgin Mary. There he had built houses, churches, and other dwellings, planted vineyards, and brought fields under cultivation, [Note: [Col. 0962D] Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals*, book XXIV, no. 86, reads “and had received meadows from fiscal officials and the lords of the places.”] and had received meadows from the revenues of our faithful, [lacuna] men.

As he asserts, he has continued until now to hold and possess these things lawfully and equitably, without opposition from anyone. He therefore petitioned our majesty that we should grant and confirm to him and his monks, as an alms from us, the aforesaid place, with all its adjacent lands or appurtenances, wherever he and his monks are presently known to possess property lawfully and reasonably.

We did not wish to deny his petition; rather, know that we have granted and confirmed everything for the increase of our reward.

Therefore we order that neither you nor your subordinates or successors presume at any time to disturb the aforesaid venerable man, Abbot Nimfridius, or his successors, concerning the aforesaid places where he and his monks are presently known to be established lawfully, equitably, and reasonably, or to bring any legal claim against them, or to remove or diminish anything from them [through injustice].

[Note: [Col. 0963D] The words enclosed in brackets could not be read.]

Rather, by this authority and confirmation of ours, let them possess these things as an alms from us for all time, so that they may be more pleased to pray earnestly to the mercy of the Lord for us, our sons and daughters, and the entire household of our house. [lacuna]

And so that this authority may be held more firmly and preserved better through the ages, we have decreed that it be strengthened below by the seals of our hands and ordered it sealed with our ring.

[Note: [Col. 0963D] The rest is missing, as the first editor attests, from the nearly worn-away original. Mabillon nevertheless states in the place already cited that this decree was issued at the royal palace of Compiègne, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of February, in the eleventh year of King Charles’s reign. These chronological details cannot be reconciled with what the annalist of Lorsch relates: “The king came from Herstal, where he had wintered and where he had celebrated Christmas and Holy Easter; at the beginning of spring he set out and came to Compiègne.”]

### XL. Decree of Charles the Great for the monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés (year 779)

*(From D. Bouquet, same work.)*
Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards, [Col. 0963C] and patrician of the Romans, to all our bishops, abbots, counts, and junior officials. If we do not cease to grant suitable benefits to the places of holy churches or to priests, we confidently believe that this will unquestionably be repaid to us with eternal blessedness. Therefore let your greatness or utility know how the venerable man Hrobert, abbot of the basilica of Saint Vincent or of the lord Germanus, where that precious one rests bodily, brought a petition to the clemency of our kingdom and showed us for rereading a precept of our lord and father, King Pippin of blessed memory. In it we found inserted how, for the name of the Lord and moved by his merits, he is known to have granted a benefit, namely that every year, wherever within our kingdom the merchants of that holy [Col. 0963D] place wished to travel—as this same Abbot Hrobert seems to deserve—whether to purchase lamps or while traveling for any other necessity, both beyond the Loire and this side of the Loire, or in Burgundy, even in Provence or in Francia, as also in Austrasia, wherever, with Christ’s favor, they wished to travel within our kingdoms, their traveling agents should not have to pay any toll, nor any charge on pack animals, carts, boats, or any other exaction from there to the account of our treasury.

Therefore, by this present precept [Col. 0964A] we decree, and command that it remain perpetually in force, that at no ports, nor in cities—whether at Rouen or Wicus, at Amiens, at Tournai, at Dorestad, or through all the ports—and at Saint-Maixent, nor anywhere else, nor in the Parisian territory, nor at Amiens, nor in Burgundy, in the county of Troyes, nor in the Sénonais, nor in any cities likewise, wherever in our kingdoms, with Christ’s favor, or in counties or territories, tolls may be demanded: neither a charge on ships, nor on carts, nor on pack animals, nor on the transport of goods, nor a wheel-tax, bridge-tax, dust-tax, landing-tax, turf-tax, nor any other exaction which our treasury could hope to receive from there. Neither you nor your junior officials or successors shall demand or compel them to pay these charges; rather, in every respect, for the name of the Lord, the abbot himself or his successors, or the aforesaid church of Saint Vincent or of the lord Germanus, shall have this exemption granted, so that it may contribute to the increase of the lamps of that holy place.

We also add the toll which Count Gerard appeared to have received from the court of Villa Nova of Saint Germanus, so that henceforth the portion belonging to Saint Germanus may receive that toll in its entirety, as our alms, for the lamps of that church, without anyone’s opposition. We have decreed that this grant, valid by whatever authority and for perpetual times, be strengthened by our own hand.

**Sign of Charles, most glorious king.**

Optatus, acting in the place of Rado, examined and approved this.

Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of April, in the eleventh and fifth year of our reign.

[Col. 0964C] Done at the public palace of Herstal.

## XLI. Diploma of Charlemagne for the monastery of Saint Marcellus at Chalon (779)

(From D. Bouquet, cited above.)

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards, and patrician of the Romans, to all our people [perhaps: officials], present and future. With the Lord’s help, who has established us upon the throne of the kingdom, it is foremost among the duties of our clemency to lend a kindly ear to the interests of all, especially to those benefits which we find were granted by our royal predecessors to ecclesiastical foundations for the welfare of souls. We ought to consider these with devoted mind [Col. 0964D] and not refuse suitable benefits, so that we may deserve to share in their reward, but rather confirm them with greater force through our royal pronouncements.

Therefore the magnificent Hubert, bishop and rector of the basilica of Saint Marcellus, which is situated beneath the town of Chalon, where that precious martyr of the Lord rests bodily, brought a petition before our exalted authority. He stated that our earlier royal predecessors, and especially our lord and father, King Pippin of blessed memory, had granted the monastery complete immunities by their full precepts [Col. 0965A], so that no public judge or any authority should enter the monastery’s estates or lands to hear cases, exact fines, take sureties, provide lodgings or provisions, or demand any exactions [requisitions]. The aforesaid Bishop Hubert also showed us those precepts of our royal predecessors and their confirmations for rereading, and asserted that these benefits had been preserved to the present day.

[Note: The precept was also published by the Sammarthani in volume II of *Gallia Christiana*, as an exercise in confirmation.]

But, seeking confirmation, he asked the clemency of our kingdom that our authority should once again confirm this for the monastery. Therefore, after examining the authorities of the earlier princes, we command that neither you nor your junior officials or successors, nor anyone at all belonging to the judicial power, should presume to enter the estates of that monastery which it presently appears to possess, or which thereafter may have been or may be granted to it by God-fearing people, to hear cases, exact fines, take sureties, provide lodgings or provisions, or demand any exactions, while its full immunity remains intact. Just as the benefit of our royal predecessors has until now been preserved for that monastery, so henceforth, by our authority, it shall remain generally undisturbed.

If in earlier times, through any negligence of abbots, lukewarmness of administrators, or presumption of judges, anything has been altered, seized, torn away, or extracted from these immunities, it shall be restored through our authority [Col. 0965C] and benefactions. Moreover, no one shall presume to infringe or violate what we have granted—not you, nor your junior officials. If, however, any lord, count, domesticus, vicar, or anyone whatsoever invested with judicial authority should presume to break or violate these provisions, whether through the indulgence of the good or the kindness of pious Christians or kings, let him acknowledge himself liable to a penalty of six hundred solidi, so that two parts shall be paid into the archive of the monastery and the third part contributed to the treasury of our chapel [Col. 0966A]. Thus it shall not be permitted that what our predecessors or good Christians have granted or bestowed should be torn apart by wicked men. Whatever our treasury might thereby have hoped to receive shall instead contribute to the increase of the people of the church of Saint Marcellus the martyr, for the stability of our kingdom and for our descendants who follow us.

And so that this authority may endure with firm stability, we have decreed that it be strengthened below with the marks of our own hand.

**Sign of [Charles], most glorious king.**

Given on the day before the Kalends of May, in the eleventh and fifth years of our reigns.

Done [Note: Wigbald, acting in the place of Rado, examined this diploma, as Mabillon reports in book XXIV of the *Benedictine Annals*, no. 90. He adds that at that time secular clergy were present in the basilica of Saint Marcellus and remained there until the tenth century, when the basilica was restored to monks under the discipline of Saint Majolus, abbot of Cluny.] at Herstal.

## XLII. Diploma of Charlemagne by which he confirms to Abbot Fulrad of Saint-Denis Lepraham and other properties of the same abbey (given at Aachen, 20 April 781)

[Note: We say nothing about the authenticity of this diploma, which Doublet claims to have derived from the original itself, or rather from the cartulary. Perhaps little faith should be placed in him, since neither Mabillon, Félibien, nor Bouquet—who were especially diligent in investigating the charters of Saint-Denis—mention it. Cointius declares it to be unmistakably fabricated, *Ecclesiastical Annals*, vol. VI, p. 214. “I would not deny,” says Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*, book III, chapter 2, p. 223, “that some things in Doublet are either wholly false, interpolated, or doubtful . . . . Doublet was a good and simple man, who brought whatever fell into his hands before the public without malicious intent, etc.” The authors of the new *Diplomatics* agree with Mabillon when they write, vol. III, p. 655: “This good man (Doublet) composed his collection from no other monuments than often faulty copies and cartularies in which the copyists sometimes rendered the originals badly”; and vol. IV, p. 415, note: “Doublet, a simple man without critical judgment, introduced into his collection several interpolated pieces taken from poor copies.” GRANDIDIER.]

(Edited from the cartulary of the abbey of Saint-Denis by Doublet, *Antiquités et Recherches de l’abbaye de Saint-Denis*, book III, p. 713.)

## XLIII. Diploma of Charlemagne by which he confirms to the abbey of Saint-Denis all the properties and privileges granted to it by Abbot Fulrad, especially “in the county of Alsace, the cell of Saint Alexander, where he himself rests bodily, with all its appendages and dependencies, together with the property and slaves of both sexes residing there” (given at Düren, 16 September 781)

[Note: The same judgment must be made about this diploma as about the preceding one. Its dating is especially false, since it says: “Given in the twenty-second and eighth year, while our lord Charles, most glorious king, was reigning.” Charles’s twenty-second regnal year among the Franks was his seventeenth among the Lombards. The twenty-second year fell in the year of Christ 790, by which time Fulrad—at whose request this diploma was issued—had already died. Perhaps, therefore, the year XIII should be read, which corresponds to the year of Christ 781 and to Charles’s eighth year of rule in Lombardy. GRANDIDIER.]

(Edited from the cartulary of the archives of Saint-Denis by Doublet, cited above.)

## XLIV. Interpolated diploma of Charlemagne by which he grants to the church of Lebrah the tithes of the lands belonging to it (781)

(From Grandidier, *History of the Church of Strasbourg*.)

[Col. 0966C]

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards, and patrician of the Romans, to all our faithful, present and future. Whatever we grant to venerable places, through love of God and for the benefit of God’s servants, after benevolent deliberation, we confidently believe will unquestionably contribute to our eternal blessedness and the salvation of our soul.

Let the whole community of the faithful, present and future, know that the venerable abbot Fulrad, our nephew [Note: Fulrad was the son of Riculfus and Ermengardis, as is clear from his will of the year 777; he was never Charlemagne’s nephew. The interpolator added this, perhaps confusing him with another Fulrad, who was abbot of Saint-Quentin at Vermand and appeared at the courts of Charlemagne and Louis the Pious. This latter had as his father Jerome, a relative of Charlemagne, who was an illegitimate son of Charles Martel and brother of King Pippin.] [Col. 0967A], came to us with the monks of the basilica of the lord martyr Denis and his companions Rusticus and Eleutherius, and asked that we grant to the church of Lebrah, situated in the county of Alsace, where the lord and holy martyr Alexander rests bodily, and to which we have granted many benefits for the salvation of our soul, the tithes of all the lands belonging to that church.

[Note: This style is entirely unknown in Carolingian charters.]

Agreeing to their pious petition, we granted them what they asked of us and handed over to them a charter sealed with our seal. Whoever should presume to oppose it shall be subject to perpetual anathema.

**Sign of Charles, most glorious king.**

Done in the city of Worms, in the thirteenth year of the reign of our lord Charles, most glorious king [Col. 0967B] of the Franks and Lombards, and patrician of the Romans.

[Note: It was then customary for archchaplains, chancellors, or others to subscribe their names in order to establish the validity of diplomas. The fact that this custom was not used in this charter of Charlemagne, among other signs of interpolation, makes it especially suspect. Félibien himself confirms this, since he did not use the supposed authority of this diploma at all in his history of Saint-Denis. Cointius states that the aforesaid charter appears spurious to him, *Ecclesiastical Annals*, vol. VI, p. 214.]

## XLV. Diploma of Charlemagne by which he declares the monastery of Honau exempt from tolls (782, 17 November)

[Note: This charter is found in Mabillon, *Annals of the Order of Saint Benedict*, vol. II, p. 699; Eccard, *Origines Habsburgicae Austriacae*, p. 104; Bouquet, *Collection of the Historians of France*, vol. V, p. 745; and Schoepflin, *Alsatian Diplomatics*, vol. I, p. 52, but not with sufficient accuracy.]

(From Grandidier, cited above.)

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards, and patrician of the Romans, to all bishops, abbots, dukes, counts, vicars, centenarii, toll-collectors, and all who administer public affairs. If we do not cease to grant suitable benefits to the places of holy churches or to God’s servants, we confidently believe that this will unquestionably pertain to our eternal blessedness.

Therefore let your greatness or utility know that, at the petition of the venerable man Beatus, abbot and rector of the monastery of Honau, constructed in honor of Saint Michael, we have wished to grant such a benefit, compelled by his merits and for the name of the Lord, that wherever the people of that monastery come within our kingdom for the purpose of trade, they should pay or give no toll or any other exaction that appears to belong to the account of our treasury.

Therefore, by this present precept we decree, and command that it remain perpetually in force, that they shall be liable neither to a toll, nor to a ship-toll [Note: *Teloneum* for ships, a freight charge], nor to a cart-toll [Note: *Teloneum* for carts, a cartage duty], nor to a transport charge [Note: *Teloneum* for horses or mounts], nor to a wheel-tax [Note: Wheel duty], nor to a bridge-tax [Note: Bridge duty], nor to a landing-tax [Note: Duty for a fortunate landing], nor to a dust-tax [Note: See above, col. 938, note t], nor to a turf-tax [Note: See above, col. 937, note n], nor to any exaction [Col. 0968A] which our treasury might hope to receive from there. Neither you nor your junior officials or successors shall demand these from them or cause them to be exacted. Rather, in every respect, for the name of the Lord and of Saint Michael the archangel, the abbot Beatus himself or his successor, or the aforesaid monastery, shall have this exemption and grant, so that it may contribute to the increase of the lamps of that holy place.

And so that this authority may be held more firmly and better observed by our faithful, we have decreed that it be strengthened with the impression of our ring.

Wigbald, acting in the place of Rado, examined and subscribed it.

Given on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of November, in the fourteenth year of our reign. Done [Note: Mabillon and others incorrectly read *Cispliaco*. Clipiacum was a royal palace, in French Clichy; concerning it, see Germanus in Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*, book IV, p. 273.] at the public palace of Clichy.

## XLVI. Precept of Charlemagne confirming the exchange of certain estates in the county of Metz, concluded between Fulrad, abbot of Saint-Denis, and Eufemia, abbess of the convent of Saint Peter in the city of Metz (782)

(From Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*.)

[Col. 0968B]

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards, and patrician of the Romans. Let it be known to our faithful, present and future, that when we confirm by our royal pronouncement what they have exchanged among themselves, we are exercising the custom of kings, and we believe that the arrangement will thereafter remain most firmly established by law.

Therefore let all your greatness know how the venerable man Folrad, abbot and archpriest of the monastery of Saint-Denis, and Eufemia [Col. 0968C], abbess of the upper monastery constructed in honor of Saint Peter within the walls of the city of Metz [Note: A monastery of virgins under the name of Saint Peter still exists at Divodurum of the Mediomatrici. Concerning Peter, or more accurately Petrus, bishop of Verdun, who presided over that church during the reign of Charlemagne, see the history of the bishops of Verdun in volume IX of the *Spicilegium*, p. 259], exchanged certain properties among themselves for the convenience of both parties.

They showed us in the present the exchanges, strengthened by the hands of good men, for rereading. There we learned that Eufemia the abbess, with the consent of the servants of God residing there, gave to Abbot Folrad two small estates in the county of Salins, on the river Salona, at Compendium—namely, in Filicione Court and in Victerneia Court—whatever property of Saint Peter there was in those courts, in its entirety, and everything belonging to those places.

Likewise Folrad gave to Eufemiana the abbess and to that congregation of Saint Peter [Col. 0969A] his own property in the county of Scarponne, at a place called Basigunde Court, whatever he had exchanged with Bishop Petrus of Verdun and with Abbot Anno, and everything that appears to belong to that place; all of it, in its entirety, he gave to Eufemiana the abbess.

But for complete security the abbot and abbess asked our exalted authority to confirm this by our authority. Know that, gladly agreeing to their petitions, we have granted and confirmed everything in every respect.

Therefore we command that, after examining the exchanges themselves, whatever one party transferred to the other, or conversely received in compensation, as the exchanges declare, shall from this day, by this authority of ours, be held, possessed, given, exchanged, or otherwise disposed of with full and most secure power in every respect, insofar as each party wishes to act for the benefit of those churches with what it received by right. Neither the aforesaid abbot and abbess nor their successors shall ever violate these exchanges.

For this reason we ordered two confirmations to be written in identical form; we confirmed them with our own hand and ordered them sealed with the impression of our ring.

**Sign of Charles, most glorious king.**

Widolaicus, acting in the place of Rado, examined this.

Given in the month of October, in the fourteenth and eighth years of our reign. Done at the public palace of Herstal, prosperously in the name of God.

## XLVII. Judicial hearing held under Charlemagne, in which Sonarciaga Court in the county of Telleau is adjudicated to the monastery of Saint-Denis (782)

(From Mabillon, cited above.)

[Col. 0969C]

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards, and patrician of the Romans. When, in the name of God, we were seated at the palace of our estate of Quierzy to hear everyone’s cases and settle them by right judgment, Ado, advocate of Saint-Denis and of Abbot Fulrad, came there and brought the following matter before us.

He said that he had appeared before Count Riferus and his *scabini* in the county of Telleau, at the public assembly called Turcarias, and had summoned certain people—Godwinus, his brother Flodoinus, and their sister Damascia, as well as Andgarius, Ercammarus, and Jonathas [Col. 0969D]. He demanded from them and stated that they had wrongfully retained in their possession a property of Saint-Denis in that same county of Telleau, at a place called Sonarciaga Court on the river Itta, which Saint Denis had acquired by his own arm.

Flodoinus, Godwinus, their sister Damascia, and also Antgarius, Ercammarus, and Jonathas were present. When they were asked whether they wished to say anything in this case against Ado, the advocate of Saint-Denis, they could never produce or establish any legal basis by which they could have possessed Sonarciaga Court, the property of Saint-Denis [Col. 0970A]. Instead, through their pledges, they invested the aforesaid Ado, advocate of Saint-Denis, with possession there in the presence of all, and there gave the required legal oath.

Accordingly, it was appropriate for Ado, advocate of Saint-Denis, to obtain and take a record of this proceeding, confirmed by the hands of good men, and by the name of Count Riferus and those who had sat there, so that for a long time he might have Sonarciaga Court adjudicated and legally cleared against the aforesaid people for the portion belonging to Saint-Denis. And so Ado, the advocate of Saint-Denis and of Abbot Fulrad, presented before us for rereading the record which he stated that he possessed according to law.

After the record had been reread, Count Riferus was asked whether this case and the record were true and accurate or not. Count Riferus then gave us his testimony in the following form: the case and the record were true and accurate.

Therefore we, together with our faithful—that is, Counts Richard, Gunthard, and Teudbald; Grifo, Gerold, Nortbold, Winegisus, Walbert, Gisold, Aroin, Teuthold, Constable, and Woraldo, our count of the palace, along with many others—appeared to have judged as follows: since Count Riferus had given us testimony that the case and the record were true and accurate, we therefore command that, because we have recognized that the case was conducted and completed in this manner, the aforesaid advocate of Saint-Denis, after examination of his record, shall have the aforesaid Sonarciaga Court adjudicated and legally cleared for the portion belonging to Saint-Denis for all time. Henceforth, all litigation between them concerning this matter shall remain settled, ended, and undisturbed forever.

[Note: It is uncertain whether Witherius was then an ordinary notary. Witherius is indeed counted among the notaries of the Emperor Charlemagne, but not among those of the king; nor do I find Chrotard as archchancellor elsewhere. This office was held by Hitherius until the twelfth year of Charles’s reign.]

Witherius, notary, acting in the place of Chrotard, examined this.

Given in the month of December, on the sixteenth day, in the fourteenth year of our reign, prosperously in the name of God.

## XLVIII. Precept of King Charlemagne for the monastery of Saint Martin at Tours (782)

(From D. Bouquet, *Collection of Histories*.)

[Col. 0970D]

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards, and patrician of the Romans, to all abbots, illustrious men, dukes, counts, domestici, *grafiones*, vicars, centenarii, our junior officials, and our traveling royal agents, present and future. It is fitting for the dignity of royal clemency to attend with diligent care to everything that priests reasonably request, not to deny them suitable or appropriate benefits, and fully to confirm the acts of earlier kings that were undertaken for the sake of God.

Therefore the venerable man Itherius, abbot of the basilica of our special patron Saint Martin, where [Col. 0971A] that precious lord rests bodily, brought before us for rereading the immunities of our glorious royal predecessors, strengthened by their hands, and those of our lord and father, King Pippin of blessed memory [where it was inserted that] the aforesaid kings, out of reverence for the most blessed Saint Martin, had confirmed the following concerning his property in our kingdoms—with God’s favor, in Austrasia, Neustria, Burgundy, Aquitaine, and Provence:

All the property and resources of that most blessed Saint Martin, peacefully located in the kingdoms mentioned above, in whatever places, great or small, whether granted through royal precepts, concessions, or immunities, or by Christian people and through various transactions, or through written instruments and charters, whether already transferred or assigned to the aforesaid house of God, the confessor Saint Martin, or to be added or assigned in future times, were confirmed, so that under our immunity those properties and the people of Saint Martin might live.

Therefore the aforesaid Abbot Itherius asked the serenity of our kingdom that we should grant the benefit of confirming this same arrangement. Agreeing to his petition and venerating the patronage of Saint Martin, know that, just as the preceding kings carried this out individually, we too have gladly granted this gift of exemption.

We therefore command that all the property of the most blessed Saint Martin, insofar as it exists in our kingdoms, with God’s favor—whether large or small estates or all the resources of the most blessed Saint Martin—shall remain under the title of immunity. No public judge [Col. 0971C] of our treasury shall presume to enter the aforesaid estates or resources of the saint to conduct business, hear cases, exact fines or penalties, collect tolls, or exercise any entry or access into the estates of Saint Martin.

Whatever our treasury had been accustomed to receive or exact from them in ancient times, whether in the past or at present, we cede entirely from our treasury, so that it may contribute to the increase of the lamps of the most blessed Saint Martin, the support of the poor, or the stipends of the monks.

No public judge of our treasury shall claim to have any authority over the aforesaid estates or resources of Saint Martin by any device whatsoever. Rather, he shall always be excluded and kept away from every fiscal authority and from the aforesaid property of Saint Martin. No one shall ever dare to seek pretexts by which the people of Saint Martin might suffer loss. Instead, after examination, the immunities of the earlier kings and our own shall be preserved in every respect.

If there should be any count, domesticus, *grafio*, vicar, tribune, or anyone invested with any judicial authority who presumes to break or violate the indulgence and kindness of our pious fathers and royal predecessors or our precept, let him acknowledge himself liable to a fine of six hundred solidi of gold, smelted pure, payable to the house of Saint Martin or its abbots [Col. 0972A]. The abbot, the monks, or the house of Saint Martin shall receive two parts, while the third part shall enter the treasury of our chapel. Thus it shall not be permitted that what has been granted to priests for the sake of God, or the immunities of earlier kings or our own, should be torn apart by wicked men.

Whatever appears presently to belong to the house of Saint Martin, or whatever in future may be given or transferred to it by God-fearing or good people, shall remain under the title of immunity. Whoever wishes to give anything to that house of God shall have permission to do so by our authority, and it shall remain peacefully under the title of immunity, without any fiscal authority. Whatever the treasury was accustomed to receive shall henceforth, as our alms, be reckoned for the lamps of that saint in the proper deduction [Col. 0972B]. The abbot himself and all his successors shall perpetually hold and possess all the property of Saint Martin under complete immunity.

If in earlier times, through any negligence or lukewarmness of abbots or the presumption of judges, anything was diminished, broken into, torn away, or damaged from this immunity, it shall be restored in every respect through these authorities and benefactions of ours.

Moreover, no one of our officials, nor any of our junior officials or successors, shall presume to break or violate what we have confirmed. Rather, as stated above, with the fullest immunity, peacefully, with God’s help and by our favor, they shall be able to possess everything that has been or will be given to them.

And so that this precept concerning that house and the venerable [Col. 0972C] church of Saint Martin may endure for future times, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and sealed it with the impression of our ring.

**Sign of Charles, most glorious king.**

Rado reread and subscribed it.

Given in the month of April, in the tenth and [Note: Correct to VIII] ninth year of our reign. Done [Note: Perhaps it should be read *Carisiago*, for Charles celebrated Easter in that estate, as the *Annals of Einhard* testify.] at the royal palace of Quierzy, prosperously in the name of God. Amen.

## XLIX. Donation of Queen Hildegard for the monastery of Saint Arnulf (783)

(From Dom Calmet, cited above.)

Hildegard, by the grace of God queen of the Franks. Whatever we grant or confirm to venerable holy places out of love for our Lord Jesus Christ, we undoubtedly believe will redound to the reward of our souls and the salvation of our bodies.

Therefore let it be known to all the greatness of our faithful, present and future, how, with the counsel, will, and permission of our lord and glorious great emperor Charles, we have granted to the basilica constructed in honor of Saint James the apostle and the other blessed apostles, where Arnulf the precious rests bodily, part of our marriage portion granted to us by that most pious emperor—namely, Vacarias and the court situated below it in the duchy of Moselle, in the county of Metz, together with its appendages and the church constructed in honor of the precious Arnulf in the aforesaid estate of Vacarias [Col. 0973A]—in its entirety, including lands, houses, buildings, resident inhabitants, slaves, woods, fields, meadows, pastures, waters, and watercourses: everything, in every respect, by this authority of ours we grant and bestow in perpetuity for possession.

We grant all these things, with their dependencies, specifically to that place because there, with God’s favor, we wish to rest bodily.

And because we know that many things first undertaken zealously later, when charity grows cold, fall into negligence, we therefore forbid all abbots or custodians of that venerable place, and adjure them by the divine judgment, ever to presume to grant the aforesaid properties as a benefice to anyone, or to lend them by precarious tenure, as is customary, or to divert them to any use whatsoever of this world [Col. 0973B]. Rather, they shall always remain subject by perpetual right in that same venerable place for the uses of those who serve God there.

If any of the abbots of that venerable place should presume to violate this will of ours, may he be unable to escape eternal condemnation, and may he find blessed Arnulf against him not as a helper but rather as an accuser.

Through Christ, the Son of God and redeemer of all, we adjure and earnestly entreat all our future successors, and judges of whatever rank, that no one dare break what we have established or alter it in any way contrary to our intention. If any of them attempts to do so, may he feel whatever he himself establishes torn down by his adversary, and moreover may he face judgment with us before the most just Judge.

And so that this authority may be held more firmly and better preserved for lasting times, our lord and most pious Emperor Charles, most willingly agreeing to our prayers, wrote his confirmation below with his own hand and ordered it sealed with his ring.

Given on the third day before the Ides of March, in the fifteenth year of our lord and most pious Emperor Charles; from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the year 783.

Done at Metz, prosperously in the name of God, in the sixth indiction.

## L. Diploma of Charlemagne for the monastery of Saint Arnulf at Metz (783)

(From Dom Calmet, *History of Lorraine*.)

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards [Col. 0973D], and patrician of the Romans. Whatever we grant or confirm to venerable holy places out of love for our Lord Jesus Christ, we confidently believe will unquestionably contribute, in God’s name, to the reward and stability of our kingdom.

Therefore, let it be known to all the multitude of our faithful, present and future, how, as an alms for our most beloved wife, Queen Hildegard, we grant to the basilica constructed in honor of Saint James [perhaps John] the Apostle and the other blessed saints, where, namely, Arnulf, precious in body, rests, our estate called Camenctum, situated in the Duchy of Moselle, in the county of Metz, together with its appurtenances and the churches that appear to belong to that estate, in its entirety: lands, houses, buildings, inhabitants, bondsmen, vineyards, woods, fields, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses—everything in full—we grant and donate by this authority of ours to be possessed perpetually.

We grant this estate, with all its dependencies, especially to that holy place so that, from its revenues, lamps may continually be maintained day and night at her tomb for the relief of the soul of our aforesaid wife. And because we know that many things which are first undertaken zealously later, when charity grows cold, fall into neglect, we therefore forbid all abbots or custodians of that venerable place, and adjure them by the divine judgment, ever to presume to assign the aforesaid estate to anyone as a benefice, or to lease it by precarious tenure, as is customary, or to turn it to any use whatsoever of this present age. Rather, as we have said, lamps are to be maintained there without ceasing for the relief of the soul of our beloved wife Hildegard; and whatever remains from those lamps is to be used to support those whom the custodians themselves shall appoint, so that, for the soul of our often-mentioned beloved wife, they may celebrate Mass daily and continually pour forth psalmody and prayers in the sight of the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 0973] Masses were being founded in the time of Charlemagne, since he himself founded them for the relief of the soul of his wife Hildegard.]

But if any of the abbots of that venerable place should presume to violate this will of ours, may he be unable to escape eternal damnation, and may he find blessed Arnulf opposed to him, not as helper but rather as accuser. We also adjure the servants of God who shall be appointed to this work, by the undivided name of the Holy Trinity, to commit no negligence; indeed, as stated above, let them diligently persevere continually in prayers, the solemn celebrations of Mass, and psalmody.

We also adjure and earnestly beseech all our future successors, through Christ, the Son of God, redeemer of all, whether judges of whatever rank, that no one dare violate what we have established or alter it in any way contrary to our wishes. If any of them attempts to do so, let him feel whatever he has decreed torn down by his adversary; moreover, he shall have to face judgment with us before the most just Judge.

And so that this authority may be held more firmly and better preserved for a long time, we have subscribed it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with our ring.

Given on the Kalends of May, in the fifteenth year of our reign, but from the Incarnation of our Lord in the year 783, on the day of the Lord’s Ascension, on the vigil of which our sweetest wife herself died, in the thirteenth year of our union. Enacted at our palace of Thionville, happily in the name of God, in the sixth indiction.

### LI. Charter of Charlemagne for the monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés (786)

*(From D. Bouquet, Collection of the Histories of France.)*

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, to all our faithful, present and future. Whatever we grant by benevolent deliberation to venerable places for the love of the Lord and for the benefit of the servants of God, we confidently believe contributes to our eternal blessedness and to the relief of our soul.

Therefore let it be known to all of you how we donate to the monastery of Saint-Germain, constructed near the city of Paris, where his precious body lies buried, and where the venerable man Abbot Hrobert appears to preside, and how we wish this donation to belong to that same holy place and to the brothers dwelling there. It is our estate called Madriolas [Maroles], in the county of Melun, on the River Seine, with all that belongs or is attached to it in its entirety, just as it has long and presently appeared to belong to that place lawfully and reasonably, or as Count Autbert presently appears to hold it by our benefice.

This includes lands, houses, buildings, inhabitants, bondsmen, vineyards, woods, fields, meadows, pastures, watercourses, movable and immovable property, and the port situated between the counties of Sens and Melun, from the estate of Alsiacum belonging to the aforesaid Saint-Germain as far as the little monastery of Saint Maurice, on both banks of the River Seine, regardless of whose land it may be. No one there is to have control of the port or the water except the aforesaid power of blessed Germain; nor may anyone collect toll, cartage duty, *vultaticum*, turf duty, riverbank duty, or passage duty. The market, too, and everything in its entirety—whatever may be said or named—we now transfer completely to that holy place and to its rectors and monks, to be possessed perpetually.

For this reason we ordered this charter of our authority to be written, by which we establish and decree absolutely that what we wish concerning that abbot and the rectors of that church shall remain perpetual: no one exercising judicial authority, no one belonging to our treasury, and no person whatsoever shall presume to disturb the aforesaid Abbot or the monks residing in that monastery concerning the estate of Madriolas or anything belonging to it, or to bring any action against them contrary to the order of justice. From this day forward, the rectors of that monastery shall have, hold, and possess it, so that the aforesaid abbot and the monks may be more eager to pray attentively for the mercy of the Lord on behalf of us, our wife and children, and the stability of our kingdom.

And so that this authority may be held firmly and better preserved in our time and in that of our successors, we have decreed that it be confirmed below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with our ring.

**Sign of Charles, most glorious king.**

I, Wigbald, have reviewed it in place of Rado.

Given on the Nones of November, in the nineteenth and thirteenth year of our reign. Enacted at the palace of Worms, happily in the name of God.

### LII. Charter of King Charles concerning hunting in the forests (788)

*(From Mabillon, On Diplomatic Matters.)*

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans. Whatever we grant or confirm to venerable holy places for the benefit of the servants of God, we confidently believe contributes beyond doubt to eternal blessedness.

Therefore let it be known to the multitude of all our faithful, present and future, how we have granted to Abbot Autland and the monks of the monastery of Sithiu, constructed in honor of almighty God and Saint Peter, chief of the Apostles, and the other saints, where the confessors of Christ, Saints Audomar and Bertin, rest bodily.

[Note: [Col. 0975C] During Charlemagne’s rule various estates were granted to the abbey of Sithiu, among which the donation of the cleric Deodatus deserves notice. For “Deodatus the cleric grants to Abbot Odland his property situated in the places of Sanctum and Ascio on the river Witbac, and in Fresinnium [Col. 0975D] on the river Capruinus, and Hildwalcurt, and in Lonastum on the river Albumfontana, in the district of Terouanne; namely, church furnishings in gold and silver, textiles of diverse appearance and kind, various books, etc., on the condition that all the property included be used to procure clothing for the monks dwelling in the monastery of Sithiu, that is, cloths for overseas shirts, commonly called berniscrist. Done publicly at Saintes. Given in August, on the third day, in the thirty-second year of the reign of our lord Charles, most glorious king.
