Gunabert the deacon wrote.” — Abbot Odland of Sithiu was succeeded by Nantharius, the second of that name, to whom Erlharius sold one manor in the place called Fletrinum, in the district of Isserctium. The deed of sale begins thus: “To the venerable lord and father in Christ, Nantharius, abbot of the monastery of Sithiu, or of the cell called Bebrona, where Ebrogerus appears to be provost . . . . . Done at Bebrona in October, in the thirty-ninth year of King Charles’s reign and the sixth year [Col. 0976C] of his empire.” The widow Lebdrudis conveys to the same Abbot Nantharius all her own property in the place called Gisna or Totingetune, in the district of Boulogne, on the river Wasconigawalla: “For this donation,” she says, “and through your kindness I requested from you [Col. 0976D] some land of your monastery in the place called Aecloum, in that district of Boulogne, on the condition that I and my three children, named Hildberta, Nidlebus, and Erpsuid, while we live, may possess those lands by your benefice in usufruct. Therefore, for that same use, every year at the feast of Saint Audomar, on the Kalends of November, we must pay two rents in cheeses; and I shall not have the power to alienate that property. Done publicly at the estate of Gisna, when October had its eleventh day, in the fortieth year of the reign and the eighth year of the empire of our lord Emperor Charles. Mark of Wendelger the centenarius +. Gumtbert the priest wrote.” Perhaps this is the same Guntbert, a monk, whose father was Goibert and mother Ebertruda, who granted to the monastery of Sithiu a certain monastery called Henetlant, which Goibert himself had built on his own property in honor of our Savior.]

That by our indulgence their men might have permission to hunt in their own forests, so that the brothers might derive support from it both for covering the volumes of books and for making sleeves and belts, while our royal forests remain protected, which we have set aside for our own use.

For this reason we ordered the present authority to be issued, by which we absolutely command and decree that neither you nor your subordinates or successors presume to disturb or bring a complaint against the venerable Abbot Audland, his successors, or their men on this account; nor to demand or exact anything from them on this matter, nor to contradict them in any way. Rather, as we have said, their men are to be permitted, by our indulgence, to hunt in their own forests.

And so that this authority may be held more firmly and preserved through the ages, we ordered it sealed below with our ring.

**Sign of Lord Charles, most glorious king.**

Given on the seventh day before the Kalends of April, in the twentieth year of our reign. Enacted at the aforesaid place of Sithiu, in the atrium of Saint Bertin, happily in the name of God. Amen.

### LIII. Charter of Charlemagne concerning the property sold by Count Hrodhard to the monastery of Saint-Denis, which the king confirms to that place (790)

*(From Mabillon, in the same work.)*

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans. We believe it known to all our faithful how, in the time of our father of blessed memory, the former King Pippin, and also of our uncle Carloman, certain properties in the Duchy of Alamannia were brought under the control of the treasury. Various men now unjustly possessed them as though by private right, and some had already dispersed them through sales, donations, and various other means.

Among these properties, Count Hrodhard formerly appears to have purchased certain holdings from Hunnidus or from other men by written deeds of sale. They are situated in the county of Breisgau, in places called Binuzl[... ]im and Romaningahoba, and in other places, with their dependencies and appurtenances. He appears to have sold or transferred them unlawfully to the possessions of Saint Dionysius the Martyr, where his precious body rests. Abbot Mainard therefore appears lawfully to have recovered them for us through his pledges.

But when we considered, for the love of God and in reverence for Saint Dionysius, for the increase of our reward, the relief of our soul, and the stability of our kingdom, we resolved henceforth, by our charter, to grant and transfer the aforesaid properties to that house of God with the readiest disposition and benevolent will.

For this reason we ordered this charter of our confirmation to be written, so that the aforesaid properties, in their entirety, with lands, houses, buildings, bondsmen, vineyards, woods, and all dependencies or appurtenances located anywhere, just as that house of God formerly appears to have possessed them, might henceforth, fully confirmed in the name of God by our charter, be held, possessed, and owned by the basilica of Saint Dionysius from this day forward, and might always prosper there as an increase of our almsgiving.

And so that this authority may be held more firmly and better preserved through the ages, we have confirmed it with our own hand and ordered it sealed with our ring.

[Col. 0978A] **Sign of Charles, most glorious king.**

I, Erkembald, have subscribed in place of Rado.

[Note: [Col. 0977] Here the era of the Lombard reign is also lacking. The matter has elsewhere been treated concerning Copsistanum, or Copsistano, the palace situated in the suburb of Mainz.]

Given on the day before the Kalends of September, in the twenty-second year of the reign of our lord Charles, most excellent king. Enacted at Copsistano, happily in the name of God.

### LIV. Charter of Charlemagne for the monastery of Saint Victor at Marseille (790)

*(From Dom Bouquet, Collection of the Histories of France.)*

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans. We believe that the protection of our kingdom is greatly increased if we respond with a freer spirit to the petitions of priests and servants of God brought before our ears, and bring them to fulfillment in the name of God.

Therefore let it be known to the multitude of all our faithful how, for the honor of the Lord, we appear to have granted the following privilege to the monastery of Marseille, which is dedicated to the blessed and ever-virgin Mary and to Saint Victor the Martyr: in whatever estates or properties, wherever situated, have been granted or transferred there through the generosity of the giver of all good things, or shall henceforth be given or transferred there by God-fearing men, and whatever appears justly and reasonably to belong there, no public judge shall at any time presume to enter for hearing cases, exacting fines, requiring lodging or provisions, distraining the men of that church, taking sureties, or demanding any public levies; nor shall he exact anything there. Rather, they are to remain under the name and protection of immunity.

For this reason we ordered this charter of our authority to be written, by which we specially decree and ordain that from now on and henceforth no one, whether an old or a new official, shall presume to enter or exact anything in the estates or properties of the aforesaid church within our kingdoms, by the favor of Christ, for hearing cases, exacting fines, requiring lodging or provisions, distraining the men of that church, taking sureties, or demanding any public levies, as we have said, at any time whatsoever.

Rather, under the name of immunity, those who now appear to be its rectors, together with their successors, shall be permitted to live and remain peacefully with all the fines granted to them. Whatever now justly and reasonably belongs to those places, or shall henceforth be given or transferred there by God-fearing men, shall, through our charity, prosper there as an increase, so that the congregation may be more eager to pray attentively to the mercy of the Lord for us and for the stability of our kingdom.

And so that this charter may be better preserved in our time and that of our successors, we have decreed that it be confirmed with our own hand and ordered it sealed below with our ring.

**Sign of Charles, most glorious king.**

[Col. 0979A] Given in the month of March, in the twenty-second and seventeenth years of the reign of Lord Charles. Enacted at the city of Quamarcia.

[Note: [Col. 0979C] From this month the beginning of Charles’s reign in Italy must be reckoned. This is the earlier reckoning of his reign; the later begins in the month of May. The earlier reckoning is confirmed by the Council of Friuli, which Saint Paulinus celebrated in 796, “in the twenty-third and fifteenth year of their most fortunate rule”—that is, of Charles and Pippin, king of Italy—as the beginning of the same council records. Thus, in April of this year Charles had already begun the twenty-third year of his Italian reign; he would have counted only the twenty-second year if the later reckoning had been used. Therefore, since, according to Anastasius, Charles subjugated various cities before the capture of Pavia, he began to call himself king from the part of Lombardy that had been conquered.]

[Note: [Col. 0979D] Corrected to “Worms,” the city where Charles celebrated the Easter solemnity in this year 790.]

### LV. Charter of King Charlemagne for the monastery of Saint Martin at Tours (790)

*(From D. Bouquet, in the same work.)*

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans. We believe it known to all our faithful how, in the time of our father of blessed memory, the former King Pippin, and also of our uncle Carloman, certain properties in the Duchy of Alamannia were brought under the control of the treasury. Various men now unjustly possessed them as though by private right, and some had already dispersed them through sales, donations, or various other means.

Among these properties, a certain former Alamannian named Fulrid appears, by a deed of sale, to have unlawfully transferred to the basilica of Saint Martin, where his precious body rests, a holding at Stamaconstat in Breisgau. Abbot Itherius therefore appears lawfully to have recovered it for us through his pledges.

But when we considered, for the love of God and in reverence for Saint Martin, for the increase of our reward, the relief of our soul, and the stability of our kingdom, we resolved henceforth, by our charter, to grant and transfer the aforesaid property to that house of God with the readiest disposition and benevolent will.

For this reason we ordered this charter of our confirmation to be written, so that the aforesaid property, in its entirety, with the church, lands, houses, buildings, bondsmen, vineyards, woods, and all dependencies and appurtenances located anywhere, just as that house of God formerly appears to have possessed it, might henceforth, fully confirmed in the name of God by our charter, be held, retained, and possessed by the portion of the aforesaid basilica of Saint Martin from this day forward, and might always prosper there as an increase of our almsgiving.

And so that this authority may be held more firmly and better preserved through the ages, we have confirmed it with our own hand and ordered it sealed with our ring.

**Sign of Charles, most glorious king.**

Ercambald in place of Rado.

Given on the second day before the Kalends of September, in the twenty-second year of Lord Charles, most excellent king. Enacted at Copsistano, happily in the name of God. Amen.

### LVI. Charter of Charlemagne by which, at the request of Abbot Anianus, he takes the monasteries of Saint John and Saint Lawrence under his protection and grants them the estate of Caunas (793)

*(From Mabillon, On Diplomatic Matters.)*

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, to all our faithful, present and future. It is right that royal power should extend protection to those whose need is found to require it.

Therefore let your greatness and advantage know that the venerable Abbot Anianus of the monasteries of Saint John and Saint Lawrence, which are constructed in places called Extorio [commonly Citou] and Olibegio, came to our synodal assembly with his monks and fully commended himself, together with all the property and men of his monastery that he appears presently to possess, to our protection. We have received and retain him and his monks under our protection, together with all their property and men, so that throughout the days of their lives they may live and remain peacefully under our protection.

[Note: [Col. 0979D] Anianus, or Annianus, the abbot praised in this charter, is the man whom Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, celebrates in a poem addressed to Benedict, abbot of Aniane. The two monasteries mentioned here, constructed by the same Annianus—one of Saint John at Extorio, the other of Saint Lawrence at Olibegio—frequently recur in these records. The monastery of Mont-Olivet, which is near Caunas, was at that time called Saint John the Baptist in the fortress of Mallast, according to the records of that place cited below. Yet it appears to be distinct from Anianus’s monastery. The other monastery, bearing the name of Saint Lawrence, is now called Saint Anianus, commonly Saint-Chinian, originally dedicated to Saint Anianus the Confessor, as appears from a charter of the emperors Louis and Lothar. Cannense is situated between this monastery and the other one, soon to be mentioned, Mont-Olivet, or Mont-Oliou, in the diocese of Carcassonne. Daniel, abbot of Caunas, subjected Caunas to Abbot Anianus, as attested by a charter of Charles the Bald to be published later. Concerning the monastery of Saint Lawrence, consult Baluze’s notes on the Capitularies and on the councils of the province of Narbonne. I return to the monastery of Saint John, which is called Saint John of Exequaurium in another unpublished Caunas original, in which the boundaries of the estate and monastery of Caunas are designated by order of Count Magnarius: “in the thirty-fourth year of the reign of our lord Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans,” that is, in the year 802. There we read of the Abbot Anianus mentioned here, who with his monks served “the monasteries of Saint John of Exequaurium and of Saints Peter and Paul, which the aforesaid Anianus built with his brothers above the Argentodublum stream, in the estate of Caunas, formerly called Bufintis, which King Charles granted to that abbot and his brothers.” Hence arose the dispute between Count Magnarius and Abbot Anianus concerning the determination of the boundaries. In the earlier charter, moreover, one should observe the formula by which Charlemagne confirms the donation of the estate of Caunas made to Anianus by Milo: “Likewise we granted him the estate of Caunas, just as Milo transferred it to his monastery by his letters.” Formulas of this kind are frequent in royal confirmation charters, as in the charter of Louis the Stammerer for the church of Nevers—as though the king were then granting for the first time a property whose donation he was actually confirming.]

For this reason we have given them these letters for the sake of confirmation, by which we absolutely command that no one among you, nor any of your subordinates, presume to touch or disturb the aforesaid Abbot Anianus or his monks, or their property or men, or to bring any complaint against them contrary to the order of justice. Rather, as we have said, they are to be permitted to live and remain peacefully under our protection with all their property and men.

Likewise, we have granted him the estate of Caunas, just as Milo transferred it to his monastery by his letters, with all its appurtenances, so that the servants of God may be more eager to pray to the mercy of the Lord for us and for the stability of our kingdom.

And if any cases should arise or have arisen against them or against their men which you are unable to settle in the province without serious loss to them, let them be reserved until our presence, so that before us they may receive a final judgment according to the order of the law.

And so that this authority may be held more firmly and better preserved by our faithful, we ordered it sealed below with our ring.

I, Widolaicus, have reviewed and subscribed in place of Rado.

Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of August, in the twenty-sixth and twentieth years of our reign. Enacted at the palace of Frankfurt, happily in the name of God.

### LVI bis. Charter of Charlemagne concerning all the property of the church of Le Mans (796)

*(From D. Bouquet, Collection of Histories.)*

[Col. 0980B]

In the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards [Col. 0981C] and patrician of the Romans. If we bring to fulfillment the petitions of priests and servants of God which they make known to us on behalf of their needs, we not only practice a lawful custom but also confidently believe that such acts will benefit us toward the blessedness of eternal recompense.

[Note: [Col. 0981D] An unusual invocation and one that must be removed.]

Therefore we wish it known to all bishops, abbots, dukes, counts, *vicedomini*, vicars, centenaries, officials, our traveling envoys, and all the faithful of the holy Church of God and of ours, present and future, that the venerable Franco, bishop of the city of Le Mans, came to our Serenity and humbly requested that we order a charter to be made for him concerning all the property of the church entrusted to him. He requested that it name specifically the cells, villages, or estates which, at the present time, he is known to hold under his own authority or that of his canons, his vassals, and others devotedly serving him or his church, both free and unfree, so that in future he or his successors might, supported more firmly by our authority and without any summons or opposition, be permitted to hold and govern them under the jurisdiction and dominion of the aforesaid church of Le Mans.

We gladly granted his request and ordered that the cells, estates, and villages be inserted by name in this charter, as he had asked. These are: the cell of Saint Vincent with everything belonging to it; the cell of Saint Albin; the cell of Saint Ouen; the cell of Saint Rigomer; the cell of Saint Almir; the cell of Saint Ulfacius; and the cell of Saint Baomad—all these with everything belonging to them—together with the four canonical villages, namely Salica, Montiniacum, Flaciacum, and Oxellum, with twelve estates and the other little estates belonging to them, as recorded in the registers of the aforesaid church: Rupiacum, Cavania, Culturas, Baliau, Aloncion, Colonicum, the old village, and Celsiacum, the canonical village; and the estate of Saint Gervasius, Aloniacum, Asinarias, Vodebris, Callemarcium, and the other little estates whose names are not presently remembered.

We ordered all these, with everything belonging to them and in their entirety, to be inserted in our charter under the protection of immunity.

We formerly also ordered another charter to be made for the aforesaid bishop and his canons concerning the monasteries, cells, villages, and estates which our faithful are known to hold by our grant. We ordered that they be named there in our charter, subject to the lawful census and to the payment of ninths and tenths and the restoration of churches. We command and order that all these be preserved by our faithful just as they are inserted in that charter. From these properties we desire, whenever the Lord grants power and opportunity, to console and increase the aforesaid church and the aforesaid bishop.

At present, however, we grant that whenever any of those who hold benefices of the aforesaid church by our grant depart from this world without male children having been born or commended to us, the aforesaid bishop, his successors, their officials, and canons shall cause those benefices to be recalled to the power and dominion of the aforesaid church without anyone’s authorization.

And whenever the occasion arises to exchange those benefices with our faithful who hold them by our grant, we wish them to be returned to the aforesaid church, so that the bishops, priests, and servants of God of that church may be more eager to pray for us, for all the people entrusted to us by God, for the stability of the kingdom, and for the peace of the entire people.

Moreover, he brought before us the immunities of our predecessors, namely the kings of the Franks, which stated how they had always held the aforesaid see, together with all its property and the men belonging to it, under the fullest defense and protection of immunity, for the love of God and in reverence for the saints whose relics are venerated there.

For the sake of confirmation, therefore, the aforesaid bishop requested that we again grant and confirm this protection around that holy place, for the increase of our reward. We did not wish to refuse his request for the love of God; rather, let all the faithful of the holy Church of God and of ours, present and future, know that we have granted and perpetually confirmed it in every respect.

Therefore we command that no public judge, no one exercising judicial authority, and none of our faithful presume at any time to enter the churches, places, fields, or other possessions of the aforesaid church which it is known presently to hold and possess lawfully in any counties and territories within the dominion of our kingdom, or which divine mercy may hereafter wish to increase in the right of that holy place, in order to hear cases, make or demand levies, exact tribute or fines, require lodging or provisions, exact tolls, take sureties, or unjustly distrain the men of that church, whether free or unfree, who appear to reside upon its land. Nor may anyone presume at any place or time to exact from those properties any public payments or unlawful exactions.

Whatever the treasury might have expected from the property of the aforesaid church, we grant in full to that church.

We also ordered the following to be inserted in this charter: no judge, count, free man, or person of any kind shall presume to accuse the ministers or advocates of the aforesaid church in the public court. Rather, he must first summon the administrators of the property and the judges of the estates and men by whom he claims to have been injured, so that he may receive from them a familiar and just judgment. If he does not wish to accept it, then he may summon the bishop of the aforesaid church, so that he may receive from him a familiar, good, and just judgment.

If he is unable to obtain justice from the bishop or his ministers, he shall thereafter have permission to pursue his complaints justly, reasonably, and lawfully in the public court.

But if, before doing these things, he should presume to accuse or summon the bishop of the church of the aforesaid see, or his ministers or advocates, then, because he has despised or violated our command, our prohibition, and our charter, let him pay our ban to us on this account, and let him pay one hundred solidi of silver to the bishop of the aforesaid church or to his ministers; thereafter he shall receive his justice without legal process or any composition.

We have granted these aforesaid judicial arrangements to the bishops of the aforesaid church and to the servants of God serving the Lord there, for the love of God and in reverence for the saints, and we wish them to remain granted in future times, just as we have discovered by investigation that they were made by our predecessors, namely the kings of the Franks.

Thus the aforesaid bishop and his successors, together with the servants of God serving the Lord there, may be more eager to pray for us and for the stability of the entire kingdom granted and preserved for us by God, together with the clergy and people subject to him.

And so that this authority of our charter may be held more firmly and preserved for future times, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and decreed that it be strengthened below by the impression of our ring.

**Sign of Charles, most glorious king.**

[Col. 0984A] Genesius, in place of Erkembald, reviewed and subscribed.

Given in the month of December, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of January, in the twenty-ninth year of our reign.

Enacted at our palace of Aachen, happily in the name of God. Amen.

### LVII. Charter of Ghisela, Charlemagne’s sister, by which she grants many estates to the monastery of Saint-Denis that she had received from her parents (798)

*(From Mabillon, On Diplomatic Matters.)

[lacuna] of the blessed martyrs Dionysius, where he himself rests bodily with his holy companions. From their estate and possessions that holy place was enriched and well [Col. 0984B] established, and is so now, and, with the Lord’s permission, will remain forever. Therefore now, in the name of God, Ghysela, most noble daughter of King Pippin and of the former Queen Bertrada, consecrated to God and ever devoted to Christ, for the sake of God and from desire for the heavenly kingdom and for the remedy of my soul, give to that holy place—and wish this gift to be presently effective—as holy Scripture admonishes us: while a person lives in the body, he should think of the eternity of life, so that from what is passing away he may deserve what is eternal. For the Lord says in the Gospel: “Make for yourselves treasures in heaven that do not fail, and from unrighteous mammon acquire for yourselves eternal dwellings.” In accordance with the statement of the blessed teacher Augustine, who says: “The world perishes, and the things that are in the world.” But that which is distributed in churches or among the poor never perishes; rather, for each person it is reckoned as righteousness leading to eternal blessedness.

Therefore, for love of him, we give to that holy place named above, where at the present time Abbot Fardulfus appears to live, rule, and govern together with a very large community of monks, our villa called Putialis in the county of [Note: [Col. 0983D] This county is Atrabatensis, as I noted in my commentary on the Life of Saint Leodegarius in the second volume of the Benedictine edition. Observe here the title “most noble,” which the royal offspring alone claim for themselves. Nor is this surprising, since kings themselves, indeed even emperors, once took pride in this name. See Gabriel Trivorius’s apologetic observation, chapter 10, and the charter of Samson, archbishop of Rheims, where he calls the younger Louis “most noble.” Compare the diploma of Charlemagne that follows immediately, issued to confirm the donation of his sister Gisela. When I read in this charter the passage from Augustine, I seem to see that Gisela for whose sake Alcuin abridged Augustine’s commentaries on the Gospel of John.] Atrabatensis, together with the churches constructed there in honor of Saint Vedast and the other saints, with their appurtenances: Gunbodecurte, or Postonevillare, or Bertinocurte, as well as Linarias, and also Hodricio, in the aforesaid county of Atrabatensis; and Magrastovilla in the county of Vermandensis; Frisionecurte and also Agnocurte in the county of Ambianensis; Vvalliu in the county of Cameracensis. These places named above, with all their entirety [Col. 0984D] and substance—that is, together with lands, manses, houses, structures, buildings, defenses, slaves, tenants, resident dependants, freedmen, and servants, both those born there and those transferred from elsewhere; fields, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses; movable and immovable property; herds with their shepherds; thoroughfares, public pastures, and their appurtenances; and every appurtenant right and all revenue that appear to look to or belong to the aforesaid places named above [Col. 0985A]—and whatever I presently possess within or outside their boundaries, whether acquired by inheritance, purchase, or any other lawful acquisition, shall from this day forward, with Christ’s protection, increase the alms and resources of the monks dwelling there. I transfer and convey it from my right into the right and dominion of that basilica, so that from this day you and your successors may have, hold, and possess it, and may freely and most firmly, with the Lord’s help in all things, have the power to do whatever you wish with it.

And so that this donation made by me may remain firm and unshaken for all time:

**Sign of Ghysela, most noble daughter of King Pippin,** [Col. 0985B] who requested that this donation be made.

**Sign of Charles, most noble son of the lord Charles, most excellent king.**

**Sign of Pippin, most noble son of the lord Charles, most excellent king.**

**Sign of Chlodoic, most noble son of the lord Charles, most excellent king.**

I, Wineradus, chancellor, at the command of the aforesaid lady Ghysela, wrote and subscribed this.

Given on the Ides of June, in the thirty-first year, and the twenty-sixth year of the reign of our lord. Enacted at our palace of Aachen, happily, in the name of God. Amen.

### LVIII. Diploma of Charlemagne confirming the donations made by his sister Gisela to the monastery of Saint-Denis (799)

*(From D. Bouquet, Collection of Histories.)*

[Col. 0985C]

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans. If we confirm by our decrees those things that are known to have been bestowed or granted by God-fearing people and by our parents upon venerable holy places, we confidently believe that this will unquestionably contribute to our eternal blessedness and increase of reward, as well as to the stability of our kingdom.

Therefore let it be known to all our faithful, present and future, how the illustrious Gisela, consecrated to God and our most beloved sister, informed our Serenity that, inspired by divine power, she had assigned certain properties of her own to the monastery of the holy martyrs Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius, where they rest bodily and where the venerable [Note: [Col. 0985D] Fulradus had already died in 784; “Fardulfus” should be read, as in Gisela’s preceding charter containing her donations.] Fulradus [Col. 0986A] was abbot, both for herself and for the salvation of the souls of our lord and father, the former most glorious King Pippin, and of our lady and mother Bertrada, after the fullest deliberation. She also showed us her deed of donation for rereading, in which it was stated that she had given to that place a villa called Puciales, situated in the county of Adrapatensis, together with the churches constructed there in honor of Saint Vedast and the other saints, and all its appurtenances belonging to it within that county: Gundhodocurte, Postinevillare, Berninocurte, and Linarias, as well as Hodricio. In the county of Vermandensis, Imuagrastuilla; and in the county of Ambianensis, Fricionecurte and Magnonecurte; likewise, in the county of Cameracensis, the place called Walin. [Col. 0986B]

But for complete security she requested our Highness that whatever she had justly and reasonably assigned, in due legal order, in the places mentioned above to the aforesaid monastery of the holy martyrs, for our common reward and eternal recompense, we should grant and confirm by our decrees. We did not wish to deny her petition for the sake of God, but, as an act of our almsgiving, we wish it to remain perpetually. Having examined her deed of donation, therefore, as it is set out therein, we decree by this authority and confirmation of ours that henceforth the aforesaid venerable man, [Note: [Col. 0985D] Read “Fardulfus.”] Fulradus, abbot, and his successors forever, whoever may be rulers of that holy place in their time, shall hold and possess these properties by the firmest legal right, so that all the things mentioned above may perpetually increase for the lights of that church and for the stipends of the servants of God. [Col. 0986C]

And so that this authority may be held more firmly and preserved better for future ages, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it strengthened with the impression of our ring.

**Sign of Charles, most glorious king.**

Genesius wrote and reviewed this in place of Ercanbaldus.

Given on the Ides of June, in the thirty-first year and the twenty-sixth year of the reign of our lord Charles. Enacted at the palace of Aachen, happily, in the name of God. Amen.

### LIX. Diploma of Charlemagne for the monastery of Centula (798)

[Note: [Col. 0985D] This diploma, granted in the year 798 of Christ, teaches us two things. First, it establishes the location of Argubium, of which Alcuin writes in his hymn on Saint Richarius:

> You founded a monastery  
> In a place near Argubium,  
> And another at Centulum—  
> Both of enduring merit.

In my notes on the Life of Saint Richarius I had conjectured that Argubium was situated near the forest of Cressi, in which the cell of Forestis was founded. This diploma confirms my conjecture, where we read that “Saint Richarius chose for himself as a dwelling the forest called Forestis, near the cistern that lies beside the place called Argubium, in the same county of Pontivo.” The monastery of Forestis is in fact still visible not far from the right bank of the Somme, between Abbeville and the town of Saint-Valery. The other notable point is that Charles was induced to grant this diploma by Angilbert’s “service and merits.” After these letters had been received, the monastery of Forestis remained subject to Centula for a long time; monks and canons were established there under the authority of the abbot of Centula. In the course of time, however, this cell was again raised to the status of an abbey, in which condition it still remains, although its revenues are extremely small and only a few monks reside there, while its buildings are collapsing. In the description of the revenues of the monastery of Centula made by Abbot Hericus we read: “In Forestis-cell there are three churches: the first of Saint Mary, the second of Saint Peter, and the third of Saint Richarius. There are five altars furnished with gold and silver, etc. There are thirty canons, who have four villas for their support, etc.,” in Book III, chapter 3, of the Chronicle of Centula.]

*(From Mabillon, Acts of the Order of Saint Benedict.)*

[Col. 0986D]

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans. Whatever we grant or confirm, after benevolent deliberation, for love of our Lord Jesus Christ and for the benefit of the servants of God, we confidently believe contributes to the increase of our reward and to the stability of our kingdom.

Therefore let it be known to all our faithful, present and future, how Angilbert, venerable abbot of the monastery of Centula, which is constructed in honor of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, his holy mother, ever-virgin Mary, Saint Peter, all the other apostles, and many saints, in which also the most illustrious confessor of Christ, Saint Richarius, rests bodily, situated in the county of Pontivo, brought to the knowledge of our Serenity that Saint Richarius himself, while still living in this present age, had chosen for himself as a place of habitation, in the forest called Forestis, near the cistern beside the place called Argubium, in the same county of Pontivo. At his request, he had received from the royal authority two or three bunuaria [Read: *bunuariis*, etc.] around that cistern, and lovers of the servants of God had endeavored to build for him there a sufficiently humble hut in which he might serve Almighty God. There, by divine calling, he departed from this world to the Lord.

Not long afterward, the brothers of the aforesaid monastery of Centula took his sacred body and buried it with great reverence in the said monastery. Through his merits, with Almighty God cooperating, many miracles were manifested in those two places. For in the dominion of one abbot there had for many years been a harmonious community of brothers, worthy in the praises of God.

For this reason he requested the clemency of our kingdom that, for love of our Lord Jesus Christ, Saint Richarius, and the other saints, and for the increase of our reward, we should, by a decree of our authority, with the fullest deliberation, grant and transfer to the monastery of Centula—where his sacred body rests—the cell in which Saint Richarius had striven to serve God. We did not wish to deny his request, compelled by his service and merits; rather, for the honor and love of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ and for eternal recompense, know that we have granted and confirmed it in every respect.

Therefore we establish and command that this arrangement, which we wish to remain forever by the firmest legal right with the aforesaid monastery of Centula, shall stand. Thus the aforesaid Angilbert and his successors forever, whoever may in their time be rulers of that monastery, shall hold and possess the aforesaid cell of Forestis, with all the furnishings of the church and all its goods, appurtenances, and adjacent properties—whatever it appears presently to possess justly and reasonably, or whatever thereafter, by the Lord’s gift, may be added or assigned there in justice and due legal order—by this decree of our Serenity, grant, and confirmation. [Col. 0988A]

Thus from now on and in the future, may the praise of God and the concord of the servants of the Lord, for the reward of our soul, under the rule of righteousness and under the name of one abbot, remain perpetually undisturbed in our times and, God willing, in times to come. May this more greatly delight those servants of God who appear to serve God there, so that they may continually entreat the Lord’s mercy for us, our children, our entire household, and the stability of our kingdom.

And so that this authority may be held more firmly and preserved better for long ages, we have resolved to strengthen it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with our ring.

**Sign of Charles, most glorious king.**

Eranbaldus reread and subscribed.

[Col. 0988B] Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of May, in the twenty-ninth year and the twenty-fifth year of our reign. Enacted at the public palace of Aachen, happily, in the name of God. Amen.

### LX. Diploma of Charlemagne confirming the New Cell to the monastery of Aniane (799)

*(From D. Bouquet, Collection of Histories.)*

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, to all bishops, abbots, dukes, counts, vicars, centenarii, and all the faithful of the holy Church of God and of ourselves, present and future.

Let it be known how the venerable Benedict, abbot of the monastery of the holy Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary, constructed at the place called Aniane, in the county whose name is Magdalonensis, informed our Serenity that he and his monks had acquired certain deserted places within our estate called Juviniacum, formerly called Fonte-Agricolae, but now called New Cell, which they had built by their own labor. They also appeared to have constructed two mills within the boundaries of that estate, on the river Leto; and between the sea and the lagoon, at the place called Porcarias, with the consent of the counts and of the other Christians living all around there, he had received a deserted tract of land. Likewise, at the place called Asogrado, he had built a cell with all its adjoining property. They also possess to this day other places, Comajacas and Caucino, on the river Araur, at the place called Ad-Salices, for the pasturing of cattle and feeding of livestock, together with their other uses. He asserts that he possesses all these things in due legal order, without unlawful opposition from anyone.

But for complete security he requested our Highness that whatever he and his monks are now known to possess justly and reasonably in the aforesaid places, we should again, by a decree of our authority, with the fullest deliberation and for the reward of our soul, transfer and confirm to the aforesaid monastery for him and his monks dwelling there under the holy rule. We did not wish to deny his request, but know that we have granted and confirmed it in every respect as an act of our almsgiving.

Therefore we command that neither you nor your junior officers or successors presume at any time to disturb or bring a charge against the aforesaid venerable man, Abbot Benedict, or his successors, concerning the aforesaid places—wherever he and his monks are presently known to be established in due legal order, justly and reasonably—or to take away or diminish anything from them contrary to justice. Rather, by this authority and confirmation of ours, let them possess these things as a grant of our almsgiving for all time, so that it may more greatly please them to entreat the Lord’s mercy attentively for us, our sons and daughters, our entire household, and all the people of our nation.

And so that this authority may be held more firmly and preserved better for long ages, we have decreed that it be strengthened below with the seals of our hands and ordered it sealed with our ring.

**Sign of Charles, most glorious king.**

Given in the month of June, in the thirty-first year and the twenty-sixth year of our reign. Enacted at our palace of Aachen, happily, in the name of God. Amen.

### LXI. Decree of Charlemagne concerning the immunity of the monastery of Corrofes, or Charroux (799)

*(From D. Bouquet, ibid.)*

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans. We believe that the defense of our kingdom is greatly strengthened if, with benevolent devotion, we grant suitable benefits to ecclesiastical places and, under the Lord’s protection, record that they shall endure securely.

Therefore let it be known to all our faithful, present and future, how the illustrious count Rotgerius, our faithful, approached our clemency and, with the fullest deliberation, appeared to transfer into our hands the monastery of his property which he had newly built in honor of our Lord and Savior at the place called Karrofum, on the river Charente, in the county of Poitiers, together with all its goods and church furnishings, books, and all its appurtenances and adjoining properties. There he appointed the venerable David as abbot.

Therefore, at his request, we have seen fit to bestow upon that holy place the following benefit for eternal recompense: in the churches, places, fields, and other possessions of that monastery which it appears presently to possess justly and reasonably, or which divine piety may hereafter wish to enlarge in the right of that holy place, no public judge shall at any time presume to enter in order to hear cases or exact fines from any quarter. Rather, the abbot himself, his successors, and the community of that monastery shall be able to exercise authority under the complete title of immunity, for the sake of the Lord’s name.

[Col. 0990A] Therefore we establish and command that neither you nor your junior officers or successors, nor anyone exercising judicial authority, presume at any time to enter the churches, places, fields, or other possessions of our aforesaid monastery to hear cases, exact fines from any quarter, impose lodging or requisition duties, take sureties, distrain the men of that church, or demand any payments. Rather, what we have granted to the aforesaid monastery for the sake of the Lord’s name and eternal recompense shall increase its resources for all time, so that those servants of God who appear to serve God there may be more eagerly pleased to entreat the Lord’s mercy for us, our wife, and our children.

[Col. 0990B] And so that this present authority may remain inviolate in our times and in those to come, we have decreed that it be strengthened with the seals of our hands and ordered it sealed with our ring. [Note: [Col. 0989D] This diploma lacks chronological notes. Since Charles describes himself in it only as king and patrician, it appears to have been issued no later than 799, and perhaps indeed at Aachen, while Charles was handing Count Rotgerius a fragment of the Lord’s Cross to be delivered to the monastery of Corrofes. So Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals*, book XXVI, no. 82.]

### LXII. Decree of Charlemagne for the monks of Saint-Martin of Tours (799)

[Note: [Col. 0990D] This diploma may perhaps be assigned to the year 800.]

*(In Martène, volume I of the* Thesaurus Anecdotorum, *column 13.)*

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, to all bishops, abbots, illustrious men, dukes, counts, household officials, grafiones, vicars, centenarii, our junior officers, and our traveling envoys, present and future.

It is fitting for the dignity of royal clemency to give careful attention to everything reasonably requested by priests, not to deny suitable and appropriate benefits, and, in accordance with the acts of earlier kings, to confirm more fully whatever has been granted for the sake of God.

Therefore the venerable man Alcuin, abbot of the basilica of our special patron Saint Martin, where that precious lord rests bodily, brought to us for rereading the immunities of our glorious royal predecessors, strengthened by their own hands, together with those of our father, King Pippin of blessed memory. They contained the following: how the aforesaid kings, out of reverence for the most blessed Saint Martin, confirmed that all the goods and possessions of that most blessed saint in the kingdom that, by God’s favor, is ours—Austrasia, Neustria, Burgundy, Aquitaine, and Provence—whether in greater or lesser places throughout the kingdoms written above; whatever had been conferred or assigned to the aforesaid house of Saint Martin by royal decrees, grants, or immunities, or by Christian people and various transactions through any instruments of charter; and whatever might thereafter be added or assigned in future times, should live under our immunity.

Therefore the aforesaid Abbot Alcuin requested from the serenity of our kingdom that, for the purpose of strengthening the same arrangement, we should bestow the benefit of our goodwill. We, consenting to his request and venerating the patronage of Saint Martin, know that we have gladly granted this gift of immunity, just as the preceding kings had individually fulfilled it.

Accordingly we command that all the property of the most blessed Saint Martin, wherever it may be in the kingdom that, by God’s favor, is ours—whether in large or small villas and estates, or among all the possessions of the most blessed Saint Martin—shall stand under the title of immunity. No public judge of our fisc shall presume to enter the aforesaid villas or possessions of that saint to conduct business, hear cases, exact fines or penalties, collect tolls, impose lodging duties, or take sureties. [Col. 0991B] Rather, whatever our fisc had been accustomed to receive or exact from them in former or present times, we entirely withdraw from our fisc, so that it may increase the lights of Saint Martin, the sustenance of the poor, and the stipends of the monks.

No public judge of our fisc shall claim to have any power over the aforesaid villas or possessions of Saint Martin by any device whatsoever. Rather, he shall always remain excluded and removed from every fiscal authority over the aforesaid property, so that he may not presume to seek any pretext by which he could cause loss to the men of Saint Martin. The immunities of earlier kings and our decrees shall be preserved in every respect.

And if any count, household official, grafio, vicar, tribune, or anyone equipped with any judicial authority should presume to break or violate the grants and benevolence of former or later kings, or our decree, he shall know himself liable to a fine of six hundred solidi, payable in refined or pure gold, to that house of Saint Martin, while another third part shall go to the chapel of our fisc. Let no one take pleasure in seeing what has been granted to priests for the sake of God, or the immunities of earlier kings or our decrees, torn apart by wicked men.

Whatever the house of Saint Martin presently appears to possess, or whatever was formerly given or conferred upon it by any God-fearing or good people, shall remain under the title of immunity. Anyone who wishes to give his property to that house of God shall, by our authority, have permission to do so, and it shall remain peacefully under the title of immunity, without any fiscal authority. Whatever the fisc was accustomed to receive shall, as our almsgiving, be counted at present among the lights of Saint Martin, together with the subsequent provisions. Both the abbot himself and all his successors shall perpetually hold and possess all the property of Saint Martin under complete immunity.

And if in past times, through the negligence or lukewarmness of abbots or the presumption of judges, anything belonging to this immunity should have been diminished, violated, removed, or broken, it shall in every respect be restored through our authorities and benefits. Let none of you, nor any of your junior officers or successors, thereafter presume to infringe or violate what we have agreed to. Rather, as stated above, with complete immunity, may they possess in peace, with God’s help and our favor, what has been granted to them.

And so that this decree concerning that house and the venerable church of Saint Martin may endure for future times, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and signed it with the impression of our ring.

**Sign of Charles, most glorious king.**

Enacted at the fortress of Laon, happily, in the name of God. Amen.

### LXIII. Decree of Charlemagne for the monastery of Gormaric (800)

[Col. 0992B]

[“In the name of our Lord God Jesus Christ” — **Note: [Col. 0991D] This invocation should be deleted.**] Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans, to all the faithful of Saint Martin who presently serve God in the holy place where the precious confessor of Christ rests bodily, and to those who will serve there in future times; to abbots, priests, deacons, and all ecclesiastical orders, senior and junior members: eternal salvation and prosperity in the love of Christ.

Let it be known to your fraternity that our beloved master Albinus, moved by pious devotion, requested from us permission to establish monks in the cell of Saint Paul, which in the rustic language is called Cormaricus, so that they might live there according to the rule and statutes of Saint Benedict. Iterius, his predecessor as abbot, acquired this place by purchase, built it, and handed it over to Saint Martin.

We considered it right to consent to his pious devotion and caused it to be confirmed by letters and by the seal of our name, so that no breach might ever afterward be made by any of his successors. For if divine piety granted our parents and us the power to give the entire monastery of Saint Martin and its possessions to whomever we wished, how much greater is our power to assign the aforesaid place perpetually to the service of God? No one may lawfully scorn a royal donation or confirmation, especially one contained in so pious and salutary a decree.

Therefore we absolutely command that this donation and order of ours remain valid and inviolate for all time. We do not wish that place to be removed from the authority of Saint Martin; rather, let the monks dwelling there live fully under the rule of Saint Benedict and receive protection and assistance from the abbots of the monastery of Saint Martin.

If any abbot in future times should scorn this decree of ours—which God forbid—let him know that he will have to render an account of his presumption to our Lord Jesus Christ on the day of his great coming. Likewise, whoever diminishes anything from the property that Abbot Iterius of blessed memory acquired or purchased, or from the property of Saint Martin that he gave to the church of Saint Paul, or if the same Abbot Albinus, at whose request we caused this confirmation to be written, should add anything, or if anyone should hereafter wish to add anything as an alms for his soul, let it serve the brothers of that place perpetually in due order.

Whoever reads this little charter should, in the fear of God, diligently strive to preserve this reasonable document, so that he may have the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ forever.

And so that this decree of ours might be more secure, we have resolved to strengthen it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with our ring.

**Sign of Charles, most glorious king.**

Given on the third day before the Nones of June, in the thirty-second year and the twenty-seventh year of our reign.

Enacted in the city of Tours, in the monastery of Saint Martin, where he himself rests bodily, happily.

### LXIV. Decree of Charlemagne for the monastery of Cormaric (800)

*(From D. Bouquet, Collection of Histories.)*

[Col. 0993B]

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans. Let it be known to all bishops, counts, household officials, vicars, centenarii, and our other faithful, present and future, that at the request of our most beloved faithful Albinus, abbot of the venerable monastery of Saint Martin, where that precious saint rests bodily, we have granted the following.

The monks who appear to live under the rule of Saint Benedict in the monastery built in honor of the apostle Saint Paul, at the place called Cormaricus, shall have permission to send two ships up and down the Loire, the Mayenne, the Sarthe, the Loir, and the Vienne, as their needs require, so that neither they nor their men shall have to pay or give any toll anywhere whatsoever, whether on salt or on any other goods.

For this reason we have ordered this present authority to be made, by which we command perpetually that neither we nor our junior officers or successors presume to disturb or bring any charge against the aforesaid venerable man, Abbot Albinus, or his successors, or the monks or their men from the aforesaid monastery of Saint Paul, on account of those ships; nor may they demand or exact from them in any way tolls, river dues, passage dues, port dues, or any other payments. Rather, this shall perpetually increase, in our times and in those to come, at that holy place of Cormaric and for those brothers, as an act of our almsgiving.

And so that this authority may be held more firmly and preserved better for future ages, we have ordered it sealed below with our ring.

Genesius in place of Hercamboldus.

Given on the fourth day before the Nones of June, in the thirty-second year and the twenty-seventh year of our reign.

Enacted at Tours, in the monastery of Saint Martin.

### LXV. Decree of Charlemagne for the monastery of Saint Anianus at Orléans (800)

*(From D. Bouquet, ibid.)*

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans. Let the prudence of all the faithful know that Fulco, abbot of the monastery of Saint Anianus, requested that we confirm by a decree of our authority the stipends and possessions assigned to the canons of the aforesaid monastery, so that the canons might possess and administer them perpetually. We granted his requests.

Therefore we ordered this decree of our Highness to be made, by which we command that, just as it has been established for the canons serving God there, so it shall be observed by the rulers of the aforesaid monastery in our times and in those to come, and the canonical order shall be maintained.

The possessions in the county of Orléans, at the villa of Apponiacum and Herbiliacum, with their small villas and appurtenances; three manses at Bercillis; one mansus at the villas of Sucarana; and in the county of Blois, at Turmo, with its appurtenances; also the plots within and outside the city, for providing lights in the dormitory of those same brothers and for purchasing firewood with which their bread may be baked each day.

If any future abbot should wish to add anything to the canons, for the love of God and in reverence for that saint, let him do so with the grace of God and presume to take nothing away. The number of canons of that monastery shall neither exceed nor fall below sixty, and so forth.

### LXVI. Decree of Charlemagne for the church of Le Mans (802)

*(From D. Bouquet, ibid.)

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Charles, most serene Augustus, crowned by God, great and peaceful emperor, governing the Roman Empire, who also, by the mercy of God, is king of the Franks and of the Lombards.

If we willingly lend an ear to the prayers of priests and servants of God, and provide assistance for carrying out their ministry, we undoubtedly believe that this will benefit us both in strengthening the stability of the kingdom and in attaining the blessedness of eternal life. Therefore we wish it to be known to all the faithful of the holy Church of God and to our own subjects, both present and future, that when, in the name of God, we were seated at our palace in Aachen to hear everyone’s cases and bring lawful judgments to completion, the priests and canonical clerics of Saint Gervasius, or the servants of God from the city of Le Mans, with the consent and permission of Joseph, their metropolitan and proper bishop, Francon, bishop of the aforesaid city, and the other bishops of the province, came into our presence and complained that our faithful, who held the property of Saint Gervasius as a benefice granted by us, either paid the ninths and tenths, or rents from which they ought to have the necessary revenues, negligently, or delayed paying them altogether.

They asked and humbly entreated that our imperial authority should ensure that the prescribed ninth and tenth portions of these properties be paid in full and without any delay to the aforesaid church, and that the buildings of the same church, as well as the episcopal residence and the houses of the brothers dwelling there in the service of God, be repaired and restored.

Moreover, they humbly requested that we order the names of the villages from which the ninths and tenths ought to be paid to the aforesaid church to be written individually into a precept of our authority, so that in future these villages or properties might not be alienated from the right of the same Church through any evil device, any kind of cunning, or the power of some rich or powerful man, nor might the ninths or tenths, rents, or restorations of the aforesaid church be taken away.

We willingly heard their prayers for the love of God, and, as they had requested, ordered the monasteries or cells, as well as the villages or estates, which our faithful are known to possess by our gift from the right of the aforesaid church, to be inserted by name in this precept, so that in future they may remain in the right and lordship of the aforesaid church with complete integrity. These are:

The monastery of Saint Peter, which Bishop Bertramnus built; the monastery or hospice of Saint Martin at Ponteleva; the monastery of Saint Victurius, in which Saint Victurius himself rests bodily; and the monastery of Saint Mary, built between the city wall and the River Sarthe, together with the little monastery of Saint Ricmirus beyond the River Sarthe belonging to it; the monastery of Saint Scholastica; the little monastery of Saint Germanus beyond the River Sarthe; the little monastery or hospice of Saint Mary, in which Lord Paduinus rests bodily; the little monastery of Saint Julian, in which he himself rests bodily; the cell of Saint Victurius within the city; the monastery of Saint Kari[.....]effus, in which that lord himself rests bodily; the monastery of Saint George; the monastery of Tillidus; the monastery of Tussiacum; the monastery of Saint John and Saint Trechius at Buxidum; the little monastery of Saint Martin at Diablenticum; the monastery of Saint Mary at Aurionnum; the little monastery of Buxidum; and the cell of Scuvillacum.

All these, as we have carefully investigated them and found them recorded in the authentic documents of Saint Gervasius, belong to it justly and lawfully.

Accordingly, we order that on the feast days of those saints in whose memories these monasteries are known to have been dedicated, every year rents shall be paid willingly by those who hold these monasteries by our beneficence to the aforesaid mother church of the city, for the use of the bishop and of the brothers dwelling there, for the restoration of the church itself, both now and in future times. On the aforesaid feast, the same abbot who at that time appears to possess the monastery shall also provide an excellent meal for the canons of Saint Mary and Saint Gervasius with willing spirit, if he wishes to have our favor and retain these benefices.

This is so that neither we nor our predecessors or forefathers may suffer any loss or danger to the kingdom through the removal or diminution of these properties belonging to the aforesaid church, but that they may remain under the jurisdiction of the Church for all time.

As for the public villages and little estates of the aforesaid church which our faithful possess by our gift, we absolutely order that the ninth and tenth portions be paid by those same faithful willingly and in full to the aforesaid mother church, and that they cause the buildings of the same church, and of the houses belonging to it within the city, to be restored there.

That is: from the estate of Taleida; from the estate of Lucdono; from the estate of Baladon; from the estate of Quebrolius, which is called Nova-Villa; from the estate of Pradellis; from Morniacum; from the estate of Quillis; from one-third of the cell of Saint Almirus; from one-third of the cell of Saint Ulfacius; from one-third of the cell of Saint Ricmirus; from the estate of Bonlidus; from Angonum; from Solemnis, both estate and village; from the cell of Jurmerus; from the estate of Apiliacum; from Alnidum; from Daucidum; from Noviliacum, Farisnonia, and Campum; Sirigicum; Luciacum; and Mons; from Comnis; the cell of Saint Leodegarius; Angon; and Bonlir; from the village of Gabron with its appendages; and Balinum, a public village; from the estate of Viviriacum; from the estate of Longa Aqua; from Campaniacum; from C[.....]nedralium; and from Geneda, public villages; from the estate of Clidis; Tredendum; Vithlena; Turniacum; Cassanum; and Villare; Adilavita; Vigra; Fontanae; Sanmurus; Brafialum; Felcaria; Domno-Jorio; and part of Fraxinedum; Maundaria; Drogiecum; Villare; Vernum; Juricium; and Camiliacum; Taxinaria; and Coctiacum, a public village; the estate of Antoniacum; the estate of Bonalfa; and all the estates belonging to the cell of Saint Martin within the city wall; Cangiacum, a public village; the estate of Limbriacum; Verincella; Verniacum; the village of Diablenticum; the cell of Arciacus; the estate of Camariacum; Civriacum; Calla; Comoriacum; the estate of Andoliacum; the estate of Griviacum; Martiniacum; Linerola; Sisciacum; the cell of Domno-Regis; and, in the district of Ardun, the one thousand settlers of Saint Gervasius; Curte-Basana; Novioma; Scomiacum; Camiliacum; Comiacum; Corma; Novi-Vicus; and Hostiliacum, public villages.

All these things which have been inserted above by name, as has already been said, we have investigated minutely and carefully, and, with the clerics themselves showing them to us, have found them recorded in the authentic documents of the same church. Other estates also, which because of the length of the document, or because the names of the estates were unknown, have not been inserted into this precept, are nevertheless known to belong justly and lawfully to the aforesaid church.

Concerning these matters we have decreed that these letters of our authority be made. Through them we establish and order that all who at the present time, or in future, have obtained or may obtain benefices from the properties of the aforesaid mother church must pay, from all the produce of the land, both [uncertain reading: “fesci”] and grain of every kind, both from their demesne and from that of their vassals, also from vineyards and the gift [or remission], from pasturage and pasture dues, from herbage dues and chickens, from fisheries and pasture payments—that is, from mast dues—from honey and agricultural produce, from what is raised in gardens, from the feeding of animals, and from the cheeses that are made, from the demesne cattle-farms, and from all payments received from the men of the aforesaid mother church, except the military levy, that is, oxen, and the contribution for constructing carts.

From all these things, we order that every year they cause the lawful rent, together with the ninths and tenths, to be rendered in full to the aforesaid mother church, without any [uncertain reading: “maritione”] or delay, or diminution.

Moreover, they must not neglect to carry out restorations, both in the aforesaid church and in the houses adjoining it, repairing the roofs and other structures according to the resources of the properties which they possess there as benefices, if each one wishes to retain our favor and these benefices.

I further will that our faithful hold the aforesaid benefices under the prescribed rent, with the consent and goodwill of the bishop of the same church, until we may exchange them with those who appear to possess them by our gift, and, with the Lord’s help, may deserve to restore and return them to the aforesaid church, to which they are owed justly and lawfully, as we have investigated.

And let this be known to all of you: if any one of you should be found who delays fulfilling this order of ours, either by despising or neglecting it, we will and order that the bishop of the aforesaid city cause these properties to be recalled into the right of the same church, or into his own power and lordship or that of his canons, until those who held the properties or benefices of the aforesaid church by our gift come into our presence.

Let him who neglects the rent lose his field; and by this authority let them lose those benefices because of their negligence or contempt.

So that this order of ours may be believed all the more truly, preserved all the more carefully, fulfilled by us in every respect, and held more firmly in future times, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with the impression of our ring.

**Sign of Charles, most glorious emperor.**

Genesius, acting in place of Erchembaudus, examined and subscribed.

Given in the month of April, on the ninth day before the Kalends of May, in the second year, Christ being favorable, of our glorious empire, and in the thirty-fourth year of our reign in Francia and the twenty-ninth in Italy. In the name of God, successfully. Amen.

## LXVII. Charles the Great’s precept confirming the privilege of immunity granted by his father Pippin to the monastery of Novientum (810)

*(From D. Bouquet, in the same place.)*

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Charles, most serene Augustus, crowned by God, great and peaceful emperor, governing the Roman Empire, who also, by the mercy of God, is king of the Franks and of the Lombards.

We believe that the honors of our kingdom are increased if, once the just petitions of priests or ministers of God have been approved by our ears, we bring them to fulfillment. For they frequently implore God’s mercy for the stability of our kingdom and the salvation of our soul.

Therefore let the diligence of all present and future generations know how Thietbaldus, abbot of the monastery called Novientum, situated in the district of Alsace on the River Ill, which the illustrious man Adalricus, also called Duke Atticus, and his wife Bersvinda built anew on their own property in the name of Christ and in honor of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, Saint Mauritius and his companions, came to our Serenity, asking that we renew the privileges which our father, of pious memory, Pippin, and his predecessors, the kings of the Franks, had granted to the same monastery and to the places belonging to the support of the brothers serving God there under regular discipline.

Therefore, by the authority of royal majesty, confirming the enactments of our predecessors, we order that in the estates of the aforesaid monastery—namely Wiswirle, situated in the district of Breisgau on the bank of the Rhine, together with its church and all its appendages; at Sulzha, Egensheim, Sigalthesheim, Burcheim, Lagelenheim, Gruzenheim, Hundensheim, Northusen, and Hollasvirle, which the aforesaid duke assigned to that venerable place, as well as in whatever may henceforth be donated—no public judge and no judicial power, spiritual or secular, dare enter forcibly, nor presume to claim the church’s possessions for itself against justice.

Rather, the aforesaid abbot Thietbaldus and his successors shall possess these properties with authority, increasing and improving them.

And so that this authority of ours may remain stable and be better preserved for future times, we have confirmed this charter, written at our command, with our own hand and ordered it sealed with the impression of our ring.

**Sign of Charles, most glorious king [emperor].**

I, Ibbo, acting in place of Erchambaldus, reread and subscribed.

Given on the day before the Ides of August, in the tenth year, Christ being favorable, of our empire, and the forty-second year of our reign in Francia and the thirty-seventh in Italy, in the third indiction.

[Col. 0998D] Done at Ferdi in Saxony, in the name of God, successfully. Amen.

# II. Privileges concerning the regions of Italy

[Col. 0997]

## I. Confirmation of immunities granted by Charles the Great to Frodoenus, abbot of Novalesa (773)

*(From Muratori, Antiquities of Medieval Italy.)*

[Col. 0997D]

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks, to our faithful men, illustrious persons.

Know this: we believe that the monument of our kingdom is greatly increased if, through benevolent deliberation, we grant suitable benefits to holy places for the repose of monks, and, with the Lord’s protection, trust that the stability of our kingdom belongs to the name of God.

Therefore let your prudence know that the venerable man Frodoenus, abbot, informed us that Abbo had formerly appeared to build a little monastery in honor of the blessed brothers and apostles Peter and Andrew and the other saints, at a place called Novalesa in the Susa Valley, and had established there a congregation of monks dwelling under the holy rule of Saint Benedict and of the other holy Fathers in the cenobitic order; and that at the present time the venerable man Frodoenus appears to preside over it.

We also appear to have granted a benefice to that holy place, as an eternal recompense, so that in the places or estates of that monastery which the aforesaid Abbo had formerly given, or which any God-fearing men had contributed there, or which divine piety might henceforth wish to add to that holy place, no public judge might at any time presume to enter to hear cases or exact fines from every direction.

Rather, the abbot of that monastery, together with the congregation, shall be able to exercise lordship over it under complete immunity, for the name of the Lord and out of reverence for the saints.

Therefore we establish that neither you, nor your subordinate officials, nor your successors, nor any public judicial authority, at any time or in any place or estate, whether in the Susa Valley itself, the Brenta Valley, the Aquese or Aquinara districts, the Mannate district, or in Burgundy, or anywhere in our kingdom where the monastery has property, whether belonging to us or received through the gift of private persons, or whatever may henceforth have been added or contributed by anyone, may enter to hear disputes, exact fines for any cause from any persons who appear to belong to that house, or take lodging, provisions, or sureties.

Rather, whatever revenue might arise from free men, public services performed by dependants, or any other dues within the places, estates, or boundaries of those properties, whether from the monks residing there or from those subject to them, and whatever the treasury might henceforth, with the Lord’s help, have been able to increase or draw from them, whether from fines or from payments of any kind, shall, by our indulgence and for the sake of future salvation, be used forever for the lights of that monastery through the hands of its agents.

What we have granted with complete devotion for the holy name of the Lord, out of reverence for that holy place, for the remedy of our soul, and for our succeeding descendants, must not be opposed either by royal majesty or by the greed of any judge.

And so that this present authority may remain inviolate, with the Lord’s help, for both present and future times, we have signed it with our own hand and sealed it with our ring.

**Sign + of Charles, most glorious king.**

[Col. 0999D] Tesius examined and subscribed.

Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, in the fifth year of our reign.

Done at Carisiac, the public palace, in the name of God.

## II. Donation of the forest and estate of Monte Longo by Charles the Great to the monastery of Bobbio and its abbot Guinibaldus (774)

*(From Muratori, in the same place.)*

[Col. 1000A]

[Note: [Col. 1000D] The title “Patrician of the Romans,” which occurs in other diplomas, is lacking in the opening. But this omission should not be made much of. For Charles had not yet begun, in the year 774, to use such a title, as the examples produced by Mabillon sufficiently show. Rather, the chronological notes create a difficulty. The diploma is said to have been issued at Pavia, in the sixth year . . . . . . of our reign. This can here give the era of his Frankish reign from the death of his father Pippin. But why is no mention also made of the Lombard reign, when the diploma is said to have been written at Ticinum and Charles is styled king of the Lombards as well? Yet one may answer here too that, because of the intervening lacuna, the first year of the Lombard reign has been withheld from us. But the sign-manual of Charolus is unusual, since in other diplomas only the sign of Carolus is written; and elsewhere occur Carolus, not Charolus, king of the Franks and Lombards, not of the Franchs and Longobards. Since, however, this concerns a copy, these slight matters seem attributable to a single scribe. Moreover, in very ancient charters I have sometimes seen Longobardorum and Longobardia written. For this reason I would not yet dare to detract from the credibility of this charter. Meanwhile, in the year 774 we have Guinibaldus as abbot of Bobbio, whom Ughelli, in *Episcopi Bobienses*, vol. IV of *Italia Sacra*, and Mabillon, in the *Benedictine Annals*, did not know. Pagi investigated in his *Critique of Baronius* for the year 774 when the victorious Charles entered the city of Ticinum, and rightly determined that it occurred in that year after the ninth day of May but before the thirteenth of June. This diploma (if one wishes to recognize it as a legitimate offspring) brings us nearer to the mark, indicating that Charles had already gained possession of that city before the Nones of June. I also saw in the archive of the archbishopric of Lucca a charter drawn up: “In the reign of our lord Carulus, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, in the twenty-fifth year of his reign in which he took Lombardy, and in the eighteenth year of the reign of his son our lord King Pippin, on the fourth Ides of June, indiction 6. It is manifest to me, Atripaldus, priest, son of the late Rapertus of the place Rocca, that by this little charter, for the remedy of my soul and in the manner that I shall decree below, I have provided to offer to God and to you, the church, to the venerable man Bishop John, my church of Saint Quiricus, built by my parents in the aforesaid place Rocca, together with houses, etc.” The charter was written in the year of Christ 798, on 10 June. Therefore, on that same tenth day of June in the year 774, Charles the Great had already gained possession of Lombardy and thus of the royal city of Ticinum. On the other hand, one may doubt whether, during May, he compelled that royal city to surrender, since another charter is preserved in the same Lucchese archive, written “in the twenty-third year of King Charles and the seventeenth of King Pippin, in the month of May, indiction five,” that is, in the year of Christ 797. In this and other charters of that age, and especially Lombard ones, I observed that the day of the month is not recorded. In addition, in the cartulary of the monastery of Saint Zeno at Verona I saw a parchment written: “In the reign of our lord Charles, most excellent king in Italy, in the seventh year, in the month of May, in the third indiction, happily. To my sweetest and most beloved and, with every honor, to be named and happy daughter, I, Felix the cleric, son of John of blessed memory, etc.” He gives her many things. That charter was therefore drawn up in the year of Christ 780, from which, as from the one indicated above, it seems clear that the Lombard era of Charles the Great had not begun in May of the year 774.]

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards.

If, from the things which divine piety continually grants eternally, we assign suitable gifts to venerable places for the benefit of God’s servants, we trust that this contributes to the increase of our reward and the stability of our kingdom.

Therefore we give to the monastery of Bobbio, where Saint Columbanus rests bodily and where Guinibaldus appears to preside as abbot, in accordance with a further petition for the future, and we wish the gift to belong perpetually to the same holy place: namely, our forest together with the estate situated there, whose name is Monte Longo, with all the lands adjoining or attached to that forest or estate, belonging to or subject to them there, together with lands, houses, buildings, dependants, vineyards, fields, meadows, pastures, waters and the courses of waters, movable and immovable property—in every respect and entirely, whatever, as we have said, appeared to belong to that forest or our estate—which we have granted with fullest consent from the present day.

Likewise, we add to the aforesaid monastery of Bobbio a certain alpine territory called ad Montem. It begins at the stream of Casa Veteri, ascending along the ridge to the summit of Lesser Cucharus above Casalegri, crossing the entire road toward Incerasiola, where it is called Banciola, where the boundary is fixed; from there the water descends to Caput Sirtaris as far as the sea. On the other side it has the boundary stream descending from Montelongo and entering the sea. From there the boundary runs from the rock of Corice over the summit of the ridge to the public road, where the boundary stands; then it descends along the boundary of Mount Petronus, over the top of the ridge, from the little valley called Castanetum, descending to the road that leads to the rock of Corice beside the mountain at Navasco. It falls into another public road leading to Castellio; from there it turns back upward beside the mountain, at a neck marked with a cross, and crosses toward the boundary of Saint Michael, running from the River Petrurius to the boundaries of Mount Harimannus above Olivetum.
