This is the public road beside the mountain, through Caunetum, as far as the wild pear tree.

All these lands, by this pragmatic act of our authority, we give and grant with one end adjoining the sea and the other extending to the boundaries of Harimannus; on one side, Gregania; on the other, Montelongo, together with its pastures, estate lands, and olive groves, just as they are known to have been possessed by Eduardus.

Therefore, by this our precept, we order that from this day forward no one exercising judicial authority, nor any other person, presume to trouble or bring a claim against the aforesaid monastery and its rectors concerning the forest, the aforesaid estate, or the aforementioned alpine territory.

Rather, the aforesaid abbot Guinibaldus and his successors shall hold the designated properties in their entirety, just as they were possessed from the palace, and shall possess, administer, and govern them. Whatever they choose to do from them for the increase of our reward or for the lights of the same church, they shall enjoy freely.

And so that this authority may be held more firmly and better preserved in our future times, we have decided to strengthen it below with our own hand.

**Sign + of the hand of Charles, most glorious king.**

[Col. 1002A] On the day of the Nones of June, in the sixth year of our reign [lacuna].

Done at the city of Pavia, in the name of God, successfully.

Enrichus examined and delivered it.

## III. Charter of an immense donation of properties made by Charles the Great to the monastery of Nonantola and its abbot Anselmus (around 774)

*(From Muratori, in the same place.)*

[Note: Whoever reads this charter and considers it attentively must either immediately consign it to the apocrypha, or remain hesitant and doubtful in contemplating it. I too hesitated, and still hesitate. It almost exceeds belief that so many properties, villages, and churches should have been poured out in a single document and on a single day to one abbot and one monastery.

Moreover, this charter has none of the appearance of a genuine diploma, and everyone knows the words and formulas with which kings and emperors were accustomed to frame their donations and privileges. One may also wonder why Duke Nortepertus should involve himself with the king in making such a donation.

These and other considerations were certainly present to my mind when I transcribed the charter. I do not claim to establish its authentic origin; I merely wish to explain my opinion of it.

I would not dare to affirm that it is a spurious product. If the ancient monks had set their minds on fabricating so magnificent a donation, it would have been much less trouble to invent a diploma, since genuine diplomas issued by kings were readily available to them and could easily be found everywhere for imitation.

Furthermore, in later times, as it appears, no traces remained of such great wealth being bestowed upon the monastery of Nonantola in Tuscany. For what purpose, then, I ask, would the monks have indulged in this imposture?

Besides, who would have invented in later centuries that district of Lucardo, about which I have spoken elsewhere, when ancient history contains not a single word about it?

There is therefore reasonable ground for thinking that the charter contains no fiction, and that it was rather a private document made by King Charles and Duke Nortepertus.

But why was so great, so extraordinary—almost, I would say, so monstrous and unusual—a donation made to the monastery of Nonantola?

I ask the readers’ indulgence if I perhaps incline too readily toward a certain suspicion, which I now dare to report. I suspect, then, that Charles’s great munificence toward Anselmus, abbot of Nonantola, arose from the fact that Anselmus himself had extended helping hands to Charles in seizing the crown of the Lombard kingdom, and received as the fruit of his well-performed service that magnificent donation of so many properties.

“But,” you will say, “Anselmus was a Lombard by birth. Who would believe that a man could abandon love for his own people and wish the kingdom of the Lombards to be transferred to the Franks?”

I will not declare this certain; nevertheless, there are considerations that seem to persuade me that matters proceeded in this way.

As is clear from the little work *On the Foundation of the Monastery of Nonantola*, Anselmus’s sister Giseltruda was married to Aistulphus, king of the Lombards. This Anselmus, moreover, is said to have governed the duchy of Friuli under the title of duke when, having renounced the world, he devoted himself to monastic life and built Nonantola and other monasteries.

He was strengthened by Aistulphus’s exceptionally distinguished generosity, to such a degree that the Anonymous of Salerno, in the continuation of his chronicle, considered it worthy to include this among the praises of that king, writing:

> “He also built a monastery in the region of Emilia, where Modena is said to be, at the place called Nonantola; for the sake of his relative, the abbot Arsenius”—Anselmus should be restored here—“a monastery of men was founded there. He also gave him many gifts in various provinces for the construction of sacred monasteries for monks,” namely, those which were later made subject to Nonantola.

After Aistulphus died, Desiderius was proclaimed king of the Lombards, but Ratchis, Aistulphus’s brother, opposed him—Ratchis being the very man who had held the kingdom before Aistulphus and was living as a monk at the monastery of Monte Cassino.

What Ratchis did, and with what effort the good monk resisted the new king, you may learn from Anastasius’s *Life of Pope Stephen II* and from the same Anonymous of Salerno, who copied Anastasius here:

> “Ratchis, formerly king and afterward a monk, the brother of the aforesaid Aistulphus, regarding the person of Desiderius with contempt, together with many other Lombard nobles, despising Desiderius, gathered a very large multitude of Transalpine troops and of other Lombard armies with him and set out to fight against him.”

Stephen II intervened in these upheavals at Desiderius’s request and established peace between the opposing parties.

But Desiderius thereafter harbored an embittered spirit and, in accordance with the condition of human affairs, raged against those whom he perceived to have conspired against him. He also turned against Anselmus, since, as a reasonable conjecture suggests, he discovered that Anselmus was connected with Ratchis, his brother-in-law, and opposed to himself.

In the *Catalogue of the Abbots of Nonantola*, Anselmus is said to have ruled “the abbey of Nonantola for fifty years; and for seven of these he suffered exile under Desiderius at Monte Cassino, as we learned from the report of many elders, because he had committed some offense—I do not know what—against Desiderius; and at that time the priest Vigilantius successfully governed the monastery of Nonantola.”

I do not know whether what is said here about the priest Vigilantius rests upon a sound basis. Among the older diplomas granted to the same monastery there is one that reads:

> “Privilege on papyrus of King Adelchis, under the abbot Silvester, confirming all the privileges noted above,” and so forth.

Thus Anselmus was not merely driven into exile; another abbot, namely Silvester, was substituted in his place to govern the monastery of Nonantola.

At the same time we learn from this that, unless Anselmus was restored to his monastery only after Desiderius had been defeated, nothing prevents us from suspecting that Anselmus himself, with all the strength he could muster, openly or secretly worked to ensure that the Lombards would welcome the arriving Charles with bowed heads and, after overthrowing Desiderius, who was hostile to him, willingly accept the Frankish prince as their king.

I would not have you invoke Anselmus’s exceptional piety here. Pope Adrian I too possessed the highest piety; yet no one should wrong him by failing to consider that he himself was hardly negligent in ensuring that, in Lombard territory, a king most friendly to himself should succeed a king detested by him. From that victory considerable benefits would also flow to the pontiff himself and to his successors.

Who Nortepertus was, the duke mentioned in the recently published charter, is unknown to me. Nevertheless, Duke Nortepertus is mentioned in a certain fictitious Bolognese charter, where he is said to have flourished during the reign of Ratchis, king of the Lombards, and is counted among the dukes of that people.

Perhaps the ancient craftsman of that charter had older monuments before his eyes, from which he could draw his knowledge of that Nortepertus.

It is therefore reasonable to believe that the abbot Anselmus, a man of great name and of exceptional standing among his own people, contributed much to the successful progress of Charles the Great’s war, through which Charles added the most illustrious Italian kingdom to his ancestral realms.

I will add no more in support of this conjecture.

As for the Roman pontiffs, matters certainly turned out well for them under Pippin, king of the Franks, and his son Charles the Great. At that time they began to dominate not only the exarchate but also Rome and its duchy.

At that time more was also apparently promised to them than the outcome demonstrated. Yet as time passed, although imperial coronation depended upon them—through which title and right were conferred upon emperors, and which some purchased with many gifts—little benefit nevertheless flowed from it into the Roman Church.

That is to say, no new territory was added to it; indeed, even its ancient possessions appear to have been diminished and taken away.

But at the beginning of the thirteenth century, under Innocent III, a pope of great spirit, and still more abundantly under Nicholas III, the Roman cause began to advance more successfully, so that the Roman Church progressed, partly through the generosity of kings and emperors and partly through armed support, to the condition in which we now see it, and for which we always desire perpetual and peaceful continuance.]

To the venerable monastery of the holy apostles situated in the castle of Nonantula, in the territory of Modena, where Lord Anselm … [lacuna] … we, Charles, king of the Franks and [Saxons?], … [lacuna] … and of the Lombards, together with Duke Nortepert, give and likewise offer all our estates and demesnes in the county of Fossola, in the county of Pistoia, in the county of Lucardo, and in the county of Lucca, in the county of Reggio, and in the county of Siena.

First, I, Lord Charles, give two of my demesne woods in the county of Fossola, lying upon the river … [lacuna], with their churches, namely Saint Mary at Advena and Saint Mary at Manum, together with one hundred of my forest holdings for each wood, along with the woods belonging to them. Also the monastery of Saint Michael in the city of Fossola, and the monastery of Saint Miniatus in that city, with their cells in the city itself and outside it, belonging to them. Also the estate of Viselle, the estate of Bibiano, the parish of Saint Gavinus, and the estate of Justinianus; Mocolidula; Colle Fenario; the estate of Tigano, in the parish of Saint Mary at Villola; the parish of Saint Jerusalem; the parish of Saint Romulus; and at the place of Bernardus; also at Grave; Saint Hilary; the estate of Praetorius; Saint Michael; the estate of Sobelinarius; Monte Miniano; Turiniano; Gorzano; Genesticlo; Spaloti; the parish of Saint Pancratius; the estate of Bergovigiano; Sculcta; Fugnana; [Col. 1003B] Saint Peter at Mauricianus; the estate of Axsinia; our estate of Spandola; our estate of Meledo, with the church at Musello, at Caprilia, … [lacuna] … niano; the tower at Pineta; also at Sexa; our estate of Novole; the estate of Fumaria; Calcinaria; Valvigne; Arzana … [lacuna] … the estate of the Monks; Simbriano; the estate of Elsa; the estate of Pesa; Campi; Ingone; Quinto; Melego; Aproniano; Susicana; … [lacuna] … ano; Popponi; Grappena; Saint Benedict; Saint George in the parish of Saint Peter at Perimone.

Also in the county of Pistoia, the estate … [lacuna] … Pinsingo; the parish of Saint Peter of Groppina; and the parish of Saint Lawrence at the place of Petriolo, which is called Bocina.

Also in the county of Arezzo, the parish of Saint Stephen, situated at Classe, and the place of Pissinale beside the river Classe.

In the county of Lucardo: our estate of Saint Peter at Mercato; also perhaps our estate of Monte Calvo; the estate of Campane; the estate of Petroniano, in the parish of Saint Leonard; the estate of Furno; the castle of Ciliano; Monte Bonici; Saint Peter with the estate of Quintolo; and beside the river Gofintia, the estate of Dominicus; Saint Donatus; the estate of Decimo, in the parish of Saint Cecilia; the estate of Penite, in the parish of Saint Mary; the estate of Meleto; the estate of Monacile; Vadolongo; Quarte, in the parish of Saint Peter; Rabuciona with the chapel of Saint Peter; the estate of Sepi with the church of Saint Mary; the estate of Caracle with the church of Saint Martin; the estate of Casentino; one of our small estates called Satri; the estate of Pinscingno with the cell of the holy apostles near the river Selice.

In the county of Lucca, Saint Mary with the estate of Pulinacho, and all our other estates in the aforesaid counties and in the territory of Tuscany, belonging to our demesne, which amounts to … [lacuna] … two thousand five hundred. And if anything more of our demesne is found written on this page, let it remain together with all the head-taxes and rent payments, and also the tithe belonging to those estates, so that it may serve for the sustenance of the poor and the monks, for the honor of religion, and so that those monks or the monastery may be subject to no one except the Roman Church.

All those estates, with their adjacent lands and appurtenances, and with their dependencies, as much as belongs to our estates within those counties, together with the woods belonging to them, the olive groves, vineyards, orchards, fruit-bearing and fruitless trees of various kinds, the rights in the rivers that flow through those counties, mountains and hills—in short, everything belonging and adjoining to them, in its entirety.

And if any of the men who neglects our commands, or … [lacuna] … gives, let the penalty be imposed upon him, his goods be confiscated, and let us send him into exile.

I had this document written by the notary Artuinus, and completed and concluded it after it had been strengthened and delivered with witnesses.

[Col. 1006A]

I, Mericho, cleric, at his request.

I, Raimpret, at his request.

I, Aldoinus, at his request.

I, Joseph, at his request.

Melchione, physician, at his request.

Signs: + + + + of the witnesses Warnifret, Artuinus, Mechois, Josephus, Stravius, Aripret, Johannes, Paulinus, Basingus, Mauro, Leo, Gumperto, Stamperto, Stabile, Da Villa, Vanielei.

### IV. Diploma by which Charles the Great grants certain privileges and rights to the monastery of Vulturnum (774)

[Note: The beginnings of the monastery of Vulturnum are narrated as follows by the Chronicle of Farfa:

“As the fame of the name of Saint Thomas, abbot [of Farfa], grew, and as the resources of this monastery were most honorably increased, in accordance with the Lord’s command, for receiving pilgrims and guests, many people from different nations began to frequent this place, either for the sake of visiting it, or for hospitality, or in order to be converted through love of God.

“At that time three noble and related men came from Benevento: Saints Paldo, Taso, and Tato. Abandoning the world and all that they possessed for Christ, they undertook a pilgrimage and reached the aforesaid Lord Thomas. The venerable Thomas then went with them to Rome and, treating them with the greatest kindness, brought them back here. Although this was contrary to the custom of the monastery, because of the ardor of their praiseworthy desire he received them within and caused them to share communally with the brothers, taking care within a few days to teach them the rule of the religious life.

“After this he indicated to them that they should go to the holy oratory of the blessed martyr Vincent in the province of Samnium, on the bank of the river Vulturnus, where at that time there was no human habitation except the lairs of wild beasts and robbers; and he promised that he would go there to them very soon. Not long afterward, however, the man of God Thomas went on foot to Benevento and proceeded to the court of Duke Gisulf, a distinguished man.

“Then one night the holy Mother of God, Mary, appeared in a vision to that duke together with the aforesaid venerable man Thomas, and commanded him, saying: ‘See to it that whatever this pilgrim asks of you, you do not refuse him, because he is a holy man and will pray for you.’ Having said this, she departed.

“When morning came, the same duke had him brought in by his servants, recognized him as he had seen him in the vision, immediately rose from his throne, and, prostrating his whole body upon the ground in worship, said to him: ‘The gracious Mother of God, Mary, showed you to me in a vision last night. Now ask me whatever you wish, and I will most willingly grant it, in devotion to your holiness.’

“But he replied: ‘I ask one small favor from the piety of your Highness: there is a certain place in the province of Samnium, on the bank of the river Vulturnus, reduced to solitude, where an oratory has been built in honor of Saint Vincent. I beg that the generosity of your piety may grant it to me, so that a monastery may be established there.’

“The duke willingly received this request and answered with a cheerful face: ‘Behold, Father: from this hour the place which you request shall remain in your power, and receive from it a charter of confirmation.’ He immediately ordered it to be written and, after it had been authenticated, handed it over to his authority.

“The man of God Thomas then restored the aforesaid men to the duke’s favor and hurried with them to the same place. After spending several days there, he gave them many instructions for salvation and showed them where they should build the refectory, dormitory, guest quarters, and all the necessary habitations. He also chose Paldo, who was gentler than all the others, to preside over them in government.” Etc.]

(From Muratori, *Scriptores rerum Italicarum*.)

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards, [Col. 1006B] and patrician of the Romans, to all bishops, abbots, dukes, counts, vicars, household officers, centenarii, and all our envoys traveling about.

Whatever we do out of love for the churches and for the peace of the servants of God, we confidently believe, with the Lord’s help, will contribute to our eternal blessedness.

Therefore let your greatness, or your benefit, know how the venerable man Probatus, abbot of the monastery built in honor of the most blessed Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary, which is called Acutianus, in the duchy of Spoleto and founded in the territory of Sabina, sent a petition to the clemency of our royal power and stated in his request that, for the increase of our reward, we ought to grant to him and to that monastery the following privilege: that this house of God should exist under such a privilege as the other monasteries [Note: The most celebrated monasteries in the Frankish kingdom, such as those in Italy were Monte Cassino, Nonantula, Farfa, and others.] of Lérins, Agaunum, and Luxeuil, where the ancient rule of the Fathers Basil, Benedict, Columbanus, and the other Fathers appears to be observed:

that none of the bishops should be permitted to accept a payment for the election of an abbot; that he should have no power to remove from the monastery crosses, chalices, patens, books, relics, or any objects belonging to the church’s sacred service; that he should have no power to place the monastery under the tribute of princes; and, finally, that he should not demand tribute or rent from the aforesaid monastery. Rather, that house of God, like the monasteries mentioned above which are within our kingdoms, should remain under the same privilege and rule of the Fathers.

We did not wish to deny his petition, out of regard for God and for the increase of our reward. Rather, know that we have confirmed or newly granted it in this manner, out of love for our Lord Jesus Christ.

Therefore we command and order that no bishop, [Col. 1007B] abbot, duke, castaldus, or any of our faithful, or your officials, or your successors, presume at any time to disturb or act contrary to justice against the aforesaid abbot, his monks, or the agents of his church concerning the property of the aforesaid monastery—property which has come to it through the generosity of kings or queens, through gifts of the people or bishops, or which has otherwise come to the monastery, or which in the future, with God’s help, may be granted to it—whether by instruments of sale, donation, cession, or other written documents. Rather, let them remain in peace under our privilege.

And whenever the abbot of that monastery departs this life, let the monks themselves have permission to elect as abbot the one whom they find most worthy according to the rule of Saint Benedict and as their order teaches and justice requires; or, if they agree together, the one whom they unanimously choose. Neither we nor our royal successors shall ever violate or break what we have granted for our reward. Rather, may they always be able to enjoy their own patrimony, so that the congregation of Saint Mary may be more eager to pray attentively for us and for the stability of our kingdom for the Lord’s mercy.

And so that this decree may be firmer for our times and for those to come, and may be better preserved through the ages, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with our ring.

Sign of Charles, the unconquered king.

Guicbaldus, acting in place of Hitherius, have examined and approved.

[Col. 1007D] Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of June, in the seventh and first year of the reign of our lord Charles, most glorious king. Done at the public palace of Carilego, happily, in the name of God.

### V. Diploma of Charles the Great for the church of Reggio (781)

(From Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*.)

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans.

Whatever we confirm or grant by our authority to venerable holy places for the love of God, we thereby exercise the royal custom, and we believe that it will remain in the future.

Therefore let the diligence of all our faithful know how the venerable man Apollinaris, bishop of the church of Reggio [Note: Apollinaris, bishop of Reggio, obtained from Charles the Great three valuable privileges in favor of his church, in which the rights and boundaries of the bishopric of Reggio are listed—those which it possessed in those ancient days.] approached the clemency of our piety, so that we might strengthen by our authority, under the protection of our immunity, all the property of that bishopric which it possessed in ancient or modern times, whether from gifts of kings or queens, from other God-fearing people, or whatever might thereafter be added or assigned to it, or whatever it is known justly and reasonably to possess.

Thus no public judge should enter there to hear cases, exact fodrum, demand lodging or provisions, take hostages, or require any public restitutions; nor, while sailing up or down the Po and collecting river dues, should he exact the ripaticum, as at Ferrara or Comacchio, where the aforesaid holy place is known to possess saltworks.

Moreover, no toll should be demanded in any market, nor river or port dues, nor should any collector presume to inflict oppression or violence.

He also requested a certain forest belonging to our jurisdiction, situated in the county of Parma, in the territory of Bismantus, at a place called Lamma Fraolaria. Its boundaries are as follows: on one side, from the river Sicla upward along the road to Mount Palaredo; from there, ascending along the road to the borders of Tuscany; thence turning toward the stream Albolus as far as the river Sicla; from there, following the Sicla downstream, it reaches the river Auzola.

Granting his petitions for divine reward, we have conceded the aforesaid forest to his church to be held in perpetuity. We have also ordered this charter of our confirmation to be made for him, by which we decree and establish that no judge may at any time exercise tyrannical authority over the estates or property of that bishopric, nor over cases to be heard, fodrum to be exacted, lodging or provisions to be supplied, hostages to be taken, or any public payments to be demanded; nor may he exercise such power or tyranny in the private houses of the priests or their clerics.

Moreover, we perpetually remit to the aforesaid holy church of Reggio, without any contradiction, all river dues, whether on salt water or fresh water, as well as tolls in all markets, and ferry dues and bridge or passage dues.

If anyone—which we scarcely believe—should attempt to oppose or violate this grant or charter of our immunity, let him be compelled to pay thirty pounds of the finest gold, half to our palace and half to the church against which he has acted; and if he has nothing with which to pay, let him pay with his life.

And so that the proclamation of our grant and immunity may remain inviolate and untouched in the present and future, and may be carefully observed by all Catholics, we have subscribed it below with our hand of confirmation and ordered it marked with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Charles, most glorious king.

C. Jac., acting in place of Radonus.

Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of June, in the thirteenth and seventh year of our reign. Done in the city of Pavia, happily, in the name of God. Amen.

### VI. Diploma of Charles the Great for the same church of Reggio (781)

(From Ughelli, cited above.)

[Col. 1009B]

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans.

We believe that the defenses of our kingdom are greatly strengthened when we confirm by our protection the suitable benefits granted or donated for the relief of the servants of God and to venerable places. In this, we exercise the royal custom, and confidently believe that it contributes, in the name of God, to the salvation of our soul.

Therefore let it be known to all your greatness how the venerable man Apollinaris, bishop of the church of Reggio, together with the clergy and people of the aforesaid church, petitioned the clemency of our royal power that we should grant the clergy the right of election in that church for all time.

He also requested that all the property of that bishopric which it presently possesses, whether from gifts of kings or queens, from other God-fearing people, or whatever might thereafter be added or assigned to it, and whatever it is known justly and reasonably to possess, should be granted or confirmed by our authority to the aforesaid holy place under the name of our immunity.

Thus no public judge should presume to enter there to hear cases, exact fodrum, demand lodging or provisions, take hostages, or require any public restitutions; nor should he exact anything at all.

We did not wish to deny his petition, made for divine worship, but it is known that we have granted the right of election to his church for all time and confirmed it in every respect.

Furthermore, we ordered our immunity to be written for him, by which we command absolutely that no one among you, nor anyone exercising judicial authority, should ever presume to enter upon the estates or property of that bishopric to hear cases, exact fodrum, demand lodging or provisions, take hostages, or require any public payments. Rather, under the name of immunity, with all the granted franchises, the aforesaid bishop and his successors shall be able to live and remain in peace for all time, so that the servants of God who appear to minister to God there may be more pleased continually to pray to the Lord’s mercy for us, for our wife, and for our offspring.

And so that this immunity may be firmer and better preserved for a long time, we have also subscribed it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with our ring.

Sign of Charles, most glorious king.

Gilibertus, acting for Radonus, have examined and approved.

Given in the month of June, on the eighth day, in the thirteenth and seventh year.

Done in the city of Pavia, happily, in the name of God.

### Diploma of Charles the Great

[Note: Perhaps it would never have occurred to me to suspect the authenticity of this production, had I not been detained by the manner in which the wax seal was attached there. For the wax was by no means impressed and spread out on the reverse side; rather, it was inserted into a slit in the parchment in such a way that it could easily be drawn out and slip readily from its place, unless it had been secured to the document by a wooden ring with a thread also applied. This gave me the suspicion that a genuine seal, taken from elsewhere, could have been introduced by someone into this parchment.

I then subjected the chronological marks to examination. The diploma is dated in the thirteenth and seventh years; these epochs, of both the Frankish and Lombard kingdoms, correctly indicate the year 781, in which year, and in the month of June, Charles the Great was indeed at Pavia. Yet in that year the fourth indiction was running; here, however, the tenth indiction is marked—a mistake which cannot be digested in any way. Moreover, *Longobardorum* is expressly written there; I do not know whether this should be counted among the errors. I will nevertheless say that in other genuine diplomas of Charles the Great which I have seen, *Langobardorum* occurs. I mean diplomas of Charles; for in other ancient records you may also find *Longobardos*, as I showed in Dissertation XXI, *On the State of Italy*. Critical method commands that these small points too be carefully observed.

But what cannot at all be whitewashed, and what finally persuaded me that this is not an authentic but a spurious diploma, is the formula of expression: “we believe that this advances us toward the summit of imperial excellence.” The diploma was issued by Charles when he was only king, and perhaps at that time did not even contemplate attaining imperial dignity. He therefore could not have spoken as emperor, nor used a form of expression later employed by Lothair I, Augustus, his grandson, and by other emperors. Accordingly, I am again moved to wonder how an opinion so different at first sight concerning this diploma could have prevailed.

Once you judge it fabricated—as I do judge it fabricated—it must certainly be said to be a very ancient fabrication of this kind; especially since on the back of the membrane, in large characters formed many centuries ago, one reads: “The boundaries of the bishopric of Reggio, granted by that same Charles to Bishop Apollinaris, and everything belonging to that bishopric.” From this privilege Ughelli, under the year 780, inserted Bishop Peter into the catalogue of bishops of Bologna, afterwards forgetting to list another Peter, likewise mentioned here, among the bishops of Parma. Yet the existence of both Peters depends upon the diploma; and I do not see who would wish to trust it.

Thus Mabillon, in the *Benedictine Annals* under the year 781, uses this document as an authentic production, and persuaded himself that he had seen Duke Gerard there, although the parchment calls him Goeradus. From this you may learn with how much circumspection and with how attentive eyes the reliability of ancient diplomas must be investigated. Therefore, if there are persons who, whenever some charter of ancient kings still furnished with its seal is presented to them, think that nothing further need be sought in order to judge it an original, they are grievously mistaken. For not even this is sufficient as a certain criterion: wax seals attached to parchments could have been removed from the reverse side, once the wax had been softened by heat, and transferred onto another document, the offspring of a forgery.

Pope Innocent III also, as is recorded in his *Life*, no. 43, with remarkable acuteness detected a defect in the seal of a privilege produced by the abbot of Scozulo; Mabillon observed this. Nor indeed are other examples of the same fraud lacking, one further example of which it is pleasant to give. In volume III of the *Italia Sacra*, under the bishops of Chiusi, Ughelli published a diploma of Ratchis, king of the Lombards, by which the monastery of Saint Saviour of Monte Amiata, situated in the same district of Chiusi, is said to have been founded. Thomasius also mentioned that document as though it were a jewel in his *History of Siena*.

Elsewhere—that is, in Dissertation LXV, *On the Establishment of Monasteries*—I shall have occasion to mention the same diploma, to be consigned among laughable fictions. Mabillon too, in the *Benedictine Annals* under the year of Christ 750, had said of it: “Ughelli reports the diploma, with a little narrative concerning the origin of the monastery (namely, of Amiata), which has the flavor of a fable. The diploma gives the year 742 as that of the monastery’s foundation, and Ughelli judged it authentic; I would very much wish it to be wholly genuine.” Thus spoke that most learned man with great moderation, although that production otherwise betrays, from head to foot, a most inept forger.

I revive this fabrication in order to add what Titius, the Sienese historian, noted upon it; his books, still in manuscript, are preserved by the heirs of my once most learned friend Hubert Benvoglienti. “This privilege,” Titius writes, “is furnished with an attached wax seal, impressed on both sides with two human figures. The letters around it cannot conveniently be read because of their antiquity. The head of each figure in the seal is crowned, and the hand of each holds a staff. This privilege is at the abbey of Saint Saviour in the district of Siena.” A seal displaying the figures of two men indicates two princes reigning together and therefore appears to have had nothing in common with King Ratchis. Nevertheless, even a forged seal once had great force in winning credence for a diploma among the ignorant.]

by which he confirms all rights and privileges to Bishop Apollinaris of Reggio and to his church (781)

(From Muratori, *Italian Antiquities of the Middle Ages*.)

[Col. 1010C]

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards [Col. 1011A] and patrician of the Romans.

If we bestow the generosity and munificence of our liberality upon the servants of God’s churches, and willingly grant their requests, we believe that this advances us toward the summit of imperial excellence; moreover—and this is more precious than all dignities—we do not doubt that we shall receive the reward of eternal recompense.

Therefore we wish all the faithful of the holy Church of God, both our contemporaries and those to come, to know that our father, the most reverend Apollinaris, bishop of the holy church of Reggio, approached our clemency and reported to us that, through negligence and carelessness, the buildings of the churches in the city of Reggio had been burned in crackling flames, and that with them certain written instruments and records had been reduced to ashes.

He had in his hands the charters of the Lombard kings, by whose authority the aforesaid church had been supported and fortified on every side, so that it might suffer neither oppression from wicked men nor the losses of invasions.

He therefore asked that, for the love of God, we should receive that church, together with all the property it had acquired up to that time or might acquire in the future through the offerings of the faithful, together with its possessions and dependents of both sexes and all the clergy serving there daily, under the protection of our defense.

This we have done, and through this page of our charter we decree and command that no person, great or small, presume in any way to disturb or molest the property or dependents of that church, or its venerable clergy.

And because the boundaries of that church lie along the borders of Mantua, Bologna, Modena, Luni, Parma, Ticinum, and Como, the property of that bishopric being situated there, the same bishop possessed an explanatory document in which, without any doubt, the property of the aforesaid church was set out by individual places and names, together with its boundaries and limits.

Therefore, to guard against the invasion of reckless presumption, and also because of the Frankish people whom we have recently introduced into Italy, he asked our Excellence to order those same boundaries to be inserted in this charter, so that the church might suffer no fraud from invaders concerning its property or boundaries.

Considering his petition worthy and reasonable, we ordered all the boundaries to be recorded according to the borders of Luni and Parma as they were set out in that explanatory document.

From the south, then, toward the west, the boundaries and limits run from Prato Mauri to Mount Mensa, thence to Centiocrucis, then to the Maritime Alps, from there to Mount Posci, descending into the stream Niteram, which flows into the river Incia; along the river Incia, as the Incia descends from the upper village of Monticulo, running transversely to Barcha; then downstream through Agida toward the north into the stream Campigenus; from there into Tegolaria, into the river Po and the Zarano, as the Po flows into the Buriana.

Likewise, toward the east on the southern side, the boundaries proceed through Prato Maggiore to Mount Rusulus, through the Alps to Fazola, and thence through the Alps as far as the Baths of Saloni.

The boundaries between Tuscany and the territory of Reggio and Modena run from the Baths of Saloni to the King’s Tent, from there to the Fountain of Silvanus, then to the Blood-red Stream, thereafter to the Lake of Carpene, then to the New Road, from there to the place called Motivus, then to the place called La Verna; thereafter, descending by Mount Lawrence, they reach the river Dullus; then through the Forest of Mallo to Collina, thereafter to Pratumlongum, and then by the stream that flows from Lupatium into the river Sigla; from there along the Sigla as far as Dullus; then ascending through Dimnaticus to Carciola; from there descending by the Serra of Maurianus, they reach the river Rasennus; then ascending to Piraniana, and from there to the mountain above Valles as far as Antiquum.

Then, descending into Piscariola, they reach the river Sigla; thereafter along the Clusa, running by Mount Cerradus, until it comes below Mount Merellus; from there it proceeds through Silvanus; then it runs through Salsula; from there through Mount Monticulus; thereafter across the Milatian Plain toward the north, through the marshes of the city of Nova as far as the road; then to Aquaprolonga, until it reaches the Buriana.

Within these aforesaid boundaries, as we have found was anciently established in that church by holy fathers and suitable and Catholic men, let every part of that church possess all its property securely and peacefully forever by our royal authority.

The aforesaid bishop also reported that a certain brother of his named Anspert had, by decree, been granted for all the days of his life certain oratories belonging to the church of Reggio: one at Luciaria, between the Po and the Bundenus, built in honor of Saint George; and another at Gabiana, likewise between the Po and the Bundenus, built in honor of Saint Andrew.

But afterward, when that Anspert sought entry into the monastery of Nonantula, he gave those oratories to the aforesaid monastery upon his entry.

The aforesaid father Apollinaris, bishop, fearing that his church might suffer loss, brought the matter to court with his advocate in the presence of our duke Goeradus, against Anselm, abbot of the aforesaid monastery.

The disagreement that had arisen between the two venerable places could in no way be settled without a hearing before the neighboring bishops. Accordingly, after an adjournment had been granted, three bishops were summoned, namely Peter of Bologna, Geminianus of Modena, and Peter of Parma, together with other suitable and Catholic men.

When they were seated in judgment with the aforesaid Duke Goeradus, Bishop Apollinaris and Abbot Anselm appeared. Their complaints were carefully examined, and the church of Reggio, to which the aforesaid oratories were subject by rightful law, acquired them according to canonical and legal procedure.

For more secure protection, the aforesaid father presented to our presence a written record, confirmed by witnesses, together with the decree, asking that we ratify it by our inviolable charter and remove every stain of dispute.

Granting his petition, by this charter we confirm the aforesaid oratories to the holy church and restore them without any contradiction.

Furthermore, at his request, we grant our Gajum estate, which lies in the same place beside the property of that church at Luciaria and is now newly cultivated, to the oratory of Saint George by this charter as its own right, for the salvation of our soul, together with the fisheries along the Po and the Bundenus and the adjoining marshes and lakes.

Likewise, to the oratory of Saint Andrew we give land and forest belonging to our royal jurisdiction, situated around the property of that church between the Po and the Bundenus at Gabiana, together with the fisheries along the Po and the Bundenus and the marshes and lakes, so that the frequently mentioned holy church of Reggio may hold and possess all these things by proprietary right, without contradiction from any authority.

We also grant that, if a dispute should arise concerning the property or dependents of that church, an investigation may be conducted through good and free men living in the surrounding area, even to the taking of an oath.

The bishops of that church shall have two or three advocates, if necessary, whom they themselves choose, who shall diligently investigate and examine the church’s case. Those advocates shall be exempt from every public exaction.

If anyone attempts to invalidate the authority of this constitution of ours, he shall be compelled to pay the fine for violating immunity—namely, thirty pounds of silver—to the party of the holy church of Reggio.

And so that this charter of our liberality, immunity, defense, investigation, and advocacy may remain firm for a long time, and may be more truly believed and more carefully observed by all, we have subscribed it below with our hand and ordered it sealed with our ring.

Sign of Charles, most glorious king.

Gilibertus, acting in place of Radonus, have examined and approved.

Given in the month of June, on the eighth day, in the thirteenth [Col. 1014B] and seventh year, in the tenth indiction.

Done in the city of Pavia, happily, in the name of God. Amen.

### VIII. Diploma of Charles the Great by which he grants a privilege to the church of Arezzo (783)

(From Muratori, *Italian Antiquities of the Middle Ages*.)

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards, and patrician of the Romans.

If we willingly heed the petitions of priests or servants of God when they are brought to our ears, and in God’s name put them into effect, we exercise the royal custom and trust that this contributes to our reward and to the stability of our kingdom. Therefore let the greatness of all our faithful, present and future, know how the venerable man Aribert, bishop of the holy church of Arezzo, which was built in honor of Saint Donatus, approached our clemency and petitioned our serenity that we should, after examining the charters of grant or confirmation, as well as the sales and exchanges, once again restore and confirm by our authority to that holy place all the property of that church which has long been and until now appears to have belonged there—both monasteries or hospices, and baptismal churches, and the remaining possessions—whatever has been given or donated there through grants or confirmations by kings, or through sales and exchanges from the generosity of good men; and also the monastery of Saint Benedict in that same city, which his predecessor, the late Bishop Cunemund, lawfully acquired or founded through his own work, together with his own property, [Col. 1014D] which he held by right of his parents and appeared to have assigned to that church of God. [Col. 1014C]

We did not wish to deny his petition out of reverence for that holy place, but let it be known that in our almsgiving we have granted and confirmed it as follows. Therefore we command that, just as it is established that the church of Saint Donatus has long been lawfully and reasonably endowed with the aforesaid property, and as the aforementioned venerable man, Bishop Aribert, appears at the present time to possess it by a rightful title, so—after examining the grants or confirmations of kings, as we have said, and the sales, exchanges, [Col. 1015A] and transfers made by good men—the aforesaid Bishop Aribert and his successors, who shall be rectors of that holy place, may henceforth, by this authority and confirmation of ours, hold and possess in undisturbed order the property mentioned above. Let none of our faithful henceforth or thereafter presume at any time to disturb or bring a claim against the aforesaid bishop or his successors concerning the property described above; rather, in our times and in those to come, let these things increase the resources of that house of God. And so that this authority may be held more firmly and better preserved through the ages, we have resolved to strengthen it below with our own hand and have ordered it sealed with our ring.

[Col. 1015B]

Sign of Charles, the most glorious king.

I, Ercambaldus, have subscribed in the place of Rado.

Given on the seventh day before the Ides of October, in the sixteenth year and the tenth year of our reign.

Done in the city of Worms, happily, in the name of God. Amen.

## IX. Diploma of Charlemagne for the church of Modena (785)

[Note: [Col. 1015D] Geminianus, under this name the second bishop of Modena, was elected in the year 785. In his favor Desiderius, king of the Lombards, confirmed as valid all the privileges of the earlier kings toward the church of Modena. After Charlemagne had subsequently defeated him and, as victor, granted various privileges to various churches, he also granted the following one to Geminianus.]

(From Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. II, p. 91.)

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards, and Roman patrician, to all bishops, abbots, dukes, counts, gastalds, and all monasteries fearing God, present and future.

[Col. 1015C]

We believe that the foundation of our kingdom is greatly strengthened by this, if we willingly and gladly comply with the petitions of priests and servants of God when they are presented to our ears, and bring them to effect. Therefore let your prudence know how, at the petition of the venerable man Geminianus, bishop of the holy church of Modena, which was built in honor of the most precious confessor of Christ, Geminianus, bishop of that church, we have granted the following benefit to that holy place: concerning the monasteries, hospices, baptismal churches, and other possessions belonging to the said bishopric, whether from the gift of a king, queens, or other God-fearing men, by which that house of God is lawfully endowed at the present time, or whatever divine piety may wish to add there, [Col. 1015D] no public judge shall presume at any time to enter there to hear cases, exact transport services from every side, or make lodging or provisions, take sureties, distrain the men of that bishopric, or demand any public payments.

For this reason we ordered this immunity to be written, by which we specifically decree and establish that none of you, nor any of your subordinates, henceforth or thereafter, as we have said, shall presume to enter the monasteries, hospices, baptismal churches, or other possessions belonging to that bishopric—whether they derive from gifts of kings, queens, or other God-fearing men—to hear cases, exact transport services from every side, make lodgings or provisions, take sureties, demand or exact any public payments, or otherwise enter or exact anything there at any time by judicial authority. Rather, under the name of immunity, with every customary due granted, let the rectors of that bishopric and their men be able at all times to live and reside in peace.

[Col. 1016A]

And so that this authority may be held more firmly and recognized through long ages, we decree that it be strengthened by our own subscription.

[Col. 1016B]

Sign of Charles, the most glorious king.

I, Vigbaldus, have recognized this in the place of Rado.

Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of October, in the fourteenth year and the ninth year of our reign.

## X. Diploma of Charlemagne for the monastery of Saint Vincent of Volturno (787)

(From Duchesne, *Writers of Frankish Affairs*.)

Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards, and patrician of the Romans, to the venerable man Paul, abbot, and to the monks of the monastery of Saint Vincent, situated in the territory of Benevento in the region of Samnium . . . . And because Desiderius’s charter was brought to us, stating how he had donated the estate of Tritae, situated in the district of Baluense, to that holy monastery for the benefit of the monks, we too issued our confirmation concerning the same charter. [Col. 1016C] But afterward it became clear that certain disputes had arisen between you and those men who claimed through charters of dukes that they were free. For this reason we sent our agents Rismus and Agilbertus there; by investigating the whole matter more clearly, they learned the entire truth concerning it. Therefore, for the increase of our reward, we order that the aforesaid men of the aforementioned estate of Tritae, just as their ancestry was bound from ancient times to render service, so also henceforth, with all freedom removed, shall perpetually perform the lawful service and obedience that shall remain forever, according to the charter of donation.

[Col. 1016D]

Another diploma in which the same emperor and king Charles granted the monks of the aforesaid monastery of Saint Vincent the free and perpetual right to appoint an abbot without any disturbance from anyone and to organize, judge, and administer the cells subject to him.

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards, and patrician of the Romans, to all bishops, abbots, dukes, counts, judges, gastalds, auction officials, vicars, centenarii, and our other faithful, present and future.

[Col. 1017A]

We believe that the foundation of our kingdom is greatly strengthened by this, if we willingly comply with the petitions of priests and servants of God when they are brought to our ears and bring them to effect. We exercise the royal custom and trust that this contributes to the increase of our reward and to the stability of our kingdom in God’s name. Therefore let your prudence know how, at the petition of the religious man Paul, abbot of the monastery of Saint Vincent the martyr, which was built in the place called Samnium on the river Volturno, we have granted the following benefit to that monastery: that, in the monasteries lawfully subject to it, whose names are these—the monastery of Saint Peter the apostle, founded near the walls of our city of Benevento, [Col. 1017B] and the monastery of Saint Mary, situated in the district of Spoleto, in the place called Apinianica—and, in addition, in the other monasteries, cells, estates, and remaining possessions that have been given or assigned there through the generosity of kings, queens, dukes, or good men, as well as in the exempted persons (*excusati*) or offered persons who are already lawfully subject to the aforesaid monasteries, or who may wish devoutly to offer themselves and their property, they shall have lawful and reasonable freedom.

Likewise, wherever that house of God is seen at the present time to be lawfully endowed by a rightful title, or whatever may henceforth be added or assigned there lawfully by God-fearing men, no public judge shall presume at any time to enter to hear cases, exact transport services from every side, make lodgings or provisions, take sureties, distrain the men of that monastery, or demand any public payments. [Col. 1017C]

For this reason we ordered this immunity to be written, by which we specifically decree that none of you, nor anyone exercising judicial power, nor any other person, henceforth or thereafter, shall presume to enter or exact anything at any time in the monasteries, cells, estates, or other possessions mentioned above, or wherever that house of God is now known to be lawfully endowed: neither to hear cases, as we have said, nor to exact transport services from every side, make lodgings or provisions, [Col. 1017D] take sureties, distrain the men of that monastery, impose any new custom, or demand any public payments.

Likewise, in God’s name, we have granted and confirmed to that holy place, insofar as human frailty permits, that whenever the abbot of that monastery departs from this life, they shall have permission, according to the rule of Saint Benedict, to choose among themselves, without anyone’s disturbance or contradiction, whichever abbot they find to be better, more worthy, and wiser; and under the name of immunity . . . . . . they may enjoy all the granted revenues. At all times, the rectors of that monastery of Saint Vincent, both they and their successors, as well as the brothers who appear to serve God there, shall be able to live and reside peacefully according to the rule, so that they may be more gladly disposed to pray earnestly for the mercy of God on behalf of us, our wives, our children, and all our people.

[Col. 1018A]

And so that this authority may be held more firmly and preserved inviolate through the ages, with God’s help, we have resolved to strengthen it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with our ring.

Sign of Charles, the most glorious king.

Sign of Jacob, in the place of Rado.

Given on the ninth day before the Kalends of April, in the nineteenth year and the fourteenth year of our reign.

Done at Capua, our city, happily, in the name of God. Amen.

## XI. Diploma of Charlemagne for the church of Benevento (783)

(From Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*.)

[Col. 1018B]

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards, and patrician of the Romans, to all our officials, present and future, with the help of the Lord, who established us upon the throne of our kingdom.

If we willingly heed the petitions of priests and servants of God that concern their peace or assistance, or bring them to effect in God’s name, we exercise the royal custom and trust that this contributes to the increase of our reward and to the stability of our kingdom in God’s name. Therefore the venerable man David, bishop of the church of the holy Mother of God and ever-virgin Mary, situated within the city of Benevento, petitioned the clemency of our kingdom [Col. 1018C] that all the property belonging to that house of God—whether from gifts of kings, queens, dukes, and duchesses, or God-fearing men, or acquired through sale, purchase, or exchange; and all judgments by which the rectors of the holy church had lawfully prevailed in court concerning its property; as well as all revenues and offerings of the faithful belonging by law to the holy church of Benevento from various churches—should be received in full by whichever bishop of Benevento existed in each period and possessed according to canonical sanction.

Whether these possessions were in various places, in cities, villages, mountains, plains, or waters, or in the open country and estates, or wherever that house of God is seen at the present time to possess and exercise dominion in lawful order, or whatever may henceforth be added or assigned there, we ought to confirm under the name of immunity. [Col. 1018D]

We did not wish to deny his petition, but let it be known that we have granted and confirmed everything in this manner. Therefore we ordered this immunity of ours to be written, by which we specifically decree that none of us, nor anyone exercising judicial authority, nor any other person, henceforth or thereafter, shall presume at any time to enter or exact anything in the monasteries lawfully subject to it, or in the estates, churches, or all the possessions described above—where that house of God is now known to be justly and reasonably endowed, or whatever it may henceforth acquire through the generosity of good men—in order to hear cases, exact transport services from every side, make lodgings or provisions, take sureties, distrain the men of that church contrary to the order of justice, impose new customs, or demand any public payments.

[Col. 1019A]

Rather, under the name of immunity, let the aforementioned David and his successors, whoever they may be in due course, live and reside peacefully, with Christ’s favor, so that they may be more gladly disposed to pray earnestly for the mercy of the Lord on behalf of us, our wives, and our children. And so that this authority may have greater firmness and be preserved inviolate in future times, we have resolved to strengthen it by our own subscription and have ordered it sealed with our ring.

[Col. 1019B]

Sign of Charles, the most glorious king.

Given on the second day before the Kalends of April, in the eighteenth year and the fourteenth year of our reign.

Done at Capua. Happily, in the name of God. Amen.

## XII. Diploma of Charlemagne for the church of Milan (791)

(From Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*.)

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards, and patrician of the Romans.

We trust that this contributes to eternal blessedness and to the stability of our kingdom, in God’s name, if we willingly comply with the just petitions of the servants of God when they are disclosed to our ears [Col. 1019C] and bring them to effect. Therefore let the greatness of all our faithful, present and future, know how the venerable man Peter, bishop of the church of the city of Milan, approached the serenity of our kingdom; how, for the love of God and the veneration of Saint Ambrose, he had established a monastery beside the bodies of the holy martyrs Protasius and Gervasius and of that most blessed confessor of Christ, and had newly established monks there under the rule of Saint Benedict, so that they might offer continual praises to God there and pray for the prosperity of the kingdom, the safety of the whole Christian people, and the condition of the holy church of Milan; and how he had appointed the venerable priest Benedict as abbot there.

He therefore petitioned the clemency of our highness [Col. 1019D] that whatever he had given to the aforesaid monastery, for the sake of God, from the property of his church of Milan, or whatever had lawfully been assigned there at the present time, and which that monastery is now known to possess lawfully and reasonably, as well as whatever might henceforth be added or assigned there by God-fearing men, with the Lord’s provision, we should fully confirm by our royal pronouncement. Thus it should remain perpetually under the government and authority of the rectors of the holy church of Milan, as it is seen to have been established by him; and whenever the abbot of that monastery should depart from this life to the Lord by divine calling, the monks of that monastery of the holy church of Milan should have permission [Col. 1020A] to choose over themselves an abbot who is wholly faithful to us, according to the sacred order and the rule of Saint Benedict.

We did not wish to deny this petition, compelled by the name of the Lord, reverence for that holy place, and the merits of the aforementioned holy bishop; rather, let it be known that in our almsgiving we have granted and confirmed everything in this manner. Therefore by this present authority of ours we decree and command that, since the monastery mentioned above, beside the bodies of the holy martyrs Protasius and Gervasius and of the confessor of Christ Ambrose, together with its adjacent properties and appurtenances, is known to have been established by the aforesaid venerable man Peter, after examination of his authority, it shall, by this command and gift of confirmation from our serenity, remain securely and most firmly established by law for all time. [Col. 1020B]

No outsider shall ever be appointed abbot there, but only someone from that congregation, as we have said, of the holy church of Milan, wholly faithful to us, whom the brothers wish to elect and who is able to govern them according to the divine laws and the rule of Saint Benedict.

We decree likewise that none of our successors, nor any successor of the aforementioned bishop, shall ever presume to violate or destroy this arrangement of ours, which we have confirmed for the love of the blessed confessor of Christ Ambrose and for the stability of our kingdom. Rather, so that the servants of God who appear to spend their lives there through the ages under the rule of blessedness may be more gladly disposed to pray continually for the mercy of the Lord on behalf of us, our wife, and our children, and for the stability of our kingdom, it shall, with God’s favor, endure and remain inviolate and irrefragable in our times and in those to come. [Col. 1020C]

And so that this authority may be held more firmly and preserved through the ages, we decree that it be strengthened below by our hand and have ordered it sealed with our ring.

Sign of +Charles, the most glorious king.

Given in the month of April, in the twenty-second year and the seventeenth year of our reign.

Done at Piacenza, from our public palace, happily, in the name of God. Amen.

## XIII. Diploma of Charlemagne for the church of Ceneda (794)

(From Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. V, p. 174.)

[Col. 1020D]

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards, and patrician of the Romans. We believe that the foundation of our kingdom is greatly strengthened by this, if we willingly heed the petitions of priests and servants of God when they are disclosed to our ears, and in God’s name bring them to effect. Therefore let the greatness of all our faithful, present and future, know how, for the sake of the Lord’s name and for eternal recompense, we have made the following confirmation . . . . of the church of Saint Titian, confessor of Christ, which was built beneath the fortress of the town of Ceneda, where that precious saint rests bodily, [Col. 1021A] and where the venerable man Dolcissimus is bishop . . . granted, and concerning all the plebes or parishes, with the jurisdictions of the places or lands of that bishop, which are included within these boundaries: namely, from the boundary of the river Limana, as the Limana flows into the Piave, and the Piave flows to the place where the Theba flows into it; then to the other place where the Nigrisalia flows into the Piave, and the Piave flows into the sea; and again from the river Limana to Mount Celicus, then to the Dead Lake, and from there to the church of Saint Florian, who formerly ruled most gloriously the rights of the same bishop in the city of Opitergium; and from there to the water where the Liquentia rises, and then as far as the transverse arch; and beyond this to the river Meduna, and the water of the Meduna flows into the Liquentia, [Col. 1021B] and again the Liquentia flows into . . . .

Therefore, considering his worthy petition, we confirm and strengthen by the page of our charter, both for him and for his successors, all the plebes and jurisdictions of the places or lands included within the aforesaid boundaries and limits. Accordingly we command that no duke, patriarch, archbishop, bishop, margrave, count, viscount, judge, sculdahis, or any person of our kingdom, great or small, presume to disturb or dispossess the aforesaid bishop or his successors of all the plebes or jurisdictions that we have granted and strengthened for them by the confirmation of our charter, just as the charters of our ancient kings or emperors were confirmed. [Col. 1021C]

Rather, let him hold everything with full authority, with every prohibition removed. If anyone—which we do not at all believe—should in future attempt to violate this charter of our confirmation, let him know that he shall pay one thousand pounds of gold, half to our treasury and half to the aforesaid bishop or his successors. So that this may be believed more truly and observed more zealously by all in the future, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it marked with the impression of our seal.

Sign of Charles, the illustrious king.

Given on the day before the Kalends of April, in the twenty-sixth year and the twentieth year of our reign.

Done at Francono fruel [reading uncertain], happily, in the name of God. Amen.

## XIV. Diploma of Charlemagne for the church of Arezzo (795)

(From Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*, vol. I, p. 412.)

[Col. 1021D]

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks, Romans, and Lombards. Whatever has been settled or defined in our presence and that of our nobles, through a just and proper process and careful examination, according to the justice of the holy Fathers, ought to be confirmed by our pronouncements, so that the purpose of Christ may remain unshaken forever.

Therefore let all bishops, abbots, dukes, counts, gastalds, and other officials, and all our faithful, present and future, know: While, under the Lord’s protection, we had come to Rome, to the thresholds of the holy chief apostles Peter and Paul, on certain affairs of the holy church of God and of the lord Pope Leo, and while we were sitting there together with those dukes, gastalds, and other faithful and nobles of ours, [Col. 1022A]

Aribertus, venerable bishop of the church of the holy city of Arezzo, came into our presence, making petition and complaint against Andrew, venerable bishop of the church of the holy city of Siena, saying:

“The diocese of his church, which his episcopal predecessors from ancient times, and he himself, had held, was invaded during the time of the late Pope Hadrian by Rodobertus, formerly bishop of the church of the holy city of Siena; afterward it was held by Haimo, formerly bishop of the aforesaid church of Siena; and until now it has been held by the aforementioned Andrew, bishop of the aforesaid church of Siena. This includes the monastery of Saint Ansanus, where he himself rests bodily, together with the other churches.”

Since a very serious dispute had arisen between them over this matter, we asked the most holy and reverend lord and Father in Christ, Leo, supreme pontiff and universal pope, to reconcile them with their priests according to canonical authority. He did so, and a judgment and charter of his authority were issued to the aforementioned Aribertus, bishop of the church of the city of Arezzo, so that henceforth he should hold and possess for the church his parish in its entirety, just as it had been from ancient times. [Col. 1022B]

[Col. 1022C]

For complete security, the aforementioned venerable Aribertus, bishop of the aforesaid holy church of Arezzo, petitioned our serenity that we too should grant to that holy church of God and should, according to what our lord Leo, supreme pontiff and venerable pope, together with all the other venerable faithful of the holy church, had defined in a just process and according to the order of equity, and confirmed by his authoritative charter, fully concede and confirm the settlement.

We did not wish to deny his petition for the sake of divine worship and reverence for that holy church, but command that it be known that we have granted and confirmed everything in this manner. Therefore we order that the aforementioned holy church of God remain forever under the firmest legal title; and, after consideration of the authority and confirmation of the aforementioned lord, of blessed memory, Father Leo, supreme pontiff and universal pope, let the aforementioned Aribertus, bishop of the holy church of Arezzo, and his successors forever, who shall be rectors in his holy church of God, possess and govern, as it was declared by him, the monasteries and baptisteries according to the holy Fathers and the order of equity, just as they have held and possessed them from ancient times. [Col. 1022D]

And so that this authority may be held more firmly and better preserved through the ages, we have confirmed it above with our own hand and ordered it sealed with our ring.

Sign of Charles the Great +, emperor.

Given on the fourth day before the Nones of March, in the thirty-third and thirty-fourth years of our empire.

[Col. 1023A]

Done at Rome, in the church of Saint Peter, chief of the apostles, where he himself rests bodily. Happily.

## XV. Letter of Charlemagne appointing his envoy Hilderic to investigate everywhere the affairs of the monastery of Farfa (797)

(From Muratori, *Writers of Italian Affairs*.)

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards, and patrician of the Romans, to all dukes, gastalds, officials, and our other faithful residing everywhere.

Let it be known to you that, at the request of the venerable abbot Mauraldus and his congregation, we command Hilderic, our faithful man, to investigate and diligently uphold the claims of the monastery of Saint Mary and of that abbot [Col. 1023B] in every place, office, or jurisdiction. Wherever your offices or jurisdiction extend, and whenever he brings before you or raises a claim concerning the rights of the aforesaid monastery, or of that abbot and his monks, you shall diligently and purely endeavor to render justice on behalf of the aforesaid monastery, without any . . . . or delay. On no account presume to inflict any disturbance or accusation upon the aforesaid Hilderic contrary to the order of reason concerning any matters, because he appears to be investigating the justice we have ordered concerning the aforesaid house of God. Rather, if you wish to have the grace of God and of us, see that he is supported in our almsgiving with justice.

And so that you may know this more clearly, we have ordered it signed below with our seal.

[Col. 1023C]

Given on the fifth day before the Kalends of September, in the twenty-fourth year of our reign.

Done in the city of Regensburg.

## XVI. Diploma of Charlemagne confirming the donation made by Ludigarus for the church of Ascoli (800)

(From Ughelli, *Italia Sacra*.)

In the name of the Lord God, our Savior Jesus Christ. Under the reign of the lord Charles and his son Pippin, most excellent kings of the Franks and Lombards and patricians, or of the Roman kingdoms, in Christ’s name, in Italy, with God’s favor, in the twenty-sixth and eighteenth years respectively; and under the same circumstances, in the eighth, most fortunate year of the duchy of the most glorious man Vinigisus, or

[Note: [Col. 1023D] Under Bishop Tuptolf of Ascoli, in the year 800, a donation was made by Ludigarus, count of the city of Ascoli, for the benefit of that church. It was confirmed by Charlemagne, king of the Franks and Lombards, and subscribed by Pippin, Charles’s son and patrician of the Romans, as well as by Vinigisus, duke of Spoleto, and by the margrave Saseprundus, Rodelantus, and Astulphus. The precious record of the donation is preserved in the archive of the cathedral church. Its script is indeed inelegant, its language barbarous, and it has been somewhat damaged by moths. Given at Ascoli in the month of June, on the second day, indiction VII, in the twenty-sixth year of King Charles in Italy, the eighteenth of Pippin, the eighth year of the duchy of the most glorious Vinigisus, and the eighth year of the *comitatus* of Ludigarus. This diploma, which some regard as suspicious, was taken by the learned Antonello from the original and sent to me.] Ludigarus, count of the city of Ascoli, [Col. 1023D] in the month of June, on the second day, indiction VI.

Therefore it is established that I, Ludigarus, count of the city of Ascoli, considering my recompense and for the reward and redemption of my soul, give and on the present day transfer to the holy mother church in the bishopric of Ascoli, or in honor of the most blessed man Bishop Tustolfus, some of my own property, namely: in the territory of Ascoli, Mount Columnate itself, with seven hundred *modii*; in Forano, four hundred *modii*; and half of the church of Saint Peter, which is now seen to stand there, together with its endowment and ornaments; [Col. 1024A] in Trisago, six hundred *modii*; and in Lomicciano and Velariana, for each parcel situated there, eight hundred *modii*; and the church of Saint Helena with its endowment and ornaments; in Valveneria, three hundred and sixty; and in Cerro, three hundred and ninety *modii*.

All the aforesaid land, with its fruits and trees, vineyards, olive groves, reed beds, and willow groves, with banks, streams, cultivated and uncultivated land, male and female slaves, *cartulati*, *praestandatii*, free men, and everything belonging to it, in its entirety. Its boundaries are: from Capo, the boundary of Umbria, and the greater ditch; on one side, the boundary of Britta; on the other side, the boundary of Claro and Clarata; at the foot, the boundary of the Tronto. All this [Col. 1024B] aforesaid land amounts altogether to three thousand five hundred and fifty *modii*.

I, the aforesaid Ludigarus, give and transfer on the present day the aforesaid property . . . to the bishopric of Ascoli, and to you, lord Bishop Tustolfus, or to your successors, for the ownership of the said bishopric and for possession without anyone’s hindrance. In exchange for this donation of mine, you, lord Bishop Tustolfus, gave me some property belonging to your bishopric, for residence within the city and outside it: namely, the castle at Isola with its appurtenance, the estate of Parignano outside the Solestanus Bridge, the estate of Casale, the estate of Prepi, and the estate of Lomenia, for the days of my life only. I have testified that I hold these things, and I promise this in return.

[Col. 1024C]

I, the aforementioned Ludigarus, count, promise this to you, the aforesaid Bishop Tustolfus, and to your descendants and successors: if at any time I should presume to remove, disturb, or bring a claim concerning these things, or should be unable to defend or uphold them against any person, I, the aforesaid Count Ludigarus, shall restore another property of equal quantity and quality, called Ferquidem, of whatever value it appears to have on that day in the aforesaid places or under the aforesaid names, to you, Lord Bishop Tustolfus, or to your descendants and successors, for possession by the aforesaid bishopric. Let this charter remain firm in its validity.

Done at Ascoli, in the place called Carrufa, in the year 874 from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ. I, Elmericus the notary, wrote this charter of donation at the request of Count Ludigarus, who asked me to write it.

[Col. 1024D]

I, Count Ludigarus, have + made with my own hand in this charter made by me the sign of the holy cross.

I, Charles the emperor, having approved and confirmed this charter at the request of Count Ludigarus, have + made the sign of the cross.

I, Pippin, patrician of the Romans and emperor, have + made the sign of the cross.

[Col. 1025A]

I, Vinigisus, duke and margrave, asked by Count Ludigarus, am a requested witness and have + made the sign of the cross.

I, Suseprundus, asked by the aforesaid Count Ludigarus, am a requested witness and have + made the sign of the cross.

I, Rodelantus, asked by the aforesaid Count Ludigarus, am a requested witness and have + made the sign of the cross.

I, Astolphus, asked by the aforesaid Count Ludigarus, am a requested witness and have + made the sign of the cross. [Col. 1025B]

[Note: Here the donation and subscriptions end.]

For a long time I was torn by hesitant thought and a doubtful mind as to whether I should publish this document, suspect and barbarous as it is, teeming with solecisms in almost every line, or whether, regarding it as spurious, I should pass over it in complete silence [Col. 1025C]; or rather whether I should spend time examining it. Its reckoning of reigns and indiction is confused, and the subscriptions give different years. If we adhere to the subscription, we are compelled to assert that the donation was subscribed by Charles the Bald, who was not yet emperor but rather the tyrant of Gaul and invader of Italy. For he was still alive at that time, and in the following year—which was 875 from the redemption of the world—when he heard of the death of Emperor Louis II, he immediately invaded the kingdom of Italy and was crowned at Rome by Pope John VIII. Yet he is never found called king of the Lombards, nor is he known to have had a son named Pepin as his associate in the kingdom. For Pepin and Charles, the sons of his brother King Pepin, who were disturbing the kingdom, had previously been captured by Charles the Bald in the year 852, tonsured, and thrust into a monastery, as Sigebert bears witness.

On the other hand, if we consider the dates of the reigns in Italy and of the indiction inserted at the beginning of the donation, we must without doubt believe that it was confirmed by Charlemagne. For in the twenty-sixth year of his reigns [Col. 1025D] in Italy, as the charter of donation states, all Latin historians testify that he honorably dismissed Leo III, set out for Italy, and in the following year was crowned emperor at Rome. Moreover, Vinigisius, duke of Spoleto, who was called as a witness to the donation, went with his army in this same year—that is, the twenty-fifth year of Charlemagne’s reign in Italy—to meet the most holy Pope Leo; receiving him reverently, he escorted him to Spoleto, as Anastasius relates. Therefore, once the error in the subscription has been dismissed, I see no reason to reject the genuine donation, nor will the ignorance of a very unskilled scribe invalidate the document. I would therefore explain and clarify the confused reckoning of the reigns as follows:

In the name of the Lord God and Savior Jesus Christ, while our lord Charles and his son Pepin, most excellent kings of the Franks and Lombards and patricians of the Romans, were reigning; the years of their reigns, in Christ’s name, in Italy, by God’s favor, being 26 and 18—that is, the twenty-sixth year of Charles’s reign and the eighteenth of Pepin’s—while the most glorious man Vinigisius was in the eighth year of his duchy, and Count Ludigari in the eighth year of his rule over the city of Ascoli; in the month of June, on the second day, in the seventh indiction. For in this indiction, in the year of Christ 799, we find that Charles undertook his journey to Italy in order to avenge the injury inflicted upon Saint Leo III by Paschalis the primicerius and Campulus the sacellarius [Col. 1026C]. At the end, where it says “Actum in Asculo,” restore it as follows:
