“Done at Ascoli, in the place called Carrufa, in the year from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ seven hundred and ninety-nine.”

Carrufa, from which that rescript of the Emperor Charles was issued, is at the extremity of the county of Ascoli. Later, that fortress was granted in 1067 by William, son of Odemund, to Bernard II; and this place is mentioned in a bull of Anastasius IV, in the year 1153, which defined it as the boundary for separating the counties of Aprutium and Ascoli. That fortress is now cut down and destroyed, but its traces still remain deeply marked along the borders of the kingdom of Naples. At a distance of two miles from its ruins the town of Ancarano was later built. It received ecclesiastical and civil jurisdiction from the bishops of Ascoli from the time when it was first established. Beneath its gate, fifteen years ago, a stone was excavated and excavated again. On it was engraved an ancient couplet, which recorded the foundation of the fortress. It was later erased so that the heraldic arms of Bishop Sigismund Donati could be carved there. But lest its memory be completely extinguished, it was copied by Giovanni Pietro Pacifico, episcopal chancellor, and bore approximately the following:

> Charles the great king founded this fortress, when  
> At that time the land of Carrufa lay in ruins.

This inscription lent authority to the writing of Count Ludigari, since it seems entirely certain that in those times Charles laid siege to that fortress; after conquering it and soon leveling it to the ground himself, he is said to have caused Ancarano to rise from its ruins on the site where formerly the magnificent temple of the goddess Ancarana had been consecrated. This fictitious and shadowy deity was venerated by the people of Ascoli as the protecting goddess of their race; Tertullian also expressly mentions it in chapter 23 of the *Apologeticum*. UGHELLI.]

.

### XVII. Diploma of Charlemagne for the church of Concordia (802)

*(From Ughelli,* Italia Sacra*.)*

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Charles, by the favor of divine clemency king of the Franks and patrician of the Romans. If we offer the assistance of our empire to religious men presiding over places devoted to divine worship, then, in proportion as we are strengthened by human aid, we confidently hope to be more readily assisted by divine aid. Therefore, let the entire community of the faithful of Holy Church, both present and future, know how, for the name of the Lord and eternal reward, and at the intervention of our faithful Radigen, we have received Peter, bishop of the holy church of Concordia, under our protection and the safeguard of our *mundeburdium*, together with the whole integrity of that bishopric: its oratories, houses, castles, villages, male and female slaves, and all movable and immovable property that can be spoken of and named, belonging or pertaining to the aforesaid bishopric of Concordia [Col. 1026A].

Moreover, we grant to the aforesaid Peter, bishop of the holy church of Concordia, and to his successors, the parishes together with all their plebes and tithes, within the boundaries or limits described below: where the river called the Tagliamento rises and flows into the sea, and where the river Livenza rises and flows into the sea.

We also grant to the aforesaid Bishop Peter and his successors the entire *fodrum*, enforcement service, compulsory labor, and every public levy throughout that bishopric, so that no one may pay *fodrum*, a collection, or any other exaction—not he himself, nor his tenant, nor anyone living or working within the dependencies of that bishopric [Col. 1026B].

We further command that none of our faithful, whether coming and entering, or traveling messengers, shall establish lodging in that bishopric or its dependencies, or demand any payment; rather, everything shall remain in the power of Peter, bishop of the holy church of Concordia, and of his successors. Supported by this authority of ours, he shall freely and securely dispose of everything entrusted to him by us.

Therefore we command that no duke, bishop, margrave, count, viscount, *sculdasius*, *gastaldus*, dean, or any great or small person of our kingdom dare disturb or molest the aforesaid Peter, bishop of the holy church of Concordia, or his successors, or demand anything from that bishopric. Rather, the aforesaid bishop and his successors shall hold these possessions peacefully and quietly, with every disturbance removed.

If anyone should therefore attempt, with rash audacity, to violate this authority of ours, or to do anything prohibited by it, let him know that he shall pay one hundred pounds of the finest gold, half to our treasury and half to the oft-mentioned Peter, bishop of the holy church of Concordia, and to his successors. And so that this may be believed more firmly and observed more diligently by all, we have ordered it to be marked below with the impression of our seal, confirming it with our own hand.

[Col. 1027B] Sign of the lord Charles, most glorious king.

Etrambaldus, chancellor, acting in place of . . . . . . . . the archchancellor, examined and authenticated this. In the thirty-fourth year of the Frankish reign and in the year 802 of the Lord’s Incarnation.

[Note: [Col. 1027] These chronological notes appear to have been placed out of order through a scribal error.]

Given on the day before the Nones of April.

Done at Frankfurt, in the twenty-ninth year of the reign.

### XVIII. Diploma of Charlemagne confirming all the possessions, privileges, and rights of the monastery of Farfa (803)

*(From Muratori,* Scriptores rerum Italicarum*.)*

Charles, most serene Augustus, crowned by God, great and peaceful emperor governing the Roman Empire, and by the mercy of God king of the Franks and Lombards. If we confirm by our edicts those things which are known to have been donated by God-fearing men to holy places, out of love for the Lord and for the benefit of God’s servants, we not only exercise the customary duty of kingship, but also confidently believe that this contributes to the increase of our reward and to the stability of our empire in God’s name.

Therefore let all bishops, abbots, dukes, counts, *castaldi*, vicars, centenarii, officials, and our other faithful, both present and future, know that the venerable Benedict, religious abbot of the monastery of Saint Mary, ever-virgin and Mother of God, situated in the territory of Sabina, in the place called Acutianus, represented to our gentleness and requested that the possessions of his monastery—which had long ago come to that holy place through the donations of various persons, namely kings, queens, dukes, bishops, counts, and *castaldi*, through the offerings of the people, or through cessions, sales, purchases, and exchanges—of which the house of God appears in the present time, that is, in the year 803 from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the third year of our empire, to have been invested and to possess peacefully, should be more fully ceded and confirmed to the same holy place by a precept of our royal authority, for the increase of our reward.

Granting his request, therefore, for the increase of our reward, out of reverence for that holy place, and because of the petition of the aforesaid venerable man, Abbot Benedict, we have granted and ordered the following to be confirmed [Col. 1028A]:

We command that this shall remain perpetually in force concerning the aforesaid place: no one whatsoever among our faithful shall ever dare to disturb or condemn the aforesaid venerable Abbot Benedict or his successors regarding the aforesaid possessions, which the aforementioned house of God is now seen to possess justly, reasonably, and peacefully—that is, those held in the year 803 from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ and in the third year of our empire—or regarding those which, with the Lord’s favor, it may hereafter lawfully acquire. Nor shall anyone at any time unjustly take away or diminish anything from them.

Rather, by this precept of our serenity and confirmation, these possessions shall contribute to the holy Church of God in our time and in the future, so that at all times, without unlawful opposition from anyone, the governors of that monastery may hold and possess the possessions described above. Thus may the aforesaid venerable Abbot Benedict and the congregation of that church be more attentive continually to entreat divine mercy on our behalf, for the stability of our empire, for our sons and daughters, and for the whole people given to us by God.

And so that this authority may be held more firmly and observed more diligently through the ages, we have ordered it to be subscribed according to imperial custom and sealed with our ring.

Given on the Ides of June, in the third year of our empire, by Christ’s favor, and in the thirty-fifth year of our reign in Francia and the twenty-ninth in Italy; in the eleventh indiction.

Done at our public palace at Aachen, happily in God’s name. Amen.

### XIX. Diploma of Charlemagne for the church of Grado (803)

*(From Ughelli,* Italia Sacra*.)*

Charles, most serene Augustus, crowned by God, great and peaceful emperor governing the Roman Empire, and by the mercy of God king of the Franks and Lombards. We believe that the principal duty of our kingship lies in this: if the petitions of priests or servants of God are brought before our ears, we should willingly grant them and, in God’s name, bring them to fulfillment.

Therefore let all our faithful, present and future, know how the venerable Fortunatus, patriarch of Grado, bishop of the see of Saint Mark the Evangelist and of Saint Hermagoras, petitioned our serenity that we should grant and confirm, by our indulgence, such a benefit to the aforesaid holy church that, under the name of immunity, he himself, the priests and other persons, as well as the slaves and tenants who dwell on his lands in Istria, Romandiola, or Lombardy, or anywhere else, might live and reside in peace.

Compelled by his service and merits, we did not wish to deny his petition, but, for the increase of our reward, know that in God’s name we have granted and confirmed the following in every respect: the bishoprics, xenodochia, and baptismal churches [Col. 1029A].

We therefore command that in villages, estates, possessions, or any other property wherever the aforesaid patriarch is presently recognized as being justly and reasonably invested, no public judge shall presume to intervene unjustly to hear cases, exact feudal dues, impose lodgings or provisions, or demand any unjust payments. Rather, while the aforesaid Patriarch Fortunatus lives, under the name of immunity, he himself, his successors, his tenants and slaves who dwell upon his lands, and all other persons shall, by our indulgence, be able to live and reside peacefully, so that they may be more pleased continually to implore the Lord’s mercy on our behalf and for the stability of our kingdom.

And so that this authority may be held firmly and preserved better through the ages, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with our ring.

### XX. Diploma of Charlemagne for the church of Como (803)

*(From Ughelli, same work.)*

Charles, most serene Augustus, appointed by God, great and peaceful emperor governing the Roman Empire, who also by the mercy of God is king of the Franks and Lombards. If, by our burden of office, we bring to fulfillment the petitions of priests or servants of God which they have made known to our ears, we confidently believe that this will unquestionably contribute to our eternal blessedness.

Therefore let the whole body of our faithful, present and future, know that our dearest son Pepin, king of the Lombards, at the petition of the venerable Peter, bishop of the church of the holy city of Como, [Note: [Col. 1029D] Peter was the first of the Franks who, at Charlemagne’s command, came to this see of Como, invested with the civil authority of that city, the ratification of all privileges, and the renewed donation of the district of Bellenzona. The same emperor, at Peter’s request, gave the county of Chiavenna as a gift to the canons of the cathedral in 803, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December, in the third year of his empire. This diploma was copied from the archive of the cathedral [Col. 1030D].] requested our serenity that all the churches and possessions pertaining to that holy place—which it presently appears to possess in an orderly, just, and reasonable manner—should be confirmed there by a precept of our authority, and especially the tolls at Meanto and Gegis, together with that place; the plebs of Berinzona, the county, jurisdiction, and port itself; and that we should grant and confirm to the clerics of Como, for canonical use, the county of Chiavenna, its sluices, and the bridge of Chiavenna belonging to our jurisdiction [Col. 1029D].

We did not wish to deny his petition. Rather, for eternal reward, know that we have granted and confirmed all these things.

We therefore command that this shall remain perpetually in force concerning the aforesaid holy place: no one among our faithful shall presume to disturb the aforesaid Peter, bishop, or his successors, or to raise any complaint against them concerning the churches or possessions described above that justly and reasonably pertain to that place. Nor shall anyone presume at any time to increase or diminish anything contrary to reason, or to take away anything from the possessions described above. Rather, by this precept of our serenity and confirmation, they shall perpetually contribute to the holy place as an eternal increase of our alms and those of the glorious king Pepin, our son.

And so that this authority may be held more firmly and preserved better for long ages, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with our ring.

Sign of Charles, most serene + and most pious emperor.

[Col. 1030B] Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December, in the third year of our empire, by Christ’s favor, and in the thirty-sixth year of our reign in Francia, in the eleventh indiction, and in the year 803 from the Lord’s Incarnation.

[Note: [Col. 1030D] If there is no error in the number of the indiction, so that XII ought to be written instead of XI, the beginning of the indiction in this diploma is not reckoned from the Kalends of September. As for the place where the diploma was issued, called Reguntiburg—a name found nowhere on geographical maps—Tattus conjectures that it is Regensburg, which is still called Regenspurg by the Germans.]

Done at Reguntiburg, in the public palace, happily in God’s name. Amen.

### XXI. Diploma of Charlemagne for the monastery of Saint Mary of Organo (805)

*(From Ughelli, same work.)*

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord, eternal God, while our lord Charles the Great was reigning as emperor, in the fourth year of his reign, in the month of November, in the thirteenth indiction, happily.

If we devote care, with just foresight, to the welfare of venerable places, we confidently hope for the future assistance of heavenly support [Col. 1030C]. Therefore, let the prudence of all the faithful of Holy Church and of our own people, present and future, observe how, graciously favoring the petition of Guadelbert, venerable abbot of the monastery of Blessed Mary, ever-virgin, the illumination of the world, situated in the suburb of Verona, in the place called Organo, we grant to that revered monastery that throughout all places established under the rule of our empire, the ships and wagons of the same monastery may travel freely and absolutely, without anyone’s resistance or opposition.

Thus they shall not be compelled to give or pay anything, whether in naval tolls, which are called *ripatici*, or in terrestrial tolls, or at the crossings of the gates or bridge of the city of Verona, or of any other city or town [Col. 1030D].

No other bishop, count, or *guastaldus*, no official, nor any person belonging to the ecclesiastical order or public administration, shall presume to demand anything from the people of that most holy monastery.

We further add and decree, for the stability of the empire and the remedy of our soul, that wherever anything belongs to the aforesaid monastery, whether in the mountains or on the plains, according to the promulgation of Roman laws, if any portion of it has been diminished, it shall be sought out, so that an inquiry into the possessions of that monastery may be made through neighboring men of good testimony and reputation; and thus it shall devolve to the right, dominion, and perpetual possession of that monastery [Col. 1031A].

As for exchanges of the immovable possessions of that monastery which have been made, whether with estates belonging to our authority or with other persons, we decree that they shall remain forever firm and stable, just as if those possessions had been granted to the monastery from the beginning of its foundation.

If anyone, therefore, presumes to devise or carry out anything against this pragmatic sanction of ours, let him know that he shall pay a penalty of thirty pounds of our public treasury, half to the palace and half to the aforesaid holy monastery.

And so that this may be believed more certainly and observed inviolably by all, we have sealed it below with our ring.

Sign.

### XXII.

[Note: [Col. 1031C] “In the name of the Lord, Amen. This is a copy or transcript of a certain writing or privilege of grant and donation of the possessions described below, found on a bronze tablet discovered in the aforesaid monastery of Saint Anastasius at Aquae Salviae, situated near the city, in the sacristy and archive of the said monastery beside the altar. I, Antonius Goioli, son of Petrus Sirete, a Roman citizen, by the grace of God and apostolic authority a public notary, copied and happily transcribed it word for word, and read it before the reverend Jacob, by the grace of God bishop of Arezzo and vicar or general commissioner of our lord the pope in the holy city, its suburbs, and its district, and before the undersigned Joannes Stephanus Maffaronis, Joannes Paulus Alictii, and the said Petrus Berte, Roman citizens, first apostolic notaries and literate witnesses. I, the undersigned notary Antonius, read it before them, and it was carefully heard. The tenor of this writing, or privilege of grant and donation, is in every respect as follows.”]

[Note: [Col. 1031D] Alexander IV expressed this noble donation of the Emperor Charles and Pope Leo III, and its cause, in a privilege granted to the same monastery. For, through the merits and aid of Saint Anastasius the martyr, whose sacred relics are preserved there, and solely through the display of that saint’s head, Charles himself and Pope Leo conquered and utterly destroyed Ansidonia, the most ancient city of Tuscia, which had been occupied by unbelievers. Therefore, to perpetuate so great a victory, they offered and permanently donated to the church of the aforesaid martyr that city, the fortress of Orbetello, the Port of Hercules, Mount Argentarius, the island of Giglio, and other fortresses and towns.

A painting vividly depicting the capture of Ansidonia, Charles and Leo as its conquerors, and their noble deed toward the holy martyr was made about four hundred years ago and was still to be seen beneath the portico of the martyr’s church outside the city, at Aquae Salviae or the Three Fountains, where the ancient monastery of Cistercian monks stands. [Note: [Col. 1031] After Ughelli’s death it was obliterated with senseless whitewash. LUC.] We now, though unworthy, hold the title of its abbot.] 

Diploma of Charlemagne and Leo III for the monastery of Triumpontium (805).

*(From Ughelli,* Italia Sacra*.)*

In the name of the Lord God, our Savior Christ. Leo, bishop, servant of the servants of God, and Charles the Great and Pious, king, on this day, with no one forbidding or opposing, but by our own free will, grant, hand over, and by a bronze tablet, gilded [Col. 1031C] in perpetuity, donate to you, blessed martyr of Christ Anastasius, for you and your monastery, which is situated at Aquae Salviae, namely the whole and entire city commonly called Ansidonia, together with the port called Baenilia; likewise the port called Hercules; also the whole mountain called Giglio, one hundred miles into the sea; and the mountain called Jannuti; and the entire mountain called Argentarius, together with the sea adjoining it for one hundred miles out into the open sea, which lies within its waters.

The aforesaid mountains called Giglio and Jannuti; also the fortress called Orbetello, with its neighboring lagoon and fishery, and with its saltworks and all its dependencies; likewise Maxiliano, with all its dependencies; and similarly the mountain called Euti, with all its dependencies, which lies between the boundaries of the aforesaid entire city.

On the first side is the great sea, and below it the waters of the sea, which extend one hundred miles, and Mount Giglio and the mountain called Jannuti, all of which belong to the jurisdiction of your aforesaid monastery. On the second side is the river called Alvenia; on the third side the water called the Elsa runs, and from there proceeds as far as the place called Serpena; and on the fourth side it runs along Serpena, proceeds by the foot of Mount Arsitius, passes through the fishpond, and comes to Burano; then, following Burano, it returns to the aforesaid great sea.

All these possessions we grant as belonging to your aforesaid holy monastery and irrevocably hand over to it, together with their mountains, hills, shores and plains, meadows, pastures, woods, marshes, wells, springs, streams full of water, adjoining ruins, vineyards, and every utility, use, and dependency.

Moreover, we grant to you, aforesaid martyr of Christ Anastasius, and to your successors in perpetuity, all the churches which are within the county and boundaries of this territory, or which shall exist there until the end of the world. You may do with them whatever you wish, you and your servants, forever: appointing rectors, removing them for their merits, sending clerics, and retaining them at all times for your benefit.

No one else, except the supreme pontiff alone, may place an interdict upon the aforesaid churches or excommunicate any cleric, unless the rector of the church of the aforesaid Saint Anastasius may do so. No one shall be permitted to construct or build within these boundaries except with the consent of the abbot of Saint Anastasius. You shall request consecrations of altars, chrism, and ordinations of your clerics from the diocesan bishop, if he is willing to give them freely and without any complaint [Col. 1033A]. If not, you shall have the power to go to any bishop you wish, provided that he is Catholic.

For our Lord Jesus Christ caused us to see in a vision through his angel that the head of the aforesaid martyr would come to his battle, which we were waging against the aforesaid city, with praises of God. It said to our enemies that we would conquer; and so we accomplished these things. Now, with God’s help and with this aforesaid martyr’s head arriving, an earthquake came upon our enemies, trembling seized them, and the walls collapsed. Our enemies fell into our hands, and all were killed.

Therefore, as has been said, we hand over, grant, and perpetually bestow upon the aforesaid monastery of Saint Anastasius, so that from this day your servants may have the power to enter upon all the possessions aforesaid for the benefit of Saint Anastasius, to use, hold, enjoy, and possess them forever and ever. Thus, through you, glorious martyr, may we deserve to hear that voice which the Lord spoke in the Gospel: “Well done, good and faithful servant; I will set you over many things. Enter into the joy of the Lord your God.” In this promise of God we place great confidence, we and all who hope in you.

And if anyone, whether ourselves or any other person whatsoever, whether priest or layman, should wish to take away or alienate from the same monastery any of the aforesaid possessions, he shall have no power to do so. Rather, on the part of almighty God, blessed Mary ever-virgin, the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and this aforesaid martyr, let him remain forever excommunicated, accursed, and anathematized, and let him become a partner with Annas, Caiaphas, Herod, Pilate, and Judas Iscariot, the betrayer of our Lord Jesus Christ. Let him be excluded here and forever from the boundaries of all the churches.

Peace be with those who observe this, the peace of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.

I, Charles, emperor Augustus, by the authority of almighty God and of our empire, decree that no human person shall have the power in any way or by any device to take away from the aforesaid monastery of Saint Anastasius all the possessions described above, to retain anything taken away, or to inflict any injury, unless, for the wrong committed, he makes appropriate satisfaction and correction within fifteen days. As a penalty, he shall pay fifty pounds of the purest gold to the Roman Empire.

This was enacted and delivered in the year 805 of the Lord’s Incarnation, in the tenth indiction, in the tenth year of the lord Leo, supreme pope, and in the fifth year of the lord Charles, emperor.

I, Leo, bishop of the Roman Church, have subscribed.

I, Charles, emperor Augustus, have subscribed.

I, Peter, bishop of Ostia, have subscribed.

I, William, cardinal of Saint Sabina, have subscribed.

I, Issae, bishop of Abien. [alternatively, Sabinen.], have subscribed.

Robert of Aachen has subscribed, and so forth.

And I, Hugh, duke of Luxovium [or Lugdunum], have subscribed.

Anastasius, archivist of the Holy Roman Church, by command of the lord Pope Leo III and of the lord Charles the Great and Pious king, completed and finished this gilded bronze tablet.

[Col. 1034A] I, Jacob, by the grace of God bishop of Arezzo, vicar general and commissioner of my lord the pope in the city and district, with authority to compel notaries and other persons possessing original writings, instruments, and other records, and indeed a certain weighty bronze tablet existing in the said monastery, was present beforehand at the hearing of this copy or transcript, written faithfully from the aforesaid bronze tablet and copied by the undersigned Antonius Gojoli, son of Petrus Sirete, a Roman citizen and public apostolic notary. It was carefully heard before me, together with the said Antonius and the undersigned Joannes Stephanus Mafferoni, Joannes Paulus Alictii, and Santolo Petrus Berte, Roman citizens and public apostolic notaries, and witnesses to the writings set forth below [Col. 1034B].

Since I have found that this copy agrees with its original in every respect, without anything added or omitted that might corrupt or alter the meaning, I subscribe myself to this copy or transcript so that henceforth it may receive full faith from all, for the perpetual remembrance of the matter. Sitting as a tribunal, I impose my decree and ordinary authority, and I have caused the sign of my greater seal to be attached or affixed, in the year of the Lord 1369, in the seventh year of the pontificate of the most holy Father in Christ and our lord, Lord Urban V, pope by divine providence, in the eighth indiction, in the month of June, on the twenty-seventh day.

And I, Joannes Stephanus Maffaron, a Roman citizen, by the grace of God and apostolic authority a notary, affirming the authenticity of this instrument or transcript faithfully written and copied from the aforesaid bronze tablet by Antonius Gojoli, son of Petrus Sirete, a Roman citizen and public apostolic notary, undersigned below, and carefully heard by me before the aforesaid lord Jacob, by the grace of God bishop of Arezzo, vicar general and commissioner of our lord the pope in the city and its district, for the matters aforesaid, together with Joannes Paulus Alictii and Santolo Petrus Berte, Roman citizens and public apostolic notaries undersigned below, and witnesses:

Since I have found the said copy or transcript to agree with its original in every respect and word for word, with nothing added or omitted that changes the substance or alters the meaning, I subscribe myself as a witness to this copy or transcript, so that henceforth it may receive full faith from all, for the perpetual remembrance of the matter, and I have affixed my customary sign, in the year, pontificate, indiction, month, and day stated above and below.

And I, Santolo Petrus Berte, a Roman citizen and public notary by apostolic authority, affirming the authenticity of this, and so forth, as above, and so forth.

And I, Antonius Gojoli, son of Petrus Sirete, a Roman citizen, by the grace of God and apostolic authority a public notary, faithfully wrote and copied the aforesaid copy or transcript of the aforesaid letters, privilege, grant, and donation from the said bronze tablet, without adding or omitting anything that changes the substance or alters the meaning. I carefully heard and read it before the aforesaid lord Jacob, bishop, vicar, and commissioner, and before the aforesaid Joannes Stephanus Maffaronis, Joannes Paulus Alictii, and Santolo Petrus Berte, Roman citizens, public apostolic notaries and literate witnesses. So that henceforth this copy or transcript may receive full faith from all, for the perpetual remembrance of the matter, I subscribe and affix my customary sign, in the year of the Lord 1369, in the seventh year of the pontificate of the holy Father in Christ and our lord, Lord Urban V, pope by divine providence, in his seventh year, in the seventh indiction, in the month of July, on the twenty-seventh day, by command of the aforesaid lord Jacob, bishop, vicar, and commissioner.

### XXIII. Renewal of the testament of Abbo the patrician for the monastery of Novalesa [Note: [Col. 1035D] The town of Novalesa, famous for its very ancient monastery, lies between Mount Cenis, *le Mont Cenis*, and the town of Susa. It is now a village commonly called *la Novalèze*.], made by Charlemagne (805)

*(From D. Bouquet,* Recueil des historiens*.)*

[Col. 1035B]

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Charles, most pious Augustus and emperor, crowned by God, great and peaceful emperor governing the Roman Empire, and by the mercy of God king of the Franks and Lombards.

Let it therefore be known to all the greatness of our faithful, both present and future, that the venerable man Frodinus, abbot of the monastery built in honor of the holy chief apostles, at the place called Novaliciis, having sent a petition through the religious monks Gislarannus and Agabertus, represented to our serenity that Abbo, once a man devoted to God, had assigned certain properties to that holy place at Novaliciis by a testament of donation. From this, it appears that that house of God, the monks residing there, and the poor and pilgrims going and returning, receive the greatest consolation. They therefore brought that testament before our presence for re-reading.

But because they had very frequently brought it for re-reading at the assemblies of the counts in various districts, compelled by necessity, it already appeared to be largely ruined. And since they had not dared to renew the testament on their own, they petitioned our highness that, by our command, it might be renewed anew, in such a form as could best be re-read from it. We, considering their need and the increase of our merit, ordered our faithful notaries to renew that testament anew within the palace, so that thereafter, for the increase of our merit, upon examination of the testament, the provision declared therein might continue to benefit that house of God in the present and future times. For we have not decided to do this according to the custom of earlier kings; rather, solely because of the necessity and the increase of our merit, we order this to be transcribed in the following manner, and we ordered it to be sealed beneath with lead.

## XXIV. Diploma of Charles the Great for the Church of Piacenza (808)

*(From Ughelli, Italia Sacra, vol. II, p. 199.)*

[Col. 1036A]

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Charles, most excellent Augustus, crowned by the Lord, great and peaceful emperor governing the Roman Empire, and by the mercy of God king of the Franks and Lombards.

We wish all the noble Catholics established in our kingdom, both of the priestly order and of the laity, to know that, as the Apostle says, we brought nothing into this world, nor can we take anything away with us from it, except what we appear devotedly to offer to the Lord for the salvation of our souls in holy places; and we undoubtedly trust that this contributes to our eternal blessedness.

Therefore let the greatness, or the entire community, of all the faithful of God and of our own people, present and future, know how the venerable Julian, bishop of the Church of the holy city of Piacenza, which was built in honor of Saints Antoninus and Victor, and also of the virgin Justina, appealed to our clemency. He asked that, for the love of God and the salvation of our soul, we might appear to grant to that church of the aforesaid saints all the judicial jurisdiction and every toll from the estate of the aforesaid church called Gusiano, with its dependencies, situated in the Piacenzan mountains within the boundaries named below, both from *arimanni* and from other free men residing within the aforesaid boundaries—all that was exacted publicly—for the increase of our merit.

Accordingly, for the sake of the Lord’s name and out of reverence for that holy place, in accordance with the petition of the aforesaid bishop, just as these dues had hitherto been exacted from the public treasury, so with the utmost devotion and in their entirety we appear to have granted to that church the aforesaid judicial jurisdiction and every toll from the aforementioned estate of Gusiano and its dependencies, within these designated boundaries and adjoining lands:

That is, on one side, from the upper ridge where the boundary is divided between the monastery of Tolla and the holy Church of Piacenza, descending as far as the Garli stream; from the Garli stream, running as far as the river Cario; from there, descending along the bed of that river as far as the head below the Maurenasca ridge; then ascending as far as the summit of that Maurenasca ridge, which is divided between it and Saderiano. From there, continuing as far as la Vegiola; on the other side, from la Vegiola as far as Castellioni; from Castellioni as far as the summit of Serra; from the summit of Serra as far as Fabricio; and from there as far as the aforesaid Costa, which is divided between the monastery of Tolla and the aforesaid Church of Piacenza.

Therefore, by this present authority of ours, we decree that we wish this grant of ours to remain perpetually in force in the name of God, so that both that bishop and his successors may have, hold, and possess the aforesaid judicial jurisdiction and toll in its entirety, within the boundaries written above and the territory included within them; and they shall have free power in all matters, with our permission, to do whatever they may wish for the benefit of their church.

Thus henceforth no duke, *gastaldius*, or *actionarius*, nor any of the officials of the public administration, shall dare to presume anything against the aforesaid jurisdiction or to interfere in any way with that toll. Rather, under the title of immunity granted by this authority of ours, with God’s help, the aforesaid venerable Julian, bishop, and those who shall perpetually be its rulers in that holy church, as we have said, shall be able to hold and possess it by a peaceful right, and continually pray to the mercy of the Lord for us and for our survivors.

And so that this authority may remain inviolate, with the Lord’s help, both for the present and for future times, we have decided to strengthen it by subscribing with our own hand and ordered it to be sealed with our ring.

The sign of Lord Charles, most pious emperor.

I, Altifredus, have subscribed in the place of Ercambaldus.

Issued on the seventh day before the Kalends of June, in the eighth year, Christ being favorable, of our empire; the fortieth year of our reign in Francia and the thirty-fourth in Italy; indiction 1.

Enacted at our palace of Aachen, happily in the name of God. Amen.

## XXV. Precept of Charles the Great Augustus by which he restored Manfred the Lombard, a citizen of Reggio, to possession of all his property (808)

[Note: The parchment of this diploma displays nearly all the features of an authentic original privilege: the characters appropriate to the period, the signs of the imperial chancery, and also the place of the lost wax seal. One thing, however, remains that raises suspicion of forgery. The eighth year of Charles’s empire indeed agrees with the first indiction, and the fortieth year of his Frankish reign also agrees; but the thirty-eighth year of his Italian reign conflicts with correct chronology, since in 808 the thirty-fourth year was running, not the thirty-eighth. Moreover, the parchment seemed to me excessively polished in execution. I am therefore forced to remain doubtful and to think that it would be safer to assign to later centuries Manfredus, the progenitor of the families Piae, Picae, Papazonae, Pedochae, and others.]

*(From Muratori, Antiquitates Italiae medii aevi.)*

[Col. 1037C]

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Charles, most serene Augustus, crowned by God, peaceful emperor governing the Roman Empire, and by the mercy of God king of the Franks and Lombards.

Let it be known to all the greatness of our faithful, present and future, how, with God’s favor and through the merits of the holy chief apostles, we acquired the kingdom of the Lombards among [lacuna], and, on account of certain accusations, had some Lombards taken out of their homeland and brought to Francia. Afterwards, at the request of our beloved son Pippin, the glorious king, we sent them back to their homeland, and ordered certain of their legitimate inheritances, which we had caused to be recalled in writing, to be restored to them.

One of these men, named Manfredus, from the royal city, approaching our clemency, petitioned our serenity that, by a precept of our authority, we should once again restore and confirm, after the fullest deliberation, all the properties which he appeared at that time to possess justly and lawfully as his legitimate inheritance when he was brought to Francia, and which we subsequently ordered to be returned to him.

We did not wish to reject his petition. Rather, for the increase of our merit and as an alms of our aforesaid son, know that we have granted and confirmed it in every respect. Therefore, issuing our command, we order that we wish this to remain permanently in his regard: as long as he faithfully serves us and our beloved son, he shall henceforth, by this authority of ours, hold and possess with the firmest legal right all the properties of his own ownership, wherever he was then lawfully vested in them when he was brought to Francia by our command and when we subsequently ordered them to be restored to him. He shall also freely enjoy complete authority to do with them whatever he may wish.

And so that this precept and confirmation may remain inviolate in our times and in those to come, we have decided to strengthen it with our own hand below and ordered it to be sealed with our ring.

The sign of Lord Charles, most pious and most serene emperor.

I, Hado, have written and subscribed in the place of E...[lacuna]anbaldus.

Issued on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of August, in the eighth year, Christ being favorable, of our empire, and the fortieth year of our reign in Francia, and the thirty-eighth in Italy; indiction 1.

Enacted at our palace of Aachen, happily in the name of God. Amen.

## XXVI. Privilege of Charles the Great for the Church of Milan (809)

*(From Ughelli, Italia Sacra, vol. V, p. 70.)*

In the name of the most holy and undivided Trinity. Charles, crowned by divine will, governing the Roman Empire, and by the mercy of God most serene, Catholic, peaceful Augustus and king of the Franks and Lombards, to all counts, *castaldi*, and all others appointed by our clemency over public affairs throughout the province of Italy: everlasting salvation in the Lord.

[Note: [Cols. 1037D–1038D] Peter Oldradus, a citizen of Milan, secretary to Pope Hadrian and a member of that city’s foremost nobility, succeeded Thomas Crassus as archbishop about the year 783. He again travelled to Gaul with Pope Leo III and, after returning to Rome, was present when that same Pope Leo acclaimed Charles the Great Augustus and emperor. Thereafter Oldradus received from him very extensive privileges favorable to the Church of Milan, outstanding among them that by which he was endowed with the political principality of Milan itself, by a munificence plainly royal. Peter also duly subdued the Arian heretics, both by writings and by the sword; hence Charles the Great bestowed on him the honorary surname “Hammer of Heretics.” A letter of this Peter to Charles the Great survives concerning the translation of the body of Saint Augustine, when it was brought from Sardinia to Pavia.]

Let all and each know how the venerable Petrus Oldradus, archbishop of the Church of Milan, approached our highness, asking that, for the love of God and the salvation of our soul, we might restore, reintegrate, and confirm by our imperial authority all the possessions of the holy Milanese Church, dedicated in honor of Saint Ambrose, confessor of Christ, and of the holy church, which had been bestowed by our imperial predecessors and by all devout men from the time of the blessed Constantine the Great and the other emperors, but afterward disturbed and taken away through the treachery of the Lombard kings.

Assenting to his pious request, and determining always to implore the aid of that most blessed bishop Ambrose and confessor of Christ, we ordered this decree and precept to be made for Petrus Oldradus, archbishop. By it we grant to him and to his lawful successors whatever appears to belong to our jurisdiction in the city of Milan: namely, lands and the entire district; public houses and the wall of that city, together with the fisc and the whole toll, and with every civil right, within and outside the city, all around as far as the boundaries.

We also grant the estates of that city, the city itself, castles, villages, farms, male and female slaves, male and female criminals [the wording is uncertain], houses, possessions, fisheries, fields, mountains, forests, waters and watercourses, and inhabited and possessed marshes, which had been held and possessed by the predecessors of that archbishop before the treachery and tyranny of the Lombard kings. We further grant, concede, and confirm all rights given and transferred under any written title or investiture, or bestowed or presented to the holy Church of Milan by any emperors or pious men.

Likewise, we grant to the venerable Archbishop Peter and to his lawful successors all those things called fiscal, comital, or vice-comital properties, which are situated or constructed in the county of Milan, both within and outside the city, all around as far as the aforesaid boundaries, so that the venerable Archbishop Petrus Oldradus and his lawful successors may have power there, personally or through their representatives, to judge, enforce, hold assemblies, bind legal obligations, release legal obligations, and do whatever their utility and advantage may require for the increase and honor of that holy Church of Milan, which shall endure forever.

Therefore, issuing our command, we order that no duke, marquis, count, viscount, *sculdasius*, *gastaldius*, or any procurator shall disturb this holy Church of God, or impose upon it lodging obligations, tolls, district dues, assemblies, or any other public charge. Otherwise, let him know that he shall pay two hundred pounds of the finest gold: one hundred to our fisc and one hundred to the archbishop himself.

And so that this may be believed more firmly and observed more carefully, we have strengthened it with our own hand and ordered it to be marked and confirmed by the impression of our ring.

Issued at Tortona on the Kalends of May, in the year of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 809, indiction 3, and in the ninth year of our empire and the forty-second year of our reign.

I, Longinus, chancellor, in the place of Odo, bishop and archchancellor of our lord Charles the Great, and of the ever-unconquered emperor Augustus, have requested and subscribed.

## XXVII. Precept of the Emperor Charles for the Monastery of Cassino (810)

*(From Tosti, Storia della badia del Monte Casino.)*

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, eternal God. Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, to all bishops, abbots, dukes, counts, judges, *gastaldi*, *actionarii*, vicars, centenarii, and the rest of our faithful, present and future.

We believe that the security of our kingdom is greatly increased if we willingly comply with the petitions of priests and servants of God when they are brought to our ears, and carry them into effect, exercising royal custom; and we trust that this contributes, in the name of God, to the increase of our merit and the stability of our kingdom.

Therefore let the prudence of all the faithful of the holy Church of God and of our own people know that the venerable Theodemar, abbot of Saint Benedict at the fortress of Cassino, where Saint Benedict consecrated in veneration the place of his bodily burial, together with the entire congregation which we know truly serves God in that place under the rule of the life-giving confessor of almighty God, Benedict, sent the monk Benjamin into our presence. They requested our highness that, out of reverence for Jesus Christ our Lord and Saint Benedict, and for the merit of our soul, we might confirm, for the enlargement and support of the aforesaid monastery, within that same holy monastery the monastery of Saint Mary at Maurinis, just as Duke Hildebrand had offered it to that same Cassinese monastery.

Recalling that their petition would contribute, for the merit of our soul, to the enlargement of so great a place, we willingly heard it. We therefore wish the aforesaid monastery of Saint Mary at Maurinis to remain perpetually within the same monastery of blessed Benedict, with its churches, cells, villages, chapels, titles, houses, male and female slaves, *cartulati*, *praefendarii*, male and female tenant farmers, male and female *aldiones*, cultivated and uncultivated lands, fields, meadows, pastures, woods, vineyards, willow groves, reed beds, waters and watercourses, fisheries, mills and mill sites, mountains, plains, valleys, marshes already acquired or still to be acquired, movable and immovable property, and whatever it may obtain.

All these things we confirm and strengthen in their entirety to the aforesaid church of blessed Benedict and to Theodemar the abbot and his successors, who shall in their time be the pastors and rulers of that monastery; and by a precept of our authority we establish that they shall have, hold, and firmly possess them according to ecclesiastical law, all contradiction by every person being removed.

We decree, moreover, that no duke, marquis, count, viscount, or any public official shall dare unjustly to compel or scourge the men of that church, take away its property, or dispossess it. If anyone wishes, or has alienated, the church’s property by false documents, the rectors of the aforesaid church shall be permitted to defend themselves justly and legally by oath and by the testimony of the good men dwelling around them, establishing that the property belongs to that church; and thus he shall restore those same properties to the church’s right and ownership.

If anyone attempts to infringe or violate this precept of our confirmation, and distrains the rectors or pastors of the aforesaid church of blessed Benedict, or their representatives, or any persons belonging to them, or does them any violence, let him know that he shall pay a composition of one hundred pounds of the finest gold: half to our treasury and half to the aforesaid venerable abbot and his successors, who shall in their time be the rulers of that church.

And so that this may be believed more firmly and observed more carefully by everyone, we ordered this present precept to be written, sealed with our ring, and confirmed it below with our own hand.

The sign of Charles, most glorious king.

Jacob, in the place of Radon.

Issued on the eighth day before the Kalends of May, in the tenth year and the fourteenth year of our reign, indiction 11.

Enacted in the city of Capua, happily in the name of God. Amen.

—Charles, by the grace of God emperor Augustus.

## XXVIII. Precept of Charles the Great for the Same Cassinese Monastery (810)

*(From Tosti, ibid.)*

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, eternal God. Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, to all bishops, abbots, dukes, counts, judges, *castaldi*, *actionarii*, vicars, centenarii, and the rest of our faithful, present and future.

We believe that the security of our kingdom is greatly increased if we willingly comply with the petitions of priests and servants of God when they are brought to our ears, and carry them into effect, exercising royal custom; and we trust that this contributes, in the name of God, to the increase of our merit and the stability of our kingdom.

Therefore let your prudence know how, out of reverence for the holy confessor of Christ Benedict, at the petition of the religious Theodemar, abbot of the Cassinese monastery, we appear to have granted the following benefit to that monastery, so that the monks serving God there may be able to live while praying for us and for the whole Christian people.

That is: the properties belonging to our sacred palace in various places, which our father Pippin, together with his brother Charles, offered to that same holy monastery. Just as they were offered and confirmed by them to that place, so we grant and confirm them to be held, possessed, and governed perpetually.

The church of Saint James at Tremiti; Saint John at Veneri, which was offered to blessed Benedict by Martin, the monk who built that church; thereafter the church of the Holy Redeemer above the river Laentus; Saint Michael on Mount Glanus; the castle of Saint Michael; the castle of Saint Peter; the estate of Saint Januarius with its dependencies, within these boundaries:

On one side, the Robbers’ Crypt, which is below the Sarracenic hillock, and from there it ascends to the *stafilum* of Majella; on the other side, as it descends into the Frassininga stream, and from there runs into the Bacinnus stream and goes to the well of Capetanus; from there the ditch of Saint Januarius and into the Rosentus. On another side, the boundary of Bisara to the road that goes to the lake above Saint Donatus; from there to Ficarium, then to the ditch of Saint Lucia; it ascends through the Cold Water to the boundary of Monte Plano, and, as it runs beneath those boundaries, to the ditch of Garifulus, and thus goes to the Alentus.

Within these boundaries we gave nothing to any man, but everything belonged to the royal fisc; we offered it all to the same monastery. Thereafter: the church of Saint Mary at Bacinno; Saint Felix at Pastoricius; Saint Benedict at Turris; Saint Vitus above the river Lavinium; Saint Elijah at Sclangarium; Saint Comitium beside the Arulus stream; Saint Felix at Pulverium; Saint Callistus at Ilianum; Saint Manumetis in the same place; Saint Mary at Potianum; Saint Mark in the same place; Saint Eleutherius at Rupi; Saint Paul in the same place, together with the castle of Calcaria; Saint Erasmus at Cerritus Planus; the Holy Redeemer and Saint Martin in the same place; Saint Benedict, Saint Mary, and Saint Comitium at Ornus; Saint Callistus; Saint Peter at Albianellus; Saint Maurus and Saint Renatus at Taratolanum, and the district of Corvarium; Saint Callistus in the valley above Loentus; Saint Mary above the *fara* of Loentus; Saint Sabinus at Trevanicus; Saint Clement at Plumbata; Saint Mary at the river Forum; Saint Peter at Lollianum; the monastery of Saint Severinus; Saint Menna at Ripa; Saint Andrew on the hill of Alba; Saint Peter at Ari; Saint Michael before the city of Ortona; the castle of Ungo; the castle of Prata; Holy Cross at the castle of Casale; the monastery of Saint Pancratius; Saint Peter in the old city of Teate; Saint Paul in the same place; Saint Thecla in the new city of Teate; Saint Theodore and the Holy Redeemer at Aternum, with its port.

In the county of Penne: the church of Saint Felix at Stabulum; Saint Benedict at Laurianum; Saint Scholastica beside the river Tabe; Saint Michael at Galbanicum; Saint Felix at Rosicola; Saint Mary at Paternus; Saint Martin at Genestrula; Saint Peter and Saint Cecilia at Castroulano; Saint Peter at Termula; Saint Benedict and Saint Mary at Maurinum, with its port; Saint Victor in the level forest; Saint Benedict and Saint Scholastica at Pinne; Saint Mary, Saint Benedict, and Saint Columba at Alarinum; Saint Mary at Cosentia and Saint Benedict at Bari; Saint Severus at Sorrentum; Saint Benedict and Saint Andrew at Caudium; Saint Sophia at Benevento; Saint Cecilia at Naples; Saint Benedict at Salerno; Saint Benedict at Gaeta; the Holy Redeemer in the same place; Saint Laurence at Majolifium; Saint Maurus at Maranisi; Saint Mary at Maritendulum; Saint Agapitus; Saint Scholastica at Teanum; Saint John at Irpinis; Saint Reparata; Saint Maximus at the Bulanus stream of Campofriddo; Saint Martin at the Vulturnus, with its port; Saint Mary at Turcinum; Saint Benedict at Benevento; Saint Michael at Alefrid.

In Cominium: Saint Victorinus and Saint Erasmus; Saint Mary and Saint Quiricus at Arce; Saint Comitium at Piscaria; Saint Peter at Ceccanum; the Holy Redeemer at Puscalle; Saint Leopardus and Saint Peter at Teczania; Saint Michael at Lalana; Saint Benedict at Casigenzana; Saint Benedict at Laurianum; Saint Benedict in Sicily; Saint Peter at Conca; Saint Benedict at Pantenum; Saint Vigilus on Mount Saint Michael; Saint Mary at Calvus; Saint Maurus at Gualdo of Liburia; Saint Scholastica at Padule; Saint Martin at Cupali; Saint Benedict at Atina.

In the county of Modena: the monastery of Saint Benedict at Adili; the monastery of Saint Martin beside the paved road; the monastery of Saint John at the estate of Trassenetula; the monastery of Saint Domninus at the estate of Argele; Saint Vitalis at the estate of Calderaria; Saint Mary at Laurentiaticum, with all their dependencies, wherever situated, whether in hamlets or farms, both demesne villages with their peasants and tenant farmers and servants of either sex, in each estate and monastery listed above, together with lands, vineyards, meadows, pastures, woods, fisheries, bird-catching grounds, cultivated and uncultivated lands, divided and undivided property, fruit-bearing and fruitless trees, and fruit trees of various kinds, together with everything above and below them in its entirety.

We have granted all this perpetually to the same Cassinese monastery. Likewise, in that same place we grant all properties offered there throughout every boundary of our kingdom, as well as whatever any person may henceforth wish to donate or offer from his own property—lands, vineyards, houses, mills, and so forth—to the aforesaid holy and venerable monastery. They shall have permission and power to donate and offer such property in whatever lawful manner they wish, without opposition from the prince, archbishops, counts, bishops, *gastaldi*, or judges.

Just as these possessions have been held by the same venerable monastery of blessed Benedict, so, by this authority of our confirmation, the abbot of that place of Saint Benedict shall firmly and inviolably hold and possess them in our times and in the future, as the ability or utility of that venerable place may require.

Thus no public judge, or anyone exercising judicial power, shall be permitted to distrain the cells, villages, fields, places, or other possessions of our monastery of Saint Benedict which, at the present time, it justly and lawfully possesses in whatever districts and territories within the dominion of our kingdom, or whatever divine mercy may thereafter wish to add to that place, for the hearing of cases, the collection of fines or tribute, the provision of lodging or transport, the taking of sureties or guarantors, or the distraining of the men of that monastery, whether free, enslaved, *cartulati*, or *afferti*, or those who dwell upon the lands of those churches. No one shall ever be permitted to demand returns or unlawful pretexts from them.

If anyone contradicts this or attempts to infringe our grant, let him know that he shall pay the penalty to the abbots of that monastery.

And so that this authority of ours may be held more firmly and, with God as its guarantor, preserved inviolate, we have decided to strengthen it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with our ring.

The sign of Charles, most glorious king.

Charles, by the grace of God emperor Augustus. Jacob, in the place of Radon.

Issued on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of March, in the thirtieth year of our reign; indiction 7.

Enacted in the city of Pavia, happily in the name of God. Amen.

## XXIX. Precept of Charles the Great for the Same Monastery (810)

*(From Tosti, ibid.)*

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, eternal God. Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, to all bishops, abbots, dukes, counts, judges, *castaldi*, *actionarii*, and all our subjects, present and future.

We take care to increase the security of our kingdom by willingly complying with the petitions of priests and servants of God when they are brought to our ears, carrying them into effect and exercising royal custom; and we trust that this contributes, in the name of God, to the increase of our merit and the stability of our kingdom.

Therefore let your prudence know how, at the petition of the religious Theuthmar, abbot of the monastery of the holy confessor of Christ Benedict, which is built in the place called the fortress of Cassino, where his most sacred body is buried, we appear to have granted the following benefit to that monastery:

Wherever water is joined to the lands of that monastery, we have granted that same water, with its bed and with both its banks, to the monastery, and we willingly confirm it, so that they may pray more earnestly for us, our wife and children, and all our people, for the Lord’s mercy; and so that this may be held by the strength of our authority and, with God’s help, preserved inviolate for long ages, we have decided to strengthen it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with our ring.

The sign of Charles, most glorious king.

## XXX. Diploma of Charles the Great for the Church of Aquileia (811)

[Note: Charles’s diploma is dated to 811, as is gathered from its chronological notes; by that time Paulinus had already died. It therefore seems to conflict with the authority of writers who assert that this dispute was settled while Paulinus was alive, in 798. Yet greater credence should be given to the diploma than to Megiserus and others. Moreover, this dispute could have arisen while Paulinus was alive, been pursued under his successor Ursus, and finally settled in the time of Maxentius, who succeeded Ursus. Or perhaps the dispute was settled once while Paulinus was alive, but was reopened under his successor Ursus.]

*(From Ughelli, Italia Sacra.)*

[Col. 1044D]

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Charles, most serene Augustus, crowned by God, great and peaceful emperor governing the Roman Empire, and by the mercy of God king of the Franks and Lombards.

Let it be known to the greatness of all our faithful, present and future, how the venerable Ursus, patriarch of the holy Church of Aquileia, and Arno, archbishop of the Church of Juvavum, came into our presence and had a considerable dispute between them concerning the province of Carantania, which ought to belong to the diocese of each of them.

For Patriarch Ursus asserted that he possessed ancient authority, and that it could be shown, through the synodal records formerly produced by his predecessors as rulers of the Church of Aquileia before Italy was invaded by the Lombards, that the cities of the aforesaid province of Carantania were subject to Aquileia.

Bishop Arno, however, asserted that he possessed the authority of the pontiffs of the holy Roman Church—Zacharias, Stephen, and Paul—by whose precepts and confirmations the aforesaid province had, in the time of their predecessors, been attached to the diocese of the Church of Juvavum.

After hearing and examining their dispute, in order to restore them to one charity and concord, and so that in future every controversy and dispute might be completely removed both between them and between their successors, we ordered the province of Carantania to be divided between them in this manner: the river Dravus, which flows through the middle of that province, was to be the boundary of both dioceses; the portion from the southern bank was to belong to the ruler of the Church of Aquileia, while the portion from the northern bank was to belong to the prelate of Juvavum.

The churches built on either bank were to retain without contradiction or dispute from either party whatever possessions they were known to have lawfully received, since we have learned that certain churches had been built on one bank of the aforesaid river.

Therefore, this settlement having been promulgated, we command and order that henceforth no controversy or question be raised by the venerable men presently in office—namely Maxentius, who has recently been substituted in the place of the venerable Ursus, patriarch, and Arno, the venerable archbishop of the Church of Juvavum [the text should read: “Arno, the venerable man, etc.”]. Rather, they shall be content on both sides with our judgment, which we have rendered according to the rule of justice for the sake of preserving the charity and peace proper between such men.

For we could not see a more equitable judgment to pronounce concerning this dispute than that the province over which both asserted authority should be divided between them. We do not wish to make the authority of either invalid or false: one excelled by antiquity, the other by the eminence of the holy Roman Church.

So that this command of our authority might possess greater force for future times and be held more firmly by those who will come after us, we ordered it, in accordance with our custom, to be subscribed and sealed with our bull.

Issued on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of June, in the eleventh year, Christ being favorable, of our empire; the forty-second year of our reign in Francia and the thirty-seventh in Italy; indiction 4.

Enacted at the palace of Aachen, in the name of God. Amen.

## XXXI. Judgment of Adalhard, Imperial Envoy, and Others, by Which the Abbot of the Monastery of Saint Bartholomew at Pistoia Was Declared Exempt from Public Burdens (812)

[Note: Adalhard, who presided over this judgment, is the celebrated abbot of Corbie, known in the annals of the Order of Saint Benedict for the holiness of his life and the fame of his deeds, and more than once administrator of the Italian kingdom.]

*(From Muratori, Antiquitates Italiae medii aevi.)*
While I, Adalard, abbot and vassal of the lord emperor Charles, was seated in the city of Pistoia to hear and deliberate the cases of individual men, Willerad, bishop; Boniface, duke [sic]; Poto and Leo, judges; Bonifred, notary of the lord king; Adaprant and Christian, abbots; Fredo, Mauro, and Peter, duke; envoys of the lord Pope Leo; Ermenfrid and Audo, scabini of Camerino; and many others being present there together, Abbot Hildepert came before us from the monastery of Saint Bartholomew, founded by a certain Gaiduald the physician near the walls of the city of Pistoia. He brought to us for rereading a charter issued by that same Gaiduald the physician, which stated how he had declared that he had built the aforesaid monastery on his own property and had conveyed property to it item by item. He stipulated that the monastery should be subject to no man’s authority or regulation, nor to that of the mother Church, except that they should always elect an abbot from that congregation itself; not from outsiders, nor from another monastery. He also stipulated that neither his son nor his heirs should have any dominion or power there, except that they should be responsible for defending its cases.

When this charter had been reread, the abbot himself stated that, in the time of the lord King Pippin, while Rotchild was still alive, he had been expelled from that monastery by the invasion of evil men and by that same Rotchild, and sent into exile without any fault and without a trial; and that the monastery had then been granted as a benefice to Nebulunko, a Bavarian by origin. When a complaint had subsequently been made by the monks of that monastery to Paulinus the patriarch, Archbishop Arno, Abbot Fardulf, Count Echerigus of the palace, and the other men of their place who were then serving as envoys here in Italy—twelve of them together—they had investigated the case in such a way that they caused the aforesaid charter to be reread in their presence. They recognized that the monastery had been unjustly taken away from me, and that no other arrangement ought to be made there except from that congregation itself, just as Gaiduald the physician himself had stipulated. Then they caused me to be recalled from that exile, expelled the aforesaid Nebulunko from the monastery, and admitted me to it thereafter.

Afterward, because of the evil custom established by that Nebulunko, from that day onward they make military service in the army, and compel all the paratae and requisitions to be made for the envoys, as well as payments to the palace—obligations which I ought not to perform according to law—because Gaiduald, who built the monastery, left heirs who perform military service.

We, hearing and recognizing how the abbot had been unjustly expelled from the monastery and had been recalled to it by the judgment of the aforesaid envoys, it appeared to us that, in accordance with the stipulations of Gaiduald the physician himself, since he left heirs who would perform military service, the abbot of that monastery should no longer perform military service, nor any parata for the royal envoys, nor any requisition, nor any payment by obligation to the palace.

Therefore I, the aforesaid Adalard, envoy of the lord emperor, to whom this matter was entrusted, and by the authority and command of our lord, have decreed that henceforth it be permitted to that abbot and his successors to serve God in that monastery with the aforesaid congregation of the servants of God dwelling there, and to pray for mercy from the Lord for our lords; and that they remain free from military service, parata, or requisition, or payments exacted by constraint from the palace—subject to the royal command should it be otherwise. Accordingly, we ordered this document to be drawn up for the security of that Abbot Hildepert and his successors.

And I, Paul, notary, wrote this from the dictation of Bonifred, in the thirty-eighth year of the reign of the lord Charles in Italy, in the month of March, in the fifth indiction.

I, Adalard.

Sign of the hand of the aforesaid Boniface, duke, who was present at these proceedings.

I, Willerad, bishop, was present at these proceedings.

+ I, Leo, vassal of the lord king, agreeing, have subscribed.

+ I, Poto, royal causidicus, was present at these proceedings.

+ Bonifred, notary, was present at these proceedings.

[Col. 1048B] Indeed, I, Peter, notary, saw and read the authentic document, copied this exemplar, and wrote it with my own hand.

### III. — PRIVILEGES CONCERNING UPPER AND LOWER GERMANY

[Col. 1047]

### I. Confirmation by Charlemagne of donations made by his predecessors to the monastery of Utrecht (A.D. 770)

*(From Heda, History of the Bishopric of Utrecht.)*

[Col. 1047B]

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks, illustrious man. If we do not deny the requests of priests in all matters, we trust that we shall thereby have the Lord as our recompense. Therefore the venerable man Gregory, bishop, brought for us to reread a confirmation by our lord father of blessed memory, Pippin, formerly king, concerning the property of his Church of Saint Martin, which is built in the village of Traiectum on the River Rhine. It concerned the property which our predecessors, the earlier Pippin, and likewise Charles and Carloman, as well as our aforesaid father, granted to that house of God or to that bishopric: namely, that they granted and confirmed to that house of God of Saint Martin the whole tithe of lands, or of slaves, or of tolls, or of commerce, or of whatever else seemed to belong to the revenues of the fisc, as we have said, the whole tenth part, so that it might be used for the lamps or the support of the monks and canons who there convert pagans to Christianity; and, by the Lord’s mercy, teach the converts whom they have, just as their Christians preserve Christianity.

Accordingly, the aforesaid Gregory requested us to renew that confirmation, which we appeared willingly to have done. Therefore, by this decree of ours, we determine and command that whatever our aforesaid predecessors justly and reasonably granted to that house of God by their charters, the aforementioned Bishop Gregory may, by our renewed confirmation, have and hold granted to that house of God without anyone’s opposition. And so that this authority of our confirmation may be stronger and better preserved through the ages, we have ordered it strengthened below with the marks of our hand.

Sign of Charles, most glorious king.

Given on the Kalends of March. Executed at the public palace of Aachen.

### II. Writ of recovery issued by Charlemagne to the monastery of Lorsch concerning the claim of Heimeric, son of Count Cancor (A.D. 771)

*(From Helwich, Lorsch Antiquities.)*

[Col. 1048C]

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks, illustrious man. When the venerable Gundeland, abbot of the monastery of Lorsch, where the holy martyr Nazarius rests bodily, came to us at the palace of Herstal, he informed us that a certain man named Heimric wished to raise a claim against that monastery, saying that his father Cancor had left him invested with it. Gundeland himself stood present and denied the entire case, saying that Heimric’s grandmother, named Williswinda, and his father Cancor had transferred or confirmed it to their kinsman, their lord Ruotgang, bishop and archbishop; and he presented us with a charter to reread on this matter.

Then Heimric himself declared before us that from that time onward he should never raise a claim concerning this matter or concerning the monastery named above, but said before us, by means of a straw, that he had withdrawn from it.

Then we, together with our faithful men—namely, Counts Hagino, Rothland, Wiching, and Frodegarius, and also our vassals Theodoric, Berthald, Alburin, Frodbert, and Gunthmar—appeared to have judged as follows: that in this matter the abbot should have full recovery and should be freed from litigation for all time, and that the dispute arising from this affair should thereafter be removed from them.

### III. Charlemagne confirms the possessions and property of the monastery of Lorsch (A.D. 772)

*(From Helwich, ibid.)*

[Col. 1049A]

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards, and patrician of the Romans. Let it be known to all our faithful, present and future, how Abbot Helmeric came into our presence and informed us that the charters of the church of Saint Nazarius had been lost and destroyed in various places, while their property was held in various places; and that consequently they were at present invested with property in our kingdom, by the favor of God, wherever they were presently invested.

At his request we issued this writ to him and to his predecessors: since that house of God is at present invested with property, they shall, by our authority and without anyone’s opposition, possess in quiet order everything which they previously held justly and reasonably by grants or exchanges, and shall be able to defend it according to law, just as royal authority has hitherto defended and now again confirmed it by an open charter. And so that this authority may be stronger and better preserved through the ages, we have sealed it below with our ring.

Sign of Charles, most glorious king.

Giltbertus, in the place of Rado, recognized this.

### IV. Charlemagne’s writ delivered to Weomad, archbishop of Trier (A.D. 773)

**[Note: [Col. 1049D]** This writ is entirely related to the Pippinian writ of the year 761, which, as regards its form, appeared to us suspicious or at least defiled by interpolations. We shall hold the same opinion concerning the present document, following the example of Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*, book II, chapter 3, § 7, and *Annales Benedictini*, volume II, p. 229; Eckhard, *Rerum Francicarum*, book XXIV, no. 149; Heumann, *De re diplomatica*, chapter 2, p. 148. In particular, the opening—“In the name of the eternal Lord God and of our Savior Jesus Christ. Charles, king of the Franks by the providential ordering of God”—imitates the formulas of Louis the Pious and Lothar. The monogram of the diploma in Brower, p. 381, which represents a saltire cross, is not appropriate to Charles; nor is the appended indiction. Suavis and Ercanbald began to serve in Charles’s chancery long after the year under discussion. Nevertheless, Mabillon and Heumann also observed in the cited places that the substance and subject matter of the diploma are by no means foreign to the style of Charlemagne’s court. **]**

*(From Hontheim, History of Trier.)*

[Col. 1049C]

In the name of the eternal Lord God and of our Savior Jesus Christ. Charles, by the providential ordering of God, king of the Franks. If we bestow some benefit from the gift of our generosity upon places dedicated to God, relieve ecclesiastical needs at the requests of our priests with assistance, and protect them with royal defense, we clearly believe that this will benefit us both in passing through mortal life and in happily obtaining eternal life.

Therefore let the discernment of all our faithful, present and future, know that the venerable man Weomad, archbishop of the holy church of Trier, presented to our sight a writ of our lord and father, King Pippin of blessed memory. In it was inserted that not only our father himself but also his predecessors, namely the kings of the Franks, had assigned to Saint Peter’s portion of the church of Trier all the property which good and holy men, out of regard for divine contemplation, had entrusted to it, and had confirmed it by their authorities, so that their kingdom might be protected by heavenly aid and that afterward they might reign in heaven with Christ, the King of kings.

For the security of the matter, the aforesaid prelate requested our Highness to follow the custom of our father and of the preceding kings and order such a writ of our authority concerning that property to be made for the love of God and the reverence of Saint Peter. We gladly granted his request and decreed that this writ of our authority be made for that church, for the love of divine worship and for the remedy of our soul. By it we command and order that all property or resources belonging to the church of Saint Peter of the city of Trier—including the cell of Saint Maximin, built in the territory of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles; the cell of Saint Paulinus; the cell of Saint Eucharius; and the monastery of Saint Mary, which Bishop Modoald of that church built from its foundations in the territory of Saint Peter and which is called Horrea; the church of Saint Martin situated in the district of Megin; and the other basilicas, castles, villages, estates, vineyards, woods, people, and whatever else, by God’s gift, is added to that church, around the Rhine and Loire Rivers, and everything existing in our kingdom—shall remain perpetually subject to the right and authority of Saint Peter’s church of Trier and its bishop.

Furthermore, we establish in the same way that no public judge, nor anyone exercising judicial power, shall dare enter, in our time or in that of our successors, the monasteries, churches, castles, villages, fields, lands, or other possessions of the aforesaid church, whether beyond or beside the Rhine or Loire Rivers, in the districts or territories within our royal power which the aforesaid church possesses, or which divine power may thereafter wish to increase in the right of that holy place, in order to hear cases, exact fines, tributes, or requisitions, impose lodging or parata, take sureties, distrain the men of that church, demand unjust exactions, or collect tolls; nor shall anyone presume to exact anything whatsoever of those matters listed above.

Rather, it shall be permitted to the aforesaid prelate and his successors to possess all the aforesaid monasteries, estates, villages, and castles, with their appurtenances, in their entirety and in perpetuity, in quiet order, for the remedy of our soul and those of our parents, as is contained in the writ of our most pious father, and faithfully to obey our command.

Therefore, so that this writ of our authority may obtain fuller force in the name of God, be more truly believed by the faithful of the holy Church of God—namely, those of the present and future—and be more diligently preserved by our successors, we have confirmed it with our own hand and ordered it sealed with the impression of our ring.

Suavis, in the place of Ercanbald, recognized this.

Given on the Kalends of September, in the sixth year of the reign of Charles, most pious king, indiction 9. At the palace of Herstal, in the name of God. Amen.

### V. Writ of Charlemagne, king, by which he donates the town of Hamalo in Saxony, with its appurtenances, to the church of Fulda (A.D. 774)

**[Note: [Col. 1051D]** The autograph of this notable donation was until recently still preserved in the Fulda archive. The person who once prepared and corrected this copy beside it knows this best, although he omitted what was most important: the chronological notes. Because these are lacking, it must be concluded that this gift came to the church of Fulda only after Charlemagne’s first expedition into Saxony and not before the year of Christ 774, when he called himself king of the Lombards and patrician of the Romans. **]**

*(From Schannat, History of Fulda.)*

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans. Whatever we grant to venerable places for the love of God and for the welfare of the servants of God, we trust will contribute to the increase of our reward and the stability of our kingdom.
