Therefore let it be known to the greatness of all our faithful how we donate to the monastery of Fulda, built in the district of Graphelt in honor of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, where the precious body of the martyr Boniface rests and where the venerable Abbot Hurmio appears to preside over the administration, certain property of our ownership, namely Hamalo, situated in the district of Saxony, with all its entirety: that is, with all its appurtenances and dependencies, both cultivated and uncultivated lands and buildings, woods, meadows, pastures, roads and trackless places, waters and watercourses, male and female slaves, animals, and all the movable and immovable possessions of its people.

We donate and transfer it, wish it to be donated in perpetuity, and confirm it by a writ of our authority: this property of ours to the aforesaid monastery of Fulda, in honor of the holy Savior and the most holy martyr Boniface, as perpetual property, for the use of the monastery and of the venerable brothers devoutly serving God there.

Therefore we also caused a charter of our writ and authority to be written concerning it. By it we decree and wish it to be decreed forever from this day that no one presume to inflict any injury or violence upon the aforesaid place or anything belonging to it. Rather, the abbot of the aforesaid monastery, his successors, and the brothers living regularly under them shall transfer the aforesaid property from our ownership into their control, possess and cultivate it, and turn it to their use in whatever manner they wish. Thus may we be more pleased to commend ourselves frequently to God in their prayers. And so that this authority of our donation and confirmation may be held more firmly in future times and observed more diligently by all the faithful, we caused this charter to be written and marked with the impression of our ring.

### VI. Writ of Charlemagne, king, by which he donates the monastery of Holzkirchen to the church of Fulda (A.D. 775)

**[Note: [Col. 1051D]** The autograph of this notable donation was until recently still preserved in the Fulda archive. The person who once prepared and corrected this copy beside it knows this best, although he omitted what was most important: the chronological notes. Because these are lacking, it must be concluded that this gift came to the church of Fulda only after Charlemagne’s first expedition into Saxony and not before the year of Christ 774, when he called himself king of the Lombards and patrician of the Romans. **]**

*(From Schannat, ibid.)*

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans. Whatever we suitably grant or confirm to venerable places of the saints for the love of God, we trust will accrue to us as reward and to the stability of our kingdom.

Therefore let it be known to the greatness of all our faithful how, for the name of the Lord and the salvation of our soul, we donate and wish to be donated in perpetuity to the monastery of Saint Boniface—built in the district of Graphelt on the River Fulda, where the precious lord martyr Boniface rests bodily and where the venerable Abbot Hurmio appears to preside over a community of monks—the little monastery called Holzkirchen, situated in the district of Waldassin on the River Albstat.

Troandus appears to have built it from new foundations as his own property in honor of the most glorious Virgin and other holy martyrs, and appears to have assigned his own property to that place. Later, by an act of authority, he transferred that little monastery to us in its entirety, with its appurtenances and dependencies, and confirmed to us everything that he or other men had assigned to it: lands, houses, buildings, slaves, vineyards, woods, fields, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, movable and immovable property, money, fortifications, mills, dependencies, appurtenances—everything that can be said or named—entire and complete.

As we have said, what the aforesaid Troandus transferred to us, we have donated and transferred to the portion of Saint Boniface, and wish it to be granted in every respect, on the condition that from this day the church of Saint Boniface or its rectors shall have, hold, and possess that little monastery in its entirety, and freely enjoy it according to the opportunity of the church, so that it may contribute to the increase of that holy place in our time and in future times. May the community also be more pleased to implore the Lord’s mercy attentively for us, for our wife, and for our offspring. And so that this authority may be held more firmly and better preserved through the ages, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with our ring.

Sign of Charles, most glorious king.

Rado, in the place of Hitterius, recognized and subscribed.

Given in the month of November, in the eighth year of our reign. Executed successfully at the public palace of Düren. Amen.

### VII. Immunity granted by Charlemagne to the monastery of Prüm (A.D. 775)

*(From Hontheim, History of Trier.)*

[Col. 1053A]

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, etc. To all bishops, abbots, dukes, counts, household officials, vicars, centenarii, and all our envoys traveling about.

We believe that the defense of our kingdom is greatly strengthened if, after benevolent deliberation, we grant suitable benefits to the places of the saints or to churches, and, with the Lord’s protection, trust that they will happily endure.

Therefore let your discernment know how we appeared to have granted the following benefit to the monastery called Prüm, which our lord and father of blessed memory, Pippin, formerly king, built anew in honor of the holy Savior, where Abbot Assuerus appears to preside: for eternal recompense, we have granted its estates, those which at the present time appear to be held by royal, our own, or anyone else’s gift, and those which divine piety may thereafter wish to increase in the right of that monastery and its rectors.

No public judge, without our command or that of our heirs, shall enter them to hear cases, or exact fines from everywhere.

**[Note: [Col. 1053C]** *Freda* is a kind of fine, or the third part of a composition, which was usually paid to the fisc and sometimes also to judges. It frequently occurs in old charters of Marculf, book III, forms 2, 3, and so on. There, as here, by virtue of a privilege and immunity granted by the prince, judges are forbidden to exact fines in ecclesiastical possessions, so that whatever the fisc might have hoped to receive from them may be converted to the use of the churches, for the lamps of sacred places, and so forth. **]**

Nor shall he take sureties.

**[Note: [Col. 1053D]** *Taking sureties.* When a judge compelled someone summoned to court, or accused of a crime, to provide a guarantor who would present him before the law on the appointed day, he was said to “take sureties.” Du Fresne observes that this formula occurs frequently in privileges and immunities granted to churches. It is generally added that judges are forbidden to enter their lands to hear disputes, exact fines for any causes, or impose lodging or parata. See Marculf, book I, forms 3, 27, 28, and so on. By this circuit of words nothing else is meant than that the judge is not to pronounce judgment or administer justice in the lands where immunity has been granted. **]**

Nor shall he impose *scaras*,

**[Note: [Col. 1053D]** *Scaras.* Angariae, whether involving horses or other services. Hence, for Caesarius of Heisterbach, *scaram facere* means to serve one’s lord when he commands and to carry his messenger or letters to the place assigned to one. **]**

or lodging payments,

**[Note: [Col. 1053D]** *Mansionatici.* The inhabitants of the provinces were burdened with receiving envoys and royal legates, counts, dukes, and their officials, and with providing them provisions according to each person’s rank and condition. *Mansionatici* more commonly means the expenses for receiving such persons, as in Aimo, book V, chapter 10, and under the right of hospitality which the aforesaid persons enjoyed. **]**

or requisitions,

**[Note: [Col. 1054C]** *Conjecta.* A contribution or collection, especially that which was paid by the people to royal envoys on their journey. **]**

whether requisitions for cartage

**[Note: [Col. 1054D]** *De carrigio.* Transport by cart, which subjects provided to their lord. **]**

or for riding horses;

**[Note: [Col. 1054D]** *De parafredos.* Horses customarily supplied for riding by public officials. *Capitularies of Charlemagne*, book II, chapter 16: “Those who either receive envoys sent to us badly in their lodgings, or do not pay the sum established by us, or refuse to provide *paravreda*.” **]**

nor shall judicial power presume at any time to enter for these purposes. Rather, we have granted this to that monastery and its rectors: that under the name of immunity, or under our protection or that of our heirs, they shall remain in peace.

Likewise, we have granted to that same holy place that the people who appear to dwell on the land of that monastery—both free Franks and ecclesiastical dependents—

**[Note: [Col. 1054D]** *Franci.* Here *Francus*, as often elsewhere among the ancients, is used for a free and ingenuous man. See Eckhart, *Rerum Francicarum*, book XXII, no. 9, p. 377. **]**

shall not be required to pay any *heribannum* or *bannum*.

**[Note: [Col. 1054D]** *Heribannum*, or *bannum.* A compound word from *heer*, “army,” and *bannum,” which means a summons, command, or proclamation. The word *heribannum* is used for the fine imposed on one who refused to go to the army after the proclamation and summons. **]**

Rather, this has been granted and conceded to that holy place for the increase of our reward.

We therefore decree and command that neither you nor your juniors or successors, nor any public court or authority, at any time enter the estates of the monastery of Prüm situated anywhere in our kingdoms—whether granted by royal or private generosity, or those which, by Christ’s favor, may hereafter be granted—to hear disputes; nor exact fines for any causes; nor take lodging payments, parata, or sureties; nor impose *scaras* or requisitions, whether for cartage or from those who dwell within the fields or boundaries, or upon the land of the aforesaid monastery.

Whatever the fisc, or fines, or anything else could have hoped to receive by our indulgence shall, for the sake of future salvation, be applied forever to the lamps of the aforesaid monastery through the hands of its agents.

What we have granted with full devotion to that monastery, in honor of the holy Savior, for the name of the Lord, the remedy of our soul, and that of our succeeding offspring, neither royal majesty nor the savage greed of any judge shall attempt to oppose.

And so that this authority may remain inviolate, with God’s help, in present and future times, we have determined to strengthen it below with the subscriptions of our hand and ordered it sealed with our ring.

Sign of the lord Charles, most glorious king +.

Given in the month of November, in the eighth year, the second year of our reign.

Executed at the public estate of Diedenhofen, successfully in the name of God. Amen.

**[Note: [Col. 1054D]** These provisions were later confirmed in the year 826 by the emperors Louis and Lothar. **]**

### VIII. Another privilege granted by Charlemagne to the abbey of Prüm (A.D. 775)

*(From Hontheim, ibid.)*

[Col. 1054C]

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards and also patrician of the Romans. Let it be known to all bishops, abbots, dukes, counts, vicars, centenarii, and our other faithful, present and future, how our lord and father of blessed memory, Pippin, formerly king, appears to have built anew the monastery called Prüm in honor of the holy Savior. He appears to have assigned and confirmed in every respect to that holy place fiscal property and property of his own, where he appointed the venerable man Assuerus as abbot and rector, together with a company of monks, and ordered him to govern that holy place according to the sacred rule.

Therefore the aforesaid abbot and the monks residing in that monastery petitioned the clemency of our kingdom that the people whom our lord and father of blessed memory, Pippin, formerly king, granted or assigned to that monastery should remain at the aforesaid place in the same tenure and custom as before, as our other fiscal dependents do, both in their legal responses and in every other law or custom, as other fiscal dependents throughout our kingdoms have and as they formerly had custom in each district.

**[Note: [Col. 1055D]** *Fiscalini.* Fiscal men or slaves enjoyed, in some respects, a more favorable law than the slaves of private persons. They were admitted to give testimony; injuries inflicted upon them were punished more severely; and they had greater power to dispose of their property among the living, although they could donate or sell their goods only to certain churches, and so forth. Compare Pottgießer, *De statu servorum*, book I, chapter 4, no. 7. **]**

For the sake of the Lord’s name and the remedy of our soul, we could not deny their petitions, but, as you are to know, granted and confirmed them in every respect. Therefore we command and decree that none of our faithful, nor anyone exercising judicial authority, presume in any way to disturb the aforesaid house of God or its rectors, or the people serving that holy place whom our lord and father granted to it, or to raise a claim against them in this matter. Rather, as we have said, in our time and in that of our successors they shall serve that house of God in the same way as they served their own masters before our lord and father assigned them to the aforesaid house of God.

In the same manner they shall serve that holy place under the same status, both in giving legal responses and in every other law and custom, as the other fiscal dependents appear to do.

And so that this decree may be held more firmly and better preserved through the ages, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with our ring.

Sign of Charles, most glorious king.

Given in the month of November, in the eighth and sixth year of our reign.

**[Note: [Col. 1055D]** In this place Martène and Durand rightly observe a copyist’s error, who inserted VI instead of II; for the chronological notes of Charlemagne’s reign must be distinguished in such a way that the beginning of his reign in Francia precedes the beginning of his Lombard reign by six years. The death of Weomad, metropolitan of Trier, is recorded under the year 776, according to Mabillon, *Annales Benedictini*, volume II, book XXIV, no. 67. After him Richbod was appointed bishop, as is read in the *Acts of the Bishops of Trier*, chapter 40; no other mention of him is made there. **]**

Executed publicly at the estate of Diedenhofen, successfully in the name of God. Amen.

### IX. Charlemagne grants the monastery of Lorsch a privilege of liberty, together with free election of its abbot (A.D. 775)

*(From Helwich, Lorsch Antiquities.)*
Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks, an illustrious man, to all bishops, abbots, counts, your vassals, and our traveling envoys: Whatever we establish for the needs of the churches or the peace of God’s servants, we confidently believe will, with the Lord’s help, undoubtedly contribute to our eternal blessedness.

Therefore, since it is known to your diligence how the archbishop [bishop] Ruotgangus, of blessed memory, gathered a considerable company of monks in the monastery called Lauresham, which had come to him through the transfer of Williswinda and Cancrinus—where, out of complete devotion, he placed the holy body of the most blessed Nazarius, and above which he also appears to have left Gundelandus as abbot and heir of the monastery in that same holy place after him—it happened later that the aforesaid abbot Gundelandus, seeing danger threatening that holy place and fearing that, through the designs of wicked men, desolation might also befall the monks, appears to have come into our presence. He handed the monastery itself over to our authority and fully entrusted both himself and his entire community to our protection and defense. We received him with gladness, both for the increase of our reward and for the salvation of that same flock.

The aforesaid abbot and his monks also asked us for such an authorization that, whenever the abbot of the aforementioned monastery should happen to depart from this world to the Lord, they should unanimously be able to choose from among themselves whoever they found worthy of this honor. Out of love for God and for the increase of our reward, we could not deny their petition; rather, know that we have granted and confirmed it in every respect.

Therefore, issuing our command, we order—for we know that this community desires to live under proper discipline and to conduct itself according to the rule of Saint Benedict—that, with our permission, they may always choose as their abbot from within their own community one who is acceptable to God. Thus, since good men have been gathered together there into one flock, they may enjoy their own patron, and no adversary may come to seize him from them.

For we do not wish that, on any pretext, those monks whom the lord Ruodgangus and Gundelandus gathered for the work of God should at any time thereafter, either they or their successors, be alienated or dispersed. Rather, just as it is contained in the testament of that donation which they obtained through Williswinda and Cancrinus, so in every respect let the arrangement concerning that community be preserved, so that they may perpetually observe the rule of Saint Benedict, as the order teaches and the frailty of the body permits, and may live or reside peacefully in that monastery under our protection—or, as we have said, under our defense.

For this reason we have given them this order of ours, by which we expressly command that no one whatsoever from among the bishops, in whose diocese the monastery is known to have been founded, nor any other person, presume to disturb or molest the aforesaid abbot Gundelandus, or the monks of that monastery, or the men who justly and reasonably appear to belong to them, or to act against the order of justice. Rather, under our protection, or under that of our heirs, may they always, as we have said, remain in peace and fully enjoy in every respect the things which we have granted them for the name of the Lord, so that the abbot and the monks of that monastery may be pleased to pray more earnestly for us, for our descendants who follow us, and for the Frankish people, for the Lord’s mercy.

And so that this authority may be held more firmly and preserved more effectively through the ages, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with our ring.

**Sign of Charles, the most glorious king.**

I, Witigowo, have examined and authenticated it.

## X. Charter of Charles the Great by which he grants Hamalumburc, with its appurtenances, to the church of Fulda (year 777)

*(From Schannat, History of Fulda.)*

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans: Whatever we grant to venerable places out of love for the Lord and for the needs of God’s servants, we confidently believe to pertain to the increase of our reward and to the stability of our kingdom. Therefore let it be known to the greatness of all our faithful how we grant to the monastery of Fulda, which is built in the Gau of Grapfeld in honor of the blessed Peter and Paul, where the precious body of the martyr Boniface rests, and which the venerable abbot Sturmio appears to govern, the following possessions of ours: Hamalumburc, situated in the Gau of Salecgau on the river Saale, with its entire integrity and its appurtenances or dependencies—Achynebach, Thinpersbach, and Itarital—that is, everything that you appear to possess in the places named above, namely lands, houses, buildings, inhabitants, slaves, vineyards, woods, fields, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, movable and immovable property. We have transferred all these things, in their entirety and without exception, to the aforesaid holy place, to possess perpetually.

For this reason we have ordered this charter of our authority to be written, so that from this day onward the aforementioned abbot Sturmio, as well as his successors who shall govern that holy place, may have, hold, and possess the aforesaid properties for the benefit of the aforementioned church, and may freely enjoy whatever course of action they choose for the advancement of that holy place. No one whatsoever, whether from the judicial authority or any other person, may at any time presume to cause disturbance or bring a claim against the aforesaid abbot Sturmio, his agents, or his successors concerning the properties mentioned above. Rather, by our charter, may they possess them under the firmest legal right, so that the community may be more pleased continually to implore the Lord’s mercy for us, for the stability of our kingdom, and also for our wife and offspring.

And so that this authority may be more firmly established, we have resolved to strengthen it below with the marks of our hand and ordered it sealed with our ring.

**Sign of Charles, the most glorious king.**

Vuigbaldus, acting in the place of Rado.

Given on the seventh day before the Ides of January, in the ninth and third year of our reign. Enacted at the public palace of Heristal, happily, in the name of God.

> **Note:** Rudolfus, the very celebrated monk of Fulda, in his *Life of Rabanus* in Brower, *Fulda Antiquities*, p. 230, led astray by I know not what error, writes that the estate of Hamalburg, formerly a royal fiscal estate and now a town, was conferred upon the possessions of Saint Boniface the martyr through the generosity of Pippin, king of the Franks. From this it perhaps seemed to some unskilled person that this elegant and excellently preserved diploma of Charles the Great contained the original donation of the village of Hamelen in Saxony, rather than that of Hamalumburc. He therefore erased the final syllable *burg* of this word as superfluous; later another person, no less rashly, restored it. Both would have acted more wisely had they left untouched the parchment, venerable by reason of its age and of the sign of that most munificent prince.

## XI. Transfer by Charles the Great of Lisiduna to the monastery of Utrecht (year 777)

> **Note:** Transfer of Charles concerning Lisiduna. This donation contains the whole tract around the river Hem, where Emersfurt and Leusden extend as far as Dorestad, together with the forests called Milderuissen and Denen, which are still visible near Amerongen, Elst, Wageningen, and Ecde. In these places the bishops of Utrecht—or, by their donation, the provost of Saint John—hold tithes and other rights, especially at Ecde, Wageningen, and Weelchmourhout. A certain impostor recently did not hesitate to corrupt and distort this document in order to flatter a prominent foreign man, replacing Lisiduna with Lindinium, a place in Betuwe. Such men are truly pests in ancient history and ought to be hated by all lovers of ancient truth.

*(From Heda, History of the Bishops of Utrecht.)*

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans. If, from those things which divine mercy has deigned to bestow upon us, we grant anything to venerable places, we confidently believe that this will undoubtedly contribute to our eternal blessedness.

Therefore let it be known to the greatness of all our faithful how we grant to the basilica of Saint Martin, which is built in Old Utrecht below Dorestad, where the venerable man Albricus, priest and elected rector, appears to preside, our estate called Lisiduna, in the Gau called Flehite, on the bank of the river Hem, with its entire integrity and its appurtenances or dependencies, namely lands, manses, houses, buildings, inhabitants, slaves, woods, fields, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, movable and immovable property—in short, everything that Count Wiggerus held there through our benefice.

We likewise grant those forests whose names are Hengestschate, Tornhese, Mokoroth, and Widock, which lie on both sides of the Hem.

Likewise we grant to the basilica of Saint Martin, which is built above Dorestad and is called Ubkirica, from every side one hundred perticae of land, so that the aforesaid basilica may possess at all times a tract of land measuring one hundred perticae, together with the riparian due on the river Lek and that island near the church, on the eastern side between the Rhine and the Lek.

> **Note:** *Ubkirica*: that is, the upper church which stood above Dorestad. I do not know precisely what place is designated by these words.

> **Note:** *The riparian due on the Lek*: they believe that *ripaticum* is the toll owed for preserving or fortifying the riverbank.

> **Note:** *That island*: The pagi of Doorn and Cothen are indicated here; they lie between the old bed of the Rhine and the Lek. For when the Rhine once flowed east of the town of Dorestad toward Utrecht, between the villages of Doorn, Wereunde, Odijk, and Vechten, while the Lek proceeded westward below Dorestad as only a small stream, it enclosed all the aforesaid and adjoining villages as though they were on an island.

We transfer all these things from the present day to the aforesaid holy places, to possess perpetually.

> **Note:** *Therefore this charter*: Thus it is written below, “our charter of generosity,” and in the *Formulas of Marculf*, Book II, “the denarial charter,” and so forth. Gregory of Tours, Book IX of the *History*; Aimon, Book V, chapter 36: “He made a charter confirming the entire abbey according to the custom of princes.”

For this reason we have ordered this charter of our authority to be written, so that from this day onward the aforementioned priest Albricus, or his successors who shall be rectors of that holy place, may have, hold, administer, govern, and dispose of the aforesaid places for the benefit of the aforementioned basilica, and may freely enjoy whatever course of action they choose for the advancement of that holy place.

No one whatsoever, whether from the judicial authority or any other person, may at any time presume to disturb the aforesaid priest Albricus or his successors concerning the things already mentioned, or to act against the order of justice, or to bring a claim against them. Rather, by our charter of generosity, may the aforesaid basilica possess them under the firmest legal right.

And so that this authority may be held more firmly and preserved for long ages, we have resolved to strengthen it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with our ring.

**Sign of Charles, the most glorious king.**

Given on the seventh day before the Ides of June, in the ninth year of the same most glorious king.

Enacted at the public palace of Nijmegen, happily, in the name of God.

## XII. Privilege of Charles the Great concerning the immunity of the monastery of Lauresham (year 779)

*(From Helwich, Lauresham Antiquities.)*

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks, an illustrious man, to all our faithful, both present and future. When the rightful petition of priests, relating to the needs of holy places, has reached the ears of our clemency, it is fitting that, once heard, it should be carried into effect in the name of God, so that we may deserve to obtain the forgiveness of the eternal Requiter, and that they may be pleased continually to pray for the stability of our kingdom and faithfully to assist us in every matter.

Therefore let your greatness and prosperity know that, for its merit, we appear to have granted to the monastery called Laurescham—built in honor of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and the other saints, where the precious lord and illustrious holy martyr Nazarius rests bodily and shines forth in power, and where the venerable man Gundelandus appears to preside as abbot together with the community of monks—in the Rhine Gau, on the river Weschnitz, complete immunity, with full and entire grace, for the increase of our reward and for its peace and that of its successors.

Accordingly, by this special charter we decree, and wish it to remain perpetual, that neither you, nor your vassals or successors, nor anyone invested with judicial authority, may presume to enter the courts or villages of that monastery or of its church, situated in whatever pagi or territories, whether those which it appears now to possess or control, or those which it may thereafter increase, improve, or acquire through gifts from kings or queens, through grants made by the people, through purchase, or through any other acquisition, in order to hear cases, exact fines everywhere, take sureties, impose lodgings or requisitioned provisions, compel the men belonging to it—whether free, dependants, or residents of the monastery—to appear before the court, or demand or exact any public payments which are rendered from those places to our treasury.

Rather, under the name of immunity, the judicial authority or our traveling envoys must not enter any of its villages at all. The abbot himself and his successors may, in the name of God, possess and control all their villages, together with all fines, levies, and public payments granted to them, exactly as stated above.

Let no one whatsoever among our faithful, present or future, ever or by any device appear to violate what we have granted to that house of God for our reward and, with God’s help, for the stability of the Frankish kingdom. Rather, as we have stated above, we wish it to be preserved and granted in every respect to the aforesaid monastery in our times and in those to come, without any opposition.

And so that this authority may be held more firmly and preserved more effectively through the ages, we have resolved to strengthen it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with our ring.

**Sign of Charles, the most glorious king.**

Rado, acting in the place of Riutbertus, has authenticated it.

Given in the month of May, in the fourth year of our reign.

Enacted happily at Theodonis Villa, the public palace.

## XIII. Privilege of Charles the Great by which he receives the monks of Saint Maximinus under his protection and grants them free election of their abbot (year 779)

*(From Hontheim, History of Trier.)*

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Let it be known to all who faithfully believe in Christ—to kings, bishops, and dukes—that I, Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, for the remedy of my soul and the stability of our kingdom, wish the monasteries of the saints established under my rule to remain unharmed through the succession of ages, just as I have found them secured by the privileges of my predecessors.

Therefore, because I found the abbey of Saint Maximinus established under the protection of my father Pippin by my father’s privilege [Note: Grave marks of fabrication attach to this account, both in its tenor and in its appended seal. Hence a serious presumption of similar fabrication arises against the present document, which reports it, since it is not probable that Charlemagne was shown his father’s diploma, visibly disfigured by defects. Several further features in this document are also contrary to the chancery of Charlemagne; these are discussed individually by Heumann, *De re diplomatica*, p. 149 and p. 26 ff., and by Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*, book III, chapter 1, § 4.], I too resolve to make a testament by which that place and the monks living there may be able to live peacefully under our protection and devote themselves to prayer.

Accordingly, by royal authority and power, we grant to Verinolfus, abbot of that monastery of the aforesaid confessor of Christ, which is built in the suburb of Trier and dedicated in honor of Saint John the Apostle and Evangelist, and to the monks serving Christ in that place, the free power for all future ages after us to elect an abbot from among those same monks. If one cannot be found there, they may choose one wherever they wish.

Moreover, by our charter we establish and irrevocably confirm that no king succeeding us, nor any other person whatsoever, presume to exercise any authority against that place or its monks throughout the entire abbey, nor exact toll anywhere from their ships, nor hold a court without the abbot’s order and request. Rather, let that place remain securely and peacefully under our protection.

So that the authority of this charter may be held more firmly through the ages, we have resolved to confirm it with the marks of our hand and ordered it strengthened with our ring.

> **Note:** *We ordered it strengthened with our ring.* The attached seal, accurately depicted by Zyllesius, shows the beardless face of Charles the Great and has occasioned considerable controversy as to whether it is spurious or genuine. Those who insist that Charles’s chin was always adorned with a beard reject it, relying on the image of this emperor which Eckhart reproduces from Petavius’s *Gnorismate*, *Frankish Affairs*, vol. I, book XXIV, p. 628; on the Roman mosaic carefully examined by Spon and Le Blanc and published in Eckhart’s book XXV, p. 78; on the lead seal of the bearded Charles the Great, which is owed to the same Le Blanc; and on other seals of Charles in Mabillon, *On Diplomatics*, book V, p. 389; Heineccius, cited treatise, plate 4; Struvius, *Corpus of German History*, vol. I, plate 1, no. 1; and the coin in Bunau, cited work, part II, p. 307.

> But is it not possible that Charles sometimes, at least, laid aside his beard in his portraits, seals, and coins? This seems to me by no means implausible. For Bunau, in the work cited on p. 307, produces a beardless coin of Charles the Great. Nor did Charles thereby do anything unfamiliar to the Franks, since he was, according to Einhard, extremely observant of ancestral custom. His father Pippin, just like the kings of the Merovingian line, was accustomed sometimes to appear bearded and sometimes shaven. In particular, Pippin’s chin, elsewhere covered, can be seen bare on the San-Maximinus agate, which I have examined with my own eyes more than once and which Eckhart reproduces in the cited volume I, p. 597. The same is true of several seals and coins reproduced by him on p. 599 and by Mabillon in the cited book V, plate 23.

> We also see many beardless images of Merovingian kings engraved in copper in the first volume of Eckhart’s celebrated *Frankish Affairs*: Childeric I, p. 36; Childebert I, p. 87; Chlothar I, p. 90; Charibert, p. 98; Sigebert, p. 105; Childebert II, pp. 140 and 156; Guntram, p. 149; Theuderic II, p. 172; Chlothar II, p. 195; Dagobert I, p. 208; Clovis II, p. 238; Childeric II, p. 254; Theuderic III, p. 290; Clovis III, p. 303; and Childebert III, p. 315.

> Yet if we see in these places that the Merovingians laid aside their beards, we also observe that some of them—especially Dagobert I and Clovis II—put them on again in other coins edited by Eckhart in the cited work. This clearly indicates a custom that alternated according to personal preference.

> Nor did these changes in bearded and beardless appearance cease with Charles the Great. His brother Carloman is shown with an entirely bare face on a coin in Menestrier, *History of the City of Lyons*, book III, p. 219. Louis the Pious, already emperor, appears sometimes bearded in Mabillon, cited book V, plate 99, and sometimes beardless in Bunau, *German History*, part III, p. 3. Charles the Bald is bearded in Bunau, book IV, p. 3, and beardless in Mabillon, *On Diplomatics*, p. 407. Emperor Arnulf appears sometimes bearded and sometimes beardless in Bunau, part IV, p. 180. Conrad I is similarly represented in the same part IV, p. 410.

> It is therefore easily concluded that the shaven face on the San-Maximinus seal of Charles the Great cannot by itself be regarded as a certain sign of forgery, provided that the remaining text of the diploma is sound. But who doubts that a seal of good quality could be attached to a document not legitimately produced?

**Sign of the most glorious king.**

Rado, I have reread it.

Given in the month of August, in the fortieth year of our reign.

> **Note:** In the original: “Enacted.” Zyllesius publishes “in the fortieth year of our reign”; Lambecius and Papebrochius read “in the eleventh year” in the original. This gives rise to a new basis for suspicion, since in the year 709 Verinolfus was not yet abbot of Saint Maximinus; Vothilradus was still abbot.

> I had already written this when, in August 1745, there appeared at Trier the *Assertion and Defense of this San-Maximinian Diploma*, established in three dissertations, by the most distinguished J. Phil. Praetorius, electoral court councillor and ordinary professor of history and public law at the University of Trier. Although it is filled with much learning, it nevertheless did not move me to change the opinion about the forgery of the diploma set out here.

Enacted at Patresbronna, at our treasury, above the same [Mabillon: *Lipsa*].

## XIV. Charter of Charles the Great by which he grants to the church of Fulda whatever the king’s vassal Otkarius held as a benefice (year 779)

*(From Schannat, History of the Diocese of Fulda.)*

Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans. Whatever we grant or confirm by grant to the venerable places of the saints for the name of the Lord, we confidently believe to pertain to the salvation and advancement of our soul and to the stability of our kingdom.

Therefore let it be known to the greatness of all our faithful how, for the name of the Lord and the salvation of our soul, we grant and transfer to the monastery of Fulda, where the most precious martyr of Christ Boniface rests bodily and where the venerable abbot Surmio appears to preside over a company of monks, certain properties of ours, which we wish to be granted permanently.

These are in the Gau of Worms: whatever our faithful Otkarius appears to have held through our benefice, namely, in the city of Mainz, twenty-five manses, sixty-six and sixteen slaves, dependants, and vineyards belonging to those benefices; likewise, in another place beyond the Rhine, in the place called Lubringouva; and, in a third place called Nuvenheim, whatever the aforesaid Otkarius held there, both lands and fields, vineyards, and cultivated and uncultivated gardens; and, in a fourth place, namely Gunzinheim, whatever our aforesaid faithful appears to have held there; and, on the river Naha, one meadow.

All these things mentioned above we grant and transfer to the holy monastery of Fulda, in honor of the martyr Saint Boniface, and wish them to remain granted forever, so that there, with the Lord’s assent, they may contribute to the increase of the brothers serving God, in our times and in the future. Thus the community may be pleased to implore God’s mercy more earnestly for us, for our wife, and for our offspring.

And so that this transfer may be held more firmly and preserved more effectively for future ages, we ordered this charter of our command and authority to be written and marked with the impression of our ring.

**Sign of Charles, the most glorious king.**

I, Egilbertus, chancellor, have authenticated it.

> **Note:** I believe this Egilbertus to be the same man who, in Mabillon, *On Diplomatics*, VI, no. 53, authenticated a charter of Charles the Great dated 778, where he is called Giltbertus.

Given on the Ides of November.

## XV. Charter of Charles the Great by which he grants to the church of Fulda the field called Hunefeld (year 761)

*(From Schannat, History of the Diocese of Fulda.)*

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans. Whatever we grant to venerable places out of love for the Lord and for the needs of God’s servants, after benevolent deliberation, we confidently believe undoubtedly to pertain to eternal blessedness and to the remedy of our soul.

Therefore let it be known to the greatness of all our faithful how we grant to the monastery of Saint Saviour, which is built within the Vast Forest of Bochonia on the river Fulda, where the body of Saint Boniface rests buried and where the venerable Baovulfus appears to govern, the field called Unofeld, together with its woods, to possess perpetually.

For this reason we ordered this charter of ours to be written, by which we specifically decree and establish that no one whatsoever among our faithful or successors presume to disturb the aforesaid abbot Baovulfus or his successors concerning the place already mentioned, or to act contrary to justice, or to bring a claim against them. Rather, with God’s help, may it perpetually contribute to the increase of that house of God in our times and in the future.

And so that this authority may be more firmly established, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with our ring.

> **Note:** The seal has been torn away from this original document.

**Sign of Charles, the most glorious king.**

Widolaicus, acting in the place of Rado, has authenticated it.

Given in the month of December, in the fourteenth and eighth year of our reign.

Enacted at the palace of Carisiacum.

## XVI. Donation by Charles the Great of various estates to the abbey of Prüm (year 790)

*(From Hontheim, History of Trier.)*

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans. Whatever we cede or bestow upon the venerable places of the saints, out of love for the Lord or for the needs of God’s servants, after benevolent deliberation, we confidently believe in the name of God to pertain to the increase of our reward and to the stability of our kingdom.

Therefore let it be known to the greatness of all our faithful, present and future, how, out of regard for God and for eternal recompense, we grant to the monastery of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ— which the lord Pippin, our father and formerly king, together with the lady Bertrada, our mother and queen, appear to have built anew from its foundations, for future salvation, at the place called Prüm—certain properties of ours. The venerable abbot Asoarius presides there, and we wish these properties to remain permanently granted to that holy place.

> **Note:** In the Gau called Longonahe, in the Gau called Heinrichi, and in Angrisgau. All these pagi lie beyond the Rhine. Angrisgau lies between the Rhine and the Sieg, on the opposite side from Andernach, where today the county of Sayn is situated. Longonahe extends broadly around the river Lahn. Einrich, which is also part of the Gau of Longonahe, occupies the tract now held by Nassau, Dillenburg, Diez, Katzenelnbogen, and Idstein.

These are the properties which the aforesaid abbot and Ahardus, our envoys, had acquired from a certain man named Alpad by lawful procedure according to the law in a case belonging to us, at the places called Nasongae, Squalbach, Haonstat, Caldenbach, Boumhaim, Tabernae, Heringae or Aendrichae, Villare or Theodissa, Abothisscheid, and Larheim.

> **Note:** *At the places named Nasongae, etc.* Of the places named here, Nassonga is known, now Naflau on the Lahn; Squalbach, or Schwalbach, famous for its mineral springs; Heringae, also called Heigrehe, now Hayger above Dillenburg; and Willare, which also occurs in Waltrada’s charter of 821, in the *Fulda Deeds*, p. 134, perhaps Weil on the stream Weil below Reifenberg; Larheim lies between Katzenelnbogen and Diez.

And on the *Hrenum* [*Rhenum*, the Rhine], the portion which our aforesaid envoys appear to have lawfully vindicated against the aforementioned Alpad for our benefit, with lands, houses, buildings, inhabitants, slaves, vineyards, fields, woods, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, movable and immovable property—in its entirety and without exception—we have granted to the aforesaid monastery, as an alms of ours, under the firmest legal right, to possess for all ages.

Therefore, by this present authority of ours, we decree and command—and wish it to remain perpetual—that the venerable man Asoarius, abbot, and his successors who shall in future govern the monastery of Saint Saviour may hold and possess the properties written above, in their entirety and as we have described them, for that holy place, in our times and, with God as our protector, in the future.

No one whatsoever among our faithful or the successors of our kingdom may at any time presume to bring any claim against the agents of that monastery concerning the properties described above or to diminish them. Rather, may the servants of God who appear to serve God there be more pleased to pray earnestly for us, our wife and children, and the stability of our kingdom.

May what we have granted to the aforesaid monastery of our Lord and Saviour, as a gift from our generosity for eternal recompense, through this charter of our serenity and gift of confirmation, with Christ’s favor, contribute perpetually to the increase of the lamps of that church and to the provisions of God’s servants.

And so that this authority may be held more firmly and, with the Lord’s help, preserved more effectively through the ages, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with our ring. Moreover, whatever we ought to have stated above, we have remitted to that holy place the entire legal payment and composition which the aforesaid Alpad was required to pay for those properties.

**Sign of Charles, the glorious king.**

Ercambolt, acting in the place of Rado, has authenticated it.

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of June, in the twenty-second and seventeenth year of our reign.

Enacted at the city of Mainz, happily, in the name of God. Amen.

## XVII. Privilege of Charles the Great for the monastery of Kremsmünster (year 791)

*(From Rettenpacher, Annals of Kremsmünster.)*
Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards, and patrician of the Romans. If we willingly heed the petitions of priests or servants of God when they are brought to our ears, and bring them to fulfillment in the name of God, we exercise the royal custom and trust that this contributes to our reward and to the stability of our kingdom. Therefore let all our faithful, present and future, know how the venerable Fater, abbot, reported to the clemency of our kingdom that Tassilo, formerly duke of the Bavarians, had caused a monastery to be built as a new work in honor of the holy Savior within our forest, at the place called Chremifa, in the district called Traungaev, and by a charter of donation had granted certain places to that holy foundation in the aforesaid district or within the aforementioned forest: namely Sulzpach, Syppach, Liubilinpach, and whatever is seen to lie between the two rivers called the Ipfae; likewise one decania from those slaves over whom Taliub and Sparuna had been placed as administrators; also, beside the river called Todicha, thirty slaves and the territory belonging to the aforesaid decania, as Physso swore, and as Bishop Arno and Abbot Fater, together with Count Hleodro and Judge Chunibert, traversed and inspected; furthermore, that land at Todicha and Sirnicha which those slaves had cleared without the permission of Duke Tassilo.

Likewise, at another place called Eporestal, that land which had similarly been cleared without Tassilo’s permission, and which his agents Saluhho, Wanilo, and Gaerbertus had surveyed. The men, however, living at Eporestal upon that land, if they wished to retain the said land in order to serve the aforesaid house of God, were to retain it; but if they wished, they were free to depart. He also gave at Petenpach the land extending from that spring to the river called Albina, as Tassilo had marked it out, and from there to the Alps, where he had granted them pasture. Likewise, the village called Alinchofa, in its entirety, together with its appurtenances and dependencies; at Albarch, a chapel built in honor of Saint Martin, with the properties belonging to it; at Sulzpach, another church with all that belonged to it; and at Nordfilusa, a third church with the properties belonging to it, in Tonahgaae.

In the aforesaid district of Drungaae, at the place called Aschaha, two vineyards with two vinedressers; and at another place called Raotola, three vineyards with three vinedressers; likewise two fishermen, and in addition two other men who look after bees, and six smiths. The aforesaid Abbot Fater asserts that he holds and possesses all these things listed above peacefully on behalf of the aforementioned monastery. But since the grant of the aforementioned Tassilo could by no means remain firm and secure, he therefore asked our serenity that we should once again, as an act of our almsgiving, by our authority, fully grant and confirm these things to that holy foundation, just as we have done.

Therefore, after examining Tassilo’s grant, we command that, in accordance with what it declares, the aforementioned Abbot Fater and his successors who shall be superiors of that monastery of the holy Savior may henceforth, by this precept of our serenity and gift of confirmation, hold and possess all these things in their entirety, without anyone’s hindrance and in peaceful possession, so that in our time and in that of our successors they may perpetually increase the resources of that house of God, for the increase of our reward.

And that this authority may be held more firmly and, with Christ’s favor, be better preserved through the ages, we have confirmed it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Charles, most glorious king.

[Col. 1067A] Given on the third day before the Nones of January, in the fourteenth indiction, in the twenty-third year of the reign of our lord Charles, most serene king.

Enacted at Worms, in the name of God, successfully. Amen.

### XVIII. Diploma of Charlemagne confirming the donation made by his brother Carloman to the Abbey of Echternach (794)

(From Hontheim, *History of Trier*.)

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards, and patrician of the Romans. Whatever we grant or confirm to venerable holy places for the love of the Lord, we trust contributes to our reward and eternal recompense.

Therefore let all our faithful, present and future, know how the venerable man [Col. 1067B] Berneradus, archbishop of the holy church of Sens,

[Note: [Col. 1067D] Berneradus, archbishop of the holy church of Sens. Berneradus—Alcuin dedicated the *Life of Saint Willibrord* to him—is said to have governed the monastery from 777 to 798, as the brief manuscript *Chronicle of Echternach*, written by Theoderic around 1190, records. Since, however, Berardus is recorded as having presided among the bishops of Sens at approximately this time, from 793 to 795, we conjecture that the two were one and the same person. See also Heuman, *On Diplomatic Matters*, chapter 2, section 66, no. 11.]

who is rector of the monastery where Saint Willibrord rests bodily, situated at the place called Echternach, informed the clemency of our kingdom that Carloman, our brother of blessed memory, for the increase of his reward, had apparently donated to the aforesaid monastery certain estates in the district of Bitburg, at the place called Droise [Dreyls] on the river Salmana, and Officinas on the Lisura,

[Note: [Col. 1068D] Officinas on the Lisura. Martene, Calmet, and Bertholet read *Officinus*, but incorrectly.]

together with lands, houses, buildings, inhabitants, slaves, vineyards, woods, fields, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses—everything in full, whatever by law appeared to belong to those places. But, owing to negligence, no charter of grant had ever been received from that brother of ours concerning them. Therefore, the aforesaid Archbishop Berneradus asserts that he holds those properties peacefully on behalf of the aforementioned monastery; but for the security of the entire matter he asked our highness that we should once again, as an act of our almsgiving and of that brother of ours, grant and confirm these things to that holy foundation by our authority.

We do not wish to deny his petition, for the sake of God and out of reverence for that holy place; rather, know that we have granted and confirmed this in every respect for the increase of our reward. Accordingly, by the present decree we have determined and command that no one whatsoever among our faithful, nor anyone exercising judicial authority, shall at any time presume to disturb the aforementioned Archbishop Berneradus, or his successors who shall be rectors of the monastery of Saint Willibrord, concerning the aforesaid properties, or bring any legal claim against them, or take away or diminish anything from them.

Rather, for the increase of our reward and for the soul of our brother King Carloman, the properties shall in our time and in that of our successors, with Christ as guide, perpetually increase the resources of that holy place through the hands of those who read, for the lights of that church and for the support of the servants of God who appear to serve God there.

And that this authority may remain inviolate for all time, with God’s help, we have decided to strengthen it below with our own hand and to seal it with our ring.

Sign of Charles, glorious king.

### XIX. Donation of Charlemagne granting the villages of Lauriacum and Catiacum in the district of Angers to the Monastery of Prüm (797)

(From Hontheim, cited above.)

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards. Whatever is done by due process in our presence or that of our nobles, and is justly concluded, ought to be strengthened by a written record for the knowledge of future people, so that thereafter it may remain unshaken under the firmest legal title.

Therefore let all our faithful, present and future, know how Asoarius, abbot of the monastery of the holy Savior—which our lord and father of holy memory, Pippin, formerly most glorious king, and our lady and mother, Queen Bertrada of good memory, built as a new work at the place called Prüm—repeatedly petitioned our serenity concerning certain properties situated in the district of Angers, the villages called Lauriacum and Catiacum. He asserted that these ought by law to belong to him through his mother Wilharana and his grandmother Teodilda, but that in times past, together with other properties which had been transferred to the fisc because of the disloyalty of certain men and his relatives, they had been wrongfully and unjustly appropriated.

Considering his priesthood and faithful service, we believed that his account was entirely true, ordered him to be fully reinvested with those properties, and resolved to confirm them to him by a precept of our authority. After some time, however, it was clearly established by Odilhard, bishop of the holy church of Nantes, and by other truthful men living in that region, concerning the aforesaid village of Lauriacum, that it was due by law and justice to our inheritance, and that Abbot Asoarius ought to have no legal claim to it. Standing in judgment before us and in the presence of many of our nobles, he returned the aforesaid villages, as the Roman law teaches and as his assessors had adjudged to him,

[Note: [Col. 1068D] Roman law. By “Roman law” here the Theodosian Code is meant; the *Digest* and Justinian law were not yet known in the West. This is the first evidence that has come to my notice of Roman law already being used in Francia.]

to our possession, together with our precept of confirmation.

Of these properties, we assigned one, called Lauriacum, for the future salvation of our lord and father, Pippin, formerly most glorious king of blessed memory, as an act of almsgiving, to the aforesaid monastery of the holy Savior by a precept of our authority. The other, called Catiacum, because the people of that district testified that they had seen it held by the grandmother of Asoarius, Teodilda, we confirmed by our authority as her allodial property.

Again, after some years, a dispute arose concerning certain dependencies belonging to that village between the aforementioned Abbot Asoarius and our Count Nuno. When they came before us to argue their case, we established with complete certainty, both through truthful men and through documents, that his grandmother Theodelhildis had previously given the aforesaid village of Catiacum, together with other property of hers, to our lord and father. Therefore, by law and justice, it ought to belong more fully to us than to Abbot Asoarius through his mother Wilharana.

These matters having been established, it pleased our highness, for the love of God and out of reverence for him, since he is recognized as a man of God, and from a pure heart and sincere will—for he had reported one thing to us as another and had appeared both culpable and convicted—to forgive him everything as an act of our almsgiving. Moreover, after fullest deliberation, we decided to grant and confirm to the aforesaid monastery, for the salvation of the souls of our lord and father and of our lady and mother, the villages named above, Lauriacum and Catiacum, with their dependencies, from our own bounty.

Therefore we establish and command—and wish this to remain forever—that from now on and henceforth the often-mentioned venerable Abbot Asoarius and his successors in perpetuity, who shall be shepherds of the aforesaid monastery of the holy Savior, shall hold and possess the aforesaid villages of Lauriacum and Catiacum, together with lands, houses, buildings, inhabitants, slaves, vineyards, fields, woods, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, movable and immovable property, dependencies and appurtenances—in every respect and in their entirety, insofar as they appear to belong to those places and insofar as our possession appears, by God’s gift, to be legitimate—on behalf of that holy place, by this precept of our authority, grant, and confirmation, as an act of our almsgiving.

Thus may these properties increase the resources of that house of God in our time and in that of our successors, so that the servants of God who serve him there may be more gladly moved to implore continually the Lord’s mercy for us and our children, for the stability of our kingdom, and for the souls of our father and mother.

And that this authority may remain inviolate, with God as its author, we have confirmed it with our own hand and ordered it sealed with our ring.

Sign of Charles, most glorious king. Ercanbaldus, acting in the place of …, acknowledged it.

Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of March, in the twenty-ninth [XXIX] and twenty-fourth years of our reign.

Enacted publicly at our palace at Aachen, in the name of God, successfully. Amen.

### XX. Donation of Charlemagne, emperor, granting Cervia with its forest to the archbishop and church of Trier (802)

(From Hontheim, cited above.)

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Charles, by the favor of divine clemency, august emperor and patrician of the Franks. To the counts and dukes dwelling both beyond and on this side of the Rhine and Loire, present and future.

We undoubtedly believe that it contributes to the increase and stability of our kingdom in the name of God if we grant a favorable response to the rightful petitions of priests and of the faithful of God’s churches. Therefore the apostolic man Weomadus and his brother Basinus, together with our agent Aufericus, came to us and reported that our royal predecessors, for the salvation of their souls, had transferred to Saint Peter and the church of Trier certain properties belonging to the public fisc: namely Valeniacum with all its dependencies, except the place called Cerviam (Cerff), and Serviacum with the royal forest. They had retained Cerviam and Serviacum, however, for the purpose of hunting.

[Note: [Col. 1069D] Weomadus and his brother Basinus. This charter, as regards the matter itself and its substance, does not seem at all suspect to me; as regards its form, however, it certainly appears to be such. Besides the fact that Charles’s title, “patrician of the Franks” (which ought to be “king of the Franks, patrician of the Romans”), appears truncated, the contemporary lives of Weomadus and Basinus do not agree with the thirty-fourth year of Charlemagne’s rule. Basinus and Weomadus certainly lived at the same time; both successively became abbots of Saint Maximinus and then bishops of Trier, but at an earlier date. For Basinus could not have survived so late, since he was already in office toward the end of the seventh century. It is useful here to hear Alexander Wilthemius, *Annals of Saint Maximinus*, manuscript, Book II, at the end under the year 729, where he writes:

“Now, how long Basinus continued afterward to perform the duties of abbot, I could not easily say. This much is certain: Wiomadus, whom the acts of Leotwin also insert among the abbots of Medeliacum, had a successor sooner or later. Whether Basinus, out of religious modesty, withdrew into retirement, or whether, because his age had already been bent down by long labors, he retired to rest, is certainly difficult to explain. From the records of Pippin I have learned that Basinus lived on until the sixty-second year of this century. Hence it appears either that, having become unfit through age to perform the office, he was reduced from being head of the monastery to the ranks of private persons, or—and my inclination leans more strongly this way—that just as he had recently abandoned the episcopate, so he then voluntarily relinquished the dignity of abbot. Thus, like travelers proceeding by night, we must almost test the ground with our hands to discover the path by which we may pass safely and without falling through the darkness of antiquity.”]

Therefore those faithful men petitioned us to transfer to Saint Peter the aforementioned places, Cerviam and Serviacum, together with the forest belonging to the fisc, lest the properties of Saint Peter surrounding that forest be devastated on account of it.

Accordingly, assenting to their petitions, we have transferred by lawful right to the church of Saint Peter at Trier the aforesaid places, namely Cerviam and Serviacum, together with everything belonging to them—fields, meadows, pastures, waters and watercourses, woods, cultivated and uncultivated lands, roads and trackless places, entrances and exits—and with the forest, just as it belonged to our fisc. We have transferred and sanctioned it in its entirety within the following boundaries: from the place where the river Premantia (Brimbs) rises to Bischoffsvelt; thence by the public road to Marciacum (Merzig on the Saar); and thence to Sarova (the river Saar, or Saravus), where it flows into the Moselle; from there to the place called Lyve (Leyen on the Moselle); from Lyve directly to the place where Budelschica falls into the river Troganus (Dhron); and from there directly to the source of the river Premantia.

We therefore prohibit everyone by our ban from taking any beast in this forest, which we have transferred to Saint Peter according to lawful custom, by any method of hunting, unless with the permission of the bishop of the church of Trier: no successor of ours as king, nor any other person, may presume to do so. Whoever does so shall be compelled to pay our ban.

And that this precept of our authority may be observed without violation, we have ordered this precept to be written, confirmed it with our own hand, and had it sealed with the impression of our ring.

Sign of Charles, most serene emperor. Servatius, chancellor of Arcambaldus, acknowledged it in his place.

[Col. 1071B] Given on the Kalends of September, in the thirty-fourth year, in the ninth indiction.

Enacted at the palace of Herstal, in the name of God. Amen.

### XXI. Diploma of Charlemagne, emperor, assigning his fisc at Luthosa to Saint Ludger, first bishop of Münster and founder of the Abbey of Werden under the rule of Saint Benedict, in the diocese of Cologne, as the endowment of that monastery; from it there later arose a college of canons (802)

(From Aubertus Miraeus, *Diplomatic Works*.)

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Charles, by the gift of divine clemency, august emperor. If we lend an ear to the petitions of priests and servants of God which they have made known to us for their needs, and bring them to fulfillment, we not only exercise the royal and imperial custom, but also do not doubt that the rewards of eternal recompense will benefit us.

Therefore let the understanding of all our faithful, present and future, know how Ludgerus, bishop of Mimigerdeford—commonly Münster—of blessed memory, petitioned our highness that, with the permission and aid of our piety, he might build a church on his own inheritance in the district of Rurich, at the place called Werthina, on the river Rura, in the forest of Wenneswalt, in honor of the holy Savior and the holy Virgin Mary, as well as of the holy relics which he had transferred from Rome from the apostolic pope; and that, if the opportunity were granted, he might at some time build a monastery and wished to gather monks there. He testified to this most clearly.

We gladly assent to his reasonable and just petition, commanding that, once this church has been received under our protection, it may possess more firmly and securely not only those things which have been donated to it at the present time, but also whatever shall later be bestowed upon it by the faithful of God, without any unjust harassment.

[Col. 1072A] To complete the monastery at that place and gather a community, at the suggestion of our aforesaid faithful bishop, we donate to those same relics our own property—namely our fisc called Suthosa (commonly Leuse), in the district of Brabant—in its entirety, as a possession, and by God’s grant command that it remain forever, together with everything belonging to it: lands and woods, manses and slaves, waters and meadows, buildings, cultivated and uncultivated lands. In imperial fashion, we grant and donate it by hereditary right to the aforesaid relics venerated at Werthina.

And that these things may remain unshaken in future times through the strength of our authority, with God’s protection, we confirm them below with our own hand and order them sealed with the impression of our ring.

Sign of the lord Charles, most serene emperor Augustus.

Hildegrinus, notary, acknowledged it in the place of Alcuin, archchaplain.

Given on the sixth day before the Kalends of May, in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 802; in the thirty-fourth year of his reign, in the twenty-seventh in Italy, and in the third of his empire, in the tenth indiction.

Enacted at Worms, in the name of God.

### XXII. Diploma of Charlemagne, emperor, concerning the foundation of the bishopric of Osnabrück in Westphalia (801)

(From Aubertus Miraeus, *Diplomatic Works*.)

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, Charles, emperor Augustus, governing the Roman Empire, lord and king of the Franks and Lombards, and also ruler of the Saxons.

Let it be known to all the faithful of the holy Church, present and future, that, for the increase of our reward, we have donated to Wiho, bishop of Osnabrück,

[Note: [Col. 1071D] The first bishop of Osnabrück was Saint Wiho, whom Bernardus Furmerius, in his *Frisian Annals*, says was born at Leeuwarden in West Frisia.]

and to his church—which we built first of all in Saxony in honor of Saint Peter, prince of the apostles, and of the holy martyrs Crispinus and Crispinianus—a certain wood or forest lying within these places: Farnewinckel, Rusteinstein, Angara, Osningsenethe, Dershouet, Egestervelt, with the unanimous approval of the magnates of that region, in its entirety, including wild boars, deer, birds, fish, and every form of hunting that is, under the customary ban, assigned to a forest after the model of our forest at Aachen, belonging to the wood of Osmugi; we have granted it forever for proprietary use.

[Note: [Col. 1071D] The Emperor Charles the Great established nine new episcopal seats in Germany: Münster, Minden, Halberstadt, Osnabrück, Paderborn, Verden, Hamburg, and Hildesheim; he raised two to archiepiscopal dignity, Salzburg and Hamburg.]

The condition is that if anyone should ever enter this same wood protected by our ban, without the permission of the bishop of the aforesaid see, for the purpose of hunting, clearing the forest, or doing anything else, let him know that he will incur both divine and royal vengeance, and that, for the offense, he will have to pay sixty solidi of our weight, which we have decreed to be owed to us for violation of the ban.

Moreover, we grant to that bishop and his successors perpetual freedom and release from every royal authority, unless it should happen that the Emperor of the Romans and the King of the Greeks decide to contract a matrimonial alliance between their children. Then the bishop of that church, with expenses supplied by the king or emperor, shall undertake both the labor and the honor of that embassy.

For this reason we decree that schools in Greek and Latin shall remain permanently in that place, and we trust that there will never be a shortage of clerics skilled in both languages.

[Note: [Col. 1073C] Schools. Let the reader note that formerly celebrated schools or academies existed in the palaces of bishops and likewise in cathedral churches and monasteries, especially Benedictine ones. I discussed the schools of the Benedictines in *Original Monastic Records*, printed at Cologne. Concerning Notger, bishop of Liège, who died in 1007, we read the following in the manuscript history of his life, published by Anselm in volume I of the *History of Liège*, page 217:

“His great diligence in educating boys and instructing students in the disciplines is proved by this: whenever he traveled, he always took with him, both near and far, adolescent scholars who were subject to the strictest discipline of one of his chaplains. He also had them carry a supply of books, together with the other equipment used by students. Thus it happened that those whom he had often taken from the cloister as rude and unlearned returned having surpassed those whom they had previously had as teachers in literary learning. Through the opportunity provided by this education, many of them also progressed so far under him in religious discipline and holiness that they became suitable heads of churches. Indeed, many cities rejoiced that they had such pastors: the church of Salzburg had Gunther; that of Cambrai had two, one succeeding the other, Rothard and Erluin; that of Verdun had Haimo, who, following his teacher Haimo, later built in the city of Verdun a monastery of the blessed Mary Magdalene and Saint Maurus; the church of Toul had Hezelo, and that of Utrecht had Adelbold.

Although many other churches were also reformed by men who did not attain the episcopal rank but had nevertheless been formed under him, among them Durandus, later bishop of Liège, illuminated the church of Bamberg with the discipline of religion and the arts. Ogbertus, together with certain others whom he had taken away with him from there, restored as far as possible to the condition of holy religion the life of the clergy of Aachen, which had been corrupted by the contagion of pernicious license.

What shall we say of Hulbod? Coming to Paris, he attached himself to the canons of Saint Genevieve and soon became an instructor in many schools. Later, sent by Bishop Baldric to Prague, the city of Bohemia, he gave there certain instructions in the Christian religion and returned to us once more with honor.

Many other men, educated under so great a father, likewise enlightened various places by religion and liberal studies. Their lives, distinguished by religious conduct and learning, are an evident testimony to their father’s probity.” Thus far from the manuscript *Life of Notger*.

Lietbert, bishop of Cambrai, directed the schools at Cambrai; see Book III, chapter 61, of the *Chronicle of Cambrai*.

Concerning Heraclius, bishop of Liège and an outstanding promoter of schools, who, even while bishop, was accustomed to teach, see volume I of the *History of Liège*, page 188.

For the author’s further notes, see *Notice of the Churches*, in the summary, chapter 26.]

And that this authority may be held more firmly and better preserved through long ages, we have decided to strengthen it below with our own hand and ordered it sealed with our ring.

Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of January, in the fourth year of our empire, with Christ’s favor, the thirty-seventh year of our reign in Francia, and the thirty-first in Italy.

Enacted at Aachen, in the palace, successfully. Amen.

### XXIII. Diploma of Charlemagne, emperor, donating Walemaris-villa to the Monastery of Prüm (806)

(From Hontheim, *History of Trier*.)

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Charles, most serene Augustus, crowned by God, great and peaceful emperor governing the Roman Empire, who also, by the mercy of God, is king of the Franks and Lombards.

Whatever we grant and donate to venerable places for the love of our Lord Jesus Christ, we undoubtedly trust contributes to the increase of our reward and to the stability of our empire. Therefore let all our faithful, present and future, know how we donate to the monastery of the holy Savior—which our lord and father Pippin of blessed memory built as a new work at the place called Prüm—and wish it to be donated forever, one mansus in the village called Walemaresdorpf (Wallersheim), together with a servant named Williarius, with all his peculium—that is, his personal property—or acquisitions, and the entire legal composition which, for that mansus or that servant, the venerable Abbot Tancradus and his advocate had pledged,

[Note: [Col. 1074D] Tancradus, venerable abbot. Since Asuerus, the first abbot of Prüm, still occurs in charters of the year 804, it appears that Tancradus succeeded him in that same or the following year. Mabillon says little about this Tancradus in the *Benedictine Annals*, vol. II, book XXVII, no. 67. Knauff, *Defence of the Abbey of Prüm*, p. 43, gives more, namely: “Abbot Tancradus, of the princes of Parma, a worker of great virtues and a zealot for divine worship, among the other illustrious achievements of his rule established three religious cells (or priories): one of Saint Medard in the district or territory of Speyer, another of Saint Peter at Kesseling, and a third of the Blessed Virgin Mary at Reving above the Meuse; these were to be incorporated into the monastery of Prüm, and their religious subject to it. This great abbot was especially dear to Charlemagne and Louis the Pious, who used his counsel and industry in difficult affairs. He governed and benefited it for twenty-four years.”]

[Note: [Col. 1074D] *Rewadiavit*: that is, he pledged it.]

because formerly our servant Meginfredus, having no share in the matter, had assigned it to that house of God, and our agent, Count Remicarius, had legally vindicated the case against him on our behalf.

Therefore, as an act of our almsgiving, we have once again granted it more fully to that holy place from our bounty. For this reason we ordered the present authority to be made, by which we specifically decree and command that the aforementioned Abbot Tancradus and his successors in perpetuity, who shall be rectors of that holy place, shall hold and possess the aforesaid property or mansus at Wallemaresdorp and the aforementioned servant by this authority of ours.

Thus, as we have said, it may increase the resources of the church in our almsgiving and in its lights, so that the holy congregation may be more gladly moved continually to implore divine mercy for us and our children, and for all the people granted to us by God.

And that this authority may be held more firmly and better preserved through long ages, we have decided to strengthen it below with the marks of our hand and ordered it sealed with our ring.

Sign of Charles, most serene emperor.

Amalbertus, acting in the place of Ercambaldus, wrote it.

Given on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of February, in the sixth year of our empire, with Christ’s favor, the thirty-eighth year of our reign in Francia and the thirty-third in Italy, in the fourteenth indiction.

Enacted at the palace of Theodon’s villa, in the name of God, [Col. 1075B] successfully. Amen.

### XXIV. Diploma of Charlemagne, emperor, granting various properties in the district of Angers to the Monastery of Prüm (807)

(From Hontheim, cited above.)

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Charles, most serene Augustus, crowned by God, great and peaceful emperor governing the Roman Empire, who also, by the mercy of God, is king of the Franks and Lombards.

Whatever we grant or donate to venerable holy places for the love of our Lord Jesus Christ, we undoubtedly trust contributes to eternal blessedness and to the stability of our empire [lacuna].

Therefore let all the faithful of our realm, present and future, know how we donate to the monastery which our lord and father Pippin, of pious memory and formerly glorious king, built by his own work in honor of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ at the place called Prüm, where the venerable Abbot Tancradus presides, and wish it to be donated forever, certain of our properties situated in the district of Angers, at the place called Laniacum, and likewise in the district of Rodon, at the places called Stivale and Caucina, and at Turicas, and at the New Village, and throughout all those small estates: nineteen resident holdings, together with lands, houses, buildings, inhabitants, slaves, vineyards, fields, woods, meadows, waters and watercourses—in full and in their entirety, whatever Godebertus formerly held there and lost by law for incestuous or other unlawful conduct,

[Note: [Col. 1075D] He lost it by law for incestuous or other unlawful conduct. The laws of the Franks imposed exile and confiscation of property upon those guilty of incest. *Ripuarians Law*, title 69, section 2.]

or whatever by law came to our fisc, and which Count Hugo, together with the aforementioned venerable Abbot Tancradus and several other of our faithful, acquired or legally vindicated for our side according to a judgment, in proper legal order, justly and reasonably.

[Note: [Col. 1075D] According to a judgment, in proper legal order. Since Count Hugo, together with Abbot Tancradus, presided over the judgment by which Godebertus was deprived of his property, I infer that Tancradus was a royal agent. I understand the remainder to concern the assessors, whose appointment belonged to the agents. A proceeding was finally called a lawful judgment when the count sat in the assembly with his assessors, sometimes with the intervention of an agent as well.]

Know that, for the increase of our reward, we have granted and confirmed all these things to the aforesaid holy place after fullest deliberation.
