Therefore we establish and command—and wish this to remain forever under the firmest legal title concerning the aforementioned holy place—that the aforesaid Abbot Tancradus and his successors in perpetuity, who shall be rectors of the aforesaid monastery of the holy Savior, and the monks living there under the holy Rule, shall hold and possess the aforesaid properties in their entirety, just as they came by law to our side, after examination of the judgment of our faithful Count Hugo, strengthened by the hands of good men, as it declares there—that they came to our side by justice and equity.

They shall hold and possess them by this authority of ours, so that in the lights of that holy church of God and in the support of the servants of God, for the remedy of our soul, they may perpetually increase in our time and in that of our successors.

And that this authority may be held more firmly and better preserved through long ages, we have confirmed it with our own hand and ordered it sealed below with our ring.

Sign of Charles, emperor. Amalbertus, acting in the place of Erchambaldus, wrote it.

Given on the fourth day before the Kalends of May, in the seventh year, with Christ propitious, of our empire, and in the thirty-ninth year of our reign in Francia, and the thirty-fourth in Italy, in the fifteenth indiction.

Done at our public palace at Aachen, in God’s name, successfully. Amen.

## XXV. Donation by King Charlemagne of the estate of Vargalaha to the monastery of Fulda (809)

*(From Schannat, History of the Bishops of Fulda.)*

[Col. 1076C]

Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans. Let all our faithful and Christ’s faithful know how, for the everlasting remembrance of ourselves and the pious memory of our parents, we give and transfer to our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ and to Saint Boniface the martyr, who rests in the monastery at Fulda, land acquired by us—that is, the entire district around the River Unstrut—and our own estate at Vargalaha, with all its appurtenances and with all the estates, whether near or far, that belong to it, with full ownership, just as we received it as our property from our parents. We also command concerning this that no person remove these goods from the monastery of Fulda, but that they remain as everlasting support for the brothers serving God there, in memory of us.

## XXVI. Diploma of Charlemagne confirming a pious disposition made by an illustrious man in favor of the church of Fulda (810)

*(From Schannat, History of the Bishopric of Fulda.)*

Charles, most serene Augustus, crowned by God, [Col. 1077A] great and peaceful emperor, governing the Roman Empire, and also, by the mercy of God, king of the Franks and Lombards: let it be known to all our faithful, present and future, that our faithful Bennit made known to our serenity that his father Amalangus, while the other Saxons who were his kinsmen were acting faithlessly against us, preferred to preserve his loyalty rather than persist with the other faithless men. He therefore abandoned his native place and came to us. While he was in our service, he came to an estate called Unsvisangar, which at that time appeared to be inhabited by Franks and Saxons, wishing to remain there with them, but he was unable to do so. Then he proceeded to a place called Unaldisbecchi, between the Rivers Weser and Fulda, and claimed for himself a certain portion [Col. 1077B] of the forest called Bocchonia.

[Note: Brower must have seen another charter of this donation, unknown to us, since in *Antiquitates Fuldenses*, p. 217, he observed from it that this inheritance of Bennit consisted only of cultivated land sufficient to extend two leagues in length, the same in breadth, and six leagues in circumference around the Weser. It was of the kind possessed by Adalricus, in Mabillon, *De re diplomatica*, book VI, p. 512.]

When he died, he left it to his son Bennit. Bennit, approaching our clemency, requested our highness to confirm by a precept of our authority the arrangement concerning him, so that during his lifetime he might hold and possess it peacefully, without prejudice from anyone, but that after his death it should pass to the monastery of Fulda, which Saint Boniface built. We did not wish to deny his request; rather, know that we granted and confirmed it in every respect.

Therefore we command by our authority that none of our faithful, present or future, presume in any way to deprive or disturb the aforesaid Bennit or his heirs concerning this property—which in their language is called *Bivanc*. Rather, as we have said, by this our precept he shall be permitted to hold and possess the land, however much his father claimed as his own and left to him as an inheritance, as prescribed above. And so that this authority may be firmer and may be better preserved through time, we have ordered it sealed below with our ring.

[Col. 1078B] Suavius, in place of Ercanbaldus, examined and authenticated this.

Given on the Kalends of December, in the eleventh year, with Christ propitious, of our empire, and in the forty-fourth year of our reign in Francia and the thirty-seventh in Italy.

Done at the royal palace at Aachen, successfully, in God’s name. Amen.

# APPENDIX TO THE PRIVILEGES OF BLESSED CHARLEMAGNE

[Col. 1077]

# A Testament and Certain Diplomas Falsely Attributed to Charlemagne

## I. Testament of the Emperor and King of the Franks Charlemagne, by which he distributes his treasures (811)

*(From Aubertus Miraeus, *Diplomatic Works*.)*

[Col. 1077C]

In the name of the Lord God Almighty, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Here begins the inventory and division made by the most glorious and most pious lord Charles, Emperor Augustus, in the year 811 from the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ, in the forty-third year of his reign in Francia, the thirty-sixth in Italy, and the eleventh of his empire, in the fourth indiction. He resolved to make this division with pious and prudent consideration, and, with the Lord’s assent, completed it, concerning his treasures and money that were found in his chamber on that day.

In this he especially wished to ensure not only that the distribution of alms which Christians customarily make from their possessions would also be properly and orderly carried out on his behalf from his money, but [Col. 1077D] also that his heirs, with every ambiguity removed, would clearly know what ought to belong to them and could divide it among themselves in a suitable partition, without litigation or dispute.

With this intention and purpose, he first divided all his property and furnishings that could be found on that day in his chamber—gold, silver, jewels, and royal ornaments—into three parts. Then, subdividing those same parts, he made twenty-one portions from two of them, while reserving the third intact.

The division of the two parts into twenty-one portions was arranged as follows: since twenty-one metropolitan cities are known to exist in his kingdom, each of those portions was to reach one of the metropolises, through the hands of his heirs and friends, as alms. The archbishop who at that time governed each church was to receive the portion assigned to his church and divide it with his suffragans, in such a way that one third would belong to his church, while the other two thirds would be divided among the suffragans.

Each of these divisions, made from the first two parts and corresponding to the twenty-one metropolitan cities, was separated from the others and stored individually in its own repository, with the name of the city to which it was to be delivered written on it.

The names of the metropolitan cities to which these alms or gifts were to be given are as follows: Rome, Ravenna, Milan, Forum Julii, Grado, Cologne, Mainz, Juvavum—which is also called Salzburg—Trier, Sens, Besançon, Lyon, Rouen, Reims, Arles, Vienne, Tarentaise, Embrun, Bordeaux, Tours, and Bourges.

The portion that he wished to reserve intact was to be treated as follows: after the other two parts had been distributed into the divisions described above and stored under seal, this third part was to remain available for daily use, as property clearly not alienated from the ownership of its possessor by any obligation of a vow, for as long as he remained alive or judged its use necessary.

After his death, or after he voluntarily renounced secular possessions, this same part was to be cut into four subdivisions. One of these was to be added to the twenty-one portions mentioned above; another was to be taken by his sons and daughters, and by the sons and daughters of his sons, and divided among them in a just and reasonable partition; the third was to be distributed, according to the customary Christian practice, for the use of the poor; and the fourth was likewise to be distributed as alms for the support of the male and female servants serving in the palace.

To this third portion of the whole sum—which, like the others, consisted of gold and silver—he wished to add all vessels and utensils made of bronze, iron, and other metals, together with weapons and clothing, and all other furnishings, precious or ordinary, made for various uses, such as curtains, coverlets, carpets, felt coverings, leather goods, pack saddles, and everything that might have been found in his chamber and wardrobe on that day. Thus the larger divisions of that portion could be made, and the distribution of alms could reach more people.

He ordered that the chapel—that is, the ecclesiastical equipment—both what he himself had made and collected and what had come to him from his paternal inheritance, should remain intact and should not be divided in any way.

If any vessels, books, or other ornaments were found that clearly had not been contributed by him to the chapel, anyone who wished to have them was to purchase and keep them by paying their fair assessed value. He likewise decreed concerning the books, of which he had collected a great quantity in his library, that they should be bought at a fair price by those who wished to have them, and that the price should be distributed among the poor.

Among the other treasures and money there were, as is known, three silver tables and one golden table of exceptional size and weight. Concerning these he decreed that one of them, which was quadrangular in shape and contained a representation of the city of Constantinople, should be carried to Rome, to the basilica of blessed Peter the apostle, among the other gifts assigned for that purpose. Another, which was round in shape and fashioned with an image of the city of Rome, was to be given to the bishop of the church of Ravenna. The third, which greatly surpassed the others both in the beauty of its workmanship and in the heaviness of its weight, was joined from three circles and contained, in delicate and minute representation, a depiction of the whole world. He decreed that this table, together with the golden one said to be the fourth, should increase the third portion, which was to be divided between his heirs and distributed as alms.

He made and established this disposition and arrangement in the presence of the bishops, abbots, and counts who were able to be present at that time, whose names are written here.

### Bishops

Hildebald [archbishop of Cologne], Richolf [archbishop of Mainz], Arno [archbishop of Reims], Wolfarius [archbishop of Salzburg], Bernoinus [archbishop of Besançon], Laidradus [bishop of Lyon], Joannes [archbishop of Arles], Theodulfus [bishop of Orléans], Jesse [bishop of Amiens], Hetto [bishop of Basel], Huvalcaudus [also Valcaudus, bishop of Liège].

### Abbots

Fridegisus [abbot of Saint Martin of Tours], Adalungus [abbot of Saint Vedastus of Arras], Engilbertus [abbot of Centula], Irmino [abbot of Saint-Germain of Paris].

### Counts

Walach, Meginher, Othulfus, Stephanus, Hunruocus, Burchardus, Maginhardus, Hatto, [Col. 1079D] Richuinus, Eddo, Erchangarius, Geroldus, Bero, Hildegernus, Hrocholfus.

His son Louis, who succeeded him by divine command, took care, after his death, to fulfill all these provisions with the greatest devotion and as quickly as he could, after examining the same written memorandum.

## II. Diploma of King Charlemagne confirming the possessions of the abbey of Ebersheim (770)

[Note: Schaepflin rightly included this diploma among the forgeries, *Alsatian Diplomatic History*, vol. I, p. 104. Grandidier clearly proved that it was fabricated by a forger, *History of the Church of Strasbourg*, vol. I, dissertation 4, pp. 99–101; the reader should consult him.]

*(From Grandidier, *History of the Church of Strasbourg*.)*

[Col. 1080A]

In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity. Charles, king of the Franks by the preceding mercy of God, to all the faithful of the kingdom, present and future.

We have learned from the testimony of Scripture that “the king who sits on the throne of his kingdom scatters all evil by his gaze.” We believe that this is fulfilled through us, who administer the care of so great a name, if we strive to enrich and exalt the venerable places of God’s churches by the benefit of some gift; and we have no doubt that this will be beneficial to us and to the stability of our kingdom.

Therefore, let the whole community of all our and Christ’s faithful know how Thiothbaldus, abbot [Note: In the year 770, it was not Thiothbaldus but Isenhardus who presided over the abbey of Ebersheim. The abbot Theothbaldus governed it only in the years 803, 810, and 830.] of the monastery called Noviendo or Ebersheim, in the district of Alsace on the River Ill, which the illustrious man Adalricus, also called Athicus, duke, and his wife Bersvinda [Col. 1080B] built anew on their own property in the name of Christ and in honor of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, Saint Maurice the martyr and his companions, approached our serenity. He asked that we renew the privileges which our father of blessed memory, Pepin, and his predecessors, namely the kings of the Franks, had granted to the same monastery and to the places belonging to it for the support of the brothers serving God there.

Therefore, by the authority of our principate, confirming the provisions established by our predecessors, we command that, and so forth. *(And the remainder as in the diploma of King Carloman reported above.)* But the aforesaid abbot Thiothbaldus and his successors are to possess the same properties with full authority, enlarging and improving them.

And so that this authority of our liberty may remain stable and unshaken, we have confirmed with our own hand this charter written at our command and strengthened it with the impression of our seal.

Sign of Charles, most glorious king.

[Col. 1080C] Done at the public palace at Ingelheim, in the year 770 of the Lord’s incarnation, while Charlemagne was reigning, in the eighth year of his reign. In God’s name, successfully.

Given on the Nones of March. I, Durandus, chancellor, wrote and subscribed this.

## III. Diploma of King Charlemagne for the priory of Lebrah in the diocese of Strasbourg (791)

[Note: We give this diploma after Doublet, who published it in *Antiquities and Researches of the Abbey of Saint-Denis*, book III, p. 722, and who mixed many false things with true ones in his work, printed in 1625. Felibien himself had recognized this, for in his French history of the abbey of Saint-Denis, citing only authentic evidence, he suppressed everything that bore the marks of forgery. Mabillon declared it interpolated or false, *De re diplomatica*, p. 72. For the signs of forgery, consult *History of the Church of Strasbourg*, vol. I, dissertation 4, pp. 107–109.]

*(From Grandidier, same work.)*

In the name of the supreme God and our Savior Jesus Christ, Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans, illustrious man.

If we attend to the petitions of God’s servants and the needs of the churches, and bring this to completion, we trust that we shall receive from God a very great reward on the day of necessity. Therefore, let all our faithful, present and future, understand that the venerable abbot and our faithful nephew Folradus, with his monks from the basilica of our special patron, the lord Dionysius the martyr, and his companions Rusticus and Eleutherius, where they rest bodily, fearing that after our death the church of Lebrah—which is situated in the district of Alsace, where the lord and holy martyr Alexander rests bodily—and its possessions, which we bestowed upon that saint from our benefices for the salvation of our soul, might be destroyed by wicked men and persecutors, approached our clemency. He begged and requested that we graciously issue and confirm for him a precept of our authority and confirmation concerning all the property belonging to that church, so that the aforesaid holy church might be able to hold and possess those properties perpetually, under our protection and as its perpetual alms.

Assenting to his just petition, as is just, and providing for that church, as far as we can, for the remedy of our soul, with the consent of the aforesaid abbot and on the advice of our nobles, we appoint the duke of Lorraine as advocate of that church and its possessions. By Almighty God and by the authority of our precept, we adjure him that neither he nor any of his successors in time to come usurp any unjust custom from it.

We grant this to him from the royal fisc and under the following condition: if the provost of that church is unable by himself to administer full justice against his own or other men who unjustly take away church property, he shall bring the advocate with him, and the two of them shall pursue the judicial case in accordance with what right justice requires. If those men pay anything as a result of the judicial case—what we call legal dues—it shall be divided into three parts, of which the provost shall have two and the advocate one.

If the duke himself wishes to have someone under him as a participant and assistant in this advocacy, so that what one cannot do the other may complete, we permit only one such person, and only on condition that he be free and legally qualified.

Let this also be known to the advocate: if he is summoned by the provost, he shall come three times a year, as required, to the provost’s court, bringing with him no more than twelve men and thirteen horses, at the appointed times—namely, after the feast of Saint Martin, at the feast of Saint Hilary, and in the month of May. When he comes, the provost shall prepare a meal for him.

At the feasts of Saint Martin and Saint Hilary the provision shall be the same: bread made from a measure of grain, a very good *frescinga*, and a measure of wine. For fodder for his horses, two measures of oats shall be given.

In the month of May the aforesaid quantity of bread and wine shall be provided, together with a two-year-old ram. Fodder shall be supplied for only three horses.

The provost and the advocate shall sit together at this meal. If anything more is needed there than what has been stipulated, they shall pay for it jointly: the provost two parts and the advocate one.

And lest such service seem too little to him, there will indeed be a great reward from God on the day of necessity and distress if he has acted rightly and faithfully toward the house of God and its possessions. From the benefices that we bestowed upon that church for the remedy of our soul and the stability of our kingdom, we grant ninety manses of land.

But if the advocate himself, or his successors, or any person, great or small, should presumptuously dare to act against this decree, or impose other customs upon the house of God and its possessions beyond what is specified in the register of this charter, let them know that they are bound by the chain of anathema, alienated from the kingdom of God, and condemned with all the wicked to the punishment of eternal fire.

Those, however, who observe this precept may deserve to obtain grace, mercy, and eternal life from the most merciful Lord.

And so that this petition, which the aforesaid abbot and his monks have made to us, may be held more firmly and securely, we have decided to strengthen it with our own hand below and to seal it with our ring.

Done at Rome, at the public palace, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the presence of the lord Pope Leo, in the twenty-third year—and the eighth—of the reign of our lord Charles, most glorious king.

[Col. 1081D] I, Leo, pontiff of the apostolic see, have subscribed, approving and confirming this. Sign of the lord Pope Leo. Sign of Charles, most glorious king. Wibodus, in place of Hitherius, examined and authenticated this.

[Note: *Frescinga* is a word frequently found in old Alemannic and French charters, ordinarily designating a one-year-old pig. In the region of Orléans, according to Menage, it is called in French *fresangeau*: a pig not yet fully grown, but stronger than a suckling pig.]

## IV. Diploma of the Emperor Charlemagne for the monastery of Lebrah, issued in 803 and inserted into a diploma of Emperor Charles IV from 1348

[Note: The work already cited, *History of the Church of Strasbourg*, vol. I, dissertation 4, pp. 109–111, presents the indications of forgery in this diploma.]

*(From Grandidier, same work.)*

[Col. 1082A]

In the name of God. Amen. Charles, by the grace of God king of the Franks and Lombards, illustrious man and patrician of the Romans.

Whatever we grant to venerable holy places for the love of God, we confidently believe will redound, without hindrance, alienation, or diversion of any kind, to the praise and stability of our kingdom and of our nobles in perpetuity; and we will and command this.

Therefore, let it be known to all our faithful, present and future, how we grant to the brothers serving God in the monastery of Lebrah, in the district of Alsace, in the forest of the Vosges, which our faithful nephew Fulradus, abbot, built on his own property in honor of the blessed martyrs Dionysius, Rusticus, and Eleutherius, and of blessed Alexander the pope, where that holy pope rests bodily, whatever they were in need of and whatever we know them to possess in the valley of Lebrah, extending to the boundary of the great and lofty mountain of the Vosges, commonly called the Rierst, and in the estate called Saint-Hippolyte: pastures, meadows, mills, men, rents, tithes, waters, watercourses, mountains, and forests, together with other rights and appurtenances.

We also grant the Colonmense forest and the Oak Mountain, with their hills, cultivated and uncultivated lands, meadows, waters, pastures, and the adjoining flat and wooded places. We confirm all these properties, individually and collectively, for the use and benefit of the aforesaid brothers, now and in future times.

No one shall be permitted to build houses in the aforesaid mountains, forests, places, or throughout the boundary of the entire valley, or to claim forests, lands, or other possessions there as his own by right, without the consent of the abbot and of his appointed representative, to whom it belongs, as lord of the estate, to grant such things in return for an annual rent.

In the forests of Saint-Hippolyte and in the rivers as far as the boundary of the aforesaid great mountain, they shall have and always possess by right the use and capture of wild animals, birds, and fish, and the gathering of wood.

In the aforesaid estates and places, and in Enisheim—

[Note: Ensheim, a village two leagues from Strasbourg.]

—we grant them, from the royal fisc, complete temporal jurisdiction.

Accordingly, one third of the fines shall go to the advocates, who are bound to be defenders of all the rights of the same monastery, except in criminal matters and in the confiscations resulting from theft, homicide, and other offenses for which a person is condemned to death. All the confiscated property in such cases shall come to the abbot, together with the governance of the parish churches of Lebrah, Saint-Hippolyte, and Anholzheim.

If he appoints a suitable person in his place to govern the people, and proper provision has been made for this necessity, the remainder shall accrue to the benefit of the brothers.

Moreover, in the duchy of Alamannia, above Esslingen and Hartbertlingen, we grant and wish to be conveyed annually to the aforesaid monastery, in perpetuity, one wagon of the customary size, drawn by six very good oxen and filled and laden with pure, cleaned flax, together with one sextarius of the usual coin.

We also confirm the things which our aforesaid venerable nephew Fulradus contributed to that house of God at Gemar,

[Note: A small town, Gemar.]

Anholzheim,

[Note: Ansolsheim, a village near Colmar.]

Lumersheim,

[Note: Leimersheim, a village three leagues from Strasbourg, belonging to the bishop of Strasbourg.]

Enisheim,

[Note: Today Ensheim, two hours from Strasbourg.]

Wolcksheim,

[Note: Today Wolcksheim, belonging to the bishop of Strasbourg.]

Firdenheim,

[Note: Today Firdenheim, a village of Alsace on lands belonging to the equestrian order.]

Ig marsheim,

[Note: Ingmarsheim, formerly a village near Oberhergheim, destroyed in the thirteenth century.]

Wittenwir,

[Note: Wittenweiler, a village across the Rhine belonging to the lords of Boëckel and Franckenstein.]

Marckelsheim,

[Note: Marckosheim, a town belonging to the bishop of Strasbourg.]

Grussenheim,

[Note: Grusenheim, a village belonging to the lords of Rathsamhausen.]

together with their rights, jurisdictions, and manorial courts.

We prohibit the exaction and receipt from the brothers themselves or from their men, whether transporting or carrying anything by land or water, in cities, villages, towns, fields, or any other places, whether selling or buying, of tolls, road dues, dust dues, wheel dues, bridge dues, pasture dues, customary payments, or any other contributions.

Their dependents who reside in their courts and houses, cultivate their lands and possessions, and share in them, shall pay no *styras* and shall render no other services, against their will, to the lords or advocates of those places. Nor shall they recognize anyone as a temporal judge for their offenses except the abbot, especially in matters that temporal justice customarily judges.

Those who take refuge in the same courts shall enjoy the freedom and protection of churches. Those residing in the villages shall be permitted to sell, buy, and enter into other contracts, notwithstanding any contrary command.

And so that our donation of the aforesaid and other properties, as contained in our charters and other precepts, may not be endangered, and so that our soul and the souls of our predecessor kings, and of future kings who offer anything for their salvation, may not be fraudulently deprived through any diminution of divine worship, and so that this house of God may not suffer loss of the goods which we have granted wholly free, without servitude, and completely released from every external right, we command that our often-mentioned little abbey, or house of God, remain inviolate forever.

No one, of whatever condition, great or small, shall dare or presume under any pretext to invade, arrest, occupy, obstruct, alienate, sell, buy, divert, or pledge its goods or persons, or to demand or extort *stura* or any other right from them, or impose customs upon them to their disadvantage.

If in the future some unforeseen fire, flood, or storm should occur—which may Christ not permit—for the restoration and repair of the damage, so that the error may not become worse than the original, those residing at the monastery of Lebrah at that time may, after seeking and obtaining the authority of their superior, receive something from outsiders with security for the goods received. However, once the creditors have been repaid the principal amount in full, we prohibit them from harassing the debtors further concerning our goods or their own.

[Col. 1084A] If they should presume to attempt anything contrary to this precept and should appropriate more than the just and specified amount, we call them sacrilegious before the divine judgment. At the same time, as a bodily punishment, their ordinary judges shall compel them to make restitution and reasonably condemn them to an arbitrary fine. The following words are textually corrupt or incomplete: “volentesque ex nostro proprio contulimus pro nostra nostrorumque salute cum usuris violenter aut indebite, aut alias quovis modo per manus alienas et vel sacrilegas distrahantur.”

Therefore, to you, our faithful, present and future, in the villages and cities of our empire, and to the magistrates, advocates, consuls, and citizens now present, we command that you protect and defend our holy and beloved little abbey at Lebrah, together with its persons and goods, now and in succeeding times.

Fearing that after our death they might not remain faithful in these matters, we sent the precept of our authority to Rome to be confirmed.

And so that this donation, together with the established provisions, may be more secure, and so that the house of God may rejoice in receiving protection, we appoint the duke of Lorraine as its advocate and defender.

We remember obtaining from the holy apostolic see that the venerable archbishops of Mainz and Trier, together with their suffragans and their successors, should be assistants and guardians, for sound reason, of all the foregoing, now and for future times.

We have therefore signed this present precept below with our own hand and ordered it to be marked with our ring.

Given at Aachen in the year of the Lord 803, in the first year of our empire and the fifteenth year of our reign, while our Lord Jesus Christ reigns forever and ever. Amen.

[Note: Emperor Charles IV prefaced his diploma of 1348 with the following: “We, moved by the prayers of the aforesaid abbot and convent of Saint-Denis, have seen and read through the precept of the invincible prince Charles, king, unbroken and uncorrupted in any part, sealed with the sign of his authority on a silk cord, in the form written below.”]
